->PRELIMINARY DISSERTATION ON THE USE AND ABUSE OF THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE<-

Heads of synagogues <note>original Hebrew: *Rashei Kenesiyot*</note>, inasmuch as they were considered by the Jews to be the closest peers to the "Great Men of the Generation" <note>original Hebrew: *Gedolei Ha-Dor*; a term referring to the leading rabbinic authorities of an age</note>, *Gemara Pesachim, chapter 49, section 1*, and were therefore the avowed enemies of the religion and church of JESUS CHRIST—which was removed from all worldly pomp—could not be admitted by the apostles (*). For the apostles themselves were not monarchs or princes, nor did they desire to be counted among such; rather, they were public **TEACHERS** sent by JESUS CHRIST, the supreme Lord of the church, into the whole world with the purpose of opening the way of salvation prescribed by God to mortals. Since the apostles referred everything to this primary goal of their office, they were especially careful when establishing new offices in the churches, as the necessity and utility of each case required; namely, that churches might be planted by the doctrine of the Gospel and divine mysteries might be rightly administered (*1 Corinthians 4:1*). Therefore, all other accessory offices must be measured and evaluated against this order of **TEACHERS**—the only one necessary at all times, and which must therefore remain fixed and perpetual—as if against a touchstone <note>original Latin: *lydium lapidem*; a stone used to test the purity of gold, here meaning a standard of truth</note>. For these most holy men established these offices only as circumstances required <note>original Latin: *pro re nata*; literally "as the matter arose," meaning situational or temporary</note>, and once established, they freely abolished them as the reason and character of a particular church demanded.

The **ECCLESIASTICAL ORDER**, as it existed in the time of the apostles, was best described by **PAUL** in two places: *1 Corinthians 12:28 and following* and *Ephesians 4:11*. We shall follow his footsteps, while also providing some clarity here to the other divine messages that present the offices of the apostolic church somewhat obscurely. The supreme apostle records in both places:

I. *Extraordinary spiritual gifts <note>original Greek: *charismata*</note>, unique to the primitive church,* when he names apostles and prophets. To this he also adds—specifically in the latter passage—evangelists, whom the character of the apostolic church required in a particular way. ## II. The *ordinary* office of **TEACHING**, *necessary for the church at all times*, known by the explicit name of **TEACHERS** <note>original Greek: *didaskalōn*</note>.

To this office, the apostles—when they were about to undertake various journeys for the sake of preaching the gospel—appointed **ELDERS** <note>original Greek: *presbyterous*</note> to preside in their place while absent. These were men commendable above others for their age, as well as for their prudence and gravity of character, whose duty it was to preserve the purity of doctrine and morals unstained and inviolate. Such men are already mentioned in the Jerusalem church in *Acts 11:30; 15:2, 4, 6, 22, 23*, and elsewhere; and the apostles subsequently established similar men in other churches, *Acts 14:23*. These same men, because they were most diligent inspectors of doctrine and conduct, and watched so that the Christian community <note>original Latin: *respublica christiana*</note> might suffer no harm, but that all things might be done **according to order** <note>original Greek: *kata taxin*</note>, *1 Corinthians 14:40*, were distinguished by the title of **OVERSEERS** <note>original Greek: *episkopōn*; the word from which "Bishop" is derived</note> (†): as is abundantly clear from *Acts 20:17* compared with *verse 28*. Nor are these same **ELDERS** or **OVERSEERS** any less called **SHEPHERDS** <note>original Greek: *poimenes*; often translated as "pastors"</note>, *Ephesians 4:11*, since it was their duty **to shepherd the church of God** <note>original Greek: *poimainein tēn ekklēsian tou Theou*</note>, as is explicitly stated in *Acts 20:28*. Thus, **shepherds** and **teachers** seem to be used synonymously in the cited passage of the Epistle to the *Ephesians*, since the elders also performed the office of teachers. Not only the typographical errors appended to that same praised edition, but also certain others that presented themselves to the eyes, have been carefully corrected in the text itself. These are the things which I had to truly advise regarding this new edition, at the request of the most honorable men, the booksellers.

->PROLEGOMENA (INTRODUCTION).<-

CHAPTER I.
The usefulness, indeed even the necessity, of this treatise is commended, in which the origin of the sacred rites of the *First Christian Church* is traced from elsewhere (namely from the Temple, or from the *Synagogue*). Page 1.

CHAPTER II.
The opinion of certain most learned men of both this and ancient times is related, who attempt to trace the form of government and the rites of the *Christian Church* back to the JEWISH TEMPLE; and the reasons that gave rise to this opinion are investigated. 6.

CHAPTER III.
The view of many other learned and famous men is explained, who maintain that the government of the *Christian Church* was formed according to the pattern of the JEWISH SYNAGOGUES. The reasons by which they were persuaded of this opinion, or by which it could be argued, are added. 15.

Afterward, other names of *Synagogues* are also touched upon: *hiera* (sacred places), *sabbateia* (Sabbath houses), *andrones* (men's halls), *proseukteria* (prayer houses), and *phrontisteria* (places of study or meditation), which may be found in *Philo* and *Josephus*. ## PART II.

### CHAPTER I.

The dissertation begins concerning the *Origin of Synagogues*, which, following the *Apostle James*, is traced back to ancient ages. Two intervals of time are then traversed: the first from *Adam* to the *Flood*, and the second from the *Flood* to *Moses*; the birth of *Synagogues* is sought in these periods but is not found. However, the famous passage in *Genesis* 4:26 is weighed, which deals with the public invocation of the Name of the Lord, and it is defended against the perverse interpretations of the Jews. Nor are the things omitted which *Maimonides* relates concerning *Abraham*, *Isaac*, and *Jacob* as the authors of the *morning*, *afternoon*, and *evening* prayers; likewise concerning the origin of the recitation of the **Krifmah** <note>A phonetic rendering of "Keri'at Shema," the central Jewish prayer declaring the oneness of God</note>, with the foundations of those opinions investigated. A consideration of the passage in *Genesis* 28:21 is added. 271.

### CHAPTER II.
The opinions of *Josephus*, *Philo*, and even later Teachers are weighed, who seek the origin of the explanation of the Divine Law—frequently practiced on Sabbath days—as far back as the *Mosaic* times and precepts. Testimonies from the *Law of Moses* regarding a <note>original: מקרא קדש; *miqra qodesh*</note> "holy convocation" (Leviticus 23:3) and the "sanctification of the seventh day" (Exodus 20:8) are examined; it is believed that these were the references intended by some authors (with *Grotius* not disagreeing). It is proven, however, that the origin of *Synagogues* should not be sought in either of those, both by explaining the phrase "holy convocation" and by clarifying the precept concerning the "sanctification of the Sabbath." 282

### CHAPTER III.
Consideration is given to whether *that Tent*, which *Moses* is read to have pitched outside the camp to be visited by the repentant Israelites, should be thought of as similar to *Synagogues* or the *Theological Auditoriums* <note>Places dedicated to the study and teaching of religious law</note> that were in use among the Jews of later times. Likewise, the reason is brought forth as to why that *Tabernacle* was called the TENT OF MEETING. Afterward, it is explored whether, in the famous promise found in Exodus 20:24, the *Structure of Synagogues* was silently either commanded or permitted, once the genuine meaning of that passage is produced and confirmed. 297.

### CHAPTER IV.
The opinion of the illustrious man *Hugo Grotius* <note>A famous Dutch legal scholar and theologian (1583–1645) often cited in historical debates</note> *concerning the first origin of Synagogues* is weighed, which is built upon the precept found in *Moses* regarding the reading of the *Law*, to be repeated every seven years at the *Feast of Tabernacles*. Likewise, the view of *Cornelius Bertram* on the same argument is ex-

<column-break/>

plored, and it is argued against him that *Synagogues* do not owe their origin to the dispersion of the Levites throughout the region of the land of *Canaan*, which was ordered by a singular decree of God. 308.

### CHAPTER V.
It is disputed whether the *Chaldean Interpreter* <note>The *Targum*, or Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> at Judges 5:9 appropriately mentions *Synagogues* in his *Paraphrase*; and it is simultaneously asked what should be understood in 그 text by the <note>original: חוקקי ישראל; *choqeqei Yisrael*</note> *Legislators of Israel*, after exploring the opinions of Jewish Interpreters. Further, it is asked whether *Mizpah*, which was once a famous place for the *Assemblies* of the Hebrew people, existed as a *Synagogue* in the time of the Judges—an opinion toward which the *Dutch* <note>The Statenvertaling or Dutch Authorized Version scholars</note> Interpreters seem to lean along with *Kimchi* and *Abarbanel* <note>Prominent medieval Jewish commentators</note>; to which question it is answered in the negative for various reasons that are brought forward. It is also taught that this *Mizpah* was different from the land of *Mizpah* in Joshua 11:3, near which *Joshua* defeated the Kings of Northern Canaan; and finally, the genuine meaning of the phrase <note>original: לפני יהוה; *lifnei YHVH*</note> *before the Lord* in Judges 20:1 is explained. 315

### CHAPTER VII.
The discussion concerning the public *Schools of the Prophets* is continued, and especially regarding the *regular Listeners of the Prophets*, who in *Sacred History* are usually called *Prophets and Sons of the Prophets*. Indeed, their entire way of life is described, with the help of Hebrew Commentators called upon, such as the fact that they lived together and specifically apart, ate together, and devoted themselves to study under the leadership of one or more celebrated Teachers; almost no differently than the Monastics <note>Members of religious orders, like monks</note> of following centuries. The restoration of Prophetic institutions of this kind is traced back to the times of *Samuel*, parts of whose History relating to this are illustrated, with certain glosses of *Abarbanel* <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a prominent Jewish statesman and Bible commentator</note> rejected. Finally, a comparison is established between the *Schools of the Prophets* among the Hebrews and those of the *Philosophers* among the Greeks. 349.

### CHAPTER VIII.
What duty the *Levites* had imposed upon them in teaching the Jewish people is investigated from various testimonies of Holy Scripture. It is proven, however, that they, more than other Israelites from the common people, were obligated to learn the Law and to draw out its genuine meaning; indeed, that this *knowledge* had this use: that they should respond to those asking about the meaning of the Law, determine doubtful cases, and frequently preside over the judgments of the people. It is also asserted by conjecture that the poorer among them were often received into the families of the Israelites to preside over their religious rites and take charge of instructing the household members. Subjoined to this dissertation is an exposition of *three* most noteworthy sayings of Holy Scripture regarding this matter. 362.

### CHAPTER IX.
Various arguments are produced, and once produced are illustrated and urged, sought from the Holy Scriptures, by which it is proved that *Synagogues*, as specifically so called, were by no means known or accepted under the *Jewish Kings* up until the *Babylonian Captivity*. Especially noteworthy is the remarkable History regarding the *Book of the Law*, found in the Temple by *Hilkiah*, the Chief of the Priests, and delivered to King *Josiah*, which is narrated and explained. 380.

### CHAPTER X.
An objection produced by most Learned Men from Psalm 74:8 <note>original: "They have burned up all the meeting places of God in the land."</note> against the opinion confirmed in the previous Dissertation is resolved; both by indicating the scope and argument of this entire Psalm, in determining which skilled Interpreters of Scripture disagree; and especially by explaining the *words* in which the difficulty, contrary to our opinion, is contained. 396.

### CHAPTER XI.
Certain other doubts are resolved, which are raised—or could be raised—by Jewish or Christian Doctors against the opinion approved in the previous sections, based on the interpretation of certain passages of Holy Scripture. At the end, there is also a brief discussion concerning the *Fast* that was proclaimed by *Jezebel* and observed in *Samaria*. 405.

### CHAPTER XII.
It is proposed, alongside other learned men, that *Synagogues* and their primary ceremonies originated in Canaan after the return of the Jews from the Babylonian captivity; this is confirmed by the words of *Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and Torah scholar</note>. Following this, it is argued that the precise point in time to which the origin of the Synagogues should be assigned remains uncertain, as no mention of them exists even in the *History of the Maccabees*. It is noted, however, that their primary ceremonies should be traced back to that solemn reading of the Divine Law, including the blessings joined to it, which is described in the Book of *Nehemiah*. After illustrating this text, other causes that promoted the origin of Synagogues are also reviewed. Finally, this dissertation concludes with the addition of certain passages from *Philo* and *Josephus* <note>Philo of Alexandria and Flavius Josephus, two of the most important Jewish historians from the first century</note> concerning the progress of this first *institution of Synagogues*. 413.

### PART III.
### CHAPTER I.
The meeting places of the early Church are investigated; these are divided into *Private* and *Public*, and these in turn into *fixed* and *arbitrary* <note>Temporary or occasional locations</note>. It is established from the *Acts* of the Apostles that they were *Private* for a time and *arbitrary*, after discussing the explanation of the phrase "from house to house" <note>original: "κατ' οἶκον"</note> provided by the distinguished de

<column-break/>

Dieu and *Cloppenburg*. Next, *Public* places are discussed, and it is maintained that public *Oratories* <term>Oratories: Dedicated places for prayer</term> of this kind should not be entirely denied to Christians of the first centuries, even if they were rare. The reasons are also presented for why the Christians of the earliest times both had to, and chose to, remain hidden in the exercise of their religion. Finally, some observations are made regarding those famous testimonies of the Heathens concerning the Christians: namely, that Christians "have no temples or altars." 429.

### CHAPTER II.
Several reasons are brought forward to prove that the *sacred houses* of the first Christians were *modeled* after the pattern of Jewish Synagogues; the same point is further emphasized by a brief comparison established between the *Names, Parts, and Incidentals* of both *Synagogues and Christian Oratories*. 444.

### CHAPTER III.
It is shown that the custom of praying toward the *East*, and of directing the *rear part of their Oratories* toward it—which was once observed among Christians—is not as contrary to the customs of the Jews as is commonly thought. Meanwhile, other reasons that they offered for this custom are reviewed. Finally, it is noted that the *Oratories* of the Christians grew so much in size and splendor under the rule of Christian Princes that they seemed more similar to *Temples*—whether Jewish or Heathen—than to *Synagogues*; indeed, they were frequently compared to the *Temple of Jerusalem* by the authors of those times. 456.

# BOOK TWO.

## CHAPTER I.
Following the preface regarding the difficulty of the following discussion, various passages are extracted from the *Commentaries* of *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian whose work on law and scripture was foundational for modern international law</note> on the New Testament. In these, he discusses the *Form of Governance* in both the *Synagogue* and the *Church*, as well as the similarities between the two, from which the entirety of *Grotius’s* opinion on this matter may be drawn out. ->467<-

## CHAPTER II.
It is proven that the Apostolic Churches were generally governed by a College of Presbyters <note>An assembly of elders or leaders within the early Christian community</note> of the same rank and order, certainly with some *President*, but one distinguished from the other Presbyters by no fixed mark of leadership or special privilege. Furthermore, the *right of teaching* is claimed for all the others just as much as for the President, supported both by the Holy Scriptures and the records of Ecclesiastical History. Moreover, the same and even greater weight of reasoning is applied to dismantle the distinction of *Presbyters into Teachers and Rulers*—or *Lay Elders*, as they are specifically called. On this occasion, the duty of the Presbyters of the *Early Christian Church* is explained through the history of the ancient Church, making it clear that they had almost nothing in common with our modern "elders from the common people" except for the name. ->474<-

## CHAPTER III.
Three passages—1 Timothy 5:17, Romans 12:8, and 1 Corinthians 12:28—which are commonly cited from the Epistles of Paul in favor of "Ruling Elders" from the common people, are explained at length, having searched out, presented, and confirmed their genuine meaning. Regarding the *first* passage, taken from the *First Epistle to Timothy*, it becomes necessary to ask what sort of *Teaching Presbyters* those are who are mentioned in the writings of Cyprian <note>Saint Cyprian (c. 210–258), the Bishop of Carthage and an important early Christian writer</note>, after weighing the opinion of the most learned *Dodwell* <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711), an Anglo-Irish scholar known for his works on early church history</note> concerning them. Finally, the "Elders of the people" <note>original: "Seniores plebis"</note> mentioned in the writings of the Ancients are brought onto the stage, and it is proven that they hinder the cause of "Ruling Elders" more than they help it. ->490<-

The hypothesis of *Grotius* regarding the *Governance of the Synagogue and Church* is tested against the truths already proven, and the extent to which it should be accepted or rejected is defined. ->512<-

# BOOK THREE.

### CHAPTER I.
After the <term>outline <note>original: schema</note></term> of the following treatise has been drawn, a more specific discussion begins concerning the NAMES OF THE LEADERS OF THE SYNAGOGUE, which occur in the New Testament Scriptures and can be conveniently compared with the names or titles of the Leaders of the *Early Christian Church*. Among these, the first place is given to the title <term>ELDERS <note>original: zeḳenim</note></term> or PRESBYTERS, a term common to the leaders of both the Synagogue and the Church, which is explained and illustrated from suitable authors in a manner consistent with our purpose. 609

### CHAPTER II.
After explaining the title of the Presbyters, the designation <term>SHEPHERDS <note>original: poimenon</note></term> or PASTORS is taken up, by which the leaders of the Christian Church are noted by *Paul*. This is traced back to the word <term>PASTORS <note>original: parnasim</note></term>, very well known in the modern, but especially in the Ancient Synagogue; its origin and true meaning are uncovered, and clarified as well as confirmed by many examples. Especially after examining the opinion of *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675) was a prominent English Hebraist who sought to explain the New Testament through Rabbinic traditions</note>, who attributed this role to the *Collectors of Alms*, it is proven by many arguments that in former times it was assigned by common usage to the *Governors* of such Synagogues, who were at the same time *Teachers*, excelling in learning and piety. 621

### CHAPTER III.

To the same is traced the Greek <term>presiding officer <note>original: proestos</note></term> and the Latin *Leader* [Præpositus], which are titles also given to the Presbyters of the Church. Finally, the name <term>LEADER <note>original: hegoumenos</note></term> is treated, applied to the same *Governors* of the early Church in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which is compared with the Hebrew title of the same force and usage, <term>LEADER <note>original: manhig</note></term>, known in the Synagogue. 640

->### CHAPTER X.<-
A more precise and detailed discussion is held against *Erastus* <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583) was a Swiss theologian who argued that the right to excommunicate belonged to the state, not the church; this text argues for the church's independent authority based on Jewish precedent.</note> and others, proving that *Excommunication* was received into the Apostolic Christian Church according to the example of the *Synagogue*. It is shown wherein that *Excommunication* of the ancient time chiefly consisted, after resolving exceptions or objections raised by the opposing view. It is also proven that private *Excommunication* was in use among Christians just as it was among the Jews; and finally, it is added that this power was exercised in the Church by Bishops and Presbyters <note>Elders or leaders in the early church.</note>. 752

->### CHAPTER XI.<-
A debate is held concerning *Scourging* in the *Synagogues*, which the Sacred Writers mention in more than one place. The opinions of *Theodore Beza* <note>A French Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin.</note> and *Hugo Grotius* <note>A Dutch jurist and philosopher whose work laid the foundations for international law.</note> are examined; against their views, it is demonstrated that this kind of punishment was instituted and practiced in the Synagogues in place of *Excommunication*, and it is attributed to the Presbyters of the *Synagogue*. Inquiry is also made as to whether any similar kind of coercion had a place in the assemblies of Christians. Finally, a reason is given why Christ is never read to have been Excommunicated in the Gospel histories. 768

->### CHAPTER XII.<-
the dissertation on the *Duties of the Rulers of the Synagogue* passes to the *third act* of their government: namely, the CARE of ALMSGIVING. However, before that is reached, two most noble

<column-break/>

Both of these questions are treated in such a way that many notable sayings of Holy Scripture are brought to light. Indeed, it is proven that almost every work of Christ was, and the work of Christians ought to be, <term>Gemilut Hasadim</term>. 782

->### CHAPTER XIII.<-
What *Care for the poor* was maintained by God in organizing the state of the Jewish Commonwealth is briefly indicated; the *Alms* of that nation are distinguished into *required and liberal, or voluntary*. It is conjectured that those of the latter kind only began to be solemnly collected after the end of the Babylonian Captivity, and distributed to the poor by *Collectors* <note>original: גבאים; <term>Gabbaim</term>, officials appointed to collect and distribute charity</note> established for that purpose. Again, the *Alms* are distinguished into those distributed to the *Poor of the land of Canaan*, and those given to the *Poor of any local place*. Finally, it is proven that the supreme right of distributing them belonged to both the *Leaders of the Synagogues* and the *Bishops of the Christian Churches*. 806

### CHAPTER XV.
How the *Overseers of the Jewish Elders were elected and confirmed in their office* is explained from Hebrew authors; it is taught that the customs used by Christians in this matter were derived from the Synagogue to the Church. In particular, various doubts are unraveled regarding the *Semikhah* <note>original: סמיכה; the Hebrew term for the "laying on of hands" during ordination.</note>, or the doctoral *laying on of hands* <note>original: $\chi\epsilon\iota\rho\omicron\theta\epsilon\sigma\iota\alpha$ (cheirothesia)</note> of the Jews, and its significance.
828

### CHAPTER XVI.
It is proved anew that *Bishops and Elders constituted the same College* and were of the same *Order*, not only in the Apostolic age but also in those following; this is done by setting aside the recent objections of Henry Dodwell <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711) was a prominent scholar who argued for the divine right of bishops.</note>, a most learned man, to the argument produced by David Blondel <note>David Blondel (1591–1655) was a French Protestant who argued that bishops and elders were originally the same office.</note> from the *division* <note>original: $\delta\iota\chi\omicron\tau\omicron\mu\iota\alpha$ (dichotomia); the division or classification of the clergy into distinct groups.</note> of the *Clergy* among the ancients. It is then proved that the *Presidents of the Jewish Elders* (Heads of the Academies) <note>original: ראשי ישיבות (Rosh Yeshivot)</note> were considered to be of the same Order and College as the *Assessor* Elders <note>Elders who sat in council to judge or advise.</note>. 
844

### CHAPTER XVII.
It is considered whether *particular Churches or their Rectors had any connection*

<column-break/>

*relation* <note>original: $\sigma\chi\epsilon\sigma\iota\nu$ (schesin); a Greek term for a relationship or structural link.</note> among themselves, such that the *Presbytery of one Church depended on the Presbytery or Presbyteries* of other churches as being superior in authority. It is proven that after the removal of the *Sanhedrin of Jerusalem* <note>The supreme judicial and administrative council of the Jewish people.</note>, which was fortified with Apostolic authority, all Churches and the *Presbyteries of the early churches became independent*, while preserving the necessary acts of communion which private Christian societies are obliged to cultivate by the Law of Christ. Then, the nature of those *Acts* of communion is shown; then *how and when Metropolitans* <note>Bishops of provincial capital cities who held authority over other bishops in the region.</note> *arose*, and the conformity of the *Synagogue with the Church* is demonstrated to be conspicuous in this part as well.
857

Next, the *Honoraria* or *stipends* of the Elders of both the Church and the Synagogue are discussed, again showing the agreement of the customs of both in this regard. Afterward, some points are added regarding the hereditary transfer of the office of President from father to son, again comparing the customs of the Synagogue and the ancient Church with each other.

The genuine meaning of the names <term>Chazzan</term> and <term>Shaliach Tzibur</term> is revealed and illustrated from many testimonies, and the somewhat obscure origin of the word <term>Chazzan</term> is likewise investigated. The treatment begins regarding the solemn PRAYERS and BENEDICTIONS of the Synagogue, the recitation of which among the Jews is called <gloss>by the phrase</gloss> <term>descending before the Ark</term> <note>original Hebrew: ירידה לפני התיבה (Yeridah lifnei ha-teivah). ## CHAPTER I.

> *The usefulness, and indeed the necessity, of this treatise is emphasized, in which the origin of the sacred rites of the early Christian Church is traced from other sources (whether from the Temple or from the Synagogue).*

Since human beings consider nothing more sacred or more excellent than *Religion*, it is only right that they should apply the utmost effort and diligence: first, indeed, to be properly persuaded and convinced of the truth of their religion by sound arguments; and second, to understand the rules, use, origin, and purpose of the ceremonies and rituals of their religion.

For certainly, even if it is most true that the Christian Religion does not run contrary to Reason, yet if it can be shown that Christ and the Apostles—the Authors of the Dogmas and Rituals of our Religion—ordained it according to another specific model which they themselves had before their eyes, and from which they drew their ways of speaking about matters of Religion, it cannot be denied that the Rituals of our Religion and the Form of administering the Christian Church must first be explained from this Principle, and can only finally be solidly understood through it. That Christ and the Apostles, in establishing the Sacred rites of the Church of the New Covenant, were intent upon *Jewish Sacred matters*, and especially—as will be discussed hereafter—*Synagogal matters*, there are indeed many things most worthy of observation which lead us to presume, not without reason, that:

1. In the *Worship of the Temple and the Synagogues*, certain Rites and ceremonies occur, similar in all respects to those which one may observe in our own Sacred services. For if we turn our attention to the *Reading of the Law, Psalmody <note>The singing or chanting of Psalms.</note>, Sermons, Prayers, Blessings*, and other Sacred Acts and Rites of the same kind, it is certainly established that they were no less received into use among the Ancient Jews than they are now among Christians. For one who considers this with an attentive mind, what is more natural than to think of the common *Origin* of these Sacred things?

2. In the *Temple and the Synagogues* there were *Overseers and Ministers* of sacred things, who, by reason of their *Offices* (indeed, and even their *Names*, about which more will be said shortly), are to be compared with those who *preside* in our Churches and perform ministries for them. Therefore, it is rightly asked: what is, or can be, the reason for this correspondence?

3. ### The opinion of certain most learned men of both this and ancient times is recounted, who attempt to trace the **Form of Government and Rites of the Christian Church** back to the **JEWISH TEMPLE**, and the reasons that gave rise to this opinion are investigated.

**W**e have observed that the most excellent men, who trace the *Form of Government and Ceremonies of the Christian Church* from the *Jewish Sacred Rites*, are divided—or can be divided—into two camps. There are those who refer the *Offices and Rites of the Christian Church* to the *Worship of the Jewish Temple*; there are others, again, who strive to derive the *Sacred Matters of the Christians* from the *Synagogue*. Let us extract only a single passage from Jerome. <margin>Jerome to Evagrius, Volume 2, leaf 117, column 3.</margin> He concludes that most famous letter of his to Evagrius thus: *"And so that we may know that the Apostolic traditions were taken from the Old Testament: what Aaron and his sons and the Levites were in the Temple, let the Bishops, Presbyters, and Deacons claim this for themselves in the Church."*

However, to one considering and summarizing the reasons that could have moved them to establish this comparison, these following points primarily occur; now to be listed briefly, but later to be discussed and examined more broadly in their proper place. 1. Because it cannot be denied that a great agreement truly exists between *Bishops* and *Deacons*, and *Priests* and *Levites*, by reason of the *mutual respect* which the latter had for the former. For indeed, from the earliest memory of antiquity, the *Deacons* of the Church were the *Ministers of the Bishops*, just as the *Levites* were once consecrated by God for the ministry of the Priests. 2. Because by reason of *Office*, considered both in general and specifically, a great conformity is observed between *Priests* and *Bishops*, and *Levites* and *Deacons*. In general, because *Bishops* and *Deacons* under the New Testament are considered as the overseers and administrators of sacred things, which was the same honor and duty entrusted to the *Priests* and *Levites* in the **Old Economy** <note>The religious system and social order of the Old Testament</note>. Specifically, because there are various sacred actions once proper to the Priests and Levites which have now been transferred to the *Bishops* and *Deacons* of the Christian Church, to be mentioned hereafter where convenient. 3. I shall explain the matter in a word. In former times, when the Holy Supper was to be celebrated, everyone offered what they had at hand—bread, wine, oil, incense, money, and other gifts—at the sacred

<margin>Ecclesiastical Observations, chapter 5, which concerns the Offerings of the Ancients.</margin>

and blessed with specific prayers." To this is added that a particular reason was put forward why the gifts of **bread and wine**, offered on the sacred table, should by far greater right be called **sacrifices** than any others. ...of our sins was offered to His Father. Since the *bread* and *wine* in the *Holy Supper* represent the *body* and *blood* of Christ, it seemed right to the early Church that these sacred symbols of bread and wine in the Supper could, by the highest right, be called a *sacrifice*. From this it eventually happened that the sacred *table* was called an *altar*; the Bishops and Presbyters who blessed and distributed the gifts were called *Priests*; the Deacons who served the Bishops were called *Levites*; and thus, finally, the entire *structure* <term>thesis: the systematic arrangement or institutional framework</term> of the Jewish Temple was introduced into the simple assemblies of the Christians. Just as we have already shown above from *Ignatius* the antiquity of these ways of speaking, the most learned men have likewise observed the same in *Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian, and Cyprian*—the Fathers of the first centuries. In *Eusebius* and other authors of Church History, and in the *Canons of the Councils*, such a frequency of these phrases occurs that it is abundantly clear that this comparison drove deep roots into the minds of the people of that time.

<margin>Tripartite History, book 6, chapter 29. Apology against Rufinus, Epistle Part 2, folio 72, column 3.</margin>

### CHAPTER 2. ON THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE.

B 3

*...let him light lamps, let him be excommunicated.* <note>original: "λύχνες ἅπτοι, ἀφοριζέσθω"</note> If any Christian brings oil to the sacred rites of the Pagans, or to the Synagogue of the Jews on their feast days, or lights their lamps, let him be expelled from the community. The Council of Constantinople, which sat in Trullo <note>Also known as the Quinisext Council (692 AD), it issued canons to settle discipline in the Byzantine Church.</note>, cautioned in the same way:

<margin>Canon 11.</margin>

*Let no one among those enrolled in the priestly order, nor any layman, eat the unleavened bread of the Jews, nor enter into any familiarity with them, nor call upon them in sickness and receive medicines from them, nor bathe with them in the public baths at all. If anyone attempts to do this, if he be a cleric, let him be deposed; if a layman, let him be excommunicated.* <note>The text provides this canon in both Greek and Latin; both emphasize a strict social and religious boundary between the two communities.</note>

Many similar examples could be added to these. Indeed, I ask you to read the **Orations of Chrysostom against the Jews** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD) was an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his powerful preaching; his "Adversus Judaeos" sermons are famously harsh in their attempts to prevent Christians from participating in Jewish festivals.</note>, and you will see with what earnestness, and with what force of genius and doctrine, he exhorts the Christians of his time and begs them not to admire or visit the Jewish Synagogues and their rites. On the contrary, you will see how vehemently he inveighs against those who took delight in the ceremonies of the Jewish Synagogues. Since, therefore, it was in the interest of the early Church to separate itself as far as possible from the Jewish Synagogue—and from the heretics, of whom the Synagogue had been the fertile mother since the very time of the Apostles—it is easy to understand that the early Church diligently and anxiously avoided the name "Synagogue" and the titles of the offices and rituals used within it.

7. I do not know whether it is permitted to add to what has been said that for the Gentiles <note>In this context, "Gentiles" refers specifically to people of non-Jewish, Greco-Roman pagan backgrounds.</note> converted from Paganism to Christianity, the designations derived from the **Temple** were far more familiar and pleasing than those sought from the **Synagogue**. For since the Gentiles were accustomed in their own sacred rites to name **Temples, Altars, Priests, and Sacrifices**, it undoubtedly happened most agreeably for them—or, to put it more gently, they inclined toward them because of a long habit of such names—that they would retain these words if they could find even the slightest use and analogy <note>original: "ἀναλογίαν"</note> for them in their new sacred rites, rather than exchange them for others that were entirely unknown and recent. Moreover, it is so well known that many other terms were transferred from Pagan superstition into the Christian Religion that it is unnecessary to mention it. Many names, says **Casaubon** <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), a renowned classical scholar and philologist.</note>,

Moreover, from a comparison of certain *Rites* of the modern *Synagogue* with those of ancient times, which were received around the age of Christ the Lord, it is easily established for anyone that the face of the Synagogues has not changed greatly, except that ceremonies have multiplied since that time, and their *Rule* [Regimen] has often been adapted to the varying condition of individual assemblies. But if this is indeed the case, that the *Synagogue* never changed its names and its customs for the sake of the Christians, then it must be said that the agreement which exists between the *Synagogue* and the *Church*, and their *Offices* and *customs*, either arose so greatly by some chance, or the *Christian Church* was *conformed* to the *model of the Synagogues*. All who are friends of reason will choose the latter with me.

### INTRODUCTION, ETC. CHAPTER 3.

<margin>On Matthew 4:23.</margin>
3. The most learned *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675) was an English churchman and Hebraist known for using Talmudic literature to illustrate the New Testament.</note>, in the words cited above from him, very correctly observed that the entire worship of the Synagogue was *moral*. It must be believed that he wished to say this: that the worship of the Synagogues was <term>rational</term> <note>original Greek: λογικὸς (logikos)</note>, that is, that nothing occurred in the worship of the Synagogues which could not be excellently reconciled with sound reason—indeed, even drawn from it. Since that which is called "moral" lasts through every age, he concluded most effectively that the Apostles did nothing out of place when they made the form of divine worship under the Gospel Economy conform to that model.

<margin>Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book 2.</margin>
Certainly, as soon as reason perceives *that God exists*, it simultaneously understands *that He is to be worshiped publicly with a pure, whole, and incorrupt mind and voice.* Public worship of the Divinity requires both that we venerate and celebrate God with our prayers and praises, and that we instruct and admonish one another in that mutual duty toward God and neighbor. For this to be done decently, there is a need for a place destined for these sacred rites, and for *Presidents and ministers* of the assembly, to whose care those matters may be safely entrusted. In this way, God was celebrated in the Synagogues by the Jewish nation, with only a very few Rites added on, without which almost all Religion tends to become worthless among the common people. Whatever indeed pertained to the <term>ceremonial types</term> <note>original Greek: τυπικὸν (typikon); referring to symbolic or ritual shadows of the Law</note> of the religion of the Jewish people, all of that was confined within the inner recesses of the Temple, which will be discussed a bit more broadly hereafter. The words of *Ambrose* <note>St. Ambrose (c. 339–397), Bishop of Milan and influential theologian.</note>, praised elsewhere by the most excellent *Selden* <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a polymath and scholar of ancient laws.</note>, agree strongly with our statements.

<margin>*On Natural and National Law*, book 1, chapter 10.</margin>
*Natural law has three parts: the first is that the Creator, once recognized, should be honored, and His Brightness and Majesty should not be assigned to any created thing. The second part is moral: that is, that one should live well, governed by modesty. The third part is teachable: that the knowledge of the Creator God should be handed down to others as an example of conduct.* Worship of this kind, entirely consistent with natural reason, was performed in the Synagogue. There are those who think that the Ancient Hebrews themselves bound the Gentiles to such worship by a certain precept, which is the second of the <term>Noahide Laws</term> <note>A set of universal moral laws traditionally held by Judaism to be binding on all humanity (the "sons of Noah").</note>, <term>concerning the blessing of the Name</term> <note>original Hebrew: על ברכת השם (Al Birkat HaShem); usually interpreted as a prohibition against blasphemy, but here framed as a positive duty to praise God.</note>. For according to their interpretation, that was to be translated: "Concerning the blessing, or celebration of the Divinity."

<margin>Chapter 5, Theory 17, page 335.</margin>
Thus *Schickard* <note>Wilhelm Schickard (1592–1635), a German professor of Hebrew and astronomy.</note> expressed its sense in his *Treatise on Royal Law*; and thus also...

### CHAPTER IV.

*A path is prepared for discerning which of the previously mentioned opinions regarding the Origin of Church Rites—whether they are to be sought FROM THE TEMPLE or THE SYNAGOGUE—is the truer one. To this end, the following points are addressed in advance: 1. In the Temple, in both ordinary and extraordinary cases, those ceremonies which were customary in the Synagogues were also observed from time to time. 2. Jewish authors themselves often compare the Ministry of the Synagogues in various parts with the worship of the Temple. In passing, it is investigated where the King's station or Chair was in the Temple; and also, whether there was any Synagogue within the Temple.*

Thus has been related a twofold opinion, which however seems to be contradictory, concerning the Origin of the Rites and Offices of the Christian Church. One side brings them from the Temple, the other from the Synagogue. Therefore, before we advance our step much further, it is fitting that we state which of these most appeals to us and—which is the heart of the matter here—seems to approach closest to the truth. To accomplish this properly, it will not be useless to proceed with slow and steady steps.

*First, therefore, I will state in advance that all the sacred Rites of the synagogue were also performed in the Temple; though I would wish you to interpret this correctly.* Consider with me, then: 1. That the Temple was the established and ordinary place for praying to God, praising Him, giving Him thanks, and blessing the people—acts which certainly comprise the greatest part of the Religious life of the Synagogue. That this is so is abundantly clear from the prayer of Solomon, by which the Temple was first dedicated. And you shall hear him speak thus:

I see also that the most excellent <term>Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a prominent Dutch theologian and Hebraist known for his "Covenant Theology."</note></term> translates the phrase *upon the column* <note>Hebrew: *al ha-amud* (על העמוד)</note> as *on a raised platform*. <term>Schindler <note>Valentin Schindler (died 1604), a German philologist and author of a famous five-language lexicon of Hebrew and Middle Eastern languages.</note></term> translates it in the same way: *A seat in which the Princes sat*. If, however, anyone wishes to understand by the word "column" <note>Hebrew: *amud*</note> a certain *raised platform* (as the Illustrious Cocceius does), upon which the King was accustomed to *stand* in the Temple so that he might stand out above the people, I will not argue against him with any spirit of contention. For I confess that the word "column" can be understood as a *raised place for standing*; nor does it shrink from reason that the King stood in some higher and more prominent place in the Temple. What I am chiefly disputing now is whether a *throne* was placed for the *King* in the Temple in which he *sat*, and whether that kind of *throne* is designated by the word *amud*. Neither seems to me to agree with the truth. For in the Temple, it was not the custom to *sit*, but to *stand*, which is the gesture of those *praying* and *ministering*. The Kings also in the noted texts are said to have
<margin>2 Chronicles 6:13.</margin>
*stood*, not *sat*; except that Solomon is also said to have *knelt*. Furthermore, the word *amud* cannot by any appearance be translated as a *throne* or *bench*. And my dispute could rest and end with these points. Nevertheless, let it be permitted to add this: no great reason compels us not to take the word *amud* here simply as a *column*, by which the *King*, when he participated in the sacred rites of the Temple, was accustomed to *stand*, in accordance with what is said of the *Prince* in Ezekiel. For when I carefully weigh those things brought forward by translators in favor of that commonly accepted opinion, I do not feel myself carried toward that side by any strong arguments. They suggest that by that "column" of King Joash, we should
<margin>2 Chronicles 6:13.</margin>
understand the *bronze platform* <note>Hebrew: *kiyor nechoshet* (כיור נחשת). While *kiyor* often means a basin, in 2 Chronicles 6:13 it refers to a scaffold or platform Solomon stood upon.</note> upon which *King Solomon* preached to the people and prayed to God. But on what foundation? For one may deny that with the same liberty by which others affirm it.
<margin>2 Chronicles 23:13.</margin>
On the contrary, what is proclaimed about this very King Joash in the *Books of Chronicles* seems to contradict the opinion that by "column" we should understand the *Bronze Chair* which Solomon prepared. For thus it is read there: *And behold, the King was standing in his station* (we translate it: *by his column*) <note>Hebrew: והנה המלך עומד על עמודו במבוא (*Ve-hinneh ha-melekh omed al amudo ba-mavo*).</note>

<margin>Isaiah 6:2. 1 Kings 22:19. Zechariah 3:6.</margin>
*The Seraphim stood above.* The scriptural passages agree: *And all the host of heaven stood by him*, etc. Likewise: *Among these who stand.* But if no sitting is granted to the celestial spirits who dwell in the presence of God, in what manner would it have been granted to David? There is no doubt that these words of *Abarbanel* <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a prominent Jewish statesman and Bible commentator.</note> bring much light to the present question.

For first, there is discovered in them the reason which gave strength to this opinion of the Masters <note>The Rabbis of the Talmud.</note> concerning the prerogative of sitting in the Court; then also we profit from them in that this opinion was not accepted among them without contradiction. It also does not seem very probable to me that David poured out these prayers *sitting*. We can, however, concede that point if we like, because our inquiry is mostly restricted to this: *Whether the Kings had an ordinary platform in the Temple, in which they were accustomed to sit.* I said that this was not proven by the passages which are commonly produced for that purpose. It is not absurd to suggest that the Kings, when they went up to the Temple at stated times for praying, stood in the *Inner Court*, or in the *Gate of the Inner Court* at the end of the portico of the Gate.

### CHAPTER 4. OF THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE. 37

...Parent; whether he might have gone up into the Temple and sat on a throne. I hesitate, however, whether it can be concluded from these words that he *sat* on a *throne* in some courtyard of the Temple. For the text of *Josephus* <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), the Romano-Jewish historian.</note> is satisfied if we conceive that he *sat upon a throne* after he had departed from the Temple. But I would also clearly not want to overlook the fact that the bronze platform <note>original: *concha*—literally "shell," used here to describe a raised, perhaps semi-circular platform or pulpit.</note>, constructed by Solomon, was placed <note>original Hebrew: *betok ha-azarah*</note> *in the middle of the Courtyard*. From this it also seems evident in some way that the station <note>original Hebrew: *al ha-ammud*</note> *at the column* was not the same as Solomon’s station on the bronze platform. 

I hold this reason because by that *courtyard* in which *Solomon’s rostrum* <note>original: *suggestum*</note> was set up, it seems altogether necessary to understand the *Court of the Priests*, and not the outer or greater court, as the Belgians <note>Referring to scholars from the Low Countries, likely the authors of the Dutch "Statenvertaling" Bible notes.</note> and other interpreters claim in all the notes they have given for the evidence previously observed. For once the *platform* was placed *in the middle of the Court*, before the altar, Solomon, standing on it, would have had the faces of the Israelites turned toward him as he preached, as they stood in the porticoes of that *Inner Court*. You may easily gather this from the noted text, which I cannot explain if the platform itself had been placed in the *Outer Court* or the *Porticoes of the Inner Court*. 

But if *Solomon’s rostrum* was truly located near the altar in the Court of the Priests, then I will easily prove that it is very different from the *seat* or *station* of the later Kings. For who will say that their station was in the *Court of the Priests*? Certainly, what *Solomon* did was entirely extraordinary, and his *platform* and its location seem adapted only for that specific occasion. Indeed, it was observed by the most learned *Diodati* <note>Giovanni Diodati (1576–1649), a Protestant theologian famous for his Bible translations.</note> that this *bronze rostrum* of Solomon was later consecrated to the Levites, who were appointed to praise God, even if interpreters often seem to go in all other directions. 

Furthermore, in the fact that *Solomon*, having built a *platform* or *rostrum* in the Court of the Priests, *prayed* for the people and addressed them, we must without doubt recognize a prelude to *Synagogue worship*. As is well known, this worship consists primarily in prayers being poured out from a public place and sermons for instruction being held by a public person. That this was done solemnly in this case has already been observed.

<margin>Deuteronomy 31:10.</margin>
But what the Talmudists relate concerning the duty to be performed by the King every seven years in the Temple, according to the prescription of Divine Law found in the final words of Moses, is even more relevant here. A history is related—

...the ritual of this act in the Tractate *Sotah* <note>A section of the Mishnah and Talmud; the passage cited describes the "Hakhel" ceremony performed every seven years.</note>, has already been noted by various authors. Specifically, once the first day of the Festival of Tabernacles <note>Sukkot</note> had passed, at the completion of *the seventh year and the beginning of the eighth*, they would build a wooden platform for him in the Court and he would sit upon it, as it is said (Deuteronomy 31:10), "At the end of seven years, at the set time," etc. The synagogue attendant would take the Book of the Law <note>The Torah scroll</note> and give it to the head of the assembly; the head of the assembly would give it to the deputy; the deputy to the High Priest; and the High Priest finally would present it to the King. The King, standing, would receive it, but for the reading, he sat down. He began reading from the beginning of Deuteronomy, etc. With the same blessings that the High Priest uses, the King also blessed, etc. <note>original Hebrew: *osim lo bimah shel etz ba-azarah ve-hu yoshev aleiha...*</note> *They prepared a wooden platform for the King in the Court* (*the Court of the Women*) *upon which he sat: just as it is said (Deut. 31, 10), "At the end of seven years at the fixed time," etc. Then the overseer, having taken the Book of the Law, handed it to the Head of the assembly; he reached it to the Deputy; the Deputy to the High Priest; and the High Priest finally presented it to the King. The King, however, standing, received it, but while reading, he sat. He began to read from the start of Deuteronomy, etc. With the same blessings as the High Priest, the King also blessed, etc.* You notice here the King performing exactly the same functions that those who lead the people in the synagogues are accustomed to perform. Thus, the *Temple Court* (if indeed such a thing ever existed as they depict the *Court of the Women*) was suddenly changed and converted into a *Synagogue*.

Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a pivotal Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note>, however, where he repeats and explains these same rites, expressly asserts that they were entirely similar to those used in the synagogue. *And he [the King] would look and bless in the same way that every reader blesses, and he would open the Torah in the synagogue.* <note>original Hebrew: *ve-roeh u-mevarekh ke-derekh she-mevarekh kol kore, ve-pote'ach ba-Torah be-veit ha-keneset*</note> *And he (the King) would open the book, look, and bless God with the same formula by which all those are accustomed to bless who are about to read the Law to the people IN THE SYNAGOGUES.* Again: *And he rolls up the book and blesses after it in the same way that they bless in the houses of assembly.* <note>original Hebrew: *ve-golel u-mevarekh le-akhareiha ke-derekh she-mevarekhim be-vatei kenesiyot*</note> *And he rolls up the book (after he had finished his portion) and blesses after the reading of the Law is completed in the EXACT SAME MANNER IN WHICH IT IS ACCUSTOMED TO BE DONE IN THE SYNAGOGUES.* Thus, it is sufficiently certain that at that time, in the *Temple Court*, the exact same ceremonies were performed with all the circumstances that were accustomed to be performed in the synagogues. Let it suffice to have noted this now. For other things that can be drawn from this passage of *Sotah* will be useful in the following sections.

### CHAPTER 4. CONCERNING THE OLD SYNAGOGUE. 39

<margin>Lightfoot on Luke 2:46. <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and rabbinical scholar.</note></margin>
<margin>Braun, *On Sacred Vestments*, book 2, chapter 25.</margin>
...sanctified, as has long since been observed by most distinguished men. It is recorded in the Tractates *Yoma* and *Sotah* <note>Sections of the Mishnah; *Yoma* deals with the Day of Atonement, and *Sotah* with the ritual for a woman suspected of adultery.</note> that the High Priest, once the sacred rites of the Day of Atonement were finished, read the Law <note>The Torah</note> to the people in the Temple, and having performed that ceremony, recited various *Blessings*. The words of the *Mishnah* <note>The first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions, compiled around 200 CE.</note> are:

<margin>Tractate *Yoma* ch. 7, § 1 & *Sotah* ch. 7, § 7.</margin>
**The High Priest came there to read.** <note>original Hebrew: *Ba lo Kohen Gadol likro*</note> Regarding this, *Jarchi* <note>Also known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French commentator on the Bible and Talmud.</note> notes: **The synagogue was near the Court on the Temple Mount.** <note>original Hebrew: *Beit ha-knesset hayah samukh la-azarah be-har ha-bayit*</note> The same words of *Jarchi* were noted by *Yom Tov* in his observations. However, let those who are interested see whether *Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a famous Jewish philosopher and legal scholar.</note> agrees well enough with them, since he writes that this reading was performed in the *Court of the Women*. Thus *Maimonides* says expressly regarding the aforementioned *Mishnah*:

<margin>Commentary on *Yoma* ch. 7, § 1.</margin>
**And this reading was done in the COURT OF THE WOMEN, where it is permitted for a person to sit, etc.** <note>original Hebrew: *Ve-ha-kri'ah hayetah be-ezrat ha-nashim she-mutar le-adam leyashev sham*</note> (He is speaking here of this same reading by the High Priest).

<margin>On which see also Kimchi’s Commentary on 1 Samuel 3:5-6. <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a medieval rabbi and grammarian.</note></margin>
In contrast, in the Court of Israel, no one was permitted to *sit*, as was noted in the preceding pages. But our *Maimonides* also writes the same in the *Yad* <note>The *Mishneh Torah*, Maimonides' code of Jewish law.</note>, where he discusses this same rite of the Priest:

<margin>Laws of the Service of the Day of Atonement, ch. 3, just after the middle.</margin>
**After the goat reached the desert, the High Priest went out INTO THE COURT OF THE WOMEN TO READ IN THE LAW, etc.** <note>original Hebrew: *Keivan she-higi'a sa'ir la-midbar yatza kohen gadol le-ezrat ha-nashim likro ba-torah*</note> If it is indeed certain that there was a synagogue in the Temple, then we shall best understand in what sense Christ the Lord says in *Matthew*:

<margin>Chapter 26:55.</margin>
**Every day I sat among you, teaching in the Temple.** <note>original Greek: *Kath’ hēmeran pros hymas ekathezomēn didaskōn en tō hierō*</note> But where, if not in the Synagogue of the Temple? Thus it is sufficiently proven that, in a sound sense, the same rituals were often observed in the Temple, and the same actions performed, as were celebrated in the Synagogue. In the second place, let it now be noted that the Jewish Doctors themselves recognize such agreement and conformity between the Synagogue and the Temple, and between the rituals of both, that they not only compare the worship of the Synagogues with the *liturgy* <note>original Greek: *leitourgia*</note> of the Temple, but have also ordered that various precepts pertaining to the Temple be observed likewise in the Synagogues. We shall prove this with clear arguments:

1. Thus it is read in the *Kolbo* <note>A significant anonymous Hebrew work on Jewish ritual and law, likely from the 14th century.</note>: **"Just as the Priests, who are the sons of Levi, were chosen for the temple service because that tribe was chosen by the Holy One, blessed be He, so also an upright man, who fears Heaven and clings to the ways of the Name <note>A common Jewish substitution for the tetragrammaton (the name of God).</note>, must be appointed as the Messenger of the Congregation <term>Shaliach Tzibur; the leader of prayer</term> to pray for the community; for prayer stands in the place of the temple service."** <note>original Hebrew: וכשם שנבחרו הכהנים שהם בני לוי לעבוד לפי שנבחר אותו השבט להב"ה כך יש להעמיד אדם כשר וירא שמים ודבק בדרכי השם לש"ץ להתפלל על הצבור שהתפלה במקום עבודה</note> *Just as indeed Priests of this kind were chosen for the ministry of the Temple, being descended from Levi, because that tribe constantly adhered to God; so similarly it is necessary to appoint such a man as the Minister of the assembly, who is honest, fears God, and adheres to His ways without ceasing, so that he may pour out prayers for the Synagogue; because* PRAYER OCCUPIES THE PLACE OF SACRIFICES. *You see that the Minister of the Synagogue is compared with the Priest. But another comparison also stands out in the following speech:*

### CHAPTER 4. CONCERNING THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE.

"What is the service of the heart? It is prayer." <note>original Hebrew: עבודה שבלב זו תפלה</note> *What is the worship of the heart? Prayers.* This matches the phrasing used by Paul <note>Paul the Apostle</note> in the Epistle to the Romans, where he advises the faithful to present themselves to God as **a living sacrifice, holy, and pleasing to God**, <note>original Greek: θυσίαν ζῶσαν, ἁγίαν, εὐάρεστον τῷ Θεῷ</note> an act which he calls **the rational service**, <note>original Greek: τὴν λογikὴν λατρείαν</note> or the rational worship of the faithful.
<margin>Chapter 12, 1.</margin>

But Paul's statement stands out even more clearly in the Epistle to the Hebrews: *Through him, therefore (meaning through Christ, whom the Apostle here considers as the Great High Priest), let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name.* <note>original Greek: Δι’ αὐτοῦ οὖν ἀναφέρωμεν θυσίαν αἰνέσεως διὰ παντὸς τῷ Θεῷ, τουτέστι καρπὸν χειλέων ὁμολογούντων τῷ ὀνόματι αὐτοῦ.</note>
<margin>Chapter 13, 15.16.</margin>
Indeed, the Hebrew Doctors <note>The Rabbis and Jewish scholars</note> are accustomed to describing this "rational" or logical worship in the same way. The words of Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides, the 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note> are as follows:

"The obligation of this commandment is that a person should supplicate and pray every day, declaring the praise of the Holy One, blessed be He, and afterwards ask for the needs he requires through request and supplication, and then give praise and thanks to the Lord for the good He has bestowed upon him, each according to his ability." <note>original Hebrew: חיוב מצוה זו כך הוא שיהא אדם מתחנן ומתפלל בכל יום ומגיד שבחו של הקב"ה ואחר כך שואל צרכיו שהוא צריך להם בבקשה ובתחנה ואחר כך נותן שבח והודיה לה' על הטובה שהשפיע לו כל אחד לפי כוחו</note>
<margin>Laws of Prayer and the Priestly Blessing. Chapter 1. § 2.</margin>

*That to which one is obligated by this precept (concerning the worship of God) is this: that a person should use supplications and prayers daily, and proclaim the praises of God the Blessed; thereafter, he should ask for the necessities he lacks through petitions and prayers; and finally, he should celebrate and praise God for the benefits He has abundantly bestowed upon him, as much as possible, in every detail.* (Thus Selden <note>John Selden, a 17th-century scholar of Jewish law</note> translates it: But is it not more correct to say? *Each according to his own ability.*) If we pay a little more distinct attention to these words of Maimonides, we will simultaneously perceive what the Apostle Paul means by those four species of prayer—**supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings** <note>original Greek: δεήσεις, προσευχάς, ἐντεύξεις, εὐχαριστίας</note>—which he lists in the first Epistle to Timothy, Chapter 2:1, which there will be an occasion to discuss in what follows.

I will only add this one thing to what has been said: that the Jewish Doctors are accustomed to derive the comparison they establish between prayers and the **service** <note>original Hebrew: עבודה; 'Avodah', referring to Temple service/worship</note> of sacrifices in the Temple from certain passages of Holy Scripture. Thus Maimonides says explicitly:

"It is a positive commandment to pray every day, as it is said: *And you shall serve the Lord your God.* By oral tradition they learned that this 'service' refers to prayer, as it is said: *And to SERVE him with all your heart.*" <note>original Hebrew: מצות עשה להתפלל בכל יום שנ' ועבדתם את ה' אלהיכם מפי השמועה למדו שעבודה זו היא תפלה שנ' ולעבדו בכל לבבכם.</note>
<margin>Exodus 23, 25.</margin>

*It is an affirmative precept that God must be prayed to every day, as it is said: And you shall worship Jehovah your God.* Through oral exposition, however, they learned that by this "worship" should be understood prayers, as it is said: *And to WORSHIP him with all your heart.*
<margin>Deuteronomy 11, 13.</margin>

It is therefore certain that the Jews themselves [considered] prayers...

INTRODUCTION, etc. CHAPTER V.

# CHAPTER V.

*Despite those points granted in the preceding chapter, it is proven by evident arguments that the practice of the religion of the Christian Church approaches much more closely the form of divine worship as it was celebrated in the Synagogues than the liturgy <note>original Greek: λειτουργίαν</note> of the Temple. This is because in those areas where the worship of the Synagogue differs from the ceremonies of the Temple—such as in the distinction of places, persons, clothing, age, degrees of holiness, etc.—the Church aligns with the Synagogue, not with the Temple; and furthermore, because the Hebrew Doctors <note>The Rabbis and Jewish scholars</note> themselves distinguish the worship of the Synagogue (insofar as it agrees with the Church's worship) from the religion of the Temple.*

Although these two points, which we have addressed beforehand, do not seem at all obscure, it remains certain that the *sacred worship of the Temple*, properly so called <note>original Greek: φερωνύμως</note>, retained many things unique to itself, none of which were transferred to the Synagogues. The Synagogues, in turn, had their own form and their own customs, which one would find with difficulty in the liturgy of the sanctuary <note>original Greek: ἐν τῇ λειτουργίᾳ τοῦ ἱεροῦ</note>. The principal portion of the ceremonial Law, which was observed for the most part in the Temple and could not be observed elsewhere, was excluded from the Synagogues. The Temple had its own Priests and its own Levites—men of specific families and tribes; the Temple had its own altars for various uses; it had its own sacrifices of diverse kinds; it also had its own instruments and most splendid equipment; it had its own degrees of holiness; likewise, its own secret mysteries <note>original Greek: μυστήρια</note> of religion, none of which were to be seen in the Synagogues. In the Synagogue, on the other hand, one notices a simplicity of Sacred Rites—and those entirely necessary ones—and a freedom to exercise that Rational Worship <note>A reference to the "service of the heart" or "logical worship" discussed on the previous page</note> which appears nowhere in the religion of the Temple. Prayers, as well as the reading and interpretation of the Law, are more strictly bound to the *Synagogues* than to the *Temple*; so much so that between the Temple...

### CHAPTER 5. CONCERNING THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE.

Let the separation between the Temple and the Synagogues remain manifest; and thus, through those positions we have already established, let it be seen that the inquiry has not yet been fully satisfied: does the model of the Christian Church correspond more to the *Temple* or to the *Synagogue*? Let us, therefore, speak more freely: despite those reasons for similarity that can be noted between the customs of the Christian Church and the ceremonies of the ancient Temple, it seems most certain to us that the *Worship* <note>The religious service or liturgy</note> of the New Testament Church draws its origin from the *Synagogue*, not from the *Temple*. Let us look at the reasons that can confirm this hypothesis of ours:

1. It has already been observed in the preceding sections that the *Correspondence* between *Synagogues* and the *Church* is so exact that not only the name of the *Synagogue*, but the names of *Pastors*, *Elders* <note>original: Presbyterorum</note>, the *Angel of the Church* <note>original: Angeli Ecclesiæ; a title likely referring to the presiding minister, derived from the "messenger of the congregation" or Shaliach Tzibur</note>, *Deacons*, etc., were transferred to the *Christian Church* without any change. In contrast, the name *Temple* was never so transferred; and the names *Priests* and *Sacrifices* are never applied directly and properly to the *Ministers of the Sacred Rites* and the *Worship* of the Church of the New Covenant, but always metaphorically <note>original Greek: μεταφορικῶς</note>. From this, it is safe to conclude that the form of the Christian Church aligns more with the *Synagogue* than with the *Temple*.

2. A very clear reason is derived from the fact that in those parts where the Synagogue differs from the Temple, the Christian Church sides entirely with the Synagogue, not the Temple. This becomes for us a certain and indubitable criterion <note>original Greek: κριτήριον; a standard for judgment</note> of the truth of our opinion. We must illustrate what we have said through examples.

1. The Synagogue differs from the Temple in that it can be built in any place throughout the whole world, whereas, on the contrary, the Temple was bound by God to a specific location, chosen by Divine oracle. The decree of the Teachers <note>The Rabbis and Jewish legal authorities</note> concerning the Synagogue holds thus:
<margin>Deuteronomy 12:5, 6</margin>
*In every place where there are ten free-born Israelites, there* <margin>Colbo, chapter 17 <note>A 14th-century collection of Jewish ritual laws</note></margin> *it is necessary to appoint a house in which they may gather to pour out prayers, etc.* <note>original Hebrew: כל מקום שיש בו עשרה מישראל צריך להכין בו בית שיכנסו בתוכו להתפלל וכו'</note> And yet, in this point, the Christian Church agrees entirely with the Synagogue, not the Temple. As the Apostle says:
<margin>1 Timothy 2:8</margin>
*I desire then that the men* PRAY IN EVERY PLACE <note>original Greek: Βέλομαι οὖν προσεύχεσθαι τὲς ἄνδρας ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ</note>.

Christ had already said: *The time is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.* But Malachi the Prophet had also, long before, prophesied about this in clear words: <note>original Hebrew: בכל מקום מקטר מגש לשמי ומנחה טהורה</note> *In every place a sacrifice* (incense) *is offered to my name, and a pure gift.* It is indeed worth noting that the ancient Jewish interpreters explained this prophetic saying as referring to prayers, which were to be poured out in every place. ### PREFACE, etc. CHAPTER 5.

...religious exercise, one should not even pay attention to any external decoration of clothing. In this regard, the Christian Church again aligns with the Synagogue, rather than the Temple. For even if, as superstition increased, a certain form of **Sacred Vestments** was applied to the leaders and ministers of the Church—adapted to the various orders of sacred persons—which is still observed today not only by those of the Catholic sect but also by our own in certain places, who does not know that these were of the freest institution? <note>That is, they were established by human choice rather than divine command.</note> Nothing regarding them was prescribed or commanded by the Apostles; indeed, true Christian discipline rejects toys <note>original Latin: *crepundia*, a dismissive term for trifles or children's rattles</note> of this kind. It is entirely sufficient that the bodily habit of a Minister of the Gospel be honorable and modest.

4. The same liberty exists in the Synagogues regarding *age*, and it is certainly greater than in the *Temple*. It was established by the regulations of David that a Levite must have reached the age of *twenty* years before he could perform his duties in the Temple. Regarding the age of the Priests, no explicit law exists in the Code of Mosaic laws; however, the Masters <note>The Rabbinic sages</note> constantly teach that no one was to be admitted to the Function of the Priesthood unless he was <term>of legal age</term> <note>Latin: *majorennem*; in Jewish law, this is thirteen years and one day</note>, *that is*, one who was thirteen years and *a single day* old. Let us describe a passage from *Abarbanel* <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a Jewish statesman and philosopher</note>, as noted elsewhere by the most learned *Outram* <note>William Outram (1626–1679), an English theologian</note>: <note>original Hebrew: הכהן שהיה ראוי במצוות לא היו מניחין אותו לעבוד עד היותו בן עשרים שנה</note> *A priest, as soon as he reaches the age where he is obligated to observe the commands of the law, is indeed fit for ministry; but his brother priests do not permit him to minister until he is twenty years old.* More testimonies on this have been noted by *Selden* <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a renowned English jurist and scholar of Jewish law</note>.

### CHAPTER 5. CONCERNING THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE.

Why a *minor* <note>Latin: *minorennis*, referring to someone under the age of thirteen in a Jewish context.</note> was not admitted to these later acts is due to a certain peculiar reason, which should not be overlooked in what follows. It must not be hidden that the Jewish Teachers, in selecting those for the fixed duties of the **Ruler of the Synagogue** <note>The *Archisynagogus*, the official in charge of the synagogue building and services.</note> or the Minister of the Synagogue, desired experience strengthened by a proper age; yet it remains certain that the Synagogue fixed no absolute laws regarding age. Truly, the Christian Church here again aligns so beautifully with the Synagogue that it could not be more so. For in the truly Apostolic Canons, nothing is more cautiously provided by law regarding a certain *age* than regarding the *character of the persons*. <margin>1 Timothy 4:12.</margin> Timothy, though a youth, was appointed by Paul as a minister of the Church. I am well aware, indeed, that the Church of subsequent times again prescribed a certain time for the **Priesthood**—and specifically that very age which was thought to have been assigned to the ancient Priests—a fact which did not escape the most perceptive **John Selden** <note>1584–1654, an English jurist and scholar of Jewish law.</note>; <margin>On the Succession of the Pontificate, book 2, chapter 4.</margin> but, as is the mark of difference here again, that entire determination depends entirely on the free opinion and consent of the Churches. For otherwise, it is established that every prerogative of age has been abolished under the New Covenant.

5. In addition to those things we have now observed, many others can be brought forward in which one may note a similar difference between the ceremonies of the *Temple* and the *Synagogue*. It was required of the Priests that they be free from **defects and blemishes of the body**; (although the Levites were not rejected because of bodily blemishes, as **Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note> expressly states) born of legitimate marriage; free from ceremonial impurity; and not in mourning for a relative, along with many other things that could be added from <margin>The Vessels of the Sanctuary, chapter 3.</margin> the books of *Maimonides* titled *The Vessels of the Sanctuary* and *The Entry into the Sanctuary*. Yet none of these things at all was required of him who performed the Sacred rites in the Synagogue. Not only the *lame*, but even the *blind*—notable bodily defects—are called to celebrate certain public religious acts within it. Thus holds the **Mishnah** <note>The first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions.</note>, part of which we described before: <term>A blind man</term> <margin>Megillah, chapter 4, section 6.</margin> <insert><term>recites the "Shema" and translates</term></insert>. <note>original Hebrew: *Suma pores et shema u-metargem*. The "Shema" is a centerpiece of Jewish prayer.</note> Concerning the others, there is no need to advise. For who is ignorant that the Christian Church neglects these same laws regarding its own ministers, provided only that they are sufficiently equipped for public edification?

6. The *Temple* has its own degrees of religious **Holiness**; the *Synagogue* and the **Sacred Houses** of the Christians have none, except those which common reverence toward **God** and His worship prescribes for every person. If indeed the Synagogue has something more here than the Church—which will be of small importance—nevertheless, in this case, the Church will always be closer to the Synagogue.
