### PROLEGOMENA &c. CHAPTER 5.

...than the Temple. The Temple, in turn, has its own Altars and its most sacred instruments of Divine Worship. It is also prepared with great pomp and splendor, magnificently adorned with gold and silver. Without these things, the Sacred Houses of both the Jews and the Christians—and the worship to be celebrated within them—can easily stand; as I already noted at the start of this Digression. Indeed, the Temple was honored by God with a certain glorious symbol of His presence granted to no other Sacred House in the world, even though many have falsely claimed it <note>A reference to the *Shekhinah*, or the Divine Presence, which was believed to dwell specifically in the Holy of Holies.</note>. This secret, which was the Temple’s shield <note>original Latin: *ancile*, referring to the sacred shield of the Roman god Mars, used here as a metaphor for a unique protective glory</note> and its glory, neither any Synagogue nor any Church can boast of. From this, we again conclude that the Church approaches the Synagogue much more closely than it does the *Temple*. These matters are so manifest that they affect everyone's senses.

3. It contributes much to the question we have established that the ordinary Worship performed in the Temple differs in its principal part from the Worship of the Synagogue and the Church. It is worthwhile to explain this a little more clearly in a few words. *The sacred worship of the Temple, established for the morning and evening hours, consists—on the part of the Priests—in the offering of the daily sacrifice, the burning of incense, and the Priestly blessing pronounced from the steps of the Portico; and on the part of the Levites, in the chanting of Psalms during the Priest’s drink offering.* The two main parts of the Religion of the Synagogues—**Prayers and the Reading of the Law** along with its interpretation and instruction—are lacking here.

<margin>Tractate Tamid. Laws of the Vessels of the Temple, chapter 3.</margin>
The matter is clear among the Talmudists and **Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the influential Sephardic Jewish philosopher and jurist who codified Jewish law.</note>, where they explain the perpetual worship of the Temple (<term>Tamid</term> <note>original Hebrew: *תמיד*, meaning "continual," referring to the daily burnt offerings made every morning and evening.</note>) and the **duties of the Levites**. You might ask, "Was nothing of prayer spoken at all by the Priests in the Temple?" As far as I know, nothing public was said beyond those prayers we will mention shortly. However, they performed their duty privately in the **Chamber of Hewn Stone** <note>original Latin: *Conclavi Gazith*, the hall in the Temple where the Sanhedrin met and where priests gathered for specific ritual recitations.</note>, after the parts of the sacrificial victim were already prepared for offering.

<margin>Tamid, chapter 4, section 3; chapter 5, section 1.</margin>
The text states: *And they came to the Chamber of Hewn Stone to recite the Shema.* <note>original Hebrew: *ובאו להם ללשכת הגזית לקרות את שמע*. The *Shema* is the central declaration of Jewish faith: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one."</note> **Peringer** <note>Gustav Peringer (1651–1710), a Swedish scholar who translated parts of the Mishnah into Latin.</note> says it best: *So that they might perform the morning prayers.* It is added: *The Prefect said to them: Recite one blessing, which they immediately performed; and they afterwards recited the Ten Commandments, the section "Hear, O Israel" [the Shema], and the section "And it shall come to pass if you obey," etc.* <note>original Hebrew: *אמר להם הממונה : ברכו ברכה אחת...* referring to the specific liturgy recited by the priests during the morning service.</note> I have mostly retained the translation of the most learned Peringer.

# CHAPTER 5. ON THE OLD SYNAGOGUE. 51

Among the prayers recited by the Priests before the people during those public sacred rites, Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and Torah scholar.</note> enumerates three: *True and Firm* <note>original Hebrew: *Emeth Vejatzif*; this is the blessing recited after the Shema in the morning service</note>, which is the third part of the *Shema* <note>The central declaration of Jewish faith</note> in the morning; *Be Pleased* <note>original Hebrew: *Retze*</note>, which is the sixteenth blessing of the *Eighteen Benedictions*; and *Grant Peace* <note>original Hebrew: *Sim Shalom*</note>, which is the final blessing of the *Eighteen Benedictions*. Therefore, it was not the entire *Eighteen Benedictions* <note>original: *Schemon-Esre*; the central prayer of the Jewish liturgy</note>, nor all the blessings of the *Recitation of the Shema* <note>original: *Krisma* (Keri'at Shema)</note> that were used. If the authors of the Talmud are to be believed, these were already being recited publicly in the Synagogues at that time with the same ritual by which sacred rites are celebrated in the Synagogue today; although we may rightly doubt whether the entire *Eighteen Benedictions* had been fully composed at that time. But this is discussed in the following sections. For an understanding of the matters we are touching upon here, you should consult Lightfoot in *The Hebrew Temple Service*, Chapter IX, Section V; De Veil on Maimonides’ *Treatise on the Chagigah*, Chapter III; and our own present work, Book III, Chapters XIV and XV. One thing further is added: that after these sacred rites were completed privately, the Priests were commanded to go forward to bless the people with a triple blessing, using the sacred formula: <insert>And he said, "Bless the people," etc., with three blessings: *True and Firm*, the *Service*, and the *Priestly Blessing*.</insert> <note>original Hebrew: ויאמר ברכו את וגו׳ העם שלשה ברכות אמת ויציב ועבודה וברכת כהנים</note> *Afterward, he (the Overseer) said: "Bless the people with three blessings," namely the formulas: "True and Firm," the one concerning the Worship (Service), and finally the Priestly Blessing.*

<margin>On this passage.</margin>
"Bless the people" here is the same as "bless with the people," as noted by Rabbi Yom Tov. However, on the Sabbath day, they added another prayer to those already listed: <insert>And on the Sabbath they added one blessing for the departing shift.</insert> <note>original Hebrew: ובשבת מוסיפים ברכה אחת למשמר היוצא. This refers to the "mishmar," the division of priests finishing their week of service at the Temple.</note>

<margin>Folio 11, column 2, near the end.</margin>
As to exactly which *blessing* that was, you will find it anxiously sought after and explained in the *Gemara Berachoth* <note>A section of the Talmud focusing on the rules of blessings and prayers</note>. Furthermore, what was done on the special days of either a public *Fast* or the *Day of Atonement* belongs to those specific times and does not relate as much to our current goal. It is enough for us to be certain that the worship of prayers and blessings was much more formal in the Synagogue than in the Temple. Moreover, the *Reading and Explanation of the Law*—as far as I know—was never performed by the Priests or Levites from the *platform* <note>original: *suggesto*</note> of the Court of the Priests (from which the *Levites* were accustomed to celebrate God with *song*). Yet, these were held among the primary sacred acts of the Synagogue. For this reason, there is sufficient cause to assert that the sacred rites of the Synagogue varied significantly from the ceremonies of the Temple in this <term>relation</term> <note>original Greek: σχέσει (schesis), meaning "character" or "disposition"</note>. Indeed, the Christian Church, in this area where the Synagogue departs from the Temple, aligns with the Synagogue and not with the Temple, as will become clear from the comparison to be established hereafter.

# INTRODUCTION ETC. CHAPTER 5. 52

Regarding the sacred worship of sacrifices, when they speak properly, they expressly advise that Prayers and the Reading of the Law, which constituted the religion of the Synagogues, are not **Service** <note>original Hebrew: *Avodah*; this term specifically refers to the sacrificial labor or cultic service performed in the Temple</note>; that is, they do not belong to the worship of the Temple and its ministers. These are the clear words of *Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides, the 12th-century Jewish philosopher</note> where he discusses the 
<margin>Yoma <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning the Day of Atonement</note> chapter 7, § 1.</margin> 
reading performed by the High Priest. The *Talmudic* text reads as follows: 
**The High Priest comes to read. If he wishes to read in the fine linen garments (in which he performed the worship of that day), he may read; but if it does not please him, he may read in his own white robe.** <note>original Hebrew: *Ba lo Kohen Gadol likrot...*</note> By "white robe" is understood the ordinary garment of the High Priest, which he was accustomed to wear outside of the Temple Worship. You see that the High Priest, hurrying from the sacred rites of the Temple to those of the Synagogue, was able to change his garments. For what purpose? Unless to signify that the sacred rites of the Synagogue are distinct from those of the Temple. Let us add the entire commentary 
<margin>On this Mishnah.</margin> 
of *Maimonides*: **The robe, which was his own white one, was to make known that the READING OF THE LAW IS NOT SERVICE: (that is, it ought to be considered as not at all belonging to the sacrificial worship). Indeed, it is permitted for him to read in whatever garment he wishes. As for what is said in the text—that if he wishes to read in the fine linen garments, it is allowed—this instructs you that it is permitted for him to use those very priestly garments (namely in the Temple) even at that time when he is released from the ministry of the Temple. For it is a fundamental truth among us that one may derive benefit from the priestly garments even outside the time of ministry.** <note>original Hebrew: *Itztalit lavan mishelo lehodia...*</note> That same author says exactly the same in the *Yad* <note>The *Yad HaChazakah*, also known as the *Mishneh Torah*, Maimonides' code of Jewish law</note>, where he describes the ceremonies of the Day of Atonement. 
<margin>
Treatise on the Service of the Day of Atonement, chapter 3. Folio 48, column 2, near the end.
</margin> 
These points are taken from the *Gemara* <note>The part of the Talmud containing rabbinical commentary</note> itself regarding the text of the *Mishnah* cited above. Furthermore, this clear testimony of the Gemarists greatly favors our opinion. The *Reading of the Law*, and the prayers and ceremonies pertaining to it, performed by the High Priest on the public Day of Atonement in the Synagogue, are not **Service** <note>original Hebrew: *Avodah*</note>; that is, they do not belong to the Worship and ceremonies that were prescribed for the Temple. And yet, this very religion of the Synagogues is entirely conformed to the religion of the Christian Church. From this, the conclusion arises for me that it is much better to think that the ceremonies of the Church were taken from the Synagogue rather than from the Temple; and therefore, the comparison instituted by most learned men between the Worship of Christians in their oratories and that of the Jews in the Temple falls away.

## CHAPTER VI.

*The arguments of James Ussher of Armagh* <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), Archbishop of Armagh, was a celebrated scholar who argued for the apostolic origin of the church hierarchy</note> *and of other most learned men, reviewed in Chapter 2, by which they intend to prove that the external government of the Church and the mode of Divine Worship under the Economy of the Gospel were formed by the Apostles according to the type of the Temple Religion and its administration, are discussed at length; at the same time, the importance of this question is indicated, and the testimonies produced from Holy Scripture to establish this opinion are set forth.*

<margin>Chapter 2.</margin>
After it has been proved by solid reasons and examples that *the Ceremonies of the Christian Church correspond much more closely with the Rites of the Synagogue* than with the *Worship of the Temple*, we must now respond to the arguments for the opposing view, which we reviewed in our previous discourse. Among those, what occurs to us in the *first* place is that there truly is a great similarity between *Priests* and *Levites*, and *Bishops* (or *Presbyters*) and *Deacons*. Just as the *Levites* were consecrated to the perpetual ministry of the *Priests*, so likewise the *Deacons*—as will be clearly explained in what follows, being "those who give themselves to God" <note>original Greek: Θεῷ διδόντες (*Theo didontes*); here the author suggests deacons are defined by their devotion or service to God</note>—were at the hand of the *Bishops* and *Presbyters*. But this difficulty is not among those that require an Oedipus <note>A classical reference to Oedipus solving the riddle of the Sphinx; the author means the solution is simple and does not require a genius</note> to resolve. We certainly do not deny that the *Deacons* in the early Church stood in some relation to the *Presbyters* just as the *Levites* stood to the *Priests*: for just as the latter were administrators of the *Temple* and the *Priests*, so the former were administrators of the Church and the Presbyters. 

But it must be observed that this *characteristic* alone is not sufficient to base a comparison between the *Temple* and the *Church* upon it, because there is almost no sacred or civil College or Council <note>original: *Synedrium*, the Latinized form of Sanhedrin, referring to a governing or judicial body</note> flourishing among men in which similar grades of officials and ministers are not observed. That the Councils of the Hebrews had their own **ministers** <note>original Hebrew: שליחי (*shlichi*), meaning agents, emissaries, or attendants</note> is too well known to need mentioning. In the sacred rites of the Gentiles, exactly the same system of distinction and order was maintained. There were *Priests* there: the *Greatest, Greater, and Lesser*, as among the Hebrews, and at the same time [ministers] of the *Priests*...

...of the priests: *Ministers, servants, and attendants, who bought cattle for the sacrifices, brought gifts to the altars, collected the firstfruits, begged for alms for the sacrifices, and so on.* Truly, there seems to me no reason to say either that the institutions of the Hebrews were borrowed from the Gentiles <note>The "Gentiles" here refers to the surrounding pagan nations like the Greeks, Romans, and Egyptians.</note> for this reason, or that the customs of the Gentiles were taken from the Hebrews. A sound mind easily understands that sacred affairs cannot be managed conveniently unless certain degrees of rank and order exist among their administrators. Therefore, what God ordained in His supreme wisdom regarding the discipline and ceremonies of the Temple, right reason taught the Gentiles in this regard whenever the idea came to them to worship the Supreme Power with a fixed ritual of sacrifices. Wherefore also, when we encounter in the Church certain high *Overseers of Sacred Affairs*, who have others under them of a lower grade and order as lesser *Ministers* of the sacred, we must not immediately think that this *order* was borrowed from the Temple. For if that were so, one could say with almost the same reasoning that it was borrowed from the sacred rites of the Gentiles, or from the formal proceedings of any other Sacred Sanhedrin <note>A "Sanhedrin" refers to a formal assembly or council, specifically the Jewish judicial body.</note>; unless, perhaps, other characteristic marks of agreement are found in that same example.

But regarding what contributes more to the definition of the present controversy: we do not deny that there is some degree of agreement between the *distinct orders of Priests and Levites, and the Presbyters and Deacons of the Church*. However, this agreement is such that there is a much greater similarity between the orders of *Presbyters and Deacons of the Synagogue and the Church*. If the Church agrees with the Temple in the fact that in both there are *Overseers and Ministers* of sacred things, then surely the Church agrees much more with the *Synagogue*. This is because in the Synagogue, one finds not only this same distinct order of *Overseers and Ministers* found in the *Church*, but also because the *Offices* that constitute this order are expressed by the very same names used for the offices of the *Church*. From this, it is certain that in this case as well, the Church agrees *more* with the Government of the *Synagogue* than with the order of administration of the *Sacred Temple*, even if any agreement between the *Temple and the Church* in this regard cannot be denied or hidden. It had to be demonstrated that in whatever part the *Administration of the Church’s sacred affairs* agrees with the *sacred affairs of the Temple*, in that same part it disagrees with the *Synagogue*. As long as this is not shown, the Synagogue remains the type... <note>original: *typus*; meaning the model or pattern.</note>

### CHAPTER 6. CONCERNING THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE.

...received from the Temple. *Synagogues* admitted in the past, and admit today, not only various liturgies of *prayers* and *blessings*, which are recited by the Minister of the Synagogue, either alone or with the Congregation, but also a <term>Kohen</term> <note>original: כהן; a Jewish priest descending from Aaron</note> or *Priest*, who blesses the people with uplifted *hands* (a ritual we will discuss in what follows). Therefore, if any *blessings*, of whatever nature they may have been, were in use in the *early Church* (which we rightly presume were very few and very simple, and much different from the formulas of later times), it is more believable that the Church borrowed them from the *Synagogue* than from the *Temple*. This is because the Church agrees with the *Synagogue* in all other parts where it differs from the *Temple*. 

I will propose a similar case: If someone intends to compare two structures of houses, where one is said to be the model for the other, they should not focus so much on whether they share certain common parts in which the two buildings agree. This is because certain rules of architecture are of such common and general use that their observation is not neglected in any structure at all. Instead, one should look especially at whether this building agrees with the other, of which it is said to be a model, in those *parts* in which it differs from all others. When one notices this, only then can they conclude that the one bears the image of the other. 

It is exactly the same with these sacred matters about which we are disputing. If the *Leaders of the Church* agreed in some part with the *Priests of the Temple Rituals*, and in that same part were unlike the *Leaders of the Synagogue*, then our hypothesis would surely falter. But as long as that is not proven, our cause does not suffer. 

Furthermore, this same response serves to solve the objection which is taken from the similarity of *Levites* and *Deacons*, and their *Duties*. You say: "*Deacons* had many things in common with *Levites*, therefore the *Levites* gave rise to the *Deacons*." Certainly, I would not deny that the *Deacons of the early Church* (for I am not disputing about those whom our own Church currently has) were in many ways similar to *Levites*. They served the *Presiders of the Church*; they read aloud the text of Holy Scripture; they exhorted the people to reverence and attention toward sacred things; they celebrated God through hymns and Songs; they received and arranged the holy symbols of the communion of the faithful; they guarded the Temples and chapels; they lived with the Presiders from the sacred offerings, and other things similar to these. It must be noted, however, that the *Deacons* in all these offi-

# PREFACE &c. CHAPTER 6.

...it even more agreed with the *Deacons of the Synagogue*, as will be shown in its proper place. Therefore, it is much easier to say that the *Deacons of the Church* derive their origin from the *Deacons of the Synagogue* than from the *Deacons of the Temple*. Yet, I would not be reluctant to concede that the *Deacons of the Synagogue*, who were often chosen from the Priestly order or the tribe of Levi after the destruction of the Temple, adopted many things from the *Deacons of the Temple*. Nor does this weigh against our case. For the Temple had a twofold Worship: one ceremonial and the other moral, if you consider them distinctly. However, the whole was considered ceremonial because the moral Religion of the Temple served the *ceremonial*. But that which was *moral* in the Temple ceremonies—such as praying to God, celebrating Him with song, and blessing the people in His name, etc.—was transferred to the Synagogues, and from the Synagogues to the Oratories of the Christians. It is better to say that the Church received these ceremonies from the *Synagogue* rather than from the *Temple*, because it received many other rites from the *Synagogue* while completely neglecting those ceremonies and that apparatus which were specific to the Temple. These things we now assume will become clear from the comparison itself, which is to be established hereafter.

You say that the passages of Scripture cited above stand in the way, in which the *Overseers of the Church* are called by the name of *Priests*. This is clear from those very places, even at first glance. *The Priests and Levites brought an offering to the Lord in clean vessels:* In the same way, the Ministers of the New Testament bring the *Gentiles* through the preaching of the Gospel to God, and present them to God as *sacrifices*, to be devoted to Divine honor. ### PROLEGOMENA ETC. CHAPTER 6.

To be sure, we freely grant that the **Priests and Levites, insofar as they performed sacred duties**, can be considered as <term>types</term> <note>original: "typos"; in biblical study, a "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament that foreshadows a reality in the New Testament.</note> of the **Bishops and Deacons of the Church of the New Covenant**, insofar as those men also perform sacred duties. Nevertheless, I would like two things to be observed at the same time:

1. This <term>typological</term> interpretation of the **Priests and Levites** is not only less common, but is also the weakest and most superficial of all explanations. As has already been proven, the **Sacred Rites of the Old Testament** signified various things depending on how they were viewed. The same is true regarding the **Priests**.

In former times, the **Priests** stood as types of **Christ**; they were also types of the **faithful**. For just as Christ has the right to approach God, so too do the faithful through Him. Certainly, in the ordinary **Service of the Temple**, the **Priests** (considered in an absolute sense) designated both **Christ**—who would eventually approach God on behalf of the faithful with a sacrifice of eternal power and value—and the **believers themselves**, who approach God through the continuous exercise of faith and thus through Christ and His sacrifice. However, when the **Priests** are considered specifically in relation to the **High Priest** <note>original: "Sacerdotem Maximum"</note>, they denoted only the **faithful**.

This was the primary typical meaning of the **Priests**. You might ask: "What, then, did the **Israelite people** signify?" I will say it in a word: they also signified the faithful. But you may insist that the **People and the Priests** could not conveniently signify one and the same thing. I confidently deny that. I will provide a clear and easy reason: the **Priests** were considered as a **part of the people**, insofar as they stood as types of the faithful.

For indeed, the entire **Jewish Nation** was declared by God to be a **Priestly Kingdom**. Yet it pleased God, for just reasons, that this **right of priesthood** bestowed upon all Israelites should be administered by only certain persons: the **Sons of Aaron** <note>The lineage of Aaron, Moses' brother, who held the exclusive right to the formal priesthood in Israel.</note>. Because those men exercised this right in the name and place of all Israelites, these **Common Priests** were certainly considered as a part of the people. Consequently, the people must be understood as having approached God through them. Therefore, it is false to say the **People** designated something distinct from the **Priests**, provided the Priests are understood as types of those who approach God through Christ.

Correctly observing this point is sufficient for solving all difficulties. From this, anyone can easily perceive that the certain and principal typical meaning of the **Priests** is that either **Christ** or the **faithful** are designated through them. However, if the **Priests** are taken simply as the **Ministers of the Sacred Rites of the Old Testament Church**, it is certain that they...

# Chapter 6. ON THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE.

In this respect, they can also be considered as types of the *Ministers of the New Testament*, insofar as those ministers also perform sacred duties. For they also present the *prayers and thanksgivings* of the faithful to God, like sacrifices, as it were, in the name of Christ. But this <term>typological</term> <note>Typology is a method of biblical interpretation where people or events in the Old Testament are seen as "types" or symbols foreshadowing "antitypes" in the New Testament.</note> application is the weakest and rarest of all, because undoubtedly the *leaders* of the Church have no greater right of approaching God than other believers; and therefore (strictly speaking), they were no more designated by the *Priests* than the rest of the faithful were. Thus, this is a loose and very weak application and naming, adapted to the perceptions of the Jewish people for lack of other words. I would not want such great hypotheses to be built upon it, such as those of the <term>Pontificians</term> <note>A term used by Protestant authors to refer to Roman Catholics who support the authority of the Pope.</note> mentioned above, regarding the *priesthood of Bishops and Presbyters* of the New Covenant—as if this were granted to them as a special privilege in opposition to the *common people*. Let this ambition finally be gone.

Now, a third point remains to be resolved, which was raised from the reasoning of *Paul* in his first letter to the *Corinthians* regarding the payment of *Ministers* under the <term>Gospel Economy</term> <note>The "Economy" refers to God’s plan or management of human salvation during the era of the New Testament.</note>. *Paul* intends to prove that this duty of charity is owed to him, just as it is to all other interpreters of the Divine will, by the people, so that he may live without any anxiety about seeking a livelihood. He uses this argument: <margin>1 Corinthians 9:13</margin> *Do you not know that **those who perform sacred duties** <note>original Greek: τοὺς τὰ ἱερὰ ἐργαζομένους</note>, eat those things which are from the sanctuary? and those who attend the altar <note>original Greek: τῷ θυσιαστηρίῳ προσεδρεύοντας</note>, share in the altar?* He then adds: ***So also the Lord ordained for those who announce the Gospel, that they should live from the Gospel*** <note>original Greek: Οὕτω καὶ ὁ Κύριος διέταξε τοῖς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον καταγγέλλουσιν, ἐκ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου ζῆν</note>. But, what must be carefully noted, in the text itself there is a reasoning through which we can blunt the force of this argument. *Paul* in this place compares those who *proclaim the Gospel* (for he is speaking of them) not only with *Priests*, but also with *Levites*. *To perform sacred duties* <note>original Greek: Τὰ ἱερὰ ἐργάζεσϑαι</note> must be taken entirely as a description of the office of the Levites; it is equivalent to *serving the sacred things* and being occupied in that work throughout one's whole life. <margin>Regarding this passage</margin> "For since" (this is *Theophylact’s* commentary) "what was said about the oxen had been taken by him allegorically, he says the Law now expressly commands that those who perform sacred duties should eat from the temple—that is, the **Levites**, who are lower in rank than the **Priests**: *For since he had accepted those things spoken of the oxen allegorically, he now says the Law commands in plain words that those who perform sacred duties should eat of the sacred things, that is, the Levites, who are lower in rank than the Priests.*" 

The following phrase, *to attend to the altar* <note>original Greek: τῷ ϑυσιαστηρίῳ προσεδρεύειν</note>, he correctly applies to the Priests: *that is*, he says, *the Priests and High Priests*. *After setting out the sequence of treatment for this Book, the genuine meaning of the word **SYNAGOGE** <note>original Greek: ΣΥΝΑΓΩΓΗ, meaning an assembly or gathering</note> is investigated using Hesychius <note>a 5th-century lexicographer</note>, the Seventy Translators <term>LXX: The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</term>, and the specific designation of the Hebrew word **Edah** <note>original Hebrew: עדה</note>, which has much in common with the Greek **Synagoge**. Finally, after resolving certain objections, some observations are made regarding the phrase **Qehilat Qodesha** <note>original Hebrew: קהילת קדושא</note> or **the holy assembly** <note>original Greek: ἡ ἁγία ἐκκλησία</note>, a phrase frequently used by the Apostles.*

In the First, the **NAMES AND STRUCTURE OF SYNAGOGUES** will be explained; in the Second, we will inquire into the **ORIGIN OF SYNAGOGUES**; and the Third will concern the **AGREEMENT OF SYNAGOGUES** with the **ORATORIES OF CHRISTIANS** <note>original Latin: *Oratoriis Christianorum*, referring to early Christian places of prayer</note>.

# CONCERNING THE NAMES, ETC. BOOK I. PART I.

The names, whose genuine meaning must be investigated and uncovered here, are of various kinds. For they refer either to the *Places of Jewish Assemblies*, or to the *Groups* that meet in those places, or to *both* at once. Of the last order is the word itself, **SYNAGOGUE** <note>original Greek: ΣΥΝΑΓΩΓΗ</note>, which we believe must be explained first of all, because our treatise bears it on its front.

<margin>Athenaeus, *The Learned Banqueters* <note>original: *Deipnosophist.*</note>, book 8, p. 365. See also Casaubon, *Observations* <note>original: *Animadv.*</note>, book 5, chapter 17, near the end.</margin>
The word **SYNAGOGUE**, as is well known, descends from *synagein* <note>original: συνάγειν</note>, *to gather or collect*. Hesychius <note>a 5th-century Greek grammarian and lexicographer</note> says: "*Synagein*, to drink with one another: to gather. To drink together." This is a more restricted interpretation of the word *synagein*, according to a particular use it had among the Ancients. Learn of this from *Athenaeus*: "They used the word *synagein* <note>to gather</note> for drinking together, and they called the banquet itself a *synagogion* <note>original: συναγώγιον</note>." Examples are suggested in that same place. It should be noted, however, that the word *synagein* extends much more widely than is handed down in this exposition by *Hesychius*. For *synagein* among Greek authors has the same value as *synathroizein* <note>original: συναθροίζειν</note>, *to aggregate or gather into one*. The same *Hesychius* says a little later: "*Synathroizetai* <note>is gathered together</note>, *synagetai* <note>is collected</note>."

<margin>Spanheim, *Evangelical Doubts* <note>original: *Dub. Evangel.*</note> Part 3, Doubt 87, p. 365. Isaiah 24:23. Jeremiah 31:4, 13. Leviticus 10:3. Numbers 32:15. Jeremiah 6:11.</margin>
Therefore, **synagoge** denotes *every gathering and heaping together of many into one*. Hesychius again: "*Synakterion* <note>original: Συνακτήριον</note>, a gathering." In that common sense, we see that this notion is accepted by the Seventy <term>Septuagint: the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, often abbreviated as LXX</term> who, as has already been observed by others, sometimes translate the Hebrew words **asaph** <note>original: אסף, gathering</note>, **machol** <note>original: מחוֹל, dance or chorus</note>, **am** <note>original: עם, people</note>, **qahal** <note>original: קהל, a multitude called together for an assembly</note>, and even **sod** <note>original: סוֹד, familiar association or secret council</note>, by the Greek word *synagoge*. Examples are noted in the margin; these are indeed quite rare for the other words, but frequent in the translation of the word **qahal**, as anyone easily notices from *Kircher* <note>Conrad Kircher, author of a Hebrew-Greek concordance of the Old Testament</note>. It is clear enough from these that the word *synagoge*, both by reason of its origin and by reason of its use among the sacred Greek authors, denotes every kind of gathering of *things* or *persons*; and for the latter, whether it be Civil or Ecclesiastical. It should be observed, however, that the *Septuagint Interpreters*, so called, decided by a certain particular plan to translate the Hebrew word **edah** <note>original: עדה, congregation</note> using the word *synagoge*. In a few texts, I admit, they translated the word *edah* as *parembole* <note>original: παρεμβολὴ, camp</note>, *episustasis* <note>original: ἐπισύστασις, a gathering or conspiracy</note>, and con-

### CHAPTER I. CONCERNING SYNAGOGUES.

<margin>Jeremiah 6:18, Chapter 14:8, Psalm 22:17, Numbers 23:3</margin>
...and "conspiracy," and they translated it as "all" <note>original Greek: πᾶς</note>, and they did so quite elegantly and judiciously, as will be clear to anyone who cares to look into the context of those passages. Not to mention that this same word <term>edah <note>Hebrew: עדה</note></term> was also once rendered by these same Translators <note>The "Translators" refers to the authors of the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> as "flock" <note>original Greek: ποίμνιον</note>. Nevertheless, it is certain—as far as we can judge from the diligence of *Kircher* <note>Conrad Kircher, a 17th-century scholar who created a Hebrew-Greek concordance</note>—that the word *edah* was consistently translated by them in all other places as **Synagogue** <note>original Greek: Συναγωγή</note>.

Furthermore, that Hebrew word *edah*, derived from the root *ya'ad* <note>Hebrew: יעד, meaning to appoint or meet at a set time</note>, denotes any kind of gathering or congregation of people, whether large or small, whether of the whole multitude or just a part of it. Indeed, it refers not only to *humans*, but also to other *living creatures*. In the *Book of Judges*, a swarm of *bees* is called an *edat deborim* <note>Hebrew: עדת דבורים</note>, which the Septuagint in my edition translated as: "**Synagogue** of bees" <note>original Greek: Συναγωγὴ μελισσῶν</note>. *Kircher* has it as: "A swarm of bees" <note>original Greek: Συστροφὴ μελισσῶν</note>, having undoubtedly used a different edition.

However, this word is properly and ordinarily used for assemblies of people coming together, but in such a way that no account is taken of the nature of such a gathering—whether it be *good* or *bad*, honorable or wicked, sacred or civil. Truly, David mentions the "assembly of the wicked" <note>Hebrew: עדת מרעים; original Greek: συναγωγῆς πονηρευομένων</note>, and *Moses* clearly calls the faction of *Korah*, *Dathan*, *Abiram*, and the other conspirators "the assembly of those who had conspired against Jehovah" <note>Hebrew: עדת הנועדים על יהוה</note>; here the Septuagint translators did not forget their usual word, **Synagogue**.

With these things understood beforehand, effort must now be made to understand more distinctly how much the word *edah* differs in its power and meaning from the word <term>kahal <note>Hebrew: קהל</note></term>, which itself is also sometimes translated by the Septuagint as **Synagogue**, though more frequently as **Ecclesia** <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησία, usually translated as "Church" or "Assembly"</note>. Indeed, those Septuagint translators, by never translating the word *edah* as "Ecclesia"—though they frequently use that Greek word to translate *kahal*—sufficiently indicated that they believed these two words, *edah* and *kahal*, were distinct in meaning. Yet they would have acted far better and more wisely if, just as they never translated *edah* as "Ecclesia," they had likewise never translated *kahal* as "**Synagogue**." This is because the mixing of these two concepts, when applied to one and the same Greek word, produces a certain confusion. For certainly the words *edah* and *kahal* truly have varying meanings. You may easily gather this from these words which are read in the precepts of the ceremonies...

<header>CONCERNING THE NAMES, ETC. BOOK I. PART I.</header>

<margin>Exodus 12:6.</margin>
...of the Paschal Lamb. *And they shall slaughter it*, so the text has it: <term>the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel <note>original Hebrew: kol qahal ‘adat yisra’el</note></term>. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> renders this as: <term>All the multitude of the assembly of the sons of Israel <note>original Greek: Pan to plethos synagoges huion Israel</note></term>, or, "The whole multitude (the Assembly) of the Synagogue (the gathering) of the Israelites." The Talmudists <note>Jewish scholars who compiled the Talmud, a central text of Rabbinic Judaism</note>, who never make an end to their clever subtleties, have stripped away all the impact of this way of speaking. They taught that, based on this passage, the slaughtering of the Passover lamb must be performed by *three* <term>groups <note>original Hebrew: kittot</note></term>, each consisting of *thirty men*, who were to follow one after another in the temple courtyard. To construct or establish this invention from this passage, they claim that those words—<term>assembly <note>Hebrew: qahal</note></term>, <term>congregation <note>Hebrew: ‘adat</note></term>, and <term>Israel</term>—should not be taken together as a single phrase, but separately; as if Moses had intended to say: "*An assembly, a congregation, and Israel* shall slaughter this lamb."

<margin>At this passage, in *On the Passover Sacrifice*, chapter 1, sections 9, 10, 11.</margin>
Please see the commentaries of *Solomon Jarchi* <note>Better known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator</note>, and among other writers on ritual law, *Maimonides* <note>A preeminent medieval Sephardic philosopher and jurist; the margin refers to his work, the Mishneh Torah</note>, who explains these things quite extensively. These are mere trifles! Anyone who examines the text with a clear eye is forced to recognize that the words <term>congregation <note>Hebrew: ‘edah</note></term> and <term>assembly <note>Hebrew: qahal</note></term> do not have the same meaning here, but different ones. Otherwise, there would be an obvious tautology <note>the unnecessary repetition of the same idea in different words</note>. What, then, is the distinction?

The word <term>assembly <note>Hebrew: qahal</note></term> has a more restricted and specific meaning than the word <term>congregation <note>Hebrew: ‘edah</note></term>. For it properly denotes the *entire multitude* of a certain people, joined by the bonds of society and constituting a certain republic or city-state. In contrast, the word <term>congregation <note>Hebrew: ‘edah</note></term>, by its very nature and the force of its meaning, *merely refers to any gathering or meeting of men whatsoever*, whether *smaller* or *larger*. It refers especially, however, to an *appointed* and established gathering—not of the entire people (even though its meaning is broad enough to be applied to them, as we saw in the text just cited), but of certain specific men chosen from the people, such as the *gatherings and councils of magistrates*.

And hence it happens that the word <term>congregation <note>Hebrew: ‘edah</note></term> can be applied to a specific assembly within a society, to which the notion of <term>assembly <note>Hebrew: qahal</note></term> can by no means be applied. Suppose there is some *Sanhedrin* <note>A Jewish judicial council or court</note> of twenty, thirty, or sixty men; or suppose some men are gathered from among the people to perform this or that task, whether sacred or civil—you might correctly use the word <term>congregation <note>Hebrew: ‘edah</note></term> (meaning a "Meeting"), but certainly not the word <term>assembly <note>Hebrew: qahal</note></term>. For this latter concept always designates a *common multitude* organized into a City and a Republic. Indeed, to express my meaning more correctly, <term>assembly <note>Hebrew: qahal</note></term>, taken in its broader sense, signifies the same thing that the Hebrews and Romans expressed by the word <term>people <note>original Hebrew: ‘am</note></term>, and sometimes even by <term>city <note>original Hebrew: ‘ir</note></term>. For with these names the Hebrews [refer to] the whole...

<meta>This page continues the philological investigation into the Hebrew terms 'qahal' and 'edah', specifically addressing the overlap in their usage and how the Septuagint translators rendered them into Greek. ### CHAPTER I. OF SYNAGOGUES.

...so that the words, *he frequently called an assembly* <note>original Greek: συνεχῶς ἐξεκκλησίασε</note>, signify that **Moses**, near the end of his life, **frequently preached to the people**. But these two concepts go hand in hand, and both lie hidden in the meaning of this word. <margin>See Suidas under the word: *he who gathers an assembly* <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησίαζων; Suidas was a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist</note>.</margin> It is certainly clear from the evidence brought forward that there is a living emphasis in the meaning of the word <term>qahal <note>Hebrew: קהל; usually refers to a formal assembly summoned for a specific purpose</note></term>, and a clear distinction between it and the word <term>edah <note>Hebrew: עדה; often refers to a congregation or a more general gathering</note></term>.

Nor, however, have we thus overcome every difficulty. For it is to be observed, as we touched upon before, that sometimes the **entire assembly of the Jewish people** is also called an <term>edah</term>; further, that the *Septuagint* <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> Translators themselves sometimes translate the word <term>qahal</term> as **synagogue** <note>original Greek: συναγωγή</note>, a name they otherwise usually reserve for the word <term>edah</term>; and finally, that this very notion of <term>qahal</term> sometimes seems to be applied to individual gatherings—not of the whole Commonwealth, but perhaps of a single city or Province. To each of these points, we must respond briefly.

Regarding the **first** point, I would not deny that the whole <term>qahal</term>, the **multitude of the Jewish people**, can be called and is sometimes called an <term>edah</term>, an **assembly**. This is because every society and gathering of men—whether many in number or few, whether universal or particular—can be called an <term>edah</term>, meaning an **assembly or a coming together**. Therefore, there is no formal gathering, no public meeting, which is not in reality an <term>edah</term>, an **assembly**. 

But one must pay close attention to this:
1. By the word <term>edah</term>, considered on its own without context, the entire multitude of a people is never automatically indicated. When the text says that this or that must be done **in the assembly of Israel** <note>Hebrew: בעדת ישראל (be-adat Yisrael)</note>, or *by the assembly of Israel*, that phrase—in its genuine and proper meaning—does not designate the whole **Jewish people** unless the specific circumstances of the text prove it. In contrast, the word <term>qahal</term> always and everywhere (unless I am mistaken) designates the entire Citizenry of the people. While what took place in the **assemblies of the people** can be said to have taken place in a **gathering**, it does not follow that the terms **gathering** and **assembly** mean the same thing. <margin>Exodus 12:47. Of Israel, 16:1.</margin> 

2. When the Sacred Writers strive to indicate the *entire* gathering of the people through the word <term>edah</term>, they frequently do not express it simply as the *Assembly of Israel*, but as the **WHOLE assembly of Israel** <note>Hebrew: כל עדת ישראל (Kol adat Yisrael)</note>.

...of Israel, **the entire assembly of the children of Israel** <note>original: πᾶσαν συναγωγὴν υἱῶν Ἰσראήל; a mixture of Greek and Hebrew in the text</note>. Certainly, the whole gathering of the people can mean the same as <term>qahal <note>Hebrew: קהל; usually refers to a formal assembly summoned for a specific purpose</note></term>, when the <term>qahal</term>—as often happens—is taken to mean the entire people. However, even then, the specific force of the word <term>qahal</term> is not fully satisfied, because it is sometimes used to signify a **summoned assembly** <note>original Latin: *comitia calata*, a term for Roman assemblies called specifically for religious or legal inaugurations</note>, as was just demonstrated; yet the phrase **all the congregation of Israel** <note>Hebrew: כל עדת ישראל (*kol adat Yisrael*)</note> never, by itself, denotes a summoned assembly of the people. Regarding the **second objection**, derived from the fact that the **Septuagint** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, often abbreviated as LXX</note> sometimes translated the word <term>qahal</term> as **synagogue** <note>original Greek: συναγωγὴ</note>, that point is not so significant that we must abandon our position because of it. It is true that those Septuagint translators sometimes translated <term>qahal</term> as **synagogue**, and they did so for this reason: every <term>qahal</term> can, in a healthy sense, be called an **ecclesia** <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησία; referring to a formal assembly of citizens</note> or a **synagogue**, insofar as it implies a coming together of several people to establish a **Commonwealth** or to deliberate on the highest matters of the State. However, it would have been better, in my opinion, if they had always rendered <term>qahal</term> as **ecclesia**, because this Greek concept seems formed to clearly express the Hebrew <term>qahal</term>. For every <term>qahal</term> is always and everywhere an **ecclesia**. But since it seemed otherwise to the Septuagint translators, one ought not to think that the words <term>edah</term> <note>Hebrew: עדה; often meaning a general congregation or community</note> and <term>qahal</term> differ in no way in their power of meaning. For it often happens that either the translators do not grasp the genuine meaning of words, or they translate words of varying meanings with the same Greek terms, provided there is some agreement in the meanings of those words. Therefore, we need not labor further in resolving this objection.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the Hebrew term 'qahal' (assembly). ### CHAPTER I. OF SYNAGOGUES.

...had committed a sin <term>by mistake <note>Hebrew: בשגגה (*bi-shgagah*); Latin: *per imprudentiam*</note></term>, the Law commanded that the **assembly of Israel** <note>Hebrew: קהל ישראל (*qahal Yisrael*); Greek: ἡ ἐκκλησία τοῦ Ισραὴλ (*he ekklesia tou Israel*)</note> should offer a young bull for a sin offering, to be consecrated with specific ceremonies. Jewish interpreters, however, openly declare in their Constitutions that by the word <term>qahal</term> <note>assembly</note> here, the entire assembly of the people is not to be understood, but rather each individual tribe of the people. Thus, according to their interpretation of the Law, it is not just one young bull, but **Twelve** that are to be offered by the whole Hebrew people.

<margin>So the mentioned passage.</margin>
The text of **Maimonides** <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note> states: *And if they erred regarding other commandments, they bring twelve bulls for sin offerings, and these are burnt because their blood enters the inner sanctuary. Each bull is called the "Bull for the hidden matter of the <margin>In the text it is:</margin> congregation," for it is said: "Then the assembly shall offer..." Each and every assembly and each and every tribe is called an "assembly," for it is said: "And Josaphat stood in the assembly of Judah."* One should not rashly apply any other translation here besides that most elegant version by **De Veil** <note>Charles-Marie de Veil, a 17th-century scholar who translated Maimonides' work into Latin</note>. For these words of the Law, *Then let the assembly slaughter* (or rather, *offer*), <margin>Leviticus 4:14.</margin> signify the **assembly** (<term>qahal</term>). But each tribe is separately called an **assembly** (<term>qahal</term>), since we see it written: *Josaphat standing in the assembly* (<term>bi-qahal</term>) *of Judah*." <margin>2 Chronicles 20:5.</margin> But without any doubt, this is an **unsuitable subtlety** which has no foundation in this law. For where does the **assembly of Israel** denote twelve assemblies and not the whole people, or the assembly of all the tribes together? When **Josaphat** <note>Jehoshaphat, King of Judah</note> is said to have stood in the "assembly of Judah," the assembly there is certainly to be understood as the **entire Jewish people** summoned by him to Jerusalem for a sacred gathering during a most difficult time for the Commonwealth <note>original Latin: *Reipublicae*</note>. The reason why the "assembly of Judah" there does not denote the people of Israel as a whole (constituting another state) is this: the **Ten Tribes**, having separated from the tribe of Judah, were then considered an entirely different people, distinct from the assembly or people of Judah. Therefore, this commentary on the Mosaic text is tasteless. Yet, if anyone should ask whether the multitude of each tribe could not be called a <term>qahal</term>, and thus it might be said in a sound sense that there were **Twelve assemblies** (<term>qahal</term> is not used in the plural here) of the Jewish people, the answer will be, nothing...

...signification; whereas <term>edah <note>Hebrew: עדה; generally referring to a formal assembly or a group gathered by appointment</note></term> truly corresponds to the Greek word <term>synagoge <note>Greek: συναγωγὴ; a gathering together or a congregation</note></term>, and <term>qahal <note>Hebrew: קהל; a convocation or a gathered community</note></term> to the word <term>ekklesia <note>Greek: ἐκκλησία; an assembly of citizens or, in a Christian context, the Church</note></term>.

Truly, from this dual difference in the meaning of these two Greek words, *synagoge* and *ekklesia*, I believe it is clear enough why Christ and the Apostles preferred to express the multitude of Christians by the name *ekklesia* rather than *synagoge*. This choice should not be traced primarily to the cause that they intended to distinguish the Christian Church from the Jewish one through this diversity of names—as the faithful of subsequent ages have presumed (for the Jews themselves were also accustomed to call their own gatherings *ekklesias*, as has already been observed)—but rather because the word *ekklesia* was much more suitable for designating the reality they had in mind to represent. *Synagoge*, like *edah*, always signifies a gathering *joined and assembled together*, even if perhaps bound by no other link; but the *ekklesia* designates a certain *multitude* that constitutes a people, joined together among themselves by laws and bonds, even though it may often happen that they are not gathered together in one place, or even able to be gathered. It is almost as **Justin Martyr** <note>A second-century Christian apologist and philosopher</note> expresses the matter:

<margin>
In the *Dialogue with Trypho the Jew*, page (mihi) 261.
</margin>

"For indeed, both the People and the Assembly <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησία (ekklesia)</note>, though they are many men in number, are called and addressed by a single name as if they were one thing." <note>Latin translation provided in original: *Etenim & Populus & Eccleſia ſeu Concio, permulti numero mortales, perinde atque una res forent, una voce vocantur atque appellantur.*</note>

When, for example, the faithful are dispersed through various regions of a certain land, such that the opportunity to meet is denied to them, they then indeed cease to be an <term>edah <note>Hebrew: עדה; a physical congregation</note></term>, but they do not cease to be a <term>qahal <note>Hebrew: קהל; an assembly in the sense of a corporate body</note></term>—that is, the **Church**—because they do not cease to constitute one body, which is joined together by the tightest bonds through the Spirit and faith. From this, I believe it is easy to see that the word *ekklesia* was used much more appropriately to designate the multitude of believers than *synagoge*. For certainly, one may easily gather that the writers of the New Testament did not seek or affect anything unique in the word *ekklesia* more than *synagoge* from the fact that they occasionally use this word *ekklesia* to designate a *multitude of Gentiles and secular people*.

Again, in Leviticus 4:13–14, where the Hebrew has first *edah* and then *qahal*, the Septuagint used <term>synagogue <note>Greek: συναγωγήν</note></term> in both places. And the writer of the book called Ecclesiasticus <note>Also known as the Wisdom of Sirach</note> calls a promiscuous collection of a crowd an "assembly of the rabble" <note>Greek: ἐκκλησίαν ὄχλου</note>. But for the most part, "assembly" <note>Greek: ἐκκλησία; ekklesia</note> is nothing other than the people of Israel, just as *edah* is taken in the aforementioned passage of Leviticus. Thus Stephen uses the word *ekklesia* in Acts 7:38. Caleb is said to have received his inheritance "in the assembly" <note>Greek: ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ</note> in 1 Maccabees 2:56. And in the writer of Ecclesiasticus, the terms "people" and "assembly" <note>Greek: λαὸς & ἐκκλησία</note> are used for the same thing in 24:1 and 44:15. Likewise, the same writer in the History of the Maccabees (Book 1, 4:49 and 3:13) said "the whole assembly of Israel" <note>Greek: πᾶσαν ἐκκλησίαν Ἰσραὴλ</note>, and the tablets of the covenant are said to have been read "before the assembly" <note>Greek: ἐνώπιον τῆς ἐκκλησίας</note> in 14:19, where shortly after "assembly" is explained by the word for <term>the people <note>Greek: δήμου; demou, referring to the common people or a local district</note></term> in 21:5. Nor should it be doubted that this meaning fits this passage best. For that Israelite people living in one region bore the image of the Christian multitude dispersed throughout the whole world: therefore the Christian multitude is everywhere called by the name of "people," as can be seen in Acts 15:14, Romans 9:21, and Titus 2:14. Moreover, "people" and "assembly" are the same, as we have said. Thus far Grotius; regarding whose digression we observe the following.

<margin>Matthew 16:18.</margin>
<margin>In the Lexicon at the word *Edah*.</margin>

2. It should not be stated simply and without restriction that *Edah* does not signify <term>any chance gathering <note>Greek: τὸν τυχόντα</note></term>, but only one consisting of a certain kind of men. For although *Edah*, by reason of its origin and usage, sometimes denotes a specific, determined assembly, yet at other times it very frequently signifies <term>a chance gathering <note>Greek: τὸν τυχόντα</note></term>. ...of the City and of the Kingdom, is properly called a **Qahal** <note>Hebrew: קהל; a formal assembly or gathering of the people</note>. As for the fact that the Masters of later times <note>The Rabbis of the post-biblical period</note> often interpreted and used the word **Edah** <note>Hebrew: עדה; often referring to a congregation or a body of witnesses</note> for a body of Judges, or a fixed gathering of any men, it does not hinder our opinion. Let it suffice that we hold this notion's use in the Sacred Scriptures to be general and without strict distinction. 

3. That the words **Edah** and **Qahal**, as well as **Synagogue** <note>Greek: συναγωγή</note> and **Ecclesia** <note>Greek: εκκλησία; meaning an assembly or 'church'</note>, are usually mixed in usage, specifically by the translators of the **Septuagint** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> themselves, is not so certain. We admit that the word *Qahal*, which properly denotes *Ecclesia*, is sometimes rendered by them as *Synagogue*; but it does not follow from this that the notions of *Edah* and *Qahal* differ in no way in meaning. It happens countless times <note>original: "sexcenties," literally 'six hundred times,' a Latin idiom for a very large number</note> in usage that Hebrew words of very different meaning—if you look to their origin and common use—are nevertheless translated by the same Greek or Latin words in certain cases and circumstances. A more liberal translator might convert the Hebrew terms **Qodesh** <note>Holy Place</note>, **Heikhal** <note>Sanctuary or Palace</note>, and **Beit YHVH** <note>House of the Lord</note> each in their respective places as "Temple," and not wrongly; but would anyone then conclude that these words do not differ in the power of their meaning? 

The Septuagint, however, does not mix these words, as we have already warned once and again. I confess they translate the name *Qahal* as *Ecclesia* and as *Synagogue*, because certainly every *Ecclesia* can, in a sound sense, be called a *Synagogue*; but the term *Edah*, which they are accustomed to transpose as *Synagogue*, they do not translate as *Ecclesia*, because every *Edah* is not an *Ecclesia*. Of the passages cited by **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note>, there is not one by which it is proved (which was what needed to be proved) that *Edah* signifies *Ecclesia*. Rather, they prove that *Ecclesia* is to be referred uniquely to *Qahal*.

4. Yet we grant him <note>Grotius</note> without difficulty that it is possible for the Greek word *Ecclesia* to sometimes be taken more loosely for any crowd or multitude of people; but such abuses of language <note>Latin: "catachreses"; the use of a word in a way that departs from its strict meaning</note> occur with other words too, which are often of the most constant and indubitable meaning. The interpretation of **Hesychius** <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian and lexicographer</note> seems to belong here: *"Ecclesia, Synod, Synagogue, Assembly"* <note>Greek: Έκκλησία, Σύνοδος, Συναγωγή, Πανήγυρις</note>; although it is certain that Hesychius did not have other terms at hand to designate the emphasis <note>Greek: ἔμφασιν</note> of the word *Ecclesia*. 

**Suidas** <note>A 10th-century Greek lexicographer</note>, however, is entirely on our side when he explains the word *Ecclesia* just as we previously explained *Qahal*. He takes the word *Ecclesia* for the elections <note>Latin: "comitiis"</note> and the assembly of the people. In his Lexicon regarding

The term <term>Qahal</term> <note>original Hebrew: קהל; an assembly or convocation</note> is properly used of a City and a Kingdom. But the fact that the Masters <note>The Jewish Rabbis</note> of later times have often interpreted and used the word <term>Edah</term> <note>original Hebrew: עדה; an appointed meeting or community</note> for a council of Judges, or for the established state of any gathering of men, does not stand in the way of our opinion. It is enough for us to hold that the use of this notion in the Sacred Scriptures is promiscuous and general. 

3. It is not so certain that the words <term>Edah</term> and <term>Qahal</term>, as well as <term>synagoge</term> <note>original Greek: συναγωγὴ; a gathering or bringing together</note> and <term>ekklesia</term> <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησία; a formal assembly or church</note>, are usually intermingled in usage, even by the translators of the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> themselves. We admit that the word <term>Qahal</term>, which properly denotes an <term>assembly</term> <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησίαν</note>, is sometimes rendered by them as a <term>synagogue</term> <note>original Greek: συναγωγήν</note>; but it does not follow from this that the notions of <term>Edah</term> and <term>Qahal</term> differ in no way in their meaning. A more liberal translator might convert the Hebrew terms <term>Miqdash</term> <note>original Hebrew: מקדש; sanctuary</note>, <term>Heikhal</term> <note>original Hebrew: היכל; palace or temple</note>, and <term>Beit YHWH</term> <note>original Hebrew: בית יי; House of the Lord</note> each in their own places as "Temple," and not wrongly; yet who would conclude from this that these words do not differ in the power of their meaning? However, the Septuagint does not intermingle these words, as we have already warned once and again. They translate the name <term>Qahal</term> as <term>assembly</term> <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησία</note> and as <term>synagogue</term> <note>original Greek: συναγωγή</note>, because certainly every Church <note>assembly</note> in a sound sense can be called a Synagogue <note>gathering</note>; but the term <term>Edah</term>, which they were accustomed to translate as <term>synagogue</term>, they do not translate as <term>assembly</term> <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησία</note>, because not every <term>Edah</term> <note>congregation</note> is an <term>ekklesia</term> <note>a formal assembly</note>. Truly, of the passages cited by Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a famous 17th-century Dutch scholar</note>, there is not one by which it is proved (as ought to have been proved) that <term>Edah</term> signifies <term>ekklesia</term>. Rather, they prove that <term>ekklesia</term> is uniquely to be referred back to <term>Qahal</term>.

### CHAPTER 2. OF THE SYNAGOGUES.

How the Church is to be governed in Christ’s absence. Some think reason demands 
<margin>verse 17.</margin> 
that a Prince <note>or "Leader"</note> be appointed among them. Christ counters these prejudices of theirs. He commends humility to them, following the example of a little child. He commends love, so that stumbling blocks <note>original: offendicula</note> may be avoided. Yet he teaches in what manner they should behave toward the stubborn and bold, who refuse to submit themselves to private warnings and rebukes. For this could be a matter of great doubt for the Apostles, after Christ had condemned all Lordship and mastery in his Church. Therefore, he wills that after private warnings have been tried in vain, the matter should be brought to the Church. "Tell it," he says, "to the Church" <note>original Greek: Εἰπὲ τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ / Eipē tē Ekklēsia</note>. What is the meaning of **Church** in this place? Certainly, this could be investigated at length, since, as is well known, various authors have commented on this passage in many different ways. But we must pull in our sails, lest a longer discourse bring boredom. No opinion seems to have gained more strength within the Reformed Church than that which understands "the Church" to mean its **Rulers**, or the 
<margin>1 Tim. 4:14.</margin> 
**Presbytery** <note>original Greek: τὸ πρεσβυτέριον / to presbyterion; a council of elders</note>, as they say. For it seems absurd to them to understand **the Church** in this textual circumstance as the entire multitude of believers, because they think it would follow from this that ecclesiastical censure <note>disciplinary action</note> must be exercised by the whole people of the Church—something the condition of the Church does not seem to permit. This opinion has found, among other ancient and modern writers, two very learned defenders: **John Cameron** and **Jacob Cappellus**. Cameron first argues 
<margin>
In the *Myrothecium Evangelicum* <note>A work of biblical annotations by Cameron</note> on this passage; and *Observations on the New Testament*, Psalm 82:1.
</margin>
that "Church" here can designate a specific number of persons, because the term <term>Edah</term> <note>original Hebrew: עדה; often translated as "congregation" or "assembly"</note> in Scripture denotes a Gathering of **Judges** more than once. However, he refutes those who understand "the Church" here as some Jewish Sanhedrin <note>the supreme legal and religious council of the Jews</note>, because a Jewish Sanhedrin of this kind is never called an **ekklesia** <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησία</note>, but a **synagoga** <note>original Greek: συναγωγή</note>. To defend this further, he argues that **Church** here must be referred back to the Hebrew word <term>Qahal</term> <note>original Hebrew: קהל; a formal convocation</note>. He claims this word took on a unique usage in the New Testament that it did not have in the Old. *But "Church" (Qahal), he says, signifies only a gathering of the people in the Old Testament, and indeed an external gathering, but not insofar as that gathering has a* relation <note>original Greek: σχέσιν / schesin</note> *to Religion. In the New Testament, however, "Church" signifies a gathering specifically in* relation *to religion; it does not note a* relation *to the physical meeting itself, but signifies unity. Since these things are so (he adds), what reason can be given why the Lord [would call] the Jewish Sanhedrin the "Church"?*

### CHAPTER 2. OF THE SYNAGOGUES.

...is more loosely defined than **assembly** <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησία / ekklēsia</note> in the New Testament writings. The Jews of later times, alongside the two words **Assembly** <note>Hebrew: *Kahal*</note> and **Congregation** <note>Hebrew: *Edah*</note>—which we have been busy explaining so far—frequently used two others with very similar meanings, and substituted them as if they were equivalents: **Gathering** <note>original Hebrew: *Knesiah* / כניסה</note> and **Community** <note>original Hebrew: *Tzibur* / צבור</note>. This is how Selden translates it. <meta>This page continues the philological investigation into the terminology of Jewish assemblies. Following the previous page's discussion on the terms 'Kahal' (Assembly) and 'Edah' (Congregation), the author now explores the nuances of 'Tzibur' (Community/Public) and 'Rabbim' (The Many), comparing them to Greek, Latin, and Dutch equivalents to clarify their usage in civil and religious contexts.</meta>

### CHAPTER 2. ON SYNAGOGUES.

<margin>In Menachot, chapter 1.</margin>
**Public & private sacrifices.** <note>original Hebrew: *Zivchei tzibur & yachid* / זבחי צבור & יחיד</note> The former denotes *public*, the latter *private*. Thus **sacrifices of the community** <note>original Hebrew: *zivchei tzibur*</note> are *Sacrifices of the Assembly*; **private sacrifices** <note>original Hebrew: *zivchei yachid*</note> are *individual sacrifices*. From this, **public necessities** <note>original Hebrew: *tzorkhei tzibur* / צרכי צבור</note> are *the requirements of the Commonwealth*: public business, which pertains to the benefit and advantage of the community: **To be occupied with public business** <note>original Hebrew: *asok be-tzorkhei tzibur* / עסוק בצרכי צבור</note> means *to be engaged in the affairs of the Commonwealth*. In Dutch, you cannot express the sense of this word more happily than by: *The Commons* <note>original Dutch: *'t Gemeen*</note>. That this is the genuine meaning of this name is clear from the fact that the Jews are accustomed to use **the many** <note>Hebrew: *rabbim* / רבים</note> and **the community** <note>Hebrew: *tzibur* / צבור</note> interchangeably. Indeed, the term **the many** <note>original Greek/Hebrew: *to rabbim* / τὸ רבים</note> properly denotes *a great number*, but among Hebrew authors it is used quite familiarly for the whole multitude of the people and the entire Commonwealth. Hence in the *Orach Chayim* <margin>Orach Chayim chapter 70, § 4.</margin> <note>a major code of Jewish Law</note> the term **necessities of the many** <note>Hebrew: *tzorkhei rabbim* / צרכי רבים</note> is used in place of **public necessities** <note>Hebrew: *tzorkhei tzibur*</note>. The words are: **If anyone has been occupied with the business of the community** <note>literally "the university" or collective body</note> **and the time for reciting the section "Hear, O Israel"** <note>original Hebrew: *Keriath Shema* / ק"ש</note> **approaches, etc.** If I am not mistaken, this meaning and use of the word **the many** <note>Hebrew: *rabbim*</note> is taken from the Hebrew text of the Old Testament itself. Thus the passage in *Isaiah* concerning Christ seems to be understood: <margin>Isaiah 53:12.</margin> **He bore the sin of many** <note>original Hebrew: *chet rabbim nasa* / חטא רבים נשא</note>. These **many** <note>Hebrew: *rabbim*</note> are the same ones whom Paul calls sometimes **the many** <note>original Greek: *pollous* / πολλοὺς</note> and sometimes **all** <note>original Greek: *pantas* / πάντας</note> when he treats this same point of our doctrine in the Epistle to the Romans <margin>chapter 5:18, 19.</margin>, by which he understands the whole collective body of believers. Likewise in this Law: <margin>Exodus 23:2.</margin> **You shall not follow the many to do evil** <note>original Hebrew: *lo tihyeh acharei rabbim le-ra’ot* / לא תהיה אחרי רבים לרעות</note>; here **the many** <note>Hebrew: *rabbim*</note> denotes the entire multitude of those who err. From this, **among the many** <note>Hebrew: *be-rabbim* / ברבים</note> denotes *publicly*, which Greek writers <margin>Psalm 55:19, Isaiah 53:12.</margin> express as **with openness** <note>original Greek: *parrhesia* / παῤῥησίᾳ</note>, a meaning which itself seems to have been sought from the text of Scripture. It is the same as if you said in Latin: *Among several*, <margin>2 Timothy 2:2.</margin> which the Apostle calls *through many witnesses* <note>original Greek: *dia pollon martyron* / διὰ πολλῶν μαρτύρων</note>, that is, *in the presence of many witnesses*. In Dutch we say: *In public* <note>original Dutch: *In 't publye*</note>. From these points, it is easy to gather that there is very little difference between the meanings of the words **Community** <note>Hebrew: *Tzibur* / צבור</note> and **Assembly** <note>Hebrew: *Kahal* / קהל</note>, roughly the same as between the Dutch: *The Commons* <note>original Dutch: *Het Gemeen*</note> and *The Community* <note>original Dutch: *De Gemeynte*</note>. Or in Latin: *The public thing* <note>the State</note>, *the public good*, *the community*, and *the City*, *the people*, or *the Church itself*. I admit this difference in the meaning of these words is small, and in certain cases there is none at all; yet I would hardly dare say there is no difference at all in every circumstance. Consider this passage from the *Orach Chayim*: **The Assembly** <note>Hebrew: *Kahal* / קהל</note> **whose custom it is to appoint men over the public necessities, etc.**

# CONCERNING NAMES, etc. BOOK I. PART I.

<margin>*Orach Chayim*, Chapter 53, § 26.</margin>
...where it is customary to appoint certain individuals to conduct the necessary affairs of the public entity (<term>Tzibur</term> <note>Hebrew: צבור, referring to the collective body or "the public"</note>), etc. In Dutch, you might understand this sentence thus: **"When the Congregation used to appoint some to provide for the necessities of the Public, etc."** <note>original Dutch: *Wanneer De Gemeynte eenige pleegh te stellen om de noodtsakelyckheden van 't Gemeen te besorgen ens.*</note> I do not believe, however, that this same sentence can be expressed as successfully in the Hebrew language if the words <term>Kahal</term> <note>Hebrew: קהל, usually a formal assembly</note> and <term>Tzibur</term> are swapped: *That they should appoint men of the community over the needs of the congregation, etc.* <note>original Hebrew: שנתנו למנות אנשים צבור על צרכי הקהל וכו</note>; which would nonetheless have to occur if these words were of entirely the same power. At the very least, it is certain that *Tzibur* is used more frequently in Hebrew phrases when the Commonwealth is mentioned. Thus:

**Public necessities.** <note>Hebrew: *Tzorkhei Tzibur* / צרכי צבור</note>
**Public business.** <note>Hebrew: *Oseki Tzibur* / עוסקי צבור</note>
**Public sacrifices.** <note>Hebrew: *Zivchei Tzibur* / זבחי צבור</note>
**Public fasts.** <note>Hebrew: *Ta'anit Tzibur* / תענית צבור</note>

For <term>Kahal</term> has this unique quality: that it denotes a *called assembly* <note>Latin: *comitium calatum*, an assembly formally summoned by a herald</note>, a sense of designation that is not present in the word *Tzibur*. Yet *Tzibur* has this over *Edah*: that it denotes a solemn gathering of the whole people, or at least the greatest part of them, for Sacred Rites; whereas *Edah* more signifies a pre-arranged meeting of specific men, whether they be many or fewer in number. # CHAPTER 2. OF SYNAGOGUES.

...when [of a larger body] <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's discussion of a "larger body" or community.</note> and therefore it denotes exactly the same thing as the Greek <term>synagoge</term> <note>original Greek: συναγωγή; literally "a bringing together" or assembly</note>, the frequent use of which should be derived primarily from this source. The word <term>Kneset</term> <note>Hebrew: כנשת; the root of the modern Israeli parliament, meaning "assembly"</note> does not by itself designate some whole university or City of men, but rather any kind of **Meeting** and **association**, or **gathering** of men—whether large or small, of good men or bad—depending on the circumstances of the text in which its use occurs. However, because the term <term>Edah</term> <note>Hebrew: עדה; "congregation"</note>, by the force of its origin from the root <term>Ya'ad</term> <note>Hebrew: יעד; "to appoint" or "to fix"</note>, often signifies a fixed, ordered, and composed gathering—such as that of **Judges**, **Teachers**, and others—the term *Kneset* also usually takes on that same meaning, even if it does not necessarily admit such a meaning by reason of its own linguistic origin.

<margin>Psalm 82:1.</margin>
Thus the "Congregation of God" <note>Hebrew: עדת אל / *Adat El*</note>, in which God himself is said to have stood, which was the **Great Council** of the Jews, is translated by the Paraphrast <note>The "Paraphrast" refers to the authors of the Targums, the Aramaic translations/interpretations of the Hebrew Bible.</note> as *Knishta* <note>Aramaic form of Kneset.</note>. Nothing is better known than that Hebrew writers speak *concerning the Great Synagogue* <note>original Greek/Hebrew: περὶ τῆς כנסת הגדולה / *peri tes Kneset HaGedolah*</note>, by which they understand those one hundred and twenty Theologians and Prophets who, after the Babylonian Captivity, were the authors of the "sacred judgment"—that is, the Divine Law set in order.

<margin>
Buxtorf, *Masoretic Commentary*, Chapter 10.
</margin>
These men have been discussed at length by the most learned scholars. In this usage of the word, it is clear that *Kneset* signifies a **Sanhedrin** <note>The supreme judicial and religious council of ancient Israel.</note> and a **Meeting** called for the cause of the church <note>The author uses the Latin *ecclesiæ*, here meaning the religious community or assembly.</note>.

<margin>
Morinus, *Exercitationes*, Book 2, Chapter 2, § 7.
</margin>
But elsewhere, as is known, it is accepted indifferently for any **Meeting**, whether sacred or profane. From there, as I have already advised, the word **SYNAGOGUE** is properly to be derived:

<margin>
Selden, *On the Sanhedrin*, Book 2, Chapter 26, § 7.
Spencer, *On the Laws of Moses*, Book 3, Dist. 7, Chapter 10, § 5.
</margin>
yet in such a way that we neither wish nor are able to deny that the word *ecclesia* <note>Greek/Latin: ἐκκλησία; "assembly" or "church"</note> itself has also been used in a few places by Sacred Writers with respect to this very *Kneset*. Therefore, it was not entirely off the mark when a most learned man recently said that the word *ecclesia* should be traced back to *Kneset*. However, this only holds true in a few instances, as we will argue in the following Chapter; it is not commonly true. Concerning the word <term>Atzarah</term> <note>Hebrew: עצרה; "solemn assembly"</note>, which the Greek Interpreters similarly tend to explain as a **gathering** or **meeting**—and indeed not absurdly in many places—I say nothing, because it has no use in this treatise.
