ON NAMES, etc. BOOK I. PART I.

### CHAPTER III.

*A transition to a closer consideration of the word* **synagogue** (*συναγωγή*). *It is established with solid arguments that the word has a double meaning in the writings of the New Testament: it is taken to mean either the Place of Assembly or the Gathering itself. Next, the reason is investigated as to why this word is used for the Place and the building of the assembly, even though by its origin it signifies the gathering itself. Indeed, for an easier understanding of this, it is explained that it is quite common for words which properly signify a Gathering to be transferred over time to designate the places in which the gathering is collected; examples are brought forward of the words:* **Sanhedrin** (**סנהדרין**), **synedrion** (**συνέδριον**), **curia** <note>a Roman senate house or assembly</note> (*the origin of which is sought from the Greek* **kyria** [**κυρία**] <note>meaning "authority" or "lordship"</note>), **concio** <note>a public meeting or the speech given there</note>, *and* **comitium** <note>a Roman place of political assembly</note>. *Furthermore, it is added that the word* **church** (**ἐκκλησία**) *underwent the same change of meaning among both Sacred and Secular Authors. On this occasion, the opinion of Fuller* <note>Nicholas Fuller (1557–1626), an English Hebraist and philologist</note> *is weighed concerning the genuine meaning of the word* **church** (**ἐκκλησία**) *in 1 Corinthians 11:18, 22, not neglecting Spanheim’s* <note>Friedrich Spanheim, a 17th-century Dutch theologian</note> *arguments against it. Finally, it is inquired what substance lies in what Elias Levita* <note>A famous 15th-16th century Jewish grammarian and scholar</note> *wrote regarding the word* **Kehala** (**קהלה** <note>Hebrew for "assembly" or "community"</note>).

---

Having sent before us these things which have now been abundantly examined regarding the true meaning of the words **Tzibur** (**צבור** <note>community</note>), **Qahal** (**קהל** <note>assembly/congregation</note>), **Knesset** (**כנסת** <note>gathering</note>), **Edah** (**עדה** <note>congregation</note>), **Church** (**ἐκκλησία**), and **Synagogue** (**συναγωγή**), we may now step forward and approach more closely the matter we are dealing with. Specifically, in this treatment of ours, we take the word *Synagogue* not for the *assembly* or *Gathering* of people—which we have said is the genuine and proper usage of this word—but for the place in which the gathering is collected. Because those two things differ significantly, we must investigate the origin of this more recent meaning.

That the word **synagogue** (**συναγωγή**) is taken to mean the *House of Assembly itself* is clear from the writings of the New Testament, with no one objecting, as far as I know.

Thus, I say, the discourse of Christ in **Luke** holds: *When they bring you before the **synagogues, and the rulers, and the powers**, do not be anxious, etc.* Here, "Synagogue" seems entirely to signify what is called a **House of Judgment** <note>original Hebrew: "בֵּית דִּין" (*Beit Din*)</note> among the Jews. But what, pray tell, is the reason that the word **assembly**, which properly denotes a *gathering*, changes its significance so much that it simultaneously denotes the *Place* in which that *gathering* is assembled? It is our duty now to indicate this. So that it may be done in some order, let us observe: 1. It happens not infrequently that names which signify a *gathering, meeting, or congregation* pass into the meaning of the *Place* in which such *colleges* of men are gathered. The reason for this does not seem to be obscure: since *fixed places* are usually assigned to *fixed meetings*, and since these places can hardly receive a name from anywhere else to distinguish them from other similar places than from the name and nature of the **College** which gathers in them, it follows that the names of such *gatherings* often pass into the names of the *Places* assigned to those gatherings.

A constant and unquestioned rule of proven interpretation is held by all: that one should not depart from the ordinary and most common meaning of words unless for suitable reasons. Now, that the ordinary and most common use of the word *Ecclesia* <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησία (*ekklesia*); usually translated as "Church" or "Assembly."</note> in the Holy Scriptures is that by which it is taken for a multitude of people gathered in the name of Christ, everyone—even, I think, [Nicholas] Fuller—concedes. Or, quite simply, *to meet in the Church* is to meet *among the multitude of the faithful who are in the process of gathering.*

### CHAPTER 3. ON SYNAGOGUES.

The very learned men who came before us have handed down and defended these views; anyone who clings somewhat stubbornly to their own opinion in a debate will be able to defend them easily. However, why should I hide the fact that a small doubt remains in this later passage, which I have not yet seen fully resolved to my satisfaction? For the words: *to come together in the church* <note>original Greek: συνέρχεσθαι ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ (*synérchesthai en tē ekklēsía*)</note> seem to denote something else, or something more, than merely meeting as a multitude of the faithful.

It is thus: the most excellent **Cameron** <note>John Cameron (c. 1579–1625) was a Scottish theologian and scholar known for his deep "dexterity" in judging linguistic nuances in the New Testament.</note>, with his characteristic skill in judgment, thought it should be understood not just as an assembly, but as an *assembly with a certain quality or condition*. For although, he says, *it is not customary to say one "assembles into an Assembly," it is nevertheless said that one "assembles into the Senate," even though the Senate is itself an assembly; and one "assembles into a Synod," even though a Synod is an assembly. Certainly, when **Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator and statesman.</note> complains that **Catiline** <note>Lucius Sergius Catilina, a Roman politician who led a famous conspiracy against the Republic.</note> dared to "come into the Senate," he did not understand the name "Senate" to mean a place, but rather the gathering of the Senators. For Senators are not a "Senate" in just any place they happen to be together; they are the "Senate" only when they gather for the sake of deliberating. In the same way, the pious are not said to have "assembled into the Church" everywhere they are together; but whenever they have joined together for the sake of religion, they are said to have "come together into the Church."* Therefore, the phrase *into the Church* was added to *the gathering* to designate the nature and condition of the assembly—a designation which uniquely serves the point the Apostle is making. I wanted to extract these words without any gaps, because Cameron seems to me to have come closer to the truth than all others. Yet, what prevents us from observing that *gathering together* <note>original Greek: τὸ συνέρχεσθαι (*to synérchesthai*)</note> is most optimally used in relation to a place? Let us look at examples.

<margin>Chapter 5, 16.</margin>
Thus we read in the Acts of the Apostles: *the multitude from the surrounding cities also GATHERED together at JERUSALEM* <note>original Greek: συνήρχετο δὲ καὶ τὸ πλῆθος τῶν πέριξ πόλεων εἰς Ἱερουσαλήμ (*synērcheto de kai to plēthos tōn perix poleōn eis Ierousalēm*)</note>. In the same book, **Festus** <note>Porcius Festus, the Roman procurator of Judea.</note> is introduced speaking about the Senators of Jerusalem in this way:

<margin>Chapter 25, 17.</margin>
*After they had ASSEMBLED HERE* <note>original Greek: Συνελθόντων οὖν αὐτῶν ἐνθάδε (*Synelthontōn oun autōn enthade*)</note> (in this place). Let us also compare the words of **Christ** in the Gospel of

<margin>Chapter 18, 20.</margin>
John: Jesus answered: *I have spoken openly to the world: I always taught in the Synagogue and in the Temple, WHERE the Jews always tend to gather* <note>original Greek: ὅπου πάντοθεν οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι συνέρχονται (*hopou pantothen hoi Ioudaioi synérchontai*)</note>. We notice, at any rate, that the term *to gather together* (if it is not placed alone, as often happens) continually has nouns or particles of place joined to it. If the Apostle **Paul** had said of the Church itself that it "assembled," as he does elsewhere in the Epistle, then not even the slightest doubt would remain; but...

### ON NAMES, etc. BOOK I. PART I.

Other **lexicographers** hold the same view from **Elias** <note>Elias Levita (1469–1549) was a renowned Hebrew philologist and teacher to many Christian Hebraists.</note>. **Schindler** <note>Valentin Schindler, author of a major polyglot dictionary in 1612.</note> defines <term>Kehillah</term> <note>Hebrew: קהלה</note> as: *a city, or a place where the Church dwells. Also, where the bodies of the deceased rest.* **Buxtorf** <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629) was a leading Christian scholar of Hebrew and Jewish tradition.</note> defines <term>Kehillat</term> <note>Hebrew: קהלת</note> as: *A congregation, an assembly of people, especially collected for sacred rites, a Church, a Synagogue, a place and the people gathered in that place.* He adds: *Thus when they describe the place in which someone lives, they name not the city, but the assembly:* "In the Holy Church of Venice," <note>Hebrew: בקהילה קדושה</note> etc. **Castell** <note>Edmund Castell, author of the 'Lexicon Heptaglotton' (1669).</note> provides these same definitions.

But we believe the words of **Elias** must be taken in a sensible way. Why? He says that <term>Kahal</term> <note>Hebrew: קהל, typically meaning "assembly"</note> and <term>Kehillah</term> differ in that *Kahal* denotes the *assembly*, and *Kehillah* the *place*. How can that be true, since beyond all controversy *Kehillah* is often used for the *assembly* itself? Furthermore, who could be led to believe that the Jews always designate a *place* or a *city* by the phrase "Holy Congregation"? <note>Hebrew: קהילה קדושה, "Kehillah Kedoshah"</note> I also strongly doubt whether by this phrasing: "The Holy Congregations of Prague and Venice," <note>Hebrew: קהלת ק' פראג וויניצי אה</note> the cities of Prague and Venice are actually designated. For by what right would they call the city itself *Holy*, except for Jerusalem or the Canaanite cities? (For concerning Jerusalem in writings, whether true or fictional, it is held: "Holy Jerusalem"). <note>Hebrew: ירושלים קדושה</note> 

I do not think, therefore, that what **Elias** reports is simply true. Yet I would not dare to say he writes something entirely false. For I saw in the Preface of the Jewish Calendar, edited by **Rabbi Uri**, the city of Jerusalem called absolutely the "Holy Congregation" <note>Hebrew abbreviation: ק"ק (K.K.)</note> with only this familiar epithet: "May it be rebuilt <margin>Hottinger presents this at the end of the *Booklet on Gravestones*.</margin> and established quickly in our days." <note>Hebrew abbreviation: תוב"ב (T.V.B.B.) - a common Jewish blessing for the rebuilding of Zion.</note> Let us say therefore, until this is more clearly perceived by us, that the term <term>Kehillah</term> <note>Greek: τό; Hebrew: קהלה</note> signifies a multitude of believers, of whatever sect, who dwell in this or that fixed place. Thus "Holy Congregation of Prague" denotes the Church of Prague; or, if you prefer, the city of Prague, insofar as it contains the Church of the Jews. 

As for the fact that a burial ground <note>Latin: sepulcretum</note> where many dead are buried is designated by the same name, that follows the same reasoning. We conclude that the Greek word <term>Ecclesia</term> <note>Greek: ἐκκλησίας</note> and the Hebrew <term>Kehillah</term> <note>Hebrew: קהלה</note> in certain places signify something more than a multitude; that is, a multitude in relation to a place, or a place with respect to a certain multitude gathered in it. However, when the **Apostle Paul** uses the word "church" <note>Greek: ἐκκλησία</note> in the mentioned phrase: "to come together in the church," <note>Greek: συνέρχεσθαι ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ</note> I do not think he intended his mind to focus on the Hebrew word *Kahal* or *Kehillah*. For as far as I know, it is not found among the Hebrews...

There is no need for more words to refute this comparison.

the names of Synagogues are also touched upon, such as **sacred places** <term>ἱερὰ</term> <note>original Greek: hiera</note>, **Sabbath-houses** <term>σαββατεῖα</term> <note>original Greek: sabbateia</note>, **men's halls** <term>ἀνδρῶνες</term> <note>original Greek: andrones; typically refers to the men's quarters in a Greek house</note>, **houses of prayer** <term>προσευκτήρια</term> <note>original Greek: proseukteria</note>, and **houses of study** <term>φροντιστήρια</term> <note>original Greek: phrontisteria; a term used by Philo to describe places of meditation or schools</note>, which can be found in the works of Philo and Josephus. Finally, an observation is added regarding the expression **House of Assembly** <term>בית הכנסת</term> <note>original Hebrew: Beit ha-Knesset, the standard Hebrew term for a synagogue</note>.

From those things which were brought forward in the preceding discussion, it would not be absurd to state that the word **synagogue** <term>συναγωγὴ</term> <note>original Greek: sunagoge, meaning a bringing together or assembly</note>, along with many other terms, underwent such a change in its meaning that it came to be used for a **Place** just as much as for the **Assembly** <note>original Latin: Coetu</note> that is gathered in that **Place** <note>original Latin: Loco</note>. However, it seems necessary that we demonstrate a similar usage and meaning in the **Hebrew expression** to which the concept of **synagogue** <term>συναγωγὴ</term> corresponds. Yet this is not as easy as it seems at first glance. We have said that the word **synagogue** <term>συναγωγὴ</term> corresponds with the Hebrew word **assembly** <term>עדה</term> <note>original Hebrew: Edah</note>; but in truth, that word is never used for a physical place, as far as is known. It has also been noted that the word **congregation** <term>τὸ קהל</term> <note>original Hebrew: Qahal</note> was sometimes translated by the Septuagint translators as **synagogue** <term>συναγωγὴν</term>; and yet even this word is never accepted as referring to a **place**. Whether the word **community** <term>קהילה</term> <note>original Hebrew: Kehillah</note> designates a place—as **Elias Levita** <note>A famous 16th-century Hebrew grammarian and scholar</note> teaches—we have left as almost doubtful. But even if it were so, it would not support our case, because **community** <term>קהילה</term> would then denote a **city**, not a **place of sacred assembly**.

Let us say, then, what the matter is. We have already warned before, and not in vain, that the word **gathering** <term>כניסיה</term> <note>original Hebrew: Kenisiyah</note> among the Jews has almost completely replaced the ordinary meaning and use of the root word **assembly** <term>עדה</term>. Now, **gathering** <term>כניסיה</term> or <term>כניסיא</term> signifies a **synagogue** <term>συναγωγὴν</term>, and indeed any kind of congregation; however, as it is ordinarily used, it is broader than what is usually designated by the term **assembly** <term>עדה</term>. **Elias** observes that the words **congregation** <term>קהל</term> (the **Ecclesia**) and **assembly** <term>קבץ</term> <note>original Hebrew: Qabatz, meaning to collect or gather</note> are usually translated in the **Targum** <note>Ancient Aramaic translations/paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible</note> as **assembly** <term>כנישתא</term> <note>original Aramaic: Kenishta</note>. **Philippus Aquinas** <note>A 17th-century scholar and lexicographer of Hebrew and Aramaic</note> likewise explains it through the words **to gather** <term>קבץ</term> and **to collect** <term>אסף</term> <note>original Hebrew: Asaph</note>—words for collecting and congregating into a sum total, the kind of congregations of a multitude that take place in **Sacred Assemblies**. 

Therefore, a **gathering** <term>כניסיה</term> is a multitude collected into one; it contains in the scope of its meaning somewhat more than **assembly** <term>עדה</term> and less than **congregation** <term>קהל</term>. Indeed, the Jews long ago began to apply this word to their **sacred assemblies** and to denote their congregation. For this reason, **Houses of Assembly** <term>בתי כנסיות</term> <note>original Hebrew: Battei Kenesiyot</note> or **Houses of Congregation** are called fixed places in which they are accustomed to meet to perform their sacred rites, as is well known. But even so, not every difficulty has been removed, because in the Books of the New Testament, the **Hebrew sacred places**, or their **oratories**,

### CHAPTER 4. OF SYNAGOGUES.

...they are never called **houses of synagogues** <term>οἶκοι συναγωγῶν</term> <note>original Greek: oikoi synagogon</note>, but simply **synagogues** <term>συναγωγαί</term> <note>original Greek: synagogai</note>. Therefore, it is necessary that we show that this very term **assembly** <term>כניסת</term> <note>original Hebrew: knesset</note>, when used by itself without the added word **house** <term>בית</term> <note>original Hebrew: beit</note>, is employed to refer to the place of the sacred congregation itself. Indeed, many examples of this meaning are found in the writings of **Benjamin of Tudela** <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler and explorer</note>, a man who was fond of tall tales, but whose style of writing can nevertheless be useful to us. <margin>In the *Itinerary*, page 75, edited by L. P. Empereur.</margin> Thus, he speaks in a legendary manner about the **Synagogue of the Exilarch** <term>Aichmalotarchae</term> <note>A Greek-derived term for the "Head of the Exiles" who led the Jewish community in Babylon</note> of Babylon, who resided in Baghdad: **And the large synagogue** <term>וכניסתה גדולה</term> <note>original Hebrew: ve-knesset-hah gedolah</note> **of the Head of the Exiles was built with marble columns, etc.** <margin>page 62.</margin> In another place: **But in the region of Asshur is the Synagogue of Obadiah, and the Synagogue of Jonah son of Amittai, and the Synagogue of Nahum the Elkoshite.** <note>Original Hebrew: ובתדינת אשור כנסת עובדיה וכנסת יונה בן אמתי וכנסת נחום האלקושי</note> <margin>page 96.</margin> Again in another place: **There, before a certain synagogue, Mordechai and Esther are buried.** <note>Original Hebrew: ושם לפני כנסת אחת קבורים מרדכי ואסתר</note> In the same way, the author of the *Cippis Hebraicis* <note>a work on Jewish tombs</note>, as reviewed by **Hottinger** <note>Johann Heinrich Hottinger, a 17th-century Swiss philologist</note>, writes: <margin>page 8 of the same edition.</margin> **In the middle of the city there, Abner son of Ner is buried in a cave in the Temple of the Gentiles.** <note>original Hebrew: ובתוך העיר שם אבנר בן נר בכניסיה של גוים במערה; here "knessiah" (assembly) is used for a temple or gathering place.</note> It is therefore established that Hebrew authors used the single word **assembly** <term>כניסה</term> <note>original Hebrew: knessah</note>, which denotes a congregation, to stand for the house and the ordinary place of that congregation. The Syriac Translator also frequently renders **synagogue** <term>συναγωγὴν</term> with the word **assembly** <term>כנישא</term> <note>original Syriac: knisha</note>. And what most helps our case is that the **Talmudists** <note>the ancient compilers of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish law</note> themselves long ago became accustomed to speaking in this way. You may find among them: **The Synagogue of the Alexandrians** <note>original Hebrew: כנשת של אלכסנדרייים; knesset shel Alexandriim</note>; **The Synagogue of the Coppersmiths** <note>The Latin text here links "Synagogue of Babylon" (כנשתא דבבל) with "coppersmiths," and "Synagogue of the Tarsians/Weavers" (כורסיים) with "Babylonian," which appears to be a printer's error or a specific technical reading by the author.</note>; **The Babylonian Synagogue**; etc.

However, there is still doubt whether the Hebrew word **assembly** <term>כניסה</term> <note>knessah</note> is taken to mean the **Temple of the Synagogue** by **metonymy** <note>a figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it, like "the Crown" for a King</note> or by **ellipsis** <note>a figure of speech where words are omitted but understood by the reader</note>. That is, should we say that this word "assembly" has been so shifted from its ordinary meaning of a "congregation" that it began to simultaneously designate the place of meeting; or should we imagine an "ellipsis" in this expression, such that "assembly" is said instead of **House of Assembly** <term>בית כניסה</term> <note>Beit Knesset</note>? Whoever embraces the first view defends nothing absurd, because, in the preceding chapter, we demonstrated that it often happens that words for a **group** <term>coetus</term> also designate the **place** into which the groups are gathered by metonymy. Nevertheless, we feel ourselves more inclined toward the **latter view**, that the terms *knesset* and *knessah* are used through an ellipsis for **the House of the Assembly** or **House of Assembly**, and consequently the Greek word **synagogue**...

### ON NAMES, etc. BOOK I. PART I.

<margin>
page 20.
page 32.
page 52.
Sacred Grammar on Names, book 3, Treatise 1, Canon 39, chapter 3, 1; chapter 4, 2. Revelation 3:7; Isaiah 22:22; Acts 2:27, 31.
</margin>

...**assembly** <term>συναγωγὴ</term> <note>original Greek: synagōgē</note> [is used] for the **house or temple of the assembly** <note>original Greek: oikō tēs synagōgēs</note>. There are various reasons that suggest this:

1. Because the phrase **House of Assembly** <term>Beit Ha-Knesset</term> <note>original Hebrew: בי הכנסת</note> is used much more frequently among Hebrew writers than **assembly** <term>knessah</term> or **congregation** <term>knesset</term>; from which it is certainly clear that **House of Assembly** is the full form and **Assembly** is the shortened form.

2. Because the logic of the words **assembly** <term>knesset</term> and **study** <term>midrash</term> in these cases seems to be exactly the same. For observe now that **study** <term>midrash</term>, which signifies a subtle debate or inquiry, is taken just as much for a building and School in which such inquiries are held, as for the inquiry itself. Thus you find quite frequently on Hebrew monuments: **And the second vault they call the Study of Solomon** <note>original Hebrew: והכפר השנייה קורין לחמדרש שלמה</note>. Again: **The place is very venerable, and there is a house of disputation.** <note>original Greek: οἶκος συζητήσεως; original Hebrew: ושם מדרש</note> In another place: **There is the Academy of Rabbi Simeon son of Jochai.** <note>original Hebrew: שם מדרש לר' שמעון בן יוחאי</note> It is added: **There he is also buried in his school, he and his son Rabbi Elai.** <note>original Hebrew: ושם קבור במדרשו הוא ובנו ר' אלעי</note> We see clearly in these and many other places that **study** <term>midrash</term> is taken to mean a School. Since, however, *midrash* signifies "inquiry," there is no doubt that the word **house** <term>beit</term> is missing, which is usually added to complete the expression. Therefore we believe that **assembly** <term>knesset</term> is said in place of **House of Assembly** <term>Beit Ha-Knesset</term>, just as **study** <term>midrash</term> is said for **House of Study** <term>Beit Midrash</term>.

3. Additionally, the omission of the word **house** <term>beit</term> in similar modes of speaking is very frequent. Examples were long ago observed by **Salomon Glassius** <note>1593–1656, a German biblical critic and theologian</note>; although he overlooked our term **synagogue**. Thus in Micah: **The heads of Jacob** <note>original Hebrew: ראשי יעקוב</note> for **The heads of the house of Jacob**. Likewise: **The mountain of the Lord** for **The mountain of the house of the Lord**. So too **The key of David** <note>original Greek: κλεῖς τοῦ Δαβὶδ</note> for **The key of the house of David**. Glassius adds: To this category some refer the phrase **to the [house] of Hades** <note>original Greek: εἰς ᾅδῃ</note>, meaning the **house**. Just as the Greeks say **to the [house] of the teacher** <note>original Greek: εἰς διδασκάλου</note>, meaning the home. **Euripides** <note>The ancient Greek tragedian</note> says: **Brought up in [the house] of a most pious man** <note>original Greek: Ἐν ἀνδרὸς εὐσεβεστάτου τראφεὶς</note>. And among the Latins: **At [the temple of] Ops** or **at [the temple of] Pollux**. So much from him. Let us say, then, in a similar way of speaking and writing, that **synagogue** was said for **the house of the assembly**, and **knesset** for **Beit Ha-Knesset**.

### CHAPTER 4. ON SYNAGOGUES.

<margin>Chapter 12. Fuller, Miscellany, book 2, chapter 2. From the book *That Every Good Man is Free*, page 679.</margin>
The facts concerning the **Essenes** <note>A Jewish sect known for communal living and strict observance</note>, noted long ago by Eusebius and others, are quite clear: *Coming to the sacred places, which are called synagogues, the younger men sit in rows behind the elders, according to age.* <note>Original Greek: εἰς ἱεροὺς ἀφικνόμενοι τόπους, οἳ καλῶνται συναγωγαὶ, καθ᾿ ἡλικίας ἐν τάξεσιν ὑπὸ πρεσβυτέροις νέοι καθίζονται.</note>

Among the other names by which **synagogues** are distinguished among foreign authors—though it is doubtful if the same holds true in the sacred scriptures—none is more common than **Proseucha** <term>προσευχὴ</term> <note>Literally "a place of prayer" or "oratory"</note>. This is read in the works of **Juvenal** <note>A Roman poet known for his biting satires on Roman life</note>:
<margin>Satire 3, verse 215.</margin>

> "Tell me where you are staying; in which **house of prayer** <term>Proseucha</term> should I look for you?" <note>Original Latin: Ede, ubi consistas, in qua te quæro PROSEUCHA.</note>

Most learned men now agree that *Proseucha* here refers to a Jewish **oratory** <note>A place designated for prayer</note>; however, the most literate authors of the past once hesitated over this meaning. They preferred to understand it as a "shack" or "hovel" for beggars, where those seeking alms were accustomed to hide away. For it is well established that the word *Proseucha* is formed from the Greek verb **to pray** <term>προσεύχεσθαι</term> <note>Original Greek: adprecari, vota nuncupare</note>. It did not seem that this use of the word *Proseucha* sat poorly with the goal and circumstances of Juvenal’s text. But the highly erudite **Turnebus** <note>Adrien Turnèbe, a 16th-century French classical scholar</note> taught that both meanings of the word *Proseucha* are elegantly joined in this passage. <margin>Adversaria, book 1, chapter 19.</margin> He says: *Proseuchae were the shrines of the Jews, as in Alexandria and Rome and other cities; they acquired the name because they were a kind of place for oracles or, as Christians say, oratories. ... However, since the Jews were very inclined to giving alms, a crowd of beggars would gather there. Both the Jews and the beggars themselves were hated by everyone, and because the beggars had no homes, they would sometimes occupy these places and sleep in them; therefore, the name "proseucha" fell into contempt.* **Cleomedes** <note>A Stoic philosopher and astronomer</note>, mocking the absurdities of Epicurus's philosophy, says: *...the [nonsense] from the middle of the house of prayer and from those begging there, things that are Jewish and counterfeit.* <note>Original Greek: τὰ δὲ ἀπὸ μέσης προσευχῆς καὶ τῶν ἐπ᾿ αὐτῆς προσαιτέντων ἰσδαϊκά τινα καὶ παρακεχαραγμένα.</note> This latter method of reconciliation pleases me most, because the Jews are described by Juvenal elsewhere (also in Satire 3, verse 14) as beggars. For the same poet says at the beginning of this Satire:

> *Here, where Numa used to meet his nightly lover,*
> *Now the grove of the sacred spring and the shrines are rented*
> *To the Jews: whose furniture is a basket and a bale of hay.*
> *For every tree has been ordered to pay rent to the people,*
> *And the grove **begs**, the Muses having been cast out.* <note>Original Latin: Heic, ubi nocturnæ Numa constituebat amicæ, / Nunc sacri fontis nemus & delubra locantur / Judæis: quorum cophinus fenumque supellex. / Omnis enim populo mercedem pendere jussa est / Arbor, & ejectis MENDICAT sylva camænis.</note>

<note>original Greek: τὴν προσευχὴν</note> **the prayer**, *the multitude already gathered in the Prayer House*. Later again: *He himself also, clothed in a breastplate and girded as secretly as possible with a sword,* <note>original Greek: ἦλθον εἰς τὴν προσευχὴν</note> **I went into the Prayer House**. From these accounts, it is in my judgment clear that the word **PRAYER HOUSE** <term>Proseucha: A Greek term for a place of prayer, often used by Greek-speaking Jews as a synonym for "synagogue"</term> was at that time a most common term with the meaning of *Synagogue*. For this reason, I do not <margin>Præteritor. book 1. on Matthew 21:13.</margin> fully grasp what I read in **Drusius** <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish Protestant scholar of Hebrew and Jewish antiquities</note> regarding *Prayer Houses*; *There were Prayer Houses*, he says, *properly belonging to the Jews, in which they sold fruit; from which also comes the surname Fruit-seller*. An old inscription reads: **TO PUBLIUS CORFIDIUS SIGNINUS, FRUIT-SELLER FROM THE PRAYER HOUSE.** <note>original Latin: P. CORFIDIO. SIGNINO. POMARIO. A. PROSEUCHA.</note> We know that learned men feel that *Synagogues* were not held as *sacred* in the past as they are held now, and it is possible that this is true. However, that the Jews were accustomed to *sell fruit* in their *Prayer Houses*, I do not accept as proven by *Drusius*; except that I am not unaware that *Prayer Houses* were commonly planted with trees, among which it is possible there were also *fruit-bearing* ones. *Fruit-seller from the Prayer House* perhaps simply denotes a *Fruit-seller of the Jewish Nation and Religion*. Yet, in a matter that is not entirely clear, I would not dare to speak too confidently.

In the use of this word, the same *omission* must be observed which we noted before in the word <note>original Greek: συναγωγὴ</note> **synagogue**. For <note>original Greek: προσευχὴ</note> **prayer** is used instead of <note>original Greek: οἶκος vel τόπος τῆς προσευχῆς</note> **house or place of prayer**. Hebrews 12:1. Sacred Rhetoric Tract 1. chapter 4. § 3.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ἀγὼν</note> **Contest**, refers to the place in which the contest is held. You will find more examples in **Glassius** <note>Salomo Glassius (1593–1656), a German biblical critic</note>, who did not neglect our word "prayer" among them. Indeed, "House of Prayer" is the same as what the Hebrews call <note>original Hebrew: בית תפלה</note> **Beit Tefillah**, <margin>Isaiah 56:7. Matthew 21:13.</margin> *House of Prayer*, or <note>original Greek: προσευκτήριον</note> **Oratory**. One might translate <note>original Greek: προσευχὴ τοῦ Θεοῦ</note> **prayer of God** as *prayer to God*. While the phrase is indeed somewhat unusual, we are not for that reason lacking in examples by which it may be illustrated. Thus, <note>original Hebrew: רוממות אל</note> **exaltations of God** are songs by which God is exalted. Likewise, <note>original Hebrew: יראת יהוה</note> **Fear of the Lord** is that fear which has God as its object. <note>original Greek: Ἐξουσία τῶν πνευμάτων</note> **Authority over spirits** is the power which is exercised over unclean spirits. In the same manner: "prayer of God" and "prayer toward God" are *prayers* which have God as their object. You will find more on this in **Glassius** <note>Salomon Glassius (1593–1656), a Lutheran theologian known for his work on "Sacred Philology" or the grammar of biblical languages</note>. Indeed, the phrase <note>original Greek: προσευχὴ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν</note> **prayer toward God** is found in **Paul** in the *Epistle to the Romans*; as is also, which means the same thing, <note>original Greek: ἡ δέησις ἡ πρὸς τὸν Θεόν</note> **the petition toward God**. In the Psalms it is written: <note>original Hebrew: תפלה לאל חי</note> **Prayer to the God of my life**. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> renders this as: **Prayer to the God of my life** <note>original Greek: Προσευχὴ τῷ Θεῷ τῆς ζωῆς με</note>. But it also appears in **Isaiah**: <note>original Hebrew: בית תפלתי</note> **The house of MY prayer**. That is, the house in which I am worshiped. We conclude, therefore, that nothing prevents "prayer of God" in this passage from signifying *prayers poured out to God*.

### CHAPTER 4. ON SYNAGOGUES.

Who is speaking? **St. Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople</note> says: "For it was not only where the synagogue was, but they also prayed outside, as if setting apart a particular place" <note>original Greek: οὐ γὰρ δὴ ἔνθα ἦν ἡ συναγωγὴ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἔξω ἤυχοντο ὥσπερ τόπον τινα ἀφορίζοντες</note>. For the Synagogue was not only there, but they also prayed outside of it, in a place defined for that purpose. Furthermore, just as the **Praetors** and **Duumviri** <note>types of Roman magistrates</note> (whom we shall discuss later) differed in rank, so too did a Synagogue differ from a <term>Proseucha</term> <note>a Greek term for a "place of prayer," often used for less formal Jewish meeting places where a full synagogue building might not exist</note>. Just as today, where Jews are more numerous, there are only legitimate Synagogues, properly so called. Thus, in the following chapter, it is said there was a Synagogue in Thessalonica, whereas in smaller places there were only <term>Proseuchas</term>:

<margin>verse 1.</margin>
Hence the **Syriac** translator himself called the *Proseucha* here a **House of Prayer** <note>original Syriac: בית צלותא / Beth Tselotha</note>; whereas in the following chapter, the Synagogue is called an **Assembly** <note>original Syriac: כנישתא / Kenishta</note>. Furthermore, women were not admitted to the conversation of men in the Synagogues, being separated by lattices; but here it is said: **"we spoke to the women who had come together"** <note>original Greek: ἐλαλῶμεν ταῖς συνελθούσαις γυναιξί</note>. Thus far **Heinsius** <note>Daniel Heinsius (1580–1655), a famous Dutch scholar</note>. **Beza** <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a Protestant reformer and scholar</note>, however, translates it: *where prayer was accustomed to be.* The **Dutch** <note>the Authorized Dutch translation or Statenvertaling</note> version says: **Where the prayer was wont to happen.**

<margin>In *The Ruler of the Synagogue*, chapter 13, pages 250, 251.</margin>
I would wish, however, that in reconsidering this passage I did not hesitate more now than I once did, when I defended its common version (approved by Beza and the Dutch) quite freely. At that time I wrote almost thus:

> *I find nothing to criticize in this latter interpretation, because the true and most consistent meaning of the words* **prayer** <note>original Greek: προσευχὴ</note> *and* **to be accustomed/thought** <note>original Greek: νομίζεσθαι</note> *is retained. Unless someone perhaps wants "prayer" to be taken in a broader sense, because here it signifies all the sacred worship that was performed in the Synagogues, the greatest part of which was* **Prayer** <note>original Greek: προσευχὴ</note>. *In Dutch, we might not unsuitably transpose this passage as:* **Where one was accustomed to practice Divine Service.**

And certainly, until now, I have not been fully satisfied with the explanation of the phrase: "Where prayer was thought to be" <note>original Greek: Οὗ ἐνομίζετο προσευχὴ εἶναι</note>, which Heinsius interprets as: *where by received custom there was, or used to be, a Synagogue.* For what was this "custom" <note>original Greek: νόμισμα</note>, this received practice, by which a certain Synagogue was located outside the city of Philippi by the river? Why does **Luke** <note>the author of the Acts of the Apostles</note> not say: "where there was a Synagogue of the Jews"? Why "was thought to be" or "was accustomed to be"? Or was it perhaps not there at that time? It certainly was; for **Paul** betook himself there. It is possible that the **Old Latin Translator** <note>referring to the Vulgate</note> felt this difficulty, and therefore translated "was thought to be" as "seemed to be"; since the word for "thought" <note>original Latin: νομίζομαι</note> is taken in another sense. The meaning then would be: As if Paul had conjectured that there was some Oratory or Synagogue there, in which men of the Jewish race were accustomed to meet. It is doubtful, however, whether that Old Translator, instead of "was thought"...

### ON NAMES, ETC. BOOK 1. PART 1.

...if he had not read *it seemed* <note>original Greek: ἐδόκει / edokei</note>, as **Beza** <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a primary figure in the Protestant Reformation and a biblical scholar</note> records it was written in a certain very ancient codex of his. More importantly, the paraphrase of the **Syriac** translator <note>the Peshitta, the standard Syriac version of the Bible</note> is also consistent with that version: *And we went out on the Sabbath day outside the gate of the city by the side of the river, because there a house of prayer was seen/thought to be.* <note>original Syriac: ונפקן ביומא דשבתא לבר מן תרעא דמדינתא על יד נהרא מטול דתמן מתחזיא הוא בית צלותא</note>

The Latin interpretation of the *Trostian Edition* <note>refers to the 1621 Syriac New Testament edited by Martin Trost</note> is phrased in this manner: *And we went out on the Sabbath day outside the gate of the city next to the bank of the river, where* A HOUSE OF PRAYER WAS VISIBLE. But it does not seem that the Syriac translator intended to say that some *Synagogue* was physically *visible* outside the city. It is not that this sense is more complicated than others, but because the Syriac translator would then differ greatly from all other translators and readings, with which he can easily be reconciled. The source of the error seems to me to lie in the Latin version, not in the Syriac translator. Specifically, the word *hazā* <note>Syriac: חזא</note>, meaning *he saw, he looked at, he contemplated*, in the *Etpeh'al* form *eth-hazî* <note>Syriac: אתחזי</note> (which occurs in this text), is indeed frequently taken to mean *to be looked at* or *to be seen*, but it also signifies *to be thought* or *to be considered*—just as the Greek verb *dokein* <note>Greek: δοκεῖν</note> does. This is the same variety of meaning that appears in the Latin word *videri* <note>meaning both "to be seen" and "to seem"</note>. Take some examples from our Syriac translator himself:

<margin>chapter 17, 25.</margin>

Nor can it be denied that the circumstances of the text favor them to some extent. For what necessity would **Paul** and those with him have had to *conjecture*, or to reach a mere suspicion that a **Synagogue**...

->### CHAPTER 4. OF SYNAGOGUES.<-

...to go to some place outside the city, when they could have known that for certain from even the slightest interaction with the Jews? Therefore, this interpretation also does not please me. What then? Should the words be translated: *where prayer was accustomed to be*, as the **Dutch** <note>original: "Belgae," referring to the Dutch authorized Bible translation</note> have it? We indeed established this previously, but we do not wish to deny that there is also something unusual in this expression. However, there is nothing absurd in it. Then, I confess, previously when I held this view, I did not carefully consider certain other words contained in this same historical context, in which the same word **prayer-house** <note>original Greek: προσευχή / proseuchē</note> is repeated, and is not absurdly translated as **Oratory** <note>a small chapel or room for private prayer</note>. <margin>verse 16</margin> *It came to pass as we were going to prayer,* <note>original Greek: Ἐγένετο δὲ πορευוμένων ἡμῶν εἰς προσευχήν</note> or *It happened that while we were traveling to the place of prayer.* So says **Beza** <note>Theodore Beza, a major 16th-century biblical scholar</note>. Similarly the Dutch: *And it happened, as we went to the prayer.* Everyone indeed agrees that here, by "prayer-house," we should understand by metonymy <note>a figure of speech where a location is called by the action performed there</note> the place where prayers were accustomed to be made; yet who would deny that in this text the word is more clearly and distinctly translated as **Synagogue** or **Proseucha** <note>a Greek term for a Jewish place of prayer</note> than merely as **Prayer**? It is certainly more appropriately said that someone is heading toward a Synagogue than toward a prayer or a petition. For this reason, **Diodati** <note>Giovanni Diodati (1576–1649), translator of the Bible into Italian and French</note> translated this passage entirely correctly: *As we were going to the place of prayer.* Not to mention that the **Syriac Translator** repeated his **House of Prayer** <note>original Syriac: בּית צלוּתָא / bêth ṣelûtā</note> here. But if that former text admitted an equally easy interpretation, I would have no reason why I should not also translate the word *proseucha* there as a **House of Prayer** or a **Synagogue**.

But this sentence seems more obscure to me: *where, according to received custom, there was a House of Prayer.* For what should you understand by that "received custom"? Was it that it was not permitted for the Jews to have a Synagogue within the cities themselves? Most learned men seem to have thought so, and I confess it is probable that in certain cities the magistrates did not permit the Jews to hold public assemblies. Indeed, it is certain that it was not at all unusual for Jews to have their synagogues outside cities, at any place of more celebrated memory. However, in the meantime, who would deny that many other cities, even the most famous ones throughout the **Roman Empire**, admitted synagogues? Or did Luke <note>the traditional author of the Book of Acts</note> mean this: that according to received custom, the Synagogue was **BY THE RIVER**? But neither does that produce a sense free from doubt. For even if Jews frequently built Synagogues near rivers (about which more later), who would deny that others...

<header>ON NAMES etc. BOOK I. PART I.</header>

...that many [prayer houses] of this kind were built in places that were not washed by river waters? Does that which the most learned **Diodati** <note>Giovanni Diodati (1576–1649), a Protestant theologian famous for his Italian translation of the Bible</note> suggested please you more? In the text, he translates the words "where it was thought prayer was" <note>original Greek: οὗ ἐνομίζετο προσευχὴ εἶναι</note> as: *Where the ordinary place of prayer was*; <margin>Note in Fragments p. 25.</margin> but in the margin he explained it thus: *Where it was, namely by public ordinance and authority: to protect the Jews from popular riots, and also to separate them from others.* You consider whether the Greek phrase bears such an explanation, and decide on this passage as you please. For me, so much light does not shine here as is required to fully resolve the matter. Rather, I willingly confess that I am now more hesitant regarding the common translation than I once was.

However, regarding those things cited from **Drusius** <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish scholar of Hebrew and the Old Testament</note> and **Heinsius** <note>Daniel Heinsius (1580–1655), a famous Dutch scholar of the Renaissance</note>, what I previously disapproved of, I still disapprove of now for the same reasons. They distinguish between a **Proseucha** <note>a Greek term for a house of prayer</note> and a **Synagogue**. **Drusius** asserts that **Proseuchas** were frequented *for the sake of praying*; but in **Synagogues**, *Moses and the Prophets were read.* **Scaliger** <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a leading scholar of historical chronology</note> also leans toward this view. *Whether Proseuchas differ from Synagogues,* he says, *or are the same thing, I do not affirm, and my mind inclines more toward the idea that a Proseucha and a Sabbation <note>a term for a place of Sabbath rest or assembly</note>, or Synagogue, were not the same thing.* I do not clearly perceive, however, what reasons led them to decide this way. For why should *Moses and the Prophets* not be read in those places called **Proseuchas** just as they are in **Synagogues**? I admit that **Proseucha** denotes prayer, and by **metonymy** <term>metonymy: a figure of speech where a location or object is called by the name of an activity associated with it, such as calling a church a "house of prayer"</term> an **oratory** <note>a small chapel or room for private prayer</note>, but what is more common than for a thing to be named from its *principal part*? Among the Hebrews, a **Synagogue** is called both a **House of Prayer** <note>original Hebrew: בית תפלה / beit tefillah</note> and a **House of Assembly** <note>original Hebrew: בית הכנסת / beit ha-knesset</note>; yet it would be foolish to conclude from this that no *reading of the Law and Prophets* is celebrated there.

As for **Heinsius**’s attempt to distinguish Synagogues from **Proseuchas** by the name—claiming that the former were much more famous than the latter—this can be sufficiently refuted by the fact that **Philo** <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Jewish philosopher</note> and **Josephus** <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37 – 100 CE), a Jewish historian</note> call even the most famous Synagogues **Proseuchas**. Nor does it help **Heinsius** that the **Syriac Translator** renders "prayer-house" <note>original Greek: προσευχὴν / proseuchēn</note> as **House of Prayer** <note>original Syriac: בית צלותא / beit tzelota</note> and "synagogue" <note>original Greek: συναγωγὴν / synagōgēn</note> as **Synagogue** <note>original Syriac: כנישתא / knishta</note>, because the **Syriac Translator** had to adapt his version to Greek idioms; this in no way prejudices the meaning of the Hebrew or Greek words among the people by whom their use was accepted. Furthermore, **Heinsius** also labors to build his hypothesis on the idea that they were not admitted indiscriminately into Synagogues...

### CHAPTER 4. ON SYNAGOGUES.

...women, for whom seats distinct from the men were assigned in the **Synagogues**, who nevertheless here seem to be gathered together with the men in the same place; yet that does not much advance the cause of his argument. For what evidence is there in the text from which one might conclude that women in this **Proseucha** <note>a Greek term for a house of prayer</note> did not occupy their own seats separately from the men? That the Synagogue at **Thessalonica** was large was conceded by **Heinsius** <note>Daniel Heinsius (1580–1655), a Dutch scholar who argued that "proseuchae" were informal, open-air prayer sites</note>. And yet, in that very place, Paul turned his discourse to the women just as much as to the men. You may gather this from the following chapter. For after it was related there by the historian <note>Luke, the author of the Book of Acts</note> that Paul had frequently debated in the Synagogue of the Thessalonians, he continues: <margin>Acts 17, 4.</margin> *And some of them believed, and joined Paul and Silas; and of the devout Greeks a great multitude, and of the leading women not a few.* <note>original Greek: γυναικῶν τε τῶν πρώτων οὐκ ὀλίγαι</note> <margin>Compare Acts 13, 50, and see the commentary by Grotius there.</margin> Paul therefore spoke in this **Proseucha** to the **women** as well as to the men; yet you cannot easily conclude from this either that the women in this Synagogue were not separated from the men, or even that this Synagogue was not among those which **Heinsius** chooses to call "legitimate" <note>meaning officially recognized or formal synagogues</note>.

Furthermore, besides this name of **Proseuchae**, **Synagogues** are designated by other names by **Josephus** <note>Titus Flavius Josephus (37–c. 100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian</note> and **Philo** <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BC–50 AD), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher</note>. Larger Synagogues are called, by way of emphasis, *hiera*, or TEMPLES. <margin>On the Jewish War, book 7, chapter 21.</margin> Thus **Josephus**, where he describes the state of the Jews in Antioch after the death of **Antiochus Epiphanes** <note>The Seleucid king whose persecution of Jews led to the Maccabean Revolt</note>: *Those who took up the kingdom after him returned all the bronze offerings that had been made to the Jews living in Antioch, dedicating them in their SYNAGOGUE.* He continues: *Being treated in the same way by the kings who followed (according to the version by Rufinus), they increased in number, and by the construction and magnificence of the gifts, they made the TEMPLE more illustrious.* It is manifest that what he previously called a **Synagogue** is here called a **Temple** (*Hieron*); doubtless on account of the magnificence and splendor of the building, which was constructed in the form of a Temple. The Hebrew word *Miqdash*, or **Sanctuary**, does not differ much from this meaning of the word *hieron*. <margin>Ezekiel 28, 18.</margin>

### ON NAMES etc. BOOK 1. PART 1.

<margin>Isa. 16:12.</margin>
...sanctuary, which in some places is translated as *hieron* <note>Greek: temple or holy place</note> by the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>. And indeed, it seems that the word *miqdash* <note>Hebrew: מקדש, sanctuary</note> is also understood as a place destined, among other things, for prayers, according to **Isaiah** prophesying concerning Moab: *And he shall enter into his sanctuary to pray.* <note>Original Hebrew: ובא אל מקדשו להתפלל</note> Here, *miqdash* is a *proseuchterion* <note>Greek: house of prayer</note>, an Oratory, in which God's help is implored. It is certainly the same in its general meaning as *hieron*; although it may extend more widely <margin>Spencer, *On the Theocracy of the Jews*, ch. 5, § 2.</margin> according to the opinion of a certain most learned man. But this word *hieron* was so common among the Greeks that any sacred buildings of the Jews could easily be designated by it. Perhaps it is also to be understood in this way: that **Onias**, the founder of that famous Egyptian Temple, <margin>Antiquities, Book 13, ch. 6.</margin> writes in a letter to **Ptolemy and Cleopatra** that the Jews in **Coele-Syria, Phoenicia, and Leontopolis** "possess temples contrary to what is fitting" <note>Original Greek: παρὰ τὸ καθῆκον ἔχειν ἱερὰ</note>, or *possess TEMPLES contrary to right and divine law.* What? Did **Onias** mean to say that the Jews had temples for themselves in all those places, in which sacrifices were offered at altars in the likeness of the **Jerusalem Temple**, and the ceremonies of the *carnal Law* prescribed by Moses were observed? Truly, I can hardly believe that the Jews commonly broke out into such excess, contrary to the entire institution of the nation. **Onias** built a temple <margin>The Jewish War, Book 7, ch. 30.</margin> in Egypt, modeled after the one in Jerusalem, in which Priests and Levites performed their duties, as **Josephus** relates. But that was an entirely new and unheard-of deed. Therefore, I think it not absurd to understand this writing of **Onias** as referring to **Synagogues**, which appeared to be certain "lesser temples," about which **Onias** likely spoke with greater boasting to **Ptolemy and Cleopatra**, so that he might more easily draw them into his <margin>Compare also Josephus, Antiquities, Book 14, ch. 17.</margin> wishes. There is also another passage in the same **Josephus** which I thought should be referred to this matter, as long as I adhered more than was proper to the translation by **Gelenius** <note>Sigismund Gelenius (1497–1554), a scholar known for his Latin translations of Greek classics</note>. But having examined it thoroughly, I found myself deceived. We shall describe the whole passage, because it is very relevant to the matter we are discussing. **Josephus** is about to report the edict of the **Emperor Augustus**, by which the privileges of the Jewish nation in the cities of the Roman Empire are <margin>Antiquities, Book 16, ch. 10.</margin> confirmed. <header>CHAPTER 4. OF SYNAGOGUES.</header>

...by the decree of the sworn Senate, *the Jews may use their own rites and laws, just as they used them in the time of Hyrcanus <note>John Hyrcanus I, High Priest and ruler of the Hasmonean dynasty (reigned 134–104 BCE).</note>, the High Priest of the Most High God,* and that the right of asylum remains for their TEMPLES; and that they are permitted to send votive money to Jerusalem through specific men. At first glance, it might seem that he [Josephus] interpreted "the sacred things" <note>original Greek: τὰ ἱερὰ (*ta hiera*)</note> here as *Temples*, and therefore understood the meaning of the edict to be that the shrines of the Jews enjoyed the right of asylum. But if he was of that opinion, he wandered completely from the true sense and intent of the edict. For if you take "the sacred things" here to mean *shrines* or *Temples*, to what, I ask, will you refer the relative word "them" <note>original Greek: αὐτὰ (*auta*)</note>, which cannot be traced back to anything other than "the sacred things"? Furthermore, I do not know on what basis it could be believed that the Synagogues of the Jews enjoyed the right of *Asylums* <note>A legal protection where a person could not be forcibly removed from a sacred space.</note>? Certainly, I do not accept this until I see it supported by definite reasons. I would prefer to believe, however, that **Gelenius** <note>Sigismund Gelenius (1497–1554), a scholar known for his Latin translations of Josephus.</note>, who in his translations usually expresses the intent of **Josephus** more than the literal words, translated the text more freely here because sacred money was usually kept in the Synagogues. 

You should rather conceive the meaning of the edict in this way: *It pleases me that the Jews should enjoy their own rites according to their ancestral Law, and that their sacred things should be safe, and that these should be sent to Jerusalem and delivered to the treasurers of Jerusalem.* By "the sacred things" <note>original: τὰ ἱερὰ</note> we must actually understand *money*, or the *Sacred* tribute, which every Jew, wherever they might be, was bound to pay to God as long as the Commonwealth stood, and to transmit to the Temple in Jerusalem; which money in this same edict and those following goes by the name of *the sacred funds* <note>original: τῶν ἱερῶν χρημάτων</note>. From the beginning of this Chapter, it is clear enough that a controversy arose regarding these sacred funds. For they [the Jews] were accused by the Greeks of *exporting money*. 

Yet there is something in this Rescript of Caesar that relates more closely to our subject. It continues thus: "*But if anyone is caught stealing the sacred books or the sacred money, either from a sabbateion or from an andron <note>The Greek text uses 'andron,' typically meaning a men's apartment or assembly hall.</note>, let him be considered a committer of sacrilege*"; which means: *If anyone is found stealing sacred books or sacred money from their* RELIGIOUS PLACES, *this person is held guilty of sacrilege.* What **Josephus** expresses with the double term *sabbateion* and *andron* <note>original: σαββατεῖον & ἀνδρεῶν</note>, **Gelenius**, looking at the sense, translates as *Religious Places*. Rightly so. However, I believe these words should be considered as having distinct meanings. *Sabbateion* <note>original: Σαββατεῖον</note> seems to denote the *Synagogue*, into which men and women used to gather together on the *Sabbaths* (from which it takes its name) to meet—

> Rabbi Dosa, the son of Harcinas, says: 
> Morning sleep, midday wine, childish chatter, and sitting in the

Here you see that *Beth Ha-Knesset* is taken for a **society of profane men**, who *gather together and waste time dealing with vain and futile things.*

...and to the Greeks, **Synagogues**. Other names as well, by which **Philo** and **Josephus** <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> denote the *Places of Sacred Assembly*, have not been neglected. Before I proceed further, I must point out more precisely that the word **Synagogue** <note>original Greek: Συναγωγὴ (*Synagoge*), meaning a gathering or assembly.</note>, when used for a *sacred building*, is taken either in a broader or a narrower sense. 

In the broader sense, this word simultaneously includes the meaning of an **Academy** or a **Public School**, in which Doctors <note>In this historical context, "Doctors" refers to learned teachers, rabbis, or scholars of the law.</note> dispute the meaning of the Divine Law. In the narrower sense, it refers only to **Oratories** <note>Places dedicated specifically to prayer.</note>, in which the people gather on Sabbaths and Feast days to celebrate sacred rites. 

Certainly, **Lightfoot** <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), a prominent English Hebraist and clergyman known for using Rabbinic literature to explain the New Testament.</note>, when discussing the different academies of the Hebrews, was convinced that the notion of the *Synagogue* is also accepted for **Schools** and **Academies** in the writings of the **New Testament**. 

<margin>
*Hebrew Hours on Matthew 4:23.*
</margin>

Regarding this, he says: *The word Synagogue is used in this sense at times in the New Testament; you may certainly safely suppose that Christ sometimes preached in these Theological Schools, just as he did in the Synagogues.* Nor does he think this only regarding the Greek word *synagoge*, but also the Hebrew word **Keneset** <note>original Hebrew: כנסת (*Keneset*), meaning assembly.</note>. Thus he says in the same place: The **Beit Midrash** <note>original Hebrew: בית מדרש (*Beit Midrash*), literally "House of Study."</note> or *School* is also not infrequently called **Tzibur** <note>original Hebrew: צבור (*Tzibur*), meaning "community" or "public."</note> and **Keneset** or **Synagogue** by the Talmudic writers. 

We do not wish to contradict Lightfoot, because we have already anticipated the same point in the preceding pages, where we spoke in passing about the Synagogues of the **Alexandrians** and **Libertines** <note>A group mentioned in the Book of Acts, likely former slaves or their descendants who had been freed.</note> mentioned in the **Acts of the Apostles**.

Prologue, chapter 4, page 28.
</margin>

We proposed it to be likely that "Synagogue" there denotes a **Gymnasium** <note>In the classical sense, a place for both physical and intellectual training—here referring to a school or academy.</note> or an **Academy**, forming a single building along with the Synagogue, in which the **Alexandrians, Libertines, and Cyrenians** were accustomed to perform their sacred rites and, at the same time, study the humanities. 

Indeed, a **Gymnasium**, called a **Beit Midrash**, was joined to the more famous Synagogues, into which learned men gathered to teach or debate; these schools, as appendages of the Synagogues, were sometimes designated by the name of **Synagogue** itself. Furthermore, it is probable that in less populated places, one and the same **building** served for both **common religious exercises** and **scholarly instruction**. For the Jews were not everywhere so fortunate as to have a Gymnasium distinct from the Synagogue. Such a building was called a **Keneset** from its greater and more common use. 

Therefore, when it is preached of Christ in the Gospel histories that *he taught in the synagogues of the Jews* <note>original Greek: ἐδίδαξε ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς τῶν Ἰουδαίων (*edidaxe en tais synagogais ton Ioudaion*)</note>, I do not object to the word **Synagogue** being taken in its broadest sense for all **houses of sacred assembly**, so that by that name at once...

# CHAPTER 5. AND OF SCHOOLS, ETC.

...be included under the terms **Schools**, or **Gymnasia** <note>In this context, *Gymnasia* refers to places of intellectual training or academies, rather than athletic facilities.</note>, especially in those locations which did not have *Schools* distinct from *Synagogues*. In such places, the *Synagogues* were used for both *Scholastic* and *Ecclesiastical* purposes—that is, for teaching, disputing, and praying. It is reasonable to believe that in the **Villages** and **Smaller Towns** of the land of **Canaan**, as well as in the cities of the Roman Empire that supported Jewish citizens, things were so arranged that they allowed only a single **House**, consecrated for mixed religious exercises. Indeed, many of the names by which **Philo** and **Josephus** designate the *Sacred Houses* of the Jews are to be referred entirely to this **Dual** use and dual type of *Sacred Building*. Furthermore, the Jews of this time use the terms *Synagogue* and *School* interchangeably in daily speech, very frequently and familiarly calling the *Synagogue* itself a **School** (in *German*, **Schul** <note>original Hebrew/Yiddish: שול (*Shul*), which is still the common term for a synagogue in many Jewish communities today. The Latin text notes the German usage.</note>). For this reason, **Buxtorf** <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a prominent Hebraist whose book *Synagoga Judaica* described Jewish customs.</note> himself, when treating the *Synagogues* and adapting himself to the language of the Jews, confuses these terms throughout his work: *Commonly, indeed,* he says, *the terms Synagogue and School are used mixedly and indifferently, which we ourselves have often followed in this book.* I would prefer to believe, however, that **Christ**, as long as he performed his public ministry, was more often engaged in **Synagogues** than in **Schools**, where the *Synagogues* were distinct from the *Schools*. This is despite the fact that in the *Synagogues* he always conducted himself before the people as a **Teacher** <note>original: *Doctor*, implying a learned instructor or rabbi.</note> of the highest authority. Where the *Synagogue* and *Schools* were merged, I believe he adapted himself to the customs of his time and mixed *Scholastic* behaviors with *Ecclesiastical* ones. This seems likely because **Christ** was accustomed to preaching during the most crowded gatherings of the people, specifically on **Sabbath** days, when a great multitude of people flocked to the **Places of Prayer** <note>original Latin: *Proseuchas*, from the Greek *proseuche*, meaning a place dedicated to prayer.</note>. The fact that **Christ** taught the people in this **Nazarene Synagogue**, and specifically on the **Sabbath** day, was an *Ecclesiastical* matter. But the fact that while teaching, after the text was read, he **sat down** <note>The author refers to the custom where a reader might stand to read Scripture but sit to provide the sermon or commentary, a posture associated with formal teaching.</note>, suggests the custom of the **Schools**, unless I am mistaken. In the *Synagogues*, however, that freedom of teaching and speaking to the people flourished, which **Christ** enjoyed...

# CHAPTER 5. AND OF THE SCHOOLS, ETC.

We would not err if we take the term *Synagogue* so broadly here that it simultaneously includes the public *Schools* attached to *Synagogues*. And the same thing may perhaps be observed in practice elsewhere. I do not deny, however, that the word *to reason* or *dispute* <note>Greek: *dialegesthai*</note> can and—where the occasion warrants—indeed must sometimes be explained as referring to the sermons delivered by *Paul* in the so-called *Synagogues*. This is because Paul's sermons were primarily directed toward the Jews to convince them of certain truths through arguments; and what else is this but to dispute?

However, that *Paul* taught and disputed not only in the *Synagogues* strictly so-called, but also in *Schools*, is most clearly evident from the following history, in which Paul's stay at *Ephesus* is described: 
<margin>Chapter 19, 8.</margin>
*He separated* (these are the words concerning *Paul*) *the disciples, daily* REASONING *in the school of a certain Tyrannus.* <note>The author cites Acts 19:8, though this specific description is found in verse 9. The Greek phrase used is *kath’ hēmeran dialegomenos en tē scholē tyrannou tinos*.</note> Without a doubt, "School" here refers to a *House of Study* <note>Hebrew: *Beth Midrash*</note>, a *house of investigation and reasoning* <note>Greek: *oikos syzētēseōs & dialogismou*</note>. *Luke* used the word *schola* [school], however, because it had already been adopted into the Hebrew language by that era. It is found in the *Midrashim* <note>Ancient Jewish commentaries and interpretations of the Hebrew Bible</note> and is written as *Aschola* or *Ascholi* <note>Hebrew: אסכולא & אסקולי</note>. The most learned *Cohen de Lara* <note>David Cohen de Lara (1602–1674) was a famous Sephardic rabbi and philologist known for his work on Talmudic vocabulary.</note> explains it as a *House of the Book* <note>Hebrew: *Beth Sepher*</note>, that is, a *primary school*.

The *Syriac* translator, truly, did not neglect the use of this word, which was frequent enough at that time, in his version; it is expressed in this manner: *And every day he was speaking with them in the school of a man named Turnos.* <note>Original Syriac: וכל יום ממלל הוא עמהון , באסכולא דגברא דשמה טורנוס</note> Very well indeed. For *Tyrannus* <note>Greek: *Tyrannos*</note> is a proper name here, the same as *Turnus*, which is common enough among the *Talmudic* writers, as *Drusius* <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616) was a prominent Flemish Protestant scholar of the Bible and Hebrew.</note> has already observed before us. Thus, you have Paul here separating himself *with the disciples* <note>Greek: *syn tois mathētais*</note>—who among the Hebrews are called *Talmidim* <note>Hebrew: תלמידי, meaning scholars and learned men</note>—and debating in the *School of a certain Turnus*. 

However, what we have said so far is not fully sufficient for understanding the distinction between *Schools and Synagogues* among the Jews; therefore, it would not be entirely out of place to discuss the condition of the *Schools* somewhat more clearly, though briefly.

*Schools* or Academies within the institutions of Jewish Law and Religion are usually called, as already mentioned, HOUSES OF DISQUISITION <note>Hebrew: *Batei Midrashot*</note>. By this name, they are distinguished from the HOUSES OF SACRED GATHERING <note>Hebrew: *Batei Knesiyot*</note>, properly so called, which are the models for Christian Churches or Oratories, and which are our primary subject. *Midrash* <note>Hebrew: מדרש</note> indeed signifies *investigation* or *disputation*,

<meta>This page continues the philological investigation into the Hebrew root word *darash* (to seek or investigate) and its evolution into the concept of "Midrash" or scholarly study within the synagogue and school context, following the discussion of Paul's reasoning in the school of Tyrannus.</meta>

### ON THE DISTINCTION OF THE SYNAGOGUE, BOOK I, PART I.

From the Hebrew <term>darash <note>original: דרש</note></term>, which means *to seek, to inquire, to weigh a matter with the greatest accuracy and to judge it;* the meaning of this word was later transferred to the *investigation of the sense of Holy Scripture*.

<margin>Ezra 7:10.</margin>
There is one primary passage in the Book of Ezra that undoubtedly provided the occasion for this word to be used so frequently with this specific meaning. There it is written of Ezra: "For Ezra had prepared his heart to SEEK THE LAW OF THE LORD <note>Hebrew: *lidrosh et Torat Yehovah*</note> and to do it." (The text should be translated this way if you simply consider the most common meaning of the word *darash*). The Dutch <note>The author refers to the *Statenvertaling* or Dutch States Translation</note> translate this as: *De wet des Heeren soecken* <note>To seek the Law of the Lord</note>. In their margin, however, they noted nothing further. But what does it mean *to seek the Law of Jehovah?* Without a doubt: to judge, compare, and accurately weigh the text of the Law; then to inquire into the genuine meaning of the Law, and to explain it carefully to others.

<margin>In the Lexicon at the word *darash*</margin>
The distinguished Johannes Cocceius <note>A famous 17th-century Dutch theologian and Hebraist</note> says: *In the context of historical events, "darash" means to follow along closely* <note>Greek: *parakolouthein*</note>. To the Rabbis, a <term>Midrash <note>original: מדרש</note></term> is a *consideration of the Sacred text, or a sermon or reading regarding the sacred text;* and *to darash* is, for them, *to laboriously unpack, or to explain diligently with words*.

<margin>Luke 1:3.</margin>
Whether Luke had this specific passage in mind, I do not know. However, the explanation of it by Jacob Alting <note>A German-born professor of Hebrew at Groningen</note> is well-known: *darash* indicates an extensive explanation, such as is observed in sermons to the people, through which everything is applied to practice; this seems to be why the phrase *to do it* <note>original: *la’asot*</note> was immediately added.

<margin>History of Academic Promotion, p. 219.</margin>
I wonder, however, if this observation is not perhaps too subtle. It is more likely that we should say that *darash* here denotes the critical review of the text and the investigation of the Law's true meaning. It is well established that later Jews accepted *darash* in the same sense that Alting does. Furthermore, since it often happens in the diligent investigation of truth or meaning that we propose our doubts to others, weigh their opinions, and—in order to find the truth which usually lies in obscurity—debate by comparing reasons, the word *darash* (to seek) was transferred among the Chaldeans, Syrians, and Arabs from the sense of "seeking" to that of "inquiring and disputing."

<margin>Schindler in the Lexicon at this word.</margin>
Thus, the Syriac version <note>The Peshitta</note> commonly uses this word in the New Testament. We will give one example from the *Acts of the Apostles*: "But there arose some from the Synagogue, which is called the Synagogue of the Libertines etc., *disputing* with Stephen."

<margin>Acts 6:9.</margin>
The Syriac version reads: *And they were disputing* <note>Syriac: *v’darshin hon*</note> *with Stephen*. Among the Jews, however, in their own language, the word *darash* began to be familiarly used for any profound or exquisite speech, or dissertation on [the Scri]ptures...

### CHAPTER 5. AND OF SCHOOLS, etc.

S 2

<margin>Concerning Book 3, Part 1, chapter 5.</margin>
...[Scri]pture or any text of the institutions of Jewish Law. Because, however, among the Doctors of subsequent centuries, that alone was considered profound speech which was filled with subtle trifles—sought out with the singular genius of that nation from this or that principle—hence <term>Midrash <note>original: מדרש</note></term> began to be called an *allegorical exposition*. In this style of interpretation, some deeper sense of Sacred Scripture is sought, and this same sense is illustrated by pleasant fables and stories. We deal with that kind of discourse in the following part of our work, where the nature of Ancient Sermons is explained. We believe, however, that the <term>Batei Midrashot <note>original: בתי מדרשות; Houses of Inquiry</note></term> received their name not so much from this more subtle *practical* mode of commenting, as from the established custom of debating, or even explaining the text by way of *Questions and Answers* (which was the method of Talmudic *discussions* <note>Greek: συζητήσεων</note> and Scholastic *explanations* <note>Greek: ἐξηγήσεων</note>), or from a more accurate investigation into the meaning of Holy Scripture.

<margin>2 Chronicles 13:22; 24:27. <note>The Latin text cites 1 Chronicles, but these references to "Midrash" are found in 2 Chronicles.</note></margin>
Once or twice the term *Midrash* is found in the Scripture of the Old Testament, where it denotes an *historical commentary*, such as: <gloss>The Midrash of the Book of Kings <note>original: מדרש ספר המלכים</note></gloss>, meaning a *Commentary or inventory of the Book of Kings*.

<margin>In the Tishbite. <note>A dictionary of Talmudic Hebrew by Elias Levita.</note></margin>
Elias Levita writes: <gloss>A book in which the words or deeds of Kings and Prophets are written is called a Midrash <note>original: ספר שכתוב בו דברי המלכים: והנביאים נקרא מדרש</note></gloss>. He adds the reason: <gloss>because everyone who desires to know those matters accurately will find them accurately explained there <note>original: כי כל הדורש אותם הדברים וימצאם שם</note></gloss>. The Dutch <note>The author refers to the Dutch "States Translation" of the Bible.</note> translate this as: *History*. Therefore, a *Midrash* is an accurate and exquisite review and investigation, through which an involved or obscure matter is made clear. Say then that *Batei Midrashot* are, by the reasoning of their etymology, *Buildings* in which the genuine sense of Divine Law or the opinion of Jewish Jurisprudence is sought with singular effort and accuracy. But let us see what the Jewish authors themselves say regarding the interpretation of the word. Elias writes in *The Tishbite*: <gloss>And also the house or the room set apart for the study of the Law is called the HOUSE OF INQUIRY <note>original: וגם הבית או החדר המיוחד ללמוד תורה נקרא בית המדרש</note></gloss>.

<margin>Gemara Berachot, folio 16, column 1, near the end. Isaiah 32:9. Hebraic Hours on Matthew 4:23.</margin>
Elsewhere it is called the <term>Beit Rabbanan <note>original: בית רבנן</note></term>, the *House of the Teachers*, which is surely explained as a *House of Inquiry*. We trace the footsteps of the Talmudists: <gloss>Greater is the promise that the Holy One, Blessed be He, made to women than to men, as it is said: "Rise up, you women who are at ease; hear my voice, you confident daughters; give ear..." [Isaiah 32:9]. I said—Rav said to Rabbi Hiyya: By what do women merit [reward]? By bringing their children to the synagogue to read [the Scripture] and to the [study house]... <note>original: גדולה הבטחה שהבטיחן הקדוש ברוך הוא לנשים יותר מן האנשים שנאמר נשים שאננות קומנה שמענה קולי בנות בוטחות האזינה: אמרתי אמר ליה רב לרבי חייא נשים במאי זכיין באקרויי בנייהו לבני כנישת׳ ולבו׳</note></gloss> <insert>(it can be read: "to the Rabbi," as will be clear from the Gloss)</insert>

### ON THE DISTINCTIONS OF THE SYNAGOGUE, BOOK 1, PART 1.

<margin>This phrase is found in [Tractate] Shabbat, folio 119, column 1, in the middle. This passage will perhaps be used later.</margin>
<gloss>By bringing their sons to the house of the teachers to study, and waiting for their husbands until they return from the house of the teachers.</gloss>
*The Holy and Blessed God granted a greater degree of hope and trust to women than to men, according to what is said: "You tranquil women, rise up; hear my voice, you confident daughters; give ear to my speech" [Isaiah 32:9]. Rav said to Rabbi Chaya: "What is the righteousness of women?" (I would prefer to translate it this way, rather than with Lightfoot—who noted part of this passage elsewhere—as: "What is the women's <term>justification <note>original Greek: δικαίωμα (dikaioma); a legal or moral entitlement</note></term> through which women commend themselves to God?"). It is that their sons read in the Synagogue, and their husbands devote themselves to Talmudic study in the Academy, and that they wait with respect for their husbands returning home from the Academy. On this passage, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator</note> says:*

<gloss>To the house of the assembly [the Synagogue]. The schoolchildren were accustomed to learn before a Master in the house of the synagogue.</gloss>
*In the House of the Synagogue. The young students are accustomed to learn before a Master in the house of the synagogue. Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot, a 17th-century English scholar of Hebrew and the New Testament</note> raises a doubt whether Rabbi Solomon meant that children are catechized in the synagogue. But if we consider the Talmudic text, the commentator simply seems to say that boys often practice reading the Divine Law in synagogues in the presence of their Master, and are*

<margin>Regarding the Gemara <note>the commentary portion of the Talmud</note> of Megillah, folio 28, column 2.</margin>
*instructed by him, if they make any error. Certainly, Rabbi Solomon says this clearly in another gloss:*
<gloss>The children were accustomed to read in the house of the assembly [Synagogue].</gloss> *He continues:* <gloss>The house of the teachers is the House of Inquiry [Beit Midrash].</gloss> *THE HOUSE OF DISQUISITION, in which they learn the Mishnah <note>the early collection of Jewish oral laws</note> and the Gemara.*
<gloss>And they wait for their husbands: They wait for their husbands and give them permission to go and learn the Law in another city.</gloss> *They wait for their husbands: They wait for their husbands and grant them the power of going away and learning the law in another city. What laudable indulgence of women toward their husbands!*

<margin>Occurs in the Gemara of Shabbat, folio 119, column 2, at the end. And in Maimonides, Laws of Torah Study, chapter 2.</margin>
*I would like you to observe from this passage something useful to note: that the Academy is called here <term>Beit Rabban <note>literally "House of our Teacher"</note></term>, the House of the Teachers, and the primary school <note>Latin: "Schola trivialis," referring to the basic level of education</note> is called <term>Beit Rabban</term>, the House of the Master. The latter <term>phrase <note>original Greek: φράσις (phrasis)</note></term>, "children of the house of the teacher" <note>Tinokot shel Beit Rabban</note>, by which the boys who attend primary schools are designated, is common enough in the writings of the Jews. In this phrase, I believe the ending "-nu" in the word "Rabbenu" should be taken as the Aramaic suffix for the first person plural, so that "Rabban" signifies "our Master"; according to the form "Rabbenu" [our teacher] or "Morenu" [our guide], which familiarly take this ending in many cases,*

### CHAPTER 5. AND OF THE SCHOOLS, ETC.
