...they inquire, even though it often contributes almost nothing in terms of *force* <note>original Greek: *ἐνεργείας* (energeias); meaning the active power or emphasis of a word</note> to the meaning. <term>Rabban</term> <note>Hebrew: רַבָּן</note>, however, seems to me to be a plural with an Aramaic suffix of the same kind, and carries the same weight as <term>Rabbotenu</term> <note>Hebrew: רַבּוֹתֵינוּ; "Our Rabbis"</note>. Furthermore, <term>Rabban</term> is said, if I am not mistaken, instead of <term>Rabbona</term> <note>Hebrew: רַבּוֹנָא; "Great Master"</note>, with the final letter being absorbed, as almost always happens among the Talmudists. Johannes Buxtorf <note>A prominent 17th-century Christian Hebraist</note> indeed thinks it is a feminine plural termination; this, however, is less pleasing to me. Although it is certain that <term>Rabbanim</term> <note>Hebrew: רַבָּנִם</note> in the plural is not always used for doctors of the highest dignity, I hardly doubt that the title <term>Rabbanim</term>, though now quite common, denotes a certain higher degree of honor than <term>Rabbot</term>. Certainly, in this passage, an elementary school <note>Latin: Schola trivialis; referring to the basic level of education in the liberal arts</note> is called <term>Beit Rabban</term> <note>Hebrew: בית רבן; "House of the Teacher"</note> in the *Gloss*, and an *illustrious school* is called in the text <term>Beit Rabbanan</term> <note>Hebrew: בית רבנן; "House of the Rabbis"</note>, taking into account the lesser and greater dignity of each. Furthermore, the *Gloss* describes the phrase <term>Beit Rabbanan</term> as a <term>Beit Midrash</term> <note>Hebrew: בית מדרש; "House of Study"</note>, *a House of Disquisition, and one consecrated to the studies of the Mishna and the Gemara* <note>The two primary components of the Talmud</note>; in which surely there is no difficulty. Undoubtedly, an *Academy* is called <term>Beit Rabbanan</term>, the *House of the Doctors*, because the Doctors spend a great part of their lives in it, being occupied and dwelling there; unless one prefers to say <term>Beit Rabbanan</term> is an *ellipsis* for *Beit Midrash Rabbanan* [The House of Study of the Rabbis].

Let us not, however, neglect the Jewish acumen even in these minutiae; for elsewhere they explain this very *phrase* <term>Beit Rabbanan</term>. An external ruling <note>Latin: constitutio exotica; likely referring to a Baraita, a tradition outside the official Mishna</note>, immediately following the *Mishna*, held as follows: <term>Regarding Synagogues, they do not derive benefit from them</term> <note>Hebrew: בתי כנסיות אין נאותין בהם</note> *They do not derive any personal benefit from Synagogues.* (Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> says: <term>They do not adorn themselves within them</term> <note>Hebrew: אין מתקשטין לתוכו</note>). To explain those words, the following is found in the progress of the *Gemara*:* <term>And they do not derive benefit from them. Rabba said: For the Sages and their disciples it is permitted, according to that which Rabbi Joshua Ben Levi says: what is Beit Rabban? The House of the Rabbis.</term> <note>Hebrew quoted from the Talmud</note> *That is, it is permitted for the Rabbis to conduct themselves in their school as if they were in their own homes.* Rabbi Solomon explains this clever point thus: <term>Why do they call Academies the 'House of the Rabbis'? Because it is their home for every purpose.</term>

### CONCERNING THE DISTINCTION OF THE SYNAGOGUE, BOOK I, PART I.

...[sub]jection is its genuine and proper meaning. No; rather, the disciples of the Teachers were arranged in rows like a vineyard. <margin>Mark 6:40</margin> Lightfoot brought forward the same explanation of the word from Solomon Jarchi <note>Also known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator</note>, illustrating from there the phrase "in groups" <note>original Greek: πρασιαὶ, πρασιαὶ (prasiai, prasiai); literally "garden beds," used in the Gospel of Mark to describe people sitting in ranks</note> in Mark. I would also not want to pass over the fact that the name <term>Bei Rav</term> <note>Hebrew: בי רב; "House of the Master"</note> is likewise applied to Academies. <margin>Chapter 3, page 44</margin> Regarding this, the author of the *Halichot Olam* <note>The "Pathways of Eternity," a 15th-century guide to the methodology of the Talmud</note> advises thus: "Wherever <term>Bei Rav</term> is mentioned, it does not literally mean a specific Master, but rather the House of Study, or a place of debate" <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: ממש : וכל היכי דאתאמר בי רב לאו רב ממש אלא בית המדרש הוא; original Greek: συζητήσεως (syzeteseos), meaning discussion or inquiry</note>. Therefore, <term>Bei Rav</term> is the school of any public Teacher: and accordingly, it is the same as <term>Bei Rabbanan</term> mentioned above, and <term>Bei Rabbi</term>, of which the author says in the same place: "By the masters of the Teacher’s school, we should understand the learned men who apply themselves to letters in the Academy." <note>original Hebrew: כלהו דאמרינן רבנן דבי רבי : ר"ל התלמידים בני הישיבה</note>. Therefore, the expressions <term>Bei Rav</term>, <term>Beit Rabbi</term>, and <term>Bei Rabbanan</term> are of almost the same value in Talmudic literature. Indeed, the scholarly lecture hall <note>original Greek: ἀκροατήריον (akroaterion)</note> itself is frequently designated by the single word <term>Beit</term> <note>Hebrew: בית; "House"</note>, <margin>Alting, *History of Hebrew Academies*, page 289</margin> as is clear from the common Talmudic phrases "House of Shammai" and "House of Hillel" <note>original Hebrew: בית שמאי & בית הלל; referring to the two famous rival schools of thought in the 1st century</note>. "House" in this phrase is used metonymically <note>original Greek: μετωνυμικῶς; a figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it</note> to denote the scholars and learned men who followed the sect or school <note>original Greek: αἵρεσιν (hairesin)</note> of Hillel or Shammai. Truly, the word "House" is to be understood as an abbreviation for <term>Beit Midrash</term> <note>House of Study</note>, mentioned before, or <term>Beit Talmud</term> <note>House of Learning</note>, a phrase <note>original Greek: ῥῆσις (rhesis)</note> that appears in the Jerusalem Gemara; unless you prefer to interpret it as "family." Among the Greeks, gyms of this kind were called schools, places of meditation, or places of teaching <note>original Greek: σχολαὶ (scholai), φροντιστήריה (phrontisteria), διδασκαλεῖα (didaskaleia)</note>, <margin>Codex Megilla, chapter 3, folio 73, column 4</margin> as was noted before. So much for the Names.

<margin>Selden, *Prolegomena to the Book on Succession to the Property of the Deceased*</margin> Moreover, these schools, or <term>Batei Midrashot</term> <note>Houses of Study</note>, or rather Lecture Halls, destined for the sacred exercises of the Teachers, about which I am speaking, were either Private or Public. Private ones were again of two kinds: either for single individuals or for several. <margin>*Orach Chajim*, chapter 151, § 2</margin> Regarding the Academy, or the private or domestic school, there is a clear passage in the *Orach Chajim* <note>The "Path of Life," a central code of Jewish law</note>: "An individual who establishes a study house in his own home for his own convenience, it possesses no sanctity whatsoever." <note>original Hebrew: יחיד הקובע מדרש בביתו לצורכו אין לו קדושה כל כך</note> That "House of Study for an individual" <note>Hebrew: בית מדרש של יחיד</note> is opposed to the "House of Study for the many" <note>Hebrew: בית מדרש של רבים</note>, the public school, which maintains its own sanctity, as can be seen from that passage. Let us speak briefly of each, so that once this mass [of terminology] is cleared away, we may thereafter discuss the Synagogues more freely.

<header>CHAPTER 6. CONCERNING SCHOOLS AND ORATORIES, ETC.</header>

## CHAPTER VI.

*A discussion concerning private Schools and Oratories and their use among the Teachers of the Jewish nation. The true meaning of the terms <term>Aliyah</term> <note>Hebrew: עליה; literally "ascent" or "upper room"</note>, <term>Hyperōon</term> <note>Greek: ὑπερῷον; an upper story or room</note>, <term>Anōgeon</term> <note>Greek: ἀνώγεον; a room above the ground</note>, <term>Cœnaculum</term> <note>Latin: "dining room" or "upper room"</note>, and <term>Chalcidicum</term> <note>Latin: a portico or large hall; here referring to a specific architectural space</note>, which pertain to this subject, is investigated. The use of such sacred upper rooms is demonstrated from the writings of the Old and New Testaments as far as is sufficient, not omitting the opinion of the illustrious De Dieu <note>Louis de Dieu (1590–1642), a Dutch Protestant theologian and orientalist</note> regarding the upper room in which the Apostles were gathered on the Feast of Pentecost. The windows of these upper rooms and their use are also discussed. Finally, private study halls, which were numerous, are described.*

Among the Jewish nation, the practice and logic of their Religion were such that those devoted to wisdom, and others of a more prosperous status and holier life, would reserve some part of their houses specifically for the exercises of piety and learning. This was situated in the *upper parts of the house*, closest, it seems, to the *roofing*, with *open windows* facing that cardinal point of the heavens in which the Temple was located; furthermore, it was furnished with those aids which the study of piety or letters required. They would retire there, not only whenever they were alone—with God and conscience as witnesses—to cultivate fellowship with the Divine through intimate prayers, or to apply themselves to serious meditations on divine matters, but also when they wished *with others* to converse about the divine Law, to debate its meanings, and to devote themselves to other sacred exercises. You have here a brief sketch of the *Schools*, or if you prefer, *domestic houses of prayer*. What we have said must now be proven and illustrated.

To pave the way for this digression, we shall set aside an ancient and well-known tale, long since excerpted by the most learned men, which nevertheless will lead us to the knowledge of these *Upper Rooms*; for the rest, we care nothing. The words of **Rabbi Gedaliah:** <note>Likely Gedaliah ibn Yahya ben Joseph, author of the 16th-century work "Shalshelet Ha-Kabbalah" (The Chain of Tradition)</note>

<margin>lia</margin>Rabbi Abuia, the father of Elisha "the Other" <note>Elisha ben Abuyah, a famous rabbi who later became an apostate, hence the nickname "Acher" or "The Other"</note>, was immensely wealthy. This history is certainly composed in such a way as if the Jewish writers either retained a faint memory of, or were gripped by envy toward, the miracle that Luke records as happening to the Apostles on the day of Pentecost in the **upper room** <note>Greek: *en tō hyperōō*</note>, where they were gathered in a certain sacred chamber; <margin>Acts 2, 3.</margin> of which we shall speak shortly. ...designation, this is quite clear not only from the cited testimonies in which the Doctors are said to have **ascended** into it, but it can also be understood from the word itself, *Aliyah* <note>original Hebrew: עליה</note>, since it derives from *alah* <note>original Hebrew: עלה</note>, meaning "to ascend." In Greek, this is translated as *hyperōon* <note>original Greek: ὑπερῷον, meaning an upper room or chamber</note>. A learned dissertation exists regarding the power and genuine meaning of both these terms by **John Gregory**.

<margin>
*Notes and Observations*, chapter 3. P π´. regarding sketches, page 138.
</margin>

Gregory observes that Eustathius <note>A 12th-century Byzantine scholar and archbishop</note> teaches that the word *hyperōon* descends from the Spartan word *oa* <note>original Greek: ᾠὰ</note>, as they were accustomed to call the high parts of houses "the lofty things," or **the uppermost parts of the homes**. He adds: Moschopulus <note>A Byzantine grammarian</note> says that a *hyperōon* is **a room built under another**, which among the Athenians is called a *dieres* <note>original Greek: Διῆρες</note>, meaning **a chamber built upon a chamber**. He interprets *hyperōon* by the term *dieres*, just as Hesychius <note>An Alexandrian lexicographer</note> interprets *dieres* as *hyperōon*, and interprets "stairway" <note>original Greek: κλίμαξ</note> and *hyperōon* as *anōgeon* <note>original Greek: ἀνώγεων, literally "above the ground"</note>. In my own records it is read thus: *hyperōïon, hyperōon, anōgaion oikēma, hyperōa, anōgaia*. This is correct. For the learned advise that it can be written both as *anōgeōn* and *anōgaion*, unless perhaps *anōgeōn* and *anōgaion* are being confused. Suidas <note>The *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> has this: *Anōgeon*. A room. *Anōgaion* and *katagaion* <note>an underground room or cellar</note> are written with a diphthong and a small "o." *Anōgeon* is a **dining room situated in the upper part of the house.**

<margin>
On this word *anōgeōn*.
</margin>

**But *anōgaion* and *katagaion* are written with a diphthong and a small "o"** <note>referring to the Greek letter omicron</note>. Let us also add the other things that Suidas says: **As for the word *anōgeōn*, even if perhaps the rules themselves dictate it be written with a large "o"** <note>the letter omega</note> **and a plain "e," yet that hunter of words and accurate craftsman of the art of correct writing, Master Coprogenius** <note>original Latin/Greek: *Coprogenius*, a name meaning "dung-born," likely a humorous or polemical nickname for a grammarian mentioned in the Suda</note>**, who observed the accurate and correct method of exchanging these letters, handed down that these are written with a plain "e" and a small "o."** The word descends, as they believe, from *anō* <note>above</note> and *gaia* or *gē* <note>earth</note>, because it signifies a chamber higher than the earth. It is called a **dining room** <note>original Latin: *cænaculum*</note> by Roman writers. Indeed, the Romans in ancient times were accustomed to **dine** in the lower parts of their houses, but afterwards, when they built their houses to a greater height, they thought it more worthy and magnificent to celebrate their feasts in some upper part of the building. From that time, the upper chambers of the house were called *cænacula*.

<margin>
Besides Gregory, see Stuck, *Antiquities of Feasting*, book 2, chapter 11.
</margin>

Whether the same custom was observed among the Jews is doubtful. From the examples of Jewish history just cited, you might not wrongly conclude that the Hebrews dined in...

**Beza** adds in his annotations that *the Jews were accustomed to dine in that part of the house*; this is utterly rejected by the recently praised **Gregory**, because he judges that the sacramental supper must be entirely distinguished from common and ordinary reclining at table. Indeed, **Gregory** even critiques these words: *That the Jews were accustomed to have dining chambers of this sort, both for the reception of travelers and especially for the Passover.* I am not surprised by the error, he says, however great it may be. For if the sense of the *upper room* <note>Greek: τοῦ ὑπερῴου</note> was not correctly understood, it could hardly happen that they would not err; but it was very poorly done to designate the same place for both uses, not to say profanely. <margin>in the place cited.</margin>
For who is unaware that dining chambers were destined for guest-quarters? **Stuckius** will provide the evidence. But you say: were the dining chambers, or the *upper rooms* <note>Greek: τὰ ἀνώγεα ὑπερῷα</note>, rooms consecrated to sacred exercises? Some were, certainly, but not all. For who could persuade us that the houses of all **Jews** were equipped with such dining chambers? And, if that were granted, who would assert that the houses of the **Jews** were only of two stories? It certainly seems altogether likely that **Paul** spoke words to the faithful at **Troas** in a chamber of the third story. <margin>Acts 20:9.</margin>
*he fell down from the third story* <note>Greek: ἔπεσεν ἀπὸ τοῦ τριστέγου κάτω</note>. Therefore, if there was some *upper room* <note>Greek: ἀνώγεον</note> on the second story, who could deny there was another, more sacred one on the third? Or if anyone refuses that, let him at least concede that the same story contained several rooms, among which nothing prevents one from being destined for sacred exercises and others for other uses. By another name, the *upper room* <note>Greek: τὸ ὑπερῷον</note>, or the **chalcidicum** <note>a term for a portico or a grand hall</note> dining chamber, is sometimes so-called by Latin authors, although the **chalcidicum**, as described by **Isidore**, seems to differ from our *upper room*. ### CHAPTER 6. ON PRIVATE ORATORIES.
<meta>catchword: house</meta>

<margin>According to the common division of chapter 3. For the Hebrew text lacks these divisions.</margin>
...the upper room of the house, intended for prayers and other sacred exercises, where the windows were opened toward Jerusalem. <note>The author is referring to the practice of Daniel (Daniel 6:10), who prayed toward Jerusalem.</note> Another passage consistent with this one, from the story of *Tobit*, was suggested by *John Gregory* <note>An English orientalist and scholar, 1607–1646</note>. In that narrative, *Sarah*, the daughter of *Raguel*, is introduced; weary of her troubles, she is said to have prayed to God in her father's upper chamber, which was equipped with windows. These are the words as they appear in the edition by *Paulus Fagius* <note>A 16th-century Hebraist</note>, which is the only one I currently possess: *Then she went and fell prostrate BEFORE THE WINDOW, praying and saying: "Blessed be the Lord our God, and blessed be his great name," etc.* <note>original Hebrew: אז הלכה ותפלה נגד הלון ותאמר ברוך יהוה אלהינו וברוך שמו הגדול וגו</note> Gregory reports that in other Hebrew copies it is written: *she went up* <note>original Hebrew: עלתה</note> *to the upper room of her father.* But we need not concern ourselves too much with that, because in what follows, the mention of the upper room is clear enough: *Likewise, Sarah descended FROM THE UPPER ROOM IN WHICH SHE HAD PRAYED.* <note>original Hebrew: וכמו גם כן שרה ירדה מן העליה אשר התפללה</note> The fact that a window is likewise attributed to this upper room is consistent with what we just noted regarding Daniel's upper room. Let us see if we can find these same upper rooms in the writings of the New Testament.

<margin>Chapter 6.</margin>
Indeed, I believe the words of Christ in *Matthew* should be referred to here first. *But you*, He says, *when you pray, enter into your INNER CHAMBER,* <note>original Greek: εἴσελθε εἰς τὸ ταμεῖόν σου</note> *and having shut your door, pray to your Father in secret, and your Father, who sees you in secret, will reward you openly.* <note>Matthew 6:6</note> *Beza* <note>Theodore Beza, a major Protestant reformer and scholar</note> correctly translates this as *Inner Chamber* <note>original Latin: *Conclave*</note>. The Old Interpreter <note>The Vulgate</note> has *Bedroom* <note>original Latin: *Cubiculum*</note>. In this case, the Greek terms for "chamber" <note>original Greek: ταμεῖον and ταμιεῖον</note> are the same as the Hebrew word for an "innermost room," <note>original Hebrew: חדר / cheder</note> 
<margin>In his Paraphrase.</margin>
which is the word *Jachaides* <note>Likely Joseph ben Yahya, a Jewish commentator on Daniel</note> used to translate the term for "upper room" <note>original Hebrew: עליה / aliyah</note> in the book of *Daniel*. It is worth noting that the Lord Christ contrasts these private Oratories with public ones. The *Pharisees* made a singular display of their piety with their prayers *in the Synagogues*, or *Public Oratories*. Christ, who seeks to drive out all hypocrisy, recommends *private Oratories*. It is clear from the *Acts of the Apostles* that the disciples of Christ by no means neglected these precepts of their Master. Whether they were alone or had others of their profession as companions, they frequently retired into private Oratories of this kind. # CHAPTER 6. ON DOMESTIC ORATORIES.

However, even more beyond controversy are the things which the same historian *Luke* records concerning the upper room of the *Troadians* <note>The people of Troas, an ancient Greek city in Asia Minor</note>, in which the Apostle Paul <margin>Acts 20:8.</margin> preached. "And there were," he says, "many lamps in the upper room where they were gathered together." <note>original Greek: "Ἦσαν δὲ λαμπάδες ἱκαναὶ ἐν τῷ ὑπερῴῳ οὗ ἦσαν συνηγμένοι"</note> *There were indeed many lamps* IN THE UPPER ROOM, *in which they were gathered.* This upper room, as I have said, belonged to the *Troadians*, in a private house, where Paul held a discourse until late at night, as is narrated in the same place.

It must still be explained for what purpose these upper rooms, or *private oratories*, were equipped with *windows*; though this is not difficult to understand. For this custom is based on both *precept* and *example*. On precept, indeed, because from the time the Temple was built by *Solomon*, all Israelites were obliged to turn themselves in prayer toward <margin>1 Kings 8:44.</margin> that region of the world in which the *Temple* was situated—a matter that will be discussed more extensively in what follows. From this, it was fitting that they had *windows* in their chambers open toward that quarter of the world. On *example*, indeed, because this was already observed by Daniel, that most holy man, whose customs it cannot but be praiseworthy and proper to imitate. Hence that rule among the Talmudic scholars, which *Rabbenu Asher* <note>Asher ben Jehiel (c. 1250–1327), a prominent Talmudic scholar known as "The Rosh"</note> did not neglect in his *Definitions*: <margin>In definition 24, chapter 5 of the Book of Berachoth.</margin> *Rabbi Chaya, the son of Abba, <margin>Daniel 6:11. On the Book of Berachoth, folio 34, column 2, at the end.</margin> said that Rabbi Yochanan said: A man should not pray except in a house equipped with windows; according to that which is said: "And he had windows open in his upper room facing Jerusalem."* <note>original Hebrew: אמר רבי חייא בר אבא אמר רבי יוחנן אל יתפלל אדם אלא בבית שיש שם חלונות שנאמר וכיון פתיחן ליה בעלית' לקבל ירושלם</note> However, the reason given by *Solomon Jarchi* <note>Better known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud</note> is slightly different, though it may be reconciled with the preceding ones without difficulty: *The windows will be the cause for him to rightly direct his heart, for he looks toward the heavens and is humbled.* <note>original Hebrew: החלונות גורמין לו שיכוין לבו שהוא מסתכל כלפי שמים ולבו נכנע</note> So much for *Domestic Oratories and Schools*. I will now only add at the end that secret upper rooms of this kind were not unknown even to the Gentiles <note>Non-Jewish people, particularly Romans and Greeks in this context</note>. Thus we read concerning *Augustus* <note>The first Roman Emperor</note>: *Whenever he intended to do anything in secret and without interruption, he had a* **UNIQUE PLACE IN A HIGH POSITION,** *which he called "Syracuse" and his* "little workshop"; <note>original Greek: τεχνύφιον (technyphion)</note> *he would withdraw to this place, <margin>Suetonius in "Life of Augustus," chapter 72. Lampridius in "Life of Alexander [Severus]," chapters 29 and 31.</margin> or to the suburban estate of one of his freedmen.* Indeed, the Gentiles also had their own domestic shrines, in which they worshipped the gods of their family—

### CHAPTER 7. OR ON ACADEMIES.

->U 3<-
<meta>catchword: First</meta>

*The opinion of Abraham Ben David <note>Abraham ben David of Posquières (c. 1125–1198), a famous Provencal rabbi known as the Ravad.</note> states that it was not permitted for the Interpreter to deviate from the opinions of the preaching Teachers. These individual points are confirmed by the famous history of the disagreement that once arose between Gamaliel and Joshua <note>This refers to the dispute between Rabban Gamaliel II and Rabbi Joshua ben Hananiah in the Talmud (Berakhot 27b), which resulted in a restructuring of the academy's leadership.</note>.*

---

I now move to the public **Schools**, in which **Teachers** of the highest reputation, fortified by the public authority of the entire **Nation** or **City**, specialized in the Divine Law and ancestral traditions <note>original Greek: πατροπαραδότους (patroparadotous)</note>. Let me describe those schools as **Lecture Halls**, which were larger or smaller depending on the status of the Teachers and students. They were furnished with **Chairs** <note>original Latin: Cathedris</note> in which the **Teachers** sat and **preached** or disputed through **Interpreters** <term>Interpreter: Known in Hebrew as a Meturgeman; an assistant who repeated the teacher's quiet words loudly for the audience, often explaining them further.</term>. Furthermore, these halls were adorned with other **benches**, occupied by the Colleagues of the Teacher and other learned men or those studying the Divine Law. These **seats** were protected by **lattices** <note>original Latin: cancellis; a physical barrier or railing</note>, outside of which other listeners from the common folk were allowed to **stand**, finding pleasure in hearing the disputes or sermons of the Teachers.

To establish a **School** of this more famous sort (as the face of the Jewish Commonwealth before its destruction by the Romans is painted in the **Talmud and Jewish Histories**), these necessary **People** were generally required: The **Teacher**, who was **promoted** to that dignity through the authority of the **Sanhedrin** <term>Sanhedrin: The supreme council and judicial body of ancient Israel.</term>; the **Interpreter**, himself lower in wisdom and rank, who explained the teacher's **words** to the listeners; the **Colleagues**, who raised doubts to the teacher and who sat with him in the **Sanhedrin** or **Forensic Court** (though I would have this understood only regarding the most famous **Academies**); the **Students**, who devoted themselves to his discipline; and the **Attendants of the Academy**, who looked after the needs of the **School** and performed other necessary duties for the Teacher and students.

The method of teaching was as follows: the **Colleagues**, who were learned men, and the young **Students** would raise a question on this or that argument; the **Teacher**, through the **Interpreter**, would **respond** more at length to the question; or even the **Teacher** himself would explain more broadly a question he had raised, and in that explanation, he would range widely into any similar arguments. Let these things be said briefly as a sketch of the **ancient Schools**, each of which must now be illustrated more diligently—even if, certainly, not every difficulty in every part of this subject has been removed for us. Nevertheless, let us see how far it is possible for us to proceed.

# ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS, BOOK I. PART I.

First, it seems certain from the customs of the *Talmudists* <note>Scholars and teachers of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> that every *Sanhedrin* <term>Synedrium: a Greek-derived term for a high council or court of justice</term> had its own *lecture hall*, in which the *Divine Law* was explained. The duty of teaching and explaining in that *lecture hall* was primarily performed by the Prince, or the President of the Senate, who for that reason was honored both as the *Rector of the Academy* and as the *President of the Senate*. Let us consider the words of *Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar</note>, which we believe contain the proof of our opinion. He writes as follows:

<margin>
Treatise on the Sanhedrin, chapter 3, section 1.
</margin>
*How much of the day did the Judges spend in hearing and deciding cases? The Small Sanhedrin and the Court of Three sat from the end of the set morning prayer until the end of the sixth hour of the day; but the Great Sanhedrin of seventy-one men sat from the time of the morning sacrifice until the time of the evening sacrifice. On Sabbaths and festival days, however, they sat in the Academy (the house of inquiry) which was on the Temple Mount.* <note>Original Hebrew: "עד אימתי יושבין הדיינין... יושבין בבית המדרש שבהר הבית"</note> This definition by Maimonides is founded on the words of the *Gemara* <note>The component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis and commentary</note>:

<margin>
Babylonian Gemara, Sanhedrin, folio 88, column 1.
</margin>
*On Sabbaths and festival days they sit at the rampart.* <note>Original Hebrew: "בשבתות ובימים טובי' יושבי' בחיל"</note> In this testimony it is clearly established that the places designated for Judgments were distinct from the *Academies*. Reason seemed to require this, yet I will not hide the fact that this doubt troubled me for some time. For anyone who weighs the *Talmudic* institutions or the histories of the succession of famous Doctors among them might doubt whether the very place designated for judgments was not the same one designated for Academic disputes. Certainly, the same person who was called the <term>Nasi: Prince or President</term> in the *Sanhedrins* is called by another name, the <term>Rosh HaYeshiva: Head of the Academy</term>, and in almost every instance is associated with the <term>Beth Midrash: House of Study or Discussion</term>. Furthermore, the *Rector of the Academy* is even today distinguished by the title <term>Av Beit Din: Father of the Sanhedrin</term>, even though the Jews now enjoy no Sanhedrins except for the *Academies* in which they teach the law. Then, one may also notice that "to speak the law" and "to teach" are very frequently conflated in their writings. Not to mention that the same manner of speaking is observed in secular writings when they touch upon the affairs of the Jews.

<margin>
Law 17, concerning Jews and Sky-worshippers.

...you should lead them all, and *the Sanhedrin once again consisted only of Israelites (Senators of the Pharisaic sect) to make the day a festival.* Therefore, matters were sought out and debated within the Sanhedrins themselves whenever doubtful cases came before the Senators. Nor do I think the reason is to be sought elsewhere for why, in the Sanhedrins of Twenty-Three <note>Smaller local courts consisting of twenty-three judges</note>, three ranks of Candidates sat on the lower benches (if this tradition deserves credit, which I will not dispute now), except so that they might diligently observe various legal cases and thus gradually become accustomed to the judgments. I might also mention that if the votes of the Senators were tied or insufficient, some of these very Candidates were joined to the Senators to help define the legal opinion along with them. It also pertains to this that among the Senators of the Sanhedrin, according to the Canons of the Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note>, none were admitted who were not equally fit for teaching the law as they were for pronouncing it. I have no doubt, therefore, that matters were discussed and disputed in the Sanhedrins, yet in such a way that a notable distinction always remained between the *Chambers of Judgment* and the *Academies* while the Hebrew Republic was standing and flourishing. However, when jurisdiction was cut short or taken away from the Jews by the Romans and their Republic was overturned, then I confess that the *Sanhedrins* and the *Academic Auditoriums* became confused <note>In the sense of being merged or blended together</note>. # ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS, BOOK I. PART I. #

*...difference. Indeed, those same Judges deserve to be called Professors, since the power of teaching was granted to the same people to whom jurisdiction was entrusted.* If these words of that most learned man <note>referring to John Selden, mentioned on the previous page</note> are to be understood regarding that interval of time following the destruction of the Jewish State by the Romans, then I subscribe to them in every respect. But if, as it seems, they are to be applied to all periods of the State, even when it was flourishing, then I confess I hesitate at them. Jewish writers sometimes speak of this point so unclearly that I have often been pulled now in this direction, now in that, before I could satisfy my mind in defining it. For they are accustomed to speak of the <term>Synedria</term> <note>Sanhedrins, or high courts</note> as they were when the State flourished in the same way they actually functioned after the State was overturned. However, I would by no means believe—not even based on the impressive sayings of the <term>Talmudists</term> <note>The ancient rabbinic scholars of the Talmud</note>—that while the State was flourishing, the Sanhedrins of the Jewish nation conducted themselves in the manner of *Schools*, as I have already declared. Furthermore, what the *form* of these *Schools* was is not obscure in itself, and you will understand it properly from those things which we will soon intersperse in the discussion on *Teachers and the Method of Teaching*. For it is not our purpose to deal with this matter formally, but to touch briefly upon those things that are currently relevant and need illustration. <margin>See Jerusalem Talmud, Tractate Berachot, folio 7, column 4.</margin> They were equipped with a *Chair of Honor* <note>original: cathedra; Hebrew: כסא, kisse</note> in which the *Rectors* <note>The heads or leaders of the school</note> sat while teaching or explaining, and *benches* <note>original: subsellia; Hebrew: ספסלים, safsalim</note> in which sat the *Colleagues of the Rector*, men learned and devoted to wisdom; at the same time, there was often a <term>fence</term> <note>Hebrew: גדר, geder</note> or railing, outside of which other listeners stood together. All things will be clear from the evidence that will soon be brought forward. Truly, how great is the *sanctity of the Schools*, as they even surpass the *sanctity of the Synagogues*: how much reverence must be shown to them; namely, that *one must not sleep in them*; *nothing but sacred matters are to be meditated upon in them*; *one is not to bless someone who sneezes* <note>Referring to the custom of saying "God bless you," which was forbidden in the study house to prevent distraction from the holy word</note>, and many similar things; you will find these handed down in a simple style by *Maimonides* <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note>.

<margin>Maimonides, Laws of Torah Study (Hilchot Talmud Torah), chapter 4, near the end.</margin> In these *Academies*, the supreme power of *teaching* and the chief exercise of that power belonged to the *Rector of the Academy*, or the *Prince* <note>The Nasi</note>, who was required to be so practiced in all the minutiae of the traditions that he was able to respond promptly to all questions proposed and immediately resolve and discuss any difficulties raised. Familiar is the <term>Gloss</term> <note>A commentary or explanatory note</note> on that famous passage cited a little earlier from the Tractate *Horayot*: <note>original: נשיא הוא היה בעל הדרשה : ומלמד תורה ברבים</note> *The Prince is he who possessed the supreme power of preaching and taught the Torah in public.*

Our masters say: **FROM THE DAYS OF MOSES UNTIL RABBAN GAMALIEL THEY DID NOT LEARN THE LAW EXCEPT STANDING: but FROM THE TIME RABBAN GAMALIEL DIED, a disease descended into the world, AND THEY LEARNED THE LAW SITTING;** and this is what they say: *From the time Rabban Gamaliel died, the Glory of the Law ceased.* These last words are found in the *Mishnah Sotah* <note>A tractate of the Mishnah; original: *Misna Sota*</note>. Regarding the "disease" <note>or "weakness"</note> that they say had invaded the world since Gamaliel's time, you should understand it to mean that the bodies of the disciples had become so weakened that they were thereafter by no means sufficient to endure such standing positions. But I certainly doubt whether this tradition rests on reliable evidence. For the more I weigh it, the more it seems to me to be of the genre of exaggerations <note>Greek: *tōn hyperbolōn*</note>. In the history of the New Testament, it is recorded regarding the listeners of our Lord both that they *sat* and that they *stood*.

<margin>Chapter 13, 2.</margin>
You have an example of standing in the Gospel of *Matthew*, in these words: **On that day Jesus went out of the house and SAT BY THE SEA, and a great crowd gathered to him, so that he got into a boat and sat; AND THE WHOLE crowd STOOD on the shore.** <note>original: *ὥστε αὐτὸν εἰς τὸ πλοῖον ἐμβάντα καθῆσθαι· καὶ πᾶς ὁ ὄχλος ἐπὶ τὸν αἰγιαλὸν εἱστήκει*</note>. The same is found in *Mark*.

<margin>Chapter 4, 1.</margin>
No other example of standing is brought forward from the writings of the New Testament as far as I know. But who does not see that this case is entirely unique? For since Christ was sitting in a boat—a place certainly not very elevated—it could hardly have happened that the listeners, who occupied the nearby shore, could have understood his words unless they received them standing on their feet. Otherwise, it seems established from the whole of Scripture that the disciples sat on lower benches, or lay down on mats at the feet of the Teachers, who sat in a higher chair.

<margin>Chapter 3, 32.</margin>
The clearest testimony of this is in *Mark*, who narratively relates that Christ taught a *sitting crowd*. **And they sat**, so the text of *Mark* has it, **a crowd around him, And THE CROWD SAT AROUND HIM.** <note>original: *Καὶ ἐκάθητο... ὄχλος περὶ αὐτὸν*</note>. And yet this certainly happened before the death of Gamaliel <note>The author is pointing out a chronological contradiction in the Jewish tradition</note>; nor is it likely that the listeners of Christ the Lord showed less reverence to their Teacher than was customary at that time.

<margin>Luke 2, 46.</margin>
Nor do I doubt that this same custom of disciples sitting can be clearly proven from the SITTING OF CHRIST **in the midst of the doctors, in the midst of the Teachers, hearing them and asking them questions.** <note>original: *ἐν μέσῳ τῶν διδασκάλων... ἀκούοντος αὐτῶν καὶ ἐπερωτῶντος αὐτοὺς*</note>. # ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS BOOK I. PART I. #

There are some men who believe that Christ the Lord appeared in this assembly of Teachers <note>or "Doctors"; original: *Doctorum*</note> not as a *disciple*, but as a *Teacher*. However, they do not gain my agreement. For although I would not wish to take away anything from the supreme progress made by Christ at such a tender age, I find it harder to believe that a twelve-year-old youth, unknown as it seems to the Teachers and appearing in the *School* by chance, would have been received by them as a Teacher. *To listen was the role of the Teacher, and to ask was the role of the disciple.* <note>In this context, the author refers to the formal structure of a lesson where the teacher listens to the student's inquiry to guide the instruction.</note> Christ indeed questioned the Teachers as a disciple, and *heard* their responses, examining and debating them as the occasion allowed—a practice permitted to any student of truth in the Jewish Schools. He sat, therefore, as a disciple, not as a *Teacher*. Nor am I easily persuaded that the Apostle Paul meant anything else when, in his defense before the people of Jerusalem, he says he was <margin>Acts 22, 3.</margin> *educated at the feet of Gamaliel* <note>original Greek: *ἀνατεθραμμένον παρὰ τοὺς πόδας Γαμαλιήλ*</note>. For what could you understand more simply by that phrasing than that the Apostle Paul sat at Gamaliel’s feet as a *disciple*?

The most learned <margin>Observations, book 3. chapter 2.</margin> *Petit* <note>Samuel Petit (1594–1643), a French scholar of ancient law and scripture.</note> certainly argues at length to the contrary; he thinks these words indicate only that Paul was *nourished* in Gamaliel’s house, and thus reclined at the same table at his feet. What shall I say? To me, the speech seems much clearer and simpler if I take it to mean his instruction. The most excellent <margin>In *Sotah*, chapter 9. p. 994.</margin> *Wagenseil* <note>Johann Christoph Wagenseil (1633–1705), a German Hebraist.</note>, who generally grants *Petit* the truth of this Talmudic tradition regarding the standing of disciples until the death of *Gamaliel*, instead judges that *this is a modest self-deprecation by Paul. He does not arrogantly boast that he was a companion and intimate of Gamaliel, sharing all things sacred and profane with him, but rather humbly and submissively professes that he sought his "food" [knowledge] while cast down at the feet of the great Teacher.*

Nevertheless, it is certain that *Petit* less successfully resolved another difficulty that might easily be raised against this view from a quite familiar phrase: *to cover oneself in the dust of the feet of the wise*. ...rather than to prostrate oneself on the very *ground* which the Teachers sprinkle with the dust of their feet; or to *sit* at the feet of the Teachers, who are positioned in a higher chair, and in this manner receive their sayings? This is much like what is declared concerning *Mary*: <note>original Greek: Παρακαθίσασα παρὰ τοὺς πόδας τοῦ Ἰησοῦ... ἤκουε τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ</note> Sitting AT THE FEET OF JESUS, she heard his word (Luke 10:39). What does *Petit* <note>Samuel Petit (1594–1643), a scholar of ancient law.</note> say regarding this phrase? He claims that the Hebrew term *hit’abaq* <note>Hebrew: התאבק, often interpreted as "to powder oneself with dust," but here Petit links it to "wrestling."</note> is equivalent in its meaning to *wrestling*. He suggests that by this metaphor it is indicated that *even in times of relaxation and play, nothing should be relaxed regarding the wisdom and Doctrine which they have acquired for themselves from constant association with the wise.* But *Petit* proves this significance of the word *abaq* <note>Hebrew: אבק, meaning "dust."</note> with no example. Furthermore, there is no reason in the words themselves to suggest this explanation. Indeed, what is more, by a quite crude and unpolished metaphor, the relaxation of labors would be compared with wrestling matches. The illustrious *Wagenseil* <note>Johann Christoph Wagenseil (1633–1705), a German Hebraist.</note> rather believes that *humility* is recommended to disciples by this expression. But that is not contrary to our opinion. It was an act of humility to *sit on the ground* before one’s Instructors and to adopt that posture for oneself while learning.

We therefore embrace with both arms the opinion of *Scaliger* <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a leading scholar of the Renaissance.</note>, who interprets this phrase as referring to disciples *prostrating themselves on the ground*, and he illustrates this from other sources as well. We have seen *Buxtorf* <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a famous scholar of Hebrew and the Talmud.</note> concede to these same views. If, however, you compare what he has learnedly gathered for the explanation of the phrase <note>Hebrew: מבין רגליו, *miben raglav*</note> "from between his feet," which forms part of the prophecy of the Patriarch *Jacob* concerning *Shiloh* <note>Genesis 49:10, a messianic prophecy.</note>, you will observe that so many passages of Scripture as he has cited cannot be conveniently satisfied if you suppose that disciples in ancient times *stood*. For even if you imagine the Teacher sitting in a Chair, if you conceive of the disciples *standing*, how could you say that the *Teacher* or *Lawgiver* <note>original: τὸν מחוקק (*mechoqeq*)</note> is "between the feet" of the disciples? How much more easily the whole matter is perceived if you establish that the disciples sat, or prostrated themselves on the ground, and that the Teachers had their chairs placed among their feet? Truly, as far as I am concerned, I believe that the Author of the *Commentary on the Epistle to the Corinthians*, who bears the name of *Ambrose* <note>This refers to "Ambrosiaster," an anonymous 4th-century commentator whose works were long attributed to St. Ambrose.</note>, hit the nail on the head <note>original: *rem tetigisse acu* — literally "touched the matter with a needle."</note> when he recorded these words:

Commentary on 1 Corinthians 14.
</margin>

> This is the tradition of the Synagogue: that they dispute while sitting, the elders of higher dignity in Chairs, those following on benches, and the newest on the floor upon mats.

What does *Petit* say regarding this phrase? He claims that the Hebrew term *to cover oneself with dust* <note>original: התאבק (ha’it’abek)</note> means the same in its significance as *to wrestle*. For *Maimonides* hands down the common and established law in his definitions, not caring much about what was done on this or that singular occasion against the common customs of the School. That it was indeed among the customs of the School for the <term>Interpreter</term> <gloss>Meturgeman</gloss> to be of lower rank than the explaining <term>Teacher</term> <gloss>Rav or Chacham</gloss>, and that he was not permitted to deviate from the Teacher’s opinions, may be clearly gathered from those things preached in the treatise *Sotah* regarding the rare gentleness of the famous Teachers *Rabbi Abba of Acre* and *Rabbi Abbahu*. ### CHAPTER 7. OR, ON THE ACADEMIES. ###

<margin>
**Masters of Shields**
<note>original Hebrew: בעלי תריסין (Ba'alei Terisin)</note>
The wise men who conquer one another in matters of Law <note>original Hebrew: חכמי המנצחים זה את זה בהלכה</note>. Wise men who, by disputing, strive to prove one another wrong.
</margin>

As the history in the *Jerusalem Gemara* <note>The Jerusalem Talmud, a collection of Rabbinic tradition and law compiled in the Land of Israel around the 4th century.</note> records, and as is related by *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and Hebraist known for his work on the Talmudic background of the New Testament.</note>, the illustrious *Wagenfeil* <note>Johann Christoph Wagenseil (1633–1705), a German Hebraist.</note> also drew it from the *Babylonian* version. Therefore, it will suffice to represent a summary of it in English. *Rabban Gamaliel II*, who served as the President of the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme rabbinic court and legislative body.</note> after the destruction of the Jewish State, did not get along very well with *Rabbi Joshua*, the son of *Hananiah*, who was called the "Father of the Court" <note>Av Beit Din, the second-highest ranking member of the Sanhedrin.</note> of that same Senate. This led Gamaliel to frequently abuse his authority against this very *Joshua*, who was next to him in dignity within the Senate. Among other incidents, it happened that a certain *disciple* (a man skilled in Jewish discipline, who at the end of this history in the Gemara is said to have been *Simeon, Son of Jochai*) raised a doubt to *Rabbi Joshua*: *Whether the evening prayers were a matter of free choice or of necessity?* <note>original Hebrew: תפלת ערבית רשות או חובה (Tefillat Arvit reshut o chovah?)</note>. *Rabbi Joshua* defined them as being of free choice. Not satisfied with this, the student went to *Gamaliel* and repeated the same question to him, to which *Gamaliel* replied: *the evening prayers are a matter of necessity*. When the student countered that *Rabbi Joshua* had answered to the contrary, *Gamaliel* ordered that he should raise this same dispute in the public School, in the presence of the sharp and practiced scholars. So it was done. The student stood up and asked *Gamaliel* in public: *Are the evening prayers performed by choice, or indeed by necessity?* *Gamaliel* persisted in his response, that they are *performed by necessity*; and, turning to his colleagues, he asked if any of the teachers present called this into doubt? *Rabbi Joshua* answered: no one disagrees. "But," said *Gamaliel*, "it has been reported to me that you disagree. Stand up on your feet, then, so that testimonies may be produced against you." *Rabbi Joshua* stood up, and, being convicted, he easily yielded. To this, *Gamaliel* began to recount this argument at great length, until the people—weary of *Rabbi Gamaliel's* severe domination over *Rabbi Joshua*—shouted

<margin>
**Huzpit**, the Interpreter, in the Kabbala of Rabbi Abraham among those of his age, page 59, column 2.
</margin>

to *Huzpit the Interpreter* <note>The Meturgeman, whose job was to repeat the Rabbi's whispered words loudly to the crowd.</note> to be silent, and they removed *Gamaliel* from the Presidency. After long deliberations, they substituted him with *Rabbi Eleazar*, a youth of eighteen (in the Jerusalem version: sixteen) years. He, in turn, soon gave permission to any disciples to enter the *Auditorium*, removing the *Doorkeeper* <note>original Hebrew: שומר הפתח (Shomer ha-Petach)</note>—is this the same, or another, as that *Rabbi Zenon the Cantor*, who is so named in the Jerusalem version? ...of the nation on benches <note>original Hebrew: ספסל (safsel)</note>, besides their number (as added in the *Jerusalem Talmud*) who stood behind the railings. It appears clearly from this history what form, what system, and what customs of disputing existed in the ancient Academies. If indeed you desire to know more regarding what order the *Interpreter* <note>The Meturgeman, an official who stood by the lecturer to translate or amplify the teaching for the audience.</note> should observe in responding to the questions proposed, you will find satisfaction in Maimonides' *Tractate on the Doctrine of the Law* <note>Referencing Maimonides' Hilkhot Talmud Torah.</note>. As for our current purpose, enough has been said of these things.

## CHAPTER VIII.

->*The principal parts of the Synagogue’s structure are recounted, and two of them, the Book-Ark and the Platform, are more distinctly described. Furthermore, the names of the Ark (Tevah, Heikhal, Aron) are set forth, along with its placement, origin, and use. Likewise, the various names of the Platform are first declared: Tower, Throne, Bimah, Pirgulah, Dukhan, Pergula, and Pulpit; then its form, placement, origin, and use are briefly discussed, illustrating Nehemiah 8:4.*<-

<margin>Gemara Megillah, chapter "The People of the City" <note>Hebrew: Benei Hair</note>, folio 73, column 4, near the end.</margin>
Next, we must pass to the description of Synagogues, strictly and properly so-called, and explain their parts, form, and the necessary requirements of structure which are determined in the Canons of Jewish law. Once these are completed, it will be convenient to add a few other things about their *Utensils*, and to declare certain surrounding circumstances which pertain here. We establish that there are four *major parts of the Synagogue* which concern our purpose—or the *sacred instruments of that ministry*, which are also called in the *Jerusalem Talmud* "the vessels of the house of assembly" <note>original Hebrew: כלי בית הכנסת (Klei Beit HaKnesset)</note>: 1. **THE ARK**, in which the Book of the Law is kept. 2. **THE PLATFORM**, from which the Divine Law is read before the people, chanted, or explained. 3. **THE BENCHES** of various order and use. 4. **THE LAMPS**, by which the Synagogues are illuminated.

I. By **THE ARK** of the *Synagogue* we understand the *box or chest in which the Book of the Law is placed*. It is called *Aron* <note>original Hebrew: ארון</note>, "Ark," in the statutes of this nation:

*They do not build the door of a Synagogue except opposite the side toward which they pour forth prayers in that city. <margin>Shulchan Aruch, Title 153, § 2.</margin>

*The inhabitants of a city who sell a Synagogue shall be able, with its price, to provide for themselves a* <term>Tevah</term> <note>A chest or ark</note>, *which is the Ark in which they store the book of the law, or a table upon which they place the Book of the Law.* <margin>Chapter 4, § 1. Regarding the Sanhedrin, book 3, chapter 16, § 1.</margin> In this place, it is explained parenthetically what is to be understood by *Tevah* in the text of the *Megillah* <note>A Talmudic tractate regarding the Scroll of Esther and synagogue practices</note>, the words of which are repeated in the earlier part of this Canon. <term>Tevah</term>, says *Rabbi Joseph Karo*, is the <term>Heikhal</term>, *that sacred shrine of the Synagogue* (thus elsewhere <margin>Notes on the Arba Turim, in this place.</margin> the word *Heikhal* was most elegantly translated by *Selden* <note>John Selden, a 17th-century English polymath and scholar of Jewish law</note>) in which the Book of the Law is stored. He adds, however, that this word also denotes the table upon which the Book of the Law is placed. Indeed, as he himself says elsewhere, the disciples of *Rabbi Jonah* are the sources for this meaning of the word *Tevah*, where it is taken for a table or a reading desk: *But the disciples of Rabbi Jonah say that the desk upon which they place the Book of the Law throughout the whole year is called a* <term>Tevah</term>. <note>original Hebrew: ופי' תלמידי הר' יונה...‏</note> On what foundation they have done this, however, I do not know. <margin>John 12:6. Drusius, book 2, Hebrew Questions, chapter 74.</margin> For certainly it cannot be denied that the more common use of the word *Tevah* is that it be taken for an *ark*, whence it is also compared by other Authors with the Greek <margin>Waser, On Ancient Hebrew Coins, book 1, chapter 19.</margin> *glossonkomon* <note>original Greek: γλωσσόκομον (glossokomon); originally a case for mouthpieces of flutes, later a money-box or casket</note>, <note>In the Megillah it is written as דלוסקמי (deluskami)</note> which signifies an ark, a chest, or a money-purse. <margin>Megilla, folio 36, column 2, after the middle.</margin> Nor do I think, where mention is made of a Synagogue in the writings of the Jews, that it is ever more suitably explained than as a *Book-Ark*. And I greatly approve that *Constantine l'Empereur* <note>A 17th-century Dutch Hebraist</note> thus interpreted this word in the writings of *Benjamin* <margin>In the Itinerary, p. 78.</margin> while occupied in describing the Synagogue of Ezekiel. The words of Benjamin are: *And in the courtyard of the Synagogue is the Ark...* <note>original Hebrew: ובחצר הכנסת התיבה</note>

Other common names already reviewed are **Aron**, **Tevah**, **Heikhal**, and **Argaz** <note>original: ארון (Ark/Closet), תיבה (Box), היכל (Palace/Sanctuary), and ארגז (Chest).</note>, of which the first two directly express the *Book-Ark* itself, while the latter more generally denotes that entire *sacred shrine*, often large and grand (as you may see in the *Portuguese Synagogue of Amsterdam*), which was built for the sake of this *Repository*. *Tertullian* <note>An early Christian author (c. 155–220 AD).</note> called this sacred instrument of the Synagogue an **Armarium** <note>A cupboard or closet.</note>. His words are: <margin>On the Dress of Women, chapter 2, near the end.</margin> *I know that the Scripture of Enoch, which assigned this order to the angels, is not received by some, because it is not admitted into the* **Jewish Armarium**. I believe he is correct. For to Latin writers, *Armarium* denotes a *place* in which books are stored. I learned this from *Lotichius* <note>Johann Peter Lotichius (1598–1669), a German physician and scholar.</note>, whose words on *Petronius* are these: *An Armarium is a place where books are kept; just as an* <margin>Page 213.</margin> *Armamentarium is a place for weapons.* He further employs the authority of *Perrottus* <note>Niccolò Perotti (1429–1480), an Italian Renaissance humanist.</note>, whose words serve us excellently: *In addition, he says, Armaria are inserted into the walls of houses, and Armamentaria no less usefully than elegantly. Armaria are properly those things in which books are stored.* For certainly those Synagogal *Repositories* are also commonly built into the very walls of the synagogues. Nor would you use the word *Arca* <note>Chest or Ark.</note> here inappropriately; for by this word *Livy* <note>Titus Livius, a Roman historian (59 BC–17 AD).</note> <margin>History, Book 40, Chapter 29.</margin> designated that compartment in which the *Books of Numa Pompilius* were stored and preserved. Elsewhere, *Epiphanius* <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 315–403), a Church Father.</note> mentions the Jewish *gazophylakia* <note>Greek: γαζοφυλακίων; treasuries or storehouses.</note>, in which, besides other books, those *Acts of the Apostles* written by Luke were preserved in his time. His words: "And some have said that the Gospel of John and the Acts of the Apostles were translated from the Greek tongue into Hebrew and are kept in the <margin>Heresies, Book 1, vol. 2, p. 127. Heresy 30.</margin> treasuries of the Jews, I mean those in Tiberias, and are stored among the hidden books," as some of those who believed from among the Jews...

# CHAPTER 8. OF SYNAGOGUES.

<margin>In the place cited.</margin>
And Raba said here: The word **Argaz** <note>original Hebrew: ארגז; a chest or box</note> is explained by Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi, the celebrated 11th-century French rabbi and commentator.</note>. The words of the Tractate Megillah are: **The wrappers of the Pentateuchs and the cases of the Books are ritual objects and must be hidden away.** <note>original: זכילי דחומשי וקמטרי דספרי תשמיש קדושה נינהו וגניזון; from the Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 26b. "Hidden away" refers to the practice of *Genizah*, where worn sacred texts are stored rather than destroyed.</note> And Raba said: *The wrappers of the five books of Moses and the small chests of the sacred Books are to be considered as holy instruments and therefore must be stored away.* Rabbi Solomon, in his explanation of the word **Kamtar** <note>original: קמטר</note>, says: **By 'Kamtar' you should understand a Chest, which they call an 'escrain' <note>original: אשקרי' ניין; an Old French word for a cabinet or casket.</note> and a 'tebah'.** By this term, you should understand a cabinet, which they call a *scrinium* <note>a Roman term for a cylindrical box used for holding scrolls.</note> (for so, if I am not mistaken, this foreign word should be rendered), a meaning that is frequent in the *Targum of Jonathan* <note>An Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, the son of Uziel. But, as I have said, **Argaz** and **Kamtar** can be used here for any *case* in which the Book of the Law is stored in the Synagogue. Other familiar names, already listed, are **Tevah**, **Aron**, and **Heikhal** <note>original: תיבה (Chest), ארון (Ark), היכל (Palace/Shrine).</note>. The first two of these terms directly describe the Book-Chest itself, while the last one more generally denotes that entire *sacred shrine*, often large and majestic—as you may see in the Portuguese Synagogue of Amsterdam—which was built for the sake of this repository. Tertullian <note>An early Christian author (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) from Carthage.</note> called this sacred instrument of the Synagogue a **CABINET**. His words are:

<margin>On Female Fashion, chapter 2, near the end.</margin>
> *I know that the Scripture of Enoch, which assigned this order to the angels, **is not received by some, because it is not admitted into the** **JEWISH CABINET**. <note>original Latin: ARMARIUM JUDAICUM</note>*

Rightly so, in my opinion. For to Latin writers, a *Cabinet* <note>Armarium</note> signifies a place in which books are stored. I learned this from *Lotichius* <note>Johann Peter Lotichius, a 17th-century physician and scholar.</note>, whose words regarding the author *Petronius* are these:

<margin>Page 213.</margin>
> *A 'Cabinet' is a place where books are stored; just as an 'Armory' <note>Armamentarium</note> is where arms are kept.*

He further employs the authority of *Perrottus* <note>Niccolò Perotti, a 15th-century humanist scholar.</note>, whose words serve us excellently:

> *Furthermore, he says, Cabinets are built into the walls of houses, and Armories no less usefully than elegantly. Cabinets are properly those things in which books are stored.*

Certainly, those Synagogal repositories are also commonly enclosed within the very walls of the synagogues. Nor would you inappropriately use the word *Chest* <note>Arca</note> here; indeed, it was with this word that *Livy* <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian.</note> designated that compartment in which the Books of *Numa Pompilius* <note>The legendary second king of Rome.</note> were stored and preserved.

<margin>History, book 40, chapter 29.</margin>
*Epiphanius* <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Salamis known for his works against heresies.</note> elsewhere mentions the Jewish *gazophylakia* <note>Greek for treasuries or storehouses.</note>, in which, among others, those books of the *Acts of the Apostles* written by Luke were preserved in his time. His words:

<margin>Against Heresies, book 1, vol. 2, p. 127. Heresy 30.</margin>
> *Indeed, some have said again that the Gospel according to John, translated from the Greek dialect into Hebrew, is contained in the treasuries of the Jews—I mean those in Tiberias—and is stored among the secret books, as some of those who believed from among the Jews [testify]...*

<note>original Greek: ὑφηγήσαντο ἡμῖν κατὰ λεπτότητα...; followed by Latin: Atque rursus ab aliis relatum...</note> They have described this to us in detail. Furthermore, it is reported by others that the Gospel of John also, translated from the Greek language into Hebrew, was brought into the Jewish treasuries—specifically those in Tiberias <note>A city on the Sea of Galilee that was a major center of Jewish scholarship in the early centuries AD.</note>—and was laid up there in secret, as certain individuals who converted from the Jewish nation to Christ have accurately told us. But anyone who compares the following words of Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Salamis known for his writings against heresies.</note>, and what he later says concerning the treasury of Hillel the deceased Patriarch <note>Hillel II, a 4th-century leader of the Jewish community in Roman Palestine.</note>, will see that *Epiphanius is speaking about the private storehouses of learned men,* not about the *Arks* of the Synagogue, which are our current subject.

But truly, *Chrysostom* <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> makes express mention of those arks in his Orations against the Jews, in the third section. Allow me to excerpt certain parts: *Do not tell me (in defense of the Synagogues) that the Law and the books of the Prophets are stored there. That is not enough to make a place holy.* Again: *In short, if you think the place is holy because the Law and the books of the Prophets are kept there...* But, what is especially worthy of observation is that *Chrysostom* gives that same name to that Synagogal <term>theca</term> <note>a case or container</note>, calling it a <term>kibotos</term> <note>original Greek: κιβωτός; meaning an Ark or Chest</note>, or an **Aron** <note>original Hebrew: ארון</note>, the name by which Jews even today designate it. Perhaps he read <term>chrisma</term>, but incorrectly) *no tablets of the covenant, no Holy of Holies... nor the other things which once made that Ark venerable. To me, this Ark which the Jews have now seems no better than the chests sold in the marketplace; indeed, it is in much worse condition.*

### CHAPTER 8. OF SYNAGOGUES.

...if it is built to the east of the land of Canaan <note>The biblical Land of Israel.</note>, its *ark* <note>The *Aron Kodesh*, the chest where the Torah scrolls are kept.</note> should be placed on the side that faces the West; if, on the other hand, a Sacred Oratory <note>A synagogue or house of prayer.</note> is built in the West, as is frequently the case in these regions, it is necessary that the chest for the sacred books be placed on the eastern wall, with the door directly opposite it to the west. ### ON THE STRUCTURE, BOOK I. PART I.

<meta>catchword: gracious</meta>
<meta>vocabulary: propitiatory (ἱλαστήριον), mercy seat (כפרת), atonement (ἱλασμὸς), redemption (ἀπολύτρωσις), propitiatory (propitiatorium), throne of grace (thronus gratiæ)</meta>

...a propitiation <note>original Greek: ἱλαστήριον (*hilastērion*), referring to the "mercy seat" or the place where atonement is made.</note> through faith in his blood, for the demonstration of his righteousness; *Whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood.* The <term>mercy seat</term> <note>original Hebrew: כפרת (*kapporet*), the golden lid of the Ark of the Covenant.</note>, or <term>propitiatory</term> <note>original Greek: ἱλαστήριον (*hilastērion*).</note>, a *covering*, was under the Old Testament behind a certain most precious veil, because the <term>ransom</term> <note>original Greek: λύτρον (*lytron*), the price paid for release.</note> had not yet been brought, through which <term>atonement</term> <note>original Greek: ἱλασμὸς (*hilasmos*).</note> and <term>redemption</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπολύτρωσις (*apolutrōsis*).</note> were to be made. But under the New Testament, the veil having been torn—that is, according to the Apostle, the flesh of Christ broken on the cross—that entire ark, and the <term>propitiatory</term> ark, and all things that were in that most holy place, *were publicly exposed to the eyes of all.* A passage from the Revelation of John is entirely to be compared:

<margin>Chapter 11, 19.</margin>
And the temple of God was opened in heaven, and the ark of his covenant was seen in his temple. *Then the Temple of God in heaven was opened, AND THE ARK OF HIS COVENANT WAS SEEN IN HIS TEMPLE.* John also, intending the same thing, called Christ the <term>atonement</term> <note>original Greek: ἱλασμὸς (*hilasmos*); see 1 John 2:2.</note>; and he is the atonement for our sins, *He himself was made, he himself is the atonement and the propitiatory.* 

<margin>Epistle [1 John] 2, 2.</margin>
Upon him God dwells, just as formerly he dwelt above the mercy seat. In him God is reconciled with the sinner, as formerly in the propitiatory. In respect to him and through him, it is fitting for God to speak with the sinner, just as formerly from above the mercy seat God announced the way of salvation. In him it is fitting for God to hear the sinner, just as formerly he heard those praying at the Propitiatory. Since this is so, it is also not fitting at this time to address God with prayers, or to ask anything from God, except by looking toward this <term>propitiatory</term>, in which God has uniquely fixed his gracious Throne. This the ancient Israelites did, as we have understood, and it is fitting for us to do the same under the New Testament, signified by those Cherubim who were looking intently toward this propitiatory. 

<margin>Epistle [1 John] 2, 1. 2.</margin>
Saint John seems to refer to this here with these well-known words: *But if anyone should sin, we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the Just, and he is the atonement for our sins, who is the propitiation for our sins.* That is, if anyone has fallen into sins, let him know that God has erected a certain <term>propitiatory</term>, at which and in which it is permitted to ask him for forgiveness.

<margin>Chapter 4, 16.</margin>
We believe Paul intended the same in his Epistle to the Hebrews: Let us therefore come with boldness to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace for timely help; *Let us approach therefore with confidence the throne of grace.* The throne of grace under the Old Testament was above the propitiatory <note>The golden lid of the Ark.</note>; under the New Testament it is with Christ, who was made the <term>propitiatory</term>, and without whom it is not fitting for God to [show] himself gracious...

### CHAPTER 8. OF THE SYNAGOGUES

<header>CHAPTER 8. OF THE SYNAGOGUES.</header>

...to present. These things [I say] in passing <note>original Greek: ἐν παρόדῳ (*en parodō*)</note>, because of the importance of the subject matter. Let us take up our thread again: the following sections are also of the same character:

<margin>§. 2.</margin>
If anyone prays toward one of the other directions, let him turn his face toward the Land of Israel if he is outside the land; toward Jerusalem if he is in the Land of Israel; and toward the Sanctuary if he is in Jerusalem. <note>This is the author's translation of the quoted Hebrew text from the Rabbinic tradition.</note>

<margin>§. 3.</margin>
One who cannot determine the directions should direct his heart to his Father who is in heaven. In the same way, Christ the Lord—since He did not wish the faithful of the New Testament to look toward any specific direction of the sky in their prayers—taught them to say at the beginning of their prayer: *Our Father who art in heaven* <note>original Hebrew: אבינו שבשמים (*Avinu she-ba-shamayim*); original Greek: Πατὴρ ἡμῶν ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς (*Patēr hēmōn ho en tois ouranois*)</note>. Indeed, following these precepts, the entire Synagogue today prays toward the *Ark*, which, outside the land of Israel, always looks toward it [the Holy Land].

Truly, there is no doubt that this *Arca* <note>The Ark or Cabinet where Torah scrolls are kept, known as the *Aron Kodesh*.</note> of the Synagogues was constructed in imitation <note>original Greek: μίμησιν (*mimēsin*)</note> of that most sacred ancient one, which was crafted by the skilled <term>Bezalel</term> <note>The artisan chosen by God to build the Tabernacle (Exodus 31).</note> by God's command, and placed first in the Most Holy place of the Tabernacle, and later in the Temple. This is clear since Jews usually take care to make the Synagogue as similar to the Temple as possible. Furthermore, they designate this *Ark* of their Synagogue by the same names, *Aron* <note>original Hebrew: ארון (*Aron*), meaning chest or ark.</note> and *Heikhal* <note>original Hebrew: היכל (*Heikhal*), meaning palace or sanctuary.</note>, which are perfectly suited to renew the memory of the Temple and the *Ark of the Covenant*. This also seems to be confirmed by the argument that, as noted before, those entering the Synagogue are accustomed to bow toward this *ark*, as if it held the most present Divinity, just as the ancient Ark once did. And certainly, the *ark of the Ancient Temple* was properly a *chest* for the Holy Books, and thus was of the same use as this Synagogal *Cabinet*. The Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>, the summary of all the Precepts according to which the celebrated Republic of the Israelites was formed and governed, was enclosed in this *chest*. The other books, which contained the fuller interpretation of the divine will, were placed <margin>Deuteronomy 31:26</margin> *at the side of this Ark* <note>original Hebrew: מצד (*mi-tzad*)</note>. Whether there was another specific repository for the sacred Books in the Temple is unknown to me. <term>Maimonides</term> <note>A 12th-century philosopher and one of the most prolific and influential Torah scholars of the Middle Ages.</note> indeed speaks of the *Book of the Temple Court* <note>original Hebrew: ספר העזרה (*Sefer ha-Azarah*)</note>, a most corrected version, which <margin>Laws of Tefillin, etc. chapter 7, § 2; On the Right of the King chapter 2, § 5.</margin> <term>Schickard</term> <note>Wilhelm Schickard (1592–1635), a German polymath and scholar of Hebrew law.</note> calls the most sacred and original volume, preserved by the Levites: "And the king is commanded to write another scroll of the Law for himself and place it..."

Following this example, the Volumes of the Mosaic Law, along with their appendages and ornaments (which we shall discuss later), are stored in the *Cabinets* of the Synagogue. ...should ascend, he who is to read the Divine Law, or who is to deliver a sermon to the people, so that his words may be heard by all. When they set up the Ark, in which the Book of the Law is usually kept, they place it in the middle, so that the back of that Ark is toward the Temple <note>The author is discussing the orientation toward Jerusalem</note>, while the front is toward the people. The latter words of this text might perhaps present some difficulty, because the word <term>Heichal</term> <note>original Hebrew: היכל, literally "Palace" or "Sanctuary"</note> in this text of Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a famous Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note> seems to have an ambiguous meaning.

<margin>§. 2.</margin>
For in the preceding paragraph, he had used the word <term>Heichal</term> <note>original: היכל</note> to mean the sanctuary or cabinet of the synagogue, with these words: <term>And they build in it a sanctuary in which they place the Book of the Law, etc.</term> <note>original Hebrew: ובונין בו היכל שמניחין בו ספר תורה וכו'</note> But by <term>Heichal</term> in this later text, it seems that the Temple of Jerusalem must be understood entirely, toward which direction the back of the library-Ark ought to be aligned, so that its front would face the people, as will be observed in the following paragraph, to be cited hereafter.

<margin>§. 4.</margin>
Unless perhaps Maimonides understands by <term>Tevah</term> <note>original Hebrew: תיבה, usually meaning a box or chest</note> a certain mobile Ark separate from the sacred sanctuary, which is placed between the <term>Heichal</term> and the <term>Bimah</term> <note>The raised platform for reading the Torah</note>, and before which the Minister of the Synagogue stands to pour out prayers. I do not deny, reader, that the passage is somewhat obscure to me. However, I think no one doubts that the Hebrew word <term>Bimah</term> <note>original: בימה</note>, which Maimonides uses, is the same as the Greek <term>bēma</term> <note>original: βῆμα, a step or raised platform</note>, derived from the verb <term>bainō</term> <note>original Greek: βαίνω, "to step"</note>. Cohen de Lara <note>David Cohen de Lara, a 17th-century scholar and lexicographer</note> says: <term>Bimah means the seat of judgment where the judge sits.</term> <note>original Hebrew: בימה פי' כסא המשפט ששם ישב השופט</note> A <term>Bēma</term> is the seat of judgment occupied by a Judge.

<margin>
In Ir. David p. 25.
Romans 14:10.
2 Corinthians 5:10.
Laertius in *Life of Solon*, book 1, page 37.
</margin>
Thus <term>bēma</term> is frequently understood by various authors, even the Sacred ones <note>The author cites the New Testament letters to the Romans and Corinthians where "the judgment seat" is mentioned</note>. Among the laws of Solon <note>Solon was an ancient Athenian lawmaker</note> was this: <term>To bar from the platform (bēma) anyone who was notorious for wickedness and disgrace.</term> <note>original Greek: Τὸν ἡταιρηκότα εἴργειν τοῦ βήματος</note> Indeed, it should be observed that the word <term>Bamah</term> <note>original Hebrew: במה</note>, though written with the same letters, pronounced in almost the same way, and having nearly the same meaning among the Hebrews (for it denotes a "high place," whether a Temple or an altar), has nevertheless contributed nothing to the origin of the word <term>Bimah</term> <note>original: בימה</note> which Maimonides used here. This is despite the fact that I have no doubt that the Greek <term>bōmos</term> <note>original Greek: βωμὸς, meaning altar or platform</note>—which is used for an "altar," but also for a "Temple" by authors, and is likewise derived by Eustathius <note>A 12th-century Greek scholar and bishop</note> from <term>bainō</term>—descends directly from this very Hebrew word <term>Bamah</term>.

It is clear from this testimony that by "tower" and "throne," sacred instruments of the same use are denoted, except that the former is the ordinary one and the latter is used for extraordinary occasions. Indeed, Maimonides employs three terms to describe the platforms of the Synagogues: *bimah*, *migdal*, and *kisse*. Of these, the first denotes the lowest part of the platform, which is raised from the ground and where one stands, while these latter denote the pulpit, placed as if on top of that platform, in which the Scroll of the Law, to be read in the Synagogue, is placed. It is worth knowing that these words of Maimonides are drawn from the Gemara of *Megillah* in both the Babylonian and Jerusalem Codes. After I reflected on the fact that the *Book of the Law* <note>original: *Librum Legis*</note> is sometimes placed upon it (without a cloth <note>original Hebrew: *b'lo mappah*</note>, as Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, also known as Rashi, a premier medieval commentator</note> says), I have determined that this pulpit must also be counted among the sacred instruments, and that it is forbidden to sell or dispose of it indiscriminately. Rabbi Solomon explains the word *throne* <note>original Aramaic: *kursaya*</note>, which is called *chair* <note>original Hebrew: *kisse*</note> in the text of **Maimonides**, as a **Wooden Platform** <note>original Hebrew: *bimah shel etz*</note>. This should be understood in a more general sense, as he means this very **Chair** <note>original: *Cathedra*</note> in which the Scroll of the Divine Law is placed in the Synagogue; this is the upper part of the platform. For the lower part, which is strictly called the **platform** <note>original: *bimah*</note>, is not counted among the sacred instruments, even though it shares in that common holiness which belongs to the entire Synagogue building; as noted in the Jerusalem Talmud, and repeated from there by Maimonides' critic, Rabbi Abraham <note>Rabbi Abraham ben David, known as the Ra’avad, who wrote famous "Animadversions" or critiques of Maimonides' work</note>.

<margin>
Place cited.
Animadversions on the Laws of Phylacteries, etc. chapter 10. §. 4.

Chain of Tradition, page 101.
On Plautus’s *Pseudolus*. Act 1. Scene 2. line 79.
