I have used the word *Pulpit* more than once, although this term is also of broad meaning and denotes any raised place from which the ancients were accustomed to declaim. A Pulpit, says a learned man, *is the place in which authors recited*; called a *speaking place* <note>original Greek: *logeion*</note> by the Greeks. Ancient Glosses state: *Pulpit*, an *altar-step* <note>original Greek: *thymele*</note>, a *level boarding* <note>original Greek: *sanidama epipedon*</note>. Rabbi Gedaliah calls it a *pergula* <note>a gallery or balcony</note>: *The ancients say that Ezra was the first who began to preach from a pergula, which means a high place.* The Chronicles report that *Ezra was the first of those who began to interpret the law from a pergula, that is, an elevated place*. However, what a *pergula* actually is, is not agreed upon by learned men. **Scaliger** <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a famous Renaissance scholar</note> says they were *appendages of buildings that looked out into the public space*. He continues: *And because of this, craftsmen and teachers who were less known used to first display their work or teach in them, so that they might become known to the people*. **Juvenal** <note>A Roman satirist</note> says:

> But there shall be no builder to whom every 
> *Pergula* <note>here referring to a school or gallery</note> must yield.

But **Salmasius** <note>Claude Salmasius, a renowned 17th-century classical scholar</note> disagrees, and contends that all public rooms in which professors of all arts and doctrines spoke publicly were called *pergulas*. This matter is not so important to us that we should waste our efforts <note>literally "consume oil," referring to the oil in a scholar's lamp</note> in examining it more diligently. For us, a *pergula* is a *projection* <note>original Greek: *probolē*</note>, any structure somewhat higher and projecting, from which speeches and declamations are conveniently recited. The Talmudists are accustomed to call the platform of the Priests' Court, in which the Levites stood accompanying the sacrifices with sacred songs, the **platform** <note>original Hebrew: *duchan*</note>. This platform, according to the description of the Talmudists, was one hundred and thirty-five cubits long, built to the east of the Priests' Court (strictly so called), on the floor...

several *Teachers* were accommodated at once. In this way, it seems to me entirely necessary to understand what follows in the text: *“And there stood upon the platform of the Levites Jeshua & Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Binnai, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani, and they cried out with a loud voice to the Lord, their God.”* I believe they all stood together, yet in such a way that only one prayed at any given time, with the others standing by him and also praying to God in their own turn. I see, however, that this interpretation greatly displeases the Dutch Translators <note>original: "Belgis Interpretibus," referring to the translators of the Dutch Authorized Version or Statenvertaling</note>. I, for my part, readily concede that those who stood on this chair did not speak to the common people all at once—as that would hardly suit the preservation of order in the Assembly—yet I see no absurdity in several Teachers standing together on one platform, who each in their own place and time spoke either to God or to the people. Indeed, I believe that the present text teaches this most clearly, and the rites of the Ancient Hebrews confirm the same.

<margin>Chapter 8:1.</margin>
To say, however, that several platforms were erected here and the people were divided into many groups is something that, in my opinion, contradicts the historical text. For it is clear from the text that the whole people were gathered into one place, forming only one <term>Qahal</term> <note>original Hebrew: קהל; a congregation or assembly</note> or <term>Ekklesia</term> <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησίαν; an assembly</note>, and only one <term>wooden platform</term> <note>original Hebrew: מגדל עץ (migdal etz), literally a 'wooden tower' or pulpit</note> was erected. We cannot conceive how it could have happened without significant <term>confusion</term> <note>original Greek: συγχύσει (synchysei)</note> for the people, gathered in one place, to be divided into distinct parts and listen to different Teachers simultaneously.

<margin>Nehemiah 8:4.</margin>
Our opinion is further confirmed by the fact that the narrative itself expressly states, *“Ezra stood on a wooden platform, and there stood beside him”* <gloss>original Hebrew: ויעמוד אצלו (va-ya'amod etzlo)</gloss> *“Mattithiah & Shema, & Anaiah,”* and the other Levites and experts in the Law. What then? Do you think Ezra alone stood in an elevated place, while the others stood lower down? Certainly not; rather, they stood at Ezra's side on the same platform for the same purpose, each in his own place and order, just as is clearly stated here. I will say briefly, therefore, how I have conceived it in my mind, and how the events narrated in this place should be understood according to Hebrew customs. In my judgment, a wide *wooden platform* was constructed, on which several Teachers stood together. Once the assembly had gathered, Ezra brought out the book of the Law, and after the blessings were performed, he read a portion of it before the entire assembly of the people in a clear voice, so that everyone understood the reading. <header>OF THE STRUCTURE BOOK I. PART I.</header>

*...did not interpret what had been read, or illustrate it with a longer commentary.* For as much as can be gathered from this historical account, the one who stood in the middle of the platform read, while those who stood at his side interpreted what was read, so that each person read and commented in his own place. In this way, not even Ezra himself, when he read, explained the portion he had pre-selected; rather, the other Teachers and <term>Scribes</term> <note>original Greek: γραμματεῖς (*grammateis*)</note>, who were standing nearest to his side, did so. We seem to be able to conclude this from the fact that Ezra is said to have read, while the Levites *made the people understand the Law and attend to it, so that they might understand it* <note>original Hebrew: מבינין את העם לתורה (*mebinim et ha-am la-torah*)</note>. For such is the force of that phrase. Thus, there was one who read *distinctly and clearly* <note>original Hebrew: מפורש (*meforash*)</note>, another who *gave the sense to what was read* <note>original Hebrew: שום שכל (*sum sekel*)</note>, and yet another who heard what was read and understood it—three things which are specifically affirmed regarding the Persons of that Church. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, also known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval commentator</note>, who is quite skilled in ancient customs, explains that word "understanding" which is said here of the Levites in this way: *that they were translating the words of the Law for the people* <note>original Hebrew: שהיו מתרגמן לעם דברי תורה</note>. Indeed, in the Ancient Church, the Interpreter was a different person from the Reader. And let these things now suffice regarding the Platforms of the Synagogues.

Thus, the faces of all the people are toward the Sanctuary, toward the Elders, and toward the Book-Chest.* <note>original Hebrew: כיצד העם יושבים בבתי כנסיות הזקנים ויושבים ופניהן כלפי העם ואחוריהם כלפי ההיכל וכל העם יושבים שורה לפני שורה ופני של שורה לאחורי השורה שלפני עד שיהיו פני כל העם כלפי הקדש וכלפי הזקן וכלפי התיבה</note> We see the whole arrangement of the benches and the distinction between those which the Elders occupied and those which the rest of the common people occupied. However, in the two Amsterdam synagogues—the only ones I have seen—this precept of Maimonides is by no means observed. In the synagogue of the Portuguese, the *seats of the Elders* are placed at the northern side of the synagogue; but the *Chair* of the Leader of the Synagogue is joined to the *platform* <note>original Latin: *suggestui*; the elevated platform or Bimah used for reading</note> in such a way that while sitting, he turns his back to the platform, but his face toward the *Ark*. In the *Prayer-house* <note>original Latin: *Proseucha*, from the Greek for a house of prayer</note> of the Germans, if I remember correctly, five seats of the Elders are joined to the *Platform* in this same place and position; the other Elders sit near the *Ark*. The same difference can be observed in the *benches of the people*, which are not arranged in rows facing the *Ark*, but along the transverse sides of the synagogue.

The seats of the Elders, wherever they may be placed, are undoubtedly the *chief seats in the synagogues*, about which Christ speaks in Matthew: <margin>Chapter 23, verse 6.</margin> "*And they love*" (he says of the Pharisees) "*the chief seats in the synagogues.*" <note>original Greek: Φιλοῦσί τε ... τὰς πρωτοκαθεδρίας ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς</note> That is, they strongly pursue that honor so that they may occupy the first place in the synagogues. The word *chief seat* <note>original Greek: πρωτοκαθεדρία (*protokathedria*)</note> agrees, if I am not mistaken, in meaning with the word *front-row seat* <note>original Greek: προεδρία (*proedria*)</note>, which designates the honored seats of the *presidents* or judges of Athens in the theaters. As Aristophanes says: <margin>The Acharnians, Act 1, Scene 1.</margin>

# CHAPTER 9. ON SYNAGOGUES

...of which we shall speak below, *if the Lord wills* <note>original Greek: εἰ θέλει ὁ κύριος</note>) should enter wearing a gold ring and splendid clothing; and a poor man should also enter in filthy clothing, and you pay attention to the one wearing the splendid clothing and say to him: "You sit here in a good place"; but to the poor man you say: "You stand over there," or "sit here under my footstool." He adds: "Have you not made a distinction among yourselves, and become judges with evil thoughts?" It is clear from the context of these words that the Apostle James is speaking about the place where the first Christians were accustomed to gather. In this place, he assumes there were distinct benches, some more dignified and honorable than others: the *more dignified* were usually designated for the wealthy, who recommended themselves by the splendor of their clothing or the dignity of their office; while the less honorable places—whether standing room or seats—were assigned to the poor, who displayed no such outward decorum or brilliance. This was almost exactly the arrangement of the synagogues among the Jewish nation. James rebukes this practice because in Christian assemblies, there ought to be more and more certain evidence of *fraternity*—that is, unity, equality, and simplicity—than in the synagogues. 

Furthermore, Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE) was a Jewish philosopher who described Jewish life and customs in Egypt.</note> provides testimony regarding this variety and distinction of seating in the synagogue when he describes the "philosophers" or "monks" of his nation, and their institutions and customs:

<margin>*On the Contemplative Life, page 691.*</margin>
"On the seventh day," he says, "they come together as if to a common assembly, and they sit in order according to age in a proper posture, keeping their hands inside [their cloaks], the right hand between the chest and the chin, and the left hand drawn back against the side." <note>original Greek: Ταῖς δὲ ἑβδόμαις, συνέρχονται καθάπερ εἰς κοινὸν σύλλογον, καὶ καθ᾿ ἡλικίαν ἑξῆς καθίζονται μετὰ τοῦ πρέποντος σχήματος, εἴσω τὰς χεῖρας ἔχοντες, τὴν μὲν δεξιὰν μεταξὺ σέρνο καὶ γενεία. τὴν δὲ εὐώνυμον ὑπεσαλμένην παρὰ τῇ λαγόνι</note> This passage from Philo was noted elsewhere by Eusebius. <note>Eusebius was a 4th-century church historian who often cited Philo to show the antiquity of Christian-like asceticism.</note>

<margin>*On the Preparation for the Gospel, Book 8, Chapter 12.*</margin>

We refer to the fact that women in the synagogues occupied benches distinct from the men—a practice still observed today in Jewish houses of prayer <note>original Latin: *Oratoriis Judaicis*</note>, and which was never neglected in the ancient Temple for the weightiest of reasons. Regarding those matters pertaining to the Temple, I remember writing elsewhere; now I shall only touch upon those things that concern the synagogues. ### ON THE STRUCTURE [OF THE SYNAGOGUE] BOOK I. PART I.

...sharing the same zeal and the same purpose. But the wall between the houses is built up from the ground to three or four cubits high, in the manner of a breastwork. The upper part reaching to the roof is left open for two reasons: so that the modesty proper to the female nature is preserved, and so that they might easily understand while sitting within earshot, as nothing obstructs the voice of the speaker. <note>original Greek: τὸν αὐτὸν ζῆλον, καὶ τὴν αὐτὴν προαίρεσιν ἔχεσαι. ὁ δὲ μεταξὺ τῶν οἰκιῶν τοῖχος, τὸ μὲν ἐξ ἐδάφους ἐπὶ τρεῖς ἢ τέσσαρας πήχεις εἰς τὸ ἄνω συνῳκοδόμηται, θωρακειοῦ τρόπον. τὸ δὲ ἄχρι τέγους ἀνάγειον ἀχανὲς ἀνεῖται, δυοῖν ἕνεκα, τοῦ τε τὴν πρέπουσαν αἰδῶ τῇ γυναικείᾳ φύσει διατηρεῖσθαι, καὶ τοῦ τὴν ἀντίληψιν ἔχειν εὐμαρῆ καθεζομένας ἐν ἐπηκόῳ, ὡς μηδενὸς τὴν τοῦ διαλεγομένου φωνὴν ἐμποδίζοντος.</note>

*This shared* <term>semneion<gloss>original Greek: σεμνεῖον; a place of worship or "shrine" used by the Therapeutae, a Jewish sect described by Philo</gloss></term>, *or Sanctuary, in which they gather every seventh day, is enclosed by a double partition, separating the gatherings of Men and women. For the women also listen together according to custom, at least those who follow the same discipline. The middle wall rises from the floor by three or four cubits, in the manner of a small parapet, while the upper parts remain open to the roof. From this arises a twin benefit: both that the modesty of the female sex is respected, and that the words of the Teacher are heard easily without any obstacles to intercept his voice. Philo was the first to state for what uses this distinction of Benches for Men and women was introduced into Synagogues. For it was granted for the sake of propriety, to which not even the slightest occasion for harm should be offered in those places held sacred to God.*

4. Regarding the <term>Nerot<gloss>Hebrew: נרות; plural of 'ner', meaning lamps or candles</gloss></term>, or LIGHTS of the *Synagogue*, a word must be added. By these we mean the lamps, cast with greater or lesser craftsmanship, suspended in the Synagogues or fixed to its walls, or even the *candelabras* by which the synagogue buildings are illuminated where it is convenient. Their use is to be traced back, if I am not mistaken, to *necessity* and *custom* <note>The author uses the word "superstitione," which in this period's scholarly Latin often referred to religious rituals or traditional customs rather than "superstition" in the modern sense.</note>. By *necessity*, certainly, because in the evening <term>liturgy<gloss>original Greek: λειτουργία; a public service or religious rite</gloss></term> of the Sabbath and Festivals they cannot do without them at all. By *custom*, however, because they are used to honor *Sabbaths and festival days* by lighting lights, whether as a sign of *joy*, designated by *light*; or in honor of the *Law*, which is distinguished by the name of *Light* in the Scriptures; or following the example of the *Sanctuary*, which was formerly illuminated by lamps; or for whatever other reasons which *custom* easily finds. Furthermore, the precept concerning *Sabbath Lamps* pertains as much to private homes as to Synagogues. Regarding these kinds of Sabbath Lights of the Jews in private homes, the verses of Persius must be understood, which have not been equally well understood by everyone:

# CHAPTER 9. ON SYNAGOGUES.

> *A tuna’s tail swims in the dish, a tall jar swells with wine:*
> *You move your lips in silence, and turn pale at the circumcised Sabbaths.*
<note>These lines are from the Roman satirist Persius (Satire 5, 183–184). He is mocking Romans who adopted Jewish customs, describing a modest Sabbath meal and the solemn, quiet prayer of the observers. "Circumcised Sabbaths" was a common, though derogatory, Roman way of referring to Jewish holy days.</note>

<margin>Commentary on this passage. Various Readings, chapter 18.</margin>
Regarding the first words of the poem, it was observed by the <term>Old Interpreter<gloss>Referring to an ancient scholiast or commentator on the works of Persius</gloss></term> that the Jews, when celebrating the birthdays of **Herod** and observing their Sabbaths, were accustomed to *place lit lamps, crowned with violets, in the windows of their houses*. However, the commentator was undoubtedly mistaken in explaining these "days of Herod" as the actual birthdays of Herod being celebrated by the Jews, as *Petitus* correctly observed following the work of *Theodore Marcilius*. Indeed, by the "days of Herod," one may most conveniently understand the feast days observed with the highest religious devotion by every Jew; Persius calls them "days of Herod" because Herod Agrippa—who was very well known to the Romans—could conveniently be presented as a type and example of the entire Jewish nation.

But it is clear from Persius’s words that the Jews, and many of the Romans captivated by their rites, were already accustomed to that same practice which still clings to them: *to light the Sabbath lamps at sunset on Friday*, to recline at well-spread tables, to have cups full of wine nearby, and to recite their particular blessings over each item. This was the custom of the Jews; and many Romans imitated it, whom **Persius** mocks. Indeed, even **Seneca** <note>A famous Roman Stoic philosopher and advisor to Nero</note> in clear words, criticizing these superstitions and customs of men that are devoid of reason, says: <margin>Epistle 95, page 604.</margin> *“Let us forbid anyone from* LIGHTING A LAMP ON THE SABBATHS: *since the gods do not need light, and men certainly take no pleasure in the soot.”*

<margin>Talmudic Tractate Shabbat, chapter 2, sections 1, 2, 3, etc. Maimonides, Laws of the Sabbath, chapter 5, section 1 and following. Orach Chayim, Titles 261, 263, 264, 265, 275, and following. Kol Bo, chapter 31.</margin>
Indeed, concerning this ritual of lighting lamps in private homes, especially at the beginning of the Sabbath and other Festivals, many precepts are found in the statutes of the Hebrews, both in the *Talmudic* code and derived from it in the works of *Maimonides* and the Ritual Books. Thus begin the precepts of **Maimonides**: <note>original Hebrew: "הדלקת נר בשבת אינה רשות אם רצה מדליק ואם לא רצה אינו מדליק ואינו מצוה שאינו חייב לרדוף אחריה עד שיעשה כגון עירובי חצרות או נטילת ידים לאכילה אלא חובה ואחד אנשים ואחד נשים חייבין להיות בבתיהן נר דלוק בשבת אפילו אין לו מה יאכל שואל על הפתחים ולוקח שמן ומדליק את הנר שזה בכלל עונג שבת וחייב לברך קוד' הדלקה בא' אמה"א אק'בו להדליק נר של שבת שמברך על כל הדברים שהוא חייב בהם מדברי סופרים"</note> *“The lighting of the lamp on the Sabbath is not a matter of choice, such that if one wishes, he lights it, and if he does not wish, he does not; nor is it merely a voluntary commandment that one is not bound to pursue diligently—such as the merging of courtyards or the washing of hands before eating—but rather it is an obligation. Both men and women are obligated to have a lamp lit in their homes on the Sabbath. Even if a person has nothing to eat, he must beg at doorways to obtain oil and light the lamp, for this is included in the ‘delight of the Sabbath.’ One is obligated to recite a blessing before lighting: ‘Blessed [are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us] to light the Sabbath lamp,’ for one blesses all things that are obligatory by the words of the Scribes.”* *The lighting of the Sabbath lamp is not left to the discretion of the individual, so that if one wants, they light it, and if they don’t want, they don't; nor is it a commandment whose observation one is not bound to pursue diligently*

ON THE STRUCTURE BOOK I. PART I.

<margin>* Regarding these matters, see Isaiah chapter 58, 13; Orach Chajim Title 263, § 3; Tractate Shabbat chapter 2, § 6.</margin>
...to pursue; such as: the *Mixing of Courtyards* <note>original: "Mixtio Atriorum," referring to the <term>Eruv Chatzerot</term>, a legal ritual that allows Jews to carry items between private and semi-public spaces on the Sabbath</note>, or the *Washing of hands* before taking food; but it is entirely obligatory—and both men and women are bound to it—that a lamp be lit in their homes for the Sabbath. Indeed, even if a person has nothing to eat, they must beg from door to door to acquire oil for themselves and light the lamp, since this also belongs entirely to the *Sabbath delights* <note>original: "Sabbathi delicias," referring to the concept of <term>Oneg Shabbat</term>, the commandment to make the Sabbath a day of joy and physical comfort</note>. * Before lighting the lamp, however, one is bound to say the blessing: *Blessed are you, O Lord, our God, Ruler of the world, who has sanctified us with your commandments and commanded us to light the Sabbath lamp; just as one blesses over all things which one is bound to observe according to the rulings of the Scribes.* However, among the Hebrews, the custom has prevailed that this task is entrusted to women, <gloss>since they are usually at home and occupied with domestic needs</gloss>, since they are accustomed to being at home and tending to domestic business. From this comes that famous passage in the body of the Talmud: <gloss>On account of three sins women die at the time of childbirth: because they are not careful regarding menstrual separation, the dough offering, and the lighting of the lamp.</gloss> *Ob three sins do women die at the time of birth; because they are not cautious in menstrual separation, the offering of the dough <note>original: "placenta," referring to <term>Challah</term>, the portion of dough set aside for the priests</note>, and the lighting of the Sabbath lamp.*

<margin>Orach Chajim, same title, § 6.</margin>
But in truth, this duty also falls upon young men separately if they have their own chambers outside the home where they devote themselves to their studies: <gloss>Young men who go to study away from their home must light a Sabbath lamp in their chamber and bless over it; but one who is with his wife does not need to light in his chamber and bless over it, because his wife blesses on his behalf.</gloss> *Young men, who apply themselves to letters away from their homes, have a necessity to light a Sabbath lamp in their chamber and to bless over it. However, he who stays with his wife in the same house while devoting himself to the study of letters has no necessity to illuminate his chamber with the Sabbath light and bless over it, because his wife performs this work on his behalf.* Indeed, even on festival days, this custom must not be neglected. This is expressly advised in the *Annotations* which are attached to the text of Maimonides:

<margin>Bezah, or Yom Tov, chapter 3. Berakhot, chapter 9. See also Orach Chajim, Title 263, § 5, in the middle.</margin>
<gloss>And so likewise on a Festival they are accustomed to light a lamp; and thus it is found in the Jerusalem Talmud in the chapter "He who brings": One who lights a lamp on a Festival is required to bless "Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to light the lamp of the Festival." And in the Jerusalem Talmud chapter "He who sees," it says to light a lamp in honor of the Festival.</gloss> *And so similarly on a feast day they are accustomed to light a lamp: For so it is in the Jerusalem Talmud, in the chapter titled "He who brings"; He who lights a lamp on a feast day is bound to bless: "Who has sanctified us with your commands and commanded us to light the lamp." Likewise in the same Talmud, in the chapter marked "He who sees," we read that the lamp is to be lit in honor of the Feast day.*

### CHAPTER 9. OF SYNAGOGUES.

<margin>Josephus, Antiquities, book 12, chapter 11.</margin>
However, it must not be overlooked that this religious practice of lighting lamps took place especially during that *Festival* which, as Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus was a first-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> testifies, was for that reason called **Lights** <note>original Greek: **Φῶτα**; Latin: **Lumina**</note>. This festival fell on those eight days of the *Dedication* <note>original: *Encaenia*, a Greek term for "renewal" or "dedication," referring here to the festival of <term>Chanukah</term></note>, during which the Jews are accustomed to celebrate the memory of the Temple’s worship, which was restored by Judas Maccabeus after the madness of Antiochus Epiphanes <note>A Seleucid king who had desecrated the Jewish Temple, leading to the Maccabean Revolt</note>. Those *eight days*, I say, which are designated for celebrating the *Dedication* of the Temple, beginning from the twenty-fifth day of the Month of *Kislev* <note>original: *Casleu*, the ninth month of the Hebrew calendar</note>, are *days of joy and praise* <note>original Hebrew: ומדליקין בהם ימי שמחה והלל</note>, and *they light lamps in the evening at the doors of their houses, every night of those eight nights, so that the miracle may be recognized and made public.* <note>original Hebrew/Latin: הנרות בערב על פתחי הבתים בכל לילה ולילה משמנת הלילות להוראות ולגלות הנס</note> These are the words of <margin>Laws of the Menorah, chapter 3, § 2. Talmudic Tractate Sabbath, folio 21, column 2.</margin> *Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides, a preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note>, describing this festival in the *Laws of the Menorah* <note>original: *Hilchoth Menuca*</note>, taken from the Talmudic Code. However, the origin of this festival is without doubt to be sought not from some divine miracle involving the *multiplying of the oil* (which the Hebrew authors story-tell was performed at that time), nor perhaps even from the singular joy which the Jewish nation then indulged in due to the unexpected and sudden restoration of sacred and civil affairs (as *Josephus* would have it, though we do not entirely exclude that), but rather from the fact that the lampstands of the Temple were restored during those days and, being refilled with oil, illuminated the Temple with their light—which was surely a most brilliant sign of the restored religion and Temple worship. <margin>Chapter 4, verse 50.</margin> This is the view suggested by the text in the First Book of Maccabees <note>original: *Hasmoneorum Primo*</note>, which narrates this restoration of sacred worship: *And they burned incense upon the altar, and they lit the lamps that were upon the lampstand, and they gave light in the temple.* <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἐθυміяσαν ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον, καὶ ἐξῆψαν τοὺς λύχνους, τοὺς ἐπὶ τῆς λυχνίας, καὶ ἐφαίνοσαν ἐν τῷ ναῷ</note> <margin>Notes on the 1st Book of Maccabees.</margin> *Drusius* <note>Johannes Drusius, a 16th-century scholar of Biblical languages</note> rightly noted on this passage, as it seems to us: *they lit the lamps* <note>original Greek: ἐξῆψαν τοὺς λύχνους; Hebrew: וידליקו הנרות</note>: *And from here come the names used in Maccabees, **Lights** and the **Lighting of Lamps**.* <note>original Greek: **Φῶτα** and **λυχνοκαΐας**</note>. *Few words, but sound ones.* But if you wish to know more about this festival, consult *Selden* <note>John Selden, a prominent 17th-century English jurist and scholar of Jewish law</note>. <margin>On the Sanhedrin, book 3, chapter 13, § 9, 10.</margin>

Furthermore, while we are discussing the sacred lamps of private homes, we must not forget the *Lamps of the Synagogues*, about which we had begun our discourse. Indeed, these private lamps themselves lead us easily to the *public* ones. For it would not be fitting for the house of the Synagogue to lack sacred lights at the same time when the dining rooms of private individuals were illuminated by them. *Various utensils are reviewed, which pertain either to sacred worship or to the ornament of the synagogue. 1. Sacred books with their appendages. 2. Trumpets and horns. 3. Indeed, it is proper to understand these *Books of the Law* according to the customs of the Jewish people as *Scrolls* <note>Hebrew: מגלות (*megillot*)</note>, consisting of calf-skin parchments sewn together *lengthwise* to a span of several cubits. *Thus you learn from their words that every one of these things invalidates a Torah scroll; and if even one of these faults occurs in it, it is like a "Chumash" <note>A single book or a non-sacred copy of the Pentateuch</note> from the five-part volumes used for teaching children; it does not possess the sanctity of a Torah scroll, and they do not read from it in public.* 

*We have received the teaching that there are twenty things, any one of which renders the Book of the Law profane; if any of these occurs, it becomes like a fifth part of the Pentateuch (De Voisin <note>Jean de Voisin, a 17th-century French Hebraist and theologian</note> translates this as "It becomes as the Pentateuch," but this does not seem to be Maimonides' meaning. The word "Chumash" <term>Chumash: a Hebrew term meaning "fifth," usually referring to one of the five books of Moses or a printed copy, as opposed to a ritual scroll</term> does not denote the [entire] Pentateuch, but a fifth part of the Pentateuch, whose sanctity was far below the sanctity of the entire volume of the Law—that is, all five books of Moses contained in one continuous volume), from which boys are taught; it lacks the sanctity of a Book of the Law, nor do they read from it publicly.* 

Lest we seem to say nothing at all, we will briefly present the sum of these twenty conditions in English words only, referring the curious reader to the work of the aforementioned De Voisin, who translated and illustrated them. Therefore, <margin>In the place cited above.</margin> a codex is <term>Pasul: Hebrew for "disqualified" or "invalid"</term> profane if:

I. *It is written on the skin of an unclean animal.* 
II. *It is written on the skin of a clean animal, but not properly prepared.* 
III. *It is written on skin not specifically prepared for the purpose of being a Book of the Law.* 
IV. *It is written on the part of the skin where it should not be written—that is, on the "membrana" [inner layer] on the side that faced the flesh, or on the "pergamenum" [parchment/outer layer]* <margin>See Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf, a renowned Hebraist</note> under this word.</margin> *on the side that had the hair.* 
V. *It is written partly on the inner layer and partly on the outer layer.* 
VI. *It is written on "diphthera"* <note>original: διφθέρᾳ, a type of hide prepared with salt and flour but not gall-nut</note>. 
VII. *It is written on "duchsustos"* <note>original: דוכסוסטוס, the middle layer of a split hide</note> *otherwise than exactly according to the rules.* 
VIII. *It is not written with permanent ink.* 
IX. *It is written in other languages.* 
X. *It is written by a heretic or similar profane persons.* 
XI. *The Divine Names are written without holy intention.* 
XII. *Even one letter is missing.* 
XIII. *Even one letter is redundant [extra].* 
XIV. *One letter touches another.* 
XV. *The shape of any letter is corrupted so that it cannot be read properly, or if it resembles another letter, or if the writing is torn, perforated, or stained.* 
XVI. *A letter is separated from another by too great a distance, so that a word appears doubled; or if they are moved too close, so that two words appear as one.* 
XVII. *The form of the Sections [Parashiyot] is changed.* 
XVIII. *The form of the Songs [poetic portions] is changed.* 
XXIX. *The rest of the writing is written in the style of a Song.* 
XX. *The sheets are sewn together without using the sinews of a clean animal.* 

The Hebrews judged these twenty conditions to be supremely necessary in a *Volume of the Divine Law*,

# OF THE STRUCTURE BOOK I. PART I.

...intended for the use of the Synagogue. The accuracy and exactness required in the sacred Scrolls <note>Latin: *Codicibus sacris*</note> is more to be praised or wondered at! Certainly, Christ the Lord described this class of men with the greatest justice when he said, in <margin>Matthew 23:24.</margin> *straining out a gnat, but swallowing a camel* <note>original Greek: διυλίζον τὸν κώνωπα, τὴν δὲ κάמיλον καταπίνον</note>: even if one might certainly disapprove of such painstaking care and fastidious exactitude regarding the text of Holy Scripture—upon which the highest importance of our happiness depends—given the great perversity and laziness of the human race.

But we must not pass over the ornaments of these Scrolls. Among them are included the *mantles* <note>Hebrew: מטפחות, *mitpachot*</note>, which are linens stretched more in length, like bandages, than extended in width, with which the <margin>Orach Chajim Title 154. § 4.</margin> sacred Scroll is wrapped. Regarding these, it is written in the Hebrew statutes: *The linens of a Book of the Law that have worn out may be used to make shrouds for the dead, and this commandment constitutes their hiding away* <note>The Latin translates the Hebrew *genizatan* as *occultatio* (hiding/sequestration) and provides the Greek equivalent *ἀπόκρυψις* (*apokrypsis*), referring to the practice of Genizah, where sacred objects are buried or hidden rather than thrown away.</note>.

<margin>Regarding the Code Megillah, Canon 43, folio 40, column 1. Laws of the Scroll, chapter 10, § 3. Torah.</margin>
The same Rule <note>Latin: *Canon*</note> is found in the definitions of Rabbenu Asher and in Maimonides. Mention is also made of the *case* <note>Hebrew: תיק, *tik*</note> in which the Book of the Law is stored, in these same statutes, as well as the golden and silver apparatus with which the Book of the Law is adorned. Besides the passage cited above from Maimonides, let us describe only a part of the Rule of Rabbenu <margin>Laws of Tephillin [Phylacteries] etc., chapter 10, § 5. Regarding Code Megillah, Canon 40.</margin> Asher: *Holy utensils, such as the case for sacred books, Tephillin [phylacteries], and the Mezuzot <note>Hebrew: מזוזות; the Latin explains these as "sheets fixed to doorposts"</note>, and the Book of the Law, and the straps of the <margin>Definition 43.</margin> phylacteries <note>original Greek: τῶν Φυλακτηρίων</note>, are to be hidden away* <note>original Greek: ἀποκρύπτονται</note>. *The hiding away* (Genizah) *of a Book of the Law is described in the following sections:* *A Book of the Law that is worn out by age is hidden in the grave of a student of Hebrew Law who repeats the statutes, and it is placed in an earthen vessel.* These Rules mean that these holy utensils should never be discarded in such a way that they could eventually be applied to profane uses. The same is read in the *Yoreh De'ah*.

<margin>Title 282. § 12. & 16.</margin>
But other ornaments of manuscript Pentateuchs <note>The first five books of the Bible</note> are also mentioned there, which are added to them for the sake of beauty; so it is in the text: *The silver or gold apples <note>Hebrew: תפוחי, *tappuchei*. 2. *Let us note the use of the horn in proclaiming the New Year.* [John] Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675) was an English churchman and Hebraist known for using Talmudic sources to explain the New Testament.</note> says of it: **The trumpet was sounded in every city in which there was a judicial assembly, at the entrance of the new year; but this only occurred after the destruction of the Temple.** <margin>Chapter 4. §. 1.</margin> He supports this opinion from the tractate *Rosh Hashanah* <note>The "Head of the Year," the Talmudic tractate dealing with the Jewish New Year.</note>, although the specific words of the text are not cited. But indeed, these statements by Lightfoot are so ambiguous and obscure that they could easily lead into error someone who does not examine the matter more carefully. I will therefore speak a little more clearly: it was provided by commandment that on the very first day of the new year, which are the Calends <note>The first day of the month.</note> of the month *Tishrei* <note>The seventh month of the Hebrew calendar, usually falling in September or October.</note>, a loud blast should be raised by the blowing of the Trumpet (the Horn, I mean, or the **Shofar** <note>original: שופר (*shofar*), a ritual musical instrument made from a ram's horn.</note>, if we wish to speak accurately) in all assemblies of the Israelites, whether they were within or outside the land of Canaan. <margin>Laws of the Shofar. chapter 1. §. 1.</margin> Let us hear Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal scholar.</note>:
**It is an affirmative commandment of the Torah to hear the blast of the shofar on the New Year, as it is said: "It shall be a day of blowing for you" [Numbers 29:1]. And the shofar which is blown, whether on the New Year or during the Jubilee, must be a curved ram’s horn, etc.** <note>original: מצות עשה של תורה לשמוע תרועת השופר בראש השנה שנאמר יום תרועה יהיה לכם ושופר שתוקעים בו בין בראש השנה בין ביובל הוא קרן הכבשים הכפוף וכו</note>
*It is an affirmative commandment of the law to hear the sound of the Horn at the beginning of the new year, according to that which is said: "It shall be a day of blowing for you" [Numbers 29:1]. ### CHAPTER 10. OF THE SYNAGOGUES. 207

If the New Year fell on the Sabbath, in the *Sanctuary* <note>The Temple in Jerusalem</note> or in *Jerusalem, the ram's horn would be blown*; however, after the Jewish State was overturned, *this Horn was only blown in every place* where the *Great Sanhedrin* <note>The supreme council and tribunal of the ancient Jewish people</note> held its seat, whether in *Yavne* <note>A center of Jewish learning after the destruction of the Second Temple</note> or elsewhere. *Rabbi Eliezer* indeed thought that this privilege was given to the city of *Yavne* alone, for as long as the Great Sanhedrin sat within it, but the opinion of the wise men prevails. Since, however, in this current time, every image of the ancient Sanhedrin has perished—which survived for a long time in the land of *Canaan* after the destruction of the Jewish Republic—it follows that today the ram's horn is not to be blown if this festival of the New Year falls on the *Sabbath*. Thus it is read in the express words of the Hebrew statutes:

<margin>
*Orach Chayim*, Laws of Rosh Hashanah. Title 588. §. 8.
Laws of the Shofar, chapter 2. §. 6.
</margin>
**On the festival day of the New Year that happens to fall on the Sabbath, they do not blow the shofar.** <note>original Hebrew: יום טוב של ראש השנה שחל להיות בשבת אין תוקעין בשופר</note> <margin>Annotations to the Mishnah 2. chapter 4. *Rosh Hashanah*.</margin> *Maimonides* <note>A famous 12th-century scholar</note> writes in the same sense. Regarding the prudence and watchful care of the Great *Sanhedrin*, as *Maimonides* notes, they presume that it *would not misuse the Horn on the Sabbath day*, a matter to which they attended most cautiously. Thus, a permission was granted to the *Great Sanhedrin* which was forbidden to all other assemblies.

# CHAPTER 10. ON SYNAGOGUES. #

...solemn <note>Completing the word "solen-neus" from the previous page.</note> use of Trumpets and Horns in Synagogues, so however, that at the same time regard is had to the double use of each of these instruments, and that this use differs in two different circumstances. For thus the Glossator <note>Likely referring to a traditional commentator like Rashi or a commentator on the Mishnah.</note> holds: *Where there is a Horn; that is, on the Feast of the New Year and the Jubilee.* <note>original Hebrew: מקום שיש שופר כגון ראש השנה ויובל; Latin: "Ubi est Buccina; seu in Festo Novi anni & Jubileo."</note> *Where there are trumpets: as on Fast days.* <note>original Hebrew: מקום שיש החצוצרות כגון התענות; Latin: "Ubi sunt tubae: uti in diebus Jejuni."</note> I doubt, however, whether this is the true intention of the tradition. Concerning this trumpet of the Fast, it is without a doubt to be understood as what **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an early Christian bishop known for his powerful preaching and his "Adversus Judaeos" (Against the Jews) orations.</note> refers to when he is occupied with deterring his Christian listeners from the sacred rites of the Jews.

3. Let us mention in a single word another certain sacred ornament of the Synagogue, namely the most splendid **Curtain** <note>The Parochet, which hangs in front of the Torah Ark.</note>, which is usually hung before the *Book Ark*. For the Jews strived, as much as it could be done, to make the Synagogue as similar to the Temple as possible.

4. We must by no means overlook the **Alms-Boxes** or **Charity Chests**, which may be found in Synagogues or at their doors, so that an opportunity is given to those about to pray to exercise their liberality toward the poor, and thereby more easily earn divine grace. The *Alms* chest is usually called a *kuppah* <note>original Hebrew: קופה</note>, from which come the *Collectors of the chest* <note>original Hebrew: gabbai ha-kuppah</note> among the Jews, who are distinct from the *Collectors of the tray* <note>original Hebrew: gabbai tamchui; the "tray" was for collecting and distributing food rather than money</note>. And indeed, that chest of which Maimonides <note>The 12th-century philosopher and legalist Moses Maimonides.</note> speaks was carried around by those very Collectors to gather alms, which were immediately cast into it; except that those *Alms* were sometimes also collected into a certain *Purse* or pouch, called by Maimonides, using a Talmudic phrase, <margin>Bava Batra folio 8. column 2. Maimonides, same title §. 9.</margin> a *charity bag* <note>original Hebrew: arnaki shel tzedakah</note>. Indeed, this does not produce a difference in meaning; nevertheless, it is certain that the word *arnaki* <note>original Hebrew: ארנקי; likely derived from the Greek "arnakis," meaning a sheepskin or a leather pouch.</note> signifies a **purse**, **pouch**, or small box in which coins are stored. However, the **chests** into which money was thrown for various uses in the Temple were called *shofarot* <note>original Hebrew: שופרות, literally meaning "trumpets."</note>, of which six were designated for coins of voluntary offerings.

<margin>Chapter 6. § 9.</margin>
One may read about these in the Code *Shekalim* <note>The tractate of the Mishnah and Talmud concerning the "shekel" tax and Temple administration.</note>. The Talmudic interpreters agree that the name was taken from the external shape of these **Chests**, for they were narrow at the upper part and wider at the lower part to prevent temple-theft <note>original Greek: ἱεροσυλίαν (hierosylia); the trumpet-like shape made it easy to insert coins but difficult for a hand to reach in and steal them.</note>.

<margin>Mark 12:41–42. John 8:20.</margin>
Undoubtedly, these same chests go by the name of *treasuries* <note>original Greek: γαζοφυλακίων (gazophylakion)</note> in the Gospels, into one of which Christ the Lord saw the **widow** throwing **two small coins**, praising her piety toward God. However, those **small boxes** of the Synagogues—placed either at their doors or within the **Synagogues themselves**—have nothing unique about them as far as I know, except that they are of two types distinguished by the use of the **alms** that are **placed in them**. For some receive alms to be sent to the land of **Canaan** <note>The Holy Land/Israel.</note> to support the poor who dwell there to this day for the sake of piety; others receive alms to be distributed by the *collectors* <note>original Hebrew: גבאים (gabba'im), the officials responsible for communal charity.</note> to the poor of that **church** or **Jewish community** to which those synagogues belong. But on the small boxes that receive alms for the poor of the land of **Canaan**, there is inscribed **Land of Israel** <note>original Hebrew: לא"י, an abbreviation for "Eretz Yisrael."</note>, or something similar (which my memory has not retained with enough tenacity), by which they are easily distinguished from the others.

Besides these **instruments**, we have also seen in a modern **German** <note>Meaning the Ashkenazi Jewish tradition.</note> synagogue suspended **tablets** <note>original Hebrew: לוחות (luchot).</note>, and among them **one** on which was marked the name of an **excommunicated person**, or someone **publicly denounced** for their crimes; of which ritual, God willing, we shall speak more in the following pages.

CHAPTER II. ON SYNAGOGUES.

## CHAPTER XI.

*A transition is made to the explanation of the circumstances <note>original Greek: τῶν περιστατικῶν (ton peristatikon); refers to the external or incidental details surrounding a subject.</note> that must be considered regarding the construction, use, transfer of ownership, and destruction of Synagogues. Regarding the first category, it is noted that Synagogues ought to be built in the highest places of a city at a conspicuous height; the rules of that regulation are produced from the writings of the Hebrews, with reasons also added. Then it is noted that Synagogues were formerly established outside cities, whether for reasons of necessity, convenience, or holiness. On that occasion and by that path, it is explained why and how Synagogues were once frequently built near rivers and cemeteries, citing various examples and reasons from the traditions of this people that are not entirely unworthy of note.*

Having considered the **major parts of the Synagogue, the Utensils, and certain Ornaments**, it will be not unwise to move on to certain **circumstances** <note>original Greek: περιστατικὰ (peristatika)</note> which deserve to be observed regarding the **construction, use, and the alienation <note>The legal transfer of the property to another owner or purpose.</note> or destruction of Synagogues.**

<margin>Laws of Prayer, chapter 11, § 2.</margin>
**I.** Regarding the **construction of a Synagogue**, the Teachers have especially emphasized this precept, to be fulfilled with the greatest religious care: that the **Synagogue be built in the highest place of the City**, and that its building be more elevated than all other buildings of that City. Thus it is written in **Maimonides**: <note>original Hebrew: כשבונין בית הכנסת אין בונין אות' אלא בגבהה של עיר שנאמ' בראש הומיות תקרא ומגביהי' אות' עד שתהא גבוהה מכל חצרות העיר שנ' ולרומם את בית אלהינו</note> *“When they build a Synagogue, they do not build it except on the height of the city, as it is said: **She cries out at the head of the noisy streets** <note>Proverbs 1:21</note>. And they raise the building to such a height that it is higher than all the courtyards of that city, according to what is said: **And to exalt the house of our God**.”* <note>Ezra 9:9</note>

<margin>Proverbs 1:21. Ezra 9:9. Gemara on chapter 1, folio 2, column 1, at the beginning.</margin>
The foundation of this decree is found in the **Tractate Sabbath**: <note>original Hebrew: ואמ' רבה בר מחסיא אמר רב חמא בר גוריא אמר רב כל</note> *“And Rabbah bar Mehasia said, Rav Hama bar Guria said, Rav said: ‘Any [city whose roofs are higher than the synagogue...]’”* <note>The text continues onto the next page, but refers to a Talmudic warning that a city where houses overshadow the synagogue is destined for ruin.</note>

ON STRUCTURE BOOK I. PART I.

**"Every city whose roofs are higher than the synagogue is ultimately destined to be destroyed."** <note>original Hebrew: כל עיר שגגותיה גבוהים מבית הכנסת סופה ליחרב</note>

Rabba Bar Machasia says: Rabbi Chamma, son of Goria, says: Rav says: **"Every City whose roofs are higher than the houses of the Synagogue, its end is devastation."** It is, however, soon added in the marginal annotations to this text of Maimonides: <note>Maimonides (1138–1204) was a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> "And our Rabbi Tam <note>Rabbeinu Tam (c. 1100–1171) was a famous French Tosafist and grandson of Rashi.</note> explained that this refers specifically to roofs that were flat and used for activity; there are times when people use the space above the Synagogue. But our roofs, which are not made for use, are considered similar to towers and steeples."

Rabbeinu Tam interprets this simply as referring to flat roofs that provide utility to the inhabitants of those houses. For it would be shameful to use a certain part of a house that was higher than the **HOUSE OF THE SYNAGOGUE**. But as for our roofs, which are not formed for use, they are held in the same category as castles and towers. Castles and towers are permitted in the text of the Gemara <note>The Gemara is the component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis and commentary.</note> to be higher than Synagogues. Understand the whole matter more clearly from the *Shulchan Aruch*: <note>The Shulchan Aruch ("The Set Table") is the most authoritative legal code of Judaism, authored by Joseph Karo in the 16th century.</note>

<margin>
Laws of the Synagogue <note>original: Hilchoth Beth Hacceneseth</note>. Title 150. §. 2. o. Rabbi Karo in the margin.
</margin>

**"One does not build a Synagogue except at the height of the city, and they raise it until it is higher than all the residential buildings of the city that are used—this excludes fortresses and towers which are not used. A roof that is sloped and not fit for use is measured up to the place where it is fit for use; that is, if there is an upper chamber under the roof, it shall not be higher than the Synagogue."**

<margin>
To the windows; the translation of "visions" <note>original: לכוי תרגו' שכוית. This refers to the translation of the Hebrew word 'sh'khuyyot' in Isaiah 2:16.</note>

One does not build a Synagogue except in the highest place of the City; indeed, they exalt it until it has become higher than all buildings of the City from which some use is derived. But regarding lookouts and towers from which no use is derived, as well as a sloped roof which is likewise not adapted for use, they are accustomed to measure those up to that place which is suitable for use; in such a way that if some upper room is made under the roof, it should not be higher than the house of the Synagogue. <margin>

**"Some say that he who has raised his house higher than the Synagogue is compelled to lower it."** <note>original Hebrew: יש אומרים מי שהגביה ביתו...</note> He who has built his house higher than the Synagogue, according to the opinion of some, must be forced to make it lower. From where this regulation took its origin is clear enough from the testimonies that have been cited. First, they judged that so much reverence is owed to their houses of prayer that they should stand out above the rest of the City's structures. Indeed, it contributes to the dignity of a Divine House that its structure be higher and more excellent than any human buildings. Then also, as has already been observed by us several times, since they consider their Synagogues as being like the Temple...

### CHAPTER II. CONCERNING SYNAGOGUES.

<margin>
On the Syrian Goddess.

It is not surprising that they strove to make these as similar as possible, and assigned a notable height to the synagogues. For the Temple, as was the custom for those people, was built on a mountain, whose *peak* was sufficiently elevated. Indeed, the Gentiles, when building temples and shrines in high places, imagined that they were closer to heaven, and therefore their prayers would be heard more easily "from nearby," <note>original Greek: ἀγχόθεν</note> as *Lucian* says. <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125–180 AD) was a Hellenistic satirist who wrote on religion.</note> Whether the same opinion settled in the minds of the Hebrews is a question that is not absurd. For it is certainly certain that from the time they entered the land of Canaan, they affected a desire to worship God on the highest slopes and mountains. Nevertheless, I do not doubt that later it also occupied their minds that this pertains most of all to the *honor and splendor* of the Temple: that it should stand out above whatever buildings were adjacent to it. It was in the prophecies that *the mountain of the house of Jehovah would be raised up above the mountains.* 
<margin>
Isaiah 2, 2
</margin>
And it is indeed established that Mount *Akra*, <note>original: Arcam. This refers to the fortress hill in Jerusalem.</note> which according to the testimony of *Josephus* was higher than Mount *Moriah*, was lowered in the times of the Maccabees, with its peak taken away from it, "so that the Temple might also tower over it." <note>original Greek: ὡς ὑπεרφαίνοιτο καὶ ταύτῃ τὸ ἱερόν</note>
<margin>
Josephus, *Jewish Wars*, book 6, ch. 6, or book 5, ch. 13.
</margin>
But we remember writing more copiously about that elsewhere.

# ON CONSTRUCTION, BOOK I. PART I.

Every city whose roofs are higher than the synagogue is ultimately destined for destruction. <note>original Hebrew: כל עיר שגגותיה גבוהים מבית הכנסת סופה להחרב. This is a famous passage from the Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 11a.</note> *Rabba Bar Machasia says: Rabbi Chamma, Son of Goria, says: Rav says: Any City whose roofs are higher than the buildings of the Synagogue, the end of that city is devastation.* However, it is immediately added in the marginal annotations to this text of Maimonides: <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> "And our teacher Tam <note>Jacob ben Meir, known as Rabbenu Tam (c. 1100–1171), a leading French Tosafist.</note> interprets this as specifically referring to roofs that were flat and level, which people used; it is a disgrace that people should use space higher than the synagogue. But roofs that are not made for use are like towers and ruins." <note>original Hebrew: ופי' רבינו תם דווקא כעין גגותיהן היו שוין ומשתמשין בהן ויש בזיון שמשתמשין למעלה מבי' הכנס' אבל גגותיהן שאין עשויים להשתמש בהן דומיין לאקשקושי ואבדורי</note> *But Rabbenu Tam interprets this simply regarding flat roofs, which provide use to the inhabitants of those houses: for it would be shameful to use a certain part of the houses that was more elevated than the* HOUSE OF THE SYNAGOGUE. But as for our roofs, which are not shaped for use, they are held in the same place as fortresses and towers. Fortresses and towers, in the 
<margin>Laws of the Synagogue. Title 150. Section 2. Rabbi Karo in the margin.</margin>
text of the Gemara, <note>The component of the Talmud containing rabbinic commentary on the Mishnah.</note> are permitted to be higher than Synagogues. Understand the whole matter more clearly from the *Schulchan Aruch*: <note>The "Set Table," the most widely consulted code of Jewish Law, compiled by Joseph Karo in the 16th century.</note> "They do not build a Synagogue except on the height of the city, and they raise it until it is higher than all the structures of the city’s houses that are used—this excludes fortresses and towers that are not used, and a sloped roof that is not suitable for use. They measure up to the place that is suitable for use in buildings; that is to say, if there is an upper room under the roof, it should not be higher than the synagogue."
<margin>For beauty; the Aramaic translation of "pleasant sights" [from Isaiah 2:16] is "beautiful towers." So the Aramaic Interpreter [the Targum]: "desired lookouts" he translates as "beautiful little fortresses," section 3.</margin>
*They do not build a Synagogue except in the highest place of the City: indeed they exalt it until it becomes higher than all the buildings of the City from which any use is derived. But regarding lookouts and towers from which use is not derived, as well as a sloped roof, which is likewise not adapted for use, they are accustomed to estimate those up to that place which is suitable for use; so that, if any upper room is made under the roof, it is not higher than the house of the Synagogue.* It is added shortly after in the following paragraph: "One who has raised his house higher than the synagogue—some say they compel him to lower it." <note>original Hebrew: מי שהגביה ביתו יותר מבית הכנסת יש אומרים שכופין אותו להשפילו</note> *Whoever has built his house higher than the Synagogue, he, according to the opinion of some, must be forced to make it lower.* From where this regulation drew its origin is clear enough from those testimonies that have been cited. First, they judged that so much reverence is owed to their Houses of Prayer that they should stand out above the other structures of the City. For it certainly contributes to the honor of a Divine House that the structure be higher and more excellent than any human buildings. Then also, since, as has already been observed by us several times, they compared their Synagogues to the Temple...

### CHAPTER II. OF SYNAGOGUES.

Since they strove to make [synagogues] as similar [to the Temple] as possible, it is not surprising that they assigned them a conspicuous height. For the Temple, as was the custom among many nations, was built on a mountain whose *summit* was sufficiently elevated. Indeed, the Gentiles, when constructing Temples and shrines in high places, imagined themselves to be closer to heaven, and therefore believed their prayers would be more easily heard *from nearby*, as *Lucian* <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125–180 AD), a Syrian-Greek satirist and rhetorician.</note> says.
<margin>On the Syrian Goddess. See Spencer, *On the Laws of the Hebrews*, Book 1, Chapter 6, Section 1.</margin>
Whether the same opinion took hold of the minds of the Hebrews is a question not without merit. For it is certainly established that from the time they entered the land of Canaan, they were inclined to worship God on the highest slopes and mountains. I do not doubt, however, that later it also occupied their minds that it pertained greatly to the honor and *splendor* of the Temple that it should stand out above all buildings adjacent to it. It was in the prophecies that *the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be raised above the mountains*.
<margin>Also Isaiah 2:2</margin>
And it is quite well known that Mount *Acra*, which according to the testimony of *Josephus* was higher than Mount *Moriah*, was leveled during the time of the Maccabees, <note>The Maccabees were Jewish leaders who led a rebellion against the Seleucid Empire in the 2nd century BCE. Acra was a fortress overlooking the Temple.</note> with its peak removed *so that the Temple might also tower over it in this way*. <note>original Greek: ὡς ὑπεרφαίνοιτο καὶ ταύτῃ τὸ ἱερὸν</note> But we remember writing about this more extensively elsewhere.
<margin>Josephus, *The Jewish War*, Book 6, Chapter 6, or Book 5, Chapter 13.</margin>

<margin>Psalm 119:164.</margin>

->### CHAPTER II. OF SYNAGOGUES.<-

...that not *all* synagogues in the past were located *in the fields*, but certainly *some* were. However, I have three reasons why synagogues were often *not built within cities*. 1. Because Jews in exile were often not permitted to have *synagogues* within the *cities themselves*. 2. because a location *outside the cities* was considered *more convenient* for establishing synagogues. 3. because that same location *outside the cities* was often deemed *holier*. We must speak briefly about each of these.

1. Since the Jews were remarkably *hated* and *detested* <note>The author uses the strong Latin terms "invisi & exosi," reflecting the historical reality of anti-Judaism in the Roman and early modern eras.</note> by other peoples, it does not seem likely that all nations would have granted the Jews the faculty of constructing synagogues within their cities. For it is possible that in certain parts of the empire, the Jews suffered the same fate that later befell the Pagans, whose superstition—after the Christian religion prevailed throughout the world—was banished *to the villages* <note>original Latin: "ad pagos." This is a linguistic play on the word "pagan," which derives from "pagus" (village/rural district), as the old Roman religion lingered in rural areas after cities converted to Christianity.</note>. But I do not have at hand right now clear and explicit testimonies to support this hypothesis of mine, except that this very same reason seems to have been behind why the Jews had a synagogue not in the City of Rome itself, but outside of it.

2. The location for building synagogues outside the city was often much *more convenient* than in the city itself. The reason for this convenience can be sought from the fact that outside the cities, the *view of the sky* <note>Seeing the sky was important for determining the timing of prayers and the appearance of the new moon.</note> was much more open, the place itself was quieter, further removed from crowds, and therefore more suitable for the exercises of religion; and also because of the *water*, or rather the *rivers*, near which synagogues were most conveniently built. This was because the Jews were required *to wash their hands* before offering prayers. We assume this now as something certain and well-known, as we undertake to prove it in the following pages. Furthermore, they preferred synagogues to be established near *rivers* rather than near other bodies of water because rivers provide purer, running water. I believe we should refer here to what is read in the Acts of the Apostles concerning the *synagogue* which is said to have been outside Philippi:

<margin>Acts 16:13.</margin>
*And on the Sabbath day we went outside the city by a river, where a place of prayer was customarily located* <note>original Latin and Greek: "extra urbem APUD FLUVIUM, ubi ex recepto more erat Proseucha." The Greek term "proseucha" refers specifically to a house of prayer.</note>.

<margin>Book I. Part 1. chapter 4.</margin>
I remember discussing this testimony in the preceding pages. Let it suffice now to call to mind that specific part: that the synagogue, by established custom, was said to be *at the river*.

<margin>Annotations on Numbers 32.</margin>
What was the reason for that location? The highly esteemed Dutch Interpreters <note>Refers to the "Interpretes Belgæ," likely the scholars behind the Dutch Authorized Version (Statenvertaling) or similar reformed scholarship.</note> believe that the leaders of Philippi *did not grant the Jews a synagogue within that colony*. I would not deny

...It is possible, however, that Luke intended to speak here as much about the location of the synagogue by the river as about its location outside the city. <margin>On the word Fontinalia.</margin>
Without a doubt, we should recall here what we read in the poet *Juvenal* concerning a synagogue built outside the gate of the city of Rome called *Capena*. Near this gate there were abundant waters, which is why it was called the *damp gate* and was named the "gate of fountains" <note>original Latin: *fontinalis*</note> by Festus. Juvenal writes:
<margin>Satire 3, lines 11–12.</margin>

> ->to the Jews.<-

Part of these words has already been described above. In our judgment, the most learned *de Dieu* <note>Ludovicus de Dieu (1590–1642), a Dutch orientalist.</note> correctly observes that the origin of this custom can be traced back to what is recorded in sacred history about Isaac. 
<margin>On Acts 16:13.</margin>

<margin>Genesis 24:62, 63.</margin>
who is said to have gone out into the field, and specifically to a well or spring, <term>to pray</term> <note>original Hebrew: לשוח (*la-suach*). While modern scholars often translate this as "to meditate," the author follows the "Chaldean" (Aramaic Targum) interpretation of "to pray."</note> according to the Chaldean interpreter, whom Pagninus follows. *From this the custom seems to have arisen, so that places of prayer <note>original: *Proseuchae*</note> were erected outside the cities in the fields, and almost always near rivers, springs, torrents, and other streams of water.* 

Whether this custom gained strength from the superstitions of the Gentiles—who worshipped not only God by the torrents, but the torrents themselves as gods—I would not dare to say. The illustrious *de Dieu* thinks the idolaters were more likely to have imitated the Jews. Yet who can say that the Jews of later 
<margin>Isaiah 57:6.</margin>
times did not imitate the Gentiles, even if they did not fully cross over into their superstition? For it is certain that they borrowed many things from the Gentiles. The testimony of *Epiphanius* <note>A 4th-century Church Father who wrote about various religious sects.</note> concerning the synagogue of the Samaritans, which was outside the city, will be useful to observe as our dissertation proceeds.

3. We have added that this could be an underlying reason why synagogues were built outside *cities*: because that location was sometimes judged to be *holier*. It was considered holier because of the tombs of distinguished and most upright men located there. Indeed, it is abundantly clear that the Jews had a custom of erecting synagogues and academies near the tombs of highly praised men, as seen in the writings of *Benjamin of Tudela* <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler from Spain who documented Jewish communities across Europe, Asia, and Africa.</note> and in the *Hebrew Gravestones*, which were translated into Latin and illustrated by the most learned *Hottinger*. <note>Johann Heinrich Hottinger (1620–1667) was a Swiss philologist and theologian.</note> In this latter treatise, examples are so common that it would be tedious to describe each one. -> These are the journeys of the children of Israel who go from strength to strength, <-

<margin>In the Preface of the Book on Gravestones, near the end.</margin>
The most excellent Hottinger <note>Johann Heinrich Hottinger, a Swiss orientalist.</note> made a summary of a remarkable story pertaining to this from a certain Hebrew Manuscript. The Jews had been accused before the Muslims <note>original: "Mu-hammedanos."</note> that their impiety was holding back the long-awaited rains. For this reason, a space of *three days* was granted to them to obtain rain from God through prayer, under the threat that if the outcome failed, they would all undergo the most certain danger of death. The Jews, forced to accept this harsh condition, first decided among themselves that if divine grace denied them help, they would rather rush into mutual slaughter after the three days—falling by the hands of their fathers and brothers—than give their enemies pleasure and mockery by their death. With this decree, they approached the *monument of Zechariah the Prophet* <note>original Hebrew: כוון זכריה הנביא (Kivun Zechariah ha-Navi).</note> *to pray and supplicate* <note>original Hebrew: להתפלל ולתחנון (le-hitpallel u-le-tachanun).</note> with manifold pomp and processions. ### CHAPTER II. OF SYNAGOGUES.

"What is the difference between them? The difference between them is the graves of heathens." <note>original Hebrew: מאי בינייהו איכא בינייהו קברי גוים. This is a standard Talmudic formula used to determine the practical difference between two legal or theological opinions.</note> *Why are prayers performed at burial grounds?* Rabbi Levi, the son of Chamma, and Rabbi Chamma, the son of Chanina, disagree on this. One says: *We are before you, O God, like the dead;* the other, however, says that it is done for the purpose that the deceased might pour out prayers on our behalf. What is the heart of this controversy? The primary dispute concerns the graves of "those outside" <note>original Greek: τῶν ἔξω (ton exo), a term used to refer to Gentiles or those outside the Jewish faith.</note>. For Rabbi Levi, the son of Chamma, did not want the burial grounds to be visited on days of fasting for the sake of obtaining help from God through the intercession of the saints, but only to rouse humility in the souls of the supplicants and to place their present condition vividly before their eyes—which is to say, a condition not far removed from that of the dead. He supported this argument by the fact that Jews, at the time of a fast, visit not only the burial grounds of Israelites, but also those of Gentiles, if the former are not available. And yet, it is not probable that they would wish to ask for help from the hands of Gentiles.

<margin>
Maimonides, Laws of Fasting (Hilchot Taanith), chapter 6, § 17.
</margin>
Maimonides, in the work cited above, continues: <note>original Hebrew: ובוכין ומתחננין שם כלומר הרי אתם מתים כאלו אם לא תשובו מדרכיכם</note> *they weep and supplicate there (at the graves), as if they were saying: "Behold, you are all dead just as these are, if you do not turn back from your ways."* Truly, even if certain individuals among the Jews held this view, like Rabbi Levi and Rabbi Chamma, I do not doubt that the opinion of Rabbi Chamma, the son of Chanina, was much more widely accepted.

<margin>
Spencer, On the Laws of the Hebrews (De Legibus Hebraeorum), book 3, chapter 1, dissertation 6, § 5.
</margin>

This was proved at length by

<margin>

# ON STRUCTURE BOOK I. PART I.

<margin>Annotation on Virgil, Book 6 of the *Aeneid*, verse 875.</margin>
It is easy to reconcile what we were just discussing—that synagogues were often built on the banks of *rivers*—with the fact established from ancient records that it was the *custom of the ancients to establish tombs along the banks of streams.* It is enough to point this out using the words of the learned *Cerda* <note>Juan Luis de la Cerda (1560–1643) was a Spanish Jesuit scholar famous for his extensive commentaries on the Roman poet Virgil.</note>, who supports this with many suitable testimonies.

<margin>
Bava Kama <note>A tractate of the Talmud dealing with civil matters and damages.</note>, folio 16, column 2 & folio 17, column 1.
*On Royal Law*, chapter 6, Theorem 19, page 173. *On Hebrew Mourning*, chapter 3, section 13.
2 Chronicles 32:33.
</margin>
3. In the records of the Hebrews, one can read that such gatherings were often established at the tombs of distinguished men *for the sake of honor*. Pertinent here is the testimony from *Bava Kama*, observed before us by *Schickard* <note>Wilhelm Schickard, a 17th-century polymath and professor of Hebrew.</note> and *Geier* <note>Martin Geier, a 17th-century Lutheran theologian and Hebraist.</note>: <note>original Hebrew: כבוד עשו לו במותו מלמד : שהושיבו ישיבה על קברו כפי' ישיבה תלמידים לעסוק שם בתורה לפי שחרבה תורה בישראל כדאמר שבדקו מדן ועד בארשבע ולא מצאו איש ואשה תינוק ותינוקה שלא היו בקיאים בטומאה וטהרה ולא על קברו כמש אלא ברחוק ארבע אמות ;</note> "They showed him honor at his death"; this teaches that they established a <term>yeshiva</term> <note>An academy for the study of the Torah and Rabbinic literature.</note> at his grave. According to the explanation, a *yeshiva* refers to students gathering to engage in the study of the Torah there, because the Torah had been diminished in Israel—as it is said that they searched from Dan to Beersheba and did not find a man, woman, boy, or girl who was not an expert in the laws of ritual impurity and purity—and [they sat] not directly upon his grave, but at a distance of four cubits. The words of the text concerning Hezekiah <note>A King of Judah known for his religious reforms.</note>, "they did him honor," imply that a scholarly assembly gathered at his tomb—that is, students, so that they might learn the Scripture there. This was because he had multiplied the Law in Israel to such an extent that when they investigated the progress from Dan to Beersheba, not a single man or woman, nor even a small boy or girl, was found who was not well-trained in the distinction between the pure and the impure.

<margin>2 Chronicles 30:5.</margin>
However, they did not sit directly upon the tomb (lest they be defiled, *Schickard* adds, because it is considered a sacrilege to handle sacred matters next to a corpse), but remained at a distance of four cubits <note>original: ulnarum (ells/cubits)</note> from it. In this way, as later generations hand down, the Jews were accustomed to honoring the tomb of a King.

<margin>Laws of Mourning <note>original: Hilchot Evel</note>, chapter 14, section 13. See Geier, chapter 6, section 11.</margin>
Whether this account be true or false, it is at least easy to gather from it that for the sake of honor, the Jews often instituted religious or academic assemblies at the funerals of distinguished men. Otherwise, *Maimonides* <note>The influential 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legal codifier.</note> himself teaches that it is not permitted to read, learn, wear <term>phylacteries</term> <note>Small leather boxes containing Torah verses worn during prayer, also called tefillin.</note>, or pray at tombs, unless at a distance of four cubits.

## CHAPTER XII.

*The discussion continues regarding the circumstances to be considered in the construction of Synagogues; accordingly, libraries, guesthouses, and trees near the Synagogue are examined. It also addresses the necessary condition of the ten-man requirement of Israelites, which the Hebrew Canones require for a Synagogue to be established, investigating the reasons for that statute. Regarding the <term>circumstances</term> <note>original Greek: τὰ περιστατικὰ (ta peristatika), referring to the external conditions or requirements surrounding a building.</note> that concern the building of a Synagogue, it will not be useless to mention, thirdly, that LIBRARIES were sometimes joined to Synagogues. Indeed, Benjamin of Tudela <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler from Spain who documented Jewish communities across Europe, Africa, and Asia.</note> speaks expressly concerning the Synagogue of Ezekiel: <margin>Travels, page 79.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: ושם בית גדול הקדש והוא מלא ספרי' ומבית ראשון ומבית שני יש שם ספרים וכל שאין לו בן ,יקדיש ספרו לשם</note> *"And there is a great holy house, full of books, where books from both the first and second temples are preserved; and whoever lacks children consecrates their books there."* Such libraries are often united with the Academies and Schools, which themselves were joined to Synagogues, together constituting what was once a single <term>Gymnasium</term> <note>In the early modern period, this term referred to a place of higher learning or an academy.</note>. A modern example of this is the Portuguese Synagogue of Amsterdam, which has an attached *Gymnasium* with a *Library* adjacent to it. Otherwise, Synagogues may be content with their own *scroll-cases*, which we discussed in previous sections. However, the splendor of this Synagogue of Ezekiel was rare, if one is to believe *Benjamin*.

4. It seems entirely likely that certain GUESTHOUSES were located very near to Synagogues, in which it was convenient for travelers who came from elsewhere to stay. I have gathered this from the *Observations on Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note>, where he disputes whether it is permitted to eat <margin>Laws of Prayer, chapter 1, § 6.</margin> and drink in Synagogues. An example of Rabbi *Ashi* seemed to stand in the way of those who argued against it, for elsewhere the contrary seems to be stated about him; to which it is answered in these Observations: <margin>Bava Bathra, folio 3, column 2.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: והא דפרק קמא רבבא בתרא דרב אשי עאל לבי' כנישת' במתא מחסיא לאו לבית הכנסת ממש אלא סמוך לבית הכנסת מקום שהאורחים רגילים</note> *"And as for what is mentioned in the first chapter of Bava Bathra—that Rav Ashi entered the synagogue in the city of Mata Mehasia—this does not mean the synagogue itself, but rather a place near the synagogue where travelers were accustomed to stay."*

# CHAPTER 12. OF SYNAGOGUES.

As for this testimony of Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis, a 4th-century bishop who wrote against various heresies.</note>, I admit, based on his authority, that the Jews and Samaritans of old sometimes had such <term>places of prayer</term> <note>original Greek: τόπος προσευχῆς (*topos proseuchēs*)</note> outside cities. I admit this even more willingly because it aligns well with what we presented shortly before regarding "Rural Synagogues." Furthermore, I easily presume that the Jews, being more devoted to their religion, were eager to imitate their forefather Isaac <note>Genesis 24:63 describes Isaac going out to the field to meditate/pray in the evening.</note>; besides the fact that the condition of certain locations might not have allowed for the construction of a more grand Synagogue building. However, whether the word <term>prayer-house</term> <note>original Greek: προσευχὴ (*proseuchē*)</note> designated only these types of prayer locations—and specifically those distinct from the more spacious buildings for which the name "Synagogue" would have been reserved—is a point I still hesitate on. The writers of the New Testament, along with *Philo* and *Josephus*, stand in the way. The former use the word <term>synagogue</term> <note>original Greek: συναγωγῆς (*synagōgēs*)</note> everywhere in the widest sense for all places of public assembly, whether intended for prayers and the reading of the Law, or for instruction. The latter two, as has been proven by us with the clearest evidence, also apply the name *Proseucha* [prayer-house] to the most grand Synagogues. Therefore, I do not easily abandon the opinion defended above: that the word *Proseucha* once enjoyed a very broad meaning and was applied to any Jewish meeting place without distinction. In the Roman language, such a place as Epiphanius describes, we would call a *sacellum* [shrine], unless I am mistaken. For *Festus* <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian.</note> says of it:

<meta>This page continues the discussion of communal obligations and the legal mechanisms by which a Jewish community "compels" its members to support the synagogue.
