# CHAPTER 12. OF SYNAGOGUES.

[If a man] should speak out, and because of this discord the daily prayers should cease, and no standard of Justice be observed, and truth and peace should fail in the city, and even in the entire Kingdom that follows their faction, it certainly seems to me that care must be taken that all the fathers of families who bear the burden of paying taxes should assemble in one place. They should bind themselves by an oath that each will express his opinion for the glory of God and the greatest benefit of the society, and that he will follow the votes of the majority, whether in choosing the leaders of the assembly, or in appointing the Ministers of the Synagogue, or in organizing the alms box, or in appointing the collectors of alms, or in building or destroying parts of the synagogue house, adding or subtracting, and so on. The sum of the matter is that whatever pertains to the needs of the assembly shall be done according to the decision of the majority.

But if the minority refuses to submit and to observe all these things we have written, the majority—or those elected to the Magistracy by the majority—has the power to constrain and compel them by any means, whether in a court of the Israelites or even in the courts of the gentiles <note>This refers to using secular or non-Jewish legal systems to enforce communal Jewish bylaws</note>, until they say: "We consent." If they find it necessary to spend money on this legal matter, those who constitute the minority shall bear their share of those expenses. However, if anyone refuses to give his opinion according to the formula of that oath, his vote is null. Thus, the votes of the majority who took the oath upon themselves are followed. We see clearly from these words what that "compulsion" is of which Maimonides speaks.

But what is the reason that the number ten is placed among the necessary conditions for building a House of Prayer? Certainly, if you demand a reason, the Teachers will give you a "meager" one, as Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and Hebraist</note> says, and a "false and forced" one, as Vorstius <note>Willem Willemzoon Vorstius, a 17th-century scholar of Rabbinics</note> says. And what is that reason? It is this: that certain prayers pertaining to the sanctification of the Divine Name, such as the <term>Kaddish</term> <note>A prayer of praise and sanctification of God's name</note> and the <term>Barechu</term> <note>The formal call to prayer, literally "Bless [the Lord]"</note>, may not be recited without a count of ten men. 

And what is the cause of this? Because it is written elsewhere: *I shall be sanctified <term>in the midst</term> of the Children of Israel* (Leviticus 22:32). The word <term>midst</term> <note>Hebrew: *betoch*</note>, they say, refers to the gathering of the assembly and here signifies the number ten. But why so? Because that word is found elsewhere joined with the word <term>assembly</term> <note>Hebrew: *edah*</note>. For it is said: *Separate yourselves <term>from the midst of this assembly</term>* (Numbers 16:21). Now, they say that "assembly" (<term>edah</term>) signifies ten men, because the ten Spies of the land of Canaan—Joshua and Caleb being excluded—are called an "assembly" (<term>edah</term>) in that same Mosaic history <note>This refers to Numbers 14:27, where God asks, "How long shall this evil *assembly* [the ten unfaithful spies] murmur against me?"</note>.

I would wish it to be considered here first that Hebrew writers defined any solemn and legitimate assembly—not only a sacred one (though this most of all), but also a civil one—by at least ten men. *“If ten or more Hebrews were present (a number they frequently employ to define assemblies) then...” etc.* These are the words of *Selden* <note>John Selden, a 17th-century English jurist and scholar of Jewish law</note>. <margin>Book 2, chapter 10, *On Natural and International Law*. *Hilkhot Issurei Biah* <note>Laws of Prohibited Intercourse</note>, chapter 12.</margin> The matter is certain and well-known, confirmed previously by the testimony of *Maimonides*, but it should be illustrated by certain examples observed by us here and there. But how many men? *Ten*, according to the opinion of *Maimonides*, because that many make up an assembly; when they are not present, a matter is not considered to have been done **publicly** or **in public** <note>Hebrew: *be-farhesya, be-rabbim*</note>. <margin>See Selden, *On Natural and International Law*, book 4, chapter 4; and Wagenseil, *Fiery Darts* <note>original: *Tela Ignea*—a collection of Jewish polemics</note>, page 301.</margin> A similar example to this concerns the *sanctification of the Divine Name among the Gentiles*. Namely, if any Gentile should force an Israelite to the transgression and violation of certain commandments of God (they except the crimes of idolatry, adultery, and murder) and *ten* were not present (**ten from Israel** <note>Hebrew: *asarah mi-Yisrael*</note>, who constitute a **congregation** <note>Hebrew: *edah*</note>), it was entirely permitted by their own laws to transgress the commandment; indeed, he who did not yield to the will of the Gentile was judged **guilty of his own life** <note>Hebrew: *mitḥayyev be-nafsho*</note> <note>Meaning he was responsible for his own death by refusing to comply when the law would have allowed him to save himself</note>. If, however, ten were present in such a case, he was absolutely obligated to sanctify God by death instead...

Synagogues were built using money collected from the congregation: <note>original Hebrew: גבו מעות לבנין בית הכנסת ובא להם דבר מצוה מוציאין בה המעות : קנו אבנים וקורות לא ימכרום לדבר מצוה אלא לפדיון שבויים אע"פ שהביאו האבנים וגררום ואת הקורות ופסלום והתקינו הכל לבנין מוכרים הכל לפדיון שבויים בלבד אבל אם בנו וגמרו לא ימכרו בית הכנסת אלא יגבו לפדיון מן הצבור</note> **IF THEY COLLECTED MONEY FOR THE BUILDING OF A SYNAGOGUE, and a situation arises where they are obligated by Divine command to spend money, they may spend the collected money on it. If they have already purchased stones and timber, they shall not sell them for any other such case, except for the <term>redemption of captives</term> <note>Pidyon Shvuyim; a high-priority religious duty in Jewish law to ransom those held for money.</note>. Indeed, even if they have already brought the stones and polished them, and hewed the timber, and prepared everything for the construction, they may sell everything for the sake of redeeming captives. However, if they have completely finished the building, they do not sell the house of the Synagogue, but rather they collect money anew from the congregation.** Compare the preceding sections, from which it will also be clear in § 5. 7. that money is sometimes collected from elsewhere. So much for the circumstances that were to be considered regarding the founding of synagogues.

### CHAPTER XIII.

**The surrounding circumstances <note>original Greek: τὰ περιστατικὰ</note> regarding the Dedication and the Reverence due to consecrated Synagogues are described, citing the relevant decisions from the Talmud and Ritual codes. Then, the canons of Jewish Law concerning the destruction of Synagogues and the honor to be maintained even for destroyed Synagogues are explained; the distinction established between the Synagogues of Babylonia and those of the land of Canaan is not overlooked. Finally, the alienation of Synagogues—that is, their sale and donation—is addressed, along with the conditions for both.**

After the building of Synagogues, the circumstances of their sacred and religious **Use** must be observed, as is appropriate. Two matters come to mind for us to report here: 1. The Dedication of Synagogues. 2. The Reverence due to them.

<margin>On the Sanhedrin, book 3, chapters 14, 15, 16; chapter 16, section 1, page 260.</margin>
1. How ancient a custom the dedication of Temples, altars, statues, and any other things serving Religion may be, has been pursued so extensively by *Selden* <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a renowned English jurist and scholar of Jewish law.</note> that anyone wishing to avoid useless labor may rightly rest here. However, he wrote very little concerning Synagogues, and this is essentially all of it: *“Regarding those places, however, in which the use of prayers occurs only by chance (such as the solemnity during Fasts for rain, held in the city square, into which they even carried the Ark of the Synagogue containing the book of the Law, as well as private dwellings and courtyards where the people happened to gather for prayer without any preceding formula of sacred Dedication), they say:* <note>original Hebrew: אין בהן קדושה מפני שלא קבעו אותם לתפלה בלבד אלא עראי מתפללין בהן כאדם שמתפלל בתוך ביתו</note> *'There is no holiness in them, because they did not establish them for prayer alone, but rather they pray in them temporarily, just as a person prays within his own home.'”* *Selden* then adds: *“And from these things it is not difficult to conclude that the Synagogues of the Jews also obtained a certain Dedication through their permanent establishment,* <note>original Hebrew: קביעות (Kevi'ut)</note> *consecration,* <note>original Greek: ἀφιδρύσει</note> *or constitution for 'prayer alone,'* <note>original Hebrew: לתפלה בלבד</note> *by which they were separated from common uses...”*

Section 21. *If they have simply built a house, and afterwards consecrated it as a house of the Synagogue, that house enjoys the full law of a house of the Synagogue:* **YET IT IS NOT HOLY UNTIL THEY HAVE POURED OUT PRAYERS IN IT,** <note>original Hebrew: "אבל אינו קדוש עד שיתפללו בו"</note> *not even if they built it under that name and title, so that it might be a House of the Synagogue. But after they have prayed in it, even travelers entering it as the occasion allows, it is considered holy, since it was already previously destined for public prayers.* One can clearly see from this rule <note>original Latin: "Canon"</note> in what the Dedication of Synagogues consists. First, the Masters <note>The Rabbis or legal authorities.</note> require that a house be built either under that name and title so that it may serve for public prayers, or at least, after it has been built, it should be designated for those public prayers by those to whom this right belongs. Once that is done, they then require in the second place that someone pour out their prayers in it, as in a house consecrated for this use, even if a traveler does so. And only then are such buildings considered holy, and enjoy all the prerogatives of a Sacred Building. Almost nothing else is read in the definitions of Rabbenu Asher <note>Asher ben Jehiel (c. 1250–1327), a prominent Talmudist and legal authority.</note>:

<margin>
Rule 41. On the Tractate *Megillah*, folio 40, column 1.
</margin>

*Even if indeed he has built a building, and afterwards consecrated it as a Synagogue building, its status is that of a Synagogue building. Yet it is not holy until it has served such sacred uses; not even if it was constructed from the beginning in the name of a Synagogue (for this purpose, title, and intent).* This is, of course, a very simple method of consecrating, and most agreeable to reason, if very little is to be granted to superstition. How the Gentiles, however, established the consecrations of Sacred Buildings may be learned from Alexander ab Alessandro <note>A 15th-century Italian humanist jurist known for his work on Roman customs, *Geniales Dies*.</note>: *The consecration of a temple was performed so that he who was to dedicate the Temple and building, holding the doorpost, having lit a small brazier, and having called upon the Deity to whom the Temple and buildings are sacred, [withdrew] himself from profane use and human law,*

Now a word must be added concerning the **ALIENATION OF SYNAGOGUES**, which occurs either through **SALE** or **GIFT**. To rightly understand this subject, it must first be noted that the Jews distinguish their Synagogues into those of *Fortified Cities*, which may be called **PUBLIC**, and those of *Villages*, which we shall call **PRIVATE**. It was not permitted to sell the Synagogues of fortified towns or those held in common. The primary source of doctrine and debate on this argument is in the Tractate Megillah, from which **Maimonides**, **Rabbi Jacob** <note>Likely Jacob ben Asher, author of the Arba'ah Turim, a seminal code of Jewish law.</note>, and almost all other compilers of rituals have extracted the relevant points. The chapter "Megillah" begins thus:
<margin>Chapter "Bnei Ha'Ir" (Sons of the City), which is the fourth in some volumes and the third in others, folio 26, column 1.</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: בני העיר שמכרו רחובה של עיר לוקחין בדמיו בית הכנסת בית הכנסת לוקחין תיבה וכו'</note> *The Sons of the City (the community of Israelites living in a certain place) who sell the city square may use its price to acquire a Synagogue; those who sell a Synagogue may use its price to acquire an Ark, and so forth.* Regarding those words, the <term>Gemara</term> <note>The component of the Talmud consisting of rabbinical analysis and commentary on the Mishnah.</note> states: <note>original Hebrew: בני העיר שמכרו רחובה של עיר אמ' רבה בר בר חנה אמר רבי יוחנן זו דברי רבי מנחם בר יוסי סתימתאה אבל חכמים אומרי' הרחוב אין בו משום קדושה ור' מנחם בר יוסי מאי טעמי' הואיל והעם מתפללין בו בתעניות ובעמדות ורבנן ההוא אקראי בעלמא</note> *Regarding the inhabitants of a city when they sell the city square: Rabba bar bar Channa said that Rabbi Yochanan said, "These are the words of Rabbi Menachem bar Jose, the Authoritative Teacher; however, the Sages say that no sanctity resides in the city square at all." What is the reasoning of Rabbi Menachem bar Jose? It is because the people pray there during fasts and stationary assemblies. But the Sages hold that such use is merely accidental.*

# CHAPTER 13. CONCERNING SYNAGOGUES.

<margin>Chapter 4, Section 1, 2.</margin>
What argument did Rabbi Menachem produce in support of his opinion? It was this: that the people pray in these places during fasts and on solemn communal watches <note>The Latin *stationibus* refers to the Hebrew *Ma’amadot*, groups of laypeople who represented the community at the Temple; here it refers to special prayer gatherings.</note> (concerning which, see the Tractate *Taanit* <note>The section of the Talmud dealing with fast days.</note>). The Sages, however, reply that such occurrences are rare in the world. Rabbi Menachem believed that the very streets of the city should be regarded as sacred places, because it occasionally happens that the people, if the synagogues cannot hold the crowd, gather in the streets to pray. Examples of this can certainly be found in the 
<margin>2 Chronicles 32:6.
Ezra 10:9.
Nehemiah 8:2, 4.</margin>
Holy Books. But it has already been determined in the *Gemara* <note>The part of the Talmud that contains rabbinic commentary and analysis.</note> itself that the opinions of the Sages differ from that of Menachem. This doubt is resolved in the same way by Maimonides: <margin>Laws of Prayer and the Priestly Blessing, Chapter 11, Section 21.</margin> 
<note>original Hebrew: רחובה של עיר אע"פ שהעם מתפללין בו בתעניות ובמעמדות מפני שהקבץ רב ואין בתי כנסיות מכילין אותן אין בו קדושה מפני שהוא עראי ולא נקבע לתפלה וכן בית וחצרו שהעם מתקבצין בהם לתפלה אין בהם קדושה מפני שלא קבעו אותן לתפלה בלבד אלא עראי מתפללין בהם כאדם שמתפלל בתוך ביתו</note> *The open square of a city, even though the people pray in it on fasts and communal standing days because the gathering is so large that the synagogues cannot contain them, possesses no holiness. This is because its use is temporary and it was not permanently established for prayer. Likewise, a house or a courtyard where people gather for prayer possesses no holiness, because they did not establish them for prayer alone; rather, they pray in them by chance, just like a man who offers his prayers within his own private home.* As for what concerns the city square, although the people may pray there during fasts and communal watches—since the crowd is larger than the synagogues can hold—there is no inherent sanctity in it. This is because it only happens by chance that the square is used for such a purpose, and it was not properly ordained for regular prayers. And so it is with houses and courtyards in which people gather to offer prayers; no sanctity resides in them, because they did not ordain such places solely for prayer, but they pray in them incidentally, like a man who pours out his prayers in a private residence. Therefore, the opinion of Menachem falls, and <note>original Hebrew: הלכה כחכמים</note> *the law follows the Sages.* What has been pronounced by the Sages is here considered to be the Law, says Bartenora <note>A famous 15th-century commentator on the Mishnah.</note>. Let us now proceed to the *Gemara*: <margin>On this passage.</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: אמר רבי יוחנן: בית הכנסת לוקחין תיבה: אר"ש שמואל בר נחמני אמר רבי יונתן לא שנו אלא בית הכנסת של כפרים אבל בית הכנסת של כרכים כיון דמעלמא אתו ליה לא מצו מזבני ליה דהוה ליה דרבים</note> *Rabbi Yochanan said: If they sell a synagogue, they must buy an ark <note>A chest for holding Torah scrolls.</note> with the proceeds. Rabbi Samuel, son of Nachmani, said that Rabbi Jonathan says: This is only **TO BE UNDERSTOOD CONCERNING VILLAGE SYNAGOGUES**, but as for **CITY SYNAGOGUES**, since people are accustomed to come to them from all over the world, they may not be sold, because they are considered to belong to the public.* In Maimonides and others, this limitation is repeated in almost the same words. Thus Maimonides says: <margin>Laws of Prayer, Chapter 11, Section 16. Way of Life (Orach Chajim), Title 153, Section 6, 7.</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: במה דברים אמורים שמותר למכור בית הכנסת בבית הכנסת של כפרים שלא עשו אותה אלא על דעת בני הכפר לבדם שתהיה להם להתפלל בה</note> *To what do these words apply? That it is permitted to sell a synagogue only in the case of village synagogues, which were built solely with the intent of the villagers themselves, so that they might have a place to pray.*

<header>CONCERNING THE STRUCTURE BOOK I. PART I.</header>

How should we understand the rule regarding whether it is permitted to sell a Synagogue? *Regarding the Synagogue of Villages, which they did not build except by the will of the villagers alone, so that they might pour out prayers within it.* <note>The author is distinguishing between small local synagogues and large urban ones.</note> The reason why it is not permitted to sell the synagogues of large towns is given in the text: because people from the entire world are accustomed to gather there for prayer, and thus the right of ownership belongs to many. Let us learn what these things mean from the *Tosafot* <note>original Hebrew: כיוון דמעלמא קאתו לה נראה לפרש הכי כיון שרוב בני אדם רגילים ללכת שם להתפלל אף על פי שאין נתנים כלום בבנינו מכל מקום כיון דלדעת אותן רבים נעשה חמורה קדושתו ואינן יכולין למכרו , ועוד יש לפר' כיון שרבים נתנו בבנינו ובשאר צרכיו</note> <note>The *Tosafot* are medieval commentaries on the Talmud, often providing clarifying legal definitions.</note>:

The words: *“Since they are accustomed to gather there from everywhere,” should be explained thus: Because a great multitude of men is accustomed to frequent it for the sake of prayers. For even if they perhaps contributed nothing of their own toward its construction, nevertheless, because that Synagogue was made for the benefit of those many people, its sanctity must be considered more serious, and therefore it is not permitted to sell it.* Or perhaps these words also allow for this meaning: that many people contribute something toward the maintenance of its building and other necessities. *Rabbenu Asher* <note>Asher ben Jehiel (c. 1250–1327), a prominent Talmudic scholar also known as the "Rosh."</note> binds and urges this *Gemaric* <note>Relating to the Gemara, the component of the Talmud containing rabbinic analysis.</note> tradition even more strongly:

<margin>To this place, folio 37, column 2.</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: ואפי' היה ידוע שבני הכרך בנו אותה ולא סייע להם מחוץ לעיר בהוצאות בניינה אפילו הכי כיון דמעלמא קאתו לה בני העולם, העיר הקדישוה לדעת כל העולם.</note> *Even if it is well known that the townspeople built that Synagogue from their own resources, and no assistance was brought to them* from those outside of their city <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῶν ἔξω τῆς πόλεως αὐτῶν</note>; *even if, I say, the matter stands thus, nevertheless, because men are accustomed to gather from everywhere to frequent it, the inhabitants of the City are considered to have consecrated it for the public benefit of everyone.* Rabbi Asher adds that in the *Jerusalem Talmud*, the words of which he describes, this decree is confirmed.

By <term>Kepharim <gloss>villages</gloss></term> we should understand here *pagi*, so called, or societies of those who live in the countryside, further removed from the towns. By <term>Kerakim <gloss>towns</gloss></term>, however, we mean the celebrated and fortified cities, which men from various regions of the world are accustomed to frequent. It must be well noted, however, that what is said here concerning the *Synagogues of Towns* allows for some restriction, which is expressly mentioned in the following context of the *Gemara*. For after mention was made of the Synagogue of the *City of Machazia* <note>Likely referring to Mahoza, a major center of Jewish learning in Babylonia.</note>, which by the grant of *Rabbi Ashi* <note>A primary redactor of the Babylonian Talmud.</note> is said to have been able to be sold, because the men who frequented that city

### CHAPTER 13. CONCERNING SYNAGOGUES.

<note>original Latin: CAP. 13. SYNAGOGARUM</note>

Because some were accustomed to frequent it only for the sake of Rav Ashi <note>A prominent Babylonian rabbi and primary editor of the Talmud</note>, a *new* objection is brought forward concerning the Synagogue of the Coppersmiths <note>original Latin: Synagoga Ærariorum; original Hebrew: טורסיים (Torsiyim)</note>, which was in Jerusalem—a city indeed most strongly fortified—and yet it is said to have been sold. An objection was raised:

<margin>Rabbi Solomon [Rashi] on this passage: *Torsiyim* means copper-smiths.</margin>

*Rabbi Judah said, it happened that the SYNAGOGE OF THE COPPERSMITHS, which was in Jerusalem, was sold to Rabbi Eliezer, and he performed all his necessary business in it.* <note>original Hebrew: מתיבי: אמר ר' יהוד' מעשה בבית הכנסת של טורסיים שהיה בירושלים שמכרוה לרבי אליעזר ועשה בה כל צרכיו</note> Yet, the objection is resolved:

<margin>"And this is it, and we made it." <note>This marginal note refers to the claim of the builders' ownership.</note></margin>

That Synagogue was small, and they themselves had built it. It follows that if a certain society of men in any city had built a Synagogue or an Academy, it is always considered to be under the power of its masters, so that they were free to sell it whenever it pleased them. Therefore, what is proclaimed in these Canons <note>Referring to the religious laws or "Mishnayot"</note> concerning the Synagogues of fortified cities is to be understood only regarding those Synagogues which truly belong to *those cities* and form a part of them. But even on this point, not all the doctors agree. Indeed, *Rabbi Isaac of Vienna*, as found in the *Annotations to Rabbenu Asher*, believes that every Synagogue can be sold when it is established that it was built by the citizens at their own expense alone. Let us review the text:

<margin>In the Observations on Rabbenu Asher.</margin>

*But in the Or Zarua <note>The "Sown Light," a major legal work by Isaac ben Moses of Vienna</note> it is written: that every Synagogue which is known to have been built by the inhabitants of the city, and not with money collected from the world, can be sold by the authority of the seven good men of the city, etc.* <note>original Hebrew: אבל באור זרוע כתוב דכל בית הכנסת שידוע שבני העיר בנו אות' ולא גבי זוזי מעלמא יש לה מכר על פי שבעה טובי העיר וכו'</note> Let us also relate the rest, which follows:

*And likewise, when A PRIVATE INDIVIDUAL HAS BUILT A SYNAGOGUE, and has given it to the inhabitants of the city absolutely, granting them also the power of repairing the house and expanding the building, so that neither he nor his heirs can prevent them, then such a Synagogue is considered the property of the whole congregation, and it is permitted to sell it by the authority of the seven good men.* <note>The "seven good men of the city" (Shivah Tuvei Ha'Ir) were the elected lay leaders or city council of a Jewish community.</note>

<sig>Ii 2</sig>

*But if he gave it in such a way that the good men do not have the power to prevent him from coming into it to pray—but rather he reserved for himself the right that no one has the authority to repair the damage to the house or add to the building except him or his heirs—then it cannot be sold except by the authority of the congregation and by his own authority or the authority of his heirs.* <note>original Hebrew: וכן יחיד שבנה בית הכנסת ונתנו לבני העיר לגמרי... אבל אם נתנו כך שאין לטובים כח למחות מלבא אל תוכו להתפלל אלא ששייר לעצמו... אין לו מכר כי אם על פי הקהל ועל פיו או על פי יורשיו</note>

<vocab>Synagoga, R. Isaac de Vienna, R. Ascher, Or Saruah, Synagoga Ærariorum, Hierosolyma, divenditio, coetus propria, Viros Civitatis</vocab>

### ON THE STRUCTURE [OF THE SYNAGOGUE] BOOK I. PART I.

<note>original Latin: DE STRUCTURA LIB. I. PARS I.</note>

...the men of the city. But if a person gave it on the condition that the "Good Men" <note>community leaders or trustees</note> have no power to prevent anyone from entering it for the purpose of prayer, but reserved for themselves the right that no one except themselves and their heirs should have the power to repair cracks in the house or to advance its building, that Synagogue cannot be sold except by the decision of the congregation, or of that person, or of their heirs. From these words, it is established that Synagogues could be established by *private individuals*, and once established, could be *given* to the Church <note>The author uses the Latin "Ecclesia" here to refer to the Jewish religious assembly or community</note>, either absolutely or with certain conditions. This seems to do much to illustrate <margin>Luke 7:5.
On this place: Orach Chajim, Title 153, § 14. <note>A section of the Shulchan Aruch, the code of Jewish law</note></margin> the *Gospel History*, in which a Centurion is said to have built a *Synagogue* for the people of Capernaum, as was observed before us by *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and rabbinical scholar</note>. Just as someone could donate an entire *Synagogue* to the community, so too could they give the land, or anything else that is among the necessities of the Synagogue.

Let us now discuss *under what conditions it was permissible for Gentiles to alienate their Synagogues*. Specifically, for *Gentiles* <note>original Latin: Paganis. In this context, it refers to non-Jews (Gentiles) who funded or built Jewish places of worship</note>, if they had built a Synagogue at their own expense, it was lawful to *alienate* <note>to transfer ownership or sell</note> it in two ways: either it was permitted for them to sell it privately to anyone, or it was sold through the *Elders*, or the *seven Good Men of the congregation* (the local Magistrates) in an *assembly of the whole people*. If the former occurred, then these two conditions had to be observed: **1.** It was not permitted to sell the Synagogue for any uses that were base or ignoble. **2.** It was also not permitted to convert the price of the sold Synagogue to other uses than *sacred* ones; and, what is more, another religious instrument, more sacred than a Synagogue, had to be purchased with that price. But if the Synagogue were sold in a *public assembly of the whole people* by the elders of that society, then indeed it was sold so absolutely that the Synagogue building could be applied by any buyer even to the most base uses and services. Let us again prove these things we have said with internal testimonies. Thus says the *Mishnah* <note>The first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions</note>:

<margin>Megillah chapter 3, § 1.</margin>

> They may not sell a Synagogue except on the condition that, if they wish, they may take it back; these are the words of Rabbi Meir. However, the Sages say they may sell it in a permanent sale, but with these four things nevertheless excepted: so that it is not converted into a bathhouse, or a tannery, or a place for immersion <note>a laundry</note>, or a water-house <note>a latrine</note>. Rabbi Judah, however, says they may sell it under the name of a Courtyard, and whoever acquires it for themselves may do with it whatever they please. <note>original Hebrew: אין מוכרין בית הכנס' אלא על תנאי שאם ירצו יחזירוהו דברי רבי מאיר וחכמי' אומרי' מוכרין אותו ממכר עולם חוץ מארבעה דברים למרחץ ולבורסקי לטבילה ולבית המים ר' יהודה אומר מוכרין אותה לשם חצר והלוקח מה שירצה יעשה</note>

### CHAPTER 13. ON SYNAGOGUES.

->If all the villagers agree, or if the elders of the place sell it in the presence of all the people of the place, they are able to sell it, and may even make of it a stable <note>or "tavern"</note> in which to drink wine constantly; and the law follows neither Rabbi Meir nor Rabbi Judah. <note>original Hebrew: אנשי הכפר כולם בהסכמת... This holds true when the villagers have sold it without approval or consent <note>meaning without the specific communal authorization required for sacred property</note>. However, if all the Seniors <note>Elders or community leaders</note> of that place sell it in a public assembly of the entire people, then they can sell it for such a purpose that it is lawful for the buyer to turn it into a tavern. The statements of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Judah do not carry the force of law in this matter.

<margin>Bartenora notes the same. <note>Obadiah ben Abraham of Bertinoro (c. 1445–1515), a famous commentator on the Mishnah.</note></margin>

This explanation by **Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> is taken from the **Gemara** <note>The portion of the Talmud containing rabbinic commentary and analysis.</note> on the first **Mishnah** of this same chapter. Megillah chapter 3, § 1.</margin> if they sell wraps or a chest, they must buy the Five Books of the Law <note>the *Chumash*, or volumes containing the individual books of the Torah</note>; if they sell the Five Books, they must use that price to acquire for themselves a Book of the Law (the five Books of Moses written together in one scroll). But if they sell a Book of the Law, it is necessary to buy another Book of the Law with that price, <margin>Same place, § 15.</margin> because no holiness is greater than the holiness of the complete Mosaic volume. And so, if the people have collected a certain sum of money to build a School or a Synagogue, or to acquire an Ark, wraps, or a chest for the Book of the Law, and they wish to convert the collected sum to another purpose, they may not convert it except to buy something holier than what they first proposed to buy. However, if they have accomplished the purpose for which they collected that money and some coins remain, they may spend those on whatever they wish, etc. But if those coins were subject to a specific condition <note>such as a donor's restriction</note>, that condition must be fulfilled.

There follow now two rules concerning the sale of a Synagogue, which have already been explained. The text continues: <margin>§ 18.</margin> And so, if the Seven Good Men of the City <note>a board of seven community trustees</note> in an assembly of the entire city sell the Synagogue on the condition that the remaining money should be common <note>original Greek: κοινὸן (*koinon*), meaning secular or non-sacred property</note>, let it be common. Therefore, when they have received the money for the sold property and they build another Synagogue from it, or acquire any other religious instrument for themselves, the remainder—as per the condition—shall be common; and they may do with it whatever they please. But if all the members of the community, or the majority of them, confer their right upon one man, <margin>§ 19. § 20.</margin> whatever he does is valid. He alone may sell it or give it as a gift, adding whatever conditions please him as he sees fit, according to what is found in the **Orach Chayim** <note>The section of the *Shulchan Aruch* (the standard code of Jewish Law) dealing with daily ritual life.</note>. <margin>Chapter 153, § 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.</margin> Thus far regarding the sale of Synagogues and its conditions; which one may read in similar opinions in the **Shulchan Aruch**.

# ON STRUCTURE, BOOK I, PART I.

They were imbued with the discipline of the Law of the Fatherland under the guidance of the learned. I would favor the latter view <note>that these were schools as well as places of prayer</note>; both because the Jews record that a **Beit Midrash** <note>original Hebrew: בית מדרש</note>, or *Academy*, was joined to every individual Synagogue in Jerusalem, and because those learned men who are said to have disputed here with Stephen <note>Referencing the account in Acts 6:9 regarding the trial of Saint Stephen.</note> are far more likely to have emerged from scholastic training than simply from a [standard] Synagogue. We can best understand the whole matter like this: notable *Jews* living in various parts of the world outside of Canaan almost always made an effort so that those who shared a region, province, district, or famous city would have a school <note>Latin: *Gymnasium*</note> established in Jerusalem in their name and at their expense. This was done both to send their sons there to be educated in their native language and traditions, and also so that those staying in Jerusalem for the sake of religious rites might have a fixed and permanent place to practice their religion. For the Temple could not hold all the synagogues. To further illustrate this passage, *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), a prominent English Hebraist and clergyman known for using Rabbinic literature to explain the New Testament.</note> appropriately cited from the Jerusalem Talmud this very *Synagogue of the Alexandrians*, which the *Alexandrians are said to have built there in Jerusalem at their own expense*.

<margin>In the place cited.</margin>

Otherwise, no difficulty remains in this text, except that it is obscure who those *Libertines* <term>Libertini: A Latin term for freedmen—formerly enslaved people who have been legally granted their freedom.</term> might be, whose Synagogue is listed here first. If *Libertinus* <note>original Hebrew: המשרר; likely a variant or error for *Ha-meshuhrar*, meaning "the freedman."</note> is to be understood here as a *Freedman*, properly so called, who has been manumitted <note>released</note> from slavery into liberty—about which we have no doubt (*for we do not accept the view of some that this is the name of a specific ethnic group*)—then the word has, if I am not mistaken, a fourfold meaning.

For a *Libertine* can be:
1. A *Jew* by birth and race who was sold into *slavery* to a Hebrew master in the land of Canaan, either by himself or by the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme council and tribunal of the Jews.</note>, and was subsequently granted freedom by that same master.
2. A *Jew* by birth and race who served a Gentile master (of which kind there were *many* in Italy and Rome) and was given freedom by him.
3. A *Gentile* by birth who, after performing service for a Hebrew master, was sent into *liberty* by him, and at the time of manumission was co-opted into Judaism as a <term>Proselyte of Righteousness: A convert who has fully embraced the Jewish faith and all its requirements.</term> (both of which were done through the ritual of *baptism* <note>Referring to the *tevilah*, or ritual immersion required for converts.</note>).
4. A *Gentile* who was subject to a Gentile master and, having been manumitted by him, embraced *Judaism*.

From which of these classes of *Libertines* is the Synagogue in this text to be claimed? The most learned and practiced men certainly differ. *Lightfoot* places *Libertines of the first order* among—

The opinions of *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), a prominent English Hebraist</note> and *Selden* do not please me. I agree with *Grotius*, whose judgment I find more and more to be the healthiest when he is not bound to received assumptions. As for *Lightfoot*, who could believe that Jews—who had either sold themselves into slavery due to the pressure of poverty or had been sold by the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme rabbinic court</note> because of theft, and whom *Lightfoot* himself calls the **"dregs of the populace and a lice-ridden crowd"**—would have been capable, after their manumission <note>The formal act of freeing a slave</note>, of building and sustaining an Academy <note>Latin: *Gymnasio*</note>? And even if they were capable, what suitable reason would they have had for doing so in Jerusalem? Once they were restored to their former liberty and all their legal rights, there was no reason for them to separate themselves from the public Synagogues of Jerusalem. As for *Selden*, I could hardly bring myself to believe that the Jews had freed so many Gentile slaves and received them into their religion in the land of Canaan that these men could have borne the expense of building and maintaining an **Academy**; especially since the Jews, as *Lightfoot* observes, were quite reluctant to manumit Canaanite slaves. See <margin>*Maimonides*, Laws of Servants, chapter 9.</margin> *Maimonides*. 

But even if there had been a large enough number of these men, what cause would there have been for these freedmen to separate themselves from the common sacred rites of Jerusalem, into which they had now been received, and to withdraw into a peculiar Synagogue of their own? I admit they were inferior in certain prerogatives to Jews born of the true stock of Jacob, but surely that was no obstacle to them practicing the same rites in the same Synagogues with the rest of the Jews. Indeed, the more they separated themselves from the others, the more they rendered their own condition lowly and ignoble. Let us therefore think, along with *Grotius*, that this passage refers to *Jews* by origin who had been held in the service of Gentiles in *Italy* or *Rome* and were granted liberty by them, and along with them, the *Roman* or *Italian Libertini* <note>Freedmen</note> who had been initiated into Judaism as **Proselytes of Justice** <note>Full converts who took on the whole Law of Moses</note>. For if Luke had simply wanted to translate the Hebrew <term>the freedman</term> <note>original Hebrew: המשוחרר, *ha-meshuchrar*</note>, as Selden and Lightfoot contend, he undoubtedly would have used the Greek word <term>freedman</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπελεύθερος, *apeleutheros*</note> or another of similar power, but certainly not that Roman or Italian word *Libertinus*. ### CHAPTER 14. OF SYNAGOGUES

...that they did not have a synagogue. There are, as far as we understand, two responses to this objection. 1. We might say that the word *Pagi* <note>original Latin: *Pagi*; Hebrew: *Kapharim* — meaning villages or small settlements</note> is sometimes used with greater or lesser emphasis; that is, the word sometimes denotes *larger villages*, which are also called *Cities* or Societies, and sometimes refers to rural villas located in the immediate territories of a City. 2. We might establish that Villages did not always have fixed Synagogues, or indeed might not have had them at all. However, let us wander a bit more freely to provide a clearer explanation of this whole matter.

<margin>Chapter 1 §. 1. 2. 3.</margin>
It is established in the Code Megillah <note>The *Megillah* is a tractate of the Mishnah and Talmud concerning the reading of the Book of Esther</note> that the *Reading of the Megillah* (the small book of Esther) can and must occur at various times depending on the different status of places and societies. For *Towns* that were enclosed by a wall from the time of Joshua, called *Kerakim*, it was a decreed duty to read the book of *Esther* on the fifteenth day of the month of Adar. The words state: *Towns, surrounded by a wall from the times of Joshua the Son of Nun, read on the fifteenth.* <note>original Hebrew: כרכין המוקפין חומה מימות יהושע בן נון קורין בחמשה עשר</note> Besides these *towns*, mention is made of **LARGE CITIES** <note>original Hebrew: עיירות גדולות — *Ayarot Gedolot*</note> and **VILLAGES** <note>original Hebrew: כפרים — *Kapharim*</note>. *Large Cities* were those Jewish societies in which were found the so-called *ten Idle Men*, about whom we shall speak hereafter. <note>term: *ten Idle Men* — from the Hebrew *Asarah Batlanim*; these were ten men of leisure who were supported by the community to ensure a quorum was always available for synagogue services</note> Moreover, it is determined in the *Megillah* that these cities enjoy this prerogative: that they may read on the fourteenth, which is the day closest to the 15th. *Great Cities read on the fourteenth.* <note>original Hebrew: עיירות גדולות קורין בי"ד</note> If, however, there was another society that lacked such *Ten Idle Men*, it did not read the book of *Esther* except *on the day of the Synagogue Assembly*, <note>original Hebrew: ביום הכניסה — *Be-yom ha-kenisah*</note> that is, on Monday or Thursday. This was because on those days legal judgments were given and the Synagogue was well-attended, which we will discuss more broadly shortly.

Suppose, for example, there was a society of Jews in which the ten idle men were not found, and the ordinary time for reading the *Megillah* (the fourteenth day) fell on a Tuesday or Wednesday; it was the duty of that society not to read the *Megillah* on that fixed Tuesday or Wednesday, but to move the reading earlier to the preceding *Monday*. If the 14th fell on a Wednesday, this Monday would be the twelfth; if the 14th fell on a Tuesday, it would be the thirteenth. This was the very same time at which the *villagers* were accustomed to go into the city, who...

<header>CHAPTER 14. ON THE SYNAGOGUES.</header>

Truly, nowhere were safer locations more necessary than on the seacoasts, where it was essential for stored goods to be protected from robbers and for the men guarding them to be safe from the untimely surges of the waves; for this reason, the most famous fortifications and citadels of the ancients were situated by the sea.

In these various places, however, there was a different celebration of the *Festival of Purim* <note>The Jewish holiday commemorating the saving of the Jewish people from Haman, as told in the Book of Esther</note>. The Jews who lived in Shushan observed this festival on the *fifteenth day* [of the month of Adar]. Indeed, because *Shushan* was a fortified city, this privilege was extended *to the fortified cities* of the land of Canaan, and it was decreed that in all of them the *Festival of Purim* should be celebrated on the *fifteenth day* of the month of Adar. But why is this decree restricted to cities fortified since the time of Joshua? *Maimonides* <note>The 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note>, *Asher* <note>Likely Asher ben Jehiel, a prominent medieval Talmudist</note>, and all the authors of the Rituals provide the reason: because many cities in the land of Canaan were destroyed at that time [during the Persian period of the Purim story], so that very few would have enjoyed this privilege if they had only considered the cities fortified during that specific period. Therefore, it seemed more advisable to grant this privilege to all those cities which could be believed from history to have been fortified since the time of Joshua [son of Nun].

Furthermore, since the ancient Jews understood by the term <term>medina</term> <note>original Hebrew: מדינה — usually meaning a province or district, but here interpreted as an unfortified populated area</note> any places where mixed societies of people lived but which were not surrounded by a wall, it followed that all Jewish communities living in places not enclosed by a wall should be able to read the Book of *Esther* on the *fourteenth day*, because they were considered to enjoy the same privilege as the <term>medinot</term> <note>plural of medina</note> or districts in the land of Media and Babylonia. And this is true to the extent that today, in any communities outside the land of Canaan, the *Megillah* <note>The Scroll of Esther</note> is read on the 14th day of the month of Adar. However, the ancient Sages did not conclude it exactly this way. What, then, is the reason for this? Namely, that *Large Cities and Towns* had <term>kepharim</term> <note>original Hebrew: כפרים — villages</note> around them in their district; by these, you should understand smaller societies of men living in the countryside within the district of a City or town, from whom the townspeople received their provisions. These *villagers*, having neither a *Synagogue* nor a *tribunal* (for they lived in the district of a City or town), used to travel to the Town or City twice a week—that is, on *Monday* and *Thursday*—to set out their wares there, and [await] judgments...

<header>CHAPTER 14. OF SYNAGOGUES.</header>

**Synagogues of the Villages** <note>original Hebrew: *Kenesiot shel Kepharim*</note>—is it possible that **Villages** (as mentioned in **Chapters 3 or 4**) were formerly destitute of Synagogues? Certainly, this difficulty can be resolved in this manner: by stating that the word *village* <note>original Hebrew: *Kephar*</note> in the text of the *Megillah* <note>The Talmudic tractate concerning the Book of Esther</note> is used in a more restricted sense to mean *smaller rural societies*, such as those found in the districts surrounding cities and towns. Regarding these, it is indeed true that they did not ordinarily enjoy the presence of a Synagogue. However, as for the larger and more numerous rural societies, they were very often equipped with Synagogues.

Certainly, this restricted meaning of the word *village* <note>Hebrew: *Kephar*</note> is explained by the scholar **Kimchi**: "Houses," he says, "outside the city for villagers and those who till the earth." <note>original Hebrew: *Batim chutz la-ir le-kepharim u-le-ovdei adamah*</note>. **Philippus Aquinas** <note>A 17th-century philologist and convert from Judaism</note> says: "A few houses together outside the city." <note>original Hebrew: *Batim me'atim yachad chutz me-ha-ir*</note>. In every respect, the word *Kephar* has exactly the same meaning as the Latin word *tugurium* <note>a hut or cottage</note>. For just as the Latin word comes from "covering" <note>Latin: *tegere*</note>, so does the Hebrew. The Dutch use a similar word: **Boerehutte** <note>Farmer's hut</note>. 

However, just as a whole City or society of men is eventually formed from many such rural huts, so the word *Kephar* over time also began to be applied to **larger villages**, which are otherwise usually called *Vici* <note>townships or neighborhoods</note>, though this is not as frequent in the Biblical text as it is among the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> translations. This is why the Chaldean Translator rendered the phrase **unwalled cities** <note>original Hebrew: *eri perazot*</note>, which appears in the text of **Esther**, as *Pagos* <note>Villages; original Aramaic: *Kuphrana*</note>, as **Elias** <note>Elijah Levita, a Renaissance Hebrew scholar</note> records. Indeed, the *unwalled cities* in the text of Esther signify very large **neighborhoods**, even if they are not surrounded by a wall, in which there is a frequent gathering of people. The Dutch call these **Dorpsteden** <note>Village-towns or open towns</note>. 

The term <term>komopolis</term> <note>a Greek word meaning "village-city," describing a place with the status of a village but the size of a town</note>, which appears in the Gospel of **Mark**, agrees entirely with this phrase; it is found nowhere else in the New Testament. It says in Chapter 1, verse 38: "Let us go into the neighboring **country towns**" <note>original Greek: *komopoleis*</note>. The Dutch translate this as **Vlecken** <note>Market towns or hamlets</note>. But perhaps they would have rendered it better with the same word used in the Book of Esther: **Dorpsteden**. 

On that passage, there is a rather elegant paraphrase by **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius, a famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note>, which it would be a shame to leave out. He says that **Tacitus** <note>A Roman historian</note>, in the fifth book of his *Histories*, when he mentions "works of a long peace being destroyed, built not far from the camp in the manner of a municipality," was describing a *komopolis*. Such a *komopolis* had been **Bethsaida**, which had recently acquired the appearance of a town; **Luke** called these "cities" here more loosely, as also in verse 12. Certain **Masters of the Hebrews** think that the *unwalled towns* <note>Hebrew: *perazot*</note> are *komopoleis*. There are some who disagree. Nor do the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translate it that way. It is clear from **Josephus** <note>A first-century Jewish-Roman historian</note> that there were "villages no less than the size of a city." From this, so often...

<meta>Catchword: ties (completing the word "often")</meta>

<summary>This page analyzes the linguistic definitions of "villages" in Jewish law and scripture, arguing that while small hamlets lacked synagogues, larger "village-towns" (komopoleis) were substantial enough to have them.</summary>

# THE STRUCTURE OF THE FIRST BOOK, PART I.

...that our writers use the Greek words *polis* <note>original: *πόλιν*, meaning city</note> and *kome* <note>original: *κώμην*, meaning village</note> interchangeably. Pollux and Harpocration <note>Ancient Greek lexicographers who explained difficult terms</note> note that the Greek poets use the word "city" for what are actually "villages," and they bring forward an example regarding Euboea <note>A large Greek island</note> about which Euripides <note>The famous Athenian tragic playwright</note> said: "Euboea is a certain city neighboring Athens." <note>original Greek: *Εὐβοὶ Ἀθήναις ἐστί τις γείτων πόλις*</note> I believe what Hugo Grotius <note>A foundational Dutch jurist and theologian</note> teaches here is most true: that the Hebrew phrase *unwalled cities* <note>original Hebrew: *arei perazot*</note> designates "village-cities" <note>original Greek: *κωμοπόλεις*</note> or *villages* <note>original Greek: *κώμας*</note>—namely, country towns formed in the likeness of cities, even though they lack defensive walls. These latter ones were often called *villages* <note>original Hebrew: *kepharim*</note> by the Jews, which is also translated by the Septuagint translators <note>The 70 scholars who translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek</note> as *villages* <note>original Greek: *κώμας*</note>. Therefore, a "village-city" <note>original Greek: *Κωμόπολις*</note> is a *village* <note>original Hebrew: *kephar*</note> in a broader sense. From this, it came about that this word *kephar* was so frequently joined in a compound with the proper names of places or people who were famous in such a village, in almost exactly the same way as the word *Ville* <note>French for "city" or "town"</note> is used by the French, and as the word *polis* <note>city</note> was formerly used by the ancient Greeks. The most frequent example is the name CAPERNAUM, which was a city of Galilee.

<margin>chapter 4, 31.</margin>
Thus we read in the Gospel of Luke: "And he went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee." <note>original Greek: *καὶ κατῆλθεν εἰς καπερναοὺμ, πόλιν τῆς Γαλιλαίας*</note> But as for Capernaum being the same place which is called by the Talmudists *Kfar Nahum* <note>original Hebrew: *כפרנחום*</note>—a word composed of our word *kephar* <note>village</note> and *Nahum*—who can doubt it? Of similar construction are: *Cephar-chenanja*, *Cephar-barkai*, and *Cephar-Azis*, as noted by Johannes Buxtorf <note>A celebrated 17th-century Christian scholar of Hebrew and the Talmud</note>. And, it is worth noting, in that same place he translated the word *kephar* as both "city" and "village." But many other examples besides these noted by Buxtorf were collected by the distinguished Wagenseil <note>Johann Christoph Wagenseil, a German scholar known for his work on Jewish texts</note>.

<margin>In the Annotations to the Excerpts of the Gemara on Tractate Sotah, Chapter 3, page 464.</margin>
Therefore, *kephar* is a "village" <note>original Greek: *κώμη*</note> and *kepharim* are "village-cities" <note>original Greek: *κωμοπόλεις*</note>, or *unwalled cities* <note>original Hebrew: *arei ha-perazot*</note>. John Lightfoot <note>A prominent English Hebraist of the 1600s</note>, commenting on the passage from Mark mentioned earlier, thought that the word "village-cities" <note>Greek: *κωμοπόλεις*</note> corresponded to the word for "towns" <note>original Hebrew: *ayarot*</note> among the Hebrews. We certainly believe that the word *polis* <note>city</note> in the New Testament Scripture is often taken for a "village" or "village-city," and when that happens, it refers back to the Hebrew word *ir* <note>city</note>, which we have said elsewhere denotes any Israelite society coming together as one. However, I think it most certain that "village-city" <note>Greek: *κωμόπολις*</note> has a meaning too specific and limited to refer simply to the word *ir*. *Ir* is a general term and is applied to hamlets, cities, or the largest towns; thus all these places are called *towns* <note>original Hebrew: *ayarot*</note> or *cities* <note>original Greek: *poleis*</note>. But if a restriction is added by the adjoining word "village" <note>Greek: *kome*</note>, then I believe the Sacred Writers intended the word *kephar* <note>village</note>. Just as you have *unwalled cities* <note>original Hebrew: *arei perazot*</note> in the Book of Esther, so you have the *unwalled cities* <note>Hebrew: *arei perizi*</note> and *village of the Perizzites* <note>Hebrew: *kephar perizi*</note> in the Old Testament Scriptures with the same meaning. ...in the writings of Moses; where our Dutch <note>original: *Belgæ*</note> translators put it best: **Unwalled cities.** <note>original: *Onbemuyrde steden*</note> The latter term appears in the First Book of Samuel, where they have: **Land-hamlets.** <note>original: *Land-vlecken*</note> It must be admitted, however, that no word is as frequently used to signify *villages* of any kind as the Hebrew term *Chatzerim*. <note>original: חצרים; this term literally means "courtyards" but refers to open settlements or suburbs</note> It is contrasted with *city* in every sense when the division of *cities* and *villages* of the land of Canaan is discussed in the Book of *Joshua*. *Symmachus* <note>An ancient translator of the Old Testament into Greek</note> thought that *suburban fields* were denoted by this word, but *Masius* <note>Andreas Masius, a 16th-century scholar of Near Eastern languages</note> holds the opinion of *Solomon Jarchi* <note>Commonly known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note>, who contends that it signifies *smaller villas*. We approve of *Masius’s* judgment; for it is not inconsistent with the style of Scripture for *smaller villas* to be called *Fields*. Indeed, there is a most famous passage in Mark: *and wherever he entered into villages, or cities, or fields.* <note>original Greek: ᾗ ὅπε ἂν εἰσεπορεύετο εἰς κώμας ἢ πόλεις ἢ ἀγρός (Mark 6:56)</note> Beza <note>Theodore Beza, a major Protestant reformer and linguist</note> translates this: *And wherever he entered into* **Hamlets**, *or* **Cities**, *or* **Fields.** <note>original Latin: *Vicos, aut Urbes, aut Agros*</note> The Dutch translators mark this distinctly as: **Hamlets, Cities, Villages.** <note>original: *Vlecken, Steden, Dorpen*</note> The Vulgate <note>The standard 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> goes entirely astray with its translation of *Hamlets, villas, or States*. We have no doubt that this interpretation arose from a variation in the reading. Similarly, in Luke there is mention of *the surrounding hamlets and fields*, <note>original Greek: τῶν κύκλῳ κωμῶν καὶ τῶν ἀγρῶν (Luke 9:12)</note> that is, *the Hamlets and Villages that were in the circuit of the City*. This certainly matches the phrase found in the First Book of Chronicles: *Fields, cities, and villages.* <note>original Hebrew: שדה ערים וכפרים (*Sedeh arim ve-kefarim*)</note> In other places, *Cities* <note>original Hebrew: ערים (*Arim*)</note> are certainly contrasted with *villages* <note>original Hebrew: חצרים (*Chatzerim*)</note>, and I would think that by this contrast, fortified cities are understood. Moreover, these fortified cities appear in Scripture under more distinct names, among which the frequent ones are: *Fortified town*; <note>original Hebrew: עיר מבצר (*Ir mivtzar*)</note> *City of a wall*; <note>original Hebrew: עיר חומה (*Ir chomah*)</note> or *a city fortified with gates and bars*; <note>original Hebrew: עיר בצורה חומה דלתים ובריח</note> *a city which has a wall*; <note>original Hebrew: עיר אשר לו חומה</note> *a strong city*; <note>original Hebrew: עיר מצור (*Ir matzor*)</note> while *a fortified city* <note>original Hebrew: עיר מצורה</note> and *the fortifications* <note>original Hebrew: הבצרות (*ha-betzurot*)</note> in Daniel have the same meaning.

# ON THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE

## BOOK ONE.

## PART II.

### Concerning the Origin of Synagogues.

### CHAPTER I.

*A dissertation begins regarding the Origin of Synagogues, which is traced back to ancient times following the testimony of the Apostle James. <note>original: "cum Jacobo Apostolo arcessitur"; a reference to Acts 15:21, where James the Just states that Moses has been read in the synagogues "from ancient generations."</note> Two intervals of time are then surveyed: the first from Adam until the Flood; the second from the Flood until Moses. Nevertheless, a famous passage is examined, Genesis 4:26, which deals with the public calling upon the Name of the Lord, and it is defended against the distorted interpretations of the Jews. Included also are the reports of Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and Torah scholar.</note> concerning Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as the authors of the morning, afternoon, and evening prayers, as well as the origin of the recitation of the Shema <note>original: "Krismah," referring to the Keri'at Shema, the centerpiece of the daily morning and evening prayer services</note>, after investigating the foundations of those opinions. Finally, a consideration of the passage in Genesis 28:21 is added.*

-># CONCERNING THE ORIGIN BOOK I. PART II.<-

That it [the synagogue] is of ancient use and custom is clear from the Speech which James delivered at the Council of Jerusalem: <margin>Acts 15:21</margin> *For Moses*, he says, *from ancient generations has in every city those who preach him, being read in the synagogues every Sabbath*; <note>original Greek: "Μωσῆς γὰρ ἐκ γενεῶν ἀρχαίων κατὰ πόλιν τοὺς κηρύσσοντας αὐτὸν ἔχει, ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς κατὰ πᾶν σάββατον ἀναγινωσκόμενος"</note> **FROM ANCIENT AGES** *Moses has those who preach him city by city, since he is read in the Synagogues every Sabbath.* The Vulgate <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible.</note> punctuated this text differently, though with a very slight distinction, and referred the words *in the synagogues* to the preceding context rather than the following, in this manner: *For Moses from ancient times has in each city those who preach him in the Synagogues: where he is read every Sabbath.* The Syriac version <note>The Peshitta, the standard Christian Bible in the Syriac language.</note> does the same; but, as I said, that difference in reading is of very little importance. The sense remains the same: that Synagogues and their worship had already long since been established by use among the Hebrew nation. For the phrase *from ancient generations*, <note>original Greek: "ἐκ γενεῶν ἀρχαίων"</note> which corresponds to the Hebrew <margin>Job 8:8. Malachi 3:4</margin> *from ancient years* <note>original Hebrew: משנים קדמוניות (mishanim kadmoniyot)</note> or *from former generations*, <note>original Hebrew: מדורות ראשונים (midorot rishonim)</note> can signify nothing less than that Synagogues had already been accepted among the Jews for a long time, and the reading of the Law practiced in them was of a sufficiently ancient custom. This, I say, is entirely what is <margin>verse 8.</margin> signified by this phrase, even if I am not unaware that a very similar expression, *from ancient days*, <note>original Greek: "ἀφ' ἡμερῶν ἀρχαιῶν"</note> which occurs in the speech of Peter reported shortly before, is to be explained with less emphasis. # CHAPTER I. OF SYNAGOGUES.
<meta>Mm 3</meta>
<meta>catchword: with</meta>

In both sacred and secular literature, nothing is so precisely defined that you can provide an answer without anxious hesitation and a fear of being corrected. Even learned writers, who have published brilliant examples of their diligence to the world, are either silent on this matter or, if they speak, they contradict one another. Some trace the birth of the **Synagogues** back to <term>Moses</term><note>The traditional prophet and lawgiver of Israel.</note>, others to a later time, and still others only to the period following the <term>Babylonian captivity</term><note>The 6th-century BCE period when the elite of the Kingdom of Judah were deported to Babylon.</note>. In order to discuss all these views more clearly and successfully, and at the same time to avoid confusing the reader with a useless and intrusive pile of various opinions—as often happens—we have proposed to run through each interval of time in the world and the Church in order. In these periods, we shall seek the origin of the Synagogues until we finally find it. Let us begin, even if it might seem unnecessary, from that most ancient age which flowed from the creation and restoration of man: first, up until the Great Flood, and from there to the age of Moses.

<margin>Genesis 4:1, 2.</margin>
In the history written by Moses, which encompasses that first interval of time, one example of public worship of the Divine is mentioned, but no specific command is recorded. Much less is any mandate mentioned regarding a *place* in which the public worship of God was to be celebrated. We read that *Cain* and *Abel*, the first pair of brothers (so very different from each other), performed *sacrifices*; but whether they offered them in some established and consecrated place, or whether they joined prayers to them, remains uncertain. Nothing of that sort is mentioned in the Holy Scripture. Therefore, the only thing for our consideration regarding this timeframe is what <margin>Genesis 4:26. The Hebrew doctors believe, as has long been observed by most learned men, that this passage concerns the *origin of idolatry*. They translate these words as: *Then there was profanation in calling upon the Name of the Lord*; namely, by transferring the Divine Name to those things which are not God. <term>Selden</term><note>John Selden (1584–1654), a renowned English jurist and scholar of Jewish law.</note> defended their opinion, as he frequently does. ## ON ORIGINS BOOK I, PART II.

<margin>
Laws on the Worship of Stars and Constellations <note>original: *Hilkhot Avodat Kokhavim u-Mazalot*</note> chapter 1, § 1.
</margin>
In this matter, one should certainly consult *Dionysius Vossius* <note>A 17th-century Dutch scholar known for translating and commenting on Jewish texts.</note>, who followed this treatise of *Maimonides* <note>The preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist (1138–1204).</note> with a very brilliant commentary. We deliberately set aside many things that we could describe in great detail from this and other authors. We will only provide the reasons for which we believe the Hebrew interpreters are in error on this point. 1. The very logic of this version destroys itself. For *to call upon the name of the Lord is not a profane act*; and therefore *it cannot be profaned by calling upon the name of the Lord*. On the contrary, *to call upon the name of the Lord is a holy work*, both laudable and most appropriate for a reasoning creature. If you say, through this phrase, "it was profaned by calling upon the name of the Lord," that it indicates that the name of the Lord began to be *invoked* in a profane and God-dishonoring way, I believe I have a solid reason for denying that such a sense can lie hidden within the power of these words. For someone speaks very obscurely and unclearly who, when they wish to say that men began to worship idols, says that *the divine name was profanely invoked*. As I have said, that is an unusual and involved way of speaking, the like of which one will perhaps not be able to find in the Divine Scripture. For he who worships idols *does not call upon the name of the Lord*, and therefore does not profane the name of the Lord *by* calling upon it. If *Moses* had wished to say that, he would have said it better this way: **אז הוחל לקרא בשם אלהים ,אחרים**, *Then it was profaned by calling upon other gods* <note>original Hebrew: *Az huchal likro be-shem elohim acherim*</note>. 2. This was also quite correctly observed by *Dionysius Vossius*: if the meaning of the words were that which the Hebrew interpreters choose—"in calling upon"—then it would have been written in the Hebrew text as **בקרא** <note>original: *be-kro*</note>, rather than **לקרא**, <term>to call</term> <note>original: *li-kro*</note>. For although I am not unaware that the letter **ל** <note>The Hebrew letter 'Lamed,' acting as a prefix.</note>, when joined to infinitives, often has the same power as **ב** <note>The Hebrew letter 'Bet,' meaning 'in' or 'with'.</note>, yet as far as this passage is concerned, it would be said much more clearly and conveniently according to the sense that the Jews attach to this place: *Then it was profaned* **in calling** *upon the Divine Name*; rather than **to call** *upon the Name of the Lord*. Yet I do not think it can be stubbornly denied that **הוחל** <note>original: *huchal*</note> can be translated as "it was profaned." Our colleague *Drusius* <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish Protestant scholar of Hebrew.</note> did not deny that either. But I maintain that this meaning of the word is entirely inconsistent with this passage and its circumstances. Therefore, let the words be rearranged as we have already established: *Then it was begun to call upon the name of the Lord*; or, *then it was begun to be named by the name of Jehovah*, as *Aquila* <note>A 2nd-century Greek translator of the Old Testament known for his literalism.</note> has it: *Then it was begun to be called by the name of the Lord* <note>original Greek: Τότε ἤρχθη τοῦ καλεῖσθαι ἐν ὀνόματι κυρίε</note>. The Hebrew phrasing allows for either version. Which of them should be chosen is a matter of doubt. He who [chooses] the latter...

For someone who does not worship God cannot be named after God. Indeed, *to be named after God* is nothing other than to be held, recognized, and called the *people of God* and *sons of God*—that is, worshipers of the Divine Name.

Furthermore, the interpretation <note>original Greek: *exēgēsis*</note> "to invoke the name of the Lord" signifies in the Holy Scriptures a public invocation and petition to the Deity. I should not overlook that what is said in this text as *before evening* <note>לפנות ערב</note> is read in the printed edition of *Maimonides* as *at the turn of the day* <note>לפנות היום</note>, as both *Schickard* and *Selden* read it when they cite this very passage of *Maimonides*. However, *Selden* noted in the margin that in a manuscript copy of *Maimonides*, it is read as *before evening*, which is undoubtedly to be preferred. If *Maimonides* truly wrote *at the turn of the day*, then he seems to have taken the word "turn" <note>פנה / panah</note> to refer to the declining of the day, a sense in which it is sometimes used in Scripture. But

<margin>
Jeremiah 6:4. Psalm 90:9. Genesis 30:16.
</margin>

this is a minor point. As for what they further add regarding *Jacob* as the author of the evening prayer, this seems to be extracted by them from the fact that *Jacob* is said to have *COME FROM THE FIELD* **IN THE EVENING**. Rather, they sought it from the passage in *Genesis 28:11*, in which it is said of *Jacob* that he "interceded" <note>original: ויפגע / vayifga; often interpreted by the Sages as "prayed."</note> or prayed in that place (namely *Bethel*) and stayed there overnight. See *Buxtorf* in *The Jewish Synagogue, chapter 10, page 220.* <note>Johannes Buxtorf was a leading 17th-century Christian Hebraist.</note> That *Jacob* meditated and prayed in the field following the example of his father—that, I confess, the text does not explicitly state, but it is by no means absurd to suggest it is implied.

Beyond these things, there is also a tradition circulated among the Hebrew nation that *Jacob* and his sons began, by their own example, to teach their descendants that solemn profession of the *Unity of God*, which is part of the **reading or recitation of the Shema** <note>original Greek/Hebrew: τῆς קרית שמע / tēs Keriath Shema</note>—that is, the section "Hear, O Israel" (about which, God willing, more will be said later) to be repeated every morning and evening by every Israelite. The Israelites wished for this article on the *unity of God* to be deeply fixed in the minds of their people. But let us collect the whole text of *Maimonides* on this matter: *Laws of the Recitation of the*

<margin>
*Shema*, chapter 1. §. 4.
</margin>

"One who recites the Shema, when he finishes the first verse, says in a whisper: 'Blessed be the name of the glory of His kingdom forever and ever.' And then he returns and reads in his usual way 'And you shall love the Lord your God' until the end. And why do we read it this way? It is a tradition in our hands that at the hour when our father Jacob gathered his sons in Egypt at the time of his death, he commanded them and urged them regarding the Unity of the Name and the way of the Lord in which Abraham and Isaac his father walked. And he asked them and said to them: 'My sons, perhaps there is a defect among you—someone who does not stand with me in the Unity of the Name?' as he said..."

### BOOK I. PART II. ON THE ORIGIN.

<note>The following is a translation of the Hebrew passage at the top of the page, which recounts a traditional Midrashic story about the death of Jacob.</note>
For our teacher Moses said to us: "Lest there be among you a man or woman, etc." <note>Deuteronomy 29:18</note>. They all answered and said: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One" <note>The *Shema*, Deuteronomy 6:4</note>. That is to say: "Hear from us, our father Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is One." The elder <note>Jacob</note> opened his mouth and said: "Blessed be the name of the glory of His kingdom forever and ever." Therefore, all Israel is accustomed to say the praise which the elder Israel praised after this verse.

<margin>Deuteronomy 6:4.</margin>
He who recites the section <note>original Latin: *Pericopam*</note> "Hear," etc., having recited the first verse, silently adds the words: **BLESSED BE THE NAME OF THE GLORY OF HIS KINGDOM FOREVER AND EVER.** He then repeats the text, and continues to recite in his usual manner:
<margin>verse 5.</margin>
*And you shall love the Lord your God* etc., until the end of it. But what is the reason for this manner of recitation? It has been handed down to us from long ages ago that at the time when the Patriarch Jacob gathered his sons in Egypt, being near his death <note>original: *fato suo proximus*</note>, he commanded them and spoke very seriously concerning the article of the Unity of God, and concerning the way of the Lord in which Abraham and Isaac, his father, walked. He asked them and said to them: "My sons! Perhaps there is one among you whose soul is profane, who does not receive this article of the Unity of God with a well-founded faith as I do?" This was much like how Moses warned the Israelites in his own time:
<margin>Deuteronomy 29:17.</margin>
*Lest there be among you man or woman,* etc. They all responded and said: **HEAR, ISRAEL, THE LORD, OUR GOD, THE LORD IS ONE.** It was as if they wished to say: "Hear, our father Israel, from us: The Lord, our God, the Lord is one." To which the elderly parent opened his mouth, returning these words: *Blessed be the name of the glory of His kingdom forever and ever.* For this reason, indeed, all Israelites have become accustomed to offer this praise after that solemn profession of the Unity of God from this verse, following the example of Jacob, their father.

We see here how deep the Jews lay the foundations of their rituals—deeper, certainly, than they ought. For that this entire tradition is legendary <note>original: *fabulosa*</note> and crafted by an overly sharp wit from the words of Moses: *Hear, Israel* <note>original Hebrew: שמע ישראל / Shema Yisrael</note>, which they took into their minds to interpret as "Hear, [the Patriarch] Israel"—this is so clear to anyone paying attention and considering the whole matter that nothing could be more so. However, the plan of our undertaking will require us to say more about this in our following discussion.

Moreover, just as modern Jews trace the prayer customs of a later age back to the very birth of their nation, so too it is not established for me with certain and fair reliability whether they assigned fixed places of prayer to this age of the Patriarchs. It deserves to be weighed, however, that after Jacob...

# CHAPTER I. CONCERNING SYNAGOGES.

<margin>Genesis 28:21.</margin>
Moses attributed this saying to Jacob, who had sensed the presence of the Divine Power at Bethel:
<note>original Hebrew: והאבן הזאת אשר שמתי מצבה יהיה בית אלהים</note>
"And this stone, which I have set as a pillar, shall be the house of God," <note>Genesis 28:22</note> *and of all that you give me, I will give a tenth back to you.* It is truly remarkable that "the **HOUSE OF GOD**" <note>Hebrew: *Beth Elohim*</note> is already mentioned in this place. Ibn Ezra <note>A famous 12th-century Spanish rabbi and biblical commentator</note> in his commentary on this passage understood it as: <note>original Hebrew: מקום קבוע לתפלה</note> **A FIXED PLACE DEDICATED TO PRAYERS**; which is essentially how <term>Proseuchae</term> <note>From the Greek word for "prayer," often used in antiquity to describe Jewish prayer houses before the term "synagogue" became standard</note> or Synagogues are defined. However, the simplicity of the text is satisfied if we say that *Jacob* intended to build an *altar* in this place and publicly profess the worship of the Divine Name, which is called the *invocation of the name of Jehovah*. For temples, or sacred buildings, seem to owe their origin to later centuries.

<margin>Genesis 35:1, 7.</margin>
Indeed, subsequent events confirmed this explanation of Jacob’s words; furthermore, it is certain that the ancients were accustomed to pour out their prayers at the *altars* they had built.

<margin>See Pierius on Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book 8, verse 719.</margin>
Therefore, "the House of God" must signify here a place where God was deemed to be present in a singular way, to be worshipped by Jacob and his descendants with sacrifices, prayers, and thanksgivings. The main point is this: during the interval of time from the restoration of the world after the flood until Moses, the Patriarchs worshipped God through sacrifices, prayers, praises, and other domestic sacred exercises. They followed that same simplicity of worship which reason, exercised through faith, had already introduced before the flood. Thus, the worship of the Synagogues—which does not differ greatly from common reason—was lightly foreshadowed, though the foundations of the Synagogues and their specific, private customs were by no means yet laid.
