-># CONCERNING THE ORIGIN, BOOK I, PART II.<-

<margin>
Exodus 27:21 <note>The author likely intends Exodus 33:7, which describes Moses pitching the tent outside the camp.</note>
Commentary on this passage.
Chapter 36:1, 2, 3.
Exodus 18:7.
</margin>

What pertains to us in this narrative is that Moses pitched a certain tent outside the camp and called it <note>original Hebrew: אהל מועד</note> **the Tent of Meeting**, to which every pious Israelite who wished to consult God is said to have gone out. But what kind of tent was this, and of what nature? Would you call it the **Tabernacle**, which is usually called the *Tent of Meeting*? **Ibn Ezra** <note>A renowned 12th-century biblical commentator</note> rightly denies this. Indeed, we read that the construction of the Tabernacle was only completed later. Therefore, it is better to understand this as **Moses' own tent**, which is mentioned elsewhere, or some other tent erected by Moses for the time being until the Tabernacle—the form of which God had prescribed—was fully built. The former view seems to come closer to the truth.

However, the question that chiefly concerns us is: why was this tent called <note>original Hebrew: אהל מועד</note> **the Tent of Meeting**? Was it perhaps because the **Israelites** were accustomed to **gather** there to pour out their prayers to God at fixed hours? Or was it because the people **gathered** there so that they might be **taught** by Moses and instructed in the knowledge of the secret precepts of the Law? Certainly, if that is true, then this *Tent* can not inaptly be compared to a **Synagogue** or some kind of **Lecture Hall** sacred to the explanation of the Law.

And this was the view of the **Paraphrasts** <note>Translators who created the Aramaic Targums, which often added explanatory details to the biblical text</note> and certain other interpreters, both ancient and modern. **Onkelos** <note>The author of the standard Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> seems to have had something similar in mind, rendering the text thus: *Moses took the Tabernacle and pitched it outside the camp, far from the camp,* <note>original Aramaic: וקרי ליה משכן בית אולפנא ויהי כל דתבע אולפן מן קדם יי נפק למשכן בית אולפנא מברא למשריתא</note> *and he called it the* **Tabernacle of the House of Teaching**, *and everyone who sought* **instruction** *from the presence of the Lord went out to the* **Tabernacle of the House of Teaching**, *which was outside the camp.*

But the **son of Uziel** <note>Referring to the Targum Pseudo-Jonathan, an expansive Aramaic paraphrase</note> is much clearer: <note>original Aramaic: ברם ית משכנא נסב מתמן ופריסיה ליה מברא למשריתא אדחיק יתיה מן משרית עמא דאתנרון תרין אלפין אמין והוה קרי ליה משכן בית אולפנא והוי כל מאן דחזר בתתובא בלב שלים קדם יי הוא נפיק למשכן בית אולפנא דמברא למשריתא מודי על חוביה מצלי על חוביה ומצלי ומשתבק ליה</note> *But he took the Tabernacle from there and extended it for himself outside the camp, moving it far from the camp of the people—a distance of two thousand cubits* <note>This distance corresponds to the "Sabbath day's journey," the maximum distance one was permitted to walk on the holy day</note>—*and he called it the* **Tabernacle of the House of Teaching**; *and everyone who returned in repentance with a whole heart before the Lord would go out to the* **Tabernacle of the House of Teaching** *outside the camp, confessing his sins and praying regarding his sins, and he would pray and be forgiven.* But...

### CHAPTER 3. CONCERNING SYNAGOGUES.

<margin>On this passage.</margin>
...converted with repentance and a whole heart before the Lord, he would go out to the **TABERNACLE OF THE HOUSE OF INSTRUCTION** <note>original Latin: TABERNACULUM DOMUS DOCTRINÆ</note>, which had been pitched outside the camp, confessing his sins and asking for their forgiveness; and to the one who asked, the sin was pardoned. **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Rabbi Solomon Isaaci, known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval French commentator</note> does not deviate far from this view here, where he interprets "Tent of Meeting" <note>original Hebrew: אהל מועד (Ohel Moed)</note> as a **House of assembly for those seeking the Law** <note>original Hebrew: בית ועד למבקשי תורה (Beit va'ad le-mavakshe Torah)</note>.

<margin>On this passage.</margin>
<margin>On chapter 3, 1.</margin>
<margin>2. 3.</margin>
<margin>Commentary on Exodus 28:21.</margin>
Examples of this exposition are also found in the **Baal Ha-Turim** <note>A commentary by Jacob ben Asher (c. 1269–1343)</note>: *And it came to pass that everyone who sought the Lord went out.* <note>original Hebrew: והיה כל מבקש יהוה יצא</note> *From this you may gather that it is necessary for a man to go out into the public* <note>The Hebrew "לגלות" (laglot) implies wandering or going into exile to find a teacher</note> *in order to learn the Law.* <note>original Hebrew: מכאן שצריך אדם לגלות כדי שילמוד תורה</note> Similar things can be read in the **Targum of the Song of Songs** <note>An Aramaic paraphrase and expansion of the biblical book</note>. Observe, however, that the Paraphrasts **Onkelos** and **Jonathan** <note>Authors of the standard Aramaic translations of the Pentateuch and Prophets</note> are accustomed to translate this name *Ohel Moed*, when used for the Divine Tabernacle, as the **Tabernacle of the Appointed Time** <note>original Aramaic: משכן זמנא (Mishkan Zemana)</note>, which is rendered by some interpreters as the *Tabernacle of Time* and by others as the *Tabernacle of the Covenant*; but you might translate it as the **Tent of the Stated Assembly**. For there is one and the same meaning for the word *Zemana* <note>Aramaic for time/appointment</note> among the Chaldeans as there is for the concept of *Moed* <note>Hebrew for appointed time/place</note> among the Hebrews. **Münster** <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a prominent Christian Hebraist</note>, not indeed on this passage but on another where the *Tabernacle of God* is first called the *Ohel Moed* or *Tent of Meeting*, writes thus concerning the reason for the name: **THE TABERNACLE OF TESTIMONY** *was so called because the congregation of Israel would assemble there for praying and sacrificing.* The annotations of the **Tremellius** <note>Immanuel Tremellius (1510–1580), a Jewish-born Calvinist scholar</note> text tend toward the exact same point: *He proclaimed to all who would consult God that they must come to that place, from which the name* **TENT OF MEETING** *was derived.* I would not say for certain whether the **Belgian Interpreters** <note>Translators of the Dutch "Statenvertaling" Bible</note> intended something else when they transposed this expression as: *The tent of the coming-together* <note>original Dutch: De tente der t'samen-komste</note>.

<margin>Exodus 29:42, 43.</margin>
But although there is nothing inconsistent in this tent being called the *Tent of Meeting* because the Israelites were accustomed to gather there to consult the mouth of Jehovah through Moses—indeed, even if that can be truly predicated of this Tent—it is nevertheless certain that this Tabernacle was not named the *Tent of Meeting* for that reason above all others. For in the very history of Moses, another reason for that name is given by God Himself, one that is clear and involved in no shadows. Recall with me these words: *A perpetual burnt offering throughout your generations at the door of the* **TABERNACLE OF MEETING** *before Jehovah,* **WHERE I WILL MEET WITH YOU** <note>original Hebrew: אשר איועד לכם שמה (asher iva’ed lakhem shammah)</note> *to speak to you there,* where **I WILL BE PRESENT BY APPOINTMENT**

## ON THE ORIGINS, BOOK I, PART II.

<margin>On the Laws of the Hebrews, Book 2, Chapter 5.</margin>
"In every place where I shall cause my name to be remembered, I will come to you and bless you." <note>original Hebrew: בכל המקום אשר אזכיר את שמי אבוא אליך וברכתיך; original Latin: In omni loco, ubi recordari fecero nominis mei, veniam ad te, & benedicam tibi. This is a translation of Exodus 20:24.</note> A man of undoubted learning, **John Spencer** <note>John Spencer (1630–1693) was an English theologian and scholar, often considered the father of comparative religion</note>, has recently been laboring to shed some light on this text; for it is somewhat obscure. He observed that the word *Zakar* <note>Hebrew: זכר</note> was accepted in antiquity not only with the meaning of **remembering and recollecting**, but also of **worshipping, performing a sacred duty**, and (especially in the *Hiphil* <note>The "Hiphil" is a causative verb form in Hebrew grammar; here it would mean "to cause to remember" or "to cause to be worshipped"</note> form) of **celebrating**.

<margin>
Isaiah 66:3.
Amos 6:11.
1 Chronicles 16:4.
</margin>
He adduces certain passages from the sacred Authors to confirm this. He adds that if this opinion remains firm, it lends support to the view of those who believe that the word for **Priest** <note>original Latin: Sacer. The author is referencing an etymological theory linking the Latin word for sacred/priest to the Hebrew root for memory or male</note> is derived from *Zakar*, meaning memory or worship. We, however, leave that point undecided. He continues, judging that this sense of the word in this text is to be preferred over its other meanings, as it is simple and fits the context perfectly; so much so, that those words—"In every place where I shall have placed the memory of my name"—would, according to him, be understood thus: **Wherever I shall present myself to be worshipped and celebrated.** What prevents us, however, from pointing out that this opinion is burdened by some difficulty? For *Hizkir* <note>Hebrew: הזכיר, the causative form of the root</note> indeed signifies **to mention, to praise**, and, if you like, **to worship and to pray** (though this is rarer), yet never **to present oneself to be mentioned or worshipped in some place.** Those two things—to worship, and to present oneself to be worshipped—differ entirely. Furthermore, the meaning of these words: "where I shall present myself to be worshipped, there I will come to you," is not very plain or clear. For according to the mind of the **distinguished Author** <note>Referring again to John Spencer</note>, it would mean this: **Where I have caused you to pour out your prayers to me, there I will present myself to be present with you.** But in truth, God would thus indicate no specific place in these words where He wished to be worshipped by the Israelites; which, nevertheless, He seems to wish to indicate by this precept. For it has remained obscure and doubtful until now where God wished to present Himself to be worshipped and to be adored by the Israelites; whereas, as I have already noted, God seems in these words to altogether designate and define the places of His worship by certain characteristics, so that the Israelites would not remain in doubt as to where they should worship God. Therefore, it has pleased others instead to conceive the Lawgiver's intention thus: **Wherever you pray to me and celebrate my name, there I will come to you and bless you.** And the **Vulgate** <note>The 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible used by the Western Church</note> seems to tend toward this, for which reason it has already been criticized by **Fagius** <note>Paul Fagius (1504–1549) was a German Renaissance scholar of Hebrew</note>: "In every place where the memory of my name shall be..."

<meta>The catchword "veniam" (I will come) indicates the first word of the next page, continuing the quotation: "...I will come to you."</meta>

<summary>This page debates the interpretation of Exodus 20:24, specifically focusing on whether the Hebrew root Z-K-R (to remember) implies a specific physical place for worship or a more general act of prayer and celebration. The author critiques John Spencer's causative interpretation, arguing it fails to clearly identify where God commanded the Israelites to worship.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of sacred spaces and the "Tent of Meeting," transitioning from the Rabbinical interpretations of the House of Instruction to the biblical precedents for establishing altars where God manifests His presence.</meta>

->### ON THE ORIGIN, BOOK I, PART II.<-

...is it? These things, if I am not mistaken [are the meaning]: *Wherever I shall have demonstrated by certain arguments that I am present, there I will come to you, and I will bless you.* The words, therefore, seem to be translated as follows: *Wherever I have celebrated* (or, made famous) *my name, there I will come to you.* The word *hazkir* <note>original Hebrew: הזכיר</note> means *to be remembered* and *to cause to remember*, and by consequence *to celebrate* or *to make famous*. Hence it is quite rightly used regarding men who worship God, but especially regarding those who celebrate God and proclaim His praises. 

But God Himself can also *celebrate* Himself. God, I say, can Himself make His name famous in a certain place. This occurs when He causes signs and evidence of *His presence* to exist in a certain place, especially indeed of His *glory* or His *grace*, because signs of Divine Grace most of all attract the sinner to show reverence to God in this or that place. So that we may perceive this better, it will be useful to observe that the Ancients were accustomed to worship God most especially in those places where God had *previously* appeared to them—that is, where He had given them some unique proof of His presence. Thus we read in the history of Abraham:

<margin>Genesis 12:3, verse 7.</margin>
*The Lord appeared to Abraham and said, to your seed I will give this land.* What follows? HE BUILT AN ALTAR THERE TO THE LORD, WHO HAD APPEARED TO HIM. Then indeed, in the context of the following history, it is recounted that Abraham pitched his tent anew not far from that place (for he had moved away from there) and again invoked the Divine name there—that is, he professed it in public.

<margin>Chapter 13:4.</margin>
The words are: *At the place* <note>original Hebrew: אל המקום (el ha-makom)</note> OF THE ALTAR, WHICH HE HAD BUILT THERE IN THE BEGINNING, <note>original Hebrew: ויקרא שם אברהם בשם יהוה (va-yikra shem Avraham be-shem Yehovah)</note> AND Abraham INVOKED the name of the Lord THERE. In this place, God had shown Himself present to *Abraham*, which is why he built an altar there, so that it might exist as a perpetual monument of that apparition. Therefore, having returned again to that same place, he *invoked* the name of God, who had once shown Himself favorable there. I think we should refer to nothing else what is told of Jacob in the same history.

<margin>Chapter 28:15.</margin>
God appeared to him as he slept at *Bethel*, which was called *Luz* <note>Bethel means "House of God"; Luz was its earlier Canaanite name</note>: Having woken up, he said: <note>original Hebrew: אכן יהוה במקום הזה (akhen Yehovah ba-makom ha-zeh)</note> *Surely the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.* What more? Jacob placed a *stone* there as a <note>original Hebrew: מצבה (matzevah)</note> *pillar*, and poured oil over it, and vowed that this stone would be <note>original Hebrew: בית אלהים (Beit Elohim)</note> *the House of God*—that is, that he [would worship] God at this stone...

### CHAPTER 3. CONCERNING SYNAGOGUES.

"...I will come to you." As if, **Fagius** <note>Paul Fagius (1504–1549) was a German Renaissance scholar of Hebrew and a Protestant reformer</note> adds, *God wished to find favor wherever men might establish worship for Him according to their own judgment.* The **Syriac** <note>The Peshitta, the ancient Syriac translation of the Bible</note> version openly gives itself to this sense: *In every place where you shall remember my name, I will come to you and bless you.* <note>original Syriac: בכל אתר דתדכר שמי : אתא לותך ואברכך</note> The **Arabic** version says: *And in whatever place you remember my name, I will hear you and come to you.* We must not overlook the **Author of the Jerusalem Paraphrase** <note>The Targum Yerushalmi, an Aramaic translation and expansion of the Torah that often adds interpretive detail</note>, who writes: *In every place where you mention <term>MY HOLY NAME</term>, my Word will be revealed to you and will bless you.* <note>original Aramaic: בכל אתר דתדכרו ית שמי קדישא מימרי הגלי עליכון ומברך יתכון</note> But perhaps the Author, by the term <term>שם קדישא</term> (*Holy Name*), understood the name **Jehovah**, and intended to say (as is evident from **Solomon Jarchi** <note>A common Latinization for Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator</note>) that the glorious presence of God is revealed to His people in the place where the <term>HOLY NAME OF GOD</term> is lawfully pronounced.

<margin>In the Annotations on this passage.</margin>
**Diodati** <note>Giovanni Diodati (1576–1649), a Swiss-born Italian Protestant theologian famous for his Bible translations</note> differs little from these: *Let it not be a matter of permanent altars, as if to attach my grace to some specific place by imagination; I will hear you in any place indifferently, wherever I give you the command or the occasion to be invoked.* <note>original French: "Ne basti point des autels perdurables, comme pour attacher, a la phantasie, ma grace en quelque lieu: je t'exaucerai en tout lieu indifferemment, ou je te donnerai commandement, ou occasion d'estre invoqué."</note> If this interpretation holds, and the Lawgiver truly commanded **His worship**, adoration, and the celebration of His name in any place whatsoever by these words, then surely what more impressive evidence could be produced for the <term>Construction of Synagogues</term> from the <term>Mosaic Laws</term>, or indeed from the entire Old Testament?

<margin>On this passage.</margin>
It is certainly not irrelevant to note here that **Baal Hatturim** <note>Jacob ben Asher (c. 1269–1343), a pivotal Jewish legal authority often cited by his book title, the "Ba'al Ha-Turim"</note> (whether moved by this reason, I do not know) has, in a way, applied this text to synagogues. He annotated it thus: *The word <term>Abô</term> ("I will come") contains the number ten, as if God wished to signify that if I find ten men in the Synagogue, I will come to you and bless you.* <note>original Hebrew: אבוא עולה עשרה לומר שאם אמצא עשרה בבית הכנסת אבוא אליך וברכתיך. This is an example of Gematria, where the numerical value of the Hebrew letters in "I will come" (אבוא) totals ten, the minimum number (Minyan) required for communal Jewish prayer.</note> However, I do not believe this latter sense, which we have discussed thus far, is actually present in the words. For it does not say, *where you celebrate my name, there I will come to you*, but where **I** *cause my name to be remembered; there I will come to you and bless you.* These two meanings differ greatly, as this latter interpretation sufficiently proves that God is speaking not of every place, but of a specific place. For He does not cause His name to be remembered everywhere, but in a certain place or in certain places. What, then, is the true and genuine meaning of this gracious promise?

### CHAPTER 3. CONCERNING SYNAGOGUES.

...to bless. But **Onkelos** <note>The author of the most famous Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Torah, traditionally a convert to Judaism</note> and **Uzielides** <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, to whom an Aramaic translation of the Prophets and a later Targum on the Torah are attributed</note> explain God's mind more distinctly. <margin>
Spencer, *On the Reason for the Laws of Moses*, Book 3, Chapter 3, Section 1.
</margin>
And certainly, since in the entire Law of Moses there exists no explicit commandment regarding the offering of prayers—as has been observed by others long ago—who would wonder that nothing is found in the statutes of that Law regarding the **Structure of Synagogues**, which are primarily dedicated to prayers? The ancient Israelites were certainly not slow in pouring out prayers to God, for indeed, reason itself incites and impels every man to this in times of great necessity. One may also find examples of those praying, as well as formulas for prayers and thanksgivings, in the Law. Sacrifices also were always held by them and by all other peoples as aids to prayer. Nevertheless, you will not easily find an express command regarding prayers themselves in the Law. Therefore, you would search there in vain for any precept regarding **Synagogues**.

I am only disputing this now: whether there were public places scattered throughout the land of **Canaan** in which the people gathered on *Sabbaths* and *Feast days* to offer prayers and hear the reading of the Law, with the *Levites presiding?* I do not think this can be proven to have existed among the Jews in the time of Joshua and the Judges, which is the period under discussion. 

As for **Bertram's** conjecture that what were later called the *High Places* <term>original Latin: "Excelsa"; referring to the biblical "Bamoth"</term> perhaps flowed from this—because he considers it likely that these places were in a more elevated part of the City—just as he did not dare to place confidence in that conjecture himself, so he is, beyond all doubt, mistaken. I would not want to deny that Prophets and other men dedicated to sacred studies lived in elevated places both inside and outside the cities. Truly, I cannot bring myself to believe that the name *Bamoth* <note>original Hebrew: "במות"</note>, or *High Places*, originated from that. 

For those *High Places* were consecrated to idols, built on high mountains and precipices. For the closer the Gentiles were to heaven, the more easily and more presently they believed they would have the *Divine Presence* <term>original Latin: "Numen"</term>. 

<margin>
Leviticus 26:30.

</margin>

How, then, shall we believe that the *High Places* originated from that ritual of gathering, praying, explaining the Word of God, and sacrificing in high places which Bertram mentions? # CHAPTER 4. OF SYNAGOGUES.

<margin>Judges 6:26; 13:19</margin>
...Manoah <note>The text reads "noah," the end of "Manoah," the father of Samson.</note> are said to have offered sacrifices upon a rock (in the former passage the Hebrew word *Sela* <note>original: סלע (*sela*), meaning a crag or cliff</note> is used; in the latter, *Tzur* <note>original: צור (*tzur*), meaning a rock or boulder</note> is used), who would conclude from this that there were certain fixed places where the people were accustomed to gather for prayers, instruction, and sacrifices? For that is what would need to be proven from those examples. The cases and circumstances of both these sacrifices were altogether unique. Who would deny that the people often sacrificed on rocks, mountains, hills, and various steep and high places as long as God had not yet clearly designated a specific place for His worship? Indeed, it is clear from these very examples that they often sacrificed outside the location of the Tabernacle, with God not only permitting it but even **commanding** it. This might be seen as contrary to the written Law, except during that period when the **Ark** wandered outside the Tabernacle and was kept in private homes. But God Himself could grant exceptions or waivers regarding His own law—which decided the modes and circumstances of His worship—according to His good pleasure and the various conditions of His people’s state. However, it does not immediately follow that there were fixed places where the people were solemnly gathered into an assembly at stated times for sacred rites; much less does it follow that the people were gathered in this way to pray and hear an explanation of the Law.

Indeed, you cannot even conclude this from the evidence that **Bertram** <note>Bonaventure Corneille Bertram (1531–1594), a scholar of the Hebrew Republic</note> produced from the history of **Samuel**. 
<margin>1 Samuel 9:12; 16:2</margin>
<margin>1 Samuel 7:9, 17</margin>
Samuel ascended to **high places** (called a *Bamah* <note>original: במה (*bamah*), a local altar or "high place" often used before the Temple was built</note>) outside the Tabernacle to perform sacrifices with the people, to celebrate a banquet prepared from those sacrifices, and to bless them. It cannot be denied that he did this often (even if the first passage noted by Bertram is understood by some to refer merely to a banquet held in a prominent part of the City). But who would conclude from this that **Sacred Buildings** were constructed in those places, similar to the **Synagogues** of today? It is certain that *Altars* were built by Samuel and others, but it is not established that *Synagogues* were built. 

If that cannot be proven from those facts, by what logic will you argue that these places were intended for prayers and the explanation of the Law, for which the people were gathered solemnly on fixed days? 
<margin>1 Samuel 16:2</margin>
In fact, it is clear that the instance of sacrifice described in the last piece of evidence produced by Bertram is entirely unique. Therefore, that evidence has no power to prove that solemn sacrifices outside the Tabernacle were an established custom, performed at set times within a congregation of the people. 
<margin>1 Samuel 20:6</margin>
More weight might be given to what is read in that same history concerning the fixed, annual sacrifice of the family of **Jesse**. But, as I said, from...

<meta>This page continues the author's argument that early Israelite gatherings outside the central Tabernacle do not constitute "synagogues" in the formal sense. ### ON THE ORIGIN, BOOK I, PART II.

Through these and similar examples, it is indeed proven that sacrifices were offered and prayers were poured out outside the Tabernacle; however, it is not proven that there were *Synagogues*, which is the sole point under dispute. Truly, whatever the case may be, it is relevant to my point to observe that any place in which prayers are combined with *sacrifices* is not categorized by me as a Synagogue; rather, I carefully distinguish such places from Synagogues and their form of worship. That sacred place which is called a *Synagogue* must be uniquely consecrated to prayers and the exposition of the Law. For in this respect a Synagogue differs from a Temple: the latter is designated for *sacrifices*, while the former is for *prayers*. The latter requires a *physical* <note>original Latin: *carnalem*, literally "fleshly," referring to the animal sacrifices and physical rituals of the Temple</note> worship, while the former requires a *spiritual worship*. If you join sacrifices to prayers in a certain place, then I would call that place a *Temple*, or a shadow and prelude of a Temple, but I would not call it a *Synagogue*. 

Therefore, if it is true, as Bertram <note>Bonaventure Corneille Bertram (1531–1594), a Genevan Hebraist who wrote extensively on the "Republic of the Hebrews."</note> contends, that there were certain specific places outside the Tabernacle where the people used to gather for prayers and sacrifices, those places had nothing in common with *Synagogues* and their worship. Instead, they imitated the Tabernacle and the worship established there by God. Since it was burdensome for the people to travel to the Tabernacle of the Lord, they sought at home what they ought to have sought abroad.

It is therefore more relevant to consider what the same author mentions regarding the company of Prophets gathered on a certain hill, which is called *Bamah* <note>original Hebrew: במה, usually translated as a "High Place" or "shrine"</note>, and is referred to as the *Hill of God*.
<margin>1 Samuel 10:5</margin>
But we shall explain that passage in the place where we treat specifically the manner of institution observed in this state of affairs among the Israelites. For although these were confused times for the Jewish Republic, during which the people worshipped God quite neglectfully, who would believe that they lacked all knowledge and instruction in the Law? But, as mentioned, more on this in what follows.

...the people interpretations of the Law, and that they should bless and celebrate the Lord. Thus says the Paraphrast <note>original: *Paraphrastes*; a term for the author of the Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note>, who in his version of this and other Books is accustomed to wander somewhat freely. But in the Hebrew text, as anyone can see, there is absolutely no mention of Synagogues. The legislators and the noble-minded who were among the Jews are stirred up by *Deborah* to give praises to God for the immense benefit which had been granted to them by the singular grace of the Divine Power. But no appearance of an argument present in the text would persuade you that those praises ought to be said to God in Synagogues. 

But the Paraphrast—who shares this trait with all his fellow countrymen who were nurtured in the doctrine and love of ancestral traditions <note>original Greek: *πατροπαραδότων* (patroparadotōn); referring to the oral traditions passed down through generations</note>—everywhere imagines things for himself. He thought that by the words *choqeqim* <note>original Hebrew: חוקקים; literally "lawgivers" or "governors"</note> and *hamitnadbim ba'am* <note>original Hebrew: המתנדבים בעם; "those who offered themselves willingly among the people"</note> one should understand the *Presidents of the Academies and Synagogues*, those most studious Interpreters of the Divine Law. 

But by what art can that be elicited from the text? Indeed, even if I were to grant that by "the lawgivers" and "those who offered themselves willingly" one should understand *Doctors and Scholars skilled in the Divine Law*—the kind of men who were never lacking in the Jewish Commonwealth, as will be shown in its proper place—it does not follow from this that either the *Academies* or the *Synagogues* of that age were similar to those which the later times of that Commonwealth finally saw. 

We have no need for more words to tear down this supposition. It will be our choice, even if not at all compelled to do so, to add to what has been said: that by "the lawgivers" it seems that in this place, we should not designate the *Teachers of the Law* so much as the *Judges*, nobles, and magistrates of the people, who prescribe Laws to their subjects and define punishments for those who transgress them. 

For the speech of *Deborah*, as is fitting, is directed especially to those who, through her command <note>original Greek: *κέλευμα* (keleuma); a call or summons</note>, had been roused to aid the wretched affairs of the people and to fight against the Canaanite enemies. *Indeed, it occurs to me that those* **lawgivers of Israel** <note>original Hebrew: חוקקי ישראל (*choqeqi Yisrael*)</note> *are actually Scribes, whose duty it is to record in a Book the more notable deeds and events of the times, as well as the causes and outcomes of wars; Deborah indeed advises them to bless the Lord, and when they come to record this war in writing, they should primarily attribute its outcome to Divine Grace. <meta>catchword: ascen-</meta>

<margin>
In the Lexicon <note>Likely referring to a Hebrew dictionary of the time</note> at the word פא <note>Hebrew: *Pe*, the letter or root for "corner/side"</note>

**THE PEOPLE**, all the tribes of Israel in the assembly of the people of God; *four hundred thousand men, on foot, prepared to draw the sword*. By these פנות העם <note>Hebrew: *pinnoth ha'am*</note> **"Corners of the people,"** I say, certain writers have understood the Magistrates and the supreme Prefects <note>High-ranking officials or leaders</note> of the people. But from the text itself it is clear that this exposition is of no value. For these פנות כל העם **"Corners of all the people"** are explained by the phrase כל שבטי ישראל **"all the tribes of Israel,"** and they are said to make up this very number of four hundred thousand soldiers. It is certain, therefore, that not the Prefects of the people, but the people themselves are designated by this phrase. But in what sense is the people called the *Corners of the people*, you ask? I will respond with *Cocceius* <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a prominent Dutch theologian and Hebraist</note>, that it is because the whole people, gathered into one, stood in a formation exhibiting the shape of a house having corners. This is, without a doubt, the true reason for the expression. Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a Jewish statesman and commentator</note>, who indeed thinks with us that the Prefects of the people are by no means indicated by the word "Corners," enters upon this path of explanation: that by "Corners of the people" are denoted the tribes of the people, standing separately each in its own place or corner and pitching camp. The Dutch translators <note>Latin: *Interpretes Belgæ*, referring to the translators of the *Statenvertaling* or Dutch Authorized Version</note> took the Hebrew words as if, instead of "Corners of all the people," it were written *from the corners of all the people*: *And (from) the corners of all the people, all the tribes of Israel presented themselves in the Assembly of God's people.* <note>Original Dutch: "Ende (uyt) de hoecken des gantschen volcks stelden sigh alle de stammen Israels in de Vergaderinge van Godts volck."</note> But this version of theirs is somewhat harsh, nor does it satisfy the Hebrew phrase. That interpretation of the words which we have brought forward is the simplest, and for that reason is to be preferred over the others. In any case, it is beyond doubt that this passage is not dealing with the Prefects of the people, gathered in a certain place apart from the commoners; and therefore, the objection which rests on this foundation is of no value.

Indeed, I would also wish it to be observed in the *second* place that there is a reason in the text from which you may conclude that the people at this time and occasion did not meet at *Mizpah* to pray, but to take counsel in a grave and anxious matter. If this can be proven, then the whole hypothesis collapses upon which this **"Mizpah Synagogue"** is built. Evidence for my words is found in the following account of this history, where it is said,
<margin>
Chapter 20, verse 18.
</note>
that the people, intending to pray to God and consult Him, *ascended to Bethel*, or into the *House of God*. Let us cite the very words of the sacred text: *And they arose,* ויעלו בית-אל <note>Hebrew: *vaya'alu Beit-El*</note> *and they ascended to the house of God, and they questioned God, and the Children of Israel said, "Which of us shall go up first to the battle—"*

It is certainly clear from these testimonies that the people went up to the House of God to pray, to perform sacrifices, and to consult the mouth of the Lord <note>To seek divine oracular guidance</note>; from this it is gathered that *Mizpah* was at that time a place of counsel <note>A political or military meeting place</note>, but *Shiloh* <note>original: *Silunta*</note>, where the Tabernacle was, was considered the place sacred for prayers and sacrifices. For we do not read that the people prayed *at Mizpah*. On the contrary, we read that the people went elsewhere to pray. What reason remains, then, to conclude from this history that there was a Synagogue at *Mizpah*? The place, indeed, into which the people went up to pray, is called <note>original Hebrew: בית אל</note> *Bethel*, which may be translated: *The House of God.* Interpreters have made it a matter of doubt as to which place this was. Some think it is *Shiloh*, or rather the Tabernacle of God built at *Shiloh*. Others think it was *Bethel* <note>The specific city of that name</note>, a place sacred due to frequent divine appearances and for that reason famous enough in the sacred history of the earliest times. We, along with most distinguished men whose judgment it is right to value highly, incline toward the first opinion. We think, I say, that by *Bethel* or the *House of God*, the Tabernacle is entirely to be understood here, which was still standing at *Shiloh* at that time. There is a clear reason for this in the same account. For where the historian had recorded the prayers poured out to God by the people for the third time in this place, he continues: *And the children of Israel inquired of the Lord,*

He argues, I say, that it should be understood as referring to the *Ark*, which must then be conceived as having been transported to that place where the people are said to have assembled *before the Lord* or *to the Lord*. Among other passages, he cites this one of ours from the *Book of Judges*, in which the people are said to have gathered at Mizpah <note>original Hebrew: אל יהוה</note> *to the Lord*. *Adrichomius* <note>Christian van Adrichom (1533–1585), a Dutch priest and cartographer</note> agrees entirely with this same opinion; in his description of this town, he states expressly: *The Ark of the Covenant was once there, and for that reason the people of Israel assembled there for prayer*, citing this very same testimony whose meaning we are investigating. But I truly do not know what compelled these learned men to that conclusion? For nowhere in Sacred History is it said, as far as I know, that the *Ark was at Mizpah*. To wish to deduce that solely from that expression, *before the Lord*, seems to me to be too weak an argument. For who doubts that someone can be said to *appear before the Lord*, and to *come to the Lord*, even if he does not come *to the Ark*? It is true that he who appeared *before the Ark* was said, in the style of the Sacred Writers, to appear *before the Lord*; yet you cannot conclude from this—except rashly—that no one can be said to *appear before the Lord* unless he appears *before the Ark*. 

I will, therefore, state what seems to me to be the most excellent reason for the expression by which the Israelites are declared to have assembled at Mizpah <note>original Hebrew: אל יהוה</note> *to the Lord*. For therein lies the whole difficulty. Great and solemn assemblies and gatherings of the people of God were not only called together, as it were, in His name, but God was held and considered to be present in them in a singular way. For it is not merely a common popular belief, but a clear doctrine of the Word of God, that God is present in a peculiar and particular way at every established congregation that is instituted in a public place for a public cause; even more so if 그 congregation is called in the name of God, and is indeed an assembly of the people of God, in whose midst God has professed His will to dwell. Indeed, whatever is done publicly is considered to be done *before the Lord*, because—although nothing escapes God of those things which are done in the most private places—the conscience of every man teaches him that those things which do not even escape the notice of men can in no way escape God. Let us prove what we have said from the Scriptures.

...of the covenant made at Hebron between David and the people: *And (as the sacred history records) all the Elders of Israel came to the King at Hebron; and King David struck a covenant with them in Hebron* <note>original Hebrew: לפני יהוה</note> **BEFORE THE LORD.** This covenant ratified between David and the people at Hebron is said to be *before the Lord*. But for what reason? Was it because there was a Synagogue at Hebron? Or an altar? Or because the Ark had been brought to Hebron? Certainly, no such reason is expressed in the text, nor indicated in any way. On the contrary, it is said of the Ark in the context of this same history <margin>2 Samuel 6:3.</margin> that it was only afterwards brought out from the House of Abinadab <note>A Levite in whose house the Ark was kept for twenty years after its return from the Philistines.</note>. What else, then, does that phrase signify in this place, other than that this covenant was struck publicly, having invoked the name of God and implored His help and vengeance? This expression was taken in exactly this way in the history of the confirmation of Saul's rule at Gilgal: <margin>1 Samuel 11:15.</margin> *And the whole multitude of the people came to Gilgal, and there they established Saul as King* <note>original Hebrew: לפני יהוה</note> **BEFORE THE LORD,** *and there they offered peace offerings* <note>original Hebrew: לפני יהוה</note> *before the Lord.* The Lord was present here. Was it because the Ark had been transported to Gilgal? Nothing is said of it. Indeed, if one considers the history of the Ark diligently, the opposite is clear. For the Ark, after it was redeemed from the Philistines to their misfortune, remained in Kiriath Jearim in the house of Abinadab. <margin>1 Samuel 7:2; 1 Chronicles 13:6.</margin> Nor do we think the sacred <term>Historian</term> <note>Referring to the biblical author.</note> would have shrouded these migrations of the Ark in silence if the Ark had truly been brought here. For after God showed—first by one, then by another example—how much reverence He wished to be shown to the Ark <margin>1 Samuel 6:19; 2 Samuel 6:7.</margin>, they were not so casual in carrying the Ark from one place to another. Nor, therefore, can the Israelites be said to have stood at Gilgal *before the Lord* simply because perhaps some altars were erected there and sacrifices offered upon them. For one can learn from the text that the sacrifices were offered <note>original Hebrew: לפני יהוה</note> *before the Lord*. The singular presence of the Lord moved the Israelites to offer sacrifices; but the sacrifices were not the cause of the divine presence. Let us say, therefore, that the phrase <note>original Hebrew: לפני יהוה</note> *before the Lord* signifies nothing else here than God being present in the assembly, gathered in the name of God, and acting as one representing the cause of God. Thus, then, understand it when Moses addressed these same Israelites, gathered in the plains of Moab: <margin>Deuteronomy 29:10.</margin>

## CHAPTER VI.

The transition to another period of time for the Judean Commonwealth, as it was governed by Kings until the Babylonian captivity; the question is asked: did that era give birth to Synagogues? To this question it is answered that Synagogues indeed, strictly so-called, do not seem to have arisen during all that time, but nevertheless the Jewish people did not lack for all forms of public instruction. Before that first proposition—which denies Synagogues to this interval of time—is proven, the nature and method of public instruction is discussed in advance. In particular, the public **Schools of the Prophets** are described, in which the prophets were accustomed to preach before the common people, as illustrated by various texts of Holy Scripture. It is then proven that such institutions were not entirely absent even under the Judges, although at that point in time they were very rare. On this occasion, the meaning of a praiseworthy and obscure passage—2 Chronicles 15:3, 4, 5 <note>This passage describes a time when Israel was "without a teaching priest and without law," which the author uses to discuss the history of religious education.</note>—is investigated, after examining the commentaries of the Hebrew Interpreters.

# ON THE ORIGINS, BOOK I, PART II.
<meta>catchword: de- (of)</meta>

It is well-attested that David gave new life to the Jewish Commonwealth, which before his time had been afflicted in various ways and on many occasions. Since he was no less famous for his piety than for his courage, you might rightly ask: did his age and reign not give rise to the Synagogues? It is likewise known that the affairs of the Hebrews were at their most flourishing under the rule of *Solomon*. The question then arises: did *Synagogues* come into being in that golden age, or indeed in the following centuries, during which the Jewish people were ruled by Kings descending from the family of *Jesse* <note>Jesse was the father of King David; this refers to the Davidic dynasty.</note>, until the Babylonian Captivity? This is a quite difficult and obscure question, and in defining it, we do not wish to deny that we remained uncertain for some time. However, having weighed the evidence that we encountered, it seemed best to answer it in this way: *first*, we concede that during that entire interval of time some kind of public instruction existed, the manner and method of which we shall set forth as we understand it; *second*, we shall argue with various reasons that it is not sufficiently clear that *Synagogues*, specifically so-called, were in use among the Jewish nation during all this time; and finally, *third*, we shall weigh those points which have been or could be argued to the contrary by learned men.

I. To one reading the Histories contained in the Volume of the Sacred Books, it is not hidden that some kind of public instruction flourished among the Jewish people. # ON THE ORIGIN, BOOK I, PART II.
<meta>catchword: de- (the beginning of the next page's first word, "deinceps" or similar)</meta>

It is well-attested that David gave new life to the Judean Commonwealth <note>original: "Reipublicæ Judaicæ"</note>, which before his time had been afflicted in various ways and at different turns. However, since he was no less famous for his piety than for his courage, you might rightly ask: did his age and reign give rise to *Synagogues*? It is equally well known that the affairs of the Hebrews were at their most flourishing under the rule of *Solomon*. You may insist, then: was it in that golden age, or perhaps in the following centuries—during which the Jewish people were subject to Kings descended from the line of *Jesse* <note>The "line of Jesse" refers to the Davidic dynasty, as Jesse was the father of King David.</note> up until the Babylonian Captivity—that *Synagogues* were born?

This is a sufficiently difficult and obscure question, and in defining it, I will not deny that I have remained in doubt for some time. However, having weighed the evidence that has come before me, it seemed best to respond in this way: *first*, we concede that throughout that entire interval of time, there existed *some kind of public instruction*, the manner and nature of which we shall explain to the best of our understanding; *second*, we shall argue with reasons why it is not sufficiently clear that *Synagogues*, specifically so called, were in use among the Judean nation during all this time; and finally, *third*, we shall weigh those points which have been either debated by learned men to the contrary, or which could be debated.

In this school, he nurtured and instructed certain disciples—his constant followers—both in the knowledge of divine matters and in the precepts of holiness. ### ON THE ORIGIN BOOK I, PART II. 332

*...they make sweet talk with their mouths; their heart goes after their gain. To them you are like a singer of sweet songs, one who has a beautiful voice and plays well, and they hear your words, but they do not do them.* <note>original: "suaviloquia in ore ipsorum ipsi faciunt..." — a translation of Ezekiel 33:31-32.</note>

God assumes in this entire speech of His to the Prophet that the people were accustomed to coming to Ezekiel at fixed times; to sit in his presence; to receive his rebukes with reverence; and to be solemnly instructed by him in the knowledge of the ways of God. The Prophet Ezekiel was therefore regarded as a **Public Teacher** of the people, who, in his own house—as if in a certain public *School*—established assemblies, and there, before a crowded gathering, interpreted the Divine will with eloquent speech. Anyone who pays careful attention to the words of the text I have cited will sense this meaning lying beneath the surface. For those hypocrites, of whom God speaks to the Prophet, are said to come to him **AS THE PEOPLE ARE ACCUSTOMED TO COME** <note>Hebrew: *ke-mavo am*</note>, that is, solemnly, and putting on a show of reverence toward the word of God and the Prophet: **just as men who are students are accustomed to come**, according to the Chaldean <note>The "Chaldean" refers to the Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, whom Kimchius <note>Rabbi David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), a preeminent medieval Jewish grammarian and biblical commentator.</note> follows. Those same hypocrites are also said to sit before his face and to hear his words. From these things it is clear that such assemblies at the Houses of the Prophets were fixed and solemn. For it was not just this or that individual man—incited either by a true affection for God or by some personal desire of the mind—who went to the Prophet and cursorily sought out the true sense of the Divine will; rather, an entire multitude of the people gathered solemnly to the Prophet and sat before him, which was the custom of **disciples** before a **Master**. Ezekiel, moreover, did not discharge his duty toward the people in just a few words, but preached among them in a composed oration. This is evident from the fact that those hypocrites are said to receive the words of the Prophet as a "pleasant sound," with which an eloquent orator or a skilled flute-player charms the ears.

<margin>Chapter 14, 3.</margin>

But the memory of this custom is found not only here, but also elsewhere in Ezekiel. These are the words:
> Thus says the Lord Jehovah: every man from the house of Israel who sets up his idols <note>original: "stercora sua" — literally "his filth" or "dung-idols," a derogatory Hebrew term for idols.</note> in his heart, and puts the stumbling block of his wickedness before his face, **AND COMES TO THE PROPHET**; I, Jehovah, will answer him in that matter according to the multitude of his idols.

For the homes of the Prophets are rightly compared to public workshops of knowledge and virtue, which any student of the Divine Name was permitted to visit. Moreover, if I am not mistaken, what we read in the *Books of Kings* regarding the story of **Elisha** contributes greatly to proving and illustrating these points. He used to stay frequently with the **Shunammite** lady, who, because of the kindness she showed the Prophet, obtained a male child through a singular divine blessing. But when this son died quite unexpectedly one day, the troubled and grieving mother soon decided to go to the Prophet Elisha, and accordingly asked her husband for

<margin>2 Kings 4, 23.</margin>
the use of a boy and a donkey. To which the story continues: **And he (the husband) said; "Why are you hurrying to him today?** IT IS NEITHER THE NEW MOON, NOR THE SABBATH." <note>Hebrew: *Lo chodesh ve-lo Shabbat*</note> This is indeed a simple narrative, but of great importance to our subject. For in that response of the husband to the wife, it is clearly assumed that it was customary for the people to visit the Prophets and public Teachers on the days of the **Sabbath** and the **New Moon**, so that they might be instructed by them and imbued with both the knowledge of God and true piety. Therefore, the homes of the Prophets were **Schools**, or, if you prefer, **Synagogues**, in which the people were accustomed to gather in that state of affairs. You may see this observed everywhere by the commentators on this passage.

<margin>Isaiah 23:18.</margin>
> *And her merchandise and her gain shall be holy to the Lord; it shall not be placed in treasuries, nor stored up:* <term>For her merchandise shall be for those who sit before the Lord</term> <note>original Hebrew: כי ליושבים לפני יהוה יהוה סחרה</note> *but* **for those sitting before the Lord** *shall her merchandise go, so that they may eat to satiety, and for lasting clothing.* Who are these "sitting before the Lord" here? The disciples of God, who were nurtured in the School of God; the phrase is taken from the custom of sitting before Teachers and Prophets, which was most common in those centuries.

Even if we believe these public Schools of the Prophets flourished most after the times of David and Solomon, who could convince themselves that there were none at all before then? I admit they were few, but that some existed will become clear from what we shall say in the following chapter. However, I wish to prove that they were few and rare from a certain notable passage in the *Chronicles* of the Kingdom of Israel. It is related there that in the time of King Asa, *Azariah*, the son of Oded, being stirred by God, spoke thus to Judah and Benjamin:

<margin>2 Chronicles 15:3, 4.</margin>

There are those who believe that the times indicated are those which had passed just before the reign of Asa. For Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, after he had persisted for a short time in the worship of the true God, abandoned Him along with the Jews, whom his son *Abijah* imitated. At that time, God afflicted the Jews somewhat more severely by sending the King of Egypt <note>This refers to Shishak, who invaded Judah and plundered the Temple around 925 BCE</note> to strip the Temple and the Royal Palace of its ornaments. That wound was healed when King *Asa* succeeded his father, for by his piety he reconciled the favor of the Divine once more to himself and his subjects. 

Some, however, are of the opinion that this text vividly describes the state in which the Jewish Commonwealth and Church existed under the Judges. And their judgment pleases me now more than the others, and I shall provide reasons why those other interpretations do not equally satisfy me. The first interpretation, which seeks the truth of this saying in that future captivity of the Israelites or the Jewish people—into which they were led by the Assyrians or Babylonians—is approved by *Kimchi*, *Aben Melech*, and others. <note>David Kimchi (Radak) and Solomon ben Melech were influential medieval Jewish grammarians and biblical commentators.</note> The words of Aben Melech, who recites a part of Kimchi’s commentary and discusses it more explicitly, are these:

<margin>Isaiah 1:27.</margin>
The Prophet speaks concerning the *state of the restoration of the Israelites from Captivity*: "And I will restore your judges as in the beginning" <note>original: "Et reducam Judices tuos ut in initio"</note>; for as long as they are in exile, they are considered to be deprived of their true and honest judges. I have already mentioned that Kimchi suggested this interpretation. As for the fact that this author cites Onkelos <note>Onkelos was a famous convert to Judaism whose 2nd-century Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Torah is still studied today.</note> to confirm the hypothesis—that the Scripture speaks of those who live among idolaters as if they themselves worshiped idols—it is explained as follows. Moses, toward the end of his ministry, predicted the future defection of the Israelites from God and their removal into the Babylonian Captivity, as well as their idolatry during that captivity and their eventual conversion.
<margin>Deuteronomy 4:27, 28. See Solomon Jarchi <note>Also known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator.</note> on this passage.</margin>
In that speech, these words occur: *And you shall serve there gods, the work of human hands* <note>original: "ועבדתם שם אלהים מעשה ידי אדם"</note>. These are rendered by *Onkelos* as: *And you shall serve there the peoples, the worshipers of idols* <note>original: "ופלחתון תמן לעממיא פלחי טעותא"</note>. The son of Uzziel <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, traditionally credited with the Aramaic translation of the Prophets.</note> follows the same path of interpretation. Both undoubtedly sought to free their nation from the hatred that might be fueled by these words.

It should not be overlooked, however, that the translator of the *Vulgate* <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible, which became the standard for the Catholic Church.</note> also interprets this testimony we are discussing as referring to a future time. For he says: *But many days shall pass in Israel without the true God—and when they shall have returned in their distress to the Lord God of Israel, and shall have sought Him, they shall find Him.* The Greek Translators <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> seem to have been of the same mind, expressing certain words of this text in the *future tense*. Thus, in the fourth verse:
<margin>Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, Book 8, chapter 6.</margin>
*And he will return to the Lord God of Israel, and he will be found by them* <note>original: "Καὶ ἐπιτρέψει αὐτὸς ἐπὶ Κύριον Θεὸν Ἰσραὴλ, καὶ εὑρεθήσεται αὐτοῖς"</note>. In the following verse, however, they retain the *present tense*: *And in that time there is no peace* <note>original: "Καὶ ἐν ἐκείνῳ τῷ καιρῷ οὐκ ἔςιν εἰρήνη"</note>. He describes a coming time when neither a truthful prophet nor a priest devoted to justice would be found among the people. Then their cities would be subverted, and the Nation dispersed throughout all lands, leading a life in the manner of vagabonds with no fixed home. But I do not believe that these translators, and those who follow them, have grasped the truth. For certainly the Hebrew words *Vayyashev* and *Vayvakshuhu* <note>original: "וישב וביקשהו"</note>, as they are currently punctuated in our text, absolutely demand a *past tense* meaning. "The days," <note>original Hebrew: 'הממים', likely a scribal error for הימים (ha-yamim), meaning "the days"</note> which are found in the sixth verse. Next, it must be observed that an argument based on the *past tense* carries much more weight in the Prophet's speech than one drawn from the future. This conviction is far more appropriate: *Worship God, because your fathers, by not worshiping God for a long time, suffered many evils*, rather than: *worship God, because your fathers will at some point for a long time not worship God, and therefore they will fare badly.* Anyone who examines this text a little more closely will notice this. Certainly, everything within it leads us to the *past*. As for the fact that *Kimchi* and *Aben Melech* <note>David Kimchi and Abraham ibn Ezra (Aben Melech), two of the most influential medieval Jewish biblical commentators.</note> suggest that the word *Gods* <note>original: אלהי (Elohai)</note> can be explained here as *Judges*, anyone who rereads the text will easily reject that. For both the phrasing and the connection of the entire speech demonstrate clearly enough that the *true God* <note>original: אלהי אמת (Elohai emet)</note> is intended. The Jews seek "refuges" <note>original Greek: κρηסφύγετα (krēsfygeta), a hiding place or technical loophole</note> to divert the odium of these words away from themselves.

Indeed, those who think the Prophet is depicting the state of the *Israelites* from the time *Jeroboam* <note>The first king of the breakaway Northern Kingdom of Israel, who famously set up golden calves for worship.</note> led them astray into idolatry cannot be judged to have hit the mark of this passage's purpose any more successfully. The author of the Chaldean Paraphrase <note>Also known as a Targum, an Aramaic translation and expansion of the Hebrew Bible used in ancient synagogues.</note>, edited through the care of the most learned *Beckius*, conceived the meaning of these words in this way:

> *And there were many days for the House of Israel since they were divided from the house of Judah, and they turned aside after Jeroboam; they did not worship the true God, but they worshiped golden calves, nor was there a Priest among them teaching righteousness, but rather idolatrous priests who offered incense in a foreign cult, nor were they occupied with the Law.* <note>original Aramaic: ויומין סגיעין לבית ישראל דאית פליגו על דבית יהודא וסטובתך וירבעם לא פלחו לאלהא קשוט והוו סגדין לאגלין דדהב ולא הוו להון כהין מלפי זכו אלהן כומריא דמסקין קטורתא לפלחנא נכריתא ולא אתעסקו באוריתא</note>

The most illustrious Beckius, whose version we have followed, gets stuck on the word וסטובתך (*wastobteka*). *I do not entirely grasp it*, he says; *the meaning is indeed clear, but the words are obscure, especially the latter part. For no one fails to see that there are two words here that should be separated.* He rightly judges that the reading should be restored from a manuscript codex. In the meantime, he thinks it should be read as: וסטון בתך (*wa-stun betok*) and they withdrew through the middle, or, by means of Jeroboam. But it seems hardly doubtful to me that it should be read as: וסטו בתר ירבעם (*wa-stu batar Yerovam*), meaning: *and they turned aside after Jeroboam*. For the letter ך (*kaph*), poorly written at the end of the word בתר (*batar*), could easily have been mistaken for a final ך. These opinions of the Paraphrast...

### CHAPTER 6. ON SYNAGOGARUM.

Regarding the past tense of the recipient, the illustrious *Beckius* <note>Matthias Friedrich Beck (1649–1701), a German Orientalist and theologian.</note> aligns himself with *Rabbi Solomon* <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note>, *Abendana* <note>Isaac Abendana, a Jewish scholar known for his work in England and his translation of the Mishnah.</note>, and *Tremellius* <note>Immanuel Tremellius, a Jewish convert to Christianity and a major biblical scholar of the Reformation.</note>. Rightly so. However, the first two interpret the passage as referring to the state in which the Kingdom of Judah existed under *Rehoboam* and *Abijah* <note>The first two kings of Judah after the kingdom split into North and South.</note>, as we shall soon see; whereas *Tremellius* applies it to the *Israelites* <note>The Northern Kingdom.</note>. For he translates it thus: *For many days the Israelites have been without the true God.* Indeed, his annotations prove this even more clearly. Yet, for my part, I do not see at all what foundation exists in the text for this opinion. On the contrary, I see arguments occurring within it that overthrow this interpretation.

For, 1. There is not only a commemoration of the falling away of the Israelites, but also of *their conversion from that falling away*. In verse 4, the Israelites are said, *when they were in distress, to have returned to Jehovah, the God of Israel, and to have sought Him.* When was this ever done by the Israelites of the ten tribes, considering the time from the beginning of Jeroboam’s reign until this time of King *Asa*? I certainly find no such conversion of theirs to God in history. As for the fact that the Jews repented under King *Asa*, I do not think this can be applied to the Israelites of the north. Tremellius, however, sensing this difficulty, rendered the *fourth* verse into Latin as follows: *But if they had turned, when they were in distress, to Jehovah, the God of Israel, and sought him, he would have been found by them.* Yet the text does not use a conditional phrasing, but an absolute one. The text sounds like this: *And when they were in distress, they turned to the Lord, and he was found by them.* It is not permitted for an interpreter to turn an absolute proposition into a conditional one.

2. The condition of this time is depicted in the text such that there was no peace for those going out or returning; that there were violent disturbances; that nation clashed against nation; that God pressed the inhabitants of these lands with every kind of distress. But what reader of sacred history could extract these <term>criteria</term> <note>original Greek: κριτήρια, meaning distinguishing marks or standards of judgment.</note> of the time of Jeroboam’s reign from the record? 

<margin>2 Chronicles 13:2</margin>
It is well known that the Jews and Israelites occasionally clashed with one another. It is also clear that the hearts of the Kings of Judah were not reconciled with 

<margin>1 Kings 14:30</margin>
the hearts of the Kings of Israel until this time. Nevertheless, the riots, disturbances, distresses, and collisions of this time are described with too much emphasis to fit exactly the state of Jeroboam’s reign.

3. It must be observed above all that the time assigned to this disturbed state of affairs is expressed as <term>many days</term> <note>original Hebrew: ימים רבים (yamim rabbim).</note>. This description denotes a long period of time, provided there are no circum-

...circumstances, which restrict the designation of this phrase. Otherwise, we concede that the phrase, taken *comparatively* and *restrictively*, does not always enjoy that breadth of meaning. But let us compare this text with another testimony, very similar to it, in the Book of *Hosea*, except that the latter is to be understood regarding the future time, while our current text refers to the past: <margin>Hosea 3:4.</margin> "For the Israelites shall sit **MANY DAYS** <note>original: *yâmim rabbim*</note> without a King, and without a Prince, and without a sacrifice, and without a sacred pillar." Who are these "many days"? Let *Kimchi* <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), also known as Radak, a major medieval Jewish commentator and grammarian.</note> answer, whose explanation of these words—though well enough known—is nonetheless worthy of being related:

> **THESE ARE THE DAYS OF EXILE IN WHICH WE LIVE TODAY,** *during which we have neither King nor Prince from Israel; indeed, we are in the power of the nations and in the power of their Kings and Princes.*

It is clear, at any rate, that the long time of Israelite exile and servitude, which they are now passing through, is expressed by the phrase "many days." From this, at the very least, we may conclude that this expression, if the text does not restrict it, signifies an interval of a long time. However, from the time of the Israelites' rebellion under *Jeroboam* until the time of King *Asa*, only twenty years had elapsed. <margin>1 Kings 15:10.</margin> Consider now whether those years deserve to be called "a long time," when the text suggests no argument for a restricted explanation of this phrase. I, at least, believe that these words indicate a longer interval of an age than that which is completed in the course of twenty years.

The same difficulty presses even more upon *Rabbi Solomon* <note>Rashi, the 11th-century French rabbi and commentator.</note>, and *Abendana* <note>Isaac Abendana, a 17th-century Jewish scholar.</note> who followed him, who referred this case to the times that had already elapsed from the third year of King *Rehoboam* until the beginnings of the reign of *Asa*. Let us hear *Abendana*:

> *And Rashi explained the verse "And for many days Israel was without the true God" <note>2 Chronicles 15:3</note> as referring to the time until you [Asa] arrived. For it is written regarding Rehoboam: "And it happened, when Rehoboam had established the kingdom and had strengthened himself, he forsook the law of the Lord, and all Israel with him." And regarding Abijah it is written: "And he walked in all the sins of his father which he had done before him." And regarding this, he said that there were many days for Israel in which they had no true God and no teaching priest, because there was no one who would ask a priest for a matter of the Law; therefore, he did not teach until now.*

The time that the Israelite Nation spent under the Judges is approximately *three hundred years*. Other very learned and highly skilled men establish many more years than this; for now, we will be content with the minimum, nor will we pursue the matter more accurately at this moment, because our interpretation will remain consistent even if this number of years is either shortened or extended. Nothing more is required to strengthen our hypothesis than to show, part by part, that the things said by the Prophet *Azariah* concerning a certain past time can be applied to this era skillfully and without any force. It is certain that this era is best and most significantly expressed by the phrase <term>many days</term> <note>original Hebrew: *yamim rabbim*</note>. *One hundred, two hundred, and three hundred years are indeed truly* <term>many days</term>—a long span of time, which is the genuine meaning of this expression. Is this not true of that long period which the Jews lived through before, and even after, the times of *Eli*? Indeed, nothing is more certain. In the history of the most desperate affairs of this people after the death of Phinehas, when God was accustomed to bring them help through the *Judges*, there is absolutely no mention of a Priest or High Priest performing his office—that is, teaching the people, reminding them of their duties, warning them away from idolatry, urging them toward the worship of the true Deity, and deciding lawsuits and controversies if any arose. For all of that pertains to the duties of the High Priest. After Phinehas, no one is mentioned except *Eli*, who was descended from the line of *Ithamar*. And yet, as we have said, between Phinehas and *Eli* there is a void of nearly two hundred years.

<margin>1 Chronicles 24:3, 6.</margin>

Perhaps it would not be absurd to say that the *Priesthood*, in that most turbulent state of the Jewish Commonwealth which we are discussing, was deserted or profaned by the sons or grandsons of Phinehas, and that for this reason God entrusted the Priesthood to *Eli*, even though he was produced from the lineage of *Ithamar*. These Sons of the Prophets were indeed in many cities, so that they might correct the people of Israel in every town. But because their prophecy was only for specific times (that is, given when the opportunity arose or in specific, incidental cases), it was not recorded in writing. We are more clearly informed about these Sons of the Prophets from the history of Elisha. They lived with the Prophet, their teacher, in a specific place, and were instructed by him there in the knowledge of sacred things. Such a place was either within a city or outside of it, and here again, it was either in the wilderness or in the mountains, locations removed from human society and company. ### CHAPTER 7. ON SYNAGOGUES.

*And the Sons of the Prophets said to Elisha: See now, the place where we sit before your face is too narrow for us to hold us.* **PLEASE, LET US GO TO THE JORDAN, AND LET EACH OF US TAKE ONE BEAM FROM THERE,** <note>original Hebrew: ונעשה לנו שם מקום לשבת שם</note> **and let us make a place for ourselves to dwell there,** A PLACE WHICH WE MAY INHABIT, **or in which we may sit; and he said: Go.** The *Place* prepared for the Sons of the Prophets in the desert was a kind of <term>monastery<note>The Latin uses "coenobium," referring to a communal religious house where members live and study together under a rule.</note></term> in which sacred disciplines were cultivated. Indeed, Saint Jerome <note>Eusebius Sophronius Hieronymus (c. 347–420 AD), a Church Father best known for his Latin translation of the Bible.</note> compared these Sons of the Prophets to the monks of his own time.

<margin>Jerome, Letter to Rusticus on the form of living. From the edition of Erasmus, p. 16 at letter f.</margin>
I will extract his words, which are read in his *Letter to Rusticus*: **THE SONS OF THE PROPHETS, WHOM WE READ WERE MONKS IN THE OLD TESTAMENT,** *built themselves little huts near the streams of the Jordan, and having left behind the crowds of the cities, they lived on polenta and wild herbs.* Not, says <term>Erasmus<note>Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536), the famous Dutch Renaissance humanist and editor of Jerome's works.</note></term>, *that they were distinguished from others by a certain dress or titles, as is the common crowd of monks today; but because, removed from the bustle of towns, they led a life in solitude—whereas today's monks prefer to be nowhere more than in the thickest crowds of men, especially among the wealthy and the gluttonous.*

<margin>Jerome to Paulinus, folio 37.</margin>
Again, in his *Letter to Paulinus*: *Our (the monks') Prince is Elijah, our Elisha; our leaders are the* **SONS OF THE PROPHETS, WHO DWELT IN THE FIELDS AND WASTES,** *and made themselves tents near the streams of the Jordan.* It must be held, however, that the Sons of the Prophets were not all strangers to marriage. For we read specifically in this same history about the wives of the Sons of the Prophets.

<margin>2 Kings 4:1.</margin>

I agree, therefore, with what Jerome wrote to Eustochium concerning them: *Elijah was a virgin, Elisha a virgin,* **MANY SONS OF THE PROPHETS WERE VIRGINS.**

<margin>On the Guarding of Virginity, f. 50. col. 4. Abarbanel on this passage.</margin>

Furthermore, I have said it is likely that these Prophets also opened their schools on mountains or in the high places of various towns. # ON THE ORIGIN, BOOK 1, PART II.

...and who can doubt that they flourished at one time or another among the Israelites? A single <term>Doctor<note>In this context, a learned teacher or master of theology.</note></term>, or Prophet, raised up by God, who made himself famous among the people through instruction and miracles, could often plant the seeds of true virtue and knowledge in many disciples. Once he had passed away, who does not easily understand that such zeal cooled over time, and sacred studies once again collapsed? I am not far from the opinion of **Abarbanel** <note>Don Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a renowned Jewish statesman, philosopher, and biblical commentator.</note> that with **Samuel**, literature and learning revived after that lukewarm exercise of Divine worship of which we spoke in the previous Dissertation. <margin>1 Samuel 10:5</margin> 

*Afterward you shall come (Samuel is speaking to Saul)* <note>original Hebrew: אל גבעת האלהים</note> to the **HILL OF GOD**, *where the Philistine garrisons are; and it will happen that, when you have come there to enter the city,* <note>original Hebrew: ופגעת חבל נביאים ירדים מהבמה ולפניהם נבל ותף וחליל וכנור והמה מתנבאים</note> **YOU WILL HAPPEN UPON A CERTAIN SOCIETY OF PROPHETS** *descending from that high place, who will have with them a harp, a tambourine, a flute, and a lyre, and they will be prophesying.* The truth of this prediction was proven by the event. 

Another similar passage occurs in this same history. Saul had made manifest his plan to kill David. David, having been informed of this, fled to Ramah to the Prophet Samuel; regarding which the text says: 

<margin>1 Samuel 19:18</margin>

*And they went, he and Samuel,* <note>original Hebrew: וישבו בניות</note> *and they dwelt (stayed)* **IN NAIOTH.** Now, *Naioth* was a certain well-known place in Ramah, as is clear from the following verse: 

<margin>19</margin> 

*And it was told to Saul, saying: "Behold, David is in Naioth in Ramah."* But Saul, not deterred from his purpose by reverence for Samuel, sent messengers to Ramah to capture David. Regarding them, it is said: 

<margin>20</margin>

Thus, when these messengers frustrated Saul's expectations a first, second, and third time, Saul himself finally followed in their footsteps with the same result. For he himself, having been brought to that same place, is said to have prophesied with the others. Moreover, this notable circumstance is added: *And* **HE ALSO STRIPPED OFF HIS CLOTHES**, *and he also prophesied* **BEFORE SAMUEL**, <note>original Hebrew: ויפל ערום כל היום ההוא וכל הלילה</note> *and* **HE LAY DOWN NAKED ALL THAT DAY AND ALL NIGHT.** <note>In biblical terms, "naked" often means stripped of one's outer royal or professional robes, wearing only an undergarment, symbolizing a total loss of worldly status before God.</note> 

The Jewish Interpreters teach that there was a celebrated **Academy** in both of these places; indeed, they write that <note>original Hebrew: נוית</note> *Naioth* was the name of the **Academy of Ramah**, so named because it was a seat of doctrine and piety. This has been learnedly demonstrated by **Alting** <note>Jacobus Alting (1618–1679), a Dutch linguist and theologian who specialized in Hebrew antiquities.</note>, whom I praised above in his <margin>History of the Hebrew Academies.</margin>

...event. It is my purpose, for the confirmation and illustration of those points which were addressed in our preceding discourse, to examine certain aspects of these texts more closely.

1. That which we supposed—that those ancient *Gymnasia* <term>Gymnasia<note>In this context, the author uses the Greek-derived term to describe schools of higher learning or academies for spiritual and intellectual training.</note></term> or monasteries of the Wise <note>original Latin: *Sophorum*</note> were built long ago in *lofty places*, whether inside the city or outside the city, acquires singular strength from these testimonies. I believe that *Naioth*, which is rendered by the Paraphrast <note>Referring to the Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note> as the *House of Learning* <note>original Aramaic: בית אולפנא, *Beit Ulpana*</note>, denotes *habitations* or *small dwellings*. These, moreover, were placed in *Ramah*, in a high place. For the word *Ramah* <note>original Hebrew: רמה</note> itself indicates this, as those who have traveled through these regions can attest. And indeed, reason bids us believe that such places were preferred by these students of wisdom over others because they are most suitable for a solitary life and the meditation of Divine things.

2. From these testimonies, we may recognize more distinctly what grade, office, and order these Prophets held. Among the Hebrews, every *Interpreter* of the Divine will is called a *Prophet* <note>original Hebrew: נביא, *Navi*</note>—everyone, I say, who discourses on Divine matters and recounts them more freely, whether he owes his knowledge of them to God directly <note>original Greek: ἀμέσως, *amesos*, meaning without an intermediary</note>, or even to other holy men who were instructed by God. Thus, a *Prophet* is exactly the same as what we call a *Theologian* <note>original Latin: *Theologus*</note>. But because it happened very frequently under the economy of the Old Covenant that those who interpreted God's will to the people were duly instructed for that task by God Himself, without any human labor or ministry intervening, hence the word *Prophet* was more frequently applied to those Theologians who were taught truths, whether of present or future things, by God Himself without any other effort. And the word *to prophesy* <note>original Hebrew: נבא, *nava*</note>, which gave origin to the term "Prophet," is taken in exactly the same sense. For *to prophesy* properly signifies to explain any matter—especially Divine truths—with a free mouth, and to discourse eloquently upon them. For the Prophets, being moved by the Spirit, were commonly distinguished by this character,

...distinguished, so that they poured forth words in the most elegant ways with a great flow of speech. The prophet Isaiah was not content to respond in simple words to Hezekiah, who was asking for his own safety and that of the city of Jerusalem, but he reduced his words, as it were, into musical modes, and interpreted the counsel of God to Hezekiah quite eloquently with an elegant circuit of words.
