# OF THE ORIGIN. BOOK 1, PART 2.

...of whom how many are mentioned here and elsewhere? In the first <margin>1 Samuel 10:5, 10; Chapter 19:20.</margin> text, a <term>hevel nevi'im <note>original Hebrew: חבל נביאים</note></term>, or *chorus of Prophets*, is presented; in the latter, a <term>lahakat nevi'im <note>original Hebrew: להקת נביאים</note></term>, or *assembly* <term>(kehillat) <note>original Hebrew: קהלת</note></term> *of Prophets*. Who would believe that God wished to impart the knowledge of future events—which is a most rare science and not for constant use—to so many men at once? It is more satisfactory, therefore, to understand by these "Prophets" and "Sons of the Prophets" men most studious of Divine wisdom and true piety. These were men who trained themselves in knowledge and virtue through continuous exercise, and who spent a great part of their leisure in praising God and recounting His perfections and blessings through song and musical instruments. Indeed, it is relevant here to consider: 1. That the word <term>nava <note>original Hebrew: נבא; meaning to prophesy or speak under inspiration</note></term> is clearly found in the writings of the Old Testament with the meaning of praising God through musical instruments.

<margin>1 Chronicles 25:1.</margin> Thus it is in the Books of Chronicles: *And David and the captains of the army separated for the ministry the sons (or with the sons) of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun*, <term>who should prophesy with harps, with lutes, and with cymbals <note>original Hebrew: הנבאים בכנרות בנבלים ובמצלתים</note></term>. Again,

<margin>2.</margin> it is repeated concerning Asaph in the *following verse*: *under the hand of Asaph, who PROPHESIED under the hands of the King; that is, the seer closest to the King.* <note>original Hebrew: על ידי אסף הנבא על ידי המלך</note> Again, concerning Jeduthun:

<margin>3.</margin> <note>The source text marks this as margin 4, likely a typo for verse 3</note> *Under the hands of their father Jeduthun with a harp, who PROPHESIED in giving thanks and praising the Lord.* <note>original Hebrew: על ידי אביהם ידותון בכנור הנבא על הודות והלל ליהוה</note> The word <term>hitnabbe <note>original Hebrew: התנבא</note></term> here seems to signify as much as singing sacred hymns, or, as it is said in the text itself, *to praise and celebrate the Lord.* <note>original Hebrew: הודות והלל ליהוה</note> <term>Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the famous 11th-century French rabbi</note></term> and <term>David Kimchi <note>Radak, a 12th-13th century grammarian and commentator</note></term> in this passage distinguish the act of prophesying from the act of playing musical instruments, because the text says: *they prophesied with harps.* Therefore, for them, playing the harp is not itself prophesying; rather, prophesying is the modulation of sacred songs to the praise of God with one's own voice.

<margin>Notes on the Paraphrase of 1 Chronicles, chapter 25, 1.</margin> Their words were excerpted by the most learned <term>Beckius <note>Matthias Friedrich Beck (1649–1701), an Orientalist scholar known for his work on the Targums</note></term>. I would easily concede this point to them and other learned men, because even in that history which we are illustrating, it is said that *the Prophets prophesied*, while those who handled musical instruments preceded them. It is one thing, therefore, to prophesy, and another to play musical instruments.

<margin>2 Kings 3:15.</margin> The Prophet <term>Elisha</term> is also said to have prophesied while a minstrel played. Nor do I understand differently what is told of <term>Saul</term>, prophesying in his house while David played the lute. Thus the very words of the sacred history sound:

# CHAPTER 7. OF SYNAGOGAGES.

<margin>1 Samuel 18:10.</margin>
**HE PROPHESIED IN THE MIDST OF HIS HOUSE, AND** *David* **STRUCK THE STRINGS** *on this day, as on any other* <note>original Hebrew: ויתנבא בתוך הבית ודוד מנגן בידו כיום ביום; original Latin: VATICINABATUR IN MEDIO ÆDIUM SUARUM, & David PULSABAT FIDES hoc die, ut quovis alio.</note>. There are quite a many interpreters, both Jewish and Christian, who explain the act of "prophesying" in this specific passage as a mere empty display or a pretense of the act of prophesying, through both words and gestures. However, I am of the opinion that the meaning of this word in this text does not vary at all from those instances we have already indicated in the passages cited previously. In my judgment, *to prophesy* here means to modulate sacred songs with the voice—an act which Saul seems to have performed frequently while David played upon the strings.

What, then, does Abarbanel say here? <term>He means that they thought about what would be in the end of days; for every herald of the future is called "one who prophesies." It is useful to know, however, that there is a great difference between a "Prophet" and "one who prophesies." For a Prophet is one truly influenced by the Blessed Name, while "one who prophesies" is any man who prepares himself and diligently applies himself to knowing the future <note>original Hebrew: ר"ל שחשבו במה שיהיה באחרית הימים כל מגיד העתי דורת נקרא מתנבא' וראוי שתדע שיש הפרש גדול בין נביא ובין מתנבא' כי הנביא הוא מושפע באמת מהשם יתברך והמתנבא הוא האיש המכין עצמו ומשתדל לדעת העתידות</note></term>. <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508) was a prominent Jewish statesman, philosopher, and Bible commentator.</note> We shall not transcribe more of his words, lest by disputing a matter of no great importance we consume more ink and time than is proper. Let it only be noted that the term <term>hitnabbe <note>original Greek/Hebrew: τὸ התנבא</note></term>—meaning "to act as a prophet" or "to prophesy"—is used in the Scriptures even for those Prophets who were truly moved by the Spirit of God;

<margin>1 Kings 22:8. 1 Samuel 10:10, 11.</margin>
and in the very history of Samuel, the words <term>Navi <note>Prophet</note></term> and <term>hitnabbe <note>to prophesy</note></term> are used interchangeably, referring to the same subjects in the same circumstances. Therefore, we do not accept this observation of Abarbanel. 2. Yet among the Greeks, all these things are considered both pleasing and worthy of praise.* Having prefaced this, he writes of Epaminondas: *He was so well educated that no other Theban...*

### CHAPTER 7. OF SYNAGOGUES.

...their own specific traits, by which they could be distinguished no less than the Philosophers of the Gentiles; there is no reason for us to doubt this, as the entire historical Scripture of the Old Testament proclaims it loudly. Whether that is actually what is signified here, I am uncertain, and I leave it to the reader to consider.

One might, not without reason, compare these Schools of the Ancient Prophets in many respects with those of the Ancient Philosophers among the Gentiles—except that the former, being truly established by God, passed down heavenly wisdom to their disciples, while the latter, having searched the secrets of nature and stirred the seeds of truth lying hidden in their consciences, imbued excellent minds with secular learning and equipped them for every noble pursuit. <margin>In the biography of Menedemus, Book 2, pages 175, 176.</margin> If you wish to know the arrangement of the *Schools* in which the Philosophers were accustomed to teach their listeners in ancient times, consider these words of *Laertius* <note>Diogenes Laertius, a 3rd-century biographer of Greek philosophers.</note> regarding *Menedemus*: <note>original Greek: Ἦν δὲ (φασί) καὶ ἐκκλίνης καὶ τὰ τῆς σχολῆς ἀδιάφορα. ὄυτε γοῦν τάξιν τινὰ ἦν παρ᾽ ἀυτῷ βλέπειν, ὄυτε βάθρα κύκλῳ διέκειτο, ἀλλ᾽ ὃ ἂν ἕκαστος ἔτυχε περιπατῶν ἢ καθήμενος, ἤκουε, καὶ ἀυτὸ τοῦτον τὸν τρόπον διακειμένος;</note> *His discipline was of a looser sort, and he was, as they say, rather indifferent regarding the School;* FOR YOU WOULD NOT HAVE SEEN ANY ORDER AROUND HIM, NOR WERE THERE BENCHES ARRANGED IN A CIRCLE, *but each person listened while walking or sitting, however they happened to be, with the teacher himself moving about with equal freedom while teaching.*

Indeed, it was permitted for any student of wisdom to open a school of this kind, just as I believe was done in the past by the Prophets among the Jews. This is certainly to be gathered from the same *Laertius*: <margin>Laertius in the biography of Theophrastus, Book 5, page 325.</margin> <note>original Greek: Σοφοκλέους τοῦ Ἀμφικλείδου νόμον εἰσενεγκόντος, Μηδένα τῶν Φιλοσόφων σχολῆς ἀφηγείσθαι, ἂν μὴ τῇ βουλῇ καὶ τῷ δήμῳ δόξῃ, εἰ δὲ μὴ θάνατον εἶναι τὴν ζημίαν;</note> *A law was proposed by Sophocles, son of Amphiclides, that no one of the Philosophers should lead a School unless it seemed good to the Senate and the people; if anyone did otherwise, he was to be condemned to death.* However, this law was repealed the following year. It is not clear to me from any evidence that these Prophets of the Jewish nation were supported by public expense; though I am aware that this was sometimes done among the Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans.

But we must define what kind and what manner of institution that was, and on what occasions it was exercised by them.

**1.** I would estimate that it pertained to the Levites to respond to Israelites who were struggling with difficulties arising from the wording of the law, and who approached them to consult on sacred law. Very many doubtful cases, which easily arise in the daily commerce of men, were not determined in the Mosaic law. Therefore, various questions could arise every day concerning the consequences of the Divine Law and their various applications, in a manner not unlike what happens in human courts. In Roman laws, the foundations of justice and equity are expressed clearly enough, beyond doubt. Yet, for all that, they are not so precise—nor could they be made precise by any human art or genius—as to cut off all disputes that can be moved concerning the sense of words or the consequences of the law. The **Talmudic Constitutions** <term>Talmudic Constitutions: Refers to the Mishnah and Gemara, which expanded the brief biblical laws into a comprehensive legal code</term> composed in later times sufficiently prove that the nature of the Mosaic Laws is not different; for these are essentially so many definitions of Jewish Law regarding what should be done or omitted in various cases not determined in the Mosaic law. On the Sabbath, it is forbidden to work. Certain examples of prohibited works were also noted. You would swear that the Legislator [Moses] had expressed his mind so...

But the reliability of the **Talmudists** <note>The Jewish scholars who compiled the Talmud.</note> in those matters they have left behind concerning the **Sanhedrins** has long been suspect to the most learned men. The first clear history concerning the institution of the **Great Sanhedrin** is in the Mosaic accounts. <margin>Numbers 11:1, 2.</margin> Whether that council continued through all the intervals of the Jewish Republic, who can say, and who would believe the one saying it? It is likely that it was restored by **Jehoshaphat**. <margin>2 Chronicles 19:8, 9, 10.</margin> Concerning the **Sanhedrin of Twenty-Three Men** and the **Sanhedrin of Three Men**, of which the Talmudists speak so voluminously, **Holy Scripture** and **Josephus** <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> say not even a "mu" <note>original: "μυ," a Greek expression meaning the slightest sound or word.</note>, as far as I know. Indeed, Josephus expressly mentions **Sanhedrins of Seven Men**. Whom should we believe, Josephus or the Talmudists? It is certain that there were some smaller Sanhedrins, but of what number of judges remains uncertain to me if one rejects the testimony of Josephus. For his assertion seems more probable to me than that of the Talmudists. But my discussion now does not wander so much around the number of the Sanhedrins as around their qualities and origins. The point of dispute is whether the **Priests** and **Levites** alone from the descendants of Jacob were chosen for the seats of the **Judges**? I, for my part, would believe that they were for the most part preferred over others; both because God had entrusted this duty to them, so that they might be equipped for pronouncing the Law by their knowledge of the statutes, and because it seems likely that they were generally more learned than the other Israelites, and therefore held to be more fit for exercising such an office. Yet I do not think that the way to attaining this dignity was closed to other Israelites, if their fitness was established; but, as I said, for the sake of fitness, I consider that the Levites were for the most part preferred over other Israelites, especially in the earliest times of the Jewish Republic. Let our opinion, therefore, stand within these bounds; and let us now observe further that "pronouncing the law," which I have chiefly ascribed to the Levites—

### CHAPTER 8. OF THE SYNAGOGUES.

...we wrote of the office; in the Hebrew style, it is <note>original: הורות</note> **TO TEACH**; because those who pronounced justice were required to interpret the doubtful and more obscure Laws. I will present an argument from the Mosaic institutions: <margin>Deuteronomy 17:8.</margin> *“If a matter should be too difficult for you,”* (these are the words of the Lawgiver) *“a matter to be discerned in judgment, between blood and blood, between law and law, and between stroke and stroke, concerning which there is usually a dispute within your gates, you shall arise and go up to that place which the Lord your God shall choose. And you shall come to the Priests, the Levites, and to the Judge who shall be in those days, and you shall inquire, and they shall indicate to you every word of judgment. And you shall do according to all that word which they have indicated to you from that place which the Lord shall choose: and you shall be careful to do <note>original: כל אשר יורוך</note> according to all that they **TEACH** you: <note>original: על פי התורה אשר יורוך</note> according to the decree of the Law **WHICH THEY SHALL TEACH YOU**, and according to the judgment which they shall pronounce to you, you shall do.”* I would like it to be noticed that in this passage it is presupposed that the land of Canaan was furnished with Sanhedrins <note>The Sanhedrin was the supreme council and tribunal of the Jews, responsible for interpreting religious and civil law.</note>. For whatever the cause or legal action, it did not always demand an appeal to the Judges in Jerusalem; rather, many common matters could be settled in the cities and villages where Judges of a lower bench had been appointed to administer justice—provided that the case in question was determined in the Law, or at least could be determined from it by clear logical consequences. But if some more serious question was to be decided by the Judges, which was neither declared in the Law itself, nor had that higher Tribunal of the Priest or Judge exercised authority over it until then, one had to go up to the place chosen by God. There, the Priests and Judges who were present, constituting the supreme Sanhedrin, were to be consulted; to depart even a little from their opinion, or from their **Teaching** and Law, was a capital offense.

This Law was renewed by Jehoshaphat. <margin>2 Chronicles 19:10.</margin> And thus we understand in what sense Levi is called in Malachi <note>original: מלאך יהוה צבאות</note> the **Messenger of the Lord of Hosts**. <margin>Chapter 2:8.</margin> The word "Messenger" <note>original: מלאך</note> has the same value as the word "Ambassador" among the Romans. Indeed, in my opinion, Levi is called the *Ambassador of the Lord of Hosts* because he gave the Laws in the name of God, and as if in the place and stead of God, and explained them once they were given. So it is: *They sat in the Chair of Moses <note>The "Chair of Moses" was a symbolic term for the seat of authority occupied by those authorized to interpret the Law.</note>, and whatever they commanded to be done concerning the circumstances of the Mosaic Law, <margin>Matthew 23:3.</margin> had the force of Law.* I will add that Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra was a famous 12th-century Spanish rabbi and biblical commentator known for his grammatical approach to the text.</note> interprets in the same way, and rightly so, what is said in this same passage concerning the Levites, <margin>Commentary on this passage.</margin> or concerning Levi: <note>original: תורת אמת היתה בפיהו</note> **The law of truth was in his mouth**

...sacred persons and instructed in the knowledge of the Law, and therefore were fit for educating children, they were often taken by the Israelites into their own families. But this was as much as I had decided to write about the office of **teaching**, which was committed to the Levites.

<margin>1 Chronicles 12, 32.</margin> Yet the reader, a student of the Divine Word, will not take it poorly if I add a few things to these meditations of mine, not foreign to the matter I have been occupied with so far. In the Book of Chronicles, famous men are listed who defected from the Kingdom of Saul to David, and among them the men of Issachar, marked with this title: <note>original Hebrew: ומבני יששכר יודעי בינה לעתים לדעת מה יעשה ישראל</note> *And of the children of Issachar, those who had **PRUDENT UNDERSTANDING** of the opportune times, to know what Israel ought to do.* This is indeed a magnificent praise of the men of Issachar. Nor can it be denied that it has some merit. Yet others, and those most learned interpreters, think that here only secular prudence is hinted at, by which one discerns what is best to do or not do in the various cases of human life, and likewise in the various businesses of the State in different <margin>Commentary on this passage.</margin> times. ### CHAPTER 8. OF SYNAGOGUES.

...they incline. Rabbi Jonah thinks that by this phrase are designated Men most skilled in the Law and excelling in the dexterity of judging what was appropriate for them to act and decree according to the Laws of the Jewish people. But Kimchi <note>David Kimhi (1160–1235), a fundamental medieval Jewish biblical commentator and grammarian.</note> refutes this opinion as follows: <note>original Hebrew: אבל לדעת מה יעשה ישראל אין טעמו דבק לזה הפי' כי היה לו לומר לדעת מה יעשה המלך</note> *But regarding the phrase "to know what Israel should do," its meaning does not stick to this interpretation, for it should have said "to know what the King should do."* **The words of the text: TO KNOW WHAT SHOULD BE DONE BY ISRAEL, do not correspond to this interpretation, since it rather should have been expressed thus: to know what should be done by the KING.** 

I, however, cannot bring myself to believe that the science of Astrology is hinted at here, but rather I side with those who think the passage should be explained as referring to **secular prudence** <term>secular prudence: Practical wisdom and political foresight used to navigate worldly affairs and governance.</term>. The illustrious Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian and famous Hebraist.</note> in one place <margin>Lexicon on the word *yada* [to know], page 295.</margin> in his Lexicon under the word *yada* [to know] explained the phrase in this way: *Those who know how to distinguish at opportune times.* <margin>On the word *et* [time].</margin> *Those who knew how to judge according to the circumstances of the times;* those who know how to judge according to the various conditions of the times. In another place he puts it thus: *Understanding how to distinguish prudently regarding the times.* 

He seems to me not to be far from the truth. The Hebrew phrase *yode’e binah* <note>original Hebrew: יודעי בינה</note> [knowers of understanding], which is common enough in the Sacred Scriptures, denotes knowing something with prudence and wisdom, or to know prudently and wisely; or, if you prefer <margin>2 Chronicles 2:11.</margin> to stick strictly to the Hebrew phrasing: *to know prudence and wisdom.* <margin>Proverbs 6:10.</margin> Moreover, that human faculty was referred to by the ancients as **practical judgment** <term>judicium practicum: The ability to apply general moral or legal principles to specific, real-world situations.</term>, by which it is discerned what ought to be done, or not, at various times, cases, and circumstances, whether by a single man or by the whole people. 

As this is indeed an excellent faculty, supposing and indicating a great capacity of mind that very quickly perceives what is good and bad in every matter, so it cannot be successfully exercised except by one who has a mind most highly instructed in every kind of knowledge and trained by experience in various matters. <margin>Genesis 3:4.</margin> In Scripture, this is called *knowing good and evil;* which is to separate good from evil in every matter presented to the mind by a sharp act of judgment, and to be furnished with the knowledge necessary for the exercise of such a faculty. 

It is added in the text, *yode’e binah la-ittim* <note>original Hebrew: יודעי בינה לעתים</note>, *knowing prudence for,* or *according to the times,* that is, when times are pressing in which there is need for the counsel of prudent men. Thus I think that "for the times" should be explained, as "at the times" is used elsewhere in the Psalms: <margin>Psalm 9:10.</margin> *And the Lord shall be a high place for the oppressed,* <note>original Hebrew: משגב לעתות בצרת</note> *a high place, where TIMES of distress press.* Again: <margin>Psalm 10:1.</margin> *Why, O Lord, do you stand far off...*

[...] I owe to the industry of the most distinguished men, de Dieu and Cocceius. Let it only be allowed to reverently point out that the Dutch interpreters, by translating it thus:

> *The words of the wise are as goads and as nails, deeply driven [by] the masters of assemblies, etc.* <note>original Dutch: "De woorden der wyſe zyn als prichelen en nagelen, diep ingeſlagen (van) de meeſters der Verſamelingen." This refers to the Dutch States Translation of Ecclesiastes 12:11.</note>

have not attained the genuine meaning of the Hebrew expression; this is all the more worthy of attention because the passage is so frequently on everyone’s lips. Specifically, these most excellent interpreters took the <term>descriptive term</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπίθετον (epitheton)</note> <term>masters of assemblies</term> <note>original Hebrew: בעלי אסיפות (Ba'ale Asuppot)</note> as if it referred to the *Doctors* or *Wise Men*, in this manner: *The words of the wise are like goads and nails driven in by the masters of assemblies.* So too did the most renowned Alting—

<margin>History of the Hebrew Academy, page [my copy] 284.</margin>
otherwise highly skilled in the knowledge of this language—interpret it. *All these* (he had been speaking of *Doctors of various kinds*) *were called by the common name* <term>Masters of Assemblies</term>, *because they would gather and congregate many disciples for the academic body by teaching; or else because they gathered many scattered opinions into a single system and shared them with their listeners.* But it must be observed, 1. In the text it does not say <term>from the masters of assemblies</term> <note>original Hebrew: מבעלי אסיפות (mi-ba'ale asuppot)</note>, but simply <term>masters of assemblies</term>, in this way: *The words of the wise are like goads and driven nails, masters of assemblies.* 2. If <term>masters of assemblies</term> designates the *Doctors* and *wise men*, then the speech loses all its force and elegance. Try it, if you please: *The words of the wise are like nails, driven in by the wise.* What force, what beauty is in such a sentence? *The words of the wise are like nails, driven in by the teachers.* Therefore, note that the <term>descriptive term</term> <term>masters of assemblies</term> does not belong to the *wise men* or teachers, but to the *nails*, and you will have the easiest interpretation of this passage: *The words of the wise are like nails, the masters of assemblies.* The nails themselves are here called <term>masters of assemblies</term>, or as the renowned Cocceius puts it: *those holding the collections*; and de Dieu: *by which joinings are made*. For the word <term>Baal</term> <note>Master, Lord, or Owner</note>, which is translated as *Dominus* among the Latins, enjoys a very broad meaning among the Hebrews and has a singular and emphatic use in certain phrases. He who *possesses* something as *his own* is called the <term>Baal</term> (master) of that thing, or the holder and possessor of that thing; and hence something of which an attribute or a certain property is truly predicated as belonging to it is called its <term>Baal</term>, its master or holder.

Even the celebrated Altingius, otherwise most skilled in the knowledge of this language, does the same. <note>Jacob Alting (1618–1679) was a Professor of Hebrew at Groningen.</note> *All these* (he had been speaking of the *Teachers of various kinds* in his *History of the Hebrew Academy*, page 284) *were called by the common name* <term>Masters of the Gatherings</term> <note>original Hebrew: בעלי אסופות (ba'ale asuppot)</note> *because by teaching they would collect and gather many disciples into an Academic body; or also, because they gathered several scattered opinions into one system and communicated them to their listeners*. 

But it must be observed: 1. In the text it does not say <term>from the masters of assemblies</term> <note>original Hebrew: מבעלי אסופות (mi-ba'ale asuppot)</note>, but simply <term>masters of assemblies</term> <note>original Hebrew: בעלי אסופות (ba'ale asuppot)</note>, in this way: *The words of the wise are as goads and nails driven in, the masters of assemblies*. 2. If the *Doctors* and *Wise Men* are designated by "masters of assemblies," then the speech loses all its force and elegance. Try it, if you please: *The words of the wise are as nails, driven in by the wise*. Where, I ask, is the beauty of this sentence? *The words of the wise are as nails, driven in by the teachers*. 

Therefore, note that the epithet <term>masters of assemblies</term> does not belong to the *wise men* or *teachers*, but to the *nails* themselves, and you will have the easiest interpretation of this passage: *The words of the wise are as nails, the masters of the gathering*. The nails themselves are here called <term>masters of assemblies</term>, or as the celebrated Cocceius puts it: *those holding collections together*; and de Dieu: *by which joinings are made*. For indeed the word <term>Master</term> <note>original Hebrew: בעל (Ba'al)</note>, which is translated as *Dominus* among the Latins, enjoys the broadest meaning among the Hebrews and has a singular and emphatic use in certain phrases. He who possesses something as his *own* is called the <term>master</term> of that thing, or the holder and possessor of it; and from this, any thing of which a certain attribute or property is truly predicated as belonging to it is called its <term>master</term> or <term>possessor</term>. <margin>According to Cocceius in his Lexicon on this word.</margin> Thus, a <term>Master of hair</term> <note>original Hebrew: בעל שער (ba'al sa'ar)</note> means *hairy, or having hair*; a <term>Master of shrewdness</term> <note>original Hebrew: בעל מזמה (ba'al mezimah)</note> means a *Master [of thought]...*

<summary>The author critiques the common translation of Ecclesiastes 12:11, arguing that "masters of assemblies" refers to the "master-nails" (the strength of the arguments) rather than the teachers themselves.</summary>

# ON ORIGINS BOOK I. PART II.

...or if he were held captive in foreign lands, then he would indeed be prevented by necessary circumstance from visiting this Temple and performing the customary religious duties toward God. What counsel then? In that case, clearly the people would *turn* <note>original Latin: "converteret"</note> in whatever place they were toward that quarter of the heavens in which the Temple was built; and in pouring out prayers, they would conceive in their mind as present that from which the body was separated by a great distance. 

This is indeed to *pray* **by way of the city and the house**, <note>original Hebrew: דרך העיר והבית (derekh ha-ir ve-ha-bayit)</note> which may be translated: *toward the city and the Temple*. But if no such circumstance detained the people, then it was their duty to go to this Temple and there supplicate God as if present. Those who did this were said to *pray* **toward the house, at the Temple** or **in the Temple**. <note>original Hebrew: אל הבית (el ha-bayit)</note> Indeed, the small word **toward** <note>original Hebrew: אל (el). The author is arguing that this preposition can mean "in" or "at" in this context.</note> (not to mention other 
<margin>verse 30.</margin>
examples easily found elsewhere) is understood in this very context: *And you shall hear* (prayers poured out to You) **IN THE PLACE OF YOUR DWELLING IN HEAVEN; and You will hear and show Yourself merciful.** <note>original Hebrew: אל מקום שבתך אל השמים (el meqom shivtekha el ha-shamayim). The author notes the Hebrew uses "el" (toward) to mean "in".</note> What is said as **toward heaven** you should properly translate as *at heaven*, which is to say *in heaven itself*; an elegant mode of speaking often favored by the Sacred Writers. 

As far as I can perceive, Solomon, in this entire scope of words, proposes the Temple alone as a **public oratory**. <term>oratory: a building or room set apart for private or public prayer (from the Latin "oratorium")</term> Jehoshaphat certainly repeated this 
<margin>2 Chronicles 20:9.</margin>
privilege of the Temple, himself praying to God in this Temple: *If some evil befalls us* (this is a fragment of his words), *the sword, judgment, or pestilence or famine;* **we shall stand before this house and before You.** <note>original Hebrew: נעמדה לפני הבית הזה ולפניך (naamdah lifne ha-bayit ha-zeh ve-lifnekha)</note> You see here only the Temple proposed as a public **house of prayer**, <note>original Greek: προσευκτήριον (proseukterion)</note> and no other sacred places besides it come into consideration. 

Indeed, what is said here—**to stand before this house** <note>original Hebrew: עמוד לפני הבית הזה (amod lifne ha-bayit ha-zeh)</note>—agrees with the phrase **at this house**, which has already been explained. Moreover, since the nations—whose ceremonies the Jewish people imitated with great zeal—boasted of their own temples everywhere at that time, as is clear from sacred history, who would think that the Jews of that age did not prize the religion of the Temple more than that of Synagogues? And that after building that most magnificent Temple, they would have wanted to diminish its value, splendor, and majesty by the construction of Synagogues? As far as I can see, this does not quite fit with the character of the Jews of that time.

### CHAPTER 9. ON SYNAGOGUES.

<margin>

**Fourthly**, when we weigh the fact that from the reign of Rehoboam <note>The son of Solomon whose reign saw the kingdom split into Israel and Judah.</note> onward, idolatry dominated among the people—sometimes more, sometimes less—and that even the efforts of pious Kings were continually interrupted and disturbed, either by the wicked inclinations of the people or by the policies of succeeding Kings, how can we believe that the worship of **Synagogues** flourished at that time? Or that the Jewish people, in such a state of affairs, devoted any effort to founding Synagogues? The very House of the Temple itself was at times so neglected that it had to be repaired at great expense. The people, on the contrary, were carried with such monstrous zeal toward the **High Places** <note>original: *Excelsa*; these were unauthorized hilltop shrines used for sacrifice, often associated with pagan worship.</note> that even the most pious Kings were hardly able to overthrow them. By **High Places**, you should understand not only the higher peaks and summits of mountains, but also certain smaller shrines <note>original: *sana*</note> built upon them. This was the love and the delight of the people, who were rivals to the superstitions of neighboring nations right up until the Babylonian Captivity. How well does it fit this state of affairs to imagine that synagogues were established? Indeed, if we contemplate the face of the Church during that interval a little more closely, we will find it much more afflicted and foul than we would dare to think or believe without the explicit testimony of Holy History—and even more so than we are commonly accustomed to believe.

I. I would like it to be noted what the Sacred History relates concerning **Jehoshaphat**, a most pious Prince. He is indeed praised as a Prince not only for this reason, that he destroyed and overthrew the **High Places**, but also because, surpassing his ancestors in zeal and piety, he sent out the **Levites and Priests** through the whole land of Canaan to teach the people. 

<margin>2 Chronicles 17:6.</margin>

The words of the text are: *And in the third year of his reign, he sent his princes, Ben-Hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah,* **TO TEACH IN THE CITIES OF JUDAH** <note>original Hebrew: ללמד בערי יהודה (*lilmod be-arei Yehudah*)</note>: *and with them were the Levites Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, and Tob-Adonijah, the Levites; and with them Elishama and Jehoram, the Priests.* **AND THEY TAUGHT IN JUDAH, AND WITH THEM WAS THE BOOK OF THE LAW OF THE LORD** <note>original Hebrew: וילמדו ביהודה ועמם ספר תורת יהוה (*va-yelamdu bi-Yehudah ve-immam sefer Torat Yehovah*)</note>; *and they went around all the cities of Judah,* **AND TAUGHT THE PEOPLE** <note>original Hebrew: וילמדו בעם (*va-yelamdu ba-am*)</note>. From every circumstance of this history, it is clear that this act of King Jehoshaphat was altogether singular. This distinguished Prince informed his subjects of the meaning of the Divine Law...

### CHAPTER 9. ON SYNAGOGUES.

If copies of the Law of Moses had been kept <note>original: "Mosaicæ exemplaria reservata sint"</note> as a matter of course, why would these Teachers carry a copy of the Mosaic Law with them? Indeed, why would the author of this history record that detail so pointedly? The fact that these *Priests and Levites*, along with the Princes, are said to have traveled through *all the cities of Judah* clearly reveals that this practice of instruction was not a continuous or permanent institution. For if it were otherwise, certain Teachers ought to have been assigned to every city by the King, who would devote themselves to educating the people on every occasion. However, it appears from this text that the Teachers chosen by the King traversed the entire region of Judah, and it is not equally clear that others succeeded them in their place. Thus, from this case—rare and notable as it is—we may conclude that the common people in that age enjoyed no such ordinary reading and exposition of the Divine Law as is now practiced in the Synagogues.

### CHAPTER 9. ON SYNAGOGUES.

For who would believe, as **Kimchi** <note>David Kimchi, a 12th-century biblical commentator and grammarian</note> rightly suggests, that Sacred History would have neglected to record such a thing in praise of Manasseh? <note>Manasseh was a king of Judah known for a long, largely idolatrous reign before a late-life repentance.</note> Everything leads us rather to believe that he only repented at the very end of his life, as he was drawing near to old age. From this, **Kimchi** easily concludes that although he may have put some effort into uprooting idolatry, he was by no means capable of restoring the worship of the true God or reviving the study of the sacred scriptures, which were by then almost entirely buried. This interpretation does not seem to stray from sound judgment.

**Abarbanel** <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century statesman and philosopher</note>, however, even while conceding that there is no solid foundation for attributing thirty-three whole years to Manasseh's repentance, does not find satisfaction in this interpretation. He thinks that one cannot conceive of such a total scarcity of the Codes of Divine Law as is necessary to assume here, especially since Jeremiah and other Prophets flourished at that time. He, therefore, following other older teachers of his nation, imagines that Manasseh and Amon—the grandfather and father of King Josiah—sought out all copies of the Law in Judea and tried to corrupt them by changing the memorial names of God <note>original Hebrew: האזכרות (*ha-azkarot*), refers to the sacred names of God</note> into the *names of idols*. When the Priests noticed this, one of them was so pious and concerned that the wicked King might also try to corrupt that specific copy which Moses had written with his own hand and placed at the side of the Ark; therefore, he removed this copy from there and hid it within the walls of the building. Later, when Josiah was reigning and restoring the public worship of God to its original state, the Priests searched for this volume with great care but could not find it. It happened by chance that those occupied in repairing the Temple found it.

This is a fable, as anyone can see, which **Abarbanel** felt compelled to believe out of necessity. He offers no argument from the text except that it is written as: *The* Book of the Law <note>original Hebrew: ספר התורה (*Sefer ha-Torah*)</note>, with the demonstrative "the," and not simply *a* book of the law. He also argues at length about the reverence with which such a Code—written by the very hand of Moses—should be venerated and preserved. He adds that if the people of the modern age were allowed to either see that same Code with their own eyes or touch it with their hands, there is no doubt they would be affected in a way not much different from the High Priest Hilkiah <note>referred to here by the Latinized name Chilkias</note>. ### CHAPTER 10. OF SYNAGOGUES.

<margin>In the Lexicon under the word *Mo'ed* <note>The Hebrew word for "appointed time" or "meeting place."</note>; *Sacred Miscellany*, Book 2, chapter 9. Psalm 74:8.</margin>
The assemblies of God <note>original Hebrew: מֹועֲדֵי אֵל (*mo'adei el*)</note> **Synagogues**. *Luther* translates this as **Houses of God**. But we must especially cite *Fuller*, a most learned man indeed, who takes this as proof for the most ancient constitution of synagogues and their divine origin. These are his very words: *“The Prophet confirms that the establishment of synagogues was begun not by human effort, but by divine command, calling them ‘the synagogues of the Mighty God’* <note>original: συναγωγὰς ἰσχυρᾶ (*synagōgas ischura*), from Aquila’s Greek translation</note> *; not only because of their purpose, being dedicated to divine worship, but also because of their source, being built according to the will of God.”* And certainly, it must not be hidden that this argument is not without some appearance of truth; if other facts aligned with it, it could be used quite aptly to support the opposing view. However, since the other facts do not align, and we have proven with suitable arguments—at least with probability—that synagogues were unknown until the migration to Babylon <note>original: τὴν μετοικεσίαν βαβυλῶνος (*tēn metoikesian babylōnos*)</note>, it would be a sign of laziness not to try and see if we are equal to removing this difficulty.

<margin>On Synagogues, Dissertation 1, section 6.</margin>
The famous *Burmann*, defending the same hypothesis as us, tried to loosen the knot in this way: he determined that this Psalm does not describe and mourn the present calamity of the Jewish people, but a future one. He argued it does not refer to one specific time of the Old Testament Church, but to various times; and especially, that the things predicted in this Psalm find their fulfillment in certain highly afflicted conditions of the New Testament Church. Thus he says: *“And one could easily escape all these difficulties if it is admitted—as Cocceius wishes—that since neither Antiochus burned the Temple, nor is Nebuchadnezzar recorded to have burned synagogues (even though he burned the Temple), it follows that this Psalm should not be restricted to the time of the Old Testament. Rather, it should be attributed to the time of the later Church—namely, from after the times of Solomon until the end of the age—lamenting not just one calamity, but pitying one affliction of itself and public worship piled upon another.”* He adds: *“Whatever the case may be, it is enough for us that nothing can be concluded here regarding the times of David, and thus nothing regarding synagogues being already built at that time.”* However, although I greatly venerate the memory and labors of Burmann and usually follow his judgment most willingly, I may be permitted to think differently from him here. ...the author intended to express future events through such *signs*, or through such voices and phrases, which were known and understood at the time he issued this prophecy. For this is the custom of the Prophets. When they speak of future things, they usually express them with the words and phrases commonly used at the time they publish their prophecies. Since I have discussed this in the preceding pages, I have no need to deal with it at length now. Imagine that at the time the Prophet wrote these things, *Synagogues* did not exist. Therefore, neither he nor the people of that time had any concept of "Synagogues." Now, it is truly rare for the Holy Spirit to hand down future events using words that designate things of which the people of that age have no idea; for in doing so, He would make the understanding of His word too difficult. Instead, He is accustomed to representing future things through words or emblems <note>Used here as symbolic representations or "word-pictures."</note> drawn from *matters* known and understood in the age when His word is published.

<margin>Malachi 1:11.</margin>
Thus, when foretelling that prayer houses <note>The Latin *oratoria* refers to places set aside specifically for prayer.</note> were eventually to be built for God throughout the whole world, and that Gentiles were to be chosen as Ministers of the Church, he says *in every place a pure offering must be offered to God, and Priests must be taken from the Gentiles*, etc. If, therefore, it is granted—as the most learned *Burmann* <note>Frans Burman (1628–1679), a Dutch Reformed theologian.</note> seems to grant—that the "assemblies of God" <note>original Hebrew: מועדי אל (*mo'adei el*)</note> designated the *Synagogues* of later times, such as the Oratories and Temples of Christians, then it becomes entirely probable that *Synagogues* already existed at that time. For it seems that if they had not existed, the Prophet would have used a different phrase that would have sparked a easier concept in the readers for a thing unknown at that time.

Indeed, when we consider the Psalm diligently, it seems to us to deal entirely with a certain time of public calamity, and specifically with the most miserable state of the Jewish Commonwealth, when the people were led away into the Babylonian Captivity. In this Psalm, I say, the deplorable face of the Jewish Republic and Church is *prophetically* depicted: the time when the Temple, by order of the King of Babylon, was turned to ashes, and Judea having been laid waste by the Chaldeans <note>The ancient people of Babylonia who conquered Jerusalem in 586 BCE.</note>, the Nation sacred to God was deported to foreign regions. ### CHAPTER 10. ON SYNAGOGUES.

...in the days of Nebuchadnezzar. But those first two <note>Referring to the prophets mentioned on the previous page.</note>, along with *Jeremiah* and *Ezekiel*, flourished only during the very first years of the Babylonian Captivity; regarding *Daniel*, enough has already been said. Therefore, it is rightly said of that interval of time that *there were then no Prophets.* 2. As for what is further added: *Nor is there any among us who knows for how long*; this too admits a suitable interpretation. To be sure, seventy years were predetermined by God for the Babylonian Captivity, but since all future events that do not depend on human planning and care are held as uncertain by the common people, the author of these laments describes the end of this calamity as if it were unknown; even more so because this span of *seventy* years was long, and thus the hope of the miserable Jews was drawn out into a state of uncertainty. Furthermore, although seventy years were indeed prescribed for the Babylonian Captivity, the end of the calamity and the afflicted state of the people—which was to last far beyond that span of time—was rightly considered uncertain. What of the fact that the *Angel of the LORD* in the book of Zechariah, under [King] *Darius*—whether it was *Darius Hystaspes* or *Darius Nothus* <note>Darius I or Darius II; the author is unsure which Persian king is intended.</note> is doubted—intercedes before God with these very words:

<margin>Zechariah 1:12</margin>
*How long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, against which you have been angry these seventy years?* <note>Original Hebrew: עד מתי אתה לא תרחם את ירושלם ואת ערי יהודה (*Ad-matai atah lo-terakhem et-Yerushalayim ve-et arei Yehudah*).</note>

You see then that even at a time when the people had long since been freed from the Babylonian prison, the end of the miseries with which they had struggled for so many years was still regarded as unknown. How much more, therefore, in *laments* <note>Original: "threnis," referring to the style of the Book of Lamentations or mourning poems.</note>—in which it is considered an art to conceal even those things that might mitigate the pain—is the end of this affliction presented as uncertain?

I think, therefore, that these words, when properly considered, do not present an obstacle to interpreting this Psalm as referring to the calamity of the Babylonian Captivity. Certainly, the whole of that text argues that it should be referred to a specific time in the Old Testament. Those who interpret it as referring to the affliction of the people under *Antiochus Epiphanes* <note>A Hellenistic king who persecuted the Jews in the 2nd century BCE, leading to the Maccabean Revolt.</note> are no less burdened by this final difficulty than we are, since the end of this calamity was also fixed by the Prophet *Daniel*;

<margin>Daniel 8:14. 1 Maccabees 7:16</margin>
even though I am aware that after the restoration of the Temple's worship, the people still struggled with a thousand miseries. However, I do not wish to overlook the fact that the *Author of the First Book of Maccabees* [cites] *Psalm Seventy-Nine*, which almost...

With these things established, we must now come closer to the difficulty presented to us by the words of this Song. Namely, among the calamities which are recounted in it in a long series, this also is mentioned: that **THEY HAVE BURNED ALL THE ASSEMBLIES OF GOD IN THE LAND** of Canaan <note>original: "כל מועדי אל OMNIA CONVENTICULA DEI IN TERRA"</note>. If by "all the assemblies of God" <note>original: "כל מועדי אל"</note> we must understand *Synagogues* here, of the kind that existed in later times, then this dispute is settled. For what did not exist cannot be described as having been burned. It must be seen, therefore, as I have already warned, whether "all the assemblies of God" are indeed *Synagogues*. 

Certainly there were ancient Translators who found no *Synagogues* here. The Septuagint <note>The earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, often abbreviated as "οἱ ὁ."</note> says: *Let us cause the feasts of the Lord to cease from the earth* <note>original: "καταπαύσωμεν τὰς ἑορτὰς κυρίου ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς"</note>.

Jerome suggests that it should be read as: *let us burn* <note>original: "κατακαύσωμεν"</note>. Theodotion translates: *They set on fire all the seasons of the Strong One in the land* <note>original: "Ἐνεπύρισαν πάντας καιροὺς ἰχυροῦ ἐν τῇ γῇ"</note>. Symmachus: *They burned all the festivals of God on the earth* <note>original: "Ἐνέπρησαν πάσας τὰς ἑορτὰς Θεῦ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς"</note>. The Old Latin Translator: *Let us cause all the FEAST DAYS of God to rest in the earth.* If it is uncertain what these translators intended by these versions of theirs, this at least is certain: they found no mention of *Synagogues* in this text. 

I would believe, indeed, that through a certain metonymy <note>A figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it; here, the "festivals" stand for the "Temple" where they are celebrated.</note> they understood the "feast days" to mean the *Temple*, since all the feasts were to be celebrated therein. Therefore, with that being *burned*, the *festas* themselves are considered burned. I admit, however, that the expression is a little *harsh*, by which feast days are said to be *burned* or *consumed*. 

There are, therefore, other most learned men who think this phrasing refers solely to the Temple. They think the Temple, I say, is called here **All the assemblies of God**.

<margin>In the Lexicon at the word *mo’ed* <note>The Hebrew word מועד means an appointed time or place.</note>.</margin>
...they have burned all the **PLACES OF GOD** <note>original: "כל מועדי אל"</note>: that is, the *Temple*, which consisted of many parts. Indeed, this interpretation is neither absurd nor to be despised. For in this same Psalm, the *Temple* is called **PLACES OF ASSEMBLY** <note>original: "מועדים"</note> and **SANCTUARIES** <note>original: "מקדשים"</note> (using the plural number, as they say, according to the custom of the Hebrews and even the Belgians <note>The author likely refers to Dutch scholars or the Dutch language’s use of plurals for grand buildings.</note>). <margin>verse 4.</margin> *Your enemies roar* **in the midst** *of your* **PLACES OF ASSEMBLY** <note>original: "בקרב מועדך"</note>; <margin>verse 6.</margin> *They have cast your* **SANCTUARIES** *into the fire* <note>original: "שלחו באש מקדשך"</note>. It has already been stated that the Hebrew interpreters read *your assembly* <note>original: "מועדך"</note> and *your sanctuary* <note>original: "מקדשך"</note> as *your assemblies* and *your sanctuaries*, where the letter *yod* <note>The Hebrew letter י , which often indicates a plural form.</note>, the marker of the plural, is omitted. <margin>Psalm 73, 8.</margin> Nor does any difficulty remain in this, since it is established beyond doubt that the *Temple* is sometimes called **SANCTUARIES** <note>original: "מקדשים"</note>. <margin>Jeremiah 51, 15.</margin> <margin>See also Isaiah 63, 18.</margin> *Aben Esra* <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra, a 12th-century Spanish rabbi and scholar.</note>: <margin>according to those who read it there</margin> "The Sanctuaries (referring to the Temple) are called *meeting places* <note>original: "מועדים"</note> because the Israelites were accustomed to gather there during the festivals; and in the same way, the following should be understood: 'They have burned all the **meeting places of God**' <note>original: "מועדי אל"</note>." Do you see how *Aben Esra*, in this passage as well as the preceding one, understands "all the meeting places of God" to mean the *Temple*? <margin>Commentary on this place; Exodus 25, 22.</margin> *Jarchi* <note>Also known as Rashi, a famous 11th-century French rabbi.</note> says likewise: "Your meeting places; this is the Holy Temple, concerning which it is said: *And I will meet with you there*." It will therefore be permissible, following the most excellent interpreters, to understand by these words "**all the meeting places of God**" the most august *Temple* with its splendid courts and magnificent structures of side-chambers, as it was prepared by *Solomon* at great expense. These were "all the meeting places of God in the land of Canaan," because in them God showed Himself present to His people. Yet what forbids us from extending the emphasis of this expression even further, if it can be done? Let us observe, therefore, that by a "**meeting place of God**" <note>original: "מועד אל"</note>, by the virtue of the Hebrew phrase, should be understood any *place* in which God either now shows Himself present, or formerly showed Himself present, and which He decorated with some appearance of His own and a manifestation of His grace. If I am not mistaken, "meeting place of God" most properly denotes among the Hebrews a place, not where men gather together, but in which God appears as if by appointment, and gives clear evidence of His presence and grace. For the phrase, as correctly noted by *Jarchi*, is taken from those words of God to *Moses* concerning the space in the middle of the Ark between the two *Cherubim*: "And **I WILL MEET** with you there..."

### ON THE ORIGIN, BOOK I, PART II.

<margin>
Book I, Part 2, Chapter 3.
</margin>

**AS AGREED WITH YOU:** We have dealt with this matter more at length above, where we discussed the meaning of the name <term>Ohel Moed</term> <note>Hebrew: אהל מועד</note> or **Tent of Meeting**. Indeed, that place in which **God** presents Himself as present is properly called <term>Mo’adei El</term> <note>Hebrew: מועדי אל</note> or **THE PLACE OF THE ASSEMBLY OF GOD**. I do not deny that God is usually present in the gathering of His people, and therefore every congregation of the people of God can be called, in a certain sound sense, a **PLACE OF THE ASSEMBLY OF GOD**. However, I do not think that such a meaning for this phrase fits the simplicity and character of the Hebrew language. For formerly, under the conditions of the Old Testament, God wished to be sought and worshipped by the people in specific places chosen **by Himself**, and not by the people. It was the people’s duty to observe **where God appeared**, and to seek God **there**. Therefore, by "Places of the Assembly of God," as I have said, it is believed that those locations are most appropriately designated in which God was accustomed to **manifest** Himself in a singular way.

And what were those places, you ask, **besides the Temple**? Various ones indeed. For they were places of this kind where God appeared to the Patriarchs and other holy men, even outside the Tabernacle. 

<margin>
Genesis 35: 1, 3, 7.
Joshua 8:30.
Judges 6:24.
Chapter 13:20.
Chapter 21:4.
1 Samuel 14:35.
</margin>

Moreover, it was an accepted custom that in such a place, which God had celebrated with such a singular example of His grace, a marker or **altar** would be placed. By this, the **grace of God** exhibited in those places at some time was recalled to those passing by, and they were reminded to worship God **there** rather than elsewhere. And I believe these places can certainly be understood as <gloss>Mo’adei El</gloss> **places of the assembly of God**. For although after the Temple was built, the people were especially required to worship God in that most sacred place, nothing prevents those other places from being honored by holy recollection—the memory of ancient blessings, of course, winning them veneration. 

Nor is this interpretation foreign to the context of the passage. For in this Psalm, **Asaph** <note>The traditional author of Psalm 74, often depicted as a levite musician reflecting on the destruction of the Temple.</note> complains that the enemies wanted to destroy all worship of the true God and completely erase the memory of Him from the minds of men. What would achieve that more than if they devastated all those places in which the memory of God’s name had been worshipped, and where the signs of that memory stood? Moreover, he complains that those places were burned, because the most famous of these places—namely, the **Temple**—suffered this fate. And indeed, **Jarchi** <note>A common Latinization for Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> comes very close to this interpretation:

Commentary on this passage.
</margin>

# CHAPTER 2. ON SYNAGOGUES.

"They destroyed Shiloh; Nebuchadnezzar destroyed the First House [Temple]; the Romans destroyed the Second House." <note>original Hebrew: הֶחֱרִיבוּ שִׁילֹה נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר הֶחֱרִיב בֵּית רִאשׁוֹן רוֹמִיִּים הֶחֱרִיבוּ בַּיִת שֵׁנִי</note> *All the places of God’s Assembly in the land: All the houses of assembly which He had. The Philistines destroyed Shiloh; Nebuchadnezzar destroyed the First Temple; the Romans the later one.* Jarchi <note>The influential medieval Jewish commentator Rashi</note> agrees with us in that he interprets these words as referring to several places of assembly; however, he differs because he applies this Psalm to several afflictions of the Jewish Nation simultaneously. Yet, as you see, he finds no mention of *Synagogues* in this text. If, however, our explanation does not satisfy someone, and they are entirely persuaded that the "shadow" of Synagogues lurks beneath these words, let them also understand—and I would not object—that this phrase could refer to the *Schools and Academies of the Prophets*. We previously mentioned that the people used to gather in such places and the youth were instructed in the liberal arts; even though no necessity forces us to accept that interpretation here. Surely, the more prudent will not think that a single passage with such a doubtful meaning is enough to overturn all the arguments we presented in the **previous Chapter** for the opposing view.

If certain women—for I think it would be difficult to prove that all or even the majority of them did so, or were obligated to do so—frequented the Temple with their husbands on some solemn feast, they seem to have stayed by their husbands' sides and performed their duties along with them.

### CHAPTER II. OF SYNAGOGUES.

Finally, I will not conceal a difficulty that occurred to me while occupied with these matters, drawn from the history of the stolen vineyard and its murdered owner, **Naboth**. <margin>1 Kings 21:8, 9, 10, etc.</margin> Jezebel, the most wicked wife of Ahab, had conceived in her mind the crime of thrusting her husband into possession of Naboth's vineyard by most unjust force—a vineyard which Naboth had refused to surrender to Ahab, as it had descended to him as an inheritance from his ancestors. Therefore, she sent letters to the elders and leading men of Samaria, and to the governors and magistrates of the people, in which she commanded *a fast to be proclaimed, and Naboth to be placed* AT THE HEAD OF THE PEOPLE <note>original Hebrew: בראש העם (berosh ha'am)</note>. That this was diligently carried out and managed by these men is suggested by the following context of the story. This fast was celebrated in Samaria. But where? For it seems clear that it was celebrated in a specific place designated for that purpose, since each person had a seat according to their dignity in that solemn act.

This seems entirely indicated by the words: *and you shall set Naboth at the head of the people* <note>original Hebrew: והושיבו את נבות בראש העם (ve-hoshivu et Navot berosh ha'am)</note>. Was there, then, a **Synagogue** in Samaria in which the people were accustomed to gather at the time of a **Fast**? I think not. For how can it be imagined that there was one where such great impiety reigned? You might then ask, where was this Fast observed? I answer, either in some public square of the city, or in the **Temple** that had been built by Ahab in **Samaria**. In ancient times, when fixed places for the exercise of religion in such acts were not yet designated, fasts seem to have been celebrated in **public squares and streets**. 

Nor do I doubt that this was observed in the **Mizpah Fast** <note>original Latin: "Jejunio Mispitico," referring to the assembly called by Samuel in 1 Samuel 7</note>, which we have discussed elsewhere. Indeed, even after the Temple was restored, that solemnity did not fall into disuse. <margin>1 Samuel 7:5, 6; Nehemiah 8:1, 2, 3.</margin> A most famous example is that **Fast** held in the presence of **Ezra** *in the street of Jerusalem*. Furthermore, Maimonides <note>The 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legal scholar.</note>, in accordance with the statutes of the ancients, teaches that this same ritual for celebrating a fast was observed by his ancestors in the past and would be observed again if they were to govern their own Republic according to their own judgment. <margin>Hilchot Ta’anit <note>original: "Hilcoth Tanioth," the Laws of Fasts</note>, chapter 4, § 1.</margin> He says: *On each day of those seven final fasts, which are established to request rain, they pray in this manner. They bring out* THE ARK INTO THE PUBLIC SQUARE OF THE CITY <note>original Hebrew: מוציאין את התיבה לרחובה של עיר (motsi’in et ha-teivah li-rehovah shel ir)</note>, *and all the people gather, and cover themselves in sackcloth, etc.* What is so strange, then, if we say that the Fast established by Jezebel...

## CHAPTER XII.

*The origin of Synagogues and their primary ceremonies is placed after the Return of the Jews from the Babylonian Captivity to Canaan, as supported by learned men and confirmed by the words of Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note>. *Following this, it is argued that the exact point in time to which the origin of synagogues should be assigned is uncertain, given that no mention of them exists even in the History of the Maccabees. It is noted, however, that their principal ceremonies are to be traced back to that solemn Reading of the Divine Law, with the associated Blessings, described in the Book of Nehemiah. Once this text is illustrated, other causes that promoted the origin of synagogues are also reviewed. Finally, this dissertation is concluded with the addition of certain passages from Philo and Josephus concerning the progress of this first institution of Synagogues.*

<margin>
Spencer, *On the Laws of the Hebrews*, Book 1, Chapter 4, Section 10, p. 54.
Sigonio, *The Hebrew Republic*, Book 2, Chapter 8.
See also Schindler in his *Lexicon* at the word *Migdal* <note>original Hebrew: מגדל; meaning "tower" or "pulpit," referring to the wooden platform used by Ezra.</note>.

But since *prayers* fulfill the greatest part of Synagogue religion, it will be useful to learn from *Maimonides* how much Ezra advanced the institutions of the Synagogues in this regard. He had said that prayers are commanded in the Law by these words: <note>original Hebrew: ועבדתם את ה' אלהיכם</note> *and you shall serve the Lord your God.* <note>Exodus 23:25.</note> For it is established from the most ancient oral tradition <margin>Laws of Prayer and the Priestly Blessing [Hilcoth Tephilla Ubircath Cohanim], chapter 1, § 1.</margin> that by <term>service</term> <note>original Hebrew: עבודה, "Avodah." <header>PART II OF BOOK I: ON THE ORIGIN.</header>

<margin>Neh. 8:1.</margin>
The Hebrew word *meforash* <note>original: מפורש</note> means that which is *explained*, *declared*, or *expressed in writing*. This is not, in truth, a dispute of any great weight; however, I am of the opinion that when it says, *And they read in the Book, in the Law of God* <note>original Latin: ויקראו בספר בתורת יי'</note>, it is sufficiently indicated that Ezra read from the Law written by Moses, which the people had requested. Thus, it was not necessary to indicate this with another rare and infrequent word. This is especially true because those oral traditions do not seem to have been widespread or to have held any authority at that time. Indeed, I find it hard to believe that a people returned from the Babylonian Captivity—whose affairs were in total disarray and who had almost forgotten the *written* Law—would have given any thought to unwritten *traditions*. Such things were only later devised by overly imaginative minds after the deaths of the Prophets and were then covered with the cloak of venerable antiquity. I therefore retain the *Common Version* <note>The Vulgate</note>, in which there is no difficulty.

However, a certain *learned man* <note>likely referring to the Hebraist Immanuel Tremellius</note> rightly addressed that last phrase, *and they understood the reading* <note>original: ויבינו במקרא</note>, which *Tremellius* had translated as: *They gave understanding through the scripture itself*. The Dutch translated it as: *So they made it so that it was understood in the reading*; they rendered it: *And they understood the Scripture—namely, the Listeners*. For if the version by *Tremellius* and the *Dutch* were to hold, the same thing would be said twice in a short historical <term>perigraphe</term> <note>original: περιγραφή — a summary or sketch</note>, and in such a way that the second part would be less emphatic than the first. Furthermore, the Hebrew word *hebin* <note>to understand</note> is constructed here with the preposition *be* (ב); in such cases, it ordinarily signifies *to understand*, not *to make someone else understand*. We therefore conceive of distinct actions in this verse concerning two types of people: the *Teachers*, naturally, and the *Listeners*. Of the *Teachers*, it is told that *they read and gave the meaning*; of the *Listeners*, it is said that *they understood what was read*.

It is still a matter of doubt whether those who read the Law before the people were the same ones who interpreted it or "gave the meaning." Certainly, if we consider the eighth verse, it is clear that the *Levites*, whose names are even listed, instructed the people in the Law. Therefore, Ezra did not do this alone, but rather the Levites, who had been taught by Ezra and stood at his side. Nor should it be imagined that *Ezra* alone read here, although that action is ascribed to him as the primary <term>nomikos</term> <note>original: νομικῷ — a legal expert or jurist</note> in the fourth verse; for those *Levites* who stood by him *read* as well, as we clearly gather from **Chapter 9:3–4**, each in his own place and order, as was fitting. Truly, we must describe more distinctly from this text those features which the Synagogues of subsequent times held in common.

$\beta$. Standing upon it are *Ezra* with other *Doctors* <note>scholars or teachers of the law</note>.
$\gamma$. Reading the Law—

These were bought by students of the divine law and read more diligently than had been done before the Jews were carried away to Babylon. Handwritten <term>books</term> <note>original: *codices*</note> seem to have been rare, interpretation scarce, and studies of the Divine Law lukewarm before the times of the Babylonian Captivity. ...as we find. In what circumstance, therefore, were they born? In the *Captivity* <note>The Babylonian Captivity (6th century BCE), when the Jewish people were exiled from Jerusalem to Babylon.</note>, I believe. The experience of all ages has taught that the sacred rites of Religion tend to be treated lukewarmly and negligently when their exercise is free and unimpeded; on the contrary, where Religion is oppressed by force or confined within narrow boundaries, then it is that the zeal for it thrives most. 

It happened almost exactly thus with the Jews. As long as they lived in Canaan, enjoying their Prophets and Priests, they continually slipped from the worship of the true God into foul idolatry, from which they could be deterred by no promises or threats. But when they were led away into the Babylonian Captivity, and when they seriously called to mind their misery and its causes, they first conceived such a hatred for all idolatry that they detested no crime more than this from that time forward; then they also began to handle the Word of God more diligently, and to examine and investigate its meanings, as is evident from *Ezra*, who is most celebrated by this name among the Captives. 

<margin>A. A. 43 the discipline of the laws</margin> 

From this study was born the public reading of the Divine Law, instituted among the Jews returning from Captivity in Jerusalem, in the square which was before the Temple, about which we were just briefly explaining. Moreover, the reading of the Divine Law could have been repeated and more frequently continued in this same way among the returning Jews on the more solemn festivals or even on Sabbaths in the Temple, or if there were too great a gathering of people, in the square before the Temple, without any *Synagogues* <note>The author distinguishes between the act of communal reading and the formal institution of the synagogue building.</note>. 

But those Jews who lived outside of Canaan among the Gentiles, undoubtedly affected by the example of those who were in Canaan and by a singular zeal for the Divine Law and the religion of their fathers, when they wished to imitate the piety and zeal of their fellow tribesmen, they had to seek out *places* in which they might handle these sacred matters. For since they lived among the Gentiles, where they had no Temple they could use for this purpose, nor any place of their own where they were free to gather, they were driven by the greatest necessity to establish certain *places* for this religion of theirs. 

But since it can easily be believed that Kings and Magistrates, most devoted to the established worship of their own idols, would have been reluctant to consent to the public building of *places* to be consecrated for the exercise of a religion so different from their own, and which condemned all other religions, and therefore...

# ON ORIGINS BOOK I. PART II.
<header>DE ORIGINE LIB. I. PARS II.</header>

Since the Jews were despised and hated by all other nations, it seems most likely to me that those living outside of Canaan in the midst of the Gentiles first chose private homes for their sacred gatherings. Or, perhaps they designated a part of certain private houses—inhabited by the most noble men of their community—for these sacred rites, meeting there on fixed days to devote themselves to prayer, reading, and the interpretation of the Law. 

However, after the Jews began to distinguish themselves greatly in certain Kingdoms and Republics, as much by their numbers as by their wealth, and often directed their affairs so prudently that their friends flourished in the Courts of Kings and Princes, they eventually obtained this grace (among other favors granted to them with a liberal hand): they were permitted to build public *Synagogues and Houses of Prayer* <note>The author uses the terms Synagogas and Proseuchas; the latter is a Greek term for a place of prayer often used in the Diaspora.</note>. 

Perhaps these were first granted to them in Egypt, which they inhabited in incredible numbers. From there, they might be considered to have been transferred to other regions and, as it seems to me, to Canaan itself. This can only be reached through conjecture. Indeed, in the history of *Susanna* <note>A story found in the Greek additions to the Book of Daniel.</note>—whoever its author may be and with whatever reliability it was written—I found mention of a *Synagogue* or *Auditorium* which was in the house of *Hilkiah*, a most noble man among the inhabitants of Babylon, where the Jews of that place were accustomed to <margin>Chapter 1, 4. Antiquities Book 13, chapter 6.</margin> convene. 

It is more uncertain whether we may trace back to this point what *Onias* (son of *Onias III*) says in a petition offered to *Ptolemy Philometor*. He states that while traveling through various regions, he noticed that in *Coele-Syria*, *Phoenicia*, *Leontopolis*, and other places, the Jews <term>had temples contrary to what is proper</term> <note>original: "παρὰ τὸ καθῆκον ἔχειν ἱερὰ"</note> **HAD TEMPLES CONTRARY TO WHAT IS DECOROUS**. 

We discussed above whether *Temples* in the proper sense are to be understood here, or rather *Synagogues*? And certainly, we are still hesitating. If they were *Synagogues*, why does he say it was "contrary to what is proper"? If they were *Temples* properly so called, under what pretext does he criticize in others the very thing he himself aspires to do? There are other difficulties which might cast doubt on the reliability of Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian.</note>. If, however, by <term>sacred places</term> <note>original: "ἱερὰ"</note> we should understand *Synagogues*, then from these words we can gather that even then, *Synagogues* flourished in great numbers in the regions neighboring Canaan. But if you understand them as *Temples*, specifically so designated, why would you not admit the existence of *Synagogues* where you admit *Temples*?

### CHAPTER 12. ON SYNAGOGUES.

established *Synagogues*, I would not wish to exclude others. For what wonder is it that many other factors converged here? Therefore, I believe: **1.** The commandment given by Moses concerning the reading of the Law every seventh year during the *Feast of Tabernacles* before the whole assembly of Israel could 

<margin>Deuteronomy 31:10. Book 1. Part 2. chapter 4.</margin>

provide the occasion for the buildings of Synagogues. To be sure, this commandment itself, as noted above, does not mandate the construction of Synagogue buildings. I even doubt whether it was diligently, or even frequently, observed while the Republic <note>Referring to the sovereign Jewish state.</note> stood before the Babylonian Captivity. Yet the reading of the Law ordered there could hardly be performed without certain ceremonies, which are not entirely unlike those that were later accepted in the Synagogue. Indeed, the worship of the Synagogues is simple, and consists almost entirely of prayers, reading, and interpretation of the Law. And it is possible that the people, upon returning from Babylon, were driven by this commandment 

<margin>Nehemiah 8:1.</margin>

and ordered *Ezra* to bring forth the Law at the Feast of Tabernacles; and thus this very commandment gave rise to certain primary ceremonies of the Synagogue. ### CHAPTER I. WITH SYNAGOGUES ETC.

...of men. Erasmus had translated the phrase *house by house* <note>original Greek: κατ᾽ οἶκον (kat’ oikon)</note> as "through individual houses." However, Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a French Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin.</note> rightly warns that this interpretation should be rejected due to its *ambiguity*. For we should not think that meetings were held and the Holy Assembly <term>synaxis: from the Greek for "gathering," referring here to the formal liturgical assembly of the early Church.</term> was celebrated in the private homes or small huts of every individual believer. Rather, the true meaning of the expression is fully satisfied if we understand "house by house" to refer to *private houses*—not every single one belonging to every person, but the larger and more spacious ones that were suited for these uses. To be sure, the Church at Jerusalem was divided into several parishes <note>original Greek: παροικίας (paroikias)</note>, whose residents <note>original Greek: πάροικοι (paroikoi)</note> were accustomed to meet at certain specific and more spacious houses <note>original Greek: οἴκους (oikous)</note>. These houses are clearly contrasted with the Temple, into which all the disciples of Christ used to flow together without distinction. This same distinction can be observed in the following context of this history:

<margin>Acts 5:42</margin>
> *And daily in the TEMPLE and FROM HOUSE TO HOUSE, they did not cease teaching and preaching Jesus Christ.* <note>The author provides the Greek here: ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ καὶ κατ᾽ οἶκον (en tō hierō kai kat’ oikon).</note> *The Temple is manifestly distinguished from the houses.*

Since these matters are quite easy and explicit, I do not know what drove those most learned men of refined judgment, De Dieu and Cloppenburg <note>Louis de Dieu and Johannes Cloppenburg were 17th-century Dutch theologians and scholars of biblical languages.</note>, to take a different path here.

He believes there were many such rooms open for the use of sacred assemblies and sacrificial feasts, especially on feast days. At last, however, he surrendered himself entirely to his friend in this doubtful matter, perhaps out of regard for kindness and friendship more than for his arguments. ...severely accusing their enemies, because they *did not blush to speak about the mystery of the Lord’s Supper in the presence of the Catechumens <note>Those receiving instruction before baptism but not yet fully admitted to the sacraments</note> and even Greeks and Pagans*. Because of this, it happened that Christians nurtured the unfair suspicions of the Gentiles regarding their sacred rites, as is evident from the accusations of *Celsus* <note>A 2nd-century philosopher and author of "The True Word," one of the first major intellectual attacks on Christianity</note>. It is very easy to understand how this method of handling the mysteries could strongly drive the Christians toward a *secret and quiet practice of their religion*. For since those who are protected by no power or authority in the State are forced to admit random spectators to what they perform in public, the Christians of the earliest times—possessing almost no authority until they finally acquired some among the Gentiles through long habit in the *third century*—do not seem to have wanted to expose themselves to this disadvantage in the beginning, even if there were no other reason to deter them from public practice of their sacred rites. And these things move me to believe that in the first two centuries, *public places* where Christians openly professed their faith were *rare*. However, I would not dare to claim that none existed at all. For the situation in certain cities could have been different, whether because they were located at the edges of the Roman Empire, or because they had Governors or inhabitants a bit more indulgent toward Christians, so that they could meet publicly there without danger.

The Christians, when they were choosing and arranging the places for their own Assemblies, could have imitated these examples. But who would believe that they kept the *Temples* or *Schools* of the Gentiles <note>original: "Gentilium" — referring to non-Jewish, polytheistic peoples, often called Pagans.</note> in their sights?
