The *Temple*, which was specifically called by that name, was a *House* in which God was thought to *dwell*; it was not intended for the congregations of men, but for the *indwelling of God*. The Israelites, who desired to meet with God, were only received in the *Porticoes* <note>original: "Porticibus" — the covered porches or walkways surrounding the main sanctuary.</note> of the Temple, and it was there that they poured out their prayers. <margin>Acts 7:48</margin> Truly, the Church of the Christians has no house of this kind, built of wood and stone, of which God is the inhabitant. For God to dwell in such a way in a specific place, or in any place at all at this time, is repugnant to the profession of the Christian faith. <margin>1 Peter 2:5</margin> The Church itself—the very assembly of the believers—is the *House of God*. Therefore, the first Christians, when they were arranging the *places* of their assembly, did not look back to the Temple, since it was utterly opposed to their sacred rites. <margin>Psalm 82:13, 14</margin> It is added that they knew God did not wish to tolerate any other *house of His dwelling* except for the one in *Jerusalem*. If, however, under the name of the "Temple" you also include the *porticoes* in which the Israelites were accustomed to worship God, I confess there was something about the Temple which could have given the Christians an occasion for building oratories <note>small chapels or places designated for prayer.</note>. Truly, since it was permitted to worship God not only in the Temple but also in *every other place*, it should not be thought that Christians, in establishing *sacred* places for the exercise of their Religion, had the Temple more in mind than any other *places* which were similar to the Temple in this respect. Therefore, nothing remains except that we cast our eyes upon the *Schools* or *Synagogues* (which were often conflated among the Jews), and inquire whether the Church of the early times, when about to organize the *places* of its worship—whether in *private* or in *public*—wished to shape them to this *type* rather than to any other. So I believe: and the following points will persuade you of it.

->### CHAPTER 2. COMPARISON WITH SYNAGOGUES, etc.<-

1. I would like it to be considered that *Synagogues* were extremely suitable and well-adapted for the practice of the Christian Religion. *Synagogues are public or private places* in which Jews are accustomed to gather, both for praising God and praying, and for hearing the reading and interpretation of the *Divine Law*. For this practice, which certainly does not require a grand display, they were primarily intended, and were equipped with the very few instruments necessary for that purpose. Indeed, what else did the first Christians do, or what ought they to have done, in their own *Places of Assembly*? To pray to God, to sing hymns to Him, and to build up and strengthen one another in that truth which they professed—this was their work, this was their practice. *Add a table* upon which the sacred symbols of bread and wine—commended to His Church by Christ through a specific command—may be arranged, and you will be permitted to call that place, which you previously called a *Synagogue* when it was dedicated to Jewish rites, a *Church* now that it is possessed and used by Christians. Since, therefore, *Synagogues* are most fitting for the sacred worship of the New Covenant and were established by the Jews for the same purposes for which *Oratories* <note>original: "Oratoria" — literally "places of prayer," used here to describe early Christian meeting spaces.</note> were to be established by the Christians, it is indeed very likely that the *Houses of the Christians were shaped according to the pattern of Synagogues*. This reasoning will gain greater strength if we consider:

2. That the first *Apostles and Teachers* of the early Church were *Jews* by both race and profession, who had been accustomed to the *Synagogues* and their practices from infancy. Indeed, that truly great and excellent man, *Hugo Grotius*, elsewhere not only concedes that Christian Churches are referred to by the name of *synagogues* in the book of James, but teaches further that in the Churches of the Christians, almost the same rites were observed as those known to be observed in the Synagogues. Moreover, those other names by which Synagogues are designated were likewise formerly attributed to the meeting houses of the first Christians. ...the things which were cited above from the book *Kol Bo*: <note>original Hebrew: כל מקום שיש בו עשרה מישראל צריך להכין לו בית שיכנסו בתוכו להתפלל</note> "In every place where there are ten Israelites, it is necessary to establish a **HOUSE**, in which they may **GATHER**, for the sake of **PRAYING**." <note>original Latin: "In omni loco, in quo sunt decem Israelitæ, oportet constituere DOMUM, in quam CONGREGENTUR, ad ORANDUM."</note> Observe that the Synagogue is called a *house* here, and indeed a house of gathering, for the sake of prayers. ### CHAPTER 2. WITH SYNAGOGUES, ETC. 451

...from the throne or *Exedra*, which was in the *chancel*, they were accustomed to exhort the people through *sermons*. Regarding the Episcopal *exedra*, one should understand what the Fathers of the Synod of Antioch said concerning <term>Paul of Samosata</term><note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Antioch who was deposed for heresy and criticized for his worldly, autocratic behavior.</note> in the writings of <term>Eusebius</term>: <margin>Ecclesiastical History, book 7, ch. 30.</margin> <note>original Greek: Βῆμα μὲν καὶ θρόνον ὑψηλὸν ἑαυτῷ κατασκευασάμενος, οὐκ ὡς Χριστοῦ μαθητής, σηκρήτον δὲ, ὥσπερ οἱ τοῦ κόσμου ἄρχοντες, ἔχων τε καὶ ὀνομάζων; παίων τε τῇ χειρὶ τὸν μηρὸν, καὶ τὸ βῆμα ἀράττων τοῖς ποσί;</note> "He prepared for himself a platform and a high throne, not as a disciple of Christ, but having and naming it a 'private chamber' <note>original: *secretum*</note>, just like the rulers of the world; striking his thigh with his hand and stomping on the platform with his feet." For he constructed for himself both a **TRIBUNAL** and a **HIGH THRONE**, *not as a disciple of Christ;* and he held a **PRIVATE CHAMBER**, *named just like that of a secular magistrate. In addition to this, he was accustomed to strike his thigh with his hand,* and *stomp on the* **TRIBUNAL** *with his feet.* The Fathers of Antioch criticized this in *Samosata* because he built a *throne* in the chancel higher than others, in the likeness of a *Tribunal*. <margin>See Valesius on this passage.</margin> Ruffinus expressed the sense quite well: *In the Church he ordered a* **TRIBUNAL** *to be built for himself much higher than it had been, and a throne to be placed in the highest parts.* <margin>The City of God, book 22, ch. 8, near the end.</margin> Is this not the same thing that **Augustine** called an exedra? *On the steps of the exedra, **IN WHICH I SPOKE FROM A HIGHER POSITION**, I made both brothers stand while their petition was being read.* <margin>Note on this passage; On the Crown of Hippolytus, book 4, Epistle 5, page 126.</margin> Prudentius, however, called the <term>Ambo</term><note>An elevated pulpit or lectern used for reading the Gospel or preaching.</note> itself a *tribunal*:

->*At the opposite front, a high* **TRIBUNAL** *is raised by steps,*<-
->*from which the Bishop proclaims God.*<-

<margin>ch. 2, 3.</margin>
He imitated Cyprian, who likewise called this same place **TRIBUNAL**—the place *from which the readers read the Sacred Scripture, and because it was higher than others, it was called an ambo*, from the Greek word *anabaino* (to ascend). We wish to compare this with the *raised platforms of the Synagogues*. **β.** In the *Buildings* of the Christians, the *seats* were no less arranged, some more honorable than others, *with those for women indeed being distinct from those for men*, just as they were formerly in the Synagogues of the Jews. A clear memory of them is found in the words of **James** cited above, where he blames Christians because, when a wealthier man entered their meeting house, they said: **SIT HERE COMFORTABLY** <note>original: *SEDE HIC καλῶς PULCRE*</note>; but to another, whose clothing was less splendid: *You stand there, or sit here under my footstool.* <margin>Book 2, ch. 61.</margin> One may learn that the matter was handled in a similar way in the Christian Churches of following centuries, with distinct *benches* for men and women as is done in the Synagogue, from the so-called *Apostolic Constitutions* of Clement. <margin>Book 2, ch. 1.</margin> On this, see *Hospinian, On Temples*, who noted various testimonies useful for clarifying this comparison. <margin>Ecclesiastical History, book 10, ch. 4.</margin> In **Eusebius** we read specifically concerning the Temple of the Tyrians that it was adorned with <note>original Greek: βάθροις ἐν τάξει τοῖς καθ’ ὅλου κατὰ τὸ πρέπον</note> **BENCHES arranged in order throughout the whole Temple in a fitting manner**.

### ON THE AGREEMENT OF HOUSES OF PRAYER, BOOK 1, PART 3. 452

The most learned <term>Valesius</term><note>Henri Valois (1603–1676), a distinguished French classical scholar and historian of the early Church.</note> argues against <term>Leo Allatius</term><note>A Greek scholar and librarian of the Vatican (1586–1669) who sought to demonstrate the historical unity of the Eastern and Western Churches.</note> that the **benches** <note>original: *subsellia*</note> mentioned here should be understood as those prepared for the ministers of the Church, rather than for the laity. However, I hold with Allatius that by "benches," the seats not only of the Ministers of the Church but also of the laity are signified. For the author of the *Panegyric* <note>Referring to the famous sermon for the dedication of the Church of Tyre, recorded by the historian Eusebius.</note>, being about to repeat every detail he had spoken regarding this Temple so that he might apply them to the spiritual Temple—that is, the Church—explains his mind in the following words: <note>original Greek: “Ἔνεισι δ' ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ καὶ θρόνοι. βάθρα τε μυρία καὶ καθιστήρια;</note> “**In this Temple there are also thrones, and countless benches and seats.**” Who would believe that those "innumerable" benches of which this author speaks were intended only for the deacons and the other Ministers of the Church? This is especially true since it is certain, and Valesius himself admits, that the Laity also sat in the Church.

<margin>chapter 20, verse 8.</margin>
γ. Who does not know that lamps were lit in the ancient Church, first indeed for practical use, and then also for decoration (which was certainly a great abuse)? Regarding their **use**, we already have a clear passage in the Acts of the Apostles: <note>original Greek: Ἦσαν δὲ λαμπάδες ἱκαναὶ ἐν τῷ ὑπερώῳ, οὗ ἦσαν συνηγμένοι;</note> **There were many lamps in the upper room where they were gathered.** For <term>Luke</term> had noted that <term>Paul</term> had extended his sermon at <term>Troas</term> even until midnight. However, that lamps subsequently began to be lit in the Temples of Christians for the joy and honor of the martyrs—a custom by no means to be approved—can be learned from that bitter and immoderate dispute of the most learned <term>Jerome</term> against <term>Vigilantius</term><note>Vigilantius was a priest who criticized the growing cult of martyrs, relics, and the use of ritual candles, which Jerome defended with characteristic ferocity.</note>, who had rightfully criticized this abuse.

<margin>Volume 2. Letters. folio page 44. column 4.</margin>
> **As for the candles, Jerome says, we do not light them in the bright light of day, as you fruitlessly allege: but so that we may temper the darkness of the night with this comfort, and keep watch by the light, lest we sleep in the darkness, blind like you. But if some, on account of the ignorance and simplicity of worldly men, or certainly of religious women—of whom we can truly say: "I confess they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge"—do this for the honor of the martyrs, what do you lose by it?**

Then, after a few intervening words, he continues:

> **For even without the relics of martyrs, throughout all the Churches of the East, when the Gospel is to be read, lamps are lit, even when the sun is already shining: certainly not to drive away the darkness, but to show a sign of joy.**

Indeed, just as among the Jews the piety of those who light lamps in the Synagogues is praised, so no less was the humility of those in the Christian Churches commended, who performed this duty for the house of God—

### CHAPTER 2. COMPARISON WITH SYNAGOGUES, etc. 453

...they did not deny God. Worthy of observation on this matter is what <term>Sozomen</term><note>Salamanes Hermias Sozomenus (c. 400–450 AD), a historian of the early Christian Church.</note> reports concerning Melas, the Bishop of <term>Rhinocolura</term><note>An ancient city on the border between Egypt and Palestine, now known as El Arish.</note>.

<margin>Church History, book 6, chapter 31. See also Hospinian, *On Temples*, book 2, chapter 32.</margin>

Those who had come to him—as he was an opponent of the <term>Arian faction</term><note>A major theological movement in early Christianity that argued Jesus Christ was distinct from and subordinate to God the Father; it was declared heretical at the Council of Nicaea.</note>—intending to drive him from his seat, are said to have found him **preparing the lamps of the church, like the lowliest servant, having a belt stained with oil over his cloak and carrying the wicks.** <note>original Greek: τὸς λύχνος τῆς ἐκκλησίας παρασκευάζοντα, οἰάγε ὑπηρέτην ἔχατον, ἐπιῤῥύπον τῷ ἱματίῳ ὑπὸ τῷ ἐλαίῳ τὴν ζώνην ἔχοντα καὶ τὰς θρυαλλίδας ἐπιφερόμενον</note>

δ. <term>Casalius</term><note>Giovanni Battista Casali (1576–1648), an Italian antiquarian who wrote on ancient Christian and Roman rites.</note> relates from Paulinus, the Bishop of Nola, that there were small rooms in Christian temples in which the sacred books were kept.

<margin>*On Ancient Christian Sacred Rites*, Part 3, chapter 33, p. 169. *Letters*, Volume 2, folio 43, column 1.</margin>

And yet these seem in some way to be able to represent the **Arks**, or even the **Libraries of the Synagogues**. Certainly **Jerome** expressly mentions the **Libraries of the Church** in his writing to Pammachius: "**Turn over the commentaries of all whom I have mentioned above, and make use of the LIBRARIES OF THE CHURCHES, and you will reach your desired goal with a swifter step.**" **Erasmus** notes: "**It appears that even then there were public libraries.**" I know, however, that these belong to the end of the *fourth* or the beginning of the *fifth century*, when everything in the churches was already arranged not only for use, but also for splendor. But since the **reading of the Divine word** was practiced in the Church even from the time of the Apostles, it is clear that the Church must have had its own sacred books, wherever they might have been kept.

It happened conveniently that I found an excellent testimony regarding these volumes in the letters of **Constantine** to **Eusebius**. Constantine had decided to erect several churches in **Constantinople**; he therefore commands Eusebius to see that fifty <term>Codices</term><note>The "codex" was the ancestor of the modern book, consisting of folded sheets bound together, replacing the older scroll format.</note> be prepared, which would serve for the Ecclesiastical **Readings**. A part of the letter reads as follows:

"For it appeared proper to signify to your wisdom, that you should order **FIFTY CODICES OF THE DIVINE SCRIPTURES**, the preparation and use of which you know to be especially necessary for the instruction of the Church, **TO BE WRITTEN ON WELL-PREPARED PARCHMENT BY ARTISTIC SCRIBES WHO ACCURATELY UNDERSTAND THEIR CRAFT, IN A BEAUTIFUL AND READABLE HAND, AND IN A PORTABLE FORM...**" <note>original Greek: Πρέπον γὰρ κατεφάνη... This famous request led to the production of high-quality Bibles, such as the Codex Sinaiticus or Codex Vaticanus.</note>

<margin>*On the Life of Constantine*, book 4, chapter 36.</margin>

### CHAPTER 2. WITH SYNAGOGUES etc. 455

<margin>Concerning the Sanhedrin, book 3, chapter 15, section 5.</margin>
**PRIVATE CHURCHES** <note>The Latin "Catæ Ecclesiæ" refers to early domestic or designated prayer spaces rather than public basilicas.</note> signified nothing at all beyond the *houses of prayer* <note>original Greek: εὐκτήρια (eukteria), meaning places dedicated to prayer.</note> themselves, which, according to the whim of the owners from whom they were leased or permitted, could be converted to other uses if nothing stood in the way. The simple performance of sacred rites in a newly built Temple was regarded as a Dedication. Yet, who does not know that from this very time, as superstition and luxury grew, Christian Temples began to be named and consecrated after the manner of the **Jewish**, or rather the **Pagans**? They were dedicated not only to God and Christ the Lord, but to the *Virgin Mary*, the martyrs, and *Holy Men*, and were inaugurated with various ceremonies in their honor. It is certain that these Dedications were established following the example of both *Jewish* and *Pagan Temples*; for just as the former was dedicated to the true God, the latter were inscribed and named for false gods. However, we strongly doubt whether this ritual can be traced back to the Synagogues by any appearance of evidence. For, as far as we know, the Synagogues rejected all such formal namings and solemn Dedications. # ON THE FORM OF GOVERNMENT, BOOK II.

<header>ON THE FORM OF GOVERNMENT, BOOK II.</header>

...greatly differ from one another, so that they are not easily reconciled. It is easy, however, to note the causes of this disagreement. *First*, the *constitution of the Ancient Synagogue* itself is a matter of difficult investigation. Then, the very *form of Government of the Christian Church* is fiercely disputed among *Christian Doctors* <note>In this context, "Doctors" refers to learned theologians and scholars of the church.</note>, a dispute that remains undecided to this day. Therefore, as each scholar adopts a different hypothesis regarding the *Government of the early Christian Church*, he likewise fashions for himself a corresponding image of the *Government of the Synagogue*. Since human judgment tends to vary even in the clearest matters, let each person consider how easily it can happen here that those who set the same goal for themselves nevertheless hasten toward it by different paths. 

However, since it is our purpose—notwithstanding this difficulty, which might rightly have deterred us from this work—to modestly attempt what we can contribute to the elucidation of this argument, it will be absolutely necessary that we define the MODE OF GOVERNMENT of both the SYNAGOGUE and the ANCIENT CHURCH before we descend to the comparison of *Individual Offices*. Since truth is struck out from the disputes of Doctors (which are conducted candidly for the sake of seeking truth alone) just as fire is struck from flint, it will be pleasing above all to weigh on the scales of right judgment certain opinions of *Learned Men* who have occupied themselves with this matter before us. We shall select or reject from them what seems to agree more or less with the truth, so that finally, having properly examined everything that seems relevant to the best of our ability, we may be free to conclude something certain regarding the *constitution* of both the *Synagogue* and the *Ancient Church*, and in this way proceed rightly to the treatment of individual details. 

Since, in truth, *Hugo Grotius*, a man illustrious by his own merit, is (as far as I am aware) easily the leader among the learned who have assumed and illustrated the hypothesis of the *conformity between the Government of the Synagogue and the Church*, it would be a good deed to hear him speaking in the first place and to dwell a little upon his words.

<margin>On the word *Ruler* (*Archon* <note>original: Αρχων</note>). Matthew 9:18 and Luke 8:41.</margin>

Thus, Hugo *Grotius* writes in his *Commentaries on Matthew*:
> "*Ruler* <note>original: Αρχων</note>. Namely, 'of the synagogue' <note>original: τῆς συναγωγῆς</note>, which Luke adds. It must be noted that those SET OVER THE JEWISH SYNAGOGUE were men of esteemed integrity, who were called by the Chaldean name *Parnasim* <note>original: פרנסים</note>, that is, 'those who shepherd' <note>original: οἱ ποιμαίνοντες</note>, a term which is read more than once in the Itinerary of Benjamin <note>Refers to the travelogue of Benjamin of Tudela, a 12th-century Jewish traveler who documented Jewish communities worldwide.</note>,"

The Chief of THESE later began to be called "THE BISHOP" <note>original Greek: ὁ ΕΠΙΣΚΟΠΟΣ; transliterated: ho Episkopos</note> by way of excellence, as seen in the Canons called Apostolic, in the letters attributed to Ignatius, in Tertullian, and others. This is "the angel" <note>original Greek: ὁ ἄγγελος; referring to the "Angels of the Seven Churches" in Revelation</note> in the Apocalypse; elsewhere in Paul, he is "the one who presides, laboring in the word" <note>original Greek: ὁ προεστὼς, ἐν λόγῳ κοπιῶν</note>; and similarly in Justin [Martyr], "the president" <note>original Greek: ὁ προεστὼς</note>. In like manner in the Synagogue, he who was the Chief was called the *Ruler of the Synagogue* <note>original Greek: ὁ Ἀρχισυνάγωγος; transliterated: Archisynagogos</note>, or *ruler of the synagogue* <note>original Greek: ἄρχων τῆς συναγωγῆς</note>, or *the president* <note>original Greek: ὁ πρόεδρος</note>. According to
<margin>On Matthew 9:18.</margin>
Philo, he was the Hebrew *Head of the Assembly* <note>original Hebrew: רֹאשׁ הַקָּהָל; transliterated: Rosh Ha-Kahal</note>, or in Syriac, the *Head of the Congregation* <note>original Syriac: רֵישׁ כְּנִישְׁתָּא; transliterated: Reish Knishta</note>. But here, as we have said, "oversight" <note>original Greek: ἐπισκοπὴ</note> refers to the honor of the Elder; here the Syriac uses "eldership" <note>original Syriac: קְשִׁישׁוּתָא; transliterated: Keshishuta</note>. It is certainly clear from these words that Grotius compares the Ruler of the Synagogue with the Bishop, and the Elders of the Synagogue with the Elders of the Christian Church. This, I say, seems clear enough. Yet, what is that obscure and ambiguous word he uses when speaking of the Elders of the Christian Church: *The Chief of these* LATER *began to be called "the Bishop" by way of excellence*? What does this "later" mean? Does it mean that, according to Grotius's hypothesis, in the first institution of the Elders of the Christian Church, no Chief of the Elders was appointed? Not at all. Grotius means that this Chief of the Elders—whom he supposes was indeed elected from the beginning along with the others in the ordering of the Church—only later began to be called "Bishop"; a name he acknowledges was previously common both to himself and to the other Elders. That *Grotius* truly felt this way can be gathered without difficulty from other parts of his commentary. Thus he says expressly on the Epistle to the Philippians:
<margin>On verse 1, chapter 1.</margin>
HE WHO HELD THE FIRST RANK IN THE ORDER OF ELDERS was called "the bishop" <note>original Greek: ὁ ἐπίσκοπος</note> by way of excellence. From this it happened that the name remained his by a certain proper right, just as the name "ELDERS" <note>original Latin: SENUM</note> was used for the First of the Bishops in Africa. Moreover, the Chief of this Philippian presbytery seems to have been Epaphroditus himself. He says as much in the Epistle
<margin>On verse 5, chapter 1.</margin>

Just as in the **SYNAGOGUES THE FIRST AMONG THE ELDERS WAS THE ONE** who taught the people, and was called *Rabbi* or *Appointed Officer* <note>original Hebrew: ממנה; transliterated: Memunneh</note>, so in the Christian Church the role of **THE PRESIDING OFFICER** <note>original Greek: ΤΟΥ ΠΡΟΕΣΤΩΤΟΣ; transliterated: tou proestotos</note> was the same: these are the "elders who labor in the word" <note>original Greek: πρεσβύτεροι οἱ κοπιῶντες ἐν λόγῳ; referencing 1 Timothy 5:17</note>. In large cities, such as *Antioch*, just as there were many Jewish Synagogues—because everyone could not gather in one place, being divided by such large distances—so there were multiple assemblies of Christians: each had its own **MASTER**, who was also called "the bishop" <note>original Greek: ὁ ἐπίσκοπος; literally, "the overseer"</note> by way of excellence <note>original Greek: κατ’ ἐξοχὴν; meaning a title used in its highest or most specific sense</note>, just as among the Hebrews he was called "The Great Elder" <note>original Hebrew: הזקן הגדול; transliterated: HaZaken HaGadol</note>. *Hammond* and *Thorndike*, most learned men, follow him, though I have never used the former of these. <note>Henry Hammond and Herbert Thorndike were 17th-century English theologians who sought to justify the Anglican hierarchy by finding its roots in the primitive church and Jewish tradition.</note>

However, although *Grotius* seems to express his mind clearly enough in these matters, there is still something that makes me hesitate. Specifically, a significant doubt has arisen for me as to whether what he writes concerning the entire Body or College of Elders <note>original Latin: Presbyterorum</note>—whose President was called the "Head of the Assembly" <note>original Hebrew: ראש הקהל; transliterated: Rosh HaKahal</note>—is intended to be understood as a "homogeneous" Body or College (that is, one made up of the same kind of people), or rather as a College made up of men of different types and ranks. A University, for example, is governed by a College of men of the same kind, all of whom perform the duty of teaching within it, even if the highest care of business is committed to one of them under the title of *Rector*, serving as a President. Political and Judicial Senates among us usually consist of men of a single type and rank, even though they are directed here and there by some President, whether permanent or temporary. Therefore, I call such groups "homogeneous colleges." 

But our churches at this time are governed by a "heterogeneous" college—that is, one of different ranks and kinds, consisting of Pastors and Lay Elders; who, although they constitute one body, remain distinct in name, duty, and dignity. Indeed, even today the synagogues of the Jews are governed by men of different kinds, namely by some **MASTER**, called a *Rab* <note>original Hebrew: רב; the general title for a Jewish teacher or master</note> (about whom more will be said in the following pages), and the *Parnasim* <note>original Hebrew: פרנסים; community leaders who managed the physical and financial needs of the synagogue</note>, or **SHEPHERDS**; of these, the governance of sacred things is almost entirely committed to the *former*, while to the *latter* is entrusted the care of "circumstantial matters and the things outside of the assembly" <note>original Greek: τῶν περιστατικῶν καὶ τῶν ἔξω τῆς ἐκκλησίας</note>, or the Jewish Polity. These two groups sometimes unite into one body and exchange counsel with one another. ...is required. Therefore, that body, or *College of Synagogue Rulers*, is *heterogeneous* <note>composed of different types of officials with distinct roles, rather than a group of equals</note>. Now, if you look at the words of *Grotius* regarding the Governance of the Ancient Synagogue through several *Presbyters* <note>Elders</note> along with a *President*, or *Prince of the College*, it seems entirely likely that they should be understood as referring to a homogeneous college—a *Senate*, I mean, of *Elders* of almost *one* kind. However, when we pay attention to the phrases that Grotius used in his commentaries on this subject, the opposite might seem to be the case. 

For Grotius seems to have taken those expressions of his about the *one President of the Synagogue*, who is called *Rav* <note>original Hebrew: רב</note>, **MASTER**, and about the other *Rulers*, who are called *Parnassim* <note>original Hebrew: פרנסים; often translated as "providers" or "stewards"</note>, **PASTORS**, partly from *Benjamin of Tudela* <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish traveler who recorded the customs of Jewish communities across the world</note> and partly from the governance of the *modern* Synagogue. And yet, the *Synagogues* over which *Benjamin* says individual *Rabbis* <note>original Hebrew: רבני</note>, **MASTERS**, were placed, were certainly not ruled by a homogeneous college of *Teachers* and *Rulers*, but by *one Master*, either alone or joined with Elders of another order; and *modern Synagogues* are likewise governed by Rulers of different orders and duties. 

It is possible, however, that Grotius, in using these names, looked more to their true meaning than to the use they have in the modern Synagogue. Therefore, so that we may proceed in these matters clearly and with certainty, as is our purpose, we will first lay this foundation: *Grotius’s hypothesis regarding the Governance of the Ancient Synagogue* as a model <note>the "type" or original pattern</note> for the Governance of the Church is in no way to be accepted, unless it is understood to refer to *Elders of the same kind and order*, or to a *homogeneous College of Elders*. This is because it can be certainly and unbeatably demonstrated that the First Christian Churches were everywhere ruled by Elders of the same kind. We will therefore provide proof for this point, since much depends on it, and then we will speak more freely our opinion regarding the remaining part of the Grotian hypothesis.

GROTIUS'S OPINION ON THE FORM [OF CHURCH GOVERNMENT], BOOK II.

### CHAPTER II.

*It is proven that the Apostolic Churches were everywhere governed by a College of Elders of the same kind and order. Although there was indeed some sort of President, he was not distinguished from the other Elders by any certain mark or prerogative of his presidency. Furthermore, the right of teaching is claimed for all the others just as much as for the President, based both on the Holy Scriptures and on the records of Church History. Moreover, a greater force of arguments is applied to dismantle the distinction of Elders into "Teaching" and "Ruling" (or "Lay" elders, as they are specifically called). On this occasion, the office of the Elders of the Early Christian Church is explained from the history of the Ancient Church, to make it clear that they had almost nothing in common with our modern "lay" elders <note>The author is referring to the Reformed practice of having non-ordained "Ruling Elders" as part of a church consistory, arguing that this modern role does not actually match the historical office.</note> except for the shared name.*

**A** At the time when the Church of the Reformed Name <note>A common historical term for the Protestant churches arising from the Reformation</note> made its separation from the Roman Papacy, and this Reformed Church itself adopted a different form of Government, it burned so intensely with disputes concerning the true model of the Apostolic Church’s Government that almost no other controversy has occupied the pens of learned men for so long, so seriously and persistently, and with such great zeal and contention on both sides—and with as much hope of victory as desire for it—as this very one. 

One side defends the view that the Apostles, in organizing the Government of the Church, placed a certain common College of Elders <note>original Latin: "Collegium Presbyterorum"</note> over individual Christian assemblies, but that *one* specific person was placed over them with singular dignity and power, like a *President* or *Prefect*, bearing the title of *Bishop*. The other side contends that the Apostolic Churches were ruled by a certain common Senate of *Elders*, who were equal in name, dignity, and office, without the kind of President and Leader who held a rank higher than the other Elders. And indeed, this latter opinion was favored by those celebrated Doctors of France and Germany who devoted their efforts to purging the Church of the vices of Popery, and the confession...

### CHAPTER 2. ON THE GOVERNMENT OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

<margin>
Blondel, *Defense of the Opinion of Jerome on Bishops and Presbyters.*
Walo Messalinus <note>A pseudonym for Claude Saumaise</note>, *On Bishops and Presbyters.*
Salmasius, *Apparatus for the Books on the Primacy of the Pope.*

...they composed a confession of faith received by our assemblies; these same men also applied themselves with all their might to defending it. However, as those disputes perpetually flared up again, in our own age *Salmasius* and *Blondel* exercised themselves in this arena—above and among all others—with the highest praise for their learning and sharp insight. Of these, *Blondel* defended the opinion of *Jerome* <note>St. Jerome, a 4th-century Church Father who famously argued that in the New Testament, "bishop" and "elder" were different names for the same office</note> *concerning Bishops and Presbyters*, which does not differ even a thread from the view of our churches. *Salmasius*, however—first under the cover of the name *Walo Messalinus*, then openly in his *Apparatus for the Books on the Primacy of the Pope* against *Petavius* <note>Dionysius Petavius, a Jesuit scholar who argued for the divine right of the papacy and the early distinction of bishops</note>—strenuously championed the same view.

For my part, having re-read and examined as much as is sufficient the disputes of the learned on this matter—and especially having weighed, properly and without prejudice, those texts of the New Testament that deal with the Government of the Apostolic Church, and having compared the records of Church History—I am naturally drawn toward this opinion:

1. Throughout the time of the Apostles and according to their ordination, the churches were everywhere governed by a **common Senate of Presbyters** <note>In this context, "Senate" refers to a governing council or "college" of elders</note> of the same kind and order, who were not distinguished by **name, office**, or even by **dignity**.

2. Those Presbyteries <note>The organized bodies of elders</note> were indeed headed by a **permanent President**, who was more eminent than the others either by civil dignity, or by learning, age, or wisdom; but otherwise, he was a man of the same order and office, and distinguished from the other Presbyters by no special name.

3. To this man, as is fitting, the duties of speaking, teaching, and administering the sacred rites were commonly entrusted as the senior, or wiser, or more worthy member; however, this was done in such a way that the **other Presbyters** were by no means excluded from this service.

4. To **him**, as the **First** and **President** of the Presbyters, the business of the Church—both more serious and more trivial—was referred for the **sake of order**; yet, he decided nothing regarding the more serious matters except **by consulting the Senate of Presbyters**.

5. That eminence of the **President of the Senate of Presbyters** in the common churches of the first Christians appeared as hardly anything notable, **both** because the affairs of Christians were initially quite meager, **and** also because love <note>original: "ἡ ἀγάπη" (agape)</note> prevailed over vainglory <note>original: "τῇ κενοδοξίᾳ" (kenodoxia)</note>—which, when it finally broke into the churches, corrupted everything.

6. A more notable eminence, however, soon appeared in the larger churches, over whose **Senates of Presbyters** the **Apostles** themselves or **Apostolic Men** presided; since their authority was distinguished, it could not happen that it...

# THE OPINION OF GROTIUS ON THE FORM OF GOVERNMENT, BOOK II.

...that [authority] was recognized by both the Elders <note>Presbyters</note> and the entire Church. 7. Following the example of those Apostles and Apostolic men, other *Presidents of the Presbyteries* <note>The presiding officers of the local councils of elders</note> also assumed a greater dignity and authority over time. Thus it happened that those *Presidents* were soon distinguished from common Elders by name and rank, and the *Episcopacy* <note>The office of a single Bishop ruling over a city or region</note> was introduced into the Christian Church. Whoever accepts these hypotheses with me regarding the *Form of Government of the Early Church* will, on the *one hand*, satisfy the records of Holy Scripture, in which we are instructed concerning the Government of the Early Church—namely, in the Acts and the Apostolic Epistles. On the other hand, they will perceive without difficulty how the *Episcopacy* was received and established in the Church in such a short time after the departure of the Apostles, and perhaps even before the departure of some of them. Otherwise, there is a great deal of labor spent in trying to reconcile these two facts. However, I must now primarily prove the *first and third* of these hypotheses; I will discuss the others more fully in their proper place.

And so, two opinions stand in our way here, against which we must argue. The *first* is held by those who think that, from the very beginning, *Bishops* were *placed over* the Elders by the Apostles with unique authority and dignity, as being distinct from them in rank, order, and office—a view from which Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch polymath who argued for a middle way between high-church episcopacy and radical presbyterianism</note> is not far removed. The *second* opinion belongs to those who think that the Elders of the Early Christian Church were divided into *Teachers and Rulers*, such as our "Lay Elders" <note>Members of the congregation who hold office to govern but do not preach or administer sacraments</note>. At any rate (especially the latter group), they deny that there was a *homogeneous Senate of Elders* <note>A council where all members held the same spiritual office</note>, by which we maintain the early churches were governed everywhere. But because, as I have already noted, the first of these controversies has been debated extensively and learnedly by many Scholars, I may spare myself the unnecessary labor here and briefly and clearly propose only the main points of the arguments for our opinion. In the *second question*, I may be more extensive.

<margin>Acts 20:17</margin>
Let us therefore consider, *in the first place*, what is handed down concerning the constitution of the Ephesian Church in the *Acts of the Apostles*. *Paul*, hurrying to Jerusalem, wished to greet the *Leaders of the Church of Ephesus* in passing, both to say farewell to them and to diligently commend to their care the flock committed to them. Regarding this, the text says: *But sending from Miletus to Ephesus*, he called for the elders... <note>original Greek: μετεκαλέσατο τοὺς πρεσβυτέρους (metekalesato tous presbyterous). The OCR cuts off the word, which is completed by the catchword on the next page.</note>

# CHAPTER 2. THE GOVERNMENT OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

...elders of the church <note>original Greek: πρεσβυτέρȣς τῆς ἐκκλησίας</note> he summoned the **ELDERS** of the *Church*. By this one name, all the *Rectors* <note>Leaders or governors</note> of that *Church* are designated. He addresses them in the following context as men of the same rank and office, with absolutely no indication that among those *Elders* there was *one* more excellent in grade than the rest, to whom Paul's speech was specifically directed, or to whose care the *Church of Ephesus* was singularly committed. Those who have read the so-called *Epistles of Ignatius* <note>Ignatius of Antioch, an early Christian writer who strongly advocated for the authority of a single Bishop</note>, and have noticed from them with what perpetual anxiety their author observes and inculcates that famous distinction between *Bishops* and *Elders*, do they sincerely believe that the *Apostle Paul* could or should have spoken in such a general way to the *Elders of the Ephesian Church* without making even the slightest mention of a *Bishop* (so designated afterward by way of excellence <note>original: κατ’ ἐξοχὴν</note>), if indeed there had been any such *Prince of Elders* in the *Church of Ephesus* at that time, or if that distinction between a *Bishop* and *Elders* was of such great importance as the *Author of the Ignatian Epistles* considers it to be—whether that author was Ignatius himself or someone else? 

But these words of Paul, by which he specifically warns them of their duty, remove all doubt: <margin>verse 28.</margin> *Take heed therefore diligently to yourselves, and to all the flock*, in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops, to shepherd the church of God, which he purchased with his own blood <note>original Greek: ἐν ᾧ ἡμᾶς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἔθετο ἐπισκόπȣς, ποιμαίνειν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τῷ Θεȣ͂, ἣν περιεποιήσατο διὰ τȣ͂ ἰδίȣ αἵματ@</note>, in which *that Holy Spirit has appointed you* **BISHOPS**, *to* **FEED THE CHURCH** *of God, which he acquired with his own blood.* Those whom Paul had called *Seniors* <note>original: πρεσβυτέρȣς, or "Elders"</note> out of consideration for their dignity, he calls *Bishops* <note>original: ἐπισκόπȣς, meaning "Overseers"</note>, *Prefects, Inspectors*, or *Curators of the Church* out of respect for their office, attributing to all of them the equal task of shepherding <note>original: τȣ͂ ποιμαίνειν</note>, that is, of feeding the Church as a flock. 

Those who are not distinguished by name, and who likewise are not distinguished by office—by what reasoning, finally, shall they be distinguished? At the very least, in this whole speech of Paul, in which there was a most convenient occasion for mentioning such a distinction if any had existed, not even the smallest indication of it is to be found. <margin>Commentary on Acts 20:17.</margin> All the *Rectors of the Ephesian Church* are called equally, without any note of discrepancy, **BISHOPS, ELDERS, and PASTORS**. Indeed, if we review those places in the History and Epistles of the New Testament Scripture in which the *Leaders* of the Christian Church are mentioned in various and distinct cases, they everywhere appear to us as equals in name and office, with no distinction whatsoever observed between them. Acts 11:30 compared with chapter 12:25; 14:23; Acts 15:2, 4, 6, 22, 23.

Barnabas and Saul [were sent] to the **elders**, <note>original Greek: πρὸς τοὺς πρεσβυτέρους; original Latin: ad Presbyteros Hierosolymæ</note> that is, to the Elders of Jerusalem. These same men are said again to have appointed **elders**, or *Seniors*, <note>original Greek: πρεσβυτέρους; original Latin: Seniores</note> in every church. <note>original Greek: κατ' ἐκκλησίαν; original Latin: in singulis Ecclesiis</note> In the Acts of the Synod celebrated at Jerusalem, as recorded by the same Luke, there is frequent mention of the **Apostles and Elders**, <note>original Greek: τῶν Ἀποστόλων καὶ πρεσβυτέρων; original Latin: Apostolorum & Presbyterorum</note> as those who constituted its most distinguished part. Of **Bishops**, as distinct from **Elders**, there is no mention at all. Furthermore, where Paul discusses the *Governors of the Church*, he designates them by one common name: **those who are over you**, or *Overseers*. <note>original Greek: προϊσταμένους; original Latin: Præpositos</note> Indeed, that passage is well known, yet no less remarkable, which <margin>1 Thessalonians 5:12.</margin> occurs in *Paul's First Letter to the Thessalonians*: *But we beg you, brothers, to recognize those who labor among you, and* **ARE OVER YOU IN THE LORD**, *and* **ADMONISH YOU**. <note>The author quotes the Greek: εἰδέναι τοὺς κοπιῶντας ἐν ὑμῖν, καὶ προϊσταμένους ὑμῶν ἐν κυρίῳ καὶ νουθετοῦντας ὑμᾶς; and Latin: ut agnoscatis eos, qui laborant inter Vos, & PRÆSUNT VOBIS IN DOMINO, & ADMONENT VOS</note> All here are called **Overseers**; <note>original Greek: προϊστάμενοι; original Latin: Præpositi</note> the duty of all is mentioned as being to labor—namely, *in the word*—and to admonish. <note>original Greek: κοπιᾷν ... ἐν λόγῳ ... νουθετεῖν</note> There is no special privilege of one over another here.

But why do we hesitate to seek a notable argument for our opinion from Paul’s Letter to Titus? He writes thus at the beginning of that Letter: <margin>chapter 1:5.</margin> *For this reason I left you in Crete, that you might set in order what remains, and appoint* **ELDERS TOWN BY TOWN**, *as I directed you.* <note>The author quotes the Greek: καὶ καταστήσῃς κατὰ πόλιν πρεσβυτέρους, ὡς ἐγώ σοι διεταξάμην; and Latin: & constituas OPPIDATIM PRESBYTEROS, sicut ego tibi ordinavi</note> Under the care of Titus, acting as an extraordinary legate of the Apostle Paul, several **elders** <note>original Greek: πρεσβύτεροι</note> were to be appointed in each of the many towns of Crete. Again, no distinction between one Elder and another occurs here. On the contrary, from the following context of Paul's discourse, it is clear that these Elders are the same as **Bishops**. For after Paul had reviewed the qualities required for those to be ordained as Elders in the following sixth verse, he continues his <margin>verse 7.</margin> speech as follows: *For it is necessary for a* **Bishop** *to be blameless, as God's steward.* <note>The author quotes the Greek: Δεῖ γὰρ τὸν Ἐπίσκοπον ἀνέγκλητον εἶναι, ὡς Θεοῦ οἰκονόμον; and Latin: Oportet enim Episcopum irreprehensibilem esse, tanquam Dei dispensatorem</note> Those whom he had called Elders a little before, he here calls **Bishops** in an alternating phrase, <note>original: alternata ῥήσει</note> requiring the same qualities in both. Paul knows of no Elders other than Bishops, and therefore it is the same to him whether he speaks of Elders or Bishops, or <margin>1 Peter 5:1, 2.</margin> whether he describes the virtues of the former or the latter. Indeed, Peter also is unaware of this distinction, for he demands one and the same thing from all Elders.

<meta>This page continues the argument that the New Testament does not distinguish between the offices of "Elder" and "Bishop." ->### GROTIUS’S VIEW ON THE FORM OF GOVERNMENT, BOOK II.<-
<meta>catchword: that</meta>

Setting aside prejudices and passions, how shall we lead our minds to believe that neither Luke in the *Acts*, nor Paul, nor the rest of the Apostles in any of their *Epistles* made even the slightest mention of any *Chief of the Elders* <note>original Latin: *Presbyterorum Principis*</note>, if truly such a *Chiefdom* or dignity, or special duty, or unique title for one of the *Elders* had been established and known in their own time? For they often had to speak, and did speak, of the *Churches* and the *Government of the Churches*. The fact that they write frequently about all other offices, but are entirely silent about this office of the *Episcopate* <note>The office of a Bishop; original Latin: *Episcopatus*</note>, as it was later called, is proof to us that at that time such a name for a duty or dignity was not yet in use. Nor is it necessary here to repeat the lengthy objections that the defenders of the opposing view produce here and there, whether regarding this or earlier testimonies, because in a matter so clear, those objections can be of no value or weight. They only do this so that they may scatter the light of so many arguments—which shines more strongly when united—into various parts, and break the force and brilliance of that light once it is thus divided. Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), a scholar and Church Father best known for translating the Bible into Latin</note>, most skilled in reading the Scriptures, saw this truth and did not fear to frequently and boldly urge and press it home at a time when the *Episcopal* dignity had already grown to its highest peak;

<margin>In the *Antidote* to Jerome's Letter to Oceanus, Part 2, Epistle, folio 116, column 2.</margin>
whose testimonies certainly ought to carry the most weight among the Papists <note>The author uses the term *Pontificios*, referring to the Roman Catholic Church</note>, because the *Decrees*, as Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536), the influential Dutch humanist and theologian</note> says elsewhere, *approve the writings of Jerome without exception*. Let us hear from the man himself, truly a most learned man, as he discusses this in certain places.

It seems very relevant to me that Jerome seeks an example from <term>Deacons</term> to illustrate this question. These men, as no one denies, were all instituted in the beginning as equals in office and dignity. Yet the following centuries saw <term>Archdeacons</term> no less than <term>Archpresbyters</term> <note>Chief Elders</note>, as is well enough known. Indeed, it is certain enough that all <term>Bishops</term> in ancient times were held to be equal in office and authority, whether they were in charge of a greater or a smaller Church.

Lest I call upon other witnesses again (of whom I could call very many, because this same question has been sufficiently discussed by learned men), I will remain with this same Letter of Jerome. "Wherever there is a <term>Bishop</term>," he says in the course of that letter, "whether at Rome or at Gubbio <note>A small Italian city, used to contrast with the power of Rome</note>, at Constantinople or at Reggio, at Alexandria or at Tanis: he is of the same merit and of the same <term>priesthood</term> <note>original Latin: *sacerdotium*</note>. The power of riches or the humility of poverty does not make a <term>Bishop</term> either higher or lower. For all are successors of the Apostles." Jerome intends that one <term>Bishop</term> is not greater than another in authority; rather, all are equally to be considered successors of the Apostles. This was entirely the opinion of the Ancient Church. Therefore, he who wonders how it happened that one of the <term>Presbyters</term> was in time preferred over the others, even though the Apostles instituted all <term>Presbyters</term> as equals in name and office, should consider within himself how it happened that one <term>Bishop</term> was placed over several, or even...

I will not dwell longer on this *first question*, lest I seem to want to "re-cook twice-cooked cabbage" <note>original Latin: *crambem toties coctam recoquere*; a common proverb for tiresome repetition of an old argument</note>. I transition, therefore, to the *second* question, which is of the greatest usefulness and importance for the present matter.

Namely, I maintain this: that from the testimonies noted above, one may in good faith conclude not only that there were no *Bishops* of a higher grade than *Elders* <term>Presbyters</term> in the early Church, but also that no *Elders* were known in that same Church who were distinguished in their office from other men of their own order. We notice, at any rate, that the *Churches of our homeland* <note>Referring to the Dutch Republic and the Reformed Church of the Netherlands</note> are governed by *Elders* of two kinds: *Teachers* <term>Docentes</term>, as they are called, and *Rulers* <term>Regentes</term>. By *Teachers*, we mean *Ministers of the Gospel*, to whom the care of proclaiming the Divine Word and administering the Sacraments is especially committed. By *Rulers*, we mean men of esteemed dignity, chosen from the body of the Church, who are joined to the *Ministers of the Gospel* so that they may participate with them in all affairs regarding the sacred counsels to be taken for the benefit of the Church. 

However, these *Ruling Elders* are quite notably distinguished from the *Teachers* in various ways. For they do not have the power of teaching or administering the sacraments. Neither are they financially supported by the Church. Nor do they preside over the Church in perpetuity; rather, when they have devoted themselves to this office for a certain defined time, they make room for other successors. This, I say, is the condition of the *Ruling Elders* among us, who are sufficiently distinguished from the *Teachers* by their order and office. I would personally judge that no such Elders existed in the Ancient Apostolic Church. However, the opinion of certain most learned and diligent men—

# THE OPINION OF GROTIUS ON THE FORM [OF THE CHURCH], BOOK II.

...to temper [it]; provided that nothing is added, and nothing is *taken away* from that *Form of Governance* of the Apostolic Church, such that it would invert or disturb it, or contrary to the economy of the New Covenant <note>original Latin: *Novi Foederis*</note>. Indeed, it is far from the case that the *Elders* <term>Presbyters</term> of our Churches, whom they call *Laymen* <term>Laicos</term>, disturb the order of Church Governance—or that which was to be established according to the general precepts of Christ (which we have in the Gospels) and was ordained by the Apostles—but on the contrary, they greatly promote the counsel of Christ and the Apostles regarding the *Governance of the New Covenant Church* in their own way. Therefore, I do not blame these *Lay Elders*; rather, I acknowledge and approve of them as much as anyone. However, lest I sin against the laws of brotherhood <note>Grotius is navigating a delicate line here, trying not to offend his fellow Dutch Reformed colleagues while disagreeing with their historical interpretations</note> of which I am a part, I must state plainly that I find no such *Elders* in the *Apostolic Church* of the earliest times, nor any in the Church of the following ages, nor in the writings of the Apostles, nor in the monuments of subsequent eras, as far as they have been surveyed by me or by others. Indeed, this opinion has sat with me for so long that I have been most fully confirmed in it as time progressed; and I do not consider it a fault that I publish it quite freely, even if it is not equally in harmony with the common opinion of our Churches. For since this question is of the slightest importance among the articles of *our faith*, and it is therefore free for anyone to discuss it modestly and reverently—and since the truth on the other side charms me quite openly—no one who is a student of equity and truth will begrudge me, I think, the freedom of defending an opinion which no other reason or presumption, except the force of truth, has compelled me to embrace. Let us therefore come to the matter, and see whether our opinion is consistent with itself and the Scriptures, or not.

3. Truly, it seems to me that the opinion regarding *Lay Presbyters* cannot be more clearly refuted from any other source than from the history of the Governance of the Christian Church which followed the times of the Apostles. What kind of *Presbyters* did the Churches have after the times of the Apostles (as far as one may judge from ancient records)? In what way and by what form were they governed? Certainly, nothing is more certain, nothing more well-established in all ancient history, than that the *Presbyters*, though distinguished from the so-called *Bishop*, constituted the most distinguished part of the *Clergy*. They were considered like the *Bishop*, or, if you prefer, like the *Ministers of the Divine Word* of our own time, as being entirely consecrated to caring for the Church. They were not admitted into the *clergy*—that is, into the order of sacred persons—except with the intention that they should persevere in it for their whole life, renouncing all other worldly cares, offices, and dignities. They had the power of teaching in the *Church* and in other places, both public and private (for it was considered a singular and exceptional thing if this power were denied to a Presbyter). They likewise had the power of administering the sacraments: to anoint the baptized at the fonts with chrism <note>original: "chrismate", a consecrated oil used in initiation rites</note> in the absence of the Bishop; to preside over the Lord's Supper and distribute its Symbols <note>the bread and wine</note>; and to recite blessings and prayers as usage required in such cases. From this, they were considered as *Priests* <term>Sacerdotes: those who perform sacred rites</term>, men of the same order as the Bishop, who was himself also a Priest. They lived off the sacred offerings no less than the *Bishop*. Indeed, *what does a Bishop do*, WITH THE EXCEPTION OF ORDINATION, *that a Presbyter may not do?* says *Jerome* <note>original: "Hieronymus". Jerome was a 4th-century Church Father who argued that bishops and presbyters were originally the same office</note>. ...the exception to fall by itself. 2. It must be carefully observed that these two things, which are being compared, differ greatly from each other. Namely, it is not difficult to perceive from our hypotheses how the so-called *Bishops*, even if they did not appear in the Apostolic Churches, could have been born in the Churches within a short interval of time. For I would certainly believe it happened not infrequently that, due to a lack of other candidates, men were chosen into the same order of *Elders* who were highly venerable for their strictness of character, experience, and piety of life, and were therefore appointed to rule the assembly with full right, but were less fit for teaching. And so I easily conceive that certain *Elders of the Church* taught, while others taught more rarely, or even abstained from teaching altogether—either because they were less fit to teach, or because they had others in the same assembly who were more abundantly equipped through practice for *teaching* and speaking, while they themselves in the meantime diligently attended to some other part of the *Elder’s* duty. *Paul*, therefore, does not deny the right of teaching to any *Elders* in this passage; he only supposes that some *do not teach*. He would wish, however, that all should teach; indeed, he incites and exhorts all to teach, since he proclaims those who teach as especially worthy of double honor. This is the simple, clear, and least ambiguous sense of *Paul's* words. Therefore, Deacons or *Subdeacons* might have been assigned to informing the *Catechumens* <note>Those receiving basic instruction before baptism.</note> (though it is certain that *Presbyters* often did not consider even this duty unworthy of themselves), while the *Presbyters* devoted their labor to teaching the exercises of the faithful, or the clergy itself—the Deacons, Readers, and Subdeacons. Certainly, I do not think it is a new thing in the *History of the Ancient Church* that *Bishops*, and by their permission *Presbyters*, were free for the instruction of others, much as *Teachers* who are put in charge of educating the Youth do now.

# GROTIUS'S OPINION ON THE FORM OF THE CHURCH, BOOK II.

<margin>Catalog of Ecclesiastical Writers, on Pantaenus.</margin>
Who is ignorant of the fact that at least in Alexandria, schools were open in which certain so-called "Doctors" <note>In this context, a "Doctor" is a formal Teacher of doctrine, not a medical professional.</note> explained the mysteries of the Christian religion? Jerome (who described these things from Eusebius, and should be cited for the sake of brevity) had said regarding Pantaenus that, *according to a certain ancient custom in Alexandria, from the time of Mark the Evangelist, there were always* ECCLESIASTICAL TEACHERS. And indeed, Clement, a PRESBYTER <note>An Elder or priest in the early church hierarchy.</note> of the Church of Alexandria, succeeded this Pantaenus.

<margin>On Clement.</margin>
So says Jerome: *Clement, a Presbyter of the Alexandrian Church, and a pupil of the Pantaenus whom we mentioned above, held the* ECCLESIASTICAL SCHOOL *at Alexandria after his death*, and was a master of instruction <note>original Greek: κατηχήσεων; referring to catechesis, the systematic instruction of new converts.</note>. Here you have a Presbyter-Teacher. Afterward, Origen flourished in the same school, having been appointed as its head by Demetrius, the Bishop of the city of Alexandria, in the eighteenth year of his age.

<margin>Jerome on Origen. See also Huet’s Origeniana, chapter 2, section 12. Ecclesiastical History, book 6, chapters 15 and 26. In the Catalog of Ecclesiastical Writers, on Origen.</margin>
Moreover, Origen continued in that duty after he was ordained a PRESBYTER by Theoctistus and Alexander, the Bishops of Caesarea and Jerusalem, until he was forced to depart from Alexandria; upon leaving Alexandria, he handed his school over to Heraclas, who was at that time a Presbyter, and who was later raised to the Bishopric of Alexandria after the death of Demetrius—having already been called by Origen to share in some part of his duty due to the great number of students. Eusebius records both of these facts in distinct places. Jerome writes: *It is well known that, before he moved to Caesarea, he was at Rome under Bishop Zephyrinus, and immediately upon returning to Alexandria, he made* HERACLAS THE PRESBYTER, *who continued to wear the philosopher's garb, his assistant in* instruction <note>original Greek: κατηχήσεων</note>. Later, the same Jerome says of Dionysius: DIONYSIUS, *Bishop of the city of Alexandria, held the school of* instruction <note>original Greek: κατηχήσεων</note> as a PRESBYTER *under Heraclas*. Here, certainly, we have Presbyter-Teachers. I know, indeed, that this institution and succession of Doctors in the Alexandrian Church is often proclaimed as if it were almost unique to that Church. However, I do not think that should be taken too strictly. For since everywhere among the Gentiles <note>The non-Christian Greco-Roman world.</note> of those times the very accepted custom of opening schools and teaching various disciplines in them prevailed, and since the Christian faithful entirely needed some instruction besides those public exhortations of the Bishops, what forbids us from believing that the Presbyters of various Churches opened schools of this kind and taught Christian discipline in them? Certainly Origen, as a Presbyter, taught no less at Caesarea than at Alexandria. Let the Alexandrian

### CHAPTER 3. ON THE GOVERNANCE OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

Even if the Church [at Alexandria] claimed a specific succession of certain *Teachers* <note>Latin: *Doctorum*; referring to formal instructors of Christian doctrine</note> from the time of *Mark the Evangelist* <note>The traditional founder of the Church of Alexandria</note> onward, we are not therefore compelled to deny that other Churches had their own *Teachers* among their *Presbyters* <note>Elders</note> or *Deacons*. What if some from the order of *Presbyters* were distributed through the districts and villages to instruct those Churches and imbue them with the mysteries of the faith?

<margin>Eusebius, Church History, Book 7, chapter 24.</margin>
Indeed, this can be gathered from the clear words of *Dionysius*, Bishop of Alexandria, in his books against *Nepos* <note>Nepos was an Egyptian bishop who promoted a literal thousand-year reign of Christ on earth</note>, which were preserved by *Eusebius*: *When I was,* he says (these are the words of Dionysius), *in the Arsinoite Prefecture* <note>A region in Egypt, now the Faiyum</note>, *where, as you know, this opinion had long since become so widespread that it caused schisms and the desertion of entire Churches, having called together the presbyters and teachers of the brothers in the villages* <note>original Greek: συγκάλεσας τὲς πρεσβυτέρως καὶ διδασκάλες τῶν ἐν ταῖς κώμαις ἀδελφῶν</note>, *and with those brothers present who wished to attend, I urged them to examine that doctrine (of Nepos) publicly.* Who are these *Teachers* here distinguished from the *Presbyters*? Without doubt, they were those same *Presbyters* who were tasked with imbuing the catechumens <note>those being instructed in the faith before baptism</note> or the faithful with the knowledge of the Christian Religion. Whatever the case may be—whether the *Presbyters* in that text of Cyprian were in charge of the *Clergy* or of instructing the faithful—we are by no means forced to imagine some extraordinary spiritual gift <note>original: *charisma*</note> of teaching with which these Presbyters were uniquely equipped. They were more *learned*, more fit, and more practiced than other Presbyters, but I would not suggest they were distinguished from the rest by some extraordinary grace. Furthermore, if that testimony of *Possidius* <note>A friend and biographer of St. Augustine</note> does not deserve as much trust as is commonly granted to it by learned men, it would be easy to interpret *Presbyter-Teachers* as *Senior Presbyters*—those closest to the Bishop—to whom it was granted by the Bishop to speak words to the people in public, and who were held to be more fit and better trained for this than the other Presbyters.

<margin>Notes on the Letter of Polycarp, page 35.</margin>
*The business of preaching,* says that most learned man and my teacher of blessed memory, *Le Moyne*, *belonged to the Apostles, Bishops, and* FIRST PRESBYTERS. *Hence, in the times of the Ancient Church, the Bishops always preached; the lower Presbyters did not take up this duty unless the Bishops and the leading Presbyters nodded their heads and granted permission.* He himself goes on to confirm this with a long series of witnesses. So it is: Not all Presbyters took upon themselves the burden of preaching and expounding the word of God. Some were free for administering the Sacraments, investigating scandals, comforting the sick, strengthening the weak, and looking after and promoting the interests of the Church.

Or is the *honor* to be shown to the Elders of the Church to be considered as that reward which Paul proves is owed to them for their labor, through these testimonies: *You shall not muzzle the ox while it treads out the grain*; and: *the laborer is worthy of his wages*?

Does Paul reason in this way: "You shall not put a muzzle on the ox, therefore the Elder of the Church is to be honored above others"?

Certainly, unless by *honor* we simultaneously understand the provision of goods which are necessary for sustaining life, in my judgment we will make this reasoning of Paul ridiculous and weak.

Indeed, that the word *honor* <note>Greek: τιμὴ</note> here not only includes, but in the first place signifies a *stipend* <note>Greek: ὀψώνιον; literally "provisions" or "pay"</note> owed to the ministers of the Gospel,

### CHAPTER 3. ON THE GOVERNMENT OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH. 499

*...widows, who are truly widows.* <note>Latin: *viduas, quae vere sunt viduae*; quoting 1 Timothy 5:3</note> Does Paul mean to say here: "follow the widows, who are truly such, with honor and reverence?" Certainly, from the entire context that follows, it is clear that he intends to say this: SUPPORT *widows, who are truly widows.*
<margin>verse 16.</margin>
To "honor" here is to support, or, as Paul himself subsequently interprets his own meaning, to provide for <note>original Greek: ἐπαρκεῖν (*eparkein*)</note> and assist the needs of someone. Indeed, Paul had dealt with this duty of charity, to be shown to widows, in the words preceding the text we are currently treating; to which he then adds:
The Elders <note>original Latin: *Presbyteri*</note> who rule well are worthy of **DOUBLE HONOR**.
He means to say: double, that is, a greater stipend, a double support. Paul wants more of a stipend, support, or nourishment to be granted to the Elders of the Church than to the widows, both because their families are more burdensome, and because they deserve more by virtue of their labor. Paul does not divide external honor or veneration between the Elders and the widows. It would be foolish to think so.
<margin>Erasmus: Annotations on this place.</margin>
Erasmus says: *“Elder” here is a term for the office of Bishop <note>original Latin: *Episcopi*</note>, not for age. And “honor” signifies SUPPORT <note>original Latin: *SUBSIDIUM*</note>, not that common sort of honor—stepping out of the way, uncovering the head, or bending the knee; just as Saint Jerome noted in more than one place.* Every most excellent Interpreter has recognized and approved this meaning of the word “to honor” <note>original Greek: τιμᾶν (*timan*)</note>, and has strived to illustrate it from elsewhere, especially from the Hebrew meaning of the word *kabed* <note>original Hebrew: כבד; meaning to be heavy, weighty, or to honor through provision</note>. But we do not require their help now, because the truth shines so clearly in this passage that it can easily defend itself without any external aid. Therefore, we rightly establish without any ambiguity that if Paul deals in this place with such Elders whom he wants to be supported by the Church, it follows that he in no way refers by these words to Lay Elders <note>original Latin: *Presbyteros Laicos*</note>, such as our Churches have received. For certainly: 1. They are not supported by the Church. 2. No stipend is owed to them by the Church. Indeed, a stipend is owed from the Church only to those Elders who must consume such a large part of their life in the ministry and care of the Church that time is not left to them to provide for the necessities of this life in a proper way through any other labor. This cannot be said of our Lay Elders, as is well known. The Elders, therefore, of whom Paul speaks, were the ordinary, fixed, and perpetual Pastors and Bishops of the Church—as they were still called at that time—to whom the care of the Church was entrusted; to these men this [duty], to others

Therefore, since <term>to distribute</term> <note>original Greek: μεταδιδόναι (*metadidōnai*)</note> is most familiarly used with this meaning, it seems we should not rashly depart from it. But that which is added—<term>IN SIMPLICITY</term> <note>original Greek: ἐν ἁπλότητι (*en haplotēti*)</note>—confirms this exposition even more. It has indeed already been observed by most learned men, and not overlooked by **Grotius**, that Paul’s use of this word is singular and emphatic, signifying <term>liberality in giving alms</term>. In this sense, <margin>2 Corinthians 8:2; 9:11, 13</margin> it occurs more than once in Paul’s *Second Epistle to the Corinthians*. The Dutch translate it as: **Charity** <note>original Dutch: *Goeddadigheyt*, meaning beneficence or doing good deeds</note>. **James** likewise confirms this use of the word when he says of God that He gives to all <term>SIMPLY</term> <note>original Greek: ἁπλῶς (*haplōs*)</note>, <margin>James 1:5</margin> that is, *liberally*. The Dutch have it as: **generously** <note>original Dutch: *mildelyck*</note>. Moreover, there is a great elegance in this meaning. There is no other cause for liberality pleasing to God than a pure and <term>unfeigned</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνυπόκριτος (*anypokritos*); literally "without hypocrisy" or "non-acting"</note> love of God and the brothers. Where there is charity and <term>unfeigned faith</term> <note>original Greek: πίστις ἀνυπόκριτος (*pistis anypokritos*)</note>—a faith that is pure, candid, and simple—there will be a liberal mind. Conversely, when someone communicates his gifts to the needy with a sparing and grasping hand, it is born <term>out of hypocrisy</term> <note>original Greek: ἐξ ὑποκρίσεως (*ex hypokriseōs*)</note>, which is the opposite of <term>simplicity</term> <note>original Greek: τῇ ἁπλότητι (*tē haplotēti*)</note>. In <term>hypocrisy</term> <note>original Greek: ὑποκρίσει (*hypokrisei*)</note> there is a double will: of giving and of not giving. The man fights with himself over whether he *wants* to give or *does not want* to; he debates within himself how much he ought to *give* to his brother, and how much he should *retain* for himself. He is finally led by carnal reasons to help his needy brother, yet in such a way that he does not expend as much as he ought; and even that which he does expend, he would rather retain for himself than impart to his brother, if the laws of external decency would allow it. I do not doubt, along with the **Celebrated Cocceius**, that **Paul** studied to adapt this use of the Greek word to a similar mode of speaking found in the Scriptures of the Old Testament. <margin>1 Chronicles 29:9</margin> For at the end of the *First Book of Chronicles*, the liberality of the *leaders and the Jewish people*, exercised for the building of the Temple, is described in the same style: *And the people rejoiced over their liberal offering;* <term>FOR WITH A WHOLE HEART THEY OFFERED WILLINGLY TO THE LORD</term> <note>original Hebrew: כי בלב שלם התנדבו ליהוה (*Ki be-lev shalem hitnadvu l'Yhvh*)</note>. You might translate this as: <term>in simplicity of heart</term> <note>original Greek: ἐν ἁπλότητι τῆς καρδίας (*en haplotēti tēs kardias*)</note>; <term>THEY CONTRIBUTED MUNIFICENTLY TO THE LORD.</term> From these things, I believe it will be manifest to anyone that <term>simplicity</term> <note>original Greek: τὴν ἁπλότητα (*tēn haplotēta*)</note> pertains to those who expend something of their own for the use of God and the Church. But if it is proved that by "the one who distributes," we are not to understand the Deacons of the Church, but any of the wealthier faithful who relieve the poverty of the Church with their resources,

### CHAPTER 3. CONCERNING THE GOVERNANCE OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

...we will have made much progress in the true understanding of this passage. For then:

1. It will be certain that **the Apostle Paul** (whose words the authors of the opposing view use as the foundation for their hypothesis) is not here enumerating those specific kinds of *spiritual gifts* <note>original Greek: χαρίσματα (charismata)</note> that pertain to the formal governance of the Church, but rather any gifts whatsoever, in which even the common ranks of the faithful participated. Every kind of gift, I say, is enumerated here by the Apostle Paul—both those belonging to *teachers* and *students*, and those belonging to *leaders* as well as the other members of the Church.

<margin>verse 8.</margin>
This is also confirmed by the final words of this sentence: *the one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness* <note>original Greek: ὁ ἐλεῶν, ἐν ἱλαρότητι (ho eleōn, en hilarotēti)</note>. For whatever the authors of the opposing opinion may assert, it is impossible for the phrase *the one who shows mercy* <note>original Greek: τὸν ἐλεῶντα (ton eleōnta)</note> to describe a specific class of church officials.

2. If the interpretation we have given is admitted, then it is very probable that by *the one who presides* <note>original Greek: τὸν προϊστάμενον (ton proistamenon)</note>, we should not understand the *Elders of the Church* <note>the Presbyters</note>. For who would believe that the Apostle Paul observed so little order in listing the gifts of the Holy Spirit that, having just spoken of the gift of *liberality* in giving alms, he would immediately begin speaking about the gift of *governance* for the entire Church? *The one who presides* is placed here in the middle, between *the wealthy believer who distributes* <note>original Greek: τὸν μεταδιδόντα (ton metadidonta)</note>—who pays out something from his own resources to the poor—and *the one who shows mercy* <note>original Greek: τὸν ἐλεῶντα (ton eleōnta)</note>—who provides particular aid and help to the wretched according to his ability. Therefore, it is entirely fitting that we believe *the one who presides* designates someone with a similar kind of *gifted function* <note>original Latin/Greek: κεχαρισμένον (kecharismenon)</note>. Otherwise, what order or connection would there be in Paul’s discourse? Why would the *gift of church governance* be placed in the middle, between the *gift of liberality* and the *gift of compassion*? 

Therefore, I gladly follow the opinion of **Theophylact** <note>an 11th-century biblical commentator and Archbishop of Bulgaria</note>, that by *the one who presides*, those members of the Church are designated who assist and oversee the care of the poor and needy, whether in their own name or on behalf of the Church. Only one thing is required to confirm this interpretation: that we prove the term *presiding* <note>original Greek: προϊστάμενος (proistamenos)</note> can be suitably explained in this sense.

<margin>1 Thessalonians 5:12</margin>
And here indeed, I do not deny that the concept of *presiding* is used once by Paul to refer to the *leaders* of the Church; but the word *patroness* <note>original Greek: προστάτις (prostatis)</note>, which shares the same origin and meaning (varying only in gender), is used by Paul himself in this very same Epistle in the sense we are emphasizing.

<margin>Romans 16:1, 2</margin>
"I commend to you," he says, "**Phoebe**, our sister, a *minister of the Church at Cenchreae* <note>original Greek: διάκονον τῆς Ἐκκλησίας τῆς ἐν Κεγχρεαῖς (diakonon tēs ekklēsias tēs en Kenchreais)</note>."
