->GROTIUS’S OPINION ON THE FORM [OF THE CHURCH], BOOK II<-

*That you may receive her in the Lord, in a manner worthy of the saints, and assist her in whatever matter she may have need of you, for she herself has been a patroness of many, and of myself as well.* <note>This is a quote from Romans 16:1-2 regarding Phoebe; the original Greek for "patroness" is προστάτις (prostatis)</note>. Beza <note>Theodore Beza, a 16th-century French Protestant theologian</note> translates this as: *For she has both* PROVIDED HOSPITALITY *to many, and to me personally.* The Dutch version says: *A Protectress* <note>original Dutch: Een Voorstandster</note>.

<margin>Commentary on this passage</margin>
Therefore, in the judgment of distinguished interpreters, the term *patroness* <note>Greek: Προστάτις</note> here indicates a *woman* who had performed many duties of charity for both *Paul* and other holy men. Let us hear *Beza*: *It should be known that the term "patrons"* <note>Greek: προστάτας (prostatas)</note> *refers to those specifically called "proxenoi"* <note>Greek: πρόξενοι; a Greek term for official hosts who looked after foreign visitors</note>, *that is, those chosen by a city to receive guests and travelers into their home and protection. This is what Eustathius* <note>a 12th-century Byzantine scholar</note> *means by "presiding over strangers"* <note>Greek: προϊσταθαι τῶν ξένων (proistasthai tōn xenōn)</note>. *The Apostle therefore means that the home of this Phoebe, a servant of the Church of Cenchreae, was open to traveling brothers as if it were a public hostel for the saints—virtues which he requires in a widow.*

Certainly, the term *the one presiding* <note>Greek: ὁ προϊστάμενος (ho proistamenos)</note>, by the force of the word and its origin, is the same as a *patron* <note>Greek: προστάτης (prostatēs)</note>. Accordingly, I am entirely convinced that *Paul* in this text, by "the one who presides," meant men who, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, were moved to offer and provide help to the needy and afflicted with singular love, care, and wisdom. I believe this to be the genuine sense of this text, and I have chosen it not out of necessity, but by reason. 

For if I were to concede that "the one who presides" in this passage must be understood as the Leaders of the Church, who could then conclude from that that "Lay Elders" <term>Presbyteros Laicos; a term used in Reformed theology for church elders who are not ordained ministers but assist in governance</term> exist? You would only conclude that there are Elders who, through the Holy Spirit, received a singular gift for wisely ruling and caring for the Church more than others. Just as there were *Elders* who—during that singular *dispensation* <note>Greek: οἰκονομίᾳ (oikonomia); referring to the era of the early church</note> of the abundant distribution of various gifts of the Holy Spirit—were more suited for teaching; just as there were those more fit for *exhorting*, convincing, rebuking, and comforting; so too there were those more prepared by the Holy Spirit for governing the Church and offering it help in various situations. 

Each of the *Elders* contributed his own gift for the benefit of the Church. However, there was only one order, one condition, one and the same *office*, a common care, and a common counsel among these *Elders*. For if a new kind of order of "presiding elders" <note>Latin: Presbyterorum προϊσταμένων (proistamenōn)</note> were to be created from these words, why shouldn't we also invent other orders of Elders, such as "exhorting" <note>Greek: παρακαλούντων (parakalountōn)</note> elders or "teaching" <note>Greek: διδασκόντων (didaskontōn)</note> elders? Therefore, let us hold to this: There was one order of *Elders* in the *Early Church*, upon whom generally fell the burden of the Church...

...to feed the flock. Each person contributed his own *gift* to this end. This man was more suited to teaching, another to exhorting. That man, in turn, was more effective in care and counsel. <margin>Chapter 12, verse 28</margin>

We wish the following points to be weighed: **1.** *In this passage, Paul the Apostle is dealing with* gifts <note>Greek: *χαρίσμασι* (charismasi)</note> *of the Holy Spirit, not with the ordinary offices of the Church, as is evident from the entire context of Paul's discourse.* Indeed, he himself describes them as *gifts* in verse 31. To perform *miracles* <note>Latin: *virtutes*</note>, to heal the sick, to speak in various tongues, to foretell the future, or to explain prophecies about future events, should not be considered ordinary offices of the Church, but *gifts*—extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit. *But, you say, were the Apostolate and the position of Teacher* <note>Latin: *Doctoratus*</note> *not duties of the Church?* I certainly admit that the Apostolate and the position of Teacher—if you consider these terms outside the circumstances of this text—can be called offices of the Church just as much as gifts of the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, as they occur here, it is most certain that those names are used by Paul to mean *gifts* rather than *offices*. Where Paul says in this place that God has given some as *Apostles*, he means that God *equipped* certain men *with such gifts* as were required for the Apostolate, a most weighty duty. Again, when he says God gave some as *Teachers*, he means to say that the Holy Spirit bestowed upon certain faithful people an *aptitude for teaching*, just as he gave to others the gift of publishing or explaining prophecies, to others a knowledge of languages, and to others other things. Paul is primarily dealing with *gifts*, not *offices*. Therefore, regarding what the same Paul declares here—that God has established certain *governments*—that is (assuming for now that the word "government" <note>Greek: *κυβέρνησις* (kybernēsis)</note> here refers to the governance of the Church, such as that of the Elders)...

### THE OPINION OF GROTIUS ON THE FORM [OF THE CHURCH], BOOK II. ###
<meta>catchword: Spirit-</meta>

...it can be understood in this way: that God granted this grace of the Spirit to certain members of the Church so that they might excel in *prudence, counsel, and care* for governing the Church. The office of the *Elders* was once the same; distinguished by the same honors and burdened by the same *duties*, if you consider the office in itself. However, as God worked in various ways by His Spirit in the early Church, He distributed various *gifts* <note>Latin: *dona*</note> to these same Elders. He equipped this man with the gift of *teaching*; to others He imparted the gifts of *exhorting, comforting, debating, healing, performing miracles, and the gift of tongues*; to others again He conferred the grace of governance <note>Greek: *κυβερνήσεως* (kybernēseōs)</note>, for which *prudence and counsel* are required. Each of the *Elders*, and indeed every member of the Church, employed these gifts of theirs for the benefit of the believers of the entire Church. If someone, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, was strong in the gift of *teaching and exhorting*, and was chosen into the order of *Elders*, he applied this gift of his to the building up of the Church; if someone else, in turn, excelled in *prudence and counsel*, he was applied to the governing and care of the Church. Moreover, that one person excelled another was not due to their office—which was the same for everyone—but to a *singular grace of the Holy Spirit* which was more clearly visible in him than in another.

The most excellent and *first* of all the spiritual gifts was the grace of the *Apostleship*. The last and *lowest* of all was kinds of tongues <note>Greek: *γένη γλωσσῶν* (genē glōssōn)</note>, that is, *to express the thoughts of one's mind in various languages*. Paul urges this point more because there were those in the Corinthian Church who were quite proud of this gift. Now it must be considered, 1. <note>The original text uses the Hebrew letter *א* (Aleph) to denote the first point.</note> that Paul places this *gift* of governance in the next-to-last place in his list of various spiritual gifts. And yet, the *gift of governing the Church* ought to be counted among the greatest and most excellent gifts of the Spirit—

# CHAPTER 3. ON THE GOVERNMENT OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH. #

...of the Holy Spirit. For in order to govern the Church, there is a need for wisdom <note>Greek: *sophia*</note> and understanding <note>Greek: *phronesis*</note>, as well as prudence and counsel. Since wisdom and prudence are the highest human perfections, they must also be considered the most excellent gifts of the Holy Spirit. If, therefore, Paul had intended to designate the gift of governing the Church by the word "governance" <note>Greek: *kybernesis*</note>, it seems he would have given it a more honorable place among the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are listed here by him in a distinct order.

2. Paul places this gift of governance <note>Greek: *kybernesis*</note> after the gift of "helping" <note>Greek: *antilepsis*</note> in this list. According to the view of those interpreters against whom we are now arguing, *helping* <note>Greek: *antilepsis*</note> signifies either the gift or the office of caring for and assisting the poor. Therefore, according to their hypothesis, "Deacons" would be understood by these *helps*. However, since the office or gift of governing the Church is much more excellent than the gift or office of caring for the poor and providing them with aid and assistance, it seems inconvenient to understand the gift or office of governing the Church by the word "governance" here. This is because it is well-established that Paul lists the gifts of the Spirit in this passage in an order that places more excellent gifts before those that are less excellent. For this reason, other experienced interpreters of Scripture have moved away from this meaning of the word and interpreted it quite differently. Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and influential biblical commentator.</note>, whose work we have just used with profit, writes as follows:

> *Helps, governments: That is, to support the weak, and to govern, or rather to manage the affairs of the brothers. Even if these things are part of our own diligence, he says they are still gifts of God, persuading us to be grateful and to look toward Him and not to be puffed up.* <note>Original Greek/Latin: *Ἀντιλήψεις, κυβερνήσεις... Opitulationes, gubernationes: Hoc est, fovere infirmos & gubernare...*</note>

Therefore, for Theophylact, governance <note>Greek: *kybernesis*</note> is the same as "presiding" <note>The word used in Romans 12:8, often translated as "he who leads."</note> in the Epistle to the Romans. If this interpretation by Theophylact is accepted, then the Apostle’s speech will be consistent.

<margin>Proverbs 1:5; chapter 11:14.</margin> Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English scholar famous for explaining the New Testament through Jewish tradition and language.</note>, who also exercised his talent here, understood by "helps" <note>Greek: *antilepsis*</note> the companions of the Apostles who assisted them in baptizing believers and, as he says, were sent here and there to places the Apostles could not reach while occupied with other matters. ### CHAPTER 3. THE GOVERNANCE OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH. ###
<meta>catchword: Spirit-</meta>

...of the Holy Spirit. For the purpose of governing the Church, there is a need for wisdom and prudence <note>Greek: *σοφίας & φρονήσεως* (sophias & phronēseōs)</note>, or *prudence and counsel.* Indeed, since wisdom and prudence are the highest perfections of man, they must also be regarded as the most excellent gifts of the Holy Spirit. If, therefore, Paul had intended for the word governance <note>Greek: *τὴν κυβέρνησιν* (tēn kybernēsin)</note> to designate the gift of *governing the Church*, it seems he would have given it a more honorable place among the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are listed here by him in a specific order.

2. Paul places this gift of governance <note>Greek: *κυβερνήσεως* (kybernēseōs)</note> after the gift of helps <note>Greek: *ἀντιλήψεως* (antilypseōs)</note> in this list. According to the view of those interpreters against whom we are now arguing, "Helps" indicates either the gift or the office of caring for and relieving the poor. According to their hypothesis, these helps <note>Latin: *adjumenta*</note> should be understood as the Deacons. However, since the office or gift of *governing the Church* is much more excellent than the gift or office of caring for the poor and providing them with aid and assistance, it seems improper to understand "governance" here as the gift or office of *governing the Church*. This is because it is well-established that Paul lists the gifts of the Spirit in this passage in such an order that he places the more excellent ones before the less excellent. For this reason, other experienced interpreters of Scripture have moved away from this definition and have interpreted the word quite differently.

Theophylact <note>A significant Byzantine biblical commentator from the 11th century.</note>, whose works we have recently used with some profit, writes as follows: *Helps, governments: That is, to support the weak, and to govern, or rather to manage the affairs of the brothers. For even if these things are the result of our own diligence, he nevertheless affirms that they are gifts of God; persuading us to be grateful, and to look toward Him, and not to be proud.* In Theophylact’s view, therefore, "governance" means the same as "leadership" <note>Greek: *προϊστασις* (proistasia)</note> in the Epistle to the Romans. If this interpretation by Theophylact is accepted, then the Apostle’s speech remains consistent.

Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English cleric and scholar famous for using Rabbinic knowledge to explain the New Testament.</note>, who also applied his own talent to this passage, understood "helps" to mean the companions of the Apostles who assisted them in baptizing believers and who, as he says, were sent here and there to places where the Apostles themselves could not go while occupied with other matters.

### GROTIUS'S OPINION ON THE FORM, BOOK II. ###

...which the Hebrew word *tachbulot* <note>original Hebrew: תחבולות; typically referring to "wise counsel" or "guidance" in the Book of Proverbs</note> denotes as profound *skillfulness*. However, *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675) was a prominent English Hebraist and clergyman known for using Rabbinic literature to explain the New Testament.</note> thinks that by this word "governments" <note>Greek: *kybernesis*</note>, the Apostle Paul intended to designate that *gift* which he elsewhere calls the "discerning of spirits" <note>Greek: *diakrisin pneumaton*</note>; since skill, sagacity, and *acuteness* of mind and judgment are required for such discernment. Indeed, this most learned man believes that the gifts of the Holy Spirit, <margin>verses 8, 9, 10</margin> which *Paul* had listed at the beginning of this same *Chapter*, should be compared *in order* with those he lists in the words just described. If this comparison is made, the *gift* of "discerning of spirits" mentioned there will correspond to the gift of "governments," which appears in this latest list.

But that hypothesis has not been approved by us so far, because according to it, the gift of "prophecy" <note>Greek: *propheteias*</note> would have to be matched with the gift of "helps" <note>Greek: *antilepseos*</note>; which, even if *Lightfoot* attempted it in some way, is not accepted by us. *Paul* indeed lists gifts of the same kind at the start of this Chapter that he mentions at the end, and which therefore can and should be compared with each other; yet it is not clear enough that *Paul* enumerates these *gifts* in the *earlier* passage in precisely the same order as in the *later* one. In this later list, he observes a very accurate order, as is evident from the particles *first*, *second*, *third* <note>Greek: *proton, deuteron, triton*</note>. In the *earlier* list, however, he does not entirely neglect the order, yet he is not as observant and careful of it as he is in this later passage.

Nor do we agree with Lightfoot that by "helps" <note>Greek: *antilepseis*</note> in this text, the *ministers of the Apostles* are to be understood. It is not an absurd opinion, I admit. It is also certain that the Apostles had such ministers at hand. However, I believe there is something else that can be brought forward with greater evidence for the genuine explanation of this word. *Paul*, after he had listed the gifts of the Holy Spirit in this later passage, immediately <note>Greek: *amesos*</note> repeats them in the verses following; except that instead of the *eight* gifts he had numbered, he repeats *seven*; perhaps by repeating one *gift* he includes *two* previously listed ones, or otherwise. From this diagram it is clear that the individual gifts listed in verse 28 are repeated by their own names, except for *those* of helping <note>original Greek: ἀντιλήψεως; antilepseos</note> and governing <note>original Greek: κυβερνήσεως; kyberneseos</note>; however, in place of those two, the *gift* of interpretation <note>original Greek: διερμηνείας; diermēneias</note> is substituted. Yet the gifts of helping and governing—or rather the different *offices*—are distinct if you pay attention to the meanings of the *words*; nor do they seem capable of being explained by any single common *name*. It must therefore be said (for I do not see how this difficulty can be removed by any other more convenient reasoning) that *Paul*, in this repeated list, omitted one of those two mentioned *gifts* and substituted the word "interpretation" for only one of them.

Moreover, this gift of interpretation <note>original Greek: τῆς ἑρμηνείας; tēs hermēneias</note> is much more appropriately referred to the gift of "helps" than to that of "governing." For certainly, those who interpreted languages in the Church were an *aid* both to the Church and especially to those members or leaders of the Church who were speaking in an unknown tongue; and therefore, by the greatest right and the most fitting expression, they are called <term>helps</term> <note>original Latin: opitulationes; original Greek: ἀντιλήψεις. The author argues this refers to administrative or linguistic assistance rather than a specific office like the Diaconate.</note>. Let "helps," therefore, no longer be considered as referring to *Deacons*, but to *Interpreters of foreign languages*.

Now we must come to the gift of governing <note>original Greek: κυβερνήσεως; kyberneseos</note>. I have said that in this repeated census it seems to have been omitted by the Apostle, which is why it is more difficult to explain. For even if we were to reject that part of Lightfoot’s hypothesis—namely, that Paul repeats the various gifts of the Holy Spirit at the end of this *Chapter* in the *same order* in which he had listed them at the beginning—we nevertheless do not deny that he repeats the same species of those gifts, even if the order is changed in some instances.

Reasoning, moreover, favors this opinion. ## GROTIUS’S OPINION ON THE FORM [OF GOVERNMENT], BOOK II. ##

...skill and cleverness, of the kind that usually comes into use in war; who would doubt that those whose duty it was to distinguish and judge various Spirits had need of this sort of skill and wisdom? Therefore, let <term>governance</term> <note>original Greek: κυ-βέρνησις; kybernēsis, often translated as "administrations" or "governments."</note> be a gift of skill, wisdom, and cleverness, granted by the Holy Spirit to certain faithful individuals in the early Church for the purpose of discerning the operations of true and false spirits. ### CHAPTER 3. CONCERNING THE GOVERNANCE OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH. ###

That the *elders*, whose judgment has been strengthened by experience, should be consulted regarding more serious matters—as seen in the <term>song of indiction</term> <note>original Latin: "carmine indictionis." This refers to the ritual formula used by the Roman fetial priests to declare war, mentioned by Livy.</note> <margin>History, Book 1.</margin> in the works of *Livy*—cannot but be judged a fair and useful practice. <margin>chapter 32.</margin> However, the crux of the matter is this: just as there is no mention of such *Seniors* in the *Scripture* (a point upon which the dissenting parties in this case will easily agree), so too were they entirely distinct from our <term>Lay Presbyters</term> <note>Non-ordained church elders who handle administrative rather than sacramental duties.</note> in every respect and manner. 1. These *Seniors*, specifically so called among the Ancients, did not form part of the *clergy*—that is, the ecclesiastical order—but of the *laity*. They were not with the *Clergy* (the *Bishops, Presbyters, and Deacons*) in the <term>Presbyteries</term> <note>The governing councils of the local church.</note>, in the *chancel*, or in the *Councils*, but they remained with and among the *laity*, and constituted a part of it, albeit a respected and distinguished one. 2. These *Seniors* are for that reason ranked after the *Deacons*, as is also clear from the testimonies we have noted. 3. Consequently, the Ancients even took care that they were not called PRESBYTERS <note>original Greek: πρεσβύτεροι; presbyteroi</note>, lest anyone through ignorance should confuse them with the *Presbyters of the Church* mentioned in Scripture, but rather SENIORS, and *elders* <note>original Greek: γέροντες; gerontes</note>. <margin>In the Code of Canons of the African Church, canon 100. See Forbes in the cited passage.</margin> 4. The *care of the Church* was not demanded of them; for it was no more incumbent upon them than upon all other members of the Church to admonish, exhort, or instruct the *laity*—if not publicly, then at least privately. They had no role in excommunicating sinners or admitting penitents. I will put it in a word: they were not part of the *Ecclesiastical Senate*, to which the care and ministry <margin>“And we have in the Church our own Senate, the assembly of Presbyters.” Jerome, Commentary on Isaiah, book 2, on chapter 3.</margin> of the Church were entrusted. They were a distinguished part of the laity, removed and distinct from the Clergy and its *Senate*, and performing no duties of the clergy or the ecclesiastical ministry. Nevertheless, this was done, I say—as reason teaches it is fair and good to do—so that the *Bishops and Presbyters* of the Church did not neglect to employ the advice, help, and testimony of these *Seniors* (the distinguished men of the laity) in certain cases. Indeed, in that early age of the Church, where there was a greater integrity of mind, a more ardent charity, and less ambition, a much greater interaction flourished between the *Clergy and the Laity* than thereafter. So that no one may further confuse these *Seniors* with the *Apostolic Presbyters*, I will say in a single word: they were not the *Overseers* or *Rulers* of the CHURCH, but the SENIORS OF THE PEOPLE. Beware, therefore, of believing that there is any mention of such *Seniors of the people* in the writings of the *Apostles*...

Even if I were to assume that the Governance of the Apostolic Church was formed according to the *model of Synagogue Governance*, many things nonetheless stand in the way of my admitting that the *Governance of the Apostolic Church* was similar to the *Governance of the modern Synagogue*, and was fashioned after such a model. ### CHAPTER 4. OF THE GOVERNMENT OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.
<meta>catchword: CHAPTER</meta>

Who would venture to compare things of such a different kind and order—distinct in both their names and their duties—with the **Bishop and Elders** of the Apostolic Church? For even those who wish for these offices to be most distinct in rank and dignity would not say that they differ from one another in as many ways as the <term>Master of the Synagogue</term> <note>Hebrew: *Rav*; the primary teacher or head of the school</note> differs from its <term>Pastors</term> <note>Hebrew: *Parnasim*; communal administrators or providers</note>; and I will not even bring forward more examples of their dissimilarity at this time. Therefore, if Grotius intended to compare the **Bishop and Elders** of the Early Church with the **Master and Pastors of the modern Synagogue**, he has undoubtedly strayed from the truth. However, if he conceived in his mind that the **Ancient Synagogues** were often ruled by a **Council of Learned Men**, of a single kind and rank (about which we shall discuss more extensively in the following pages, <note>original Greek: *Theou didontos*</note> God willing), then Grotius’s words can easily be reconciled with that view. In that case, we have nothing to criticize in this part of the Grotian hypothesis; indeed, we shall do our best to support and illustrate it in its proper place.

Second, I would wish it to be observed that Grotius—being too intent, it seems, on his <term>Chazzan</term> <note>Hebrew: *חזן*; originally an overseer or attendant, later a cantor</note>, or **Bishop of the modern synagogue**, to whom almost all the care of the synagogue's sacred rites is entrusted—attributes more to the **Bishops of the Apostolic Churches throughout his Commentaries** than is right, and **elevates them too far above the Elders**. We acknowledge that in the earliest churches there was some **President of the Elders**, who would soon become conspicuous with greater dignity than the other Elders due to his age, the gravity of his office, and his spiritual gifts; yet we do not acknowledge that the **Bishop** and the **Elders** of the early church were truly different in the **nature and function of the Eldership** from the very beginning of their institution. However, Grotius’s Commentaries lead us to that conclusion, as far as I can see, even though Grotius initially and not unwillingly concedes that the word **Bishop** had a more general meaning. What the difference was between the **President and the common Elders**, we shall clearly teach in its proper place, investigating it from the structure of the **Synagogue** itself. Since the order of our discussion forbids us from anticipating other matters now—beyond what we said in the preceding **second Chapter of this Book**—we will not add more regarding this example of the Grotian Synagogue. How much we differ from Grotius will become manifest from the end of this section and the **first Part of the following Book**.

### CHAPTER V.

*The structure of the Synagogue, which the most learned Petit built up from the Body of Civil Law, is examined: in which context it is debated how various titles of dignity—such as Patriarchs, Primates, Leaders, Chiefs, Archisynagogues <note>Greek: "rulers of the synagogue"</note>, Fathers of the Synagogues, High Priests, Priests, Presbyters <note>Elders</note>, and Seniors—are to be understood in the Roman Laws that deal with the Jews.*

<margin>Various Readings, book 2, chapter 1.</margin>
Leaving Grotius aside, let us turn to *Samuel Petit*, also a most learned man. He intended to explain from the Digests <note>original Latin: *Pandectis*; a comprehensive collection of Roman legal writings</note> of the Law certain obscure names by which the Hebrews, after the destruction of the Temple, expressed the more noble *offices* of their nation. He attributed almost as many distinct functions to the Synagogue as there are names of dignity found in the Imperial Rescripts <note>Official letters or decrees issued by a Roman Emperor</note>. Mentioned in the Legal Codes are the names *Archisynagogues, Fathers of the Synagogues, High Priests, Priests, Presbyters, etc.*, who are called the *Primates of the Jews* and are said to dominate in their *Sanhedrins* <note>original Latin: *Synedriis*; high councils or assemblies</note>. Mention is also made of the *Azanitae* <note>likely referring to the *Chazzan* or synagogue attendants</note>, who were ministers of the Synagogue according to the interpretation of *Epiphanius*. However, the most learned Petit, as I have already said, formed his arguments as if these distinct names designated just as many distinct offices and duties within the Synagogues. He judges that the <term>Archisynagogues</term> presided over the ecclesiastical gatherings that meet in the Synagogues; however, the <term>Fathers of the Synagogue</term> were second in dignity within the Synagogue and were the deputies of the Archisynagogues. He draws his conjecture for this from the fact that in the Jerusalem Sanhedrin, the <term>Father of the House of Judgment</term> <note>original Hebrew: <term>אב בית דין</term> (*Av Beit Din*); the second-highest ranking member of the Sanhedrin</note> was first after the <term>Prince</term> <note>original Hebrew: <term>נשיא</term> (*Nasi*); the presiding chief of the Sanhedrin</note>, as is established by the Talmudists. By a similar reasoning, he says, we believe that the Fathers of the Synagogues are first after the Archisynagogues. *And perhaps it is for this reason that several Archisynagogues are named for a single Synagogue: not because there were actually several Archisynagogues, but in each Synagogue there was an Archisynagogue and another after him, the Father of the Synagogue, his deputy, who is honored with the same name; just as among those same Jews, although there was only one High Priest, his deputy also...*

prove the contrary from the fact that Priests are given the first place in the Synagogue for reading the Divine Law according to the accepted Canon found in the Jewish Statutes: <note>original: "כהן קורא בתורה ראשון אחריו לוי אחריו ישראל"</note> *The Priest reads first; after him the Levite; and after him the Israelite.* However, the Israelites read in this order: <note>original: "בשבת ויום טוב ויום הכפורים קורים אחר לוי תלמידי חכמים הממונים על הצבור..."</note> *On the Sabbath, the Festival, and the Day of Atonement, after the Levites, there shall read: the Disciples of the Wise who are appointed over the congregation; after them the Disciples of the Wise who are worthy to be appointed as governors over the congregation; then the sons of the Disciples of the Wise whose fathers preside over the Synagogue, and finally the <term>Leaders of the Assembly</term><note>original: "ראשי כנסיות" (Rashei Knesiyot)</note> and the whole people.* For attention must be paid to the reason why the first place in reading is assigned to the Priests and Levites in the Synagogues. It is established from the Sacred Book of the Old Testament that the Priests and Levites were once specifically designated by God for this purpose: to read and teach the Law, and they continued in that office until the destruction of the Temple. From this alone must the origin of the rite be sought—that the first turns for reading in the Synagogue are granted to the Priests and Levites. Nevertheless, you should beware of concluding from this that the Priests and Levites are superior in rank to the Rulers of the Synagogue. <header>CHAPTER 5. THE GOVERNANCE OF THE SYNAGOGUE IS EXPLORED.</header>

<margin>
See the *History of the Emperors and Princes, etc.* by Monsieur Tillemont <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a French ecclesiastical historian known for his meticulous accuracy.</note>, from page 987. *...that privileges [be granted] to those who are subject to the authority of the Illustrious* PATRIARCHS: *to the* RULERS OF THE SYNAGOGUE, *and the* PATRIARCHS, *and the* ELDERS, *and the others who serve in the sacred rites of that religion, etc. Who could believe that in this Law, the Patriarchs are made subordinate to the Rulers of the Synagogue? And indeed, these Patriarchs seem to be of another kind, far lower in dignity than those aforementioned leaders?* Petit <note>Samuel Petit (1594–1643), a scholar who specialized in reconciling ancient laws.</note>, and others who followed him, considered this passage to be "ill-affected" <note>A scholarly way of saying the text is likely corrupted or mistranscribed by ancient scribes.</note> and therefore only to be corrected through emendation. But so far, no emendation has been brought to light that carries any weight of probability. Very recently, a certain most learned man contended that the name "Patriarch" among the Hebrews of that time had an ambiguous meaning; it designated both the Prince of the Jewish Nation and certain Prefects of the Synagogue who were lower in dignity than the so-called Rulers of the Synagogue. Thus, the Emperor would have used the word "Patriarch" in the same sense as he elsewhere uses the title "Fathers of the Synagogues." I would easily admit the latter point. I admit, I say, that in this Law of Arcadius and Honorius <note>Roman Emperors ruling in the late 4th and early 5th centuries.</note>, the titles of "Patriarch" and "Fathers of the Synagogues" are confused. But it has not yet been clearly proven that the Jews themselves at that time took the word "Patriarch" in that double sense, nor can it be proven from Roman Laws. For who can say whether the founders of Roman Law knew the true and distinct use of these titles, and did not occasionally confuse them with one another? If, however, that double explanation of the word Patriarch of which I just spoke is to be admitted, then I feel quite strongly that the name Patriarch, taken in the second sense, corresponds to the honorary title* <term>Ab Bet Din</term> <note>Hebrew: אב בית דין. Literally "Father of the House of Judgment," referring to the vice-president of the Sanhedrin or a high-ranking judicial officer.</note>, *the Father of the Sanhedrin among the Jews.*

*But even if it were true—and we most especially desire it to be true—that the Roman Emperors, in their Laws and Rescripts addressed to the Jews, always used the names of that nation's dignities and synagogue administration in their genuine significance and listed them in a distinct order, one still could not easily conclude that as many honorary offices existed in the Synagogues as there are names of dignities found in the Roman Laws. For just as some of those names have a more general meaning and use, so there is no doubt that in the Roman Laws they are accepted in that general and common sense. Nor does Petit himself deny that this is the case regarding the titles of* LEADERS, NOBLES, *and* ELDERS— <note>Original Latin terms: *Primatum*, *Procerum*, *Majorum*.</note>

# PETIT’S OPINION ON THE FORM, BOOK II.

...[REASON]ING. Therefore, in other matters, it does not seem necessary to work so hard at distinguishing so carefully between *Rulers of the Synagogues, Fathers of the Synagogues, Teachers, Presbyters, and Elders*. However, it will be useful to review each of these titles of dignity that appear in the Laws and to briefly and candidly offer our judgment on their use and meaning.

<margin>See Morin, *Biblical Exercises*, Book 2, Exercise 3, Chapters 1 and 2.</margin>

*First*, Petit <note>Samuel Petit (1594–1643), a French scholar of law and antiquity.</note> discusses the PATRIARCHS, whom he says correspond to the <term>Reshei Galuyot <note>Hebrew: ראשי גליות; literally "Heads of the Exile."</note></term> or *Aichmalotarchs* <note>From Greek: Princes of the Captivity.</note>, the Princes of the Jews in Captivity. We do not disagree with him on this point. Therefore, we will not repeat at length what he, as well as Morin, Hottinger, Alting, Vorstius, L’Empereur, and recently Tillemont and Pezron, have written regarding this supreme office—an office which the Jews enjoyed for several centuries after the destruction of their commonwealth, by the indulgence of the Roman Emperors. These Princes were the heads of all *Sanhedrins* <note>Jewish high courts or assemblies.</note> and *Synagogues* of their *province* <note>original: ἐπαρχίας (eparchy).</note>, whether in the land of *Canaan* or in Babylonia. They held authority *first* in matters of RELIGION, of which they were the supreme arbiters, and *then* also in *Civil and Criminal* matters, insofar as the Roman Emperors did not restrict the exercise of that power or tolerated it. Indeed, for a time, the Emperors were most indulgent toward those *Patriarchs*, whom they addressed as *Illustrious, Spectable, and Most Distinguished Men* <note>These were formal ranks of the Roman senatorial and equestrian orders (Illustres, Spectabiles, Clarissimi).</note>.

<margin>Law 8 and 15, *Theodosian Code*, regarding Jews and Heaven-worshippers, page 243.</margin>

This is evident from many other proofs, but especially from the remarkable testimony of *Origen* <note>A prominent early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD).</note> in his *Response to Africanus*:

> *Even now, for instance,* he says, *while the Romans are reigning and the Jews are paying the didrachm <note>A silver coin representing the half-shekel tax formerly paid to the Temple.</note> to them, how much the ETHNARCH (Patriarch) is able to do among them by the permission of Caesar! We who have experienced it know that they live no differently than if their nation were still reigning.* Origen continues: *Trials are also held secretly according to the Law, and some are even condemned to death; this happens neither with full and open authority for this purpose, nor yet entirely in secret from the reigning Emperor. Having spent a long time in that nation’s country, we have learned and are fully certain of this.* <note>original: Origen provides the quote in Greek, followed by a Latin translation in the manuscript.</note>

### CHAPTER 5. THE GOVERNANCE OF THE SYNAGOGUE IS EXAMINED.

...what do the words **Heads of the Assembly** <note>original: *Archiperecitæ*, a Latinized term likely derived from the Hebrew *Resh Peraka*, referring to leaders of public lectures or academies.</note> or **Elders** mean? Is the finger not pointed here at the **Rulers of the Synagogue** of the Jews? But what does this also mean: PERHAPS also **Masters**. Surely nothing is more evident than that the Emperors understood very little of the difference between those titles—if there was any—or at least they did not distinguish these titles from each other very scrupulously in their Laws?

<margin>Maimonides, [Laws of the] Sanhedrin, chapter 1, § 3.</margin>
<margin>Law 4 of the Theodosian Code, under this title.</margin>
Following these in order are the **FATHERS OF THE SYNAGOGUES**, whom Petit <note>Samuel Petit (1594–1643) was a French scholar of ancient law.</note> identifies as **VICARS OF THE RULERS OF THE SYNAGOGUE**, in the likeness of the <term>Father of the House of Judgment</term> <note>original: אב בית דין (*Ab Bet Din*), the second-highest ranking member of the Jewish high court.</note> in the *Sanhedrins*, and the <term>Vicar</term> <note>original: סגן (*Sagan*)</note> of the High Priest in the Temple. And indeed, in the Great Sanhedrin, some *Father of the Sanhedrin* was subordinate to the President, who was called the <term>Prince</term> <note>original: נשיא (*Nasi*)</note> and <term>Head</term> <note>original: ראש (*Rosh*)</note>. However, in the *Synagogue*, we have not encountered such *Fathers of the Synagogue* of the type Petit describes; nor is any other evidence produced by *Petit* to defend these "Fathers of the Synagogues." Therefore, we believe that by "Fathers of the Synagogues" in the Decree of *Constantine*, we should understand either the **Elders** of the Synagogue themselves (elsewhere called "Seniors"), or the **Rulers of the Synagogue** themselves, or the **Leaders of the Academies**, who in later centuries claimed the title of <term>Fathers of the House of Judgment</term> <note>original: אבות בתי דין (*Abot Batte Din*)</note> for themselves. Thus, you frequently find in the titles of the Doctors of the Jewish nation: **FATHER OF THE HOUSE OF JUDGMENT**, and **Head of the Academy in the Holy Congregation**. Also: **FATHER OF THE SANHEDRIN**—that is, of the House of Judgment—of the Holy Congregation. But the same phrase *Father of the House of Judgment* can be translated as: **FATHER OF THE SYNAGOGUE**. For *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a foundational Dutch legal scholar and theologian.</note> was the first to observe on another occasion that among Greek and Latin authors, both sacred and secular, *House of Judgment* was often explained not only as "Sanhedrin" but also as "Synagogue," and almost all learned men now grant this. If we admit this interpretation of the title, then it must be said that in the Decree of *Constantine*, titles of the same meaning are confused with one another; a thing which we have above supposed and defended as not being absurd when it occurs in the Imperial Laws.

Next follow the **PRIESTS** <note>original: *Hierei* (from the Greek ιερεῖς)</note>, or **SACERDOTES**. And indeed, the *Synagogue* of old had *Priests* just as the modern one does. To whom this honor is granted, not only by reason of their lineage, so that they are the first to read the **Mosaic Law** in the Synagogue, but especially because the duty is entrusted to them of blessing the assembly gathered in the Synagogues after the sacred rites are finished, **with uplifted hands** <note>original: בנשיות כפים (*Nesiat Kappayim*), the Priestly Blessing or "Birkat Kohanim."</note>; concerning which ceremony,

What do the words **Chief of the Assembly** <note>original: *Archipericite*. Next in order are the **Fathers of the Synagogues**, whom **Petit** <note>Samuel Petit (1594–1643) was a French scholar who attempted to reconcile Roman law with Jewish tradition.</note> identifies as the **Deputies of the Rulers of the Synagogue**, modeled after the **Father of the House of Judgment** <note>original: אב בית דין (*Ab Bet Din*)</note> in the *Sanhedrins* <note>The high judicial councils of ancient Jewish communities.</note>, and the **Deputy** <note>original: סגן (*Segan*)</note>, the *Deputy of the High Priest* in the Temple. Indeed, in the Great Sanhedrin, some *Father of the Sanhedrin* was subordinate to the President, who was called the **Prince** <note>original: נשיא (*Nasi*)</note> and **Head** <note>original: ראש (*Rosh*)</note>. However, in the *Synagogue*, we have not so far encountered such *Fathers of the Synagogue* as **Petit** describes; nor does **Petit** produce any other testimony from elsewhere to support these "Fathers of the Synagogues" of his. Therefore, we believe that by the *Fathers of the Synagogues* in the Decree of *Constantine*, we should understand either the *Elders* of the Synagogue themselves, or the *Seniors*—as they are called elsewhere—or the *Rulers of the Synagogue* themselves, or the *Heads of the Academies*, who in later centuries claimed for themselves the title of **Fathers of the Houses of Judgment** <note>original: אבות בתי דינין (*Abot Batte Dinim*)</note>. Also: **Father of the House of Judgment of the Holy Congregation** <note>original: אב בית דין דקהלה קדושה (*Ab Bet Din de-Kehilla Kedusha*)</note>. I say **Father of the House of Judgment**. But this same phrase **Father of the House of Judgment** <note>original: אב בית דין</note> can be translated as **Father of the Synagogue**; for **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), the famous Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> was the first to observe on another occasion that *Ab Bet Din* was often explained by Greek and Latin authors not only as *Sanhedrin*, but also as *Synagogue*—a point both sacred and secular authors make, and which nearly all learned men now concede. If we admit this interpretation of the title, then it must be said that in the Decree of *Constantine*, titles of the same meaning are confused with one another; as we previously supposed and defended, it is not absurd for this to happen in the Imperial Laws.

We affirm the same regarding **CHIEF PRIESTS** <note>original: *Archiereis*</note> as we do regarding the Priests. There is no mention of them in the Laws cited by Petit; I doubt they ever appear in the *Corpus Juris Civilis* <note>The body of Roman civil law compiled under Justinian</note>. However, this notion exists in this sense in the writings of *Aelius Lampridius* <note>A presumed author of the Augustan History</note>, concerning the Emperor Alexander: *He wanted to appear to trace his origin from the Roman race, because he was ashamed to be called a Syrian; especially because at a certain festive time, as is their custom, the people of Antioch, Egypt, and Alexandria had provoked him with insults, calling him a Syrian* **CHIEF OF THE SYNAGOGUE** *and a* **CHIEF PRIEST**. That the word *Chief Priest* <note>original: *Archiereus*</note> here means the same as that other term *Ruler of the Synagogue* <note>original: *Archisynagogus*</note> is clear from the first consideration of the words. For why? Did the Egyptians wish to say that Alexander was either a High Priest or some Prince of the Jewish Priests? I do not think so. Rather, it is likely that those Eastern peoples wanted to mock his Syrian and Jewish origins in jest; for the sake of [mocking] his dignity and honor, they compared him with the most noble leaders of the Jewish nation, whom they understood were called *Rulers of the Synagogues* and *Chief Priests* by the Jews themselves. 

From this, therefore, you should by no means conclude that there was a certain Prince of Priests in every Synagogue. Indeed, whether that dignity of the <term>Chief Priests</term> <note>original Greek: *Αρχιερέων* (Archierēōn), meaning the high-ranking members of the priestly order</note>, the *Princes of the Priestly Order*, continued after the destruction of the Temple, I freely admit I do not know. I am more inclined to think that it became extinct with time. Nevertheless, those **Priests** who were promoted to the Government of the Synagogue were able to claim this title for themselves in a way, because they were leaders not only of the Synagogue, but of all the priests—as many as belonged to the <term>administration</term> <note>original Greek: *διοίκησιν* (dioikēsin)</note> of that Synagogue. But I do not concede, as Petit would have it, that besides the *Rulers of the Synagogue of the Priestly Order*, each synagogue had a *Chief Priest* presiding over the common Priests of the Synagogue.

### PETIT’S OPINION ON THE FORM, BOOK II. 528

<meta>catchword: fa-</meta>

Furthermore, regarding the **PRESBYTERS & ELDERS** <note>original: *Presbyteris & Senioribus*</note>, *Petit* feels that they were the most noble and wise men of the Jewish People, who presided over the *Synagogue* along with the *Leader of the Synagogue* <note>original: *Archisynagogo*</note>, the *Father of the Synagogue*, the *High Priest*, and the *Priests*; these men clearly corresponded to those *Elders* who were chosen from among the people for the *Sanhedrin* <note>original: *Synedrium*</note> of the 71 members <note>original: *τῶν LXXI*</note>. We accept this interpretation in those Laws in which the *Presbyters* are distinguished from the *Leader of the Synagogue*. Otherwise, it should be observed that these titles have a more general meaning. For not only were they the *Chiefs* of the Synagogues, but especially the *Assessors of the Sanhedrins* <note>A term for legal advisors or council members</note>—such as the Jews maintained in many places after the destruction of their republic—who bore the name of *Elders* <note>original: *זקנים* (Zekenim), *Presbyterorum*, or *Seniorum*</note>.

<margin>Law 15. Code on Jews & Heaven-worshippers.</margin>
Thus, the name *Elder* <note>original: *Senioris*</note> must certainly be understood in this way in this Law of Honorius and Theodosius: *If there be any dispute between Christians and Jews, it shall be decided not by the ELDERS OF THE JEWS, but by the ordinary Judges.* In this Law, judges are set in opposition to judges. However, judicial matters among the Jews, even in exile, were entrusted to the *Sanhedrins*, whose *Assessors* were called *Elders*. Nevertheless, even today Synagogues have their own *Elders* <note>original: *זקנים* (Zekenim), *Presbyteros*</note>, but they are very different from those Senators of the ancient Sanhedrins. I will not deny that such *Chiefs of the Synagogues*—if they were indeed granted that name at that time—are also included under the name of *Presbyters* in the Laws. But I am fully persuaded that those ancient heads of the greater Synagogues were all honored with the title of *Doctors* <note>Teachers or learned scholars</note> and, together with their *President*, formed a complete *Sanhedrin*. I believe the government of the Synagogue was entrusted to this same Sanhedrin, with the President of the Sanhedrin specifically bearing the name *Leader of the Synagogue* by way of distinction <note>original: *κατ’ ἔμφασιν*</note>. And so we will not find it necessary to assign different kinds of *Presbyters* to those more famous Synagogues of ancient times. The same *Presbyters* who held authority in the *Sanhedrins* ruled the *Synagogues* in the larger cities; and these same men are called *Presbyters* in the Imperial Decrees. But I must deal with this matter with specific effort in the following sections, since it is upon this point that the entire weight of the comparison to be established between the government of the *Synagogue* and the *Church* will rest.

Therefore, either *Petit's* "Synagogue" must be reformed, or the hope of properly comparing the **Officials of the Synagogue** and the **Church** must be abandoned.

->LIGHTFOOT’S OPINION CONCERNING BOOK II.<-

## CHAPTER VI.

*The structure of the Ancient Synagogue, as conceived in the mind of the famous John Lightfoot, is here presented to the eye. In this model, it is assumed that the sacred duties of the Synagogue were divided among Ten Men, who are called <term>Batlanim</term> <note>Hebrew: בטלנים, literally "idle ones" or "men of leisure"</note>, or Idle Men. Consequently, we first present the primary passages from the Jewish Legal Code regarding these Ten Idle Men; then, two interpretations of this title are provided: one by Lightfoot and Cappel, and the other by Buxtorf, which is more widely accepted among translators of the Talmudic Code.*

<margin>Commentary on Matthew 4:21.</margin>
We must finally come to *John Lightfoot*, a man universally recognized as most skilled in Hebrew affairs, whose memory for this reason ought to be honored by all scholars of literature after his death. When he observed that in the *Body of Jewish Law* mention is sometimes made of the <term>Ten Idle Men</term> <note>original Hebrew: עשרה בטלנים, *Asarah Batlanim*</note>, he first determined that these Ten Idle Men should not be regarded as *lazy* or *slothful* men, present in the Synagogue only in body but not in spirit. Instead, he argued they should be understood as learned and literate men who were "at leisure" from worldly business to manage the affairs of the Synagogue and were devoted to the study of the Law. 

Next, he determined more explicitly by conjecture which and what kind of duties of the Synagogue were distributed among these Ten Idle Men. He makes THREE of them <term>Synagogue Rulers</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀρχισυναγώγες, *Archisynagōgoi*</note>, the presiding officers of the Synagogue; commonly, as he himself thinks, called the <term>Court of Three</term> <note>original Hebrew: ב"ד של שלשה, *Beth Din shel Shloshah*, or "House of Judgment of Three"</note>. ONE is the Synagogue MINISTER, known by the name <term>Messenger of the Congregation</term> <note>original Hebrew: שליח צבור, *Sheliach Tzibbur*</note>, or the *Angel of the Church*, or the <term>Chazan</term> <note>Hebrew: חזן, an official with oversight or liturgical duties</note>, or <term>Overseer</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπισκόπες, *episkopous*</note>, as he himself believes. THREE are DEACONS, to whom the care of the poor was entrusted. The *eighth* he conjectures was an INTERPRETER of the DIVINE LAW in the Synagogue. The *Ninth* and *Tenth*, he added, "it is not readily apparent what we should name them from the triumvirate." Let us assume they are the **THEOLOGICAL SCHOOL-LEADER** and his **INTERPRETER**, about whom there will be a more extensive opportunity for inquiry elsewhere. To proceed in order, we will *first* inquire into the certain-

*Lightfoot’s hypothesis is twofold*: 1. That the ancient synagogues had Ten Men, who were called <term>Batlanim</term> <note>original: בטלנין; literally "idle ones" or "men of leisure"</note>, or *Idle Men*. 2. That the duties of governance and the ministry of the Synagogue were distributed among them. Regarding the first point: it is clear enough from the <term>Body of the Talmud</term> <note>the central text of Rabbinic Judaism</note>, in passages long ago noted by Rabbi Nathan and Buxtorf, that the ancient synagogues of the larger cities had Ten *Idle Men*. These <term>Ten Idle Men</term> <note>original: עשרה בטלנים, *Asarah Batlanim*</note> are mentioned only once in the <term>Mishna</term> <note>the first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions</note> of the tractate *Megilla* in both the Babylonian and Jerusalem Talmuds, in exactly the same words and circumstances in both places. The words of the Mishna relevant to this matter in both Talmuds are these: *Which is a LARGE CITY? Every one IN WHICH THERE ARE TEN IDLE MEN. If there are fewer than that, behold, it is a VILLAGE.*

<margin>Gemara Sanhedrin, folio 17, column 2. Gemara Megilla, folio 5, column 1. and Bava Kama, folio 82, column 1. Regarding Section 6, chapter 1 of Megilla.</margin>
Similarly, in the <term>Gemara</term> <note>the component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis and commentary on the Mishna</note>, mention of these *Ten Men* is quite infrequent. They occur, however, in the tractates *Sanhedrin*, *Megilla*, and *Bava Kama*. In the tractate *Sanhedrin*, they are listed simply as members of the city: <term>TEN IDLE MEN OF THE SYNAGOGUE</term> <note>original: עשרה בטלנים של בית הכנסת</note>. In the Gemara of *Megilla*, regarding the passage of the Mishna just cited, you will find this noted: <term>TEN IDLE MEN WHO ARE IN THE SYNAGOGUE</term> <note>original: עשרה בטלנים שבבית הכנסת</note>. In *Bava Kama*, they are only mentioned briefly. From this, one can gather little else than that ten Idle Men belonged to an ancient synagogue that was properly established. Furthermore, what kind of men these were, what business they had in the Synagogue, or for what reason they were distinguished by this title, is more often assumed as known in the Talmud than it is declared. See, however, if you can gather more from the Jerusalem Gemara. These words are read there: *It is taught: Ten who cease from their work for the house of the synagogue.* <note>original: תני עשרה בטולים ממלאכתן לבית הכנסת</note>. It is therefore sufficiently certain that the ancient synagogue had Ten Men who were called *Idle*.

<margin>As cited.</margin>
But what kind of men these were, and of what office and rank, remains, as I have said, in the dark until now. Therefore, the illustrious Lightfoot, intending to enter this deep water more profoundly, took it upon himself to define and explain it a little more accurately. He did this by interpreting these <term>Batlanim</term> <note>original: בטלנין</note>, the *Idle Men*, as learned and studious men who, as he himself says...

### LIGHTFOOT'S OPINION ON BOOK II.

<margin>In the Lexicon at the word *Batlan* <note>original: בטלן; Hebrew for "idle man" or "man of leisure"</note></margin>
They are *not to be regarded* as SLUGGARDS *or* IDLE; *but* <term>Batlanim</term> <note>original: בטלני; those who have ceased from work</note> from all their crafts and occupying themselves with the needs of the community, *for whom (as those who were not entangled in worldly affairs) there was* LEISURE *to care only for the matters of the Synagogue and to devote themselves to the study of the Law. This most deserving man [Lightfoot] would have done very well if, in such an ambiguous matter, he had used more words and had cited the authors or foundations of this interpretation of his. It is true that the Hebrew Doctors, who interpret the ancient customs and the terms of Jewish law, commonly use this same formula of words in explaining the title of the "Idle Men" as Lightfoot does. For thus specifically Rabbi Nathan, whose words the celebrated Lightfoot seems to have adopted, explains* <term>Batlan</term> and <term>Batlanim</term> <note>singular and plural forms of "Idle Man"</note> *as* <gloss>Ceasing from their work and devoting themselves to the needs of the congregation</gloss>. *It is also certain that these words of Rabbi Nathan can support the explanation given by Lightfoot. However, I do not believe that Lightfoot was unaware that there is another, more widely accepted interpretation of this title. Rabbi Solomon Jarchi <note>also known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most famous medieval Jewish commentator</note>, a famous and skilled interpreter of the Talmud, explains these Ten Idle Men as ten Israelites hired for pay to pass their leisure time in the synagogues from morning until evening. This was primarily for the end that those who wished to visit the synagogue for the sake of prayer might find there the number of ten men <note>the "minyan," or quorum of ten adult males required for communal Jewish prayer</note>, without which it was considered unlawful to recite certain prayer formulas.*

They receive a stipend so that they may always be present in large numbers during prayers and other sacred assemblies in the synagogue, remaining from start to finish with the* PRIEST *or the* CHIEF OF THE PRIESTS, *so that the synagogue is never empty during sacred rites, nor the Priest left alone. <header>CHAPTER 6. ON THE GOVERNMENT OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH, ETC.</header>

That this was not unknown to *Lightfoot* seems to be concluded both from the fact that he so expressly took care in his description of these *Idle Men* that they should not be taken for lazy and unoccupied men, and also because he elsewhere explained related material on the distinction between <term>Krakhim</term> <note>original: כרכים; large walled cities</note>, *Towns*, <term>Kfarim</term> <note>original: כפרים; villages</note>, *Hamlets*, and <term>Ayarot</term> <note>original: עיירות; small cities</note>, not only from the Talmudic text but also from the *Glossary* attached to it. That he did this at *Mark 1:38*—such that the related *Glossary regarding the Ten Idle Men* would have escaped his eyes—I would not easily believe. Very recently, however, I noticed that *Jacob Cappellus*, a most learned man, has moved toward an opinion that hardly differs from that of *Lightfoot*.

<margin>
Observations on the New Testament, p. 26. regarding Matthew 18:15.
Sanhedrin Code, chapter 1, section 10.
</margin>
The words of *Cappellus* are these: *THESE TEN MEN, whom (Maimonides) <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar</note> says represent the Synagogue, seem altogether to teach us that EVERY SYNAGOGUE HAD A COUNCIL OF TEN, BY WHOSE JUDGMENT MATTERS PERTAINING TO THE SYNAGOGUE WERE CONDUCTED. This assembly dealt neither with civil nor capital cases. For he who dealt with civil cases belonged to a council of three; he who dealt with capital cases belonged to a council of 23, as Maimonides teaches in the same place. It remains, therefore, that this COUNCIL OF TEN was an ECCLESIASTICAL SENATE.*

And this very explanation of the *Idle Men* did not seem so absurd to me when I was first commenting more freely on the sacred rites of the Synagogue, that I not only approved of it, but even took pains to defend it later when it was under attack. Now, placed outside the heat of dispute, I will not stir up a quarrel long since put to rest, but will only briefly repeat the reasons which I produced elsewhere to either excuse or illustrate *Lightfoot’s* explanation, so that my reader may have the means to judge this question correctly and freely. For since I have no reason to wish to thrust *Lightfoot’s* opinion upon any mortal—as I myself once followed it not as certain, but as probable—it will suffice for me to have shown that it does not shrink from reason. If I have provided that, I shall be little concerned about the rest. For just as the ceremonies of ancient times are covered in much darkness, so undoubtedly many things cannot be boldly defined without rashness.

## CHAPTER VII.

*Evidence is brought forward to illustrate the opinion of Lightfoot and Cappellus concerning the Ten Idle Men, and to support it with probability; namely, 1. That Benjamin of Tudela interpreted the "Ten Idle Men" as ten literate men devoted to teaching and judicial matters. 2. That not only in Hebrew, but also in other languages, studious and literate men are commonly called "Idle." 3. That the periphrasis <note>A roundabout way of speaking; a descriptive phrase</note> of these Idle Men—"those occupied with the needs of the community"—perfectly matches Lightfoot's exposition.*

---

<margin>1. Page 70+</margin> It has been established that Benjamin of Tudela <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler from Spain who documented Jewish communities across Europe, Asia, and Africa</note> understood the word <term>Batlan</term> <note>original: בטלן; often translated as "idle" or "unoccupied"</note>, or **Idle Man**, to mean a **literate man**; indeed, he interpreted the phrase *Ten Idle Men* as referring to the very Prefects of the Sanhedrins and Schools. This is how the city of *Baghdad* was described and illustrated by that most learned man, *Constantine L’Empereur* <note>A 17th-century Dutch Hebraist and scholar</note>: *Furthermore, nearly a thousand Jews live in Baghdad, who enjoy tranquility and peace, and indeed great glory under the rule of the Great King. Among them are very wise men* <gloss>original: וראשי ישיבות מתעסקים בתורה, ומשרי; and the heads of the academies occupied in the Mosaic Law, and princes</gloss> *and the heads of the Assemblies (the Rectors of the Academies) occupied in the Law of Moses. In that city there are ten* <gloss>original: ישיבות; Yeshivot</gloss>, **Assemblies** (Academies and Sanhedrins). *And the head of the supreme Sanhedrin is the teacher Samuel, son of Eli, the head, I say, of the most eminent Sanhedrin. The Deputy* <gloss>original: סגן; Sagan</gloss> *of the Levites is the head of the second; Master Daniel is the President of the third Sanhedrin; Master Eleazar is an associate, the President of the fourth Sanhedrin; Master Eleazar, son of Tsema, the Procurator of the Order—whose genealogy is traced back to the blessed Prophet Samuel—is the head or President of the fifth Sanhedrin; Master Hasdia, the glory of the scholars* <gloss>original: חברים; Chaverim or "Associates"</gloss>, *is the President of the sixth Sanhedrin; Master Haggai is the Prince of the seventh Sanhedrin; Master Ezra of the eighth; the teacher Abraham, called Abou Tahir (Holy Father), is the head of the ninth Sanhedrin; and finally, Master Zacchæus, son of Bustanai, their general treasurer, is the President of the tenth Sanhedrin.* He then adds the following, which I urge you, my reader, not to ignore: <gloss>original: הם הנקראים בטלנים שאין מתעסקים בדבר אחר אלא בצרכי צבור ובכל ימי השבוע הם נכון לכל; They are the ones called "Idle Men" because they occupy themselves with nothing else but the needs of the community, and through all days of the week they are ready for everyone.</gloss>

<header>CHAPTER 7. ON THE GOVERNMENT OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH, etc.</header>

<margin><unclear>In the Itinerary, page 71, etc.</unclear></margin>
> <note>Hebrew original: לכ"ל אנשי הארץ היהודים חוץ מיום ב' שבאים כלם לפני הרב שמואל ראש ישיבת גאון יעקב ועומד עם העשרה בטלנים ראשי הישיבות לדון לכל הבאים עליהם וכו'</note>
> *These* IDLE MEN *are so called because they are occupied in no other thing than the necessary business of the people. AND THEY ADMINISTER JUSTICE TO ALL THE JEWS OF THAT REGION every day of the week, except for the second day <note>Monday</note>, when they all meet with Rabbi Samuel, the head of the Sanhedrin <note>The high council or court</note>, which bears the name of the "Pride of Jacob"; and he himself is present WITH THOSE TEN IDLE MEN, the Heads of the Sanhedrins, so that he may administer justice to all who approach without distinction.*

It is certainly clear from this testimony that **Benjamin of Tudela** <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler whose journals provide vital information on medieval Jewish life</note> interprets an **Idle Man** <note>original: Otiosus</note> as a *literate man* who *devotes his leisure* to studies for the benefit of the *commonwealth*. Furthermore, it is evident that he speaks not only of *Idle Men* in general, but also of the *Ten Idle Men*, by whom he understands the *Ten Leaders of the Sanhedrins*, or the *major schools of Baghdad*. Who could now doubt that *Benjamin*, when speaking of the *Ten Idle Men*, was referring to the accepted phrase used by the *Talmudists* <note>Scholars and commentators of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish law</note> regarding the *Ten Idle Men*? Nevertheless, the interpretation of this title given by *Benjamin* differs greatly from that of *Jarchius* <note>Rabbi Solomon Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most famous medieval commentator on the Talmud</note> and more recent *interpreters of the Talmud*. From this, it seems we must conclude that in *Benjamin’s* time, several different interpretations of this title were in use. For if a fixed and defined interpretation of the <note>original Greek: τῶν; of the</note> *Ten Idle Men* had existed in *Benjamin’s* day, what could have possessed *Benjamin of Tudela* to knowingly and willingly depart from it without necessity, going against the common authority of the Doctors, and devising another explanation of his own that would be entirely new and unwelcome to his people? If this is the case, I do not see why *Benjamin’s* reasoning should not be held in equal regard to that of *Jarchius* in explaining this title. For they were men of the same century—the twelfth since the birth of Christ. To be sure, our *Tudelensian* was prone to inventing and believing fables. I admit it; but *Jarchius* was also a man of fables, if ever there was one. Yet who would believe that *Benjamin*, however inclined toward fables and fictions, would wish to introduce new meanings for words into the Hebrew language for no benefit and no reward to his nation? I repeat, therefore, that in the time of *Benjamin*, not only did the interpretation of the title *Ten Idle Men* vary, but even then, that name was explained by some as *Literate and Learned Men*, who were entirely devoted and dedicated to divine matters, whether in the Sanhedrins and Schools, or in the Synagogues.

# LIGHTFOOT’S OPINION ON BOOK II.

2. It must be observed that this very word **Idle** <note>original: *Otiosus*</note> most appropriately—indeed, quite elegantly—carries the meaning attributed to it by **Benjamin of Tudela**, whether one considers its use among Hebrew authors themselves or compares it with words of equal power in other languages. Among Hebrew authors, I have found that "Vacation" or "Leisure" <margin>In Sanhedrin, on chapter 1, § 10.</margin> <note>Hebrew original: בטל, *Batlan*</note> is ascribed to Judges when they are occupied in the exercise of their duty. Thus we read in the decisions of **Rabbi Asher**: *The Judge may receive the reward of his leisure <note>original: "vacationis suæ (Otii sui)"</note> for that work which he had to cease, so that he might be intent upon judgment.* In the Greek and Latin languages, indeed, the words *to have leisure* <note>Greek original: $\sigma\chi o\lambda\alpha\zeta\epsilon\iota\nu$</note>, *to be idle*, and *to be vacant* do not signify mere rest in which you do nothing at all, but rather rest from harsher and servile works which tire the body more than the mind. As I might say with **Plato**, it is "leisure from one's own labors" <note>Greek original: $\mathrm{T}\hat{\omega}\nu$ $\mathrm{o}\imath\kappa\epsilon\acute{\imath}\omega\nu$ $\grave{\epsilon}\rho\gamma\omega\nu$ $\grave{\alpha}\rho\gamma\acute{\imath}\alpha\nu$</note>. Of this rank are literate and studious men, such as the Doctors of the Churches and Academies; since the common people see that they are immune from servile labor and perform such tasks that the commoners themselves only do when they are "at leisure," the people call them "Idle." And among the Greeks, the term *to have leisure* <note>Greek original: $\tau\grave{o}$ $\sigma\chi o\lambda\alpha\zeta\epsilon\iota\nu$</note> corresponds exactly with the Hebrew *Batlan* <note>original: בטל</note>: for it denotes *to be idle*. But this very *leisure* signifies applying oneself to the doing of some thing, or seizing the opportunity to do something. **Suidas** <note>A 10th-century Greek lexicographer and encyclopedist</note> says under the word *leisure* <note>Greek original: $\sigma\chi o\lambda\acute{\eta}$</note>: *Leisure is either doing nothing, or being occupied with something. Instead of "to be at leisure," they say "to have the opportunity."* <note>Greek original: $\sigma\chi o\lambda\acute{\eta}, \hat{\eta} \tau\grave{o} \mu\eta\delta\grave{\epsilon}\nu \delta\rho\hat{\alpha}\nu \hat{\eta} \tau\grave{o} \pi\epsilon\rho\acute{\iota} \tau\iota \sigma\chi o\lambda\acute{\alpha}\zeta\epsilon\iota\nu. \grave{\alpha}\nu\tau\grave{\iota} \delta\grave{\epsilon} \tau o\hat{\upsilon} \sigma\chi o\lambda\acute{\alpha}\zeta\epsilon\iota\nu \lambda\acute{\epsilon}\gamma ov\sigma\iota \tau\grave{o} \epsilon\grave{\upsilon}\kappa\alpha\iota\rho\epsilon\hat{\iota}\nu$</note> *It is to be vacant for some matter and to give effort to it; as if one were "idling" about something.* That is, to spend all one's leisure on a specific matter. However, for *to have leisure*, many say *to have opportunity*. **Hesychius** <note>An influential Greek grammarian and lexicographer</note> says: *Leisure. Not only does it denote doing nothing, but also being vacant for a certain thing and giving effort to it, and also a way of spending time.* <note>Greek original: $\sigma\chi o\lambda\acute{\eta}. \mathrm{O}\grave{\upsilon} \mu\acute{o}\nu o\nu \tau\grave{o} \mu\eta\delta\grave{\epsilon}\nu \delta\rho\hat{\alpha}\nu, \grave{\alpha}\lambda\lambda\grave{\alpha} \kappa\alpha\grave{\iota} \tau\grave{o} \pi\epsilon\rho\acute{\iota} \tau\iota \sigma\chi o\lambda\acute{\alpha}\zeta\epsilon\iota\nu \kappa\alpha\grave{\iota} \grave{\eta} \delta\iota\alpha\tau\rho\iota\beta\acute{\eta}$</note> In **Herodian** <note>A 3rd-century Roman historian who wrote in Greek</note> you have: *To give effort to spectacles and festivals*, *to be vacant for sacred rites*, *to give oneself to luxuries*, *to spend one's leisure in exercising tyranny.* <note>Greek originals: $\Theta\acute{\epsilon}\alpha\iota\varsigma \kappa\alpha\grave{\iota} \grave{\epsilon}o\rho\tau\alpha\hat{\iota} \sigma\chi o\lambda\acute{\alpha}\zeta\epsilon\iota\nu$; # CHAPTER 7. ON THE GOVERNMENT OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH, ETC. 537

...the practice of Youth and Masters in places destined for it, was called **Leisure** <note>original Greek: σχολὴ (*schole*); original Latin: *Otium*</note> by Ancient Authors, from which at last the place itself, the **School** <note>original: *Schola*</note>, began to be named after that "leisure." Indeed, it is so fitting that **literary men, scholars, and those devoted to sacred matters** should be named **the Idle** <note>original Hebrew: בטלנים (*Batalnim*); original Greek: σχολάζοντες (*scholazontes*)</note>. Hence, in the works of **Suidas** <note>A 10th-century Greek lexicographer and encyclopedist.</note>, the word for "school" <note>original: σχολεῖον</note> is explained as a "place of learning" <note>original: διδασκαλεῖον</note>, and "acting as head of a school" <note>original: σχολαρχήσας</note> is explained as "one who rules a school, or a place of study," that is, "one who presides over a school or the literary exercises of students." We pass over other examples. However, the words **to be vacant** <note>original: *vacare*</note> and **to be idle** <note>original: *otiari*</note> are clearly of the same power among the Latins. It would be commonplace to dwell on the proof of this meaning in the word *vacare*, since nothing is better known to schoolboys than that "to be vacant for letters and studies" <note>original: *literis studiisque vacare*</note> is the same as "to spend one's leisure in learning letters and to devote effort to studies."

<margin>Letter to Celantia on the instruction of a mother of a family. Volume 1, folio 4, column 1.</margin>
**Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century scholar and Bible translator.</note> elegantly takes the word **vacation** <note>original: *vacationis*</note> to mean "every sacred occupation." Thus he advises **Celantia**:
> Have such care for the home, that you still grant some **vacation** to the soul.
After a few things interspersed:
> Let there be such study of Divine reading there, such frequent turns of prayers, such firm and deep thought of things to come, that you may easily compensate for all the occupations of the remaining time with this **vacation**.

<margin>Book 3 of On Duties <note>original: *De Officiis*</note>.</margin>
It is quite certain that the notion of **leisure** <note>original: *otium*</note> among the authors of the Latin language signifies something no less honorable than shameful "idleness." **Cicero’s** <note>The famous Roman orator and statesman.</note> most famous sentiment is: *Scipio used to say that he was never less idle than when he was **idle**, nor less alone than when he was alone.*

<margin>On the Nature of the Gods, Book 3, at the beginning.</margin>
**Plutarch** <note>A Greek philosopher and biographer.</note> says: *When he was at leisure, he did more?* <note>original Greek: ὁ πότε σχολάζοι πλείονα πράττειν</note> Again, **Cotta** in Cicero’s work excellently supports our point: *For we are both **idle**, and we are dealing with those matters which are even to be preferred to business.*

<margin>In Caesar, chapter 4.</margin>
**Suetonius** <note>A Roman historian.</note> says of **Julius Caesar**: *But after the civil rebellion was settled, he brought a charge of extortion against Cornelius Dolabella, a man of consular and triumphal rank; and once Dolabella was acquitted, Caesar decided to withdraw to Rhodes, both to avoid resentment and so that **through leisure** and rest he might devote himself to Apollonius Molon, the most famous master of oratory at that time.* Caesar's "leisure" <note>original: *otium*</note> in this case was to give his effort to studying under Apollonius Molon.

<margin>See Furetière in the word "Academic."</margin>
Nor would it be out of place here to note that the members of the **Academy of Bologna** are even now called the **Idle Ones** <note>original: *Otiosos*</note>. Say therefore, according to this familiar and accepted use of the word, that the **Idle Men** are <margin>In the Travels, page 6.</margin> *those who have separated themselves from the affairs and cares of the world and stand over the book day and night* <note>original Hebrew: שנתפרשו מעניני העולם ועומדים על הספר יומם וliלה; quoting Benjamin of Tudela's description of scholars.</note>; as **Benjamin** [of Tudela] says elsewhere. Or, if anyone desires an even more extensive [meaning] of the "Idle Men"...

# LIGHTFOOT’S OPINION ON BOOK II.

<margin>Chapter 61, 5. The phrase: *to stand upon that book* (of the Law) <note>original Hebrew: עמד על הספר (*amad al ha-sefer*)</note> is the same as that used by Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:1: *Moreover, brethren, I make known unto you the Gospel, which I preached unto you, which you also received, and in which you stand.* <note>original Greek: ὃ καὶ παρελάβετε, ἐν ᾧ καὶ ἑστήκατε (*ho kai parelabete, en ho kai estēkate*)</note></margin>

If anyone desires a description [of these men], let them turn their mind to these words of **Kimchi** <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a prominent medieval Jewish commentator and grammarian, often called the Radak.</note>, as he explains the "Spiritual Priests" of **Isaiah**: *And you shall live; you will not need to work for a sage, for the sons of the stranger will do them [the labors], and you will be free to serve the Name [God] like the priests who were ready and prepared for the service of the Temple; so you will be free from worldly business, and you will occupy yourselves with the Law of God and in the words of wisdom to know the Lord.* <note>original Hebrew: ואתם תחיו לו צריכים... לדעת את ה' (*Ve-atem tichyu lo tzerichim... lada'at et Hashem*)</note> Specifically: YOU SHALL NOT HAVE NECESSITY TO BEND OVER YOUR SERVILE WORKS, BECAUSE THESE SHALL BE COMPLETED BY FOREIGNERS, BUT YOU SHALL BE ENTIRELY DEVOTED TO WORSHIPPING GOD, LIKE THE PRIESTS, WHO ARE ARRANGED AND PREPARED for the ministry of the Sanctuary; thus you shall be turned away from worldly business, and you shall give your effort to the Divine Law and the study of wisdom to know the Lord. Let us repeat the saying from before: **The Idle Men are those who give their effort to literature** <note>original Latin: *Otiosi sunt, qui literis dant operam*</note>, or **those who occupy themselves with the Torah** <note>original Hebrew: העוסקים בתורה (*ha-oskim ba-Torah*)</note>.

3. The phrase **to occupy oneself with the needs of the community** <note>original Hebrew: עוסק לצורכי צבור (*osek le-tzorkhei tzibur*)</note>, by which almost all Interpreters define the office of these "Idle Men," seems to signify something slightly more than what the interpretation of **Jarchi** <note>An older name for Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, 1040–1105), the foremost medieval commentator on the Bible and Talmud.</note> contains. I confess it is indeed of a more general meaning and is used for all those who serve the public interest in any way; for the more someone does, the more right they have to be said **to care for the needs of the Synagogue**. Yet, who would doubt that such Idle Men, who preside over the Sacred Rites of the **Synagogue**, promote the benefit of the Church more than those who merely lease the presence of their bodies to the Synagogue buildings for an accepted salary? But let us pay closer attention to the phrases which the Interpreters use throughout in describing these **Idle Men**.
