# CHAPTER 7. ON THE GOVERNMENT OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH, ETC.

<margin>According to the Lexicon, under this word.</margin>
**"That ten men are idle from their own business and occupied with the needs of the community,"** <note>original Hebrew: שעשרה אנשים בטלים מעסקיהם ועוסקין בצרכי צבור (*she-asarah anashim betelim me-iskeyhem ve-osekin be-tzorchei tzibur*)</note>. *According to the Lexicon, you should understand the "Idle Men" as ten men ceasing from their own private affairs and* INTENT UPON THE ADVANTAGES OF THE PUBLIC GOOD.

Let us see now what the phrase **"occupied with the needs of the community"** <note>original Hebrew: עוסק לצרכי צבור (*osek le-tzorchei tzibur*)</note> signifies. The word **"community"** <note>original Hebrew: צבור (*tzibur*)</note> properly denotes *the entire assembly of people gathered in the House of Prayer*; and because all the people of a single district were accustomed to come together in the synagogue on Sabbaths and feast days, the term was eventually taken more broadly to mean the *Commonwealth* or *Republic*, as it is translated elsewhere by **Selden**. <note>John Selden (1584–1654) was a brilliant English jurist and scholar who wrote extensively on Jewish law and its influence on European systems.</note> <margin>Selden, *On the Sanhedrin*, book 2, chapter 4, section 4.</margin> This was discussed in previous sections. Indeed, the phrase **"the necessities of the congregation"** <note>original Hebrew: צרכי צבור (*tzorchei tzibur*)</note> is very frequent in the writings of **Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a foundational Jewish philosopher and legal codifier whose works were studied by Christian scholars to understand biblical law.</note> and others, <margin>Book 1, Part 1, chapter 2.</margin> and it signifies any *offices and duties which are imposed on someone in the name of the Congregation for the public benefit*. Hence, **"to be occupied with the necessities of the congregation,"** or **"with the needs of the many,"** <note>original Hebrew: בצרכי רבים (*be-tzorchei rabbim*)</note> is the same as being intent upon the public interest and fulfilling the duty committed to you with the highest faith and diligence. *Since, however, it is certain that the advantages of the Commonwealth, or the Necessities of the Synagogue Assembly, are primarily managed by the Overseers of the City or Synagogue and the public Ministers of the Synagogue*, it follows that Judges, Pastors, Deacons, Teachers in the Academy, and Synagogue Ministers are usually described by this phrase. <margin>As cited above.</margin>

In this way, indeed, **Benjamin of Tudela** <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler whose travelogues provided Christian scholars with vital information about the Jewish diaspora.</note> correctly described the Judges of Baghdad: **"They are those called 'Idle Men' because they apply themselves to no other matter than the needs of the community,"** <note>original Hebrew: הם הנקראים בטלנים שאין מתעסקים בדבר אחר אלא בצרכי צבור (*hem ha-nikraim batlanim she-ein mitasekim be-davar acher ela be-tzorchei tzibur*)</note>. <margin>In the *Tishbi* <note>A dictionary of Talmudic and Rabbinic Hebrew by the 16th-century scholar Elias Levita.</note>.</margin> Regarding the **"Minister of the Synagogue,"** <note>The *Chazan*, often translated as "cantor" today, but historically an overseer or sexton.</note> Elias Levita says in the same way: **"And he is also called an Inspector, because it is his duty to see what the necessities of the congregation are,"** <note>original Hebrew: ונקרא גם כן חזן לפי שהוא צריך לראות מה הם צורכי צבור (*ve-nikra gam ken chazan lefi she-hu tzarich lirot mah hem tzorchei tzibur*)</note>.

<margin>Title 53, section 26.</margin> Regarding the **Deacons** <note>The author uses "Deacon" to translate the Hebrew officials responsible for communal welfare and charity.</note> there is a passage, already noted by others, in the *Orach Chajim* <note>The "Way of Life," the first section of the *Shulchan Aruch*, the definitive code of Jewish law.</note>: **"When a congregation is accustomed to appoint men over the public needs, whether as a Synagogue Minister, or for the charity chest, or for other appointments needed by the community, etc.,"** <note>original Hebrew: קהל שנהגו למנות אנשים על צורכי הצבור בין לחזן בין לקופה של צדקה בין לשאר מינויים הצריכים לצבור וכו' (*kahal she-nahagu limnot anashim al tzorchei ha-tzibur ben le-chazan ben le-kupah shel tzedakah ben li-shear minuyim ha-tzrichim la-tzibur etc.*)</note> WHEN THE ASSEMBLY IS ACCUSTOMED TO PUT CERTAIN PEOPLE IN CHARGE OF PUBLIC BUSINESS (the necessities of the whole group) — *whether it appoints a* SYNAGOGUE MINISTER, *or* COLLECTORS OF ALMS, *or distributes other duties for the public good, etc.*

It appears, certainly, from these few documents, that the phrase **"occupied with the needs of the community"** means to be intent on the necessary business of the Commonwealth; in Jewish Law, this refers everywhere to those Synagogue officials who bring more benefit to the Commonwealth, or the Church, than ten men to whom this [task]...

# LIGHTFOOT’S OPINION ON BOOK II.
<meta>catchword: per</meta>

then it is supposed that business is given to them, so that they may *be at leisure*. However, I am not unaware that there is a great breadth of meaning in this phraseology, and the force of the words is either intensified or diminished according to the judgment of the writers.

As indeed these individual points seem to suggest, more honor or duty should be attributed to these *Ten Idle Men* than has been given by *Jarchi* <note>original: Jarchio. "Jarchi" refers to Solomon ben Isaac, better known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note>, so too various things could be brought forward to diminish the weight of Jarchi's authority in this case. For what Jarchi maintains here, he must hold from tradition; for you will find nothing about it in the Talmud itself. Moreover, that tradition would have been of a very long time and therefore more uncertain, because
<margin>Maimonides, *Laws of Megillah*, chapter 1, section 9. And in the Commentary on the Code of the Megillah, chapter 1, section 1.</margin>
the *distinction between Major and Minor Cities*, which the *Ten Idle Men* formerly served, and the varying reading of the Book of Esther subordinated to this distinction of cities, according to the testimony of the Teachers themselves, only took place in *Canaan* while the *Republic flourished*. After the Republic was overturned, and the distinction between *Major and Minor Cities* perished, the use of the *Idle Men* themselves seems also to have gradually perished, though the name, as often happens, was preserved. But, what is more, it is sufficiently clear that the tradition of the Teachers concerning the interpretation of this title is not constant and perpetual. We mentioned above that *Benjamin of Tudela* <note>Benjamin of Tudela (1130–1173) was a Jewish traveler whose itineraries provide valuable historical information about Jewish communities across Europe and the Middle East.</note> asserts that the Presidents of the *Ten Sanhedrins of Baghdad* were called the *Ten Idle Men*. Benjamin would not have done this unless he had understood from elsewhere that the name *Idle* most especially applied to the leaders of the Schools and Synagogues, who, being entirely devoted to sacred things, live altogether free from worldly business.
<margin>To Alfasi, folio 360, column 2.</margin>
**Rabbi Nissim** <note>Nissim ben Reuben (c. 1310–1375), a famous Talmudist and philosopher from Girona.</note>, on the other hand, having rejected a large part of Jarchi's commentary, says that they are called *Idle Men* who: 
> ALL THOSE WHO ARE FOUND DILIGENTLY IN THE SYNAGOGUE IN THE MORNING AND EVENING AT THE HOUR OF PRAYER. <note>original Hebrew: כל שמשכימין ומעריבין להיות מצוין, בשעת תפלה לבית הכנסת (*kol she-mashkimin u-ma'arivin lihyot metzuyin, b'sha'at tefillah l'veit ha-knesset*)</note>

This explanation, I confess, stands in opposition to Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675) was an English churchman and Hebraist who sought to use Jewish sources to explain the historical context of the Bible.</note>; but it also stands in opposition to the patrons of Jarchi’s explanation. It is enough for us to have gathered from this that the tradition regarding the true interpretation of the name *Idle Men* fluctuates among the Hebrew interpreters themselves, and therefore Jarchi is not to be trusted too much in this case. And indeed, men most practiced in Hebrew letters have frequently acted so as to abandon the glosses of the Talmudic interpreters and of Jarchi himself, when they saw that those glosses relied on no suitable foundations and reason suggested otherwise; and this all the more so because the Talmudic glossators [tend] to forge fables without necessity...

As for what is said, that this *Number of Ten Idle Men* <term>Batlanim; Jewish men of leisure who were paid or supported to be present in the synagogue to ensure a quorum (minyan) was always available for prayer</term> was required in the Synagogues to recite the more sacred prayer formulas, I certainly do not deny that the Jews require a number of *ten men* to recite certain prayer formulas; however, they can certainly fulfill this duty of theirs without *ten men* specifically hired for that purpose so that they might sit *Idle and Lazy* in the Synagogues for the greatest part of the day and wait for those praying. For even today, it is so accepted among their customs that if seven, six, or even just one (for the Masters disagree here) enter the Synagogue after the blessings of the **Shema** <term>Shema; the central declaration of Jewish faith, beginning "Hear, O Israel..."</term> have already been recited, and if they find enough others remaining in the Synagogue to complete the *number of ten* with them, then those remaining are forced to wait until they have recited the *Shema* <note>The original text uses the Greek article "the" (τὸ) before the Hebrew "Shema," which the transcription misspelled as "Schemab."</note>. *Rabbi Tam (for it is clear that "R.T." And this same thing is also stated in the Treatise Sopherim <note>Maseket Soferim; a minor tractate of the Talmud regarding the rules for scribes and public liturgy</note>: In a place where there are nine or ten who have heard the Kaddish and Barechu, if there is even one among them who has not heard them, and he recites the Kaddish and Barechu and they answer after him, he has duly fulfilled his duty. With these views, my Lord and Parent Rabbi Asher <note>Asher ben Jehiel (c. 1250–1327), a prominent Talmudist and the father of Jacob ben Asher</note> (of blessed memory) agrees.*

### THE OPINION OF LIGHTFOOT REGARDING BOOK II.

They belonged to the *City*, and were considered its *Officials*. For we recognize no office of the Synagogue unless it concerns the sacred rites of the Synagogues themselves and is administered within the Synagogue itself. For this must be noted beforehand, lest this whole dispute turn into a *logomachia* <term>logomachia; from the Greek, a dispute over words or terminology rather than substantive facts</term>. However, this duty of the *Collection of Alms*, as it was exercised outside the Synagogues, is consistently referred by Hebrew Authors to the **City** <note>original: "עיר" (Ir)</note>, that is, to the Society of Jews in any given place, insofar as it is considered by us not as a *Sacred* entity, but as a *Civil* one. **Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal scholar whose codification of Jewish law, the Mishneh Torah, is cited here</note>:

<margin>Chapter 9, § 1. Code: Laws Concerning the Poor</margin>
**EVERY CITY** in which there are Israelites is bound to appoint from among them **COLLECTORS OF ALMS**, men well-known and trustworthy, who go around among the people from the eve of the Sabbath to the eve of the Sabbath, taking from each and every person what is appropriate for him to give and the amount assessed for him. And they distribute the money every Sabbath eve, giving to every single poor person food sufficient for seven days; and this is what is called the **KUPPAH** <term>Kuppah; literally a "basket" or "chest," referring to the communal fund used to support the local poor with weekly distributions</term>.

**EVERY CITY**, *in which there are Israelites, is bound to appoint* **FROM ITS INHABITANTS COLLECTORS OF ALMS**, *men known and faithful, who go around the people from the evening of the Sabbath until the evening of the Sabbath, receiving from each one as much as is appropriate for him, and as much as has been imposed upon him. They indeed distribute the money each evening of the Sabbath, and give to individual poor persons food which suffices for seven days; and this is called the* **KUPPAH**, *the Charity Chest*. It is clear from this testimony that Maimonides ascribes the *Collectors of Alms* to the *City*; and he does so consistently throughout this entire Treatise. Thus, he calls the Overseers of Alms, or the Magistrate, or the universal Society of inhabitants—to whom he ascribes the power of disposing of collected Alms according to their judgment—

<margin>Chapter 8, § 11.</margin>
**THE MEN OF THE CITY** <note>original: "אנשי העיר" (Anshei Ha-Ir)</note>. I say the Men of the City, not of the **Synagogue** <note>original: "בית הכנסת" (Beit Ha-Knesset)</note>. By the same reasoning, the *Poor* who are supported are called

<margin>Chapter 7, § 13.</margin>
**THE POOR OF THE CITY** <note>original: "עניי עיר" (Aniyei Ir)</note>, as they are surely to be considered *members* of the City in this case. Indeed, these very *Collectors of Alms* are named

<margin>Chapter 257, § 8.</margin>
**COLLECTORS OF THE CITY** <note>original: "גבאי העיר" (Gabbai Ha-Ir)</note>. *There is a passage in the Yoreh De’ah* <note>The Yoreh De’ah is one of the four constituent sections of the Shulchan Aruch, the authoritative code of Jewish law</note>: *If any poor person has relatives who are wealthy and able to support him, the* **COLLECTORS OF THAT CITY** *are not bound to nourish him; even though these relatives themselves contribute to the communal fund according to their means*. Behold, they are not called...

### CHAPTER 8. ON THE GOVERNMENT OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH, ETC.

...are called <gloss>Gabbai Beit HaKnesset</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: גבאי בית הכנסת; literally "Treasurers of the House of Assembly"</note>, Collectors of the *Synagogue*. Why then, I ask, are they called <gloss>Gabbai Ir</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: גבאי עיר</note>, Collectors of the **CITY**, if these Collectors of Alms belong to the *Synagogue* and not to the *City*? Indeed, I am well aware that the word *Ir* <note>original Hebrew: עיר; City</note> enjoys a very broad meaning among Hebrew authors and can designate any Society of Jews dwelling in any place. I also know that the *City* and the *Church* <note>The author uses "Ecclesia" to mean the religious assembly or congregation</note> among the Jews of old did not constitute two separate bodies of men as is the case with us, but merged into one *Society*. However, just as every *Society* has a dual aspect—either in how it fulfills its religious duty toward God in *Sacred Places*, or in how it strives for its own preservation and well-being, which truly makes it a *City*—so too was it arranged with Jewish *Societies*. They fulfilled their religious duties toward God in the *Temple* and *Synagogues*. The duties administered outside the Temple and Synagogues were regarded as *Civil*; and the word *Ir* [City] itself properly denotes the Society of Jews insofar as it constitutes a *City*, and that *City* strives to preserve and defend itself. Refer to this, then: those Collectors of Alms were appointed by the *Sanhedrin* <note>The Jewish high court or local council of elders</note> itself, insofar as it managed the care of the *City* or the *Civil Society*, and that the *Sanhedrin* prescribed to every *Citizen* the manner of exercising this grace; those who resisted this mandate were to be corrected with lashes.

<margin>Note on Chapter 9 of Maimonides, § 4.</margin>
Let us hear **Prideaux** <note>Humphrey Prideaux (1648–1724), an English scholar and divine</note>, the learned interpreter of this *Treatise of Maimonides*: > *It was not decreed how much each should give to the Dish <term>Tamhui; a collection dish for daily food donations for the poor</term>, and therefore three Collectors were appointed who, having the authority of Judges, might judge during the collection whether each was giving according to his means.* However, the **ALMS OF THE CHEST** <term>Kuppah; a weekly collection for the local poor</term>, since it was a fixed matter, being **IMPOSED BY THE SANHEDRIN OF THE CITY**, was not collected by more than those to whose care it was to be committed.

<margin>Chapter 7, § 10.</margin>
Maimonides himself writes in this manner: > <gloss>If there is anyone who does not wish to give Alms, or gives less than is fitting for him, the court coerces him and strikes him with the strike of rebellion until he gives what they estimated he should give, etc.</gloss> <note>Original Hebrew: מי שאינו רוצה ליתן צדקה או שיתן מעט ממה שראוי לו בית דין כופין אותו ומכין אותו מכת מרדות עד שיתן מה שאמרוהו ליתן וכו'</note> *If there is anyone who does not wish to give Alms, or gives less than is fair,* the **SANHEDRIN** *shall compel him and strike him with <term>lashes of rebellion; a discretionary physical punishment used by Jewish courts to enforce communal obligations</term> until he gives as much as they judge must be given by him, etc.*

It is clear that this entire matter pertained to the care and direction of the *Sanhedrin* of the City, which commanded each Citizen to give as much as his condition allowed. Thus Maimonides again advises elsewhere that the Collectors of Alms—

<margin>Chapter 9, § 1.</margin>
<gloss>—take from each and every one what is fitting to give and the fixed amount [assessed]—</gloss> <note>Original Hebrew: לוקחין מכל אחד ואחד מה שהוא ראוי ליתן ודבר הקצוב</note>

...upon him, *they receive from individuals what it is appropriate for them to give,* **AND WHAT HAS BEEN IMPOSED UPON THEM.** That is, by the Sanhedrin. Indeed, the *Collectors of the Dish* <note>Latin: *Collectores Catini*; refers to the Hebrew *Tamchui*, a vessel for collecting food for the poor</note>, which I think should be noted here, belong to the same body as the *Collectors of the Chest* <note>Latin: *Collectores Cistae*; refers to the Hebrew *Kuppah*, a fund for collecting money</note>; as is again very clearly evident from Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist</note>:

<margin>Chapter 9, Section 2.</margin>
<gloss>And likewise they appoint collectors who take every single day from each and every courtyard, etc.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: וכן מעמידין גבאין שלוקחין בכל יום ויום מכל חצר וחצר וחצר וכו׳</note> *In the same way* (he had been speaking of the *Collectors of the Chest* to be established in the City) *they appoint Collectors, who receive [alms] every single day from each house, etc.* And from this, the <gloss>Kuppah</gloss> & <gloss>Tamchui</gloss> <note>Hebrew: קופה & תמחוי; the "Chest" and the "Bowl"</note>, the *Chest and the Bowl* or *Dish for Alms*, could be interchanged and mixed together if public interests required it:

<margin>Yoreh De'ah, chapter 256, section 4.</margin>
<gloss>The residents of the city have the right to make the chest into a bowl, and the bowl into a chest, and to change them for whatever they wish for the needs of the community.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: רשאים בני העיר לעשות קופה תמחוי ותמחוי קופה ולשנותן לכל מה שירצו לצרכי צבור</note> **THE INHABITANTS OF THE CITY HAVE THE POWER TO CONVERT the Alms of the CHEST into the Alms of the DISH and the Dish into the Chest, and to spend them on all those things which they shall judge to pertain to the public good.** Now who would say that the *Collectors of the Dish*, so called among the Hebrews, are to be referred to the *Synagogue*? Therefore, it was thus established of old in the State of the Jews. The *Collectors of the Chest and the Dish* were appointed by the same Magistrate. Both collected their alms through the town at the doors of the citizens. The collected alms were frequently interchanged at the discretion of the Magistrate. What then, you ask, was the difference? What was the reason that Overseers of the poor with different names were established? The difference is exceedingly small; so much so, that the *Collectors of the Dish* were often neglected in the Cities and their duty entrusted to the *Collectors of the Chest*. However, where in larger cities these Collectors were established by the Sanhedrin as distinct in office and name, this distinction between them took place: the *Collectors of the Chest* provided only for the needs of the poor of that City and Town, while the *Collectors of the Dish* cared for any other poor people arriving from elsewhere, who stayed in the city for one or a few days, coming and going. This is the reason why these *Collectors of the Dish* were required to go from door to door every single day and distribute to each person their daily portion, whereas the *Collectors of the Chest* would go from door to door only every Friday and distribute money to the poor of the City for the entire week. This is also why *the former* would receive any kind of food in the bowl, while *the latter* would collect only money. For indeed, the *Collectors of the Chest* and they themselves

# CHAPTER 8. ON THE GOVERNMENT OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH, etc.

and that they themselves gathered alms by going from door to door in the City is again clear from *Maimonides*. <margin>chapter 9, §. 8. 9.</margin> He explicitly warns that the *Collectors of Alms* should not separate from one another while going through the city; they should place money—whether found or received from others—into their own sack in the marketplace to avoid suspicion, and other similar instructions. From this, again, what else can you conclude than that the *Collectors of Alms* belong to the City, **not to the Synagogue**? For whoever performs his duty in the *City* is undoubtedly to be counted among the *Officials of the City*, not those of the *Synagogue*. Since among the Ancient Jews the City and the Church constituted one and the same communion and society, it is hardly possible to distinguish the Officials of the City from those of the Synagogue by any other mark than this: the Synagogue Officials must perform their duty within the Synagogues, while those who perform their duties outside of them are to be referred to the Officials of the Civil Society. Let us add to this, as a finishing touch, another decree of a similar kind from the *Yoreh De'ah* <note>The *Yoreh De'ah* is a section of the *Shulchan Aruch*, the foundational code of Jewish law</note>, which strengthens our previous points regarding the collections in no small way: <margin>Yoreh De'ah chapter 256. §. 5.</margin> <gloss>If anyone has lived in a province for thirty days, they compel him to give charity to the chest along with the people of the province; if he has stayed three months, they compel him to give to the food bowl; if he has stayed six months, they compel him to give charity for the clothing with which they cover the poor of the city; if he has stayed nine months, they compel him to give charity for the burial with which they bury the poor and perform all the needs of burial, etc.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: מי שישב במדינה ל' יום כופים אותו ליתן צדקה לקופה עם בני המדינה ושב ג' חדשי' כופין אותו ליתן תמחוי ושב ששה חדשים כופין אותו ליתן צדקה בכסות שמכסים בה עניי העיר ושב ט' חדשים כופין אותו ליתן צדקה לקבורה שקוברים בה את העניים ועושי' להם כל צרכי קבורה וכו'</note> *If anyone has stayed in some city (in any place) for thirty days, they* COMPEL *him to give Alms to the Chest along with the inhabitants of that place. If for nine months, they compel him to give Alms for providing for the burial of the poor, and for all those things which pertain to it.* You see that the collection of Alms is restricted to the City and all its inhabitants, with no account taken or mention made of the Synagogue. Furthermore, the inhabitants of each city are compelled (by the Sanhedrin) to pay out Alms for the benefit of the City. These points shall suffice to demonstrate the truth, which will provide great light in what follows for our opinion on the Pauline Deacons <note>Refers to the office of Deacon established by St. Paul in the early Christian Church</note>, which will then be explained more fully.

Furthermore, I now assume that the supreme power of arranging *sacred matters* and the exercise of Divine Worship to be celebrated in those places lay equally with these *Courts* <note>original Latin: *Curias*, referring to the local governing councils or assemblies</note> of each city. For *civil and sacred* affairs among the Jews were not distinct, except in theory. Indeed, God formed the Jewish Republic in such a way that sacred matters were mixed with civil ones, and the *City* was by no means distinct or to be distinguished from the *Church* <note>original Latin: *Ecclesia*, here used in the sense of a religious assembly or community</note>. Civil and Sacred laws were merged by the Legislator, and obedience to them is urged by the same arguments. The *Magistrates* were established as the Interpreters and Defenders of the whole body of these Laws, sitting in the *chair of Moses* <note>original: *sella Mosis*, a term for the seat of authority and teaching in the synagogue</note>, and called by the common name *Elohim* <note>original Hebrew: אלהים; while usually meaning "God," it is also a biblical term for judges who act with divine authority</note>. These magistrates, therefore, had no less right and power to establish the Church and order sacred matters than they did to rule the city. Whether a Synagogue should be built in the city over which they presided, where it should be built, at what times sacred rites should be celebrated, which rites should be preferred over others, what kind of people should be admitted to the communion of those rites, and who should be kept away and excommunicated from them—it stood with these men to define such things, just as much as it did to decide which people they wished to grant the right of citizenship to, and to whom they would deny it. Indeed, since the *City* was the same thing as the *Church*, being added to the *City* was of the same value as being admitted to the communion of the *Church*. ## ON THE TRUE FORM, BOOK II.

...the power of sacred matters resided with the <term>Beth Din</term> <note>original Hebrew: בית דין</note>, the **Sanhedrin**, or the **Senate** of each place; which lesser Senates were nevertheless subject to the <term>Beth Din ha-Gadol</term> <note>original Hebrew: בית דין הגדול</note>, the **Great Senate of Jerusalem**. From these premises, which I believe no one will easily doubt, I now finally conclude that this Sacred **Senate** of each city, called by the Hebrews the <term>Beth Din</term> <note>original Hebrew: בית דין</note>, presided in the more famous **Synagogue** of that city and held the first place there.

### CHAPTER 9. THE GOVERNMENT OF THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE.

In the story of Susanna <note>An addition to the Book of Daniel found in the Apocrypha</note>, two among others are mentioned as <term>Zequenim</term> <note>original Hebrew: זקנים</note>, or **ELDERS**, of the Jewish people dwelling in Babylon. These men were accustomed to meet with the whole people at the house of Joakim—a man of chief dignity among them—to handle legal and forensic matters. Even if the history itself were fictional, it is nevertheless probable that its author wished to adorn his drama with circumstances that smelled of the truth and could be easily reconciled with accepted customs. Whatever the case may be regarding the rest of the story, there seems to be at least this much truth underlying the tale: that the multitude of Jews living in the more famous places of the Exile were governed by certain **Presbyters** <note>Elders</note> of significant authority and power.

Just as the larger Senates in Judea had a President who was the most learned and honored man of that Council, so too the most grand Senates outside of Judea—such as those of *Alexandria, Antioch* (and perhaps even *Damascus*), *Babylon*, and later *Baghdad*—were distinguished by a **President**. This leader, like a Prince, protected the rights and the honor of his nation in those foreign places with the greatest splendor. They were called **Ethnarchs** <note>original Greek: Ἐθνάρχαι, meaning "ruler of a people"</note> by the Greeks, and **Patriarchs** or **Primates** by the Latins. To these Sacred Senates of the Jews and their Princes, we again assign the first parts, the first place, and the first honor within the Synagogue; for no one denies that the supreme power regarding sacred matters resided with them.

Up to this point, we have been largely occupied with explaining our own opinion regarding the government of the famous ancient synagogues. Now, it will be necessary to establish these suppositions from the monuments of the Ancients, to reconcile them with those records, and finally to apply them to those passages of Holy Scripture which treat the government of the Synagogue. Let us begin with **Philo** and **Josephus**. Philo the Jew <note>A Hellenistic Jewish philosopher from Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE)</note> nowhere outlines the form of the ancient synagogue more distinctly than where he discourses on the **Essenes** <note>original Latin: Effaeis</note>, those practical philosophers, their customs, and their entire way of life. In the following context of this book, Josephus mentions another riot that arose in *Caesarea*, caused by the Jewish Synagogue, which was treated irreverently by the Caesareans. In this history, there appear the influential men of the Jews <note>original Greek: hoi dynatoi tōn Ioudaiōn</note>, **THE LEADERS OF THE JEWS** living in Caesarea, who offered eight *talents* <note>A talent was a massive unit of weight used as a measure of gold or silver; eight talents represented a very large fortune.</note> to *Gessius Florus* so that he might use his authority to remove a building of shops that was an insult to the Synagogue. The same Josephus, speaking of *Antiochus*, the author of the calamity that pressed upon the Jews of Antioch, says he was an honored man of his own race, since his parent had been the ruler of the Jews at Antioch <note>original Greek: archōn tōn ep' antiocheias Ioudaiōn; Latin: **PRINCEPS JUDÆORUM ANTIOCHENORUM**</note>, **THE CHIEF OF THE ANTIOCHENE JEWS**. I would think, however, that this Chief of the Jews of Antioch, whom *Josephus* mentions, was an *Ethnarch* <term>Ethnarch: A governor or "ruler of a nation," specifically a leader who represented an ethnic group within a larger empire, such as the Roman or Seleucid empires.</term>. We have said that such Chiefs of their own race were granted to the Jews by the Magistrate in every celebrated city, both for the purpose of administering justice to their fellow countrymen (like a *Praetor* <note>A high-ranking Roman official responsible for the administration of justice.</note>), and for advocating for and sustaining the cause of their race before the Magistrate, as well as for caring for and establishing other matters that concerned the interests of the Jewish City and Church.

From this, you may gather quite distinctly what the manner of governing the Synagogue and what the order of sacred rites was. Indeed, one may observe therein a certain *Jesus*,

<margin>
Josephus, *The Life*, pages 1020 and 1022.
</margin>
whom *Josephus* calls a <term>Ruler</term> <note>original Greek: archonta</note> or <term>Prefect</term> <note>original Latin: Praefectum</note>, and a <term>Council</term> <note>original Greek: boulēn</note> or <term>Senate</term> <note>original Latin: Senatum</note> deliberating on the public affairs of the Tiberians in the Synagogue. He calls them <term>the ten most powerful of the Tiberians</term> <note>original Greek: tous deka tōn Tiberieōn dynatōtatous</note> or <term>TEN MOST POWERFUL of the Tiberians</term>; <term>ten leaders of the multitude</term> <note>original Greek: deka tou plēthous proestōtas</note> or <term>TEN OVERSEERS OF THE PEOPLE</term>; <term>the ten first men of the Tiberians</term> <note>original Greek: deka prōtous Tiberieōn</note> or <term>TEN PRIMATES OF THE TIBERIANS</term>: yet Josephus does not explain the basis of that dignity or excellence, nor does it please me to inquire into it too anxiously because of the uncertainty of the matter. *His Life*, page 1021.

That is to say, *Jesus the Prefect*, according to his own will, admitted this man into the Synagogue and excluded another. Indeed, compare also the other things that follow. Besides this *Jesus* and the *Senate*, no other Prefect or Prefects of the Synagogue of the Tiberians are named; on the contrary, the judgment of all things is left to them, as the highest Prefects of the Tiberian people.

Maimonides shows the *Ancient Synagogue* nowhere perhaps more clearly than in the *Treatise on Fasts*; a type of assembly that corresponds in every way to our hypotheses. His words are these: *On each of these later days of Fasting instituted for the sake of rain, they pray according to this rule. They bring the Ark out into the city square, and all the people gather, covering themselves with sackcloth and scattering burnt ashes on the Ark and on the Book of the Law to further provoke sorrow and to humble their souls:* <note>original Hebrew: ואחד מן העם נוטל אפר מקלה ונותן בראש הנשיא ובראש אב בית דין</note> *and one of the people takes some of those ashes and places them on the head of the* <term>PRINCE</term> <note>the Nasi, or highest leader</note>, *and on the head of the* <term>FATHER OF THE SYNEDRIUM</term> <note>the Av Beit Din, or second-in-command of the court</note> *in that very place where the* <term>Phylacteries</term> <note>Tefillin; small leather boxes containing scripture worn on the forehead</note> *are fixed, so that they may be shamed and return to their senses; and everyone follows this example by placing ashes on their own head.*

<margin>Section 2</margin>

<margin>Section 3</margin>
<margin>Section 4</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: ואם היה אותו שאומר דברי הכיבושין ראוי להתפלל מתפלל ואם לאו מורידין אחר</note> *And if he who delivered that penitential speech is fit to pray, then he himself performs this duty; if not, it is entrusted to another.* But who is considered fit to pour out prayers in such cases? *etc.* Behold, the true form of the ancient Jerusalem Synagogue! The entire congregation <note>original Latin: Ecclesia</note> meets in one place. Over it presides, according to our hypotheses, the great Sanhedrin <note>the high court</note> of Jerusalem, and indeed the <term>PRINCE OF THE SANHEDRIN</term>; following this example, the Presidents of the smaller Sanhedrins presided in other cities. Furthermore, other men of distinguished appearance and skill could be deputed both for this work and for pouring out the extraordinary prayers of this time.

# CHAPTER 9. ON THE GOVERNANCE OF THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE, 563

In addition to these, one can find excellent examples of this kind of Synagogue Governance in the writings of *Benjamin of Tudela*, who, in almost all the major places where the descendants of Israel stay in greater numbers, identifies <term>YESHIVOT</term> <note>Hebrew: ישיבות; translated by the author as "Assemblies of Learned Men"</note> (or <term>Presbyteries</term>, following the style of Scripture <note>original Greek: πρεσבυτέρια</note>), by whose collective counsel both the academic and ecclesiastical sacred affairs of that place are directed. It will be useful to extract certain examples from him for our use, because upon this hypothesis the entire comparison we will later establish between the Governance of the Synagogue and the Church will be built. Let us first hear our *Tudelan* traveler on the Jews of *Damascus*:

<margin>p. 56.</margin>
And there is the Head of the Academy of the land of Israel, whose name is Rabbi Ezra; and his brother Sar-Shalom, the <term>FATHER OF THE HOUSE OF JUDGMENT</term> <note>Hebrew: Av Beit Din, the deputy head of the court</note>; and Rabbi Joseph, holding the fifth place in this Academy; and Rabbi Masliach, the Head of the Order, the <term>PREACHER</term>; and Rabbi Meir, the Glory of the Wise; and Rabbi Joseph ibn Falat, the <term>FOUNDATION OF THE ACADEMY</term> <note>The Hebrew text provided is כור (Kuer), but a margin note suggests it should be יסוד (Yesod/Foundation)</note>; and Rabbi Heman the <term>PARNAS</term> <note>A community leader or administrator, translated here as "Pastor"</note>; and Rabbi Tsaddik the Physician.

And there is the PRINCE OF THE SENATE of the land of *Israel*, whose name is *Rabbi Ezra*; and his brother *Sar-Shalom*, FATHER OF THE HOUSE OF JUDGMENT; and *Rabbi Joseph, holding the fifth place in this Senate*; and *Rabbi Masliach, the Head of the Order*, PREACHER; and *Rabbi Meir, the Glory of the Wise*; and *Rabbi Joseph, the "admirable stone,"* * THE FOUNDATION OF THE ASSEMBLY; and *Rabbi Heman*, PASTOR; and *Rabbi Tsaddik*, the Physician. Here is a SENATE OF TEN LEARNED MEN, whom *Benjamin* reports moderated scholarly and ecclesiastical matters in *Damascus*.

<margin>* L’Empereur <note>A famous 17th-century Hebraist</note> undoubtedly read <term>Yesod</term> <note>Hebrew: יסוד, meaning "foundation"</note> which, if it be the genuine reading, can be compared to Paul's phrasing in Galatians 2:9: <note>original Greek: Οἱ δοκοῦντες στύλοι εἶναι</note> "Those who seemed to be pillars."</margin>

### OF THE TRUE FORM, BOOK II. 564

...there are nearly three hundred Jews. — **CHURCH** <note>Hebrew: קהל (*Kahal*)</note> according to L'Empereur; <note>Constantijn L'Empereur was a noted 17th-century scholar who translated Benjamin of Tudela’s travels.</note> or **COLLEGE**) **ONE** *sits at the lower shore of the sea; while the other likewise sits at the shore of the sea, but in a tower above:* <note>original Hebrew: וְהֶם יְשִׁיבָה גְדוֹלָה וְתַלְמִידוּ הַכַּמִים</note> *and they have a great Academy and wise students: Rabbi Simeon, son of Rabbi Antoli, and Rabbi Jacob his brother, and Rabbi Levaro; and these are the heads of the upper [assembly],* *and they constitute a* **GREAT ASSEMBLY**, (which L'Empereur calls "venerable") and *these Learned Men—Rabbi Simeon son of Rabbi Antoli, and Rabbi Jacob his brother, and Rabbi Levaro—are presided over that upper Church or college.* <note>original Hebrew: וּבְרֹאשׁ הַקָּהָל שֶׁל מַטָּה רַבִּי יַעֲקוֹב פִּרְפִּינוּ הֶעָשִׁיר וְר' אַבְרָהָם וְר' מֵאִיר וַחֲתָנוֹ וְרַבִּי יִצְחָק וְר' מֵאִיר</note> *But presiding over the lower* **COLLEGE or CHURCH** *are Rabbi Jacob Phirpicnus, a very wealthy man, Rabbi Abraham, and his son-in-law Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Isaac, and another man named Rabbi Meir. You see here a Church—or rather, two Churches in a single place—governed by several Learned Men who, as is clear from these words, share the same rank and office.*

Indeed, it was a very common custom among the Jews in the various places of their Exile where they settled in large numbers to immediately establish a <term>YESHIVA</term> <note>Hebrew: יְשִׁיבָה; literally a "sitting" or session</note>, an Assembly or an ecclesiastical Sanhedrin, appointed to lead and teach the community. This is a well-known fact from their history, in which testimonies of such <term>YESHIVOT</term> (Assemblies, Sanhedrins, or Consistories, both academic and ecclesiastical) appear everywhere. Regarding this very word <term>YESHIVA</term>, *Elias Levita* <note>A famous 15th-century Hebrew grammarian.</note> writes: <note>original Hebrew: יְשִׁיבָה קוֹרִין לְמָקוֹם שֶׁיֵשׁ שָׁם מַרְבִּיצֵי תוֹרָה וְתַלְמִידֵי רַבִּים</note> *“They call a place where there are those who 'make the Law lie down' (that is, those who teach it) and many students, a* <term>YESHIVA</term> *or Assembly; as when they say: 'It is the custom in the two Assemblies,' etc. And in the same way, they are accustomed to call the* **HEAVENLY CONSISTORY** *or Sanhedrin a* <term>YESHIVA</term>, *as when they say:* **IN THE HEAVENLY CONSISTORY AND THE EARTHLY CONSISTORY.**”

A formal gathering of Learned Men, who handle sacred matters and sit together while doing so, is called a <term>YESHIVA</term>. This is because the presiding teachers sit while they teach, and their disciples also sit while receiving their instructions. This is the primary meaning of the word; it was subsequently applied almost exclusively to the Doctors themselves and their formal sessions within a Sanhedrin, or a scholarly or ecclesiastical Consistory. 

We believe these proofs are now abundantly sufficient to support our position. Let no one be deterred by the accounts cited from Benjamin of Tudela; for even if we should not grant our Traveler blind faith in all matters...

...should be applied, yet I see no reason why, in these matters where he relates nothing absurd, credit should be denied to him. Even if he had most desired to deceive us in these very things, it is not to be presumed that a man, sufficiently equipped with talent and seeking the favor of his own people, would want to pass down false information about *the very form of Government of the more celebrated Synagogues of his Nation*, as this would have rendered him hated by his fellow countrymen.

## CHAPTER X.

*Proof that other Synagogues—either because they were less celebrated and subordinate to larger ones, or because they lacked a sufficient number of Learned Men—were governed by a single* **MASTER OF SACRED THINGS**, *called a* **RAV** <note>Hebrew: רב</note>; *his character and duties are described in considerable detail. To these is added a description of the* **PARNASSIM** <note>Hebrew: פרנסים</note>, *the Pastors of the modern Synagogue. Many other matters regarding titles of honor for Masters are interspersed, such as* **CHACHAM, RABBI, RAV, CHAVER** <note>Hebrew: חכם, רבי, רב, חבר</note>, <note>These titles translate roughly to: Wise Man, My Teacher, Master, and Associate.</note> **WISE MAN, SCHOLAR, ACQUAINTANCE**, *etc.* <note>The original text includes the Greek terms: σοφὸς, σοφισטὴς, γνώριμος.</note>

That same traveler from Tudela <note>Benjamin of Tudela, the 12th-century Jewish traveler.</note> relates another form of Synagogue government, widely accepted among the Jews today, in which the Sacred Rites of the Synagogue are directed in public by *one* man skilled in Divine matters. His words regarding the Synagogues of the Baghdad district are as follows:
<margin>Travels, page 73. +</margin>
> *The Head of the Exile* <note>The "Exilarch," or political leader of the Jewish community in Babylon.</note> *gives them permission in all these communities to appoint over each and every congregation a* **MASTER** *and a* **MINISTER**, *who come to him to receive ordination* <note>literally: "the laying on of hands"</note> *and authority.*
Where L’Empereur <note>Constantijn L’Empereur, a 17th-century scholar who translated Benjamin’s work into Latin.</note> translates *Professor* or *Preacher*, the text expresses this as **RAV** <note>Hebrew: רב</note>, meaning **TEACHER** or **MASTER**, and **CHAZZAN** <note>Hebrew: חזן</note>, meaning **MINISTER**. <margin>page 115.</margin> He subsequently calls them **RABBIS AND MINISTERS** <note>Hebrew: רבנים וחזנים</note>. Indeed, our Benjamin writes that sometimes the entire government and administration of the Synagogue was committed to *one* man of proven integrity and learning. ...nurtured by rewards. From that time, there were either invented (though I am not unaware that the Jews seek more ancient origins) or more frequently used certain *titles of dignity* with which students of *Jewish Law* were decorated by their Teachers after completing their course of study. However, the common title of this kind, and one already very well-received in the age of Christ the Lord, was that of רבּי, *Ribbi*, or *Rabbi Doctor* <note>The author uses "Doctor" here in the traditional sense of "Teacher" or "one who is learned."</note>, sought with great ambition by students of Jewish Law so that they might distinguish themselves from the common crowd of men. Indeed, Christ the Lord rebuked the Pharisees because they desired to be honored by men as <margin>Chapter 23, 7. 8.</margin> *Rabbi*, *Rabbi*, and He warns his own disciples to guard themselves against that vice of arrogance; *But you*, He says, *are not to be called Rabbi*. <note>original Greek: Ὑμεῖς δὲ μὴ κληθῆτε, Ῥαββί</note>. Furthermore, this dignity of Mastery was usually conferred through <term>SEMICHA</term> <note>Hebrew: סמיכה, the "leaning" or "imposition" of hands</note>, or the *Imposition of hands* (ordinarily; for it was also conferred without this rite through the simple pronunciation of words) by another who had himself received this title from another *Doctor* through the <term>CHEIROTHESIA</term> <note>Greek: χειροθεσία, the laying on of hands</note>, or *imposition of hands*. I will not add more on this now, because these things have long since been diligently described by most learned men.

<margin>Selden, *On the Sanhedrin*, book 1, chapter 14, section 1.</margin>
Nevertheless, it must not be overlooked that these Doctors were of diverse qualities and offices. <margin>Alting, *History of Academic Promotions*, page 325.</margin> *Some*, says Selden, (Presbyters, or *Doctors*) *they created into the* Dignity *of teaching, and of* BINDING, *or forbidding, and* LOOSING, *or Permitting—that is, of defining cases of conscience and sacred doubts, as if into the dignity of a Doctorate of Universal Theology. Others they created with the faculty of explaining certain particular Chapters of Theology, which were called* דברי יחידים <note>Hebrew: *Divrei Yechidim*, literally "the words of individuals," referring here to specific or private opinions in law</note>, *as if circumscribed within the singular limits of a Doctorate of Theology. Others, which was most frequent, they gifted with the Power, License, or rather the capacity for hearing cases of any kind, thus creating Doctors of Law and Theology simultaneously. Others, finally, were permitted only some cases, such as those involving money, but not Capital cases.*

<margin>Alting, *History of Academic Promotions*, pages 318, 321 in the Lexicon at the word סמיכה. *Laws of the Sanhedrin*, chapter 4, throughout.</margin>
Alting warns of the same thing in words that are not obscure, though briefer; Buxtorf also warns of this, following Maimonides, whose text he cited and interpreted. This title of *Doctor* was therefore conferred upon them according to the judgment of the Promoter and the aptitude or desires of the Candidates, as Maimonides expressly states. To some was given the faculty of hearing monetary cases; to others, more serious *punitive* cases <note>Hebrew: דיני קנסות, *Dinei Knasot*, involving fines or penalties</note>; to others, again, the license for teaching what is permitted and what is forbidden. *The Sanhedrin can promote that man (one very highly trained in the Law of God) and grant him the power of* **JUDGING**, *but not of* **TEACHING** *what is permitted and forbidden; or they give him the authority to pronounce on the permitted and prohibited, but not to judge monetary cases; or they grant both the right to teach and to hear monetary disputes, but not to judge cases involving fines, and so forth. However, just as those who were declared fit for *judging* exercised this ability whenever a suitable opportunity arose, so those promoted to *teaching* not only responded when asked about various cases of conscience regarding forbidden and permitted things, but also, *having obtained permission* from their Promoters, opened *Schools* and interpreted the Divine Law within them. I say "with permission obtained from their Promoters" because otherwise it was by no means permitted to them as long as the Promoter was still living. Since this faculty was indeed recognized in those who, in later times, were called חכמים <note>Hebrew: *Chachamim*, meaning "Sages" or "Wise Men."</note>, **Doctors**, they were for this reason rightly honored with the title of "the wise" <note>original Greek: σοφῶν</note>. Jerome speaks aptly to our point:

<margin>To Algasia on the Eleven Questions, Part 3, folio 59, column 4.</margin>
> *Therefore (he says, speaking of Jewish traditions), Jewish observations among the unskilled and the common folk seem to have an image of reason and human wisdom; hence their* **DOCTORS** *are called* "the wise," <note>original Greek: σοφοὶ</note> *that is,* **WISE MEN**. *And whenever they explain their traditions to their disciples on certain days, they are accustomed to say,* "the wise repeat the traditions," <note>original Greek: οἱ σοφοὶ δευτερώσιν. The term *deuterōsin* refers to the Mishnah or "repetition" of the law.</note> *that is,* **THE WISE** *teach traditions; or, the Wise hand them down in this way.*

Thus, every **Doctor** of the Jewish Nation—whether he had merely attained the faculty of teaching, or was actually exercising that faculty from the Chair—was called a חכם <note>Hebrew: *Chacham*, a Sage.</note>. Let us recall just one or two sayings of Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal scholar.</note>. He writes thus at the beginning of the treatise titled *Talmud Torah* <note>Study of the Law.</note>:

<margin>Talmud Torah, chapter 1, §. 1.</margin>
> ולא בן ובן בנו בלבד אלא מצוה על כל חכם וחכם מישראל ללמוד את כל התלמידים אף על פי שאינן בניו וכו', *It is not only the duty of every man to teach his sons and grandsons the meanings of the Divine Law, but it is a commandment upon every* **Sage** *in Israel to instruct any disciples, even though they are in no way his own sons, etc.*

Again in the same treatise:

<margin>Chapter 5, §. 3.</margin>
> וכן חכם שהגיע להוראה ואינו מורה הרי זה מונע תורה ונותן מכשולות לפני העוורים, *And so a* **Sage** *who has attained the fitness to teach, and yet refrains from teaching, surely he withholds the Law and places stumbling blocks before the blind.*

From this usage of the word, you may now interpret the passage of Paul to the Corinthians:

<margin>1 Corinthians 6:5.</margin>
> Οὕτως οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν ὑμῖν σοφὸς, οὐδὲ εἷς, ὃς δυνήσεται διακרῖναι ἀνὰ μέσον τοῦ ἀדελφοῦ αὐτοῦ; *Is there not even one* **Wise Man** *among you who can bear judgment between his brothers?* By "wise man" in this place, Paul does not mean just any prudent man of proven judgment, as I see it, but rather a **Doctor** or an Interpreter of the Divine Word nearly equal to a **Doctor**, such as those who were usually consulted by the Jews in the Provinces for cases of conscience and questions of law, as will be noted in what follows. By another name, these **Sages**, or those studious of **Divine Wisdom**, were called חברים <note>Hebrew: *Chaverim*.</note>, **Colleagues**, or **Associates**. # CHAPTER 10. ON THE GOVERNMENT OF THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE.

<margin>Notes on the Treatise *Talmid Chacham* <note>Disciple of a Sage</note>, Maimonides on the Firstlings of Animals, chapter 2, section 10, page 84.</margin>
Indeed, any person distinguished by the name of *Doctor* <note>In this context, "Doctor" refers to a learned teacher or scholar, from the Latin *docere* (to teach), rather than a medical doctor.</note>, and anyone who is learned and refined in doctrine, is called a **חבר** <note>Hebrew: *Chaber*, meaning "Associate," "Companion," or "Fellow."</note> by the Hebrew writers. Thus it is: any **תלמיד חכם** <note>Hebrew: *Talmid Chacham*, literally "Disciple of a Sage," a term for a Torah scholar.</note>, a man of letters—especially one who had recently been elevated to the rank of *Doctor* and who therefore did not yet possess full power or authority in issuing legal opinions because his Master or Mentor was still living—was called an **Associate** <note>Hebrew: *Chaber*</note>.

<margin>On the word *Chaber*. See L’Empereur on Benjamin, page 188. Cocceius in Notes on the Gemara Sanhedrin, chapter 11, page 113. Pococke, *Porta Mosis*, Appendix, pages 396 & 420. *Trihæresium*, chapter 5, page 265. Rabbenu Asher, decisions on Sanhedrin, section 2.</margin>
Elias Levita <note>A famous 16th-century Hebrew grammarian.</note> writes: **אדם שהוא נסמך לרבנות אבל אינו ראוי עדין להיות מורה הוראה להקרא מורנו הרב קורין אותו חבר והרב פירוש נתחבר אל מי שהוא מורנו הרב** <note>Hebrew original translated in the following Latin/English text.</note> *A man upon whom hands have been laid for the rank of the Rabbinate, but who is not yet fit to be a Teacher of the Law <note>original: "Doctor of dogma"</note> so as to be called "Our Great Teacher," they call him an "Associate" of that Great One (his Mentor). The meaning is: he is associated with him who is known as our Great Teacher.* I will pass over other points brought forward by learned men to illustrate this word; however, I will grant this to *Scaliger* <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a renowned Renaissance scholar.</note> by transcribing his own words.

> After the laying on of hands,—the Jewish Doctor, he says, *was not immediately called* MASTER, *although he had been advanced to the rank of the Mastership, but was only called* **חבר** <note>Associate</note>; *which in the same sense among the Greeks is* **γνώριμος** <note>Greek: *gnōrimos*, an "acquaintance" or "intimate associate"</note>: *as, "Speusippus the associate of Plato" signifies a disciple—not a mere beginner, certainly, but one who is able to teach.* Cicero translates it as **FAMILIARIS** <note>Latin: an "intimate friend" or "member of the household."</note>. *Therefore, **Associate** is never used except with its relative term, such as "Rabbi Ishmael the associate," or **חבר**, of Rabbi Eleazar.*

<margin>In the place cited above.</margin>
In that last point which *Scaliger* asserts—that **Associate** is never used except in relation to someone else—he is clearly in error; this has already been observed by *L'Empereur*, though he did not mention *Scaliger* by name. But where *Scaliger* compares the word **חבר** with the Greek **γνώριμος** <note>Associate/Intimate</note>, he is quite correct. Among the Greeks, *gnōrimos* denotes a disciple who is intimate with the Master. I have observed the use of this vocabulary several times in the works of *Philo* the Jew. I will select one or two passages.

<margin>On the Sacrifices of Abel and Cain, page 111.</margin>
**Τὸν γὰρ Θεοῦ φοιτητὴν, ἢ γνώριμον, ἢ μαθητὴν, ἢ ὅ τι ποτε χρὴ θεμένους ὄνομα καλεῖν αὐτὸν, ἀμήχανόν ἐστιν θνητῶν ὑφηγήσεων ἀναχέσθαι;** *For the student of God, or his* **ASSOCIATE** <note>original Greek: γνώριμον</note>, *or disciple, or whatever other name you please to call him, it is impossible to endure the petty instructions of mortals.*

<margin>That the Worse is Wont to Plot Against the Better, page 27. On Drunkenness, page 200.</margin>
Again: **Ὁπότε γὰρ πατὴρ υἱὸν τύπτει σωφρονίζων, ἢ διδάσκαλος γνώριμον, ἕτερος ὁ τύπτων καὶ ὁ τυπτώμενός ἐστιν;** *For when a father strikes his son to discipline him, or a Master his* **ASSOCIATE**, *is the one who strikes someone other than the one who is struck?* Elsewhere he again joins together "students and associates." Thus, the **Associate** <note>Hebrew: *Chaber*</note> is greater than the common...

It seems truer that the word **Associate** <note>Hebrew: *Chaber*</note> carries a double meaning among Hebrew authors. Sometimes it is used for a **Teacher's Colleague**, as we have already described (specifically when it is used with respect, whether expressed or implied, to the titles *Rav* or *Rabbi*). At other times, it refers to a member of a specific society of men who bound themselves by certain laws to mutual purity and the holiness of life. "These Associates were," says Guisius, "as it seems to me, a class of men who were significantly more scrupulous than the common people regarding the details of ritual uncleanness; they had entered into a society and obligated themselves to certain laws so that they might conduct themselves more safely among their own and avoid the uncleanness arising from commerce with the common folk." This was elegantly stated and explained by Guisius, and we embrace it with both arms. We also embrace the idea that these "Associates" are nearly the same men who, in the Gospel...

### CHAPTER 10. ON THE GOVERNMENT OF THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE.

In the Gospel, they are called *Pharisees*. We readily grant that the word **Associate** <note>original Hebrew: *Chaber* (חבר)</note> is to be explained this way in the passages of the *Demai* <note>a Talmudic tractate regarding produce where there is doubt if it was tithed</note> and *Bechorot* <note>a tractate concerning firstborn animals</note> illustrated by Guisius. Certainly, Bartenora <note>a famous 15th-century commentator on the Mishnah</note> saw more acutely into the passage of *Demai* than Maimonides did; and after him, the celebrated Coccejus had already excellently interpreted the words of the Code *Demai*: 
<margin>
In the Excerpts of the Gemara of the Sanhedrin, page 113.
</margin> 
*He who takes upon himself to be an* **ASSOCIATE** <note>original Hebrew: *Ha-mekabbel alav lihyot chaber* (המקבל עליו להיות חבר)</note> etc., according to the mind of Guisius as: *He who receives into himself that he will be an* **ASSOCIATE**, that is, *that he will be* **from the brotherhood and society of those committed to ritual purity** <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῆς ἀδελφότητος καὶ ἑταιρίας τῶν πεπιτευμένων περὶ καθαρότητος</note>. According to this interpretation of the word, it was possible for someone to be a *Learned Man* and yet not an **Associate** <note>Hebrew: *Chaber*</note>; although such cultivators of doctrine were held in low esteem among the Jewish nation. However, it is a different matter when the name **Associate** is attributed to *any Doctor* with respect to the **Master** or **Excellent Teacher** <note>original Hebrew: *ha-Rab* (הנ רב)</note>; it has been stated and proven from certain passages that in this latter sense, the term is used very frequently in Hebrew history. Concerning another title of related significance, **Disciple of a Wise Man** <note>original Hebrew: *Talmid Chacham* (תלמיד חכם)</note>, I have nothing separate to advise at this time.

<margin>
"Those who are considered to interpret the laws with precision." *The Jewish War*, Book 2, Chapter 7.
</margin>
Furthermore, it is clear from Gospel history how great a supply of these *Doctors*, *Scribes*, and *Students* of Divine Wisdom existed in the land of Canaan around the age of Christ the Lord, while the study of traditions was flourishing. In these accounts, we see Christ the Lord surrounded and besieged by them in every place. How great then was the multitude of *Pharisees*, of whom Josephus says that they *interpreted the Divine Laws more accurately?* Jewish history records that around that time there was such an abuse of **Promotions** <note>the formal granting of the title of "Rabbi" or "Doctor"</note> that it had to be corrected by suitable laws. From this, it happened that these Doctors were not only scattered throughout Canaan, but were also diffused through all other regions of the world inhabited by Jews.

<margin>

In various smaller locations of the **Exile** <note>original: *Exilii*; the Jewish Diaspora outside the Land of Israel</note>, where Jews lived in small numbers and were poor, **Synagogues** were content with a single such **Doctor** <note>a scholar or teacher of the law</note>, skilled in sacred matters, to whom they committed both the resolution of cases of conscience and the administration of Synagogue rituals. Similarly, in the land of Canaan itself, although there were several **Synagogues** in the more prominent cities and the high Senate of that city presided over the most grand Synagogue of that place, in those smaller and less famous **Prayer-houses** <note>original: *Proseuchis*, from the Greek for a place of prayer</note>, the care of practicing religion seems to have been entirely entrusted to a certain individual Master or **Doctor**, or even, quite simply, to a certain **Synagogue Minister**, who could also be a **Doctor**, as we understood from Benjamin <note>Benjamin of Tudela, a 12th-century Jewish traveler</note> and as the matter itself sufficiently demonstrates. It was enough for such a **Doctor** to be promoted to the **dignity of the Mastership** <note>original Hebrew: *Ravnut* (רבנות)</note>, which consisted of solving cases of conscience, distinguishing between the permitted and the forbidden, and teaching and interpreting the dogmas of religion; while others, meanwhile, were promoted to the **judicial art** <note>original Hebrew: *Dayyanut* (דיינות)</note> to decide **lawsuits of lesser importance**, and were employed as **arbitrators** to decide those cases outside the form of a formal judicial process.

### CHAPTER 10. ON THE GOVERNANCE OF THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE.

It is observed that the word **Rav** <note>Hebrew: רב</note> or **Rabba** <note>Aramaic: רבא</note> among the Chaldeans <note>speakers of Aramaic</note> signifies a **Prince, Leader, Prefect, Lord, or Master**, which is confirmed by suitable arguments. Thus it is; **Rav** denotes *the greater one* <note>original Greek: τὸν μείζονα</note>, a superior, and hence is conveniently applied to any *Prefect*. Christ the Lord, when he warned his disciples that none of them should arrogantly claim the title of *Teacher* <note>original Greek: καθηγητοῦ</note>, immediately added to his words: 
<margin>Matthew 23:11.</margin>
*He who is* GREATEST *among you shall be your servant*, <note>original Greek: Ὁ δὲ μείζων ὑμῶν, ἔσται ὑμῶν διάκονος</note> that is, he who thinks he ought to be called by the EXCELLENT title of **Rav** by the highest right, let him be the Minister of you all. Thus, the **Rav** (the greater) and the **Minister** (the servant) are placed in opposition to one another. However, when the word **Rav** is used for *Masters*, the presiding officers of the Synagogue religion, it certainly carries a greater force and emphasis than when it is simply attributed to any *promoted Doctors*. It is much like in Germany, where the title of *Doctor* is common to both *Professors* of sciences and all those who have been *promoted* <note>granted a degree</note>, yet the title usually shines with a greater *force of expression* <note>original Greek: δυνάμει τῆς φωνῆς</note> when applied to the former. Indeed, perhaps this very word **Rav**, when granted to the *Prefects of the Synagogue*, could not ineptly be considered in relation to the word **Keneshta**, meaning *Synagogue*. 
<margin>Mark 5:35, 38.</margin>
<margin>Luke 8:49.</margin>
For the Syriac language usually translates the Greek *archisynagogos* <note>ruler of the synagogue</note> as **Rav Keneshta**, meaning the *Prince or Prefect of the Synagogue*. It is used in the same sense and with the same force of meaning, if I am not mistaken, as **Rav Bayta** <note>Aramaic: רב ביתא</note> is said among the Syrians to be the *steward* <note>original Greek: ὁ οἰκονόμος</note> or *Prefect of the house*; and as the word MASTER was used by Roman writers, both ancient and more recent, as has long been observed by learned men. Thus we find among them *Masters of the People*, *Masters of the Districts, of Societies, of Villages, of Colleges, of the Knights, of Offices, of Letters, of the Palace, etc.*

If the word **Rav**, used for the *Prefect of the Synagogue* as we have described, admits this latter interpretation, then it would entirely agree in meaning with the title **Rosh HaKnesset** <note>Hebrew: ראש הכנסת</note> or **Reish Keneshta** <note>Aramaic: ריש כנישתא</note>, the *Prince of the Synagogue*. We shall deal with the former title further below; the latter, which differs from the former only in the inflection of the words, we shall take from *Echa Rabbatha* <note>a Midrashic commentary on the Book of Lamentations</note>, from which certain excerpts are taken in the *Brief Observations on the text of Maimonides*. The words of Maimonides <note>a preeminent 12th-century Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> are these: 
<margin>Laws of Fasting, chapter 3, section 3.</margin>
**In any fast where they eat while it is still day, if he ate and ceased and finished intending not to eat, he may not return and eat even though there is still time in the day.** <note>original Hebrew: וכל תענית שאוכלין בה מבעוד יום אם אכל ופסק וגמר שלא לאכל אינו חוזר ואוכל אף על פי שיש שהות ביום</note> *In every fast where the license to eat remains while it is still day (understand "day" as the evening from which the fasts [begin])*...

# CHAPTER 10. ON THE GOVERNMENT OF THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE.

In the Hebrew writings, he is called <term>Ab Beth Din</term> <note>Hebrew: *Av Beit Din*, literally "Father of the House of Judgment," the second-ranking member of the Sanhedrin</note>, the Father of the Council or of the Senatorial Order, and <term>Mischneh</term> <note>Hebrew: *Mishneh*, meaning "second" or "deputy"</note>, the deputy to the Prince, who stood at his right side. This is not a bad description as far as this passage is concerned. For since the Apostles established a Senate, over which a Patriarch presided like a Prince, and this "Apostle Joseph" excelled in authority among the assessors of the Senate of the house of Hillel <note>The Hillel family provided the Nasi, or Prince, of the Sanhedrin for several generations</note>, it is possible that the Joseph mentioned by Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Salamis who wrote about Jewish-Christian history</note> was honored as the Father of the Hillelian Sanhedrin. However, lest anyone be led into error by these words of Hottinger <note>Johann Heinrich Hottinger, a 17th-century Swiss scholar of Oriental languages</note>, it must be advised that the word **Apostle** has a much broader meaning than that of the <term>Ab Beth Din</term>, the "Father" of the Sanhedrin. For according to Epiphanius’s interpretation, all the assessors of the Patriarchal Sanhedrin were called **Apostles**.

<margin>Heresies, Book 1, Vol. 2, Heresy 30.</margin>
*For this Joseph was in the number of those men who are outstanding in dignity, namely those who are closest to the Patriarchs, called **Apostles**. These sit with the Patriarch, and spend time with him continually, often both night and day, for the sake of giving counsel and supplying those things which ought to be done according to the Law.* <note>The author provides this quote first in the original Greek of Epiphanius, followed by a Latin translation; both are rendered here in English.</note>

<margin>See Petit’s *Various Readings*, chapter 24.</margin>
Hottinger seems to have interpreted Epiphanius’s words as if there were only *one* Apostle for each Patriarch, but to me, following the view of others, it seems far more suitable to explain it this way: that there were several Senators for each Patriarch, called **Apostles**, who were from time to time sent by him with full authority as legates to visit or reform the synagogues under his jurisdiction. And certainly, while the Republic <note>The "Jewish Republic" refers to the period of Jewish self-governance and theocratic rule in Judea</note> was still standing, **Legates** were often sent by the Sanhedrin on more serious business to various regions of the land of Canaan, or to the **Synagogues outside of Canaan**. These men, according to their own judgment and the greatness of the power granted to them, made decisions concerning the republic; indeed, Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> left memorable examples of this in the *History of His Life*.

<margin>In his *Life*, pages 1013 and 1015.</margin>
What is recorded there happened, it is true, during the final times of the Republic, when the Sanhedrin could already be considered to have vanished; nevertheless, if you attend to the text—in which all things are said to have been managed chiefly by **Simon, son of Gamaliel** (who is known from other sources to have been the President of the Sanhedrin at that time)—and to the state of the Jewish Republic, which was then attempting to claim its freedom by shaking off the Roman yoke, you will not deny the [appear-]

BOOK II. ON THE TRUE FORM.

<margin>Observations on Luke 6:13.</margin> ...at least the appearance of the Sanhedrin survived in that age. Heinsius <note>Daniel Heinsius (1580–1655), a famous Dutch scholar</note> has already observed, based on Eusebius, that the Apostle *Paul*, before embracing the Christian faith, was an *Apostle* <note>original Latin: *apostolus*, used here in the sense of a commissioned envoy</note> of that kind; and I need not repeat what other learned men have argued, that the Apostles of Jesus Christ himself—the supreme Prince and Patriarch of the Church—are not undeservedly compared with these Jewish Apostles. This title <term>Ab Beit Din</term> <note>Hebrew: *Av Beit Din*, "Father of the House of Judgment"</note>, or *Father of the Sanhedrin*, was adopted by the <term>Gymnasiarchs</term> <note>Heads of the academies or schools</note> and the teachers of famous schools, who, together with other doctors or learned youths, formed the appearance of a <term>Yeshivah</term> <note>Hebrew: *Yashivah*, an academic assembly or session</note>. Since the President of the Academic Assembly usually presided over the synagogue at the same time, the title *Father of the Sanhedrin* subsequently became attached to the directors of the synagogues. They seem to have preferred this title over <term>Rosh Yeshivah</term> <note>Hebrew: "Head of the Academy"</note>, *Head of the Senate*, or <term>Nasi</term> <note>Hebrew: "Prince"</note>, because those terms sounded more grand and excellent, and properly belonged only to the directors of the most famous Sanhedrins or schools. <margin>On the year 833, 4th millennium, page 97.</margin> In the writings of Ganz <note>David Gans, a 16th-century Jewish mathematician and historian</note>, I read that *Rabbi Joshua, son of Hananiah, was Father of the Senate and the Precentor on the platform* <note>The "Precentor" or *Chazzan* led the liturgical singing from the raised platform or *Bimah*</note>. Clearly, the name *Father of the Senate*, as far as I can gather from that passage, is not used there in an absolute sense for the supreme President of the Academy, but for the President's Assessor <note>An assistant or deputy judge</note>, a meaning of the word we were just discussing. For that *Rabbi Joshua* is called there the *Colleague of Rabbi Eliezer the Great*, who, unless I am mistaken, acted as the supreme President of the Academic Assembly and the Synagogue congregation.

It remains to be noted that, besides this <term>Parnas</term> <note>Hebrew: *Parnas*, a leader or provider</note>, or *Prefect of Sacred Matters*, the Jews in larger places where they live in greater numbers have a certain *Political Senate* of <term>Parnassim</term>, *PASTORS*, or *CONSULS*. Maimonides <note>The influential 12th-century Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> calls these <term>Memunnim al ha-Tzibur</term> <note>Hebrew: "Those appointed over the community"</note>, <margin>Laws of Prayer, chapter 11, section 4. Laws of Fasting, chapter 1, section 17; chapter 3.</margin> *OVERSEERS OF THE CHURCH*, and elsewhere, if I am not mistaken, <term>Zekenim</term>, or *ELDERS*. I described them sufficiently at the beginning of this book. With them lies the supreme power regarding *matters outside the synagogue* <note>original Greek: *ta exo tes synagoges*, referring to civil or secular affairs</note>. They govern the Jewish community in the manner of *Consuls*. They ensure that the place of religion and its instruments are kept in good repair. They impose monetary taxes on their subjects according to each person's means, to be spent for sacred or civil use. They bring the disobedient back into order through Excommunication and other penalties, no doubt having first obtained the consent of the *Master of the Synagogue*. Of the poor...

<margin>Synagogue, Chapter 44.</margin>
It seems to me that in certain more famous locations of their **Exile**, such a **Senate** of respected men from the common people was established by the Jews, partly because they could not find a sufficient supply of learned scholars everywhere, and partly because the synagogue assemblies were not wealthy enough to support many learned men. Indeed, these **Synagogue Senates** should, in my view, be considered as a shadow and a <note>original Greek: *schēma*, meaning "form" or "outline"</note> form of those **Judicial and Civil Senates**—those **Presbyteries**, I say—by which we have already said the Jews were formerly governed, both in their own Homeland and in the more famous places outside their Homeland. I have various arguments for this. 

First, the names <term>Parnassim</term> and <term>Elders</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Parnasim* and *Zekenim*</note>, by which these modern "consuls" are honored, belong to learned and wise men according to the most ancient usage of those terms. 

Second, the teacher of a Synagogue or Academy is still called, with respect to this Senate, the <term>Father of the Consistory</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Av Beit Din*, "Father of the House of Judgment"</note>. For even if he does not preside over a **Senate** of men of his own kind and rank in the Synagogue, it nevertheless happens at times that he is called into this Senate by these "pastors" or rectors of the Synagogue, both to deliver a legal opinion in more difficult cases and to deliberate with them on public affairs. And since there is no other <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>A Jewish judicial council</note> for him to preside over, this Senate of "consuls" is regarded at least as a shadow and a type of the <note>original Greek/Hebrew: *tō Beit Din*, "the House of Judgment"</note> council. 

Third, these **Parnassim** even take up certain rights that were formerly proper to the **Houses of Judgment**. For unless I am mistaken, they also exercise the power of both fining and excommunicating, and even of corporal punishment where that custom prevails, against those who shamelessly transgress the statutes of the city and of their religion. ### CHAPTER XI.

->*What things occur in the History of the New Covenant, the Statutes of Roman Law, in Epiphanius, and elsewhere regarding the Governance of Synagogues, are brought forward to illustrate the preceding hypotheses, and are reconciled with them. Primarily discussed is the genuine meaning of the terms* **HEAD OF THE SYNAGOGUE** <note>Hebrew: *Rosh HaKnesset*</note> *among the Hebrews, and **ARCHISYNAGOGI** among the Greeks and Latins.*<-

Before I now proceed to define to which of these types of Synagogue Governance the Form of Governance of the Christian Church should be referred, I have decided to examine both the History of the New Testament and other monuments of Antiquity, in which some memory of this kind has perhaps been left for posterity, and to consider whether those things can be reduced to our hypotheses concerning the **Various Governance of the Synagogue**, and receive light from them.

<margin>Luke 4:16</margin>

it is clear, because Christ the Lord is said to have entered this *Synagogue* on the *Sabbath day*, **as was his custom** <note>Greek: *kata to eiōthos autō*</note>. Indeed, on Sabbath days, the *Synagogue*—so named because it is a place of assembly—is most commonly visited. The sacred solemnities of the *reading* <note>The public reading of scripture</note> performed while standing, and the subsequent *explanation*, fit well with the nature of the *Synagogue*. However, the fact that Christ sat down to teach suggests a **School** <note>Latin: *Schola*; a place for instruction and study</note>. Perhaps, therefore, we will not err if we conclude that this *Nazarene Synagogue* served the inhabitants as both a *School* and a *House of Prayer* <note>Latin: *Proseucha*; a term often used for a place of assembly or prayer, particularly where a formal synagogue building might not exist</note>. For we have elsewhere assumed that this was often done in smaller places.

Now, in this entire history, no official of the *Synagogue* is mentioned except for one *attendant* <note>Greek: *hyperetēs*</note>, the **Minister** of the Synagogue, by whom the 
<margin>verse 20.</margin> book was **given** to Christ, and to whom it was **returned**. In the following 
<margin>verse 28.</margin> context of the narrative, the **eyes of all** are said to have been **fixed** on him, and **all were filled with wrath**; yet, besides this *Minister of the Synagogue*, no *Ruler of the Synagogue* <note>Latin: *Praefectus Synagogae*</note>, nor any other member of the Synagogue distinguished by a specific title, is found here. However, those who are not strangers to the customs of the Synagogue will not wonder at this. For the Presidents of the Synagogue had almost no duty in the ordinary solemnities of religion (unless the President of the Synagogue himself was teaching) other than to protect their own dignity in the Synagogue by their presiding presence, and, if anything out of the ordinary happened, to moderate and settle it by their authority. When nothing out of the ordinary was done in the Synagogue, they had almost nothing to do. Indeed, many acts of religion could be performed even in their absence, and today in Synagogues, sermons are not infrequently held while they are away. Therefore, what prevents us from considering the absence of the Rulers of the Synagogue in this case as well? 

But there is no difficulty here, since elsewhere express mention is made of **several Rulers** <note>Greek: *Archisynagogoi*</note> as well as **one**. Luke indeed shows several in his **History of Paul**: <margin>Acts 13, 14.</margin> *But they (Paul and his companions), having passed through from Perga, came to Antioch of Pisidia, and having entered the Synagogue on the Sabbath day, they sat down. After the* **reading of the Law and the Prophets**, *the* **rulers of the synagogue** <note>Greek: *hoi Archisynagogoi*</note> *sent to them, saying: Men and brothers, etc.* It is clear that Luke is speaking of the Synagogue so named. He mentions that in it *the Law and the Prophets were read*. Whether there was **one** reader of the Law and Prophets in the Synagogue, or **several**; whether the *Minister of the Synagogue read the Law and Prophets*; or whether [he called upon] others...
