# CHAPTER II. ON THE GOVERNMENT OF THE OLD SYNAGOGUE, 583

...records that it is watered by a <note>original: *Pēgē potimōtatē*</note> **"most drinkable spring, which the locals call CAPERNAUM."** This location is noted in the works of *Adrichomius* <note>Christiaan van Adrichom (1533–1585), a Dutch priest and geographer known for his maps of the Holy Land</note> and *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English scholar and clergyman who specialized in interpreting the New Testament through Rabbinic literature</note>. *Lightfoot* further mentions that a place called *Kepharnōmē* is cited in the *Life of Josephus*, though he expresses doubt as to whether it should be identified with our *Capernaum*.
<margin>Book 2 of the *Jewish War*, chapter 25.</margin>
Certainly, it is well established that *Josephus* elsewhere—when describing all the more illustrious cities of Galilee over which he had been placed in command—mentions no *Capernaum*. But what of this? Is it truly believable that *Josephus*, who describes every famous location in his district, would make no mention of this place at all if it could be compared to other sites in fame and size? He states it was a spring, rising in a pleasant stretch of land, which we may believe first attracted a few dwellings; subsequently, through frequent habitation, a **Village** <note>Latin: *pagus*</note> was formed there, flourishing greatly in the time of Christ, but later diminished again according to Christ’s prophecy. We have no doubt that this decline had already occurred by the age of *Josephus*. Indeed, *Lightfoot* was persuaded—and I am quite thoroughly convinced as well—that *Josephus* was speaking of no other *Capernaum* than this very one, because our *Capernaum* was situated in the same location where *Josephus* records this spring to have bubbled up. Furthermore, the historians of the New Testament speak of *Capernaum* in such a way that it is difficult to accept there was more than one **Synagogue** there. For besides the fact that, although *Capernaum* is mentioned quite frequently, multiple *Synagogues* are never counted there, we believe the words of *Luke* lead us to this conclusion. He relates that the **Centurion**—a man who was not a Jew, but who wished to save his dying servant—sent the ELDERS OF THE JEWS (<note>original: *tous presbyterous tōn Ioudaiōn*</note>, that is, as we shall soon explain more clearly, the **rulers** or **rulers of the synagogue** <note>original: *tous archontas, tous archisynagōgous*</note>, one of whom was *Jairus*) to Christ to intercede for him. 
<margin>Chapter 7, verse 5.</margin>
These men said: **"For he loves our nation, and he himself built the SYNAGOGUE for us."** <note>original: *Agapa gar to ethnos hēmōn, kai tēn synagōgēn autos ōkodomēsen hēmin*</note> Consider this: is it likely or even probable that the inhabitants of *Capernaum* would owe the benefit of a built synagogue to a Gentile man if *Capernaum* had been such a grand and famous city? Does it not rather suggest that it was a more celebrated **hamlet and village**? The dying servant belonged to a single Centurion;

### CHAPTER II. ON THE GOVERNMENT OF THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE.

...reports that it is watered by a **most drinkable spring** <note>Greek: *Pēgē potimōtatē*</note>; the locals call it **Capernaum**. <note>Original Latin: *Fonte dulcissimo, quem accole CAPERNAUMUM vocant.*</note> This location is noted by *Adrichomius* and *Lightfoot*. Furthermore, *Lightfoot* mentions that a place called *Kepharnome* is recorded in the *Life of Josephus*, though he doubts whether it should be identified with our Capernaum.

<margin>Book 2 of *The Jewish War*, chapter 25.</margin>
Certainly, this much is established: *Josephus*, in describing all the more illustrious cities of Galilee over which he was placed in command, mentions no city by the name of Capernaum. Why is that? Can we believe that *Josephus*, who describes every famous place in his administrative district, would make no mention of this place at all if it could be compared to other locations in fame and size? He says it was a spring, rising in a pleasant stretch of land, which we can believe first attracted some dwellings; then, through frequent habitation, a **village** <note>Latin: *Pagus*; a rural district or village</note> was formed there, which flourished greatly in the time of Christ, but was afterwards diminished again according to the prophecy of Christ. We have no doubt that this decline had already occurred by *Josephus's* time. For *Lightfoot* was convinced—and I am indeed most firmly convinced—that *Josephus* was speaking of no other Capernaum than this very one, because our Capernaum was situated in the same location where *Josephus* reports this spring bubbled forth.

Moreover, the historians of the New Testament speak of Capernaum in such a way that it is difficult to accept that there was more than one **synagogue** there. For besides the fact that, although mention of Capernaum is made very often, multiple synagogues are nowhere numbered, we think the words of *Luke* lead us to this conclusion. He recounts that a Centurion <note>A Roman military officer in charge of one hundred men</note>—a man who was not a Jew at all—wishing to keep his dying servant among the living, sent the **ELDERS OF THE JEWS** <note>Greek: *tous presbyterous tōn Ioudaiōn*</note> to Christ to intercede for him. These elders, as we shall soon state more clearly, were the **rulers** <note>Greek: *tous archontas*</note>, the **synagogue leaders** <note>Greek: *tous archisynagōgous*</note>, of whom **Jairus** was one. These men said:

<margin>Chapter 7, verse 5.</margin>
**For he loves our nation, and he himself built the synagogue for us.** <note>Greek: *Agapa gar to ethnos hēmōn, kai tēn synagōgēn autos ōkodomēsen hēmin*</note>

What then? Is it likely, or even probable, that the inhabitants of Capernaum would owe the benefit of a built synagogue to a Gentile man if Capernaum had been such a famous city? Does not everything rather point toward the idea that it was a more celebrated **village** <note>Latin: *pagus*</note> or **township** <note>Latin: *vicus*</note>? Are these facts such that we would dare to count Capernaum among the more celebrated cities? In the Gospel of John, only a *single Synagogue of Capernaum* is mentioned. **"These things he said in the synagogue, as he taught in Capernaum"**; <note>original Greek: *Ταῦτα εἶπεν ἐν συναγωγῇ, διδάσκων ἐν Καπερναούμ*</note>. Does this mean, **"in one of the synagogues"** <note>original Greek: *en miā tōn synagōgōn*</note>, as Luke says elsewhere? But even <margin>Book 1, Part I, Chapter 14.</margin> the name itself, *Kephar* <note>original Hebrew: כפר, meaning a village or hamlet</note>, indicates that *Capernaum* was a **Village** or a more prominent **town**, of the sort called *Cities* <note>original Hebrew: עיירות (*ayarot*)</note>—for so *Capernaum* is called a "city" <note>Greek: *polis*</note> by the Evangelist—as described in the preceding sections. And did these villages have more than one synagogue? I will say it as it is: when I consulted the learned works of *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English Hebraist who mapped the geography of the New Testament using Rabbinic sources</note> regarding *Sacred Chorography*, it seemed altogether clear to me that *Capernaum* was a village near *Tiberias*, situated by the Lake of Gennesaret. At first, as can be gathered from Christ's words, it was small; later, it became more celebrated when a synagogue was built there. It was very close to *Tiberias*, and it is unlikely that on one and the same shore, at such a small distance between locations, there were two towns <margin>On Matthew 9:18; 11:23; 7:5.</margin> competing with each other in fame. Therefore, *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a towering Dutch jurist and theologian</note> rightly advised even before me that **"There was only ONE SYNAGOGUE IN CAPERNAUM."** Let us establish, therefore, that there was one synagogue in *Capernaum*, and that there were several *Presidents* of that synagogue, one of whom was a man named *Jairus*. And who were those *Presidents* if not those **Elders of the Jews** <note>original Greek: *tōn Ioudaiōn Presbyteroi*</note> whom Luke records as interceding with Christ the Lord on behalf of the Centurion’s servant? These men were the Judges and Rectors of that place according to our hypothesis, and they presided in the synagogue, constituting a *Council of Elders* <note>original Greek: *gerousian*</note> or some kind of *Yeshiva* <note>original Hebrew: ישיבה, meaning a session or religious assembly</note> or *Presbytery* <note>original Greek: *Presbyterion*</note>. The very name of "Elder" <note>Latin: *Presbyter*</note> easily leads us to this conclusion. Indeed, in the <margin>Acts 18:8, 17.</margin> *Corinthian* synagogue, TWO **Rulers of the Synagogue** <note>original Greek: *Archisynagōgoi*</note> are also expressed by their names: **Crispus** and **Sosthenes**. It does not appear that there were multiple *synagogues* in *Corinth*; and it seems, therefore, that *Crispus* and *Sosthenes* were presidents of one and the same synagogue at one and the same time. Both of them also seem to have given their names to Christ <margin>verses 8, 17.</margin> <note>i.e., converted to Christianity</note> upon the preaching of *Paul*. This is stated openly regarding *Crispus*, but more obscurely regarding *Sosthenes*. For certainly this *Sosthenes* seems to be <margin>Chapter 1, 1.</margin> the same man as the one the Apostle mentions in the *First Epistle to the Corinthians*...

The concept of the **RULER OF THE SYNAGOGUE** is used in both the Law and by various other authors in either a broader or a narrower sense. In the broader sense, it designates in general all those set over the Synagogue, whether they be Elders or Learned Men, whom we have said preside in the more distinguished seats in the Synagogue; it was in this sense that I just mentioned the word *Archisynagogus* was used by Luke in the Acts of the Apostles. This use of the word is manifest in the Decree of the Emperors Arcadius and Honorius: *“It is a matter of unworthy superstition that* **RULERS OF THE SYNAGOGUE** <note>original Latin: *Archisynagogi*</note> *or* **ELDERS OF THE JEWS**, *or those whom they call* **APOSTLES** <note>In this Jewish context, *Apostoli* refers to the *Shlichim*, official messengers or envoys sent by the Jewish Patriarchs to collect taxes or deliver instructions</note>, *etc.”* Here, "Rulers of the Synagogue" are explained as "Elders"; and from these Rulers and Elders, the "Apostles" are distinguished by the disjunctive word *or*. Thus, the Emperors designate by this title all those *who, by the Law of the Nation, preside over the Nation itself*, and those whom the *Patriarchs have set over the rest*. Therefore, all members of the Sacred Senate, the assessors of each synagogue, are generally and quite correctly called **Rulers of the Synagogue**. Yet, more often, this very word **Ruler of the Synagogue** is taken in a narrower sense, when it denotes either the **PRESIDENT** of the Synagogal Elders in those places where a **Session** <note>original Hebrew: *Yeshiva* (ישיבה), a traditional seat of learning or judicial assembly</note> or a certain sacred **Council of Elders** <note>original Greek: *gerosia* (γεροσία)</note> was established, or simply the **Head** <note>original Hebrew: *Rosh* (ראשׁ)</note> or Master of the Synagogue described above. For even if that entire Senate presided in the synagogue, it was primarily the duty of the President—in the name of the whole Consistory, and by his own prudence and authority—to act as the first and chief not only of the Senate, but also...

But in those places where no such sacred **presidency** <note>original Greek: *proedria*, referring to a seat of honor or leadership</note> resided, that person alone who was the Master of the Synagogue’s Sacred Rites was called the **Ruler of the Synagogue** <note>original Latin: *Archisynagogus*</note>, as we were just describing. Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century bishop and writer on heresies</note> accepts this word in either of these two meanings when he says that Joseph the Apostle removed the **Rulers of the Synagogue**, **Priests**, and **Elders** from their office. For where he distinguishes **Rulers of the Synagogue** from **Elders**, with **Priests** placed between them, he shows clearly enough that by "Elders" <note>original Latin: *Presbyteros*</note> he here designates either the assistants and colleagues of the Rulers of the Synagogue in the Sacred Council of Elders, or those very Seniors of the Synagogue who elsewhere are called *Memunim al ha-tsibur* <note>Hebrew: ממונים על הצבור, meaning "those appointed over the congregation"</note>—the Officials of the Synagogue—and *Parnasim* <note>Hebrew: פרנסים, meaning "providers" or "pastors"</note>, as described in the previous chapter. Once this is admitted, nothing remains but that by **RULERS OF THE SYNAGOGUE** we understand either the **PRESIDENTS** of the Sacred Councils of Elders, or those **MASTERS OF THE SYNAGOGUE** to whom the management of the Synagogue’s sacred rites was entrusted alone. And the concept of **RULERS OF THE SYNAGOGUE** is taken in one of these two meanings by most other authors.

<margin>Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho*, page 366.</margin>
Here is a passage from Justin Martyr <note>A 2nd-century Christian apologist</note> concerning Rulers of the Synagogue who teach. *Therefore*, he says, *when you meet and talk together, do not attack the Son of God with insults, nor, by obeying the* **PHARISAIC TEACHERS** <note>original Greek: Φαρισαίοις πειθόμενοι διδασκάλοις</note>, *ever mock the King of Israel with taunts; such as those your* **RULERS OF THE SYNAGOGUE TEACH** <note>original Greek: ὁποῖα διδάσκουσιν οἱ Ἀρχισυνάγωγοι ὑμῶν</note> *after the prayers are finished*. By these teaching Rulers of the Synagogue, we must understand either the Presidents of the Elders, or those particular Masters of Sacred things who are called *Didascali* <note>Teachers</note> in the Constitutions of Roman Law, and *Rabbanim* <note>Rabbis</note> among the Jews.

Alexander was a Syrian, and he also favored the Jewish people and religion; therefore, as a rather bold insult, he was called a "Syrian Ruler of the Synagogue" and "High Priest" by the people of Antioch and Alexandria—these being names of dignity accepted among the Jews. For it is certain that Severus, the best of the Roman Emperors, was also devoted to the Jewish religion...

### CHAPTER II. ON THE GOVERNMENT OF THE OLD SYNAGOGUE.

<margin>
Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, Book 1, *Against the Ebionites*; and the Theodosian Code, concerning the Jews and the Sky-worshippers.
</margin>
There were also among the Jews certain FATHERS OF THE SYNAGOGUES; likewise PRIESTS and ELDERS and DEACONS of the Synagogues, whom the Jews call *Azanitas* <note>original: *Azanitas*, from the Hebrew *Chazzan*, meaning a sexton, cantor, or communal official</note>. There were also APOSTOLI <note>The *Apostoli* were official envoys sent by the Jewish Patriarch in Palestine to collect taxes and maintain communication with the Diaspora</note>, and placed above all these were the PATRIARCHS. But in this passage by Dionysius, the word *archisynagogus* <note>Greek: ἀρχισυνάγωγος, ruler of the synagogue</note> signifies something else, which is obscure to me. We shall pass over the remarks that Valesius <note>Henri Valois, a 17th-century French scholar of ecclesiastical history</note> added here regarding the Government of the Ancient Synagogue, drawn from Epiphanius and the Imperial Constitutions. They agree with what we noted in the previous sections from Petit; we discussed then to what extent those views were true or false.

Now, we only need to consider that Valesius says it is obscure to him what the word *Archisynagogus* means in this passage. This doubt, it seems to me, can be easily resolved if we say that Dionysius, the Bishop of Alexandria—where the common use of the term *Archisynagogus* was familiar—used it rather than any other term to indicate that Macrianus <note>Fulvius Macrianus, a high-ranking official under Emperor Valerian, whom Dionysius associated with Egyptian magic and the persecution of Christians</note> was a sort of *Prince* and *Prefect* of several Egyptian magicians. This is especially likely since the word *synagoga* <note>Greek: συναγωγή, assembly or gathering</note> had already begun to be used frequently in a negative sense among Christians of that time to refer to a gathering of wicked men, following <margin>Revelation 2:9, 3:9.</margin> the example of the passage in the Apocalypse which mentions the *synagogue of Satan* <note>Greek: τῆς συναγωγῆς τοῦ σατανᾶ</note>. For Dionysius, therefore, the *Archisynagogus* here is the Prefect and Prince of any assembly of wicked and criminal men, in whose ranks the Jewish *Teachers* and *Rulers of the Synagogue* <note>original: *Didascali & Archisynagogi*</note> were commonly placed by Christians at that time. Jerome calls these same men the *Overseers* <note>Latin: *Præpositos*</note> of the Synagogue. <margin>Letter to Algasia, Part 3, folio 59, column 3.</margin> He says: *They have OVERSEERS for the SYNAGOGUES, most wise men chosen for a foul task: so that if they cannot discern with their eyes whether the blood of a virgin or a menstruating woman is clean or unclean, they may taste it beforehand.* <note>Jerome is here repeating a polemical and likely fictitious anti-Jewish trope regarding the determination of ritual purity</note>. Who does not see that Jerome intended to describe those *Rulers of the Synagogue* of that final sort, whom we have called the *Masters of Synagogue Rituals*?

Let us now briefly touch upon the remaining names by which the dignity of the *Synagogal Prefecture* is expressed in Roman Laws. ### CHAPTER II. ON THE GOVERNANCE OF THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE.

Thus far we have said nothing about the title **Head of the Synagogue** <note>original: *Rosh Ha-Knesset*</note>, which corresponds most closely to that of the **Archisynagogue** <note>original: *Archisynagogos*</note>. This title occurs in the records of both ancient and more recent Teachers. We will provide one example from the Mishnah <note>The Mishnah is the first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions, compiled around 200 CE</note> and another from Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar</note>. The Mishnah tractate *Sotah* <note>Tractate *Sotah* discusses the ritual for a woman suspected of adultery, but also outlines other public ceremonies</note> records it thus: "The blessings of the High Priest—by what ritual are they performed?" <margin>Chapter 7, §. 7.</margin> **The Minister of the Synagogue takes the scroll of the Law and gives it to the Head of the Synagogue** <note>original Hebrew: *Chazan ha-Knesset notel sefer Torah ve-notno le-Rosh ha-Knesset*</note>; the **MINISTER OF THE SYNAGOGUE** receives the book of the Law and hands it to the **LEADER OF THE ASSEMBLY**.

Maimonides writes elsewhere in this manner: <margin>Laws of Prayer, Chapter 12, §. 7.</margin> **And even the Minister of the Synagogue or the Head of the Synagogue does not read of his own accord until the congregation, or the greatest among them, tells him to read.** <note>original Hebrew: *Ve-afilu Chazan ha-Knesset o Rosh ha-Knesset eno kore me-atzmo...*</note> Indeed, not even the **MINISTER OF THE SYNAGOGUE** or the **LEADER OF THE SYNAGOGUE** read by themselves unless the Synagogue, or a man of the highest authority within it, has called them to read. But who is that **Head of the Synagogue** in both of these places? Certainly, in the first passage from *Sotah*, by the **Head of the Synagogue**, one may understand either the Prince of the Sanhedrin <note>original: *Synedrium*, the supreme legal and religious council of ancient Israel</note>—the Primary Man of the Synagogal Assembly who undoubtedly was present alongside the Holy Senate of Seventy Men during the solemn reading by the High Priest and the King mentioned there—or perhaps a specific Teacher who was specially appointed by the Sanhedrin over a particular synagogue of the Temple. 

But the first option seems much more likely to me, because this reading took place not in the Temple synagogue itself, but in the Court <note>The inner courtyards of the Temple complex</note> by the High Priest and the King on the festival days of Atonement <note>Yom Kippur</note> and Tabernacles <note>Sukkot</note>. In the Court, however, whom else should we conceive as the Leader of the entire Assembly of Israelites than the Prince of the Great Sanhedrin, or his Deputy if he himself were absent? For he was truly the primary figure of the Assembly, or the "Prince of the Gathering," <margin>On *Sotah* Chapter 7, §. 7, 8. On *Yoma* Chapter 7, §. 1.</margin> as Wagenseil <note>Johann Christoph Wagenseil (1633–1705), a Christian Hebraist and scholar of Jewish law</note> and Sheringham <note>Robert Sheringham (1602–1678), an English linguist and translator of the Mishnah</note> have interpreted this title; and it was according to his judgment and that of the High Senate that these sacred rites were to be performed. Nor was it beneath the dignity of the President of that Great Presbytery to perform this duty for the Sagan <note>The *Sagan* was the deputy or associate High Priest</note> and the High Priest—firstly, because the High Priest and his deputy, the Sagan, were truly notable for possessing the highest rank after the King among the Jewish people; secondly, because these rites were celebrated in the Temple, where the authority of the High Priest was undoubtedly greatest; and finally, because the High Priest and his deputy were delegated to God on the public Day of Atonement in the name of the Sanhedrin and the entire Jewish people, and therefore the highest honor was to be paid to them during that festival. Likewise, in Maimonides, by **Head of the Synagogue**, you may understand either the specific Overseer of the Synagogue, elsewhere called the **Parnas** <note>original: *Parnas*, a community leader responsible for administration or charity</note>, or the [Head] of the Holy Senate...

### CHAPTER XII.

*Various models of Synagogue Governance, proposed in the preceding sections, are compared with the form of Governance of the early Christian Church; it is proved by solid arguments that none of them can be applied to the form of the Apostolic Church’s Governance, except for that first model, by which the more prominent Synagogues are assumed to have been ruled by a Senate of several Doctors <note>In this context, "Doctors" refers to learned teachers or scholars of the law, not medical physicians.</note>, who constituted a certain sacred Consistory <note>A formal council or administrative body.</note>, or Presbytery <note>A body of elders (presbyters) who shared leadership responsibilities.</note>.*

We would have exhausted ourselves in vain up to this point in describing the *Various models of Synagogue Governance* if we were unable to apply any of them to the true form of Governance of the Christian Church, which we defended in the *second Chapter* of this Book. Therefore, let us finally address this and demonstrate that genuine image according to which the Governance of the Christian Church was modeled. However, since this is of the greatest importance in our entire treatise, so that it is not done rashly or unadvisedly, we shall carry it out in due order and by parts. Thus, we assume here *First*:

->The Governance of the Christian Church *was not formed according to that model of Synagogue Governance in which only one person presided over the Synagogue*, <term>Rav <gloss>Master</gloss></term>, *or* TEACHER; *which was discussed in* Chapter 10.<-

Even when the Episcopacy <note>The office or government of the Church by bishops.</note> was already established in the Church, no matter of greater importance was acted upon by the Bishops without the counsel of the Presbyters...

Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654) was a famous English jurist and scholar of Jewish law whose work is frequently cited in debates about church structure</note> elsewhere most diligently investigated the genuine sense of this passage, and after establishing its true reading, he observed that this word—entirely unknown to secular Greek authors—appears among ecclesiastical writers with a dual meaning: it denotes both the *dignity itself, or the* HONOR OF THE ELDERSHIP <note>original: τὴν τιμὴν τοῦ πρεσβυτερίου</note>, and the ASSEMBLY OF ELDERS, or *Meeting*. As if it had been said: ‘Which was given to you by Prophecy with the laying on of hands, by which you were made an Elder’: just as if one were to say ‘by the laying on of hands’ of a Doctorate, of Marriage, of Baptism, of Confirmation, or* <term>בסמיכת הזקנים</term> <gloss>be-semikhat ha-zekenim</gloss> <note>literally "by the leaning of the elders," referring to the Jewish practice of ordination through the laying on of hands</note>, *by the Laying on of hands by which Elders were usually created.”* The Pauline words should therefore, according to Selden, be explained as the *Laying on of Hands* by which someone *was made an Elder*. For the *Genitive Case* <note>A grammatical case usually indicating possession or origin</note> in this construction of words leads us much more clearly to consider the *Presbytery* <note>original Greek: τὸ Πρεσβυτέριον</note> here as the *cause of the Laying on of Hands*, rather than as *its effect*. And in the Hebrew phrase <term>סמיכת זקנים</term> [Semikhat Zekenim] **THE LAYING ON OF THE ELDERS** (with which I would readily grant this Pauline phrase can be compared), the <term>זקנים</term> [Zekenim] or Elders also function, unless I am mistaken, as the *cause of the Laying on*; so that <term>סמיכת זקנים</term> denotes the *Laying on of Hands, which was performed by the Elders*.

<margin>* In this way also the phrase <term>סמיכת זקנים</term> [Semikhat Zekenim] is interpreted in the Commentary on Section 3, Chapter 1 of the Code Sanhedrin <note>The Sanhedrin is the section of Jewish law dealing with courts and leadership</note>.</margin>

* Therefore, I interpret the words of the Apostle in this way: that hands were laid upon Timothy by the assembly of Elders, just as Theodoret, Chrysostom, and Theophylact <note>Prominent early Christian theologians and commentators from the 4th to 11th centuries</note>, as is now my judgment, correctly understood them. By this *Assembly of Elders*, I then understand the Apostle Paul joined with other Teachers and Rulers of the Christian Church, who laid hands on Timothy in a public gathering of the Elders and perhaps the whole Church, and in this way ordained him to the dignity and work of the Ministry. This certainly does not conflict with, but can be most amicably reconciled with, what Paul proclaims elsewhere—that *he himself laid hands on Timothy*.

<margin>2 Timothy 1:6.</margin>

* "I remind you," he says, "to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands <note>original Greek: ᾿Αναμιμνήσκω ᾿αναζωπυρεῖν τὸ χάρισμα τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὅ ἐστιν ἐν σοὶ διὰ τῆς ἐπιθέσεως τῶν χειρῶν μου</note>." For certainly the *Personal Pronoun* "my" <note>original Greek: ἐγὼ</note> here, in the same word construction, denotes the acting cause; and therefore the term *presbytery* <note>original Greek: τὸ πρεσβυτέριον</note>, being constructed similarly, must also be explained in the same way. And indeed, this notion of a <term>presbytery</term> is a common meaning among Ecclesiastical writers, even in Ignatius <note>Ignatius of Antioch, an early Christian martyr and bishop writing c. 100 AD</note> himself. Thus he writes to the Trallians: *What is a PRESBYTERY other than a sacred assembly, counselors and assessors to the Bishop?* <note>original Greek: Τί δὲ πρεσβυτέριον ἔστιν ἀλλ᾽ ἢ σύστημα ἱερὸν, σύμβουλοι καὶ συνεδρευταὶ τοῦ ἐπισκόπου;</note> Again: *Elders as the COUNCIL of God* <note>original Greek: Πρεסβύτεροι ὡς Συνέδριον Θεοῦ</note>. Therefore, since the Jewish Sanhedrins—which were responsible for judging and caring for sacred matters—were called by the specific word *Presbytery* by Luke, and the very same name is given by Paul to the Assemblies of Rulers in the early Christian Church, we rightly conclude that Christian Presbyteries were established according to the model of those Jewish ones.

Moreover, the letters are drafted in the name of the Prince in roughly this manner: Let it be known to you that I have agreed with my colleagues that such and such days should be added to this year.*

...it is observed that in those places where the *Jews* lived under foreign power, the ecclesiastical system was commonly the same as the scholastic. The same *Learned Men* who established an Academy in exile, who explained Divine Law, and who *professed Jewish Jurisprudence*, were those same men who commonly presided in the *Synagogue*. Indeed, since they were not permitted in every place to have *Schools* distinct from *Synagogues*, for this reason the *Synagogues* themselves in many places were regarded as *Gymnasia* <note>original: "Gymnasiis"—referring here to places of mental exercise or study rather than physical athletics</note>, or, if you prefer, the *Schools* were merged with the *Synagogues*; with the same *Teachers* presiding over the *Synagogue* and the *School* at the same time. Philo <note>A Jewish philosopher from Alexandria who lived during the time of Christ</note> is to be understood as speaking of such *Scholastic Synagogues* in various passages when he discusses and describes synagogues. Benjamin <note>Benjamin of Tudela, a 12th-century Jewish traveler</note> is equally clear regarding such *Assemblies*—both *Scholastic* and *Ecclesiastical*—in the testimonies already cited. Certainly, in the land of *Canaan* itself, the Presidents of the Academies held theological inquiries in the public lecture halls of their discipline, just as they preached while the people were present. But where the Jews lived subject to foreign rule, it was sufficient for them to have *Learned Men* constituting a single ישיבה <term>original: *Yeshivah*, meaning a "Session" or "Senate"</term>—a *Senate* managing the *affairs of the School & Synagogue*; or rather, the affairs of the *Synagogue*, which was itself like a *School*. The *Christians*, since they always lived under foreign power, whether in the land of *Canaan* or outside it, imitated this same pattern. And we have a shining example of this in the Acts of the Apostles, where it is preached concerning the Apostle *Paul*, **Acts 19: 8, 9.** that he separated the **Disciples** at Ephesus, *disputing daily in the* **School** *of a certain man named Tyrannus.* The manner of management by the *Teachers* of the first *Christian Church* was so *Ecclesiastical* that it participated not a little in the *Scholastic* style. Indeed, as I have just said, the *Schools & Synagogues* in many places outside the land of *Canaan*—and perhaps also in less famous places within the land of *Canaan* itself—were merged among the Jews, and the Government of both was easily entrusted to the same persons. So far is it from this difficulty slowing us down, that on the contrary, from this very hypothesis and no other, the duties and circumstances of the leaders of the early Church can be explained: as we shall see in what follows.

2. Perhaps you might object to me that all the ancient ישיבות <term>original: *Yeshivot*, the plural of *Yeshivah*, meaning "Sessions" or "Assemblies"</term>—both *Scholastic* and *Ecclesiastical*—had their own ראש <note>original: *Rosh*, meaning "Head"</note> or *President*, who is usually called the ראש ישיבה <note>original: *Rosh Yeshivah*, meaning "Head of the Assembly"</note>, or the **Prince of the Synedrium** <note>A council or assembly, derived from the Greek *Sanhedrin*</note>, whether *Scholastic* or *Ecclesiastical*; and that therefore this hypothesis opposes our positions concerning the Rulers of the early Church being of the *same Kind and Order*, which we established in the Second Chapter of this Book. # ON THE TRUE FORM, BOOK II.

...God; and I admit that each had its own **Scholastic Assembly** <note>original: "Confessum Scholasticum"</note> and its own **President**, who was called the <term>Head of the Academy <gloss>original Hebrew: ראש ישיבה, "Rosh Yeshiva"</gloss></term>. Regarding the dignity and authority of such a President in the **Greater Assemblies**—such as those that flourished before and after the destruction of Jerusalem in the land of Canaan, and in the more famous places outside Canaan like Alexandria, Antioch, Damascus, and subsequently also in **Babylonia**—I would not deny that his status was distinguished above the other **Elders** <note>original: "Presbyteris"</note> with whom he constituted the **Council** <note>original: "Synedrium"</note>. 

But it must be observed: 

**1.** That such a **President of the Senate** was always considered to be of the same **order and office** as the whole **Senate**, of which he was the most distinguished part; and, what is more, he was always subject to the **Senate**, which could remove him from his office whenever it wished. Therefore, this **President of the Jewish Presbyteries** <note>The councils of elders</note> should be compared with the **Presidents of Civil** or **Legal Senates**, which have been established in many places. To be sure, the dignity of the **Presidency** wins them greater authority and reverence, and gives them certain prerogatives; yet they are not, by virtue of it, removed from the **order and class** of men of the Senate over which they preside—as can be seen even from the single example of the **Rectors of the Academy** <note>meaning the heads of universities</note> in our own time. In any case, all the assessors of the greatest and most majestic Senate of Jerusalem—the President not excepted—were called <term>Sanhedrin <gloss>original Hebrew: סנהדriן</gloss></term>, <term>Elders <gloss>original Hebrew: זקנים, "Zekenim"</gloss></term>, <term>House of Judgment <gloss>original Hebrew: בית דין, "Beit Din"</gloss></term>, <term>Council of Elders <gloss>original Greek: πρεσβυτέριον, "presbyterion"</gloss></term>, <term>Senate <gloss>original Greek: γερουσία, "gerousia"</gloss></term>, and whatever other names were attributed to that Senate. From this it is certain enough that those Sacred Colleges constituted **homogeneous bodies** of men of the same class and order. For if there was any greater dignity belonging to the President, it was reflected back upon the whole **College** from which it was conferred upon him. 

But besides these things, **2.** I would wish it to be observed that in those common <term>Academies <gloss>original Hebrew: ישיבות, "Yeshivot"</gloss></term> or **Sacred Presbyteries**, such as resided indiscriminately in less populous places, the dignity of the <term>Head of the Academy <gloss>original Hebrew: ראש ישיבה, "Rosh Yeshiva"</gloss></term>—the **President of the Senate**—was hardly greater than the dignity of his **Colleagues**. He was the **First** and **perpetual President** of this **Senate**, of the same **order, office, and power** (since he was required to exercise all power with them and through them) as his other colleagues; nor did he excel them in any dignity, except that he was the first among a class of men of his own kind and office. Let the testimonies we cited from **Benjamin** <note>Benjamin of Tudela, the 12th-century traveler mentioned on the previous page</note> be compared again, with reason itself supporting this. For the dignity of the **President** in smaller Senates is always less and less conspicuous. To which is now added **3.** that **Christ the Lord** [placed] his Disciples...

...seriously warned his own followers about avoiding the <term>Principate <gloss>A position of supreme authority or dominion</gloss></term>, and more than once recommended to them an equality of governance. Since these warnings of Christ were still fresh, the **Presidents of the Christian Presbyteries** in the origins of the Church seem to have used their dignity and authority so moderately that they were distinguished from the other Elders by hardly any visible mark. 4. Nevertheless, it is sufficiently clear that the **Presbyteries of the Primitive Church** truly had their own **Presidents**, from the fact that **Bishops** <note>original: "Episcopi"</note> acquired great authority and dignity for themselves over the other Elders a short time after the birth of Christianity. But concerning this, we shall speak more extensively in the **following Book**, in its proper place.

3. A difficulty might perhaps arise from what I said: that the **Presbyteries** of the Christian Church were established after the model of those **Jewish** ones consisting of **literate men** <note>original: "Viris literatis," referring to scholars or those trained in the Law</note>, since it entirely appears that many Elders of the early Church were chosen from the common people, out of the congregation itself.

This objection may be addressed in a few words. I do not deny that in certain Churches of the earliest times, due to a lack of others, **unlettered** Elders from the common people were appointed as overseers—that is, those who before that time had not devoted effort in the Schools to the study of Jewish Religion and Law, and had not brought back the title of **Doctor** <note>original: "Doctoris," meaning a formal teacher or master of the Law</note> from their masters. However, I utterly deny that any men from the common people were promoted to that most grave office who had not been advanced in knowledge to the point where they could honorably maintain this dignity, whether through the extraordinary grace of the Holy Spirit or through Apostolic instructions. Moreover, even if they were not "Doctors" at that time, by that very **Apostolic Laying on of Hands**, they were set apart from the common people and into the order of Doctors; from which, finally, proceeded the distinction—observed all too strictly in the Ancient Church—between the **Clergy** and the **Laity** <note>original: "Clerum & Plebem," literally the Clergy and the People</note>.

Finally, if you ask what should be determined regarding the <term>Pastors <gloss>Hebrew: פרנסים, Parnasîm</gloss></term> or <term>Elders of the Synagogue <gloss>Hebrew: זקנים, Zeqēnîm</gloss></term> of the present day? I answer: They are a shadow and image, though a somewhat dim one, of **that Council** by which the **Ancient Synagogues** were governed when there was a more abundant supply of learned men. Literate men could not always be had; wherefore necessity often demanded that the **Senate** of the Synagogue be constituted from the members of the **Synagogue** themselves, who were often not so skilled in their own Religion and Law. To them, however, was given the same name of **Pastors and Elders** <note>original Hebrew: "Parnasîm & Zeqēnîm"</note>, which belongs to the Overseers truly so-called, and to the dignity of the office...

However, even if sometimes regarding the same business one aspect belongs to the Ecclesiastical forum and another to the Civil forum, this takes place in few instances, and because of those few, there was no need to establish two different judgments. If, therefore, the Civil and Sacred matters were submitted to the one and the same Sanhedrin <note>the high council or court of the ancient Jewish people</note>, then surely the first place in the Synagogue, and thus the supreme government of the Synagogue, must be granted to that Sanhedrin."

For suppose it happened that some member of the Synagogue assembly committed a crime worthy of Censure, Excommunication, or Flogging; who would stand to hear the case and pass sentence on it? Would it be some *Ruler of the Synagogue* <note>original: "Archisynagogo"</note>, distinct from the Sanhedrin, or perhaps an *Ecclesiastical Consistory* of that place? Was there then among the Jews, while their Republic flourished, Sacred Tribunals of different kinds in one place, which could hear and judge the same offenses committed against Religion? For everyone who has learned Hebrew letters knows that the Sacred Tribunals, which are called **בתי דינין** <note>original Hebrew: Batte Dinin; literally "Houses of Judgment" or Law Courts</note>, heard cases of Excommunication and exercised the power of Excommunication. Shall we then attribute the same right and the same power in one and the same place to the *Rulers of the Synagogue*, as distinct from these Elders of the Sanhedrins? And if perhaps the assessors of the Sanhedrins themselves should do wrong, would they also be considered subject to the judgment of the *Rulers of the Synagogue*? Certainly, since these things are entirely contrary to the Laws of a well-constituted Republic, nothing remains except that our hypothesis, consistent with itself in all...

The common <term>NAME</term> by which the Rulers of the Synagogue are designated, both in Holy Scripture and outside of it, is <term>Archisynagogos</term> <note>original Greek: *Ἀρχισυνάγωγος*</note>, the **CHIEF OF THE SYNAGOGUE**. We have already dealt with the meaning of that term when we discussed the Form of Government of the Ancient Synagogue. This compound word is expressed by Luke through its simple components: *Ruler of the synagogue* <note>original Greek: *Ἄρχων τῆς συναγωγῆς* (Archon tes synagoges)</note>. Such a construction is familiar, as is evident from words like <term>Chief Judge</term> <note>original Greek: *Ἀρχidikasthhs*</note>, <term>chief of laws</term>, <term>chief observer</term>, <term>chief cup-bearer</term>, and <term>chief architect</term>, which were well known in the flourishing period of Greece.

<margin>
Luke 19:2.
1 Peter 5:4.
2 Samuel 3:4.
Numbers 31:13.
32:2.
</margin>
In the writings of the New Testament, you find names constructed in a similar way, such as <term>chief tax collector</term> <note>original Greek: *ἀρχιτελώνης* (architelones)</note>, <term>chief shepherd</term> <note>original Greek: *ἀρχιποίμην* (archipoimen)</note> (which also appears in the Septuagint translation), and others. Furthermore, what the Greeks call <term>Archisynagogos</term>, or *ruler of the synagogue*, can be expressed in Hebrew in various ways. The Septuagint translators <note>The 70 scholars who translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek.</note> rendered the phrase **Princes of the Assembly** <note>original Hebrew: *נשיאי העדה* (Nesi'e ha-edah)</note> as *Rulers of the synagogue*. Nor did they err, surely; even if it is quite certain that the writers of the New Testament, by using their word *archisynagogos*, did not intend to express the Hebrew phrase *Princes of the Assembly*.

<margin>
See Kircher’s Lexicon <note>Conrad Kircher’s 1607 Hebrew-Greek Concordance.</note> at the word **Head** (**ראש**)
</margin>
It is more likely that with this term they were referring to the titles **Head of the gathering** <note>original Aramaic: *ריש כנישתא* (Resh Kenishta)</note>, **Head of the assembly** <note>original Hebrew: *ראש הכנסת* (Rosh ha-Knesset)</note>, or **Head of the community** <note>original Hebrew: *ראש הקהל* (Rosh ha-Qahal)</note>, which seem to have been already accepted among them at that time. It should not seem new that the word **Head** <note>original Hebrew: *ראש* (Rosh)</note> is rendered by them as *ruler* <note>original Greek: *archonta*</note>, since the Septuagint paved the way not just once, but several times. **Assembly** <note>original Hebrew: *כנסת* (Knesset)</note> indeed, which has almost the same meaning as **congregation** <note>original Hebrew: *עדה* (Edah)</note>, is conveniently rendered as *synagogue*; and even the word **Community** <note>original Hebrew: *קהל* (Qahal)</note>—which, however, is more conveniently translated as *church* <note>original Greek: *ἐκκλησίαν* (ekklesian)</note>, as we have shown before—is often rendered by the Greek Septuagint translators as *synagogue*, as can be seen from the examples collected by Kircher.

<margin>
Leviticus 4:13, 14.
Deuteronomy 5:22.
10:4.
</margin>
Moreover, this title is most suitable for signifying the thing to which it is applied. For whether **Knesset** denotes the assembly itself, gathered in the House of the Synagogue (which seems most probable to me, and can be seen from the plural **Heads of the assemblies** <note>original Hebrew: *ראשי כנסות* (Rashe Knessetot)</note>), or whether it denotes the Synagogue building itself, it is most fitting that the person to whom the care of the sacred rites—to be handled by the multitude in a certain place—is entrusted, be called <term>Archisynagogos</term>, the **RULER OF THE SYNAGOGUE**. However, the Early Christian Church, as should now be noted, left this title to the Synagogue. It did not call its leaders *rulers of the church*; but rather *Presbyters* <note>Elders</note>, *Bishops* <note>Overseers</note>, *Pastors*, *Doctors* <note>Teachers</note>, as will be discussed...

However, I would think that the Prefects of the Synagogue are described *indirectly* under the name of **the leading men of the Jews** <note>original Greek: τῶν πρώτων τῶν Ἰουδαίων (tōn prōtōn tōn Ioudaion)</note> in the *Acts of the Apostles*. For it happened—so the words of the text go—*that after three days Paul called together* **THE FIRST OF THE JEWS** <note>original Greek: τοὺς ὄντας Ἰουδαίων πρώτους; original Latin: JUDÆORUM PRIMOS</note>. But I believe it must be carefully observed that the text does not simply say, *the first of the Jews* <note>original Greek: τοὺς πρώτους τῶν Ἰουδαίων; original Latin: primos Judæorum</note> (which could be taken generally for Jews of more distinguished reputation—the principal and leading Jews, I mean, who were staying in Rome, in the way the Greek word <term>First</term> <note>original Greek: πρῶτος (prōtos)</note> is often used); rather, it says, *those who were the first of the Jews*. By this, as far as I can discern, it is clearly hinted that the Jews summoned by Paul were truly then established in some more eminent dignity, and were known and recognized by that name. Paul did not merely call together the *Principal* men of the Jews who were such in their own opinion or that of others, but those who, because they held a Magistracy, were truly regarded and honored by all Jews as *Leaders*. Certainly, the **First Men** <note>original Greek: οἱ πρῶτοι (hoi prōtoi)</note> are often the same to the Greeks as the <term>Rulers</term> <note>original Greek: ἄρχοντες (archontes)</note>, the Princes or Magistrates of the People. Thus **Luke** himself used this voice elsewhere: *But the Chief Priests and Scribes sought to destroy him,* **AND THE LEADERS OF THE COMMON PEOPLE** <note>original Greek: καὶ οἱ πρῶτοι τοῦ λαοῦ; original Latin: PRIMORES PLEBIS</note>; the Dutch <note>original Latin: Belgæ</note> translate this as: *The rulers of the people* <note>original Dutch: De Overste des volks</note>. **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch legal scholar and theologian</note>, who is less favorable to this interpretation, says this excellently for our purpose in his *Annotations on Acts*: *Those who are elsewhere called "the rulers" [archontes], and in the following chapter "elders" [presbyteroi], that is, Senators of the Great Sanhedrin, as the Syrian translator understood it: For the Priests are named specifically because of the excellence of their dignity, and the Lawyers because of the fame of their learning.* Therefore, the *leading men of the Jews* in Luke’s former passage will, without a doubt, have the same signifying force as the *rulers of the Jews*, or the [rulers] of the synagogue of the Je—

# ON THE NAMES OF THE PREFECTS BOOK III. PART I.

<margin>verse 21.</margin>
...of the Jews <note>original Greek: Ἰουδαίων (Ioudaion)</note>. The following context illustrates and confirms this interpretation. For after Paul had pleaded his case before them, these **Leading Men** <note>original Latin: Primores</note> replied to him:
> *We have received no letters about you from Judea, nor have any of the brothers who arrived reported or said anything evil about you.*

Clearly, all synagogues outside of Canaan were subject to the Great Senate of the entire Nation <note>The Great Sanhedrin, the supreme council in Jerusalem</note>, which sat in Jerusalem. Therefore, whatever was of concern to that high Sanhedrin was written in its name to the **Prefects** of each synagogue. Furthermore, these "leading men" <note>original Greek: πρῶτοι (protoi)</note> clearly indicate that such letters from the High Sanhedrin should have been delivered to them, if any had been sent to Rome; they certainly would not have claimed this honor for themselves if it did not belong to them by reason of their **office**. However, Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note> takes a different view, writing on this passage: "The leading men of the Jews" <note>original Greek: τῶν Ἰουδαίων πρώτες (tōn Ioudaion prōtes)</note> means the MORE EMINENT ONES. For the Jews do not seem to have had a synagogue in Rome at that time. Grotius does not add a reason; yet it is undoubtedly to be sought in the fact that **Claudius expelled all Jews from Rome.**

<margin>
Chapter 18, 2.
See his Annotations on chapter 18, 2.
In the time of Augustus, more than eight thousand Jews inhabited the city. Josephus, Antiquities, book 18, chapter 12.
</margin>
Grotius therefore doubts whether the Jews who returned to Rome after the edict of **Claudius** (and Grotius does not deny that they returned) **had a synagogue**. For my part, however, I have no doubt of it. For even if it is uncertain whether the Jews at that time had a grand building in or outside of Rome known by the name and title of a **Synagogue**, I still believe that the Jews living in Rome—considering their **number**, which seems to have been significant—consecrated some place for celebrating their sacred rites according to the accepted custom, in which they **assembled** on the Sabbath days. Certainly, if it was permitted for Paul, staying in Rome as a **prisoner**, to receive many Jews in his lodging and to discuss the secrets of the Jewish religion with them, I see no reason why the **Jews** living in Rome would have been prevented from meeting together and practicing their religion. Nevertheless, this title of "the first men" is with the greatest justice excluded from the Church and its **Overseers** because of the clear saying of Christ to his disciples when they were arguing about supreme dominion in the Church:

<margin>Chapter 20, 27.</margin>
> *And whoever wants to be* **FIRST** <note>original Greek: πρῶτος (prōtos)</note> *among you, let him be your* **SERVANT** <note>original Greek: δοῦλος (doulos)</note>.

In addition to this title of "the first," I would think that the **Prefects of the Synagogue** are sometimes simply hinted at in the writings of the New Testament by the name of **Rulers** <note>original Greek: ἀρχόντων (archontōn)</note>.

<margin>Chapter 7, 48.</margin>
As in this saying of the Pharisees in **John**: *Has any of the* **RULERS** <note>original Greek: ἀρχόντων (archontōn)</note> *believed in him?*

Therefore, let us finally begin the matter itself, starting with the name **elder** <note>original Greek: πρεσβύτερος (presbyteros)</note>.*

# CHAPTER I. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

...the received meaning of the word. **The Diviner**: *Understand this to mean the King*, *according to what is said*: <margin>Proverbs 16:10.</margin> *A divine sentence is in the lips of the King; his mouth shall not transgress in judgment.* **The Elder**: *Someone of this kind*, WHO DESERVES TO SIT <note>original: *be-Yeshivah* ( בישיבה )</note> IN THE ASSEMBLY OF LEARNED MEN. **The Captain of Fifty**: *This is one who knows how to speak strictly regarding those things contained in the five Books of Moses.* *Receive also another interpretation.* **The Prefect of Fifty**: *Rabbi Abbu says*, *look here for the reason why it is not appropriate to appoint any Interpreter of the Synagogue younger than fifty years of age*, etc. You have here, in any case, that which we were required to prove: that <term>ELDER <note>Hebrew: *Zaken* ( זקן )</note></term> is properly used by the Jews for one who constitutes part of the Sacred Consistory, which is here called the <term>ASSEMBLY <note>Hebrew: *Yeshivah* ( ישיבה ), referring to a traditional school or council of scholars</note></term>. Nor does it stand in the way that this exposition is "mystical" or allegorical; rather, this confirms our opinion all the more, because in their mystical expositions, the greatest account is taken of those meanings of each word that belong to it properly and with emphasis. 

Let us take an example from the word itself for <term>PROPHET <note>Hebrew: *Navi* ( נביא )</note></term>, which is explained in this very testimony. This is commonly taken to mean a man who maintains a singular commerce with God and is informed of the Divine will through extraordinary revelations. This, I say, is the common definition of this word; because no meaning is *stronger* or *more effective*, it retains its interpretation in this *allegorical explanation*. To be sure, the word *Prophet* can admit a less emphatic meaning and be explained as any *Interpreter* of the Divine Will; but, as I have already said, in allegorical interpretations, the *most effective* explanations of words are required. 

The case is entirely the same with the word <term>ELDER <note>Hebrew: *Zaken* ( זקן )</note></term>. Taken simply, it denotes *any old man*. But it is taken in a far more august and effective sense for a *Learned Man*, and thus an *honored* one, who makes up a part of the <term>ASSEMBLY <note>Hebrew: *Yeshivah* ( ישיבה )</note></term>, just as one may read in the words cited. And certainly, it was most accepted among the Jews around the time of Christ our Lord to call those men who were outstanding in wisdom—and especially those who had been promoted and co-opted into the Sanhedrin or Academic Assembly—<term>PRESBYTERS <note>from the Greek *presbyterous*, meaning "elders" or "seniors"</note></term>, or SENIORS. <margin>On the Ancient Sanhedrin of the Hebrews, Book I, Chapter 14, page 304.</margin> <term>Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654), an English jurist and polymath who wrote extensively on Jewish law and its influence on Christian institutions</note></term> observed this long ago, and here he has left hardly anything for our diligence to uncover. # ON THE NAMES OF PREFECTS BOOK III, PART I.

...the teaching of a Man; the Chaldean Paraphrasts <note>The Targumists, who translated the Hebrew Bible into Aramaic</note> also not infrequently translate the word **Elder** <note>Hebrew: *Zaken* ( זקן )</note> as **Wise Man** <note>Aramaic: *Hakima* ( חכימא )</note> and **Wise Men** <note>Aramaic: *Hakimaya* ( חכימיא )</note>. <margin>Leviticus 19:32.</margin> 
regarding the words: *Before the hoary head rise up, and honor the face of the Elder* <note>Hebrew: *Zaken*, often translated simply as "old man"</note>, the Jews believe there is contained a precept regarding the honoring of a **Wise Man**. Thus 
<margin>Law 222. from the edition of Hottinger, page 330.</margin> 
it is written in the *Laws of the Hebrew Rights* by Rabbi Levi <note>Referring to the *Sefer HaChinuch*, a work on the 613 commandments often attributed to Aaron ha-Levi of Barcelona</note>: **To honor the Sages and to rise before them, as it is said: "Before the hoary head rise up." And the Translation of Onkelos <note>The standard Aramaic Targum of the Pentateuch</note> renders it: "Before him who is expert in the Law, rise up." And "honor the face of the Elder." Our Teachers of blessed memory explained: "There is no Elder except him who has acquired wisdom." And the reason why the Scripture expresses "the Wise Man" using the term "Elder" is because a Wise Youth sees through his wisdom what an Old Man sees through his many years.**
<margin>Leviticus 19:32.</margin> 
**The Sages must be honored, and one must rise for them, because it is said: "Rise before the hoary head."** Which *Onkelos* translates thus: *Rise for him who is skilled in the Law.* **And honor the face of the elder.** Our Masters teach: **No one is an Elder, except he who has acquired Wisdom for himself.** The reason, moreover, why the Scripture expresses the **Wise Man** by the word **Elder**, is because *a Wise Youth sees by his Wisdom that which an Old Man sees by the multitude of his years.* Other interpretations of this text, which are built upon the ancient glosses of the Pharisees, are consistent with this. *Jonathan* <note>Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic paraphrase</note> says: 
<margin>On this see Cartwright, *Mellificium Hebraicum*, book 1, chapter 3, Folio 32, column 2.</margin> 
**Before Elders, who are prudent in the Law, you shall rise, and you shall show honor to the face of the Wise Man.** This explanation is asserted most clearly in the Volume *Kiddushin* <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning marriage and status</note>; the text of which, brought forward for this purpose, was translated by Cartwright <note>Christopher Cartwright, a 17th-century English Hebraist</note>. Indeed, Maimonides himself, who earnestly champions the honor of *Wise Men*, repeats this same precept concerning the reverence to be shown to Learned Men, and he bases it upon this same 
<margin>Laws of Torah Study (*Hilkhot Talmud Torah*), chapter 6, § 1.</margin> 
Mosaic Law. His words: **It is a commandment for every disciple of a Sage to be honored, even if one has not used him as a Teacher; as it is said: "Before the hoary head you shall rise and you shall honor the face of the Elder." That Elder is one who has acquired wisdom. And from what distance is one bound to stand up before him? Consistent with these points, and confirming and illustrating what we have said (which must be repeated here, even though we have already noted it above), in the writings of the New Testament, the assessors of the **Sanhedrins** <term>Sanhedrin: A council or assembly of Jewish leaders acting as a court or senate</term> or the **Academic Senates**—for both are called *Yeshivot* <note>original Hebrew: ישיבות; literally "sittings" or sessions of study</note> among the Jews; indeed, almost all Jewish Sanhedrins after the destruction of the Republic were converted into Academic Senates—are very familiarly called **Elders** <note>original Greek: πρεσβυτέρους (*presbyterous*)</note>. It shall suffice to have noted that the most distinguished Senate of the Jewish people—the Great Sanhedrin, I mean—is called twice by Luke the **Presbytery** <note>original Greek: πρεσβυτέριον (*presbyterion*)</note>, or the **College of Elders**. So it is in the Gospel: *And as soon as it was day, the* **Presbytery** (*the Council of Elders*) *of the people was gathered together.* So again in the Acts: *As also the High Priest is my witness, and all the* **SENATE OF ELDERS**. By "Presbytery," Luke understands, as I have already said, the Great Sanhedrin, which consisted of Elders. Since, however, no one at that time was admitted into such Sanhedrins unless he was approved in **learning and character** and **promoted** to the **Doctorate** <note>Referring here to the status of a certified teacher or Master of the Law</note> by a solemn rite, it is clear from this that the title and name of "Elder," where it is applied to the Overseers of the Christian Church in the New Testament writings, is to be understood as referring to a **learned and literate man**, or at least to an upright and wise man, who had been **promoted** to the dignity of the Elders through solemn rites and added to some Senate of Elders by election. Our hypothesis is clearly confirmed by the New Testament Scripture when it ascribes to the Elders of the Christian Church the **imposition of hands** <note>original Greek: ἐπίθεσιν χειρῶν (*epithesin cheiron*); the ritual of laying hands on a person to ordain them</note>; concerning which, God willing, we shall discuss in the following pages.

Furthermore, if we look more closely into the matter itself, it is not at all surprising that it became established through long usage that whatever men excelled in dignity and wisdom—and especially those who were admitted into some judicial or doctrinal Sanhedrin—were called **Elders** or **Seniors**, even if they were often not very advanced in age. Cicero says in his work **Cato the Elder**: *Unless wisdom, reason, and judgment existed in old men, our ancestors would not have called the supreme council a* SENATE.

Thus it has been sufficiently proven, unless I am mistaken, that around and after the time of Christ and the Apostles, those who were chosen for the college of learned and advanced men—which the Jews call a <term>Yeshivah</term> <note>original Hebrew: ישיבה; a traditional school or assembly for the study of sacred texts</note>—were called <term>Presbyters</term> <note>from the Greek *presbyteros*, meaning "elder"</note>. Since the leaders of the early Church adopted this same title for themselves, and since it is unlikely they did so against the common usage of the word at that time, we rightly conclude that the Presbyters of the early Church constituted a certain *Council* of learned men, or men distinguished by wisdom and dignity. This was formed after the pattern of the <note>original Greek/Hebrew: των ישיבות</note> *Assemblies of Literate Men* which we mentioned previously. Indeed, it was defined by the Church Canons of later times that any man approved in doctrine and character could be admitted to the order of Presbyters after the age of thirty; it was merely cautioned that this dignity should not be conferred on anyone under thirty. This is found in the Canons of the Council of Neocaesarea, held before the Council of Nicaea: *A Presbyter shall not be ordained before thirty years...* <note>original Greek: Πρεσβύτερος πρὸ τῶν τριάκοντα ἐτῶν μὴ χειροτονεί-</note>

# ON THE NAMES OF THE LEADERS BOOK III. PART I.

We will not dispute with the Teachers now. This much is certain and accepted by all: Paul uses the term PASTORS to designate the ordinary Leaders of the Church; those same ones, I say, who are elsewhere called Elders and Bishops. Because this is clear from the meaning of the name itself and proven by the consensus of all Interpreters, it is also clearly established from those testimonies in which the office of Bishops and Elders is said to be *poimainein*, to SHEPHERD or FEED. Take this passage from the Acts of the Apostles:

<margin>Chapter 20, 28.</margin>
*Pay attention therefore to yourselves, and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you as BISHOPS TO SHEPHERD the church of God.* <note>The Greek phrase "poimainein ten ekklesian" means to feed or act as a shepherd to the church.</note> This "shepherding" is here assigned to Bishops and Elders. <margin>Chapter 5, 1. 2.</margin>

It follows: *Until God reveals the one who is to Govern you.* <note>original Greek: "archein," meaning to rule or lead.</note>

Furthermore, there is no reason for it to be unclear to anyone why Paul wanted to designate the ordinary Leaders of the Church by the name of PASTORS. For, 1. the comparison between the Church and a Flock, and likewise between the Rectors of the Church and Shepherds, is quite easy and clear. For just as shepherds nourish, lead, and protect the flock committed to them, so it is the duty of Church Leaders to provide spiritual food to the believers committed to them, to rule them by their counsel and prudence, and to fortify them against the corruption of doctrine and morals: things which are clearly hinted at by Paul in that passage we noted from the Acts of the Apostles.

"Indeed, shepherding has been considered so venerable and beneficial a task that the class of poets is accustomed to call kings the **SHEPHERDS OF THE PEOPLE**. But does the lawgiver <note>Philo refers to Moses as the "Legislator" or "Lawgiver."</note> not also bestow this name upon the wise, who alone are kings in truth?" For just as a shepherd leads a flock, God governs—according to justice and law—the earth, water, air, fire, and all things contained within them, whether plants or animals, both mortal and divine. Furthermore, He governs the nature of the heavens, the circuits of the sun and moon, and the revolutions and harmonious dances of the other stars, acting as Shepherd and King. Over these He has appointed His **RIGHT REASON, HIS FIRSTBORN SON**, who, like the **DEPUTY** <note>original: "Pro-Rex" or "Hyparchos," meaning a viceroy or high official acting on behalf of a king.</note> of a great king, shall take up the care of this sacred flock. For he speaks thus: The Lord shepherds me and nothing shall be lacking to me. Indeed, let each person repeat this for himself. For it is fitting for every friend of God to meditate on such a song, but especially for the whole world. For just as a shepherd leads a flock, God—as Shepherd and King—governs by right and law the earth, water, air, fire, and whatever is contained in them, whether plants or animals, mortal or divine; and additionally the nature of the heavens, the circuits of the sun and moon, the revolutions of the other stars, and their most harmonious dances. Over these He has placed His **RIGHT REASON, HIS FIRSTBORN SON**, to take upon himself the care of this sacred flock as a great **DEPUTY KING**. For thus it is written in a certain place:

# ON THE NAMES OF OVERSEERS. BOOK III. PART I.

<margin>Exodus 23:20.</margin>
It is written: *Behold! I am; I WILL SEND MY ANGEL BEFORE YOUR FACE, that he may guard you on the way.* In these words, it is clearly established by Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher, often interpreted the Old Testament through the lens of Greek philosophy.</note> that the title of **Shepherd** is the most honorable for any form of Governance, since not only the **Wise** and **Kings**, but even **God** himself is distinguished by it in the sacred writings. From this, you may easily conclude that it is for the sake of honor that the same title is granted to the **Leaders and Rectors** of the Church, which is our primary concern now. We do not wish to overlook—as it certainly deserves careful attention—that Philo speaks of the <note>original Greek: Λόγῳ, *Logos*</note> **WORD** as the **FIRSTBORN SON** of God, and as the **Shepherd** of the World and the Vicar <note>A "vicar" is one who acts as a representative or deputy for a higher authority.</note> of the Church. It is as if he were aware of the mystery of our faith regarding the Father and the Son, or even as if he intended to say one and the same thing as

<margin>John 10:14. Hebrews 13:20. 1 Peter 5:4.</margin>
John, Peter, and Paul, who call the **Second Person of the Deity** the **Word**, the **Firstborn Son**, and the **Chief Shepherd**. Indeed, it is truly marvelous that Philo interpreted that **Angel** mentioned in the Book of Exodus—whom we also teach was the **Only-Begotten Son of God**—as being that same **WORD**. For even if Philo drew other ideas from Plato, he seems to have held this particular point from the ancient <term>Traditions of the Fathers</term>. But let these things be said <note>original Greek: ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ, *os en parodo*</note> **in passing**. We proceed. 3. The **Rectors of the Church of the New Covenant** were long ago set forth and promised under the name of **Shepherds**. For it is expressly read in **Jeremiah** concerning those who would return to Jerusalem from the Captivity:

<margin>Chapter 3:15.</margin>
*And I will give you* <gloss>original Hebrew: רעים, *Ro'im*</gloss> **SHEPHERDS**, *according to my own heart, and they shall feed you with knowledge and prudence.* From what follows, it is clear that this speech refers primarily to the times of the **Messiah**; as does another 

<margin>Chapter 23:4.</margin>
similar prophecy, in which this same promise is repeated. This means the Israelites returning from Babylon would no longer be governed by the harsh scepter of **Kings**, but would be led by the advice of **Leaders** and especially **Priests**,

<margin>Josephus, Antiquities, Book 11, Chapter 4.</margin>
(as Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus was a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> himself testifies) until finally all **Political Rule** in the Church was abolished and all care for it was entrusted to **Teachers**, who would rule it by their instruction and admonitions. This is what it means to **feed with prudence and intelligence**: and who could deny that this was more suited to the first **Rectors of the Christian Church** than to any other **Overseers of the Jewish Church**?

And since these things are so, no difficulty remains in the fact that the **ordinary Rectors of the Christian Church** are called by Paul...

# CHAPTER 2. OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

Pastors; nor should that be considered something new or foreign. I do not know, however, what light might shine upon this matter when we notice that the **OVERSEERS OF THE SYNAGOGUES** were both called in the past and are still called today *Parnasim* <note>original Hebrew: פרנסים</note>, **PASTORS**? Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a Dutch jurist and theologian who often compared Christian and Jewish communal structures.</note> observed this several times in his Annotations on the Epistles of Paul, from which we have already selected some parts in the preceding pages. But since he, as far as we can tell, neglected to discuss the derivation of this word more extensively, it will be convenient to treat its <gloss>Ephesians 4:11</gloss> origin and genuine meaning somewhat more distinctly.

The word *Parnas* <note>original Hebrew/Syriac: פרנס</note> most consistently signifies **PASTOR**, a shepherd <note>original Greek: ποιμένα</note>, from the word *parnes* <note>original: פרנס</note>, which denotes *to feed* or *to pasture*, among both the Ancient and Modern Syrians, with whom the Talmudic writers agree <unclear>likewise</unclear>. You will find countless examples in the Chaldaic Paraphrases <note>The Targums, which are ancient Aramaic translations and interpretations of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, as noted by lexicographers. <margin>Chapter 34, 8.</margin> In *Jeremiah* you have: *And those Pastors fed themselves, but they did not feed my people.* <note>original: ופרנסו פרנסיא ית נפשיהון וית עמי לא פרנסו</note> <margin>Chapter 34, 23.</margin> In *Ezekiel*: *He himself shall feed them, He himself shall be to them for a* **PASTOR.** <note>original: ויתן יפרנס יתהון, הוא יהי להון לפרנס</note>

I omit the rest. The most learned *Casaubon* <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614) was a renowned classical scholar and philologist.</note> observed in his elegant notes on *Persius* that the name of Mount **PARNASSUS** is derived from this very word *Parnas* <note>original: פרנס</note>, taken in this meaning. He says that the Greek Grammarians are talking nonsense when they claim **PARNASSUS** was called that as if it were *Larnassus*, because the *larnax*—that is, the ark—of the Flood had come to rest on that mountain. We have said elsewhere that *both Boeotia and most of the neighboring places in Phocis were founded by Cadmus and other Phoenicians or Syrians.* Even if *Plutarch* and other historians had remained silent on this matter, the names themselves would provide clear evidence. The name of this mountain comes from that origin. *Parnas* to the Syrians is *to pasture* <note>original Greek: νέμειν</note> and *Parnasin* <note>original: פרנסין</note> are <term>Pastors</term> <note>In the Jewish tradition, the *Parnas* was a communal leader responsible for the physical and spiritual "feeding" or maintenance of the congregation.</note>. Hence *Parnassus* is "the pastures" <note>original Greek: αἱ νομαί</note>. They called the mountain this because it was where they pastured their flocks. <margin>On Sacred Animals, Book 2, chapter 44.</margin> *Samuel Bochart* <note>A French scholar (1599–1667) famous for his work on biblical geography and zoology.</note> confirmed Casaubon's conjecture as most certain when he proved from various documents that Mount *Parnassus* is extremely abundant in grass. <margin>Delphi Phoenicians, page 8, section 2.</margin> Indeed, I am not unaware that *Dickinson* <note>Edmund Dickinson (1624–1707) was an English physician and orientalist.</note> brings forward another etymology for this famous rock of **PARNASSUS** (namely from *Perets* <note>original: פרץ</note> and *Vachash* <note>original: וחש</note>, as if you were to say, *the chasm of Divinations*), but anyone who weighs it with judgment and compares it with the preceding one will undoubtedly prefer the former over this far-fetched and poorly sounding one.

Thus the *first* meaning of this word is certainly established; but what, I ask, is its origin? I once toyed with this idea in my mind, that...

# ON THE NAMES OF THE OVERSEERS, BOOK III. PART I.

The word *Parnas* <note>original Hebrew/Syriac: פרנס</note> perhaps descends from *Paras* <note>original Hebrew: פרס, meaning "to divide" or "to break"</note> by the insertion of the letter *N* <note>the Hebrew letter Nun (נ)</note> to create a weightier and more elegant pronunciation of the word. Since the sound of the letter *N* is soft, simple, easy, and delicate, the Syrians—a people devoted to pleasant sounds—have loved it in every age. It is for this reason that they terminate the final letter of masculine plural words with an *N* <note>the suffix -in</note>, whereas the Hebrews use an *M* <note>the suffix -im</note>. It is also why they explain the Hebrew *Dagesh* <note>a diacritic mark indicating a doubled consonant</note> through the use of an *N*. Thus, where the Hebrews say *attah* <note>original: אתּה, meaning "you"</note>, the Syrians pronounce it *antah* <note>original: אנתּה</note>. Furthermore, they reduce the weightier and coarser letters found in other languages to an *N* in their own tongue. So it is that the Greeks' *psalterion* <note>original Greek: ψαλτήριον, a stringed instrument</note> is expressed by them as *psanterin* <note>original: פסנתרין</note>. And from this, I thought it came to pass that they inserted the letter *N* into the word *Paras* <note>פרס</note> after the letter *P* <note>פ</note>. I might even say that the nature of the letter *N* demanded this in some way, as it does not strike the ears as strongly in *Paras* as it does in *Parnas*. I believe something of this sort also occurred in the word *Parnak* <note>original: פרנק</note>, which signifies a small piece of cloth or a rag. I have no doubt that this was related to a foreign root *Parnak* by the most learned Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a celebrated Hebraist</note>, when it properly descends from *Parak* <note>original: פרק</note>, meaning "to break"—from which the Dutch word *breecken* <note>to break</note> takes its origin.

As this construction did not seem contrary to the spirit of the language, so too the meaning was not far removed from the word *Paras*. The term *Paras* in a general sense denotes the act of dividing and separating, but among the Ancient Hebrews, it specifically signified *breaking bread at a banquet and distributing it to the other guests.* It is certainly used this way in *Isaiah* in the 
<margin>Chapter 58, 7.</margin>
words: *Is it not by* DISTRIBUTING <note>original Latin: DISTRIBUENDO; Hebrew: פרוס</note> *your bread to the hungry?* David Kimchi <note>A famous medieval rabbi and grammarian, often called the RaDak (1160–1235).</note> says in his Commentaries: *This "distribution" is the "breaking" of bread, well-known in the words of our Masters (of blessed memory) in the sense of dividing a loaf: One says the blessing and afterward breaks the bread, etc.* But we must not omit the Chaldean paraphrase <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation/interpretation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, which is even more notable here. For in this passage, the Paraphrast translates *Paras* as *Parnas*, as if pointing a finger to show that *Parnas* arose from *Paras*. It says: *Will you not* FEED <note>original Latin: pasces; Aramaic: תפרנס</note> *the hungry with your bread?* The Seventy <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> use the word *didomi* <note>original Greek: δίδωμι, meaning "I give"</note> here, perhaps having regard to a similar passage in 
<margin>Chapter 18, 7.</margin>
Ezekiel: *He will give his bread to the hungry.* Otherwise, you would say a *perusah* <note>original: פרוסה, a slice or portion</note> for the hungry or for the poor, which is a familiar expression in the writings of the Hebrews, as Kimchi himself noted in his *Lexicon*.

### CHAPTER 2. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.
