Nor is this version of the Elders <note>the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> to be blamed. For among the ancients, those who broke the bread would give it, broken and divided, to the other guests. You find both actions in the Gospel according to Matthew: *While they were eating, Jesus took bread, and when he had blessed it, he broke it and gave it to the disciples* <note>original Greek: ἔκλασε καὶ ἐδίδου τοῖς μαθηταῖς; Latin: FREGIT & DEDIT discipulis</note>. From this, the "breaking of bread" <note>original Greek: κλάσις τοῦ ἄρτου</note> was taken to represent the entire Banquet in the writings of Luke. Indeed, there is another passage in the Prophecies of Jeremiah which seems to support our conjecture: *Neither shall men break bread for them in mourning, to comfort them for the dead* <note>original Hebrew: ולא פרסו להם על אבל לנחמם על מת</note>. The Septuagint translates this as: *And bread shall not be broken in their mourning for consolation over the deceased* <note>original Greek: Και ου μη κλασθη αρτος εν πενθει αυτων εις παρακλησιν επι τεθνηκοτος</note>. For "to them" <note>original Hebrew: lahem</note>, they read "bread" <note>original Hebrew: lechem</note>. The meaning is this: so great will be the calamity of that time that no food will be distributed even to the mourners to refresh their spirits. The following words also illustrate this thought: *Neither shall they give them the cup of consolation to drink for their father or their mother* <note>original Hebrew: ולא ישקו אותם כוס תנחומים על אביו ועל אמו</note>. For it seems to me that we must conclude from these words that the ancient Hebrews instituted funeral feasts after the burial of the deceased for the consolation of the mourners. Jerome seems to have believed the same thing. Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a prominent medieval Jewish scholar and grammarian</note> certainly reports in his *Book of Roots* that this was the opinion of nearly all the ancients regarding this passage, although he himself takes a different view. He says: *The commentators explain "they shall not distribute to them" as "they shall not distribute in mourning," just as they distribute to a grieving person and break bread for him to revive him* <note>original Hebrew: המפר׳ פירשו ולא יפרסו להם לא יפרשו על אבל כמו שפורסים לאכל והבצעם לו הלחם שמברין אותו</note>. Since, indeed, the one who distributes bread to the family *nourishes and feeds* them by this very act, it seems to me that the word *Parnas* <note>original Hebrew/Syriac: פרנס</note> gradually acquired that meaning of *feeding* or *providing* which it now possesses.

<margin>
In *Ir David* ("City of David"), or on the *Agreement of Rabbinic words with Greek*, at this passage.
</margin>
Such was my view for a long time. However, I should not hide that the most learned man, David Cohen de Lara <note>a 17th-century Sephardic scholar known for connecting Rabbinic Hebrew with Greek and Latin</note>, derives the word *Parnas*—which in the Chaldean Paraphrase <note>the Targum</note> signifies "Food and Nourishment"—from the Greek word *pyrnos* <note>original Greek: πύρνος</note>, which is accepted with the same meaning. Suidas <note>a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> defines *pyrnos* as "the broken piece of bread" <note>original Greek: τὸ ἀπόκλασμα τοῦ ἄρτου</note>. Hesychius says the same. Furthermore, according to the lexicographers, *pyrnos* comes from *pyrinos* ("wheaten"), which in turn is derived from *pyros* ("wheat"). If this is the case, I would not wish to object; the word *Parnas* could be traced back to this very Greek word *pyrnos* and derive its meaning from there.

### CHAPTER 2. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

This Governance is Spiritual: it concerns souls, rather than bodies. Furthermore, *shepherding* is explicitly related by Peter to the *flock* <note>original Greek: ποίμνιον (*poimnion*)</note>. But since the faithful are called a *flock* not in a literal sense, but metaphorically, it is clear that the word *to shepherd* must also be explained not literally, but metaphorically, as the Pasturing and Governance of souls. Again: the Elders <note>original Latin: *Presbyteri*</note> of the Church are called *shepherds* by Peter in the same sense that Christ the Lord, in that same context, is called the *CHIEF SHEPHERD* <note>original Greek: ἀρχιποίμην (*archipoimen*)</note>.

<margin>verse 4.</margin> Now, Christ the Lord is certainly not called the Chief Shepherd with respect to Alms or Ecclesiastical estates—which the illustrious Dodwell understands by the word *inheritance* <note>original Greek: κλῆρος (*kleros*); often translated as "lot" or "heritage"</note>—but because the supreme Governance of the entire Church has been committed to Him. And how cold and lifeless, I ask, would Paul's speech become if you were to understand the "Shepherds" in the Epistle to the Ephesians <margin>Chapter 4, 11.</margin> as merely Collectors of Alms or Managers of the Church's temporal goods? For what gift can we consider more excellent or more becoming of Christ the King to bestow upon mortals: to feed bodies and administer temporal goods, or to nourish and direct the minds of men? Certainly, while the former is not to be despised, the latter is to be far preferred over the former. Not to mention that *to shepherd* is elsewhere attributed to the Elders of the Church in such a way that we are entirely certain that the direction, guidance, and care <margin>Acts 20, 28.</margin> of the souls of believers—which is a Spiritual pasturing—is indicated by it. We are not ignorant, of course, that the Management of Alms and temporal goods was not neglected by the Bishops of the early Church—a matter we shall explain in what follows, *with God's help* <note>original Latin: σὺν Θεῷ (*syn Theo*)</note>—but we rightly deny that this was the true or even the primary reason why Bishops or Elders were called Shepherds.

Indeed, it is certain and placed beyond doubt that the word <term>Parnas</term> <note>Hebrew: פַּרְנֵס; a provider or sustainer</note>, besides the primary and ordinary meaning it has of "feeding," most commonly denotes among the Jews a *Leader*, *Prefect*, *Governor*, or *Rector* of any kind. Philippus Aquinas <note>A 17th-century scholar and converted rabbi who authored a Hebrew-Aramaic-Latin dictionary</note> states: *A Parnas is a leader and a shepherd of men, who has some authority over them, and they listen to his voice.* <gloss>original Hebrew: פַּרְנֵס הַמַּנְהִיג והרועה בני אדם ויש לו ממשלה מה עליהם ושומעים לקולו</gloss>

### ON THE NAMES OF THE PREFECTS, BOOK III, PART I.

**PARNAS** is the kind of man who leads and feeds people, who possesses a certain authority over them, and whose voice they obey. This word is undoubtedly understood in this way in that common proverb:

> <note>original Hebrew: כשנתמנה אדם פרנס מלמטה נקרא רשע מלמעלה</note>
> *When a man is appointed as a* **SHEPHERD** <note>original: *Parnas*</note> *here below, he is called wicked above.*

By this saying, they hinted that Prefectures and High Offices are dangerous for a just and good man, since they are hardly conducted without falling into sin. And thus also the *word* **Parnas** is used more than once in the *Seder Olam* <note>The *Seder Olam Rabbah* is a 2nd-century CE Hebrew chronology detailing history from the creation to the Bar Kokhba revolt.</note>, for example:

<margin>Chapter 12.</margin>

# CHAPTER 2. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

"A *Parnas* <note>original Hebrew: פרנס, a community leader or provider</note> appointed over the community." Our teachers <note>original Latin: *Doctores nostri*</note> generally understand the term **PASTOR** to mean the **PREFECT OF THE SYNAGOGUE**. This is exactly what we intended to show. For if those men who were appointed to rule the assembly (especially those living in exile <note>original Hebrew: בגלות, *ba-galut*</note>) were called "Pastors" by the Jews, there is no doubt that the Apostles, in attributing this same name to the leaders of the early Church, borrowed it from the Synagogue.

However, a difficulty arises here that must be resolved, which easily occurs to anyone reflecting on how this name is used in the synagogues of our own time. In the preceding pages, we have proposed that the *governance of the early Church* was modeled after the *governance of the Synagogue*, which consisted of several learned men promoted to that dignity through the <term>Laying on of Hands</term> <note>original Latin: *Manuum Impositione*, a ritual of ordination</note>. Yet, the synagogues of this time are indeed governed by several **Pastors** <note>original Hebrew: פרנסים, *Parnasim*</note>, but they are men more celebrated among their countrymen for their wealth, nobility, and authority than for their wisdom and learning. They constitute a *political* or civil council rather than an *ecclesiastical* one; they leave the legal jurisdiction and instruction of the congregation to other judges and teachers; and finally, they step down from their office each year, handing it over to others who succeed them through new elections. Certainly, these "Pastors" are very different from those Pastors of the early Church whom we have described. 

This is indeed how things stand if modern leaders represent those ancient ones (who shared the same name) in every respect. But I hold quite the opposite view. For although the meaning of the name *Parnas* <note>original Hebrew: פרנס</note>—by its etymology and common use—is so broad and flexible that it can be applied without hesitation to any leaders or teachers of a multitude, and is thus not out of place when applied today to any kind of moderators and leaders of Jewish assemblies, I believe that in former times it was primarily attributed to those directors of the community who excelled not so much in lineage and wealth as in learning. They were recognized as learned and literate men, fit for both Judging and Teaching. Even if it is not in my power to prove this with explicit Hebrew testimonies, I have various points that support my opinion, which I will now present in due order.

To this end, it first seems relevant to consider a passage I noted from

-># ON THE NAMES OF THE PREFECTS BOOK III. PART I.<-

The *Beginning of Wisdom* <note>original Hebrew: *Reschit Chochma*, a 16th-century moralistic text</note>, taken from the admonitions of *Resh Lakish* <note>Rabbi Simeon ben Lakish, a 3rd-century sage</note>—which I wish I could reread now, but I do not have the book at hand—contains these words: <margin>Chapter 3.</margin> "But if he is not learned enough to read the Scriptures or repeat the Traditions, what shall he do that he may live? Let him go and establish himself as a **PASTOR** over the **COMMUNITY**." <note>original Hebrew: *Parnas al ha-tzibur*</note>. 

Certainly, if I understand the meaning of this passage correctly, it suggests that one who is personally unfit for reading the Scriptures or the Traditions can compensate for this deficiency by appointing a **Pastor** over the Synagogue along with others—specifically, one who can explain the Scriptures and Traditions. This would indicate that in former times, a **Pastor** was considered a **Learned Man** who was capable of expounding on the Law.

A saying of similar weight occurs to me in the *Master of Rows* <note>original Hebrew: *Baal Turim*, the famous commentary by Jacob ben Asher</note> regarding Numbers 14:19, where the prayers of Moses for the rebellious people are recorded. This tacitly implies that the duty of the <term>Parnas</term> <note>the Hebrew term for a community leader or provider</note> is to **pray for the assembly**. The words are these: "This is what they say: **TWO GOOD PASTORS** arose for Israel, Moses and David, **WHO KNEW HOW TO PRAY FOR THEM.**" <margin>In the Talmud, tractate *Taanith*, folio 9.</margin> 

Elsewhere, they make mention of **THREE GOOD PASTORS**: "Three **GOOD PASTORS** stood forth for Israel: Moses, Aaron, and Miriam." <margin>Chapters 10, 11.</margin> One may notice here the phrase **GOOD PASTOR** <note>original Hebrew: *Parnas Tov*</note>, which was used by our Lord regarding Himself in the Gospel of Saint John: <margin>There is likewise a clear mention of the "Good Pastor" in the Talmud, tractate *Berachoth*, folio 55, column 1, after the middle.</margin> "**I am the good shepherd; the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.**" <note>original Greek: Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός...</note> 

Indeed, if the opinion cited from the *Master of Rows* is of such antiquity, why should we not say that our Lord was contrasting and comparing Himself to Moses and David, who were commonly called "Good Pastors" by the Jews? We say this without denying that there is also a reference here to that **PASTOR** who was promised by God to the Israelites in the books of Ezekiel, Hosea, and Zechariah.

Furthermore, *Jarchius* <note>Rabbi Solomon Isaac, better known as Rashi</note> implies elsewhere that the office of the **Pastors** is to **admonish** the people and urge them toward **repentance**. He writes: <margin>On Isaiah, chapter 56, verse 10.</margin> "Their Pastors are like the blind, all of them; they do not see what is coming, like a watchman appointed to see the sword approaching and warn the people, yet he is too blind to see the sword and too mute to warn the people—like a dog appointed to guard the house who is too mute to bark. So are the Pastors of Israel; they are not..."

# CHAPTER 2. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

...they do not warn them to return to the right path. <note>original Hebrew: *einam mazhirin otam lachzor le-mutav*</note> **All of their PASTORS** (**Governors**) **are like the blind, because they do not pay attention to the things that are happening. They are like a watchman stationed to see coming destruction and to pre-warn the people about it, but who is blind, so that he does not see the destruction approaching, and mute, so that he cannot warn his people. Like a dog appointed to guard a house, who is mute so that he cannot bark—as Hylax on the threshold** <margin>Virgil, *Eclogues* 8</margin> <note>Hylax is the name of a dog in Virgil's poetry; the author uses this classical reference to illustrate a "silent watchdog."</note>—**so the PASTORS OF ISRAEL do not urge the people to change themselves for the better.** And thus we have shown that almost all parts of the office of the Teachers of the Synagogue are attributed to the <term>Parnasim</term> <note>the Hebrew term for community leaders or "providers"</note>, the Pastors. From this, we conclude not without reason that the <term>Parnasim</term> anciently designated learned and pious men who were employed in offering prayers, giving exhortations to the people, and explaining the Holy Scriptures.

Let us take another example of that ancient meaning of this word from the fact that both the Talmudic and other writers are accustomed to distinguish by the name of **Pastors** those who are well known to be celebrated among them for their learning and sanctity of life. So it is said in Micah: <margin>Chapter 5:5</margin> "And we will raise up against him seven shepherds" <note>original Hebrew: *ve-hakimonu alav shivah ro'im*</note>, which they explain in the tractate *Sukkah*, as mentioned by Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, also known as Radak, a medieval biblical commentator</note>: **Who are these SEVEN PASTORS? David in the middle; Adam, Seth, and Methuselah at his right; Abraham, Jacob, and Moses at his left.** <note>original Hebrew: *Man ninhu sheva ro'im...*</note> Wherever the ancient Jews may have obtained this exposition—which Solomon Jarchi <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator</note> confesses he does not know—it is nevertheless clear that they themselves designate by the name of <term>Parnasim</term> those whom they otherwise proclaim to be the Rectors of the Academies, or those certain to have excelled in knowledge and holiness. In addition to this, it should be observed that the determination of doubtful opinions is ascribed to the <term>Parnasim**, the Pastors; since this properly belongs to the Rectors of the Synagogues, they most certainly seem to be understood by the term <term>Parnasim</term>. We take an example of this from the book *Kol Bo* <note>a 13th-century collection of Jewish laws</note>, in which, when the disputes of the Masters regarding a doubtful matter occur, it is finally said: <margin>Chapter 55</margin> **For thus the PASTORS of the first generation of Israel preached**, and so forth. <note>original Hebrew: *she-kach amru parnesei ha-dor ha-rishon...*</note> And in this same way I understand what is found in Rabbi Meir in the *Apod. Kodesh* <note>likely *Avodat HaKodesh* by Meir ibn Gabbai, a 16th-century Kabbalist</note>: <margin>Part 3, Chapter 23</margin> **All differences of opinion and conflicting views were given by one God and spoken by one Pastor.** <note>original Hebrew: *kol chilukei ha-deot... El echad natnan u-parnas echad amran*</note>

### ON THE NAMES OF THE OVERSEERS BOOK III. PART I.

...[re]igning, one God gave, and one PASTOR spoke forth. <note>The text likely concludes a citation from the previous page regarding Ecclesiastes 12:11, "given from one shepherd."</note> God is here called *Pastor* with respect to the pronunciation of a sentence regarding the heads of religion. Indeed, the <term>Parnasim</term> <note>Hebrew for community leaders or providers; here equated with pastors</note> are also joined with the <term>Chachamim</term> <note>Hebrew for "wise men" or Sages</note>, whose task it was to terminate theological controversies.

<margin>See *Seder Olam Rabba*, p. 15. <note>A 2nd-century CE Hebrew-language chronology.</note></margin>
So in the *Sepher Toledoth Adam* <note>The Book of the Generations of Adam</note> it is recorded that God showed the first man, among other things, **"Each and every generation and its Sages and its PASTORS."** <note>original Hebrew: *dor va-dor ve-chachamav ve-parnasav*</note> I will only add that this very word *Parnasim* is applied also to **Judges**, who ought to be learned and practiced men. The passage already cited by us above does not need to be repeated here.

Indeed, even clearer proofs of this hypothesis remain for me. In the Tractate *Taanith* <note>A volume of the Talmud dealing with fast days</note>, where in the *Mishna* <note>The foundational legal text of Rabbinic Judaism</note> there is mention of a **Fast** of the <term>Iechidim</term> <note>Hebrew for "individuals" or "distinguished ones"</note>, the writers of the Gemara <note>The commentary on the Mishna</note> strive to define who is to be understood as a "Singular Person," and how much he differs from a <term>Talmid</term> <note>a student or disciple</note>, or a "Learned Man," simply so-called. They define a "Singular Person" as one who is worthy to be appointed as a <term>Parnas</term> (PASTOR) over the Synagogue.

<margin>Codex *Taanith*, folio 10, column 1, at the beginning.</margin>
> Our Rabbis taught: Let no man say, "I am a DISCIPLE, I am not worthy to be considered a SINGULAR PERSON." Rather, all DISCIPLES of the SAGES are SINGULAR PERSONS. Who is a SINGULAR PERSON, and who is a DISCIPLE? A Singular Person is anyone worthy to be appointed as a PASTOR over the community; a Disciple is anyone who, when they ask him about a matter of Jewish Law <note>original: *Halakha*</note> in his studies, can answer it—even if it is regarding the Tractate *Kallah*. <note>A minor tractate of the Talmud; the author implies that a Disciple must at least know the basics of his curriculum to hold the title.</note>

The meaning of these words is clear: a "Singular Person" (<term>Iechidim</term>) is distinguished by that name from a "Disciple" because his **Learning** excels that of other disciples, and thus he is fit to administer the Office or Pastorship of the Synagogue. From this, it is most clearly evident that in order for someone to be a Pastor of the Synagogue, it was formerly most required that he excel in **Learning** and erudition among his peers, and thus

### CHAPTER 2. OF THE SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

...so much so that he is adorned with the title of **Teacher** <note>Latin: *Doctor*</note> among them. This proof will become even more evident if we compare what is read concerning this same argument in column 1 of folio 114 of the 
<margin>Tractate *Sabbath*, folio 114 (not 104, as found in Lightfoot), column 1.</margin>
Tractate *Sabbath*: "And Rabbi Yochanan said: Who is that **Wise Disciple** <note>Hebrew: *Talmid Chacham*</note> whom they appoint as a **Pastor** <note>Hebrew: *Parnas*</note> over the community? He whom they ask concerning a matter of Law in every place and he answers, even in the **Tractate of the Bride** <note>Hebrew: *Massekhet Kallah*; a minor tractate of the Talmud often considered obscure or difficult, thus serving as a test of deep knowledge.</note>." **Who is the Wise Disciple** (**Learned man or Teacher**) **whom they set over as a Pastor of the Synagogue? He whom they ask concerning a decree of Hebrew Law in every place, and who is ready to answer regarding it, even in the Code of the Bride.** The most learned Lightfoot, who noted both these 
<margin>Lightfoot's Commentary on Luke 2:45.</margin>
passages elsewhere, punctuated and divided the latter poorly in his version when he translated it thus: *Who is the disciple of the wise? He whom they set over as the Pastor of the Synagogue: he who, if they ask him about tradition, has an answer in any place.* Anyone can see that these parts do not fit together well. For what does that double "he" mean? The first part of the context should be translated thus: **Who is that Wise Disciple whom they appoint as the Pastor of the Synagogue?** Then it is answered: **He who is fit to respond to all doubtful cases of Hebrew Law.** Indeed (as is supposed here), there are various degrees of those called **Wise Men** <note>Hebrew: *Talmidei Chachamim*, literally "disciples of the wise."</note>. The question in this passage is to what degree of learning such a "Disciple of a Wise Man" must have advanced to be appointed as a **Pastor** of the synagogue. This is then answered in what follows. In the same way, the following words should be punctuated and divided: **Who is that learned Disciple for whose work his fellow citizens are obligated to perform? He who, having set aside his own desires, is intent on fulfilling the will of God.** It is certainly clear from the cited words that such a Learned Man is only to be adorned with the **title and office of Pastor** if he is most skilled in Jewish Law and extremely quick in answering. We pass over the difficulties raised and resolved in the *Tosaphoth* <note>Medieval Hebrew commentaries on the Talmud that often harmonize conflicting passages.</note> regarding the comparison of this text with the one in the Tractate *Taanith*, as they do not significantly serve our purpose. Let us only ensure that we do not deny Lightfoot the praise he deserves here. For he, having explained the words "Disciple" and "Individual," added this: **I seem to see here some shadow of Pastors and Teachers** <note>original Greek: *poimenōn kai didaskalōn*, a reference to Ephesians 4:11</note>...

### CHAPTER 3. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

...is not infrequently attributed to Christian [leaders], and is commonly compared with the two preceding terms [Elder and Pastor]. This is certainly the case in the speech of Paul, already mentioned several times, addressed to the
<margin>Acts 20:28.</margin>
**ELDERS** <note>Latin: *Presbyteros*</note> of the Ephesian Church: *Take heed therefore to yourselves, and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you as* **OVERSEERS** <note>original Greek: *episkopous*</note>, *to* **SHEPHERD** *the Church of God, etc.* Likewise, in the words of Peter, speaking to the
<margin>1 Peter 5:2.</margin>
**Elders** in this manner: **SHEPHERD** *the flock of God which is among you, exercising* **OVERSIGHT** <note>original Greek: *episkopountes*</note>, *attending to its care, or performing the duty of a Prefect and Curator, not by compulsion, but willingly.* Therefore, it will be useful to investigate the true meaning of that word, which we shall most conveniently achieve by this method: 1. By indicating its use among Greek writers. 2. By investigating its origin from the Ancient Synagogue.

No one reading Greek doubts that the word **Overseer** <note>original Greek: *Episkopos*</note> is derived from *to inspect* or *to attend to* <note>Greek: *episkopein*</note>; and this in turn from *to visit* and *to look at* <note>Greek: *episkeptesthai* and *skeptesthai*</note>, words of similar meaning. An **Overseer** <note>Greek: *Episkopos*</note> is therefore an **Inspector** in Latin; while among the Greeks, according to the lexicographer Hesychius, he is a **listener**, a **guardian**, an **observer**, or a **surveyor** <note>Greek: *epēkoos, phylax, epoptēs, metaskopos*</note>. In my judgment, Hesychius is referring to the Athenian **Overseers** <note>Greek: *episkopous*</note>, whom Suidas describes in this way: *Those sent by the Athenians to subject cities to inspect the affairs of each were called* **Overseers** <note>Greek: *episkopoi*</note> *and* **Guardians** <note>Greek: *phylakes*</note>; *whom the Spartans called* **Governors** <note>Greek: *harmostas*</note>. Those who were sent by the Athenians into subject cities to inspect what was being done by each were called **OVERSEERS**, **Inspectors**, and **Guardians** (note the same words used by Hesychius), **Custodians, whom the Spartans called** **Governors** <note>original Greek: *harmostai*, literally "orderers" or "compositors"</note>. Suidas speaks clearly enough when he compares the Athenian Overseers with the "Harmosts" of the ancient Spartans. For it is well known that **Harmosts** were the Moderators of provinces or cities: *The leaders who were sent by the Spartans into the cities subject to them,* as the same Suidas says elsewhere. Indeed, there was another Spartan magistrate who, in name at least, clearly corresponded to these Overseers: namely, those five most famous **Ephors** instituted by King Theopompus. For the commentator on Thucydides teaches us that they were called **Ephors** <note>Greek: *ephoroi*</note> *because they oversaw the affairs of the city.* See, if you please, Cragius and Meursius <note>Niels Krag and Johannes Meursius, 16th/17th-century scholars who wrote on Spartan history</note>, who wrote about Spartan affairs. Nor should we omit here the **Suffetes** <note>The chief magistrates of Carthage, similar to Roman Consuls</note>, the highest magistrates of the Carthaginians, whom *Livy* mentions several times. They are
<margin>book 28, chapter 37; book 39, chapter 60.</margin>

### CHAPTER 3. OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

...is not rarely attributed to the Christian church, and it is everywhere compared with the two preceding terms. This certainly occurs in the speech of Paul, *already frequently mentioned*, to the ELDERS of the Church at Ephesus: <margin>Acts 20:28.</margin> *Take heed therefore to yourselves*, Acts 20:28, *and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you overseers* <note>original Greek: ἐν ᾧ ὑμᾶς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἔθετο ἐπισκόπους</note>, in which that Holy Spirit appointed you OVERSEERS, TO FEED <note>original Latin: *ad pascendum*; literally, to shepherd or pasture</note> the Church of God, etc. Likewise in the words of Peter, speaking to the *Elders* in this manner: <margin>1 Peter 5:2.</margin> FEED *the flock of God, which is among you, overseeing it* <note>original Greek: ἐπισκοποῦντες</note>, *DEVOTING THEMSELVES TO ITS CARE*, or *carrying out the duty of a Prefect and Curator, not by compulsion, but willingly*. Therefore, it will be useful to investigate its true meaning, which we shall most conveniently achieve in this way: 1. If we indicate its use among Greek writers. 2. If we investigate its origin from the Ancient Synagogue.

That the word <term>Episcopus</term> <note>often translated as Bishop, but literally meaning "Overseer"</note> is derived from *episkopein* (*to inspect, to attend to*), and this in turn from *episkeptesthai* and *skeptesthai* (words of similar meaning), no reader of Greek doubts. The *Episcopus* is therefore what the Latins call an *Inspector*: and to the Greeks, an *overseer, a guard, a supervisor, or a scout* <note>original Greek terms: ἐπήκοος, φύλαξ, ἐπόπτης, μετάσκοπος</note>, according to the interpreter Hesychius <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian who compiled a famous dictionary of obscure words</note>. In my judgment, Hesychius is referring to the Attic <term>Episcopi</term> <note>officials from Athens</note>, whom Suidas <note>The author of the Suda, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> describes in this way: *Those sent by the Athenians into subject cities to inspect the affairs of each were called overseers and guards; whom the Spartans called Harmosts. Those who were sent by the Athenians into subject cities to inspect what was being done by each were called* <term>Episcopi</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπίσκοποι</note>, *INSPECTORS, and* <term>Phylakes</term> <note>original Greek: φύλακες; note the same words used by Hesychius</note> *Guards, whom the Lacedæmonians <note>Spartans</note> called* <term>Harmostai</term> <note>original Greek: ἁρμοσταὶ</note>, *Compositors*. Suidas speaks clearly enough when he compares the Attic Overseers with the Harmosts of the ancient Spartans. For it is established that the *Harmosts* were the Governors of Provinces or Cities, *the rulers sent by the Lacedæmonians into subject cities*, as the same Suidas says elsewhere. ### ON THE NAMES OF THE PREFECTS BOOK III. PART I.

Indeed, I confess, there are those who wish that word <note>Referring to the Carthaginian title *Suffetes*</note> to be formed from the Hebrew *Shophetim* <note>original: שופטים; meaning "Judges"</note>, with the Punic pronunciation only slightly altered; however, the most excellent of Learned Men follow *Joseph Scaliger*, who in his observations on *Festus* derives the word *Suffes* from *Tsaphah* <note>original: צפה</note>, *Isuffe*, or *Suffe*, which means a *speculator* <note>in the sense of an observer or watchman</note> (for *Tsaphah* signifies "to watch" among the Eastern peoples, from whom the Carthaginians originated), just as *Ephorus*, *Episcopus*, *Epoptes*, and <term>skopos</term> <note>original: σκοπὸς; a lookout or scout</note>. Therefore, they are the same as the *Tzophim* <note>original: צופים; watchmen</note>, who are <term>episkopoi</term> <note>original: ἐπίσκοποι; overseers</note>, <term>ephoroi</term> <note>original: ἔφοροι; guardians or overseers</note>, *Inspectors*, *Moderators*, and *Rulers* of peoples. The word <term>epoptes</term> <note>original: ἐπόπτης; an overseer or eyewitness</note> is used with the same meaning. For although it commonly denotes to the Greeks one who, after a full initiation, is allowed to look into the *mysteries* <note>original: μυστήρια; the secret rites of ancient Greek religion</note> themselves, nonetheless it not rarely signifies the Curator of a work, whether sacred or civil. Pollux <note>A 2nd-century Greek grammarian</note> says: *Managers of games, ephoroi, epoptai, leaders, and episkopoi.*

<margin>Book 2. Against Apion.</margin>
But there is an elegant passage on this in Josephus, in his books *Against Apion*, concerning the Priests:
> For these men, there was a strict care both of the law and of other pursuits; for the priests were appointed as *INSPECTORS* of all things, and *Judges* of disputed matters, and *Punishers* of those who had been condemned. <note>original Greek: Τούτοις δ' ἦν καὶ τὠνόμῳ καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἐπιτηδευμάτων ἀκριβὴς ἐπιμέλεια: καὶ γὰρ ἐπόπται πάντων καὶ δικασταὶ τῶν ἀμβισβητεμένων, καὶ κολασαὶ τῶν κατεγνωσμένων οἱ ἱερεῖς ἐτάχθησαν;</note>

What has been said so far regarding the word <term>episkopos</term> <note>overseer</note> itself, as well as its related terms through which it is explained by Hesychius <note>A 5th-century lexicographer</note>, tends chiefly toward this point: that *Episcope* <note>oversight</note> and *episkopein* <note>to oversee</note> ordinarily denote a type of *Inspection* that is joined with Governance and Prefecture. Thus, <term>episkopoi</term>, by the force of this word’s ordinary meaning, are distinguished from the lowlier ministries, to which even themselves some *care and inspection* of certain things is sometimes committed; these are called by the Greeks <term>speculatores</term> <note>original: σπεκουλάτορες; scouts or military spies</note>, *diopteres* <note>watchers</note>, *diangeloi* <note>messengers</note>, *dioptai* <note>observers</note>, or *ereunetai* <note>investigators</note>, as observed elsewhere by Casaubon and Salmasius <note>Prominent 16th and 17th-century scholars</note>.

<margin>On Suetonius' life of Caligula. On Spartianus' life of Hadrian.</margin>
Ordinarily, I say. For I would not support an absolute denial that the word is also used for lowlier ministries, who merely *attend* to what others do, and report it to the supreme power. Certainly, a clear example of this meaning occurs to me in Josephus, when he records with what great solicitude and anxiety *King Herod* observed the Jews (from whom he expected no good for himself), and how he inquired into their opinions and conversations about him.

<margin>Antiquities book 15. chapter 13. p. m. 541.</margin>

> *They were stationed both in the city and along the roads, who*

### CHAPTER 3. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

...who should ATTEND to those who gathered for this purpose, or observe them. So, it is by no means universally true what <margin>In the Scholia on the Epistles of Jerome to Evagrius, Epistle Volume 2, folio 117, column 4.</margin> Erasmus noted elsewhere:
> "To oversee [*Episkopein*] <note>original: Ἐπιſκοπεῖν</note> is not to inspect for the sake of knowing—which is what that word signifies to the Latins—but to watch over so that you may provide for necessary things."

On the contrary, to oversee [*episkopein*] in the passage we quoted from Josephus is precisely to inspect for the sake of knowing. I concede, however—indeed, I have already conceded—that it commonly holds among the Greeks that an "overseer" [*episkopos*] <note>original: ἐπίſκοπος</note> signifies that kind of Inspector and Curator who is simultaneously a Prefect and Ruler. In this sense, Herodian very elegantly called God <margin>Book 7, chapter 10.</margin> the "witness and overseer [*episkopos*] of things done," the WITNESS and INSPECTOR of those things carried out among men. And King Antiochus in the <margin>Book 1, chapter 1, 55.</margin> Books of Maccabees is said to have appointed overseers [*episkopoi*] over all the people, INSPECTORS over the whole people. Nor does this word embrace any other meaning when it is used by the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> or the writers of the New Covenant <note>The New Testament.</note>, for whom an overseer [*episkopos*] is a Prefect or Curator, and overseeing [*episkope*] <note>original: ἐπιſκοπὴ</note> is a Prefecture. Thus, where Peter—after Judas the Betrayer was removed by a <margin>Acts 1:20</margin> sad fate—exhorts the others to substitute another in his place, and proves at the same time from the Prophecies that this ought to be done: "For it is written," he says, "in the Book of Psalms, *let another take his office* [*episkopen*]"; <note>original: τὴν ἐπιſκοπὴν αὐτοῦ λάβοι ἕτερος</note> that is, let another take his PREFECTURE (the Bishopric of Judas). The Belgians <note>Referring to the Dutch States Translation</note> render this: *Syn Opzienders ampt* <note>original: Dutch; "His overseer's office"</note>.

These words are taken from the version of the Seventy at Psalm 109:8, where the Hebrew context has: *let another take his office* <note>original: פקדתו יקח אחר - Pekudatho yikkach acher</note>, agreeing well enough with the version just related. For indeed, *Pekudah* <note>original: פקודה</note> signifies a Prefecture of any kind in general, and the duty of caring for a thing. Thus in the Book of Numbers: <margin>Chapter 4:16</margin> "And Eleazar, Son of Aaron the Priest, was PREFECT over the oil of the light, etc." The Seventy: "Overseer [*Episkopos*] Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest." Perhaps because they also observed that *Pekudah* is very frequently taken in Sacred Scripture not only for the Prefecture itself, but also for the Prefect, which happens not infrequently in other languages as well. Thus the passage in Isaiah is to be understood: <margin>Chapter 60:17</margin> "And I will make your oversight peace," <note>original: ושמתי פקודתך שלום - Ve-samti pekudatekha shalom</note> that is, I will give you peaceful overseers [*episkopous*]. Again elsewhere: "And the Priest placed oversight [*pekudoth*] over <margin>2 Kings 11:18 (referred to as 1 Reg. in text)</margin> the house of Jehovah," that is, Curators. The Seventy: "and the priest established overseers [*episkopous*] in the house of the Lord." But also the *Pekidim* <note>original: פקידים; officials or overseers</note> are "overseers" [*episkopoi*] to the Seventy...

### ON THE NAMES OF PREFECTS BOOK III. PART I.

**Prefects, Curators.** In Dutch: *Chiefs, Commanders.* <term>epistatai [superintendents]</term>, <term>epitropoi [guardians]</term>, or in Hebrew <term>pakidim [officers]</term> <note>original: פקדים</note>, which would be easy to prove with many documents if they were not already found everywhere in the Lexicons. For our part, we can very easily understand from these why the *Apostleship* is called <term>episkopē [oversight]</term> <note>original: ἐπισκοπὴ</note>; for the <term>apostoloi [apostles]</term> were <term>overseers of the whole church</term> <note>original: ἐπίσκοποι ὅλης τῆς ἐκκλησίας</note>, the *Inspectors and Curators* of the entire Church. Let these remarks suffice concerning the true meaning of the word <term>episkopos [overseer]</term> among Greek authors, both secular and sacred.

Therefore, we must now consider in the second place whether this word <term>episkopos [overseer]</term> derives its origin from the Synagogue, as do the other two terms we have explained. This seems to be the presumption, both because other names of Ecclesiastical discipline conform to those received in the Synagogue, and because this term is very frequently joined with others taken from the Synagogue. Let us search, then, until we find that which is obscure or lost.

However, in his *Annotations* on *Paul’s Epistle to the Philippians*, he explicitly refers the word <term>episkopos</term> to the Hebrew words <term>pakid</term> or <term>pakud</term>. This observation by Grotius is not to be despised, insofar as it is certain that the word <term>episkopos</term> agrees entirely in its power of meaning with the Hebrew <term>pakid</term>, as is most manifest from what has gone before; yet I do not rest in this conclusion, because the term <term>pakid</term>, as far as I know, was not a standard or customary term used within the Synagogue. At the very least, Grotius produced no passage to prove it.

**Memuneh** <note>original: ממונה</note>, the word by which the Hebrews express the very same thing that the Greeks do by their terms: **overseers** <note>original: ἐπίσκοποι</note>, **presidents** <note>original: προεστῶτες</note>, and **leaders** <note>original: προΐστάμενοι</note>. If you wished to render this into **Greek**, you could certainly not translate it more diligently or significantly than by *episkope*. Certainly, the titles **Appointed One** <note>Memuneh</note>, **Pastor** <note>Parnas</note>, **Overseer** <note>Episkopos</note>, and **President** <note>Proestos</note> are of entirely equal value and power in their meaning.

### CHAPTER 3. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

Let us not close this discussion, however, before we have added a word about the title **Leaders** <note>original Greek: ἡγούμενοι (hegoumenoi)</note>, with which Paul twice or thrice designates the Elders, or *Prefects of the Christian Church*, in the Epistle to the Hebrews. <margin>Hebrews 13:17.</margin> "Obey," he says, "your **Leaders**, and submit to them: for they watch for your souls, as those who must give an account." We translate that word as **Leader** <note>original Latin: Ductorem</note>, as it carries a similar emphasis among the Latin writers. Virgil writes:
<margin>Aeneid, book 2, verses 13–14.</margin>
> *Broken by war and repelled by the fates,*
> *the* **Leaders** <note>original: Ductores</note> *of the Greeks.*

Servius <note>A 4th-century grammarian and commentator on Virgil.</note> remarks: "**Leaders** [Ductores] is more resonant than 'Guides' [Duces]: just as one might say 'Ruler of Asia.'" Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a famous Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> attempts to explain this term from the Hebrew word *alluphim* <note>original: אלופים</note>, which he says is used in the Old Testament to designate **Leaders and Princes** of armies or peoples. And it is indeed true what Grotius claims about the meaning of this word. In fact, the word *alluph* <note>original: אלוף</note> is used among the Jews today with the meaning of **Teacher** <note>original: Doctoris</note>, as is clear from other sources and specifically from the title of Abarbanel's book, titled *Miphaloth Elohim* ("The Works of God"). I previously compared this very name **Leaders** <note>original Greek: ἡγούμενοι</note> with the Hebrew word *nagid* <note>original: נגיד</note>, in roughly these words: *The Apostle calls them Teachers, that is,* **negidim** <note>original: נגידים</note>, *or Forerunners.* For in this way, every *Teacher* is at the same time a *Leader*, just as the study of knowledge and the conduct of life is both a *playing field and a path*. The Syriac and Arabic translators indicated this well enough when they translated the word *kathegetes* <note>original Greek: καθηγητὴς</note>, which signifies *Teacher*, as *Leader*. <margin>At Matthew ch. 23:10.</margin> On this passage, Louis de Dieu <note>A Dutch orientalist and theologian.</note> rightly observed that the term *nagid* <note>original: נגיד</note> in the Holy Scriptures is used not only for political Prefects, but also for ecclesiastical ones, just as Azariah is called the *nagid* of the House of Jehovah, or the **Overseer of the House of the Lord**. <margin>2 Chronicles 31:13; 4:4.</margin> Hence even Christ is called our *kathegetes*, our **Teacher**. *Nagid* is a "Leader and Forerunner," or a **Leader** <note>original Greek: ὁ ἡγούμενος</note>, or a **Chief** <note>original Greek: ὁ ἡγεμὼν</note> as seen in Isaiah. And indeed, the title **Leader** <note>original: ἡγούμενος</note>, meaning "Forerunner and Guide," is most fitting for the Elders of the Christian Church, since it is their duty as *Pastors* to lead and govern the flock, not only by teaching well, but also by living blamelessly, <margin>Isocrates, To Nicocles.</margin> which is *to lead the younger ones toward virtue, not only by exhorting them, but also by showing them through their own actions what kind of men good men ought to be.* Thus far I have excerpted my own words. But even though I still maintain that Paul's use of **Leader** <note>original: ἡγούμενος</note> can be compared just as beautifully to the Hebrew *nagid* <note>original: נגיד</note> as to *alluph* <note>original: אלוף</note>, I now believe with better reason that the term **Leaders** <note>original: ἡγούμενοι</note> is entirely...

### BOOK III, PART I: CONCERNING THE NAMES OF THE PREFECTS

...should be referred to the word *Manhig* <note>original Hebrew: מנהיג</note>, which itself signifies both a **LEADER** and a **Governor**, both because there is an exact agreement in the meaning of these two words, and because this title is not unknown to the *Synagogue*. I happen to find this word used in a very general sense by *Abarbanel* <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century Jewish statesman and philosopher.</note>, in his commentary on the *Third Chapter of Isaiah*, with these words:

<margin>Commentary on Isaiah 3:1</margin>
> The general intention in this prophecy is to predict the punishments of the children of Judah and Jerusalem for two crimes for which they were held guilty: the first being the wickedness of the **LEADERS** <note>original Hebrew: המנהיגים (ha-manhigim)</note>, and the second the haughtiness of the tranquil women, etc.

*The general intent of this prophecy is to announce the punishments of the Jews on account of two crimes of which they proved themselves guilty: namely, the impiety of the* **LEADERS**, *and the pride of the tranquil women.* You may find it in a more specific sense
<margin>Folio 31, column 2, near the end.</margin>
in the *Bereschit Rabba* <note>A midrashic text on Genesis.</note>, from which a testimony is taken in the *Seder Olam Rabba* <note>A 2nd-century Hebrew chronicle.</note>: *God showed to the first Adam*, "each generation and its leaders" <note>original Hebrew: דור ודור ומנהיגיו; original Greek: καὶ τοὺς ἡγεμόνας αὐτῆς</note>, and **ITS LEADERS**, etc. Other parts of this passage will be cited below.

*Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius, the Dutch theologian previously mentioned.</note> applies this title only to the *Bishop*; but for what reason, I do not clearly see. From the end of *Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews* it is gathered quite clearly
<margin>verse 24.</margin>
that by that term all those are designated who are elsewhere called *Presbyters* <note>Elders</note> and *Bishops* <note>Overseers</note>. For what else does it mean when he says: *Greet all your Leaders?* Who would deny that the *Presbyters* are *Leaders*? Who would claim that *Paul* intended only the *Bishops* to be greeted? Nor is this discovery solely the work of *Grotius*. For I have seen that *Origen* <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD).</note> interpreted this same 
<margin>Luke 22:26. Commentary on Matthew, Huet edition, Volume I, page 420.</margin>
word *Hegoumenos* <note>original Greek: ἡγέμενοϛ (leader/guide)</note> in the speech of *Christ* found in *Luke* as meaning "Bishop." *But the leader:* (so he says) *I think the one called Bishop in the churches is named thus, as one who serves those being served;* but **LEADER**: (*this is the word from Luke, which Origen explains*) (*I think he who is called Bishop in the Churches is so named*) as one who ministers to those who minister; or who becomes the *Servant of servants*, as Huetius <note>Pierre Daniel Huet, a 17th-century French bishop and scholar.</note> rightly notes. But this interpretation has no other foundation than the preference of the interpreters.

More names for the *Provosts of the Church* that might receive light from the *Ancient Synagogue* have not occurred to me. It is possible, however, that others exist, to be reserved for the industry of others. But as for the other names which the *Synagogue* gives to its *Prefects*, which differ from the denominations of the *Provosts of the Church* and therefore provide no guidance for them, we shall not concern ourselves.

->CHAPTER 4. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.<-

# CHAPTER IV.

The QUALITIES, *or Conditions, which Paul requires in the first Epistle to Timothy for the selection of* **BISHOPS** <note>original Latin: *Episcopis*</note> *are reviewed and divided into certain classes. Then, two of these are set apart for more extensive explanation: one, that it is necessary for a Bishop to be* **apt to teach** <note>original Greek: διδακτικὸν (*didaktikon*)</note>, *which it is proved should be translated as "suited for teaching"; the other, that it is necessary for a Bishop to be* **the husband of one wife** <note>original Greek: μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα (*mias gynaikos andra*)</note>. *It is demonstrated with many arguments that by this phrasing not only so-called "successive" polygamy* <note>remarrying after the death of a spouse</note> *but also "simultaneous" polygamy* <note>having multiple wives at the same time</note> *is excluded. Furthermore, the extent to which both of these conditions were observed among the Elders of the ancient Jewish Assemblies is investigated through the Hebrew Scriptures.*

Having completed the discussion of *Names*, let us now proceed to the QUALITIES or *Virtues* that were required in the proper appointment of any *Bishop*, and indeed in any *Prefect of the Synagogue* <note>a leader in the Jewish house of worship</note> of the ancient sort, before it was appropriate for them to be promoted to this honor. These *Qualities of a Bishop* are fully listed by Paul in his *Epistles to Timothy and Titus*.
<margin>1 Timothy 3:1. Titus 1:6.</margin>
We see that these qualities can be conveniently distinguished into *Internal and Absolute* [qualities] and *Relative* [qualities]. Among the *Internal and Absolute*, I include *Vigilance* <note>original Greek: νηφάλιος (*nephalios*), meaning sober or clear-headed</note>, *Temperance and Prudence* <note>original Greek: σώφρων (*sophron*)</note>, *Dignity of person* <note>original Greek: κόσμιος (*kosmios*), meaning orderly or respectable</note>, *Equity* <note>original Greek: ἐπιεικὴς (*epieikes*), meaning gentle or fair</note>, and APTITUDE FOR TEACHING <note>original Greek: διδακτικός (*didaktikos*)</note>. I distinguish the *Relative* qualities into *Negative and Positive*. The *Negative* qualities are further divided into *General and Specific*. The *General Negative* quality is *Irreproachability* <note>original Greek: ἀνεπίληπτος (*anepileptos*)</note>. The *Specific* ones are: *Abstinence from immoderate and constant wine-drinking* <note>original Greek: μὴ πάροινος (*me paroinos*), literally "not a brawler over wine"</note>; likewise from *Violence* <note>original Greek: μὴ πλήκτης (*me plektes*), literally "not a striker"</note>; from *Excessive greed for gain* <note>original Greek: μὴ αἰσχροκερδὴς (*me aischrokerdes*)</note>; and thus from [the love of] *Money* <note>original Greek: ἀφιλάργυρος (*aphilargyros*), "not a lover of silver"</note>. Also, a mind *Averse to fighting* <note>original Greek: ἄμαχος (*amachos*), "not a fighter"</note>, and similarly one that is *Well-established* <note>original Greek: μὴ νεόφυτος (*me neophytos*), literally "not a novice" or "not newly planted"</note> in the profession of Christian Doctrine. Finally, the *Positive* virtues (which are also relative) arise either from a regard for *others* or for *his own family*. Toward *others*, for instance: *Hospitality* <note>original Greek: φιλόξε- (catchword for *philoxenos*, "loving strangers")</note>...

However, the Vulgate <note>the standard Latin Bible used by the Western Church</note>, which was named such after Jerome's time, translates "apt to teach" as **A TEACHER** <note>original Latin: *doctorem*</note>, although in another place it uses "able to be taught."

<margin>2 Timothy 2:24. Book 1, in the place noted before.</margin>
I have no doubt that this translation also comes from Jerome, because Jerome himself elsewhere translates this word as *teacher*. Thus he writes in his work *Against Jovinian*, where he touches upon these words of Paul with a brief commentary: **A TEACHER**: For it is of no use to enjoy a conscience full of virtues unless one **IS ALSO ABLE TO INSTRUCT** the people committed to them, so that they may be strong enough to exhort in doctrine and refute those who contradict it. Thus, Jerome perceived the sense of the Greek word well enough...

### CHAPTER 4. OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH, 651

...we established, but when he <note>Referring to the translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> wished to express it with *a single Latin word*, he found none more suitable than that of *Teacher* <note>original Latin: *Doctoris*</note>; nor will you easily find another. For what is called *teachable* <note>original Latin: *docibilis*</note> in Latin (a word employed by Erasmus) does not mean *fit or able to teach*, but rather *to be taught*: *teachable*, I say, signifies one who *can be taught*, not one who *can teach*. Nevertheless, the most learned interpreters now agree that the true sense of this word—which is found *only twice* in the *Epistles* of Paul (and whether it appears in other genuine Greek writers, I do not know)—is to denote one who is *apt* or *well-suited for teaching*.

<margin>In the Lexicon on this word.</margin>
Suicer <note>Johann Caspar Suicer, a 17th-century Swiss theologian and lexicographer</note> thinks it possible that the Old Latin translation used before Jerome understood the same thing by its word *docile* <note>original Latin: *docilis*</note>. For, he says, "skilled in DECEPTION" <note>original Latin: *FALLENDI DOCILIS*</note> *in the works of Silius*, and "skilled in DANCING" <note>original Latin: *SALTANDI DOCILIS*</note> *in the works of Claudian*, means an expert in deceiving and dancing. However, if Suicer’s observation were to be applied to this case, then the *Old Translator* ought to have written: *Docile in teaching*. For certainly *docile* properly denotes one who *readily receives instruction*, not one who *teaches*, as is clearly evident from even a single passage of *Plautus*:

<margin>Bacchides, Act 1, Scene 2, verse 57.</margin>
> *In those matters you are a much more* TEACHABLE <note>original Latin: *DOCILIOR*</note> *student,*
> *Than in those things I taught you, where I wasted my effort.*

Let us say, therefore, if we wish to depart from the modern Vulgate, that *apt to teach* <note>original Greek: διδακτικός (*didaktikos*)</note> signifies *skilled in teaching, or fit for teaching*, and I believe we shall not be far from Paul's intent. For it seems altogether likely that what is called *apt to teach* here is explained in the Epistle to Titus—where Paul is equally intent on describing the qualities of Bishops—by the phrase:

<margin>Titus 1:9.</margin>
*Holding fast to that faithful word which is according to doctrine* <note>original Greek: ’Αντεχόμενον τῷ κατὰ διδαχὴν πιςῷ λόγῳ (*Antechomenon tō kata didachēn pistō logō*)</note>, *so that he MAY BE ABLE both to exhort with sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict it* <note>original Greek: ἵνα δυνατὸς ᾖ καὶ παρακαλεῖν τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ τῇ ὑγιαινούσῃ καὶ τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν (*hina dynatos ē kai parakalein tē didaskalia tē hygiainousē kai tous antilegontas elenchein*)</note>. This is truly what it means to be *apt to teach*.

Furthermore, this very quality which Paul requires in a Presbyter or Bishop is also entirely desired by the Jews in those men who are chosen by them for their *Yeshivot* <note>original Hebrew: ישיבות (*Yeshivot*) — scholarly or ecclesiastical assemblies</note>, or *Scholarly Assemblies*.

<margin>Book 2, chapter 10.</margin>
It is certainly established from those things discussed above that the leaders of the Jewish Academies were in the habit of decorating certain of their disciples—who had completed their course of study with honor—or other men whose *learning and character* were sufficiently proven after established examinations, with the title of *Teacher* <note>original Latin: *Doctoris*</note>, much as is now the custom

### CHAPTER 4. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

<margin>In the Lexicon on this word.</margin>
...we [can], but when he <note>Referring to the translator of the Vulgate or an early Latin commentator</note> wanted to express it with *a single Latin word*, he found none more suitable than that of **Teacher**; nor will you easily find another. For what is called in Latin *docibilis* <note>Original Latin: *docibilis*—a term used by the humanist Erasmus to mean "able to teach," though the author disputes this usage</note>, (a word used by Erasmus) is not *fit or skilled for teaching*, but rather "able to be taught": *docibilis*, I say, signifies one who can be taught, not one who teaches. However, the most learned interpreters now agree that the true sense of this word, which is found only *twice* in the *Epistles* of Paul (I do not know if it appears in other genuine Greek writers), is to denote someone *apt*, or *fit* for teaching. Suicer <note>Johann Caspar Suicer (1610–1684), a Swiss theologian known for his dictionary of Greek ecclesiastical terms</note> thinks it possible that the Old Latin Translation before Jerome understood the same by its word *docilis*. For, he says, "EAGER TO DECEIVE" *in the works of Silius*, and "SKILLED IN DANCING" *in Claudian*, means one who is an expert in deceiving and dancing. Yet if Suicer’s observation were applied to this case, then the *Ancient Translator* ought to have written: *Teachable in teaching*. For certainly *docilis* properly denotes one who easily receives instruction, not one who teaches, as is clearly evident from even a single passage of *Plautus*:

<margin>Bacchides, Act 1, Scene 2, line 57.</margin>
> *You are a pupil far more* TEACHABLE <note>Original Latin: *docilior*</note> *in those matters,*
> *Than in those things I taught you, where I wasted my effort.*

<margin>Titus 1:9.</margin>
Let us say, then, if we wish to depart from today’s *Vulgate* <note>The 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible that became the standard for the Catholic Church</note>, that *didaktikos* <note>Original Greek: διδακτικόν—apt to teach</note> signifies *skilled in teaching*, or *apt for teaching*, and we will not be far, I think, from Paul’s mind. For it seems entirely that what is said here to be *apt to teach*, is explained in the *Epistle to Titus*—where Paul is equally intent on describing the qualities of Bishops—as: *Holding fast the faithful word according to the doctrine* <note>Original Greek: ’Αντεχόμενον τοῦ κατὰ διδαχὴν πιστοῦ λόγου (*antechomenon tou kata didachēn pistou logou*)</note>, *so that he* MAY *be able both to exhort by sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict* <note>Original Greek: ἵνα δυνατὸς ᾖ καὶ παρακαλεῖν τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ τῇ ὑγιαινούσῃ καὶ τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν (*hina dynatos ē kai parakalein tē didaskalia tē hygiainousē kai tous antilegontas elenchein*)</note>. This is what it truly means to be *apt to teach*.

# ON THE QUALITIES OF RULERS, BOOK 3, PART 1.

...is accepted in our Academies; among those *Teachers* <note>original Latin: *Doctorum*</note>, some are ordained to teach and to solve cases of conscience, others to judge, and others again generally for any acts, whether of teaching or judging, with a testimony of their fitness and power to exercise those acts, should a solemn calling come to them. With such <term>Rabbis <note>original Hebrew: רבנים (*Rabbanim*)</note></term>, or *Teachers*, of whom there is such frequent mention in the Gospels, the <term>Assemblies <note>original Hebrew: ישיבות (*Yeshivot*)</note></term>, both *Scholarly* and *Ecclesiastical*, were furnished in the time of Christ. 

<margin>Matthew 23:7-8.</margin>
Indeed, Christ the Lord speaks of the *Scribes* and *Pharisees* in this same manner: that they aspired to be called by men, *Rabbi, Rabbi* <note>original Greek: *ῥαββὶ*</note>, and that they simultaneously loved *the first seats in the synagogues* <note>original Greek: *τὰς πρωτοκαθεδρίας ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς*</note>, **THE CHIEF SEATS IN THE SYNAGOGUES**. He was suggesting, if I am not mistaken, that these men sought after the leadership positions of the Schools and Synagogues, which were often joined together. Therefore, since the Jews especially require this in a *President of the Synagogue* and *Academy*—that he be a <term>Master <note>original Hebrew: רב (*Rav*)</note></term>, a *teacher* <note>original Greek: *διδάσκαλος* (*didaskalos*)</note>, or *one taught* <note>original Greek: *διδακτὸς* (*didaktos*)</note>, and (what is simultaneously implied by this word) that he be *apt to teach* <note>original Greek: *διδακτικὸς* (*didaktikos*)</note>, (which is still observed by them today)—we see from this with how much greater right *Paul* required an aptitude for teaching in the <term>Elders <note>original Hebrew: זקנים (*Zekanim*)</note></term> or *Christian Presbyters*. These were to administer that duty of teaching somewhat more diligently than the *Presidents of the Jewish Synagogues*. However, we do not wish anyone to take this to mean that, in the early times, no one was to be promoted to the Presbyteries or *Assemblies of the Christian Church* unless they had already been honored by the Apostles or some other Council of particular churches with the public title of *Doctor* <note>In the 17th century, "Doctor" simply meant a highly learned teacher.</note> as a testimony of their fitness. 

<margin>Matthew 23:10.</margin>
For since Christ the Lord had blamed the abuse of the mere title of *Doctor* among the Jews, it is not unreasonable to feel that the Christian Church hardly conferred that *title* on any others except those who were actually exercising the office of teaching, and who received the position of teaching along with the title, and indeed through the *Laying on of Hands*. It was more rarely conferred on those who merely sought a testimony of their fitness and desired to distinguish themselves from others by that title of honor; however, we shall discuss this more extensively in the following sections. It is enough, therefore, that we hold this firmly: that no one was admitted into the <term>Christian Councils <note>original Latin: *Synedria*, referring to governing bodies modeled after the Jewish Sanhedrin.</note></term> unless they were *learned* and literate men, or were *regarded as such*; whether they excelled others through a singular *grace of the Holy Spirit*, or had acquired the faculty or aptitude for teaching through their own study and labor. For that is what *the quality of being apt to teach* <note>original Greek: *τὸ διδακτικός*</note> signifies.

What *Paul* says—that a *Bishop* must be the *Man of One Wife*—many Doctors have long observed can be understood in two ways. Either that a *Bishop* or *Presbyter* at one and the same time maintains *only one wife*, not two or more in his family, which they call SIMULTANEOUS bigamy or polygamy; or, that a *Bishop*, having been released from the bond of one marriage, adds another or more wives to himself successively, which is called SUCCESSIVE bigamy or polygamy. Since, indeed, the bond of marriage is dissolved in two ways, either by *divorce* or by *death*, it is clear from this that the *Man of One Wife* can be spoken of in this latter sense as one who either does not bring in a new wife over one who has been divorced, or who does not take another wife for himself in the place of one who has died. Which of these *Paul* intended must now be examined.

The Apostle Paul desired the kind of monogamy <note>original Greek: μονογαμίαν</note> in Bishops that is opposed to *simultaneous polygamy*, in which someone is bound by a marital covenant to two or more women at the same time...

Indeed, what reason would there be to deny it? Therefore, in my judgment, **Calvin** was more prudent in this matter; passing over the **Greeks** in silence, he writes that **polygamy** was commonly prevalent among Eastern peoples, thereby sufficiently indicating that he was not convinced of the same regarding the **Greeks**.

# ON THE QUALITIES OF RULERS, BOOK III, PART I. #

**THE MATTER.** And this is the **first** reason for me why I do not think that Paul, in the words "husband of one wife," <note>Original Greek: *μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα* (mias gynaikos andra)</note> was focused on **Bigamy** <note>In this context, "Digamia" or bigamy refers to marrying a second time, even after the death of a first spouse.</note> or **Polygamy**, which they call **Simultaneous**.

<margin>1 Timothy 5:9.</margin>
But I have a **second**, no less clear reason from what follows. Paul, in the course of this **Epistle**, regarding widows to be chosen for the **ministry** <note>Original Greek: *διακονίαν* (diakonian); service or deaconship</note> of the Church and simultaneously supported by the same, likewise requires that they have been the wives of one husband. A widow, he says, is enrolled, not less than sixty years of age, **having been the wife of one husband**, <note>Original Greek: *γεγονυῖα ἑνὸς ἀνδρὸς γυνὴ* (gegonuia henos andros gynē)</note> that is, who has been the **WIFE OF ONE HUSBAND**. Certainly, the phrase "Wife of One Husband" means just as much as that other related to it, the meaning of which we are now debating: "Husband of One Wife." But what is said—"Who has been the Wife of One Husband"—is undoubtedly not to be understood this way: "She who did not acknowledge multiple husbands at one and the same time," (for that would be completely absurd), but it should be taken thus: "She who was not joined to multiple husbands **successively**" <note>This refers to what we might call serial monogamy—marrying again after a husband has died or after a divorce.</note>. And therefore, by the same reasoning, what the same Apostle requires of Bishops with the same phrase—that they be **husbands of one wife**—seems in no way to be explained concerning those who have wives **simultaneously**, but with far better justification concerning those who have not shared themselves with two or more wives **successively**. We conclude, therefore, that the words of the Apostle are to be explained not as regarding **simultaneous Polygamy**, but rather **successive**; although, as must be noted here, the latter includes the former. For in those from whom it is required that they do not marry multiple wives successively, it is especially required that they do not have multiple wives at the **same time**.

But now a new inquiry arises: whether the Apostle wants Bishops to be such "Husbands of One Wife" as those who, having **divorced** <note>Latin: *repudiata*</note> a former wife (whether rightfully or wrongfully, as commonly happens) while she is still alive, do not entangle themselves in new bonds of marriage; or indeed those who do not choose another partner for their bed in place of a deceased wife. The most learned **Beza** <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a prominent Protestant reformer and successor to John Calvin.</note>, whom we just noted, completely concedes that Paul's words can also be taken in the former way. He concedes, I say, that those who marry a new wife after a former one has been divorced (rightfully or wrongfully) are unworthy of the **Episcopate** <note>The office or rank of a bishop.</note> according to these Pauline canons. "And those things," he adds, "are **Bigamies** severely forbidden by the ancient Canons, so much so that it was not even permitted for clerics to be present at such [wedding] banquets." ## CHAPTER 4. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES. ##

...did not know how to interpret it except as being about a woman who, having been repudiated by her husband, had married another while her former spouse was still living. Listen to him: *"But I,"* he says, *"would consider those men to be properly called **digamous** <note>Original Greek: διγάμους (digamous); literally "twice-married."</note> who,* WHILE THEIR WIFE IS LIVING, WHETHER SHE IS STILL LEGALLY JOINED OR SEPARATED BY AN UNJUST DIVORCE, *bring in another wife; and those women **digamous** who, having been undeservedly rejected by their husbands, later married others."* And these views are not entirely without merit. Since Divorces among the Greeks, and even more so among the Romans and Jews (especially those who followed the **School of Hillel** <note>A famous school of Jewish law known for its more lenient interpretation of the grounds for divorce.</note>), were not only permitted but were accepted by very frequent custom, and since it was common practice for those who were single to quickly choose new arrangements, who would think it unreasonable for the Apostle to advise or command that such "digamy" or polygamy should not be tolerated in the **Presbyters** <note>Original Latin: Presbyteris; elders or priests in the early church.</note> of the Church?

Indeed, I certainly grant fully that such Digamy or Polygamy is by no means to be tolerated in a **Bishop** <note>Original Latin: Episcopo; an overseer or leader in the church.</note> of the Church, and that this very principle lies hidden within Paul’s precept concerning the **Monogamy** of a Bishop. But the question is more specifically this: should we stop at this meaning, or should we proceed further? The question is asked whether that form of **Successive Digamy** or **Polygamy**—where one invites another spouse into the vacant bed of a deceased wife through a new marriage covenant—is not also excluded and prohibited by these words: **husband of one wife**? <note>Original Greek: μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα (mias gynaikos andra)</note> Is it therefore not a violation of this rule of Paul’s for a man to marry another after his wife has died? 

**Beza** <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a prominent Protestant reformer and successor to John Calvin.</note> believed that it was not a violation, and that this latter form of "digamy" or "polygamy" was not prohibited by Paul’s words. I feel differently, and I am convinced that Paul intended to exclude this latter form of remarriage by these words just as much as the other two types already discussed. Thus, he would wish that no **twice-married** or **multi-married** man—whether he contracted a new marriage while his wife was living or after she died—be appointed as a **Leader of the Church**. 

The reason for my interpretation is abundantly clear to me because the related phrase used by the same Paul—**WIFE OF ONE HUSBAND** <note>Original Latin: UNIUS VIRI UXOR; referring to 1 Timothy 5:9.</note>—which we have already mentioned more than once, must be explained not only regarding a wife who does not enter a new marriage while her husband is still living (having been rejected or separated by divorce), but especially regarding a wife who, after the death of her husband, has rejected a second love. That this is the genuine interpretation of this latter...

### ON THE QUALITIES OF RULERS, BOOK III. PART I. ###

...of the previous phrase, then confirmed by the fact that a woman was called a <term>UNIVIRA</term> <note>Latin: "a woman of one husband."</note> or <term>UNIVIRIA</term> (a term with the same meaning) among the <term>Romans</term>. Their customs, which were then accepted throughout a great part of the world, were not unknown to Paul. Such a woman was one who had acknowledged *only one husband* and had not been joined with two or more, whether simultaneously or successively. Two notable testimonies of this have occurred to me, which I shall not hesitate to describe, as they shed light on this matter.

<margin>History, Book 10, Chapter 23.</margin>
*The first is found in Livy* <note>Titus Livius, a Roman historian who wrote a monumental history of Rome.</note>, who records that on the occasion of a public prayer service established in <term>Rome</term>, a dispute arose in the Shrine of Patrician Chastity, which is located in the <term>Cattle Market</term> <note>Original: "Foro Boario," the ancient Roman marketplace for livestock.</note> near the <term>Round Temple of Hercules</term>. Let us understand the whole matter from <term>Livy</term>: *The matrons had barred Virginia, daughter of Aulus, a Patrician woman married to the Plebeian Consul Volumnius, from the sacred rites because she had married outside the Patrician class.* A brief altercation followed, which flared up from womanly anger into a heated contest of spirits, as *Virginia* boasted that *she had entered the Temple of Patrician Chastity as both a Patrician and a chaste woman, and as* <term>A WOMAN MARRIED TO ONE MAN, TO WHOM SHE WAS LED AS A VIRGIN</term>; *nor was she ashamed of her husband, his honors, or his achievements.* Following this distinguished deed, she added magnificent words. In the Long Street where she lived, she partitioned off a part of her house—enough room for a modest shrine—and placed an altar there. *And having called together the Plebeian matrons, she complained of the injury done by the Patrician women; "I dedicate this altar," she said, "to Plebeian Chastity: and I exhort you that, just as a contest of valor occupies the men in this city, so should a contest of chastity exist among the matrons. Strive so that this altar may be said to be honored more holily and by more chaste women than that other one, if such a thing is possible."* <term>Livy</term> adds: *This altar was honored with nearly the same ritual as that older one, so that no matron—unless her chastity was proven and* <term>SHE HAD BEEN MARRIED TO ONLY ONE HUSBAND</term> (<note>original Greek: γεγαμία ἑνὸς ἀνδρὸς γυνή</note> <gloss>a woman who has been the wife of one man</gloss>)—*had the right of sacrificing there.* What, I ask, does it mean here to be "married to one husband"? Does it mean to be married to only one husband at a time, toward whom you behave chastely and modestly, even if he is perhaps your second husband? Certainly not. <term>Livy</term> himself interprets it: *To be married to one husband means to be with the one to whom you were led as a virgin.* Therefore, any woman who was *joined* to *multiple* husbands over time, whether after a divorce or after the death of a former husband, was rightly excluded from this shrine of chastity.

The *First Canon* of the Council of Laodicea is eloquent in this sense: *Regarding the fact that, according to the ecclesiastical rule, those who have been freely and legally joined in second marriages—not having married in secret—after a short time has passed and they have devoted themselves to prayer and fasting, should be granted communion by way of concession.* <note>The author provides the text in both Greek and Latin to emphasize the legality of these second marriages.</note> Do you see how this canon speaks of digamists of this sort, who contracted second marriages freely and *legally* <note>Greek: "νομίμως"</note>? You will see more in the works of Beveridge; indeed, read also, if you please, the interpretation of <term>Zonaras</term> <note>Johannes Zonaras, a 12th-century Byzantine chronicler and theologian.</note>.

...of the soul, or the offending of others? It is so. Nor is this discussion of mine intended to pronounce all **twice-married** <note>original: *digamos*; those who married a second time after the death of a first spouse</note> men of our time as unworthy of the Bishopric of the Church, as if they were transgressors of the Pauline precept. For since carnal lust does not reign among us in the same way as it once did among the Greeks and Romans—who were commonly persuaded that second marriages were a certain sign of a dominating lust (which they truly are not)—no mortal among Christians today is offended by the second marriage of any most holy man, if it is contracted properly between equal partners of a fitting age. Therefore, I do not think a man sins much against the **Pauline Canons** <note>The rules for church leadership established by the Apostle Paul in the New Testament</note> who, for sufficiently weighty reasons, takes a second wife. Rather, those rules are to be prudently tempered according to the various cases and customs of the peoples who have received the discipline of the Gospel. Thus, it was only a zeal for the truth (which is delightful and beautiful to investigate even in the smallest matters) that caused me to wander more widely into an inquiry of the meaning of Paul's words.

# ON THE DUTIES OF THE PREFECTS BOOK III. PART I.

Under GOVERNANCE, I include these three things:
1. MODERATING THE ACTIONS OF THE SYNAGOGUE.
2. EXERCISING DISCIPLINE TOWARD THE DISOBEDIENT.
3. HAVING CARE FOR THE DISTRIBUTION OF ALMS.
Let us begin by speaking of the first office of Public Instruction.

It is abundantly clear, both from the writings of the New Covenant <note>The New Testament</note> and from the records of the Hebrews, that besides the reading of the Law and the Prophets, a certain sacred prayer or sermon was delivered to the people gathered in the Synagogue buildings on the Sabbath day. We read concerning Christ the Lord, that he preached and taught throughout all parts of the Land of Judea in the synagogues. <margin>Chapter 4, 23.</margin> *It is thus in Matthew:* <note>original Greek: Καὶ περιῆγεν ὅλην τὴν Γαλιλαίαν ὁ Ἰησοῦς, διδάσκων ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς αὐτῶν, καὶ κηρύσσων τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον τῆς βασιλείας</note> *Jesus went about all Galilee, TEACHING IN THEIR SYNAGOGUES, and preaching the Gospel of the Kingdom.* You may easily find similar accounts in the other Evangelists. Concerning the rest of Christ's <term>Talmidim</term> <note>Hebrew: תלמידים; meaning "disciples" or "students"</note>, the Disciples and Apostles, the same is clear from their <margin>Chapter 13, 5.</margin> Acts, which Luke recorded. Let the account of Barnabas and Paul serve as evidence: *And when they had come to Salamis,* <note>original Greek: κατήγγελλον τὸν λόγον τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς τῶν Ἰουδαίων</note> THEY ANNOUNCED THE WORD OF GOD IN THE SYNAGOGUES OF THE JEWS. Nor should we overlook the saying of Saint James in <margin>Chapter 15, 21.</margin> those same Acts of the Apostles: <note>original Greek: Μωσῆς γὰρ ἐκ γενεῶν ἀρχαίων κατὰ πόλιν τοὺς κηρύσσοντας αὐτὸν ἔχει, κατὰ πᾶν σάββατον ἀναγινωσκόμενος</note> *For Moses from ancient generations has those who preach him in every city, being read every Sabbath.* Here, "preaching" <note>original Greek: τὸ κηρύσσειν</note> is expressly distinguished from "reading" <note>original Greek: τοῦ ἀναγινώσκειν</note>. Indeed, we do not see how Christ and the Apostles would have been admitted to this exercise by the Jews if it had not been a familiar and widely accepted practice in all sacred assemblies at that time. For since the Jewish Doctors were often burning with great envy toward Christ, they do not seem likely to have granted Christ an action that promoted his own authority, unless they were bound to it by the order established in the synagogues at that time. For we do not read that this liberty was ever taken away from Christ, not even when their hatred had already reached its greatest height. Let the testimony of Christ be heard <margin>Chapter 26, 55.</margin> in the Gospel of Matthew: *In that hour Jesus said to the crowd: "Have you come out as against a robber with swords and clubs to seize me? Daily I sat with you,"* <note>original Greek: διδάσκων ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ</note> *Teaching in the Temple—that is, if I am not mistaken, in the synagogues which were in the Temple.*
