### ON THE DUTIES OF PREFECTS, BOOK III, PART I.

...to consider more deeply the power of this word *Darash* <note>original Hebrew: דרש</note>, as it expresses this matter best and most familiarly of all.

<margin>chapter 13, 14.</margin>
Among the Hebrews, *Darash* denotes *to inquire*, or in Greek, *to seek* <note>original Greek: ζητεῖν</note> and *to examine* <note>original Greek: ἐτάζειν</note>. Thus, for example, in the writings of Moses: *And you shall INQUIRE, and search out diligently, and ask well.* <note>Deuteronomy 13:14; original Hebrew: ודרשת היטב</note> *Darash* here means to inquire into a matter studiously and industriously. When this is applied to the study of Holy Scripture, as it often is, it denotes *inquiring into the true, genuine, and profound sense of Scripture, and at the same time discussing it, whether this is done through a formal discourse (either literal or figurative), or through mutual questioning and public or private debates.* In these few words, almost everything contained in the power of this term is encompassed.

<margin>chapter 1, 20.</margin>
The Apostle Paul clearly refers to this meaning of the word in his first Epistle to the Corinthians, saying: *Where is the wise man? where is the Scribe?* <note>original Greek: ποῦ συζητητὴς τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου;</note> Where is the <term>DISQUISITOR</term> <note>The term "disquisitor" refers to a formal investigator or a debater who searches out the meaning of the law or nature.</note> OF THIS AGE? So says the venerable Theodore Beza <note>A major 16th-century Protestant theologian</note>. The Dutch translate it as: **Where is the Searcher of this age.** <note>original Dutch: Waer is de Ondersoecker deser eeuwe</note> Drusius <note>Johannes Drusius, a Flemish Old Testament scholar</note> thought this term should be referred to the *Chachame Mechkar* <note>original Hebrew: חכמי מחקר</note>, the "Wise Men of Research," whom Jerome calls "Searchers of natural causes."

Properly speaking, the *Wise Men of Research* or *Men of Research* <note>original Hebrew: חכמי מחקר & אנשי מחקר</note> among the Jews were called *Philosophers*, who scrutinize and investigate the causes of natural things, as can be seen from the evidence collected by <margin>Drusius, *Additions to the New Testament*, book 6, on this passage.</margin> Drusius. However, that is not exactly "to dispute" <note>original Greek: συζητεῖν</note>, which signifies "to debate and dispute" among the authors of the Greek language and the Holy Scriptures. It is therefore more pleasing that our countryman John Lightfoot and, before him—if I am not mistaken—Nicholas Fuller in his *Sacred Miscellanies*, referred this to the Hebrew *Dorshim* <note>original Hebrew: דורשים</note>, which is equivalent to the Greek *disputers* <note>original Greek: συζητηταί</note>. Lightfoot brought forward a passage where this word is used from the *Genesis Rabbah* and *Avodah Zarah* <note>Two significant works of ancient Jewish rabbinic literature</note>, which I encountered <margin>folio 31, column 2, near the end of the booklet *Seder Olam Rabbah*.</margin> near the end of the booklet *Seder Olam Rabbah*, and which I have excerpted here as it is read:

> The Holy One, Blessed be He, showed to the first man, Adam, each and every generation and its LEADERS; each and every generation and its PROPHETS; each and every generation and its DISQUISITORS; each and every generation and its WISE MEN and PROVIDERS; each and every generation and its JUDGES; the wise men of each generation, the prophets of each generation, the number of their names, the count of their days, the calculation of their hours, and the total of their footsteps, as it is said: *For You count my steps.* <note>This Hebrew passage lists the types of leaders God revealed to Adam, highlighting the role of the *Dorshim* or "Searchers" of the Law.</note>

# CHAPTER 5. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

...and every Generation and its Judges. "The wise men" <note>original Greek: Τοὺς σοφοὺς</note> of every Generation; the Prophets of every Generation; the number of their names; the number of their days; the calculation of their years; the sum of their steps, as it is said: *For you count my steps.* **Job 14:16.**

The <term>disquisitor</term> <note>original Greek: Συζητητὴς; a formal seeker or debater of the law</note> is therefore here the *dorēsh* <note>original Hebrew: דורש</note> or *darshan* <note>original Hebrew: דרשן; a preacher or interpreter</note>, since to "reason together" <note>original Hebrew: דרש; original Greek: συζητεῖν</note> is the same as to inquire. I doubt whether "to search" <note>original Greek: τὸ ἐρευνᾶν</note>, which is found in the Gospel of John, should also be traced back to this word, where Christ says: *Search the scriptures* <note>John 5:39; original Greek: Ἐρευνᾶτε τὰς γραφὰς</note>. **SEARCH the Scriptures.** Which the Dutch translated with the same word: **Ondersoeckt de Schriften.** It should have been translated—as is clear from the whole context, at the urging of the venerable Beza <note>Theodore Beza, a major Reformer and linguist</note>, and with the Dutch themselves warning in the margin: **You search the scriptures.** <note>The author is discussing a grammatical nuance: whether Jesus was giving a command to "Search!" or stating a fact: "You [already] search the scriptures [but miss the point]."</note> To "search" <note>original Greek: Τὸ ἐρευνᾶν</note> is to *investigate* <note>original Hebrew: חקר</note> and *inquire* <note>original Hebrew: דרש</note> into the Torah, to track down the true and genuine sense of the Law by applying diligent study, whether this is done through private exercises or through discussions held with others. 

Indeed, from this word the terms "subject of inquiry" <note>original Greek: τὸ ζήτημα</note> and "investigation" <note>original Greek: ζήτησις</note> owe their origin, which properly signify the subject of a legal or scholarly search, or that over which a *darshan* <note>original Hebrew: דרשן</note> disputes and inquires. These terms occur frequently in the Books of the New Covenant. The words of Gallio in the Acts of the Apostles are: <margin>Chapter 18, 15</margin> *If it is a question* <note>original Greek: ζήτημά</note> *of words and names and your law, look to it yourselves.* Also the words of Claudius Lysias in his letter to Felix, <margin>Chapter 23, 29.</margin> the Governor of Judea: *Whom I found accused concerning questions* <note>original Greek: ζητημάτων</note> *of their law.* And Paul's words to King Agrippa in that most elegant Speech: <margin>Chapter 26, 3.</margin> *Especially because you are an expert in all the customs and questions* <note>original Greek: ζητημάτων</note> *among the Jews.* The "question" <note>original Greek: τὸ ζήτημα</note> or **QUESTIO** is taken here for the argument of the inquiry upon which a discussion is established, which, if I am not mistaken, the Hebrews call a *derush* <note>original Hebrew: דרוש</note>. 

Philippus Aquinas <note>A 17th-century scholar of Hebrew</note> states: "A *derush* <note>original Hebrew: דרוש הדבר שעלי נבנה הויכוח או ההלכה</note> is the matter upon which a dispute or a legal ruling is built." The *derush* <note>original Greek transcription: τὸ דרוש</note> is the thing over which a dispute or discourse is constructed. "Investigation" <note>original Greek: Ζήτησις</note> occurs in the Epistle to Titus: <margin>Chapter 3, 9.</margin> *But avoid foolish questions* <note>original Greek: ζητήσεις</note>*, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law.* 

Where the Apostle clearly alludes to the discussions—sometimes vain and foolish—which are celebrated in the Synagogues by the "reasoners of this age" <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῶν συζητητῶν τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου</note>, the Disputers of this world; that is, those belonging to the Synagogue and the administration of the Old Testament. But it will be necessary for us to track the nature of those first investigations and reasonings <note>original Greek: συζητήσεων</note> a little more carefully, so that we may come closer to the power of this word...

# ON THE DUTIES OF PREFECTS BOOK III, PART I.

<margin>
Book I. Part I. chapter 6.
</margin>
It was a very ancient custom among the Hebrews that learned men would sometimes retire to a place consecrated to study to exercise one another through modest inquiries into the understanding of the Word of God. These private dissertations of the Teachers were discussed above, where we described the Upper Chambers <term>Cænacula</term> <note>Private upstairs rooms often used for scholarly or religious gatherings</note> of the Teachers and their use. And this same method of instruction was celebrated in public *Schools* and *Academies*, especially those called *Batei Midrash* <note>original Hebrew: בתי מדרשי; Houses of Study</note>, namely, with the Disciples asking questions and raising difficulties, and the Teachers resolving the doubts raised through an Interpreter <note>An assistant, often called an Amora or Meturgeman, who communicated the teacher's thoughts to the audience</note>. This is most clearly established from the *Talmudic Gemara* <note>The part of the Talmud containing rabbinical commentaries and debates</note>, which consists entirely of questions and answers, and the opinions of disputants, in the correct discernment of which much depends for the interpretation of the Gemara. 
<margin>
See Halichot Olam Treatise 2. chapter 2.
</margin>
Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note>, whose words were cited above when we discussed the houses of debate <note>original Greek: περὶ τῶν οἴκων τῆς συζητήσεως</note>, explains this ancient custom of teaching very clearly. Nor do we lack examples of this ancient custom in the Gospels themselves, in which both the Disciples and other Teachers often approached Christ with their questions—the former indeed so they might profit through him, the latter so they might cause trouble for him. 
<margin>
Chapter 10, [verses] 1, 2.
</margin>
A notable example of this is found in Mark: *And rising from there, he came into the borders of Judea by the side of the Jordan, and the crowd gathered to him again*, and as he was accustomed, he taught them again <note>original Greek: καὶ ὡς εἰώθει πάλιν ἐδίδασκεν αὐτοὺς</note>, *and as he was accustomed*, he TAUGHT them once more: *Then the Pharisees approaching*, asked him <note>original Greek: ἐπηρώτησαν αὐτὸν</note>, QUESTIONED HIM: *Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?* 
<margin>
Chapter 2, [verse] 46.
</margin>
Truly, nothing is more eloquent than that which we read concerning the boy Christ in Luke: *And it happened after three days that they found him in the Temple, sitting in the midst of the teachers, both listening to them and asking them questions* <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἐγένετο μεθ’ ἡμέρας τρεῖς εὗρον αὐτὸν ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ καθεζόμενον ἐν μέσῳ τῶν διδασκάλων, καὶ ἀκόοντα αὐτοὺς, καὶ ἐπερωτῶντα αὐτοὺς</note>; *And it happened three days later, that they found him in the Temple* SITTING in the midst of the Teachers and LISTENING TO THEM AND QUESTIONING THEM.

Furthermore, because it most often happened that Teachers sitting in the Chair <term>Cathedra</term> <note>The official seat of a teacher or professor</note>, either questioned by their disciples or challenged by their colleagues through raised difficulties, would respond somewhat more at length to that question or objection and would range more widely into the proposed argument, it resulted from this that *darash* <note>original Hebrew: דרש</note> in Talmudic writings also denotes *to discuss, to discourse, to hold a sermon upon some matter*, or, to sum it up in one word, TO PREACH. Thus, it is familiar in the whole Talmudic Corpus: "Our Rabbis taught/expounded" <note>original Hebrew: דרשו רבותינו; Darshu Rabboteinu</note>, which

### CHAPTER 5. OF SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

...as they commonly explain it: *Our Teachers instruct*. <note>original Hebrew: ר' יוחנן דרש</note> *Rabbi Jochanan taught and explained*, and other phrases similar to these. From this, the <term>Darshanim</term> <note>original Hebrew: דורשים; teachers or preachers</note> are those sorts of *Teachers* who discourse more at length upon a specific argument. Observe the use of the word, if you please, from these words found in the Tractate *Chagigah*: <margin>Chapter 2, 1.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: אין דורשין בעריות בשלשה ולא בממעשה בראשית בשנים ולא במרכבה ביחיד אלא אם כן היה חכם ומבין מדעתו</note> *They do not explain the laws of forbidden relationships before three people, nor the Work of Creation before two, nor the Work of the Chariot before one, unless he be a wise man and understands by his own knowledge.* <note>The "Work of Creation" refers to the mysteries of Genesis, while the "Work of the Chariot" refers to the mystical vision of Ezekiel; both were considered dangerous for the uninitiated.</note> It is clear enough that the word *darash* <note>original Hebrew: דרש</note> in this place signifies *a clear and profound explanation of any difficult theological argument, proceeding from a Teacher*. And from this, it follows that the most learned men—not without merit—translate the word <margin>In the Book on the Sanhedrin. On the passage of Maimonides in The Guide for the Perplexed, Part 2, chapter 39.</margin> *darash* as *to preach* <term>concionari</term>. Certainly *Selden* <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a renowned English jurist and scholar of Jewish law</note> does so, as do others; and it is in this latter sense that we most especially desire this word to be understood and used. Yet even these definitions are not sufficient. It is necessary to go further, because just as words gain strength through usage, it is certain that an even greater force of meaning lies within this term.

Undoubtedly, the discourses, disputations, and inquiries concerning the Law established by the ancient Teachers were of such a nature that not only was the literal sense of Holy Scripture explained in them, but also a certain *higher* and deeper sense. This sense was more *spiritual* and more, so it seemed, in harmony with Divine Wisdom. From this practice, it came about that the word <term>Midrash</term> <note>original Hebrew: מדרש</note> began to be used in the writings of the Jews for an *Allegorical Dissertation or a Sermon filled with Allegories*. Maimonides in his *Guide for the Perplexed*, Ibn Ezra in his *Commentaries*, and others already noted by Hottinger and Buxtorf, have written on the nature of these. Elijah <note>Elijah Levita, a famous 16th-century Hebrew grammarian</note> says: <note>original Hebrew: קראן מדרש פירוש שאין על דרך פשוטו</note> *Midrash is the name for an explanation that does not follow the literal path.* <note>The "literal path" refers to the Peshat, or plain meaning of the text.</note> This, however, must be understood in such a way that the term also encompasses every instruction through *similitudes, enigmas*, parables <note>original Greek: παραβολὰς</note>, proverbs <note>original Hebrew: משלים; meshalim</note>, and all other discourses in which one ranges into spiritual and sublime matters. One cannot truly deny that this method of teaching was in use among the ancient Jews, since their Teachers constantly hand it down and the Sacred monuments confirm the same. It would have been a pleasure for us to support this with certain arguments, had not Pierre Daniel Huet <note>A French bishop and intellectual giant of the 17th century</note>—a truly distinguished man and far greater than our praises—and Joannes...

For most things are handed down among them THROUGH FIGURES in the manner of the ancients.

The same Philo speaks explicitly again regarding the "Theoreticals" <note>The Therapeutae or "Theoretical" Essenes, a contemplative group described by Philo.</note>: *For reading the most sacred writings, they philosophize upon their ancestral philosophy by allegorizing, since they believe the symbols of the literal interpretation belong to a hidden nature, revealed in underlying meanings <note>original Greek: ὑπονοίαις; "hyponoia" refers to the deeper or hidden sense beneath the surface of the text.</note>. They also have the commentaries of ancient men, who, having become the founders of the sect, left many monuments of the form found in allegories, using which as certain archetypes, they imitate the manner of their choice.* Handling the sacred volumes (this is the version by Gelenius <note>Sigismund Gelenius (1497–1554), a scholar known for his Latin translations of Greek classics and Philo.</note>), they devote effort to the PHILOSOPHY RECEIVED BY HAND FROM THE ELDERS, BY SEARCHING ITS ALLEGORIES, *since they believe that beneath the open words lie secrets of nature, to be explained by probable conjectures* (better translated as: *to be explained tropically or allegorically.*) They also have the commentaries of the ancients, who as authors of this sect left many monuments concerning ALLEGORIES OF THIS SORT, to whose imitation the descendants accommodate themselves.

Yet I would not wish that you, who hear Philo discoursing on the supreme antiquity of "Allegorical Study" (in the sense that he himself understands it and practiced this study in his writings), should give him blind faith in all things. # CHAPTER 5. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

<margin>Preface to the Talmud, folio 6, column 4.</margin>
<margin>See also Carpzov, *Introduction to Jewish Theology*, etc., preceding Raymond Martini’s *Dagger of the Faith*, chapter 8, page 36.</margin>
In my opinion, they did not follow the Law and the Prophets in this manner until after the times of *Alexander the Great*, when they began to learn the *Philosophy* cultivated among the Greeks. Because this study of *Philosophy* was pleasing and delightful to them due to its novelty, they loved it vehemently; and consequently, they mixed it with the decrees of the Law and the Prophets. They did this all the more because they saw that the *Practical or Moral Philosophy* of the Gentiles <note>The "Gentiles" here refers to the non-Jewish Greek and Roman world.</note> was highly consistent with the *practical commandments* found in *Moses and the Prophets*. At least, this is what they convinced themselves. Furthermore, the Jews who associated with the Gentiles believed (an error of mind by which *Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy through allegory.</note> himself was shamefully deceived) that it would greatly help in commending the wisdom and authority of the Divine Law to the Gentiles if they led them to believe that beneath the simple and clear words of the Law, deep and sublime truths lie hidden—truths that can only be truly explained through the secret dogmas of Philosophy.

Moreover, I do not believe that those *Allegorical* dissertations—truly quite foolish and useless—which the later crowd of Hebrews thrust upon us in the *Talmud* <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara.</note>, originated from the Ancient Sages, even though they were approved and praised by Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the most influential medieval Jewish philosopher.</note>. In my view, those ancients treated such spiritual matters with greater solidity and weight. However, there is no need for me to argue this point at length now. We will satisfy this argument if we provide one or two examples of this kind of deeper *midrash* <note>original Hebrew: מדרש; a method of exegesis or interpretation that goes beyond the literal sense of the text.</note> dissertation, as it seems most relevant to the present subject.

<margin>Chapter Hechalil <note>Referring to "He-Chalil" (The Flute), the fifth chapter of Tractate Sukka.</note></margin>
In the Jerusalem Talmud, in the *Tractate Sukka* <note>A volume of the Talmud dealing with the Festival of Tabernacles (Sukkot).</note>, where mention is made of the *joy* that the Ancient Jews displayed during the *drawing of water* <note>Referring to the "Simchat Beit HaShoeivah" or "Rejoicing of the Water-Drawing House," a ceremony held during the Temple period.</note> at the Festival of Tabernacles, *Rabbi Joshua* comments as follows:

"Rabbi Joshua, Son of Levi, said: Why is it called the 'House of Drawing'? Because from there they draw the Holy Spirit; according to that which is written: *With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation* (Isaiah 12:3)." <note>original: "Dixit R. Josua, Filius Levi: Quare vocatur nomen ejus locus haustionis? QUIA INDE HAURIUNT SPIRITUM SANCTUM: secundum id, quod scriptum est: Et haurietis aquas cum gaudio ex fontibus salutis."</note>

It is certainly clear from this testimony that the Ancient Hebrews interpreted WATER here as the HOLY SPIRIT, and the drawing and pouring of water as the outpouring or distribution of the gifts of the *Holy Spirit*. This is indeed an *Allegorical* interpretation, falling under the categories of *midrash* <gloss>original Hebrew: מדרש; homiletic interpretation</gloss> and *derash* <gloss>original Hebrew: דרש; the "sought" or deeper meaning of a text</gloss>.

This *explanation* is drawn from the force of Scripture and confirmed by Christ the Lord in the Gospel of John. Specifically, the condition of the Church of the New Covenant is elegantly compared to living in tents—just like that of the Jews during the Festival of Tabernacles <note>Sukkot, a harvest festival where Jews live in temporary booths to remember the wilderness wanderings.</note>—and this concept has already been put forward by Zechariah. 
<margin>Chapter 14, 16.</margin>
For just as during that festival the Israelites left their fixed homes and, wherever they pleased in the fields and public places, they built "Tabernacles" (a mobile type of dwelling decorated with branches), and drew water with the greatest joy and the blaring of trumpets and horns from the spring of Siloam <note>A ritual during Sukkot called Simchat Beit HaShoevah, the "Rejoicing of the Water-Drawing."</note> and poured it out; so too would it be with the state of that future Church, and especially in its final age. It would leave the **Father's House and Family** <note>original Hebrew: בית אביו (*Beit Aviv*)</note>; it would abandon the Temple (which was a fixed dwelling) along with all its sacred rites and furnishings; it would renounce external kinship and relations; and it would live dispersed throughout the field—that is, the entire world

(*the field is the world* <note>original Greek: ὁ δὲ ἀγρὸς ἐστὶν ὁ κόσμος</note>). It would worship God in Spirit and in truth within this born-again and, as it were, renewed and flourishing age, where **all things are new** <note>original Greek: πάντα καινὰ</note>, thriving and turning green. It would not be bound to a specific location, but would have obtained the **possession** <note>original Hebrew: אחוזה (*achuzah*)</note>, the **inheritance of the world** <note>original Greek: τὴν κληρονομίαν τοῦ κόσμου</note>. This would be the age in which *knowledge of divine things* would multiply, once the outer bark and all veils were removed, and the greatest abundance of the *Holy Spirit* would be poured out. This Spirit flows from Christ, who sits at the right hand of his Father (that is, reigning with his Father), which is why it is called the "Spirit of Christ" and "of the Son." "*For these,*" he says, "*are the two covenants: one indeed from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery, which is Hagar. The latter produced no sons except for slavery <note>original Greek: δουλείαν (douleian)</note>. Paul argues these things in accordance with the customs of the Hebrews, among whom it was held that offspring were judged to be *free* or *enslaved* according to the status of the mother. # ON THE DUTIES OF PREFECTS BOOK III. PART I.

...that is, *Midrashim* <note>original Hebrew: מדרשים, meaning "expositions" or "investigations"</note>, *discourses and dissertations*, in which a certain deeper sense of the mysteries of the Law is drawn out. Of this kind are the things the Apostle writes concerning *Melchizedek*, the *Priests*, the *Sacrificies*, the *Altar*, and the *Tabernacle*—with even the Hebrew interpreters not disagreeing—in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which is indeed most learned and most worthy of the Apostle Paul. Among the Hebrew commentators, you will find many *Allegorical Discourses* of this nature, which they call *Midrash* <note>original Hebrew: מדרש</note>, not only in those books that carry this title (of which there are many), but also in many others which you will find in the archives of the Hebrews, as well as in the *Talmud* <note>A central text of Rabbinic Judaism consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara</note>, where they are mixed with many little stories, regardless of how others might defend them.

But not only that method of instruction which is through *allegories* <note>original Greek: ἀλληγορίας</note> belongs to the *Darash* <note>original Hebrew: דרש, the process of deep interpretation or searching a text</note>, but also that which is through *parables* <note>original Greek: παραβολάς</note>, or *Meshalim* <note>original Hebrew: משלים, meaning "proverbs" or "parables"</note>, *similitudes, and enigmas*. This method of teaching through parables or *proverbs* <note>original Greek: παροιμίας</note> (which Cicero called *Comparisons*, because in them two things are brought together and compared) is both very simple and pleasant, and also very ancient. Among the ancients, says Seneca:
> *a speech aimed at applause was not yet sought: those who spoke simply and for the sake of demonstrating a thing were full of parables, which I judge to be necessary—not for the same reason as they are for Poets—but so that they might be supports for our weakness, and bring both the speaker and the listener directly to the matter at hand.*

<margin>See our Observations book 3, chapter 19.</margin>
This is especially true of the Palestinians, Syrians, Arabs, and the other peoples produced by the land of the Orientals, who are the leaders and providers of all Wisdom; indeed, this is abundantly clear not only from the testimony of Jerome, who lived in those places, but also from the monuments of all the Orientals (not neglecting those of which a great supply has been given to us in the Holy Scriptures). But since we are dealing only with those Jews whom the age of Christ saw, we shall contain our discourse within those limits.

<margin>chapter 9. section 15.</margin>

# CHAPTER 5. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

...of our Lord lived, and therefore it is gathered from this testimony that from those times and thereafter, the Wisdom of the Teachers <note>Referring to the Jewish Rabbis of the period</note> diminished in the elegant crafting of **parables** <note>original Greek: $\pi\alpha\rho\alpha\beta o\lambda\tilde{\omega}\nu$</note>, which a little before had greatly flourished. This method of instruction through **parables** <note>original Greek: $\pi\alpha\rho\alpha\beta o\lambda\dot{\alpha}\varsigma$</note> pertained to the *Darash* <note>original Hebrew: דרש, the process of searching out deeper meaning</note>, or to Dissertations and sacred Oratory. We know this because parabolic fictions as well as allegorical commendations are everywhere expressed in the Talmud by the same word, *Darash*, as is known to anyone who is not a total stranger to Talmudic writings. Robert Sheringham, <margin>See Carpzov.</margin> a most learned man, took great care in his Preface to his translation of the *Codex Joma* <note>A volume of the Mishnah concerning the Day of Atonement</note> to record specimens of such parables—similar to those <margin>Raymond Martini, p. 35.</margin> found in the speeches of Christ—drawn from the *Derashot* <note>original Hebrew: דרשות, sermons or homiletic discourses</note> of the Hebrew Teachers. He drew these from the *Gale Razia* <note>Hebrew for "Revealer of Secrets"</note> of Conrad Otto, a man who converted from Judaism to Christianity and was thereafter a Professor of the Hebrew Language at the Academy of Altdorf; however, Otto later "returned like a dog to his vomit" <note>A biblical idiom used here to describe Otto's return to Judaism</note>, though he did not fail his readers in the specific passages he cited from the Talmud. Let us present one or two specimens of this kind of parabolic teaching from the *Reshith Chochma* <note>The "Beginning of Wisdom," a 16th-century work of Jewish ethics and mysticism</note>:

<margin>folio 3, column 2.</margin>
*And our Sages, of blessed memory, said: Repent while your strength is still with you, while the* **LAMP BURNS, GIVE IT OIL SO THAT IT IS NOT EXTINGUISHED.** *If the lamp is extinguished, the oil is of no use to it. This is explained such that the oil is to the lamp what the Law and <margin>Ecclesiastes 9:8.</margin> the Commandments are to a man, according to what is said: "Let not oil be lacking upon your head."* It is added:

*Furthermore, our Teachers say in the Midrash: The Holy God, Blessed be He, said to Israel: My children, while the gates of repentance are open, perform repentance; for I accept a gift* <note>In this context, the "gift" is the act of repentance</note> *in this world, but when I sit in Judgment in the world to come, I will accept no gift. He who has labored to the point of exhaustion in this world shall eat on the Sabbath.* <note>The Sabbath here represents the eternal rest of the afterlife</note> *This world is like a vestibule, and the world to come is like a dining hall; prepare yourself in the vestibule so that you may enter the dining hall.*

### ON THE DUTIES OF THE PREFECTS, BOOK III, PART I.

<margin>Thomas <note>Likely a reference to a specific commentary or author, possibly a misreading of "ibid." in the original source, as the quote follows from the previous discussion.</note></margin>
> This world is like a vestibule, and the world to come is like a dining room. Prepare yourself in the vestibule, so that you may enter the dining room.

<margin>See John 9:4; 11:9; [Matthew] chapter 25:1.</margin>
This latter saying is recorded by Rabbi Jacob in the *Pirke Avoth* <note>original: "Pirke Avoth," meaning "Ethics of the Fathers," a fundamental collection of rabbinic ethical teachings</note>. Here you see a method of teaching and persuasion through parables, the likes of which you may also find in the speeches of Christ. For the parable of the *Virgins*, in which Christ commends them to keep their lamps constantly supplied with oil—a symbol of the gifts of Grace and Evangelical truths—accords perfectly with that earlier parabolic exhortation.

Our Lord Christ greatly loved this manner of teaching, whether through **parables** <note>original Greek: παραβολὰς</note> and **fables** <note>original Greek: αἴνους</note>, or through **allegories** <note>original Greek: ἀλληγορίας</note> or **proverbs** <note>original Hebrew: משלים (mashalim)</note>, both long and short, in *His* sermons. He did this not only to follow the Teachers of that age and to accommodate Himself to the understanding of the people, but also to fulfill the prophecies of the ancient Prophets and to serve that hidden Divine plan regarding the **unbelief** <note>original Greek: ἀπιστίᾳ</note> of the Jewish nation, and following that unbelief, their **hardening** <note>original Greek: πωρώσει</note>, and finally their final **rejection**, which are the very reasons He cites in *Matthew*.

<margin>Chapter 13, [verses] 13, 14.</margin>
For indeed, **Jesus spoke to the crowds in parables, and without a parable He did not speak to them** <note>Matthew 13:34</note>; *And* **WITHOUT PARABLES** he did **NOT SPEAK** to them, that is, he did not preach to them. For "to speak" <note>original Greek: Τὸ λαλεῖν</note> here is the same as the Hebrew word **to say** <note>original Hebrew: אמר (amar)</note>, meaning **to discourse**, a sense in which it is frequently used among the Hebrews, so that **to say** <note>original Hebrew: אמר (amar)</note> and **to search or preach** <note>original Hebrew: דרש (darash)</note> correspond to each other in this passage.

<margin>On the various uses of the word "to say" [amar], see Sheringham on chapter 1 of the *Codex Joma*, section 1; chapter 1 in the Excerpts of Johannes Cocceius, section 7; 2 Timothy 3:17; book 1, part 2, chapter 7.</margin>
Thus you frequently find in the Talmudic Gemara <note>the portion of the Talmud containing rabbinic commentary</note>: **Resh Lakish said** <note>original: אמר ריש לקיש</note> (meaning "he spoke" or "he preached"). **Rabbi Huna said** <note>original: אמר ר' הונא</note>. And the term for **discourse** <note>original: אמורא (amora)</note> is also taken for a **sermon**, and **interpreter** <note>original: אמוראה (amora'ah)</note> for a **Preacher**. So it is said in the Gemara of Sanhedrin: **The members of the Prince's household had appointed a Judge who was not PERFECT** <note>The author equates the Hebrew concept of a judge who "had not learned" with the Greek terms for being "complete," "fit," or "approved"—meaning someone not yet fully trained in the science of ancestral traditions, whom they only then considered "perfectly instructed."</note>. **They said therefore to Judah bar Nachmani, the interpreter for Resh Lakish: STAND BY him DURING THE SERMON.** For it was the custom, as we have already explained, that the Teachers had an **Interpreter** <term>Amora<gloss>a speaker who stood by a Rabbi to repeat and explain his teachings loudly to the crowd</gloss></term> attached to them who would explain their words to the people in somewhat greater detail.

Indeed, however much this method of **preaching** was common among the Hebrews—and hence the word **to search/preach** <note>original: דרש (darash)</note> is used so familiarly in that sense—one must not think that this method of **teaching** was in every...

### CHAPTER 5. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

It is established from the writings of the Hebrews that any *sacred inquiry or discourse* is designated by this term, as we have noted in the preceding pages. It may be observed that in those books which contain the *sermons and discourses of the Hebrew Doctors* <note>The author refers here to the Rabbis of the Talmudic and Midrashic eras.</note>—of which there are many—either the more illustrious texts are explained, or the duties of piety and the more notable virtues are proposed **for training in righteousness** <note>original Greek: πρὸς παιδείαν τὴν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ</note>, alongside the applications of **teaching, correction, reproof, and exhortation** <note>original Greek: διδασκαλίας, ἐπανορθώσεως, ἐλέγχου & παρακλήσεως; these are the four purposes of scripture mentioned in 2 Timothy 3:16.</note>. And so we read in the Gospel history that Christ sometimes *preached* in this way, when he either proposed more illustrious truths, or admonished his listeners of their duty, or responded to the objections of his adversaries, or finally, when he refuted the vices and errors of those times.

<margin>Chapters 5, 6, 7.</margin>
Although some shorter parabolic sentences were occasionally mixed into these discourses, they were not always full parables, which we discussed shortly before. Certainly, that most excellent sermon of Christ delivered on the mount and preserved by *Matthew* is of this kind; in it, he laid the most solid foundations of the **Kingdom of Heaven**—that is, of his Kingdom, the Church of the New Testament—yet it does not contain full parables of that sort.

<margin>Chapter 4, [verses] 21, 22.</margin>
Nor does the sermon he gave at Nazareth regarding the famous passage of *Isaiah* seem unlike that one; of which *Luke* says: *And all bore witness to him*, **and they wondered at the words of grace that proceeded from his mouth** <note>original Greek: καὶ ἐθαύμαζον ἐπὶ τοῖς λόγοις τῆς χάριτος, τοῖς ἐκπορευομένοις ἐκ τοῦ στόματος αὐτοῦ</note>, *and they marveled at* the WORDS OF GRACE *which came forth from his lips*. He preached, therefore, with grace, so that he pleased the people. The Hebrew Doctors, if I am not mistaken, are accustomed to express this through the word *hirtzah* <note>original Hebrew: הרצה</note>, which carries the meaning of *preaching*.

<margin>See Buxtorf on this word.</margin>
Thus they say: **Rabbi Joshua explained certain matters before Rabban Jochanan** <note>original Hebrew: רבי יהושוע הרצה דברים לפני רבן יוחנן</note>. And again: **Rabbi Akiva preached before Rabbi Joshua** <note>original Hebrew: רבי עקיבא הרצה לפני רבי Joshua</note>. Since the word *hirtzah* <note>to preach</note> is derived from *ratzah* <note>to be well-pleased or to favor</note>, it appears that to preach is to do so **with grace** <note>original Greek: μετὰ χάριτος</note>, so that you may please your listeners.

<margin>Chapter 4, [verse] 2.</margin>
The Apostle expresses this in the second Epistle to the Corinthians as **commending himself to every human conscience by the manifestation of the truth** <note>original Greek: συνιστάνειν ἑαυτὸν πρὸς πᾶσαν συνείδησιν ἀνθρώπων τῇ φανερώσει τῆς ἀληθείας</note>, which the Dutch <note>original Latin: "Belgae," referring to the translators of the Dutch Authorized Version or Statenvertaling.</note> have translated: *making himself pleasing through the revelation of the truth*, just as they also transposed "words of grace" as *the pleasant words*.

For Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal scholar.</note> drew this phrase—which he also uses elsewhere—from the Talmudic tractate *Taanith* <note>The Hebrew word for "Fast."</note>, where the ceremonies to be observed during a **public fast** are described: <note>original Hebrew: סדר תעניות כיצד מוציאין את התיבה לרחוב של עיר ונותנין אפר מקלה על גבי התיבה ובראש הנשיא ובראש אב בית דין וכל אחד ואחד נותן בראשו הזקן שבהן אומר לפניהם דברי כיבושין אחינו לא נאמר באנשי נינוה וירא אלהים את שקם ואת תענותם אלא וירא אלהים את מעשיהם כי שבו מדרכם הרעה ובקבלה הוא אומר וקרעו לבבכם ואל בגדיכם</note> **What is the procedure for observing a public fast? Each person likewise places them upon their own head. Then the Elder among them speaks a discourse intended to subdue the hearts of the people, roughly in this form: "My brothers; it is not said of the people of Nineveh: 'And God saw their sackcloth and their fasting and afflictions,' but rather: 'And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way.' Furthermore, in the Prophetic exhortations (which in this text are called Kabbala)** <note>In this context, *Kabbala* refers to the "tradition" of the Prophetic books, not the mystical system.</note>**, it says: 'Rend your hearts and not your garments.'"** I have presented these words here all the more gladly because in them we have a most clear specimen of a Synagogue sermon from ancient times.

<margin>See regarding this Rabbi Solomon and Bartenora. "And in the tradition, in the words of the Prophets."</margin>
Furthermore, as to what **words of subduing** <note>Hebrew: דברי כיבושין, *divrei kibushin*</note> are—which we have translated as *a discourse intended to subdue the hearts of men*—this is by no means obscure from our version and the context of the text itself. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most famous medieval commentator.</note> writes: <note>original Hebrew: כבושין לשון עציר כמו מכבש בלעז פרי"שא שכובשין את הלבבות להחזירם למוטב ואלו הן דברי כיבושין כו'</note>

<margin>In the Gloss on this passage.</margin>
The word **subduing** [kibushin] has the meaning of pressing (**constraining, or restraining**) like a **press** [machbesh], which in the common tongue is called a *Presse* (in Dutch: *Een presse*. I believe I have correctly followed the mind of Jarchius <note>Jarchius is a Latinized name for Rashi.</note>); because, namely, those words subdue the hearts of men to turn them toward the better. Such "subduing words" are those very ones in the text: "My brothers, etc."

<margin>In this passage.</margin>
Bartenora <note>Obadiah ben Abraham of Bertinoro (c. 1445–1515), a famous commentator on the Mishnah.</note> says: <note>original Hebrew: דברי כבושין דברים שכובשין לבו של אדם להחזירו למוטב</note> **Subduing words: Words that subdue the heart of man to lead it back toward what is good. I shall add no more.**

### CHAPTER VI.

*A more specific discussion on the circumstances of holding sermons among the Jews; namely, the Place, Time, and Occasions on which this act was celebrated in the synagogue. In particular, a twofold kind of Synagogical sermon is observed, one of which was mixed with the reading of the Divine Law, and the other followed it.*

Since we have sufficiently discussed the *manner of preaching*, it will best serve the purpose of this treatise to now *secondly* examine the *Circumstances of holding sermons*, that is, the *Places, times, and occasions* in which such sacred discourses were held; thereafter we shall proceed to the *Persons* to whom this task was entrusted.

From what has been said regarding the genuine meaning of the word *Darash* <term>Darash: A Hebrew root meaning to seek, inquire, or expound upon scripture</term>, it is clear enough that such discourses or sermons on divine matters could be established in any *Places* where learned and pious men desired to gather. Men excelling in wisdom even had a certain part of their homes dedicated to these sacred exercises, where they frequently withdrew; these were called *Aliyot* <note>original Hebrew: עליות, meaning "upper chambers" or lofts</note> by Hebrew writers, and in the Sacred Scriptures they are called an *Upper Room* <note>original Greek: ὑπεרῷον</note>, as was indeed proven in previous sections. However, the act of *Exposition* <note>original: τοῦ דרש (of the Darash)</note> properly belonged to the *Schools and Academies*, in which the Doctors <note>Teachers or Rabbis</note> instructed either their disciples or even the common people through *Interpreters*, as we have already mentioned; for this reason, they were also called *Batei Midrashot* <term>Batei Midrashot: Houses of Study or Academies</term>. For the Interpreter, standing by the Doctor, explained his words to the people or the disciples; this *Interpreter* was then specifically said to **PREACH**.

<margin>Chapter on the Laws of Money [Diné Mammon], folio 7, column 2.</margin>
Thus it is found in the *Sanhedrin* <note>The Talmudic tractate concerning the high court and legal procedures</note>: *The interpreter stood up beside him to make the sermon heard by the assembly; that is, specifically, what the Doctor had whispered to him.* <note>original Hebrew: קום עליה באמורא להשמיע</note>. And a little later, more clearly: *When the Interpreter* **PREACHED**, *the assembly sat on the ground, and anyone walking between them to sit in his place—passing through the middle of their ranks—appeared as if he were walking over their heads.* <note>original Hebrew: שכשהיה המתורגמן דורש היו הצבור יושבין לארץ והמפסיע ביניהם לילך ולישב במקומו נרא' כמפסיע על ראשין</note>.

However, beyond the fact that the *Teachers* and their *Interpreters* formerly preached in the *Academies*, often with the common people listening, it must be firmly held that *sermons* were also delivered to the public in the *Synagogues* themselves—a point proven most clearly above. Even if someone, reading simply that *Christ* and the *Apostles* preached in the *Synagogues*, might reasonably doubt whether "Synagogues" does not often refer to the more illustrious *Schools* connected to the synagogues; there are nevertheless other passages in the *New Testament* beyond all exception that speak of *Synagogues* in the proper sense of the word. 

For instance, when it is said that *Christ*, according to his custom on the Sabbath day, *entered* the synagogue <note>original Greek: εἰς τὴν συναγωγὴν</note>, *and stood up* to read <note>original Greek: ἀναγνῶναι</note>, *to read from the book handed to him by the Attendant of the Synagogue*, and after the *Reading* was finished, *he taught* and explained the passage he had read, showing the fulfillment of that famous prophecy. This is certainly of such a nature that it must be referred to the *Synagogue* specifically so-called: the place where the *Reading of the Law* was performed (though I admit this reading was done specifically to provide a text for the sermon), where a public *attendant* was appointed to guard the Book of the Law, and the people were gathered in great numbers on the *Sabbath* day. Similarly, the *History* narrated in the Acts of the Apostles concerning *Paul* and his companions leaves no room for doubt:

> But they, having traveled from Perga, came to Antioch, a city of Pisidia, and entering the Synagogue on the Sabbath day, they sat down. After the Reading of the Law and the Prophets, the Prefects of the Synagogue sent to them, saying: "Men, brothers, if there is any WORD OF EXHORTATION (<note>original Greek: λόγος παρακλήσεως, *logos parakleseos*</note>) for the people among you, speak."

Regarding this, Luke further reports that *Paul* preached: the summary of which sermon he has preserved for us in that same place. Indeed, for this purpose, a *Pulpit* or *Platform* (<term>Bimah: A raised platform in a synagogue used for reading the Torah and addressing the congregation (בימה)</term>) was erected in the Synagogues, as Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the influential medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> testifies, from which words could conveniently be addressed to the people. Since we have dealt with this previously, we shall say nothing more of it now.

...regarding the *Time* at which *sermons* of this kind were established. For this is everywhere called in the *Gospel History and the Acts* "the day of the Sabbaths" <note>original Greek: ἡ ἡμέρα τῶν σαββάτων</note>, or the *Sabbath Day*. Philo the *Jew* also testifies to this, and it is a practice preserved in modern customs; however, one should include under the notion of the *Sabbath* also the *Fast Days and Festivals*, on which the people gather in the *Synagogue buildings* as they usually do on the *Sabbath*. Nor should you exclude certain other *extraordinary times* for delivering orations, such as those designated for the *circumcision of an infant, weddings, or the funerals* of Eminent Men, which are celebrated with orations to be recited in the Synagogue. We do not think anything else should be gathered from those words which are read in the *Acts of the Apostles*:

<margin>Chapter 13, 42.</margin>
> *As they were going out of the Synagogue of the Jews, the Gentiles begged that these same words might be spoken to them on the following Sabbath <note>original Greek: τὸ μεταξὺ σάββατον</note>.*

For the phrase *into the intervening Sabbath* <note>original Greek: εἰς τὸ μεταξὺ σάββατον</note> is correctly translated here as: *on the next following Sabbath*. <margin>The Jewish War, book 6, chapter 6. Spicilegium and in this place.</margin> *"Towards the next Sabbath,"* <note>original Dutch: Tegen den naesten Sabbath</note> just as *the intervening* <note>original Greek: τὸ μεταξὺ</note> is understood in Josephus and other Greek authors, as observed by those most worthy men Cappel and de Dieu. <note>Louis Cappel and Louis de Dieu were 17th-century scholars of biblical languages.</note> <margin>On the Emendation of Time, book 6, p. 559.</margin> Therefore, the illustrious Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a famous Renaissance scholar of chronology.</note> acts too rashly in wanting *the Sabbath* <note>original Greek: τὸ σάββατον</note> to be changed to *of the Sabbaths* <note>original Greek: σαββάτων</note>, and wanting the expression *into the intervening of the Sabbaths* <note>original Greek: εἰς τὸ μεταξὺ σαββάτων</note>—taken as *during the interval between two Sabbaths*—to be translated as *the time between two Sabbaths*. In Hebrew: *during the secular days of the week* <note>original Hebrew: בחוֹל השבת</note>. I say the illustrious man acts too rashly, because that emendation not only relies on the authority of no manuscripts, but it is also not necessary. Indeed, what is called *the intervening Sabbath* is subsequently called in this same historical context *the coming Sabbath* <note>original Greek: τὸ ἐρχόμενον σάבβατον</note>. <note>The printer has used a Hebrew Beth (ב) in place of the Greek double beta (ββ) in the word σάבβατον.</note> <margin>verse 44.</margin> The words are:

> *On the following Sabbath, almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of God.*

And it is not surprising that the *Gentiles* also wished to be instructed on *Sabbath* days with the *Jews*, because there was no more convenient place for instruction than the *Synagogue*. But we must come closer and distinguish more specifically *by what Order or occasion* this act of preaching was celebrated among the other sacred acts of the Synagogue. I believe this order varied *according to the twofold method of preaching* used in the synagogues of old.

The simplest method of *preaching*, which obtained in the most ancient synagogues and sacred gatherings of the people, was this: that the *Levites, Priests, and legal experts* <note>original Greek: νομικοὶ, referring to scholars of the Divine Law</note> would read the *Divine Law* aloud, and [explain] the part read

### CHAPTER 6. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

...they would interpret and explain before the people by way of a kind of perpetual commentary. Thus, those assemblies were not merely certain orations or public speeches <note>original Greek: δημηγορίαι (demegoriai)</note> regarding some argument established after the reading of the Law and the Prophets—the kind which later began to be in use (and which we are now chiefly investigating)—but rather interpretations <note>original Greek: ἐξηγήσεις (exegeseis)</note> or paraphrases <note>original Greek: παραφράσεις (paraphraseis)</note> of certain illustrious or obscure parts of the Law, woven into the reading of Scripture for the purpose of teaching the people. Indeed, it cannot be doubted that under the leadership of Moses, Joshua, and other excellent men who, driven by the Spirit of God, frequently restored the troubled affairs of the Jews, the Levites and Priests—specifically appointed by God for this task—not only read the divine Law to the people, but also explained it. However, you cannot gather this ritual more clearly from anywhere else than from those things which are read in the book of Nehemiah concerning the events after the return from the *Babylonian Captivity*. 
<margin>Chapter 8, 1.</margin> 
There, the *Priests and Levites* are described as being stationed on a high platform, *interpreting and explaining the Divine Law*. But because this passage was cited and largely declared above, I will now observe this one thing: in this case, it was not the one who *read*, but the one who *stood beside the reader* and illuminated the more obscure words of the Law with a shorter or longer commentary, who was considered to have *preached*. This act of *preaching* is quite conveniently expressed here by the Hebrew word *to make someone understand* <note>original Hebrew: הבין (habin)</note>. So also in the following verses, the *Levites* are said to 
<margin>Chapter 8, 16.</margin> 
*make the people understand* <note>original Hebrew: מבינים את העם (mevinim et ha-am)</note>, that is, to educate and instruct the people. For a *teacher* <note>original Hebrew: מבין (mevin)</note> is he who is contrasted with a *disciple* <note>original Hebrew: תלמיד (talmid)</note>. So it is in the first book of Chronicles: 
<margin>Chapter 25, 8</margin> 
*The teacher with the disciple* <note>original Hebrew: מבין עם תלמיד (mevin im talmid)</note>. The Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> renders this: *Of the mature and the learners* <note>original Greek: Τελείων καὶ μανθανόντων (Teleion kai manthanonton)</note>. For the word *mature* <note>original Greek: Τέλειος (Teleios)</note> is also used in the writings of the New Covenant for one who has arrived at a perfect knowledge of things (which they call *maturity* <note>original Greek: τελειότητα (teleioteta)</note>), who in the writings of the Hebrews is called *completed* <note>original Hebrew: גמיר (gamir)</note>. The Chaldean <note>The Aramaic translation or Targum</note> has: *The scribe with the disciple* <note>original Aramaic: ספרא עם תלמידא (saphra im talmida)</note>. Indeed, a *scribe* <note>original Aramaic: ספרא (saphra)</note> is a *teacher*. Thus, many scribes <note>original Greek: γραμματεῖς (grammateis)</note> are called simply *Teachers* <note>original Hebrew: מבינים (mevinim)</note> in the book of *Ezra*. It is the same thing that is said in this same context: *to give the sense* <note>original Hebrew: שום שכל (shum sekel)</note>, or to *place* (to apply to the text being read) *understanding*. For I believe this phrase should be explained in exactly this way. To be sure, the Talmudists <note>Jewish scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism</note> disagree; they want the entire task attributed here to the Priests and Levites to have consisted in the *Hebrew text being translated by them into Chaldean* <note>Aramaic, which was the common spoken language of the Jews after the exile</note>.

### ON THE DUTIES OF OFFICIALS, BOOK III, PART I.

...since the people had already forgotten the Hebrew language during the Babylonian Captivity, accents—both those which serve to guide the reading and those which distinguish the sense of the sentences—were eventually added. This was observed long ago <margin>Commentary on the Masorah, chapter 8.</margin> from both Talmuds by Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629) was a leading Christian scholar of Hebrew and Jewish tradition.</note>. But who is unaware, or who denies, that it is a settled custom among the Jews to bend the meaning of Scripture with an affected cleverness to suit the hypotheses they most want to be accepted?

For besides the fact that the term *interpreted* <note>original Hebrew: מפורש (meforash)</note> does not conveniently denote a verbal paraphrase <note>original Greek: παράφρασιν (paraphrasin)</note>, any more than the phrase *and giving the sense* <note>original Hebrew: ושום שכל (vesum sekel)</note> denotes the arrangement of accents, perhaps it is not so much a true opinion as a common one among the Doctors <note>Academic or religious scholars.</note> that the Hebrew language fell into disuse among the people returning from Babylon. Indeed, the starting point of this interpretation was most successfully overturned by the renowned Alting <margin>Philosophical Dissertation on the Version of Scripture, chapter 1.</margin> <note>Jacob Alting (1618–1679) was a Dutch linguist and theologian who challenged the idea that Hebrew was lost in Babylon.</note>, who showed through a comparison of the entire Sacred History that all the Jews spoke Hebrew after their return from Babylon. He argued they loved and used that dialect until the times of the *Seleucids* <note>The Greek-Macedonian dynasty that ruled the Near East after Alexander the Great.</note>, and specifically *Antiochus Epiphanes* <note>The king whose Hellenizing policies led to the Maccabean Revolt around 167 BCE.</note>, when they became intermingled with the Syrians. 

I do not deny, however, that after the Syriac dialect <note>Also known as Aramaic or "Chaldean."</note> invaded the entire land of Judea—to the point that the Hebrew nation could no longer understand the text of Scripture read in its own language—those same preachers I just mentioned, who commented on the words read by their brothers, were also tasked with translating the words of the Law from the Hebrew language into the Syrian language (which they commonly call Chaldean). This was truly to *make them understand* <note>original Hebrew: מבין (mevin)</note> what had been read, and *to give understanding to the text* <note>original Hebrew: ושום שכל (vesum sekel)</note>.

For this same reason, those Interpreters <note>original Hebrew: מתרגמים (meturgemanim) — the OCR text reads 'מתרגמיס' which is likely a transcription error for the plural 'interpreters'.</note> stood at the *side of the reader*, just as in this case the Commentators or Preachers flanked the side of Ezra while he read. For the Jews rarely deviate from the customs of their ancestors. Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal scholar.</note> writes: <margin>Laws of Prayer, chapter 10, section 10.</margin> *From the days of Ezra* <note>original Hebrew: מימות עזרא נהגו שיהא שם תורגמן מתרגם לעם מה שהקורא קורא בתורה כדי שיבינו ענין הדברים</note> *it was the custom for an interpreter to be present, explaining to the people what the reader was reciting from the Law, so that they might perceive the meaning of the words.* Just as an interpreter who assisted a Teacher in a school or academy was properly said *to preach* <note>original Hebrew: דרש (darash)</note>, so the same may be said of this ecclesiastical Interpreter <note>original Hebrew: תורגמן (turgeman)</note>, who is quite distinct from the academic one; for perhaps this meaning is not far removed from the notation of the word *to preach* <note>original Hebrew: דרש (darash)</note>.

<summary>This page argues that while some believe Hebrew was lost in Babylon, it likely remained the vernacular until the Greek Seleucid era, necessitating the eventual role of the 'Turgeman' to translate Hebrew scripture into Aramaic for the public.</summary>

### CHAPTER 6. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

<margin>Chapter 1, Section 6.</margin>
**To Expound** <note>original Hebrew: דרש (Darash)</note> And one might refer here to a passage from the *Codex Yoma* <note>A volume of the Talmud concerning the rituals of the Day of Atonement.</note>, where mention is made of the High Priest preparing himself for the ministry of the Day of Atonement on the preceding night: *If he was a Sage <note>A scholar or wise man.</note> himself, he would expound; but if not, the disciples of the Sages would expound before him.* That is, if he himself was well-versed and learned in the Law and the decrees of the ancestors, he would exercise himself that night by reading, interpreting, and explaining the Holy Scripture.

For here, **to expound** <note>original Hebrew: דרש (Darash)</note> means to commentate while reading. And there was certainly a reason why this *action* of preaching was attributed to them, since those interpreters, while interpreting, frequently wandered into obvious arguments, either by explaining and illustrating the meaning contained in the words more clearly, or even by applying it to the present condition of the people for **exhortation** <note>original Greek: παράκλησιν (paraklesin)</note> and **correction** <note>original Greek: ἐπανόρθωσιν (epanorthosin)</note>. Let us now turn our eyes to the **Aramaic Paraphrases** <note>original Latin: Chaldaeas paraphrases</note>, (which they call **Targumim** <note>original Hebrew: תרגומים (Targumim) — Aramaic translations of the Hebrew Bible that often include expansive commentary.</note>), which were born, it seems, from ecclesiastical interpretations and later shared commonly for private use when the knowledge of the Hebrew dialect had perished among the Hebrews themselves; if not in full, as they had been spoken from the mouth of the interpreter, then at least in a shortened form. We see, in any case, that in those Paraphrases, not only were the Hebrew words converted into the Syriac <note>A dialect of Aramaic.</note> language, but the difficulties of the context were removed, metaphorical expressions were explained, parables were set forth, and types were illustrated, and this was done through a rather lengthy established commentary; though not everywhere with equal success and ease, because many of them belong to later times, in which fables increased, but true knowledge of divine things decreased.

### CHAPTER 6. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

**To Expound**. <note>original Hebrew: דרש (Darash), meaning to search out, explain, or preach.</note> And here one might refer to a passage from the *Tractate Yoma* <note>A volume of the Talmud focusing on the rituals of the Day of Atonement.</note>, where mention is made

I would like to point out that the first reading—that of the <note>Latin</note> Vulgate—is approved by me. In my judgment, its genuine meaning is this: the Gentiles searched through the Holy Scriptures for the *names of their idols* for the purpose of learning the Jews' opinions of them, thereby finding even weightier reasons to vent their rage against the Jews and their religion. For there is no foundation for the claim or belief (as I see some learned men interpret this passage) that the Gentiles investigated the *names of their idols* in the Scriptures so that they themselves might be further confirmed and hardened in their own superstitious worship. 

However, I have now primarily cast my eyes upon the *first part* of this text, which says: *and they unrolled the book of the law* <note>original Greek: καὶ ἐξεπέτασαν τὸ βιβλίον τοῦ νόμου</note>, which is commonly translated into Latin as: *And they explained the Books of the Law*; and it is explained in this manner: that the Gentiles *revolved*—that is, *unrolled*—the *volumes of the Law*, which were *rolled up* according to the custom of volumes at that time.

Le Moyne says: *Exepetasan* <note>unrolled</note> is the same as the word *aneptyxan* <note>opened</note> used in Luke. *Ptysso* means *to roll up, to wind, or to reduce into a volume* <note>original Hebrew: גלל הספר, 'to roll the scroll'</note>. Conversely, *anaptysso* denotes *to explain and unroll*, just as *ekpetannymi* means *to extend*, from which comes *exepetasan*. 

But for what purpose, I ask, were the *volumes of the Divine Law* unrolled and revolved during this solemn Fast, which was celebrated by Judas Maccabeus and the rest of the Jews when the affairs of the Republic were utterly desperate? The illustrious Le Moyne gives this reason: *So that they might represent the injuries inflicted upon God, the people, and sacred things.* I do not despise this reason. Yet I think it could also have been conveniently done for this purpose: so that ashes might be sprinkled upon the *Book of the Law (perhaps unrolled)* as a sign of the deepest mourning.

### CHAPTER 6. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES,

He begins his speech from the reading of a specific passage of Scripture, which he sets as the <term>theme<gloss>original Hebrew: נושא (noshe); literally 'subject' or 'burden'</gloss></term>, or the subject and argument of his discourse. Then he adds a certain saying of the Rabbis, which they call a <term>dictum<gloss>original Hebrew: מאמר (ma'amar); a formal statement or teaching</gloss></term>. Taking occasion from these, he chooses a theme that conforms to the aforementioned reading, which he then discusses more at length, bringing in various passages of Scripture and the authorities of the Rabbis to support the matter. But beyond this, you will understand the entire method of preaching accepted in today's Synagogues most clearly from those things which <note>Johann Christoph Wagenseil (1633–1705), a prominent Christian scholar of Jewish law and custom.</note> Wagenseil, mentioned above, wrote on this subject. 

Indeed, I assign the origin of such sermons primarily to that age which preceded the birth of Christ, our Lord, by a hundred years or more, during the reigns of <note>These were rulers of the Hasmonean dynasty in Judea.</note> Hyrcanus, Aristobulus, and Alexander Jannaeus. For that was the time when wisdom—although fallen and corrupt—began to be valued and restored along with the restored Republic [of the Jews]. Teachers also began to become famous, and ambition, honors, and the reputation of both the teachers and the disciples who were dedicated to the study of wisdom and piety began to increase. And from this, it also seems to me to have happened that certain Teachers, excelling in learning and holiness—especially those who were devoted to the <term>sect of the Pharisees<gloss>original Greek: τῇ αἱρέσει τῶν Φαρισαίων</gloss></term>—wanted to instruct the common people with their precepts, parables, and allegories beyond the ordinary <term>interpretation<gloss>original Greek: ἐξήγησιν (exegesis)</gloss></term> of Scripture. They wished to exhort them to virtues through their sacred speeches, so that through this opportunity they might show their skill in speaking to the people and commend themselves to all by their learning and holiness.

### ON THE DUTIES OF THE OFFICIALS. BOOK III. PART I.

*...they granted great liberty to any* **Doctors** <note>In this context, "Doctors" refers to learned teachers or scholars of Jewish Law, rather than medical practitioners.</note> *; hence the reason is sought why Christ and the Apostles preached so familiarly in the Synagogues.*

After we have attempted to explain the method of preaching, this discussion of ours will finally lead us to a more diligent investigation of the **Persons** who performed this office of preaching; which we now undertake.

If anyone understands that in certain Jewish Synagogues there were appointed certain **Darshanim** <gloss>original Hebrew: דרשנים; Preachers</gloss>, who were famous and celebrated among their fellow countrymen by this name, I would not want them to think that either the custom of all *modern Synagogues* is such, or that the custom of the *ancient* ones was so. Concerning the fact that this act of preaching belonged first of all to the **Archisynagogoi**, of whom we spoke in the preceding Chapter—or rather, the right to perform that act—it is clear enough from the fact that they were the *Leaders* of the *Synagogue*, by whom all the duties of the Synagogue were distributed. Since they had the power of granting the exercise of that act to others, as will be indicated more broadly later, it is clear enough that it belonged to them and pertained to them first. # ON THE DUTIES OF PREFECTS, BOOK III. PART [X]

...[those who are] called **ARCHIPERECITAE**, or perhaps **ELDERS** <note>original: *Presbyteri*</note>, or **MASTERS** <note>original: *Magistri*</note>, are forbidden to prevent this <note>likely referring to the reading of Scripture in the vernacular mentioned in the decree</note> by any clever tricks or excommunications, 
<margin>Novella 146. Issued in the 25th year of Justinian, 548 AD. See Morin, Exercise 6, chapter 2, book 2.</margin>
unless they wish to be punished for these things with physical penalties, and furthermore to suffer the confiscation of their private property, being <unclear>fined</unclear> against their will; for we desire and command things that are better and more pleasing to God. Thus the Old Translator has it. The Greek words are: *“Nor do those among them called **Archipericitae**, or perhaps **Elders**, or **Teachers**, have the authority to prevent this through certain machinations or excommunications.”* There is hardly any learned man who has not discussed this word and its true meaning. The most erudite conjectures of Hugo Grotius, Johannes Gerardus Vossius, Dionysius Gothofredus, Nicolaus Serarius, Samuel Petitus, John Selden, and also Jean Morin <note>These were prominent 16th and 17th-century scholars of law, theology, and history.</note> are found concerning it. Almost all, as I said, agree that this word designates the **Archisynagogoi** <term>Archisynagogue: From the Greek for 'ruler of the synagogue,' the official responsible for the building and the arrangements for services.</term>, or the leaders of the Jews in the Synagogues and in public readings—whether of the Sacred Scripture itself or of the body of the Talmud—since the meaning is easily determined from the context of the text. They are accustomed to derive the word, which appears to be a compound, from the Greek *archē* <note>meaning 'rule' or 'beginning'</note> and the Hebrew **פרק** (*Perek*), which denotes a Chapter, section, text, or part of a sacred Book, or of the Talmud, whose chapters are called **פרקים** (*Perakim*) (which is the opinion of Morin), upon which the commentary of the Teacher was to be established. Whence *Archipericites*, following the example of **ארכירוקי** (*Archi-Rokei*) and **ארכי הדיינים** (*Archi-HaDayanim*) <note>Hebrew titles for 'Chief of the Physicians' and 'Chief of the Judges.'</note>, would signify the **Chief of those Commentators**, or, as learned men have it, the **Prince of Preachers**, in whose 
<margin>Various Readings, book 2, chapter 10.</margin>
power it is to interpret such a chapter first of all, or to give it to others to be interpreted. Samuel Petitus, however, proceeds slightly differently. “But it is not approved by us,” he says, “that they derive the latter part of the word from the *Perakim* [Chapters] of the Talmud. For how would the **Archiperrecitae** be approved if they publicly read and interpreted the titles of the Talmud, or *Perakim*, in the Synagogues, when by this very Constitution Justinian forbids the public reading of the **Deuterosis** <term>Deuterosis: A Greek term (meaning 'repetition') used by Christians to refer to the Mishnah, the Jewish oral law.</term>, which they call **משנה** (*Mishnah*), and which is the principal part of the Talmud?” The words of the Constitution [Justinian's decree] are these: *“But that which is called **Deuterosis** by them, we interdict in every way, as it is not joined to the sacred books, nor handed down from above by the Prophets, but is an invention established by men speaking from the earth alone, and having nothing divine in them. Therefore, let them read the sacred words themselves, rejecting those books [the Mishnah], yet not hiding what was said through them, but in vain using those things handed down from outside without writing, which were devised by them for the sake of the simpler [people]...”*

### CHAPTER 7. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

...destruction. However, there is no great force in this reasoning of the illustrious Petitus. For besides the fact that it is not likely that the Emperor, when he used the word *archiperekitēs* <note>original Greek: ἀρχιφερεκίτης; likely a Greco-Hebrew hybrid title</note>, understood its genuine meaning—which would have to be sought from a knowledge of the Hebrew language—it is certain enough that in using names, we are not accustomed to attend so much to their original meaning (if they are broken down into their simple root parts) as we are to the usage they have among the people of the time in which we live. Among those people, since this word *archiperekitēs* generally denoted the Leaders of the Jews, the Patriarchs, the Elders <note>original Greek: πρεσβύτερος (*presbyteros*)</note>, and the Rulers of the Synagogue <term>Archisynagogoi: The presiding officers of a Jewish congregation</term>, Justinian also adopted it for the same people, perhaps not noticing the specific meaning inherent within it.

It would be the same as if someone were to call a certain Judge, who belonged to the Jewish Senate but had not yet reached thirty or forty years of age, an "Elder" <note>original: *presbyteron* or *Seniorem*</note>; such a person surely would not recall the true literal notion of the word "Elder" <note>original: πρεσβύτερος</note> in his mind, but would accommodate himself, as is done, to the common usage in human interaction, where it is most familiarly accepted as a title for a Judge. In the same way, even though the Emperor Justinian had forbidden the Jews from the public reading or explanation of the "Oral Law" <note>Referring to the Mishnah or Talmudic traditions which Justinian's Novella 146 sought to suppress in favor of Biblical Greek/vernacular readings</note> in the Synagogues—by which name you should here understand their Schools—he could still rightly call the Prefects "Archiperecites," even if this word itself expressed the very act of explaining the Oral Law. This is because the Rulers of the Synagogue were commonly known by this name among their own people, and the performance of this duty had been entrusted to them until that time. 

But let us hear Petitus himself, as he conjectures about the origin of this word. He continues thus:

> The reason for the name is this. Its first part is Greek <note>*archi-*, meaning 'chief' or 'head'</note>, but the second is Hebrew, from *perek* <note>Hebrew: פרק</note>, when it signifies to survive evils and be liberated from them; and in those times they called *perakah* <note>Hebrew: פרקה</note> those remnants of the Jews who survived in various places and had lived through so many evils, which had overtaken their entire race and nation. A *perakah* was therefore a band of Jews gathered into the same Synagogue, so named because it survived the destruction, just as the *perukah* <note>Hebrew: פרקוה</note> were found everywhere on earth. Archiperecites, therefore, are those who preside over their *perakah*; that is, the Rulers of the Synagogue.

The meaning of the words in the *Seder Olam Zuta* <note>A small Hebrew chronicle from the 8th or 9th century</note> is no different, which we shall report from the work *The Faith* <note>original: *Fide*</note> by Serarius: "He went up to the land of Israel, and they appointed him *Le-Resh Perake* <note>Hebrew: לריש פרקי; literally 'Head of the Sections' or 'Chapters'</note>." So Serarius reads it, and he explains it as "Head or Prince of the *Perakim*" <note>referring to sections of the law or communal groups</note>; but he does so falsely. For as from his...

That most learned man says: *Pirka* <note>original Hebrew: פרקה</note> signifies the "hands" or the "remnants" of the Jews, snatched from many evils and finally gathered into certain Synagogues. But on what foundation does this etymology rest, since it relies on this assertion alone? Indeed, I strongly doubt whether this use of the word occurs anywhere among Hebrew writers. ### CHAPTER 7. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

For what is called here the *Resh Pirka* <note>original Aramaic: ריש פרקא; literally "Head of the Section" or "Head of the Lecture"</note> is called by other Jewish historians recounting this same history the *Rosh Sanhedrin* <note>original Hebrew: ראש סנהדרין; "Head of the Council"</note>, as was observed by Morinus <note>Jean Morin (1591–1659), a French scholar of biblical criticism and Jewish history</note>. And in this way, you may very easily understand 

<margin>Sacred Exercises, p. 297.</margin>

another passage from the same *Minor Chronicle* noted by Morinus, which is likewise found *at the end* of that Chronicle: 

<margin>page 36, column 2.</margin>

*The Judge of the Prince of the Captivity* <note>original Aramaic: *Resh Galuta* or Exilarch, the political leader of Jews in Babylon</note> *went into the City in which Rabbi Chanina was the Scholarch* <note>Head of the School</note>, *and he* STUDIED TO ESTABLISH A SCHOOL THERE, (*Morinus translates: And he sought to make a head*) but the Scholarch did not permit him to do so. You see that *Pirka* <note>original: פרקא</note> is most conveniently understood here as a *School*. And this same meaning fits well enough with other passages added by Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a famous Hebraist</note>, in which the word *Pirka* is commonly rendered in Latin as *Reading* or *Sermon*: such as the phrase *he came to the Pirka*, which is said to mean *he came to the sermon*, but could best be translated as *he came to the School*. 

<margin>p. 44.</margin>

Indeed, in the *Halicoth Olam* <note>A 15th-century handbook on Talmudic methodology by Yeshuah ben Joseph ha-Levi</note>, *in the Pirka* is rendered as *publicly*; from which you may conclude that *Pirka* denotes a *public place*, a multitude gathered in public, or something similar; perhaps derived from *perek*, meaning *to break forth*. Unless you would rather derive the word *perek*, as it enters the composition of the Greek title *Archipherekites*, from the root *perek*, which to the Talmudists also means *to solve an objection*; so that an *Archipherekites* would be the *Leader of the Disputants in the Academy*, that is, the *highest Master and Rector of the School*. However, if *Pirka* is taken here either for a *Chapter* to be explained, or for an *Academic or Synagogal Sermon*—toward which the very common and by no means negligible opinion of learned men aims—then surely from this word you might rightly conclude (as we were contending) that the Rulers of the Synagogues held the highest *authority for teaching and preaching* in the Synagogues.

***

Yet what we have been guessing at from these arguments, we may recognize more directly and clearly from others. 

<margin>On the Contemplative Life, p. 691.</margin>

Philo the Jew <note>A Hellenistic Jewish philosopher from Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE)</note>, besides those things noted from him above, after he had described the *Weekly Sabbath Assembly of the Essenes in the Synagogue*, proceeds thus regarding the *Sermons* held there: *And coming forward, the eldest and most experienced in the doctrines speaks* (he teaches), *with a steady gaze and a steady voice, with reason and wisdom; not displaying a cleverness of words, as do the Orators or the sophists of today, but having searched out and interpreting the exact meaning of the thoughts.*
