->### ON THE DUTIES OF OFFICIALS, BOOK III, PART I.<-

The **Rulers of the Synagogue** <note>original Latin: *Archisynagogi*</note> did not always or ordinarily perform this act of preaching. Indeed, this has been proven above from the *Code of the Scribes* <note>original Latin: *Codice Sopherim*; a collection of scribal laws and traditions</note> and can be clearly gathered from the history of the New Testament. For if the act of preaching had been performed as a matter of course by the **Rulers of the Synagogue** themselves, there certainly would not have been such frequent opportunities for Christ or the Apostles to preach. Consider the history, already cited several times from the Acts of the Apostles, <margin>Chapter 13, 15.</margin> the reading of the Law and the Prophets had been celebrated—that is, the ordinary duties of the Synagogue had just been completed. All the people, therefore, were preparing to depart, and it is not read that the Rulers of the Synagogue had any intention of *preaching*. But when they saw Paul with his fellow soldiers <note>The author uses a military metaphor for Paul's companions in the ministry</note> entering the Synagogue outside of the regular order, taking the seats of the **Teachers** <note>original Latin: *Doctorum*; referring to those authorized to teach the Law</note>, and perhaps signaling a desire to speak through their gestures and body movements, they were willing to grant them the opportunity to speak. Whether the neglect of this *Act* arose from the incompetence of certain **Rulers of the Synagogue**, or from the frequency of *Academic* institutions, or from the multitude of **Teachers** offering themselves to hold *sermons* besides the **Rulers of the Synagogue**, or indeed from the growth of the liturgy of *Prayers and Blessings*, is unclear to us.

Indeed, the *third adjustment*, which we cannot pass over "with a dry foot" <note>An idiom meaning to pass over something without due attention</note>, is that the *Act* of preaching in the Synagogues was not exclusive to the **Rulers of the Synagogue** alone, but was exercised most freely by any other **Teachers** besides them. The Hebrew people were divided into <margin>1 Corinthians 14, 24.</margin> men whom Paul calls *laymen* <note>original Greek: $\iota \delta \iota \acute{\omega} \tau \alpha \varsigma$ (*idiotas*); referring to common people or those without professional training</note> and whom the Hebrews call the *people of the land* <note>original Hebrew: עם הארץ (*Am ha'aretz*)</note>—the Romans call them the *common folk*—the most despised plebeians who were not imbued with the knowledge of the Divine Law; and the *Disciples of the Wise* <note>original Hebrew: תלמידי חכמים (*Talmidei Chachamim*)</note>, by which name all those were generally noted who had devoted their efforts to the Divine Law, being the most noble and generous part of the people, dedicated to sacred studies from infancy. These latter were handed over to the discipline of Teachers famous in their age, and when they had reached the proper measure of years, they sought with great zeal this same title of **Rabbi** <note>original Hebrew: רבי; meaning "Doctor" or "Teacher"</note>, and they obtained it either by their own fitness and progress in the knowledge of the Law of their Fatherland, or by the favor of their instructors. ->If there is no Elder and Wise Man there, they appoint a Wise Man; if there is neither<-
->an Elder nor a Wise Man there, they appoint a man of integrity.<-

<margin>folio 16, column 1.</margin> *If there is no* **Wise Elder** *present, they appoint a* **Wise Man** (*that is, a Teacher*, although he might not be advanced in age). *If there is neither an Elder nor a Wise Man present, they appoint* **a man of distinguished form and integrity**. <note>The Hebrew *adam shel tzurah* (אדם של צורה) literally means "a man of form," referring to someone of high moral character and respected appearance.</note> *These words are taken from the Gemara Taanith <note>The portion of the Talmud discussing fast days</note>, from which it is certainly clear that Synagogues did not commonly maintain specific, fixed* **Preachers** <note>Hebrew: *Darshanim* (דרשנין)</note>. *Furthermore, in cases of extreme necessity, it was permitted for certain men of the Common People—for such was the one called a* **man of integrity**, *who is contrasted here with the* **Wise Man**—*to speak words to the people in the Synagogues, with the greatest liberty, as anyone can see.* <margin>cited above.</margin> Indeed, this same freedom of preaching persists in the **Synagogues of the present day**, as is established by the writings of *Leone de Modena* <note>A famous Venetian rabbi and scholar, 1571–1648</note>. *Wagenseil* <note>Johann Christoph Wagenseil, a 17th-century Christian Hebraist</note> *notes: For common sermons are given in the vernacular tongue of whichever Jewish nation it might be, nor are they usually held on fixed days, except that the* **Rabbi**, *the* **Presider of the Synagogue**, *is accustomed to speak on rituals before the Passover holidays, and before the Day of Atonement he discusses something regarding Repentance; likewise, when a famous man among them has died somewhere in the world, he combines a funeral oration with supplications. At other times, perhaps a traveling guest, or anyone else who has confidence in his own learning and believes he has thought of something worthy of recitation, undertakes to discourse upon it.*

Since this is the case, what harm would there be in ascribing this same freedom and power of preaching to the **Ministers of the Synagogue**, especially the more honorable ones? These men often governed the **Synagogue** solely by their own authority. Certainly, if other more suitable men were not present—who were better suited to the task—these ministers themselves would use special occasions like **Fasting** or **Thanksgiving** to stir the people to humility or joy, and to remind them of their duty. ### CHAPTER 7. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

Now there were in *Antioch*, in the Church of that place, PROPHETS and TEACHERS <note>original Greek: διδάσκαλοι (*didaskaloi*); Latin: *doctores*</note>: *Barnabas*, *Simeon*, and *Lucius*; likewise *Manahem* and *Saul*. What prevents us from believing that these men were truly admitted into the order of Teachers according to the Jewish rite <margin>Book 2, chapters 10 and 11.</margin>, and recognized as such in the Jewish Schools and Synagogues, as long as the Christian Church had not yet completely separated itself from the Jewish one? Who would doubt that *Paul* was a *Teacher*, considering that an office of honor was entrusted to him even before his conversion? For we gather from the *Acts of the Apostles* <margin>Chapter 9, verses 1, 2.</margin> that he was sent by the Priest and the Jerusalem Sanhedrin <note>The supreme judicial and religious council of the Jews</note> to all the synagogues. Indeed, I believe that he was an Apostle of the Sanhedrin <note>original Greek: Ἀπόστολον τῆς συνεδρίᾳ (*Apostolon tēs synedria*)</note>; from these Apostles of the Sanhedrin <note>original Hebrew: *Shelichei Sanhedrin* (שליחי סנהדרין), meaning authorized messengers or delegates of the council</note> undoubtedly arose the *Apostles of the Patriarch* after the destruction of the Temple, those most famous in Law whom we discussed previously. From being an Apostle of the Sanhedrin, he indeed became an Apostle of Jesus Christ <note>original Greek: Ἀπόστολος Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ</note>, who was considered here in the likeness of a *Patriarch* <note>The author compares the authority of Jesus over the Church to the authority of the Jewish Patriarch over the Diaspora</note>. Moreover, besides the office of *Patriarch*, which was the greatest of all, there was no more worthy or honorable duty among the Jews than that of *Apostle*, just as the matter also stood in the Christian Church.

Indeed, it is clear that *Paul* was a public Rabbi and *Teacher* <note>original Hebrew: רבי (*Rabbi*)</note> among the Jews from the laying on of hands performed for Timothy, by which he also declared him a *Teacher*. But regarding this, as has been treated previously, so it shall be discussed more extensively in the following parts, if it pleases God. I only wish to observe this one thing now: that the title Rabbi <note>original Greek: Ῥαββὶ</note> refers only to the laying on of hands <note>original Greek: ἐπίθεσιν τῶν χειρῶν (*epithesin tōn cheirōn*), the formal ordination rite</note>. Surely, if this title had been very common, why would the Pharisees, who were accustomed to high aspirations, have sought it with such zeal and ardor, and why would Christ the Lord have so carefully forbidden its use to his disciples?

Certainly, the writings of the Hebrews record this nowhere, nor does it suggest...

Hence, the chairs for teaching and judging are here called the *Chair of Moses*, which the *Pharisees* had now occupied. Their faction (according to the witness of *Josephus* <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish historian</note>) was then prevailing, which is why the Great Sanhedrins and the Academies were filled with them. Therefore, the Chair of *Moses* is also that which the *Doctors* and other legal experts and disciples <note>original Greek: *μαθηταὶ* (*mathētai*)</note> who were considered fit for *teaching* occupied in the Synagogues and Academies.

# ON THE OFFICES OF THE PREFECTS BOOK III. PART I.

<meta>catchword: diju.</meta>

Luke records: "After the reading of the Law and the Prophets, the Prefects of the Synagogue sent to them, saying: *'Men, brothers, if there is any word of exhortation in you, speak.'*" What would have been the reason for the Leaders of the Synagogue <note>original Latin: *Archifynagogi*</note> to invite these men—who, as it clearly appears, were total strangers—to speak, if they had simply occupied the common benches of the crowd? By what sign would the leaders have been made certain of their fitness and their intention to teach? And what could that sign have been other than their *sitting* <note>original: *sessio*</note>, since nothing else is reported of them except that they entered the synagogue and sat down? Since the mere act of sitting cannot, by itself, be an indication of being a *Doctor* <note>A "Doctor" here refers to a formal teacher of the Law, from the Latin *docere*, "to teach."</note> or of an intention to teach, it seems altogether likely that a different kind of *sitting* is signified here—one belonging to the *Doctors*.

<margin>In Schillo book 3, chapter 6.</margin>
The famous Altingius <note>Jacob Alting (1618–1679), a Dutch linguist and theologian.</note> writes regarding this same case: *"And by this practice (of sitting) they were recognized as Doctors by the Leaders of the Synagogue, who, once the reading of the Law and Prophets was finished, allowed them to speak in the assembly if they had come prepared with a meditation."* For you cannot rightly conclude from this that such a thing was granted to just any traveler to speak publicly. Rather, when these travelers identified themselves as Masters by the privilege of SITTING, the Prefects of the Synagogue—who had sometimes heard of such men arriving from Jerusalem—granted them that honor. However, it should not be overlooked that 

<margin>verse 16.</margin>
Paul, *STANDING UP* <note>original Greek: *ἀναστάς* (*anastas*), though the OCR incorrectly transcribed this as *διναζᾶς*</note>, delivered this sermon. Indeed, Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note> also requires this standing posture for one giving a sermon, even though we know that Christ ordinarily sat while teaching. From this, I admit, a doubt might arise for some whether Christ taught more in the Schools than in the Synagogues, because it is certain that *the sitting of Masters while teaching was the most accepted custom in the Schools.* Yet, to remove this scruple, I would like it noted that it is certain from New Testament history that 

<margin>Luke 4:20.</margin>
Doctors who were teaching sat not only where it was convenient in the Schools, but also in the Synagogues. Certainly, in the Gospel of Luke, Christ taught in the synagogue, and yet *HE SAT DOWN* <note>original Greek: *ἐκάθισε* (*ekathise*)</note>. We find the same thing clearly in the *Acts of the Apostles*: <term>On the Sabbath day we went outside the city by the river, where it was thought there was a place of prayer; and sitting down, we spoke to the women who had gathered</term> <note>original Greek: *Τῇ τε ἡμέρα τῦ Σαββάτων ἐξήλθομεν ἔξω τῆς πόλεως παρὰ ποταμόν, ἕ ἐνομίζετο προσευχὴ εἶναι· καὶ καθίσαντες ἐλαλῶμεν ταῖς συνελθέσαις γυναῖξι*</note>; *"When we 

<margin>Chapter 16:13.</margin>
HAD SAT DOWN, we discussed things before the women who had convened."* To "sit down" here again means to sit in the Chair of the Doctors. From this, the women and the others who had gathered for the sacred rites understood that they were Doctors, and they also delivered their sermons while sitting. This interpretation also applies to a notable passage in Paul's first 

<margin>Chapter 14:30.</margin>
Letter to the Corinthians: *"Let two or three prophets speak, and let the rest..."*

# CHAPTER 7. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

711

XXX x 2

<meta>catchword: CHAPTER.</meta>

...let them judge. <note>original Latin: *dijudicent*, likely referencing 1 Corinthians 14:29: "Let the others judge."</note> *But if something is revealed to another* WHO IS SITTING BY, *let the first be silent.* <note>The author is quoting 1 Corinthians 14:30. Original Greek: *Ἐὰν δὲ ἄλλῳ ἀποκαλυφθῇ καθημένῳ, ὁ πρῶτος σιγάτω*; original Latin: *Quod si quid alii retectum fuerit SEDENTI, prior sileat*.</note> To *sit* here again signifies *to occupy the Chair of the Prophesiers*, or of the *teachers*. Indeed, those who believe that no order was maintained in this Assembly—as if there were a liberty of speaking and teaching for everyone indiscriminately, even the unlearned and those not sufficiently practiced—seem to be mistaken. For I maintain it should be held as certain that Paul, in this chapter, presents to us the image of the Ancient Synagogue—no longer the Judean one, but the Christian one—which retained the Ancient *model* <note>original Greek: *τύπον* (typon)</note> in all things. Since in the Ancient Synagogue all those well-educated were admitted to speak, this ought not to have been done with less liberty in the Christian Church, which had obtained such an abundance of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. But just as *order* was to be preserved in all things, so these Men and Doctors, who were moved by the Holy Spirit, were bound to claim the benches of the *teachers* for themselves, and to communicate their gifts to the Church in due order, so that all *confusion* <note>original Greek: *σύγχυσις* (synchysis)</note> might be avoided. And I believe this is the most certain reason that can be given for why *Christ* and the *Apostles*—though not specifically designated for this office among the Jews—once had the liberty of speaking, teaching, and preaching in the Synagogues, without anyone wondering at it or disapproving.

However, if we compare this liberty of speaking with that of the *Leaders of the Synagogue*, <note>original Latin: *Archisynagogorum*</note> of whom we spoke before, we find this distinction between the two: that the *Leaders* not only possessed the primary right of preaching, but they could also grant themselves the power to preach, whereas it was not permitted for others to perform this act *by right* unless it was *conceded* by them. They, therefore, just as they distributed all the more honorable offices of the Synagogue, also disposed of this act of *preaching* according to their own pleasure and judgment, so that no one would dare to perform it unless permission had been granted by the Leaders of the Synagogue: a clear proof of this matter is found in the Acts of the Apostles, a history we have already brought to light and illustrated many times.

<summary>This page argues that the early Christian church adopted the organized speaking order of the Jewish synagogue, where "sitting" in designated seats signaled a teacher's authority. It explains that while educated members had liberty to speak, the Leaders of the Synagogue (Archisynagogi) held the ultimate authority to grant or withhold permission to preach.</summary>

## CHAPTER VIII.

*The sermons of the Teachers of the Christian Church are compared with those of the Synagogue—from which they derive their origin—in terms of their name, method, and various circumstances; certain phrases of Holy Scripture pertaining to this matter are also explained.*

In the earliest gatherings of Christians, sermons <note>original Latin: *Conciones*</note> were delivered by the leaders and teachers of those assemblies. This was done so closely according to the example of the Synagogue sermons that the matter is so well known and familiar that it is almost unnecessary for a scholar to discuss it. Indeed, to anyone reading the Acts of the Apostles and comparing them with the Gospel history and the Epistles, it will be clear: 1. That the Apostles preached in the Synagogues just as Christ the Lord had led the way, and as other men of their order—that is, the Doctors <note>Teachers or learned scholars of the law</note>—were accustomed to do at that time. 2. That the Apostles handed down this same form of preaching, as if by hand, and commended it by their instructions to the overseers and teachers of the Christian Church in the following times. Thus, it is most certain and well known that the sermons of the early Church draw their origin from the Synagogue.

<margin>
Justin Martyr, *Second Apology to Antoninus Pius*, pages 97, 98; and Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 39.
</margin>
That this practice of preaching was subsequently continued in the assemblies of the Apostles is equally clear from the explicit testimonies of Justin Martyr and Tertullian (who will be called upon later), as well as from the principal authors of Ecclesiastical History. Nevertheless, so that our treatise does not fall short in this area, we must briefly see how well the Church's sermons agree with those of the Synagogue in terms of their Name, Method, Circumstances, and the People who performed that act. If these points do not satisfy the reader, they may be easily supplemented by a diligent student from the singular treatise by Bernardino Ferrari, *On the Rite of Sacred Sermons of the Ancient Church*. This work was made available for the public benefit and recommended quite recently—after we had already committed these thoughts of ours to paper—by the most learned and celebrated Johannes Georgius Graevius, the prince and father of letters among us.

<margin>
Acts 17:2.
</margin>

Paul entered among them, and for three Sabbaths **DISCOURSED** <note>original Greek: διελέγετο (dialegesto)</note> with them from the Scriptures, **EXPLAINING AND DEMONSTRATING** <note>original Greek: διανοίγων καὶ παρατιθέμενος (dianoigon kai paratithemenos)</note> that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer. This occurred in the Synagogue of Thessalonica. Here you find three notions expressing the same act: reasoning, demonstrating, and opening. The first of these, "to reason" or "discourse," occurs again with this same meaning in verse 17 of this chapter, and in other places. In its power and significance, it corresponds to the Hebrew word <term>Darash <gloss>to seek, study, or expound</gloss></term>, as it is the same as to discuss or dispute. The *Dutch* <note>original Latin: Belgæ</note> rightly translate it as *handelen* <note>to handle or deal with a subject</note>; to dispute by discussing. And it has already been noted and proven by us in the previous sections that Hebrew sermons were called <term>Derashot <gloss>expositions or inquiries</gloss></term> from this very Hebrew word *Darash*.

Since this phrasing is not entirely explicit, let us hear what the most learned man, Nicholas Fuller, contributed to its illustration. He says it is familiar to the Chaldeans, Syrians, and Jews to use the word <term>Piska <gloss>to cut or divide</gloss></term>, which signifies to cleave or cut. From this, the verses of the Bible received their name, being called <term>Pesukim <gloss>divisions</gloss></term>, that is, segments, sections, or small parts. Nothing was better known than this to Timothy, who had been taught the Holy Scriptures from childhood. Moreover, those who devoted their labor to these verses (*Pesukim*)—that is, to the entire doctrine of the Law and the Prophets, or the written Word of God—were called <term>ha-posekim ba-Torah <gloss>those who cut the Law</gloss></term>, that is, those who were occupied in treating the Law, being well-versed or practiced in it. For Rabbi Moses Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note> uses "those who are occupied" and "those who cut" (or decide) in the Law as synonyms. However, I do not know if my memory fails me, or if rather that most learned man errs, when he says that *Posek ba-Torah* is a familiar term for Hebrew writers and especially Maimonides in that specific sense...

# ON THE DUTIES OF PRESIDENTS, BOOK III, PART I.

...[continued]... and *the commentaries of the Apostles, or the writings of the Prophets are read as long as time permits. Then, when the reader has finished,* THE PRESIDING OFFICER <note>original Latin: Antistes</note> DELIVERS THE SERMON, *by which he instructs the people, and urges them to the imitation of such beautiful things. Nevertheless, since the exercise of sacred acts was quite free, both in the Church and the Synagogue, I judge that nothing can be absolutely determined about it.

<margin>Regarding the variation of the sacred customs of the Church, see Sozomen, book 7, chapter 19; and Socrates, book 5, chapter 22.</margin>
The methods of these sacred *Acts* often varied in their circumstances and ways, according to the natural talent of the *Teachers* who presided over them. Some of these were better suited to the *explanation* of the Divine Word, others to the *exhortation* of the common people, and others to *disputations*. Indeed, although the method of teaching in the Synagogues was quite free, the method of instructing and building up the Church under the New Covenant ought to be even freer and more abundant, because in it would be revealed the greatest abundance of *Teachers* and an admirable variety of the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

<margin>chapters 2, 3.</margin>
For it was foretold in this way by the visions of the Prophets. In Isaiah, for instance, it says that <term>in the latter days <gloss>Hebrew: bacharit hayamim</gloss></term> (a phrase which the Hebrew commentators say refers to the *times of the Messiah*), THE LAW WOULD GO FORTH <note>original Latin: LEX EGRESSURA ESSET</note> *from Zion*, and THE WORD OF JEHOVAH *from Jerusalem*. This means that the Teachers, instructed in the Word of the Gospel, would go out from the land of Judah to spread it through all other parts of the world.

<margin>Chapter 52, verse 7.</margin>
Again, it says that *the feet upon the mountains would be beautiful* for the <term>one who proclaims <gloss>Hebrew: mashmia; Greek: tō kēryssonti</gloss></term>, *making peace heard*, for the <term>one who brings good news <gloss>Greek: tō euangelizomenō</gloss></term>, MAKING SALVATION HEARD.

<margin>See Guillaume Budé.</margin>
For <term>to proclaim <gloss>Greek: kērýssein</gloss></term> (which is derived from the Hebrew <term>kara <gloss>קרא</gloss></term> or <term>karaz <gloss>כרז</gloss></term>) is to announce something publicly with the voice of a herald; and that word was used not only <term>in war <gloss>Greek: en polemō</gloss></term>, as Suidas <note>a 10th-century Greek encyclopedist</note> says, but also in sacred matters, from which we get the <term>sacred heralds <gloss>Greek: hierokērykes</gloss></term>.

# ON THE DUTIES OF THE PRESIDING OFFICERS, BOOK III, PART I

...ce, <note>original: "mis," likely completing "peace" from the previous page</note> <term>the women who bring good news are a great host <gloss>Hebrew: ham'vasserot tzava rav</gloss></term>, <term>of those who proclaim <gloss>Greek: tōn kēryssontōn</gloss></term>, A GREAT ARMY OF PREACHERS, a most ample multitude. In order to satisfy these illustrious prophecies, it is clear that the *Church of the New Testament* required a more abundant, freer, and more extensive method of teaching in public assemblies—commensurate with the magnitude of the gifts of grace granted to her—than was commonly the case in the *Jewish Synagogues* before the time of the appearance of Christ the Lord. Indeed, how great the *liberty, abundance, and variety* of such acts were in certain assemblies of the early Christian Church—acts which contributed greatly to the edification and progress of the Christian people in the *Doctrine and Discipline* of life—one may certainly learn from the fourteenth chapter of the *First Epistle to the Corinthians*, in which Paul represents the face of that Church most clearly. There you will find many traces of the ceremonies of the *Synagogue*; likewise of the freedom of teaching, prophesying, and interpreting, but which were nevertheless entirely adapted to the *condition of the Faithful of the New Testament*, which varied greatly from that of the Old.

Furthermore, just as the method of the sermons delivered corresponds with the manner in which this act was carried out in the *Synagogues* (yet in such a way as to be tempered to the condition of the Church), so the method of teaching and instruction observed in the *early Church* was not very different from that of the *Synagogue*. It has already been handed down and proven by us that Christ, according to the custom of the Teachers of his time, taught through <term>parables <gloss>Greek: parabolos</gloss></term> and <term>allegories <gloss>Greek: allegorias</gloss></term>. The former kind of instruction was aimed more at the common people (to whom Christ the Lord accommodated himself in many things), while the latter was aimed at the *Learned*. Since, however, the Spirit was given to the Apostles after Christ's ascension into heaven so that they might clearly and transparently explain the mysteries of the *Kingdom of heaven*, it is not surprising that they did not follow that first method of teaching as much. But the latter method, through allegories—which consisted in searching out the secret and mystical sense of *Holy Scripture*—was thoroughly preserved among them, as is abundantly clear from the *Epistles of Paul*. For it does not seem that Paul taught differently by word of mouth than he did in writing. A bright argument for that method of teaching is also provided by that so-called *Epistle of Barnabas*, the first part of which consists almost entirely of allegories and declarations of certain types of the *Old Economy* <note>The "Old Economy" refers to the religious system and laws of the Old Testament.</note>. Although we do not believe it was written by Barnabas, we do not...

### CHAPTER 8. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

...we nevertheless define it as a venerable monument of Christian antiquity to be cherished. Even so, it must always be held that just as there was the greatest liberty in the *manner of teaching*, so the Doctors of the Church followed their own natural inclinations in their way of teaching.

<margin>Sacred Observations, Book 3, Chapter 19, pp. 2, 65.</margin>
However, it has been confirmed by me elsewhere—and is known to anyone somewhat experienced in reading the surviving works of the first Doctors of the Church—that *allegorical expositions of the Scriptures* were commonly received and praised in the Church, following the model of *Jewish interpretations*. In a later age, however, the Doctors who were to preach in the churches, having rejected the simplicity of the Divine word and set aside the gravity befitting a Minister of the Gospel, often arranged their sermons so that they turned out as similar as possible to *Scholastic or Forensic Declamations*, or *Jewish Haggadot* <note>original: "Agadis Judaicis," referring to Jewish homiletic stories or non-legal traditions used to illustrate a point</note>.

<margin>Against the Luciferians, Epistle, Volume 2, folio 51, column 1.</margin>

I wish that Bernardino Ferrari, whom I mentioned above, had not praised this manner of preaching under the name of *prudence*. 
<margin>On Ancient Sermons, Book 2, Chapter 18.</margin>

Well then, let us turn to the CIRCUMSTANCES of holding *Sermons* among the Christians; and let us demonstrate that these also do not differ from those of the Synagogue. Therefore, as pertains first to the PLACE; those who were accustomed to teach the people in this manner in Christian churches occupied a higher and more eminent place, the *Cathedra* <note>The bishop’s teaching chair or throne</note>, located in the *middle part of the Temple* (and soon in the *furthest part*), distinguished by steps and railings from the main body of the Temple where the common people took their place, and destined for the Bishops, Priests, and Deacons alone. Hence there is constant mention of the *Pulpitum* (Pulpit), *Tribunal* (Platform), *Suggestum* (Dais), *Gradus* (Steps), and *Cancelli* (Railings or Chancel) among the Latins; and of the *platform* <note>Greek: βήματος, bematos</note> and *ambo* <note>Greek: ἄμβωνος, ambonos</note>—from the word for *ascending* <note>Greek: ἀμβαίνειν, ambainein, or ἀναβαίνειν, anabainein</note>—among the Greeks, whether in the Church Fathers or the authors of Ecclesiastical History. Still, one must carefully distinguish between this *Cathedra* or *Episcopal Tribunal* erected in the *Choir*, of which we are especially speaking, and the *Ambo of the Readers* in the nave of the Temple itself, from which the Bishops spoke more rarely; regarding which, if it pleases you, you may see Ferrari discussing it more at length.

<margin>Book 3, On Ancient Sermons, chapters 8, 9.</margin>

### ON THE DUTIES OF PREFECTS, BOOK 3, PART 1.

...the day called THE DAY OF THE SUN <note>original: "γομένην ἡμέραν DIEM, QUI SOLIS DICITUR." One can easily gather from the Sermons of Ambrose and Augustine that this practice mostly prevailed in this way. And so it was also decreed in the *Sixth Council*, which was celebrated in the *Trullo* <note>The Council in Trullo (692 AD), also known as the Quinisext Council, was held in the domed hall—or *trullus*—of the imperial palace in Constantinople to establish disciplinary canons for the Church.</note>.

<margin>Canon 19.</margin>
It begins as follows: "That those who preside over the churches must, on every day, but especially on Sundays, teach all the clergy and the people the words of piety, gathering the thoughts and judgments of truth from the Divine Scripture, and not transgressing the limits already set or the tradition of the God-bearing fathers." <note>This is a translation of the Greek text provided in the source: "Ὅτι δεῖ τοὺς τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν προεστῶτας..."</note> *It is necessary that those who preside over the Churches, on all days indeed, but especially on the Lord’s Days, teach all the Clergy & the people the words of piety & right Religion, gathering the understandings & judgments of truth from Divine Scripture, and not transgressing the already established boundaries, or the tradition of the Divine Fathers.*

It was indeed permitted for *Bishops* and considered praiseworthy to teach the people several times a week; indeed, it was long ago observed by learned men that Bishops often instituted daily sermons for the people. However, those who devoted themselves to instructing the common people on *Sundays and Feast Days*, as they call them, were considered to have fulfilled their duty. Yet, it must not be overlooked that in the *Apostolic Canons* <note>A collection of ancient ecclesiastical decrees regarding the government and discipline of the early Christian Church.</note> no certain time is predetermined for holding sermons: the necessity of teaching is merely imposed upon *Bishops* and *Presbyters* <note>term: Presbyters (elders/priests)</note>.

<margin>Canon 58.</margin>
Thus one may read in them: *A Bishop or Presbyter who does not take care of the Clergy or the people and does not teach them piety, let him be separated.* <note>original: "Ἐπίσκοπος ἢ πρεσβύτερος ἀμελῶν..." / "Episcopus aut Presbyter, qui Cleri vel populi curam non gerit..." Specifically, just as in the Synagogues the Prefects allowed themselves the greatest liberty in performing this act—so much so that sermons were often neglected and omitted and were not counted among the *ordinary* and fixed sacred rites of the Synagogue—so it is fair to believe that the Bishops and Presbyters of certain Churches were somewhat negligent in preaching. This was despite the fact that, in other respects, reason suggests that this part of Divine worship should be observed with much greater care and industry in the Christian Churches than it was formerly observed in the Synagogues. For the Gentiles, of whom by far the largest part of the Christian Church consisted, were unrefined in Religion and therefore greatly in need of public and private instruction; and the nature of the New Testament, as now...

What is surprising, however, is that in the Roman Church in the most ancient times, absolutely no public *sermons* <note>original: "conciones"</note> were held. <margin>Ecclesiastical History, book 7, chapter 39.</margin> Sozomen <note>Salminius Hermias Sozomenus (c. 400–450 AD), a historian of the early Christian Church.</note> says regarding the City of Rome: "Neither the bishop nor anyone else teaches here in the church;" <note>original Greek: "Οὔτε δὲ ὁ ἐπίσκοπος οὔτε ἄλλος τις ἐνθάδε ἐπ' ἐκκλησίας διδάσκει;"</note> *For neither the Bishop nor anyone else teaches in the Church there.* That Sozomen testified to the truth in these words is proved by many things already brought forward by the most learned de Laroque. <margin>Adversaria, book 2, chapter 21.</margin> I truly believe that both the act of preaching itself, as used in the Church, and this neglect of it—or rather, the supreme *liberty* observed in exercising it—should be traced back to the *Synagogue*.

### CHAPTER 8. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

...as expressed: "What sort of things does he also send out those bishops of the neighboring fields and the presbyters who flatter him to discuss in their addresses to the people?" <note>This quote is from Philostorgius, a 4th-century church historian, describing how certain leaders used their subordinates to spread their particular doctrines.</note> *He also sent out the Bishops of the neighboring villages and cities, and also the Presbyters, his flatterers, so that they might preach* <margin>Book 3, chapter 17.</margin> *the same things about him in their* SERMONS TO THE PEOPLE. Furthermore, what shall I say regarding the *posture of the body*? Teachers of great name and authority among the Jews delivered their orations while sitting; it is likely that others, either possessing less authority or for whom standing was more convenient than sitting, remained standing. I believe that *Christian Teachers* reserved the same freedom for themselves. Generally, however, it happened that *Teachers of the Church* preached **while sitting**, following the example of the *Teachers of the Synagogue*.

## CHAPTER IX.

*This chapter deals with the GOVERNMENT OF THE PREFECTS OF THE SYNAGOGUE, which is divided into three actions: the Management of Synagogue proceedings, the Correction of the disobedient, and the Care of Alms. For the sake of order, we shall divide these into: 1. **THE MANAGEMENT OF THE RITES AND SACRED SERVICES OF THE SYNAGOGUE.** 2. **THE CORRECTION OF THE DISOBEDIENT.** 3. **THE CARE OF ALMS.** We will also add a few remarks **CONCERNING THE JUDGES**.

*Regarding the first point:* That the Prefects of the Synagogue were charged with the task of **managing the sacred acts to be performed in the Synagogue** follows so clearly from the very notion of their name and **Office** that I <margin>Annotations on section 7, chapter 7 of the Code Sotah.</margin> require no further proof here. Rabbi Solomon <note>Also known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval French rabbi and author of comprehensive commentaries on the Talmud and Tanakh.</note>, in explaining the title **Head of the Synagogue** <note>Hebrew: *Rosh Ha-Knesset*</note>, says: **The Head of the Synagogue is the one by whose word the affairs of the synagogue are determined: who shall read from the Prophets; who shall recite the Shema <note>A centerpiece of Jewish prayer services</note>; and who shall descend before the Ark <note>The chest where the Torah scrolls are kept; "descending" refers to leading the prayers from a lower platform</note>.** Reason, as I have said, demands this. For if these sacred matters of the Synagogue were not arranged according to the will of the Prefects (for what Rashi attributes here to "the" Prefect—meaning either one of the group or their president—undoubtedly pertains to them all), why would they bear the title of Prefects or Shepherds? We have an illustrious example of what Rashi says in the history already cited several times from the <margin>Acts 13:15.</margin> **Acts of the Apostles**. Paul and Barnabas entered the Synagogue of Antioch, and the **Prefects of the Synagogue** gave them the opportunity to speak. It is indeed true that in the Gospel history, it is not recorded that Christ obtained permission to preach and read from the Heads of the Synagogue. But let us consider that in the Gospel history, many circumstances of events are often omitted because they are assumed to be known to the people of that age. Christ was a Teacher of the highest reputation, and thus occupied the Chair <note>The "Seat of Moses" or teaching position</note> with greater authority than others; furthermore, at that time there was such liberty of teaching in the synagogue that the Head of the Synagogue might remain silent...

...the consensus of the elders was sufficient for celebrating certain sacred acts. You may clearly gather the nature of these Synagogal Corrections from the Constitutions of Justinian. Thus it is stated in the Rescript of the Prince in the place already noted: <margin>Novel 146.</margin> *Neither shall those who are called by them "the greatest of all," the "Archiperecitae" <note>A term likely referring to the "Archipherekites," the heads of the schools or those who led the recitation of the Law.</note>, or "Presbyters," or perhaps "Masters," have the license to prohibit this by any **penalties** or **excommunications**.* The Greek words are: *Neither shall the Archiperecitae, or Presbyters, or perhaps teachers, have authority among them to prevent this through certain penalties or excommunications.* <note>original Greek: Οὐδὲ ἄδειαν ἔξουσι παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς Ἀρχιφερίται ἢ Πρεσβύτεροι τυχὸν ἢ διδάσκαλοι προσαγορευόμενοι περινοίαις τισὶν ἢ ἀναθεματισμοῖς τοῦτο κωλύειν (*Oude adeian exousi par’ autois Archipheritai ē Presbyteroi tychon ē didaskaloi prosagoreuomenoi perinoiais tisin ē anathematismois touto kōlyein*)</note>. Here, the *Synagogal Corrections* are mentioned.

The first of these species are the "anathematismoi," *Excommunications*; the second are certain "perinoiai," *certain punishments*, *corrections, or censures*, such as were often exercised by the Heads of the Synagogue in various cases, perhaps by the indulgence of the Princes. <margin>On the Sanhedrin, book 1, chapter 7, page 89.</margin> "I am certainly persuaded," says Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654) was a famous English jurist and scholar of ancient laws and Jewish history.</note>, "that by *perinoiai* are signified animadversions and censures or punishments of any kind, which were then in use among the Jews by imperial permission." The standard Rabbinic Hebrew term for "retribution" or "calamity."</note> instead of *perauot*. As for the first type, it would be entirely superfluous to discourse at length on the nature, types, degrees, use, purpose, and effects of Hebrew EXCOMMUNICATION, since the most learned Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654) was a famous English jurist and scholar of Jewish law.</note> (among others) has treated this matter extensively and with singular effort, first in his books *On the Law of Nature and Nations*, and then in his books *On the Sanhedrins*. Regarding the first point, I wish it noted beforehand that the Jews introduced this reasoning: they asserted they were bound by a certain Commandment of Divine Law toward their fellow tribesmen—sharers of the same Religion and State—to rebuke, warn, and correct them if they stumbled in their morals or caused scandal to the weak; *first* indeed privately, then *publicly*, so that they might lead the sinner back to the right path and to a sounder mind. This constitution is found fully in the Jewish Precepts according to the guidance of *R. Because Scripture says: *Rebuking, you shall rebuke him.* <note>Leviticus 19:17: "You shall surely rebuke your neighbor."</note> From this, our Masters say in the Gemara <note>The Gemara is the component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis and commentary on the Mishnah.</note>: *Rebuking, you shall rebuke him*, even a hundred times. But do you wish for clearer examples? Read those which follow.

> At the start of the rebuke, it is appropriate to rebuke in secret and with soft language and pleasant words so that he is not ashamed. There is no doubt that if he did not turn back by this, they shame him for his public sin, and they publicize his sin and mock him until he returns to what is good.

—**AT THE BEGINNING OF THE REPRIMAND, it should be done PRIVATELY, with a soft tongue and peaceful words, lest he blush with shame. Without a doubt, however, if by this method he does not return to the right path, THEY SHAME THE SINNER PUBLICLY, making an example of him <note>original Greek: παραδειγματίזונτες (*paradeigmatizontes*) — to make a public example or spectacle of someone.</note> and harassing him until he returns to his senses.** Those things which the Jews have in their constitutions regarding *public correction* are not far from this. Thus it is read in the *Yoreh De'ah* <note>A segment of the Shulchan Aruch, the authoritative code of Jewish law, dealing with forbidden things and communal ethics.</note> in that same chapter where *Excommunication* is treated:

<margin>

> A rebuke <note>original Hebrew: נזיפה (*Nezifah*) — the mildest form of social distancing or formal "shaming" in Jewish law.</note> is when a great man scolds someone, saying "How impudent is so-and-so!" and the like. This is his judgment: that he should hide and sit in his house and be ashamed, and not see the face of the one who shamed him; he should be rare in laughter and speech, nor too occupied with his business, and he should carry himself humbly before the eyes of those who see him. Yet it is not necessary for him to distance himself from all people—neither in eating or drinking, nor in greeting—and he does not need to observe any of the laws of formal mourning, nor does he need to appease the one who put him to shame.

**That REPRIMAND consists of this: that a Great man (and who in the Synagogue is greater than the Ruler of the Synagogue? <note>original Latin: *Archisynagogus*.</note>) scolds someone, saying, "How impudent is N.!" and things of that sort. This, indeed, is the manner of it: that he (who has sustained the reprimand) hides himself and sits at home, covered in shame, nor should he see the face of the one who put him to shame. He should be sparing in laughter and speech, nor should he be too occupied with his ordinary business; he should also behave humbly in the sight of those who see him. Yet it is not necessary for him to remove himself from the company of men, either in eating or drinking or in greeting, nor should he adopt any formal mourning rituals, nor must he appease the person who shamed him.** It seemed right to Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675) was an influential English scholar who studied the Jewish context of the New Testament.</note> to refer to two passages here, which he noted from Maimonides <note>The preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> regarding **Proclamation** (<gloss>announcement</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: הכרזה (*Hachrazah*)</note>) in the Synagogue; these must be fully described by us as they are read in Maimonides, before we give our own opinion on them:

<margin>
Commentary on Matthew 18:17.
Laws of Marriage, chapter 12, near the middle.
</margin>

> Just as a man is obligated for the sustenance of his wife, so he is obligated for the sustenance of his small sons and daughters until they are six years old; from then on, he feeds them until they grow up, according to the regulation of the Sages. If he does not want to, they scold him and shame him and urge him; if he still does not want to, they make a proclamation about him in public and say, "So-and-so is cruel!"

...[shamed] women, and they say: *So-and-so <note>The letter 'N.' serves as a placeholder for a specific name.</note> is rebellious against her husband; after which proclamation the Sanhedrin <note>The high court or council of elders.</note> sends messengers to her a second time, saying: "If you persist stubbornly in your rebellion, you have forfeited your dowry," etc.* Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> says that this *proclamation* was made every day for four entire weeks, but this is not universally accepted, as you will see in the marginal notes. It seems more probable that it occurred only on *four Sabbaths*, when the people gathered in the synagogues. Furthermore, you certainly see in these words that some *proclamation* or notification of a crime was made in the synagogues, directed at shaming someone and bringing them back to their duty through shame; yet, this public shouting is not described in the text as being joined with *Excommunication*. This was the only action taken, as far as appears from the text: the crime was publicized for the disgrace and shame of the sinner who stubbornly persisted in their sin. Yet perhaps it would not be absurd to think that this *public shouting* was sometimes joined with Excommunication—specifically with that type of excommunication called *Niddui* <note>A 30-day formal ban or temporary excommunication.</note>. You might first gather this from the fact that it continued for *four weeks* (that is, thirty days), which was the exact time designated for a *Niddui*. Secondly, in the *Yoreh De'ah* <note>A section of the *Shulchan Aruch*, the standard code of Jewish law, dealing with forbidden things and communal discipline.</note> where Excommunication is described, a *Hachrazah* <note>Hebrew: הכרזה; a formal public proclamation.</note> or *proclamation* is mentioned as something to be applied if the crime of the excommunicated person was more serious.

# ON THE DUTIES OF THE PREFECTS BOOK III. PART I. 734 #

<margin>Matthew 18:15, 16, 17.</margin>
It may come to mind that Christ the Lord had these or similar customs of his own time in view in that famous passage of the Gospel of Matthew, and likewise the Apostle Paul in *his Epistles*. Those famous words of Christ in *Matthew* are as follows:

> *If your brother sins against you, go and REBUKE HIM BETWEEN YOU AND HIM ALONE. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen to you, take with you one or two others, so that by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established. But if he refuses to listen even to them, <note>original: εἰπὲ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ</note> TELL THE CHURCH. And if he neglects to hear even the Church, <note>original: ἔστω σοι ὥσπερ ὁ ἐθνικὸς καὶ ὁ τελώνης</note> LET HIM BE TO YOU AS A GENTILE AND A TAX COLLECTOR.*

<margin>Book 1, chapter 2. II.</margin>
Learned men have raised doubts regarding these words as to what this *Church* <note>The term "Ecclesia" can mean a local assembly or a formal religious body.</note> is that Christ speaks of, and what the meaning is of: *Let him be to you as a Gentile and a Tax Collector*; and these questions have been solved in various ways according to the hypotheses that each scholar has adopted. We remember touching upon the first part of this dispute in the preceding pages: however, we have reserved for this place certain matters that contribute to a true understanding of this passage, where they properly belong.

The common opinion of the Doctors <note>Learned theologians and church authorities.</note> holds that these words of the Lord refer to Christian *Excommunication*, and that the foundations for it were laid here by Christ. Thus, the sum of the Precept comes to this: a sinning brother who stubbornly persists in sin after private warnings must be reported to the *Prefects of the Church*, and by them—if he refuses to cease from sin after being warned—he must be declared unworthy of the Ecclesiastical Society; unworthy also of the symbols of the sacred *Union* of the faithful with Christ and with one another. Yet this interpretation has not been so equally accepted by everyone that it has not suffered contradiction. It is well known that a most learned man, *Thomas Erastus* <note>A Swiss physician and theologian (1524–1583) who argued that the state, not the church, should punish sins.</note>—a *Physician* by profession, but no less skilled in theological matters—attacked *Ecclesiastical Excommunication* as it is commonly practiced in a distinct and learned dispute during the last century. He did this (with the approval of the most celebrated theologians of Switzerland) against *Theodore Beza* <note>A French Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin in Geneva.</note>, a fierce defender of *Excommunication* as it is received in the churches among us. We shall not hide below what we have gained and what we approve of from the *Erastians*, which we have read with the greatest pleasure. Now it simply hap-

It is necessary to point out that *Erastus* <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583) was a Swiss physician and theologian who argued that the sins of Christians should be punished by the state rather than by the church through excommunication.</note> exerted great effort to explain this passage of *Matthew* in such a way that no support for the common practice of *Excommunication* remains in it. However, he did not carry this out so successfully that a practiced reader would not perceive that he is, to some extent, stuck. I will provide his own words, so that nothing of their value seems diminished. *The genuine Erastian sense of this passage and Chapter is as follows: a brother, that is, a Jew, does you wrong; strive to be reconciled with him alone. If you achieve nothing alone, try the same after taking two or three others with you. If even so you cannot free yourself from the injury, report it to the SYNEDRIUM <note>The Sanhedrin, or Jewish high council.</note>, that is, to the MAGISTRATE of your people or YOUR RELIGION.* But if he refuses to listen even to this body, *you may then proceed against him without causing offense to anyone, just as you would against a Tax Collector or a Gentile who brings an injury upon you*, (who do not allow themselves to be dragged to any court other than the ROMAN TRIBUNAL).

<margin>See his Theses on Excommunication, § 41.</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians Chapter 6, 6.</margin>
<margin>Matthew Chapter 16, 18.</margin>
<margin>See Erastus, § 48.</margin>
<margin>Book 1, chapter 2.</margin>

Erastus therefore believes that Christ's warning in this place completely aligns with *Paul's* instruction in the *First Epistle to the Corinthians regarding avoiding the tribal courts of the Gentiles*, to which the Jews were already subject, until extreme necessity compelled them to flee there because of the obstinacy of the opposing brother. 

But who does not see: 1. The word <term>ekklesia</term> <note>original: ἐκκλησία; in Christian contexts, the Church; in Greek civil contexts, a public assembly.</note> is used in this place in the Gospel of *Matthew* with the manifest meaning of the *Universal body of believers*; would it not be quite incongruous and contrary to its inherent meaning to take it here for a *legal assembly or Sanhedrin*? I know how other Learned Men, who have explained the word <term>ekklesia</term> here as an *Ecclesiastical Sanhedrin*, have tried to defend their hypothesis by pretending that the word <term>ekklesia</term> here corresponds to the Hebrew word <term>edah</term> <note>original: עדה; often translated as 'congregation' or 'assembly' in the Old Testament.</note>; and that this word is used everywhere for a *Judicial Sanhedrin, whether Political or Ecclesiastical*. 

But this supposition was sufficiently refuted in the preceding pages. I believe it will never happen that a student of Greek and Hebrew letters will be fully satisfied with this interpretation, or be convinced—without some internal struggle—that the word <term>ekklesia</term> can be comfortably taken for a *Sanhedrin*, let alone a *Judicial Sanhedrin*. The Greek word <term>ekklesia</term> corresponds to the Hebrew <term>qahal</term> <note>original: קהל; a general assembly of people.</note> and <term>tsibur</term> <note>original: ציבור; the community or public.</note>, which (at least the former) are foreign to that [judicial] meaning. 2. Whether it was a public shaming of someone in the *qahal* <note>original: קהל, a Hebrew term for a congregation or assembly</note> or *tzibur* <note>original: צבור, a Hebrew term for a public community or congregation</note>, or a multitude of believers gathered to celebrate sacred rites (for I consider the Greek word *ekklesia* <note>original: ἐκκλησίᾳ, meaning assembly or church</note> to correspond to those terms here), among the Hebrews it either preceded ***Excommunication*** or was considered as a kind of part of it. Surely Christ could not have mentioned and recommended a rite so closely related to ***Excommunication*** without at the same time looking toward ***Excommunication*** itself, and approving of it, if not openly, then at least silently. It is indeed true, as we also concede, that Christ did not command public ***Excommunication*** here; but I think a clear reason can be given for that. Specifically, it does not seem that ***Excommunication*** itself was practiced so frequently in those most ancient times, nor does it seem that the distinction between ***Greater Excommunication*** ( *cherem* <note>original: חרם, the most severe form of exclusion or banishment</note> ) and ***Lesser Excommunication*** ( *nidui* <note>original: נדוי, a temporary or less severe distancing</note> ), which later became established, was in frequent and accepted use. I would judge it more probable that in ancient times, those who were *expelled* from the ***Synagogues*** were completely separated from the ***Jewish Church*** by a more severe form of ***Excommunication***, which was later called *cherem*, and that *nidui* was used almost exclusively among *private individuals*, where one person separated another from their fellowship by this type of ***Excommunication*** until they were satisfied. In other cases of *scandal*, they seem to have employed *corrections, rebukes, shamings*, and *public proclamations*. These things appear likely to me from the character of the *Gospel History*, in which mention of ***Excommunication*** is very rare. Whoever assumes these things with me will easily see the reason why Christ the Lord also did not speak directly about ***Excommunication*** itself, but rather about *Correction* and public *Shaming*, which at that time fulfilled the role of a lighter ***Excommunication***. And I believe that what Paul writes in his

Yet these words contain more than those of Christ. For in this place, Paul commands that the social interaction of the one who neglected Paul’s precepts should be avoided by the *entire Church*; this indeed comes very close to ***Excommunication***. Briefly, I say, because these things have been recorded with sufficient care by others.

<margin>Yoreh Deah section 6, § 1.</margin>

Doubtless, after that **REBUKE** <note>original Hebrew: נזיפה (*nezifah*), a formal reprimand</note> which used to last seven days, there followed **EXCOMMUNICATION** <note>original Hebrew: נדוי (*nidui*)</note>, a separation from the sacred assembly. This was done so that in every place, the person was bound to keep a distance of four cubits <note>about six feet</note> from his brothers according to the Law and the Constitution of the *Elders* <term>the Sages or Rabbinic authorities</term>; they hold that the separation of *nidui* <note>original Greek: τὴν נדוי separationem</note> primarily consisted of this. The one set apart <note>original Greek: ἀφωρισμένος</note> by this excommunication remained in this state for thirty days, at the end of which he would seek forgiveness <note>original Hebrew: מחילה (*mechilah*)</note> and pardon for his offense from those who had excommunicated him. Upon this petition, having shown signs of repentance, he was readmitted to the communion of the Church with the formula: **MAY YOU HAVE** release <note>original: שרוי לך (*sharui lach*), Greek: *aphesis*</note>; and "It is forgiven you" <note>original Hebrew: מחול לך (*machul lach*)</note>, which is called the *Release of Excommunication* <note>original Hebrew: התרת נדוי (*hatarat nidui*)</note>. But if he were stubborn and led to no repentance for the offense, nor submitted himself to those excommunicating him according to the decrees of the *Elders*, that *Excommunication* or *nidui* was continued for another thirty days, or for a time established by the excommunicators, if it were defined according to their pleasure. But if, in the meantime, the *Excommunicated person* gave no evidence of true repentance, but on the contrary persisted in his stubbornness, there followed—after another thirty days had passed (*Maimonides* <note>a preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> does not require this latter period)—the **BAN** <note>original Hebrew: חרם (*cherem*), Greek: *anathema*</note>, a total separation from the Church, which was the final type of Excommunication. For those are mistaken who think there were more levels, and who establish that *shamta* <note>original Hebrew: שמתא</note> was a more severe degree of Excommunication than the *cherem*, since in reality only two types are found among the Ancient Jews, and *shamta* coincides with *nidui*. And these things are explained clearly enough throughout that entire Chapter titled *Excommunication and the Ban* <note>original Hebrew: נדוי וחרם (*Nidui ve-Cherem*)</note> in the *Yoreh Deah* <note>a section of the Shulchan Aruch, the code of Jewish law</note>.

In these matters there is indeed no great difficulty, except that it is somewhat obscure in what sense Excommunication mentioned in the Scripture of the New Testament (whether it be *nidui* or *cherem*, which is all the same to us now, though the latter seems more likely) was expressed—

<margin>John 9:22; 12:42; 16:2.</margin>
...is expressed by the phrase **to be put out of the synagogue**, <note>original Greek: ἀποσυνάγωγον γίνεσθαι (*aposynagōgon ginesthai*)</note> that is, to be driven away or removed from the Synagogue. This occurs twice in the Gospel of John, while the phrase **to make one an outcast from the synagogue** <note>original Greek: ἀποσυνάγωγον ποιεῖσθαι</note> occurs once in that same Author. The middle passage reads as follows: *Nevertheless, many even of the authorities believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they did not confess it, lest they should be put out of the synagogue.* <note>John 12:42; original Greek: ἵνα μὴ ἀποσυνάγωγοι γένωνται</note> Truly, this phrase can admit a twofold interpretation, based on the dual meaning of the word **synagogue** <note>original Greek: συναγωγή (*synagōgē*)</note>. It might mean that someone is expelled from the very building of the Synagogue by a decree of the Sanhedrin <term>the high council of Jewish leaders</term>, being denied the ability to frequent it according to custom or to celebrate sacred rites within it. Or, it might mean that someone is declared unworthy of the company of his own people, placed in such a state that *no one is allowed to sit within four cubits <note>about six feet</note> of him, nor may he participate in the usual social gatherings.* Thus, **to be made outside the Synagogue** or **to be an outcast from the synagogue** would denote *being deprived of the common society of men, even of one’s own countrymen, and being banished or driven away.*

Selden defends his opinion chiefly with this argument: that it was permitted for those who were excommunicated to enter the Temple (specifically by turning *to the left* through the gate known as the **Gate of the Mourners**). This reasoning, supported by Selden’s authority, once persuaded me of this interpretation so thoroughly that I did not even call it into doubt. Now, however, I confess my mind is burdened by several scruples. Therefore, those Hebrew words are much more suitably expressed as **to be set apart from the church**. <note>original Greek: ἀφορίζεσθαι ἀπὸ τῆς ἐκκλησίας</note>

...of the assembly, or to become an outcast from the assembly <note>original Greek: ἀπεκκλησιαστὴν (*apekklēsiastēn*)</note>. Certainly, the translators of the Septuagint <note>the Greek version of the Old Testament</note> retained the word **assembly** <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησία (*ekklesia*)</note> here. They have: *He himself shall be separated from the assembly of those who returned from exile.* <note>Ezra 10:8; original Greek: ἀυτὸς διασαλήσεται ἀπὸ ἐκκλησίας τῆς ἀποικίας</note> However, it must not be concealed that Maimonides <note>a preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist</note>, when dealing with excommunication, employs the phrase:

<margin>Laws of the Study of the Torah, chapter 7.</margin>

**separated from the congregation**, <note>original Hebrew: נבדל מן הצבור (*nivdal min ha-tsibbur*)</note> which has much in common with that passage in Ezra and comes very close to the phrase: *to be put out of the synagogue.* But it should be observed that **congregation** <note>original Hebrew: צבור (*tsibbur*)</note> is rendered even more appropriately as **synagogue** <note>original Greek: συναγωγή (*synagōgē*)</note> than the word **assembly** <note>original Hebrew: קהל (*qahal*)</note>, because by its very root, *tsibbur* denotes *a multitude of people gathered in a certain place*. Let us, therefore, leave this matter undecided for now, until we have brought forward the other points that pertain to it.

What Selden <note>John Selden, a 17th-century English jurist and scholar of Jewish law</note> says regarding the **Temple** is not without merit! Yet it is not fully sufficient to complete this proof. For the nature of the **Temple** and of the **Synagogues** was not one and the same in all respects. The **Temple** was a kind of common refuge for the entire Jewish nation, and it seems that no one was prohibited from entering it except for those who were **impure**, or those known to have sinned publicly against the whole Jewish nation, or to have profaned and dishonored the Temple itself, which was held to be sacrosanct: such a man as Paul was judged to be.

<margin>Acts 21:27, 28.</margin>

But the nature of the **Synagogues** seems to me to be different; they comprised just as many distinct societies of Jews, or the multitude of Jews of a single district. Consequently, the judgment regarding the life and morals of those who constituted their society properly belonged to them. Indeed, they could maintain that judgment or jurisdiction more easily than could be done in the **Temple**, into which the entrance of all circumcised men was both mixed and frequent. However, lest I seem to have begun this discussion out of a certain intellectual whim rather than necessity, I will set forth the reasons that have shaken my confidence in the former opinion.

<margin>On the Customs of the Jews, Book 2, chapter 3.</margin>

First of all, Leo de Modena <note>a famous Venetian Rabbi of the 17th century</note> explicitly asserts that *the excommunicated are expelled from the Synagogue itself*. His words are: *When they excommunicate someone, they signify it publicly: after which time it is not permitted for any Jew to mingle in conversation with the excommunicated person, nor to approach within four cubits of him*; (the French version says: a fathom) **ENTRANCE INTO THE SYNAGOGUE IS PROHIBITED TO HIM**, *and he is obliged to sit with bare feet on the ground, as if some relative of his had died, until he has been absolved by one or more Rabbis, and restored to his former state through a blessing.*

For, what he says regarding the *prohibition of conversing with the Excommunicated person* belongs entirely to the more severe Excommunication according to the accepted Canons <note>established religious laws</note>. Indeed, social interaction with an Excommunicated person, in the simple sense, was not strictly forbidden; rather, it was every *unnecessary* conversation with one struck by an Anathema <note>a formal curse or total ban</note> that was prohibited. Even then, it was permitted to speak with him in necessary cases, unless the Sanhedrin <note>the supreme Jewish judicial council</note> had specifically issued a caution to the contrary. So it is written in the *Yoreh De'ah* <note>a major section of the Shulchan Aruch, the code of Jewish Law</note>: *It is permitted to speak with the excommunicated and the anathematized, unless the court has explicitly aggravated his status in this regard.* <note>original Hebrew: מותר לדבר עם המנודה ועם המוחרם אא"כ החמירו עליו ב"ד בפירוש</note> But it is likely that these two distinct types of Excommunication were not strictly observed in all Synagogues, but were often confused with one another. For even in the Jewish Canons, this entire practice of excommunication and its method is left to the discretion of the Leaders of the Synagogue.

<margin>Cited Title, *Yoreh De'ah*, Section 8.</margin>
And without doubt, the penalty of Excommunication—given the current state of Jewish affairs among the Nations—is inflicted by them with greater severity than is defined in the common Canons. They do this to better keep their subjects in line with their duties and, since no other power of enforcement is available to them, to at least place this barrier against license and moral offenses. This is much like the practice that prevailed among Christians while Paganism was still dominant <note>referring to the early Church's use of social exclusion before it had state legal power</note>. But even if Leo <note>likely Leone da Modena, a 17th-century Venetian Rabbi</note> speaks of the more severe Excommunication, which is usually called **Cherem**, it does not greatly differ from our hypothesis. We believe that almost only this severe type was in use among the Jews around the time of Christ, as we have previously declared. This also agrees with what is found in the booklet erroneously attributed to Athanasius <note>a 4th-century Church Father</note> regarding the *Passion of the Image of Our Lord*. # CHAPTER 9. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES. #

...afflicted with many and various tortures, they **THREW** him out of the SYNAGOGUE while *half-dead*.

Beyond these things, it deserves attention, *secondly*, that the act of *Excommunicating* occurs in the New Testament Scripture under the concept of *ekballein* <note>original Greek: ἐκβάλλειν</note>, meaning to **EXPEL** or **EJECT**. This is certainly how it seems to be taken in the Gospel of John regarding that blind man healed by Christ, of whom it is notably said: <margin>Chapter 9, verse 34.</margin> *And they threw him out* <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἐξέβαλον αὐτὸν ἔξω</note> and they **THREW** him out. And again: <margin>verse 35.</margin> Jesus heard *that they had thrown him out* <note>original Greek: ὅτι ἐξέβαλον αὐτὸν ἔξω</note>, that they had **THROWN HIM OUT**. This *throwing out* <note>original Greek: ἐκβάλλειν</note> altogether seems to refer to a certain place, which is most conveniently established as the *Synagogue*, into which this blind man previously had free entry. This is especially likely if we consider that this took place on the *Sabbath day*, when the Elders <note>the members of the council or Sanhedrin</note> were occupied either in the Synagogue or the Academy. <margin>verse 14.</margin>

To these things is added *thirdly*, that the very nature of the *Act of Excommunication* seems to imply that the *Excommunicated person* was barred not only from the communion of the *assembly*, but also from the *Place* where the *assembly* was gathered. For to be *separated* from the *Assembly* itself, what else is it than to be *separated* from the *Place* in which that *assembly* meets? Concerning the *menuddeh* <note>original Hebrew: מנודה; a person under a formal ban or excommunication</note>, or him who had been struck by the lightning-bolt of the *Severer Excommunication*, there is no doubt here. For it was not even permitted to *live with* him, or to have commerce with him in eating and drinking; indeed, according to the canons of the strictest discipline, it was not permitted to stay under the same *roof* with him. For this reason, a *small hut* was built for him in which he might be sustained, removed from human company. <margin>Yoreh De'ah <note>a code of Jewish Law</note>, the cited chapter, section 11.</margin> Nor was there much business in the *Synagogue* for the *menuddeh* <note>original Hebrew: מנודה</note>—the *Excommunicated person*, so simply called—since it was not permitted for him to sit near his fellow people (except for his wife and children) in any place within a *space of four cubits* <note>approximately 6 feet or 2 meters</note>, and it was a sin for others to sit with him in turn. For how easy was it to transgress this *Law* in the *Synagogues*, where there was a promiscuous gathering of *many people*, if an *Excommunicated person* frequented them? Therefore, I believe that in the age of Christ the Lord, that type of *Excommunication* prevailed by which someone was removed not only from the *assembly*, but also from the *Place* where the *assembly* usually gathered. Therefore, I think this act of *Excommunicating* is expressed in the New Testament Scripture by the terms: *separating*, *reproaching*, and *throwing out* <note>original Greek: ἀφορίζειν, ὀνειδίζειν, ἐκβάλλειν</note>. <margin>Luke 6:22.</margin> And I feel more inclined toward this view because, given this, there is a clear reason for the manner in which *excommunication* was practiced in the early Christian Church.

The same occurs in those passages which <term>Seldenus: John Selden (1584–1654), a famous English jurist and scholar of ancient Jewish law</term> excerpted from Elias ben Moses Karao: *To place under anathema, to excommunicate, or to separate someone from the assembly of Israel according to the sentence of the sages who are in the* HOUSE OF JUDGMENT.

It is doubtful, however, what is to be understood here by the **House of Judgment**. It is commonly accepted that this expression implies a Judicial Senate consisting of several learned men, whether in the Land of Israel or in Exile. I do not think it should be understood otherwise here, as I reconsider what I once meditated upon regarding this argument. For a *Senate of Learned Men* of this kind held the highest power both in the *State* <note>original: *Politia*</note> and in the *Church and Synagogue*; as much in *civil* as in *sacred* matters. And from here the reason must be sought why the penalty of Excommunication was inflicted on someone as much for *civil* as for *sacred* (if I may speak so) faults.

<note>original Hebrew: "אם לא חזר בו יש מי שאומר מתירין לו לאחר שלשים יום והוא שיבא לבית דין ומבקש שיתירו לו אבל אם מזלזל בנידויו ואינו מבקש שיתירו לו מניחין אותו בנידוי עד שימות"</note>
**IF EXCOMMUNICATION** *has been issued on account of* **FINANCIAL MATTERS**, *or insolence, and the person has been reconciled with the one who brought the suit against him, they release him immediately. ...[it] is, because it does not only originate from the Sanhedrins <term>Synedriis: High councils or courts of justice in ancient Judea</term>, but also has regard for the Commonwealth of the Jews, insofar as that is civilly governed.

&emsp;&emsp;However, it is something to wonder at, that the Judicial Senate (or <term>Beth Din: House of Judgment</term> <note>original Hebrew: בית דין</note>), which had the power to punish—whether by monetary fines, or by flogging and beating with rods, or by other more severe penalties—those who either did not show them due obedience or transgressed the laws and statutes of their ancestors, fled to Excommunication in civil cases. By this, I confess, the accused suffered a certain loss of status <term>capitis diminutio: A Roman legal term for a reduction in civil rights or status</term>, not properly as citizens, but as members of the Synagogue. But this difficulty is removed if one considers: 1. That the State and the Church—and hence the Political and Ecclesiastical Senates, as well as civil and sacred offenses and punishments, which are distinct among us—were blended together among the Jews, as we have proved above. 2. Many of the things said by Jewish authors concerning Excommunication are to be understood as Excommunication practiced by Jews subject to a foreign empire, where almost no other punishment remained for them to restrain the disobedient except this one. For certainly, just as Excommunication was born in Exile, so its greatest use is found in Exile. For to add this here as an aside <note>original Greek: ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ</note>, Excommunication is not based on Divine law in the writings of the Old Testament, but seems to have been born during the Babylonian Captivity. The praiseworthy author Elias ben Mose (noted above) was of this mind, as cited in [John] Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a renowned English jurist and scholar of Jewish law often cited in early modern legal texts</note>:

> <note>original Hebrew: כן הוא ראוי בזמן הגלות שכל מי שלא קבל דברי תורה ודברי החכמים היוצאים מכח התורה להחרימו ולנדותו ולהבדילו מעדת ישראל על פי החכמים אשר בבית דין הנמצאים בזמן ההוא על כל הקהל ומשמם אחרי גזרת החכמים הנמצאים בזמן ההוא דור דור</note>
> "Thus it was appropriate in the time of exile, that whoever did not accept the words of the Torah and the words of the Sages, which proceed from the power of the Torah, should be banned, excommunicated, and separated from the congregation of Israel, according to the decree of the Sages present in the House of Judgment at that time over the whole community; and they were so named after the decree of the Sages existing at that time, from generation to generation."

And thus it was fitting and necessary **IN THE TIME OF CAPTIVITY**, that if anyone did not take upon himself the words of the Law or the words of the Sages, which are drawn from the very force of the Law, **TO PLACE HIM IN CHEREM AND IN NIDDUI** <note>Cherem and Niddui: Two levels of Jewish excommunication; Niddui is a temporary social distancing, while Cherem is a more severe, total exclusion from the community</note> **AND TO SEPARATE HIM FROM THE ASSEMBLY**, or the community of Israel, by the decree of the Sages who then presided over whatever judicial administration existed. And the Assembly, or the entire gathering, followed or willingly accepted the decree of the sages of this kind throughout all ages. And this is according to that example which occurs in Ezra <margin>Chapter 10, verse 8.</margin>: "*Whoever does not come within three days according to the decree of the princes and the elders, all his substance shall be forfeit...*"

## CHAPTER 9. SYNAGOGUE AND CHURCH. ##

...his substance, <note>original Latin: "tia ejus", completing "substantia" from the previous page</note> **and he himself shall be separated from the assembly of the exile** <note>original Hebrew: והוא נבדל מקהל הגולה. This is a reference to Ezra 10:8, regarding the punishment for those who did not return to Jerusalem.</note> **AND HE HIMSELF SHALL BE SEPARATED FROM THE ASSEMBLY OF THE CAPTIVITY.** *Reason supports this.* For when the Israelites were in the Babylonian Captivity, subject to the Kings and Governors of that jurisdiction, no bond remained for them to preserve their society except *Religion*, which was practiced by them in that most afflicted state more ardently than in former times when affairs were flourishing in the Fatherland. 

But since almost every Religion has its own sacred rites, which cannot be properly performed except by many in a common assembly and through a mutual consensus of minds; or at the very least, since a community of Religion binds men to mutual love as strongly as possible, and it is pleasing to everyone to have partners in Religion, it follows that it is a punishment of the gravest sort to be barred from the sacred rites of Religion, and to be removed from the fellowship of those who are bound together with us by the bond of Religion. This must necessarily have been even more the case in the Jewish Religion than in other vain and futile Religions, because the Jews everywhere were most fully persuaded of the truth of their Religion, and boasted of their Religion as the greatest privilege on this earth. 

And since they everywhere held their Sages in great veneration, it could not but seem to them a supreme foreshadowing of the future judgment <note>The author suggests that being cast out by the community was seen as a terrestrial preview of being cast out by God in the afterlife.</note> if someone had so offended that *he should be banished from the communication of prayer, and the assembly, and all holy commerce.* From this, if the *Prefects of Sacred Things* <term>Præfectis Sacrorum: Religious leaders or officials overseeing worship</term> in the Captivity were denied their due reverence and obedience, they could bring the disobedient back to their duty by no more convenient means than if they pronounced them unworthy of the communion of their society and repelled them from common sacred rites—that is, *Excommunicated* them. 

And it is probable that this was already introduced during the Babylonian Captivity. For as for what the Author of the *History of Susanna* <note>An ancient story often included in the Book of Daniel in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, but considered apocryphal by Protestants and Jews.</note> wished to persuade us—as if the Jews in that Exile had retained their other Forensic Tribunals <term>Tribunalia Forensia: Civil or public courts of law</term> and were permitted to carry out punishments for capital crimes—no wiser men among Christians will accept this. Since, moreover, in other respects sacred causes were not distinct from civil ones among the Jews, these very Presbyteries <term>Presbyteria: Councils of elders</term> of the Jews in Exile took cognizance of any causes whatever, both civil and sacred (without prejudice, however, to the Political Forum of their captors, and only by its indulgence). Hence it seems to have happened that in those famous *twenty-four causes of excommunication*, whether their origin is from the first, or from the second Jewish...
