...tune to be recovered from exile (which I do not dispute), political matters were constantly mixed with ecclesiastical ones, because both the civil administration and the leadership of the Church <note>The author uses "Ecclesia" (Church) here to refer to the Jewish religious assembly or community.</note> were entrusted to these Presbyteries <note>The term "Presbytery" here refers to the Council of Elders or the local governing body of the synagogue.</note>. <margin>
Theodosian Code, book 2, title 1, law 10.
</margin>

Even though the Sanhedrins <note>The supreme councils of the Jewish people.</note> of Palestine, after the Republic was restored, were again made masters of their own rights and could punish transgressors of the Mosaic Laws with other types of penalties—such as flogging, whipping, monetary fines, and even death itself—they nevertheless did not neglect this Excommunication. This was because this Ecclesiastical penalty, joined as it was with ignominy, contempt, and various inconveniences, was to many more grave and troublesome than a civil penalty. This was especially true if we accept the hypothesis that in Canaan itself, while the Republic flourished, almost no form of public Excommunication existed except for the most severe kind. 

But when the Republic was overturned again by the Romans, almost this type of punishment alone was left to the Ecclesiastical Presbyteries, by which they could bring the disobedient members of their religion back into order and recall them to their duty. For the Romans certainly allowed them to settle those controversies which pertained to their *superstition* <note>The Roman legal term "superstitio" was used to refer to non-Roman religions, including Judaism, without necessarily carrying the modern purely negative connotation.</note>, and they easily tolerated the punishment of Excommunication to be inflicted by them upon the disobedient, unless perhaps they abused it against Imperial Edicts. Clearly famous in this regard is that Constitution of *Arcadius and Honorius* <note>Roman Emperors of the late 4th and early 5th centuries.</note>, which more than one learned man has brought to light before us: *Jews* (it states) *living under Roman and common law regarding* THESE MATTERS, WHICH DO NOT PERTAIN SO MUCH TO THEIR SUPERSTITION, *as to the court, the laws, and rights, shall approach the courts by solemn law, and shall bring and receive all actions according to Roman Laws.*

*Finally, let them be under our Laws. To be sure, if any, by mutual agreement and in the likeness of arbitrators, should think it necessary to litigate before the Jews or Patriarchs by the consent of the parties—provided it is only in a civil matter—they shall not be forbidden by public law to seek their judgment; even the Judges of the Provinces shall execute their sentences.* <note>The author is quoting a Roman legal decree—likely from the Theodosian Code—which allowed Jewish communities a degree of self-governance in private civil matters.</note> *Clearly, from this constitution it is manifest that the Hebrews dispersed under the Roman Empire had Sacred Consistories, councils <note>original Greek: συνέδρια</note>, and synagogues, in which only those matters were settled by the Elders and Teachers—or Wise Men <note>Hebrew: חכמים, Hachamim</note>—which pertained to their superstition (that is, their Religion); not, of course, those matters which belonged to the Roman forensic Tribunals and were to be decided according to their Laws and constitutions. Nevertheless, they granted to them what is granted to all men: to choose Arbitrators from their own People—men who were Learned and proven—or to designate Judges by Agreement for deciding disputes of lesser weight. Since these Arbitrators were chosen from men of a more honorable rank, it seems that the Rectors of the Academies and Schools and the Pastors of the Synagogues were the ones who primarily performed this duty, because they were considered the most skilled in the law of the Hebrews. Thus, the face of Synagogue Governance in the Second Exile was again the same as it was in the First. You may gather the same from the Justinian Edict, which was cited at the beginning of this Chapter. The sum of it is that the Rectors of the Academies and Synagogues, together with literate men, constituted a House of Judgment <note>Hebrew: בית דין, Beit Din</note> or Academy <note>Hebrew: ישיבה, Yeshiva</note>—an assembly or Ecclesiastical Sanhedrin—whose members were called Masters, Elders, Pastors, and Teachers. These individuals held the highest Power of Excommunication among the Jews at all times.*

*But indeed, since in Jewish Societies during the Exile such a great abundance of literate men was often not available as was required to compose the Presbyteries <note>Councils of elders.</note>, and since a Synagogue often took for itself only one Wise Man <note>Hebrew: חכם, Hacham</note> as the Doctor of the Academy and the Church <note>The author uses "Ecclesia" (Church) here to refer to the Jewish religious assembly.</note>, and since, furthermore, the civil governance of the Synagogues was often committed to certain prudent men from the common people—even if they were not sufficiently instructed in Doctrine—it happened that the power of Excommunication devolved by law most closely upon these men. And so the custom of the modern Synagogue carries on, so that the right of exercising this act resides with the Rabbi <note>Hebrew: רב, Rav</note>, the Teacher of the Synagogue or Academy, and, unless I am mistaken, also with the Community Leaders <note>Hebrew: פרנסים, Parnassim; literally "providers" or "administrators"</note>. However, the former, as one skilled in ancient customs and representing the whole—*

### CHAPTER 9. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH. ###

...he must trouble himself to seek them out for as far as a *parsa* <note>A Persian unit of distance, roughly 2.5 to 3 miles</note>. If he does not find them, then ten men who study the Mishnah <note>The first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions</note> may release him. If he does not find these, then ten who know how to read the Torah may release him. If he does not find these, even ten who do not know how to read may release him. If he does not find ten in his location, even three may release him.

When someone is *Excommunicated* by means of a dream, this must certainly be held as a true *Excommunication*, and the *Excommunicated* person must be formally released from it. Even if he is absolved within a dream, this is of no consequence. Furthermore, even if the person knows the specific individual who *Excommunicated* him in the dream, that individual does not have the power to release him. It is therefore necessary that a COUNCIL OF TEN be present, men who are practiced in the *Talmudic* <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism</note> constitutions, to absolve him. If he cannot find such men, the burden is on him to seek them out up to the distance of a *Parsa* (4,000 paces). If he truly cannot find them even then, ten men who are learned in the *Mishnah Study* may release him (Maimonides omitted this part), 
<margin>Laws of Torah Study, chapter 6.</margin>
and even if these cannot be found, ten men who are skilled in *Biblical* reading may release him. If these too cannot be had, ten others may lawfully release him, even if they are not well-versed in *Biblical Reading*. But if he cannot find even the number of ten in his own place, then even three men will suffice for this business. Do you see how necessary the number of ten learned men was considered in this place, and how carefully they were to be sought out? And for what reason, I ask, other than because it was anciently believed and accepted that a perfect Assembly of Learned Men must consist of at least ten people? But since we have discussed this quite extensively in the preceding sections, I do not wish to enter into that dispute anew. Let these words suffice concerning *Jewish Excommunication*, specifically public excommunication. For it is indeed known from those same *Jewish Constitutions* that a private person could *Excommunicate* another private person—indeed, anyone could even excommunicate themselves—but that is not our concern at present, especially since it has been abundantly explained by Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a famous English jurist and scholar of Jewish law</note>. Let us now see what we reserved for the third place: the similarities between *Christian* and *Jewish Excommunication*.

## CHAPTER X.

*A more precise and extensive argument against Erastus and others, showing that Excommunication in the Apostolic Christian Church was adopted following the example of the Synagogue; it is taught in what way that Excommunication of ancient times principally consisted, while resolving the exceptions or objections of the opposing view. It is also proven that private Excommunication was in use among Christians just as among Jews; and finally, it is added that this power in the Church was exercised by Bishops and Presbyters <note>church elders or ministers</note>.*

It was stated in the previous sections that *Erastus* <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583), a Swiss physician and theologian who argued that the state, not the church, should punish sins; his views led to the term "Erastianism."</note> contends that for *Excommunication*, as it is practiced in our Churches, there is no precept or example in the writings of the New Testament, but that it should be regarded as a *human invention*, which has brought a great deal of harm to the Church of Christ. As I have weighed his argument and turned it over in my mind, I believe it must be granted to him—and can be granted without any inconvenience—that that specific part or type of *Ecclesiastical Excommunication* by which someone is barred from the use of the sacred symbols of *bread and wine* in the Lord’s Supper, is not expressly commanded in the Scripture of the New Testament, nor is its practice recorded as having been exercised.

Since many, however, place the greatest part of *Christian Excommunication* in that act, and explain the passages of Scripture that might be thought to deal with *Excommunication* according to that hypothesis of theirs, it is inevitable that Erastus seems to many to argue with the highest probability. But it must be observed against Erastus and others who follow him (among whom I place Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654), an English polymath and jurist who argued that early church discipline was modeled on Jewish legal traditions.</note>) that even if Christ and the Apostles do not speak explicitly regarding this part or type of *Ecclesiastical Excommunication* by which someone is barred from the *Sacraments* <note>Specifically the Eucharist or Lord's Supper</note> (which I admit Erastus has solidly proven), nevertheless, the precepts given by them concerning *Excommunication* entirely include this very forbidden use of the Sacred Symbols. Specifically, the precepts of Christ and the Apostles aim at the fact that all fellowship <note>original: "commercium"</note>...

# CHAPTER 10. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

...dealings with stubborn sinners must be avoided, whether by private members of the Church or by the Church as a whole. If this latter point can be clearly demonstrated, then it will simultaneously be proven that the symbols of sacred communion must be denied to those same persistent sinners, whatever Erastus <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583) argued that the Church did not have the scriptural authority to exclude people from the sacraments.</note> may strive for to the contrary. For (to use the words of Aurelius of Cillani in the Council of Carthage found in the works of Cyprian) <margin>Acts of the Council of Carthage in Cyprian, page 348.</margin> *how can such people be admitted into the House of God (I add: how can they be admitted to the table of the most holy Christian communion) who are prohibited from being admitted into our private home?* But it will be necessary for us to trace this matter from the very beginning <note>original Latin: "ab ovo," literally "from the egg."</note> from the writings of the New Testament, and to show more clearly the conformity between Christian and Jewish Excommunication.

We understood above that Christ the Lord teaches that a sinning brother must be rebuked privately first, then publicly; and if he refuses to yield, <margin>Chapter 18, verse 15 <note>Referring to the Gospel of Matthew.</note></margin> *he is to be held as a Gentile and a Tax Collector.* These words, according to what we then said, can signify nothing less than that the familiar social association with such a man is to be avoided. But by whom? By the Church, to whom that crime became known through the rebuke? That is not stated in the text. Certainly, if it were expressly stated in the text (although no one could absurdly conclude it from there), then there would be no reason why we should not directly apply this passage of Christ to *Public Excommunication*. But it is said in the text: **Let him be to Thee.** By which it is strictly implied that for that person against whom he had sinned, he is to be held *as a Gentile and a Tax Collector*; and because we do not wish to draw more from those words of Christ than lies clearly within them, let us admit this interpretation, which we also admitted above. Yet it is not easily denied that Christ the Lord here looked back to the *Neziphah* <note>original Hebrew: נזיפה, a term for a "shaming" or minor disciplinary rebuke lasting seven days.</note>, *Correction*, or *Tokhechah* <note>original Hebrew: תוכחה, a "reproof" or formal warning given to a sinner before legal action.</note>, *Rebuke for sin*, which was in use among the Jews. Nor can it be denied that the Lord here, as a remedy against scandals, advised *private Excommunication*, such as seems to have been in use among the Jews at that time. For in what, I ask, did that *private Jewish Excommunication* (concerning which there are so many Canons) consist, other than in this: that one person would treat another as a *Gentile and a Tax Collector*? That is, he would flee his fellowship and familiar company? That someone would separate himself (I am looking now at the term *Niddui* <note>original Hebrew: נידוי, a formal distance or "casting out" that usually lasted thirty days.</note>) from the dealings of the other? And that *private Excommunication*, as it prevailed among the Jews,

### ON THE DUTIES OF PREFECTS, BOOK III. PART I.

...was held to be very much in agreement with reason, and at the same time a most useful remedy, perfectly suited to the character of the Christian Church, against scandals. For tell me, please, what would you want to do, or what could you do against your brother who offends you, in the arrangement of the New Covenant <note>The author uses "economy of the New Covenant" to describe the era of the Gospel, contrasting it with the legalistic structures of the Old Testament.</note>, where no coercive authority holds place, but reason and charity rule? This is by far the safest path, this is consistent with reason and in harmony with the Law of charity: that you first warn him privately, then publicly, and if after being warned he refuses to return to a right mind with you, you should avoid social interaction with him. What is this very thing other than to *privately excommunicate* him, as the *Jews* were accustomed to do? But if indeed it is permitted for an individual to *privately excommunicate one’s brother*, who would deny that the *entire Church* has the same right, if a brother has sinned against the *whole Church*? Certainly, it is not at all far-fetched to derive public *Excommunication* from this *private* form. But a word must still be said about those things which Christ adds to this precept of his,

<margin>verse 18.</margin>
because their interpretation seems doubtful or obscure: *Truly I say to you*, <note>original Greek: "ὅσα ἐὰν δήσητε"</note> WHATEVER YOU BIND ON EARTH, SHALL BE BOUND IN HEAVEN, and <note>original Greek: "ὅσα ἐὰν λύσητε ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς"</note> *whatever you loose on earth, shall be loosed in heaven.* It is well known that from the most ancient times of the Church, these words have been understood as if they contained a confirmation of what Christ had said previously: that is, as if Christ were granting even more clearly to the Church the power of Excommunicating—which, according to these interpreters, is *binding*—and of *loosing*—that is, admitting the excommunicated person back to the communion of the Church after satisfaction has been made. Indeed, this interpretation does not deserve to be rejected on the grounds that it deviates from the Hebrew ways of speaking; for they also sometimes (though more rarely) express *Excommunication* by the name <term>issur <note>Hebrew: איסור</note></term>, or "BINDING," and are commonly accustomed to call the restoration of an excommunicated person a <term>heter <note>Hebrew: היתר</note></term>, or "loosing." But this fact stands in the way: that Christ does not say <note>original Greek: "ὅσους"</note> "whomever" [referring to people], but <note>original Greek: "ὅσα"</note> "whatever" [referring to things]. From this it is clear that he is speaking about *matters*, not about *persons*.

...in the Church; as if he had said: Whatever you have pronounced lawful or unlawful; whatever you have commanded or prohibited, those things are to be ratified in the Heavenly Court <note>original: "Curia Cœlesti." <margin>2 Thessalonians 3:14</margin>
After this passage from Matthew, the words of Paul in the second Epistle to the *Thessalonians* further deserve consideration; where he orders that those refusing obedience to his commands should be MARKED, and forbids <note>original Greek: "συναναμίγνυσθαι αὐτοῖς"</note> ASSOCIATING WITH THEM, SO THAT THEY MAY BE ASHAMED. <margin>Chapter 16:17</margin>

AVOID THE ADMONITION <note>original Latin: "ADMONITIONEM DEVITA." A reference to Titus 3:10: "A man that is an heretic after the first and second admonition avoid."</note>. Beware lest you interpret the final word "AVOID" <note>original: "DEVITA," here clipped as "DEVI-".</note> wrongly, alongside that old and severe theologian <note>original: "theologo," here clipped as "Theo-".</note> of his time, who argued from it that *heretics ought to be punished with death*. You might believe it to be a fable <note>original: "fabulam," here clipped as "Fa-".</note>—and I confess I have believed it until now—but Erasmus relates <note>original: "narrat," here clipped as "rat".</note> it in good faith in his Commentaries on this passage. But to the matter at hand. Paul deals <note>original: "agit," here clipped as "git".</note> here with "instruction," <note>original Greek: "νουθεσίαν" (*nouthesian*), meaning a warning or disciplinary advice.</note> one and another ADMONITION regarding a factious man <note>original: "hominem," here clipped as "minem".</note>. Moreover, "instruction" in this place is the same, unless I am mistaken <note>original: "nisi fallor".</note>, as "rebuke" <note>original Hebrew: נזיפה (*nezifah*), a rabbinic term for a formal disciplinary reprimand.</note>. Christ requires "reproof," <note>original Greek: "ἐλέγχον" (*elenchon*), an evidentiary conviction of error.</note> which we say <note>original: "dicimus".</note> is the same as the Hebrew "correction" <note>original Hebrew: תוכחה (*tokhekhah*).</note>. But if a disturber of this kind does not come to his senses after admonitions <note>original: "admonitiones".</note>, Paul wants him to be avoided. "Avoid," he says <note>original: "inquit".</note> <note>original Greek: "Παραιτοῦ" (*paraitou*).</note>.

Yet the Greek word "to avoid" <note>original: "παραιτεῖσθαι" (*paraitéisthai*)</note> signifies to repel someone, to repudiate, that is to expel, to cast out <note>original Greek: "ἐκβάλλειν" (*ekballein*)</note>, and to send away <note>original Greek: "ἀποπέμπειν" (*apopempein*)</note>; whence among Greek authors it is not infrequently accepted in the sense of the repudiation of a wife, which, as is known, did not only consist in the denial of social interaction, but in the dismissal of the wife <note>original: "uxoris".</note> and her expulsion from the home. What else is this than to excommunicate, just as Excommunication was in use among the Jews at that time <note>original: "tempore".</note>. For Paul in this place does not [simply] <note>original: "tempore" or "temere".</note> establish a form of Excommunication such as was defined in that Excommunication which was called "shunning" <note>original Hebrew: נידוי (*niddui*), the formal thirty-day social exclusion in Jewish law.</note>, but simply says that a man of this kind is to be repelled, repudiated, sent away, and expelled, according to the customs <note>original: "moribus".</note> used among the Jews at that time. Nor does it seem doubtful that <note>original: "quin".</note>, just as exclusion from social interaction is meant here, so also is exclusion from the place in which the faithful were accustomed <note>original: "solebant".</note> to gather. For since Christians in those first times often <note>original: "saepe".</note> gathered in private houses and were enclosed in narrow spaces <note>original: "spatiis".</note> to celebrate their sacred rites, and at the same time cultivated all the honorable duties of fraternity <note>original: "fraternitatis".</note> and charity toward one another, who can conceive that they tolerated in those conventions <note>original: "conventibus".</note> men from whose social interaction they were required to separate themselves according to the canon <note>original: "canone".</note> of their discipline? Who would believe that the first Christians of pure faith <note>original: "fidei".</note> admitted into their assemblies those whom it was necessary to avoid <note>original Greek: "παραιτεῖσθαι" (*paraitéisthai*)</note> according to the Pauline command? But if you object that the command was given to *Titus* alone and not to others, I shall refute this from the constitutions of the Jews <note>original: "constitutionibus".</note>: that a man was considered Excommunicated from the entire Church if he was Excommunicated by the *Leader of the Church*. This passage, therefore, may finally <note>original: "demum".</note> be the first of those in which Christian Excommunication is clearly and expressly <note>original: "diserte".</note> commanded.

To this discussion, let us now add the instructions of Paul in the first Epistle to the Corinthians. There was a man in the Corinthian Church who had committed a great crime, one most unworthy of the Christian religion: *he had taken his stepmother as a wife*. Yet, he was still tolerated by the Corinthians in their brotherly communion. Paul is rightly incensed by this, and he chastises the negligence of the Corinthians with a heavy and severe discourse. He rebukes them because they did **NOT MOURN**, so that the one who committed that deed might be **TAKEN AWAY FROM THEIR MIDST**. That is to say, they had not demonstrated their own *grief* over the scandal through a necessary "punishment" <note>original Greek: ἐπιτιμίαν (*epitimian*), a legal or ecclesiastical penalty.</note>, admonition, and rebuke toward the sinning brother to the point of separating themselves from his communion, nor had the man himself been expelled from the communion of the Church by their mourning and rebuke. It is quite clear from this entire *Chapter* that this was Paul’s intention. Furthermore, it should be carefully noted that Paul says here: *ek mesou hymōn*, **FROM THE MIDST OF YOU**; we should clearly perceive that Paul is dealing here with Church communion, not with the removal of a man from the world through death—a sense in which the phrase is sometimes used in the writings of the Old Testament <note>original Latin: "T. V." standing for *Testamenti Veteris*.</note>. Indeed, *Paul* further declares that he has already decided (if the Corinthian Church would agree) **TO DELIVER SUCH A MAN TO SATAN** *for the destruction of the flesh* <note>original Greek: εἰς ὄλεθρον τῆς σαρκὸς (*eis olethron tēs sarkos*).</note>. Regarding this "handing over to *Satan*" (even if the opinion is not absurd that this refers to the *Synagogal anathemas* <note>formal curses of excommunication.</note> by which someone is subjected to the power of *Satan*, provided that such or similar formulas as they have now were already accepted back then), I now readily allow it to be understood that a person is handed over to the Devil to be tortured with *bodily afflictions*. After all, it is not absurd to think that demons were subject to the Apostles to that extent. He warns the Corinthians to purge out this *leaven*, which could easily corrupt the whole mass. # ON THE DUTIES OF PREFECTS BOOK III. PART I.

<margin>Chapter 2, verses 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10.</margin>
...we speak regarding the intention and genuine purpose of Paul's words; likewise, the same is clear from what the *Corinthians*, in accordance with this Pauline admonition, did toward this brother of *theirs*, who had caused that *scandal* to the Church. They had rebuked him in public, they had severed the bond of charity and of their own communion previously maintained with him, they held his sin against him <note>original: *peccatum ipsi reservaverunt*, meaning they did not grant him absolution</note>, and thus they had left him in a state of *extreme grief and sorrow*: all of which can be concluded from the *Second Epistle to the Corinthians*. But what do these things mean, other than that this man had truly been Excommunicated—that is, separated from Ecclesiastical communion by a public sentence of Paul and the Church, until he had shown clear signs of repentance? 

However, Erastus <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583) was a Swiss physician and theologian who argued that the Church did not have the scriptural authority to exclude people from the sacraments.</note> objects that not even a word is read here (nor elsewhere) regarding this man being barred or excluded by the sentence of the Church from the use of the Sacred Symbols of communion, *the bread and the wine*. Erastus constantly harps on this same string <note>original: *hac chorda... oberrat*, a musical metaphor for repeating a flawed argument</note>, and fights along these lines—to use the words of Tertullian <note>An influential early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155–220 AD).</note>—and he repeats this same objection to other passages as well, whether cited so far or to be cited below, which might seem to deal with *Excommunication*; therefore, it would be wrong to overlook this evasion. 

I grant Erastus, then, that this specific part or type of *Excommunication*, by which someone is barred from the use of the Sacred Symbols of the *bread and wine*, is not directly addressed in the writings of the New Testament; and I also confess that I have perceived this more clearly from the Erastians. Yet, even with this conceded, *Excommunication* as it is now received is not undermined. For the *exclusion* from the use of the *Sacred Symbols* must be considered a necessary and indubitable consequence of *Excommunication* as it was practiced in the age of the Apostles. 

For *Apostolic Excommunication* consisted in the same thing as *Jewish excommunication*: that someone should be separated from the communion of their brothers, and consequently also be excluded from the *Place* where that communion was practiced, and from the *Sacred Rites* <note>original: *Sacris*</note> celebrated there. Thus, *Excommunication* truly and properly consisted only in this: that someone was separated from the sacred assembly, as was the custom in the *Synagogue*. From this, however, it necessarily followed that the person was at the same time barred from the Symbols of Sacred communion. For it would be absurd to offer the Symbols of Sacred communion to one who, by the sentence of the Elders <note>original: *Presbyterorum*</note>, had been declared unworthy of the very communion of the brothers. It would have been absurd to sit with him at the *sacred table*, when it was not permitted to sit at a *common* [private] table...

### CHAPTER 10. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

Indeed, as I have already stated, because the **Sacred Symbols** <note>original: *Symbola Sacra*; referring specifically to the bread and wine of the Eucharist</note> are not distributed except in the very place of sacred **communion**, it follows that the Sacred Symbols must be denied, and were denied, to anyone who was excluded from the Place and the Communion of the brothers where those symbols were distributed. And so, I easily concede that **Excommunication** does not properly consist in the mere denial of the Sacred Symbols of Union, but rather in the denial of any familiar social interaction with the faithful. But in turn, I demand it be conceded to me that this denial of the Sacred Symbols necessarily follows **the Separation** <note>original Greek: *τὸν Ἀφορισμὸν* (ton Aphoismon); a technical term for being set apart or excluded from the community</note> or exclusion from fraternal communion.

Now, one or two further testimonies must be cited to confirm what we have said. Truly, the admonition of John in his second Epistle is entirely relevant here: <margin>verse 10.</margin> *If anyone comes to you and does not bring this Doctrine, **do not receive him into your house and do not say "greetings" to him.*** <note>original Greek: *μὴ λαμβάνετε αὐτὸν εἰς οἰκίαν καὶ χαίρειν αὐτῷ μὴ λέγετε*</note> What is Excommunicating if this is not it? John adds: *For he who says "Greetings," **shares in his evil works.*** <note>original Greek: *κοινωνεῖ τοῖς ἔργοις αὐτοῦ τοῖς πονηροῖς*</note> Therefore, John commands that those who do not profess Christian Doctrine purely and sincerely must be excluded entirely from all familiar communion; one should not say "Greetings" to them, nor receive them into the House. What then? Is someone to be received into the public **House** <note>The church building or assembly</note> whom it is not permitted to receive into private ones? Or is fraternal communion to be practiced with him in the **Love Feasts** <note>original: *Agapis*; communal meals shared by early Christians</note> and the **Lord’s Supper**, which in the past were certainly celebrated together, when it is a sin even to announce a **greeting** to him? 

But nothing confirms our opinion so well as what we read in the third Epistle of the same John (or at least by that *John the Elder* of most ancient memory) concerning Diotrephes, whose ambition and malevolence are rebuked: <margin>verse 10.</margin> "**Neither does he himself**," it is said, "**receive the brothers, and he hinders those who wish to, and casts them out of the church**"; <note>original Greek: *Οὔτε αὐτὸς... ἐπιδέχεται τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς καὶ τοὺς βουλομένους κωλύει καὶ ἐκ τῆς ἐκκλησίας ἐκβάλλει*</note> he does not receive the brothers, he prohibits those wanting to admit them, and HE THROWS THEM OUT OF THE CHURCH. What is this **casting out of the church** other than **casting out of the synagogue**? Certainly, as has already been observed by the most Learned Men, the phrases are in complete agreement. To me, it is almost the same whether you understand by **the church** the Building in which the Church was accustomed to meet, or the **Church** itself—that is, the multitude of the faithful coming together in a certain place—because, as we have shown above, the one is contained within the other. However, I believe it should be observed that this **private excommunication** was a type and model for **public excommunication**. For if, in ancient times, a **private individual** excommunicated another in such a way that he utterly avoided his company and even excluded him from his own prayers, who could believe that **public excommunication** was any less rigid? Indeed, I believe it can be safely concluded that in those first ages of the Church, this particular form of excommunication—whether public or private—was primarily in use, which we have shown was designated among the ancient Hebrews by the terms **separation** <note>original Greek: ἀφορισμός (aphorismos)</note> and **casting out** <note>original Greek: ἐκβολή (ekbole)</note> from the synagogues.

### CHAPTER 10. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

...[excom]munication, which is called **Niddui** <note>original: נידוי; a minor form of Jewish excommunication involving thirty days of social distancing</note>, they had another more serious form called **Cherem** <note>original: חרם; a severe ban or "devoting to destruction," involving total exclusion from the community</note>, because by it someone was completely separated from the Body of the Church. (Though it is uncertain, as I have often said, whether these two types of **Aphorismos** <note>original: ἀφορισμός; a Greek term for "separation" or "cutting off"</note> were sufficiently distinct in the age of Christ, or so distinctly practiced, and whether instead a single intermediate type between *Niddui* and *Cherem* might have prevailed then). Thus it is known that among Christians, that same type of Excommunication was received by which a person is completely torn away from the communion of the Church, called **Anathema** <note>original: ἀνάθεμα; something "set aside" or cursed</note>, which is the same as the *Cherem*.

For this is how we Christians are accustomed to call the sentence pronounced against those who speak impiously, when we set it up publicly for all to see and know, as if it were inscribed on a monument.* <note>The author provides this quote in both the original Greek and a Latin translation; I have rendered it here as a single English passage.</note>

<margin>Apostolic Canons, 28; edited by Beveridge.</margin>
In the Canons of the Church, this kind of *separation* is said to be "to be cut off entirely from the Church," or to be utterly excised from the Church.

From this, we can easily gather that it was composed long after the time of Christ. Christian Bishops, however (especially the Roman ones) of later times, applied the same industry in fashioning anathemas, the better to seize the minds of the common people and to terrify their adversaries, whom they struck with this bolt of lightning. Indeed, even in more ancient times, the Church Fathers were quite studious and ingenious in decorating and extending these anathemas of theirs, as can be seen in the example of the anathema of the **Synod of Sardica** <note>A council held in 343 AD to address the Arian controversy.</note>, pronounced against the **Arians** <note>Followers of Arius, who taught that Jesus Christ was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father.</note>, as found in Theodoret.

->### CHAPTER 10. OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.<-

<margin>Notes on Eusebius, pages 132 and 136.</margin>
*The elders of the assembly, sitting with these men, and no others among the Christians, would rightly excommunicate anyone.* But Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a renowned English jurist and scholar of Jewish law.</note>, in writing these things, does not seem to have paid attention to those examples of *private* excommunication which were produced by us a little earlier. Certainly, the custom prevailed among Christians just as much as among the Jews, where a private person could excommunicate another private person. We assert this with greater confidence because that distinguished man, Henri Valesius <note>Henri Valois (1603–1676), a French classical scholar and historian.</note>, has confirmed us in this opinion. Indeed, a singular example of *excommunication* serves this point—one exercised by a private citizen against *Theodosius the Younger* <note>Emperor Theodosius II (r. 402–450 AD).</note>, as related by Theodoret, but presented here by us from Cassiodorus's *Tripartite History*.

<margin>Tripartite History, book 10, chapter 27.</margin>
The words are as follows: *Truly the Prince himself was adorned with many other virtues, but especially with mercy, gentleness, and tranquility of mind. It is fitting for us to show a clear proof of this.* A CERTAIN MAN INDEED OF THE MONASTIC LIFE <note>original: "CONVERSATIONIS QUIDEM MONACHICÆ"; referring to a monk's way of life or discipline.</note>, *but of a rather harsh disposition, approached the Emperor to petition him regarding a certain matter. When he had done this frequently and had not obtained the things he requested*, HE FORBADE HIM FROM ECCLESIASTICAL COMMUNION <note>This is a formal act of excommunication.</note>, *and, having imposed this bond upon him, he departed. Truly the most faithful Emperor, having returned to the Palace at the hour of the midday meal while guests were present, said he would not take food until his bond was first loosened. For this reason, he sent to the Bishop of the City, asking that he command the one who had bound him to loosen his bonds. And when the Bishop said that a binding should not be accepted from just anyone, and sent word that he was loosened, the Emperor nonetheless would not accept the release until the man who had bound him—having been sought out with much effort—restored to him the communion he had forbidden. Behold, a Prince and Emperor himself excommunicated and released by a private citizen!* And let these things now said about the act of excommunication itself suffice. A word must be added concerning the persons in whose hands the power to exercise this act resided in the Christian Church.

<margin>See Tertullian's Apology, 39.</margin>
To be sure, just as among the Hebrews this power was in the hands of the **בית דין** <term>Beth Din: House of Judgment; a rabbinical court</term> or **ישיבה** <term>Yeshiva: an assembly or academy of scholars</term>, the *Consistory of Elders*, or even in the hands of a single **רב** <term>Rav: a Rabbi or master</term>, the *President of the School and Synagogue*, so likewise this faculty of excommunicating has been exercised by the Bishops and Presbyters of the Christian Church from the most ancient times. We have understood this from the words of Selden just noted, and the same can be gathered from all the ancient Canons of the Church that deal with this subject, besides the fact that supreme reason demands the same. As an example, examine the Canons of the Councils of *Elvira* and *Nicaea* <note>The Council of Elvira (c. 305 AD) and the Council of Nicaea (325 AD) established early Christian laws regarding discipline and heresy.</note>.

Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a prominent Protestant reformer and translator</note> correctly translates this: *And I said, Lord, they know I dragged to prison and inflicted lashes* **THROUGHOUT EACH SYNAGOGUE** <note>original Latin: *PER SINGULAS SYNAGOGAS*</note> *upon those who believed in you.* The Dutch <note>The "Belgae," likely referring to the Dutch States Translation (Statenvertaling) of the Bible</note> translate it: *Flogged in the synagogues* <note>original Dutch: *In de Synagogen geesselde*</note>. Each of these points will acquire its greatest strength when we shortly demonstrate that such Flogging truly took place within the synagogues.

Entire tribes, cities, the High Priest, and even, according to some, the King himself, were subject to this judiciary. This was the only and sole body to which one could appeal in the weightiest matters. To this body was committed the right of War and Peace. It was their role to establish new laws for the public good, to repeal those already established, to set up local Sanhedrins, and other matters pertaining to supreme power. Nor was a Senate of greater authority ever assembled, unless all their records are misleading.

...of those times, it seemed beautiful to speak about the customs of their own Republic following the example of the Greeks and Romans, undoubtedly so that its dignity would not be diminished in the eyes of foreigners. Therefore, such testimonies must be taken **with a grain of salt** <note>original Latin: *cum grano salis*</note>, and should not be accepted until they are conveniently reconciled with the universal customs of the people and other passages. Nor do we accept the idea that the word <term>Kahal</term> <note>Hebrew: קהל; often translated as "assembly" or "congregation"</note> denotes the kind of Legislative Assembly of Nobles among the Jews as Grotius suggests. For from those points argued above regarding its genuine meaning, it is clear that it signifies **the whole multitude of the people**, **gathered** for festivals or other solemnities, and certainly **not the Delegates of that multitude**. It is translated by the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> as <term>Ecclesia</term> <note>Greek: ἐκκλησία – assembly or church</note> and **multitude** <note>Greek: πλῆθος – plethos</note>, just as the term <term>Edah</term> <note>Hebrew: עדה – another term for congregation</note> is translated as **synagogue** <note>Greek: συναγωγή</note>. It is far from the case that the meaning proposed by that illustrious man <note>referring to Hugo Grotius</note> holds true.

And I beg you, as a third point I would like noted: what reason would there be here to distinguish **councils** <note>Greek: συνέδρια - synedria</note> from **synagogues**, and to believe that for the purpose of examining the Apostles, special entire assemblies had to be instituted among the Jews? Especially since it is well known from the statutes of the Hebrews <margin>Chapter 1.</margin> that a **False Prophet** <note>Hebrew: נביא השקר – *Navi ha-Sheker*</note> must be judged by the Great Sanhedrin. So it is stated in the tractate *Sanhedrin*: <margin>Maimonides, Laws of Foreign Worship, chapter 10.</margin> **A lying prophet is not to be judged except in the Sanhedrin of seventy-one men.** No greater crime was charged against Christ and the Apostles than that they were **False Prophets** <note>Latin: *Pseudoprophetae*</note>; indeed, this was by far the most serious accusation. If the judgment belonged to that supreme Senate, what need is there to imagine larger assemblies here in which this business would have to be decided? 

But as a fourth point, where the Great Man <note>Grotius</note> appeals to History, he undoubtedly errs in no small way. Who would believe that **the Sanhedrin and all the Senate of the sons of Israel**, <note>Greek: τὸ συνέδριον καὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γερουσίαν τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ</note> mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles <margin>Chapter 5, 21.</margin>, indicates anything other than the **Sanhedrin** mentioned in the preceding Chapter IV? This is especially true since Josephus usually calls this same Sanhedrin a <term>Gerousia</term> <note>Greek: γερουσία – a Council of Elders or Senate</note>, and these names do not signify different things. It seems to me that Luke’s meaning is this: since it often happened that the **Senate** was poorly attended, the Prince of the Senate would convoke all its members with more diligent care...

§. 607.

<margin>See Selden, *On the Sanhedrin*, book 1, chapter 7, page 105.</margin> <note>John Selden (1584–1654) was a renowned English polymath and jurist who wrote extensively on Jewish law to understand English common law origins.</note>
On the eve of the Day of Atonement <note>Yom Kippur</note>, it is customary for everyone to be flogged in a solemn rite as a sign of repentance. The words of Rabbi Jacob Ben Asher <note>1269–1343, an influential German-Spanish rabbi and author of the *Arba'ah Turim*, a foundational code of Jewish law</note> are as follows:

<note>original Hebrew: נהגין באשכנז שכל הקהל לוקין מלקות ארבעים בבית הכנסת אחר תפלת המנחה שמתוך כן יתן אל לבו לשוב מעבירות שבידו.</note>
> It is the custom in Germany that the entire congregation receives forty lashes in the synagogue after the afternoon prayer, so that by this means, one may take it to heart to repent for the transgressions in his hand.

*It is the custom in Germany, that the entire congregation* **BE FLOGGED WITH FORTY LASHES** *in the synagogue after the evening prayer, so that having been thus chastened, he might firmly resolve to withdraw from the sins that clung to him.* Here you have a chastisement in the synagogue of the ancient Hebrews entirely similar to [judicial] floggings, since those too were limited to forty lashes. Joseph Karo <note>1488–1575, the author of the *Shulchan Aruch*, the most authoritative legal code in Judaism</note> expressed it thus:

<note>original Hebrew: כל הקהל מלוקים מלקות ארבעים אחר תפלת המנחה שמתוך כן יתן על לבו לשוב מעבירות שבידו.</note>
> The entire congregation is lashed forty times after the afternoon prayer, so that by this means, one may take it to heart to repent for the transgressions in his hand.

*The sense is the same: except that what Rabbi Jacob restricted to the Germans, Karo expresses more generally. Yet there is something you might object to: that this flogging is penitential, not unlike the penances of the Papists* <note>The author is likely a Protestant scholar comparing Jewish penance to Catholic practices of self-mortification common in his era</note>. *Indeed, I do not deny or hide this; but I easily reply that the Synagogal chastisement or flogging of which we treat was likewise inflicted for this purpose: that the sinner might be led by it to a right mind—that is, to repentance for his deed. Let us note, however, for a clearer solution to our doubt, that Jewish writers speak openly of a certain Synagogal flogging, and indeed one substituted for Excommunication, concerning which we spoke in the preceding chapter.*

<margin>Laws of Excommunication and Ban, chapter 334, §. 42.</margin> <note>original Hebrew/Latin: Hilcoth Niddui Vacher. [Hilkhot Niddui v'Cherem]</note>

*A wise Elder, experienced, or a Father of the House of Judgment, if he has acted perversely, they never publicly Excommunicate, unless perhaps he has perpetrated a crime of the sort committed by Jeroboam, Son of Nebat, and his associates. But when he has committed some other sin, they are accustomed to* **FLOG HIM PRIVATELY**, *and so also the matter stands...*

...even to the Scribes and Elders themselves, yet with no one excommunicating him? And for what reason, I ask? Certainly, one would not rashly offer any other reason than that they regarded Christ as a Sage <note>The Latin *Sapiens* here refers to a 'Hakham' or a scholar of the law.</note> of the highest renown, one who, among them, was not to be rashly excommunicated. Nor is it difficult to investigate from where that custom originated among them. At every age, the Jewish nation held itself in high regard—both because of the privileges it had specifically obtained from God and because it was subject to the common contempt of others—and for that reason, they covered up the crimes of their fellow tribesmen before the Gentiles <note>The term 'Gentiles' here specifically refers to the non-Jewish Roman authorities.</note> with the greatest zeal. This was especially done during that time when the Romans had occupied their land. Since the Romans lived in the midst of the Jews, they were able to perceive both political and ecclesiastical matters quite accurately. 

Certainly, when the Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> go to give a reason for the cessation of the Great Sanhedrin <note>The supreme judicial council of the Jews.</note> before the subversion of the Republic, they do not trace it to a prohibition of capital cases by the Romans, but to the multitude of murderers; so much so that the Sanhedrin judged it did not suit the dignity of the nation to inquire into the most foul deeds of all in the presence of the Romans. This was primarily because they came there unwillingly to condemn an Israelite to death, as that was most clear from their laws. 

Thus, they also seem to have avoided excommunication as much as possible, lest they incur the reproach of the Gentiles. But the common order of the Rabbis intervened to prevent this from happening to a Sage. For they believed that all the glory of Wisdom and the luster of the Rabbinate would perish if any illustrious Doctor were excommunicated for his own actions. Yet if extreme necessity perhaps demanded it, they did it with such an appearance as to entirely preserve the honor of their order. This is established in the Babylonian Gemara <note>The component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis and commentary.</note> 

<margin>Moed Katon, folio 17, column 1.</margin>
from the example of *Mar Zutra* <note>A prominent 5th-century Babylonian Jewish scholar.</note>, preserved by various followers of this science, who excommunicated himself before he excommunicated a junior Sage: <note>original Hebrew: זוטרא חסידא כי מחייב בר מ רבנן שמתא ברישא משמית נפשיה והדר משמת ליה כי הוה עייל באושפיזא שרי ליה לנפשיה והדר שרי לדידיה אמר ר׳ גידל תלמיד חכם מנדה לעצμο ומותר לעצμο</note> **Mar Zutra the Pious, whenever any distinguished man among the Sages was to be excommunicated according to the merit of his sin, would excommunicate himself first; then he would excommunicate him. Rabbi Giddal said: A disciple of the wise may excommunicate himself and release himself.** *Mar Zutra the Saint*, as often as any of the more distinguished Sages was to be excommunicated by merit of sin, [he placed] himself first...

### CHAPTER II. OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH. 781

...excommunicated him and afterwards [absolved] him. *Returning thereafter to his home, he first absolved himself, and afterwards absolved the other.* For even Rabbi Gidel said: *A learned man <note>original: "Vir Doctus," likely referring to a Talmid Hakham or Torah scholar</note> may excommunicate himself, and also absolve himself.* Therefore, Christ, as a distinguished Sage <note>original: "Sapiens"</note> and a Teacher of the greatest reputation among the Jews, was not to be excommunicated for these same reasons. We do indeed read in the Book of Sanhedrin, in the Venetian Edition, a story of Jesus the Nazarene being excommunicated by four hundred trumpets by his Teacher. But who does not know that this was concocted out of envy and hatred by later Jews, since they had nothing they could charge against Christ? The Gospel histories clearly teach us that Christ the Lord taught in the synagogues and public places right up to the days destined for his passion—something that could not take place for an excommunicated person. Regarding the disciples of Christ, consider what should be thought. Christ had predicted their expulsion from the synagogue in the Gospel of John: 

<margin>Chapter 16, 2.</margin>
*they will make you outcasts from the synagogues* <note>original Greek: ἀποσυναγώγους ποιήσωσιν ὑμᾶς</note>; yet in the history of the following times, we do not read in express words that such an excommunication took place, except that as time went on, the Church separated itself from the Jewish community. 

<margin>Acts 5, 40.</margin>
We understand that the Apostles and Disciples of Christ were flogged, beaten, sent to prison, suffered persecution, were killed, and stoned, but it is not recorded in so many words that they were "excommunicated." Indeed, in the entire history of the New Testament, we do not read of anyone else being excommunicated except for that blind man whom Christ had healed, 

<margin>John 9, 34.</margin>
of whom it is said: *they cast him out* <note>original Greek: ἐξέβαλον αὐτὸν ἔξω</note>, a phrase which is consistently understood to signify excommunication. And this very fact, which is narrated here concerning the blind man, strongly confirms our earlier opinion. For as much as one may gather from this history, it seems this blind man was a person of more humble fortune, <gloss>from the people</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: מעם (*mi-am*)</note>, <term>people of the land</term> <note>original Hebrew: עם הארץ (*am ha-aretz*); a term used by the Jewish elite to describe the unlearned or common folk</note>, regarding whose excommunication they were not so concerned as they were regarding the excommunication of Christ and the Apostles, who were celebrated for the praise of their wisdom, virtues, and miracles, and who were very influential by grace of their teaching. Rightly, therefore, Christ says, *they are to be flogged in the synagogues.* Especially if we maintain that <term>Flogging</term> alone was practiced in the land of Canaan, while Excommunication was practiced outside the land—that is, in Babylonia—or, what is more true, Floggings.

# Chapter XII.

*The discussion on the duties of the Synagogue Rulers <note>Archisynagogi</note> moves to the third act of their governance, namely the CARE OF ALMS. Before reaching that point, however, two very noble questions are discussed and settled: why Alms among the Jews are called <term>Tzedakah</term>, meaning JUSTICE; and how much difference there is between this <term>Tzedakah</term> and another duty of piety and charity, which among them is designated by the name <term>Gemilut Hasadim</term>, meaning liberal Beneficence or acts of loving-kindness. Both questions are handled in such a way that many notable sayings of Holy Scripture are brought to light. Indeed, it is proven that almost every work of Christ was, and the work of Christians ought to be, <term>Gemilut Hasadim</term>.*

WE pass now to the third Act of Synagogue Governance, which concerns Alms; the supreme power of distributing these resided with the rulers. It is a pleasure in this dissertation to bind ourselves to the following order: 1. That we may first say something in general about the true meaning of the terms <term>Tzedakah</term> and <term>Gemilut Hasadim</term>, which are frequently used in the writings of the Jews when they distinguish between Alms and other duties of charity. 2. We shall prove that the supreme care of Alms, or the power of distributing them, was entrusted to the Synagogue Rulers. 3. We shall compare the Elders, or Bishops of the Church, with the Synagogue Rulers in this regard.

...than in all other *Affirmative* precepts. <note>The "Affirmative" or positive commandments are those that require a specific action to be performed.</note> Yet the reason for this naming is not immediately apparent. Two points deserve to be weighed in this discourse by that most Learned Man before we examine the actual reason for the comparison of these two words, *Justice* and *Alms*. First, that he asserts the word <term>Tzedakah</term> is never taken for *Alms* in the Scriptures; second, that he writes this name was only assigned to *Alms* at the time when the Talmudic regulations were organized into order after the destruction of Jerusalem. For so I understand his mind, and what follows forbids me from understanding it otherwise: *Maimonides speaks as if this meaning of the word were not only received among the* **RECENT JEWS**, *but even that the same was in primary and ancient use.* Prideaux clearly feels that this use of the word only became prevalent after the destruction of Jerusalem, when the Talmudic regulations began to be compiled. It is surprising, however, that it did not occur to the Learned Man that this word <term>Tzedakah</term> was already received in familiar and frequent common speech for *Alms* in the age of Christ the Lord.

...treasures of gold and silver, because justice delivers from death. <note>original Latin: *justitia liberat a morte*. But it overcomes every objection that the <term>LXX</term> <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> sometimes translated the word <term>Tzedakah</term> <note>original Hebrew: צדקה, which usually means "righteousness" or "justice."</note>—both in the Mosaic Law and in the other writings of the Old Testament—as *mercy* <note>original Greek: ἐλεημοσύνη (*eleemosyne*).</note>, to be exercised by God; and indeed as *mercy* in the true sense of **Almsgiving**, as it is now understood by us, namely for a **gift** bestowed upon the poor out of compassion. Let us bring forth one or two examples. Thus it is in Deuteronomy, in the laws concerning a pledge:
<margin>Chapter 24, 13.</margin>
*You shall surely return the pledge to him (your poor brother) about the setting of the sun, and he shall sleep in his garment and bless you:* **and it shall be righteousness for you before the Lord your God.** <note>original Hebrew: ולך תהיה צדקה לפני יהוה אלהיך (*ve-lekha tihyeh tzedakah lifnei Adonai Elohekha*).</note> The Septuagint renders this: **And it shall be alms for you before the Lord your God.** <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἔσται σοι ἐλεημοσύνη ἐνάντιον κυρίου τοῦ Θεοῦ σου.</note> For my part, I would have rendered this place better: *And it shall be a righteous deed for you before the Lord.* <note>original Greek: δικαίωμα (*dikaioma*), suggesting a legal standing or justification.</note> It is nevertheless sufficiently clear from this specimen how deeply that notation of the word *Tzedakah*—by which it is taken for **mercy**—clung to the translators. The following are also of that same kind:
<margin>Psalm 24, 5.</margin>
From the Psalms: **He shall receive righteousness from the God of his salvation.** <note>original Hebrew: ישא צדקה מאלהי ישעו (*yissa tzedakah me-Elohei yisho*).</note> The Greek says: **He shall receive mercy from God his Savior.** <note>original Greek: Λήψεται ἐλεημοσύνην παρὰ Θεοῦ σωτῆρος αὐτοῦ.</note>
<margin>Psalm 33, 5.</margin>
Again: **He loves righteousness and judgment.** <note>original Hebrew: אוהב צדקה ומשפט (*ohev tzedakah u-mishpat*).</note> The Greek: **He loves mercy and judgment.** <note>original Greek: 'Αγαπᾷ ἐλεημοσύνην καὶ κρίσιν.</note>
<margin>Chapter 59, 16.</margin>
From Isaiah: **And his righteousness, it supported him.** <note>original Hebrew: וצדקתו היא סמכתהו (*ve-tzedakato hi samkhat-hu*).</note> The Greek: **And by mercy he was supported.** <note>original Greek: Καὶ τῇ ἐλεημοσύνῃ ἐστηρίσατο.</note>
<margin>Daniel 4, 24.</margin>
Indeed, in Daniel, they translated this word specifically as a gift of mercy to be conferred upon the poor: **Redeem your sins through righteousness.** <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: חטיך בצדקה פרק (*hatayakh be-tzedakah perok*).</note> The Greek: **Redeem your sins through almsgiving.** <note>original Greek: τὰς ἁμαρτίας σου ἐν ἐλεημοσύναις λύτρωσαι.</note>
And thus it has been sufficiently proved that this meaning of the word *Tzedakah* did not first arise in the Schools of the <term>Talmudists</term> <note>The ancient Jewish rabbis who compiled the Talmud.</note>, but was already accepted in use among the Jews before the birth of Christ the Lord. Whether it was done correctly and in keeping with the nature of the word or the Biblical style (which we observed Prideaux denied) we shall soon see.

But what is the reason for this meaning? For since a **charitable gift** <note>original Latin: *stips*</note> is usually paid to the poor out of **mercy**—whence it is called *eleemosyne* among the Greeks—and since **justice**, strictly taken, is many times opposed to mercy, what is the underlying reason that the name **Tzedakah**, or **Justice**, was bestowed upon **Almsgiving**? We have certainly noticed that learned men find this difficulty...

<header>CHAPTER 12. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.</header>

...are bound; for they are not entirely free from ambiguity or obscurity, because those authors do not explain the force of the word *Justice*, and how much it differs from kindness or benevolence. Let us therefore discuss this a little more clearly and distinctly, so that we may finally arrive at the true reason for this naming.

*Justice* is not badly defined by the Philosophers as a virtue, or a habit of the Will, by which one grants each person their *Right* <note>original Latin: *Jus*</note>. But truly that *Right*, unless I am mistaken, can be considered in two ways: it is either taken *strictly* for a *Right* which is prescribed and defined by the Laws of each City or Society; or, under the name of *Right*, is broadly included every duty to which equity and reason bind us to perform <margin>On the Law of War and Peace, book 1, chapter 1, §10.</margin>, even if by chance it is not expressed in the Laws of the Society; or, as Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a Dutch jurist whose works laid the foundations for international law based on natural law.</note> puts it, *every dictate of right reason*. According to this twofold acceptance of *Right*, *Justice* likewise denotes either that habit of the human mind by which it strictly conforms to the Laws of Society, giving each citizen of the Commonwealth his due according to what has been established—or, in the Pauline phrase <margin>Romans 13:7.</margin> *render to all their dues: taxes to whom taxes are due, custom to whom custom, fear to whom fear, honor to whom honor* <note>original Greek: ἀπόδοτε πᾶσι τὰς ὀφειλάς· τῷ τὸν φόρον τὸν φόρον· τῷ τὸ τέλος, τὸ τέλος· τῷ τὸν φόβον τὸν φόβον· τῷ τὴν τιμήν, τὴν τιμήν</note>; or *Justice* will denote more loosely and generally that virtue or disposition of the will by which a person obeys all the dictates of right reason and *natural* equity, and especially carefully arranges all their actions toward their neighbor according to the rules of common equity. 

By the Laws of Society, each person's right is narrowly and strictly defined. But it often happens that if someone interprets that right just as *strictly* in all circumstances, they may do an injury to another; whence, if I am not mistaken, arose that saying: *The highest right is the highest injury* <note>original Latin: *Summum jus, summa injuria*. This legal maxim warns that the law, when pushed to its extreme and without the tempering of equity, can become a tool of injustice.</note>. Opposed to this *strict right* and narrow interpretation of law is *equity*; or, opposed to that cunning and crafty law—as Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman statesman and orator.</note> puts it <margin>For Caecina.</margin>—is *the equitable and the good*. This is right reason, imbued with perfect love for one's neighbor, and interpreting that *Civil Right* in favor of the neighbor as much as can be consistent with one's own safety and that of the entire Commonwealth—interpreting a right which, if explained cunningly and craftily, would result in harm to the neighbor, or from which at least no benefit would ever flow to the neighbor. This *equity* of mind, or the will to exercise that equity of mind toward another with a demonstration of sincere love for them, is often called, according to the style of Scripture...

...is called <term>Tzedakah</term> <note>Hebrew: צדקה; traditionally translated as "righteousness" or "justice," but frequently used in post-biblical Hebrew to mean "almsgiving."</note>, **Justice**. Indeed, **Justice** is also used [in this sense] by Latin authors; which is entirely useful to observe for a genuine understanding both of the matter we are now discussing and of other texts of Holy Scripture. For, to come closer to the point, **Almsgiving** is not given to the poor out of that strict Civil Law—for we are not concerned here with Alms commanded by the Governors of a State, but only those bestowed upon the needy out of liberality—the observance of which makes a Citizen of the Republic <term>politically just</term> <note>original Greek: πολιτικῶς δίκαιον; referring to one who obeys the specific laws of a city-state</note>, and which is so often called <term>justice</term> <note>original Greek: δικαιοσύνη</note>. Instead, it is bestowed out of **equity**—that is, that virtue of the mind by which one grants to another as much as right reason, combined with a most broadly expressed love for the other, suggests. And for this reason I believe **Almsgiving** was called <term>Tzedakah</term> (**Justice**) among the Hebrews. For although that mental **equity** or **equanimity** may perhaps be demonstrated in many other acts of human life, in no act of man is there so clear and obvious a demonstration of a fair, upright, and virtue-loving mind as in a work of charity—or of equity and **Justice**, to speak now with the Hebrews—by which Alms are distributed to the needy. # CHAPTER 12. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

...observed regarding this use of the word <term>Tzedakah</term> <note>Hebrew: צדקה; usually "righteousness," but here argued to mean "liberality" or "abundance"</note> are worthy of the closest attention. Certainly, "sow for righteousness" in Hosea means *to sow generously and abundantly*, just as "reap according to mercy" <note>Hebrew: חסד (Chesed)</note> means *to reap generously and abundantly*; and in that same place, the phrase "rain for righteousness" <note>Hebrew: מורה לצדקה (Moreh l'Tzedakah)</note> denotes *copious rains*. Likewise, "rain for righteousness" in Joel is excellently rendered by him as *rain after a copious sowing, or rain that suffices abundantly.* The common translation of that phrase as *Teacher of Justice* is indeed pious and consistent with the <note>original: "τῇ ἀναλογίᾳ τῆς πίστεως" (tē analogia tēs pisteōs)</note> **analogy of faith**, but it does not satisfy the spirit of the language and the circumstances of this text as well as that Drusian interpretation does. Yet, by this we in no way deny that either this passage should be understood as referring to **Christ the Lord**, or to the **Doctrine of Christ and the Apostles**; for what is more familiar and better known in the style of Scripture than comparing the instructions of Teachers to *rains*? But as for the fact that <term>Tzedakah</term> in these two places denotes something *large, copious, and abundant*, it must undoubtedly be traced back to this: that among men it signifies that *virtue*, or the exercise of that virtue, by which they satisfy their neighbor in all duties of human charity prescribed by the Law, according to the *fairest and most generous* interpretation of that Law. The remaining passages, excerpted in the margin from the commentaries of learned men, we leave to the reader’s own consideration, because to re-examine each of these texts and build our hypothesis from there with arguments would bring weariness to the reader. Let us at least be allowed to add from our own records this remarkable sentiment of **Solomon**, preserved in the **Proverbs**, where the word <term>Tzedakah</term> seems to be taken in exactly the same sense.

<margin>Proverbs 21:21.</margin>
The words are: <note>Hebrew: רדף צדקה וחסד ימצא חיים צדקה וכבוד (Rodeph tzedakah v'chesed yimtza chayim tzedakah v'kavod)</note> *He who pursues* **JUSTICE** *and the study of the good, shall find life*, **JUSTICE**, *and honor*. The word <term>Tzedakah</term> is joined here, as in other places, with the word <term>Chesed</term> <note>Hebrew: חסד; loving-kindness or mercy</note>, and therefore seems entirely to denote something related to *mercy*. If, however, you interpret <term>Tzedakah</term> here as *strict right* <note>original: "jus arctum"; legalistic justice</note>, then it would be opposed to *mercy*. Therefore, reason suggests that it be explained in this place as the exercise of natural equity according to its most generous interpretation: the effect of which equity is **beneficence** toward others. Nor do I doubt that the word <term>Dikaiosyne</term> <note>Greek: δικαιοσύνη; righteousness or justice</note> is attributed to God with this meaning in the first Epistle of John, in these words:

<margin>1 John 1:9.</margin>
> *If we confess our sins*, <note>original: "πιστός ἐσι καὶ δίκαιος, ἵνα ἀφῇ ἡμῖν τὰς ἁμαρτίας"</note> **He is faithful and Just, to forgive us our sins**.

Whatever to this...

# ON THE OFFICES OF PREFECTS, BOOK III, PART

Regardless of what the Commentators say about this passage, it is clear to me that the interpretation of the word **Justice** <note>original: "Justitiæ"</note> best fits that which I explained quite extensively above and confirmed with subsequent examples. Indeed, God remits the sins of the believing and repentant person by **right** and **justice** <note>original: "jure & justitia"</note> because of the obedience of Christ the Lord; nevertheless, the **Justice of God**, which we consider as the virtue of pursuing His own glory through the punishment of sin—even in Christ the Lord Himself as the Surety <note>original: "Sponsore"</note> for the sinner—is by no means among the "impulsive causes," as they call them, for pardoning sin. Rather, it is the **highest equity** <note>original: "summa æquitas"</note> of God, if I may put it that way, demonstrated in the most kind governance of the sinner. God now exercises this **equity** most justly, without any detriment to His glory, following the passion and obedience of Christ the Lord. In this way, the healthy sense of the passage remains firm.

<margin>
Book 5 of *On the Ends of Good and Evil* <note>Cicero’s *De Finibus*</note>.
</margin>
We must not overlook what we mentioned before: that among Latin authors themselves, the word **JUSTICE** was accepted with a similar meaning. What is clearer than the words of Cicero describing Justice? **Justice**, he says, **is a habit of the mind, preserved for the common utility, giving to each his own, and GENEROUSLY AND EQUITABLY GUARDING THE FELLOWSHIP AND UNION OF HUMANITY.** What does **Justice** have in common with **generosity** <note>original: "munificentia"</note> unless **Justice** denotes that virtue by which one exercises natural equity to the highest degree or, in Cicero’s phrase, **generously**? Indeed, this meaning of **Justice** is manifest here in Terence:

<margin>
*The Self-Tormentor* <note>Heauton Timorumenos</note>, Act 4, Scene 1, line 33.
</margin>

->Now I beseech you,<-
->As your mind is more mature by age and more forgiving,<-
->That my folly may find some protection in your **JUSTICE**.<-

<margin>
In *Aristides*, chapter 2. Sallust, chapter 9. Fabricius on the word *Equity*. Bos on Nepos regarding this same word.
</margin>
And thus, it has long been observed by students of the **Latin Language** that **Justice** is used for **equity**, and for that which is the companion and effect of equity—**clemency** <note>original: "clementia"</note>—provided it is just and consistent with reason, by Nepos and Sallust.

Now, indeed, no doubt remains in my mind why, metonymically <note>original: "μετωνυμικῶς"; a figure of speech where a concept is called by the name of something associated with it</note>, the word **Justice** <note>original: "צדקה" (Tzedakah)</note> is used first for the virtue or act by which one gives alms to the poor, and then for the **gift** itself bestowed upon the poor. For since that common virtue which we distinguish by the name of **equity** is demonstrated by no other act so clearly (as we have already warned above) as by this very act in which one shows oneself generous to the poor, it is not surprising that this usage prevailed among the Hebrews and Chaldeans...

This justice is said to *remain forever*, which means that the fruit of this pious action will endure for all eternity.

However, it is not only the *act* itself by which one helps the poor, but also that very *gift* (the very sign of equity) which is bestowed upon the poor by that act, which is thereafter <term>μετωνυμικῶς</term> <note>metonymically; using the name of one thing for that of another associated with it</note> called <term>צדקה</term> <note>Tzedakah: Justice/Charity</note>, and from there among the Greeks, <term>ἐλεημοσύνη</term> <note>eleemosyne: almsgiving or mercy</note>. # CHAPTER 12. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

...kindness toward one who is indeed worthy of a benefit, but not to such a great extent. And it is in this sense especially that he <note>Referring to Maimonides, the 12th-century Jewish philosopher mentioned on the previous page</note> contends this word should be understood when it is attributed to God in the Scriptures.

<margin>Psalm 89:9, Exodus 34:6.</margin>
There is no reason for us to strongly resist Maimonides. *Chesed* <term>Hebrew: חסד; usually translated as "loving-kindness" or "steadfast love"</term> generally denotes an intense, fervent, devoted, and overflowing zeal or deed; and thus, it is applied in Holy Scripture both to the *will* and the *exercise* of overflowing kindness—God's toward humans and humans' toward one another—the kind of *zeal or deed* otherwise called *grace* <term>Greek: χάρις; charis</term>. Indeed, every *overflowing zeal* of a human toward God, by which one clearly shows themselves most intent on promoting Divine Glory, is referred to by this very word *Chesed*. But it is most frequently and familiarly used in the former sense, where it signifies the *exercise of unmerited and overflowing kindness from God to humans, and from humans to one another*; and it is this very meaning that serves us best now.

### CHAPTER 12. OF THE SYNAGOGUES AND THE CHURCHES.

...he was obligated. Specifically, of his own accord, without waiting for the Judge's sentence. And I certainly noticed that both Louis de Dieu and Buxtorf favor this interpretation of Fagius. <margin>On Psalm 4:4.</margin> De Dieu translates the words of Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a prominent medieval Jewish biblical commentator and grammarian.</note>, described above, thus: a <term>Chasid</term> <note>Hebrew: חסיד; a pious or beneficent person who goes beyond what is required.</note> is said to be one who practices beneficence toward his neighbor BEFORE HE OWES IT BY LAW. <margin>In the Lexicon at the word <term>Shurah</term> <note>Hebrew: שורה; meaning a line or row.</note>.</margin> Buxtorf [writes], "He is holy who acts BEFOREHAND, OUTSIDE THE LINE or ORDER OF JUDGMENT." That is, he adds, one who acts well of his own will, before the Judge decrees it and imposes such action upon him; for those who do well only because they are forced are not truly pious or holy. They therefore took the word <term>Lifnim</term> <note>Hebrew: לפנים; often meaning "before" or "within."</note> as if it were vocalized as <term>Lifnim</term> <note>Hebrew: לִפְנִים</note>, and rendered it as *beforehand*. Against this version of Fagius, Nicholas Fuller <note>An English orientalist and philologist.</note> offers this critique: He (Fagius) took those words as if it were written <term>Before the measure of judgment</term> <note>Original Hebrew: לפני משורת הדין</note>, that is, BEFORE THE MEASURE OF JUDGMENT, namely, before the Judge's sentence has been passed; whereas the uncorrupted and genuine way of writing and reading it is this: <term>Beyond the line of the law</term> <note>Original Hebrew: לפנים משורת הדין</note>, that is, BEYOND THE LINE OF THE JUDGMENT or THE LAW itself. This is correct, if I am any judge. 

Moreover, if the word <term>Lifnim</term> <note>The author uses a Greek article "τὸ" with the Hebrew word.</note> were translated here as *beforehand*, as Buxtorf proposed, how forced and unusual is this expression: *beforehand, outside the line of the law*? And furthermore, I ask you, how can this translation be adapted to other places where this phrase is used, such as when Rabbi Ishmael in the tractate *Berakhot* <note>A volume of the Talmud dealing with blessings and prayers.</note> prays to God that He might act kindly with His people, <margin>See the famous Cocceius in the place cited.</margin> <term>and enter with them beyond the line of the law</term> <note>Hebrew: והכנס להם לפנים משורת הדין; a prayer for God to treat people with mercy rather than strict justice.</note>. Certainly, the word *Lifnim* is not only completely redundant in this version but also disturbs the elegance of the entire phrase. Nor indeed is the famous Buxtorf consistent with himself here, or the son with the father. For in the *Smaller Rabbinic Lexicon*, he had equipped the Hebrew phrase with these vowel points: <term>Lifnim mishurat hadin</term> <note>Hebrew: לִפְנִים מִשּׁוּרַת הַדִּין</note>, and had rendered it much as the famous Cocceius later did: *Within the measure of Judgment*. 

But these vowel points on the word <term>Mishurah</term> <note>Hebrew: משורה; referring to a measure.</note> are undoubtedly false; for the word <term>Mishurat</term> here is not to be considered as a simple construct form derived from <term>Shur</term> <note>Hebrew: שור; wall or line.</note> with the vowel point on the left horn of the letter *Shin* [making it an 's' sound], but rather a composite of the prefix <term>Min</term> [meaning "from"] and the word <term>Shurah</term> [line] with the point on the right [making it a 'sh' sound]. What then? Nothing remains for me to think or say except that the word <term>Lifnim</term>, which I believe should be vocalized as <term>Lifnim</term> <note>Hebrew: לִפְנִים</note> (for whether the word <term>Lifnim</term> ever occurs elsewhere in this construction to mean *within* is unknown to me), should be rendered in Latin as either *by all means* or *outwardly*, along with Fuller (and it could easily be shown, if it were worth the effort, that both translations suit this word well enough), and that the letter <term>M</term> in the word <term>Mishurat</term>...

...[hamar]toloi <note>original: "τωλοὶ"; the end of the Greek word for "sinners."</note> SINNERS, Christ died for us. This is an extraordinary force of discourse. Paul distinguishes all men, however many there may be, into three classes: SINNERS, the JUST, and the GOOD. He calls those "Sinners" who, by their life and habits, overstep the boundaries of Divine Law; the "Just" are those who fulfill the Law prescribed for them, not entirely neglecting the principle of equity; but the "Good" are those who do good to others far beyond the dictates and rules of the Written Law or even common equity. Concerning this distinction between Justice and Goodness, we shall speak more clearly in its proper place below. And this accurately agrees with what is found in the *Pirke Avoth* <note>original: "Pirke Avoth," the "Ethics of the Fathers," a compilation of ethical teachings from the Mishnaic period.</note>: *He who says, "What is mine is yours, and what is yours is yours,"* <note>original: האומר שלי שלך ושלך שלך</note> is called a <term>Chasid</term> <note>Hebrew: חסיד; a pious man or one who practices loving-kindness.</note>.
