<meta>This page continues the investigation into the Jewish concept of "Gemilut Hasadim" (acts of loving-kindness), specifically contrasting it with "Tzedakah" (charity or alms) based on the Talmudic tractate Sukkah and Pauline theology.</meta>

### ON THE DUTIES OF PREFECTS BOOK III.

...I BESTOWED MANY ACTS OF KINDNESS UPON ALL MY BROTHERS, *and my people, and the entire multitude of captives who were led away with me into exile to the land of Assyria, to Nineveh.* <note>original Latin: *multas contuli benignitates*; this is a quotation from the Book of Tobit 1:3/1:16, describing Tobit's secret acts of charity and burial of the dead.</note> Indeed, regarding how much <term>Gemilut Hasadim</term> <note>Hebrew: "the bestowing of acts of kindness"</note> differs from <term>Tzedakah</term> <note>Hebrew: "righteousness," commonly used to mean charity or alms</note> or *Almsgiving*, it is carefully handed down by the Jews <margin>Folio 49, column 2. See Fagius's Commentary on Pirkei Avot chapter 1, section 2, and Wagenfeil's Notes on the Excerpts of the Gemara Sotah, chapter 1, section 52, page 343.</margin> in the Tractate *Sukkah*, the summary of which—since it has already been described by others—we shall provide here:

1. *Almsgiving* consists only of money, but *Beneficence* encompasses every kind of duty.
2. *Almsgiving* is performed only for the poor, but *Beneficence* is shown to both the poor and the rich.
3. *Almsgiving* has a place only among the living, but *Beneficence* regards both the living and the dead <note>This refers to the "true kindness" of burying the deceased, an act for which no repayment can be expected.</note>.

These points are indeed correct; however, not every difficulty is yet removed. We established in the preceding pages that *Almsgiving* is called *Justice* by the Jews because *Justice*—that is, natural equity—commands that the poor be helped. Yet, in those points we brought forward to explain <term>Gemilut Hasadim</term>, it was observed that through <term>Gemilut Hasadim</term> there come those duties of benevolence which one is not obligated by any law to observe; and yet *Almsgiving* is referred to <term>Gemilut Hasadim</term> just as much as it is to <term>Tzedakah</term>. These things seem not to be entirely consistent with one another.

But I respond briefly: the boundaries of equity and benevolence are not very strictly defined or circumscribed. Therefore, there is no reason to wonder why men often ascribe the same act sometimes to *equity* (that is, *justice*) and sometimes to *benevolence*. For *Equity*, insofar as it relates to strict law, is called *kindness*; but when relating to broad law, it is called *Justice*.

From this, however, can it not also be said in a sound sense that although the broad and abundant exercise of *Almsgiving* should be referred to <term>Gemilut Hasadim</term> (to which no human is bound by any legal right), nevertheless, *Almsgiving*—when it is simply distributed by someone according to their means for the necessary support of the poor—is properly called <term>Tzedakah</term>? The former truly belongs to *liberal benevolence*, while the latter belongs to *equity and Justice*; although I would not deny that these two approach each other very closely. This is why they are often joined together among the Jews, except that the exercise of <term>Gemilut Hasadim</term> is held to be more excellent and noble than that of <term>Tzedakah</term>.

And to speak plainly, I believe we should also include here the fact that our Lord attended and celebrated the wedding at Cana in Galilee. Jesus was invited there with his disciples, as we read in the history. But what business had my Lord in the solemn celebration of a wedding, where many lighthearted things and many follies were usually committed—even if we have passed over what happened there in silence? I myself reflect on it this way: that the Lord Christ was here exercising <term>Gemilut Hasadim</term>—an office of piety, I say, which was held in high honor among the people of that age. The portion of land in Canaan was sufficient for a family's support; however, because many people lack the industry and prudence to maintain themselves in their current state, and since the Israelites were not forbidden from alienating <note>selling or transferring ownership</note> their goods and possessions (though they were to be restored in the **Jubilee** <note>The Jubilee was a year of release every 50 years when, according to Mosaic law, alienated lands were returned to their original owners and debts were forgiven</note>), poverty and want—great evils—could no more be avoided in their State than in other Republics. Therefore, the most wise Legislator <note>referring to God or Moses</note> ensured that nothing would be lacking for his State in this regard, prescribing effective remedies in his Laws against this evil. These remedies were of two kinds: either **fixed and established by law**, or **voluntary**; both are reviewed and declared by **Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note> in his *Treatise on Gifts to the Poor*.

Indeed, such a strict accounting of these Alms was subsequently held that Israelites who were negligent in this equity or *charity* were warned by the Magistrate or the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme judicial council of the ancient Jewish people</note> with **lashes of rebellion** <note>original Latin: verberibus rebellionis; a disciplinary punishment used for those who refused to follow a rabbinical command</note> for this neglect of their duty, as Maimonides again testifies.

The **Alms**, however, which are collected by the Jewish *Churches* <note>The author uses "Ecclesiis" (Churches) here to refer to organized Jewish congregations in the diaspora</note> in exile outside the land of Canaan, or which are cast into the *Alms Chests*, are of two kinds, according to their two uses: namely, those destined for sustaining the *poor of the land* of Canaan, or those for the relief of the poverty of the individual poor of *those specific Churches*. As for what concerns the **Alms of the Dish** <term>original Latin: Catini; referring to the *Tamchui*, a communal bowl or vessel used to collect food or donations for immediate distribution to the wandering poor</term>, as they are called among the Jews (consisting not only of money, but of all kinds of food collected in a *dish* and distributed to the poor arriving from anywhere), these were not accepted in all places and are considered by the Jews themselves to be of a different category, as we have discussed in previous sections. To these two types of *Alms* correspond **two small Chests**, located in the Synagogues (as I mentioned before) and distinguished by their own inscriptions.

<margin>Jerome's Letters, book 2, folio 45, col. 4.</margin>
1. Vigilantius had criticized the custom of sending *money to the land of Canaan* for the holy poor who lived there in significant numbers for the sake of Religion, among whom was Jerome himself. Jerome was ready to bring forward in defense of that ritual the examples of the Apostolic age, the memory of which is preserved both in the Acts of the Apostles and in the Pauline Epistles. When he had done so, he continued thus:

> *It would be a long task now if I wished to go through all the testimonies from all his (Paul's) epistles, in which he deals with this and hastens with his whole mind that to Jerusalem and to the holy places...*

### CHAPTER 13. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

This seems to draw its origin partly from piety and affection toward the land of Canaan—which the Jews of the *Diaspora* <note>original: "τῆς διασποרᾶς" — the dispersion of Jews outside the ancestral Land of Israel</note> could declare by no surer argument—and partly from the Statutes of the Scribes. ### CHAPTER 13. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

...it would be permitted, *that Paul, by the same institution while the Sabbath was still in force, ordered the Corinthians to defer their collections to the following day, which was the first day of the week. By this very act, he considered that first day not as a feast, but as a workday <note>original Greek: "εργασίμον" (ergasimon) — a day on which it is lawful to work</note>, and therefore the opposite of a feast, and destined for the work of the collection.* I approve of the first and more important part of this observation: that Paul, in relation to Jewish custom, wanted the Alms <note>original: "Eleemosynas" — charitable gifts</note> to be set aside not on the Sabbath—which was undoubtedly still observed by the Corinthians—but on the first day of the week. In Paul’s words, you will find nothing except concerning the *setting aside of money*, nor do I think Paul intended anything else.

<margin>1 Corinthians 16:2.</margin>
> *On the first day of the week,* he says, *let each of you* SET ASIDE BY HIMSELF, STORING UP (accumulating) *whatever he has prospered, so that when I come, no computations, or collections, may then be made.* <note>original Greek: "Κατὰ μίαν σαββάτων... ἕκαστος ὑμῶν παρ’ ἑαυτῷ τιθέτω, θησαυρίζων ὅ, τι ἂν εὐοδῶται˙ ἵνα μὴ ὅταν ἔλθω, τότε λογίαι γίνωνται"</note>

Paul is speaking about money to be set aside by individuals in private, and gathered into some private treasury; not about a collection to be established in the Church. To be sure, the word *collections* <note>original: "λογίαι" (logiai)</note> is usually interpreted in this sense, as if it noted *gatherings* to be established in the Church; but its meaning is obscure because it is found only in this context (twice, in fact) and nowhere else in Scripture. If it is to be translated as *collection*, as Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin</note> insists, then in this place it will denote that very *collecting* of money which private individuals performed when they added some sum of coins to the total every week, and thus made a kind of *gathering of coins* (*a treasury, or a heap*, according to Paul). Nevertheless, it does not seem absurd to us to translate *the collection* <note>original: "τὴν λογίαν" (tēn logian)</note> as *financial accounts or computations*, in the sense that *account* <note>original: "λόγος" (logos)</note> is used by Paul in

his *Epistle to the Philippenses*. <margin>Book 2. chapter 8. See Maimonides, chapter 9. § 1.</margin> 
It must be known, however, that while the Alms were in the power of the *Collectors*, the supreme power of distributing them nevertheless resided with the <term>Beit Din <note>original Hebrew: בית דין — "House of Judgment," the local judicial and ecclesiastical senate</note></term>, or the *Supreme Judicial and Ecclesiastical Senate* of each place. You may see this in the writings of the same Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent Jewish philosopher and jurist whose legal code, the Mishneh Torah, is cited here.</note>, or even (which is our primary consideration now) in the hands of the *Doctor of highest authority*, to whom the care of the Synagogue’s sacred matters is committed. 

<margin>In the mentioned Treatise, chapter 7. § 10.</margin>
This person represents in his own person (as we suggested before) the *Ecclesiastical Senate*; I mean to say, the power lies with the *Prefect of the Synagogue*. It is easy, in turn, to prove this from that same *Treatise* of Maimonides, in three places where he explicitly mentions it.

<margin>Chapter 6. § 17.</margin>
Maimonides had said that it is not permitted for someone to distribute the tithes of the poor as general *Alms*; however, he soon restricts this as follows: <gloss>And if he were a great sage, he may give it to the 'Doctor of the City' as a favor,</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: ואם היה חכם גדול, אותו לחבר עיר בטובת הנאה</note> *They give those to the* DOCTOR OF THE CITY (so called, it seems, based on the opinion of Nathan, because on account of his supreme authority, everyone *gathers to him*; whether this is correct, I will not dispute now) so that they might receive some grace from it. The Tithes were to be handed over to the *Doctor of the City* to be distributed and paid out, unless I am mistaken. 

Afterward, again, dealing with the use of *Alms* imposed upon merchants: 
<margin>Chapter 7. § 14.</margin>
<gloss>But if a 'Doctor of the City' is there, they shall give it to the 'Doctor of the City,' and he shall divide it as it seems best to him.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: ויש שם חבר עיר יתנה לחבר עיר, והוא מחלקה כמו שיראה לו</note> *If indeed the* DOCTOR *of the City is there, they shall hand those (Alms) over to the Doctor of the City, who shall distribute them as he sees fit.*

### CHAPTER 13. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

<margin>On the Ceremonies of the Jews, Book 1, Chapter 14. Synagogue of the Jews, Chapter 44.</margin>

But if such a *Prefect* <note>original: "Praefectus" — a high-ranking official or supervisor</note> is not present, then reason suggests that this power falls back to the <term>Parnasim <note>original Hebrew: פרנסים — community leaders or providers, often translated as "pastors" in this period</note></term>, the *Pastors of the Synagogue*. These men, without a doubt, frequently deliberate on the use of those funds together with the *Prefect of the Synagogue* or the *Appointed Collectors of Alms*. This aligns with what is found in the writings of Leone de Modena and Buxtorf <note>Leone de Modena (1571–1648) was a famous Venetian rabbi; Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629) was a renowned Christian Hebraist. Let us come now at last to the *Christian Church*, and let us prove that its ancient *Bishops* agreed in this regard with the *Presidents of the Synagogue*. It is well known that in the early Church, singular care was taken for the *poor* from the times of the Apostles until a later age, when charity grew cold and the gifts owed to the poor were consumed by the Bishops and Priests of the Church for the construction of grand buildings and empty sacred pomp. Otherwise, the ancient and purer Church surely commended itself so greatly by this virtue of charity toward the poor that Julian himself <note>Emperor Julian "the Apostate" (r. 361–363), who attempted to revive Roman paganism.</note>, though no small patron of Paganism, showed himself a rival of it in his letters to Arsacius, the Priest of Galatia. He proposed that charity should be imitated by his fellow Pagans with earnest zeal. <margin>Sozomen, Ecclesiastical History, Book 5, Chapter 16.</margin> "For it is shameful," he said, "if none among the Jews have to beg, and the impious Galileans <note>Julian's derogatory term for Christians.</note> support our people in addition to their own, while our own people appear to be destitute of aid and help from us." <note>original Greek: "Αἰσχρὸν γὰρ... εἰ τῶν μὲν Ἰουδαίων οὐδεῖς μεταιτεῖ, τρέφουσι δὲ οἱ δυσεβεῖς γαλιλαῖοι πρὸς τοῖς ἑαυτῶν, καὶ τοὺς ἡμετέρους; οἱ δὲ ἡμέτεροι, τῆς παρ’ ἡμῶν ἐπικουρίας ἐνδεεῖς φαίνονται;"</note> <margin>page 184.</margin> This was the case, unless we consider that at no time in the Church were there ever lacking greedy and stingy people among the Christians themselves, as you can easily see from *Cyprian’s Sermon on Alms*. However, the highest care and the greatest power for disposing of those alms (or liberal gifts) which the Christian people contributed with a generous hand—both for the support of sacred persons and for the poor—resided with the Bishop of the Church, or the *President*. It shall suffice for now to prove this with the single testimony of Justin Martyr, because, God willing, in the following Book concerning the *Minister of the Synagogue*, the method of administering alms in the early Church will be discussed more at length. Justin’s words on this matter are very clear <margin>Apology 2, page 33.</margin> and memorable: "Those who are prosperous and willing, each according to his own choice, gives what he wishes, and that which is collected..." <note>original Greek: "Οἱ δὲ εὐποροῦντες δὲ καὶ βουλόμενοι κατὰ προαίρεσιν ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ, ὃ βούλεται, δίδωσι, καὶ τὸ συλλε-" — the text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

The Councils did, in fact, often claim for themselves the power of ruling on civil cases, and they sometimes attempted to force the disobedient to acknowledge their jurisdiction through <term>Anathemas <note>original: "Anathematismos" — formal excommunications or religious curses</note></term> or Ecclesiastical *Penalties*. I believe that no other jurisdiction was tolerated among the Jews in Exile than that of **Compromisory Arbitrators** <note>original: "Arbitrorum Compromissariorum" — private mediators chosen by mutual agreement of both parties whose decisions are legally binding by contract</note>. <margin>Book 9, Title on the Jews and the Caelicolae <note>A title in the Theodosian Code regarding Jews and a specific sect called "Heaven-worshippers."</note></margin>

If, however, any of them, by common agreement, think they should litigate before the Jews in the manner of Arbitrators in* **CIVIL BUSINESS ONLY,** *they shall not be forbidden by public law from choosing their judgment. Judges shall even execute their sentences, as if they had been given by the sentence of a court-appointed arbitrator.* Through this Law, all formal jurisdiction was taken away from the Jews. And in general, it is certain that after the destruction of the Jewish State, a likeness of Government and Jurisdiction remained in the *Sanhedrins* <note>original: "Synedriis" — the governing councils or courts</note>, but the actual power was far from them, as 
<margin>On the Sanhedrin, Book 2, Chapter 4.</margin>
*Selden* <note>John Selden, a famous 17th-century legal scholar and Hebraist</note> also acknowledges; although a greater or lesser degree of liberty in Judgments was granted to those Sanhedrins by the Emperors (and is still granted today in various Kingdoms or Republics), as is easily clear from the Laws concerning the Government of Synagogues compiled by *Petit* and *Morin*. And in the same way, the matter stood with the Councils of the first Christians. In Criminal and Civil matters, no jurisdiction belonged to them, because the Christians established their Societies while living under a foreign Empire and Jurisdiction, from which they could not withdraw themselves without falling into the crime of disturbing the Divine Order. The principles upon which Christian Society was founded concern solely the Government of the mind; and therefore, the Rectors of those Churches have no more right or business in

He permitted litigants to appeal to the judgment of bishops if they wished to decline secular magistrates; and he decreed that their verdict should be authoritative and superior to that of other judges, as if it had been issued by the Emperor himself. He further ordered that the provincial governors and their subordinate soldiers should carry out the judgments rendered, and that the decrees of the synods should be unalterable. *Furthermore,* he **PERMITTED LITIGANTS TO CHOOSE THE EPISCOPAL JUDGMENT** *if they wished to refuse secular judges, and ordered that the* **SENTENCE OF THE BISHOPS SHOULD BE RATIFIED**, *no differently than if it had been delivered by the Emperor himself; and that the Rulers and their officials should commit the sentences delivered by the Bishops to execution; and finally, that the judgments of the Ecclesiastical Assemblies should be firm and inviolable.* Nor were the Bishops slow in exercising and claiming this right of theirs. # CHAPTER 14. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

After having discussed the primary duties of the **Rulers of the Synagogue** and the **Overseers of the Church**, we shall proceed, with God’s favor, to explain the **CIRCUMSTANCES** <note>original: "ACCIDENTIA" — in this context, the specific qualities, requirements, and incidental details pertaining to an office</note> of both; which are indeed varied and of differing importance. We will first look at the **ORDINATION** of the Rulers of the Synagogue and the Church; then we will examine their *relationship, both toward one another and toward other councils of elders of their kind.* Here it will be necessary to investigate whether all the Rulers of the Synagogue were equal in dignity, or if some were subject to others. Afterward, we must discuss their number, and by what means they maintained and supported themselves and their families in that position of dignity. The word **ORDINATION** is a general term, denoting both the **ELECTION** and the **CONFIRMATION** of a sacred office, encompassing both the *voting* <note>original Greek: "χειροτονίαν" (cheirotonia) — literally "stretching out the hand," referring to election by a show of hands</note> and the *laying on of hands* <note>original Greek: "χειροtheσίαν" (cheirothesia) — the ritual act of placing hands on a person to confer authority or blessing</note>.

We learn from Lampridius <note>Aelius Lampridius, one of the supposed authors of the *Historia Augusta*, a collection of biographies of Roman Emperors</note> that the Jews and Christians followed one and the same method in ordaining their sacred Overseers:

<margin>In the *Life of Alexander Severus*, chapter 46.</margin>
> Whenever he <note>the Emperor Alexander Severus</note> wished, he says, *to give Rulers to the Provinces, or to appoint Governors, or to* **ORDAIN** *Procurators (that is, financial officers), he would post their names, urging the people that if anyone had a charge against them, they should prove it with clear evidence; if they did not prove it, they would face the death penalty. He used to say that it was a serious matter that, while* **CHRISTIANS AND JEWS DID THIS IN PROCLAIMING THE PRIESTS WHO ARE TO BE ORDAINED,** *it was not done for the Rulers of Provinces, to whom the fortunes and lives of men were entrusted.*

This testimony of Lampridius is notable, if anything is, because from it we are informed not only of the *agreement* between Christians and Jews in ordaining their sacred Overseers, but also of the manner in which they were to be ordained. Both points must now be explained more fully and confirmed with reliable documents.

The Overseers of the Christian Church in the most ancient centuries after the departure of the Apostles were chosen and ordained almost in this manner. At least three Bishops of the same Province gathered at that Church where a Bishop—either a new one or one to be ordained in place of the deceased—was required. In the assembly of believers, they openly proposed the names of certain worthy men whom they judged fit for the vacant government of the Church. If these men were displeasing to the Clergy or to the Church (that is, the assembly of believers),

But if the Church had nothing to justly criticize in the persons proposed by the ordainers, then the ordaining Bishops immediately designated that same man whose name they had proposed as the *Bishop* of the Church, and they immediately inaugurated him into his office through *prayers and the laying on of hands*. Indeed, sometimes the Clergy and the People took the lead in the proposal itself with their votes, or the ordaining Bishops asked for the votes of the Clergy and the People concerning the Bishop to be ordained, with confirmation soon to follow. 

And indeed this whole action, with all its circumstances, was called *cheirotonia* <note>original Greek: χειροτονία — literally "stretching out the hand," referring to election by a show of hands</note> by the Greeks, and ORDINATION by the Latins, of which a certain part was the *laying on of hands* <note>original Greek: ἡ ἐπίθεσις τῶν χειρῶν — cheirothesia</note>, or the IMPOSITION OF HANDS. The creation or ordination of a Presbyter <term>Presbyter: from the Greek 'presbyteros,' meaning elder; a leader in the early church</term> was carried out with fewer complexities. For only the *Bishop* of each place recommended him to the Clergy and the Church for this office, and, with no one else intervening, consecrated him in this office or dignity through the *Laying on of Hands*. It is sufficiently certain that these practices were held not long after the departure of the Apostles, and this is now to be proven by us. But whether the Apostles themselves established this precedent deserves to be weighed and debated.

From the history of the New Testament and the Pauline Epistles, it is clear enough that the *Apostles*, or *Apostolic Men* <note>Leaders in the early church who were contemporaries of the Apostles or directly influenced by them</note>, designated and chose their own *Pastors* for each Church, and *ordained* them through the Laying on of Hands and inaugurated them into their new office; but it is not equally clear, nor can it be gathered from any certain and suitable argument, whether the names of those to be chosen were proposed by the Apostles to the Church to be approved or rejected by the same. # CHAPTER 14. OF THE SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

<margin>
From *On the Sanhedrin*, book 1, chapter 14 and book 2, chapter 7.
Chapters 10, 41.
</margin>
...they had chosen. And in the same way many others, who either preceded them or followed them, held this view. Those versions of the word *to choose by show of hands* <note>original Greek: χειροτονεῖν (cheirotonein)</note> tend toward this: as if the Apostles had proposed the *names of the Presbyters <term>Presbyter: an elder or minister in the early Christian church</term> to be chosen* to each Church, and the Churches themselves, through *outstretched hands* as signs of their votes, had chosen their own Presbyters from the proposed names. But it was long ago demonstrated at length and invincibly by the most learned Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654), an English jurist and scholar of Jewish law and antiquities</note> that such an exposition of the notion of *choosing by show of hands* cannot hold here. For the action of *the choosing* <note>original Greek: τῆς χειροτονίας (tēs cheirotonias)</note> in this passage is ascribed not to the people, but to Paul and Barnabas themselves. When *the act of choosing* denotes that action of the people by which they testify their assent with extended hands, then it must be ascribed to the people themselves, and not to others. For *to choose by show of hands* is not to *make* someone else extend their hands, but it marks the very action of the person who extends their own hands as a symbol of their vote. Therefore, since Luke <note>The traditional author of the Acts of the Apostles</note> declares that Paul and Barnabas *had chosen* <note>original Greek: κεχειροτονηκέναι (kecheirotonēkenai)</note>, it certainly cannot be explained as if Paul and Barnabas had merely caused the Church to extend its hands. Rather, if one were to insist on the proper meaning of the word, it would have to be interpreted as Paul and Barnabas themselves choosing the Presbyters through the symbol of their own outstretched hands. However, because this is far from all probability, nothing remains but for us to simply translate *the choosing* here as *to elect*, *to decree*, *to designate*, or *to ordain by election*. It is well known that it is often used this way by the purest Greek authors, as proven by Selden, and Luke himself had used the word in this same Book of the Acts of the Apostles. According to this interpretation, nothing else will now be gathered from this passage than that Paul and Barnabas themselves designated and chose the leaders for each Church. In what manner this was done, and whether with the intervening votes *of the multitude of the disciples* <note>original Greek: τοῦ πλήθους τῶν μαθητῶν</note>, is not stated.

# CHAPTER 14. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

...they were indeed asked what they desired in the person proposed by the Ordainers <note>The presiding clergy who performed the ritual of appointment</note>; whether they judged him worthy of this office or not? To such an extent, in fact, that the *election* is generally attributed to the Christian People by ecclesiastical authors, and the *Bishops*, acting only as *Ordainers*, approved and, as it were, ratified the election with their consent.

<margin>Annotations on Canon 4 of the Council of Nicaea.</margin>
I do not, therefore, entirely approve in all respects of what the most learned Beveridge <note>William Beveridge (1637–1708), an influential English bishop and scholar of church law</note> says when he attributes the *election* to the Ordaining Bishops and only *consent* to the Christian People in the elections of the ancient Bishops. For although I do not deny that the Ordaining Bishops also interposed their own judgment in the elections, it was nevertheless their duty in these elections to follow the common desire of the whole Church, unless some matter of great importance stood in the way; and therefore, the *Election* is ascribed with greater right to the Church than to *them*. Moreover, since much exists among the ancient writers on this argument, and the nature of our project <note>original: *nostri instituti ratio*</note> prevents us from wandering too far afield, it will suffice to examine only Cyprian <note>St. Cyprian (c. 210–258 AD), Bishop of Carthage and a foundational figure in early Christian theology</note> and bring forward what we have noted from him on this subject.

<margin>Letters, book 4, section 2, page 3.</margin>
Let us begin with an elegant letter of Cyprian regarding the schismatic Novatian <note>An early Christian priest who claimed the papacy by force, leading to a split (schism) in the church</note> to Antonianus, where he defends the election of Cornelius <note>Pope Cornelius (reigned 251–253 AD), whose legitimacy was challenged by Novatian</note> as the Bishop of Rome.

> For as for Cornelius, he says, *our dearest brother, who is commended by the praiseworthy testimony of God, of Christ, and of His Church, as well as by all his fellow priests, he did not reach the Bishopric suddenly, but* HAVING BEEN PROMOTED THROUGH ALL ECCLESIASTICAL OFFICES <note>original: *per omnia ecclesiastica officia promotus*</note>, *and having often served the Lord in Divine administrations, he ascended to the sublime peak of the Priesthood through* ALL THE RANKS OF RELIGION. *Then, thereafter, he neither demanded the Bishopric itself, nor desired it, nor (like others, whom the swelling of their own arrogance and pride inflates) did he invade it by force, but being quiet and modest—the sort who are usually chosen by God for this position—he suffered violence, so that he might receive the Bishopric against his will. And* HE WAS MADE BISHOP BY MANY OF OUR COLLEAGUES <note>original: *a plurimis collegis nostris*</note>, *who were then present in the city of Rome, and who sent us honorable and praiseworthy letters, distinguished by the testimony of their proclamation, regarding* HIS ORDINATION. *Moreover, Cornelius was made Bishop by the judgment of God and His Christ, by the* TESTIMONY OF ALMOST ALL THE CLERGY, BY THE VOTE <note>original: *suffragio*</note> OF THE PEOPLE *who were then present, and by the College of ancient Priests and good men.*

Behold this whole rite described clearly enough! The Bishops (whom Cyprian calls his colleagues) MADE Cornelius BISHOP.

### CHAPTER 14. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

If something was done against the law and the prerogatives of the Christian People, it cannot serve as a rule. From these things it now appears what kind of examination it was that Severus Alexander <note>Roman Emperor (reigned 222–235 AD), known for his religious tolerance and interest in the organizational structures of Jews and Christians.</note> was seen to praise above regarding the appointment of *Leaders* of the Jews and Christians. Truly, Severus praised the fact that the people were consulted by the Ordaining Bishops to see whether they had any grounds for reproach in those who were proposed or recommended for the Bishopric, and that the testimony of their lives, morals, and virtues was demanded from the people. Lampridius <note>One of the traditional authors of the *Augustan History*, a collection of Roman imperial biographies.</note> himself will be the best interpreter of Emperor Alexander’s mind, when he reports in another place with what zeal the Emperor himself observed this custom.

<margin>In the *Life of Alexander*, chapter 15.</margin>
Lampridius says: *He never made a Senator without the advice of all the Senators who were present*, SO THAT HE WAS CREATED BY THE OPINIONS OF ALL, (or: *sworn in* <note>original Latin: *gyraretur*</note>) *and the highest men gave their testimony*. Then: *He did not make these same Senators except by the vote of the highest men in the Palace, saying: it is necessary for him who* MADE A SENATOR *to be a great man himself*. Therefore, Severus himself did not strictly "make" the Senators, nor did he wish to be seen doing so; rather, those who cast their votes and testified to the dignity and suitability of these distinguished men did the making, in much the same way as the Christian People act in choosing Bishops.

*Election* is followed by the second part of <term>cheirotonia <note>Greek: χειροτονία; literally meaning "stretching out the hand," originally used for voting but later for the ritual of ordination.</note></term> (in the sense that the word was used among the Ancients), that is, <term>the laying on of hands <note>Greek: ἡ ἐπίθεσις τῶν χειρῶν (*he epithesis ton cheiron*)</note></term>, with prayers and hymns of praise directed toward that purpose. And although the word <term>cheirotonia</term>, when considering its original use and etymology, truly signifies the act of election itself, custom nevertheless prevailed so that among the Greeks it denotes exactly what the Latin term *to Ordain* (*Ordinare*) means. This Ordination consists primarily in the confirmation of the designated Bishop through Priestly Blessings and the *Laying on of Hands*.

<margin>On the 1st Apostolic Canon.</margin>
Zonaras <note>Joannes Zonaras, a 12th-century Byzantine historian and theologian who commented extensively on church law.</note>: <gloss>Now indeed, it is called CHIROTONIA, which is the completion of the prayers of consecration for one who has been allotted to perform sacred rites, and the invocation of the Holy Spirit; it is so named because the HIGH PRIEST EXTENDS HIS HAND, BLESSING THE MAN TO BE CHOSEN FOR SACRED DUTIES.</gloss> <note>original Greek: "Νῦν μὲν χειροτονία καλεῖται ἡ τῆς καθιερώσεως τῶν ἱερᾶσθαι λαχόντος τελεσιεργία τῶν εὐχῶν καὶ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος ἐπίκλησις· ἀπὸ τοῦ τὸν ἀρχιερέα τείνειν τὴν χεῖρα εὐλογοῦντα καὶ χειροτονούμενον"</note> Therefore, the Ancient Translator [was] not absurd...

### THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF RULERS, BOOK III. PART...

It was surely by a certain singular <term>chariti; grace or favor</term> of God toward the descendants of Israel to name and choose these Elders according to His own will, whereas in other matters all things are subject to [human] judgment. And we see in the Sacred Books that God never neglected this majestic right of choosing Rulers and Judges, whether He did so by Himself through an extraordinary 
<margin>1 Samuel 10:21</margin>
sign of His will—as was done in the election of Saul—or 
<margin>Numbers 11:16</margin>
through His delegate and Minister, Moses—as was done in the first Great Council of the whole nation—or even if God waived this right of His Majesty and permitted the people themselves in each city to choose their own Rulers; which He seems to have granted in the formation of the Republic 
<margin>Deuteronomy 16:18</margin>
under the Law <note>original Latin: "Lege concessisse videtur," referring to the commandment to appoint judges and officers in all gates.</note>. When later the Jew, as if spurning the command of God, wished to be ruled by men who would be substituted for the Supreme Ruler, and God Himself consented to these persistent desires on account of the great stubbornness of the people, then the supreme power in sacred and civil matters devolved to the King, as far as the final form of that Republic was concerned. This is most clearly evident from the histories of David, Solomon, and the kings who followed. And so, under these Kings, such a Senate was to be established either immediately by the King’s own 
<margin>2 Chronicles 19:5-6</margin>
command, or he granted the people the power to establish them in each city. This was done by *Jehoshaphat*, though it is uncertain whether it was in the former or latter manner. When the Israelites were later subjected to the empire of the Babylonians <note>The author likely means the Persians, as Artaxerxes was a Persian King.</note>, King Artaxerxes, claiming this right of sovereignty for himself, committed its exercise to his delegate, 
<margin>Ezra 7:25</margin>
Ezra; as Ezra himself left written. Gabinius also, the Roman governor of Syria, after Judea was conquered by Pompey, claimed this very power of supreme command for 
<margin>Antiquities of the Jews, book 14, chapter 10</margin>
himself; and he established five Sanhedrins throughout all Judea, as Josephus testifies. And after the destruction of Jerusalem, the *Emperor Titus* is said to have appointed *Rabbi Jochanan, son of Zakkai*, as the Prince of the Sanhedrin. 
<margin>R. Gedaliah, Shalshelet Ha-Kabbalah, folio 27, column 1.</margin>
However, the Talmudic Doctors and their followers commonly assert that the Great Sanhedrin of Jerusalem held the supreme 
<margin>Selden, On the Sanhedrins, book 2, chapter 15.</margin>
power of arranging sacred matters, even to the furthest reaches of the Republic, and that all other Sacred Senates dispersed throughout Canaan depended upon this Most Noble Sanhedrin. Indeed, they claim that delegates of this Sanhedrin chose men throughout the cities of Canaan who were proven for their skill in judging and elected them into the local Sanhedrins, to be promoted thereafter to the Senates of Twenty-Three Men.

### CHAPTER 15. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

They sat on the Mount and in the Court of the Temple. <term>Maimonides; the prominent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist</term> writes: <note>original Hebrew: אמרו חכמים... "The Sages said: From the Great Sanhedrin they would send throughout all the land of Israel and examine everyone they might find to be wise, fearing of sin, and humble—and they would make him a judge in his city."</note> *Laws of the Sanhedrin, chapter 2.*
*The Sages thus handed down, that from the Great Sanhedrin they sent into all the land of Israel, and* SEARCHED, *and whoever they found* WISE, *and fearing sin, and humble... they* MADE *him a member of the Sanhedrin of his city.* Therefore, according to the views of the <term>Talmudists; the scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism</term>, the supreme right of establishing Sanhedrins throughout the land of Canaan belonged to the Great Sanhedrin of Jerusalem. This Talmudic doctrine can be reconciled with what was previously discussed in this way: the Kings or Princes of the Jewish Nation, who for the most part were ignorant of the subtleties of Religion, gave the Great Sanhedrin of Jerusalem the most ample power in sacred matters. They committed all major controversies of Religion to its Judgment and subjected the Sanhedrins of other cities to this Great Senate. Although it is not entirely clear whether this was always the rule, it is certain from history that after the Jewish state was restored by the <term>Hasmoneans; the priestly family that led the Maccabean revolt</term>, the authority of the Jerusalem Senate was supreme and was often to be respected by the Kings or <term>Ethnarchs; provincial governors or rulers of an ethnic group</term> themselves. Therefore, the most Honorable Jerusalem Senate itself chose its own members from the Minor Sanhedrins to replace those who had died, and it had the right to form similar councils in any other places and to furnish them with members according to its own pleasure.

<margin>See <term>Selden; John Selden, a 17th-century English jurist and scholar of Jewish law</term> *On the Sanhedrin*, book 2, chapter 6, § 3 and book 2, chapter 15, § 15.</margin>
However, whether this Great Sanhedrin always exercised its right throughout the whole of Canaan is not equally clear. Nor is anything explicitly read about this in the text of either <term>Talmud; referring to the Jerusalem and Babylonian Talmuds</term> from which Maimonides derived that ruling of his. To me, it seems much more probable that the Sanhedrins of any cities, if no delegates of the Great Sanhedrin were present, did this by themselves, and undoubtedly after consulting the people in the Synagogue. Certainly, the words of the Babylonian Talmud suggest this. And even if this business was carried out by delegates of the Great Sanhedrin, then it is also possible that this custom was observed: that they did almost nothing in this matter without consulting the people in the Synagogue. For it was there that the <term>bedikah; investigation or examination</term> of everyone could be best conducted. And I could hardly bring forward any more eloquent arguments for this matter...

ON THE INCIDENTS OF RULERS, BOOK III, PART

<margin>Josephus in his *Life*, p. 1020.</margin>
...arguments, such as those various ones found in the *Life of Josephus*, described by himself. There we see all public matters handled in the Synagogues, by the council of the people, and also by the very delegates of the <term>Sanhedrin; the supreme legal and religious council of the Jewish people</term> and the People of Jerusalem, who had come into Galilee to remove Josephus from his office of the Prefecture. Josephus reports that they deliberated with the People of the Tiberians, assembled in the Synagogue, so that, once Josephus was removed, they might claim the supreme Prefecture for themselves. And certainly, Josephus speaks everywhere of the Republic of his nation in such a way as if no business of great importance was conducted therein without the council of the people.

After the Republic was later overturned by the Romans, and the power of the Sanhedrin was diminished and cut short, the face of things nevertheless did not change significantly. Throughout the whole land of Canaan, there remained a great number of <term>Gymnasia; here referring to schools of religious study</term> and Synagogues, as also in Babylonia, Egypt, and other more famous regions of the world. Moreover, this custom was preserved by the High Sanhedrin of Canaan: that it would elect its own Presidents, yet not without consulting the people. This is clear, unless I am mistaken, from a comparison of two passages of Hebrew history which deal with one and the same event concerning the election of a President of the Sanhedrin. Specifically, Hebrew history records that when Rabban Gamaliel, the grandson of the elder Gamaliel, carried himself too insolently toward Rabbi Joshua, the son of Hananiah, the Fathers and Elders of the Sanhedrin deposed him from the dignity of the Presidency, and substituted Eleazar, the son of Azariah, in his place. Thus Rabbi Abraham writes of it in the *Kabbala*:

# ON THE APPOINTMENTS OF THE GOVERNORS, BOOK III, PART [A]

Those matters of the synagogue, of which we spoke above, are chosen by a *Committee of Five*, who are designated by the entire synagogue assembly in the following manner. Each member of the synagogue writes the *name* of some honored man, to whom he would entrust the election of the Pastors, on a slip of paper and casts it into an urn. After this is completed, the slips are examined by the *Chazzans* <note>original Latin: *Chazzanis*; referring to the synagogue overseers or cantors</note> and three men from the assembly, who are found to have the most votes to confer this duty of choosing the Magistrate, then select two others at their own discretion. These men, now *five* in number, complete the election together. A certain Jew reported that the <term>Gabbaim</term> <note>original Hebrew: *gabbaim*; those responsible for collecting and distributing charity</note> or *Collectors of Alms* are similarly designated by the synagogue assembly only through votes written on slips. However, he claimed that the *Masters of the Synagogue* are invited to this office under honorable conditions by the Pastors, acting as the highest Magistrate who represents the entire synagogue assembly. If this is truly the practice observed, it must nevertheless be thought that this power was given to the Magistrate by the people. For it is certainly certain that in modern synagogues—which are entirely independent and recognize no <term>Patriarch</term> <note>The *Nasi*, or head of the Sanhedrin</note>—everything depends on the free votes of the synagogue people.

<margin>Chapter 53, Section 19.</margin>
This is manifest from the *Orach-Chajim* <note>A central code of Jewish Law, the "Way of Life"</note>, where the common consent of all members of the synagogue is required to establish a Synagogue Official. Behold two <term>Canons</term> <note>rules or laws</note> regarding this business:
> <term>A single individual can also delay the election of an Official and say: "I object to so-and-so being the Cantor [Chazzan]"; unless, by chance, he already consented to his election at the beginning.</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Yachid ve-yakhol le-akev...*</note>

<margin>Section 21.</margin>
> <term>No MESSENGER OF THE COMMUNITY FOR THE RECITING OF PRAYERS is to be appointed by the order of a Prince (the Magistrate under whose authority the Jews live), even if he should please the greatest part of the Church.</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Ein memanin sheliach tzibur...*; the *Sheliach Tzibur* is the person leading the congregation in prayer.</note>

But for those synagogues that were under the jurisdiction of the Patriarchs, the same liberty was not always present, even if this *right* belonged to them. The words of <term>Benjamin</term> <note>Benjamin of Tudela, a 12th-century Jewish traveler</note> must be considered. For he speaks thus of all the synagogues subject to the Patriarchate of Baghdad:

<margin>Travels, page 73.</margin>
> <term>Authority was given to them in all these communities to appoint a Master for every single congregation, for they come to him to receive ordination and authority.</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Nitan lahem reshut...*</note>
The <term>Exilarch</term> <note>original Latin: *Aichmalotarcha*; from the Greek for "Leader of the Captivity," the head of the Jewish community in Babylon</note> gives to them (the Jews of the Baghdad jurisdiction) the power in all those assemblies to appoint a MASTER over each Church.

### CHAPTER 15. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

MINISTER; for they shall approach him, so that they may receive from him the **Imposition of Hands and License**. Within these words, a sense may lie hidden: that the <term>Aichmalotarcha</term> <note>From the Greek *Aichmalotarches*, meaning "Leader of the Captivity," or Exilarch—the political and religious head of the Jews in Babylon.</note> of Babylon grants license to all the assemblies of his province to appoint a Master and Minister for themselves, and thereafter confirms the Governors elected by the assemblies in their office; thus, the right of **Election** is reserved for the assemblies themselves. Whether this means he gave Governors to each synagogue according to his own judgment—since he was best informed regarding the qualifications of the Teachers—or whether he *ordained* them (for the word *hakim* signifies this much here) and confirmed them in their office with the consent of the assemblies intervening, which is more probable. For the Jewish assemblies were subject to these Patriarchs in precisely the same way as the Christian Churches were to the Apostles of Christ; although the Apostles were endowed by the Lord with the power to appoint Pastors over the Churches according to His pleasure, it is nevertheless probable that they wished to do nothing in that regard without the consent of the people. <margin>\* Theodosian Code, *On the Jews and Heaven-Worshippers*, book 15. "All privileges which [have been granted] to distinguished men, to Patriarchs, or to OTHERS WHO HAVE BEEN PLACED IN CHARGE," etc. Also book 12, Chapter under the same title. "That privileges [be granted] TO THOSE WHO ARE SUBJECT TO THE AUTHORITY OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS PATRIARCHS," etc. Book 2, chapter 9.</margin> And so we shall easily understand how, in the Roman Laws, the Patriarchs are said to give Governors to the synagogues under their jurisdiction, \* and how **Epiphanius** records that **Joseph**, the Apostle of the Patriarch of the Jews of Tiberias, exercised this same power. Unless, however—and this is not to be doubted—certain Patriarchs conducted themselves more imperiously in their government and claimed more power for themselves than was fitting. In general, it is certain that the Patriarchs were not accustomed to thrust Governors upon the assemblies under their jurisdiction against their will, but rather consulted the people on the matter; this is abundantly clear from the points above, as well as from the illustrious testimony of the Emperor Severus.

Having shown the agreement between the Synagogue and the Church in the Rite of **Choosing Governors**, it will be easy to observe the same in the **CONFIRMATION** or the **Ordination** itself, which was performed through the **IMPOSITION OF HANDS**. For most celebrated men have long since pointed out that this ceremony was derived from the Synagogue into the Church; yet, those things which pertain to this subject have not been fully explained by them.

### ON THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF RULERS, BOOK III, PART I.

<margin>
Jacques Basnage, *Sacred and Ecclesiastical Exercises*, Year 35, Number 13.
</margin>
The ceremony of the **Imposition of Hands** was most familiarly used among the Jews during the height of their prosperity, and indeed in various cases. Since these have recently been reviewed with no small diligence by a certain learned man, there is no need to linger on repeating them. It suffices, therefore, to mention that among other things, this **Rite** was solemn for the Jews in **Ordaining Teachers** or **Judges**, and in **Confirming** those same men in the **Exercise of their Ecclesiastical Office**. These matters, however, must be discussed more distinctly.

1. It is a matter of tradition that around the age of Christ the Lord, this custom prevailed: that the <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>The supreme judicial and religious council of the Jews.</note> or the Prince of the Sanhedrin, and all the Teachers to whom that faculty had been granted by the Prince of the Sanhedrin, conferred upon other students of Divine Wisdom and men well-trained in Jewish Law the **faculty of teaching or judging** through the <term>Imposition of Hands</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Semikhat Yadayim*</note>. I say "faculty" in such a way that after this Promotion, they became capable of holding judicial leadership and were considered worthy to be co-opted into the established Sanhedrins. For even if the Teachers promoted to exercise certain **Particular Acts**, whether of Teaching or Judging (of which I spoke in the previous Book), achieved this through that Imposition of Hands—so that they could resolve cases of conscience proposed to them and pass sentence on certain lawsuits for which <margin>a <term>Court of Experts</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Beit Din shel Mumchin*</note></margin> three approved and literate men were required—nevertheless, by that very **Promotion** or **Imposition of Hands**, they were not actually co-opted into **any specific Sanhedrin of the City**, but achieved that only through **Election**, about which I have spoken in the preceding pages.

<margin>
See Buxtorf under the word *Semikhah* and Selden, *On the Sanhedrins*, book 2, chapter 7 and chapter 13, section 3.
</margin>
But while these things are certain and long observed from Hebrew authors, I have nevertheless seen certain learned men of our time—following <term>Lightfoot</term> <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and Hebraist known for using Talmudic concepts to interpret the New Testament.</note> too securely as he discussed these things elsewhere—who have not quite correctly understood them. Specifically, Lightfoot convinced himself from <term>Maimonides</term> <note>A preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal scholar.</note> (doubtless misunderstood) that around the age of Christ the Lord, the Jews no longer promoted learned men to the degree of Doctorship through the **Imposition of Hands**, but through a bare **Declaration**, by which one Doctor is pronounced so by another without any added symbol or ceremony. Thus Lightfoot expressly states in his work on *Acts*: *In this matter, therefore, this action agrees with the custom...*

### CHAPTER 15. SYNAGOGUE AND CHURCH.

...according to the custom common in the Synagogue, that THREE [men]—Simeon, Lucius, and Manaen—IMPOSE [hands] on the two who were to be sent out, Paul and Barnabas; yet, in the fact THAT THEY IMPOSE HANDS, they even depart from the common custom. Now follow these words of Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a foundational Jewish philosopher and legal scholar.</note> in the works of Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English scholar who specialized in using Rabbinic literature to explain the New Testament.</note>, upon which he builds his opinion: IN WHAT MANNER IS THE ORDINATION OF ELDERS <note>original Latin: *Presbyterorum*</note> [done] through the ages? NOT SO THAT THEY IMPOSE HANDS upon the head of the Elder, BUT THAT THEY CALL HIM RABBI, and they say to him: "Behold, you are ordained, and you have the power of judging." Then Lightfoot ties himself in knots [asking]: why would the Jews have abandoned the Imposition of Hands? Why would the Church have adopted a rite abandoned by the Jews? All this is in vain, because Lightfoot did not grasp the sense of Maimonides' words in a matter otherwise quite familiar. These are the Hebrew words of Maimonides:

<margin>Laws of the Sanhedrin, chapter 4, section 2.</margin>
"How is the <term>Semikhah</term> <note>The Hebrew term for ordination, literally meaning "leaning" or "laying" [of hands].</note> performed for the generations? Not that they should lean their hands on the head of the elder, but that they call him 'Rabbi' and say to him, 'Behold, you are ordained, and you have the authority to judge.'"

How then was ordination done in all previous ages? NOT (*that is:* **Not only**) SO THAT THEY IMPOSE HANDS TO PROMOTE [someone], but also that they declare him a Teacher by a spoken voice, and say to him: BEHOLD, YOU ARE PROMOTED, and, you have the power of judging. Maimonides wants to say clearly and simply that in ancient times a double method of promotion prevailed among the Jews; one indeed through the Imposition of Hands, joined with the Spoken Declaration, and the other through that Declaration alone, by which someone is pronounced a Teacher. This is so much the case that the word "NOT" <note>Hebrew: *Lo*</note> in the text of Maimonides is to be understood as "NOT ONLY" <note>original Latin: *non tantum*</note>, in opposition to the word "BUT." This mode of speaking was so familiar to the Jews that various examples of it also exist in the writings of the New Testament; such as:

<margin>John 6:27. see also verse 26.</margin>
Do not work <note>original Greek: *μὴ*</note>, NOT (Not only), to obtain the food that perishes, but <note>original Greek: *ἀλλὰ*</note>, BUT, for the food that remains unto eternal life. Again in the following Chapter:

<margin>Chapter 7:16.</margin>
My doctrine is not <note>original Greek: *οὐκ ἔστιν*</note>, NOT (not only) mine, but his who sent me. Again:

<margin>Chapter 12:44.</margin>
He who believes in me, DOES NOT believe in me, BUT in him who sent me. Nor should there be doubt about the truth of our interpretation, because Maimonides certainly did not wish to establish anything different in this argument from the <term>Gemara</term> <note>The section of the Talmud containing rabbinical commentary and analysis.</note> and the common opinion of the Teachers. In the Gemara, however, Rav Acha, the son of Rabba, is said to have told Rav Ashi:

<margin>Sanhedrin, folio 13, column 2.</margin>
"Is the ordination performed with the actual hand? He said to him: [No,] it is performed by calling him by the name 'Rabbi.'"

Does this *Laying on of Hands*, which was customary in Doctoral Promotions among the Jews, give the origin to the *Laying on of Hands* received in the Ordination of Pastors in the Early Church? This is certainly something that deserves to be weighed more accurately. Through Doctoral Ordination, no one was actually admitted into the Consistory <note>A governing council or assembly.</note> of the Church among the Hebrews, but they only obtained a testimony of their own fitness. The Bishops and Presbyters <note>Elders.</note> of the Early Church, however, were actually placed into the possession of the Office of Ministry and *oversight* <note>original Greek: *ἐπισκοπῆς* (episkopēs)</note> through the *Laying on of Hands*. ### CHAPTER 15. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.
#### PAGE 839

To prove that the rite of **Ordaining** judges and Rabbis was continued according to the Jewish opinion, the author produces the testimony of Benjamin of Tudela <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler from Spain who recorded the customs of Jewish communities across Europe, Asia, and Africa.</note> to demonstrate that this rite was observed by the Jews up until the year 1170 AD. Indeed, the words of Benjamin are quite remarkable; though we have cited them before, they must necessarily be repeated here. He speaks of the Synagogues that were subject to the Babylonian Exilarch <note>The "Aichmalotarcha" or Head of the Exile, who led the Jewish community in Babylon.</note>:

<margin>Travels, page 73.</margin>
"The Head of the Exile <note>original Hebrew: *Rosh HaGolah*</note> gives them authority in all these congregations to appoint over each and every congregation a **MASTER** and a † **DEACON**; for they come to him to receive the **LAYING ON OF HANDS** <note>original Hebrew: *Semikhah*</note> and authority." The election by the Church, and the confirmation of the elected leaders and ministers by the Patriarch of Baghdad <note>The Exilarch.</note>, seems to be assigned by these words. Both of these points align beautifully with Ecclesiastical Ordinations. And since the Exilarchs seem to have followed the accepted customs of their own community in this rite, perhaps we may conclude from this that while Jewish affairs were flourishing in Canaan <note>The Land of Israel.</note>, the leaders and ministers of the Synagogues—who were dependent on the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme judicial and religious council of ancient Israel.</note>—were confirmed in their office by the President of the Sanhedrin through the Laying on of Hands.

<margin>Acts 6:6.</margin>
In the same way, we see that the Apostles not only inaugurated Bishops and Deacons into their offices through the Laying on of Hands, but they also applied this Rite of the Laying on of Hands in every other **Ordination** for any kind of extraordinary function. Furthermore,

<margin>Acts 13:2.</margin>
Benjamin writes that on the day the Exilarch himself was **initiated** into his duty with great

<margin>page 74.</margin>

### CONCERNING THE INCIDENTALS OF RULERS, BOOK III, PART.
#### PAGE 840

I believe it can be very well compared and reconciled with how those in the Church are inaugurated into their office, even if only a single, rather than a double, *Laying on of Hands* was used among the Jews for their Senators <note>The members of the Sanhedrin or high councils.</note>.

Indeed, let us consider what is most true: that the Rite of *Laying on of Hands* was not, in its first and genuine use, applied except in such *Ordinations* by which someone was *actually* initiated into some office. However, as literary studies flourished, more people rendered themselves capable of office than there were positions of Judging or Teaching to be committed to them. Then, finally, it was devised—and clearly done through an obvious *abuse of this Rite*—that *Hands* were also laid upon certain Learned Men as a testimony of their fitness and learning, without them being *actually* ordained by that laying on of hands to any specific status or office of Teaching and Judging. For all the learned agree, if I am not mistaken, that the *Laying on of Hands* was adopted by the Jews following the example of that act by which *Moses*, at God’s command, *laid his hands upon Joshua* and, through this symbol, publicly *confirmed* him before all the Israelites in the most serious office of Rule and Judgment. 

<margin>Numbers 27:18.</margin> Certainly, Joshua did not merely receive a testimony of his fitness here, but was *Ordained* by Moses through this rite to that very Magnificent Prefecture over the Jewish People. Therefore, according to this example, hands were properly to be laid on no one except those who were *actually* to be ordained to some status, office, or duty through this symbol. And it is by no means to be doubted that it was so in the beginning, after the rebirth of learning in Judaism following the restoration of the Commonwealth by the *Hasmoneans* <note>The Maccabean dynasty that ruled Judea from approximately 140 BC to 37 BC.</note>. 

At that time, none were promoted through the *Laying on of Hands* except those who were actually placed in the Sanhedrins <note>The supreme councils or courts of justice.</note> or appointed over Schools. But as studies thrived and the number of scholars increased, along with an eagerness for empty glory, the Presidents of the Academies and Sanhedrins were forced to distribute honorary titles to satisfy their students and simultaneously to bring honor to their studies. Thus, there suddenly appeared **Doctors** upon whom **hands** were laid without there being a School for them to preside over, or a Sanhedrin in which they might determine the law. Yet, even so, that *Ordination* was not entirely without fruit. For they were able to resolve cases of conscience and settle disputes—for the termination of which men of proven learning were required—if they had been ordained by the Sanhedrin for those particular *Acts*. Nevertheless, they were not, by this Ordination, placed in the Sanhedrins or the Chairs of authority; this is what I said was a departure from the original use of this rite and occurred through its abuse.

<summary>This page discusses the historical evolution of the "laying on of hands" from a functional appointment to a specific office (like Joshua's) into an honorary academic or legal title given to "Doctors" without specific posts.</summary>

->### CHAPTER 15. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.<-

With these points established, it will be easy to understand how these matters are to be reconciled with the customs of the early Christian Church. When the Apostles or Apostolic men established Churches everywhere, both within and outside of Canaan <note>The Holy Land</note>, they found it necessary to place Leaders over them, and they seem to have instituted them in this manner. After consulting the Church—that is, the gathered multitude of believers—they selected men who were prudent, upright, and practiced beyond others in the knowledge of the Ways of God; they chose, if I may be permitted to speak this way, the **best of their disciples**, whom they had formed in that Church. These men they then **ordained through the Laying on of Hands** (<term>samkhu</term> <note>original: סמכו; the Hebrew term for the act of ordination</note>) to the office and honor of the **Presbyterate** <note>The council of elders or "Presbytery."</note>. With a single and same act of the Laying on of Hands, I say, they ordained them to the office of **oversight** <note>original: ἐπισκοπῆς (episkopēs); the Greek term from which "Episcopacy" or "Bishopric" is derived</note> of that Church, and placed them in the Sacred Consistory <note>A governing council or assembly</note> of that Church.

Just as Joshua was not first declared capable of leadership through some preliminary Ordination and then later actually appointed as the Leader and Teacher of the people through a second ordination, but rather achieved both at once through one and the same Ordination—so too **Pastors**, Leaders, or Presbyters attained both through one and the same act of Ordination. For those who were initiated into that office by the actual act of the Laying on of Hands were by that very act deemed capable of it. I have already argued that the practice in the Jewish Schools—whereby some were declared **Doctors** <note>Teachers or learned authorities</note> simply through this Rite of the **Laying on of Hands** so that some public testimony of their fitness might exist—was done as an **abuse** of this symbol, driven by the great number of disciples and a desire to honor their studies. 

Christianity, in its early beginnings, had no obvious reason for such an **abuse**, since at that time many Ecclesiastical Sanhedrins <note>Church councils modeled after the Jewish high courts</note> had to be formed in various places. Men capable of the Ordination of the Doctorate or Presbyterate could be immediately co-opted into these councils, so that there was no need to separate the title of "Doctor" or "Presbyter" from the office itself. And, to avoid using more words than necessary on this matter, I would even suggest that the organization of nascent Christianity was exactly as Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> imagines the state of Judaism would be, hypothetically, if only a single Doctor who had been legitimately promoted by the Laying on of Hands remained in it.

<margin>Sanhedrin, chapter 4, section 2.</margin>
His words from that same treatise on the Sanhedrin <note>The legal code regarding the Jewish high courts.</note> are as follows:

> "Suppose there were no one left in the Land of Israel except one ordained person: he would seat two others beside him and ordain seventy at once, or one after another; and afterward, he and the seventy would form the Great Sanhedrin and ordain others."

### ON THE ATTRIBUTES OF LEADERS, BOOK III, PART I.

**And other courts ordained...** <note>original Hebrew: וסמכו בתי דינים אחרים (ve-samkhu batei dinim acherim)</note> If it should happen that in the land of Israel there remained only a single legitimate **Promoter** <note>An authorized person who bestows ordination</note> (one who himself had been lawfully Promoted), he, with two others joined to his side, could **ORDAIN SEVENTY OTHERS**, whether all at once or individually, one after another. Once this was completed, **HE HIMSELF, TOGETHER WITH THOSE SEVENTY, WOULD FORM A GREAT SANHEDRIN** <note>The supreme legal and religious council of ancient Israel</note>, which could then **ORDAIN OTHER MINOR SANHEDRINS**. Just as these promoted individuals were constituted as both Teachers and Senators <note>Members of a governing council</note> through that single act of Ordination, and were placed into Sanhedrins by that very act, so too those Presbyters <note>Elders</note> of the primitive Church achieved both through a single act of Ordination, according to the first and genuine use of this **Symbolic Rite**. If we arrange matters in this way, we will simultaneously perceive most clearly how Ecclesiastical Ordinations—of both the **Episcopate** <note>the office of Bishop</note> and the **Presbyterate** <note>the office of Elder</note>—truly descended from these **Doctoral Ordinations** adopted from the Jews.

Whether other **Doctoral Promotions** modeled after those Jewish ones existed among the first Christians—beyond those ordinations by which someone was actually promoted to the office of governing a specific Church—is a matter we shall be less concerned with for now. Furthermore, in the writings of the Church Fathers, **Teachers** are occasionally mentioned who were not always clearly members of the Clergy. Tertullian notably wrote: *What then if a Bishop, if a Deacon, if a widow, if a virgin, if a TEACHER, or even a Martyr should fall from the rule [of faith], shall heresies therefore seem to possess the truth?* Later in the same treatise: *There is surely some brother who is a TEACHER, gifted with the grace of knowledge*, etc. By "Teachers," I mean those who either received a singular testimonial of their learning through some Bishop or were specifically ordained to this duty of **Teaching**. In this manner, Jerome testifies that Origen was **CONFIRMED BY DEMETRIUS, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF ALEXANDRIA, IN THE PLACE OF CLEMENT THE PRESBYTER**, and taught for many years before he was ordained as a Presbyter. ### CHAPTER 16. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES. 845

<margin>Book 2, chapter 2.</margin>
All the Elders <note>original: *Presbyteri*</note> of every Church in ancient times held that mutual relationship <note>original Greek: *σχέσιν* (schesin)</note> with one another, such that they all together constituted a certain **Body or College**, which directed the affairs of the Church by common counsel. However, I would by no means want this to be understood as if no one in that College had any prerogative over another. For we have already established in the **previous Book** that all Christian Presbyteries <note>the governing councils of elders</note> from the times of the Apostles had *fixed* and ordinary **Presidents**, who were for the most part more eminent than the other Elders in age and wisdom. These men convened and dismissed the assemblies, proposed matters for deliberation, and their opinions carried the greatest weight in those discussions. Indeed, these **Presidents** of the Ecclesiastical Senates, who eventually came to be called **Bishops** <note>original: *Episcopi*</note> alone, acquired and claimed such great *authority* over time that they greatly excelled above the Elders. Almost everything in the Churches was conducted according to their prescription, and nothing was done against their will. Thus, they seemed to differ from the Elders not only in *dignity*, but also in *rank* and *office*. Nevertheless, in the most serious matters, the Bishops always maintained the policy of deciding nothing without the council of the Elders.

By these hypotheses, which we explained more fully in the previous Book, one can satisfy the requirements of both Scripture and the remaining monuments of Christian antiquity. For if you should perhaps maintain that Christian Presbyteries, from their very first institution, had Presidents who were distinct in *rank and office* from the other Elders (an opinion which the most learned men in England <note>a reference to Anglican scholars defending the "divine right" of the episcopacy</note> persist in defending), you will never satisfy the history of the Acts of the Apostles <note>original: *Actuum Apostolicorum*</note> or the Pauline Epistles. In those texts, the government of the Church is generally attributed to several **Bishops, Elders, and Pastors** (using the names confusedly and without distinction), without any mark of difference. It would truly be a wonder if those distinct orders of Bishops and Elders left no trace in the history of Luke or the letters of Paul, if they were indeed instituted by the Apostles. If, on the other hand, you defend the idea that those Elders of the Apostolic age were so equal to one another in every way and form that no constant order was observed among them in sitting and deliberating, or that the dignity of the Presidency was not stable but "ambulatory" <note>rotating or temporary</note>, then the reason will forever escape you as to how, in such a short interval of time after the departure

# CHAPTER 16. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

The teachers of the Church, having lost the true images of things, substituted false ones in their place. For since the Apostles were sufficiently instructed by the Spirit that the <term>τὴν καθαίρεσιν</term> <note>original Greek: "tēn kathairesin" — the abolition or tearing down</note> of ancient ceremonies was imminent, they ought to have been careful not to promote or silently recommend an opinion of their superiority and usefulness through the titles of Church offices derived from them.

Indeed, what is more, I do not concede that in the second and third centuries—when the dignity of the Bishop had already grown not a little above that of the common priests—there appeared as great a distinction between a Bishop and the Presbyters as there was under the Old Covenant between the High Priest and the Priests. For:

**1.** <note>original: א (Aleph), the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet used as a list marker</note> If that were the case, how could Jerome, a Doctor of the fourth and fifth centuries, still say or dare to say in his own time: <margin>Letter to Evagrius</margin> **With the exception of ordination, WHAT DOES A BISHOP DO THAT A PRESBYTER DOES NOT DO?** A Bishop ordained Presbyters; he was not ordained by Presbyters. In this alone did he differ from them, according to the opinion of Jerome. But how small a thing is this, if one considers the degree of difference that existed between the High Priest and the Priests?

**2.** <note>original: ב (Bet), the second letter of the Hebrew alphabet</note> Bishops and Presbyters were so closely joined to one another that the Bishops were not permitted to do anything in more serious matters without the Presbyters. Thus Cyprian writes: <margin>Book 3, Letter 10</margin> **As for what OUR FELLOW-PRESBYTERS Donatus, Novatus, and Curdius wrote to me, I COULD NOT WRITE BACK ALONE, since from the beginning of my episcopacy I determined to do nothing by MY PRIVATE OPINION WITHOUT YOUR COUNSEL and without the consent of the people.** <margin>Book 3, Letter 19</margin> He says the same thing frequently in other letters.

**3.** <note>original: ג (Gimel), the third letter of the Hebrew alphabet</note> Far more frequently, Bishops and Presbyters are referred to as belonging to one and the same Sacerdotal Order <note>The "priestly" rank or class</note>, rather than being distinguished from one another as High Priest and Priests. This is clear from Cyprian himself and the Canons of the ancient Church, as well as from many passages in the Justinian Code <note>A collection of laws compiled under the Roman Emperor Justinian I</note>.

<margin>See Ziegler on Deacons, chapter 2, section 7. 3rd Council of Carthage, chapter 29.</margin> **4.** <note>original: ד (Dalet), the fourth letter of the Hebrew alphabet</note> Moreover, that very title of "Supreme Priest" <note>original: Summi Sacerdotis</note> was denied to the Bishops of the First See in the African Church, after experience had shown that some had interpreted this title too loosely to suit their own ambition, and had claimed for themselves more dominance over their fellow bishops than was right. The words of the Canon state: **The Bishop of the First See shall not be called CHIEF OF THE PRIESTS, nor SUPREME PRIEST, or anything of this kind, but only the Bishop of the First See.**

### ON THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF RULERS BOOK III. PART I.

<margin>The Bishop of the See.</margin> When, nonetheless, Bishops in the records of the ancient Church are either called "High Priests," or are compared with the Highest—or as they put it, the *Presiding Priests*—that comparison must be taken with a grain of salt, and it must not be pressed too far. (I do not deny that this happens, though very rarely, even in the writings of Cyprian himself.) <note>St. Cyprian of Carthage (3rd century) was a key figure in defining the role of the Bishop, often emphasizing the unity of the church through the episcopal office.</note> For in my judgment, they intended to suggest nothing else by this than that there is nothing higher than a Bishop in the Church, just as the Temple had no one higher than the High Priest. Anyone who labors to extract more from this comparison will run into other clear statements of the Church Fathers regarding the close <term>arrangement</term> <note>original Greek: "θέσει" (thesei) — position or structural relationship</note> which existed in the most ancient times between the Bishop and the Presbyters.

But since in every dispute, effort should be made to argue not about words but about *realities*, I really do not know if these lengthy quarrels might eventually be settled, if only the stubbornness of interpreting words according to one's own whim were absent. For we, who defend the <term>single order</term> <note>original Greek: "μίαν τάξιν" (mian taxin) — one rank or class</note> of Bishops and Presbyters, do not deny, however, that the Presbyteries <note>the councils of elders</note> of the Apostolic age had their own perpetual *Presidents*, to whom the primary care of governance and business was entrusted. And what more could the advocates of the opposing view demand? Let us hear [Henry] Dodwell: <margin>Cyprianic Dissertations 10. §. 9.</margin> <note>Henry Dodwell was a 17th-century scholar who defended the necessity of the episcopacy for the validity of the sacraments.</note> *Blondel grants the power of convening and dismissing assemblies, which we have proven is sufficient on its own in our English tract on* SCHISM. <note>David Blondel was a French Protestant scholar who argued that Bishops and Presbyters were originally the same rank.</note> But if that is truly *sufficient*, why then is there a dispute about the *name*, when we agree on the facts themselves? Elsewhere, that learned man <margin>Dissertation I. §. 5. In the same place.</margin> calls those first Presbyters of the Apostolic age PRESIDENTS OF THE PRESBYTERIES, a name by which we likewise designate them. He also concedes in the same place that those Presidents of the Presbyteries were only called BISHOPS by the later Church, which is the same thing we assert. 

The question will finally be asked, then: should the stable Presidents of Senates, who have the power of convening and dismissing meetings, be said to be of the same *order* as the other Senators, or a different one? Likewise: should the Presidents of the early Presbyteries—who are distinguished from the other Presbyters by no mark of difference in the Sacred Scriptures and are consistently designated by the same names as them—be said to be of the same *order* as the other Presbyters because of the dignity of their perpetual Presidency?
