# CHAPTER 16. SYNAGOGUE AND CHURCH.

...against common usage, who here would not easily affirm both of those propositions with us? Or, if he would entirely prefer to differ from us in the use of terms, let him finally enjoy his own meaning, as we enjoy ours.

Let us see, however, what now chiefly remains for us to do: whether we can cast some light on this matter from the **Synagogue**, and contribute something toward ending this controversy (the ending of which is in the interest of the Church). Therefore, let these three things be observed with me: **1.** That Jewish <term>Presbyteries</term> <note>These were councils of elders or "senates" that governed Jewish communities, which the author argues served as the blueprint for early Christian church government.</note> had their own *Presidents*. **2.** That these Presidents were of the same rank or order as the other Elders. **3.** And although they were respected for their authority, in the *Senate* they were nonetheless required to follow the *majority vote* in more serious matters.

**1.** I should think it is beyond controversy among all who study Hebrew literature that all Jewish *Assemblies*, both Scholastic and Synagogal, had some *President*. Indeed, the mention of those *Presidents* in Jewish history is most abundant and frequent, and their *successions* <note>original Greek: "διαδοχαί" (diadochai) — the continuous line of leaders</note> through the intervals of certain ages are recounted by Hebrew historians in plainly the same manner as the successions of Christian Bishops are recounted by Eusebius. <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD) was the first great historian of the Christian Church; he famously tracked the lineage of bishops back to the Apostles.</note> Such a *President* is called by the common name <gloss>original Hebrew: "Rosh Yeshiva"</gloss> *Head of the Assembly*, <gloss>original Hebrew: "Resh Sidra"</gloss> *Head of the Scholastic Order*, and, when he is present in the Synagogue itself, <gloss>original Hebrew: "Rosh Ha-Knesset"</gloss> *Prince of the Synagogue*. Furthermore, the *President* of the greatest and most famous of all, the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme legal and religious council of ancient Israel.</note> at Jerusalem, was called <gloss>original Hebrew: "Nasi"</gloss> *Prince*, to whom singular honor was to be shown when he entered the Synagogal *Assembly*. Maimonides <note>A renowned 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legal scholar.</note> writes concerning the Great Sanhedrin:
<margin>Sanhedrin chapter 1, § 3.</margin>
*The one who excels among all of them in wisdom, him they appoint as* HEAD *over them, and he is the* HEAD, *or President of the* ASSEMBLY, *and he is the same one whom they call in every place the* PRINCE. <note>original Hebrew: "הגדול בחכמה שבכולם מושיבים אותו ראש עליהם והוא ראש הישיבה והוא שקוראים אותו נשיא בכל מקום"</note> Likewise, concerning the City Sanhedrins:
<margin>See Selden, *On the Sanhedrins*, book 2, chapter 6, § 1.</margin> <note>John Selden (1584–1654) was a prominent English jurist and scholar of Jewish law.</note>

# ON THE CHARACTERISTICS OF LEADERS, BOOK III, PART...

I. The Elder-Assessors <note>The word "assessores" refers to those who sit alongside a judge or leader to provide counsel.</note> are frequently called in Jewish writings <margin>Chaverim</margin> <term>Colleagues</term> of the *President* or Prince. We shall soon see how much weight this argument carries. Behold an example from the *History* of Abraham <note>original Latin: "Kabbal Abrahami," referring to the *Sefer ha-Kabbalah* (Book of Tradition) by Abraham ibn Daud, a 12th-century history of the Jewish people.</note>: <margin>Page 58, column 2.</margin> *Rabban Gamaliel, the son of Rabban Simeon, son of Gamaliel (who was killed by decree), was the* HEAD OF THE ACADEMY *and* PRINCE *after the death of Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai; and the husband of his sister was Rabbi Eliezer, the son of Hyrcanus. And* HIS COLLEAGUES *were: Rabbi Joshua, the son of Hananiah, a great sage and* FATHER OF THE SENATE <note>original Hebrew: "Av Beit Din," literally "Father of the House of Judgment," the second-highest ranking member of the Sanhedrin.</note>, *who had previously been a charcoal burner; Rabbi Jose the Priest, the Galilean; Rabbi Simeon, the son of Nathaneel; Rabbi Eliezer, the son of Arach; Rabbi Yochanan, the son of Nuri; Rabbi Yochanan, the son of Baruka, etc.*

The continuous succession of the Great Senate in the land of Canaan after the destruction of the Temple is described here. The first Prince or President of that Senate was Rabban Gamaliel; the second was Rabbi Joshua, called the *Father of the Senate*. Yet that Rabbi Joshua and the remaining Elder-Assessors are called the COLLEAGUES <margin>Page 59, column 1, at the end.</margin> of Gamaliel the President. Again, in the following succession <note>original Greek: "διαδοχῇ" (diadoche) — a sequence of leaders inheriting an office.</note>: *Rabbi Akiva was the* HEAD OF THE ACADEMY *after Rabban Gamaliel, and* HIS COLLEAGUES *were Simeon, the son of Azzai, and Simeon, the son of Suma, and Elisha Achar (or "the Other"), and Rabbi Tarphon, and Rabbi Ishmael, and Rabbi Judah, the son of Baba, etc.* And it is the same in all subsequent successions, besides the fact that this phrasing occurs frequently elsewhere.

From this, unless I am mistaken, it can be concluded with certainty that the *President of the Scholastic and Ecclesiastical Senates* was of the same order as the other Elders, his colleagues. For the word <term>Chaver</term> <note>original Hebrew: "חבר" (Chaver), meaning friend, associate, or colleague.</note> in these texts is used in the same sense as the Latin word *COLLEGA*, which is commonly used to refer to men of the same rank, as is known to everyone. Nor can this argument be evaded with any appearance of truth by those most learned men who contend that Bishops are of a different <margin>Cyprian, Letter 10, sections 1, 2, 3.</margin> *rank from Elders, because Bishops are not accustomed to calling Elders their colleagues, but only their fellow-Bishops.* Such was the position taken by the most learned Dodwell <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711) was a prominent Anglo-Irish scholar and theologian who defended the high-church view of the episcopacy.</note> in that *Dissertation* from which we just drew several points.

### CHAPTER 16. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

In the most ancient times, every **Promoted Doctor** or **Elder** <term>Presbyter</term> <note>From the Greek "presbyteros," meaning elder; used here for both Jewish and Christian officials.</note> in turn promoted others; however, when the **honor of the Doctorate** began to lose its value because of the sheer number of those doing the promoting, it was decreed otherwise. Thus, it would not be foreign to the rules of the **Christian Church**, as it was established in its beginnings, for each **Elder** <term>Presbyter</term> to ordain other **Elders**, provided the people consented. But, lest the number of Elders increase too much and the honor of the office lose its value if that power of ordaining were exercised by all Elders without distinction, its exercise was committed to the **Presidents** alone, or **Bishops** <term>Episcopis</term>, following the manner and custom already accepted among the **Jews** at that time. 

<margin>
Book 2, chapter 9.
Matthew 23:11, 12. 20:25, 26.
See Book 2, chapter 12, pages 604, 605.
</margin>

From this, however, no one can correctly infer that the **Presidents of the Elders** among **Christians** were more distinct in their "order" from the remaining **Elders** than they were among the **Jews**, because both the former and the latter exercised that power of **Ordaining** in the name of the entire council of elders <term>Presbyterii</term>. Moreover, in all other matters, since the **Presidents** shared the same office and duty as the other **Elders**, and formed the same **Senate** with them, there is absolutely no reason why they should be judged by men to be of a different order.

Furthermore, if in the **Greater Jewish Councils** <term>Consistoriis</term> <note>Referring to the Great Sanhedrin in Jerusalem.</note> the **Presidents** and the **Elders** constituted one and the same **Body**, how much more would this have been the case in the **Lesser Councils**? For in those, the dignity and eminence of the **President** was much less conspicuous, as can easily be seen from the examples we collected in the **Previous Book**. Now, it is certain that the **Christian Councils of Elders** (unless perhaps you except the one in **Jerusalem**) were not very large in the first institution of **Christianity**, and therefore they are much more to be compared with the **Lesser Jewish Councils** than with the **Greater**. Not to mention that **Christ the Lord** specifically warned His **Disciples** to be on their guard against seeking **Dominion** <term>Principatu</term> <note>original: "Principatu"; referring to Christ's command that "the greatest among you shall be your servant."</note>. Since His warnings were fresh at that time, and the affairs of the **Church** were otherwise quite humble, and the **Church’s Leaders** were bound together by the tightest bond of charity, we must think that the unique dignity of the **Presidency** in the beginnings of the **Church** vanished to such an extent that hardly any distinction was observed between the **Presidents** and the remaining **Elders**, and hardly any dignity or eminence appeared above the others.

<header>ON THE ATTRIBUTES OF RULERS BOOK III.</header>

It is very well attested among Hebrew authors that the **Elders** <term>Presbyteris</term> <note>From the Greek "presbyteros," meaning "elder." In this context, it refers to the members of a governing religious council.</note> over whom they presided were such that the Presidents could do nothing in more serious matters without their counsel, and in deliberations, they were obliged to follow the votes of the majority; this is so well known that it is almost pointless to mention it. 

<margin>
See Selden, *On the Sanhedrin*, Book 2, chapter 5, section 2, and chapter 12, section 4.
</margin>

In legal proceedings, this rule was observed: if the Senators disagreed in financial cases, the sentence was delivered according to the **votes of the majority**, even if one side won by only a single vote. But in capital cases, it was established that one side must exceed the other by two votes; I will not dwell on this now, as it pertains less to my current purpose. For I contemplate the **Sanhedrin** <term>Synedria</term> <note>The supreme judicial and administrative councils of the Jewish people.</note> of the Jews primarily in that light by which they taught and governed the Jewish **Church**, just as the Sanhedrins functioned after the **Exile**. For the Sanhedrins of the Christians, which were subject to another Supreme Power in civil and criminal matters, are to be considered exactly like the **Presbyteries of the Jews**, which were subject to a foreign power, as I have already noted several times above. Therefore, those Sanhedrins which ruled the Jewish Church, taught, and determined doubtful cases of Religion, were accustomed to follow the majority of the winning votes in their decisions. The **Gemara** <note>The component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis and commentary.</note> says:

<margin>
Codex Sanhedrin, folio 88, column 2. Selden, *On the Sanhedrin*, Book 3, chapter 2, section 3. See also Maimonides, *Laws of the Sanhedrin*, chapter 8. Letters, Book 3, chapter 9.
</margin>

<note>original Hebrew: שאלה בפניהם אם שמעו אמר להם ואם לאו למיניין רבו המטמאים טמאו ורבו המטהרין טהרו</note> *If a question were proposed among them (concerning what is permitted or forbidden), and something had been received by tradition, the tradition was explained. From all these things now compared, I would like it to be judged whether the Presidents of the Presbyteries in the Apostolic Church are not much more suitably said to have belonged to the same **order** as the other Elders, rather than to a different one; at the same time, for the learned...

## CHAPTER XVII.

*An investigation into whether particular Churches or their Rectors held any **relationship** <note>original: σχέσιν (schesin), meaning a connection or state of being related.</note> among themselves, such that the **Presbytery** <term>Presbyterium</term> <note>A council of elders or ministers that governs a local church.</note> of one Church depended upon the Presbytery or Presbyteries of other Churches as if they were superior in authority. It is proven that after the removal of the **Jerusalem Sanhedrin**, which was fortified by Apostolic authority, all Churches and the Presbyteries of private Churches were made independent, though still maintaining the necessary acts of fellowship, which private Christian societies are obliged to cultivate by the Law of Christ. It is then shown what those acts of fellowship are; then how and when **Metropolitans** <term>Metropolitani</term> <note>Bishops who presided over the capital city of a province and had oversight of other bishops in that region.</note> arose; and the conformity of the Synagogue with the Church is demonstrated to be conspicuous in this part as well.*

We have seen the **relationship** <note>original: σχέσει (schesei)</note> that the Elders held mutually among themselves, and especially the relationship of the Assistants to the President of the entire College—even if, in the interest of brevity, we have only touched upon the most essential and necessary points. We must therefore now investigate whether, beyond this internal structure, there was any relationship between the Presbyteries of various Churches, such that one was subject to another or one was ordained toward another, in the same way that a relationship with **Metropolitan Bishops** and **Patriarchs** <note>The highest-ranking bishops in the early church, typically associated with major cities like Rome, Antioch, or Alexandria.</note> was eventually introduced into the Christian Church. We shall speak of this briefly and freely, according to our ability.

<margin>
Acts 15:6, 22.
"Then it pleased the Apostles and Elders, with the whole church."
<note>original Greek: Τότε ἔδοξε τοῖς Ἀποστόλοις καὶ Πρεσβυτέροις σὺν ὅλῃ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ</note>

As long as the city of **Jerusalem** <note>original: Hierosolyma</note> remained the capital of Judea and the primary seat of both the Jewish and Christian religions, and while the first Apostles and the earliest believers in Christ still lived in that city, the *Presbytery* <term>Presbyterium</term> <note>The governing council of elders within the church.</note> together with the congregation of believers in Jerusalem seems to have been regarded in the early Church as the bond and the root of the entire Christian society. If any controversy arose, it was to be submitted to the judgment of this Presbytery; if a new Teacher were to be recommended to the Church, it was appropriate for him to be fortified by the authority of this Jerusalem Presbytery above all others, so that he might give full credit to his doctrine among others. Thus, when the question arose as to whether the Gentiles receiving the Doctrine of Christ should be burdened with the yoke of the **Mosaic Law**, the church at Antioch sent Paul, Barnabas, and other delegates to *Jerusalem* to the Apostles and *Elders*, so that they might look into the question and decree a legal opinion. We read in the **Acts of the Apostles** that this was done by the Apostles and Elders, not without the involvement of the Jerusalem congregation of believers. Thus Paul, although called and instructed immediately by Christ Jesus, did not deny that he held the authority to preach the Gospel; yet he explained and communicated his Doctrine to the Apostles and the more eminent Rectors of the Jerusalem Church, and based on their *consensus*, he argues for its truth in his **Epistle to the Galatians**. Therefore, according to the prophecy of **Isaiah**, the interpretation of the New Law went forth from Jerusalem and Zion. I hope that fair judges of these matters will not find me difficult to agree with on this point.

But since the authority of that primitive Jerusalem *Presbytery* was chiefly derived from the Apostles and their companions—the first witnesses of the truth, endowed by God with singular gifts of grace—and since a fixed and infallible succession of the Spirit and grace was not attached to this Presbytery nor to any other in the whole world, this singular authority and **preeminence** <note>original Greek: ἐξοχή (exoche)</note> soon ceased. This occurred as the Apostles and Apostolic men were dispersed, the Church moved across to **Pella** <note>A city where early Christians reportedly fled during the Roman-Jewish War.</note>, and the City was finally destroyed by the Romans. For although some believers, along with a leader from the **line of David**, returned to the city after it was devastated by **Titus** and restored their homes there, they never regained the singular prerogative of that formerly afflicted Church...

# CHAPTER 17. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

...as far as I know, the Ancients acknowledged thereafter. And since an infallible judgment of truth, or the certain grace of the Holy Spirit, joined with any eminence and authority over others, was not annexed to any Chair or Presbytery <term>Presbyterium</term> <note>The governing council of elders within a church.</note> (as I have said), hence all Presbyteries after the death of the Apostles were held as *equal in right, authority, and dignity*, with no Presbyter or President of a Presbytery depending upon another. That statement of Jerome is most well-known and common, written after the rights of Metropolitans <term>Metropolitanorum</term> <note>Bishops of provincial capitals who held regional authority.</note> were already established, in that famous Letter to Evagrius: <margin>Epistle Part 2. folio 117. column 3.</margin> *Wherever a Bishop may be, whether at Rome or at Gubbio; whether at Constantinople or at Reggio; whether at Alexandria or at Tanis: he is of THE SAME MERIT, and THE SAME PRIESTHOOD. The power of wealth or the humility of poverty does not make a Bishop either higher or lower.*

BUT ALL ARE SUCCESSORS OF THE APOSTLES. Correctly and in keeping with Jerome's aim, **Erasmus** observes in his *Antidote* <note>Refers to Erasmus’s "Antidotum," his scholarly commentary/defense of his editions of the Church Fathers.</note> that *Jerome here seems to make all Bishops equal among themselves, just as if all had succeeded the Apostles in equal measure.* As for what he adds later—that these words of Jerome about *Bishops* could be understood in relation to *Deacons* (namely, that the power of all Bishops over Deacons is equal)—I do not know if Erasmus wrote that quite seriously, though it does not contradict the former sentiment. For when Jerome declares that *all Bishops are Successors of the Apostles*, he certainly means that all depend immediately upon Christ Jesus, and that they recognize no one in the world as their superior in their capacity as Bishops of Christ. For Jerome here imitated the phrasing of the Ancients, who, before the titles of Metropolitans and Patriarchs arose, honored all *Bishops* as equals and as Successors of the Apostles.

<margin>Book 4. Epistle 9. page 137.</margin>
Thus **Cyprian**, after he had defended the fact that he was *a Priest from God and through God*, subsequently continuing the defense of his cause, says that *all* PRELATES HAVE SUCCEEDED THE APOSTLES BY VICARIOUS ORDINATION <note>original: "vicaria ordinatione," meaning they stand in the place of the Apostles through their appointment.</note>. And indeed, in Cyprian’s writings, you may find many other clear testimonies concerning the equality of the Ancient Bishops. I will bring forward those which are now at hand. Thus he writes in his Letter to Antonianus concerning Novatian: <margin>Book 4. Epistle 2. page 116.</margin> *And indeed among our predecessors, some Bishops here in our Province did not think that peace should be granted to adulterers, and they entirely closed the place of penance against acts of adultery; yet they did not withdraw from the COLLEGE of their FELLOW-BISHOPS, nor did they break the unity of the Catholic Church—*

<meta>This page continues the argument that early church leadership was decentralized and equal. ### ON THE ATTRIBUTES OF RULERS, BOOK III, PART I

...[unity] they broke, either through hardness or the severity of their own obstinacy, so that while peace was granted to adulterers among others, he who did not grant it was separated from the Church. Yet, while the bond of harmony remained and the indivisible sacrament of the Catholic Church persisted, **EACH BISHOP DISPOSES AND DIRECTS HIS OWN ACTION, TO RENDER AN ACCOUNT OF HIS PURPOSE TO THE LORD.** <note>original: "Actum suum disponit et dirigit unusquisque episcopus, rationem propositi sui domino redditurus." This quote from Cyprian of Carthage is a foundational argument for "episcopal autonomy"—the idea that a bishop is the supreme authority in his own diocese.</note> Certainly, Cyprian here grants to each Bishop the freest power of deciding in his own Church concerning any cases that arise, and he renders them subject to the judgment of no one <margin>Treatise on the Simplicity of Prelates, page 1641.</margin> except Christ alone. In the same sense, he says elsewhere, *The episcopacy is one, of which a part is held by each individual in its entirety.* <note>original: "Episcopatum unum esse, cujus a singulis in solidum pars teneatur." This suggests that the authority of the office is shared equally by all who hold it, rather than being a hierarchy.</note>

<margin>page 339.</margin> But our Cyprian is nowhere more precise and expressive on this point than in the opinion he delivered at the Council of Carthage, in which the question of baptizing heretics was treated. <note>The Council of Carthage (256 AD) debated whether people baptized by "heretical" groups needed to be re-baptized when joining the mainstream Church.</note> *It remains,* he said, *that we bring forth what each of us thinks about this very matter, judging no one, nor removing anyone from the right of communion because they might think differently. **FOR NEITHER DOES ANY ONE OF US APPOINT HIMSELF A BISHOP OF BISHOPS,** nor has any one driven his colleagues to the necessity of obedience by tyrannical terror, since every Bishop has his own judgment according to the license of his liberty and power, **AND JUST AS HE CANNOT BE JUDGED BY ANOTHER,** so he himself cannot judge another. But let us all await the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ, who alone and uniquely has the power both of preferring us in the government of His Church and of judging our actions.* Therefore, all Bishops are immediately <term>amēsōs</term> <note>From the Greek word meaning "without a mediator" or "directly."</note> subject to Christ Jesus, and subordinated to no higher power besides Him. 

And this is the manifest doctrine of the Ignatian Epistles, <note>Letters attributed to Ignatius of Antioch (c. 35–107 AD), an early Christian martyr and bishop.</note> in which each Bishop is established as depending immediately upon God and bearing the likeness of the most high God on earth. Thus he writes to the Trallians: 
<margin>page 6.</margin> *The Bishop exists as a representation of the Father of all; while the presbyters are as the council of God and the bond of the apostles of Christ.* <note>The original Greek text: "Ὁ Ἐπίσκοπος τῷ Πατρὸς τῶν ὅλων τύπος ὑπάρχει. οἱ δὲ πρεσβύτεροι, ὡς συνέδριον Θεοῦ καὶ σύνδεσμος ἀποστόλων Χριστοῦ."</note> **THE BISHOP BEARS THE IMAGE OF THE PARENT OF THIS UNIVERSE, while the Presbyters are as the Council of God and the Association of the Apostles of Christ.** 

To the Magnesians: <margin>page 13.</margin> *With the Bishop presiding in the place of God, and the Presbyters in the place of the apostolic council.* <note>The original Greek text: "Προκαθημένου τοῦ Ἐπισκόπου εἰς τόπον Θεοῦ καὶ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων εἰς τόπον συνεδρίας τῶν Ἀποστόλων."</note> **WITH THE BISHOP PRESIDING IN THE PLACE OF God, and the Presbyters in the place of the Apostolic Council.** 

To the Smyrneans: <margin>page 36.</margin> *All of you follow the bishop as Jesus Christ follows the Father, and follow the council of elders as the apostles.* <note>The original Greek text: "Πάντες τῷ ἐπισκόπῳ ἀκολουθεῖτε ὡς ὁ Χριστὸς Ἰησοῦς τῷ Πατρὶ, καὶ τῷ πρεσβυτερίῳ δὲ ὡς τοῖς ἀποστόλοις."</note> *Follow the Bishop, all of you, as Jesus Christ follows the Father...*

*The dignity of the priesthood is one and the same for all; and one shall not be called a High Priest at the summit, while another is an incomplete priest; but all are equally priests, all are bishops; as those who have equally received the grace of the All-Holy Spirit.* <note>original Greek: "Ὁ τῆς ἱερωσύνης αξία μία ἐστὶν, καὶ ἡ αὐτὴ ἐπὶ πᾶσι· καὶ οὐ κληθήσεται ἐν τῷ μὲν ἄκρῳ ἱερεὺς, ἐκεῖνος δὲ ἀτελὴς ἱερεὺς· ἀλλὰ πάντες ἐπίσης ἱερεῖς, πάντες ἐπίσκοποι· ὡς καὶ τὴν χάριν τοῦ παναγίου πνεύματος ἐπίσης δεξάμενοι"</note> THE DIGNITY OF THE PRIESTHOOD IS ONE AND THE SAME IN ALL: AND THIS MAN SHALL NOT BE CALLED A SUPREME PRIEST, AND THAT ONE AN IMPERFECT PRIEST, **BUT ALL ARE EQUALLY PRIESTS,** ALL ARE BISHOPS, AS THOSE WHO **HAVE EQUALLY RECEIVED THE GRACE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT.**

But although these things are so, and all Bishops of the primitive Church were of the same dignity and authority with respect to *their office*, and thus one did not depend upon another, nevertheless, not all **relationship** <note>original Greek: "σχέσις" (*schesis*) — a term meaning connection, bond, or relative position.</note> among the Bishops themselves was thereby removed. For since they were all sharers and defenders of one and the same faith, and were bound by that same faith to diligently cultivate mutual charity, friendship, and brotherhood, each of them considered it part of his duty to care for his own flock in such a way that, in the meantime, he did not neglect to practice the communion of faith with the Bishops of neighboring and other famous Churches. Indeed, Bishops often commended their faith to other Bishops and Churches through *letters, legates,* or *conferences*, with very frequent examples in Sacred History. The Churches judged this kind of exercise of union and brotherhood to be useful and necessary, lest the body of the Lord be torn into various parts, and so that the **Unity** of the Church might be preserved. Besides this, there were also other things that fostered that Episcopal Union and the mutual respect of one Church for another.

From this also arose a certain unique relationship <note>original Greek: "σχέσις" (schesis)</note> of one Church to others; the healthy communion of many churches was exercised in a unique and notable way through that act of ordaining.

3. By no argument was that mutual relationship <term>relationship <note>original Greek: σχέσις (schesis)</note></term> of Bishops with one another more clearly declared (preserving that independence which we claimed for them above) than by the fact that several *Bishops* of neighboring Churches, gathered in a Council, exercised the right and power to *depose from the office of Bishop* <note>original Latin: "ab Episcopatu deponendi"</note> their *fellow-Bishops* who had rendered themselves unworthy of the office through their teachings or conduct; which, as Christianity gained strength, happened not infrequently. Truly, if any Bishop had dared to deny or subvert the dogmas of the Faith against ecclesiastical tradition, or had prostituted his dignity with significant vices, and this had become known to neighboring *Bishops* through legitimate witnesses, the Bishops of neighboring Churches convened and were called together in a Synod. Having discovered the truth after the cause was duly examined, and after remedies for salvation and peace had been attempted in vain, they removed the unworthy Bishops from their office. This has already been declared by the notable example of Paul of Samosata <note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Antioch who was deposed for heresy regarding the nature of Christ</note> and established by the so-called Apostolic Canons.

For this reason, more prudent Bishops also invited other Bishops into council to judge the cause of Presbyters, so that the sentence passed would have more weight and authority.

# BOOK 3. ON THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF CHURCH GOVERNORS.

->Page 864<-

Although a particular Church <note>original: "Ecclesia particularis"</note> does not depend on another, it is nonetheless considered to depend on the *universal Church* insofar as it regards itself as a member of the whole and universal Church, in whose communion it must persevere with pious faith according to the rule. The same logic applies to the *Bishops* of individual Churches. Following the departure of the Apostles, all were considered to depend on no one except Christ alone; yet this was under a tacit condition: that they remained Bishops of the Christian Church. This means they were not to subvert the common doctrine of the Church and were to fulfill the necessary requirements of the Episcopacy. Since it is not presumed of any individual Church that it wishes to separate itself from the communion of the Catholic <note>In this context, "Catholic" refers to the "universal" or "whole" church rather than a specific denomination</note> Church—that is, from the other individual churches to which it is bound by its own faith—it follows that the *Bishops* and *Presbyters* <note>term: Presbyter — an elder or priest</note> of those churches are also deemed to depend on the universal Church. They are obligated by the power of their office to govern their church in such a way that it does not cease to be a member of the universal Church.

Because they were promoted to the Episcopacy of the Church under this condition, if they should openly violate that condition, the power arises for other particular churches and their Bishops to investigate the doctrine and morals of the sinning Bishop and to pass judgment on them. I admit, indeed, that the judgment of a Bishop could be entrusted to the Clergy and the People of the Church over which he presides. However, since it had already become the custom in ancient times that Bishops were ordained not by Presbyters but by the Bishops of neighboring churches, and since the judgment of the Clergy could easily be corrupted by their Bishop, and the common people <note>original: "Plebs"</note> were not sufficiently trained to render judgment due to ignorance, the judgment regarding a Bishop was entrusted to several Bishops of neighboring churches. In that act, these neighbors would represent the universal Church.

Truly, from these *acts of communion* which many individual churches and their peoples cultivated among themselves—whether regarding *Doctrine*, the *practice of Religion*, or the *morals* of the leaders themselves—new titles of ecclesiastical dignity easily arose through abuse. These titles, such as *Archbishops*, *Metropolitans* <note>Bishops of a provincial capital</note>, *Primates*, and finally *Patriarchs*, were unknown in the first centuries of Christianity. For when accusations had to be managed, letters written to summon the Bishops of the same province, and Councils convened, order required that some procedure be observed in organizing such accusations and writing letters, and even that the most worthy... <unclear>one among them should take the lead</unclear>.

<summary>This page explains that while local churches are independent, their bishops are accountable to the universal Church. It describes how the practical need for peer oversight of a bishop's doctrine and conduct led to the development of higher hierarchical titles like Archbishops and Patriarchs.</summary>

<keywords>universal church, bishop, presbyter, communion, metropolitan, primate, patriarch, councils, church hierarchy, ecclesiastical law</keywords>

...that the *Bishop* of a larger District or Province was first approached, and the duty of convening the other Bishops was laid upon him. Any particular Bishop could be considered the most worthy among *equals*—for indeed, in terms of the nature of their office and authority over their own Churches, they were all *equals*, as we previously understood from Jerome—whether he excelled others in his spiritual gifts, learning, and wisdom; or whether he preceded all other Bishops of the same Province in age or time of Ordination; or whether he governed the largest Church of all in that Province—that is, the one who was placed over the *Metropolis* <term>Metropolis: from the Greek for 'mother-city,' the capital or chief city of a Roman province</term> of that Province.

<margin>See Canon 42 of the Council of Carthage.</margin>
One may easily gather from the history of the Synods <note>term: Synod — a formal meeting of church leaders to decide on matters of doctrine or administration</note> convened regarding the Easter Controversy <note>original: "Controversia Paschalis"; a 2nd-century dispute over the correct date to celebrate Easter</note> found in the writings of Eusebius, that the latter two criteria were primarily considered here. However, the last criterion soon prevailed almost exclusively, so that the primary honor in the Episcopal Order of each Province or District was held by the *Bishops* of the more famous cities of the region, or *Metropolises*. The remaining Bishops were honored after him according to the time of their own Ordination and sat together in Councils in that order, unless some other exceptional arrangement was made. These Metropolitans, having been raised so far above the rest, did not cease as time went on to claim greater authority for themselves over their fellow Bishops and to expand this dignity of theirs by any means possible, so much so that their ambition had to be restrained by the Canons <note>term: Canons — ecclesiastical laws or decrees</note> of the Councils. And although the names *Archbishop* and *Metropolitan* were not yet in frequent use during the *second* and *third centuries* after the birth of Christ, it is most clearly evident that the practice itself had already taken hold in the Church by the end of the second and into the third century, as seen from that most famous *Canon 6 of the Council of Nicaea, the Council of Antioch, and the 34th Apostolic Canon*.

...politans; until finally, under Christian Emperors, with the form of Ecclesiastical Government shaped to match the Political Government, in the *fifth* century after the manifestation of Christ, the names and dignities of *Patriarchs, Primates, and Exarchs* <note>original: "Patriarcharum, Primatum, & Exarchorum"</note> were introduced into the Church. Patriarchs were those placed over the Bishops and Churches of several Provinces (which constituted a certain *diocese* <term>diocese: from the Greek 'dioikēsis,' originally a large administrative district of the Roman Empire containing multiple provinces</term> of the Empire), having under them several *Metropolitans*. These *Metropolitans*, subordinated to the Patriarchs, presided only over the Bishops of a single Province. Certainly, before the Council of Nicaea <note>The First Council of Nicaea, 325 AD</note>, no Patriarchs were known in the Church—at least, no Patriarchal dignity was recognized by that name as distinct from the Metropolitan rank. The dignity of Metropolitans, which had already been introduced into the Church before the Council of Nicaea, was established and confirmed by that Council; and it was only after the Councils of Constantinople <note>381 AD</note> and Chalcedon <note>451 AD</note> that Patriarchs finally emerged as distinct in name and function from Metropolitans. Since learned men such as *Ussher, Beveridge, and Spanheim* <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), William Beveridge (1637–1708), and Friedrich Spanheim (1633–1694) were prominent 17th-century scholars of church history and law</note> have already argued these points excellently and at length, there is no need to dwell on them further. We must now see, therefore, what of this kind was preserved from antiquity in the *Synagogical Government*.

<margin>Canon 4 of the Council of Nicaea. Kabbala, folio 58, column 1. Book 2, chapter 12.</margin>

*First*, there is no doubt that while the Jewish Republic still stood, the supreme authority of the Great Sanhedrin <term>Sanhedrin: the supreme council and court of justice in ancient Jerusalem</term> of Jerusalem was accepted in all the Jewish Synagogues, wherever they might be; just as the authority of the Council of Jerusalem was among Christians for as long as the Apostles presided over it. The Son of Dior, in the *Kabbala* <note>Referring to the 'Sefer ha-Kabbalah' by Abraham ibn Daud, a historical work rather than a mystical one</note>, specifically says regarding Rabbi Gamaliel: <note>original Hebrew: "רבנו שר' ג' זה ראש ישיב' והנשיא ומעשיו מקובלים בכל ארץ ישראל ובכל גליות ולא מיחה המלך ולא אדם לעולם"</note> *“We have learned that Rabbi Gamaliel was the President of the Supreme Senate and its Prince, and that his decrees were accepted throughout the entire land of Israel and in all places of the Exile, with neither the King nor any other person interfering.”* We have produced other relevant matters in the previous Book; it should suffice here only to have mentioned this. For when we compare the Government of the Church with the Government of the Synagogue, everyone understands that this pertains primarily to the Church as first established, which was the daughter of the Synagogue and drew its origin from there. I will add nonetheless: *It is necessary to recognize the one who is first among them and to regard him as the head, and to do nothing extraordinary without his knowledge.* <note>original Greek: "χρὴ τὸν ἐν αὐτοῖς πρῶτον καὶ ἡγεῖσθαι αὐτὸν ὡς κεφαλὴν μηδὲν πράττειν περιττὸν ἄνευ τῆς ἐκείνου γνώμης." This is a citation of Apostolic Canon 34, which defines the relationship between local bishops and their metropolitan.</note>

### CHAPTER 17. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

Second, all Synagogues—after the removal of the Sanhedrins <term>Sanhedrin: the supreme legal and religious assembly of the Jewish people</term> of Palestine and Babylonia, whose authority continued for several centuries after the Destruction of Jerusalem—became self-governing and independent, except insofar as they were bound by their Religion to whatever duties of fellowship and friendship were to be mutually maintained.

<margin>See Buxtorf, *Great Commentary*, chapters 6 and 7. Selden, *On the Sanhedrins*, book 2, chapter 16, section 10. Alting, *Shiloh*, book 4, chapter 5. Morinus, book 2, Exercise 4, chapter 2. Ganz, *Chronology*, at year 4979.</margin>

Christian Churches, both inside and outside Palestine, had a unique *relationship* <note>original Greek: *σχέσιν* (schesin)</note> to the *Sanhedrin of Jerusalem* as long as the surviving Apostles presided over that Sanhedrin; but after their departure, they were in no way dependent on one another. Likewise, we say that the Jewish Synagogues, which were dispersed throughout the entire world, after the removal of the *Supreme Sanhedrins*—in which the authority of the Jerusalem Sanhedrin had been preserved—entirely began to be self-governing, each independent of the other. This deserves special notice, even though the authority of the Jewish Supreme Sanhedrin was preserved for much longer (at least in some part) than that of the Christians. Specifically, after Jerusalem was destroyed, the *Supreme Sanhedrin of the Nation* was not immediately abolished; rather, although its authority was weakened in various ways, it continued for some time after that event. First, after the Destruction, that Sanhedrin (or the Supreme Academy of Palestine) sat in *Jafne* <note>also known as Jamnia</note>, then in *Tsippori* <note>Sepphoris</note>, and finally in *Tiberias*, where at last—as can be gathered from Roman Laws—it ceased in the *fifth century*. However, in the *third century* after the birth of the Lord, the Babylonian Courts or Schools (first that of *Sura*) began to flourish greatly, guided by men of the highest learning and authority among the Nation. The leadership of these schools was headed by Rabbi *Huna*, during the lifetime of Rabbi *Judah the Holy* <note>Judah ha-Nasi, the compiler of the Mishnah</note>, the Compiler of the Traditions. Nor did those leaders of the supreme Babylonian Academy yield in either teaching or authority to the leaders of the supreme Academy of Palestine. Indeed, as the former splendor of the Palestinian Sanhedrins or Schools gradually faded, the authority of the Babylonian institution grew with great increases; and those celebrated *Babylonian Ecclesiastical Sanhedrins* continued until the *eleventh century* after the birth of Christ. Benjamin of Tudela <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish traveler and chronicler</note>, a writer of the twelfth century, still recognizes the *Ethnarchs* <term>Ethnarch: a ruler over a specific ethnic group or province; here referring to the Exilarch or "Prince of the Captivity"</term> of *Baghdad*, though their authority (if Benjamin is to be believed in these matters) in teaching and deciding on the dogmas of Religion...

**SOUTHERN FRANCE** <note>original: *Gallia Narbonensis*, a Roman province in southern France including Languedoc and Provence</note>, and proclaimed all those who read the books of Rabbi Moses <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the famous philosopher and author of "The Guide for the Perplexed"</note> to be heretics. What Kimchi could not do in person, he accomplished through his letters. Indeed, in a short time, formal excommunications and thunderbolts of anathema <note>A formal curse by a religious authority, excommunicating a person or denouncing a doctrine</note> were sent not only from the leading Rabbis of those kingdoms, but **FROM ALL THE INDIVIDUAL SYNAGOGUES BY COMMON CONSENT**, by which the three men mentioned above were struck and cast down. Behold the synagogues of France and Spain, entirely free and independent <note>original: *sui juris*, "of their own right"</note>, in no way depending on one another! There was no Primate, no Patriarch, no Prince. One synagogue excommunicates another, without there being any supreme Tribunal to settle and resolve the dispute. Whatever pertains to maintaining and establishing mutual communion must necessarily occur through the *free* consent of all the academies and synagogues, such as the consent most conveniently obtained in a Synod, or an assembly of several Doctors. Through *consent*, I say, *free* and without any higher authority compelling that consent.

Nevertheless, it happens to be pleasing and joyful to me to observe, even from a later perspective, the conformity between the Church and the Synagogue.

The son of Dioris, *Rab*, and *Samuel*, distinguished disciples of *Rabbi Judah* <note>original Greek: τ' α’γ’ις, "the holy," referring to Judah ha-Nasi, the compiler of the Mishnah</note>, moved to Babylonia around the year 3979, near the end of Judah's life. There, they both restored and established the famous Babylonian Schools. They were soon followed by *Rabbi Huna*, who secured great dignity and authority for the Presidents of Babylonia, as he was said to trace his lineage back to King David. Hebrew chronologists generally agree that *Rabbi Huna* was only raised to that highest honor of the Babylonian Presidency after the death of Rabbi Judah. However, it seems clear from the Talmudic Code that *Rabbi Huna* held the leadership of the Babylonian academies and synagogues while *Rabbi Judah the Holy* was still living and flourishing. Indeed, in the Jerusalem Talmud, *Rabbi Huna* is introduced speaking thus:

<note>original Hebrew: אילו סליק רב הונא להכא אנא קאים ליה מן קדמוהי למה דהוא מן יהודה ואנא מן בנימין והוא מן דכריא ואנא מן נוקבתא</note>
"If RAV HUNA, the BABYLONIAN EXILARCH <note>original Latin: Aichmalotarcha, from the Greek for "leader of the captives"</note>, were to come up here, I would rise in his presence; because he is from the tribe of Judah, while I am from Benjamin; he is from the male line of Judah, and I am from the female line."

The author of the *Juchasin* <note>A famous 15th-century Jewish history book</note>, as noted by Morin, does not disagree. If this is true, then the Babylonian Exilarchs arose, or at least began to flourish, *at the beginning of the third century after the birth of Christ*, and not around the *middle of that century*, as common chronology holds. These Jewish leaders—whether in Palestine, Babylonia, or Egypt—are frequently called **PATRIARCHS** in Roman laws and by the Christian writers of the first centuries, as has been proven long ago by very learned men and indicated by us above.

Now, there is no doubt that while the Jewish State <note>original Latin: Republica</note> still stood, all those Jewish rulers <term>Ethnarchs<gloss>National leaders of a specific ethnic group within the empire</gloss></term>, even in the most remote regions, were subject to the Great Sanhedrin in Jerusalem. But after the Jewish State was dissolved by the Romans and the authority of that Sanhedrin was diminished, I do not believe that the leaders (or Patriarchs) of other famous regions still depended on the Sanhedrin of Palestine. Rather, I am of the opinion that the *Alexandrian* and *Babylonian* Patriarchs exercised independent authority in sacred matters within their own districts <note>original: Dioceses</note>, and were no longer subject to the Palestinian Sanhedrin. This is especially true since the Babylonian academies flourished alongside the academies of Palestine after the time of *Rabbi Judah*...

# OF THE INCIDENTAL QUALITIES OF LEADERS, BOOK III, PART [3]

It is not clear from Hebrew historians whether those Babylonian courts <note>original Latin: "curias," referring to judicial or administrative bodies</note> depended on the Palestinian Synedrion <note>original: "Synedrio Canaanitico," literally the Canaanite Synedrion</note>. On the contrary, Hebrew authors speak of the Synedrions and Princes of both those regions as if they were courts independent of one another and of the highest authority. They also attribute the same name, **Nasi** <note>original Hebrew: נשיא, meaning "Prince" or "President"</note>, to the leaders of those Synedrions, as we have said above.
<margin>Book 2, chapter 5.</margin>
Indeed, Rabbi Judah, the Prince of the Palestinian Synedrions, not only acknowledged Rabbi Huna as equal to himself in dignity, but even as his superior in terms of natural lineage.
<margin>Itinerary, page 115.</margin>
Benjamin of Tudela <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler who documented the state of Jewish communities across Europe, Asia, and Africa</note> also, in his own time, while recognizing a certain **Rosh Galut** <note>original Hebrew: ראש גלות, meaning "Head of the Exile" or "Exilarch"</note>, the Exilarch of Baghdad, nevertheless mentioned another supreme Prefect of all the synagogues of Egypt. He calls him **Sar Sarim** <note>original Hebrew: שר שרים</note>, **PRINCE OF PRINCES**, and **Rosh le-kol Kehillot Mitzrayim** <note>original Hebrew: ראש לכל קהלות מצרים</note>, **PREFECT OF ALL THE SYNAGOGUES OF EGYPT**, who was certainly not dependent on the Exilarch of Baghdad whom Benjamin had previously described. Indeed, he describes the **administration** <note>original Greek: διοίκησιν, "dioikēsin"</note> of the Baghdad leader as being very extensive,
<margin>page 73.</margin>
yet not as something that encompassed Egypt. Therefore, the Palestinian Synedrion, unless I am mistaken, had its own unique **administration**, which is designated by the name *“the Western Parts”* in a certain law of the Emperors Theodosius and Valentinian.
<margin>Book 17, Code regarding the Jews and the Sky-Worshiper Heretics. See Morin, in the place cited.</margin>
And it is clear that Cilicia <note>A coastal region in what is now southern Turkey</note> was subject to them from what Epiphanius relates concerning the Apostle Joseph. I am not unaware that Jews of later times attribute universal rule over all synagogues to the Babylonian Patriarchs. But those things are claimed regarding later times, when the Palestinian Synedrions had been extinguished, and they must be taken with a grain of salt.

By these **Jewish Patriarchs**, each of whom had their own very extensive **administration**, I would judge that a prelude was made for the **Christian Patriarchs**, who finally claimed this name for themselves in the fifth century, although the office itself existed without this name in the preceding century. Indeed, the most learned men do not doubt that the name of **Patriarch** passed over from the Synagogue.
<margin>Annotations on Canon 6 of the Council of Nicaea, page 52.</margin>

### CHAPTER 17. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

...ARCHS. So say various others who explain this name. Next, Beveridge <note>William Beveridge (1637–1708), an English clergyman and scholar of church law</note> demonstrates that it was only in the **fifth century** that this name was given to the Bishops of various dioceses. For in the Letter of Emperor Hadrian, which Vopiscus <note>Flavius Vopiscus, one of the purported authors of the *Augustan History*</note> presents in his account of Saturninus, a *Patriarch* is to be understood as a Prince, or some Ethnarch <note>A ruler of a specific ethnic group or province</note> of the Jews. This has been learnedly proven by other most learned men, and especially by the celebrated Spanheim <note>Friedrich Spanheim (1632–1701), a Dutch theologian and historian</note> in his *Historico-Theological Dissertations*. Primarily, however, the Bishops of Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem were decorated with this title.

Indeed, even if no Metropolitans <note>Bishops with authority over a provincial capital and other bishops</note> subject to those higher Patriarchs were known in the preceding fourth century at the time of the Council of Nicaea <note>The first ecumenical council of the Christian Church in 325 AD</note>, nevertheless, such extensive <term>districts</term> <note>original Greek: διοικήσεις (dioikēseis), the administrative root of the modern word "diocese"</note> were assigned to certain Metropolitan Bishops of Alexandria, Rome, and Antioch that they were far more similar to Patriarchs than to Metropolitans. Nor would I dare to deny that Christians—receding more and more from the simplicity of the Apostolic institution and introducing certain more eminent authorities into the Church with titles of honor and dignity—had the example of the Synagogal Government of that time before their eyes. For the Patriarchs of the Jews had almost as much power over the synagogues of their <term>district</term> <note>original Greek: διοικήσεως (dioikēseos)</note> as the Christian Metropolitans had already acquired for themselves over the churches of their jurisdiction in the *fourth century*. Here, therefore, I find a greater agreement between the Synagogue and the Church than I would wish.

## CHAPTER XVIII.

*It is proven that the **number** of **Presbyters** <note>original: "Presbyterorum"; Elders or leaders of the local congregation</note> in the **Presbyteries** <note>original: "Presbyteriis"; the governing councils of elders</note>, both **Jewish** and **Christian**, **varied according to the nature** of the places and circumstances. Next, the **honorariums or stipends** of the Presbyters, both of the **Church** and the **Synagogue**, are discussed, showing again the agreement of the customs of both in this regard. Afterward, some points are added concerning the **hereditary transfer** of the **Office of Leadership** from Father to Son, again comparing the customs of the **Synagogue** and the **Ancient Church**.*

We have now finished the more weighty parts of this argument. What remains may be touched upon briefly. In these matters, the prescribed order requires that we first deal with the **NUMBER OF PRESBYTERS** who constituted the **Sacred Consistories** <note>original: "Consistoria"; high councils or governing bodies</note> among the Ancients, whether Christians or Jews.

In the writings of the New Testament, nor, as far as I know, in the Canons of the **Ancient Church**, is a defined **number** of **Presbyters** for each **Church** established. The Apostles left that to the wisdom and care of each individual **Church**. And where the **Presbyters** of **Churches** are mentioned in the writings of the New Covenant, their number is nowhere defined. But since some **Churches** were larger and more crowded, and others consisted of a smaller number of believers, it is consistent with reason to think that the Apostles set many over some and fewer over others, and adapted the **Presbytery** of each **Church** to the condition of that **Church**. This is required by the order and reason according to which all things ought to be done in the **Sanctuary**.

In the **Ancient Church** now, which followed the Apostolic Church as its model, it was so received that no defined number of Presbyters was prescribed for any **Church** by the **Canons of the Universal Church**. Instead, the **Bishops** of each particular **Church**, with the consent of the **Clergy** and the **People**, co-opted <note>original: "coopta-"; the process of electing or appointing new members to a body by the existing members</note> as many **Presbyters** into the **Clergy**—

From this it finally happened that the Senate of Presbyters, especially in the larger Churches, became very large and consisted of more members than was fitting. <margin>Epistle to Evagrius, Volume 2, Page 117.</margin> Jerome says for that reason, *it is their fewness that makes Deacons honorable, while the CROWD MAKES PRESBYTERS CONTEMPTIBLE.* Indeed, in several places, as also at Rome, the Apostolic institution was observed, so that *Deacons*, properly so-called, did not exceed the number seven; on the contrary, there was everywhere a sufficiently large abundance of *Presbyters*, whereby honor grew for the Deacons, and the dignity of the Presbyters became cheapened.

Let it be an example that in the time of Cornelius, Bishop of Rome, around the middle of the third century after the manifestation of Christ, forty-six Presbyters presided over the Roman Church—if indeed those letters which Eusebius presents under this name were truly written by Cornelius. <margin>Ecclesiastical History, book 6, chapter 43.</margin> Thus Cornelius writes concerning Novatus <note>A priest in Rome who became a rival claimant to the papacy, leading to a schism</note>: *The "champion" of the Gospel did not know that there ought to be one Bishop in a universal church; in which, however, he was not ignorant—for how could he be?—that there are forty-six presbyters and seven deacons.* Therefore, that "defender of the Gospel" was ignorant that *there ought to be one Bishop in the Catholic <note>Here meaning the "universal" or "whole" church of a city</note> Church; in which, however, he knew—for how could he not know that?—THAT THERE ARE INDEED FORTY-SIX PRESBYTERS* (Valesius <note>Henri Valois, a 17th-century scholar and editor of Eusebius</note> wrote *four* by a slight distraction of mind) and seven Deacons. How large was the Roman Church even then, while Paganism was still predominant and often raging against it? <margin>Novel 3. # CHAPTER 18. SYNAGOGUES AND THE CHURCH.

<margin>1 Timothy 5:17.</margin>
...to Timothy, when among other things he proclaims that *the elders who rule well* <note>original: "τοὺς καλῶς προεστῶτας πρεσβυτέρους"</note>, are worthy of **double honor** <note>original: "duplici honore"</note>. By *honor* <note>original: "τιμὴν"</note> in this passage, the Apostle understands food and all the necessary supports of life, which are to be provided to the Overseers of the Church by the Church in the manner of an honorary gift <term>Honorarium: a voluntary fee or gift given for professional services, here referring to the support given to clergy</term>. This interpretation is established by the preceding and following verses, following a phrase common among the Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins, and it has been observed generally by both ancient and modern commentators on this passage. These supports, which are to be provided to the Overseers of the Churches, Paul calls **double honor**, having respect—unless I am mistaken—to the food and life-supports to be distributed to widows, of whom he had spoken in the preceding verse as well as in the *beginning of this chapter*. Indeed, compared to the widows, a much more generous and respectable portion of the supports of life was owed to the Overseers of the Church than to the *widows*.

Furthermore, *how much* was to be given to the Overseers and Ministers of the Church, and *in what way* they were to receive this *honorary gift* from individual members of the Church, is nowhere defined in the books of the New Testament; nor was there much need for it to be defined. For these are minor matters and could conveniently be determined by each Church individually. In the first Epistle to the
<margin>chapter 16:2.</margin>
Corinthians, Paul advises them that *on the first day of every week each of them should set aside some money*, and gradually build it into a heap, then, when Paul was present, it was to be *collected* and delivered to the faithful in Jerusalem as an *alms-gift*. But there is no mention there of the supports for the Overseers of the Church. Therefore, nothing is known of the method of giving and collecting this honorary gift except from Ecclesiastical tradition, which relates that it was very simple. Specifically, when the Christians in the most ancient times celebrated the **Sacred Supper and the Love Feasts** <note>original: "Cœnam & Agapas"; common communal meals of the early church</note>, any of the believers would offer gifts of every kind at the Lord's table as if at an *altar*, not excluding *coins*. From these, after the table had been set and the sacred rites celebrated, the remains were left in the power of the Presbytery <term>Presbytery: the council of elders or priests governing a local church</term>, and were distributed by the President, or the Bishop of the elders. These were given both to himself and the rest of the Elders and Deacons, and whoever belonged to the **Clergy** <term>Clergy: the body of all people ordained for religious duties</term>, as well as to the poor, confessors <note>those who suffered for their faith but were not martyred</note>, widows, orphans, and other wretched persons; and not only to those Christians, but also, as opportunity allowed, to the Gentiles; nor even just to the members of their own Church...

...but also of *others*. We have already heard the Martyr <note>Likely referring to Justin Martyr</note> testifying above regarding those offered gifts; now let us hear Tertullian <note>Tertullian (c. 155–220 AD) was a prolific early Christian author from Carthage</note>:

> *Each person, he says, places a modest contribution <note>original: "stipem"</note> on a monthly day, or whenever he wishes, and only if he is willing and able. For no one is compelled, but contributes of his own accord. These are, as it were, the deposits of piety. For they are not spent on feasts, nor drinking bouts, nor thankless gluttony, but for feeding and burying the poor, for boys and girls deprived of means and parents, for the elderly confined to their homes, for those who have suffered shipwreck, and for any who are in the mines, on islands, or in prisons for the sake of their Christian profession.*

Therefore, up to this point, no money was demanded from the believers, nor were fixed salaries <note>original: "salaria"</note> established for the Overseers. Indeed, Apollonius <note>An anti-Montanist writer of the late 2nd century</note> accused the Montanists <note>A prophetic Christian movement deemed heretical by the mainstream church</note> of this practice, in contrast to the Orthodox.

<margin>
Ecclesiastical History, Book 5, chapter 18.
</margin>

His words are read in Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the "Father of Church History"</note> and are of great note on this subject: "Is it not he <note>Referring to Montanus</note> who appointed collectors of money? Who, under the name of offerings, craftily manages the taking of gifts? Who provides salaries for those who preach his word, so that the teaching of the word might be strengthened through gluttony?" *Who (Montanus) appointed TAX COLLECTORS, who cleverly oversaw the taking of sordid gifts UNDER THE NAME OF OFFERINGS, and who provides salaries to those preaching his doctrine, so that his doctrine might grow strong through the foul gluttony of the belly,* as Valesius <note>Henri Valois, a 17th-century scholar of church history</note> elegantly translates. Indeed, those who wished to appear more prominent than others deposited larger sums of money with the Church as early as the second century, as seen in the example of the heretic Marcion in Tertullian. It is also clear from both Eusebius and Lactantius that by the time of the Diocletian Persecution <note>The last major persecution of Christians in the Roman Empire, beginning in 303 AD</note>, individual Christian Churches already possessed certain immovable goods <note>Real estate or land</note>, which were either given to them as gifts and legacies or purchased from the remaining funds of the ecclesiastical offerings.

# CONCERNING THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF LEADERS, BOOK III.

<margin>
See Servius and the Commentary on that passage of Virgil’s *Aeneid*, book 8, verse 721: "He reviews the gifts of the peoples." Also *Antiquities*, book 12, chapter 3; book 13, chapter 5 and 8, etc. <note>These references point to classical and historical descriptions of "Crown Gold," a customary gift given to rulers.</note>
</margin>

In Roman law, this is sometimes designated by the name *Aurum Coronarium* <term>Crown Gold: originally a voluntary gift of golden crowns to a victor, which evolved into a specialized tax</term>. Among the Romans, this term was used somewhat generally for a voluntary—yet established—payment of money made to the Patriarchs and certain Princes; for more on this, one may consult Petit and Morin <note>Samuel Petit and Jean Morin were prominent 17th-century scholars of ancient law and ecclesiastical history</note>. Indeed, the ancients called it "crown gold" because it was either offered or demanded during triumphs. The origin of the practice was that allies and friends (and even conquered peoples themselves) would offer golden crowns to the Victor, as if congratulating him and surrounding him with his due merit. These crowns were carried before him in the triumph and displayed to the people, as has been observed by other most learned men. It is also clear from Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian</note> that the **Jews** paid a tribute under this name, called *stephanitas* <note>original Greek: στεφανίτας, meaning "crown-taxes"</note>, to the Kings who were their conquerors. Since this [conquest element] did not apply to the Patriarchs, the interpretation of *Crown Gold* in this specific case must be the one I just applied <note>i.e., a voluntary but expected honorary stipend</note>. The Patriarchs maintained not only their own families in a most splendid fashion through these offerings, but they also distributed a portion of them to their Apostles and the Senates of their Sanhedrins. This is what Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century Church Father</note>, if I am not mistaken, calls *the apostolic collection* <note>original Greek: τὴν τῆς Ἀποστολῆς ἐπικα- (likely referencing the tribute sent to the Patriarch via his messengers/apostles)</note>. If those most great and celebrated Sages were sustained in this manner, it seems beyond doubt that lesser leaders, by way of *gerasia* <note>original Greek: γερασίᾳ, meaning "honorary rewards" or "dues of seniority"</note>, received some honorary payments for their own sustenance from the subjects of their *paroikia* <note>original Greek: παροικίας, meaning "district" or "parish"</note>, according to the circumstances of the place. It was a received custom that Masters should receive established salaries for certain acts of the Sacred or Civil Court. At the very least, the Jews generally gave so that they would not abandon those who devoted themselves entirely to their duties,

<margin>
Against Vigilantius.
</margin>

> according to that saying of Jerome: *This custom persists in Judea even now, not only among us, but also among the Hebrews: that those who meditate on the Law of the Lord day and night, and have no portion on earth except God alone, ARE SUSTAINED BY THE MINISTRIES OF THE SYNAGOGUES and of the whole world.*

3. However, just as the Apostle Paul made it his singular aim in promoting the Kingdom of Christ to receive nothing or very little from certain Churches for his own livelihood, so too did the Hebrew Teachers—the most perfect Sages of ancient times—boast that even if they were reduced to great poverty, they did not wish to receive anything from the community, but rather sought to provide food and clothing for themselves through their own labor. Maimonides says: *Flay the skin of carcasses [in the market for a wage] rather than [saying]*

<margin>
Laws of Gifts to the Poor, chapter 10, § 18.
</margin>

*to the community: "I am a great sage, I am a priest, support me." And in this way they commanded...* <note>This is a famous rabbinic injunction emphasizing the dignity of manual labor over dependency on communal funds for scholars.</note>

### CHAPTER 18. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

The greatest of the sages were woodcutters, bearers of beams, and water-carriers for gardens, and workers in iron and charcoal; they did not ask from the community, nor did they receive from them when they offered it to them. <note>original Hebrew: חכמים גדולי החכמים היו מהם חוטבי עצים ונושאי הקורות ושואבי מים לגנות ועושים הנפח והפחמים ולא שאלו מן הצבור ולא קיבלו מהם כשנתנו להם</note> *For it is better to skin the carcasses of beasts than to say to the People: "I am an illustrious Wise Man; I am a Priest, support me." And concerning this, the Sages have commanded: Among the most excellent Sages were those who chopped wood, carried beams, and drew water to irrigate gardens, and worked with iron and charcoal; they sought nothing from the Community <note>The Latin text uses "Ecclesia" here to refer to the Jewish congregation or "Kahal"</note>, nor did they accept anything when people offered them something of their own accord.*

Beyond these things, we do not wish to overlook that, just as those ancient members of the Jewish Elders <term>Presbyterium: the council of elders or the Sanhedrin</term> and their Presidents persevered in that office of the Elders throughout their whole lives—unless they conducted themselves unworthily or disorderly, and thus brought it upon themselves to be removed from office—so too the Presidents of those *Elders* often transferred that dignity to their **Sons**, sometimes even while they were minors. For this reason, Epiphanius says <margin>Against Heresies, 30.</margin> that the son of the Patriarch Hillel was raised into the Patriarchate, adding: *For no one else seizes the honors among the Jews, but the son succeeds the father.* <note>original Greek: Οὐδείς γὰר ἄלλος ἁרπάζει τὰς ἀρχὰς παρὰ τοῖς Ἰσδαίοις, ἀλλὰ υἱὸς, πατέρα διαδέχεται</note> This must, however, be taken with a grain of salt. For the logic regarding the Patriarchs of Palestine and Babylon was slightly different from the other Presidents of the minor Elders, since the former were considered to trace their lineage from David (or from the tribe of Judah).

Thus, where the dignity of the Babylonian **Exilarchs** <term>Aichmalotarcha: from the Greek for "leader of the captives," the political head of the Jewish community in Babylon</term> is extolled beyond measure by Maimonides in his work on the *Sanhedrin*, and their power is raised above the power of the Patriarchs of Palestine, these words are read in the margin: <margin>On Chapter 4 of the Laws of the Sanhedrin.</margin> *In the Jerusalem Talmud it is read thus: Why is the Babylonian Head of the Exile greater than the Prince in the Land of Israel? Because the former comes from the male line and the latter from the female line.* <note>original Hebrew: בירושלמי מפני מה ראש גולה שבבבל גדול מן הנשיא שבא"י מפני שהוא בא מן הזכרים והנשיא בא מן הנקבות</note> This seems to be understood as referring not only to the tribe of Judah, but specifically to the Davidic Family. And although they rarely departed from that succession of posterity, it occasionally happened nonetheless. An example occurs in Rabbi Chanina, the successor of Rabbi Judah the Holy, concerning whom Rabbi Abraham writes in this manner: <margin>In the Book of Tradition, folio 60, column 2. <note>The "Kabbala" mentioned here refers to the "Sefer Ha-Kabbalah" by Abraham ibn Daud, a historical work, not the mystical tradition.</note></margin> *Rabbi Chanina, after the death of our Holy Teacher, sat at the head; he was Rabbi Chanina bar Hama, for so our Holy Teacher commanded, and his colleagues were his sons...*

<margin>Ecclesiastical History, book 7, chapter 30.</margin>

And just as among the Hebrews the Presidents of the Sanhedrins and Academies sometimes took on colleagues in their teaching office or ordained successors, so we read in Church History that Narcissus, the Bishop of the Church of Jerusalem, took Alexander, the Bishop of Cappadocia, as his colleague in the government of the Church (as Jerome records). We also read that Paulinus,

the Bishop of Antioch, when he was about to depart this life, ordained Evagrius in his place, as Theodoret records, even if these cases were somewhat rare and unusual.

I will pause here now, lest this discussion create boredom for the reader by its length, and lest I seem to pursue this argument with too much meticulousness and unnecessary research. Otherwise, I would not lack material for raising various other questions about certain incidental matters regarding the leaders of the Church and the Synagogue, and for comparing them in those areas as well. For example: In the larger cities, when there were multiple synagogues, were there also multiple ecclesiastical <term>senates: councils of elders or presbyters</term>? Was it permitted for the leaders of synagogues and Sanhedrins to transfer from the leadership of one Academy or Church to another more honorable or larger leadership, provided a legitimate call intervened? Both seem to be answered in the affirmative, with some restriction. The Jews certainly had several ecclesiastical senates in one and the same place at times, provided that the Jews living in a single city were truly distinct groups...

## CHAPTER I.

*After the previously provided outline of the following treatise, the **MINISTERS OF THE SYNAGOGUES** of the modern day, known by the titles **Hazan** and **Sheliach Tzibur**, are described. A proven distinction is noted, however, between these titles and the persons so named in the ancient Synagogue. In the ancient setting, the **Sheliach Tzibur**, specifically called the **ENVOYS OF THE ASSEMBLY**, were those appointed to lead prayers for the gathering, whether regularly or for special occasions; while the **Chazanim**, the **MINISTERS**, performed the lowlier tasks of the synagogue.*

Here is a translation of it: the **Azan** <note>The author uses a Latinized form of *Chazzan*. ב. [2.] Just as the more learned among the Hebrews, following the mind of the Ancients, distinguish between the *Minister* and the *Legate of the Congregation*, so too they speak of the *Minister of the Synagogue* in a lowlier way, but of the *Legate of the Congregation* more honorably. Jarchius <note>The Latinized name for Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, 1040–1105).</note> elsewhere significantly describes the *Minister of the Synagogue* in this manner:

*The Chazzan of the Synagogue is the servant* <gloss>Hebrew: Shamash</gloss> *of the synagogue, upon whom lies the burden of managing all the affairs of the synagogue—namely, bringing the Book of the Law into the Ark and bringing it out from it, uncovering the Ark, and arranging everything in the synagogue correctly.* <note>The author includes the Greek term *ho Hyperetes* (ὁ Ὑπηρέτης), meaning "the attendant" or "assistant," to link the synagogue role to terms used in the New Testament.</note> Regarding the **Legate of the Congregation**, however, they speak quite honorably.

<margin>Laws of Prayer (Hilcoth Tephilla), chapter 8, section 8.</margin>

ג. [3.] Legates of the congregation of this kind functioned in this ordinary office for the purpose of pouring forth prayers, or they were appointed for it for an extraordinary occasion. The passage I just produced from the Tractate *Sukkah* <note>The author writes "Succa," referring to the Talmudic tractate regarding the Festival of Tabernacles.</note> is certainly to be understood as referring to such an *Ordinary Legate*, because there seems to be no doubt that the Alexandrian Church <note>The author uses *Ecclesia* (Church) to mean a Jewish religious assembly or congregation.</note> had a fixed and permanent administrator for reciting prayers, and common and very frequent mention of them is made in the Rituals. ### CHAPTER II.

->*The genuine meaning of the Names **Shaliach Tzibbur** <note>Messenger or Legate of the Congregation.</note> and **Chazzan** is revealed and illustrated from many testimonies, with the somewhat obscure origin of the word **Chazzan** likewise investigated. In particular, it is proven that **Chazzan** is usually used by Hebrew authors for a <term>Hyperete <gloss>an assistant or under-servant</gloss></term>, or a MINISTER OF AN INFERIOR ORDER; and **Shaliach Tzibbur** is to be translated not as MESSENGER, but as LEGATE OF THE ASSEMBLY.*<-

After we have begun to recognize those roles of the *Ministers of the Synagogue* and *Legates of the Assembly* from a distance, it is now necessary to indicate more distinctly the genuine meaning and origin of the **Names** by which we said they are called, **Shaliach Tzibbur** and **Chazzan**; for we are usually led into a clear knowledge of things through a genuine understanding of their Names.

The word **Chazzan** is quite common and familiar in Hebrew writings, and it generally denotes some *Minister of an inferior order*, such as honorable political, ecclesiastical, or academic bodies are accustomed to have ready to carry out any of their duties. It is now our task to prove this with very clear testimonies.

**Chazzan** is clearly used for a MINISTER of the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme judicial council of ancient Israel.</note> in the Code of the book *Maccoth* <note>The tractate dealing with punishments.</note>, where the ritual of scourging is described: *How do they scourge him?* <note>original: כיצד מלקין אותו</note>

### CHAPTER 2. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

...to see where the boys ought to read; yet he himself should not read. What is called *Chazzan* in the text, the most learned Schmidius <note>Erasmus Schmid (1570–1637), a German Greek scholar and theologian.</note> translates as <term>READER OF THE CHURCH</term> <note>Latin: LECTOREM ECCLESIÆ</note>. There is a twofold interpretation of this passage, as you may see in the works of Jarchius <note>A common Latinized name for Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note>, whose explanatory words I will place here:

*The Chazzan of the congregation is the one who calls forth the Seven Readers to read from the Law; and it often happens that he does not know where they ought to read on the following Sabbath morning. Therefore, he observes where the children who frequent the Master's School are reading this Sabbath. They read according to the order of the Sabbath Lessons by the light of a candle in the house of the Synagogue; from this, therefore, the Minister of the Synagogue understands which Section of Scripture must be read the following day.* <note>The text explains how the attendant used the children's Friday night study sessions to prepare for the official Saturday service.</note>

*Another Interpretation: The Chazzan* <term>TEACHES</term> *(instructs)* <term>THE BOYS</term>, *and sees where they ought to begin their reading the next day (the Sabbath), and where they should complete their legal sections.* <note>The Hebrew "Parashiot" refers to the weekly Torah portions.</note> Therefore, according to this latter exposition, the <term>Chazzan</term> is surely a <term>Schoolmaster</term> <note>Latin: Ludi Magister</note>, and he has the boys whom he teaches present with him in the Synagogue to determine where the reading should begin and end for the following Sabbath. Maimonides and Bartenora <note>Famous medieval rabbinical commentators.</note> followed this same exposition.

<margin>In the place cited.</margin>
L’Empereur <note>Constantinus L’Empereur, a 17th-century Dutch Hebraist.</note> writes well regarding this passage: *In the Code of the Sabbath it is established that in the evening, or the day before the Sabbath near the start of the Sabbath, the Chazzan should not read, but only show the boys what they ought to read: lest he perhaps adjust the lamp to see more clearly and distinctly—that is, lest by moving the lamp he pour oil onto the wick, and thus be found acting against the prohibition of lighting a fire on the Sabbath.*

**WHERE IT IS CLEAR, BOTH FROM THE CIRCUMSTANCE ITSELF AND FROM OTHER RELATED EXPLANATIONS, THAT THE CHAZZAN IS HE WHO BOTH TEACHES THE BOYS AND HIMSELF ALSO READS THE SCRIPTURE TO THE PEOPLE.**

But we are truly glad that the person we find as a *Minister of Sacred Things* in the Talmud, we find clearly mentioned in the writings of the New Testament. Specifically, this is the *servant* <note>Greek: ὑπηρέτης (hypērētēs), meaning an assistant or under-rower.</note> of whom there is most distinct mention in the Gospel of Luke, in the account of Christ preaching:

<margin>Chapter 4, verse 20.</margin>

*And when he had folded the book and given it back to the* <term>MINISTER OF THE SYNAGOGUE</term>, *he sat down.* It is the same <term>MINISTER</term>, therefore, who had the care of the Book of the Law, and of bringing it forth and returning it...
