# ON THE NAMES OF MINISTERS, BOOK III, PART
<meta>catchword: CH</meta>

...of carrying [the scrolls] into the Ark, he is called **the assistant** <note>Greek: *ho hypēretēs*</note>, which in Hebrew is the **Chazzan**.
<margin>Heresies, 30</margin> For Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his "Panarion," a treatise against heresies.</note> also correctly translated the term **Chazzan** as **deacon** <note>Greek: *diakonon*</note> and **assistant** <note>Greek: *hypēretēn*</note>, as we observed in the preceding chapter.

But what is the origin of the word? Hebrew authors, followed by Christians, commonly derive it **from the word "to see"** <note>original Hebrew: *chazah*, meaning to see or inspect</note>, because it was the duty of the Synagogue Ministers not only to attend to every necessity of the Synagogue, but also to see whether the Readers were performing their duty correctly in their reading. <margin>In the *Aruch* on this word</margin> Rabbi Nathan <note>Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome, an 11th-century Italian lexicographer who authored the *Aruch*, a fundamental dictionary of Talmudic Hebrew and Aramaic.</note> says: *In the first chapter of the Tractate on the Sabbath, it is held: Truly the Chazzan sees from where the boys ought to begin their reading.* By which is understood there the **DELEGATE** <note>Latin: *Legatus*</note> (Public Minister) **OF THE CHURCH** <note>Latin: *Ecclesiae*. Christian scholars often used this word to refer to the Synagogue congregation to emphasize parallels with Christian structure.</note>. *And in Aramaic* <note>Latin: *Chaldaice*</note> *the word "sees" is explained as "chazyah," because it is his duty to see how the reading is done, and how he calls people to the Reading of the Law.* <margin>In the *Tishbi* on this word</margin> Elias <note>Elias Levita (1469–1549), a renowned Renaissance Hebrew grammarian and lexicographer.</note> followed Rabbi Nathan, yet added something of his own: *The **Chazzan** of the **CONGREGATION** <note>Hebrew: *Hacceneseth*</note> is he who leads the assembly in public prayers (and thus ensures they fulfill their duty toward God in this regard), and he is called Chazzan from the notion of seeing, because he must **SEE** how he reads (or how the reading is done) and which men he should call up to read from the Law. Thus the author of the Aruch explains this word. And I have certainly found that the **DELEGATE** (Minister) **OF THE CHURCH**, I mean the **PUBLIC ASSISTANT** <note>Greek: *hypēretēs*; Hebrew: *shammash*</note>, is called Chazzan. And he is also called Chazzan because it is his duty to see what the needs of the Synagogue are, so that he may do what has been assigned to him.* Elias first repeats the opinion of Nathan, that the **Chazzan** is so named from the root **to see** <note>original: *chazah*</note>, because he must attend to the reading of the Law in the Synagogue and provide that worthy men are called to the Reading of the Law. Elias adds, however, that he could also be called this because it was his role in general to attend to the <margin>In the Lexicon on this word</margin> interests of the assembly and diligently procure them. Philippus Aquinas <note>A 17th-century Hebrew scholar and convert from Judaism who served as a professor in Paris.</note> states: *A delegate of the congregation; and he is so named because he is the overseer of the readers.*

# CHAPTER 2. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

The **Chazzan** <term>Chazzan: A synagogue official whose roles historically ranged from a sexton or caretaker to a leader of prayer.</term> is the **Messenger of the Synagogue**, and is so named because he pays attention to those who are reading. Among Christian scholars, this etymology was very pleasing to the illustrious **Lightfoot** <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and Hebraist known for using Talmudic literature to illustrate the New Testament.</note>, who—translating the **Chazzanim** <note>original Hebrew: *hachazzanim* (plural)</note> according to **Nathan** and **Elijah** <note>Referring to Nathan ben Jehiel and Elijah Levita, famous Jewish lexicographers.</note> as **INSPECTORS**—took the opportunity to compare the name and office of the **Chazzan** with the name and office of the **Bishop** <note>Greek: *Episkopos*, meaning "Overseer" or "Inspector"</note> in the early Christian Church. We shall discuss this, if it pleases God, in the **following chapter**. However, the illustrious **Buxtorf** <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a prominent Hebraist and author of a definitive Hebrew and Aramaic lexicon.</note> assigned no etymology to this word in his Lexicon.

Recently, a certain Learned Man contended that the word **Chazzan** should be derived from the Arabic **chazan** <note>Arabic: *khazan*</note>, spelled with the dotted *Heth* or *Cha*, which **Schindler** and **Golius** <note>Valentin Schindler and Jacobus Golius, authors of influential 17th-century Oriental dictionaries.</note> translate as **to hide and to preserve**. From this also comes **Chasin**, which according to Golius is a **Treasurer or Storekeeper**, and according to Schindler is a **Steward or Chamberlain**. He supports his opinion with probability for two reasons: first, because it is quite unusual to derive a title of office ending in *-on* from verbs whose third radical is a "resting" letter <note>A technical grammatical point referring to Hebrew roots ending in the letter He (equivalent to the root *chazah*).</note>; and second, because from that Arabic principle, the meaning would be broader than could be conveniently confined within such narrow limits of ministry. Indeed, the word **Chazzan** never denotes "inspection" joined with the care of a thing among either the Hebrews or the Chaldeans <note>Latin: *Chaldaeos*, referring here to speakers of Aramaic.</note>, but only simple vision, **beholding, etc.** Furthermore, he proves that the word **Chazzan**, in those cases where it is employed by Hebrew writers, comfortably carries the meaning of a **GUARDIAN**; for example, when Hebrew writers explain the **Chazzans of the city** <note>original Hebrew: *chazzanei mata*</note> as the **GUARDIANS OF THE CITY** <note>original Hebrew: *shomrei ha-ir*</note>.

As these arguments are plausible, they are worthy of being more diligently weighed by learned men. As for me: 1. I concede that the word **Chazzan** occurs among the Arabs with that notion which the illustrious man indicated. And it seems entirely likely that the Arabs have their word **chazan** from the Hebrew root **chasan**, by a slight exchange of the related letters *Zayin* and *Samekh* <note>The Hebrew letters 'z' and 's' are phonetically similar and often interchangeable in ancient Semitic linguistics.</note>, because that word **chasan** (as is evident from the passive *Niphal* form) formerly carried that same meaning of **possessing and storing up** among the Hebrews.
<margin>Isaiah 23:18. *Sacred Geography*, Book 2, chapter 26.</margin>
Besides Schindler, I have **Bochart** <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar.</note> as the author of this opinion, who derives from these words the Latin **Gaza** <note>Meaning "treasure" or "treasury."</note> and that word most widely accepted among the peoples of Europe today, **Magazine** <note>original: *Machazin* or *Magasin*</note>. Indeed, Schindler has already specifically noted in his Lexicon that **Chazzan** among the Arabs signifies a **STEWARD AND MINISTER**. 2. I admit that this etymology of the word **Chazzan** fits well enough for a **Minister**, or **Sexton of the Synagogue**, insofar as it is his duty to preserve and store away the **Book of the Law** <note>The Torah scroll</note> and to care for the house of the Synagogue. In Dutch: **But you shall look around.** <note>original Dutch: *Doch Gÿ siet omme.*</note>

Specifically, the verb <term>Ganaz: A root meaning to hide, store, or archive, from which the word "Genizah" (a storage for sacred texts) is derived.</term> signifies hiding and putting something away in a treasury, and thus conserving and reserving by hiding it; but *Shamar* signifies to observe something externally, and to keep watch by observing, as is done by Sentinels or Guards of the City.

3. This origin is also less conveniently applicable to this title in cases where it refers not to a place, but to a Gathering, such as when the Public Minister of the Sanhedrin is called the **Chazzan Ha-Knesset** <note>The "Minister of the Assembly" or "Synagogue Attendant."</note>, the Minister of the Congregation; it would be, I say, less fitting to call him the *Guardian of the Congregation*.

4. Regarding the point that it is unusual for the name of an Office ending in *nun* [ן] to be derived from Verbs ending in a radical *he* [ה], I confess that no similar instance occurs to me. However, it is an established rule among the Hebrews that names signifying a perpetual act are formed from participles by the addition of the termination *nun*. Following this 
<margin>Sacred Grammar by Glassius. Book 1. Rule C.</margin> 
<margin>C.</margin> observation, from *Chomes* (**Defrauding**), comes *Chomsan* (**Defrauder**); from *Gozel* (**Seizing**), comes *Gazlan* (**Robber**). In this same form, from *Chozeh* (tending, observing), could be derived **Chazzan**, a Title of Office that consists in perpetual care, attention, and observation, such as that of **Ministers**. This is further supported by the doubling of the middle radical letter, which signifies the perpetual exercise of an action. Thus, *Gonev* signifies one who is stealing, but *Gannev* signifies a **Thief**—one who has made a habit of stealing. Therefore, the **Chazzan Ha-Knesset**, according to *Rabbi Nathan's* etymology, would be the Minister of the Assembly, whose duty it is to see, attend, and observe the state of the assembly and what it requires, being prepared for all the duties of the Assembly...

Let us now add a word concerning the genuine meaning of the expression <term>Shliach Tzibbur: Literally "Messenger of the Assembly," this refers to the person who leads the congregation in prayer.</term>. It denotes a DELEGATE or a MESSENGER OF THE CHURCH. Indeed, this very interpretation allows for a twofold sense. For someone is called the Messenger *of another* either because they are ready to serve that person's every whim and command in any business and are ordered to perform various menial tasks for them; or, someone can be called a *Legate* in this way who performs a more honorable office in the name and place of another, to be held with the same dignity as the person who delegated them.

<margin>Chapter 8, Section 5.</margin>

## BOOK III. PART II. ON THE NAMES OF MINISTERS.

I shall append the commentaries of the two most excellent interpreters of the <term>Mishnah: the first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions</term> regarding these words.

<margin>Commentary on this passage.</margin> Maimonides says: <note>original Hebrew: "כשם ששליח צבור חייב ר"ל חייב בברכות ומחלוקת רבן גמליאל וחכמים אינו בתפלות ראש השנה בלבד אבל המחלוקת בכל התפלות כולם כי חכמים אומרים כשם ששליח צבור אינו יוצא ידי חובתן אלא בתפלת עצמו כך כל יחיד ויחיד אינו יוצא ידי חובתו אלא בתפלת עצמו ורבן גמליאל אומר כי בתפלת שליח צבור יוצא ידי חובתו היודע להתפלל ומי שאינו יודע והלכ' כרבן גמליאל בתפילו' של ראש השנה ושל יום הכפורי' בלבד לפי שתפילו' ארוכות בשני ימים אלו"</note> *Just as the* **MESSENGER OF THE ASSEMBLY** *is obligated: that is, he is obligated to recite the Blessings. Moreover, the disagreement between Gamaliel and the other Doctors <note>Referring to the "Sages" or "Chachamim" of the Talmudic era.</note> is not only concerning the Prayers recited on the Festival of the New Year <note>Rosh Hashanah</note>, but concerning all other prayers whatsoever. For the Sages say that, just as the* **MESSENGER OF THE ASSEMBLY** *does not rightly fulfill his duty unless he has recited those prayers himself, so also every private Israelite cannot satisfy his duty unless he also recites those same prayers. Conversely, Rabban Gamaliel said that through the prayers of the* **MESSENGER OF THE ASSEMBLY**, *satisfaction is made both for those who are skilled and capable of reciting the prayers, and for those who do not know how to pray. And this opinion of Rabbi Gamaliel holds sway only regarding the prayers of the Festival of the New Year and the Day of Atonement <note>Yom Kippur</note>, because the prayers of these two Festivals are longer.* Therefore, according to this definition by Maimonides:

1. *The Messenger of the Assembly, reciting the prayers in public, is always deemed to perform this duty for all those who are themselves incapable of reciting the prayers; by performing this public office of praying for them, he renders them all free from the obligation to pray.*

2. *On the Festivals of the New Year and Atonement, however, he renders everyone in general free from that duty, because very few Israelites are skilled in those specific Hymns of Praise <note>original Latin: "Eulogiarum"</note>. From this it follows that the Minister of the Synagogue, who is appointed to recite the prayers, sustains the Role of many people in his praying, and on those two more illustrious days, he fulfills the duty of everyone, like a common* **Messenger of the Assembly** *to God.*

<margin>In this place.</margin> *Let us now hear the paraphrase of Bartenora:* <note>Obadiah ben Abraham of Bertinoro, a 15th-century Italian rabbi and famous Mishnah commentator.</note> <note>original Hebrew: "כשם ששליח צבור חייב בין בברכות של ראש השנה בין בתפלות של כל השנה ואין יוצא ידי חובתו אלא בתפלה שמתפלל"</note> *Just as the Messenger of the Assembly is obligated, whether in the blessings of the New Year or in the prayers of the entire year, and he does not fulfill his duty except through the prayer which he prays...*

### CHAPTER 2. OF SYNAGOGUES AND ASSEMBLIES.

<note>The following Hebrew passage is a classic legal ruling from the Mishnah, the foundation of Jewish law, discussing whether a prayer leader can fulfill the religious obligations of the listeners.</note>

> Every individual who is skilled and knows how to pray must fulfill his own obligation through his own prayer. He does not fulfill his duty except through his own prayer, whether on the New Year or on all other days of the year. The Messenger of the Assembly <note>original: "Sheliach Tzibbur"</note> does not descend before the Ark <note>The prayer podium</note> except to fulfill the obligation for those who are not skilled. [However,] the Messenger of the Assembly fulfills the obligation for the many—both those who are skilled and those who are not—both in the blessings of the New Year and in the prayers of the entire year. Why does the congregation pray silently? So that the Messenger of the Assembly may arrange his prayer. The law follows the Sages regarding the blessings of the entire year, holding that the Messenger of the Assembly only fulfills the obligation for those who are not skilled; but regarding the blessings of the New Year, the Day of Atonement, and the Jubilee—which consist of nine long blessings and not everyone is skilled in them—the law follows Rabban Gamaliel, who held that just as he fulfills the obligation for the unskilled, so too he fulfills it for the skilled.

*Just as* the **MESSENGER OF THE ASSEMBLY** *is obligated both to recite the Blessings of the New Year Festival and the prayers of the whole year, and does not satisfy his office unless he himself recites those prayers, so also every private person who is fit to recite prayers does not fulfill their duties unless they themselves recite those prayers, whether on the Festival of the New Year or through the whole time of the year; and the Minister of the Synagogue, by praying, frees no one from their duty except the unlearned and incapable.* 

*The Messenger of the Assembly frees everyone from their duty (the opinion of Gamaliel): namely, both the skilled in prayer and the unlearned, both in the Blessings of the New Year Festival and in the prayers of the whole year. And why does the Assembly <note>original Latin: "Ecclesia," here referring to the Jewish congregation</note> pray silently? So that the Messenger of the Assembly may rightly order his prayers. However, here the opinion of the Sages <note>The majority of the rabbinic doctors</note> holds regarding the prayers of the whole year, for which the* **MESSENGER OF THE ASSEMBLY**, *by reciting, frees only those from their duty who are unlearned and unskilled; but as for the prayers of the New Year Festival, the Day of Atonement, and the Jubilee—of which kind there are nine longer Blessings, in which not everyone is practiced—the opinion of Rabban Gamaliel holds, that he frees from their duty both the skilled and knowledgeable of prayers, as well as the unlearned and incapable.*

*We see, therefore, from these testimonies, that this Messenger of the Assembly, so called, who recites the prayers in public, always sustains the person of the many (namely, those who cannot fulfill this duty by themselves); but sometimes also (as on the Festival of the New Year, Atonement, etc.) he sustains the person of all, and thus truly acts as a Messenger of the Assembly to God. Wherefore it is probable that this name was given to him with this very significance.* 

<margin>Note on Benjamin, p. 149.</margin>

*It is well, therefore, that Constantinus L’Empereur <note>A 17th-century Dutch Hebraist known for translating Jewish texts into Latin</note> translates* שליח צבור <gloss>Sheliach Tzibur</gloss> *as* **MESSENGER OF THE ASSEMBLY**, *performing his office in the name of the congregation. And thus also correctly the Distinguished...*

The roles of the ministry will be wretchedly entangled with one another. The term *Inspector* enjoys a very broad meaning, and can be applied both to *Rulers* and to *Ministers* according to its various interpretations, as we proved above where we dealt with the meaning of the word **Bishop** <note>original Greek: Ἐπίσκοπος; *Episkopos*</note>.

In Asia, the same number [seven] of **Angels** <note>original Greek: Ἄγγελοι; *Angeloi*, meaning messengers or envoys</note>, or **ENVOYS**, are assigned, to whom the letters and warnings of Christ the Lord, the Supreme Pastor, are directed. For these names are so similar to one another that they could not be more so. And since we do not doubt that the title <gloss>**Messenger of the Congregation**</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: שליח צבור</note> was already accepted and familiar among the Jews at that time, and since the Apostle John was born into the Synagogue and educated there for part of his life, and Christ the Lord spoke with John as such (*whether truly or in a vision, it matters not*), it seems hardly doubtful that this phrase was used in the sense then in use among the Jews.

But surely the Christian churches had no such Delegates of the Churches as the Synagogue had? Certainly, we have compared the *Presbyters* and indeed the *Presidents of the Presbyters* in the Christian Church with the *Jewish Presbyters* and their *Presidents*? How, then, can these same Presidents of the Presbyteries, the **Presidents of the Churches** <note>original Greek: οἱ τῶν Ἐκκλησιῶν Προεστῶτες</note>, be called <gloss>**Messengers of the Congregation**</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: שליחי צבור</note>, or **Angels of the Churches**; these "Angels of the Churches" who were intermediate between the *Overseers* and the *Deacons*? Since the Presidents of the Christian Churches already performed this Act themselves as a matter of course, and solemnly led the Church in prayers (as is clear from Justin Martyr <note>An early Christian apologist, c. 100–165 AD</note>), they could indeed be most appropriately called **ENVOYS OF THE COMMUNITY** <note>original Hebrew: שליחי צבור; *Sheliach Tzibbur*, the representative who leads the congregation in prayer</note>, or **ANGELS OF THE CHURCHES**. This is because they approached God for the Church solemnly and at fixed times, having been delegated, as it were, to God in the Church's name. And since the name **Bishop** <note>original Greek: Ἐπισκόπου; *Episkopou*, meaning overseer</note> does not seem to have been separately attributed to the **Presidents of the Elders** <note>Presbyters</note> at the time when John received his Revelation (for we do not place much confidence in the Ignatian epistles <note>Letters attributed to Ignatius of Antioch, often debated regarding their authenticity and dating</note>, nor do the more learned among the English), I do not see what other more convenient term the Lord could have used to designate these **PRESIDENTS**. This is because the practice of establishing prayers in the assembly was almost entirely unique to these Presidents, just as it was to the **Envoys of the Community** <note>original Hebrew: שליחי צבור</note> in the Synagogue. 

I am surprised that this was not observed by Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note>, who was otherwise most successful in comparing Jewish and Christian antiquities. For he does not seem to have thought of the **Envoy of the Community** here, but instead sought the explanation of the title **Angel of the Church** <note>original Greek: Ἀγγέλου Ἐκκλησίας</note> from Malachi, where the Priests are called **ANGELS OF THE LORD OF HOSTS** <note>original Hebrew: יהוה צבאות; *Yahweh Tzevaot*</note>. However, it is one thing to be an **Angel of the Lord**; and quite another to be an **Angel of the Church**, even if those two roles can not infrequently meet in a single person.

### CHAPTER 3. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES. 913

...the term **Envoy of the Community** <note>original Hebrew: *Tzibbur*; original Greek: *Apostolos tēs Ekklēsias*; original Latin: *Legatus Ecclesiae*</note>, a name which Paul employed twice, if I am not mistaken, in his Epistles; though whether he used it in the same sense as the synagogue is doubtful. The first passage, which appears in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians,

<margin>2 Corinthians 8:23</margin>

reads as follows: *If (a question is raised) concerning Titus, he is **MY COMPANION** <note>original Greek: koinōnos emos</note> and, as far as you are concerned, a co-worker. If the other brothers (are taken into consideration), they are **MESSENGERS** <note>original Greek: Apostoloi; original Latin: Legati</note> of the **CHURCHES**, the Glory of Christ.* Certainly, the Apostle describes with these words those three **Delegates** whom he had sent ahead to the Church of the Corinthians to prepare their collection for the sake of the poor in Jerusalem. These were Titus, Luke, and a certain other Brother whose name was not explicitly mentioned by Paul. Intending to describe them in this verse by their specific characters, he calls **Titus** **his companion** <note>original Greek: ton koinōnon autou</note>, which is the same as if he had said in Hebrew **Chaver** <note>original Hebrew: חבר; meaning a partner or associate</note>, according to that explanation of the word *Chaver* which we established in the preceding sections. The others he calls **MESSENGERS of the CHURCHES**,

<margin>Book 2, chapter 10.</margin>

which you would say in Hebrew as **Shelichei Tzibbur** <note>original Hebrew: שליחי צבור</note>, if *Tzibbur* were used in the plural; otherwise: **Shelichei Kehillot** <note>original Hebrew: שליחי קהלות; "Envoys of the Congregations"</note>. Yet I would not dare to assert that Paul intended to say by this phrase that they were *ordinary* Ministers of the Churches, or their **delegates to God** for the pouring out of **public prayers** <note>The author is distinguishing between a traveling messenger and a liturgical leader who prays on behalf of the people</note>. Rather, the sense of the passage seems to be that they were delegated by other Churches to the Corinthians to take charge of the collection that was to be carried to Jerusalem. In no other sense does Epaphroditus seem to be called by Paul an **Apostle**, or ENVOY of the **Philippians**:

<margin>Philippians 2:25</margin>

*I deemed it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my Brother, and Co-worker, and Fellow-soldier, but **YOUR MESSENGER** <note>original Greek: hymōn de Apostolon</note>, and the minister to my needs.* For he had been sent by the Philippians to Paul to supply him with necessities, and he was certainly an **Envoy of the Church** <note>original Hebrew: Sheliach Tzibbur</note> of the Philippians to Paul, but not an envoy to God. At the very least, that does not seem to be indicated by the phrase in this context.

Indeed, in the Christian Churches there were no **Envoys of the Assembly to God** <note>original Latin: Legati Coetus ad Deum; referring to someone whose primary office was to lead public prayer</note> besides the Bishops and Presbyters, or rather the Presidents of the Presbyteries. The clergy of the most ancient Christian Church consisted only of **Presbyters and Deacons**. Envoys of the Churches, such as those in the Synagogues who held a middle rank between the **Prefects and the Deacons**, existed in the Christian Church... <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page with the word "fuerunt" (were).</note>

ON THE NAMES OF MINISTERS BOOK III. PART II. 914

...[they] were, both because the office of the **Messenger of the Church** <note>original Latin: *Legatus Ecclesiae*; original Hebrew: *Sheliach Tzibbur*</note> was for the most part not a fixed and formal position in the ancient synagogues, but was freely entrusted to any of the more honorable men in the synagogue who were skilled in sacred matters, and because that **Act of Praying**, which was performed by the **Messengers of the Church** in the synagogue, was properly to be performed by the **Overseers** <note>original: *Praefectis*</note> of the synagogue themselves. This was undoubtedly practiced in many synagogues where a large number of scholars was not present. Since, therefore, in the first Christian Churches everything was arranged in the simplest possible manner, there was no need for such extraordinary messengers for praying to God; rather, it was entirely preferable that this act be carried out by the President of the Presbytery <note>the leader of the council of elders</note> as the Messenger of both the Presbytery and the whole Church.

# CHAPTER IV.

*The opinion of certain scholars is praised, who have set out to compare the* **DEACONS** *of the Church, described by Paul in the Epistle to Timothy, with the* **CHAZZANIM** <note>Hebrew: *Chazzanim*, meaning synagogue attendants or overseers</note> *of the Synagogue; and this opinion is supported by the conformity of both their* **NAMES** *and* **OFFICES**. *In particular, the genuine meaning of the terms* **servant** <note>original Greek: *diakonos*</note>, **assistant** <note>original Greek: *hypēretēs*</note>, *and* **servant of the Church** <note>original Greek: *diakonos tēs Ekklēsias*</note>, *compared with the Hebrew* **overseer of the assembly** <note>original Hebrew: *Chazzan ha-Keneset*</note> *and* **overseer** <note>original Hebrew: *Chazzan*</note>, *is discussed.*

<margin>
Prolegomena chapter 3 & book 2 chapter 1.
</margin>
However, we might perhaps more successfully discover the **CHAZZANIM**—whom every synagogue held as fixed ministers of sacred things—within the Christian Church. Certainly, most eminent men—Grotius, Morinus, Selden, Spencer, whose very clear testimonies on this matter I have produced in the preceding sections, and Hammond, who followed in the footsteps of Grotius—have long since pointed out that the **DEACONS**, whom Paul so names and describes in the first Epistle to Timothy, are conformable in both **Name** and **Office** to these Deacons <note>attendants</note> of the synagogue, and were established in the Christian Church by the Apostles (who were Jews by origin) with respect to them. Since this opinion has always seemed probable to me from the time I began to observe the **conformity of the sacred rites of the Synagogue and the Church**, it is not unwelcome that I have finally obtained an opportunity to illustrate it.

### CHAPTER 4. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.
<page-type>text</page-type>

That a certain Rite or Office was derived from the Synagogue to the Church can be proved in almost no other way than by demonstrating a very great **Agreement** between both the *Rite and the Office*. This Agreement must be observed as much in the Name and Nature of the Office as in its accidental characteristics. For since the Apostles—who ordained the Rule and Administration of the Sacred rites of the Christian Church—were Jews by origin, it should not be doubted that where the Church agrees with the Synagogue in a certain sacred Office or Ceremony, the Church received that Ceremony from the Synagogue; for the Church was born from the Synagogue, and the latter is older than the former. All learned and wise men will readily grant me this principle, and therefore I would delay in vain to demonstrate it further. Now, when I find such an agreement between the **OFFICE OF THE CHAZZAN IN THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE DEACONS OF THE CHURCH**, I shall conclude, not without reason, that the latter draw their origin from the former. And we will undoubtedly find this to be true, if we seek it out.

1. The **NAMES** of the Ministers of the Synagogue and the Church agree: the Chazzan <note>Hebrew: *Chazzan*</note> and the **DEACON** <note>Greek: *Diakonos*</note>. Regarding the meaning and origin of the word Chazzan, we saw this in the previous Chapter. It can be translated into Greek as Assistant <note>Greek: *Hypērētēs*</note> or Deacon, since there is no difference in meaning between these words, except that the latter is used more *generally* and the former more *specifically*. Otherwise, both signify any *Minister* who is at hand for one or more persons, and who performs any kind of ministry for the sake of one or many.

The **DEACON** <note>Greek: *Diakonos*</note> is so named *from serving* <note>original Greek: *apo tou diakonein*</note> or *being served* <note>Greek: *diakoneisthai*</note>, that is, *to minister*, *to serve as a handmaid*, or *to act as a minister or servant*. Its root is *Dust* <note>Greek: *Konis*</note>, from which comes *I hasten* <note>Greek: *Koneō*</note>, meaning *I hurry, I rush, or I run and stir up dust by running*. It therefore denotes any minister who performs any office or any kind of labor for another with obedience and compliance; especially those who perform the ministries of the table. This has long been proved with many examples by learned men, and I take it as a given, as it is known to all who are even moderately skilled in the Greek language. Soon, when we come to more specific details, this meaning will become sufficiently clear from the examples then to be brought forward.

**ASSISTANT** <note>Greek: *Hypērētēs*</note> among the Greeks likewise signifies any *minister and servant* who performs ministries for another, especially a *Minister* or a *public Officer* <note>original Latin: *Apparitorem publicum*</note>, as we shall soon see. The Word—

To serve <note>original Greek: ὑπηρετεῖν (hypēretein)</note> is *to minister, to be of service, and to provide labor, obedience, or duty*. The root word is "to row" <note>original Greek: ἐρέσσω (eressō)</note>, or perhaps more generally: *to move, to urge, to propel forward*; from this comes the word for "serving," which means *to be subordinate or to assist*. Having observed these points in advance—which I know no student of literature will deny me—I shall proceed to complete the proof of my hypothesis concerning the agreement of the term <term>Chazzan</term> <note>Hebrew: חזן; an official of the synagogue</note> with the term **Deacon** <note>original Greek: διάκονος (diakonos)</note> through certain propositions, to be declared in order:

<margin>Chapter 2.</margin>
1. I wish it to be accepted as certain that the word <term>Chazzan</term> <note>Hebrew: חזן</note> agrees in meaning with the word **Assistant** <note>original Greek: ὑπηρέτης (hypērētēs)</note>. We have already noted this in the preceding sections based on <margin>Chapter 4, 20.</margin> Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century Church Father</note>, who translates "Azanite" <note>a Greek form of Chazzan</note> by this very word "Assistant," and we have supported the same from the most clear testimony of *Luke*, who explicitly calls the <term>Chazzan</term> of the Synagogue an **Assistant**, a *Public Minister*. And indeed, there are many other testimonies in the history of the New Covenant from which this can be proven. <margin>Chapter 5, 25.</margin> Thus, the "Assistant" in the sermon of Christ the Lord is called a *Public Minister of Justice* in the Gospel of Matthew:
> *Lest your adversary deliver you to the Judge, and the Judge deliver you to the* **ASSISTANT** <note>original Greek: ὑπηρέτῃ (hypēretē)</note>, *and you be cast into prison.*
Who could deny that "Assistant" here carries the same meaning as <margin>Chapter 26, 58. Chapter 7, 32.</margin> the <term>Chazzan of the Assembly</term> <note>Hebrew: חזן הכנסת (Chazzan ha-Knesset)</note> in the Sanhedrin Code <note>The Jewish legal text</note>? It is used the same way later in that history: *And having entered inside, he sat with the assistants.* And in the Gospel of John: *The Pharisees and the chief priests sent assistants to seize him.* Certainly, the "Assistants" in these and other similar places are <term>Chazzans</term>, called so in *Judicial* matters among the Jews, as has long been observed by learned men and, so far as I know, has been denied by no one until now.

2. I now move forward, and I ask that it be further granted to me that the word **Assistant** <note>original Greek: ὑπηρέτης (hypērētēs)</note> agrees in meaning with the word **Deacon**, and therefore the term <term>Chazzan</term> can be rendered just as well by "Deacon" as by "Assistant." And here I will have two things to prove: 1. That among the Greeks, "Deacon" does not denote a minister of greater dignity than an "Assistant." 2. That these two terms are often used interchangeably.

A. > *Whoever wants to be* **GREAT** *among you, let him be your* **DEACON** <note>original Greek: διάκονος (diakonos)</note>, *let him be your* **MINISTER**. *And whoever wants to be* **FIRST** *among you, let him be your* **SERVANT**.
Here "Deacon" and "Servant" <note>original Latin: servus; Greek: doulos</note> are used interchangeably. Furthermore, "Deacon," as the opposite of "Great," seems to correspond entirely here to...

->### ON THE NAMES OF MINISTERS, BOOK III.<-

*To serve* <note>original Greek: ὑπηρετεῖν (hyperetein)</note> *means to minister, to attend to, or to provide labor, obedience, and service. The root word is "to row"* <note>original Greek: ἐρέσσω (eresso)</note>, *or perhaps more generally: to push or propel forward; hence "to serve"* <note>original Greek: ὑπηρετεῖν (hyperetein)</note> *means to serve under or to assist. Having observed these points in advance—which I know no student of literature would deny me—I shall primarily complete the proof of my hypothesis concerning the agreement of the word <term>Hazzan</term> <note>Hebrew: חַזָּן; a synagogue official or attendant</note> with the word <term>Deacon</term> <note>original Greek: διάκονος (diakonos)</note> by clearly declaring certain positions;*

<margin>
Chapter 2.

Chapter 4, 20.

Chapter 5, 25.

Chapter 26, 58.
Chapter 7, 32.
</margin>
1. *I wish it to be accepted as certain that the term <term>Hazzan</term> <note>Hebrew: חַזָּן</note> agrees in meaning with the word <term>Assistant</term> <note>original Greek: Ὑπηρέτης (Hyperetēs)</note>. We have already noted this in previous sections regarding Epiphanius, who translated the term "Azanite" specifically as this very word "Assistant," and we confirm the same from the very clear testimony of Luke. Luke explicitly calls the <term>Hazzan</term> of the Synagogue the "Minister"* <note>original Greek: Ὑπηρέτην (Hyperetēn)</note>, *a Public Servant. There are many other testimonies in the history of the New Covenant from which this can be proven. For instance, the "Assistant"* <note>original Greek: ὁ Ὑπηρέτης (ho Hyperetēs)</note> *in the discourse of Christ the Lord is called a "forensic and public minister" in Matthew: "Lest the adversary hand you over to the Judge, and the Judge hand you over to the officer* <note>original Greek: ὑπηρέτῃ (hypēretē)</note>, *and the Judge hand you over to the MINISTER, so that you are cast into prison." Who could deny that "assistant"* <note>original Greek: ὑπηρέτης (hyperetēs)</note> *here means the same thing as the "Synagogue Attendant"* <note>original Hebrew: חַזָּן הַכְּנֶסֶת (chazzan ha-knesset)</note> *mentioned in the Code of the Sanhedrin? Likewise, later in the same history regarding Peter: "having gone inside, he sat with the officers* <note>original Greek: ὑπηρετῶν (hypēretōn)</note>." *And in John: "The Pharisees and the chief priests sent officers* <note>original Greek: ὑπηρέτας (hypēretas)</note> *to seize him." Certainly, the "Assistants" in these and similar places are the <term>Hazzanim</term> <note>Hebrew: חַזָּנִים; plural of Hazzan</note>, so named in the judicial records among the Jews, as has long been observed by learned men and, as far as I know, denied by no one until now.*

2. *I now move a step forward and further assert that the word "Assistant"* <note>original Greek: Ὑπηρέτης (Hyperetēs)</note> *agrees in meaning with the word "Deacon"* <note>original Greek: Διάκονος (Diakonos)</note>, *and therefore the term <term>Hazzan</term> can be translated just as easily as "Deacon" as it can as "Assistant." Here, two things must be proven by me: 1. That among the Greeks, a "Deacon" was not a minister of higher dignity than an "Assistant." 2. Indeed, that these words are often used interchangeably.*

<margin>
Chapter 20, 26.
27, 28.

Thus, while every "assistant" is a "deacon," not every "deacon" is an "assistant," according to this stricter and more accepted meaning of the word "Assistant." ### CHAPTER V.

*It is established by various arguments that those Seven Stewards <note>original: Oeconomos</note> of the Church of Jerusalem, who were ordained by the Apostles **for the ministry of tables** <note>original Greek: πρὸς διακονίαν τῶν τραπεζῶν</note>, were far different from the Deacons of whom Paul speaks in his Epistles to Timothy and the Philippians, and such as were commonly known by this name in the primitive Christian Churches, as was long ago observed by Chrysostom and the Quinisext Council <note>Also known as the Council in Trullo (692 AD), which addressed matters of discipline and clerical conduct</note>. <margin>Acts 6:1, 2, 3.</margin>
The history of the appointed <term>overseers of the poor<gloss>original Greek: πτωχοτρόφων (ptochotrophon); those who nourish or care for the destitute</gloss></term> in Acts is roughly as follows: when a murmur arose among the Hellenists against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily ministry <note>original Greek: ἐν τῇ διακονίᾳ τῇ καθημερινῇ (en tē diakonia tē kathēmerinē)</note>, in the **DAILY MINISTRY**, the Apostles, having called together the multitude of disciples, proposed that *it was not right for them, having left behind the word of God,* to serve tables <note>original Greek: διακονεῖν τραπέζαις (diakonein trapezais)</note>, to **SERVE TABLES**. When this proposal pleased the people, seven men of proven faith were chosen by them, and were inaugurated into this office by the Apostles both through prayers and the laying on of hands. From these **MINISTERS OF TABLES** <note>original: διακόνοις τῶν τραπεζῶν (diakonois tōn trapezōn)</note> ordained in the primitive Church of Jerusalem, it is commonly thought that the *Office of Deacons* was derived for all other Churches of the Apostolic time. It is accepted by common faith that Paul, in his Epistles to the *Philippians and Timothy*, when speaking of the Deacons of the Churches, understands such Deacons as are narrated in Acts to have been instituted by the Apostles. Whence Cyprian already says:

> *Deacons ought to remember that because the Lord chose Apostles, that is, Bishops and Leaders,* **THE APOSTLES CONSTITUTED DEACONS FOR THEMSELVES** *after the Lord's ascension into heaven, as ministers of their Episcopacy and of the Church.*

But although I foresee that many will hold the contrary opinion to be paradoxical—being undoubtedly unaware that this view has already been defended and established by *Chrysostom* <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople</note>, and over a thousand years ago by an entire *Ecumenical Synod* <note>Referring to the Quinisext Council or Council in Trullo (692 AD), which decreed that the Seven in Acts were not deacons of the liturgy but of the poor</note>—nevertheless, fair and learned readers will easily grant me the freedom to modestly set forth my reasons for the opposing view.

<header>ON THE NAMES OF MINISTERS BOOK III. PART II.</header>

X. It is clear from the records of ancient history, and agreed upon by learned men, that the Deacons of the early Christian Church held an office quite distinct from those seven Overseers of the Poor in the original Church of Jerusalem. In fact, the ordinary Deacons of the churches were so named because they performed the required duties for the Church, the Bishop, and the Presbyters <note>Presbyters: from the Greek *presbyteros*, meaning "elders"; the leaders of the local congregation who assisted the Bishop</note> who represented the Church. This followed the practice of the Synagogue, modeled after the *Synagogal Hazzans* <note>original: *Chazzanitarum Synagogicorum*; the Hazzan was a multifaceted synagogue official who served as an attendant, caretaker, and sometimes a teacher</note>. In contrast, those *Seven-Men* of the Church in Jerusalem were *uniquely ordained by the assembly of believers for the purpose of providing daily food for widows and the poor*. These two roles differ significantly. Nor am I the first to make this observation; it was noted long ago by the Quinisext Ecumenical Synod <note>Quinisext: Also known as the Council in Trullo (692 AD), it was convened to issue disciplinary canons to supplement the 5th and 6th ecumenical councils</note>, held in Constantinople in the Trullo <note>Trullo: The domed hall of the imperial palace where the council met</note> nearly a thousand years ago, whose *Sixteenth Canon* states:

<margin>In Beveridge, volume 1, page 174.</margin>
Since the Book of Acts records that seven deacons were appointed by the Apostles, and the Council of Neocaesarea clearly argued in its published canons that there ought to be seven deacons according to the rule, even if the city is very large—convinced of this by the Book of Acts—we, having aligned the mind of the Fathers with the Apostolic word, have found that they were not speaking of the men who minister in the mysteries <note>original Greek: τοῖς μυστηρίοις διακονομένων (tois mystēriois diakonomenōn); this refers to the deacons’ role in the liturgy, such as assisting with the Eucharist</note>, but concerning the service to the needs of the tables. The Book of Acts states: "In those days..." Interpreting this, the teacher of the Church, John Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD): A prominent Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople, famous for his preaching</note>, decreed as follows: "It is a matter of wonder how the multitude did not fall into conflict over the selection of these men, and how the Apostles were not rejected by them. But what sort of rank did these men hold, and what kind of ordination did they receive? We must learn: was it that of Deacons? Yet this is not what we find in the churches; rather, is it the administration belonging to the Presbyters? And yet, as of then, no one was a Bishop, but only the Apostles. Therefore, I believe the name of 'Deacon' or 'Presbyter' was not yet clearly defined or evident [for this role]..."

Since the Book of Acts records that SEVEN DEACONS WERE APPOINTED BY THE APOSTLES, and the Council of Neocaesarea argued thus clearly in the Canons it published: *That according to the Canon there ought to be SEVEN DEACONS, even if the City be large, of which you will be persuaded from the Book of Acts: we, having adapted the mind of the Fathers to the Apostolic word, HAVE FOUND THAT THEY WERE SPEAKING NOT OF THE MEN WHO MINISTER IN THE MYSTERIES, BUT OF THE MINISTRY PERTAINING TO THE NECESSITIES OF TA-* <note>The Latin text cuts off mid-word here (*necessitatibus*) and continues on the next page.</note>

# CHAPTER 5. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.
<header>CHAPTER 5. THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.</header>
<meta>catchword: Suisse-</meta>

[NECESSI]TIES PERTAINS, since the Book <margin>Acts 6, 1.</margin> of Acts records: *In those days...* Interpreting this, the Doctor of the Church, John Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD): An influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his powerful preaching; his name means "golden-mouthed."</note>, continues as follows: *“It is worth admiring how the multitude was not divided in the election of the men, and how the Apostles were not rejected by them. However, it is necessary to know what kind of authority these men held, and what sort of ordination they received.”* WAS IT PERHAPS THE OFFICE OF DEACONS? AND YET THIS OFFICE [as it later existed] DID NOT EXIST IN THE CHURCHES. But was it the administration of Presbyters <note>Presbyters: From the Greek *presbyteros*, meaning "elders," the group of leaders who served under a Bishop.</note>? Yet there was no Bishop as of yet, only the Apostles. Therefore, I believe the NAME OF NEITHER DEACONS NOR PRESBYTERS was yet open or clearly defined. To these points, the Synod <note>Synod: Here referring to the Council in Trullo (692 AD), which clarified church laws.</note> now submits its own judgment:

“On these grounds, therefore, we also proclaim that the aforementioned seven deacons are not to be understood as those who serve in the Mysteries <note>Mysteries: The term used in the Eastern Church for the Sacraments, particularly the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>, according to the teaching previously interpreted; rather, they were those who were entrusted with the administration of the common needs of those gathered at that time; who in this regard have become for us a model of humanitarian care and zeal toward those in need.” <note>original: "Ἐπὶ τούτοις οὖν κηρύσσομεν... φιλανθρωπίας τε καὶ σπουδῆς;"</note>

Following these things, therefore, we also proclaim THAT THE AFOREMENTIONED SEVEN DEACONS ARE NOT TO BE TAKEN FROM AMONG THOSE WHO SERVE THE MYSTERIES, as the Doctrine was previously explained, but THAT THEY ARE THOSE TO WHOM THE DISPENSATION OF THOSE THINGS WHICH WERE THEN COLLECTED WAS ENTRUSTED AND HANDED OVER. *“Who in this regard have been for us a model of humanitarian care and zeal toward those who are in need.”* Behold the clearest opinion of the Synod, which is the same as our own!

<margin>See Balfour.</margin>
The Synod of Neocaesarea <note>Synod of Neocaesarea: A regional church council held in the early 4th century (c. 314–315 AD) in modern-day Turkey.</note>, in establishing Canon XV regarding the number of Deacons in each church, had supposed that *those Seven Administrators of Widows*, who are mentioned in the Apostolic Acts, were *Deacons* of the same kind as those who performed sacred ministries everywhere in the early churches, and who were noted by this name by Paul in his Epistles to the Philippians and to Timothy. But the Synod [in Trullo] denies this, following Chrysostom, by citing the very words of the Apostolic Acts. From these words, it is clear that the Seven Men ordained in the Church of Jerusalem were appointed outside the regular hierarchy to care for the food of widows, and had almost nothing in common with the ordinary *Deacons of the Churches*, such as those Paul describes in the Epistles to Timothy and the Philippians, who were held to be the *Ministers* of the Church and the *Bishops*. <margin>On Acts 6.</margin> Thus Balsamon, Zonaras, and Aristenus <note>Balsamon, Zonaras, and Aristenus: The three great Byzantine commentators on Canon Law who lived in the 12th century.</note> have advised in their interpretation of the Canon; <margin>In the Lexicon, at the word [Diakonos].</margin> so also Oecumenius <note>Oecumenius: A 6th-century author of a commentary on the New Testament.</note> has noted. Nor does the most learned <term>Deacon</term> <note>original: *Διάκονος* (Diakonos)</note> obscurely yield to them.

Suicer <note>Johann Kaspar Suicer (1619–1684): A Swiss German theologian and author of the *Thesaurus Ecclesiasticus*, a massive dictionary of Greek Church terms.</note>, when explaining the office of the Deacons of the "Apostolic Church" (as he calls it) from these very testimonies, soon adds: *THEREAFTER, THE OFFICE OF DEACONS BEGAN TO BE SOMETHING FAR DIFFERENT*; he then goes on to learnedly trace these true duties of Deacons. Yet, it did not occur to them to say that those so-called Jerusalem Deacons were entirely different from the *Pauline Deacons* <note>Pauline Deacons: The office of deacon as described by the Apostle Paul in 1 Timothy 3, which emphasizes spiritual character rather than just financial administration.</note>; instead, they preferred to say that the *office of Deacons* thereafter began to be something else. If indeed the Deacons of all the early churches were instituted after the example of these *Seven Jerusalem Stewards*, how could it be that they were so quickly removed from this office and ordained to other Ministries? What reason could be given for such a sudden change? Is it not, therefore, better and easier to say that the *Pauline Deacons*, whose order Paul describes in the Epistle to Timothy, were of a far different kind than these *Administrators of the Widows in Jerusalem*?

"...not neglecting widows, orphans, or the poor; but always providing for what is good before God and men." <note>This Greek passage is a quote from Polycarp’s Epistle to the Philippians, chapter 6. Original: "ἀμελοῦντες χήρας, ἢ ὀρφανῶν, ἢ πένητος· ἀλλὰ προνοοῦντες ἀεὶ τοῦ καλοῦ ἐνώπιον Θεοῦ καὶ ἀνθρώπων"</note> Presbyters <term>Presbyteri; elders or leaders of the local church</term> should be inclined to compassion, merciful toward everyone, bringing back those who have gone astray, visiting all the sick, **NOT NEGLECTING WIDOWS, ORPHANS, AND THE POOR, but always providing good things before God and men.** <note>original Latin: "VIDUAS, PUPILLOS, ET PAUPERES NON NEGLIGENTES, sed semper providentes bona coram Deo & hominibus."</note> Certainly, the duty that is attributed to those seven so-called Deacons in the book of Acts is attributed here by Polycarp to the Presbyters themselves. Why is this, unless it is because Deacons in the *primitive* Church were never truly ordained to this office <note>The author is arguing that caring for the poor was originally a general duty of church elders, not a specific "Deacon" office.</note>?

3. If the Deacons, as described by Paul in his Epistle to Timothy, were truly considered by him to be *Collectors and Distributors of Alms* and *Stewards of Widows' Tables*, how is it that absolutely no sign or indication of that office appears in Paul’s description of *Deacons*? Or at least, why is it that among the *qualities* Paul desires in them, no *quality* is mentioned that specifically relates to this particular duty of theirs? Elsewhere, indeed, when discussing Ministers of the Word, he says: "it is required in stewards that a man be found faithful." <note>original Greek/Latin: "ἐν τοῖς οἰκονόμοις ζητεῖσθαι, ἵνα πιστός τις εὑρεθῇ / Dispensatoribus requiri, ut quis FIDUS reperiatur" (1 Corinthians 4:2).</note> But he does not mention this virtue among the requirements for Deacons—a virtue which nonetheless seems it should have been listed among the primary ones, if the care of the poor and the duty of collecting and distributing alms had truly been mandated to Deacons. In the case of *Deaconesses*, he certainly desires that they be "faithful in all things"; but they did not manage financial matters. Therefore, that requirement must refer to something else.

# ON THE NAMES OF MINISTERS BOOK III. PART II.
<header>ON THE NAMES OF MINISTERS BOOK III. PART II.</header>

...daily <note>The text begins mid-word, completing "quotidiano" (daily), likely referring to the "daily distribution" in Acts 6:1.</note>, and the Apostles declared to the multitude that it was not right for them, having left behind the word of God, **to serve tables** <note>original Greek: *διακονῶσι τραπέζαις*</note>. Since people saw from this history that these **Seven Men** <term>Septem-Viri; the seven assistants chosen by the early Church in Jerusalem</term> were elected to **serve** <note>original Greek: *διακονεῖν*</note> tables, and the same authors observed that Paul, in his Epistles, mentions **Deacons** <note>original: *Diaconos*</note> when describing the Ministers of the Church, they concluded by comparing the two that Paul was speaking in his Epistles about the same kind of persons as Luke was in the Book of Acts. Thus, they began to likewise call those **Seven Men**, the overseers of the goods of the Jerusalem Church, **Deacons**. 

However, in my judgment, this is done incorrectly. **α.** <note>First point</note> Because Luke in Acts speaks **concerning the ministry of tables** <note>original Greek: *περὶ τῆς διακονίας τῶν τραπεζῶν*</note>, while Paul speaks **concerning the ministry of the Church** <note>original Greek: *περὶ τῆς διακονίας τῆς Ἐκκλησίας*</note>. Just as the name of *Bishop* <note>original: *Episcopus*</note> in Paul's writing refers to the *Church*, so the name of *Deacon*, which is likewise a relative term, must be referred to the *Church*—namely, to the performance of sacred functions in the Church—**not to the tables of widows**. 

**β.** <note>Second point</note> Even if I were to grant that someone who serves the tables of widows could be called a *Minister* <note>original: *Diaconon*</note> or *Servant* <note>original: *Ministrum*</note> by virtue of that office—specifically **of the tables** <note>original Greek: *τῶν τραπεζῶν*</note>—nevertheless, because the word "Deacon" was subsequently applied by ecclesiastical usage **as a specific title** <note>original Greek: *φερωνύμως*, meaning "according to its name" or "by name-association"</note> to the *ordinary* sacred *Ministers* of the Church, a great confusion in speech must inevitably arise if everyone mentioned as **serving** <note>original Greek: *διακονεῖν*</note> in any passage of Scripture is immediately called a **Deacon** <note>original Greek and vernacular: *διάκονοι, Diakenen*</note>. 

Certainly, the Apostles, up until the time these *Seven Men* were ordained in the Jerusalem Church, had performed the same duty—that is, they **had served the tables** <note>original Greek and Latin: *διηκόνησαν ταῖς τραπέζαις, MINISTRAVERANT MENSIS*</note>, for they had the ultimate care of the widows; yet they did not take the ordinary name of *Deacons* from that. Indeed, in the very context of these words, they say: **But we will persevere in prayer and the ministry of the word** <note>original Greek and Latin: *Ἡμεῖς δὲ τῇ προσευχῇ καὶ τῇ διακονίᾳ τῇ λόγου προσκαρτερήσομεν; Nos autem in precibus & MINISTERIO SERMONIS perseverabimus*</note>. The Apostles could be called *Deacons* because of this *ministry of the word* just as much as these *Seven Men* are because of the *ministry of tables*. In fact, they would have a much greater right to it, as that *Ministry* is more excellent than this one. Yet they are not called so, among other reasons, to avoid the confusion that would arise in speech; and thus there is also no just cause why these *Seven Men* should bear this name as a specific title. For in the text itself they are not called *deacons* <note>original Greek: *διάκονοι*</note>, and they are not distinguished by this name by the Apostles. Therefore, when Paul, writing to Timothy, spo-

...speak concerning the **deacons of the Church** <note>original Greek: *περὶ τῶν διακόνων τῆς Ἐκκλησίας*</note>, whom he specifically calls **Deacons**, and since in the Book of Acts mention is made of the **Ministry of the Tables of widows** <note>original: *Ministerii Mensarum vidualium*</note> being entrusted to certain persons—who are nevertheless not specifically called *deacons* <note>original Greek: *διάκονοι*</note> in the text—there is no reason why we should compare these two passages and explain one by the other. 

There are indeed, I confess, those who interpret that **Serving at Tables** <note>original Greek: *διακονεῖν ταῖς τραπέζαις*</note> so loosely that it includes every **Ministry**, not only of the common **tables of widows**, but also of the **sacred tables** in the **Lord’s Suppers** and **Love Feasts** <term>Agapae; communal meals eaten by the early Church</term>, a ministry which was specifically commanded to the Deacons of the Church. But what of it? Were the **widows of the Hellenists** <term>Hellenists; Greek-speaking Jewish Christians</term> neglected in the Ministry of the **Lord’s Supper** and the **Love Feasts**? Is **serving tables** the same as **serving the Lord's table**? Had the Apostles ever served **sacred tables**? Is the **ministry** of **sacred tables** opposed to the **ministry of the word** <note>original Greek: *τῇ διακονίᾳ τοῦ λόγου*</note>? Therefore, all circumstances suggest that by the **ministry of tables** <note>original Greek: *τὴν διακονίαν τῶν τραπεζῶν*</note>, one must understand the economic care by which food is provided in common for widows and the poor; and thus this exception fails.

# CHAPTER 5. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

...as they had done until now, they had looked after the widows and the poor. Yet the Jerusalem Church could not have lacked ordinary Deacons and Ministers of the Sacred Rites. Therefore, the great number of believers in the City of Jerusalem, the frequency of the poor, and the rare generosity of believers in that Apostolic age required *extraordinary officials* of that kind. However, in other places where such extraordinary cases did not occur, Bishops and Presbyters were able to have the care of the poor and dispense donated goods, just as was done by the Apostles before the dissension arose between the Hellenists and the Hebrews. 

β. No one should rashly conclude from the Acts that those *Seven Men* <term>Septem-Viri; a committee or board of seven men</term> performed this duty of theirs only *for a time*, because it is clear from the following context of the History that two of the more distinguished from that *Seven-Man Board*, Stephen and Philip, after that time propagated the Doctrine of the Gospel by debating and teaching—even though the Apostles had set *the ministry of the word* <note>original Greek: τὴν διακονίαν τοῦ λόγου</note> in opposition to *the ministry of tables* <note>original Greek: τῇ διακονίᾳ τῶν τραπεζῶν</note>. Indeed, we read of Stephen's debates and zeal in this very Chapter; <margin>chapter 6, 8.</margin> but concerning Philip, we read that he went away to *Samaria* and preached the Gospel, <margin>chapter 8, 5.</margin> performed many signs there, and baptized many in the name of *Jesus*. That this *Philip* was the *Deacon of Tables*, not the *Apostle* of that name, <margin>chapter 8, 14.</margin> is clear both from the fact that in the context of the History itself he is distinguished from the *Apostles*, and from the fact that he was not able to confer the gifts of the *Holy Spirit* on believers while administering baptism, since that was reserved <margin>verse 15.</margin> for Peter and John, who were delegated to the Samaritans. This Philip is later mentioned <margin>chapter 21, 8.</margin> as living in *Caesarea*, and is honored with the title of *evangelist* <note>original Greek: εὐαγγελιστῆ</note>, not *deacon* <note>original Greek: διακόνῳ</note>. The words of Luke are: *And we entered into the house of Philip the* EVANGELIST *WHO WAS ONE OF THOSE SEVEN MEN, and stayed with him.* Why does Luke not say: *of those seven deacons* <note>original Greek: τοῦ ὄντος ἐκ τῶν ἑπτὰ διακόνων</note>? Therefore, it seems that these Seven Men exercised the office of their administration only for *a certain time* and *outside the ordinary course*; for which reason it is not to be presumed that other Churches of that time took an example from them in instituting *Deacons*.

However, it favors the common opinion that *to serve* <note>original Greek: διακονεῖν</note> in the writings of the New Covenant <note>The New Testament</note> sometimes appears with the meaning of *Ministering* to the poor and exercising any duties of charity toward them; and also that *ministry* <note>original Greek: διακονία</note> is taken for the *Ministry* itself of distributing *Alms* or caring for the poor, and therefore the name seems properly for *deacons* <note>original Greek: διακόνοις</note>...

# ON THE NAMES OF MINISTERS, BOOK III.

I admit that the meaning of the words *to serve* <note>original Greek: διακονεῖν</note> and *ministry* <note>original Greek: διακονία</note> has been accepted in the writings of the New Testament in this way; as, for example, in Matthew:

<margin>chapter 15, 25. Acts 12, 25.</margin> 
Romans: *But now I am going to Jerusalem to minister to the saints* <note>original Greek: διακονῶν τοῖς ἁγίοις</note>. And several other places of this kind exist in the writings of the New Testament, which learned men use to illustrate the concept of a *deacon* <note>original Greek: διάκονος</note> in Paul's writings. 

But no one makes any progress through this, because the word *to serve* <note>original Greek: διακονεῖν</note> has many other meanings in the text of the New Covenant <note>The New Testament</note>, which are produced in vain to explain the specific office of the *deacon*. For what is more common in the same New Testament text than that *ministry* <note>original Greek: διακονίαν</note> is understood as the ministry of the word, or the preaching and administration of the Gospel? As, for example, in Paul to the Corinthians: *Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos? But ministers through whom you believed* <note>original Greek: διάκονοι δι᾽ ὧν ἐπιστεύσατε</note>. And to the

> This word is used here to include all who devote their labor to the Gospel, such as the Evangelists, and especially the Apostles themselves. 
<margin>* 2 Corinthians 3, 6; 6, 4; 11, 23. Ephesians 3, 7. Colossians 1, 23.</margin>

However, despite this quite common use of the word, no one will correctly explain to me the meaning of this same word where it is attributed to Ministers properly so called <note>Referring to the specific local church office of Deacon as opposed to the general sense of "servant."</note>. Besides these, the name of *deacon* <note>original Greek: διακόνου</note> is most commonly given to servants who serve their masters at the table, as observed above; this service of the table certainly differs from the office of distributing and dispensing alms. For although those two types of service might sometimes be performed by the same persons, the nature of the ministry and administration is nevertheless different.

### CHAPTER 5. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

Since the words *deacon* <note>original Greek: διακόνου</note> and *to serve* <note>original Greek: διακονεῖν</note> enjoy a very broad meaning, their significance in specific passages must be judged not so much by one absolute usage or another, but from the circumstances of the text and the subjects to which they are attributed. If *to serve* <note>original Greek: διακονεῖν</note> is said of servants with respect to their masters, then it denotes all *servile duties* which a servant is bound to perform for a master, especially *duties at the table*. If it is attributed to the Ministers of Christ and the Gospel, then it denotes the administration of that Word, as happens in the preaching of the Gospel. If it is applied to Priests (as in some places <margin>Antiquities, Book 3, Chapter 8.</margin> in Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note>), then it will designate all the *duties* that were to be observed by them in the Temple. If it is used with respect to Alms <term>Eleemosynas: charitable gifts or relief for the poor</term> and gifts of charity, then it signifies the spending, distribution, or collection of Alms. If the same word is used in relation to the Church, then it denotes the *Ministry* which is performed by Public Ministers in the exercise of religion, whether for the Church or for the Leaders of the Church. And in this latter relation, the word *deacon* <note>original Greek: διακόνου</note> is used by Paul in the letter to Timothy, as we proved in the previous sections.

However, we do not deny that it deserves attention that the words *ministry* <note>original Greek: διακονία</note> and *to serve* <note>original Greek: διακονεῖν</note> in the writings of the New Covenant are sometimes taken for the administration or collection of Alms, because this meaning of those words is not accepted either among the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible; the author notes they never used the specific verb "diakonein."</note> nor among secular authors, as far as I know. And even though I have not seen the Interpreters be very concerned about it, I could not help but persuade myself that there is a Hebraism <term>Hebraism: a Hebrew linguistic idiom or influence appearing in Greek or Latin texts</term> underlying this phrase. I believe I may have found this in the *Lexicon Aruch* <note>A famous 11th-century dictionary of Talmudic and Midrashic language by Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome.</note>, where under the word *SHAMASH* <note>original Hebrew: שמש; a root meaning "to serve" or "to minister"</note> the following is held: <margin>At the word SHAMASH.</margin> SHAMASH: *In the first Chapter of the Code regarding Fasting:* HE ADMINISTERED CHARITY TO THE POOR ON THE SABBATH. <note>Original Hebrew: שמש : בפרק א' בתעניות שמש בשבת צדקה לעניים. The author is linking the Hebrew word for service, "Shimmesh," to the distribution of "Tzedakah" or charity.</note> In the margin, it seems a note points to the *third folio* of that Talmudic Code, in which, however, I did not find these words, unless perhaps they escaped me because I was not reading attentively enough. But if I have grasped their genuine sense—of which I am not entirely certain—then it will certainly be established from this place that the word *SHAMASH*, which corresponds exactly with the Greek word *to serve* <note>original Greek: διακονεῖν</note>, was formerly constructed among the Hebrews with the word *charity* <note>original Hebrew: צדקה; Tzedakah</note> or *Alms*, and it is very probable

That they actually "collected" alms is not clear.

¶. The ancient Christian Church never, unless I am mistaken, recognized such fixed **Distributors of Alms** as were known in the Hebrew state, who collected **alms** from door to door. ¶. The **Collectors of Alms** among the Hebrews constitute a **Three-Man College**, whether for the **Chest** or the **Dish** <note>These refer to the two types of Jewish communal charity: the *Kuppah* (chest) for weekly money and the *Tamchui* (dish/tray) for daily food.</note>. This is because Luke speaks of a **daily ministry** <note>original Greek: διακονίᾳ καθημερινῇ, *diakonia kathemerine*</note>. 

However, see whether that can truly be said. For it was certainly the duty of the **Seven Men** to provide for the tables of **widows and the poor**, not so much for strangers (of which nothing is said in the text) but for the Hellenist <note>Greek-speaking Jewish</note> believers who belonged to that Church and were recorded on the rolls of the Jerusalem Church. Therefore, those stewards should certainly not be compared with the **Collectors of the Dish**, but with the **Collectors of the Chest**. These points will suffice, I think, to support my hypothesis; whether it is to be accepted or rejected, let the fair reader consider with reason.

->CHAPTER 6. AND OF THE MINISTERS OF THE SYNAGOGUE, etc. 935<-

But since in smaller gatherings there were not always worthy men to be found to whom that act of *Praying* could be safely entrusted, and since moreover the Jews did not easily entrust that office of prayer to anyone unless his skill, integrity, and orthodoxy were established by common testimony—and since likewise in many synagogues there was a lack of men sufficiently practiced in *Reading* and *Interpreting* the Scripture—it easily came to pass that some synagogues appointed fixed **Officials** to solemnly perform these sacred acts in the synagogue; that is, to *pour out prayers in public, read the Law, and interpret the same*. These men, because of the primary exercise of this duty, were called the **Envoys of the Assembly**. 

Furthermore, because every synagogue had need of a **Minister**, or **CHAZZAN** <note>original: *CHAZZANE*</note>, to whom the care and custody of the synagogue building and its sacred instruments were assigned, and many synagogues were not wealthy enough to support two such ministers of different kinds, it happened that those two duties—*Praying for the Assembly, etc., and guarding and caring for the Synagogue building*—were often entrusted to one and the same person. Therefore, in the Jewish Rituals, he is called indiscriminately חזן <note>original Hebrew: *Chazzan*</note>, **Minister** or **Custodian**, and ש"צ <note>original Hebrew: *Sheliach Tzibur*</note>, **Envoy of the Assembly**.

# ON THE QUALITIES OF THE ENVOYS, BOOK III.
->[The office of] praying, which was established<- in the Synagogue, was in the Christian Church ordinarily assigned to the **Chief of the Presbyters**, or the **President**. For the Christian Churches committed the Office of pouring out Prayers not to common or random persons, as in the Synagogue, but to the **presiding officer** <note>original Greek: τῷ προεστῶτι (*to proestoti*)</note>. Nor is there any doubt for us that in the ancient Synagogue the most honored men of the Synagogue were chosen for **Praying**, and even that this Act of pouring out prayers, in the first institution of the Synagogue, was performed by the **Prefects of the Synagogue** themselves.

<margin>Nehemiah 9:4</margin>
Indeed, this is clear from the History of Nehemiah. Anyone who is not a stranger to Biblical Reading knows that the Office of pouring out prayers was once observed among the Jewish people by Kings, Prefects, and Priests. But as the number of Teachers among the Jews increased daily, and Prayers began to be bound by certain **Formulas**, the Prefects of the Synagogues easily committed this Office to other **Teachers** or **Priests**, if any were present; even indeed the Prefects of the Academies

<margin>* See book 2, chapter 10, page 574.</margin>
* sometimes designated one of their **disciples** for that office of **reciting prayers**; and by that very act they sufficiently indicated that the office of Praying properly belonged to them, since they substituted others for themselves in the exercise of this duty. From these things we finally conclude that what is found in the Jewish writings concerning the <term>REQUIREMENTS OF THE ENVOYS OF THE ASSEMBLY</term> <note>The "Sheliach Tzibur," the person designated to represent the congregation in prayer</note> should be transferred to the <term>BISHOPS & Presbyters</term> of the Christian Church; and from these must be carefully distinguished those things which occur in the Hebrew writings concerning the <term>QUALITIES OF THE CHAZZANS</term> <note>The Chazzan was a subordinate official, often translated as "sexton" or "cantor"</note>; and those alone are to be compared with the <term>REQUIREMENTS OF DEACONS</term> in Paul's writings. However, this is not as easy to perform as it is to propose, because more recent Jews everywhere confuse the *Qualities of the Envoys of the Assembly* and the *Ministers of the Synagogue*. Nevertheless, let us see how far we may proceed in these matters.

---

### CHAPTER 6. AND [THE QUALITIES] OF THE MINISTERS OF THE SYNAGOGUE, etc.

to perform the duty of praying for the Assembly; which task was thereafter entrusted to the **Appointed Delegates of the Assembly**. Thus, for example, where it is said in the Code Megilla: <margin>Code Megilla, chapter 4, section 3.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: אין עוברין לפני התיבה פחות מעשרה</note> *Not fewer than ten [men] may go before the Ark;* both Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> and Bartenora have noted in their commentaries: <note>original Hebrew: ש"ץ</note> **ENVOY OF THE ASSEMBLY**. For the meaning of the statute is that it is not permitted for the Envoy of the Assembly to proceed toward the Ark to pray on behalf of the gathering unless **ten Israelites** are present in number. Therefore, whatever conditions or qualities the Ancients required in the one "descending toward the Ark," those same qualities must be transferred by us to the Envoys of the Assemblies, so called.

I. The *Jews* IN GENERAL *require that the Envoy of the Assembly be* <note>original Hebrew: הגון (*hagun*)</note>, a **WORTHY man**, *and* **SUITABLE** *to rightly perform the duty of praying.*
<margin>Orach Chajim, chapter 53, folio 45, 1.</margin>
Rabbi Jacob: <note>original Hebrew: צריך שיהיה ש"ץ הגון דכתיב נתנה עלי בקולה</note> *It is necessary, however, that the* **ENVOY OF THE ASSEMBLY** *be a* **WORTHY MAN** *and rightly instructed for that function, since it is written:* <margin>Jeremiah 12:8.</margin> *She has raised her voice against me, therefore I have hated her.* <note>The author implies that a voice raised in prayer by an unworthy person is hateful to God.</note> Rabbi Sutra, son of Tobiah, said that Rav said, and it was told to Rabbi Eliezer: This is the **ENVOY OF THE ASSEMBLY** who descends before the Ark, yet is not a worthy man and is not rightly instructed to perform this duty. These words are taken from the Gemara <note>The component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis</note> of the Code Taanith. These matters are handed down more fully in the *Colbo* <note>A 14th-century Hebrew work on Jewish ritual and law</note>; where the Author treats the Ten Days of Repentance, calculated from the Festival of the New Year until the tenth [day] of Tishri, the Day of Atonement: <margin>Folio 16, column 2. In the beginning of Colbo, chapter 65.</margin>

> It is the custom to search for an Envoy of the Assembly who is fit, worthy, and acceptable to the majority of his brothers for the prayers of these days. The reason is that he fulfills the obligation for the many if they so desire. Therefore, law and reason dictate that they should strive to have a man who is PERFECT, and of distinguished, worthy, and good character, and pleasing to the many. For even during the rest of the days of the year, when they appoint a Cantor <note>original Hebrew: חזן (*Chazzan*)</note> over the community to pray for them, they must appoint one who is fit and worthy. For prayer is called "Service" <note>original Hebrew: עבודה (*Avodah*)</note>, just as they interpreted regarding Daniel, that prayers were established to correspond to the daily sacrifices. Therefore, a man must take it to heart when he prays, before whom he is praying, etc.

They are accustomed, then, to look around diligently so that during these days of repentance they may have an **ENVOY OF THE ASSEMBLY** who is skillful and worthy, and welcome and acceptable to the greatest number of his brothers, because he can fulfill the duty of all (during these days), if it so † pleases them. And for that reason, law and justice require that they strive to have a man who is PERFECT, and of excellent
<margin>† See the explanation of these words above.</margin>

## 2. More SPECIFICALLY, other virtues and incidental qualities are now required in the Envoy of the Assembly:

### A. WISDOM.

<margin>
Laws of Prayer, chapter 8, section 9; chapter 65.

Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> says: <note>original Hebrew: אין שליח צבור אלא גדול שבצבור, בחכמתו ובמעשיו</note> *They do not appoint an Envoy of the Assembly unless he is the greatest in the Assembly, both in his wisdom and in his deeds.* The *Colbo* <note>An anonymous 14th-century Hebrew work on Jewish ritual and law.</note> states: <note>original Hebrew: במדרש עיר ואנשים בה מעט עיר קטנה זו היא בית הכנסת ואנשים מעט זו צבור ובא אליה מלך גדול זה הקב"ה ומצא בה איש מסכן וחכם ומלט הוא את העיר בחכמתו זה ש"ץ</note> They comment allegorically (on Ecclesiastes 9:15-16): *A city is sometimes small, and the men in it few.* The **small city** is the House of the Synagogue, and the **few men** in it are the Assembly (the Synagogue congregation). *The Great King returns to it;* this is God, Holy and Blessed. *And there was found in it a Poor Wise Man who delivered that city by his wisdom;* this is the **ENVOY OF THE ASSEMBLY**. Through which Wisdom one must also understand that Practical Science, which usually goes by the name of Prudence, the mother of every virtue and good work.

Wherefore, regarding the fixed and ordinary Envoy of the Assembly, they maintain it is unlawful for him to take on or substitute another Envoy for a time whose beard has not yet grown, as <term>Joseph Karo<note>A 16th-century legal scholar and author of the *Shulchan Aruch*, the most authoritative code of Jewish law.</note></term> discusses at length in his annotations to this place. A person who translated the Hebrew scripture into the vernacular (usually Aramaic) during the service.</note></term>, but is not admitted to read the Law in public, or to pour out prayers before the Ark. To the word **spreads** <note>Original Hebrew: *poreis* (פורס)</note>, this interpretation is added by <term>Bartenora<note>Obadiah ben Abraham of Bertinoro, a 15th-century Italian rabbi known for his commentary on the Mishnah.</note></term>: <note>Original Hebrew: קרועים זרועותיו נראים מבחוץ</note> *One whose clothes are torn in parts, with his arms visible and exposed.* Moreover, <term>Jarchius<note>An old scholarly name for Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki), the foremost medieval commentator on the Bible and Talmud.</note></term> and Bartenora give this reason for the statute itself: <note>Original Hebrew: מפני שגנאי הוא לצבור</note> *Because it would result in the disgrace of the Synagogue Assembly.* The <margin>1 Timothy 3:2.</margin> Apostle wishes the Bishop to be *orderly, decent, and honest* <note>Original Greek: κόσμιον</note>; which, although it refers appropriately to the internal disposition of the soul, does not exclude the external decency of the body.
