<header>CHAPTER 6. AND OF THE MINISTERS OF THE SYNAGOGUE, etc.</header>

Indeed, there are certainly some among the Jews, as Rabbi Joseph Karo points out in the *Orach Chayim* <margin>chapter 53, § 19.</margin> <note>The *Orach Chayim* is a major section of the Shulchan Aruch, the standard code of Jewish law.</note> who consider **Proselytes** <note>Converts to Judaism.</note> unfit to perform the function of the *Envoy of the Congregation* <note>Latin: *Legati Ecclesiæ*; Hebrew: *Shaliach Tzibbur*. The person who leads the communal prayers.</note>, but their opinion is nevertheless refuted by others. The summary of the disputation on <margin>Observations on Maimonides' *Laws of Prayer*, this chapter 8, § 11.</margin> this argument is found in the *Marginal Observations* on the text of Maimonides, from which I transcribe it here as being not entirely unworthy of note:

There are those who prevent a proselyte from being a public messenger because we learned in the tractate *Bikkurim* <note>Tractate on "First Fruits."</note>: "The proselyte brings [the first fruits] but does not recite [the confession], because he cannot say 'which He swore to our fathers,' etc. When he prays privately for himself, he says 'God of the fathers of Israel'; when he is in the synagogue, he says 'God of your fathers.'" But our teacher, Rabbi Joel the Levite, permitted it, for we learn in the Jerusalem Talmud at the end of the commentary of this tractate: It was taught that Rabbi Judah says the proselyte himself brings and recites. What is the reason? Because "I have made you a father of a multitude of nations" [Genesis 17:5]. Previously you were a father to Aram; from now on you are a father to all nations. Rabbi Joshua ben Levi says: The law follows Rabbi Judah. <note>original Hebrew: יש מי שמונע גר מלהיות שליח צבור מדתנן במסכת בכורי' הגר מביא ואינו קורא שאינו יכול לומר אשר נשבע לאבותינו וכו' כשהוא מתפלל בינו ובין עצמו אומ' אלהי אבות ישראל כשהוא בב''ה אומר אלהי אבותיכם ורבינו יואל הלוי התיר דגרסינן בירושלמי בסוף גמרא דהא מתני'תין תניא ר' יהוד' גר עצמו מביא וקורא מה טעם כי אב המון גוים נתתי' לשעבר היית אב לאדם (לארם scribendum) מכאן ואילך אתה אב לכל הגוים ר' יהושע אומר הלכה כר' יהודה.</note>

*There are those who* think a **PROSELYTE** *is not to be admitted to the function of the Envoy of the Congregation, an argument taken from what they pass down in the Tractate Bikkurim: The proselyte brings* (the First Fruits and Tithes) *but does not recite the formula of Confession which appears in Deuteronomy 26:13, because it is not fitting for him to say: "Which* (the land of Canaan) *you promised by oath to* **OUR FATHERS**; *etc. When a proselyte offers prayers privately, or alone, he says: "God of the Fathers of the Israelite Nation"; but when he prays in the synagogue, he says: "God of* **YOUR** *fathers."* Rabbi Joel, however, for the sake of resolving this doubt, put forward the opposing view (or rather, made it permissible), because it is read in the Jerusalem Talmud at the end of the *Gemara* <note>The portion of the Talmud that comments on the Mishnah.</note> of the Tractate *Bikkurim*: *The Tradition of Rabbi Judah: The proselyte himself brings* (the first fruits and tithes) *and recites the Formula of Confession. By what argument? Because it stands written: "I have established you as the Father of a multitude of Nations."* <margin>Genesis 17:3. Abram † Ab-Aram † As if</margin> <note>The author is noting a wordplay: Abram (Ab-Ram) is interpreted as "Father of Aram/Syria," while Abraham (Ab-Hamon) means "Father of a Multitude."</note> Up to this time you were only † Father of the Syrians; but from this time on you shall be the Father of all Nations. Rabbi Joshua ben Levi says that the opinion of Rabbi Judah prevails here.

Namely, therefore, according to the common opinion of the Teachers, *Proselytes*, as many as embrace the Jewish Religion, are so closely and deeply grafted into the stock of the descendants of Abraham, that they can call Abraham their Father, and apply to themselves all the Promises made to Abraham and his posterity. This was a point of some importance to observe. Let us not wonder, therefore, that the Church of Jerusalem entrusted the extraordinary care of widows and the poor, among others, to a certain *Nicholas*, a *Proselyte of Antioch.* Acts 6:5.

*A transition is made to the RITUALS of the Jewish Religion, the practice of which was indiscriminately entrusted to any approved and literate men in the ancient Synagogue by the Rulers of the Synagogue* <note>original: "Archisynagogis"</note>*, but in subsequent times was committed to the MINISTERS OF THE SYNAGOGUE, who also began to be called ENVOYS OF THE CONGREGATION* <note>original: "Legati Ecclesiae," referring to the Hebrew Shaliach Tzibbur</note>*. ### CHAPTER 7. ON PUBLIC PRACTICE. 947

...for our instructional purposes, we have distinguished these into two kinds of Acts. First, those which in the Ancient Synagogue could be performed by any adult men skilled in the sacred rites, chosen and appointed for that purpose. These were performed by such men, but as time passed, they were assigned to the *Chazzanim* <note>The *Chazzan* (plural *Chazzanim*) was a synagogue official or minister who served as a sexton or beadle, and later as a cantor.</note> and became a large part of their office. The other kind are those performed only by the *Chazzanim*, as Ministers <note>original: "Diaconis"</note> specifically called and destined for those services. Of the first kind are the **Reading of the Law and the Prophets**, and the **Interpretation** of both these parts of Scripture; the **Recitation of the Solemn Prayers**, under which we include those two most noble acts of **Stepping before the Ark** <note>This refers to the *Shaliach Tzibbur* or "Envoy of the Congregation" leading the service from the platform in front of the Torah shrine.</note>, and **Expounding, or Dividing the Shema** <note>The *Shema* is the central declaration of Jewish faith. "Dividing" it refers to reciting its various sections with their accompanying blessings.</note>; and also the **Blessing**, which, however, could only be performed by a Priest. Of the second kind are the duties of **Taking the Scroll of the Law out of the Ark, and returning it to the same**; **waving the cloth** <note>Likely a reference to the signal-flag used to coordinate responses in large synagogues.</note>; **blowing the Trumpet and the Horn**; **lighting the lamps**; **cleaning the Synagogue**, and other tasks of that order.

It is very clear from the records of Ancient Traditions that the sacred Acts of that first type—which today are almost all performed by the Ministers of the Synagogue and make up a significant part of their duty—were not restricted to any fixed person in the ancient Synagogue. Instead, they were performed freely by any capable man at the discretion of the Rulers of the Synagogue. The *Tractate Megillah* <note>A volume of the Talmud dealing with the reading of the Scroll of Esther and synagogue liturgy.</note> provides evidence regarding the **Reading and Interpretation of the Law and the Prophets**, as do various other authors who have described the Sacred Rites of the Hebrews. Regarding the other duties, besides what is established from that same *Tractate Megillah* and the Ritual books (as we shall see later), the description of the **Ruler of the Synagogue** by *Jarchi* <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105).</note> and *Bartenora* <note>Obadiah ben Abraham of Bertinoro (c. 1445–1515), a famous commentator on the Mishnah.</note>, produced earlier, can suffice for now as it assumes this very point.

<margin>Regarding Chapter 7, Section 7 of the Tractate Sotah.</margin>
They define the *Prefect of the Synagogue* <note>The *Archisynagogus* or Head of the Synagogue.</note> by the fact that everything in the Synagogue is arranged at his discretion; namely: "Who shall read the concluding portion of the Prophets, who shall recite the Shema, who shall step before the Ark" <note>original Hebrew: מי יפטיר בנביא מי יפרוס על שמע מי יורד לפני התבה</note>; that is, who shall pour out the most holy prayers of the Synagogue. Therefore, these Acts could certainly be assigned by the Prefects of the Synagogue to any man skilled in the Sacred Rites, and they did not constitute a fixed and ordinary part of the duty of a single person. But, as I said, this will become clearer from the description of those *Acts* themselves, which we now begin.

Regarding the **RITE OF THE READING OF THE LAW**, and how it is performed alongside certain other solemnities in the Synagogue, Jacob Alting <note>Jacob Alting (1618–1679) was a Dutch philologist and theologian known for his studies on Hebrew antiquity.</note> touched upon some points in his *Second Dissertation on Versions of Holy Scripture*. However, neither author has exhausted this material to the point that many other things worthy of observation do not remain to be recorded. Since this Rite is no less praised than it is famous and ancient, it will be well worth the effort to treat it more copiously and distinctly, observing the following order:

1. We shall discuss the **MATTER** of this *Act* <note>original: "phrasis Scholæ"; a technical term used in Scholastic philosophy to denote the subject material of a ritual.</note>.
2. We shall look at the *Act* itself and the **METHOD** of performing it.
3. We shall consider the **PERSONS** whom the Synagogue admits to perform it, and their *Requirements*.
4. We shall examine its **CIRCUMSTANCES**.
5. Finally, we shall add those **DUTIES** required by the Jewish statutes from the **OBJECT** of the act—that is, the Synagogal Assembly *to whom* this Act is directed.

1. The **MATTER** of this Act—that is, that from which the *Reading* is performed—consists generally of the *Scripture of the Old Testament*, and specifically of the **Mosaic Law** contained in five volumes, which will be the subject of our present dissertation. Regarding the *Prophetic Reading*, called the <term>Haftarah<gloss>A selection from the books of the Prophets read publicly in the synagogue after the Torah reading.</gloss></term> by the Jews, we shall deal with that separately later. However, what we have said regarding the *Mosaic Law* must be understood to apply to the whole Law, with no part excepted, which is not equally the case in the Prophetic Volumes.

Indeed, the contrary might seem true from a common reading of a notable passage in the Tractate <term>Megillah<gloss>A volume of the Mishnah and Talmud concerning the reading of the Scroll of Esther and other synagogue readings.</gloss></term>, in which the **Priestly Blessing** (found in the Book of Numbers) seems alone to be exempted from the whole Mosaic Law, and its public reading prohibited. In this passage, the **PRIESTLY BLESSING** and the Story of David and Amnon **ARE NEITHER READ** (in the Synagogue) **NOR EXPLAINED BY ORAL INTERPRETATION** <note>This refers to the *Targum*, the traditional Aramaic translation/explanation delivered alongside the Hebrew reading.</note>. <margin>Laws of Prayer, chapter 12, section 12.</margin>
And Maimonides himself <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the famous Sephardic philosopher and legal scholar.</note>, both in his commentaries on this passage and in the treatise just mentioned, includes these very histories of David and Amnon among those things which should no more be read than interpreted. Therefore our author thinks that Maimonides perhaps read the text of the *Mishnah* <note>The Mishnah is the first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions.</note> thus: *The story of the second calf is read but not translated, and likewise the Priestly Blessing.* <note>original Hebrew: "מעשה עגל השני נקרא ולא מתרגם וכן ברכת כהנים"</note> *The story of the second calf* (what is meant by this we shall say in its proper place, where we deal with the *Public Interpretation of the Law*) is read, but not explained in the vernacular, and the same applies to the *Priestly Blessing*. It is then added concerning the history of David and Amnon, that it is neither to be read nor explained in the common tongue: *The story of David and the story of Amnon are not read and not translated.* <note>original Hebrew: "מעשה דור ואמנון לא נקראין ולא מתורגמין"</note> *The history of David and the history of Amnon are neither read nor translated into the common tongue.* But, if a judgment is to be formed according to the sign from the *Gemara* brought forward above, it must be said that the text of the *Mishnah* here is likewise corrupt, and that the ancient Synagogue did indeed read the histories of the illicit loves of David and Amnon in various places, but they were by no means to be explained publicly. And so, among those things which are neither to be read nor interpreted, only the previously mentioned texts of Ezekiel should be included. Therefore, let the opinion stand: *the entire Mosaic Law was read in the Synagogue.*

it is [established], that if someone hears the Version of the Megillah <note>The Scroll of Esther, read during the festival of Purim.</note> read in a language [other than Hebrew] that is unknown to them—for instance, Latin, Syriac, or any other—they have not satisfied the duty of reading the Megillah to which they are bound on this Feast of Purim; however, they do satisfy it if they hear the Megillah read in the Hebrew language, [even if it is] unknown to them. # CHAPTER 7. IN THE SYNAGOGUE. 953

[the person] does not satisfy his duty, Rab and Samuel <note>Two of the most influential Jewish scholars (Amoraim) of 3rd-century Babylonia.</note> object, who said: *They make it lawful in Greek;* that is, they are deemed to have performed their duty who have heard the Megillah <note>The Scroll of Esther, read during the festival of Purim.</note> read in Greek. How does the matter stand? (Or: *So it seems;*) If we say that the writing of the Book itself is in Greek (that is, if someone using a Hebrew Book reads it aloud in the Greek idiom to the listeners), it is considered the same as if someone were reading the Megillah from memory, which is unlawful <note>original Latin: "nefas." Jewish law generally requires the Megillah to be read from a written scroll, not recited by heart.</note>. Rabbi Acha is reported to have said in the name of Rabbi Eleazar: *The writing must also be in the Greek language.* Certainly, Rab and Samuel, in judging that those who heard the Megillah read in Greek had satisfied their duty, were nonetheless to be understood as meaning that the Greek text was read from a Greek Book; and by no means that one who was using a Hebrew Book should read from it in Greek. In any case, whatever is contained in this version of mine exactly agrees with the decrees of Maimonides <note>The preeminent 12th-century Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note>, who dealt with the same argument and looked to this very same passage. Thus he says:

<margin>Laws of the Megillah, chapter 2, section 3.</margin>
<gloss>One who recites the Megillah from memory has not fulfilled his duty. A foreigner who heard the Megillah, which was written in the Holy Tongue <note>original Hebrew: "Lashon Ha-Kodesh," referring to Hebrew.</note> and in the Holy Script, even though he does not know what they are saying, has fulfilled his duty. And likewise, if it were written in Greek and he heard it, he has fulfilled it, even if he does not recognize it [the language], and even if the one hearing it were a Hebrew speaker.</gloss> *One who has heard the Megillah recited from memory is not thought to have satisfied his duty. A foreigner, who hears the Megillah read as it is written in the Holy Tongue and the Holy Script, although he understands nothing of those things which are said, has rightly performed his duty. And so likewise, if the Megillah were written in Greek and someone heard it read, he has satisfied his duty, even if he does not understand the meaning of the reading; and even if the person who hears that reading is a Hebrew.* It follows:

<margin>Section 4.</margin>
<gloss>If it were written as a translation <note>original Hebrew: "Targum," usually referring to the Aramaic translation.</note> or in another language of the nations, one does not fulfill his duty by reading it unless he is someone who knows that language; and this is provided that it is written in the script of that language. But if it were written in Hebrew script and he read it in Aramaic to an Aramaic speaker, he has not fulfilled it, for this reader is found to be reading from memory. and since the reader has not fulfilled his duty, the one who hears it from him has not fulfilled it either.</gloss> *If the Megillah has been turned into Chaldaic <note>A term often used by 17th-century scholars for Aramaic.</note> or translated into any other language used among the Gentiles, one is not deemed to satisfy his duty by the reading of it unless he is skilled in that language, and the Megillah itself was written in that language. But if the Megillah were written in the Hebrew language, and he himself read it in Syriac <note>Here used interchangeably with Aramaic/Chaldaic.</note>, he has not rightly performed the duty, because that reader in such a case is deemed to be reading the Megillah from memory. And since he who reads it has not rightly fulfilled the duty, he who heard it read by him has not fulfilled it either.* There are, however, other Doctors <note>Referring to other learned rabbis or scholars.</note>

# CHAPTER 7. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.

**That the Translation of the Seventy Elders was stored away with the Hebrew scrolls in the Serapeum, and that it is commonly read openly in the Synagogues.** <note>The author is quoting a common but, in his view, mistaken scholarly opinion.</note> Indeed, that learned and sharp-sighted man <note>Referring to Joseph Scaliger, mentioned on the previous page.</note>, being beset by prejudices, failed to see what is otherwise very clear in the writings of Tertullian. When Tertullian says that *“Ptolemy’s Library at the Serapeum displays the Hebrew letters themselves,”* <note>original: "Ptolomæi Bibliothecam apud Sarapæum ipsas Hebraicas literas exhibere"</note> he is referring to what he had said in the preceding lines: that Ptolemy requested from the Jews their own native writings, which they alone possessed—namely, the Biblical Codex written in Hebrew. Then Tertullian also says that, in addition to these very Hebrew Scriptures, Ptolemy was granted a translation by the **seventy interpreters** <term>LXX</term> <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible produced in Alexandria.</note>. Lest any of the Gentiles doubt whether the Sacred Books were truly published and circulated in the Hebrew language by the Prophets of old (a point Tertullian raises to establish the authority of those books), he says this can be proven by a double argument: first, that even today the Sacred Codex is displayed in Hebrew letters in the library of Ptolemy at the Serapeum; and second, that **the Jews read that codex, in Hebrew letters, openly in the synagogues.** Thus, the genuine sense of Tertullian’s words runs directly counter to Scaliger’s opinion. Furthermore, what that illustrious man adds—*“But even certain synagogues read the Hebrew along with the Greek, just as today they read Hebrew with the Targums”*—must not be passed over without comment. For I would like to know: in which synagogue of the Jews are the **Targums** <term>Targumim</term> <note>Aramaic translations or paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible used when the congregation no longer understood Hebrew.</note> read from a book? ### ON THE READING OF THE MOSAIC LAW BOOK III. PART II.

<margin>Observations on the New Testament, chapter 31. See the Prolegomena of Walton, in the place cited.</margin>
THEY WISH TO ADOPT AN EDITION FOR THE READING OF THE SACRED BOOKS, and *whichever language the local situation simply makes more convenient and suitable for the listeners.* At that time, when this Decree <term>Rescriptum</term> <note>A formal ruling or edict, specifically Emperor Justinian’s Novella 146 from 553 AD, which allowed Greek to be used in synagogues.</note> was issued by Justinian, it is possible that some Synagogues adopted a Greek Edition for the reading of the Sacred Books. However, we do not have enough evidence to know exactly what this phrase means: whether, having set aside the Hebrew text, they read the Greek text alone in the Synagogue; or whether, contrary to the common custom of the Synagogues, they added a Greek interpretation from some book to the reading of the Hebrew text. The latter view, as it is the most straightforward, is suggested by the words of Justinian’s Constitution and is approved by the learned men Crojus and Walton <note>Jean de Croÿ and Brian Walton, the latter being the editor of the famous London Polyglot Bible.</note>. If it had already been an ancient and accepted custom among the Jews to read the Greek Version in the synagogues, then this very practice of reading the Greek Version would not have provided the subject for such extensive conflict under Justinian. Yet I would deserve a mark of rashness if I were to state absolutely that the Greek Version was *never* read in Jewish synagogues before those times, because neither the specific customs of individual synagogues have been transmitted to us through reliable historical record, nor have I personally examined every single thing we have received through credible evidence. Therefore, it will be safest to suspend judgment on this matter until I see it established by more certain and solid arguments, for it remains doubtful and uncertain to me thus far.

<margin>See the Codex Megillah <note>The Talmudic tractate regarding the reading of the Scroll of Esther and synagogue procedures.</note>, chapter 1, section 8.</margin>

The literal letters as they are written in the body of the scroll.</note>, *the textual reading.*

*If an error is discovered in the Code of the Law at the time when the reading from it is being performed, another Volume of the Law is brought forward, and the beginning of the reading is made from the place in which the error was discovered: and the readers complete the reading over or in addition to those who read from the faulty Code. 4. The reading must be performed from a complete volume of the entire Mosaic Law, consisting of the five Books of the Mosaic Law. <term>Rabbi Karo</term> says **regarding a scroll that is rolled**:

> If each "fifth" [book] is written individually, even if it is on a scroll like a Scroll of the Law, they do not read from it until all five fifths are sewn together; even in villages where no "fit" Scroll of the Law is found, they do not say the solemn blessings over it.

*If any "Fifth Part" [Pentateuch] of the Mosaic Law is written separately, even if it is on parchment to be rolled up in the manner of a Volume of the Law, they nevertheless do not perform the reading from it until all those five Fifth Parts have been joined together by stitching. Indeed, not even in villages, in which no legitimate Code of the Law is held, do they pour out the solemn blessings over a single Fifth Part of the Mosaic Law.*

# CHAPTER 8. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.

### CHAPTER VIII.

*This chapter treats the **Prerequisites**, or those things that come before the **Sacred Rite of Reading the Mosaic Law**, as it is celebrated in synagogues. It discusses its methods, accompanying rituals, and consequences, presenting the statutes of the Rabbis on this subject. Among other things pertaining to this matter, the formula for the most holy prayer, the **Kaddish**, is presented from Maimonides, and the major and minor divisions of the Mosaic Law are discussed in passing.*

Let us now look further into the *Act of Reading* itself, as it is practiced in the sacred services of the synagogue. Since there are many things to be observed regarding it, we shall relate what is found in the Jewish statutes—regulations compiled on this subject—organized into these four main headings: namely, 1. its *Antecedents*, 2. the *Methods* by which it is performed, 3. the *Necessary Accompaniment*, and 4. the *Consequences* <note>original Greek: τὰ ἑπόμενα (*ta hepomena*), meaning "the things that follow"</note>.

I. Among the *Antecedents* which must precede this sacred rite of the *Reading of the Law* in the synagogue, we include:

1. *Solemn morning prayers, to be recited according to the accepted formulas, and sealed by the most holy prayer called the* **Kaddish** <note>The Kaddish is a hymn of praise to God's name, often marking transitions between sections of the liturgy</note>.

<margin>
Laws of Prayer, chapter 12, sections 20, 21, 22.
</margin>
We may understand the whole matter from Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar</note>, who explains quite clearly the order in which this *Act of Reading* occurs among the other ceremonies of the synagogue: <note>original Hebrew: כיצד סדר הקריאה בתורה עם התפלה כל יום שיש בו תפלת מוסף אחר שיגמור שליח צבור תפלת שחרית אומר קדיש ומוציא ספר תורה וקורא לאחד אחד מן הצבור ועולין וקורין בתורה</note> *"In what order, or sequence, does the Act of Reading the Law occur with the prayers? On every day when the <term>Additional Prayers</term> <note>original: *Musaf*; special prayers added on Sabbaths and festivals</note> are to be joined to the ordinary ones, after the <term>Emissary of the Congregation</term> <note>original: *Sheliach Tzibur*; the leader of the prayer service</note> finishes the morning prayers, he recites the **KADDISH**, brings out the Book of the Law, and calls the readers from the congregation one by one to read. They immediately ascend the <term>Platform</term> <note>original: *Suggestum*; the *Bimah* or raised desk where the Torah is read</note> and perform the reading. The additional prayers, as we shall understand hereafter, are recited after the reading of the Law has been completed."*

Maimonides, same place, section 21.

ON THE READING OF THE MOSAIC LAW, BOOK III

On the solemn Day of Expiation <note>Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar</note> (though not on other Festival Days), it is established that the *Evening* prayers—so called—are only offered after the Reading of the Law is completed. However, if the Reading of the Law is to be performed on a day when no *Additional Prayers* <note>term: Musaf; the additional service recited on Shabbat and festivals</note> are recited, the same order of sacred rites holds: the *Morning Prayers are poured out*, followed by the most holy formula of the *Kaddish*, and then the *Reading of the Law* follows. 
<margin>Found in Maimonides, in the *Order of Prayer* (*Seder Tephillah*), the Version of the Kaddish. Part 1, at folio 73, column 4.</margin>
The prayer which is called *Kaddish* <note>A hymn of praise to God’s name that serves as a transition between sections of the liturgy</note>, composed in Chaldean <note>Aramaic, the vernacular of Jews in late antiquity</note>, reads as follows: <note>original Aramaic: יִתְגַּדַּל וְיִתְקַדַּשׁ שְׁמֵהּ רַבָּא בְּעָלְמָא דִּבְרָא כִרְעוּתֵהּ וְיַמְלִיךְ מַלְכוּתֵהּ וְיַצְמַח פוּרְקָנֵהּ וִיקָרֵב מְשִׁיחֵהּ וְיִפְרוֹק עַמֵּהּ בְּחַיֵּיכוֹן וּבְיוֹמֵיכוֹן וּבְחַיֵּיהוֹן דְּכָל בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל בַּעֲגָלָא וּבִזְמַן קָרִיב</note> *May His Great Name be magnified and sanctified in the world, which He created according to His good pleasure, and MAY HE CAUSE HIS KINGDOM TO REIGN; may His redemption sprout forth, and may His Messiah be present, and may He deliver His people, in your lifetime, and in your days, and in the lifetime of the whole House of Israel, and that very speedily.* In translating these words, I have stayed strictly close to the literal meaning, so that none of the power of the words and phrases of this solemn formula should be lost through our rendering.

<margin>*Order of Prayer*, folio 35, column 1.</margin>
We find a shorter form of it in the *Order of Prayers* published by the Germans in Amsterdam, where the middle words are omitted: *May His redemption sprout forth! May His Messiah be present and deliver His people;* these may be considered to be included in the words: *May He cause His Kingdom to reign.* Furthermore, in this formula of the *Kaddish* prayer, we have the first two of the petitions which our Lord Jesus Christ, in the most perfect example of all prayers commended by Him to the Church, 
<margin>Matthew 6:9–10.</margin>
foreshadowed: HALLOWED BE THY NAME; and: THY KINGDOM COME. Now, what I said—that the *Kaddish* prayer is held as most holy by the Jews and is most frequently used by them—is clear from the explicit words of Maimonides: <note>original Hebrew: וכל צבור אומר אמן לעולם קודם כל תפלה ואחר כל תפלתו ואחר שאומר היום בכל עת שיאמר סדר היום יתחנן מעט ואומר קדיש</note> <margin>place cited.</margin> *The Leader of the Congregation <note>term: Shaliach Tzibbur; the person appointed to lead the community in prayer</note> always recites the Kaddish before and after every prayer that he offers in public. And anyone else who recites the prayers according to the order of that day, at whatever time he does so, should supplicate for a little while (that is, if I am not mistaken, prepare himself to recite the Kaddish through a certain petitionary meditation <note>original Greek: ἱκετικὴν (*hiketikēn*)</note>) and then recite the Kaddish.*

# CHAPTER 8. IN THE SYNAGOGUE. 963

B. *The Production of the Sacred Volume from the Ark, with the People Singing along:*
This duty falls to the Chazzan, or *Minister of the Synagogue*, as we will mention in the following sections; today he performs this task amid the acclamations and shouts of joy from the People, for which he himself usually leads the way with his introductory chants. See Buxtorf on this matter.

<margin>Jewish Synagogue, chapter 14, § 286.</margin>

C. *The Blessing to be recited after the Scroll of the Law has been unfolded.*
Indeed, it was permitted for no one to read from the Law after the Scroll was unfolded, except after the solemn *Blessings* which must precede the Reading. <margin>Laws of Prayer, chapter 12, § 5.</margin> Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides, a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal scholar of the Middle Ages</note> says: <note>original Hebrew: כל אחד ואחד מן הקורין פותח ספר תורה ומביט למקום שהוא קור' בו ואח' כך אומר ברכו את ה' המבורך וכל העם עונין ברוך ה' המבורך לעולם ועד וחוזר ומברך בא' א'מ'ה' אשר בחר בנו מכל העמים ונתן לנו את תורתו בא' א' נותן התור' וכל העם עונין אמן ואחר כך קורא עד שישלים לקרות</note> *Every reader opens the Book of the Law and looks at the place where the beginning of the reading is to be made, and afterwards utters this Blessing: "Bless the Blessed Lord!" And the whole People immediately chant back: "Praised be the Blessed Lord forever and ever." To which the Reader again adds: "Blessed are You, O Lord our God, Ruler of this World, who chose us from all nations, and gave us Your Law; Blessed are You, O Lord, who gave the Law." To which the whole People immediately respond Amen. Then the Reader begins his reading until he has finished it.* <margin>See Way of Life, chapter 89, § 4, 5, etc.</margin> These blessings must be uttered by the Reader in a clear voice, nor should the reading begin before the Synagogue Congregation has added its *Amen* to the Final Blessing, which is properly called the <term>Berakhat ha-Torah</term> <note>Hebrew: ברכת התורה; the specific blessing recited over the Torah</note>, the *Blessing of the Law*. Now, other doxologies <note>expressions of praise to God</note> had to precede the reading of other parts of the Sacred Volume. Let us take this example from the *Book of Sopherim* <note>Tractate Soferim, a minor tractate of the Talmud concerning the scribal rules and public reading of the Bible</note>, which the Reader of the Hagiographa <note>term: Hagiographa; also known as the Ketuvim or "Writings," the third section of the Hebrew Bible including Psalms, Proverbs, etc.</note> should say before beginning the reading: <margin>Sopherim chapter 14, § 4.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: ברוך אתה ה' אלהינו מ'ה' אשר קדשנו במצותיו וצונו לקרוא בכתבי הקדש</note> *Blessed are You, O Lord, our God, Ruler of this Universe, who has sanctified us with Your commandments, and commanded us in the reading of the <note>original Greek: τῶν γραφῶν ἁγίων</note> holy writings.* We see how holily and decorously the sacred exercises of the Synagogues were conducted according to the institutions of the Ancients; which, therefore, deserve no mockery or contempt, to which the famous Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf, a prominent 17th-century Christian Hebraist</note> often exposes them, although otherwise he is...

# ON THE READING OF THE MOSAIC LAW, BOOK III, PART I

<margin>Luke 4:16.</margin>
The relationship of the Synagogue to the Church is most deserving of our attention, and should be carefully considered by us. Certainly Christ the Lord also, in the synagogue of Nazareth, *stood up to read* <note>original Greek: ἀνέστη ἀנהγνῶναι</note>, and *opened the book* <note>original Greek: ἀνέπτυξε βιβλίον; original Latin: evolvit Librum</note>, which was handed to him *by the attendant* <note>original Greek: ἀπό τοῦ ὑπηρέτου</note>, that is, by the Minister of the synagogue. Specifically, he unfolded and unrolled the volume given to him, which is the proper meaning of the word *to unroll* <note>original Greek: ἀναπτύσειν</note>. Furthermore, if the Lord performed this action according to these same rites, I judge that he did nothing inconsistent with the dignity of his Person.

Let us now pass **2.** from the *preliminaries* of this act to its **MODES**; concerning which, the things I have observed, I seem able to reduce to these three: 1. Which precise parts of Holy Scripture were read; 2. **HOW MUCH** was to be read by each reader; and 3. **IN WHAT MANNER** that reading was to be performed.

Regarding the *first*: Since the volumes of Holy Scripture and the *Mosaic Law* <term>the Torah</term> are more numerous and larger than can be completed in a sacred assembly of a few hours, reason easily taught the authors of this institution to distinguish the *Divine Law* into certain parts or segments, the reading of which would correspond to the time allotted for public religious exercise and other acts of that religion. Thus it was done, and since ancient times the Law appears to have been divided into *certain larger sections* <note>original Hebrew: פרשיות (Parashiyot)</note>, each intended for a single Sabbath reading. Certainly, no student of Hebrew literature is unaware that the five Mosaic volumes among the Jews are divided into *fifty-four major sections*, or, as the Masoretes <note>The scholars and scribes who standardized the Hebrew text of the Bible</note> calculate (followed by Maimonides and Elias), *fifty-three*.

<margin>Laws of Prayer, chapter 13, § 1.</margin>
Maimonides says: <note>original Hebrew: מנהג הפשוט בכל ישראל שמשלימין את התורה בשנה אחת מתחילין בשבת שאחר חג הסוכות וקורין בסדר בראשית בשנייה אלה תולדות בשלישית ויאמר ה' אל אברם וקוראין והולכין על הסדר הזה עד שגומרין את התורה בחג הסוכות ויש מי שמשלים את התורה בשלוש שנים ואינו מנהג פשוט</note> *It is a widespread custom among all Israel to complete the reading of the Law in the space of one year, beginning on the Sabbath that follows the Feast of Tabernacles <term>Sukkot</term>. Thus, on that first Sabbath, they read the section: "In the beginning" [Genesis 1:1]; on the second: "These are the generations" [Genesis 6:9]; on the third: "And the Lord said to Abram" [Genesis 12:1]; and they proceed in this order in the reading of the Law until they complete the entire reading of the Law on the Feast of Tabernacles itself. There are also those who complete the Law in three years, but this is not a widespread custom.*

### CHAPTER 8. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.

Indeed, there are synagogues in which the reading of the entire Law is completed over a period of three years. However, that custom has been accepted by very few. Thus says Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides, a preeminent 12th-century Jewish philosopher and jurist</note>. Nevertheless, Benjamin of Tudela <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler and chronicler</note> testifies, <margin>Itinerary p. 115.</margin> that while the Babylonian and Spanish Jews complete the reading of the Law in the synagogue annually, the Canaanites <note>Referring here to the Jewish communities in the Land of Israel</note> devote three full years to that work:

*But those born in the Land of Israel do not observe the same custom, but divide each individual Section into three parts, and complete the reading of the Law in a period of three years.* <note>original Hebrew: ואנשי ארץ ישראל אינם נוהגים כך אבל עושים מכל פרשה שלשה סדרים ומסיימין את התורה לסוף שלש שנים; original Latin: At qui in Israëlitica nati sunt, eundem morem non observant, sed singulas Sectiones in tres partes dispescunt, Legisque Lectionem absolvunt trium annorum spatio.</note>

Moreover, those portions <term>Parashiot: weekly portions of the Torah</term> are marked in printed Bibles by a triple capital letter *Pe* (פ) or *Samekh* (ס); in manuscripts, they are marked throughout by larger blank spaces or intervals, just as the smaller parts of the Holy Scripture are demonstrated by a single *Pe* (פ) or *Samekh* (ס) (the first of these letters, *Pe* (פ), denotes an *open* <note>original: pethucha</note> section, while the latter, *Samekh* (ס), denotes a *closed* <note>original: sethuma</note> section). What those terms *Pethucha* and *Sethuma* mean, and what method of writing the Pentateuch <term>the first five books of the Bible</term> the Jews indicate through the symbols of those two letters, I shall not pointlessly explain here, as it does not serve my current purpose and has been extensively discussed by learned men in their proper places, albeit with varying opinions. 

I consider only this one thing useful to observe for my purpose now: that those *Minor Segments of the Mosaic Law* in no way formerly served the *Reading of the Law*, but rather served to distinguish the subject matter or arguments of the Mosaic writing. The first point is clear not only from the fact that the spaces of those divisions are quite unequal, but also because they are smaller than what ought to be assigned to various and different readers; as will be easily clear to anyone from those smaller distinctions within the *Decalogue* <term>the Ten Commandments</term>. 

The second point, however—just as any attentive reader of the Sacred Letters will be easily persuaded by considering the specific places where the Masoretes <term>scholars who standardized the Hebrew Bible text</term> applied these letters *Pe* (פ) and *Samekh* (ס)—it is sufficient for me now to support with a single specimen, taken from the *Eleventh Chapter of the First Mosaic Book* <note>The Book of Genesis</note>, in which segments marked with the letters *Pe* (פ) and *Samekh* (ס) occur to me ten times in total; but through which the matters explained in that Chapter are prudently distinguished from one another. The first *Pe* (פ) shows the history of the built Tower of Babel, and that section is—

...the greatest of all; the second marked with a פ contains the <term>genealogy</term> <note>original Greek: τεκνογονίαν (teknogonian), referring to the lineage or "begetting of children"</note> of Shem; the third the generation of Arphaxad, and so on; the last indeed marked with a ס encompasses the history of Terah. From this single example it becomes very clear that all those intervals in the writing of the Mosaic Law were applied by the <term>Masoretes</term> <note>The Jewish scholars who standardized the text of the Hebrew Bible</note> to distinguish the contents and subject matter of the things being treated, and were by no means intended to serve the ritual for reading the Law in the synagogue. Thus, for example, we see that in the Sabbath readings, the Major <term>Parashiot</term> <note>The large weekly portions read in the synagogue</note> are divided into seven sections in such a way that a new reading sometimes begins in the middle of a shorter section and ends at the end of another shorter section; sometimes, on the other hand, no account is taken of those shorter sections at all. However, if it could be done conveniently (especially in the shorter weekly readings), they preferred to start or end the reading with a shorter section, as we shall see later. 

As for the fact that the Major Sections of the Law are designated as fifty-three or fifty-four (for the ninth part <margin>Deuteronomy 31:1.</margin> of Deuteronomy, titled *Vayelech* <note>Hebrew: וילך, "And he went"</note>, is omitted by some), this was done, unless I am mistaken, with respect to the intercalated <term>lunar year</term> <note>A Jewish leap year where an extra month is added to keep the calendar in sync with the seasons</note>, which requires that many readings. Consequently, in non-intercalated common lunar years (which the Jews observe), certain portions are joined together. It mattered little which were joined, provided that the readings of certain designated portions fell at specific appointed times. Because those sections contain a rebuke of the Jewish nation, so that they might turn themselves to God through repentance. Therefore, the Jews truly confess that at this very time they are guilty of those crimes for which they are accused in this passage; and that the confession of those same crimes and the turning toward God must be established at this very time of Exile, according to the tenor and prescription of this passage. Section 8. 1. The curses found in the Torah <note>Specifically those in Leviticus 26</note> are read in one continuous sequence without pause by a single reader, starting with the verse before them and ending with the verse after them. However, regarding the curses that appear in the "Second Law" <note>Deuteronomy 28</note>, it is accepted that if someone wishes to make a pause during their reading, it is considered entirely permissible; although nowadays common custom generally dictates that they should also be completed by one reader without pause. <note>original Latin: "Execrationes, quæ habentur in Levitico, continuo filo absque pausa ab uno leguntur..."</note> Regarding the weekly readings in general, it is cautioned that no fewer than three verses should be read by any single reader, and the three readers together must read no fewer than ten verses in total. Maimonides says:

<margin>chapter 12, section 3.</margin>
They do not read fewer than ten verses in total in the synagogue—a number that includes the verse "And the Lord spoke etc." <note>original Hebrew: ודבר עולה מן המנין, referring to the common introductory formula "And the Lord spoke to Moses..."</note>. There shall not be fewer than three readers. They do not begin a <term>Parashah</term> <note>A section of the Torah</note> with fewer than three verses, nor does the reader leave fewer than three verses remaining at the end of a section, nor does any reader read fewer than three verses himself. <note>original Latin: "Non legunt in universum in Synagoga minus, quam decem versus..."</note>

<margin>chapter 4, section 4.</margin>

<margin>section 4.</margin>
three readers in the synagogue read ten verses, it is required, according to this
<margin>Orach Chayim chapter 86, section 2; chapter 13, section 4.</margin>
rule, that two of them each read *three* verses, and one reads *four*; this is the very thing Maimonides teaches in the following context. How carefully and scrupulously the Jews observe this—ensuring that in the reading of a minor section they leave *three verses* remaining—can be seen from the example of the reading appointed for the <term>New Moons</term> <note>Rosh Chodesh, the start of the Jewish month</note>, also found in Maimonides:

On the New Moons, the first reader reads three verses from the section *Tzav* <note>The Command</note>; the second reader repeats the third verse read by the first, and then reads the two verses following it, so that he leaves three verses remaining in the section; the third reader reads the three verses that the second reader left, along with "And on the Sabbath day" etc.; and the fourth reader reads "And on your New Moons." <note>original Latin: "Et in Noviluniis primus prælegit tres versus..."</note>

# ON THE READING OF THE MOSAIC LAW, BOOK III, PART II.

...and moreover reads the following verses, so that he leaves three remaining verses in that Section; the third Reader then reads those three verses together with the following verse (which alone completes one minor <term>Parashah</term> <note>A "Parashah" is a textual division or section of the Hebrew Bible; here referring to the smaller paragraph-like breaks</note>) *And on the Sabbath day*, etc. The fourth reader now begins the following <term>Parashah</term> and reads: *And in your New Moons*, etc. Indeed, it is clear from this example what reasoning the Jews followed in their Synagogue Readings regarding those *Minor Parashot* into which the Law of Moses is divided. Those sections, as I have already noted in the preceding pages, properly served to distinguish the matters and subjects discussed in the Law, without regard to the Reading of the Law, or the number of Readers, their order, or other things of that kind. But since it is necessary to conduct the public Reading with careful judgment, they desired that, once the Law had been distributed into these sections, at least such regard should be had for them in the Reading of the Law that it would not be permitted for a Reader, engaged in reading a section, to leave fewer verses remaining in it than were sufficient for the complete reading of the next Reader.

->3. Concerning the METHOD of Reading, properly so called, it pertains to,<-
->that<-

<margin>Chapter 142, Section 1. Maimonides, *Hilchot Tefillah* <note>The "Laws of Prayer," part of Maimonides' great legal code, the Mishneh Torah</note> Chapter 12, Section 6 and following; Section 2.</margin>
1. *In the Reading, the highest accuracy is required.*
*Orach Chajim* <note>The "Path of Life," the first section of the Shulchan Aruch, the standard code of Jewish Law</note>: <note>original Hebrew: קרא וטעה אפילו בדקדוק אות אחת מחזירין אותו</note> *If anyone while reading should err, even by pronouncing a single letter incorrectly according to Grammar, they command him to correct that error through a repeated Reading.* If, however, no one could be found in a particular assembly of Israelites who was fit to perform the Reading of the Law according to the rules of Grammar and the tradition of the Fathers, they allowed such a Reading even in that case. If indeed it should happen by chance that a Reader skipped some verse while reading, and this occurred on the evening of the
<margin>*Orach Chajim* Chapter 87, Section 3.</margin>
Sabbath or on Mondays and Thursdays <note>The days when the Torah is traditionally read in a shorter service</note>, and the three Readers had read ten verses besides the omitted verse, there was no need at all for the Reading to be repeated. But if an error of that kind were committed during the sacred morning services of the Sabbath, the Reading had to be repeated entirely and the error corrected, even if the end had already been imposed on the Reading and the sacred ceremonies following the Reading had been completed.

2. *It is not permitted to skip from one text of Scripture, from which the Reading is established, to another, except in the Reading of the Prophets.*
<margin>Chapter 44, Section 1.</margin>
*Orach Chajim*: <note>original Hebrew: מדלגין בנביא ואין מדלג בין בתורה מפרשה זו לפרשה</note> *They may skip in the Prophet, but one does not skip in the Torah from this section to that section.*

# CHAPTER 8. [IN THE SYNAGOGUE.]

> This [refers] to another section, and this applies to two different subjects, for we fear that the minds of the listeners might be confused; but in one subject—such as "After the Death" and "But on the Tenth" <note>original Hebrew: *Achare Mot* (Leviticus 16:1) and *Ach Baasor* (Leviticus 23:27)</note> which the High Priest reads on the Day of Atonement—skipping is permitted, provided that he does not read from memory, for it is forbidden to read even a single word except from the text. In the Prophets, however, one may skip even between two different subjects, provided that the skip does not take so long that the congregation is left standing in silence. This rule applies to a single Prophet; however, one does not skip from one Prophet to another Prophet, except in the case of the Twelve <note>The "Twelve" refers to the Minor Prophets, such as Hosea, Joel, and Amos, which were traditionally written on a single scroll and treated as one book</note>, where skipping from one to another is allowed, provided one does not skip from the end of the book back to its beginning.

*In the Reading of the Prophets, they skip from one text to another, but in the Reading of the Law of Moses they do not skip from one section to another. This, however, is to be understood as referring to texts of different subjects, lest the understanding of the listeners be confused; but in texts of a single subject—as for example when the High Priest, on the solemn Day of Atonement, reads from two different texts*
<margin>* Leviticus 16, 1. † Leviticus 23, 27. In the Section called *Emor*.</margin>
*After the Death and: † But on the Tenth; skipping is permitted, provided that he does not read aloud by heart (that is, reciting the text from memory without looking at the Book), because it is a sin to read even one word without looking at the Scripture. In the Prophets, it is also permitted to make a jump between texts of different subjects, provided it can be done in such a way that the one making the jump is not confused, and the synagogue congregation is not required to spend time waiting in silence. This again is understood to apply to different texts of a single Prophet. For it is not permitted to skip from the Reading of one Prophet to the Reading of another, except in the case of the twelve Minor Prophets; provided, however, that care is taken not to move from the beginning of the Book to its end. Almost everything contained in this rule is taken from the <term>Gemara</term> <note>The rabbinical commentary and analysis that makes up the second part of the Talmud</note> of the tractate <term>Megillah</term> <note>The section of Jewish law dealing specifically with the reading of the Scroll of Esther and other liturgical readings</note>.*

<margin>Folio 25, column 1, at section 4, chapter *Hakkore eth Hammegilla*, etc., which in some books is chapter 3 and in others chapter 4. *Hilchot Tefillah* <note>Maimonides' "Laws of Prayer"</note> chapter 12, section 8.</margin>
3. *The Reader was not permitted to recite anything from the text by heart without looking at the Book, but was required to read each word and syllable from the Volume of the Law.*

> It is forbidden to read even one word not from the writing.
*It is forbidden to read even one little word without using the instrument of the Scripture.*

### ON THE READING OF THE MOSAIC LAW, BOOK III, PART II.

...they [unroll] the Book of the Law in the Synagogue for the honor of the assembly; however, if only one Book of the Law is at hand, they unroll it anyway; <margin>chapter 12, § 23, page 70, column 1.</margin> in this case, no consideration is given to the honor of the assembly. Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note> says just as much. This Rule is taken from the Treatise *Yoma* <note>original Latin: *Codice Joma*; a volume of the Talmud dealing with the rituals of the Day of Atonement</note>. Moreover, it deserves to be observed in this place the singular use of the word <term>galal <note>Hebrew: גלל</note></term> which, although it frequently appears elsewhere with the meaning of rolling up or folding a book (as we shall see later), does not denote here the *folding or rolling up of the book*, but rather its unrolling. This unrolling of the book while searching for a text was often joined with the rolling up of some part of the volume that had already been spread out. Long ago, [John] Lightfoot <note>A 17th-century English churchman and Hebraist known for using Rabbinic literature to explain the New Testament</note> correctly observed this use of the word <term>galal</term>, and from it he illustrated the phrase of Luke concerning the Lord: <margin>Luke 4:17</margin> "and having unrolled the book, he found the place" <note>original Greek: καὶ ἀναπτύξας τὸ βιβλίον, εὗρε τὸν τόπον</note>. Unless, however, that which Luke calls "unrolling" <note>Greek: τὸ ἀναπτύσσειν</note>, in the sense it is used here regarding Christ, is properly called <term>patach <note>Hebrew: פתח</note></term> or *to open the Book* in the sacred rites of the Synagogue. This is how we heard Maimonides speaking earlier: <margin>chapter 12, § 5.</margin> *Each one of the readers* OPENS *the Book of the Law, and looks at the place he is about to read.* <note>original Hebrew: כל אחד ואחד מן הקורין פותח ספר תורה ומביט למקום שהוא קורא בו</note>

However, this very same word <term>galal</term> occurs to me in the sense of unrolling in another notable passage in [Joseph] Karo <note>The author of the *Shulchan Aruch*, the standard code of Jewish law</note>, who has it thus: <margin>chapter 140, § 3.</margin> *If anyone ascends to the platform to read, and the place to be read is shown to him, and he recites the Blessing that precedes the Reading, and then—whether he has already begun his reading or even if he has not yet started—he is reminded that another section must be read,* AND HE UNROLLS THE BOOK OF THE LAW *to that place from which the reading is to be established, there are those who say the Blessing must be repeated, and there are those who deny it.* <note>original Hebrew: העולה לקרות בתורה והראו לו מקום שצריך לקרות ובירך על התו' והתחיל לקרות או לא התחיל והזכירוהו שפרשה אחרת צריך לקרות וגלל הספר תורה למקום שצריך לקרות בו יש אומרים שאינו צריך לחזור ולברך ויש אומרי' שצריך</note> Certainly, <term>galal sefer</term> <note>rolling/unrolling the book</note> here is not the rolling up, but the unrolling of the book for the sake of finding the place—the "unrolling of the book" <note>original Greek: ἡ τοῦ βιβλίου ἀνάπτυξις</note>, or, if it were permitted to say so, the "re-rolling." 

To avoid this unrolling of a single book, several Codices <note>Scrolls or manuscript volumes</note> were brought out if the reading was to be established from different texts, which happened on Festivals or when New Moons coincided with the Sabbath. And from this comes the mention in the Rituals of two or more Codices to be used in the Reading. <margin>chapter 13, § 4.</margin> Maimonides says: *If a New Moon falls on a Sabbath, they bring out two books.* <note>original Hebrew: ואם חל ר"ח להיות בשבת מוציאים שני ספרי</note>

### CHAPTER 8. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.

They bring forth the Books of the Law, from one of which the Sabbath text is read according to the regular series of lessons, and from the other, the text for that specific festival is read. ### CHAPTER 8. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.

They bring forth the Books of the Law <note>Torah scrolls</note>, so that from one of them the Sabbath text is read according to the ordinary cycle of readings, and from the other, the text of that specific Festival. Likewise on Feast days—specifically those called the *Seven Days of Passover, the Day of Atonement, etc.*—he <note>Maimonides</note> advises that two Books be brought out into public: in one, the texts appropriate to those Festivals are recited, and in the other, that which is found written in the Law concerning the Sacrifices of those days. <margin>§. 14.</margin> Moreover, our "Moses the Egyptian" <note>Moses Maimonides, the 12th-century philosopher and codifier of Jewish law</note> did not neglect to note those cases in which three Books are brought out: <margin>§. 23.</margin> **If the New Moon of the month of Adar falls on a Sabbath, they bring out three scrolls: in one, he reads the weekly portion of the day; in the second, he reads the matter concerning the New Moon; and in the third, he reads:** <margin>Exod. 30, 12.</margin> *“When you take [a census],” etc.* <note>The portion known as Ki Tissa, original Hebrew: כי תשא</note> Between the removal of the first Book and the production of the next, the *Kaddish* <note>A prayer praising God, often marking transitions in the service</note> must be recited: <margin>§. 15.</margin> **On any day when they bring out two or three scrolls, if they bring them out one after another, when he returns the first, he says Kaddish and brings out the second; and when he returns the last, he says Kaddish.** <note>original Hebrew: ובכל יום שמוציאין שני ספרים או שלשה אם הוציאו זה אחר זה כשמחזיר את הראשון אומ' קדיש ומוציא השני וכשמחזיר את האחרון אומר קדיש</note> So much for the procedures of this act.

3. Among the *circumstances* of this ritual, this especially must be remembered: that it cannot be performed with those solemnities (some of which I have already declared) unless <term>ten adult men</term> <note>The "Minyan" or legal quorum required for communal prayer</note> of free status are present. This statute, which is contained in so many words in the tractate *Megilla* <note>A book of the Talmud concerning the reading of the Scroll of Esther and synagogue rules</note>, occurs nowhere more frequently or familiarly in their writings. Moses the Egyptian says: <margin>Megilla cap. 4. §. 3.</margin> **They do not read the Law in public unless ten adult and free men are present.** <margin>Orach Chajim cap. 143. §. 1. cap. 12. §. 3.</margin> <note>The *Orach Chajim* is a section of the Shulchan Aruch, the standard code of Jewish law</note> The reason is that for the <term>Sanctification of the Divine Name</term> <note>Kiddush HaShem; a concept of public hallowing of God's name</note>, which they intended to be joined with the reading of the Law, they judged a minimum assembly of ten men was required. However, Maimonides excepts **the eight final verses of the Torah** <margin>Cap. 13. §. 6.</margin> <note>Deuteronomy 34:5–12, describing the death of Moses</note>, because the simple nature of the text forbids believing they came from the hand of Moses in that same way, since they refer to events that took place after his death.

### CHAPTER 8. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.

They bring forth the Books of the Law <note>The Torah scrolls</note>, from one of which the Sabbath text is read according to the ordinary sequence of readings, and from the second, the text for that specific Festival. This is likewise done on Feast days—properly so-called—such as the 
<margin>§ 14.</margin>
seven days of Passover, the Day of Atonement, etc. Our author <note>Maimonides</note> advises that two Books be brought out in public: in the first, the texts appropriate to those Festivals are recited; in the other, that which is found written in the Law concerning the sacrifices of those days. Regarding the cases in which three Books are brought forth, 
<margin>§ 23.</margin>
our same "Egyptian Moses" <note>A common scholarly nickname for Maimonides, referring to his life in Egypt</note> did not neglect to note: <note>original Hebrew: ראש חדש אדר שחל להיות בשבת מוציאין שלשה ספרים אחד קורא בו סדר היום והשני קורא בו ענין ראש חדש והשלישי קורא בו כי תשא</note> *If the New Moon of the month of Adar falls on a Sabbath, they should bring out three Books: in the first, they read the Sabbath text of that day; in the second, the text that fits the Festival; and in the third:* 
<margin>Exodus 30:12.</margin>
*“When you take [the sum of the children of Israel],” etc.* <note>Referring to the portion "Ki Tissa" regarding the census and the half-shekel</note> *Between the removal of the first Book and the 
<margin>§ 15.</margin>
bringing out of the second, the Kaddish* <note>A prayer of praise often used as a transition between sections of the service</note> *was to be recited:* <note>original Hebrew: ובכל יום שמוציאין שני ספרים או שלשה אם הוציאו זה אחר זה כשמחזיר את הראשון אומ' קדיש ומוציא השני וכשמחזיר את האחרון אומר קדיש</note> *On any day when they bring out two or three Books, if they bring them out one after another, after the first is removed, the formula of the KADDISH is recited, and immediately the second is brought forth; and when the last is removed, the KADDISH is repeated. So much for the methods of this act.*

3. Among the *adjuncts* <note>Requirements or accompanying rules</note> of this act, it must especially be remembered that these solemn rites—some of which I have already declared—cannot be performed unless *ten adult men* of free condition are present. For this statute, which is contained in so many words in the Code Megillah <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning the reading of the Scroll of Esther and synagogue rules</note>, occurs nowhere more 
<margin>Megillah chapter 4, § 3.</margin>
<margin>Orach Chajim chapter 143, § 1; chapter 12, § 3.</margin>
frequently or familiarly in their writings. Maimonides states: <note>original Hebrew: אין קורין בתור' בצבור בפחות מעשרה אנשים גדולים בני חורים</note> *They do not read the Law in public unless ten adult and free men are present.* The reason is that they judged a minimum assembly of ten men to be required for the "Sanctification of the Divine Name," which they wished to be joined with the reading of the Law. However, Maimonides excepts 
<margin>Chapter 13, § 6.</margin>
the *eight final verses of the Torah* <note>original Hebrew: שמנה פסוקים שבסוף התורה</note>, specifically the last eight verses of Deuteronomy; for the simplicity of the speech forbids the belief that they came from the hand of Moses in the same manner, since they refer to the events that took place after his death.

# ON THE READING OF THE MOSAIC LAW, BOOK III, PART II.

<margin>Chapter 4, Section 3.</margin>
But this observation by Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides, the 12th-century Jewish philosopher</note> is criticized by Rabbi Abraham Ben David <note>Known as the Ravad, a contemporary and frequent critic of Maimonides</note>, his Critic, and perhaps not without probable reason. For even if it is granted to Maimonides (as all sensible men will easily grant) that those last *eight* verses of Deuteronomy did not come from the hand of Moses in the manner they are now read, they should still be considered as having been written by Joshua or another Prophet, and thus they constitute a part of the Prophetic Word. However, the Prophetic Word itself was not to be read solemnly in public in a gathering of fewer than *ten* people <note>A minyan, or the minimum quorum of ten adult males required for certain religious obligations</note>, as is known from the Book of Megillah <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning the festival of Purim and synagogue readings</note>.

<margin>Babylonian Talmud, Bava Bathra, at the end of chapter 1, folio 14, column 2.</margin>
Moreover, the Talmudic scholars record in so many words in the Book of Bava Bathra <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning civil law and the history of sacred texts</note> that Joshua is the author of those verses; where, among many other things they have regarding the writing and assembly of the Sacred Books, these words are read: <note>original Hebrew: משה כתב ספרו ופרשת בלעם ואיוב יהושע כתב ספרו ושמונה פסוקין שבתורה</note> *Moses wrote his own Book, and the History of Balaam, and the Book containing the maxims of Job. Joshua wrote his own Book, and the EIGHT FINAL VERSES OF THE LAW.* Certainly, if Maimonides derived this decree of his from the words of the Jerusalem Talmud—<note>original Hebrew: יחיד קורא אותן</note> *One reads the eight final verses of Deuteronomy*—those Talmudic words seem entirely capable of being interpreted to mean that *one* person reads those last verses of the Law, <note>original Hebrew: שאינו מפסיק בהם</note> because it is not permitted to make a pause in the reading of them, which is how Rabbi Abraham Ben David understands them. Nevertheless, Shem Tov <note>A 14th-century commentator</note> defends Maimonides based on the Chapter *Hakkometz* and the work of Alphess <note>Isaac Alfasi, an important North African legal scholar</note>, into which places I do not care to inquire now, as even the Jerusalem Talmud is not currently at hand.

4. The *Consequences* of this Sacred Rite are the *Rolling of the Book*, followed by the *Doxology* <note>A short hymn or prayer of praise to God</note> to be repeated by each of the Readers, the recitation of the *Kaddish* <note>A prayer magnifying and sanctifying God's name</note> after the final reading, and finally the wrapping of the entire volume and the *returning* of it into the Ark, or whatever other shrine from which it was taken.

<margin>Laws of Prayer, chapter 12, section 5.</margin>
Maimonides' words regarding the first two points are clear: <note>original Hebrew: אחר כך קורא עד שישלים לקרות וגולל הספר ומברך בא"י אמ"ה אשר נתן לנו תורתו תורת אמת וחיי עולם נטע בתוכנו בא"י נותן התורה</note> *Afterward he (the Reader who has been called up) reads until he completes the reading, AND HE ROLLS THE BOOK, and offers praise [original Greek: δοξολογεῖ]: Blessed are You, O Lord, Ruler of the World, who has given us Your Law, the Law of Truth, and has planted eternal life within us. Blessed are You, Giver of the LA-*

<header>CHAPTER 8. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.</header>

THE SEED OF TRUTH, & ETERNAL LIFE you have planted among us; Blessed be You, O Lord, who gave the Law. <note>This is a translation of the Hebrew blessing recited after reading the Torah. The author uses "Gem" (seed/bud) to reflect the Latin "Germen."</note> Without a doubt, it is due to the superstition of later times that the Masters <note>The Rabbis and Jewish scholars of the medieval and early modern periods</note> explain *Eternal Life* in this doxology <note>A short hymn of praise to God</note> as referring to the Traditional Doctrine <note>The Oral Law or Talmud, as opposed to the written Bible</note>.

<margin>Rabbi Karo: Orach Chajim chapter 139, § 10.</margin>
*Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who gave us the Law of truth and planted eternal life within us. Blessed are You, Lord, giver of the Law.* <note>original Hebrew: ברוך אתה יי אלהינו מלך העולם אשר נתן לנו תורת אמת וחי עולם נטע בתוכנו ברוך אתה יי נותן התורה</note>
In the final Blessing, which is added after the Reading of the Law, the "Law of truth" is to be understood as the Written Law; however, the words: "And You have planted eternal life among us," refer to the Oral Law. This Blessing was to be recited by every Reader after their assigned section was read, and meanwhile, the Scripture of the Law was to be covered with a cloth <note>original Latin: "sudario," a kerchief or ritual cloth</note> until the next Reader could continue the appointed Reading:
<margin>In the same place, § 5.</margin>
*They are accustomed to cover the writing with a cloth during the intervals between the readers.* <note>original Hebrew: נהגו לכסות הכתב בסודר בין גברא לגברא</note>

Finally, the Volume is folded, or rather rolled up entirely, by the one who read last, or by someone who has purchased this honor for a price that goes toward the use of the poor. For it is clear from Maimonides <note>The 12th-century scholar Moses Maimonides</note> that this duty of rolling the Law is considered an honorable office:
<margin>Chapters 12, 13.</margin>
*The last one who rolls the Scroll of the Law takes a reward equal to them all; therefore, even the greatest man in the congregation may go up and complete it.* <note>original Hebrew: והאחרון שגולל ספר תורה נוטל שכר כנגד הכל לפיכך עולה ומשלים אפי' גדול שבצבור</note>
The last man, who rolls up the Volume of the Law, <margin>† receives a reward. Matthew 10:41.</margin> † receives a reward <note>original Greek: λαμβάνει μισθόν</note> due to all the Readers, and therefore it is not considered a disgrace for any Great Man of the Synagogue Assembly to occupy the last place among the Readers of the Law and to bring that Reading to a conclusion.

<margin>Orach Chajim chapter 147, § 11.</margin>
Rabbi Karo says: *The most honorable of those who have read from the Law rolls the Book; and they are generally accustomed to purchase that task for a high price to demonstrate their love for the Divine Commandment.* <note>original Hebrew: שקראו בתורה גולל ורגילי לקנותו בדמים יקרי' לחבב המצוה</note> Regarding the manner of rolling the Book, and its wrappings and cloak <note>The "mantle" or decorative cover of the Torah scroll</note>, Karo includes many details there; but as they are trivial and breathe the superstition of more recent times, it would be pointless to pursue them. However, I have learned from the same Maimonides that just as the <term>Kaddish</term> formula <note>A central prayer in the Jewish liturgy focusing on the sanctification of God's name</note> is to be placed before this Sacred Rite, so it must also be added afterward:
<margin>See also Maimonides chapter 12, § 24; chapter 13, § 15.</margin>
*We have already said that the common custom is to say Kaddish whenever the one finishing the reading completes it.* <note>original Hebrew: כבר אמרנו שהמנהג הפשוט לומר קדיש אחר שקורא המשלי' לעולם</note> Maimonides continues with the rest in another place as follows:
<margin>Chapter 12, § 20.</margin>
*And when they finish, he returns the Scroll of the Law to its place and says Kaddish, and they pray the Musaf prayer.* <note>original Hebrew: וכשגומרין מחזיר ספר תורה למקומה ואומר קדיש ומתפללין תפלת מוסף; the Musaf is an additional service held on Sabbaths and festivals.</note>

*In a place where they bring out a Scroll of the Law after reading from it and carry it to another house to store it away, the congregation is not permitted to leave until the Scroll of the Law has been taken out; rather, they must stay with it and accompany it all the way to the place where it is stored.*

In the marginal notes it is recorded: <note>original Hebrew: וכן נוהגין שהגולל הולך אחר החזן ועומד לפני הארון עד שתחזור ס"ת למקומה</note>
*And so it is the established custom that the one who rolls up the Scroll of the Law follows the <term>Cantor</term><note>The person who leads the congregation in song and prayer, often called the Hazzan.</note> and stands before the <term>Ark</term><note>The ornamental cabinet or chest (Aron Kodesh) where Torah scrolls are kept.</note> until the Scroll of the Law has been returned to its place.* Regarding Christ the Lord, after the text was read in the synagogue 
<margin>Luke 4:20.</margin> at Nazareth, it is simply said: *And when he had rolled up the book, he gave it back to the attendant.* <note>original Greek: Καὶ πτύξας τὸ βιβλίον, ἀποδοὺς τῷ ὑπηρέτῃ.</note>

## CHAPTER IX.

*This chapter addresses the **Circumstances** of this sacred exercise, concerning both Time and Place. It includes an explanation of a passage by Tertullian <note>An early Christian author (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) from Carthage</note>, in which he refers to the public reading of the Law as it was performed by the Jews in his era as a "Taxed Liberty" <note>original Latin: "Vectigalem Libertatem." This refers to the taxes Jews paid to the Roman Empire for the right to maintain their religious practices.</note>. Also discussed are the qualifications and requirements of the readers, as well as the specifics of their order and number. Finally, the duties of reverence required from the synagogue assembly during the performance of this act, as recorded in the Hebrew canons, are presented.*

Thirdly, we now pass from the consideration of the *Act* itself to its **Circumstances**, of which two must be observed here: **Time and Place**.

<margin>
Luke 18:12.
"I fast twice in the week [Sabbath]." <note>original Greek: Νηστεύω δὶς τοῦ σαββάτου</note>
Laws of Prayer, chapter 12, section 2. <note>original: Hilcoth Tephil.</note>
Tractate of the Scribes, chapter 10, sections 2, 3. <note>original: Cod. Sopherim</note>
The Way of Life, chapter 85, sections 1, 2, 3; chapter 12, section 16. <note>original: Orach Chajim</note>
</margin>

The times dedicated to performing this act in the synagogue are the morning and evening hours of the Sabbath, the Day of Atonement <note>Yom Kippur</note>, and solemn fasts; the morning hours of Feast Days and New Moons; and the Mondays and Thursdays of every week, which were long ago observed with great religious devotion by the ancient Jews. Maimonides <note>The preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> states: <note>original Hebrew: ואלו הם הימים שקורים בהם בתורה בצבור בשבתות ובמועדים ובראשי חדשים ובתעניות ובחנוכה ובפורים ובשני ובחמישי שבכל שבוע ושבוע</note> *These indeed are the days on which the Reading of the Law is celebrated in public: Sabbaths, appointed Festivals, New Moons, Fasts, the Feast of Dedication <note>original Greek: Ἐγκάινια (Enkainia), referring to Hanukkah</note>, Purim, and also the second day [Monday] and fifth day [Thursday] of each and every week.* Furthermore, Maimonides indicates in the following words—which will be described in their proper place—that the Law was read during the evening hours not only on the Sabbath, but also on the Day of Atonement and fast days.

<margin>
Book 1, Part 1, chapter 8.
</margin>
As for the Place, it consists of those very synagogue buildings which were constructed for the purpose of reading the Law, among other uses. Within the synagogue, following the example of that ancient reading performed under the leadership of Ezra, there is an elevated place—a platform or pulpit <note>original: Suggestus, sive Ambo</note>—which we did not overlook when describing the structure of the synagogue. It is called a "tower" <note>original Hebrew: מגדל (migdal)</note> in the Sacred History...

## CHAPTER IX.

*The discussion concerns the circumstances of this sacred exercise, regarding both Time and Place, including an exposition of a passage from Tertullian, in which he calls the public reading of the Law—as it was performed by the Jews around his time—a "Tax-paying Freedom." It also treats the qualities and requirements of the readers, as well as the particulars of their order and number; finally, the duties of reverence required from the synagogue assembly during the performance of this act, as described in the Hebrew Canons, are provided.*

<note>Tertullian (c. 155–220 AD) was an early Christian author; his phrase "Vectigalem Libertatem" refers to the fact that Jews in the Roman Empire often had to pay a special tax to maintain the legal right to practice their ancestral customs and hold public readings.</note>

Thirdly, we now pass from the consideration of the *Act* itself to its CIRCUMSTANCES, of which two are to be observed here: *Time and Place.*

<margin>
Luke 18:12.
"I fast twice a week." <note>original Greek: Νησεύω δὶς τοῦ σαββάτου</note>
Laws of Prayer <note>Hilcoth Te-phil</note>, chapter 12, § 2.
Tractate Sopherim <note>The Scribes</note>, chapter 10, § 2, 3.
Orach Chajim <note>The Path of Life, a major code of Jewish law</note>, chapter 85, § 1, 2, 3; chapter 12, § 16.
</margin>

Regarding the times: the hours consecrated for performing this act in the synagogue include the morning and evening hours of the Sabbath, the Day of Atonement <note>Yom Kippur</note>, and solemn fasts; the morning hours of Festival Days and New Moons; and also the second and fifth days <note>Monday and Thursday</note> of every week, which were observed with great religious devotion by the ancient Jews since long ago. **Maimonides** <note>A definitive medieval Jewish scholar</note> writes: <note>original Hebrew: ואלו הם הימים שקורין בהם בתורה בצבור בשבתות ובמועדים ובראשי חדשים ובתעניות ובחנוכה ובפורי' ובשני ובחמשי שבכל שבוע ושבוע</note> "And these are the days on which the Law is read in public: on Sabbaths, Festivals, New Moons, Fasts, Hanukkah, Purim, and on the second and fifth days of every week." These are indeed the times when the public reading of the Law is celebrated: Sabbaths, appointed Feasts, New Moons, Fasts, Hanukkah <note>original Greek: Ἐγκαινία — literally "Renewal" or "Dedication"</note>, Purim, as well as the second and fifth days of each week. Furthermore, Maimonides indicates in the following words (to be described in their proper place) that the Law was read during the evening hours not only on the Sabbath, but also on the Day of Atonement and fast days.

<margin>
Book 1, Part 1, chapter 8.
</margin>

As for the Place: these are the Synagogue buildings themselves, which were constructed for the purpose of reading the Law, among other uses. Within the synagogue, following the example of that ancient reading held under the leadership of **Ezra**, there is an elevated place—a platform or pulpit <term>Ambo: A raised desk or pulpit used for reading the scriptures, ensuring the voice carries to the whole assembly</term>—which we did not overlook when describing the structure of the synagogue. In history, it is called a <term>Migdal <note>original Hebrew: מגדל — literally 'tower' or 'platform'</note></term>.
