<page-num>978</page-num>
<header>OF THE READING OF THE MOSAIC LAW, BOOK I.</header>

<margin>
Nehemiah 8:5.
Orach Chajim, chapter 141, § 7. <note>The "Path of Life," a standard code of Jewish Law.</note>
</margin>
...[on the Sabbath], the sacred rites and the statutes of the Jews [require it]; as observed in the preceding sections, the Jews built synagogues in every place, and likewise, the reading of the Law took place in every place—not only in Canaan <note>the Land of Israel</note>, but even in the most remote regions wherever a large number of them resided, provided that it was permitted to them by the Magistrate <note>the local civil authority</note>. Nor was there any fault in this. On the contrary, just as that custom was praiseworthy, so too through it, by the action of Divine Providence, the conversion of both Jews and Gentiles to Christ was promoted through preaching.

<margin>
Chrysostom, Oration 4 against the Jews.
</margin>
For this reason, I do not know what Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an Early Church Father known for his intense orations against Jewish practices.</note> is doing when he contends that it is not permitted for Jews to read the Law *outside* <note>original Latin: "foris"</note>—that is, outside the city of Jerusalem. It would be a different matter if the Magistrate forbade or impeded this religious exercise, or even burdened it with an imposed tax, as seems to have happened later under certain Emperors.

In this way, learned men rightly interpret Tertullian <note>An early Christian author (c. 155–220 AD).</note>, in my judgment, who calls the rite of publicly reading the Law a **TAX-PAYING FREEDOM**. His words, the greater part of which were described and explained above, read as follows: *But the Jews also read it openly* (referring to the Biblical Codex).
<margin>
Tertullian, Apology, chapter 19.
Samuel Petit, Various Readings, chapter 18.
</margin>
**TAX-PAYING FREEDOM** *is accessed every Sabbath.* <note>original Latin: "Vectigalis Libertas aditur Sabbatis omnibus."</note> That is, the freedom to read the Divine Law in public in the age of Tertullian was redeemed with money <note>referring to the "Fiscus Judaicus," a tax imposed on Jews in the Roman Empire for the right to maintain their traditions.</note>. From this, however, I do not conclude—as [Samuel] Petit does—that the private reading of the Hebrew Scripture was entirely forbidden. For how could it be read publicly without private practice? Or what reason would there be for granting the public reading of the Law while prohibiting the private?

And why would the Romans—who were otherwise lenient in tolerating the religions of other nations—prohibit what was in their power and not impede it through an interdict? That the persecutors of Jews or Christians, such as [Antiochus] Epiphanes, Diocletian, Maximian, etc., ordered the Books to be handed over by edicts and wanted them sought out to be given to the flames, was entirely rare and extraordinary, and departed from the common practice of the Roman Emperors. And whatever the Roman Emperors might have hostiley plotted against the Christians, I do not recall reading that they ever vented their rage against the Jewish religion with a dire persecution of that kind. And if entirely following that same example...

<summary>The author argues that the reading of the Mosaic Law was historically permitted globally, refuting John Chrysostom's claim that it was restricted to Jerusalem. He also analyzes Tertullian's phrase "Tax-paying Freedom," suggesting it refers to a fee for public assembly rather than a ban on private study.</summary>

**1. Concerning the Qualifications and Requirements of the Readers of the Law, let us note:**

**א.** <note>The Hebrew letter Aleph, used here as a bullet point.</note> *The practice of reading the Divine Law in the Synagogue was common to all Jews, with the exception of* **SLAVES, WOMEN, THE BLIND, THE FOOLISH, AND THOSE DISGRACEFULLY DRESSED**; *nevertheless,* **MINORS** *were admitted.*

א. <note>The Hebrew letter Aleph, marking the first point.</note> Although the practice of Reading could be entrusted to any skilled men in the Synagogue, nevertheless Priests, Levites, and learned men of superior dignity were generally preferred over others who were inferior in status or merit.

Furthermore, whoever is greater than another in knowledge and skill is also admitted to read before him.* Nevertheless, we should not omit the qualification added by Maimonides, in case a Priest or Levite should be missing from the Synagogue:

In the second place among the particulars concerning the Readers, their *Number* must be considered, regarding which Maimonides has encompassed nearly everything relevant in this one paragraph: <note>original Hebrew: "כמה הם הקוראין בשבת... אין מוסיפין עליהן"</note> *How many are the people appointed to the reading of the Law? During the morning hours of the Sabbath, seven read; on the Day of Public Atonement <note>Yom Kippur</note>, six; and on Festival days, five. This number they never decrease, but it is permitted to increase it. On the New Moons and the intermediate days of Festivals, four Readers are employed. On the Sabbath and the Day of Atonement during the afternoon hours, and also on the second and fifth days of each week <note>Mondays and Thursdays</note> throughout the entire year, as well as on the morning hours of the Festivals of Dedication <note>Hanukkah</note> and Purim, and during the morning and afternoon sacred services of Fast Days, only three Readers are employed; to this number they neither add nor subtract.* These rules are derived from both the Mishnah and the Gemara <note>the two components of the Talmud</note> in the tractate Megillah.

While these solemn rituals are carefully observed by the *Readers*, certain **DUTIES** of reverence and religious devotion are likewise required from the Israelite listeners and spectators, corresponding to this sacred act; among which we include:

1. *The responses to the blessings to be placed before and after this sacred act by the Reader.*

<margin>† See Maimonides, Laws of Prayer, chapter 12, § 5. Orach Chayim, chapter 141, § 5 and § 9 in the place cited.</margin>
Thus, specifically, at the first blessing of praise <term>Eulogic <gloss>from the Greek 'eulogia,' meaning a blessing or word of praise</gloss></term> directed by the Reader to the people in these words: **"Bless the Lord who is blessed,"** the people were required to respond: <note>original Hebrew: "ברוך ה' המבורך לעולם ועד"</note> **"Blessed be the Lord who is blessed for ever and ever."** Following the subsequent blessings, examples of which were provided earlier, the synagogue congregation must add: **"Amen."**

2. *Attention, joined with reverence toward the Sacred Reading.*

Maimonides states: <note>original Hebrew: "כיון שהתחיל הקורא לקרות בתורה אסור לספר אפילו בדבר הלכה אלא הכל שומעין ושותקין ומשמיעין לבם"</note> *As soon as the reader begins to read from the Torah, it is forbidden to speak, even concerning a matter of law; rather, everyone listens, remains silent, and applies their heart...*

In the handling of this matter, however, it has been decided to set a limit to the pen, because if we wished to follow each point in the same order, certain small details, already sufficiently known from what preceded, would have to be repeated. *Therefore*, those things we have to say regarding this argument we shall conveniently bring together here, so that *firstly, in general*, we may look at the *subject matter of the Reading* itself, as it is called, or the *Prophetic Word* to be read; then more specifically at the texts and parts of that Word which were to be recited before others—that is, *What and How Much from the Writings of the Prophets* was read in the *Exercise of Sacred rites*; afterwards concerning the *Manner* in which that reading was to be established; and finally concerning its *Circumstances*, as well as the *Readers* to be assigned to the *Act*, and let us add a few things *concerning the name* <term>Haphtarah <gloss>literally "dismissal" or "completion," referring to the prophetic portion that concludes the scripture service</gloss></term>, by which this Rite is designated.

<margin>
See de Voysin in the Introduction to the "Dagger of Faith" <note>original: Pugio Fidei</note> by Raymond [Martini], folio 117. 
Simon, "Critical History of the Old Testament," book 1, chapter 9.
</margin>
It is clear from the terms themselves that the subject matter of that *Reading*, which is called *Prophetic*, is <note>original Greek: τὸν Προφητικὸν Λόγον</note> the PROPHETIC WORD. By which *Prophetic Word*, however, must be strictly understood here the *Second Part of the Codex of the Old Testament*, which the Jews distinguish from the <term>Torah <gloss>the Law</gloss></term> and the <term>Hagiographa <gloss>Holy Writings, or Ketuvim</gloss></term>, labeling it with the name <term>Prophets <gloss>Nevi'im</gloss></term>. Under these they include both the *Historical Books of Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Kings* (which they certainly consider to have been written by Prophets and *therefore* call the <term>Former Prophets <gloss>Nevi'im Rishonim</gloss></term>), as well as those Writings truly and <note>original Greek: φερωνύμως</note> appropriately so-called, which have been preserved for us from the dictations of the excellent Seers *Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Twelve Prophets*, known today in the Hebrew Codex by the title <term>Latter Prophets <gloss>Nevi'im Acharonim</gloss></term>. For although some of the *Hagiographa Writings*, and specifically those well-known *five Minor Volumes of the Hagiographa* <note>The Five Megillot: Song of Songs, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, and Esther</note>, may be read in certain unique cases, nevertheless in the ordinary *Haphtarahs* which have become customary to follow the solemn Sabbath reading of the *Divine Law* according to the *List of Maimonides* (for not all Synagogues agree on the same *Haphtarahs*), no text at all is found noted from the *Hagiographa*. Moreover, it is by no means the solemn custom for these *Books of the Prophets* to be recited in their entirety from beginning to end through the *Synagogue Readings*; but, as we have already begun to point out, *certain texts* are plucked from those Books, the subject matter of which comes very close to the subject of the text to be read from the *Mosaic Law* itself. Maimonides [states]: <margin>Laws of Prayer <note>original: Hilchot Tephilla</note> chapter 13, § 3.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: "ומפטירין בכל שבת ובחג בנביא מעין שקרא בתורה"</note> *And they conclude [the reading] every Sabbath and holiday with a selection from a Prophet that resembles [the theme of] what was read in the Torah.*

On the Sabbath, a text is chosen from the Prophets of a similar theme to the one being read from the Law <note>The "Law" refers to the Torah, or the first five books of the Bible.</note>. However, on extraordinary days when a Prophetic Reading is to be celebrated—and indeed on the Sabbaths themselves upon which Feast days fall—special texts are selected from the Prophetic Books that correspond to the readings from the Law.

<margin>Isaiah 66:23.</margin>
Thus, for example, if a New Moon <term>Rosh Chodesh <gloss>the celebration of the start of the Jewish lunar month</gloss></term> falls on a Sabbath, they read the words of Isaiah: *And it shall come to pass from New Moon to New Moon*; on the New Moon of the month of July <note>likely referring to the month of Av in the Jewish calendar</note>, (during which falls that established and most famous Fast <note>Tisha B'Av, a day of mourning for the destruction of the Temple</note>) if it falls on a Sabbath, they read:

<margin>Isaiah 1:14. 1 Samuel 20:18.</margin>
*Your New Moons and your Appointed Feasts my soul hates.* If the New Moon occurs on the first day of the week, on the Sabbath of the preceding day they read:

<margin>Laws of Prayer <note>original: Hilcath Tephilla</note> chapter 13, sections 3, 4, 11, 12.</margin>
*And Jonathan said to him: Tomorrow is the New Moon.* I have described this according to Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note>, who is also the authority for the reading on the

<margin>1 Samuel 1:1.</margin>
Feast of the New Year <note>Rosh Hashanah</note>: *Now there was a certain man of Ramah, etc.*

<margin>Isaiah 57:15. Zechariah 14:1. [and following verses].</margin>
On the Day of Atonement <note>Yom Kippur</note>, in the morning hours: *Thus says the Lord, high and exalted, etc.* In the evening, from Jonah. On the first day of the Feast of Tabernacles <note>Sukkot</note>: *Behold, the day comes for the Lord, etc.* and so on for the others, for it is not my intention to write down everything. He who desires more may consult Maimonides himself, who, as is his custom, diligently lists the texts to be recited on individual festivals.

Who would not approve of or praise this institution of the Synagogue, by which they compare Moses with the Prophets and illustrate his meaning through the Prophets? For certainly Moses must be held not only as the Father and Prince of all the Prophets (<note>original Hebrew: אב כל הנביאים</note>), but also by the highest right one may proclaim of his Prophecy that it is the prototype (<note>original Greek: πρωτότυπον</note>) and model of all prophecies: not only in the sense that all prophecies are to be tested against those of Moses, but also because the Mosaic Doctrine and Prophecy contain the sum of all teachings and predictions, which were subsequently explained more broadly and copiously by the Prophets and Teachers of later times. This, unless I am mistaken, is what the Ancient Jewish Philosophers wished to say

# CHAPTER 10. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.

...you should consider whether the circumstances suggest that the word *me’ein* <note>original Hebrew: מעין; typically meaning "similar to" or "in the style of"</note> should be understood here as a *kind*, *image*, or *replica* <note>original Greek: ἔκτύπῳ (*ektypo*)</note>; in which sense it is frequently used by the Rabbis, and in which same meaning it just occurred to us in the writings of Maimonides. If we accept the word in this way in this passage, the sense will be: *The prophecy of every Prophet is a certain replica (a species or kind of image) of the Mosaic prophecy: that Moses stood as the model and exemplar, as it were, for all the Prophets, and all other Prophets were modeled after him, since they were sent by God for this purpose: to confirm and declare what Moses, the most excellent of the Prophets, had set forth.* It is fitting, therefore, that the *Writings of Moses and the Prophets* were not only read together in the Synagogue, but also that in their reading, the agreement between both was demonstrated.

Yet it seems surprising that the *Prophetic Readings* were not equally taken from the *Hagiographa* <term>Ketuvim <gloss>the "Writings," the third and final section of the Hebrew Bible</gloss></term>, especially from the *Psalms*, which are the most precious treasure <note>original Greek: κειμηλίῳ (*keimēliō*)</note> of the Hagiographa. There was undoubtedly not just one reason for this practice, but several; unless one might perhaps suspect that the Ancient Jews generally held the *Hagiographa* to be of lesser authority than the *Law and the Prophets*. However, there is no need to go that far; both because we do not have the opinions of the Ancient Jews on this matter sufficiently explored (even though it is certain that the authors of the Talmud felt this way), and because for certain of those books, other reasons are available to us, which are proposed here more safely and with a greater appearance of truth. 

Some books of the Hagiographa contain general themes of a single type, from which a specific selection could not be as easily plucked as from the Prophetic books; the *Books of Proverbs* and *Job* are of this kind. 

<margin>
See Tractate 
Sopherim 
chapter 14, sections 18, 
19. <note>Tractate Soferim is a rabbinic work focused on the preparation of sacred scrolls and liturgical reading.</note>
</margin>

Furthermore, the five smaller *Volumes—Ecclesiastes, the Song of Solomon, the Lamentations of Jeremiah, and the Histories of Ruth and Esther*—were certainly accustomed to be read during the *Feast of Tabernacles, Passover, the solemn Fast of the month of July <note>referring to Tisha B'Av, the fast mourning the destruction of the Temple, occurring in the summer</note>, the Feast of Pentecost, and Purim*. 

As for the other *Volumes of the Hagiographa*, I am easily persuaded that the *Books of Ezra and Nehemiah* were not considered by the Jews to be of the same authority as those Books of Scripture—even the historical ones—which were written by *Prophets*. Moreover, the *Historical* parts of the Book of *Daniel* have little connection with *Legal* matters <note>referring to the laws of the Torah</note>, while the *Prophetic* parts are of a loftier subject matter than the common people could have benefited from by hearing them read aloud.

# BOOK III. ON THE READING OF THE PROPHETS
<page-num>988</page-num>

<margin>
Matthew 5:17; 7:12; 11:13; 22:40. Acts 26:22.

* See Luke 24:29. † Luke 24:27, 44.
</margin>

The *two Books of Chronicles* share the same subject matter as the Books of Kings, and therefore reading them is considered less necessary. As for the *Psalms*, because of their author and subject matter, the Jews of all eras have cherished them most highly; following the example of the Mosaic Law, they are divided into *Five Books*. Because they were *chanted* <note>original: "cantillati"</note> in the sacred rites of the Synagogue, and from them especially the *Formulas for Prayers and Doxologies* <note>hymns of praise</note> were composed, they [the Jews] dispensed with a formal *public reading* <note>original: "praelectione"</note> of them. From this established custom of the Synagogue, it is easy to see why the books of the Old Testament are designated in the New Testament by the phrase <term>The LAW and the PROPHETS</term> <note>original: Νόμος καὶ Προφηטῶν (a mix of Greek and Hebrew characters for *Nomos kai Prophetai*)</note>. These were not only the primary parts of the Divine Scripture, but were also more well-known and familiar to the Jews through the Synagogue readings. I am not unaware, however, that the name of the *Prophets* sometimes included the *Hagiographa* <term>Ketuvim <gloss>The "Writings," the third section of the Hebrew Bible</gloss></term> themselves, and elsewhere in the list of the major parts of Scripture, the † Hagiographa are by no means omitted.

<margin>
Maimonides, Laws of Prayer (Hilkhot Tefillah), chapter 12, § 13.
See also the Tractate of the Scribes (Massekhet Soferim), chapter 14, § 1, 2.
Kol Bo, chapter 20, column 3, and Orach Chayim, chapter 284, § 1.
</margin>

When reading from a Prophet, the minimum requirement was *twenty-one verses*, unless the meaning of the text was completed in fewer verses, or if an interpretation of the Word being read was added. Maimonides writes: <insert>It is necessary that the reader first read in the Torah, even three verses repeating what the previous reader read; and he shall not conclude with the Prophet until he rolls up the Scroll [of the Law]; and he shall not read fewer than twenty-one verses. But if he completes the matter in fewer, he need not read more. And if he reads ten verses and the interpreter translates them, this is the law, even if he did not complete the matter.</insert> *

> *It is necessary that the Reader of the Prophet first read something from the Law—even three verses, if he pleases—repeating the text which the reader immediately before him has just read. He should not begin the Prophetic reading at all until he has rolled up the Scroll of the Law. Furthermore, he shall read no fewer than twenty-one verses; but if the sense of the text is completed in fewer verses, he is not bound by that number. If he reads ten verses and an Interpreter is present to translate them into the vernacular <note>Aramaic or the local language</note>, that is sufficient, even if the sense of the text runs longer.*

The method of the reading itself does not differ much from the reading of the Law. Specifically, the start of the reading was to be made with Doxologies (two of which pertained to the reading of the Law, and one specifically to that of the Prophets), and it was to be closed not with one, but with several Doxologies. A mention of these...

# CHAPTER 10. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.

...[Maimonides] proposes, but I have fully understood the matter from the *Tractate of the Scribes* <term>Massekhet Soferim <gloss>A minor tractate of the Talmud that outlines the rules for preparing holy scrolls and the liturgical requirements for public reading</gloss></term>, and from Rabbi Jacob Ben Asher. Truly, as we just observed from Maimonides, for the *Reader of the Prophets*, before he could begin the Reading of the Prophets itself, something from the Law <note>The Torah</note> had to be tasted beforehand; thus, those two *Doxologies* <note>formulas of praise or blessings</note> which, according to the solemn customs of the Synagogue, are usually placed before and after the Reading of the Law, were to be recited. These were then followed by the Doxology itself, from which the Reading of the Prophets was to begin. It consists, as shown in the *Tractate of the Scribes*, of these words:

<margin>
Maimonides, Laws of Prayer (*Hilkhot Tefillah*), chapter 12, § 15.
*Soferim*, chapter 13, § 9, 10, 12.

*And thus before the Reading of the Prophets they say: Blessed are You, O Lord our God, Ruler of the World, who has chosen good Prophets, and took delight in their words, which they spoke in truth. Blessed are You, O Lord, who has chosen the Law, and Moses Your servant, and Israel Your people, and the prophets of truth and righteousness.* <note>original Hebrew: וכן בנביאים אומרים ברוך אתה ה' אלהינו מלך העולם...; original Latin: "Benedictus Tu sis, Domine Deus noster, Rector Mundi..."</note>

And indeed, this Doxology was to be placed before the Reading of the Prophets; the Reading, however, was to be concluded with four Doxologies, the first of which is: *Blessed are You, O Lord our God, Ruler of the world, Rock of all ages, righteous throughout all generations, faithful God, who performs what You say, and makes firm what You speak, since all Your words are truth and justice.* <note>original Hebrew: ברוך אתה ה' אלהינו מלך העולם צור כל העולמים...; original Latin: "Benedictus sis, Tu Domine Deus noster, Rector mundi, Rupes omnium saeculorum..."</note> To which Doxology the people in the Synagogue, rising immediately, would follow with this responsory <note>original: αντιφωνίᾳ (antiphonia)</note>: *You are faithful, O Lord our God; Your words are faithful; Your name is faithful, living, and enduring, and Your remembrance is perennial among us. May You rule over us forever and ever.* <note>original Hebrew: נאמן אתה הוא ה' אלהינו ונאמנים דבריך...; original Latin: "Fidelis tu ille Domine Deus noster; fidelia sunt dicta tua..."</note>

To which responsory the Reader of the Prophets would add: *You are faithful; Blessed are You, Lord, mighty God, faithful in all Your words.* <note>original Hebrew: נאמן אתה הוא ה' אלהינו ונאמן בכל דבריך; original Latin: "Fidelis tu ILLE es; Benedictus sis tu Domine..."</note> And here the *first blessing* ended, as I perceived more clearly from Maimonides than from the *Tractate of the Scribes* itself.

The second is presented in these words: *Have mercy on Zion, for she is...* <note>original Hebrew: רחם על ציון כי היא</note>

<margin>§. 14.</margin>
Finally, the fourth Doxology follows, composed in this manner:

For the Torah, and for the service, and for the Prophets, and for this holy [N.] day <note>The "N." serves as a placeholder for the specific holiday or Sabbath being observed.</note> which You have given us, Lord our God, for holiness and for rest, for glory and for beauty; for all these things, Lord our God, we thank You and bless Your name always ... God of our salvation. Blessed are You, Lord, who sanctifies Israel and [this day]. *Because of the Prophets, and this very same holy Day N., which You gave to us, O Lord our God, for* holiness <note>original Greek: ἁγιασμον (*hagiasmon*)</note> *and rest, for glory and honor;* <margin>See Matthew 11:25.</margin> *for all those things, O Lord our God, we* give thanks <note>original Greek: ἐξομολογούμεθα (*exomologoumetha*)</note> *and celebrate Your Name always, O God of our salvation. Blessed be You, Lord, who sanctifies Israel and this day.*

However, on the [Sabbath] day it was simply said: *Blessed be You, Lord, who sanctifies the Sabbath;* and indeed for this reason:

"And the children of Israel shall keep..." etc. "For in six days the Lord made the heavens and the earth, and on the seventh day He rested and was refreshed." And they say: "See that the Lord has given you the Sabbath, which was already [established]." <margin>Exodus 31:17.</margin> *Because the Sabbath is older than Israel, just as it is written: For in six days the Lord made Heaven and earth, and on the seventh day He rested and was refreshed:* hence they say: *Direct your mind to the fact that God gave you the Sabbath, which had already existed long ago.*

In other matters, the practice was almost the same, except that the Reader of the Prophets was granted the freedom to skip from one text to another, which was not equally permitted in the *Reading of the Law* <note>The Torah</note>, as was noted above. <margin>§. 13. See also *Orach Chayim* chapter 144, §. 1.</margin> Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and Torah scholar.</note> writes:

[The reader may skip] from one matter to another, but he does not skip from one Prophet to another, except only in the Volume of the Twelve Prophets <note>The "Twelve" refers to the Minor Prophets, traditionally written on a single scroll.</note>, provided that he does not skip from the end of the book to its beginning, and provided that he does not pause in the skipping longer than it takes for the translator to finish his translation. *It is permitted for him (the Reader of the Prophets) to make a jump from one text to another of a different subject; however, he does not jump from one Prophet to another, except only in the Volume of the Twelve Prophets...*

<header>ON THE READING OF THE PROPHETS, Book III.</header>

...on the mornings of the **Day of Atonement** <note>Yom Kippur</note> and the **ninth day of the month of July** <note>This likely refers to Tisha B'Av, the fast day mourning the destruction of the Temple; early modern scholars often mapped Hebrew months to the Julian/Gregorian calendar.</note>, the third reader usually performs the duty of the **Maftir** <note>Greek: τοῦ Maphtir</note> (**Reader of the Prophets**). Although the Maftir can be counted among the total number of readers, it is generally not permitted to add anything to the established number of readers. However, on the **Sabbath**, **Festivals**, and the **Day of Atonement**, where the number of readers is not strictly limited from being increased, they are accustomed to arrange it so that on the Sabbath, the reader of the Prophets is the eighth; on a Festival, the sixth; and similarly for the Day of Atonement.

The listeners were required to receive this reading of the Prophets with the utmost
<margin>Orach Chayim chapter 146, § 3.</margin>
reverence. **Rabbi Karo** <note>Joseph Karo (1488–1575), author of the Shulchan Aruch, the foundational code of Jewish law.</note> states: *When the Maftir reads from the Prophet until he completes it, it is just as with the Scroll of the Law* <note>original Hebrew: כשהמפטיר קורא בנביא עד שישלים כמו בספר תורה</note>; it is forbidden to mingle in conversation with another while the Reading of the Prophet is being celebrated, just as is observed during the Reading of the Law. Similarly, one’s mind must be attentive to the **Blessings** which are offered by the reader before and after the act of reading from the Prophets.

<margin>Orach Chayim chapter 284.</margin>
*The blessing of the one reading the Law and the blessing of the Maftir [are significant] because on the Sabbath there are not the Eighteen Blessings, and thus one falls far short of the hundred blessings; whoever attends to all these blessings and responds ‘Amen’ after them, let it be for him the completion [of the count].* <note>original Hebrew: ברכת הקורא בתורה ולברכת המפטיר שאין בשבת י"ח ברכות וחסר הרבה ממאה ברכות כל לאלו הברכות ויענה אחריהם אמן יהא לו בהם השלומים. This refers to the Jewish tradition of reciting 100 blessings daily; since the Sabbath prayer is shorter, the Torah and Haftarah blessings help reach the goal.</note> It is every person’s duty to attend to the **Blessings of the Law and the Prophets**, because on the Sabbath, since they do not recite the **Eighteen Benedictions** <note>The Amidah, which on weekdays has 19 blessings but on Sabbath only 7.</note>, they miss several of the **Hundred Doxologies** <note>The required 100 daily blessings.</note>. Anyone who pays attention to those blessings and responds "Amen" compensates for the deficiency through them. However, it was rare for a reading to be taken from two separate prophetic books, though it did happen in certain cases.

<margin>Orach Chayim chapter 144, § 2.</margin>
As we find in **Rabbi Karo**: *On a Sabbath in which there is a Groom, it is customary to say after the Haftarah "I will greatly rejoice," or three verses from the Haftarah "I will greatly rejoice." On a Sabbath occurring on the day before the New Moon, after finishing the Haftarah of that Sabbath, they read the first and last verse of the Haftarah "And Jonathan said to him: Tomorrow is the New Moon."* <note>original Hebrew: בשבת שיש בו חתן לומר אחרי הפטרה שוש אשיש או שלושה פסוקים מהפטרה שוש אשיש בשבת ביו' א' אחר שמפטירין ההפטרה בשבת פסוק ראשון ופסוק אחרון מהפטרה ויאמר לו יהונתן מחר חודש</note> They are accustomed on a Sabbath where a **Groom** is present, after the **Haftarah** <note>The selection from the Prophets.</note> of that week, to recite two or four verses from the Prophet:
<margin>Isaiah 61:10. Compare Maimonides chapter 13, § 4. 1 Samuel 20:5.</margin>
**"I will greatly rejoice"**; and when the **New Moon** <note>Rosh Chodesh</note> falls on the first day after the Sabbath, having finished the Haftarah of that Sabbath, they add the first and last verse of the special Haftarah: **"And Jonathan said to him: Tomorrow is the New Moon."** Otherwise, when two Sections of the Law were read (which we noted previously happens on certain Sabbaths), only that Haftarah was read which corresponded to the latter portion.

This suffices for what we have reported concerning the Reading of the Prophets.

Latins otherwise say more correctly: *The assembly having been dissolved*. Yet, it seems to stand against this explanation of the word that the Synagogue assembly was not immediately dismissed after the *Reading of the Prophets*, since according to the tradition of Maimonides himself, the *Additional Sabbath Prayers* <note>original Hebrew: תפלת מוסף; Musaf prayers recited on holidays and the Sabbath</note> were only to be recited after the Reading of the Prophets was finished; and it is established elsewhere that the Priestly Blessing was to be interspersed with them; and after these were completed, the assembly was finally dismissed. Schem Tof"; likely Shem Tov ibn Gaon, a 14th-century Spanish kabbalist and scholar</note> notes in his *Migdal Oz* <note>original: "Migdal Gnoos"; referring to his commentary on Maimonides' Mishneh Torah</note>. These matters are no less clearly handed down in the *Kol Bo* <note>original: "Colbo"; a 14th-century Hebrew legal code</note>, from which I shall transcribe the parts relevant to me now: <margin>Chapter 20, folio column 4, 1</margin>

> In places where they are accustomed to appoint two cantors <note>original Hebrew: "chazzanim"</note>, one for the *Yotzer* <note>original Hebrew: "Jotzer"; the morning blessings surrounding the Shema</note> and one for the *Musaf* <note>the additional Sabbath/festival service</note>; the first reads the Torah, and after the reading of the *Haftarah* <note>the prophetic portion</note>, he says the "He Who Blessed" <note>original Hebrew: "Mi Shebarech"; a prayer for the community</note>, the "Happy Are They" <note>original Hebrew: "Ashrei"; Psalm 145</note>, and "Let Them Praise" <note>original Hebrew: "Yehallelu"</note>, and returns the Scroll to its place; and afterward the second stands up and says the "Small Kaddish" <note>a prayer of sanctification</note> and prays the *Musaf* prayer.

*But in the place where they are accustomed to appoint two Synagogue officials, one for the Jotzer (is this the blessing "He who forms Light" <note>original: "Jotzer Oor"</note>, or does the Kol Bo include the whole morning prayer under that name?) and the other for the Additional prayers; the first reads from the Law and, after the reading of the Prophets, says: "He Who Blessed"* <margin>\* You find *Ashrei* in *Sopherim* chapter 14.</margin> *\* "Happy Are They": and "Let Them Praise" (unless I am mistaken, these are the names of Blessings) and returns the Book of the Law to its place; and afterward the second one rises, and recites the "Small Kaddish," and the Additional Prayers.*

Do you see that the people were not immediately dismissed after the Reading of the Prophets? It is doubtful, however, how these things were handled in the ancient Synagogue, and whether the same custom was observed in all Synagogues. <margin>See Nehemiah chapter 8, verses 10, 11.</margin> In the sacred rites of religion as they were celebrated under the leadership of Ezra, the *Reading of the Law* seems to have occupied the final place. From the history written by Luke, it seems similarly gathered that the Sabbath rites, as they were observed in the Synagogue of Antioch in Pisidia, were terminated by the *Reading of the Prophets*, provided no sermon was held. <margin>Acts 13:15, verse 42.</margin> For *after the reading of the Law and the Prophets*, the leaders of the synagogue are said to have invited Paul and Barnabas to deliver a sermon; and it is clearly hinted in the same history that after that sermon was delivered, with no other public rites intervening, the synagogue gathering was dismissed. Also in the sacred rites of the Synagogue of Nazareth, when <margin>Luke 4:16. "And he stood up to read" <note>original Greek/Hebrew mix: "καὶ ἀνέστη ἀנאγνῶναι"</note>.</margin> Christ the Lord performed the office of the *Prophetic Reader*, Luke records that the sermon of Christ the Lord followed that reading, and with that sermon the public exercise of religion ended at that time too; unless, perhaps (which is less clear), the Lord Jesus in that case ascended the platform among the ordinary readers of the Law and Prophets for the sake of reading, or whether he read the *text* outside the usual order as the theme of the sermon he delivered, and whether he acted more as a Teacher than as a Reader. In any case, it did not deviate from the customs of the synagogue

# CHAPTER 10. IN THE SYNAGOGUE. 995

*That a sermon followed the Reading of the Prophets, given by the same Reader of the Prophets or by another, is clear from the Tractate Sopherim.* <note>The Sopherim, or "Scribes," is a minor tractate of the Talmud concerning the production of sacred scrolls and the order of the liturgy.</note> <margin>Sopherim chapter 14, § 1.</margin> *The following words are read there:* <note>original Hebrew: "וכן אתה אומר בכ"ב פסוקי'..."</note> "And so you say, concerning the twenty-two verses in the Prophet, they correspond to the readers [of the Law], three for each, and one in honor of the Minister of the Synagogue. In what case is this understood? When they do not translate into the vernacular or preach; but if they do translate and preach, the one who dismisses the congregation through the Prophet <note>original: "Ha-Maftir ba-Navi"; the person who reads the concluding prophetic portion</note> reads three, five, or seven verses, and that is sufficient." *From this we see that twenty-two verses are recited (speaking of the Reading of the Prophets) in respect to the seven Readers of the Law; specifically, three verses for each reader, and one additional for the sake of the Minister of the Synagogue.* <note>The "Minister" or Chazzan here refers to the official who oversaw the order of the service.</note> *In what case are these rules to be understood? When no Interpretation or Sermon is held. But if a translation into the vernacular <note>referring to the Aramaic Targum</note> is instituted, or a Sermon is given, the Reader of the Prophets reads three, five, or seven verses in the Prophet, and that is enough. The author of Sopherim then proceeds in this same passage to the solemnities of reciting the Shema and returning the Book of the Law to the Ark, and he seems to end the religious exercise with these.*

*From the Code of Megillah, as the words present themselves to the understanding at first sound, you might gather that the Reader of the Prophets was to perform the sacred acts of "Dividing the Shema," passing before the Ark, and the Blessing, and that these were to impose the end upon the sacred rites of the synagogue.* <margin>Megillah chapter 4, § 5.</margin> *The words are:* <note>original Hebrew: "המפטיר בנביא הוא פורס על שמע..."</note> "He who reads the portion in the Prophets also divides the Shema <note>A technical term for leading the public recitation and blessings surrounding the Shema prayer.</note>, and comes before the Ark, and blesses the people." *In this way, the Reader of the Prophets would truly be the* **Maftir**, *the "Dismisser" of the synagogal assembly. However, because the sacred rites of Dividing the Shema and proceeding before the Ark were typically celebrated* **before** *the actual reading of the Law and the Prophets, Rabbi Solomon <note>The famous commentator Rashi (1040–1105).</note>, Bartenora <note>Obadiah ben Abraham of Bertinoro, a 15th-century commentator.</note>, and Yom Tov <note>Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller, author of the Tosefot Yom Tov.</note> interpret the words to mean that, according to the sense of the Megillah, those solemnities were to be performed by the man to whom the Prophetic reading was destined; or one who was accustomed to be called to this duty of the Prophetic reading, but which nonetheless had to be performed before that reading of the Prophets. Regarding this, if it is displeasing to the reader, I will speak more extensively where I discuss the Division or Exposition of the* **Shema**. *Nevertheless, the previous points favor the opinion that the ordinary sacred rites of the ancient Synagogue were usually sealed by the Reader of the Prophets—the "ordinary" rites, I say. For in extraordinary ones (such as the reading by the Priest or the King on the Day of Atonement or the Sabbatical Seventh Year), I am not unaware that the Reading of the Law was concluded with several Doxologies and Prayers.* <margin>See Code Sotah chapter 7, § 7 & 8.</margin>

### CHAPTER 10. IN THE SYNAGOGUE. 997

The authorities seem to disagree regarding the meaning of the word *Haptir* <note>Hebrew: הפטיר, the causative form of the root meaning 'to release' or 'to open'</note>. Jarchi <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator</note> and Bartenora <note>A 15th-century commentator on the Mishnah</note> seek the explanation of the word *Haptir* from *niftar* <note>Hebrew: נפטר</note>, meaning *to be released, set free, sent away, or dismissed*. They give this sense to the words: *They do not dismiss the group of diners after the Passover—that is, after the eating of the Passover Lamb—with delicacies.* Bartenora writes: <note>original Hebrew: לאתר שאכלו את הפסח אין נפטרון מן הסעודה באכילה מינה מתוקה ופירות וכו'</note> "After they have eaten the Passover sacrifice, they do not depart (they are not dismissed) from the meal by eating sweet things, fruits, etc., as is usually done at banquets." However, you may easily gather that others take the word *Haptir* here in the sense of *finishing or pausing* (the way Elias Levita and Philippus Aquinas interpret the word in this passage) from the explanation of this rule which Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf, a famous Christian scholar of Hebrew traditions</note> produced from a commentary on the Prayer Book:

<margin>Vindication of Exercises on the Lord's Supper, page 363.</margin>

"The meaning of the words: *They do not conclude the Passover with an afikoman* <term>Afikoman: the final piece of unleavened bread eaten at the Seder, which represents the Passover lamb</term> is: *They did not CLOSE or finish this meal with types of delicacies, as happens in all other banquets; but at the end of the meal, when they were to depart (were dismissed) from their meal, they ate a portion of the Passover meat, about the size of an olive.*" Therefore, according to this meaning of the word, the Reader of the Prophets is first called the *Maftir* <term>Maftir: 'the concluder'</term> because through the *Reading of the Prophets he closes and finishes the act of the Reading of the Law* in the Synagogue; and then also because he formerly dismissed the synagogue assembly with that reading—although I do not hold this latter point to be as clearly established, as I have said.

<margin>See Maimonides, *Laws of Prayer*, chapter 13, section 25.</margin>

These are the things I had to say concerning the Rite of the *Reading of the Law and the Prophets*, as it is celebrated in the Synagogues, and as distinct from *Private Reading*. The ancient Jews did not want Private Reading to be neglected because of this Public reading, but recommended it be joined with the Public one. In this treatment, however, many unnecessary points over which the Masters dispute have been omitted or trimmed away by us, because the customs of individual Synagogues vary in certain minor circumstances. This is evident from no author more clearly than from *Kol Bo* <note>A comprehensive 14th-century collection of Jewish laws and rituals</note>, *that is, the one who published the Pandects of Sacred Rituals; for he, recording the differing opinions and customs of the Jewish Churches, concludes his discussion of those variations with this* <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword indicates the next word is 'for'</note>

### CHAPTER XI.

*The passages concerning the Reading of the Law and the Prophets that appear in the New Testament writings are indicated, not omitting the example of Christ, as the Reader of the Prophet Isaiah in the synagogue of Nazareth. ### CHAPTER II. IN THE CHURCH.
<sig>Lll lll 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: explain-</meta>

...while they are read aloud in public on the Sabbaths. For it does not say "let them read," but "let them hear," while they are read aloud with a clear voice in public. For certainly in this parable, those *Five Brothers of the Rich Man*, who was among the dead <note>original Latin: "apud inferos," referring to the underworld or Hades</note>, seem entirely to represent that most distinguished part of the Jews who lived in more remote places outside of Canaan <note>the Land of Israel</note>, having thus far been exempt from those evils which the inhabitants of Canaan <note>referring here to the Jews in Judea</note> suffered through the Roman emperors Titus, Trajan, and Hadrian <note>these emperors oversaw the destruction of Jerusalem and the suppression of the Jewish revolts in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD</note>. For God would grant the Jews living among the Nations <note>the Gentiles</note> this benefit for long ages: that it would be permitted for them to read aloud *Moses and the Prophets* publicly in the synagogues for their own conviction; to which I believe the Lord is alluding here. 

Nor is this the only such passage; it appears also in John: <margin>Chapter 5, 45.</margin> *Do not think that I will accuse you before the Father; there is one who accuses you, namely* MOSES, *in whom you have set your hope.* <note>original Greek: ἔστιν ὁ κατηγορῶν ὑμῶν Μωσῆς</note> To accuse, after all, is to charge someone in public before a Judge and to prosecute them as a defendant. Moses levels the greatest charge against all Jews whenever he is read aloud publicly in the synagogue, as he clearly presents the prophecies concerning the Messiah—which found their fulfillment in Christ—to their consciences for full conviction, as if before God (who is conceived to be present in the sacred rites of Religion where He is worshipped). 

Moreover, the Lord assumes throughout that not only the Learned, but also the common people, are diligently devoted to the private reading of the Scriptures—not only *Moses* and the *Prophets*, but also the *Hagiographa* <term>Hagiographa</term> <note>The "Holy Writings" or Ketuvim, the third division of the Hebrew Bible, including the Psalms, Proverbs, and Job</note>. And regarding the *Hagiographa* specifically: <margin>Mark 12, 26.</margin> *Have you never read in the scriptures?* <note>original Greek: Οὐ δὲ ποτε ἀνέγνωτε ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς;</note>; <margin>Matthew 12, 5.</margin> *The stone which they rejected, etc.* <margin>Ps. 118, 22.</margin> This passage taken from the Psalms proves that the Lord, by the term *the scriptures* <note>original Greek: τὰς γραφὰς</note>, understands the *Hagiographa* <note>original Hebrew: כתובימ, "Ketuvim"</note>. 

However, this Act of Public Reading of the *Law and the Prophets* is especially commended by many for this reason: that Christ the Lord himself performed the office of *Reader* in the synagogue of Nazareth, as recorded by Luke. <margin>Luke 4, 16.</margin> He entered the *Synagogue*, as was his custom, *on the Sabbath, and* STOOD UP TO READ <note>original Greek: καὶ ἀνέστη ἀναγνῶναι</note>; and having searched for the place in *Isaiah* found in chapter 61, verse 1, he read one or two verses from it. And having done this, he is said to have handed the * rolled-up Book <note>original Greek: Πτύξας τὸ βιβλίον; original Hebrew: גלל הספר, "rolling the scroll"</note> to the † attendant <note>original Greek: τῷ ὑπηρέτῃ</note>, the *Minister of the Synagogue* <note>original Hebrew: חזן הכנסת, "Chazzan ha-Keneset," the officer in charge of the synagogue's administration and maintenance</note>, and sat down to teach—that is, [explaining] the text read aloud...

...had explained, and for the sake of explanation, digressed into related matters. But it is doubtful whether Christ did not act here more as a *Teacher* and *Preacher* than as a *Reader*. For no other circumstances usually associated with the ordinary *Reading of the Law* are mentioned here. <margin>
Matthew 13:54.
Mark 6:1, 2.

The words read and explained by the Lord do not, as far as is known, enter into any Haftarah.

Whenever two Sections <note>original: 'Sectiones', referring to the Parashot or weekly Torah portions</note> are read on the Sabbath, the Haftarah <note>original: 'Haphtara', the prophetic reading</note> corresponding to the latter Section is to be recited. This is what usually happens in most places. And so most people are accustomed to reading the *Consolations of Isaiah* after the ninth day of the moon of the month of July <note>Referring to the 9th of Av (Tisha B'Av), which usually falls in July or August</note> until the beginning of the New Year. On the Sabbath after the ninth day of the month they read: *Comfort ye, comfort ye my people*, etc. On the following Sabbath they read: *And Zion said*. On the third Sabbath: *O thou afflicted, tossed with tempest*. On the fourth Sabbath: *I, even I, am he that comforteth you*. On the fifth: *Arise, shine*. On the sixth: *Sing, O barren*. On the seventh: *I will greatly rejoice in the Lord*.

<margin>
Acts 15:21. Ezekiel 38:17. Malachi 3:4. Book 1, Part 2, chapter 2. Leviticus 23:44. §. 6.
</margin>

Furthermore, just as this rite of reading the *Law and the Prophets* is laudable and suited to the condition of the People of God, so it is not to be doubted that the same is most ancient. Indeed, we have heard *Peter* <note>The author attributes the quote to Peter, though in Acts 15:21 it is spoken by James the Just</note> testifying that *Moses* was accustomed to being read every Sabbath *from ancient generations* <note>original Greek: ἐκ γενεῶν ἀρχαίων</note>, from ANCIENT ages. In Hebrew you would say: *from generations of old* <note>original Hebrew: מדורות קדמונים</note>; or according to the Biblical phrase: *from the days of old* <note>original Hebrew: מימים קדמונים</note> or *from ancient years* <note>original Hebrew: משנים קדמוניות</note>. 

Yet, what those "ancient generations" exactly were—those ancient and former ages—is not equally certain. We demonstrated in the previous Dissertation on the *Origin of Synagogues* that the Jews are commonly of the opinion that the *Reading of the Law*, to be celebrated every Sabbath, was instituted and ordained by *Moses* himself; and in the same place we discussed more accurately which of the solemnities of this act are referred precisely by the Jews to *Moses*, and which to *Ezra*. 

Certainly, in the *Mishna* <note>The first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions</note> of the *Tractate Megillah* itself, they not only make Moses the author of the institution of the *Reading of the Law* to be continued through every Sabbath, but they also boast that the same Moses commanded Israel to read the Law on Feast Days, and for that purpose to select <term>parashot</term> <note>original Hebrew: פרשות</note>, *texts*, suitable for those Festivals, which are enumerated there; they wish to find mention of this command in these words: *And Moses declared unto the children of Israel the feasts of the Lord* <note>original Hebrew: וידבר משה את מועדי ה' אל בני ישראל, citing Leviticus 23:44</note>. 

Regarding these words, the *Mishna* in *Megillah chapter 3* says: *Their commandment is that each and every one should read [the text of each festival] in its time* <note>original Hebrew: מצותן שיהו קורין כל אחד ואחד בזמנו</note>. These things are illustrated through the tradition of the <term>Gemara</term> <note>The component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis of the Mishna</note>: *Our Rabbis taught: Moses ordained for Israel that they should inquire and investigate concerning the matter of the day: the laws of Passover on Passover, the laws of Shavuot on Shavuot, [and] the laws of Sukkot on Sukkot* <note>original Hebrew: תנו רבנן משה תיקן להם לישראל שיהו שואלין ודורשין בענינו של יום הלכות פסח בפסח והלכות עצרת בעצרת הלכות חג בחג</note>.

### ON THE READING OF HOLY SCRIPTURE, BOOK III.

But these claims are surely in vain and without any foundation. We read that Moses commanded no other solemn *Reading of the Law* to the Israelites than that which was to be performed every seven years during the Year of Release <note>original: שמטה (*Shemitah*), the Sabbatical year; and Greek: ἀφέσεως (*apheseos*), meaning 'release' or 'remission'</note> at the end of the Seven-year period during the Feast of Tabernacles <note>The festival of Sukkot</note> before the entire Assembly of the Israelites. The ritual for this reading, as it was observed in later times—or at least as the Talmudic scholars wish it to have been observed—is handed down by Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> in the Treatise *Chagiga* (that is, *On the Sacred Feasts*). Since that Treatise has been elegantly translated into the Latin language by the most learned man, *Ludovico de Veil* <note>Louis de Veil (1637–1710), a scholar of Jewish descent who translated Maimonides' works into Latin</note>, and since we have already had occasion to discuss this solemnity once or twice in passing, there is no need to relate more of it here. 

Furthermore, Moses obscurely commanded another reading of the *Divine Law* which was to be instituted upon the solemn confirmation of the Covenant on the mountains of Gerizim and Ebal, established between God and the Israelites and the entire Assembly of the House of Jacob. But that was to be an extraordinary event—a recitation of the Conditions of the Old Covenant—which Joshua later carried out in the Land of Canaan according to the prescription of Moses; thus, it does not count as a regular practice here. Of a similar kind was that fixed and exemplary reading of the Divine Law instituted in the Temple by King *Josiah* himself (as far as is clear from the historical context), or at least performed by the Priests at his command. Or even that reading which is said to have been celebrated by Baruch in the Temple at the command and from the dictation of that Prophet <note>Jeremiah, whose prophecies Baruch wrote down and read to the people</note>. 

For even if I were to easily concede that these pious readings of the Mosaic Law in singular and extraordinary cases served as a prelude to the Ritual of the *Reading of the Law*—which, as is well known, was thereafter practiced in all the sacred services of the Synagogues—nevertheless, you can conclude nothing from these examples concerning a *Reading* of the entire *Divine Law* celebrated solemnly every Sabbath throughout the entire region of Canaan. Indeed, from these very examples, as it is clear from Sacred History that they were rare, and as the silence of this very argument clearly proves, what else should you conclude than...

# CHAPTER II. IN THE CHURCH. 1003

...that the Mosaic Law in those times, which preceded the event of the Babylonian Exile, was not yet customarily read aloud solemnly and every Sabbath <note>original Greek: κατὰ πᾶν σάββατον (*kata pan sabbaton*)</note>?

<margin>Chapter 8, 2. 3. Book 1. Part 2. chapter 12.</margin>
Nothing remains, therefore, but for us to trace the origin of the fixed Reading of the Law, as it is practiced in the Synagogues, to that solemn Reading of the Divine Law which is recorded in the *History of Nehemiah* as having been instituted under the leadership of Ezra in the Assembly of the Israelites at Jerusalem. Since this passage has been explained by us in previous sections—both by drawing examples of conformity between the solemn acts of the Reading celebrated at that time and the same Rite of Reading as observed in the Sacred Synagogues of a more recent era—we shall not repeat what has already been done. For even if it cannot be gathered clearly enough from that passage that the Law was read every Sabbath in the Synagogues of all cities from that time onward, it is nonetheless certain that it was read on the Feast of the New Moons <note>original: *Calendarum*</note> of the first month, and on the Feast of *Tabernacles* <note>Sukkot</note>, and during the *Fast*, which was celebrated on the twenty-fourth day of that same month. From this, it seems reasonable to conclude that the Law was subsequently read on all Feasts and Fasts in the solemn Assembly of the whole People; and, since many of the Priests and Levites applied themselves with singular industry around that very time to the study of the Divine Law, that this same Reading of the Divine Law began to be instituted throughout every Sabbath in the more frequent Assemblies of the Israelites, and was continued thereafter.

<margin>Chapter 13, 1.</margin>
Indeed, in that same History of Nehemiah, mention is made of another *Reading of the Divine Law*, though no time or circumstances are noted for it. Therefore, just as the Illustrious Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a titan of 16th-century scholarship who revolutionized the study of ancient chronology</note> was more than once too pleased with himself in his clever discoveries <note>original Greek: εὑρήμασι (*heuremasi*)</note>, I consider that he did not derive with sufficient solidity from this very History of Nehemiah the *Festival* called שמחת התורה <note>original Hebrew: *Simchat Torah*, the "Rejoicing of the Law"</note>, which the Jews celebrate on the twenty-third day of the month of Tishri as a sign of joy for the completion of the annual Reading of the Divine Law.

<margin>On the Improvement of Time <note>original: *De Emendat. Temp.*</note> book 7. p. 648.</margin>
Scaliger’s reasoning is as follows:

> *When on the first day of the Feast of Tabernacles <note>original Greek: σκηνοπηγίας (*skenopegias*)</note> the people wept because of the Moabite women they had taken as wives, and the mourning seemed to interrupt the joy of the Festival; Nehemiah, with Ezra the Scribe, forbade them to mourn as long as they were engaged in Divine matters. Therefore, from the 15th of Tishri, on which the first day of the Feast of Tabernacles is celebrated, until the eighth day of the same solemnity, which is the 22nd of Tishri, they abstained from mourning, as they did also on the following day.*

### CHAPTER II. IN THE CHURCH. 1005

The people remained attentive during that reading of the Divine Law; while the Priests and Levites read the Law before them and explained it (verse 3), the people wept. The leaders then gathered to Ezra, the expert in the Law (verse 10), so that they might be instructed by him concerning the statutes of the Divine Law. When they had been more accurately taught by him (verse 14) regarding the method of celebrating the <term>Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot): A week-long autumn festival commemorating the dwelling of the Israelites in booths during their wilderness trek.</term>, that solemnity is said to have been celebrated with greater accuracy and diligence than at any other time (verse 18).

<margin>Compare Ezra chapters 3 and 4, and Nehemiah chapter 13, verse 1.</margin>
In the same history of Nehemiah, it is narrated that at another time the people were instructed through the reading of the Law regarding the fact that <term>Moabites and Ammonites: Two neighboring nations often described as adversaries of the Israelites in the Hebrew Bible.</term> were not to be gathered into the Jewish Church. When these accounts are compared, it is clear that the Jewish common people around that time suffered from a great ignorance of the Divine Law. This kind of ignorance cannot be imagined to have had a place among the common people if, even then—according to the <note>Joseph Scaliger (1540–1609) was a famous scholar who argued that many Jewish traditions, like the weekly Torah reading, were established much earlier than other historians believed.</note> hypothesis of Scaliger—the custom had flourished of solemnly reading the Mosaic Law every Sabbath in the assemblies of the Israelites, and of celebrating the <term>Rejoicing of the Law (original Latin: *Lætitia Legis*; Hebrew: *Simchat Torah*): A celebration marking the conclusion of the annual cycle of reading the Torah.</term> on account of the completion of the reading of the entire Law. 

Therefore, it seems to us entirely likely that the Jewish people rested on this 23rd day of <term>Tishrei: The seventh month of the Hebrew calendar, occurring in September or October.</term>, which interrupted the "Great Sabbath" of the Feast of Tabernacles and the Fast to be celebrated on the 24th day. On this day, they prepared themselves for the solemn fast of the following day; for it was consistent with reason that some space of time should intervene between the joy of the Great Festival and the afflictions of the Fast. This festival of the "Rejoicing of the Law," undoubtedly of more recent origin, was subsequently assigned by the <note>The "Masters" refers to the Rabbinic authorities or teachers of the law in later Jewish history.</note> Teachers to this very 23rd day of Tishrei. Because the reading of the Law was meant to be finished on the Sabbath of the Feast of Tabernacles—since its beginning is drawn from that Sabbath which follows the Feast—they could not designate a more convenient day than this 23rd of Tishrei, which is the first to occur between these two Sabbaths after the celebration of the <note>original Greek: *skenopegias*, meaning the Feast of Tabernacles or the "pitching of tents."</note> Feast of Tabernacles. 

Furthermore, the fact that the Teachers decreed that the Sabbath readings of the Law should begin on the Sabbath following the Feast of Tabernacles could have been based on other reasons for that institution. The Feast of Tabernacles was truly regarded as the last of the year's festivals and the "seal" of the others; therefore, what could be more appropriate than for the reading of the Law to be terminated at this festival as well? At this same festival, God commanded the Law (at least Deuteronomy, or its most noble part) to be read in every <term>Sabbatical Year: Every seventh year, in which the land was to lie fallow and debts were forgiven.</term>. Once that was done, reason demanded that a new public reading of the Divine Law should follow on the succeeding Sabbath.

The people listened to that reading of the Divine Law; they remained *attentive* during the reading; as the Priests and Levites read and explained the Law, the people *wept*. Afterward, the leaders gathered around Ezra the <term>Law-expert: Historically known as Ezra the Scribe, the priest and scholar who led the returned exiles and reintroduced the Torah.</term>, so that they might be instructed by him regarding the statutes of the Divine Law. Once they had been more accurately taught the method of celebrating the <term>Feast of Tabernacles: A week-long autumn festival commemorating the dwelling of the Israelites in booths during the Exodus.</term> by him, that solemnity is said to have been celebrated with greater accuracy and diligence than at any other time.

<margin>
Compare Ezra 
chapters 3, 4. 
chapter 13, 1.
</margin>
In the same history of Nehemiah, it is recounted that at another time the People were instructed through the reading of the Law regarding the exclusion of Moabites and Ammonites from the Jewish assembly. When these facts are compared, it is clear that the Jewish common people around that time suffered from a great ignorance of the Divine Law. Such ignorance cannot be imagined to have existed among the common people if, even then—according to <term>Scaliger’s: Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a pioneer of historical chronology who argued that the Jewish reading cycles were very ancient.</term> hypothesis—the custom had flourished of solemnly reading the Law of Moses every Sabbath in the assemblies of the Israelites, and of celebrating the *Rejoicing of the Law* <note>original: *Lætitiæ Legis*, referring to Simchat Torah.</note> to mark the completion of the entire Law's reading. It therefore seems to us quite likely that the Jewish People on this 23rd day of <term>Tishri: The seventh month of the Jewish calendar, roughly September–October.</term>—which interrupted the interval between the *Great Sabbath of the Feast of Tabernacles* and the *Fast* to be celebrated on the 24th—simply rested, and through this day prepared themselves for the solemn Fast of the following day. For it was consistent with reason that some space of time should intervene between the Joy of the Great Feast and the afflictions of the Fast. This *Feast of the Rejoicing of the Law*, which is undoubtedly of more recent origin, was later assigned by the <term>Masters: The Rabbis and scholars of the Talmudic and post-Talmudic eras.</term> to this very 23rd day of Tishri. Since the reading of the Law was meant to end on the Sabbath of the Feast of Tabernacles—as its new beginning is drawn from the Sabbath that follows the Feast of Tabernacles—they could not have designated a more convenient day than this 23rd of Tishri, which is the first day to fall between these two *Sabbaths* after the celebration of the <note>original: σκηνοπηγίας (skēnopēgias)</note> Feast of Tabernacles. However, as for the fact that the Masters decreed that the Sabbath readings of the Law should begin on the Sabbath following the <note>original: σκηνοπηγίας (skēnopēgias)</note> Feast of Tabernacles, they could have had other reasons for that institution. The Feast of Tabernacles was truly considered the last of the year’s festivals and the seal of the others; therefore, what could be more fitting than that the reading of the Law should also end at this festival? At this same festival, God commanded the Law (at least Deuteronomy, or its most noble part) to be read in every Sabbatical year. Once this was done, reason demanded that a new reading of the Divine Law [begin] on the following Sabbath

...the Jewish community after their affairs were restored by the Maccabees, due to a lack of copies of the Mosaic Law, established the practice of reading those Prophetic writings in public religious exercises. However, as far as it concerns Antiochus and the enemies of the Jewish sacred rites, I would not believe that they raged any less against the *Prophetic writings* than against the *Mosaic writings*. But perhaps there is no truth underlying this Jewish tradition concerning the institution of the *Haftarah readings* <note>The Haftarah is a series of selections from the books of the Prophets read publicly in the synagogue.</note> around the time of Epiphanes, other than that the Jews, after their commonwealth was restored by the Maccabees, handled their sacred matters everywhere with greater zeal and more fervent study. From that time, they sought out, collected, and reviewed all the writings again following the work of Ezra. Since they recognized that the writings of Moses and the Prophets share the same themes and aim at the same goal, they deemed it advisable to join those two types of writings together in the readings for the Sabbath and Feast days. Previously, from the time the sacred religious rites were organized by Ezra, no reading of the parts of Scripture had included anything besides *the Mosaic Law alone*. <margin>* See Nehemiah 8:2; 13:1.</margin> At the very least, nothing is more certain or solid to us regarding the origin of the *Reading of the Prophets*.

Furthermore, as ancient as this custom of *Reading Moses and the Prophets* in the assemblies of God’s people is, it is equally praiseworthy and consistent with reason. For since those writings of Moses and the Prophets contain that very same discourse by which God revealed the way of obtaining salvation to mortals, and since the entire hope of the Church—and therefore the Church itself—is founded upon that discourse of God to humans, the highest fairness demands that those Holy Books be studied diligently by every person who desires their own salvation. And since some in the assembly of believers are unlettered and unfit to perform this duty properly, while others (far more numerous) shamefully neglect it, it is consistent with reason that in the Public Exercise of Religion—which ought to be directed toward the benefit and salvation of all believers—those same Holy Books should be read aloud for the common good.

Therefore, since this Rite constitutes part of <note>original Greek: της λογικής θρησκείας</note> *Reasonable Worship*, such as ought to be offered to God by men under the New Economy <term>New Economy: A theological term referring to the era of the New Testament or the Christian Church.</term>, it was rightly and deservedly transferred from the Jewish Synagogue into the Christian Church. This is true even though we are instructed about this practice more certainly and clearly from the history and practice of the Church than from the Books of the New Testament themselves.

In the *fourteenth chapter* of the first Epistle to the Corinthians, Paul, when reviewing the sacred *Exercises* that were celebrated in the assemblies of the believers of that time—such as: <note>original: Προφητεύειν, προσεύχεσθαι, ψάλλειν, εὐλογεῖν, εὐχαριστεῖν, λαλεῖν γλώσσαις, διερμηνεύειν</note> Prophesying, praying, singing psalms, blessing, giving thanks, speaking in tongues, and interpreting—does not mention the act of <note>original: τῷ ἀναγινώσκειν</note> reading. For when Paul elsewhere commends to Timothy <note>original: τὴν ἀνάγνωσιν</note> *the Reading*, and when Paul and Peter exhort believers to the study of the *Prophetic Word*, this can be referred equally to the private reading and meditation of the Divine Word as to the Public reading. I am not unaware that the illustrious man, Hugo Grotius, explains the statement of the Apostle James in the Assembly at Jerusalem—that *Moses is read in every synagogue on the Sabbath*—as referring to the Public Reading of the Books of Moses which was instituted on those same Sabbath days in the gatherings of Christians. Indeed, Grotius tries to prove from the records of Sacred History that the Churches of the Christians were also formerly called "synagogues," and that the Mosaic Law was read on Sabbath days in those gatherings of Christians. ...the Jewish [synagogue], after its affairs were restored by the Maccabees, instituted the public reading of those Prophetic writings in the exercise of religion because of a lack of copies of the Mosaic Law. # ON THE READING OF HOLY SCRIPTURE, BOOK III.
## PAGE 1010

<margin>
* Compare chapter 19.
</margin>

...in our assemblies no less than in Jewish ones, Moses is read, just as has been done from ancient times, and indeed on the Sabbaths. But that connection seems somewhat forced. For how was the cause of complaint for the zealots among the Judaizing Christians <note>Early Jewish converts to Christianity who believed that the Laws of Moses, such as circumcision and dietary restrictions, were still mandatory for all believers.</note> removed—namely, that Moses was being despised by Gentile Christians—if those Gentile Christians were being freed from the obligation of the prescribed Mosaic Precepts? Surely, those who honored and venerated Moses were not merely those who read the writings of Moses, but those who performed his precepts; conversely, to despise Moses was the act of those who, while wishing to be considered members of the Jewish Church, nevertheless refused to observe the Mosaic Laws.

Therefore, it does not seem that the cause of complaint for the zealots regarding Moses being neglected by Gentile Christians was removed by this Apostolic decree concerning the Gentiles. Furthermore, the explanation of <term>Grotius|Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a prominent Dutch theologian and jurist</term> does not seem to align well with the actual words of the text. For if there is mention here of the public reading of Moses in Christian assemblies, why is it said "from ancient days" <note>Original Greek: ἡμερῶν ἀρχαίων (hēmerōn archaiōn)</note>? After all, the beginnings of the Gentile Christians were still very recent. 

Why is it said that they have "those who preach" <note>Original Greek: τοὺς κηρύσσοντας (tous kēryssontas)</note>, that is, Heralds, "in the synagogues" <note>Original Greek: ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς (en tais synagōgais)</note> in an absolute sense, and not "in *their* synagogues"? For the word "synagogue," when used by itself, must be interpreted as referring to the synagogues of the Jews. Why are the preaching and reading of Moses restricted in the text to the Sabbath day? For since Gentile Christians, from the very origin of Christianity, held the first day of the week most sacred for Divine Worship; and since at that time no scriptures yet existed except those of the Old Testament, it seems entirely likely that Moses and the Prophets were read aloud in Christian assemblies on the Lord’s Day <note>Sunday</note> just as much as on the Sabbath. 

Therefore, it seems simpler and more correct to me for these words to refer to the custom of reading Moses in the Jewish synagogues, which were still frequented by the Judaizing Christians. In this way, this verse provides the reason why it was necessary to write to the Gentile Christians <margin>* and not to the Judaizing Christians</margin>, who—hearing Moses read every Sabbath in the synagogues—were already sufficiently instructed that they must abstain from sexual immorality, blood, and what is strangled <note>These requirements come from the "Apostolic Decree" in Acts 15, intended to facilitate table-fellowship between Jewish and Gentile believers.</note>.

Nevertheless, mention of this Sacred Rite of Reading Holy Scripture in Christian assemblies occurs both in <term>Justin|Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD), an early Christian apologist who described the liturgy of the early Church</term> and <term>Tertullian|Tertullian (c. 155–220 AD), a prolific North African author known as the "Father of Latin Theology"</term>, whose passages have already been described above, and frequently among other Doctors of the following times...

The author contends that Jewish-Christians already knew the Law from these weekly readings, making the Apostolic decree specifically necessary for Gentile converts.</summary>

### CHAPTER II. IN THE CHURCH.
#### PAGE 1011

...so much so that no one doubts that this rite has been accepted among the sacred things of religion since the dawn of Christianity. Let us only provide some examples of the agreement of both these rites, as celebrated in the Synagogue and the Church.

<margin>See book 3, Part 1, chapter 8, pages 715, 716.</margin>

1. **The entire Scripture was read in the Church of the Christians, including that of the Old Testament itself.**
Justin Martyr explicitly states: *“and the memoirs of the Apostles or the writings of the Prophets are read as long as time permits”* <note>original Greek: καὶ τὰ ἀπομνημονεύματα τῶν Ἀποστόλων ἢ τὰ συγγράμματα τῶν Προφητῶν ἀναγινώσκεται μέχρις ἐγχωρεῖ; original Latin: *Commentaria Apostolorum aut Scripta Prophetarum, quoad tempus fert, (die Solis) leguntur.* Justin is describing a typical Sunday service in the 2nd century.</note>. Thus, the Old Testament was read no less than the New.

2. **On Sabbath days, following the example of the Synagogue, it appears that the Mosaic and Prophetic writings alone were read.**
<term>Grotius|Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch scholar and theologian</term> proves from various testimonies in his annotations on that very passage of the Acts of the Apostles (which we have just explained) that the early Christians observed the Sabbath <note>Saturday</note> just as much as the Lord's Day <note>Sunday</note>. At the same time, he observes exactly what we have supposed here based on the Canons of the Council of Laodicea <note>A 4th-century church council that addressed various matters of discipline and liturgy</note>, the sixteenth of which states: <margin>In Beveridge, page 460.</margin> *“That the Gospels are to be read with other Scriptures on the Sabbath”* <note>original Greek: Περὶ τοῦ ἐν σαββάτῳ εὐαγγέλια μετὰ ἑτέρων γραφῶν ἀναγινώσκεσθαι; original Latin: *Quod Evangelia cum aliis Scripturis Sabbatho legenda sint*</note>. This suggests that until then, only the Old Testament Scriptures were read on Sabbath days, while it was only customary to read the New Testament Scriptures on Sundays and feast days. However, <term>Balsamon|Theodore Balsamon (c. 1140–1195), a famous Byzantine canonist</term> and <term>Zonaras|John Zonaras, a 12th-century historian and theologian</term> interpret this Canon differently; they believe it implies that the reading of Holy Scriptures on Sabbath days was entirely neglected in some churches, and therefore this Canon was written to command it. Which of these interpretations is more accurate is not sufficiently clear to us.

3. **The Scripture to be read was divided into certain "readings" or "lections," or larger texts, just as among the Jews it was divided into weekly portions.**
<note>original Greek: ἀναγνώσματα (anagnōsmata); original Hebrew: פרשיות (parashiot, the weekly Torah portions)</note>
<margin>Preface to the Royal Edition; Observations on the New Testament; Annotations on the Commentaries of Origen, pages 18, 19, 20. In the Lexicon under the words reading, chapter, and title. Critical History of the New Testament, chapter 33.</margin>
That the Holy Scripture was divided by early Christians into various parts, both larger and smaller, has long been observed and declared with many arguments and examples by the most learned men—<term>Stephanus|Robert Estienne (1503–1559), the printer who first introduced modern verse numbering</term>, <term>Casaubon|Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), a brilliant classical scholar</term>, Croy, <term>Huet|Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and editor</term>, and recently by <term>Suicer|Johann Caspar Suicer (1619–1684), author of a major dictionary of Greek Church terms</term> and <term>Simon|Richard Simon (1638–1712), an early pioneer of biblical criticism</term>. These parts occur under the names <term>perikopai|pericopes, or selections</term>, <term>kephalaia|chapters</term>, <term>titloi|titles</term>, <term>anagnōseis|readings</term>, <term>anagnōsmata|lections</term>, *Lectiones*, and *Capitula*. Regarding their industrious work, I have nothing to add to this category of research. Sometimes <term>Kephalaia|chapters</term>...
