# ON THE READING OF HOLY SCRIPTURE, BOOK III.
## PAGE 1012

...those **Sections** of each Book were sometimes called <gloss>headings</gloss> <note>original Greek: λήμματα; *lēmmata*, meaning a theme or subject for discussion</note>, which summarized the contents of that Book, varied by the nature of the material, and were prefixed to those Books themselves as introductory summaries. We see this practiced in the most elegant edition of the New Testament by <term>Robert Estienne|A famous 16th-century French printer, also known as Robertus Stephanus, who was the first to print the New Testament with verse numbers</term>, in the *Folio* edition. These same divisions were called **Titles** <note>original Greek: τίτλοι; *titloi*</note> when they were marked at the top of the pages, showing the *summary* in the manner of an **Inscription**, or a *brief account* of the material that was delivered in that **distinction** or **part**. This can be seen in that very edition by Robert Estienne. Indeed, the word **Chapter** <note>original Latin: *Caput*</note> was first used by the Latins to designate these *Brief Summaries* or *Indexes* of any book, a point long ago proven by <term>Vossius|Gerardus Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch scholar and theologian</term>, <term>Salmasius|Claude Salmasius (1588–1653), a French classical scholar</term>, and others. Later, the meaning was transferred to denote those actual divisions or **parts of the Book** that encompassed those arguments. Of such **Chapters**, or **Titles**, or, if you prefer, **Inscriptions**, the Gospel of Matthew once had 68; Mark had 49; and so on for the rest.

Sometimes, however, it happened that a <gloss>chapter</gloss> <note>original Greek: κεφάλαιον; *kephalaion*</note> was distinguished from a **Title**, and denoted the *smaller sections* into which any **Title** <margin>In the Lexicon under the word *Titles*</margin> or Section was distributed. This is how <term>Suidas|A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist</term> clearly distinguished the "chapters" from the "titles," assigning to Matthew, for example, 68 Titles but 355 **Chapters**. The numbers for these themselves are noted in the most excellent ancient editions. Furthermore, these **Smaller Sections** were also called <gloss>pericopes</gloss> <note>original Greek: περικοπὴ; a "cutting around" or a selection of text</note> among the Greeks, and **Capitula** <note>Little chapters</note> among the Latins, although the word *pericope* was occasionally accepted for any text of Holy Scripture written and defined indiscriminately, as <term>Huetius|Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar</term> learnedly discusses at length. In the same way, <margin>Acts 8:32.</margin> the term <gloss>passage of scripture</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἡ περιοχή τῆς γραφῆς; *hē periochē tēs graphēs*</note> is used in the Acts of the Apostles.

Up to this point, it was generally believed and handed down that what the Greeks call <gloss>readings</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἀναγνώσματα; *anagnōsmata*</note> and the Latins call **Lessons**, corresponded with those **Major** Sections or Divisions. These *anagnōsmata* are the portions of the Biblical Codex, whether of the Old or New Testament, which were read aloud by the Lectors in the Church. However, the most learned <term>Simonius|Richard Simon (1638–1712), a French priest and pioneer of modern biblical criticism</term> has recently taught us that the *readings* or **Scriptural Texts** to be read aloud, which are explicitly marked in certain manuscripts, are distinct from both the **Chapters** and the **Pericopes**, and were themselves larger than those **Titles** and smaller sections. Although we might easily accept this from Simon regarding the more recent Greeks, nothing can be concluded from it regarding the most ancient times...

## CHAPTER II. IN THE CHURCH.

...I think it possible. Certainly, if the **Titles** exhibited parts of Scripture distinguished by the type of subject matter, it seems that the reading of Scripture was adapted to these very distinctions of material, whether one such **Major Section** or several were read aloud. However, since nothing was publicly defined here, these practices could vary according to the judgment of the Teachers and the Churches. In distinguishing these **Sections**, whether **Major** or **Minor**, the primary consideration—as we have already suggested—was the subject matter and the distinct thoughts within that matter. A new subject in the History created a new **segment** <note>original Greek: τμῆμα; *tmēma*, a cut or division</note>. A part or a specific thought within such a segment constituted a **pericope** <note>original Greek: περικοπήν; *perikopēn*, meaning a section or passage "cut around"</note>, or a **Chapter**, consisting of a few verses. A Chapter, in turn, was resolved into **lines** <note>original Greek: στίχες; *stiches*, though usually spelled *stichoi*, refers to lines of text or verse-like divisions</note>; although scholars may dispute what exactly is to be understood by a "line" here. It is enough for us to observe here that a similar distribution of Holy Scripture into parts was received in the Christian Church as in the Jewish Synagogues. The **Major Sections** can conveniently be compared with the **Parashiot** <note>original Hebrew: פרשיות; the weekly Torah portions read in the synagogue</note> or **Haftarot** <note>original Hebrew: הפטרות; the prophetic selections read after the Torah</note>; and those **minor pericopes** of the Major Legal Sections, into which the larger parts were distributed by the **Masoretes** <note>Jewish scholars between the 6th and 10th centuries who standardized the text of the Hebrew Bible</note>, can be compared with the **Minor Sections**. However, neither the Teachers nor the Readers in the Church always bound themselves to the order of reading Scripture from beginning to end with the same religious strictness as was done in the Synagogues. Indeed, <term>Ferrari|Francesco Bernardino Ferrari (1577–1669), an expert on the rites of the early church</term> has established from very clear passages that preachers sometimes ordered readings to be done out of order so they would suit the argument of the Sermon itself; and that the Readers themselves also often read texts of Holy Scripture that they happened upon by chance.

<margin>Concerning the Sacred Rites of the Ancient Councils, chapters 17 and 18.</margin>
4. *Women in the Christian Church, following the example of the Synagogue, were not admitted to the act of reading the Law.*

We have seen what the custom was in the Synagogue. Paul circumscribes the custom of the Church: <margin>1 Corinthians 14:34.</margin> "Let your women keep silence in the churches"; <note>original Greek: Αἱ γυναῖκες ὑμῶν ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις σιγάτωσαν</note>. These words of Paul can either be accepted as a **correction** <note>original Greek: ἐπανόρθωσις; *epanorthōsis*</note> of that which he had only hypothetically stated in the preceding context of the Epistle concerning a woman praying, or <margin>Chapter 11, verse 5.</margin> **prophesying**; or they are to be understood (which seems more probable to me) as referring to the ordinary and common sacred exercise of disputing and teaching, whereas the faculty of **prophesying publicly** was entirely granted to **women prophetesses**. 6. *The Reading was performed from a Platform, or Ambo, consecrated chiefly for this use, following the example of the Synagogue*.
The temples of the Christians, in ancient times as well as in our own, had their own **Platform** <note>original: *Suggestum*</note>, placed in the middle of the temple according to the example of the Synagogues. From there, the **Reading** of both Holy Scripture and the Acts of the Martyrs was established for the people; the diptychs <note>lists of names of the living and dead commemorated in the liturgy</note> were recited; and sacred hymns and songs were chanted. That this was called the **Pulpit**, the **Ambo**, or the **Chair** <note>original: *Cathedra*</note> has been noted by us above and observed everywhere by the learned. But let us now prove by the sole testimony of Sozomen <note>a 5th-century Christian historian</note> that this Ambo served primarily for the Ritual of **Reading Holy Scripture**. In his history of the discovery of the relics of the forty martyrs, <margin>Church History book 9. chapter 2. p. 803.</margin> he describes the **Ambo**, of which he happened to make mention, as the *platform of the readers* <note>original Greek: βῆμα τῶν ἀναγνωστῶν; *bēma tōn anagnōstōn*</note>. *I imagine it was situated near the ambo; this was the platform of the readers.*

7. *The Sermon followed the Reading*.
<margin>On Sacred Assemblies book 1. chapter 15.</margin>
This is clear from Justin [Martyr], Tertullian, and the homilies of the Fathers, and Ferrarius <note>Francesco Bernardino Ferrari, an expert on early Christian rites</note> has provided further proof of it.

At any rate, it is clear from the explicit testimony of Sozomen that the **Reading of the Gospels** was reverently received by listeners standing on their feet throughout all the ancient Churches. <page-num>1017</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER 12. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.</header>

Talmudic interpreters do not agree on how the *Story of Tamar* is to be understood. Since two famous women named Tamar occur in the Biblical Scripture—one defiled through the lying-down of Judah <note>Genesis 38</note>, the other through the assault of Amnon <note>2 Samuel 13</note>—Jarchi <note>Also known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator.</note>, Rabbi Nachmanides <note>A leading medieval Jewish scholar, philosopher, and physician.</note>, and Yom Tov <note>Likely Yom Tov Asevilli, a famous 14th-century commentator.</note> understand the former to be meant here; Maimonides and Bartenora <note>Obadiah ben Abraham of Bertinoro, a 15th-century Italian rabbi.</note> understand the latter. But it seems entirely that Maimonides and Bartenora were abandoned by logic in this case. For why would the story of Tamar being forced by her brother Amnon be called the *Story* or *Deed of Tamar*, and not rather the *Story* or *Deed of Amnon*, as it is called at the end of the Mishnah? <note>The Mishnah is the first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions.</note> Tamar, having suffered the injury, was not as much at fault as her brother Amnon. Conversely, in the illicit loves of the Patriarch Judah and Tamar, his daughter-in-law, the stain did not cling so much to the Patriarch Judah as it did to his daughter-in-law Tamar: for which reason that deed is rightly called Tamar's, not Judah's. For this same reason, the Doctors permitted this story to be read aloud in the synagogue, as it did not so much harm the honor of the Patriarch Judah. It also contradicts Maimonides and Bartenora that at the end of the Mishnah, the interpretation of the story of Amnon is explicitly forbidden; and the very order of the list of Scripture texts—those which are indeed to be read but not interpreted—as established in this Mishnah, demands that the Tamar mentioned here is the daughter-in-law of the Patriarch Judah, not Tamar, the daughter of David.

By the *latter or repeated Story of the Calf*, the Gemara <note>The component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis and commentary on the Mishnah.</note> and Talmudic interpreters teach that we should understand the words of the Mosaic story concerning the *Golden Calf* which are concluded in verses 21, 22, 23, 24, and 35 <note>Exodus 32</note>; from which the *Prior Story of the Calf* is distinguished, as contained <margin>Maimonides' Commentary on the Mishnah.</margin> in the earlier verses of this same chapter. The reason why they do not publicly convert the latter story of the Calf into the vernacular is sought from the honor of *Aaron*, whose reputation they wished to protect. Bartenora writes:

> All these are read but not translated because of the honor of Aaron; <note>original Hebrew: כל אלו נקראין ולא מתרגמין משום יקרא דאהרון</note>

All these are read, but they are not translated, on account of the honor of Aaron; namely, because in that latter *Story of the Calf*, he is said to have been its author. If this custom of neglecting the translation of this latter part of the Mosaic story about the *Golden Calf* had already been accepted before the times of Josephus, perhaps a reason could be found there why Josephus, a rival for the honor of his <margin>Antiquities, book 3, chapter 5.</margin> nation, kept this entire *Story of the Golden Calf* in deep silence. By the *Priestly Blessing*, it is well known that the text of Numbers 6:24, 25, 26 is indicated; which passage in the vernacular in public con—

**He will not lift faces** <note>Hebrew: *lo yissa panim*. A phrase meaning "to show partiality."</note></margin>

By the *History of David and Amnon*, one should understand the *History of David’s adultery with Bathsheba and the History of the incest of Amnon, David’s son, committed with his sister Tamar*; and there are <margin>* See Yom Tov on these words.</margin> Jewish interpreters who arrange the matter in this way. And since it was said at the beginning of the Mishnah that *the History of Tamar is to be read entirely and explained in the vernacular* (by which they mean this same History of Tamar, the daughter of David), they reconcile these two statements by saying that where the text says *Amnon, Son of David*, those parts are passed over in the reading *for the sake of David’s honor*; but those things which are simply recorded in the text regarding *Amnon*, those are to be read as well as explained in the vernacular, because the honor of Amnon is not held in such high regard. <margin>Megillah, folio 25, column 2.</margin> The Gemara says: **The story of David and Amnon is neither read aloud nor translated into the common language. But there is no difficulty. That is to be understood regarding those parts of the history in which it is written: <margin>See also Maimonides, chapter 12, § 12.</margin> *Amnon, Son of David*: while the other refers to the remaining part, in which the name *Amnon* occurs simply. However, the first explanation seems much simpler and clearer to me.

<margin>in the place cited.</margin>

<margin>in the place cited.</margin>

### CHAPTER 12. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.

<margin>Chapter 8, 8.</margin>
<margin>Book 1, Part 2, chapter 12.</margin>
...it was required that an Interpreter should be present with the one reading from the Law, to interpret for the people what the Reader had first read from the Law, so that they might rightly understand the sense of the words. This opinion of the scholars of the Gemara <note>The component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis and commentary.</note>, whom Maimonides followed here, is based on the history of the reading of the Law under the auspices of Ezra, which we find described in the Book of Nehemiah. However, the words of the history in Nehemiah, which we have explained elsewhere, do not seem to necessarily demand that hypothesis. Indeed, it has been proven by the illustrious Alting <note>Jacob Alting (1618–1679), a Dutch linguist and theologian.</note> through solid reasoning, as mentioned at another time, that the Hebrew language had not yet ceased to be the native tongue of the Jewish people at that time. Therefore, along with that most learned man, I consider this ritual of interpretation to be of more recent origin, and I believe it should be traced back to the restoration of religious and civil affairs by the Maccabees <note>The Jewish leaders who led a rebellion against the Seleucid Empire in the 2nd century BCE.</note>. It was at this time also that the text of the Biblical codex began to be divided into <term>pesukim</term> <note>original Hebrew: פסוקים</note>, *Verses*, or *segments*; for indeed, this ritual of *Verbal Interpretation* of the Biblical text necessarily required such minor distinctions, or introduced them into the Biblical codices. Regarding the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> and Greek Paraphrases, which were born from this same institution of Public Translation, I will say nothing now, since that material has long been exhausted by learned men.

<margin>Note on 1 Corinthians 14, 2.</margin>
However, of this sacred ritual of *Interpretation* of the read Scripture, no explicit mention occurs, as far as I know, in the writings of the New Testament; nor does any appear among the Fathers or teachers of the early Church. This is because the Christian Church—in which very few individuals were found who were skilled in the Hebrew language (the Ebionites <note>A group of early Jewish Christians who maintained Jewish law and used a Hebrew Gospel.</note> being an exception)—from its very first origins, established the practice of reading aloud the *Translations* of the Holy Scripture themselves, namely the Greek and the Latin. The Greek version used was that most famous one "of the Seventy" <note>original Greek: τῶν ο', referring to the Septuagint.</note>, and the Latin was that "Old Vulgate," so called, until the time of Jerome; although there were several Latin versions publicly received. He contends that Paul in that chapter recalled the Corinthians to the customs of the Synagogues. # CHAPTER 13. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.

-> Ooo ooo 2 <-

After the rituals of reading and explaining the Holy Scripture, we must consider the *Prayers* poured out in public. The *Recitation* of these is typically noted by the phrase: <term>descending before the ark<note>original Hebrew: ירידה לפני התיבה (*yered lifnei ha-tevah*). This refers to the prayer leader moving to a lower floor level or a specific spot in front of the chest containing the Torah scrolls.</note></term>, or STEPPING FORWARD BEFORE THE ARK, as will become clear from the passages to be described hereafter. This is the case even though those *Prayers* in the Synagogue services were usually recited before these *Solemnities of the Reading of the Law and the Prophets* (with the exception of the *additional prayers*), as I have already warned several times in the previous sections. 

In this discussion, I will bind myself to the following order: first, I will put forward certain general points regarding the sacred matters of *Prayers and Blessings* as they are used among the Jews. Second, I will speak specifically about *Public Prayers* and inquire why their *Recitation* is expressed by the phrase *Descending* or *Stepping Forward before the Ark*. After that, I shall deal with the *Subject Matter, Methods, and Circumstances* of this ceremony. Finally, I will describe the *Persons* who are admitted to perform this *Ritual*, and I will report *what Duty* was required of the Common People in this part of Public Religion. At length, I will explain more distinctly that part of this ceremony which is called <term>the Exposition<note>original Hebrew: פרוסה שמע (*Parasa Shema*). This refers to a specific way of reciting or "breaking" the Shema prayer into parts.</note></term>, or the *Division* of the <term>Shema<note>The central prayer of the Jewish faith, beginning "Hear, O Israel."</note></term>. 

It happens most conveniently and gratefully that I am now given the opportunity by Divine Providence to explain all these things anew. If any matters of this kind were transmitted by me some years ago without being equally clearly perceived, they may now be declared more lucidly, and wherever I recognize an error, it may be amended. Indeed, I do this more gladly and with greater liberty because what I wrote on these arguments previously has not, as far as I know, been thoroughly examined or subjected to the criticism of the Learned until now.

By *Prayers*, in the most general sense of the word, I understand every *Orison which a man directs to God*. This kind of *Prayer* is of two types: either the *Proclamation of Divine Virtues and Perfections*, or what is properly so called, *Supplication*, by which we lay our necessities before God and implore His help and grace. *The Proclamation of Divine Virtues* is again divided into two parts: for it consists either of a simple *Commemoration of Divine Perfections*, or <term>Glorification<note>original Greek: δοξασμῷ (*doxasmo*), a hymn of praise or doxology.</note></term> of God, without a singular relation of those virtues to ourselves (in the way the Perfections and Virtues of God are often sung and celebrated in a general sense in the Psalms of David); or it consists of *Thanksgiving for Benefits* received. *Supplication* is likewise of a dual...

### ON THE RITUAL OF PRAYER, BOOK III, PART II.

...of consideration; for either through *Supplication we pray to avert* evils threatening us, which kind of *Supplications* include the *Confession of Sins*, or simply—being struck by no sense of present misery or certain fear of imminent danger—out of a perception of our dependency upon God, we *petition* with *confidence* for the goods of soul and body necessary for us.

Each of these types of *Prayers*, or rather *Orations*, distinguished by their names, I believe I have observed in the works of Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), also known as Rambam, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and codifier of law.</note> in his *Treatises* on Prayers and Blessings; as well as in the *Order of Prayers for the entire Year*, which was added by him to the last *Treatise of the Second Book*, which is titled *Ahava* <note>original: *Abava*, a typo for *Ahava* (Love), the second book of the Mishneh Torah.</note>, of the *First Part* of the work *Jad Chazaka* <note>original: *Jad Chazaka* (The Strong Hand), another name for Maimonides' code of law, the Mishneh Torah.</note>. For into these Books Maimonides collected everything pertaining to this argument—not to mention now the Talmudic volumes *Berachot* (Blessings), *Megilla* (The Scroll), *Taanit* (Fasts), and other well-known Ritual books. Specifically, *Praise*, or the celebration of God, is called among the Jews <term>Berakhah<note>original Hebrew: ברכה (*berakhah*), usually translated as "blessing".</note></term>, while *Prayer* is called <term>Tephillah<note>original Hebrew: תפלה (*tephillah*).</note></term>.

<margin>† See him in the Laws of Prayer, chapter 7, section 1, and "Praise" <note>Hebrew: שבוח (*shevach*).</note>.</margin>
Both of these terms occur distinctly in that sense in Maimonides † and others dealing with this matter. *Berakhah* is divided into two parts, <term>Praise<note>original Hebrew: שבח (*shevach*).</note></term> and <term>Thanksgiving<note>original Hebrew: הודיה (*hodayah*).</note></term>, or in Greek, <term>glorification<note>original Greek: δοξασμὸν (*doxasmon*).</note></term> and <term>acknowledgment<note>original Greek: ἐξομολόγησιν (*exomologesin*).</note></term>, just as Maimonides uses those words distinctly in describing the excellent prayer <term>Shemoneh Esrei<note>The "Eighteen Benedictions," the central standing prayer of the Jewish liturgy.</note></term> (about which we shall speak later, God willing, in its proper place):

<margin>Laws of Prayer, chapter 1, section 6.</margin>

### CHAPTER 13. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.

...it was forbidden to recite without a Congregation of Ten Adult Israelites. To this category belong the *latter part of the first Blessing* of the <term>Reading of the Shema<note>Hebrew: *Keriath Shema*.</note></term>, which is called <term>He forms light<note>Hebrew: *Yotzer Or* (יוצר אור); the first blessing recited before the Shema in the morning service.</note></term>, and that which is usually preceded by the <term>Bless!<note>Hebrew: *Barechu*; the formal call to prayer.</note></term>; likewise the <term>Kaddish<note>A prayer of sanctification and praise.</note></term> and the <term>Kedushah<note>The "Sanctification" prayer.</note></term>, or the *third Blessing* of the most holy Prayer, the <term>Eighteen Benedictions<note>Hebrew: *Shemoneh Esrei*.</note></term>, as it was to be recited by the Minister of the Synagogue. Both types are further distinguished by the time of day into *Morning*, *Afternoon*, and *Evening* prayers; in Hebrew: <term>The Morning, Afternoon, and Evening Prayers<note>Hebrew: *Tefillat Shacharit, Mincha, v'Arvit* (תפלת שחרית מנחה וערבית).</note></term>. Regarding these, likewise, in the following sections in their proper place.

However, for the *Prayers* to be recited in public and for this religious duty to be solemnly fulfilled, a certain Learned Man, skilled in sacred matters, was delegated by the <term>Ruler of the Synagogue<note>Latin: *Archisynagogos*; the administrative head of the synagogue.</note></term>. For the sake of this office, he was chiefly called the <term>Messenger of the Congregation<note>Hebrew: *Sheliach Tzibbur* (שליח צבור); Latin: *Legatus Ecclesiae*. This person leads the service on behalf of the community.</note></term>, as we have seen in the preceding pages and will have occasion to observe again in what follows.

Before I now prepare myself to describe this part of the Synagogue religion more clearly, it will be convenient to give a prior warning here: that among the Jews, the rite of *Reciting Public Prayers in the Synagogue* is commonly expressed by the phrase <term>Descending before the Ark<note>Hebrew: *Yarad lifnei ha-teivah* (ירד לפני התיבה).</note></term>, or <term>Going before the Ark<note>Hebrew: *Avar lifnei ha-teivah* (עבור לפני התיבה).</note></term>, which occurs frequently in the volumes of *Berachot, Megillah, Taanit*, and the *Rituals*.
<margin>Berachot chapter 5, sections 3, 4.</margin>
Thus Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> notes significantly regarding this phrase: <note>original: "הוא שנבנה אחד להתפלל"</note>. This means, *that someone is appointed to pray*.

<margin>
From Megillah chapter 3, sections 3, 4, 8.
Commentary on Megillah chapter 3 or 4, section 3; chapter 5, section 3; chapter 2, section 2.

Certainly, *to go before the Ark* here is the very same as *to recite prayers in public*. And that is surely as certain here as anything can be. # ON THE RITUAL OF PRAYER, BOOK III. PAGE 1028.

> *And he recites twenty-four **Blessings** <note>Latin: *Eulogias*; from the Greek *eulogia*, used here to refer to the Hebrew *berakhot*.</note> before them: those Eighteen that are recited every day, and six others added to them. Does "to descend before the Ark" mean to pray? But, as I said, the matter remains.*

Furthermore, although the meaning of this expression was very well known to Jewish interpreters, and they therefore explained it rather rarely, our own [view] formerly was that this phrase designated that solemnity by which the Synagogue brings the Book of the Law into the **Ark** <note>The *Aron Kodesh*, the chest where Torah scrolls are kept.</note> of the Synagogue, after prayers and **Blessings** have been poured out. For we were then ignorant of the nature of the "descent to the Ark" by the Ministers of the Synagogue, <margin> Chapter 21, p. 463 and chapter 27, p. 542. </margin> which we observed in the *Sacred Rites of the Portuguese Synagogue of Amsterdam*, and about which we had read a magnificent passage in two notable places in *Buxtorf* <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a prominent Hebraist and author of *Synagoga Judaica*.</note>. And it is indeed true that the act of "advancing toward the Ark" denotes the *Recitation of Public Prayers before the Ark* in which the *Book of the Law* is stored; but we quite wrongly joined this *act of reciting prayers and blessings* with the ceremony of bringing the *Book of the Law into the Ark*, since these are truly distinct and differ greatly.

The true reason for this name and the definition of this phrase is this: that he who is about to recite the *Public Prayers in the Synagogue* comes forward from the middle of the Synagogue assembly and proceeds to that *Ark of the Synagogue*, which faces toward the *Sanctuary* <note>Toward the Temple in Jerusalem.</note>, in which the *Book* is placed, and there in a lowly place <note>Many synagogues were designed with a "sunken" area for the leader to stand in, literally fulfilling Psalm 130:1: "Out of the depths I have cried to you."</note> he pours out prayers for the entire *Assembly*, while adopting specific gestures of the body. That is "to descend," and that is "to stand before the Ark." If we had applied the proper attention here, we could have observed this *Ritual of Praying* even then from *Buxtorf* and *Modena* <note>Leone di Modena (1571–1648), a Venetian rabbi and author of *The History of Jewish Rites*.</note>, beyond the fact that the true meaning of this phrase subsequently became obvious to us among other authors, as we dealt with this matter more seriously.

Thus says *Buxtorf*, although, as far as I know, he himself nowhere explains the phrase itself <margin> *Synagoga Judaica*, chapter 13, p. 269. </margin> in describing the Rite of Morning Prayers: "Which being finished (the *recitation of the **Kaddish*** <note>A prayer of sanctification.</note>), the Master of the Synagogue descends from the higher place—which corresponds to the pulpits of the Christians—and prostrates himself upon the steps before the Ark, and falls forward with his face toward the ground on the left side, which the [rest of the] assembly imitates, etc." Previously, being occupied with describing the Rite of Prayers in general, <margin> Chapter 10, p. 226. *Jewish Ceremonies*, Part 1, chapter 11. </margin> he had said: "*It is also necessary for the Precentor <note>The prayer leader or Cantor.</note> in certain prayers to stand in a deep place, and to recite prayers either from a booklet—provided the sight does not fail the letters—or to read it with [the booklet] lifted up.*" Leo of Modena: "*After ten have gathered...*"

<summary>The author corrects his previous misunderstanding of the phrase "descending before the Ark," clarifying that it refers to the prayer leader moving to a lower physical level in front of the Torah Ark to lead the congregation, rather than the act of returning the Torah to the Ark.</summary>

### CHAPTER 13. IN THE SYNAGOGA.

...the **Precentor** <note>The leader of the singing and prayers; a Cantor.</note> either ascends the **Pulpit** <note>Latin: *Pulpitum* or *Suggestum*; the raised platform or *Bimah*.</note>, or proceeds toward the **Ark** <note>The *Aron Kodesh*, where the Torah scrolls are kept.</note>, and begins to intone the prayers in another voice. Thus, the most learned Guise, in his annotations to the Tractate **Berakhot** <note>William Guise (1653–1683), an English Orientalist.</note>, explains the whole matter beautifully and accurately, encompassing much in a few words:
<margin>On chapter 5, § 3.</margin>
**שליח צבור** <gloss>Messenger of the Community</gloss>; the <term>LEGATE</term> <note>Latin: *Legatus*; the official representative of the assembly.</note>, or *MESSENGER OF THE CHURCH was delegated by the whole assembly to recite the prayers. This person would step forward a little way outside the assembly, toward the Ark: for this reason he was called* **עובר לפני התיבה** <gloss>Passing before the Ark</gloss>, *or* **יורד לפני התיבה** <gloss>Descending before the Ark</gloss>. *That is, one who steps forward before the Ark. And to "step forward before the Ark" is to take up this duty at the command of the assembly.*
<margin>* See also Lundius on the Tractate *Taanith*, chapter 1, § 2.</margin>
So it is; in the Synagogue of the German Jews in Amsterdam, the **Ark** in which the **Book of the Law** is preserved, and to which one ascends by steps, is protected by railings; in the middle of these is a lectern upon which the Book of the Public Prayer Liturgy is placed. In this very place, namely before the Ark, the prayers are recited, either from the book or even without it, if one trusts his memory. He who takes this work upon himself is called the **שליח צבור** <gloss>Shaliach Tzibur</gloss>, the *Messenger of the Congregation*, and is said to **עבור לפני התיבה**, *Step forward, or Proceed before the Ark.*

However, as far as I have observed from the records of the Hebrews, this phrase is sometimes used by writers more broadly and generally for the *ordinary recitation of all prayers*, when it also includes the recitation of those blessings which is called **פריסת שמע** <gloss>Prisat Shema</gloss>, the *Division or Exposition of the <term>Shema</term>* <note>The *Shema* is the central declaration of Jewish faith: "Hear, O Israel..."</note>. At other times, it is used more strictly for the *recitation of those prayers* which are distinct from the *Shema* and its blessings; of this kind is primarily the prayer considered holy and excellent by the Jews, the **Schemon-Esre** <note>The "Eighteen Benedictions," also known as the *Amidah* or Standing Prayer.</note>, or some of its parts. In the former way—that is, for the entire office of prayer, which also pertains to the recitation of the **Shema** and its blessings—it is clearly used by **Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> when describing the daily liturgy in words to be shown in their proper place. In those, we shall see that *to the Messenger of the Congregation, as he stands before the Ark, is also ascribed* the **פריסת על שמע** <gloss>Prisat al Shema</gloss>, the *Blessing over the Shema.* But for prayers strictly so-called, and distinguished from the Exposition of the *Shema*, which began with the *Recitation of the Eighteen*, it is used in the **Tractate Megillah**, where the act of the "Exposition of the Shema" is distinguished from the act of *Stepping before the Ark, or Praying.* **Rabbi Joseph Karo** <note>Author of the *Shulchan Aruch*, the definitive code of Jewish law.</note> explains the whole matter, citing Rabbi J.B.A., in these words:
<margin>*Orach Chajim*, chapter 69.</margin>

> **If there are men who prayed each one by himself in private and did not hear Kaddish or Kedushah, one of them stands up and says Kaddish and Barechu and the first blessing "Who forms light" <note>Hebrew: *Yotzer Or*.</note> and no more; and this is called "Dividing the Shema"** <note>Hebrew: *Poreis al Shema*.</note> **[a term meaning] a piece or a slice, because [it is] not [the whole]...**

->### ON THE RITE OF PRAYER, BOOK III, PART II.<-

<gloss>...for they do not say but a portion of it, and after they have finished the Blessing of the Creator, he says the Ancestors, the Powers, the Sanctification, and "You are Holy," and this is called Passing before the Ark.</gloss> <note>original: "שאין אומרים אלא קצת ממנה..." This Hebrew text describes the transition between the Shema blessings and the standing prayer (Amidah).</note> *If there are some people who have prayed by themselves in private, and have not heard the formulas of the Blessings of the **Shema**, the **Kaddish**, and the **Kedushah** recited, then one of them rises and says: the **Kaddish**, the **Barecu** <note>The call to prayer: "Bless the Lord who is blessed."</note>, and the first Blessing, **Yotzer Or** <note>The "Creator of Light" blessing, the first of the morning Shema blessings.</note>; but he does not add the others (he omits the rest), and he is called* **Porees al Schemah**, *which has the meaning of breaking off or cutting away* <note>original: "abrumpendi & abscindendi"</note> *(as if to say: he omits the other blessings and separates them, as it were, from the rest) because he recites only a part of those Blessings. But when they have concluded the Blessing **Yotzer**, he says the **Avoth**, the **Geburoth**, the **Kedusha**, and **Atta Kadosch**, and this man is called* **OVER LIPHNE HATTHEVA**, *meaning "one who steps forward before the Ark."*

The **Schemah**, as we shall explain in what follows, was recited daily by the Jews along with certain Blessings, and it was not only permitted but even commanded for private individuals to perform this religious duty solemnly. But a large part of that *first Blessing* of the Shema, which is called *Yotzer Or*, containing the Sanctification of the Divine Name with the formulas of the **Kaddish** and **Barecu**, ought not to be recited—according to the common opinion of the Nation—except by at least ten free adult men, who constitute an <term>עדה</term> <note>Edah; a legal "Assembly" or quorum of ten, known today as a Minyan.</note>. Therefore, the man who recited those formulas of the Blessings (which we shall describe hereafter) was said to *Divide the Shema*, namely by reciting one part of that Blessing while omitting the others that had already been recited by individuals in private. 

Furthermore, the man who recited the three prior Blessings of the **Octodenae** <note>Latin: "Octodenae" refers to the *Shemoneh Esreh* or "Eighteen" blessings, the central standing prayer also called the *Amidah*.</note>, called **Avoth** <note>Ancestors</note>, **Gevuroth** <note>Divine Powers</note>, and **Atta Kadosch** <note>You are Holy</note>, and who especially Sanctified the Divine Name through these Prayers—just as those Prayers were required to be recited by the Israelites in a public Assembly—or the man who recited the entire *Eighteen* with the additions appropriate for the circumstances of the matters and times, he was especially said to *Pray*, and to *Descend before the Ark*. He was called this because, as the <term>Jom Thoofb</term> <note>Yom Tov; likely referring to the commentary *Tosafot Yom Tov* by Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller.</note> observes, the Messenger of the Church only then moved himself to the Ark to recite these specific Prayers, whereas this was not necessary during the *Recitation of the Shema*.

<margin>Note on chapter 4, § 3 of the Tractate Megillah.</margin>
<gloss>They do not pass before the Ark: Namely, because it was the custom among them that the messenger of the community did not pass before the Ark until they reached the Prayers, properly so called, to be recited.</gloss> <note>original: "אין עוברין לפני התיבה..." In Jewish law, "Prayer" (*Tefillah*) often refers specifically to the Amidah, distinct from the Shema.</note>

In the more recent Synagogue, however, as is clear from the Liturgy of Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Sephardic philosopher and codifier of Jewish law.</note>, even the section of the **Schemah** itself with the Blessings—

The Jews, however, wished that whoever poured out prayers in public should step forward toward the *Ark*, both because that Ark looked toward the *Sanctuary* of the ancient Temple and was the shortest distance from it in the Synagogue—toward which ancient Temple it was indeed necessary for all who pray to turn by Divine Command; and because this very Ark represented that ancient, most Sacred one, which God once honored with His singular presence and before which *holy men prostrated themselves in prayer*; and finally, because they wished prayers to be poured out in a *humble place*, such as this very spot before the *Ark* to which the praying Ministers proceeded. Since this was quite recently proven by the learned man, **Daniel Lundius** <note>A Swedish scholar (1666–1747) known for his work on Hebrew antiquities.</note>, a Swede, I would repeat it in vain.

# CHAPTER XIV.

*The Formula of the Prayer* שמנה עשרה, SCHEMON-ESRE <note>Shemoneh Esreh, meaning "Eighteen," also known as the Amidah or Standing Prayer.</note>, *consisting of eighteen blessings, which is held as* Most Holy *by the Jews and to which almost all other prayers are usually referred; it is presented in its entirety from* Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the great Jewish philosopher and codifier of law.</note>, *compared with the Liturgies, and many observations are made regarding it; especially concerning the various ways it is to be recited in various cases; and concerning the author and the time of the added* Nineteenth Prayer, *which is called* ברכת המינים <note>Birkat ha-Minim, or the "Blessing concerning the Heretics."</note> *and is directed against* Heretics.

<margin>Chapter 10, 12.</margin>
<margin>Maimonides, Laws of Prayer, chapter 1, §1–2.</margin>
That all Israelites, *slaves and women* not excepted, are obligated to pray to and celebrate God daily, even though this is nowhere commanded in so many words in the Mosaic law, the Sages of the ancient age nevertheless derived from the words of *Deuteronomy*: ועבדתם את ה׳ אלהיכם, *And* **you shall serve the Lord your God** <note>Deuteronomy 23:25. The Hebrew term "service" (*avodah*) was interpreted by the Rabbis to mean "service of the heart," i.e., prayer.</note>. For **Maimonides** writes that it has been handed down through *tradition* from hand to hand that by that *Service of God*, *Prayers* are to be understood. ...whereby the Divine Virtues and Perfections are celebrated; *Supplications* for necessary things; and *Thanksgivings* for benefits received from God. He declares that these *Prayers* were originally free-form and not bound by any specific *formulas*, but after the return from the Babylonian Captivity, they were restricted both to specific *Times* and to specific *Formulas*. Indeed, he states that the Formula was established by Ezra and the Men of the Great Assembly <note>The *Anshei Kneset HaGedolah*, a traditional body of 120 elders and prophets from the start of the Second Temple period</note> as the **Eighteen Blessings** <note>original Hebrew: *Shemoneh Esreh Berachot*</note>, the summary of which Maimonides presents there. To these *Eighteen* blessings in the Liturgies, Rabban Gamaliel <note>The leader of the Sanhedrin at Yavne after the destruction of the Temple</note> added another against the Apostates <note>This nineteenth blessing is known as the *Birkat HaMinim*, directed at heretics and informers</note>. Thus, that *common Formula of Prayers*, which all adults of every condition are obligated to recite three times daily, consists in total of *Nineteen Blessings*. To these *Nineteen Blessings*, through various additions that are to be joined or inserted into them under various circumstances and times, they refer almost every kind of *Vow* and *Thanksgiving*, which he deemed his duty to explain in this manner—as I shall soon describe more extensively and clearly. The arguments for each word were brought forward in the preceding sections, where we treated the *Origin of Synagogues*.

In addition to this *Formula of Nineteen Blessings*, called the *Shemoneh Esreh*, all free Israelite males of age (*Women* and *Slaves* being excepted <note>In Jewish law, women and slaves were generally exempt from positive commandments that were tied to a specific time, such as the Shema</note>) are bound to recite another *Confession*, both of their Faith in the Unity of God and of other *Duties toward God*, along with certain *Blessings*. This religious rite is commonly called the **Recitation of the Shema**, or the Reading of the **Shema** <note>Hebrew: *Kriat Shema*</note>, or the *Selection*: "Hear, O Israel" <note>The central declaration of Jewish faith from Deuteronomy 6:4</note>. This religious act, strictly speaking, is not numbered among the *Prayers* <note>The term *Tefillah* specifically refers to the *Shemoneh Esreh*</note> by them, since all Israelites—not excepting slaves and women—are obligated to recite those others <note>The 19 Blessings</note> three times; nevertheless, taking the word *Prayer* in a broader sense, the Shema should also be reduced to that category. Therefore, since this *Act of Religion* consists largely of the explanation of these two Formulas, I believe it will be a welcome task for students of these letters if we present both *Formulas* here and discuss the manner and circumstances of *Reciting* each, as far as it pertains to the understanding of this subject; for then the things Maimonides records concerning the *Liturgy of Public Prayers* will be much more easily perceived by us. # CHAPTER 14. IN THE SYNAGOGUE. 1039

...the arrangement of Maimonides <note>original: "Maimonidis"; a 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legal scholar known as Rambam</note> is divided into three parts. Specifically, the first part of his *Laws of Prayer* <note>original: "Hilcoth Tephilla"</note>, chapter 1, encompasses three blessings consisting of **Praise to the Lord** <note>original: "שבח לח'", Shevach la-Shem</note>, the Blessed God. The final three are **Thanksgiving** <note>original: "הודיה", Hodayah</note>, a category we described in section 6 as consisting of the celebration of Divine Virtues with respect to the benefits received or to be received from God. The middle thirteen blessings, however, contain **Petitions** for all necessities, to which—as if to primary categories—all petitions of any kind can be referred, whether concerning private or public matters. <margin>Chapter 2, §. 1.</margin> And indeed, at the beginning (as the same Maimonides reminds us), this prayer consisted of Eighteen Blessings, but Rabban Gamaliel <note>A prominent Jewish leader in the late 1st century CE</note> increased it by one prayer directed against the Heretics <note>The "Birkat HaMinim," directed against those seen as deviating from Jewish orthodoxy</note>, which we have now listed as the twelfth in the usual order of the Liturgies. But so that nothing is omitted by us that serves to clarify this material, let us present the relevant points in certain theses, and then explain them.

1. These nineteen prayers (with certain adjustments, which we will mention shortly) were to be recited at every time of solemn prayer. On every weekday, Jews must pray three times: morning, evening, and night. On Sabbaths, established Festivals, and New Moons, four times; namely, when additional prayers <note>The "Musaf" or additional service</note> are to be joined to the ordinary ones in place of the extraordinary sacrifice. <margin>Maimonides, chapter 1. §. 10. of this work.</margin> On the Day of Atonement <note>Yom Kippur</note>, five times, when the "closing prayer" <note>The "Neilah" service</note> was added to those four prayers; concerning which we will speak later in its proper place. At each of these times of prayer, these Nineteen must be recited, as Maimonides is the authority: <margin>Chapter 2. §. 2. of this work.</margin> **In every prayer of every day, a person must pray these nineteen blessings according to their order.** <note>original Hebrew: "בכל תפלה שבכל יום מהפלל אדם תשע עשרה ברכות אלו על הסדר"</note>

2. This is done, however, so that in place of the thirteen middle blessings, a certain shorter prayer could be recited—and often was—which reflected a certain <term>form</term> <note>original Greek: "τύπον", typon; a pattern or model</note> and appearance of them.
The first three and the last three of this prayer were always to be poured out by private individuals without any variation, <margin>this work, chapter 1. §. 11.</note> according to what Maimonides says: **Regarding the first three and the last three, they never add to them, nor subtract from them, nor change anything in them;** <note>original Hebrew: "ג' ראשונות וג' אחרונות לעולם אין מוסיפין בהם ולא פוחתין מהן ואין משנין בהן דבר"</note> but for the thirteen intermediate blessings, a single shorter formula of supplication was substituted. This was for those who were distracted by business or less fluent in praying the rest of all...

<header>CHAPTER 14. IN THE SYNAGOGA.</header>

<margin>Laws of Prayer, chapter 13. §. 3. <note>original: "Hilc. Tephil."; referring to Maimonides' Mishneh Torah</note></margin>
...reads; just as we heard Maimonides say in the previous sections, that the Reader of the Prophets should read in the Prophet **something of the same argument as that which was read in the Law** <note>original: "מעין שקרא בתורה", referring to the *Haftarah*—the prophetic portion that matches the theme of the Torah portion</note>, *a section of the same subject matter, or kind, as that which was read from the Law.* And it is indeed very true, as Guise <note>William Guise (1653–1683), an English Orientalist and scholar</note> maintains, that the little word **like** <note>original: "מעין", *me-ein*</note> does not precisely signify a *Summary*, or *Epitome*, or *Compendium*, but rather something *which is of the same kind and subject matter*. This meaning of the word is most evident at the end of the preceding *Chapter* of this Treatise. There Maimonides says that it is permitted for anyone to add more to those fixed and solemn prayers, and to persist longer in this act of devotion than what is strictly required, as he himself has explained: but those Extraordinary or Supernumerary prayers are compared to a *Voluntary Sacrifice* <note>original: "Sacrificio Voluntario", referring to the free-will offering in the Temple</note>. He notes that the person praying should only take care that in those extra prayers, he should innovate something in the middle sections of the *Eighteen Blessings* (expressing his mind in other words) that agrees with the theme of those petitions. His words are:

<margin>Chapter 1. §. 11.</margin>
**"Therefore it is necessary that he should innovate something in each and every blessing among the thirteen middle ones, according to the theme of the blessings"** <note>original: "לפיכך צריך שיחדש דבר בכל ברכה וברכה מן האמצעיות מעין הברכות"</note>, *that is, he should innovate in each blessing of the thirteen middle ones, yet in a way that agrees with the theme of those prayers.* But even if this is the genuine meaning of the word **like** <note>original: "מעין"</note> which Guise urges, Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), a renowned English Hebraist whose work connected the New Testament to Jewish tradition</note> nonetheless did not err when he interpreted that word in the Mishnic text <note>The Mishnah, the first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions</note> as *such a thing which expresses the form of a matter in such a way that the matter is represented in a contracted form in that type*; just as truly *every compendium of a longer speech is of the same subject matter as that speech, and exhibits, as it were, its form*. From the Mishnic text itself, it is as clear as can be that this meaning of the word holds true in this place. For where Rabbi Akiva is said to have stated: *He whose prayer is fluent in his mouth should recite the Eighteen [Blessings]; if not, then* **a summary of the Eighteen** <note>original: "מעין שמונה עשרה", *me-ein shemoneh esreh*</note>, these very words certainly prove that "a summary of the Eighteen" is a form of the *Eighteen Blessings* that is more contracted and condensed than the *Eighteen* themselves. Nor do the Talmudic interpreters desert Lightfoot here. Bartenora <note>Obadiah ben Abraham of Bertinoro, a 15th-century commentator on the Mishnah</note> says: **"There are those who explain 'a summary of the Eighteen' according to the Gemara <note>The component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis</note>, where it is said that one says each and every blessing of the middle ones in a shortened form and concludes each one individually; and there are those who say it refers to 'Grant us understanding, O Lord our God, to know Your ways,' which is a single blessing that contains the essence of all the middle blessings of the Eighteen."**

There are some who explain this along with the Gemara, where it is said: *That every blessing—*

...were called <term>Minaeans</term> <note>The text reads "NAEI," a fragment of *Minaei*, from the Hebrew *Minim*, meaning heretics or sectarians</note> by Jerome * in his Letter to Augustine; perhaps the name is derived from the Hebrew מִינִים (*Minim*), by which they are accustomed to designate Heretics or Apostates. A greater difficulty, which as far as I know has not yet been resolved by the Learned, lies in the question of who that **Rabban Gamaliel** was, under whose auspices this Prayer was composed by **Samuel the Small**. Is it to be understood as that <term>Rabban Gamaliel the Elder</term> <note>original Hebrew: רבן גמליאל הזקן</note> who, according to common tradition, is said to have presided over the Sanhedrin in the years of Tiberius, Caligula, and the first years of Claudius, and who was mentioned by Luke in the Acts of the Apostles? Or was it rather the grandson of this Gamaliel (born of his son Simeon), namely **Gamaliel II**, who likewise presided over the Sanhedrin with great authority after the Destruction of the City and the Temple, in the city of **Yavne**? 

Lightfoot contends that Gamaliel the Elder, the Teacher of Paul, should be understood here. The Rabban Gamaliel in question was Paul's Master: for although the Rabban Gamaliel who is commonly called "of Yavne" was the grandson of Paul's teacher, and this matter is recorded as having taken place in Yavne, Paul’s teacher also spent time in Yavne. That he is the one referred to in the history currently under our hands is clear enough from the fact that the matter involved Samuel the Small, who certainly died before the Destruction of the City. The Hebrew chronologist **Ganz** supports this, expressly asserting that the <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>The supreme Jewish legislative and judicial council</note> moved to Yavne forty years before the destruction of the Republic, and that the Prayer against Heretics was composed there by Rabbi Samuel the Small in the presence of Rabban Gamaliel the Elder. The illustrious **Alting** defends the same opinion, and the most learned **Guisius** also follows it. 

But elsewhere, **Selden** examined these words of Ganz regarding the Sanhedrin being moved to Yavne forty years before the destruction of the Temple; he showed that in the proofs cited by Ganz from the *Yoma* and *Sanhedrin* tracts of the Talmud, that which Ganz supposes is not actually contained there. From the *Sanhedrin* codex, it is only established that Rabbi Samuel the Small had dealings with Rabbi Gamaliel the Elder regarding the matter of the Intercalation <note>The adjustment of the calendar through leap months</note>. But it is nowhere stated that this same Gamaliel the Elder presided over a Sanhedrin already moved to Yavne. Furthermore, Selden says that he has not yet read anything of the sort among the Ancients, though he thinks it cannot be doubted that there was a Sanhedrin in Yavne at that time or elsewhere; yet it was not the "Great" Sanhedrin, which had not yet migrated from Jerusalem. In any case, it is clear from the Acts of the Apostles that the Sanhedrin was still in Jerusalem under Caligula and Claudius. The Sanhedrin was not moved to Yavne—as even **Buxtorf** admits—before the Destruction of the Temple and the City; and other Jewish Doctors hold this view throughout their writings. **Rabbi Jochanan ben Zakkai** was the first...

after the destruction of Jerusalem, he presided over the <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>The supreme judicial and administrative council of the Jewish people.</note>, and was succeeded after a short space of time by Rabban Gamaliel, the grandson of Gamaliel the Elder, who was thereafter called **Rabban Gamaliel of Yavne** <note>original Hebrew: רבן גמליאל דיבנה (*Rabban Gamaliel di-Yavneh*)</note>. Therefore, we rightly grant to the Learned the task of weighing whether we should not rather say it was *this* Gamaliel in whose presence that prayer, the **Shemoneh Esrei** <note>The "Eighteen Blessings," the core prayer of Jewish daily service.</note>, and that **part of the prayer** directed against **Heretics**, was composed. Certainly, if we admit this, the reasoning behind certain petitions in this **prayer** will be established for us; as we have previously noted, they presuppose the destruction of the Temple and the City. It is also certain that the Jews never burned with greater hatred and envy toward the Christians than after the **Destruction of the Temple**. It was at that time especially that they thought about fortifying their own religion, whereas before that time, the Christians were mostly looked down upon and held in contempt by them.

In Yavne, they made <note>original Hebrew: סיגות לתורה (*siyagot la-Torah*)</note> **fences around the Law**, as the Hebrew chronicles record. Nor is it absurd to say that the same **Samuel the Small**, who flourished as a young man under the first Gamaliel, could have flourished under the grandson; for between the reigns of the two, there would have been a maximum interval of forty years—and far less if we look at the specific dates of their respective leadership. It is true, however, that this would disrupt all the reasoning of the celebrated Alting, who led us and others in a clever conjecture: that by this **Samuel the Small** we should understand **the Apostle Paul**, who before his conversion was the most bitter enemy of the Christians and who excelled among the disciples of Gamaliel. Alting supports this conjecture primarily because it seems evident from the same passage of the tractate **Berakhot** <note>The first tractate of the Talmud, dealing with prayers and blessings.</note> that this very teacher **Samuel**, who was the author of the prayer against the **Heretics**, "fell away into heresy" a year later and defected from the Jewish faith.

I do not deny that I too was among those who placed some confidence in this observation by Alting. However, it has been two or three years, perhaps a bit more, since I had a convenient opportunity to speak with a certain most learned man, a very faithful pastor of the Lord's flock in nearby Groningen. For several years, he had been laboring with laudable zeal in translating the tractate **Berakhot**, and among other excellent things, I learned that he had observed this: that this Talmudic passage concerning **Samuel the Small** had been unfortunately misunderstood and rendered by the celebrated Alting. But now, as I search the archives of my memory, it is not clearly observed by my mind what sense that Reverend and most learned man advised me was underlying the passage at that time; although I have no doubt that it is the very one which, looking at the passage more diligently now, is contained in the clearest words...

## CHAPTER XV.

->*The Rite of the* <term>RECITATION OF THE SHEMA</term> <note>Hebrew: קריאת שמע; the central declaration of Jewish faith, "Hear, O Israel."</note>, *which every male, freeborn, and adult Israelite is bound to perform twice daily, is described; the Seven Blessings are presented, with three of which the morning Shema and four of which the evening Shema must be recited, along with certain observations regarding this Rite.*<--

Beyond the **Eighteen Benedictions**, every male and freeborn Israelite must recite the so-called *Shema* twice daily, morning and evening, along with certain Blessings. This rite is usually called by them the <term>RECITATION</term> or READING OF THE <term>SHEMA</term>. It is appropriate for us to discuss this a little more distinctly, since the illustrious <term>Buxtorf</term> <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a prominent Christian Hebraist whose works were standard textbooks for studying Jewish customs.</note> treated those things pertaining to this part of the Jewish Religion somewhat briefly and <margin>See his work, chapter 10, page 205. At the letter ש (Shin).</margin> carelessly in his *Synagoga Judaica*, and no more fully or accurately in his *Abbreviaturis*.

By the *Shema* <note>original: "Schemah"; the central declaration of Jewish faith, named after its first word, "Hear."</note>, which is recited by the Jews morning and evening, you should understand three <term>sections</term> <note>original: "Pericopas"; specific passages of scripture assigned for reading.</note>, or Biblical texts, the first and most important of which begins in Deuteronomy with the word *Shema* [HEAR], and consists of these words:

> HEAR, ISRAEL, Jehovah <note>The author uses the Latinized "Jehovah" for the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God, often translated as "The LORD."</note>, our God, Jehovah is One. And you shall love Jehovah, your God, with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength. And these words, which I command you today, shall be upon your heart. And you shall instill them in your children; and you shall speak of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk on the road; and when you lie down, and when you rise. And you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes, and you shall write them upon the doorposts of your houses, and upon your gates.

The second text is the Creed beginning *And it shall come to pass if* [Hebrew: *Vehayah im shemoa*], taken from this same book of Deuteronomy, in these words:

<margin>Chapter 11:13–21.</margin>
> And it shall be if you diligently hear my commandments, which I command you today, to love Jehovah, your God, and to serve him with all your heart, and with all your soul; I will give the autumn and spring rain, and you shall gather your grain, and your wine, and your oil. And I will give grass in your field for your cattle, and you shall eat, and be satisfied. Take care for yourselves, lest your heart be seduced, and you turn away, and serve foreign gods, and bow down to them; and the anger of Jehovah be kindled against you; and he shut up the heaven, so there be no rain; and the earth yield not her fruit, and you perish quickly from this good land, which Jehovah gives you. And you shall put these words upon your heart and upon your soul; and you shall bind them as a sign upon your hands, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes. And you shall teach them to your children, speaking of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk on the road; when you lie down and when you rise up. And you shall write them upon the doorposts of your houses, and in your gates, so that your days may be multiplied, and the days of your children upon the land which God promised by oath to give to your fathers: as the days of the heavens upon the earth.

<margin>Chapter 15:37–41.</margin>
The mark of the third text is *And he said* [Hebrew: *Vayomer*] in the Book of Numbers, in these words:

> And Jehovah spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them to make for themselves fringes <note>original: "fimbrias"; refers to the tzitzit or ritual tassels worn on the corners of garments.</note> on the wings of their garments throughout their generations, and they shall put upon the fringe of the wing a thread of blue; and it shall be to you for a fringe, so that, when you see it, you may remember all the commandments of Jehovah, and do them. You shall not explore after your own heart, and after your own eyes, following which you go astray. That you may remember and do all my commandments, and be holy to your God. I am Jehovah, your God, who led you out of Egypt, to be your God: I am Jehovah, your God.

<margin>On the Ministry of the Temple, chapter 9</margin>
The RECITATION, or READING of the *Shema*, I say, consists of the reciting of these three texts. <margin>
Section 1. *Laws of the Recitation of the Shema* <note>original: "Hilcoth Keriath Shemah."</note>, chapter 1, section 3. Book 1, chapter 11, section 7. Indeed, see also the most learned Bernard on Josephus, book 4, chapter 8, section 13.
</margin>
*Those texts from Exodus, which are placed in the Phylacteries, were not actually recited in the "Keriath Shemah" <note>The formal "Recitation of the Shema."</note>; rather, in their place, a section noted from the book of Numbers was used. This error by Lightfoot <note>The author uses the strong word "hallucinationem" (hallucination/delusion) to describe Lightfoot's mistake.</note> was first observed, if I am not mistaken, by the most learned Guise <note>William Guise, a 17th-century English Orientalist.</note>, who uncovered it both from this very Code of Berakhot and from Tamid. Certainly, the words of Maimonides <note>The preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> on this matter are most clear; after noting these three texts, he adds:* "And the recitation of these three sections in this order is what is called the Recitation of the Shema" <note>original Hebrew: וקריאת שלוש פרשיות אלו על סדר זה הוא הנקראת קריאת שמע</note>. *Indeed, even Leon of Modena <note>A famous Venetian rabbi (1571–1648).</note> correctly guided us here in his explanations of the customs of the Synagogue.*

In the *Recitation*, however, this order had to be observed: the two texts from Deuteronomy were to be placed before the one from Numbers. The beginning of the Recitation was to be made from the text *Shema* [HEAR], Deuteronomy 6:4, "Because in these words are contained the articles regarding the Unity of God, and His Love, and His Study, which is the great foundation upon which everything depends. Immediately following these are those other words from Deuteronomy ["And it shall come to pass if you listen"], because they contain the commandment regarding the Remembrance of all the other Commandments; just as there is also a Commandment contained in that text from Numbers, which is recited last." <note>This explains the thematic logic of the prayer's structure: starting with the essence of God and moving to the obligation of the commandments.</note> *Thus says Maimonides.*

<margin>
*Laws of the Recitation of the Shema*, chapter 1, section 2. See the same, chapter 1, section 4. Book 1, part 2, chapter 1.
</margin>
Regarding the *Manner* of this *Sacred Rite*, it must be noted in the first place that when the first verse of the first text is recited ("Hear, Israel, etc."), a clause is to be added in a low voice: "Blessed be the name of the glory of His kingdom forever and ever" <note>original Hebrew: ברוך שם כבוד מלכותו לעולם ועד; this is a traditional response whispered during the Shema.</note>. *And this is according to the tradition which we have presented from the earlier words of Maimonides.*

# ON THE RITUAL OF PRAYER, BOOK III.

<margin>Chapter 1. Section 4.</margin>
Finally, at the end of the evening service, to be placed after the *Second Prayer* <note>The author is categorizing the blessings surrounding the Shema; this refers to the second blessing following the evening Shema.</note> of the morning-style arrangement, the symbol is "Cause us to lie down" <note>Hebrew: *Hashkivenu* (השכיבנו)</note>, and it is read in this manner:
> Cause us to lie down, O Lord our God, in peace; and raise us up again, O our King, unto life; and spread over us the tent of your peace, and direct us with your good counsel before you (and save us for your name's sake). Shield us, and remove far from us the enemy, pestilence, the sword, famine, and every cause of sorrow; and drive away the Accuser <note>Latin: *Satanam*; Hebrew: *Satan*, the Adversary or spiritual prosecutor.</note> from before us and from behind us, and hide us in the shadow of your wings, for you are God, our Guardian and our Deliverer; for you are a God who is a gracious and merciful King. And guard our going out and our coming in for life and for peace from this time forth and forevermore. BLESSED ARE YOU, O LORD, WHO GUARDS YOUR PEOPLE ISRAEL FOREVER.

This is indeed the *Short Prayer*, in respect to the preceding ones, which are called "longer" in the Volume of Blessings <note>Latin: *Codice Berachoth*; referring to the first tractate of the Talmud, *Berachot*, which deals with prayers.</note>.

<margin>Chapter 1. Sections 9, 10, 11.</margin>
The time for performing the recitation of the *Shema* <note>The central declaration of Jewish faith, "Hear O Israel."</note>, both for the morning and the evening, is debated at the beginning of the Volume of Blessings, and from there in the works of Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal scholar.</note> concerning this subject. The entire span of the night until the breaking of dawn is granted for the Evening *Shema*, and the first quarter of the day from sunrise is granted for the Morning *Shema*. The *location and physical posture of the body* <margin>Berachot, Chapter 1, Section 3.</margin> during the recitation are considered matters of personal choice. Regarding the *persons* obligated, I have already mentioned them above <margin>Chapter 3, Section 3.</margin>, and one may consult the Volume of Blessings, as well as the various temperaments and restrictions of the Precept regarding the performance or neglect of this ritual under various circumstances.

Moreover, they consider themselves bound to this part of their religion by the very words of *Deuteronomy* <margin>Chapters 6, 7 and 11, 19.</margin> cited above, which command the Israelites <margin>See Berachot, Chapter 1, Section 3.</margin>—when they lie down and when they rise up—concerning their obligation to keep God’s Precepts. <margin>Maimonides, Chapter 1, Section 1.</margin> This is primarily intended (as they interpret those words of Deuteronomy) to daily renew the memory of the *Unity of God and the Commandment to love Him*. However, since that instruction in the words of Deuteronomy is perhaps not as strictly commanded as the Teachers <note>Referring to the Rabbis or Sages of the Talmud.</note> would have it—or at least since those words of Deuteronomy allow for a broader interpretation—this very recitation of the *Shema* is to be traced back not so much to the institution of Moses himself, but to the later tradition of the time of the Scribes. Nevertheless, that this ritual was in use before the time when Christ was revealed among men seems clear from the history of the Lawyer who tested the Lord with questions <margin>Chapter 10, verse 25.</margin> in the Gospel of Luke. *Teacher, he said, what must I do to inherit eternal life? But He responded to him: What is written in the law? How do you read it?* <note>Greek: *πῶς ἀναγινώסקεις?* (pos anaginoskeis?)</note>

### CHAPTER 15. IN THE SYNAGOGUE. 1059

How do you **READ**? But he *answering said: You shall love the Lord, your God, etc.* <note>The author is quoting Luke 10:26-27, where an expert in religious law answers Jesus by quoting the Shema.</note> Those words of the Lord, "How do you read?" <note>original: Πῶς ἀναγινώσκεις (*Pōs anaginōskeis*)</note> seem to refer to a certain familiar *Reading*, which was called *the Reading* "by way of emphasis" <note>original: κατ' ἔμφασιν (*kat' emphasin*); meaning it was the primary or most important text one would read.</note>. The expert in the law easily understood the Lord’s question under this specific concept of *the Reading*, as it was commonly indicated by this name. For since many things are written and read in the Law, why was it necessary for the lawyer to understand these particular words from Deuteronomy under the general term "Reading" rather than many other similar passages, or even the Ten Commandments? It must be because these words from Deuteronomy were at that time familiarly read and recited by the Jews. Therefore, we believe that the Lord, through the words *How do you read?*, meant to say: *What do you read, or recite daily in the Shema?* For the Reading or Recitation of the *Shema* <note>The "Shema" is the central declaration of Jewish faith, beginning with "Hear, O Israel" (Deuteronomy 6:4).</note> was emphatically called "the Reading" <note>original: קריאה (*Keriah*)</note>. "What did you read in the Shema?" <note>original: מאי קראת בשמע (*Mai karata bi-Shema*)</note>. When the lawyer perceived this sense of the Lord’s words, he immediately replied: *You shall love the Lord, your God, etc.* For these words are recited in the daily *Recitation of the Shema* <note>original: קריאת שמע (*Keriat Shema*)</note>, both in the morning and in the evening. Indeed, this also seems evident from Josephus himself <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Jewish historian whose works provide vital context for first-century Judea.</note>, who, in his review of the various Mosaic Laws, alludes to these very passages of Deuteronomy and writes as follows:

DE RITU PRECATIONIS LIB. II. <note>On the Rite of Prayer, Book II.</note>

<margin>Laws of Reciting the Shema, chapter 1, § 7. <note>Referring to Maimonides’ *Mishneh Torah*.</note></margin>
...to be recited at certain times. Maimonides indeed, following the Talmudic scholars, records that Ezra and his Great Assembly <note>original: *Synedrium*; the Great Assembly (*Anshei Knesset HaGedolah*) was the legislative body of leaders at the start of the Second Temple period.</note> composed and established these **Blessings**, or **Prayers**; and he therefore maintains that those formulas should be recited by every Israelite without any change. Yet, I attribute both this Rite and several others to authors who flourished after the restoration of the commonwealth by the Maccabees. It was then that those **literal** and **strict** interpretations of the Law of Moses began to be held. This rite, along with many others of that kind, had its origin there; thus, it is possible that in the ordinary Temple Liturgy around the time of **our Lord**, some of these were recited according to the **Form of the Shema** by the Priests, as is recorded in the Tractate *Tamid* <note>A section of the Mishnah detailing the daily morning service in the Temple.</note>.

->*The whole Jewish Liturgy; that is, the Prayers and Blessings, and the order in which they are recited in the Synagogues during the Morning, Afternoon, and Evening services, is described here based on Maimonides. <margin>Laws of Prayer, chapter 8, § 1.</margin>
Before we arrive at that point, let it be observed that the **Prayers** of the Hebrew people are to be poured out in **Public Places**, or rather among a group; provided that ten adult and free men, who constitute a **Congregation** <term>עדה</term> <note>original: *Edah*; the Hebrew term for a formal gathering or community, specifically the quorum of ten (minyan) required for public prayer.</note>, are present. Maimonides is very insistent on this point, commending the virtue of prayers poured out in public over the efficacy of private ones. "The prayer of the community," he says, "is always [accepted]; and even if there are sinners among them, the Holy One, Blessed be He, does not reject the prayer of the many. Let no man join himself to any but the community, and let him not pray alone whenever he is able to pray with the community. And a man should always arrive early and stay late [at the synagogue]." <note>translated from the Hebrew text provided in the manuscript, which quotes Maimonides' *Mishneh Torah*.</note>

### CHAPTER 16. IN THE SYNAGOGA.

"And he should frequent the house of assembly <note>Hebrew: *Beit ha-Knesset*, the synagogue</note>, for his prayer is not heard at all times except in the house of assembly." **The prayers of many are always heard**; even if there are sinners among them, the ever-blessed God does not reject public prayers. Therefore, it is necessary that anyone about to fulfill the duty of praying should join the congregation; he should not pray alone when he has the opportunity to pray with the congregation. A person should ensure that he is present in the synagogue morning and evening, because prayers are not heard unless they are poured out in the synagogue. Indeed, as Petronius elegantly put it: *The rumor is that prayers joined together go forth more strongly.* This opinion of Maimonides <note>Maimonides was a preeminent 12th-century Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> on page 73 is based on the traditions of the Gemara scholars in the tractate *Berakhot* <note>The first tractate of the Talmud, dealing with prayers and blessings.</note>:

### ON THE RITE OF PRAYER, BOOK III.

<margin>Matthew 18:20.</margin> Certainly, the final parts of this passage agree with the words of the Lord to his disciples: *Where two or three are gathered in my name;* <note>original Greek: "ἐμὸν ὄνομα"</note> **FOR MY NAME;** <note>original Hebrew: "לשמי" (Lishmi)</note> (**For the glory of my cause**) **there I am in the midst of them.**

Now, the *prayers* and *blessings* <note>original Latin: "eulogiae"</note> that are performed daily in the synagogue are of two kinds. *For some constitute a necessary part of the Public Liturgy*—of the public Ministry of Prayers, I say—for which a Leader of the Congregation <term>Legatus Ecclesiae|Literally "Envoy of the Church," here referring to the Shaliach Tzibur, the person appointed to lead the community in prayer</term> is solemnly deputized. *Others do not constitute a necessary part of the Public Prayers* which are poured out by the Leader of the Congregation, but are recited by private individuals in the synagogue before the Minister of the Synagogue begins to fulfill his office. To put it another way: some prayers and blessings pertain to the Public Office, and some do not.

Both kinds are reviewed by Maimonides in the section titled *Order of Prayers for the Whole Year*, but they must be distinguished by us more carefully by comparing his treatise <margin>Chapter 10.</margin> *On Prayer* with other Ritual books. Although the celebrated Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629) was a pioneering Christian scholar of Hebrew and Jewish traditions.</note> has provided much from the ritual books regarding this part of the Jewish religion concerning *prayers*, he did not achieve certain points with equal success; he did not pass them down with enough distinction or clarity. So that this may be better understood by the reader, and to show that I say this without any boasting or desire to disparage that great man (motives I keep far from here, as I am intent only on the truth), I will follow the footsteps of the celebrated Buxtorf. I will first present the summary of what he wrote on this matter, then I will strive to shed more light upon it, omitting nothing, as far as I am able, that pertains to illustrating this argument.

Buxtorf, without employing that distinction of *prayers*—where some pertain to the *Public Ministry* and others do not (a distinction which will become clear from the following pages as necessary for forming a clear understanding of the Sacred Rite)—begins to explain the *Liturgical Prayers* in this way:

*The first prayer, composed in verse and rhythmic speech, as are most of the others, is sung and read from memory by them while standing. It sounds like this:* אדון העולם ; **MASTER OF THE WORLD, etc.** <note>original: "Adon Olam," a famous hymn emphasizing God's eternity.</note> Next they add the מאה ברכות ; **ONE HUNDRED SMALL THANKSGIVINGS,** <note>original: "Me'ah Berakhot"</note> and these are for the most part very short, **WHICH THEY RECITE TWICE EACH DAY FROM BEGINNING TO END,** the reason for which we will reveal later. Of which...
