# CHAPTER 16. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.

After he has given enough examples of blessings, he continues: *To these prayers they add two others, that they may be delivered from sins, evil men, and harmful demons. Thereafter they cast themselves down before God, confess their guilt, and hang upon His mercy alone, in the Prayer whose beginning is:* **Master of all worlds** <note>original Hebrew: "Rabbon Kol Olamim"</note>, **Lord of all ages.** . . *A short prayer follows afterwards for the giving of the Law. From there he says that the Commandments concerning Offerings are read by them, in place of the sacrifices formerly offered, along with a certain Prayer, which begins:* **Rabbi Ismael.** <note>Referring to the "Baraita of Rabbi Ishmael," a list of thirteen rules for interpreting the Torah often included in prayer books.</note> *Afterwards, a Prayer is recited for the restoration of the Temple in Jerusalem. Next, he says a Thanksgiving of similar theme is sung by them. Once this is done, he says they read a long Prayer taken here and there from the* **Psalms of David**. *That is followed by another Prayer, which they call* *Krias Schemah* <note>original Hebrew: "Kri'at Shema"</note>, **HEAR THE READING**. *When he has dealt with this in a few words, he adds: They have yet another similar Prayer, which they call* **Shemon-Esre** <note>original Hebrew: "Shmoneh Esreh," meaning "Eighteen"</note>, **EIGHTEEN**, *because it contains as many thanksgivings. This, he says, is followed by that wicked and blasphemous Prayer against Christians, etc.* <note>The author refers to the *Birkat HaMinim*, a blessing added to the Eighteen Prayers which historical Christian polemicists viewed as a curse against them.</note>

It is certainly impossible for these things not to stir a confused perception in the reader regarding the *Prayers of the Jews*, listed in such number without any distinction, aside from the fact that certain necessary and more important matters were omitted, while others were not so successfully understood by that most Learned Man <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a prominent Christian Hebraist whose works were foundational for European scholars.</note>. At any rate, if a judgment is to be formed on these matters, it should be according to Maimonides, who described the *Ritual of Prayers* quite accurately. Nor have I seen other Ritual books differ from Maimonides here. Let us therefore observe these Buxtorfian points according to the discipline of Maimonides:

1. None of those Prayers and Blessings <note>original Latin: "eulogiae"</note> which Buxtorf reviewed up to the *Shema* and *Shemon-Esre* prayers pertain to the **Public Ministry of Prayers**, which was performed by the **Minister of the Synagogue** <term>Legatus Ecclesiae|The Shaliach Tzibur, or community representative who leads the formal service.</term>. Indeed, strictly speaking, only the **Eighteen** were considered *Prayers*, to which all Israelites were necessarily bound, as we have already advised in the preceding sections. But the *Recitation of the Shema*, even if it was not strictly held to be a Prayer <note>The Shema is technically a recitation of biblical verses rather than a petitionary prayer.</note>, was also placed before the *Shemon-Esre* Prayer in the ancient Synagogue itself. And the **Public Liturgy** consisted principally of these two formulas, as we shall prove in the following sections from Maimonides.

2. As for those other Blessings and Prayers which were poured out by **Private Individuals** (one or more) in the Synagogue before the Public Ministry began (of which kind are all those listed by Buxtorf up to...

...are listed near the Shema) <note>Referring to the *Kri'at Shema*, the central declaration of Jewish faith.</note> their proper beginning is with the prayer **Master of all worlds** <note>original Hebrew: "Rabbon Kol Olamim"</note>, **Lord of all ages.** Buxtorf mentions after these the prayers he calls the **One Hundred Blessings** <note>original Hebrew: "Me’ah Berachot"</note>. For as to what Buxtorf writes, that these **One Hundred Blessings** must be recited twice daily by every Jew, in this the *Most Learned* man has first of all hallucinated <note>The author uses "hallucinatus est" to suggest Buxtorf was profoundly mistaken or dreaming.</note>. Then, although it is certain that those blessings, which make up the number of one hundred, are recited by some Jews in the Synagogues and are listed in the Prayer Books, other Doctors <note>Scholars or authorities.</note> have nevertheless warned that this was done by error. Therefore, before we proceed, it is convenient to clearly define what this whole matter of the "One Hundred Blessings" is.

<margin>
See *Leone da Modena*, book 1, chapter 9, § 3.

The Jews, as we have already observed in previous sections, consider themselves bound by the power of a Divine Precept to praise and laud God in every situation and for every thing—whether it be a manifestation of Divine virtues or something from which they perceive some convenience or utility. Such formulas of praise either begin with **Blessed** <note>original Hebrew: "Baruch"; the author translates the Latin as "Laus tibi, Domine" or "Praise to you, Lord"</note> or end with this formula, or both begin and end with it. Concerning such **Praises, or Blessings** <note>original Hebrew: "Berachot"</note>, we have already noted that a treatise by Maimonides exists, and much on the same subject is found in the Talmudic Code. 

Furthermore, it should be observed that the Jews consider themselves bound to recite at least *one hundred* such Praises or Blessings every day. If you wish to find how they extract this obligation to recite *one hundred* daily blessings from the Scriptures of the Old Testament, you will find it in the chapter of the *Kol Bo* <note>A 13th/14th-century legal compendium of Jewish law.</note> which begins this subject of the One Hundred Blessings. 

<margin>
Toward the end of chapter 10. *Orach Chayim, Hilchot Berachot* chapter 46, § 3.
</margin>

You may read these laws in Buxtorf himself. Let us now further observe the truth of this matter:

**1.** *These One Hundred Blessings are NOT recited* **TWICE** *daily by them, but rather* **ONCE** *throughout the space of a nychthemeron* <note>The Greek term "νυχθήμερον" refers to a full 24-hour period (a night and a day).</note>.

<margin>
page 228.
</margin>

It is expressly stated in the *Shulchan Aruch* <note>The "Set Table," the most authoritative code of Jewish law.</note>: **It is necessary for every man to recite at least one hundred blessings every day.** And Buxtorf himself, at the end of the chapter on these One Hundred Blessings, subjoins certain things which imply that they should recite *these One Hundred Blessings or Thanksgivings* **DAILY**, etc.

**2.** *There is no single "Formula" for the One Hundred Blessings.* <note>Meaning it is a total count of various blessings said throughout the day, not one long prayer titled "The Hundred Blessings."</note>

### CHAPTER 16. IN THE SYNAGOGUE. 1065

They do not recite them IN A CONTINUOUS ORDER in the Synagogues, as it seems should be gathered from Buxtorf, but the Precept of the ONE HUNDRED BLESSINGS is satisfied by them in this manner: that all the Blessings, which they pour out to God throughout the whole day in various circumstances (including those eighteen standard <term>Eulogies <note>The "Eighteen Benedictions" or *Amidah*, the central standing prayer of Jewish liturgy.</note></term> in this number) all those Eulogies, I say, taken together, complete the number of one hundred.

Every Jew must take care, according to the Statutes of the Nation, to pronounce at least *One Hundred Eulogies* throughout the entire <term>night and day <note>original Greek: νυχθήμερον (nuchthēmeron)</note></term>; in which number the Eulogies of the Eighteen Prayers repeated three times, the Eulogies of the <term>Shema <note>The central declaration of Jewish faith: "Hear, O Israel..."</note></term>, and the Blessings of the Table are included; not indeed as if those *One Hundred Eulogies* were recited in a continuous order, and contained within a single Formula. Let us understand the whole matter from Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal scholar.</note>:

<margin>Laws of Prayer, etc. chapter 7, § 7.</margin>
<note>The following is a translation of the Hebrew text from Maimonides' Mishneh Torah:</note>
A man is obligated to say one hundred blessings between the day and the night. And what are these hundred blessings? They are the twenty-three blessings we have counted in this chapter, and the seven blessings of the Recitation of the Shema in the morning and evening, before it and after it. And when he wraps himself in the **Tzitzit** <note>Ritual fringes or tassels</note>, he blesses: "Blessed are You, Lord, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to wrap ourselves in Tzitzit." And when he puts on **Phylacteries** <note>Tefillin; small leather boxes containing Torah verses worn during prayer</note>, he blesses: "Blessed are You, Lord, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to put on Phylacteries." And the three prayers [daily services], in each of which are eighteen blessings, which makes eighty-six blessings. And when he eats two meals of the day and night, he blesses fourteen blessings, seven at each meal: when he washes his hands first, and one over the food at the start, and three at the end, and over the wine before it and after it; behold, seven blessings. Behold, there are one hundred blessings in total.

*Every person is obligated to pronounce one hundred Blessings between the day and the night. And what are those one hundred Blessings? Twenty-three Blessings, which we have recounted in this Chapter; Seven Blessings of the Shema, morning and evening, which must be placed before and after it. To which is added the Blessing to be recited when someone puts on the* **Tzitzith** <note>original: Tzitzith</note>: *(The garment from which the legal* <term>fringes <note>original Greek: κράσπεδα (kraspeda)</note></term> *hang) Praise to you, Lord, our God, King of the World, who has sanctified us by your precepts, and commanded us to clothe ourselves in Tzitzith; And when he puts on the Phylacteries, he says: B. T. S. D. D. N. R. M.* <note>Abbreviation for: Blessed be Thou, Lord our God, King of the World</note> *who has sanctified us by your precepts, and commanded us to wear Phylacteries. # ON THE RITUAL OF PRAYER Book I

1066

here you have the Blessings; and in total ONE HUNDRED blessings, which the Jews wish to be recited daily. Since the <term>Prayer against Apostates <note>The *Birkat HaMinim*, an additional blessing added to the original eighteen of the *Amidah* prayer to exclude heretics and sectarian groups.</note></term> has been added to the <term>Eighteen <note>The *Shemoneh Esrei*, or the "Eighteen" benedictions, the central standing prayer of the Jewish liturgy.</note></term>, and the Blessings of the Table <note>The *Birkat Hamazon*, or Grace after Meals.</note> have been added, <term>Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and legal codifier.</note></term> says the Daily Blessings have increased to ninety-five. On other days, however—such as the Sabbath or Festivals—the full Eighteen are not recited, but rather seven Blessings (as explained in the previous sections); or even when it is not appropriate for someone to recite all the Blessings, Maimonides states that he ought to observe other occasions for praising God to compensate for this deficiency, so that throughout the whole day until evening he is bound to the duty of reciting One Hundred Blessings.

From this, it is clear how the matter stands with the daily Task of Blessings. Therefore, what <term>Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf the Elder (1564–1629), a famous Christian Hebraist who documented Jewish customs in his work *Synagoga Judaica*.</note></term> reports concerning the recitation of the One Hundred Blessings can only be understood as referring to those twenty-three blessings which the Jews consider themselves obligated to recite privately in addition to the Eighteen, examples of which you will find in Maimonides at the beginning of this Chapter and in Buxtorf. * But as for the fact that these Blessings are recited by some in the Synagogues (which is certain from many sources), Maimonides notes this and desires that each of those Blessings be recited in the Synagogue, but at its own place and time, when one enjoys the specific benefit for which he gives thanks to God. Anyone will realize that this is consistent with reason. For example: a Jew about to settle for sleep was required to give thanks to God, because through His wonderful Providence He provided sleep to the weary for the restoration of strength; upon waking from sleep, praise was to be attributed to God for the soul preserved while the body was overwhelmed by sleep; for the understanding granted to the <term>Rooster <note>original: *Gallo Gallinaceo*. This refers to the blessing *Hanoten lasechvi binah*, "Who gives the heart (or rooster) understanding to distinguish between day and night."</note></term> to distinguish the night; for getting up from bed, dressing, washing, and the functions of nature—

---

\* Among those are also these: <note>original Hebrew: אלהינו מלך העולם שלא עשאני גוי, עשאני גוי בא"י אמ' ה' שלא עשאני עבד</note> "Blessed art Thou, Lord our God, King of the universe, who did not make me a Gentile," and "Blessed art Thou, Lord our God, King of the universe, who did not make me a slave"; which Buxtorf, by error, assigned to the Eighteen Blessings, from which <term>Shilo <note>Likely referring to the work *Shene Luchot HaBerit* (The Two Tablets of the Covenant) by Isaiah Horowitz, often called "The Shelah."</note></term> distinguishes them in Book 5, chapter 2, § 352. ...fulfilling it in his own way, Formulas of Thanksgiving had to be recited that were appropriate to these benefits. Examples of these formulas are found in <term>Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a pivotal Jewish scholar; the author refers to his legal code, the *Mishneh Torah*.</note></term> and the Liturgies, and from them, in <term>Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, a 17th-century Christian scholar of Hebrew traditions.</note></term>. But reason entirely suggests that these Blessings should not be recited in one continuous series in the Synagogue. Instead, the Divine goodness should be praised through them at the specific time and occasion when the benefit is actually enjoyed. When that benefit is not received, it is contrary to reason to give thanks for it. For example, one who is without clothes and has none to put on cannot be bound to praise Divine grace for granted garments. One who does not hear the <term>cock-crow <note>Latin: *gallicinium*. This refers to the blessing *Birkat HaSechvi*, thanking God for giving the rooster/heart the ability to distinguish between day and night.</note></term>, or who spends a sleepless night, gives thanks to God for these benefits at an improper time. However, in this case, the judgment of Maimonides will carry more weight than my own. Hear, therefore, his words concerning these shorter *Formulas of Blessing*, which are recited daily both to complete the number of one hundred *Blessings* and as a duty according to Jewish discipline:

*In many of our cities, it is the custom to recite these blessings one after another in the synagogue, whether they have been obligated to them by receiving the benefit or not. *In what order every Israelite ought to establish and direct his Daily Prayers*, according to the customs widely received among Israelites, is indeed explicitly handed down by Maimonides at the end of *Chapter VII of the Treatise on Prayers; and in the Order of Prayers for the Whole Year.* However, of which prayers the Public Liturgy consists, and in what order they are recited, he declares in *Chapter Nine of the same Treatise.* Since these things illustrate one another, they must be sought from there and compared, at which point everything will become clear and easy.

α. <note>original Hebrew: "Ba-shachar mashkim adam u-mevarekh berakhot elu"</note> *In the morning hours a person rises and praises God with those formulas of blessing which we have reviewed in this chapter.*

These are indeed the very *Formulas of Blessing* <note>Latin: *Eulogiarum*, meaning words of praise or blessings</note> of which we have just treated. Through them, thanks are given to God for *Washing*; for the *Benefit of Nature* <note>This refers to the *Asher Yatzar* blessing, which thanks God for the proper functioning of the human body and its ability to expel waste.</note>, by which the body is fit to discharge excrement; *For the Law* <note>The Torah</note> and its study, which is joined with a prayer on that same subject; *For the Benefit of the Cock-crow* <note>The blessing *Birkat HaSechvi*, thanking God for giving the rooster (or the heart) the ability to distinguish between day and night.</note>; *For the privilege of being born an Israelite*, etc. However, according to what we have just seen from Maimonides, it is better to recite these little blessings individually at their proper times and occasions rather than in a continuous series in the Synagogue.

β. <note>original Hebrew: "Ve-kore ha-zemirot u-mevarekh lifnehem ve-acharehem"</note> *And he reads certain excerpts from the Psalms of David, to which reading he prefixes and appends a blessing.*

In these few words, <term>Maimonides <note>A 12th-century philosopher and jurist who codified Jewish law.</note></term> encompasses all the prayers to be recited before the <term>Shema <note>The central declaration of Jewish faith: "Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one."</note></term>, and he refers them to the *Reading*, or the *Chanting of Excerpts from the Psalms of David*, and the *two blessings*, the first of which is to be prefixed to that meditation, and the second to follow it. These excerpts from the Psalms of David are commonly called <term>Pesukei d’Zimra <note>original Hebrew: "psukei de-zimrot," literally meaning "Verses of Song."</note></term>, because they are truly segments, or rather certain fragments of Scriptural hymns or Davidic Psalms. These can be seen in the Liturgies after the blessing: <term>Baruch She-amar <note>Hebrew: "Blessed be He who spoke." This prayer acts as the opening blessing for the "Verses of Song" section.</note></term>; about which we shall speak soon. Moreover, these excerpts or segments of Psalms are not recited the same in all Synagogues; for here the customs of the Synagogues vary, and a great deal of liberty is granted to everyone according to the requirements of the time. In one of my Liturgies, the first fragment is composed of *1 Chronicles 16:8-37; Psalms 99:5, 9; 78:38; 40:12; 25:6; 68:35, 36;* etc. <term>Leon of Modena <note>original: "Leo Mutinensis," a famous 17th-century Venetian rabbi and scholar.</note></term> says that among the others, the last ones of the Book of Psalms starting from *Psalm 145* are especially sung, which begin with <term>Hallelujah <note>Hebrew: "Praise Yah/God."</note></term>. Maimonides, in his "Order of Prayers for the Whole Year," notes *Psalm 104:31* etc. and *146:5* until the end of the Psalms. Also *1 Chronicles 16:36 and 29:10* etc. These fragments of Davidic hymns consist of celebrations of the Divine virtues and perfections; and, as much as any other parts of the Scriptures, they are suited to awaken in our souls a profound veneratio— <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "venerationem" (veneration).</note>

This Prayer comes to be noted by us specifically because the Jewish character is perceived more clearly from no other prayer than from this very one. Its first part contains what seems to be a most absolute denial of one's own righteousness before the Lord, and it is excellent and to be praised on that account; but the latter part, as if correcting what they might have seemed to confess too liberally, exaggerates the privilege of *birth and the merit of the Fathers*. <note>This refers to the concept of *Zechut Avot*, the idea that the righteousness of ancestors like Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob benefits their descendants.</note> No one who has read the Gospels and Paul's Epistles to the Romans and Philippians is ignorant that these are placed by the Jews among the foundations of *their righteousness* before God.

<meta>This page continues the detailed analysis of the Jewish morning liturgy as described by Maimonides. ### CHAPTER 16. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.

$\gamma$. **And he reads the *Shema* and says the blessings before and after it.** *He reads the Shema and blesses before and after it.*

After the formula *Yishtabach* <gloss>May Your name be praised</gloss>, there followed the recitation of the *Shema* <note>The central declaration of Jewish faith: "Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is One."</note>, along with the blessings described in the previous chapter. There is no difficulty in this, except for what we will note hereafter regarding the variations in the recitation of the blessing *Yotzer Or* <gloss>Creator of Light</gloss> in public and private worship. Anyone who has examined the Jewish liturgy will see that the Jews have inserted these words—**Hear, O Israel** <note>original Hebrew: *Shema Yisrael*</note>—into various prayers. In these, they profess both the unity and the kingdom of God; undoubtedly, they use these very formulas to strengthen themselves against Christians, who worship their *Savior* as *God and King* along with the *Father*. Thus, you will find these words in the prayer *Ribbon* <gloss>Master of the World</gloss>, which we just mentioned, and the *Excerpts from the Psalms of David* in the German Jewish liturgy conclude with them. However, when the Jewish authorities speak of the **Recitation of the Shema** <note>original Hebrew: *Kiryat Shema*</note>, one must understand it as that formal, solemn recitation discussed in the preceding chapter.

$\delta$. **And he skips the Sanctification from the first blessing before it, because an individual does not say the Sanctification.** *And he bypasses the Sanctification of the Name of God, which is found in the first blessing of the Shema, "Yotzer Or," because a private individual is not permitted to recite it.*

The first blessing of the *Shema*, called *Yotzer Or* <gloss>Creator of Light</gloss>, contains the **Sanctification** <note>original Hebrew: *Kedushah*; a prayer describing the angels praising God</note>, which is the formal declaration and proclamation of God's holiness. Since the Jews believe this *Sanctification* of the Divine Name should not be celebrated except in a *Congregation* <note>original Latin: *Cætu*</note> consisting of at least ten men, Maimonides <note>The influential 12th-century scholar also known as Rambam</note> requires that the part of the first blessing containing that *Sanctification* be omitted by a private individual reciting the *Shema*. Yet, not all the Doctors of Law agree on this point. We shall discuss this further when we explain the act of the **Blessing over the Shema** <note>original Hebrew: *Perisat Shema*</note>.

$\epsilon$. **And as soon as he concludes the blessing "Who redeemed Israel," he should immediately stand so that he may join the redemption to the Prayer, and he prays while standing as we have said.** *And immediately after he has spoken the conclusion of the final blessing of the Shema, "Gaal Israel," let him rise, so that he may join the redemption to the Prayers; and let him pray standing, as we have advised should be done.*

The "seal" or concluding formula of the third morning blessing of the *Shema* is: *Blessed are You, [O Lord,] who redeemed Israel* <note>original Hebrew: *Baruch Atta Goel Israel*</note>; its theme is the memory of the Redemption <note>Referring to the Exodus from Egypt and the hope for future deliverance</note>.

*Formulas of Supplication and Deprecation* of this kind are found in various places in the liturgies. In these, using the most humble words, they seek from God the remission of sins, liberation from the evils of their present state, the restoration of the Commonwealth <note>original Latin: *Reipublicae*, referring here to the Jewish national state</note>, and every grace by which they might conform themselves to the Divine will in word, deed, and work. In one of these, I found again a frank denial of one's own righteousness before God, which I believe is worth noting: *O Lord, save! O King, answer us in the time when we implore Your help. Our Father, our King, grant us grace and answer us, because* WITHIN US THERE ARE NO DEEDS OF RIGHTEOUSNESS. *Act with us for the sake of Your name.* Furthermore, there is that frank confession that *Jerusalem* was laid waste because of the grave crimes of the nation: *Pray, turn back Your anger and Your wrath from Your city Jerusalem, Your holy mountain, because due to our sins and the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem and Your people have become a reproach to all the surrounding nations.* Regarding these *Supplications* and *Deprecations*, *Maimonides* wishes this bodily gesture to be observed: that the supplicant sits with his head inclined to the ground. This gesture of supplication is usually called by them *Qiddah* <note>meaning "bowing the head"</note>. Indeed, two bodily gestures for *Supplication* were accepted among the *Jews*: either for one to lie prostrate on the ground with hands and feet spread out, which is called *Hishtachavayah* <note>prostration</note>, or for one praying to incline and lower his head toward the earth, which is called *Qiddah*, from the root *qadad* <note>to bow or stoop</note>. *The entire Liturgy of Public Prayers, in the recitation of which the Legate of the Church <note>The *Sheliach Tzibbur*, or the official representative of the congregation who leads the service</note> solemnly leads the Synagogue gathering on both weekdays and festive days, is described from Maimonides <note>The 12th-century philosopher and jurist whose work codified much of Jewish law</note>, and is explained in its more difficult parts. ### CHAPTER 17. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.

We have seen which prayers every Israelite must recite daily, and in what order; at the same time, we advised that these should be recited in the Synagogue whenever the occasion allows. Now, therefore, we must further explain what we have already indicated in the preceding pages: that not all of these prayers and blessings constituted the **Public Liturgy**. That is to say, only some of them were customarily chanted by a **Public Official** <note>In Latin, *Persona Publica*, referring to the designated leader of the service</note> who was delegated for this task by the congregation. This is the role that Synagogue Ministers <note>Often referred to as the *Chazzan* or Cantor today</note> usually fulfill now.

<margin>Megillah, chapter 4, section 5</margin>
From the Book of *Megillah* <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning the reading of the Scroll of Esther and communal worship</note>, one may clearly gather that the Public Liturgy of blessings and prayers consisted of only two acts: **READING THE SHEMA WITH ITS BLESSINGS**, and **RECITING THE "EIGHTEEN" BEFORE THE ARK**. The former was called <term>פרוס על שמע</term> <gloss>to spread [the blessings] over the Shema</gloss>, or **TO BLESS OVER THE SHEMA**, and the latter: <term>עבור לפני התיבה</term> <gloss>to pass before the Ark</gloss>, or **TO STEP FORWARD BEFORE THE ARK**. To perform these acts, different persons were often delegated by the *Prefect* or *Prefects* <note>The *Parnassim* or synagogue leaders</note> of the Synagogue, as you may very clearly gather from that same Book of *Megillah*.

<margin>Section 6</margin>
Even though the more recent Synagogue now entrusts those two sacred acts to a single **Synagogue Minister**, the Public Liturgy is even now almost entirely completed by the recitation of these formulas. For this reason, we described them in the preceding sections. To make this more fully and clearly established, it will be convenient to repeat the "Ministry of Public Prayers" from the same Maimonides <note>The influential 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note>, whom we have used diligently in other matters. I will provide his text and, where necessary, illustrate it as we have been doing. These matters are found in the **Ninth Chapter of the Treatise on Prayers**.

<margin>Maimonides, Laws of Prayer, chapter 9, section 1</margin>
> ($\alpha.$) *The Public Prayers are recited in this way and order. In the morning hours, ($\beta.$) while the entire synagogue assembly is sitting, the Minister of the Synagogue (the Legate of the Congregation) ($\gamma.$) proceeds before the Ark, and stands in the midst of the people, and begins the Liturgy, saying: ($\delta.$) **KADDISH**: and the whole people immediately responding antiphonally <note>original Greek: *antiphonon*</note> answers with all their might: **AMEN: MAY HIS GREAT NAME BE BLESSED FOREVER, AND TO ALL ETERNITY**: and they answer **AMEN** again at the end of the Kaddish. Afterward, they say: **BLESS THE LORD WHO IS BLESSED**, and they respond: **BLESSED BE THE LORD WHO IS BLESSED FOREVER AND EVER**. Then he begins and "spreads" <note>leads the blessings</note> over the Shema in a loud voice, and they answer **AMEN** after each and every blessing.*

# OF THE RITUAL OF PRAYER BOOK III

**Amen** is said at the end of the **Kaddish** <note>A central prayer in the Jewish liturgy focused on the sanctification of God's name</note> recited by the Synagogue Minister, who (*the Synagogue Minister*) then says: **Barechu**, etc. <gloss>Bless the Lord...</gloss> while the Synagogue congregation sings in response <note>original Greek: ἀνטיφωνικῶς, meaning antiphonally or in call-and-response</note>: **Blessed be the Lord, the Blessed One, for ever and ever**. From there, he (the Synagogue Minister) begins (α.) **to recite the Shema with its blessings in a loud voice**, with the Synagogue congregation responding **Amen** to each **Blessing**.

α. **Public Prayers**: Doxologies <note>Hymns of praise to God</note> and prayers, as we described their order in the previous chapter, can be recited by anyone who frequents the Synagogue, or even outside the Synagogue if one does not happen to be available, even without a large gathering. However, the name **Public Prayers** refers to that part of this **Liturgy** <note>The formal public worship service</note> which was recited by the Synagogue Minister before a group. These prayers, I say, were those chanted in the Synagogue by a group of at least **ten men** <note>A *minyan*, the minimum quorum required for certain religious obligations</note> led by a Public Official. The following distinction can be observed between **Public** and **Private Prayers**: 1. Not all the blessings recited in private are recited publicly; only a part of them are recited by the delegate of the assembly. 2. Certain blessings, such as the **Kaddish**, the **Barechu**, and the **Kedustha** <note>The *Kedushah*, a prayer sanctifying God's name based on Isaiah 6:3</note> (which we will discuss soon), combine to constitute the Public Blessing; it was not permitted for individual Israelites to recite these alone.

### CHAPTER 17. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.

it should be clear that the **Shema** <note>original: "Schema"; the central declaration of Jewish faith, "Hear, O Israel..."</note> itself, along with its **Blessings** <note>original: "Eulogiis"</note>, was subsequently accustomed to be recited before the **Ark** <note>The cabinet where Torah scrolls are kept</note>, and is thus included within this phrase when taken in its broader sense.

->AND HE BEGINS BY SAYING THE **KADDISH**.<-

The Minister of the Synagogue <note>Often referred to as the Chazzan or Cantor</note> therefore assumes that the Congregation has already recited the **Morning Blessings**, **Excerpts from the Psalms**, and the blessings **Baruch Sheamar** <gloss>Blessed be He who spoke</gloss> & **Yishtabach** <gloss>May Your name be praised</gloss>; and he properly begins the Public Liturgy with the Recitation of the **Shema**: to which, however, he precedes with the **Kaddish** formula, which we have presented in the preceding pages, which is to be placed before and after almost all sacred acts; and the **Barechu**, or *Bless the Lord who is to be blessed, etc.* These two formulas are to be considered as a kind of <term>protreptikon</term> <gloss>an invitation or exhortation</gloss> to the acts of public religion that follow. However, where prayers were offered by private individuals, these two exhortatory blessings, **Kaddish & Barechu**, were omitted, because it was not permitted to recite them without a Congregation of at least *ten men* <note>Known as a Minyan, the minimum number of adult males required for communal worship</note>. Private individuals, after the **Yishtabach**, proceeded immediately to recite the first **Blessing of the Shema**, which is called **Yotzer Or** <gloss>He who forms light</gloss>. In the **Colbo** <note>A significant medieval collection of Jewish laws and rituals</note> the beginning of the **Public Liturgy** is traced from the **Yishtabach**: <margin>Chapter 5. regarding the rule of Yishtabach</margin> **And the Minister of the Synagogue stands and wraps himself in the sacred fringes and blesses the Lord, King of the Universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to wrap ourselves in the garment with fringes: and** HE PROCEEDS BEFORE THE ARK, and ordains the PUBLIC LITURGY with **YISTABBEACH**, or *MAY YOUR NAME BE PRAISED forever, O our King, etc.* After the **Yishtabach**, however, according to the **Colbo**, he finally recites the **Kaddish**: **And after the Yishtabach the Minister opens with the Kaddish.** <margin>Chapter 6.</margin>

And after the **Yishtabach** the Minister of the Synagogue recites the **KADDISH**. The **Kaddish** is, as I have said, that most holy formula of prayer which was recited at the beginning and end of any sacred acts—and perhaps the most ancient of all the prayers which the Synagogue of this time possesses. It is composed in <term>Chaldaic</term> <note>Aramaic, the common language of the Near East in late antiquity</note> so that it might be understood by the common people, who were ignorant of the Hebrew language, and even by the Gentiles <note>non-Jews</note> themselves who were skilled in the Syrian tongue, so that all might perceive from it the hope of the Jews concerning the future **Sanctification & Glorification of the Divine Name** throughout the world. This is read in the <margin>Chapter 7. regarding the rule of Kaddish.</margin> **Colbo**, where many other things concerning this **Formula** are contained. But since other things are said...

$\delta.$ AND HE BEGINS BY SAYING
->KADDISH.<- <note>original: "Kaddisch"; a prayer magnifying and sanctifying God’s name</note>

The Synagogue Minister <note>The *Hazzan* or Cantor</note> therefore assumes that the Morning Blessings, excerpts from the Psalms, and the blessings *Baruch She’amar* <note>"Blessed is He who spoke"</note> and *Yishtabach* <note>"May [Your name] be praised"</note> have already been recited by the congregation. He properly begins the Public Liturgy with the Recitation of the **Shema** <note>The central confession of Jewish faith: "Hear, O Israel..."</note>; however, he precedes this with the formula of the **Kaddish**, which we presented in the preceding pages, and which is to be placed before and after almost all sacred acts. He also includes the **Barechu**, or *Bless the Lord who is worthy of Blessing*, etc. These two formulas are to be considered as a kind of <term>protrepticon</term> <gloss>a formal call or invitation</gloss> to the acts of public religion that follow. However, when prayers were offered by individuals in private, these two introductory blessings—the *Kaddish* and *Barechu*—were omitted, because it was not permitted to recite them without a congregation of at least **ten men** <note>The *Minyan*, or required quorum for communal prayer</note>. Private individuals, after the *Yishtabach* prayer, proceeded immediately to recite the first blessing of the Shema, which is called *Yotzer Or* <note>"Who forms light"</note>. In the *Kol Bo* <note>A 14th-century Hebrew legal code regarding Jewish ritual</note>, the beginning of the Public Liturgy is traced from *Yishtabach*:
<margin>Chapter 5, in "The Law of Yishtabach"</margin>
**And the Cantor stands and wraps himself in the fringes and blesses: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to wrap ourselves in the fringes." And he goes down before the Ark and opens with: "May Your name be praised forever, our King," etc.** The Synagogue Minister stands on his feet, puts on the Sacred Garment <note>The *Tallit* or prayer shawl</note>, and praises God with the customary formula: *Blessed are You, Lord of the World, who has sanctified us with Your commandments and commanded us to put on the garment with fringes:* and HE PROCEEDS BEFORE THE ARK, and begins the Public Liturgy with **YISHTABACH**, or MAY YOUR NAME BE PRAISED forever, O our King, etc. Moreover, according to the *Kol Bo*, it is only after *Yishtabach* that he recites the *Kaddish*:
<margin>Chapter 6.</margin>
**And after Yishtabach, the Cantor begins the Kaddish.**
*And after Yishtabach, the Synagogue Minister recites the KADDISH.* The *Kaddish* is, as I have said, that most holy formula of prayer which was recited at the beginning and end of every sacred act. It is perhaps the most ancient of all the prayers that the Synagogue possesses today. It was composed in <term>Chaldaic</term> <gloss>Aramaic</gloss> so that it might be understood by the common people, who were ignorant of the Hebrew language, and even by the Gentiles <note>Non-Jewish neighbors</note> who were skilled in <term>Syriac</term> <gloss>a dialect of Aramaic</gloss>. Thus, everyone might understand from it the hope of the Jews concerning the future *Sanctification and Glorification of the Divine Name* throughout the world. So it is read in the
<margin>Chapter 7, in "The Law of Kaddish"</margin>
*Kol Bo*, where many other things are found concerning this formula. But since other things are to be sa—

<margin>Chapter 18.</margin>In the preceding sections, we presented some part of this formula:
**ומתחיל ופורס על שמע**, *And he begins and from there divides over the Shema* <note>original: "Incipitque dehinc SCHEMAM cum Eulogiis ejus"</note>. We translate this phrase as **Reciting the Shema with its Blessings**, because it is most clearly evident from the context that by *dividing over the Shema* <note>original: "pores al Shema"</note> is meant here the **Recitation of it with its Blessings**. For he adds that the Congregation responds **Amen** <note>The communal affirmation</note> to each one. Since, however, neither the Hebrew authors all agree on the exposition of this phrase, nor do the scholars among Christians who hesitate here, it will be worthwhile to investigate the true sense of this expression.

<margin>
Regarding the word *paras* [to divide].

</margin>**Buxtorf** <note>Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, a famous 17th-century Christian Hebraist</note> in his *Greater Lexicon* regarding the explanation of the phrase *pores al Shema*, wrote these words: *Among the Rabbis, "he who comes and divides over the Shema" means **He who dismisses the People in the Reading of the Prayers**, or **divides the Reading of the Shema**.* He also cites: *They do not divide over the Shema.* He continues: *The Reading of the Shema is the text from Deuteronomy 6:4, which the Jews recite every day in their morning and evening prayers; to divide it means they ought to recite only half.* Although the most learned Buxtorf explained *pores al Shema* as *To Divide*, and in this he followed **Jarchius** <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator</note> and **Bartenora** <note>Rabbi Obadiah of Bertinoro, a 15th-century commentator on the Mishnah</note>; he by no means reached the sense which those famous Doctors intended by this explanation. For what Buxtorf says—that it is not permitted to "halve" the **Shema**, that is, to recite only half the text of Deuteronomy—as if that were suggested by the words of the **Megillah** <note>The Talmudic tractate regarding the scroll of Esther and public readings</note> *They do not divide the Shema*, is entirely beside the point. If **Dividing the Shema** is interpreted as Janchius <note>Rashi</note> and Bartenora do, it was actually permitted for Jews to "Divide the Shema," because the **Division of the Shema** (in the sense the Jews understand it) was considered a **Sacred Religious Act**, which was celebrated with great ceremony. This fact could have been established by the illustrious gentleman from the very passage of the Megillah which he himself cited: *He who reads the Prophets, he it is who Divides the Shema.* Therefore, it was necessary to *Divide the Shema* in the manner the Jews did in their Sacred Acts, which they interpret through this "Division." If, however, one understands the "Division of the Shema" as a "half-recitation" of the text of Deuteronomy 6:4, it is certain that such a halving of the Shema never existed in their practice. Doubtless, the cause of this error for the illustrious gentleman...

# CHAPTER 17. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.

...because, with a hasty eye, he took a part of a sentence from the *Megillah* <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning the festival of Purim and synagogue readings</note> for the whole, which reads as follows: **They do not divide the Shema with fewer than ten** <note>original Hebrew: *Ein porsin al Shema pahot me-asarah*</note>. From this, it is so far from being a prohibited action that it is instead restricted to a Gathering of Ten men as something most sacred. Therefore, this famous scholar did not grasp the mind of **Jarchi** <note>Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), a premier medieval commentator</note> and **Bartenora** <note>Obadiah ben Abraham of Bertinoro (c. 1445–1515), a famous commentator on the Mishnah</note> when they explained **dividing the Shema** <note>original: *pores al Shema*</note> as a "Division of the Shema." Jarchi, Bartenora, and others understood the "Division of the Shema" as a Sacred Act of Religion, by which someone recites the **Kaddish** <note>A prayer of praise and sanctification</note>, the **Barechu** <note>The call to prayer</note>, and the **first blessing, *Yotzer Or*** <note>The blessing "Who creates light," which precedes the Shema</note>. It was not permitted for a private individual to recite the *Kaddish* or *Barechu*, nor even, according to these Teachers, a large part of the first blessing of the Shema, *Yotzer Or*, because it was considered to contain the **Sanctification of the Divine Name** <note>The *Kedushah*, a central part of Jewish liturgy declaring God's holiness</note>. However, since Israelites were bound to the public Sanctification of the Divine Name, if they could form a Gathering of Ten men anywhere, then—even if they had already recited the other blessings privately—they would delegate someone from the Gathering to recite the Formulas of the *Kaddish*, *Barechu*, and *Yotzer Or*. Whoever recited these blessings was said, according to Jarchi and Bartenora, **to divide the Shema**, because he separated the first blessing of the Shema, *Yotzer Or*, from the others and from the Shema itself.

This is still the custom among the Jews today: if any Jews come into the Synagogue after the Shema and the **Eighteen** <note>The *Amidah*, the central standing prayer of eighteen (now nineteen) blessings</note> have already been recited in the solemn public rites of the Synagogue (whether they were hindered by business and troubles, or time escaped them through negligence), if they can make up the number of ten, they designate someone from their company to act as the **Messenger of the Congregation** <note>original: *Legati Ecclesiæ*, equivalent to the Hebrew *Shaliach Tzibbur*</note> and lead the others in reciting the blessings of *Kaddish*, *Barechu*, and the first blessing *Yotzer Or*, as well as the Sanctification of the Divine Name found in the Eighteen. Since he separates the first blessing of the Shema, *Yotzer Or*, from the rest, he is said by those Authors **to divide the Shema**. We long ago uncovered this meaning from **R. Karo** <note>Joseph Karo (1488–1575), author of the *Shulchan Aruch*, the foundational code of Jewish law</note>, whose testimony, previously cited on this matter, we have repeated above; one may also recognize the same from Jarchi and Bartenora themselves. Bartenora: <margin>To Megillah chapter 4. section 3.</margin> **"They do not divide the Shema": ten who have come to the synagogue after the congregation has already read the Shema; one stands and says Kaddish and Barechu and the first blessing before the reading of the Shema; they "divide," a term for a "piece," meaning half of a thing from the two blessings before the reading of the Shema,** *They do not divide over the Shema; ten where*

# ON THE RITE OF PRAYER BOOK III. PART II.

...they come into the Synagogue after the Synagogue Congregation has already recited the **Shema** <note>The central prayer of Jewish faith: "Hear, O Israel..."</note> with its **blessings** <note>original Latin: *Eulogiis*; the traditional prayers surrounding the Shema</note>. One from their number stands up and says the **KADDISH** <note>A prayer of sanctification and praise</note>, the **BARECHU** <note>The formal call to prayer</note>, and the **FIRST BLESSING**, which is usually recited before the Shema. Therefore, the word <term>Porsin</term> <note>original Hebrew: פורסן, from the root meaning to break or divide</note> is to be explained in the sense of Division and Halving: for out of the two blessings that are usually set before the Shema, he recites only one blessing.

<margin>
See Wagenf. on the Excerpts of the Gemara Sotah, chapter 5, page 616, and Lund's Commentary on Taanith, chapter 1, section 2.
</margin>

And some Christian scholars have also followed this way of explaining this phrase. However, I seriously doubt whether even these famous interpreters of the Talmud have fully satisfied the matter here. For certainly the verb <term>Paras</term> <note>original Hebrew: פרס</note>, when constructed with the preposition <term>al</term> <note>original Hebrew: על, meaning 'upon' or 'over'</note>, does not, as far as I know, mean *to divide*. For that, it would need the prepositions <term>et</term> <note>Hebrew: את, the direct object marker</note> or <term>min</term> <note>Hebrew: מ, meaning 'from'</note>; yet even when constructed that way, it does not often, let alone always, enjoy the meaning of dividing. Furthermore, the expression <term>pores al Shema</term> <note>dividing over the Shema</note> is much more common than <term>pores et Shema</term> <note>dividing the Shema</note>. In the smaller edition of the **Mishnah** <note>The primary collection of Jewish oral law</note> printed in *Livorno*, it reads **they do not divide the Shema** <note>original Hebrew: *ein porsin et Shema*</note> in the first part of chapter 3 of the tractate *Megillah*, section 3. But then in section 5, it immediately says **the one who concludes with the Prophet is the one who divides over the Shema** <note>original Hebrew: *ha-maftir ba-navi hu pores al Shema*</note>. Section 6 says the same: **a minor reads from the Torah and translates, but he does not divide over the Shema**, and so it continues in the following sections. Yet in that very first place where this smaller edition has *et Shema*, the most corrected edition of the entire *Talmud* printed in *Amsterdam* (folio 33, column 2) has **over the Shema** <note>original Hebrew: *al Shema*</note>, which is also repeated in all the notes. This is also how the *Venice* edition has it, according to which this whole work was arranged. In the Amsterdam edition of the Mishnah with the notes of **Jarchi** <note>Rashi</note>, **Bartenora**, etc., this first passage does indeed contain *et*, but in the margin it is written that other manuscripts read *al*. Indeed, in the **Jerusalem Talmud**, in the last chapter of the tractate *Megillah*, section 4, where that first passage is repeated just as it is in the **Babylonian Talmud**, it clearly has **over the Shema** <note>*al Shema*</note>, although I admit that in the following paragraphs *et* is used a few times. While this does not contradict the explanation of this phrase <note>original Greek: Φράσεως</note> which we are about to bring forward, it should be known that the confusion arose because the Hebrew writers themselves wavered in its genuine explanation.

<margin>
Chapter 14, section 8.
</margin>

However, in the tractate **Sopherim** <note>A minor tractate of the Talmud concerning the rules for scribes and public ritual</note>, it is **over the Shema** <note>*al Shema*</note>. Furthermore, I would also like this to be observed: that the *Act* of **dividing over the Shema** is mentioned in the tractate *Megillah* as an *ordinary act of religion*, which is usually performed in the sacred services of the Synagogue just like the *reading of the Law and the Prophets*. But if **dividing over the Shema** were what Jarchi and Bartenora claim, it would be anything but an ordinary act of religion. For such a *halving of the Shema* as they describe was never...

### BOOK II: ON THE RITUAL OF PRAYER

Private individuals were not permitted to chant the **Blessings** in that form. <margin>Private [prayer].</margin> Regarding the fact that one ought not to recite the **Kaddish** <note>A prayer of praise and mourning that requires a quorum of ten</note> and **Barechu** <note>The call to prayer, literally "Bless ye"</note> when alone, because they contain the **Sanctification of the Divine Name**, for the proper performance of which a gathering of ten men <note>A Minyan</note> is required by the Masters, all necessarily agree according to the Rule. But regarding the Blessing **Jotzer Or** <note>original: *Jotzer Oor*; the first blessing before the Shema in the morning, meaning "Creator of Light"</note> the opinions of various men differ. **Maimonides** <note>The 12th-century scholar Moses Maimonides</note> indeed explicitly writes that for a private person reciting it, that part of the Blessing <insert>which</insert> contains the **Sanctification of the Divine Name** must be omitted; that is, the **Declaration of the Holiness of God through the words of Isaiah** chapter 6, verse 2. We can easily assume this from the Formula of that Blessing shown above. <margin>Chapter 7, § 17.</margin> Thus Maimonides expressly [states] in describing the Liturgy: <gloss>original Hebrew: וזה מן הברכה ראשונה שלפניה שאין היחיד אומ' קדושה; translation: "And this is from the first blessing before it, that the individual does not say the Kedushah."</gloss> *He passes over (when reciting the **Shema**) the Declaration of God's Holiness, which is contained in the first Blessing of the **Shema**, because it is not permitted to utter the Formulas of Blessings by which the solemn Declaration of God's Holiness is comprised.* You will see that a contrary and more widely accepted opinion is found in the **Observations** [of others], the **Colbo** <note>A medieval compendium of Jewish laws and customs</note>, <margin>* On Megillah chapter 4, § 3. † Chapter 8.</margin> **Yom Tov** <note>Refers to Rabbi Yom Tov of Seville, a 14th-century commentator</note>, and others. † **Colbo**: <gloss>original Hebrew: שה של יוצר בא לציון שהוא סדר קדושה כתב הרב ר' יונה ז"ל שנחלקו בהם הגאונים וכו'; translation: "Regarding the Sanctification in *Jotzer* and *Uva Letzion*, which is the order of the Kedushah, Rabbi Jonah of blessed memory wrote that the Geonim [heads of the academies] differed over them, etc."</gloss> <margin>† Chapter 8.</margin> *But as for what pertains to the Declaration of the Holiness of God, which occurs in the Formula of **Jotzer Or** and **Uva Letzion** (this Blessing is the second to last among the morning prayers, and precedes the one called **Alenu Leshabbeach**) in which the solemn Celebration of Divine Holiness especially stands out, Rabbi Jonah [Gerondi] of blessed memory says that the opinions of the excellent Doctors vary here, whether it is permitted for a private individual to recite it or not. There are those who say these Blessings are among the number of those in which the Name of God is solemnly Sanctified, and therefore are not to be recited without a Gathering of Ten men; and they wish that whenever a private Israelite reciting this Blessing reaches the words:* **they say in fear** <note>original Hebrew: אומרים ביראה; part of the liturgy describing the angels' praise</note>, *he should skip that solemn Declaration of the Holiness of God from the words of Isaiah which follow those words, so that he may begin again with the words* **To the Blessed God** <note>original Hebrew: לאל ברוך (*Leeel Baruch*)</note>; *and likewise that a private Israelite should skip the Declaration of the Holiness of God through Isaiah, which is found in the Blessing: **Uva Letzion**. But the most celebrated Doctors of the **Geonim** <note>The leaders of the Babylonian academies, roughly 6th-11th centuries</note> and many others go in a different direction here, judging that a Private individual can certainly recite these entire Blessings with the declaration of the Holiness of God that exists in them, because those Blessings only contain a narration of how the Name of God is Sanctified by the Angels, the servants of God: And thus certainly the Blessing **Uva Letzion** only—*

<summary>This page discusses the debate among Jewish legal authorities (such as Maimonides and the Geonim) regarding whether a private individual may recite the 'Kedushah' or Sanctification of God's name when praying alone. While some argue these parts must be skipped without a quorum of ten, others contend they are permissible because they are merely a narrative description of angelic praise.</summary>

### CHAPTER 17. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.

it contains certain verses of Scripture, which we recite. And so **Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides, the 12th-century Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> himself wrote in his *Responses to Questions*; although in the *Book of Love* <note>original: *Libro Ahava*; the second book of Maimonides' code, the Mishneh Torah</note> (that is, in that very place which we just noted, which is in the *Laws of Prayer* <note>original: *Hilcoth Tephilla*</note>, which constitute part of the *Greater Treatise of Love*), he embraced the contrary opinion. This later opinion the Author confirms with the very words of the *Tractate Sopherim* <note>A minor tractate of the Talmud concerning the rules for scribes and liturgy</note>, by which a private person is granted the ability to recite that **Declaration of Sanctity** which is in the **Blessing of the Creator** <note>original: *Eulogia Jotzer*</note>, but is denied the ability to recite the **Declaration of God’s Sanctity** which is in the **third Petition of the Prayer of the Eighteen** <note>original: *Schemon-Efre*, also known as the Amidah</note>. This is because in this latter **Sanctification of the Divine Name**, which is in the *Eighteen Benedictions*, the **Israelites** themselves profess that they are Sanctifying the name of God. But in the Blessings of **The Creator of Light** and **And a Redeemer shall come to Zion** <note>original: *Jotzer Oor & Uva Letzion*</note>, they only narrate historically, through the words of **Isaiah**, that the **Angels Sanctify God**. Therefore, the fact that the first **Blessing of the Creator of Light** is recited by those who enter the Synagogue after the **Shema** <note>The central declaration of Jewish faith</note> has already been recited (assuming they have already privately performed the duty of narrating the other Blessings of the Shema) is a practice the Doctors trace back to this: when one of those ten men <note>the Minyan, or quorum</note> says after the **Kaddish**: <gloss>original Hebrew: ברכו; translation: "Bless ye the Lord who is blessed"</gloss>, it would be improper for the Assembly to celebrate God without a subsequent **Blessing**. For it would then seem as if they had turned their minds away from the Praise of the Divine Being and were denying God. Since, however, among the **Blessings** that follow the **Barechu**, the first is **The Creator of Light**, for this reason it is recited along with the **Barechu**.

<margin>See Yom Tov <note>likely Yom Tov ben Abraham Ishbili, a 14th-century commentator</note> on this place.</margin>
Indeed, it is certain that the Jewish Doctors, in the Recitation of the **Kaddish**, the **Barechu**, and **The Creator of Light** with their responses, primarily constitute that Act which they call **Dividing the Shema** <note>original: *Perysah al Schemah*; a communal liturgical practice for a quorum</note>. From this Act, therefore, the sacred rites of the Public Synagogue take their beginning: not in the sense that those Excerpts of the Psalms with their Blessings are not sometimes also sung by one person to be **answered in response** <note>original Greek: ἀντιφωνεῖσθαι</note> by many, but because that was neither done solemnly, nor was it necessary to be done, nor did those things constitute a necessary part of the daily Ministry of the **Emissary of the Congregation** <note>original: *Legati Ecclesiæ*, referring to the Shaliach Tzibbur or prayer leader</note>.

However, distinct from this **Dividing of the Shema** (the **Blessing over the Shema**) is another certain **Exposition** or **Extension** of the Shema, of which explicit mention is made in the *Tractate Sopherim*. Specifically, in the *Tractate Sopherim*, that very passage of the *Tractate Megillah* is explained, in which the duty of **Dividing the Shema** (the **Blessing over the Shema**) is claimed for the Reader of the Prophets. That Act of the Extension of the **Shema** is not explained there as the Recitation of the **Blessings of the Kaddish and the Creator**, but as the Celebration of the Divine Name,

# BOOK III. ON THE RITE OF PRAYER.

...so that it is understood as the **Blessing** <note>original: *Eulogia*</note> with which one blesses over the **Law** <note>the Torah</note>. And there is some difficulty in the text of the **Megillah** <note>a tractate of the Talmud concerning the reading of the Scroll of Esther and synagogue rites</note>, where the **Reader of the Prophets** is said to **Spread the Shema** <note>original Hebrew: *paros al shema* (פרוס על שמע)</note>, **Explain the Shema**, and **Step forward before [the Ark]**. For in the sacred rites of the Synagogue, the holy acts of reciting the **Shema** with its **Blessings** and **Praying** precede the rite of reading the **Law**; just as the acts of dividing the **Shema** [precede it]. For elsewhere it has been observed above that the [prayers], which consisted of the recitation of the Eighteen [Benedictions], are recited after the reading of the Prophets, and indeed before the Ark; just as the **Descending before the Ark** follows the reading of the Prophets.

How then can the task of **Blessing over the Shema** and **Stepping forward before the Ark** be assigned to the Reader of the Prophets, if **Blessing over the Shema** means to recite the **Shema with its blessings**, and **Stepping forward** means to pray? This reasoning compelled the author of the Tractate **Sopherim** <note>a minor tractate of the Talmud concerning scribes and liturgy</note> not to interpret the act of **Spreading the Shema** <note>original: *Perisa al Schema*</note> as the recitation of the **Shema** with its **Blessings**, but as the solemn celebration of the Divine Name, along with the recitation of the **Section** <note>original: *Pericopa*</note> "Hear [O Israel]" etc., at the end of the sacred rite of the

<margin>
Lightfoot, *Hebrew Hours* on Luke 4:16.
See Rabbi Jacob ben Asher, *Orach Chayim* chapter 284.
</margin>

**Law**. We also formerly followed the author of this tractate, as pointed out by Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot, a 17th-century English scholar of Hebrew and the Bible</note>. And because the same author of the tractate **Sopherim**, after declaring this rite of **Spreading the Shema**, describes the ceremony by which the **Book of the Law** is returned to the Ark amidst the cheers of the people, we therefore interpreted the act of **Stepping forward before the Ark** as the ceremony by which the **Book of the Law** was returned to the Ark. This was because we found no other procession before the Ark that followed the reading of the Law and the Prophets than this one, and because the author of the Tractate seemed clearly to lead us there.

However, I will explain how the later Talmudic interpreters resolve the difficulty of the text of the **Megillah**, in which the act of **Spreading the Shema** is placed after the act of **Reading the Law**. Specifically, they interpret the words "He who reads the Prophets, he blesses over the [Shema]" in this way: that he who is accustomed to read from the **Prophets** in the synagogue is also employed to perform the **Spreading of the Shema**, even though this latter act precedes the former in the sacred religious order. Because the act of **Reading from the Prophets** was considered very honorable, the Ruler of the Synagogue would entrust the act of **Spreading the [Shema]** to the person he had designated for the reading of the Prophets.

Regarding the Prophets, the Master <note>The commentator Bartenura</note> wrote: "He who is accustomed [to read] the Prophets," and this is also the phrasing of Rashi <note>A famous medieval French rabbi and commentator</note>, meaning "the one who is destined to read the Haftarah <note>the concluding reading from the Prophets</note>." Presumably, the "Spreading of the Shema" etc. occurs before they read from the Torah.

### CHAPTER 17. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.

<margin>
Regarding **Megillah** <note>a Talmudic tractate on the festival of Purim and synagogue readings</note> chapter 4, section 5.
* The Author alludes to the passage noted from the **Sopherim** <note>The Scribes, a minor tractate of the Talmud</note>.
</margin>
"Of the Prophets," etc. Rabbi Bartenora <note>Obadiah ben Abraham of Bertinoro, a famous 15th-century commentator</note> wrote that this should be understood regarding one who is accustomed to reading from the Prophets; this is the same as the interpretation of **Jarchi** <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator</note>. It is as if they were saying: *He who is about to read from the Prophets.* Indeed, the Rite of **Spreading the Shema** <note>original: *Perifat Schemæ*</note>, **WHICH IS SO CALLED EMPHATICALLY** <note>original Greek: *κατ’ ἔμϕασιν*</note>, precedes the Ceremony of the Reading of the Law. Let us therefore finally rest in these opinions of the Teachers, since nothing better is available to us. However, one unique point deserves notice: the Jews began their Public Sacred Rites with the Recitation of the **Shema**, or the **Section** <note>original: *Pericopæ*</note>: *Hear, O Israel, etc.* This was most prudently established by the ancient Doctors because that text of **Deuteronomy** <note>Deuteronomy 6:4</note> presents the sum of the whole Doctrine of the Jewish Religion, both Theoretical and Practical. The Theoretical part was comprised in the words: *The LORD our God: The LORD is One;* the Practical part in the following words: *And you shall love the LORD your God, etc.* Therefore, by reciting this text, they were making a confession of the entire Doctrine of their religion.

<margin>
Chapter 5, section 1.
</margin>
From the Tractate **Tamid** <note>a Talmudic book regarding the daily temple sacrifices</note> it is established that the Recitation of the **Ten Commandments** <note>original: *Decalogi*</note> preceded the Recitation of the **Shema** in the Temple Liturgy, since it is **the essence of the Law** <note>original Hebrew: *ikar ha-Torah* (עיקר התורה)</note>. Bartenora writes on that passage that the same custom prevailed in Synagogues outside of Jerusalem, but it seemed advisable to the Teachers to abstain from the Recitation of the Ten Commandments <margin>See the Jerusalem **Berachot** <note>the first tractate of the Talmud, on prayers</note>, folio 3, column 3, in **Lightfoot** regarding Luke 10:27.</margin> **because of the complaint of the Heretics, who say (or perhaps would say) that the Ten Commandments alone were given at Sinai, and not the rest of the Law** <note>original Hebrew: *mipnei tar’umot ha-minim...* (מפני תרעומת המיני׳ שהיו אומרים, אלו לבדם נתנו בסיני ולא שאר התורה)</note>. Without a doubt, Christians are understood here, who teach that the Law of the Ten Commandments is distinct in nature from the Law of Rituals in its Decrees. Otherwise, it is certain that the sum of the Ten Commandments, no less than the whole Mosaic Law, is contained in the **Shema** of Deuteronomy; so that there was no great necessity for reciting the Ten Commandments. Beyond the fact that the text of the **Shema** contains a compendium of the entire Doctrine of the Jewish Religion, the Ancient Jews believed more mystery lay beneath the words: **The LORD our God, the LORD is one** <note>original Hebrew: *Adonai Eloheinu Adonai Echad* (יהוה אלהינו יהוה אחד)</note>, than those words show at first glance. <margin>Zechariah 14, 9.</margin> They undoubtedly compared the words: *The LORD our God, the LORD is one,* with the saying of **Zechariah**: *And the LORD shall be King over all the earth:* **In that day the LORD shall be ONE, and HIS NAME shall be ONE** <note>original Hebrew: *bayom hahu yihyeh Adonai echad ushmo echad* (ביום ההוא יהיה יהוה אחד ושמו אחד)</note>. They thought that these words contained a prophecy about the Kingdom of God one day being manifested through the whole world, when all Nations would acknowledge the God of Israel alone.

Behold the words of **Jarchi** <note>original: *Jarchii*; referring to Rashi, the famous 11th-century French rabbi</note>: **"The Lord our God, the Lord is one"** <note>original Hebrew: *ינו יי' אחד*</note> **"He is ours now, and not the God of the nations; but in the future He is to be the one Lord."**
<margin>Zephaniah chapter 3, verse 9.</margin>
**"For then I will turn to the peoples a pure language, so that they may all call [upon the name of the Lord]."** <note>original Hebrew: *אז אהפך אל עמים שפה ברורה לקרא כולם*</note>
*Our God; Jehovah is one: It is suggested by these words that He is now our God and is not yet the God of the Gentiles, but is to be the*
*One God [for all] in the future: As it is said: For then I will turn to the Nations,*
<margin>Zechariah chapter 14, verse 9.</margin>
*so that ALL MAY CALL UPON THE NAME OF JEHOVAH, and ON THAT*
*DAY JEHOVAH WILL BE ONE, and His Name will be One.*

<margin>Chapter 10, column 3.</margin>
So it is already written in the **Kol Bo** <note>a classic 13th-14th century collection of Jewish laws and customs</note>: **"One must prolong the letter Dalet of the word 'Echad' [One] so that they may crown Him King in heaven and on earth and in the four winds of the world, etc."** <note>original Hebrew: *יד בד' של אחד כדי שימליכוהו בשמים ובארץ וכו' רוחות העולם*</note> *It is necessary, moreover, that in reciting the* **Shema** <note>the fundamental Jewish declaration of faith: "Hear, O Israel..."</note> *the letter Dalet of the word* **Echad** <note>Hebrew for "One"</note> *be prolonged, so that they may establish Him as*
*King in Heaven, on earth, and in the four quarters of the world.*
*When one recited the Shema, he made God King: that is, in his soul*
*he acknowledged and declared Him King of the whole world; and at the same time*
*he proclaimed the future and most glorious Kingdom of God through the Messiah coming into the whole*
*circle of the lands. Nor should it be sought elsewhere why they*
*wish the letter* **ד** <note>the Hebrew letter Dalet</note> *of the word* **אחד** <note>Echad</note> *to be painted in a larger form. Thus says the* **Baal Turim** <note>Jacob ben Asher, a 14th-century authority on Jewish law</note>:
**"It is written large to tell you that you should crown Him King in heaven and on earth and in the four winds of the world, and also so that you do not mistake it for a Resh."** <note>original Hebrew: *גרוֹלה לומר לך שתמליכהו בשמים ובארץ ובארבע רוחות העולם וגם שלא תטעה בריש*</note>
*It is written in a larger form, and by this it is indicated that it is your duty to*
*acknowledge and declare Him King in heaven and earth, and the four quarters,*
*lest you take this letter for a Resh* <note>The Hebrew letters Dalet (ד) and Resh (ר) look nearly identical; mistaking "One" (Echad) for "Other" (Acher) would fundamentally change the prayer to "The Lord is another god," a heretical error</note>. *Certainly, this most ancient*
*exposition of this passage of Deuteronomy concerning the Unity of the Kingdom*
*to be manifested in the whole world, can be supported by*
*certain testimonies of Paul the Apostle, by which he demonstrates it to*
*be so: that under the Kingdom of the Messiah, one mode of justification for*
*Jews and Gentiles (and indeed without the works of the Law, through*
*faith alone) would prevail on this foundation: that God is one. This*
*demonstration rests upon the exposition of the words of Deuteronomy; when*
*compared with those of Zechariah and Zephaniah, as it was accepted among the Jews of that time.*

<margin>Romans Chapter 3, verse 30.</margin>
So, for example, in the letter to the Romans: *Since there is one God* <note>original Greek: *Ἐπείπερ εἷς ὁ Θεὸς*</note>, *Since He*
*IS GOD, who will justify the circumcised by faith, and the uncircumcised*
*through faith. Since God has declared Himself to be one also with re-*
*spect to men (as is clear from the passage in Zechariah), hence it follows by necessity*
*that He should at some time conduct Himself in one and the same way toward all*
*men who are in the world, so that He might [justify] all of them in the same manner...*

# CHAPTER 17. IN THE SYNAGOGUE. 1089

<margin>Chapter 3, § 20.</margin>
<margin>Juvenal, Satire 6, verse 15. Ovid, Metamorphoses Book I: *After Saturn was sent into dark Tartarus*, UNDER JOVE *was the world*.</margin>
<margin>Ephesians 4:3, 4, 5.</margin>
<margin>Lightfoot, *Hebrew Hours* <note>original: *Hor. Heb.*, referring to John Lightfoot’s *Horae Hebraicae et Talmudicae*</note> on Matthew 3:2.</margin>
...and should treat [humanity]; and accordingly, in the same manner, through the same medium, and by the same path, He leads them to salvation. Since this medium cannot be the **Mosaic Law**, which was given to distinguish the Jews from the Gentiles (besides the fact that it cannot be observed by all men throughout the world), it was likewise necessary that God, under the Kingdom of the Messiah, should justify all through faith. Indeed, where a man is subject to **Jehovah alone**, that is, to Him only, it is necessary that every other precept be abolished by which he is subjected or bound to other things or persons besides **Jehovah**, and that the **Precept of Love** alone should prevail, which is the very same as the **Precept of Faith**. In the same sense, [Paul writes] to the Galatians: *A mediator is not of one: but God is one.* <note>original Greek: ὁ δὲ Θεὸς εἷς ἐστιν; Galatians 3:20</note> Moses, the mediator of the old Covenant, gave the Law to the Israelites, by which they were divided from the Gentiles; but since God, notwithstanding this, has declared Himself to be **one**, reason required that He should eventually show Himself as **one** to the whole world. That is, He would **reunite the Jews and Gentiles into one People**, treat them in the same way, and lead them to glory through the same path of righteousness. Then, indeed, the whole world would again be **under Jove** <note>The author uses "Jove" (Jupiter) as a classical metaphor for the supreme God, common in Renaissance and Early Modern scholarship</note>, which the poets truly prophesied concerning the golden age—that is, concerning the state of the world either as it was first established or restored after the Flood—and God would show Himself **fair to all**. Paul’s similar saying to the Ephesians also tends toward this, which must be explained from this same principle. And this is now among the reasons why those who recited the **Shema** <note>The central declaration of Jewish faith</note> were said to receive the <term>עול מלכות שמים</term>, **Yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven** <note>original Hebrew: *Ol Malkhut Shamayim*</note>, as you will see proved at length by Lightfoot.

<margin>See the Glossary on Berakhot, folio 14, 1. Matthew 11:30.</margin>
For first, they were considered, through the profession of these words, to subject themselves to God alone as their King and Lord, having denied all other divinities besides Jehovah. Then, they expressed their hope concerning the future **Kingdom of God**, or the **Messianic Kingdom**, over the entire world, by which God would call all peoples of all lands to communion with Himself, to be subjected to Him alone through the observance of the Precept of Faith and Love. Is this same state not called by the Lord and by the Apostles, who were accustomed to this style of speech, the <term>Βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν</term>, **Kingdom of the Heavens** <note>original Greek: *Basileia tōn ouranōn*</note>, or the **Kingdom of God**? To profess Jehovah alone as one’s King, and to bind oneself to His **love**—which was done through the profession of the Creed in Deuteronomy 6:4, 5, 6—was in itself to take upon oneself the <term>מלכות שמים</term>, KINGDOM OF HEAVEN. This the Lord calls the **YOKE OF THE KINGDOM OF HEAVEN**, or **His yoke**, which is *kind* <note>original Greek: χρηστὸν (chrēston)</note> and pleasant, to be taken up eventually by all Peoples. On the other hand, to recite the text of Deuteronomy 11:13 is to receive upon oneself the <term>עול מצוה</term>, **YOKE OF THE COMMANDMENT**, because...

After the completion of the recitation of the **Eighteen Benedictions**, one had to step back by *three steps*, for the sake of reverence and honor; several ceremonies of this kind are to be observed in the recitation of this Prayer. ### CHAPTER 17. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.

...they have not prayed; (that is, so that he may lead the prayers for those who are unable to recite those prayers by themselves, and thus assist them in fulfilling their duty). Everyone, however many there are in the Synagogue assembly, remains standing on their feet, listens attentively, and responds **Amen** to every Blessing <note>original: Eulogiam; here used for the Hebrew 'Berakhah'</note>, both those who have already fulfilled this duty of prayer (that is, those who have already poured out those prayers silently) as well as those who were still bound by the debt of performing this duty.

There is no difficulty in these matters.

$\delta$. <gloss>And he says the Sanctification in the third blessing; and once the Leader of the Congregation reaches the Sanctification, everyone has permission to return to the place where he stood during the prayer, etc.</gloss> In the third Blessing, moreover, he recites the Declaration of the Holiness of God, which is contained in that Blessing. When the **Leader of the Congregation** <term>Legatus Ecclesiae: the Sheliach Tzibbur, who represents the community in prayer</term> reaches this Declaration of the Holiness of God <note>Known as the Kedushah</note>, each person is permitted to return to that place where they were standing when they previously poured out their own prayers in a silent voice. And when the Leader of the Congregation reaches the Blessing **Modim** <term>Modim: the prayer of thanksgiving, meaning 'We give thanks'</term>, the whole assembly bows down, inclining their bodies a little (but not beyond what is proper and decorous), and they say: **We give thanks to You, etc.** <note>original Greek: Ἐξομολογέμεθά σοι</note>.

The third Blessing of the **Shemoneh Esreh** <term>Schemon-Esre: the 'Eighteen' central benedictions of the Jewish liturgy</term> was recited differently by individuals and by the Synagogue assembly; a difference which we have noted and shown in the preceding sections. Specifically, as it was chanted by the Synagogue assembly, it contained the Sanctification of the Divine Name, or the Declaration of Divine Holiness through the words of Isaiah: **Holy, Holy, etc.** <note>Isaiah 6:3</note>. When the Leader of the Congregation reached this passage <note>original: pericopam</note>, anyone who had prayed silently and stepped back three paces after completing the prayer was permitted to return to that first place they occupied when they began to pray.

$\epsilon$. <gloss>And after he completes the entire prayer, he shall sit and fall upon his face, etc.</gloss> And after he finishes the entire prayer, he sits and falls upon his face, inclining slightly—both he and the entire assembly—and pours out Supplications; he prostrates himself on his face, sits, and raises his head—both he and all the people—and he supplicates for a short time in a loud voice while sitting. After these things, only the Leader of the Congregation rises and recites the **Kaddish** <term>Kaddisch: a prayer magnifying and sanctifying God's name, marking the end of a section of the service</term> for a second time, while they respond with the same **responses** <note>original Greek: ἀντιφωνίας; antiphonies</note> as at the beginning. Then he recites the prayer: **Vehu Rachum** <term>Vehu Rachum: 'And He, being merciful,' a penitential prayer</term>, and Psalm 45 <note>In the numbering system likely used here, this may refer to Psalm 46: 'God is our refuge and strength'</note>, while he stands and the others sit, repeating the Psalm with him. To these, the Leader of the Congregation adds: **Uva Letzion Goel** <term>Uva Letzion Goel: 'A redeemer shall come to Zion'</term>, **And as for me, this is my Covenant, etc.** <note>original: Vaani Sooth; from Isaiah 59:21</note>, and **You are Holy** <note>original: Veatta Kadosch</note>, and **This one calls to another** <note>original: Kara Zee el Zee; from Isaiah 6:3</note>, saying—
