# ON THE RITE OF PRAYER BOOK III. PART II 1092

...and says "Holy," and completes the *Kedushah* <term>Hebrew: "Sanctification," a prayer focusing on God's holiness</term>, that Declaration of the Holiness of God, while the congregation responds antiphonally: "Holy, Holy, Holy," etc. Then the Messenger of the Congregation <note>original: "Legatus Ecclesiæ," translating the Hebrew "Shaliach Tzibbur"</note> returns and recites that Declaration of the Holiness of God in Aramaic <note>original: "Chaldaice"</note>. After this, he then says: *Vattissaeni Ruach*. "And the Spirit lifted me up," etc. <note>referring to Ezekiel 3:12</note>, and he repeats the same in Aramaic. He then says: "The Lord shall reign forever and ever"; and he repeats this also in Aramaic so that the People may understand it. These phrases <note>original: "κόμματα" (Greek for segments or clauses)</note> of Scriptural Dictums, which are recited before and after the solemn Declaration of God's Holiness through the words of Isaiah, together with their Aramaic interpretation, are called *Seder Hakkedusha* <note>Hebrew: "The Order of Sanctification"</note>, that is, the Solemn Formula for the Declaration of God's Holiness. Afterward, he humbly pours out certain other supplications <note>original: "ἱκετικά" (Greek for prayers of a suppliant)</note> which serve to move the mercy of God, and says the *Kaddish* <term>Aramaic: a hymn of praises to God often used to mark the end of sections in the liturgy</term>, with the People chanting along according to their custom; and THE CONGREGATION IS DISMISSED.

<margin>In the German Liturgy, folio 32, column 1.</margin>
Anyone who has seen in the Liturgies the Song *Uva Letzion* ("And a redeemer shall come to Zion"), etc., which in the Liturgy of the German Jews is added to the solemnities regarding the Book of the Law <note>the Torah scroll</note> to be observed on Mondays and Thursdays, will easily understand the individual points contained in this paragraph from Maimonides. The Holiness of the Divine Name—besides what was done in the Formula of the *Kaddish*—was to be solemnly declared three times by the Synagogue Assembly. First in the *Yotzer Or* <note>Hebrew: "Who forms light," a blessing before the Shema</note>; then in the third blessing of the *Shemoneh Esrei* <note>Hebrew: "The Eighteen," the central standing prayer</note>; and thirdly in the Song *Uva Letzion*. This was done not only in Hebrew but also in Aramaic, together with the vow and profession of God’s Kingdom through the words: "The Lord shall reign (or will reign) forever and ever," etc. From this we conclude with great probability that the Lord [Jesus] adapted the first two petitions of his Prayer <note>the Lord's Prayer/Our Father</note>—and indeed the third as well—to this solemn profession of the Holiness and Kingdom of God, along with the testimony of the Angels' zeal in celebrating God, which was present in the most sacred ceremonies of the Synagogue. For the fact that this Declaration of the Holiness of God was customarily recited not only in Hebrew but also in Aramaic (the same language in which the *Kaddish* formula is composed), so that it might be understood by the common people (which are the words of Maimonides), seems to me a certain argument for its antiquity. For while the Republic <note>referring to the Jewish state</note> was flourishing before and after the times of Christ, the Aramaic or Syrian language was in use in the land of Canaan, as everyone knows. However, after the state was subverted, the Doctors of the Law, though they were rivals of the Holy Tongue <note>Hebrew</note>, seem to have used Aramaic far more familiarly and frequently in recording records for future use and in composing Sacred Formulas, as can be gathered from the Mishnaic Institutes <note>original: "Institutionibus Misnicis," the Mishnah</note> alone.

The author argues that the petitions of the Lord's Prayer were modeled after these ancient synagogue professions of God's holiness and kingdom.</summary>

# CHAPTER 17. IN THE SYNAGOGUE. 1093

Thus we have depicted from Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides, the 12th-century Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> the *Liturgy of Morning Prayers*, and we have seen it to consist of:
1. The recitation of the *Kaddish* <term>Aramaic: a hymn of praise</term> and the *Barechu* <term>Hebrew: "Bless [the Lord]," the call to prayer</term>.
2. The *Shema* <term>Hebrew: the central declaration of faith, "Hear O Israel"</term> with its *Blessings* <note>original: "Eulogiis"</note>, or the *Yotzer Or* <term>Hebrew: "Who forms light," the first blessing before the Shema</term>.
3. The *Shemoneh Esreh* <term>Hebrew: "The Eighteen," the central standing prayer</term> with the *Kedushah* <term>Hebrew: "Sanctification"</term> in the third blessing.
4. Songs of *Supplications* and *Petitions for the Averting of Evil* <note>original: "Supplicationum & Deprecationum"</note>.
5. The *Kaddish*.
6. *Vehu Rachum* <term>Hebrew: "And He, being merciful," a penitential prayer</term> and Psalm 145.
7. The *Order of Sanctification* <note>original: "Seder Keduscha"</note>, or the Formula: *Uva Letzion* <term>Hebrew: "A redeemer shall come to Zion"</term>.
8. Certain litanies <note>original: "ἐκτενειαῖς" (Greek: fervent petitions)</note> and the *Kaddish*.

This should suffice as an example. Since, however, we are on this subject, let us also briefly touch upon what the same Maimonides holds regarding the *Order of the Afternoon and Evening Services*; not using his words any longer, but our own, for the sake of brevity.

The Afternoon Public Services, to be performed with the Messenger of the Congregation <note>original: "Legato Ecclesiæ," referring to the Shaliach Tzibbur or prayer leader</note> leading the way, consisted of:
1. The chanting of Psalm 84:5 etc. and Psalm 145:1 etc. while the people are seated.
2. The recitation of the *Kaddish*, with the Messenger of the Congregation and the entire assembly rising after him.
3. The silent recitation of the *Shemoneh Esreh*, and shortly after, its recitation in a loud voice.
4. *Supplications and Petitions* with the body posture appropriate to them <note>likely referring to prostration or bowing</note>.
5. The *Kaddish*, while the Messenger of the Congregation stands.

In the Evening Services:
1. The formula *Vehu Rachum, etc.* was recited while the entire synagogue assembly sat, but while the Messenger of the Synagogue stood.
2. The Messenger of the Congregation said: *Barechu, etc. Bless the Lord!*
**S.** <note>likely "Sacerdos" or "Senior" / The Leader</note>
**B.** <note>likely "Benedictio" or "Bodes" / The Response</note> With the congregation responding according to custom: *Blessed be the Lord! Blessed forever and ever!*
3. Soon after, he added the *Kaddish* and recited the *Shema* with the *Evening Blessings*.
4. After these, the entire congregation recites the *Shemoneh Esreh* silently (first each person for himself). Silently, I say; for the Minister of the Synagogue by no means repeats this prayer in a *loud voice*, as he does in the Morning and Afternoon hours, because the Israelites are not thought to be necessarily bound to the Evening Prayers, and therefore there was no need—

so that the Minister of the Synagogue might be freed from that duty which the obligation of fulfilling his office required, except in cases of necessity. The **Sabbath Evening services** <note>original: "Vesperæ Sabbathi"</note> had this peculiarity: after the **Shemoneh Esreh** <term>Hebrew: "The Eighteen," the central standing prayer</term> was poured out by the Congregation, it was recited only once **aloud** by the Messenger of the Congregation <term>Latin: "Legato Ecclesiæ," referring to the Shaliach Tzibbur or prayer leader</term>, the formula of which is described by Maimonides in that passage.
5. The sacred rites were concluded with the solemn formula of the **Kaddish** <term>Aramaic: a hymn of praise magnifying God's name</term>.

The Sabbath and Festival rites, however, were celebrated in this order, according to the same Maimonides, during the Morning hours:
1. The **ordinary Morning Prayers** are performed according to the solemn rite, with the exception of the variation in the **Shemoneh Esreh**, concerning which we have spoken as often as necessary in the preceding pages.
2. * **Kaddish**.
3. Psalm 145.
4. **Kaddish**.
5. The **Additional Prayers** <term>Latin: "Preces Addititiæ," referring to the Musaf service</term> are recited first silently by individuals, then **aloud** by the Messenger of the Congregation.
6. **Kaddish**.

<margin>§. 13.</margin>
Having omitted from these Sabbath Morning rites the **Supplications and Petitions** <note>original: "Supplicationes & Deprecationes"</note>, as well as the **Celebration of the Holiness of God** which is contained in the formula: **Uva Letzion** <term>Hebrew: "And a redeemer shall come to Zion"</term>; these are reserved for the Afternoon rites. In those services, after Psalm 145 is sung, the **Holiness of God** is entreated through the formula **Uva Letzion**; and to these are joined the **Songs of Supplication and Petition**. After which, finally, the **Kaddish** and the **Afternoon Prayers** <note>original: "Pomeridianæ Preces," referring to the Mincha service</note> are recited.

And thus I have narrated the entire Jewish Liturgy clearly—and I hope transparently—a subject surely worthy of being considered by Christians. Would that many of them did not attend to their own sacred rites much more lukewarmly and negligently than the Jews do theirs.

### CHAPTER XVIII.

Briefly dealing with the Manners of offering Prayers, and the Circumstances of both Time and Place which ought to be observed regarding this Act of Religion. Finally, a discussion is held on the various Formulas of responses <note>original Greek: "ἀντιφωνιῶν" (antiphoniōn), referring to antiphonal or responsive singing</note> by which the Synagogue Prayers are received by the Assembly, especially concerning the little word **Amen**, and the acclamations <note>original Greek: "ἐπιφωνήμασι" (epiphōnēmasi)</note> of the **Kaddish** and **Kedusha**.

Unless this dissertation of ours on *Prayers* had grown too large, we should now proceed to discuss the MODES in which it is proper for prayers to be made according to Jewish Discipline; or rather, concerning the *Qualities* and *Accidents* which Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the influential Sephardic philosopher and jurist who codified Jewish law</note> requires in anyone praying, totaling *thirteen*. If five of these are absent, they render the prayers void and, even if the time for prayer has arrived, they *delay* <note>original: "morantur"</note> them; the other *eight*, however, although they greatly recommend the prayers, do not entirely prevent their effect.

The first five are:
α. **Purity of Hands** <term>Hebrew: "טהרת ידים" (Toharat Yadayim)</term>, which includes the laws regarding the washing of either the hands alone, or the hands and body together, before prayer.
β. **Covering of Nakedness** <term>Hebrew: "כסוי הערוה" (Kisui Ha-ervah)</term>.
γ. **Purity of the place in which prayers are to be poured out** <term>Hebrew: "טהרת מקום תפלה" (Toharat mekom tefilah)</term>.
δ. **Distracting concerns** <term>Hebrew: "דברים החופזים אותו" (Devarim ha-chofzim oto)</term>: things that urge a person to recite prayers hurriedly and anxiously, such as if one is pressed by the necessity of the bowels.
ε. **Attention of the heart** <term>Hebrew: "כונת לב" (Kavanat lev)</term>.

The latter eight are:
α. **The posture of standing** <term>Hebrew: "עמידה" (Amidah)</term>.
β. **Facing the Sanctuary** <term>Hebrew: "נכח המקדש" (Nechach ha-mikdash)</term>: that the person praying should turn toward the holy place.
γ. **Legitimate composition of the body** <term>Hebrew: "תקון הגוף" (Tikkun ha-guf)</term> in praying: namely, with the feet properly joined, the eyes cast downward, etc.
δ. **Arrangement of clothing** <term>Hebrew: "תיקון המלבושין" (Tikkun ha-malbushin)</term>: that one should present oneself for prayer properly adorned and furnished with garments.
ε. **Ordering of the place** <term>Hebrew: "תיקון המקום" (Tikkun ha-makom)</term>: that one should choose a certain place for praying, and specifically a chamber <note>original: "Conclave"</note> whose windows are open toward Jerusalem, etc.
ζ. **Leveling of the voice** <term>Hebrew: "השויית הקול" (Hashwayat ha-kol)</term>: that the person praying should not use a voice that is too high, nor should they entirely neglect the service of the voice, but should pour out their prayers in a lower and steady voice, which can nevertheless be understood by the one praying.
η. **Bowing** <term>Hebrew: "הכריעה" (Ha-kri'ah)</term>, as we have described above.
θ. **Prostration on the ground** <term>Hebrew: "השתחוייה" (Hishtachavayah)</term>, regarding which likewise in the [preceding-] <note>The text breaks off here at the catchword</note>

<margin>Chapter 5, Section 15.</margin>
Maimonides writes: <note>original Hebrew: "פשוט בכל ישראל שאין נפילת פנים בשבת ובמועדי' ולא בראש השנה ולא בראשי חדשים ובחנוכה ובפורי' ולא במנחה של ערבי שבתות וימי טובי' ולא בערבית שבכל יום"</note> *It is accepted by consensus among all Israelites that the gesture of falling on the face is not practiced on Sabbaths and solemn Festivals, nor even on the Festival of the New Year, the New Moons, the Festival of Dedication <note>Hanukkah</note>, or Purim; nor even in the Afternoon Prayers of the vigils of Sabbaths and Festivals; nor in the Evening prayers of any day.*

Among the *Circumstances* of this act, we must attend to the PLACES and TIMES. As for the Places where prayers are solemnly offered, we have seen above that besides the Temple, there are Synagogues, to be built primarily for the sake of sacred rites, where ten free and adult Israelites are present <note>a "minyan," or the quorum of ten required for communal prayer</note>; and even Academic lecture halls, which are holier seats, in which Maimonides writes that doctors of great name were accustomed to perform their duty of praying. Regarding the TIMES of daily

prayers, three fixed times are observed by the Jews: <term>Shacharit</term> (Morning), <term>Mincha</term> (Afternoon), and <term>Arvit</term> (Evening). They wish the Morning Prayers to
<margin>Chapter 1. Section 7.</margin>

The ordinary Morning Prayers must be finished before the fourth hour of the day, that is, before the first third of the day is completed. The Afternoon
<margin>Chapter 5, Sections 1, 2.</margin>

...the manner of praying solemnly did not escape the notice of Jerome and Augustine. Furthermore, Jerome notes that since on Sabbaths and Festival days other additions were made to the ordinary sacrifices in honor of the Feast, it seemed right to the Ancient Doctors that in place of the *Musaph* <term>Hebrew: "מוסף", meaning "Additional"</term> sacrifice, *Additional* prayers should also be recited. The time for these was established from after the morning prayers until the end of the seventh hour of the day: so much so, that on Sabbaths and Festivals, the Jews prayed solemnly *four times*. On the Day of Atonement <note>Yom Kippur</note>, however, they performed this religious rite *five times*, when just before sunset, *while the gates of heaven are being barred to the sun*, they repeat this act of prayer: which *Prayer* is therefore called *Ne'ilah* <term>Hebrew: "נעילה", meaning "Locking" or "Closing"</term>, according to Maimonides—or perhaps more correctly because it was customary to recite it just before the gates of the Temple courtyard were closed. The Hebrew verb *He’emin* <note>original: האמין, meaning "to believe"</note> is used with the preposition *b-* <note>the letter "bet," often translated as "in"</note>. This is useful to observe in order to understand the emphasis of the little Greek word *pistos* <note>original: πιστὸς, meaning "faithful" or "believing"</note>, which was frequently employed by the Apostles in their Epistles. For example, to the Ephesians: *To the saints who are in Ephesus and the faithful in Christ Jesus* <note>original Greek: Τοῖς ἁγίοις τοῖς οὖσιν ἐν Ἐφέσῳ καὶ πιστοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ</note>. To the Colossians: *To the saints and faithful brothers in Christ Jesus who are in Colossae* <note>original Greek: Τοῖς ἐν Κολοσσαῖς ἁγίοις καὶ πιστοῖς ἀδελφοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ</note>; and elsewhere throughout. There can be no doubt that the "faithful" <note>original Greek: πιστοὶ</note> are the *men of faith*, the *trustworthy*, or the *constant* <note>original Hebrew: אנשי אמונה, נאמנים, אמונים; original Latin: fideles, constantes</note>. The Dutch <note>original: Belgae</note> translate this as: **Faithful and steadfast**, and so those passages should be translated: **To the saints who are at Ephesus, and the steadfast in Christ Jesus.** Also: **The faithful brothers in Christ Jesus.** Yet the Dutch translators have not inelegantly rendered these passages as: **To the holy and believing brothers**, since we have already observed that the "steadfast" and "men of faith"—that is, the *faithful*—are translated by the Hebrews themselves as *believers* <note>original Hebrew: מאמינים; original Greek: πιστεύοντας; original Dutch: geloovige</note>. In this way, the word *Believers* is used by Capitolinus <note>Julius Capitolinus, one of the authors of the *Augustan History*</note>: *“And then, while everyone was attentive, he gave out the name of Antoninus* 
<margin>In the life of Marcus Augustus, chapter 3.</margin>
*Augustus. But while everyone believed that Antoninus Pius would rule for eight years, he even exceeded this number of years: and it was established among the BELIEVERS, either then or later through a Prophet, that something else was intended.”* The word *Believers* <note>original Latin: Credentes</note> is used here in an absolute sense, just as the word *believers* <note>original Greek: τὸ πιστεύοντες</note> is in the New Testament; but it must be explained with respect to that which is proposed as the object of faith in the context of the speech. Indeed, the Dutch translators have not only translated *pistos* as "believers," but in this very passage they translated the word *emunim* <note>faithful ones</note> in exactly the same way: **The Lord preserves the believers.**
<margin>Psalm 31, 24.</margin>

Nor do I wish to deny that the Hebrew commentators generally favor this opinion. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note> says: *As if to say, God guards those who trust in His salvation and lean upon Him* <note>original Hebrew: כמו שומר יי' את המאמינים בישועתו : וסומכים עליו</note>. Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval grammarian and commentator</note> agrees. Both, however, seem to have followed the ancient interpreters. Yet I would plainly think that the word *emunim* <note>אמונים</note> both here and elsewhere in Scripture is not a concrete noun <note>original: תואר, an adjective or noun describing a person</note> (meaning "faithful ones" or "believers"), but an abstract noun, signifying "faith" or "truth" <note>original Greek: πίστιν, ἀλήθεια</note>. Therefore, this passage should be translated: *The Lord preserves faith*. The Dutch: **The Lord preserves faithfulness.** That is, He is constant in keeping His faith. For this Hebraism <term>a linguistic feature or idiom characteristic of the Hebrew language</term> is to be compared with a similar passage in Isaiah: *Let the righteous nation enter, keeping the faith* <note>original Hebrew: יבא גוי שומר אמונים</note>.
<margin>Chapter 26, 2.</margin>
In the same way, a similar passage in Psalm 12:2 should be translated: *Because the faithful are diminished* <note>original Hebrew: כי פסו אמונים</note>. The Dutch: **For the...**

### ON THE RITUAL OF PRAYER, BOOK III.

...the faithful have become few. <note>original Dutch: getrouwe syn weynigh geworden</note> You see, here the word *rabb* <note>original Hebrew: רב; the author is likely discussing Psalm 12:1 where the term refers to "the many" or "abundance"</note> has been rendered as "the faithful" <note>original Latin: *fideles*; Dutch: *getrouwe*</note>, rather than as "the believers" <note>original Latin: *credentes*</note>, as it is in our current passage. **β. Amen must not be pronounced too quickly, but distinctly and slowly.**

<margin>Chapter 74, § 8.</margin>
So it is written in the *Orach Chayim* <note>The "Path of Life," a central code of Jewish law (the Shulchan Aruch)</note>: *One should not offer a "snatched" Amen—that is, an Aleph punctuated with a Chateph <note>a very short Hebrew vowel, original: חטופה</note>; this means one should not snatch it and rush to answer before the one blessing has finished. Likewise, one should not offer a "clipped" Amen—that is, a pronunciation where the letter Nun <note>the 'n' at the end of Amen</note> is not brought forth clearly by the mouth so that it is recognizable. Nor should one offer an "orphan" Amen—which occurs when someone is obligated to say a certain blessing, and his companion recites it, but he does not hear it; even if he knows which blessing the leader of the congregation <note>shaliach tzibur</note> is reciting, since he did not hear it, he should not answer Amen after him, for that would be an "orphan" Amen. Nor should one offer a "short" Amen, but rather a prolonged one; prolonged enough so that one could say the words "God, Faithful King" <note>original Hebrew: א"ל מ"לך נאמן; the first letters of these three words—El, Melech, Neeman—form the acronym AMN or Amen</note>, but do not prolong it too much, because the pronunciation of the word cannot be understood if you prolong it excessively.* It adds: *If there are some among those responding who prolong it too much, the one reciting the blessing does not need to wait for them.*

**γ. The voice should also not be raised too high when responding.**
<margin>In the place cited, § 11.</margin>
*Orach Chayim*: *And one should not raise his voice louder than the one blessing...*

### CHAPTER 18. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.

...of that Blessed One, far above all Blessing and Song, Praise, and Consolation, which are spoken in the World. And say Amen. Receive our prayers mercifully and graciously. May the prayers and desires of all Israel be accepted before their Father, who is in Heaven: And say: Amen: Blessed be the Name of the Lord from this time forth and forevermore. Let there be great peace from Heaven, and Life upon us, and upon all Israel, and say: Amen.

Let this prayer now be compared with the words of Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and Torah scholar</note>, and nothing obscure will remain.

<margin>See the Liturgy.</margin>
To the formula of praise <note>original Greek: εὐκλευστικὴν — pertaining to glory or praise</note> "Bless the Lord, the Blessed One" <note>Hebrew: *Barechu at Adonai ha-Mevorakh*</note>; the Assembly responds: "Blessed be the Lord, the Blessed One, forever and ever" <note>Hebrew: *Barukh Adonai ha-Mevorakh le-olam va-ed*</note>. Meanwhile, while the Messenger of the Congregation <note>term: Legatus Ecclesiae — the prayer leader or cantor, often called the Shaliach Tzibbur</note> draws out the *Barechu* formula, the Synagogue Assembly recites the formula "May He be praised" <note>Hebrew: *Yitbarakh*</note>, which you will find in the Liturgies next to the *Barechu* formula.

<margin>See Maimonides in the Order of Prayer (*Seder Tephil.*).</margin>
In the recitation of the third prayer of the *Shemoneh Esrei* <note>The "Eighteen Benedictions," the central standing prayer of the Jewish service</note>, which includes the Declaration of the Holiness of God, when the Minister of the Synagogue reaches the words: *And one cries out to the other, and says,* the Synagogue Assembly exclaims: *Holy, Holy, Holy, etc.* And when the Minister of the Synagogue says: *Where is the place of His glory,* the whole Assembly says: *Blessed be He, etc.* And when he says: *In our life and in our days,* all the People respond: *Amen.* And when he says: *By David,* <margin>† The Lord from His place.</margin> *your righteous Anointed,* all the People respond: *May the Lord reign forever.* In a nearly similar manner, the Synagogue sings along at the *Seder Kedusha* <note>The "Order of Holiness," a liturgical section focusing on the sanctification of God’s name</note>, which is found in the formula "And a Redeemer shall come to Zion" <note>Hebrew: *Uva Letzion*</note>, as we previously understood from the Liturgy of Maimonides. From these things it is clear that the Synagogue Assembly, in a pleasing 
<margin>Maimonides, *Laws of Prayer* (Hilchot Tephillah), chapter 9, § 5.</margin> 
harmony, continually punctuated the Blessings of the Messenger of the Congregation. Indeed, after I considered these Jewish Blessings, I no longer doubt that the Doxology <note>original Greek: Δοξολογία — a short hymn of praises to God</note> of the Lord’s Prayer—which is called a "many-named song" <note>original Greek: πολυώνυμος ᾠδὴ</note> by Lucian <margin>In *Philopatris*.</margin> <note>A satirical dialogue historically attributed to the Greek writer Lucian of Samosata</note>—was truly added to that prayer by the Lord Jesus Himself, according to the custom of that time. This was also observed before us <margin>Notes and Observations, chapter 38.</margin> by John Gregory <note>A 17th-century English orientalist and scholar</note>, who strove to illustrate it with certain similar examples taken from the Jewish Liturgy.

DE RITU PRECATIONIS LIB. III. PARS II.
<note>On the Rite of Prayer, Book 3, Part 2</note>

### CAP. XIX.

*The Rite of Prayer, as it was celebrated in the earliest Christian gatherings, is compared with the synagogal rite—both in terms of the content of the prayers and the various external circumstances of the act—demonstrating the conformity between the Synagogue and the Church in their principal parts.*

Up to now we have been occupied with the Synagogue; from which we must finally transition to the Church, which itself celebrated its religion through hymns and prayers following the example of the Synagogue. In this discussion, however, we must apply sound judgment, unless we wish to wander far into error. For it should not be expected of us here that we demonstrate all those rites of prayer which we observed in the Synagogue to have been simultaneously adopted in the early Christian Church. For aside from the fact that some of those rites are undoubtedly of more recent origin, we do not have a full knowledge of the entire liturgy <note>original Greek: Leiturgia</note> of the Primitive and Apostolic Church (for that is our only concern here). If anyone were to set out to compare the rites of the Christian Church, as they were celebrated in Divine Worship during the *fourth* or *fifth* century after Christ's birth, with the *Jewish liturgy* (which, I admit, could be done without much difficulty), he would be wasting his time and effort <note>original Latin: *oleum et operam perderet*—an idiom meaning "to waste oil and labor," referring to the lamp oil used for late-night study</note>, unless he could simultaneously show that all those rites were likewise accepted in the primitive Apostolic Church: a point that certainly will never be proven.

<margin>
In the Preface to the *Dagger of Faith* <note>original Latin: *Pugio Fidei*—a famous 13th-century polemical work by Raymond Martí</note> by Raymond, leaf 149.
</margin>

Therefore, that most learned man, Joseph de Voysin <note>A 17th-century French Hebraist and priest who edited Martí's work</note>, achieves nothing by comparing certain parts of the *Prayer Office of the Roman Church* with the *Synagogal Liturgy*; since it is established that the *Roman Office* is of a far more recent origin. After the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem <note>original: *Templum Hierosolymitanum*</note>, the Synagogue increasingly emulated the religion of the Temple over time, so that what was missing in the Temple might be compensated for through the Synagogues. The Christian Church also strove over time to conform its own worship in all things to the worship of the Temple of Jerusalem, and indeed conformed it much more so than even the Synagogue. Thus, it is not surprising that some conformity can be noted between the sacred rites of the Church of later times and those of the Synagogue—a fact that does absolutely nothing to serve our purpose. For we condemn all such agreement...

### CHAPTER 19. IN THE CHURCH.

Regarding the sacred rites of the Synagogue and the Church—not that of the later ages, but the one belonging to the Apostolic era (or, if we do not go so far as to condemn the later Church, we might still consider it of little value to our current study as it does not concern us here)—the Ancient Synagogue practiced its worship with great freedom. The primitive Christian Church acted in much the same way. And even if the Synagogues themselves undoubtedly burdened their own worship with many ceremonies, they nevertheless guarded their freedom far better than the Church, which, as time went on, began to fully model itself after the **Temple** <note>The author distinguishes between the 'Synagogue'—a place of teaching and prayer—and the 'Temple'—a place of elaborate priestly ritual and sacrifice—suggesting the later Church became too ritualistic</note>. This trend continued until the preceding century, when the worship of the Church was, in many respects, brought back to the freedom and simplicity of the Apostolic age, which is most appropriate for the Church of the New Covenant. Therefore, let us look only at whether we can identify certain traces of Synagogal worship within the practice of Hymns and Prayers in the primitive Christian Church, or the Church that most closely followed that earliest era.

<margin>
Acts 2:42.
Acts 6:4.
1 Corinthians 11:5.
1 Corinthians 14:15.
Colossians 4:2.
1 Timothy 2:1.
5:5.
James 5:17.
1 Peter 4:7.
</margin>
It is sufficiently clear from the writings of the New Testament and the ecclesiastical monuments of antiquity that prayers formed a prominent part of religion as practiced by Christians in the early Church. For instance, in the Book of Acts, only three parts of public worship are enumerated: the *Instruction of the Apostles* <note>original Greek: hē didachē tōn Apostolōn</note>, the *Communion and breaking of bread* <note>original Greek: hē koinōnia kai hē klasis tou artou</note>, and *the prayers* <note>original Greek: hai proseuchai</note>. Elsewhere, two parts are mentioned: the *Ministry of the Word* <note>original Greek: hē diakonia tou logou</note>, and *Prayer* <note>original Greek: proseuchē</note>, which are elsewhere presented under the names of *prophesying and praying* <note>original Greek: prophēteuein kai proseuchesthai</note>. I need not mention here the exhortations of Paul and the other Apostles toward this duty of **Prayer**—whether public or private—found in various places, as some of these will be illustrated shortly. Nor will I cite the testimonies of Justin and Tertullian regarding this same rite here, as they will also be brought forward by us in their proper place.

<margin>
Chapter 12, verse 10.
</margin>
Furthermore, even if those prayers of the first Christians were performed with much greater freedom and joined with far greater grace than those of the Synagogue—according to the promise of God in Zechariah regarding the pouring out of the *Spirit of Grace and Supplication*, which was realized in the primitive Church—I am nevertheless certain that the early Church, in this rite of praying, imitated the established customs of the Synagogues. They did so as far as it was consistent with the character, spiritual state, and benefits of that Church. We shall indeed attempt to demonstrate this briefly and clearly through certain arguments of similarity.

### ON THE RITE OF PRAYER, BOOK III.

1. Regarding the *Name*; Paul calls the prayers of Christians, according to the sense <note>original: "ad mentem"</note> of the Hebrew word *Berakhot* <note>original: ברכות; meaning "Blessings"</note>, "thanksgivings" and "blessings" <note>original: εὐχαριστίας & εὐλογίας</note>; in his *First Epistle to the Corinthians*, where he discusses the sacred rites of Christians: he clearly uses the same term in other places with an allusion to the Jewish rite. Thus,
<margin>1 Cor. 14:15, 16, 17.</margin>
writing to the Corinthians, he had previously called it: "To pray with the spirit" <note>original: Προσεύχεσθαι τῷ πν̅</note>, then he calls it "to bless" <note>original: εὐλογεῖν</note>, and following that "to give thanks" <note>original: εὐχαριστεῖν</note>. "He who fills the place of the layperson <note>The Latin 'idiota' refers to a common person or one uninstructed in specific spiritual gifts</note>, how will he say 'Amen' to your thanksgiving <note>original: εὐχαριστίᾳ</note>?" That is, to your *prayers*, which the Apostle calls *Thanksgiving*, because it was the custom among the Jews either to precede their prayers or at least to follow them with the formula of *Thanksgiving or Blessing*: "Blessed are You, O Lord, etc." <note>original: ברוך אתה ה' וכו'</note>, as appears from the blessings of the *Shema* <note>The central declaration of Jewish faith</note> and the *Shemoneh Esrei* <note>The "Eighteen Benedictions," a pillar of Jewish daily prayer</note>. For we should certainly think that although the entire formula of the *Shemoneh Esrei* was compiled after the *Destruction of the Temple* <note>70 AD</note>, we consider it probable that some of those *Eighteen* petitions from which that formula was constructed were already accepted in the Synagogues before that time. In this same way,
<margin>Col. 4:2.</margin>
we understand Paul in the Epistle to the Colossians: "Continue in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving" <note>original: Τῇ προσευχῇ καρτερεῖτε, γρηγορῶντες ἐν αὐτῇ ἐν εὐχαριστίᾳ</note>. The Apostle wants *thanksgiving* to be joined to, or follow after *prayer*, according to the Synagogal rite.
<margin>1 Thess. 5:18.</margin>
In the same manner, where he exhorted the Thessalonians to *prayer* through the words: "Pray without ceasing" <note>original: Ἀδιαλείπτως προσεύχεσθε</note>, he immediately adds: "In all things give thanks" <note>original: παντὶ εὐχαριστεῖτε</note>. What he says in the
<margin>Chapter 4:4.</margin>
*First Epistle to Timothy*: "Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected <note>original: "reprobabile"</note> if it is received with thanksgiving" <note>original: μετὰ εὐχαριστίας λαμβανόμενον</note>, clearly alludes to the rite received among the Jews—a practice which is highly praiseworthy—that they are not accustomed to use any creature of God, whether it serves them for the slightest utility or pleasure, without a preceding Thanksgiving using the word *Barukh*, "Blessed be the Lord of Heaven and Earth," as we mentioned above from Maimonides' <note>The influential 12th-century Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> *Treatise* on this subject.
<margin>Chapter 3:17.</margin>
Thus elsewhere to the same effect to the Colossians: "Whatever you do, in word or deed, let all things be done in the name of the Lord, giving thanks to God the Father through him" <note>original: εὐχαριστοῦντες τῷ Θεῷ καὶ Πατρὶ δι' αὐτοῦ</note>.

3. I would also estimate that the subject matter of the Church’s prayers came very close to that of the Synagogue prayers, insofar as it was consistent with the character and spiritual state of the New Testament Church.
Namely: **α.** Just as the Ancient Synagogue had its *Kadosh* and *Kedushah* <note>original Hebrew: קדוש & קדושה</note>, which are **Formulas for the Sanctification of the Divine Name**, along with a vow for the coming of the Kingdom of God (for I believe those formulas of the Synagogue prayers to be the most ancient), and which they used very frequently; so the Lord Jesus prescribed to his disciples a certain **Formula of Prayer**, which we call the "Lord's Prayer," undoubtedly for the purpose that they might use it familiarly and frequently. We are led to this clearly by the words of Luke, <margin>Chapter 11:1.</margin> who records that a disciple, seeking this prayer, addressed the Lord in this way: *Teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples.* Thus, they were to have a formula for themselves that was distinct from the formula of John and the formulas of the Pharisees. Certainly, just as the Jews have the Synagogue *Kaddish* <note>A prayer focusing on the sanctification of God's name</note>, so the Academics <note>Scholars or students in the rabbinic schools</note> also have their own *Kadosh*, or *Kaddish*, called the **Kaddish of the Masters** <note>original Hebrew: קדיש דרבנן; "Kaddish DeRabbanan"</note>, to be recited by the scholars whenever no fewer than ten individuals have labored in the Divine Law; the formula for which Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> presents after the Synagogue Kaddish. <margin>In the Example of Prayers for the Entire Year.</margin> I believe the **Lord’s Prayer** should be compared entirely with this kind of formula. For just as that *Kaddish* was accustomed to being recited more familiarly and frequently before the sacred rites—indeed, both before and after other prayers—so it was the same with the Lord's Prayer. As has been observed for a long time by the most learned men, it was customary in the Ancient Church to recite it either before or after other prayers. Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage, c. 155–220 AD</note> writes: <margin>See the venerable D. Witsius on the Lord's Prayer, Exercise 6, § 14. Book on Prayer.</margin> *Since, however, the Lord, the Provider for human needs, said separately after handing down the discipline of praying, "Ask, and you shall receive," and since there are things to be asked for according to each person's circumstances,* **THE LEGITIMATE AND ORDINARY PRAYER HAVING BEEN SENT BEFORE** <note>Referring to the Lord's Prayer as the primary foundation</note> *as a foundation, one has the right to build additional petitions from the outside.* **β.** Just as the Ancient Synagogue, besides these formulas of sanctific-

...sanctification of the Divine Name, the Church was accustomed to solemnly pray to God with **Thanksgiving** and **Blessing** for all necessities, whether of the **Body**, the **State**, or the **Church**. Just as these Synagogue prayers were gathered into one sum of **Eighteen** or **Nineteen** <note>original Latin: *Octodenarum* or *Novendenarum*; referring to the Shemoneh Esrei and the nineteenth blessing added later</note> under Rabban Gamaliel, so in the same way the Christian Church instituted its own **blessings and thanksgivings** <note>original Greek: εὐλογίας & εὐχαριστίας</note>, concerning which we have already heard Paul speaking in his Letter to the Corinthians. But there is testimony on this matter from Justin Martyr in his *Apology to Antoninus*, which, <margin>page 60</margin> though it was originally the first, is now titled the second. Justin refutes the blasphemy by which Christians were labeled as **Atheists** because they denied sacrifices to the Roman gods. He answers that Christians offer rational sacrifices to God: **Prayers, Hymns, and Thanksgivings**, the subjects of which he describes as follows: 

"For our creation, for all the means of well-being, for the qualities of various kinds of things, and the changes of seasons; and to make our request that we may live again in incorruption through faith in Him" <note>original Greek: Ὑπὲρ δὲ τοῦ γεγονέναι, καὶ τῶν εἰς εὐπο- ρων πάντων, ποιοτήτων μὲν γενῶν, καὶ μεταβολῶν ὡρῶν, πάλιν ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ γενέσθαι διὰ πίστιν τὴν ἐν αὐτῷ αἰτή- σοντες</note>. 

*Concerning Creation, by which He made us; concerning the abundance of all things for our well-being through bountiful harvest; concerning the variety of every kind of thing and the fitting change of seasons; also concerning the life that will return to us beyond all corruption because of the faith in which we rest, pouring out prayers.* 

This subject matter for prayer corresponds excellently with the **Eighteen Benedictions** <note>original: *Octodenarum*</note>. 

<margin>P. 97. 98.</margin> In the following parts of this Apology, he mentions more than once the **Public Prayers** which used to take place in the assemblies of the believers. Specifically, after administering baptism to a **neophyte** <note>original Greek: νεόφυτον; literally "newly planted," a common term for a recent convert</note> and bringing them into the assembly, he says they all prayed together "for themselves, for the one just baptized, and for all others everywhere, so that we may be deemed worthy, now that we have learned the truth, to be found through our deeds as good and dutiful citizens, and keepers of the commandments, so that we may be saved with eternal salvation" <note>original Greek: ὑπέρ τε ἑαυτῶν καὶ τ θέντος καὶ ἄλλων πανταχῆ πάντων... ὅπως τ νίον σωτηρίαν σωθῶμεν</note>. 

As we are made worthy and fit, having recognized the truth, we are found to be good and dutiful administrators of things through our very works, <margin>In Apology chapter 39.</margin> and keepers of the commands given to us. 

**Tertullian** states clearly: "We assemble in a meeting and a gathering, so that we may surround God with our prayers, as if in a massed hand, while praying. This force is pleasing to God. We also pray for the emperors, for their ministers and those in power, for the state of the world, for the peace of affairs, and for the delay of the end" <note>The "delay of the end" refers to the early Christian belief that their prayers postponed the final judgment/apocalypse</note>. These were the first [prayers] of the Christians.

I do not believe that those Prayers were restricted to fixed Formulas after the example of the Synagogue prayers (even though I am aware that a Formula of this kind exists in the *Clementine Constitutions* <note>The *Apostolic Constitutions*, formerly attributed to Clement of Rome, are a 4th-century collection of Christian discipline and liturgy</note>). 4. We can also note a various conformity between **Ecclesiastical and Synagogue Prayers regarding their Manner**; and specifically:
α. Just as the Jews were required **to wash themselves before Prayers**, so the same was received among the Christians of ancient times, a custom undoubtedly derived from the Synagogue—even though I am aware the same was also practiced among the Gentiles in their sacred rites. The renowned Suicerus <note>Johann Caspar Suicer (1619–1684), a Swiss theologian known for his "Ecclesiastical Thesaurus"</note> supports this Christian custom with many testimonies, of which I will now note one from Chrysostom: *“Then we indeed wash our hands when entering the church”* <note>original Greek: Εἶτα χεῖρας μὲν νιπτόμεθα εἰς ἐκκλησίαν εἰσιόντες</note>. Nor is there any doubt that the Apostle alluded at least to this custom of his Nation when he commanded **that men in every place should lift up holy, or pure hands** <note>original Greek: ὁσίας χεῖρας</note>; which "holy hands," according to Price <note>John Price (1602–1676), a scholar of the New Testament</note>, are *“clean and unstained”* <note>original Greek: καθαροὶ καὶ ἀμίαντοι</note>. However, it is not clearly established from where the Jews received this custom of washing themselves before Prayers. It is probable, nevertheless, that it should be derived from the fact that they were instructed by the Mosaic Law in **various washings and regulations for the body** (Hebrews 9:10), so that Sacred rites (with which prayers were ordinarily joined in those most ancient times) would not be performed without a **preliminary washing of the hands and body**. Furthermore, God occasionally required a washing of the body from the Jews in such cases, from which the Jews could understand that the Rite of body-washing is acceptable to God in those who approach Him. Certainly, this opinion commends itself to us with a much greater appearance of truth than that of the famous Spencer <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), who argued that many Jewish laws were "borrowed" from Egyptian or Gentile customs to steer the Israelites away from idolatry</note>, who contends that the Jews received this Rite from the Gentiles, and that the first mention of it occurs in the Book of **Judith**; yet even before her age, it could easily be proven from Hesiod <note>Ancient Greek poet, c. 700 BCE</note> that this was long ago received among the Gentiles. 1. It does not follow that this Rite was not accepted among the Jews at the time when the Author of the Book of Judith lived <note>The Book of Judith is a deuterocanonical work; the author argues that just because a custom isn't mentioned in earlier texts doesn't mean it didn't exist.</note>, simply because mention of it does not happen to occur during that period. 2. Even if it had been a common practice among the Gentiles before it appeared in the Sacred Records of the Jews, it would still not follow that the Jews adopted it from the Gentiles. For I would ask: from where did the Gentiles obtain it? Undoubtedly either from Reason or from Revelation. If you say it came from Tradition, then that tradition itself must ultimately be resolved back into either Reason or Revelation. Since the Gentiles were not taught by Revelation, it remains only that this Rite originated among the Gentiles from Reason. Reason judged that the highest reverence for the Divinity required men to approach God with a *pure body*, and also that a pure body was a kind of symbol and representation of a pure mind, and therefore pleasing to the Gods. Since the Gentiles reasoned this by their natural wit, why could not the Jews—who were equipped by nature with the same principles of reasoning—have had this very thought come to mind without any commerce with the Gentiles?

# ON THE RITE OF PRAYER, BOOK III
->Part<-

<meta>catchword: ali (referring to the next page's start)</meta>

Driven by a DESIRE FOR BETTER THINGS, we are compelled to advance into the Holy Place, despising the bond of the flesh with a great spirit. It is certain that a similar gesture is employed by the Jews during the recitation of the *Kedusha* <note>The "Sanctification" prayer, where participants proclaim God's holiness</note>, whether in the *Shemoneh Esrei* <note>The "Eighteen Benedictions," the central prayer of the Jewish liturgy</note> blessing, or in the formula *Uva Letzion* <note>"And a redeemer shall come to Zion," a prayer containing the Kedusha verses</note>; for the reason behind both is undoubtedly the same. 

<margin>Buxtorf, *The Jewish Synagogue*, chapter 10, page 208.</margin>
Let us hear the famous Buxtorf on this matter: *“In the section of this prayer, the Shemoneh Esrei, which they call the Kedusha, when they utter those words: ‘Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of Hosts, the whole earth is full of His glory,’ they lift their eyes toward heaven to stir up greater devotion. They move their whole body as if trembling before the awesome Holiness of God, and at the same time, they leap upward as if to equal themselves with the Angels, who were the first to bring forth this hymn, or as if to ascend to God. Yet they immediately spring back, because it is impossible either to approach God or to grasp His nature and essence in this mortal life. One egg is not more like another than these two gestures.”* Both gestures are used in the **invocation** <note>Original Greek: προσφωνήσει (*prosphonese*), meaning a formal address or call to prayer</note> of prayer for exactly the same reasons: to signify a supreme desire for heavenly things and a contempt for earthly ones, or to show reverence toward God.

<margin>*Orach Chajim* <note>The "Path of Life," a section of the code of Jewish law</note> chapter 75.</margin>
Furthermore, what Buxtorf records here is taken from the instructions of **Rabbi Jacob ben Asher**, where these are the words: <note>Original Hebrew: הגי' בני ספרד ליתן עיניה' למטה בשעה שאומרי' ק' ק' ק' ובני אשכנז וצרפת נותנים עיניהן למעל' ונושאין גופן כלפי מעלה.</note> *“It is the custom of the Spanish sons [Sephardim] to cast their eyes downward at the time they say ‘Holy, Holy, Holy’; but the sons of Germany [Ashkenazim] and France lift their eyes to the heights and raise their bodies upward.”*

δ. It is a matter of tradition that Christians, when praying, turned themselves toward the **East**. Tertullian says: *“From this arises the suspicion (namely, that the Sun is worshipped by Christians), because it has become known that we pray toward the region of the East.”* 

<margin>In *Apology*, chapter 16. See Suicer, in the place cited, page 150. The famous Huet, *On Paradise*, chapter 3, § 3.</margin>
Learned men have long investigated why the Christians established this, though it remains uncertain whether they have yet grasped the true reason for that rite. Among them are those who think that Christians wished to distinguish themselves by this rite from the Jews, who turned toward the **West** in their prayers. However, since the first Christians were from the Jews, and in other rites they followed the customs of the Synagogue willingly and sometimes tenaciously (as is clear enough from the Paschal controversy, which troubled the Asian Churches for some time)...

# CHAPTER 19. IN THE CHURCH.

<margin>
But it seems more probable to me that the Church followed this custom for the purpose of distinguishing itself from the religion of the Jews, whose Temple lay toward the West. Book 1, Part 3, chapter 3.
</margin>
...distracted others in the second century) what reason would there have been for Christians to directly oppose the Jews in this rite simply to distinguish themselves? It seems more probable, therefore, that Christians imitated the Jews in this gesture, as they did in many others. For since all those Jews who inhabited the regions of the world located to the West of Jerusalem and the Temple turned toward the East in their prayers, and since all the Jewish Christians—who lived in no small numbers in Asia Minor, Greece, Italy, and even Africa—did not abandon this custom of theirs after receiving the Gospel faith in the early days of Christianity, but turned toward the East in prayer (whether directly or indirectly, depending on the various locations) according to the discipline of the Synagogue, it is possible that the Gentile Christians followed that custom, and that the practice finally prevailed among them. But since I have discussed this in earlier sections, I will add no more now.

8. It is acknowledged by everyone that the Church received from the Synagogue the rite of the **formal address** <note>original Greek: προσφωνήσεως (*prosphoneseos*), a call to prayer or liturgical address</note> of the little word *Amen* at the conclusion of prayers poured out by the leader of the church. This is clearly mentioned in Paul’s first Epistle to the Corinthians: *Since if you give a blessing in the Spirit, how will one who fills the place of the uninstructed* **SAY AMEN** *at your Thanksgiving?* <note>1 Corinthians 14:16; original Greek: πῶς ἐρεῖ τὸ ἀμὴν ἐπὶ τῇ σῇ εὐχαριστίᾳ</note> Justin Martyr is a brilliant witness that this rite continued in the Church after the time of the Apostles, describing the sacred rites of the Christians: *And the presiding officer likewise, as far as he is able, sends up prayers and thanksgivings, and the people acclaim him, saying: AMEN.* <note>original Greek: Καὶ ὁ προεστὼς εὐχὰς ὁμοίως καὶ εὐχαριστίας... Justin Martyr was an early Christian apologist writing around 150 AD.</note> In the liturgies <note>original: Leiturgiis</note> of the ancient Church, which are nonetheless from more recent times, nothing is more familiar than this. In the works of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, this act is called: *completing the prayer* <note>original Greek: συμπληρῶσαι τὴν εὐχήν (*symplerosai ten euchen*)</note>. But it especially deserves our observation that a notable example of this **response** <note>original Greek: ἀντιφωνήσεως (*antiphoneseos*), meaning a responsive or back-and-forth chant</note> occurs in the Book of Revelation itself, where the heavenly assembly is said to respond "Amen" to the angels (acting as representatives of the Church) and the holy gathering of the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders as they lead the praises of God. *And I saw,* says John, *and I heard the voice of many angels around the throne, the living creatures, and the elders, the number of whom was thousands of thousands and ten thousands of ten thousands, saying with a loud voice: Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and...*

### ON THE RITE OF PRAYER BOOK III. PART II

...power, and honor, and glory, and blessing: And the four living creatures said: Amen: And those four animals responded: AMEN. <note>The author is quoting Revelation 5:12–14, describing a scene of heavenly worship.</note>

Here you have the Heavenly assembly formed after the manner of the Synagogue. The Angels lead the praises and Blessings of God, just like the Envoys of the Church <note>A reference to the *Shaliach Tzibbur*, the prayer leader in a synagogue.</note> in Synagogues and the Presiders in Christian Churches; and the four living creatures with the twenty-four Elders, representing the Assembly of the Church, respond antiphonally <note>original Greek: ἀντιφωνῶσι (*antiphonōsi*)</note> with that common word: AMEN.

<margin>Sermon 6 on the Lord's Prayer, page 242.</margin>
7. Just as in the Synagogue other exhortations <note>original Greek: ἐγκελεύσεις (*enkeleuseis*)</note> were also interspersed with the Sacred rites, to which the People sang in response through antiphons, so it is possible that in certain early Churches a similar Rite prevailed, even if it is more difficult to prove this regarding those first times of Christianity. However, it is clear from Cyprian <note>St. Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), an early Christian writer and bishop.</note> that there were ancient antiphonal responses <note>original Greek: ἀντιφωνήματα (*antiphōnemata*)</note> of this kind, similar to the Synagogue's exhortations: *Therefore also the Priest, before the prayer, having first delivered a Preface, prepares the minds of the brethren by saying:* LIFT UP YOUR HEARTS <note>original Latin: *SURSUM CORDA*</note>: *so that while the People respond:* WE LIFT THEM UP UNTO THE LORD <note>original Latin: *HABEMUS AD DOMINUM*</note>, *they may be warned that they ought to think of nothing else than the Lord.* In the Liturgies that later appeared under the false names of James, Chrysostom, and others, there truly occur exclamations <note>original Greek: ἐπιφωνήματα (*epiphonēmata*)</note> following the preceding exhortations, entirely similar to those of the Synagogue, but which are certainly known to belong to more recent times. Thus certainly that exclamation, which occurs more than once in the Liturgy of <margin>page 70, 71.</margin> Chrysostom: *Blessed be our God always, now, and ever, and unto the ages of ages, Amen* <note>original Greek: Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν πάντοτε, νῦν, καὶ ἀεὶ, καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων, Ἀμήν</note>; exactly corresponds with the Hebrew exclamation: *Blessed be the Lord who is blessed forever and ever* <note>original Hebrew: ברוך ה' המבורך לעולם ועד (*Baruch Adonai ha-mevorach l'olam va'ed*)</note>.

4. In the Circumstances of prayer, the Church's prayers also agreed with those of the Synagogue.

<margin>Clement of Rome, Epistle to the Corinthians, section 40, page 95, from the Colomies edition.</margin>
1. Just as the Jews conformed the Sacred rites of the Synagogue in terms of manner and time, as much as possible, to the Sacred rites of the Temple, and thus had fixed *times of Prayer* corresponding to the times of the offerings, so it seems to be inferred from Clement of Rome <note>An early Church Father and Bishop of Rome, traditionally considered the author of an epistle to the Corinthians around 96 AD.</note> that the first Christians followed the Jews in this regard. Behold his words on this matter, worthy of note: *Since, therefore, these things are clear to us, looking even into the depths of Divine knowledge, we ought to do all things in order and in their proper place, which the Lord has commanded us to perform: to fulfill the offerings and sacred services at appointed times* <note>original Greek: κατὰ καιροὺς τεταγμένους τάς τε προσφορὰς καὶ λειτουργίας ἐπιτελεῖσθαι</note>; *nor did he want these things to be done randomly or in a disordered way, but at fixed times and hours* <note>original Greek: ἀλλ' ὡρισμένοις καιροῖς καὶ ὥραις</note>, *and where and by whom he wishes them to be performed.*

β. The First Christians, following the example of the Synagogue, prayed *three times* a day, and specifically *in the morning, in the afternoon, and in the evening*, not to mention their nocturnal Prayers. Clement of Alexandria says: "But if some assign fixed and defined hours for Prayer, as for example the third, sixth, and ninth <note>These correspond to 9:00 AM, 12:00 PM, and 3:00 PM.</note>; yet he who is endowed with knowledge prays throughout his whole life." <note>original Greek: Εἰδέ τινες καὶ ὥρας τακτὰς ἀπονέμεσιν εὐχῇ, ὡς τρίτην φέρε καὶ ἕκτην καὶ ἐννατην; original Latin: Quodsi nonnulli certas & definitas horas constituunt Precationi, ut v. g. tertiam, sextam, & nonam; at is, qui cognitione præditus est, per totam orat vitam.</note> Cyprian is much occupied with this, and is too prolix for his words to be fully transcribed here. However, while Persecution was active, the Christians could not observe these times in public, and therefore this refers primarily to private Prayers.

<margin>Apology 2, page 98.</margin>
<margin>William Cave, Primitive Christianity, chapter 9. Apology, chapter 39.</margin>
γ. In Public Sacred rites, the Christians of the first age seem to have performed the *Rite of Prayer* after the Reading of the Divine Word and the Sermon, just as the Jews on Sabbaths and Feasts followed the Reading of the Law and the Prophets with <term>musaf (Hebrew: מוסף)</term>, which are *additional prayers*. Regarding the order observed in the most ancient times of Christian Sacred rites, no record is clearer than the *Apology of Justin* <note>Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD), an early Christian apologist.</note>, which we have already mentioned several times. There, Justin says that two solemn Prayers were poured out to God in the Assemblies of Christians; the *former* being those common prayers in which they included all things necessary for soul and body, the State and the Church, along with Thanksgivings; the *latter* being those by which the Symbols of the Lord’s Supper were consecrated. I do not think it can be proven from any testimony of ancient times that solemn Prayers were made by the Presider before the Reading of the Divine Word, although a certain learned man has recently inclined toward that view. Certainly, the passage from Tertullian <note>Tertullian (c. 155–220 AD), a prolific early Christian author from Carthage.</note> concerning the *Prayers of the Church*, noted above, does not support it. Tertullian is speaking of those same Prayers which Justin records as being solemnly performed *after the Reading of the Divine Word*, which was followed by the *Sermon*. Those prayers are therefore to be compared with those *Prayers* which the Jews solemnly poured forth on Sabbaths and Feasts after the Reading of the Law and the Prophets.

Because the Synagogue repeated those same prayers twice in the same sacred rites, the early Christian Church rightly avoided this as a form of idle babbling <note>The author uses the Greek word βαττολογία (battologia), referring to the "vain repetitions" Jesus warned against in Matthew 6:7.</note>.

5. Among the *Additions to Prayer* I rightly place **Hymns and Songs**, by which Christians celebrated God in their assemblies, though it seems they did so following the example of the Synagogue. For Psalms and Hymns were intended, as far as I have been able to see, to be part of the solemn worship in which a leader preceded the congregation; but they were also composed or sung by private individuals at their own discretion, though sometimes for the edification of everyone, especially while the *Agapae* <note>The 'Love-Feasts' or communal meals of the early Christians.</note> were being celebrated. For Justin Martyr, in describing the sacred rites of the Christians, *makes no mention of singing.* <margin>Apology, chapter 39.</margin> What could Tertullian write more clearly in favor of this opinion when he depicts the *Agapae*? He *says*: *“After the washing of hands and the bringing of lights, each is invited to* SING TO GOD IN THE MIDST <note>original: MEDIUM DEO CANERE</note>, *whether from the Holy Scriptures or from his own genius, as he is able.”* From this it is proven how they drank. <margin>The Tutor, book 2, chapter 4, page 122. Book 5, chapter 28. Book 7, chapter 27. Canon 59. 1 Corinthians 14:26.</margin> I am further confirmed in this opinion because I see that Clement of Alexandria requires of all Christians the duty of celebrating God with hymns and songs at their tables. Moreover, Eusebius mentions a two-fold custom of this singing, in which private individuals composed and sang hymns: first where he speaks of *Theodotus the Tanner*, and then where he speaks of *Paul of Samosata*—even if he did not think that the “private psalms” <note>original Greek: ψαλμοὺς ἰδιωτικοὺς; these refer to uninspired or non-scriptural compositions.</note> mentioned in the *Canons of the Council of Laodicea* belonged here. This custom undoubtedly flowed to the Church from that free Apostolic tradition, full of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, by which certain of the believers were moved and led to be inspired by the Spirit even outside the regular order; although in subsequent times, as the gifts of the Spirit ceased, this liberty was taken away from the believers. <margin>† See Canon 15 of the Council of Laodicea, and in Justin Martyr, Questions and Responses to the Orthodox, 57. Epistle to Trajan, book 10, Letter 97.</margin> Certain "Cantors" (Singers) were then appointed for the solemn singing of the Church, and the common people were not to recite anything outside of their prescribed formulas. Furthermore, regarding the singing of the Church which was joined with the *Eucharist*, I refer to certain words of Pliny, in which he says that *“the Christians were accustomed to meet on a fixed day before dawn, and to recite a song to Christ as if to a God antiphonally between themselves, and to bind themselves by a Sacrament* <note>The Latin word 'sacramentum' here originally referred to a Roman soldier’s oath of loyalty.</note> *not to some crime, but against theft, etc.; which being finished, it was their custom to depart.”* These things pertain to the rites of the Holy Supper, with which they joined Hymns and Songs, and undoubtedly to the hymns composed by private individuals in honor of *Christ, God and Savior*, whether they were sung by individual members of the Church or by the whole body of believers.

## CHAPTER XX.

-> *The Rite of the* PRIESTLY BLESSING, *or* <term>the Lifting of the Hands <note>Hebrew: *Neshiat Kapayim*</note></term>, *as it is usually celebrated by Priests in the Synagogues, is explained and compared with the Rite of the Church. Since this assumes that Priests descended from Aaron still survive among the Jews to this day, this fact is proven in advance.* <-

<margin>Numbers 6: 23, 24</margin>
Finally, according to our plan, we must mention the act of the <term>PRIESTLY BLESSING <note>Hebrew: *Birkat Kohanim*</note></term>, or the <term>Lifting of the Hands <note>Hebrew: *Neshiat Kapayim*</note></term>. According to Divine Institution, this was to be celebrated by the Priests in sacred religious rites; it was performed first in the Temple, then solemnly in the ancient Synagogue by the Priests, and is still celebrated in the more recent ones. Since our discussion assumes that the *Families of the Priests*, distinct from the others, have been preserved down to our own times, it is necessary to say a few words by way of introduction to clarify this argument.

It is well known from the Mosaic Writings that God, in the arrangement of the Old Covenant, chose the *tribe of Levi* to serve the religion in the Tabernacle and Temple; and within the tribe of Levi, He designated only the *Family of Aaron* to perform the sacred rites at the altar. It is likewise known that the Priests and Levites kept their families and tribe distinct from other families and tribes until the commonwealth was overthrown by the Romans.

For our purposes, therefore, I only wish it to be observed that the Hebrew nation boasts that this same *tribe of Levi and the Aaronite families* were not confused with the other tribes and families of the Israelites after that destruction of the state, but that a great part, if not all, still survive as whole and distinct from the rest. This is even explicitly assumed in *Civil Law*, <margin>Law 4. Theodosian Code regarding Jews and Sky-worshippers.</margin> in describing the leaders of Synagogues and the ministers of the **PRIESTS** <note>The author uses the Latinized Greek term *Hiereorum* to refer to the Jewish Cohanim/Priests.</note>, this...

...this makes explicit mention of *Priests* <note>original Latin: *Sacerdotum*</note>. This is assumed in two places by Aelius Lampridius in his *History of Alexander Severus* <note>Aelius Lampridius is one of the purported authors of the *Historia Augusta*, a collection of biographies of Roman Emperors.</note>, as noted long ago by Petit, where both *High Priests* <note>original Greek: *Archierei*</note> and *Priests* <note>original Latin: *Sacerdotes*</note> are mentioned concerning the Jewish affairs of that time. Then there is Maimonides <note>Rabbi Moses ben Maimon (1138–1204), a foundational Jewish philosopher and legal scholar.</note> and those who followed him; when discussing the *Reading* of the Law (in which Priests and Levites are given precedence over others in order) and the *Priestly Blessing* as it is still celebrated in the Synagogues, they assume it as a certain fact about which no one should doubt. <margin>

Jewish Customs, book 1, chapter 12.

—is observed among the Jews. This ritual was described not only by Leon of Modena <note>A famous 17th-century Venetian Rabbi and scholar.</note> but also by the distinguished Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629) was a celebrated Christian Hebraist who wrote extensively on Jewish customs.</note>. Likewise, Paul of Burgos <note>A 14th-century Spanish Rabbi who converted to Christianity and became a Bishop; he wrote influential additions to Nicholas of Lyra's biblical commentaries.</note> himself, in the Preface to his Son which he prefixed to the Bible of Lyra, states that he was descended from the tribe of *Levi*. Nor should I fail to mention other Jews of no small reputation, some of whom have adopted for themselves the name <term>Kohen <note>Hebrew: כהן, meaning "Priest"</note></term>. However, I have found that among the Ancients, Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople.</note>, and among the Moderns, Petit, opposed this Jewish boast, arguing that such *Priests* are no longer recognized among them—

<margin>Oration 3 against the Jews.</margin>
—though for different reasons. For Chrysostom does not so much deny that certain individuals among the Jews claim descent from the family of Aaron, but he strongly contends, as is his habit, that the title of *Priest* does not *apply* to them. This is because they have not been inaugurated according to the pattern of the Priests of the Law, nor does God further attest to their Priesthood through clear arguments as He once did for the Aaronite Priesthood. But Chrysostom seems to be of the opinion that the name *Priest* among the Jews is not truly used for those persons thought to be descended from Aaron, but generally for *Teachers of the Law*, who, by virtue of their office, correspond to the ancient Priests.

<margin>Place cited.</margin>
They were called *PRIESTS* <note>original Greek: *HIEREI*</note>, he says, and *HIGH PRIESTS* <note>original Greek: *ARCHIEREI*</note>, not because they were of the priestly lineage, but because they performed the task of instructing the people in Jerusalem and reading and interpreting the Law in the Synagogues—a task that had formerly belonged to the *PRIESTS* as long as the Jewish state existed. In truth, those who are called *Priests* in the Synagogue bear this name because they boast that they are the true progeny of Aaron, and many of them are regarded as such by their fellow tribesmen. Yet I have no doubt that few among them can prove the succession of their families since the Destruction of the Temple, and therefore most of them boast of this prerogative in vain, shamefully deceiving their fellow tribesmen in this regard.

However, there is a reason for us not to think that everyone who claims this name for themselves does so falsely; it is because the matter itself is not "among the impossible things" <note>original Greek: *ἐκ τῶν ἀδυνάτων*</note>, and it is established from elsewhere that Priests were always most diligent regarding their families. They always held their lineage in the highest regard because of the privileges connected to their birth. A remarkable passage on this exists from Josephus in his *Discourse Against Apion* <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD) was a Jewish historian; *Against Apion* is his defense of Jewish antiquity and law.</note>, which is entirely worthy of being transcribed here. After he had said that his ancestors carefully provided that the *priestly race should be kept unmixed and pure* <note>original Latin: *genus Sacerdotale conservarent ἄμικτον καὶ καθαρόν*</note>, *he proceeds in this manner:*

<margin>Book 1, *Against Apion*, page 1036.</margin>

For it is necessary that he who participates in the priesthood should father children from a wife of the same nation, and not look to wealth or other honors, but examine the lineage, taking the succession from the ancient records and providing many witnesses. And we do these things not only in Judea itself, but wherever there is a community of our race, and there too accurate care is preserved by the priests concerning marriages. I speak of those who dwell in Egypt and Babylon, and if in any other part of the inhabited world there are some scattered from the priestly race. <note>The author provides both the Greek original and a Latin translation for this quote; the translation provided here covers the content of both.</note>

<margin>\* Gelenius: To be born from a woman of the same nation.</margin>

<margin>† Thus Selden translates these words elsewhere: *On the Succession to the High Priesthood*, book 2, chapter 3, page 198.</margin>

If these things are truly so, it is not particularly surprising that certain priestly families have traced the succession of their race even down to later times. Yet even if this [genealogical claim] should fail, it is sufficient for us that some people present themselves as such, and that this is accepted by common faith among the Jewish nation itself.

Furthermore, just as God willed these Priests in the Old Economy <note>The "Old Economy" refers to the religious system of the Old Testament/Covenant.</note> to be mediators through whom the Israelites might approach Him, so He willed them to fulfill His own role and place in the *Blessing*, with which they were required to favor the Israelites, solemnly gathered in the Sanctuary, according to the Divine Command. Mention of that Divine Command occurs in the writings of Moses, in these words: *And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:*

<margin>Numbers 6:22, 23.</margin>

*Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying:* **Thus you shall bless the children of Israel** <note>original Hebrew: כה תברכו את בני ישראל</note>, *saying to them: The Lord bless you, and keep you: The Lord make his face shine*

*...upon you, and show favor to you: may the Lord <note>original: Jehova</note> lift up His countenance upon you and grant you peace.* <note>These are the concluding words of the Priestly Blessing from Numbers 6:24–26.</note> 
<margin>See 2 Chronicles 30:27.</margin> That this was diligently observed by them as long as the Sanctuary stood, they themselves most clearly testify in the Body of Traditions <note>The Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note>, and we have no reason to doubt it.

Indeed, not only in the Temple, but also in the Synagogue—not just in Canaan, but also outside of it—they fulfill this duty of theirs; they consider themselves bound to do so by that Divine Law which we just cited. Truly, the words of the Law contain a general command <note>Latin: *Præceptum*</note>, the observance of which is not restricted to any specific place. Since this is established both by experience and by the most clear testimonies of the Masters <note>The Rabbis</note>, the only thing that can be questioned or disputed here is how and in what circumstances and cases this Ritual is performed by them.

<margin>Regarding Sotah, chapter 7, sections 6, pages 671 & 672, and the Excerpts of the Gemara, chapter 7, number 38, page 811. However, there have been learned men who have anticipated our diligence in this matter. For not only has the celebrated Wagenseil <note>Johann Christoph Wagenseil (1633–1705), a Christian Hebraist</note> explained this ritual clearly enough in his commentary on the *Sotah* (where the difference is noted between the Priestly Blessing as it occurred in the Temple and in the Synagogues), but also the renowned Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a famous Hebraist</note> himself, in the pages added to his completed work *On the Synagogue*, gave a very accurate description of this ceremony according to the Ritual of the Jews. We rightly refer our reader to those works. We would not repeat what has been well said elsewhere without necessity; nevertheless, since we have been quite detailed in explaining other ceremonies, let us say a few things here from Maimonides regarding this ritual, including some details of the kind that are not commonly read in those other authors.

The Ritual itself is described by Maimonides in these words:

That is, outside Jerusalem. ### CHAPTER 20. IN THE SYNAGOGUE.

<margin>† The 18 Prayers <note>Referring to the *Shemoneh Esrei* or Amidah, the central standing prayer of Jewish liturgy.</note></margin>
...he has finished the † Confession <note>original: *Confessionem*; here referring to the *Modim* or thanksgiving prayer in the liturgy</note>; they immediately turn their faces toward the Synagogue Congregation, and extend their fingers, and raise their hands to their shoulders, and begin to pronounce: *The Lord bless you*, etc. And the Envoy of the Congregation <note>term: *Legatus Ecclesiæ*, known in Hebrew as the *Sheliach Tzibbur* or prayer leader</note> leads them in the words of the Blessing word for word, with them repeating, according to what is said: *And saying to them*, etc. When they have finished the first verse, the whole Synagogue assembly responds: **Amen**: which being done, the Envoy of the Congregation immediately returns to his duty and leads them through the second verse word for word, with them repeating until they have finished the second verse, when the whole Assembly again responds **Amen**: which they likewise perform in the recitation of the third verse.

To understand these words of Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Jewish scholar</note> more clearly, it should be noted that this Priestly Blessing is pronounced by the Priests toward the end of those Eighteen, or Nineteen, Prayers of which I made mention above. When the Envoy of the Congregation reaches the Seventeenth Prayer of the Eighteen, which begins: *Be pleased, O Lord*, etc. then the Priests, as many as are present in the Synagogue, proceed to the Platform <note>original: *Suggestum*, referring to the *Duchan* where the Priests stand</note>, with their faces turned toward the Ark, their hands still closed in a fist, and there they recite with the Congregation the Eighteenth Prayer, the theme of which is: *We give thanks* <note>original: *Modim*</note>, etc. After this has been recited, they perform this Rite of Blessing; so that the Priestly Blessing intervenes between the Eighteenth Prayer and the Nineteenth—or the last of those famous Nineteen—which begins with the words: <term>Sim Shalom</term>, <term>Grant peace</term>, etc. <note>original Hebrew: שים שלום</note>. Moreover, the Priests, about to pronounce the Blessing, begin it themselves with the word <term>Yevarechecha</term> <note>original Hebrew: יברכך; "May [the Lord] bless you"</note>, after which word has been uttered by them, the Envoy of the Congregation leads them through all the other words, one after another.

<margin>Orach Chajim chapter 128. <note>A section of the *Shulchan Aruch*, the standard code of Jewish law.</note></margin>
This is more clearly perceived from the *Orach Chajim* than from Maimonides: <term>The Priests begin to say "May He bless you," and afterward the prayer leader recites to them word for word and they answer after him for every word until they finish the first verse, and then the congregation answers Amen.</term> <note>original Hebrew: מתחילין הכהנים לומר יברכך ואחר כך מקרא אותם ש״צ מלה במלה והם עונין אחריו על כל מלה עד שיסיימו פסוק ראשון ואז עונין הצבור אמן</note> The Priests begin to say: *May He bless you*: and afterward the Envoy of the Congregation reads before them the Formula of Blessing word by word, and they repeat each word after him, until they have finished the first verse, when the Synagogue Assembly responds **Amen**.

Furthermore, in the act of Blessing, Maimonides says the Priests extend their fingers, which were previously turned toward the palm of the hand,
