<margin>loc. cit. <note>original: *loco citato*; in the place previously cited.</note></margin>...when he described this Gesture of the Priests in these words: *Then they expand their hands and spread their fingers, so that they make five spaces or intervals between them; namely, four between each individual finger: and a fifth between the two thumbs, so that the Divine Majesty may reside in them and have a place.*

<margin>Chapter 28. §. 12.</margin>In the *Orach Chajim* <note>The "Path of Life," a major code of Jewish Law.</note> these things are handed down slightly differently:
*And they stretch out their hands: and they intend to make five air-spaces between the sets of fingers, dividing their fingers so there is one space for every two fingers, and a space between the finger and the thumb, and between one thumb and the other thumb* —
> *And they extend their hands, and spread their fingers, and take care that there are five intervals among them: one space between two fingers of each hand: (that is, the two first fingers of each hand ought to be joined together, and likewise the two later ones; from which therefore come two spaces: namely one in the middle of the fingers of each hand) and between the finger and the thumb.* This is indeed correct. Thus we have five intervals in total: specifically, one between the middle fingers of each of the two hands, but not **four for each individual finger**. <note>The author is clarifying a technical point of "sacred geometry"—how the fingers are grouped to create "windows" through which God's presence is said to shine during the blessing.</note>

<margin>Maimonides, in the place cited. §. 1 & 14.</margin>This Rite can be carried out in Synagogues whenever the Synagogue offers solemn Prayers to God—that is, in the Morning Prayers, the Additional Prayers <note>The *Musaf* service.</note>, and the Evening Prayers <note>Referring here to the concluding service of fasts, like *Neilah*, as the Priestly Blessing is not typically performed in standard night services.</note>—with the exception only of the Afternoon prayers. In the Sanctuary <note>The Temple in Jerusalem.</note>, it was observed only in the Morning Prayers and only once per day. Afternoon prayers are excepted because there may be a fear that the Priests might have drunk a little too "cheerfully" at lunch, and would thereby be unfit to perform this ceremony with as much reverence as the Divine Majesty, whose Person they represent, requires.

<margin>Maimonides, Laws of Prayer, Chapter 15. §. 1. Chapter 14. §. 12. §. 10. §. 8. Chapter 14. §. 12. One thing we must not neglect to mention is that if by chance no Priest were present in the Synagogue, the Envoy of the Congregation <note>term: *Legatus Ecclesiæ*; the *Sheliach Tzibbur* or prayer leader.</note> would nevertheless imitate this Rite of Holy Blessing in a certain way, so that the Synagogue Gathering would not be dismissed without a Blessing. Understand this matter from Maimonides: <note>original Hebrew: ואם אין להם כהן כלל כשיגיע שליח ציבור לשים שלום אומר אלהינו ואלהי אבותינו וכו׳; "If they have no priest at all, when the representative of the congregation reaches the 'Grant Peace' [prayer] he says, 'Our God and God of our fathers...'"</note> *If there is no Priest at all in the Synagogue, when the Legate of the Assembly <term>Legatus Ecclesiæ; the Shaliach Tzibur or prayer leader</term> reaches the final prayer of the Eighteen Benedictions <note>The "Precatio Octodenarum" refers to the Amidah, the central prayer of Jewish liturgy.</note>, which begins with "Grant Peace" [Sim Shalom], he says: "Our God, and God of our Fathers, bless us with that triple blessing which exists in the Law, written by Moses, your servant, and spoken by the mouth of Aaron and his sons, the Priests, with your holy people; as it is said: 'May the Lord bless you,' etc. 'And they shall put my name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them'" <margin>Numbers 6:22.</margin> (though the people do not respond "Amen").* After which he begins the prayer: *Grant Peace*. But if the Minister of the Synagogue, who himself recites the *Prayers* before the Ark, is a Priest, and no other descendant of Aaron <margin>See Maimonides, in the place cited.</margin> is found in the entire Synagogue gathering, they wish him to abstain from pronouncing the Blessing for fear of confusion; unless perhaps he feels so confident in his presence of mind that he can skillfully perform both acts without being disturbed.

Whether the Christian Church emulated the Synagogue in this rite, as it did in most others, who can say? Justin Martyr and Tertullian, describing the public sacred rites of the Christians, make no mention of this *Blessing*. However, as the Christian rites were celebrated after the fourth century from the birth of Christ, it is quite certain that the solemn *Priestly Blessing* found a place among many other ceremonies. It was solemnly pronounced by the Bishop himself after the dismissal of the Catechumens <note>Those receiving instruction before baptism who were asked to leave before the Eucharist began.</note> and shortly before the celebration of the Lord's Supper, as is evident from the *Apostolic Constitutions* <margin>Book 2. chapter 57.</margin> that appeared under the name of Clement, where the order of sacred rites as celebrated in the Christian Church is described.

### ON THE OFFICES OF DEACONS, BOOK III, PART II.

These duties could be performed by any free and trained Israelite, and they were often performed with the *President of the Synagogue* distributing those sacred duties, as was observed above from <margin>On the tractate *Sotah*, chapter 7, section 7.</margin> Jarchi <note>Rashi, the medieval French rabbi</note>; and likewise, the Blessing could be celebrated by any Priests (whether one or several). In that ancient Synagogue, the offices of the **CHAZZANITARUM**, or *Ministers of the Synagogue* properly so-called, were of a lowlier sort, and truly diaconal <term>diakonika; service-oriented or ministerial</term>, such as one might rightly expect from *Sacristans* or *Ministers of Sacred Rites*. Although we could discuss these at greater length, we have determined to deal with them briefly, as we have long been yearning for the end of this current labor of ours. Therefore, in the Ancient Synagogue, the Offices of the **CHAZZANITARUM**, or the **DEACONS OF THE SYNAGOGUE**, were:

<margin>Chapter 4, verse 20.</margin> 1. *To bring the Book of the Law out of the Ark and hand it to the Reader, or place it before him, and to return the same to the Ark.* This duty of the attendant <note>original Greek: τοῦ ὑπηρέτου</note> has already been noted by us from the Gospel of Luke, where it speaks of the Lord about to preach in the synagogue: "And having rolled up the book, giving it back to the attendant, he sat down." <note>Luke 4:20</note> This same task is attributed to the Minister in the <margin>Chapter 7, section 7.</margin> tractate *Sotah*: <note>original Hebrew: חזן הכנסת נוטל ספר תורה ונותנו לראש הכנסת</note> THE MINISTER OF THE SYNAGOGUE *takes the Book of the Law, and hands it to the President of the <margin>Chapter 1, page 893.</margin> Synagogue.* Here, Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> confirms the same in the words we described above.

<margin>Laws of Prayer, chapter 12, section 20.</margin> 2. *To call the Readers at the command or discretion of the President of the Synagogue.* Maimonides <note>The 12th-century scholar Moses Maimonides</note> states: *When the Legate of the Assembly <term>Legatus Ecclesiæ; the prayer leader or Shaliach Tzibur</term> finishes the Morning Prayer, says the Kaddish, and brings out the Book of the Law,* <note>original Hebrew: וקורא לאחד, ואחד מן הצבור ועולין וקורין בתורה</note> *he calls the readers from the congregation one by one, who at his calling ascend the Platform <term>Suggestum; the Bimah or raised reading desk</term> and read from the Law.* It is certain and well-known that Maimonides here uses the term "Legate of the Assembly" in a more general sense to mean the *Chazzan* himself. For indeed, since all the Readers had to be called, by whom could they be more conveniently called than by the Chazzan at the discretion of the President? <margin>Maimonides, Laws of Prayer, chapter 12, section 7. Chapter 20, column 6.</margin> The *Colbo* <note>A 14th-century ritual work</note> states: <note>original Hebrew: אין הקורא רשאי לקרות עד שיאמר לו החזן לקרא</note> *The Reader is not permitted to read until the* MINISTER OF THE SYNAGOGUE *has called him to read.*

3. *To stand by the Readers, and to observe as well as pay attention to whether they read correctly.* Maimonides states: *And neither the Minister of the Synagogue, nor his* <margin>Chapter 12, section 7.</margin> *Prefect read of their own accord (without a preceding invitation), but they wait until the Assembly, or some most distinguished member of it, has invited them to read;* <note>original Hebrew: וצריך אחד לעמוד עמו בשעתי קריאה כדין חזן העומד עם הקורא</note> *And it is necessary that one should stand with him during the time of reading, just as the* CHAZZAN STANDS WITH THE READER.

### CHAPTER 21. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES.

IT IS CUSTOMARY FOR READERS. In the *Colbo* <note>A 14th-century Hebrew legal code on Jewish ritual</note> this is confirmed from the *Tosefta* <note>A collection of Jewish oral laws from the late 2nd century</note>: <margin>Colbo, chapter 20, On the Reading of the Law, column 6.</margin> **"If the Minister of the Synagogue reads, another stands by him to oversee him."** <note>original Hebrew: חזן העומד לקרות עומד אחד ומחזן עליו</note> Pay attention, I pray, my Reader, that here the word **Chazzan** <note>original Hebrew: חזן</note> means to observe and attend to the readers. Thus in the following passages on this same subject: **"But it is necessary that one of the congregation stand and oversee him,"** <note>original Hebrew: אבל צריך שיעמוד אחד מן הקהל ויחזן עליו</note> that is, it is necessary that someone from the assembly stand by him, and OBSERVE him, and assist him.

4. *Helping Readers in reading.* <margin>Chapter 20, column 4.</margin> The *Colbo* states: **"And Rabbenu Asher** <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel, a prominent 13th-century German-Spanish authority</note>, **of blessed memory, wrote that it is a commandment for each person to read for themselves; but if someone who does not know how to read accurately ascends to the platform, it is the duty of the Minister to help him quietly. Furthermore, if the one ascending is entirely unskilled in reading, let the Minister whisper every single word to him quietly, and the reader shall read aloud."** <note>original Hebrew: והר"אש ז"ל כתב מצוה לקרות... והקורא יקרא בקול רם.</note> See another passage on this from the Rituals: <margin>Orach Chajim, chapter 139, section 2.</margin> **"One who does not know how to read must be prevented from ascending to the Scroll of the Law. But if they need such a person who does not know how to read because he is a Priest or a Levite, and there is no one else besides him, if he knows how to repeat and read from the text as the Cantor prompts him word for word, he may ascend; but if not, he may not ascend."** <note>original Hebrew: מי שאינו יודע לקרות... ואם לאו לא יעלה</note> This means that he who is unskilled in reading should be stopped from going up to the pulpit. But if they have need of such a person because he is a Priest or a Levite, and no one else is present in the synagogue whom they can use, if such a Priest or Levite presumes that, with the Minister of the Synagogue leading him word for word, he can repeat it and read it along with the Scripture, he is allowed to ascend the pulpit; otherwise, he is not.

5. *To blow the trumpet and the horn in certain cases for the use of the Synagogue.* That the Trumpet <term>buccina; likely referring to the shofar or ram's horn</term> and the Horn <term>tuba; likely referring to straight metal trumpets</term> were used not only for the service of the Sanctuary <note>the Temple in Jerusalem</note> but also for the use of the synagogues, was proven in the previous Dissertation where we discussed the Instruments of the Synagogue, and confirmed by arguments in <margin>Book 1, Part I, chapter 10.</margin>. The approaching Sabbath was signaled by the Trumpet, the New Year was proclaimed, Excommunication was published, and the Horns were specifically blown on Fast days. We will not repeat what was said and proven there. This ministry, where it was not entrusted to others for the sake of honor, was undoubtedly to be performed by the Deacon of the Synagogue. Thus, the duty of signaling the approaching Sabbath by six blasts of the trumpet, on the eve—

### ON THE OFFICES OF DEACONS, BOOK III. PART ...

Regarding the Sabbath, the entire matter was Ministerial, and therefore it was to be carried out by the **Chazzans** <note>Ministers of the Synagogue</note>. Mention of this rite is found in the Tractate *Sabbath* <note>The section of the Talmud dealing with Sabbath laws</note>, and from there:

> Six blasts are sounded on the eve of the Sabbath: the first to stop the people from work in the fields; the second to stop work in the city; the third to light the lamp—these are the words of Rabbi Nathan. Rabbi Judah the Prince says: the third is to remove the phylacteries <note>original Hebrew: *tefillin*; ritual leather boxes containing scripture worn on the arm and head</note>; and he waits for the time it takes to roast a small fish or to bake bread in the oven, then he sounds a long blast, a wavering blast, and a long blast, and then the rest begins.

<margin>

Six trumpet blasts announced the approaching Sabbath on the eve of the Sabbath. With the first blast, workers in the fields were to cease their labor; with the second, workers in the city, and the shops were to be closed; at the third, the Sabbath lamps were to be lit, according to the opinion of Rabbi Nathan. However, according to Rabbi Judah the Prince, at the third blast, the Phylacteries were to be removed; and the minister then waits for about as much time as is required to roast a small fish or for bread to harden in the oven, and then he adds three more blasts—two with a long, drawn-out sound and a broken sound in the middle—and then the rest begins.

> Rabbi Jose, son of Hanina, says: I have heard that if one comes to light the lamp after the six blasts, he may light it, for the Sages gave the **MINISTER OF THE SYNAGOGUE** <note>original Hebrew: *Chazzan Ha-Knesset*</note> a short time to take his trumpet <note>original Hebrew: *shofaro*</note> back to his house and store it away.

Indeed, on the highest part of the city, there was a flat roof where the Minister of the Synagogue stood while blowing that trumpet, as is recorded in the Gemara and the Glosses of Rabbi Solomon <note>original: *R. Salomo*; referring to the 11th-century commentator Rashi</note>. We have touched upon other matters in the previous sections, so there is no need to repeat them. Thus, there seems to be no doubt that in cases of Excommunication and Fasts, the same duty was performed by this Minister of the Synagogue; though I am aware that in the Sanctuary <note>The Temple in Jerusalem</note> this was performed by the Priests, following the preliminary <unclear>summons</unclear> <note>original Greek: *keleusin*</note> of the Minister of the Synagogue. ### CHAPTER 21. OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

Those moved by a zealous devotion toward Religion considered it an honor to serve in the sacred rites out of hope for a *reward* <note>original: *mercedis*</note> that would later flow back to them. Rabbi Jacob ben Asher <note>A 14th-century authority on Jewish law</note> records that this custom is still observed among the Germans. He condemns the lukewarmness and irreverence of the Spaniards regarding sacred matters, who hire some man from the street for a fee to blow the Horn <note>original: *Buccinam*; referring to the Shofar or ram's horn used in liturgy</note>. 
<margin>Orach Chayim, chapter 585.</margin>
Certainly, since in the ancient Synagogue the *Minister of the Synagogue* <note>The Chazzan</note> was distinct from the *Messenger of the Congregation* <note>original: *Legato Ecclesiae*; the leader of prayer</note>, there is no doubt that this ministerial duty fell upon him to perform, unless someone else claimed it for themselves voluntarily and for the sake of honor.

<margin>Codex Sukkah, folio 51, column 2.</margin>
6. *The waving of a cloth in the larger Synagogues.*
Thus the Talmudic writers say concerning the *Platform of the Alexandrian Synagogue:* 
<note>original Hebrew: וחזן הכנסת עומד עליה והסודרין בידו וכיון שהגיע לענות אמן הלה מניף בסודר</note> 
*And the Minister of the Synagogue stood upon it, with a cloth <note>original: *sudario*; a linen wrap or signaling cloth</note> in his hand; and when the point was reached where the people were to respond "Amen," he would wave the cloth.* <note>In the massive synagogue of Alexandria, the building was so large that worshippers could not hear the prayer leader and needed a visual signal to know when to say Amen.</note>

<margin>Under the words *Chazzan* and *Sudar*.</margin>
In my first Dissertation on this subject, I asserted on the authority of Elijah Levita <note>A famous 16th-century Hebrew scholar and grammarian</note> that this duty belonged to the *Minister of the Synagogue*, to whom it truly pertained. But I know not what clouds later obscured my judgment, leading me to think it not improbable that the cloth was also waved in the Synagogue by the *Prefects* <note>The leaders or overseers</note>—although I have never entirely denied this role to the *Minister of the Synagogue*.

<margin>Jerusalem Talmud, Commentary on the final chapter of Hechalil.</margin>
My mind was swayed in that direction by a text of the Jerusalem Talmud, in which the *Minister of the Synagogue* <note>original Hebrew: וחזן הכנסת, Chazzan ha-Knesset</note>, standing on the Platform, seems to be distinguished from the *Appointed One* <note>original Hebrew: ממונה, Memune</note>, or *Official, who waves the cloth.* The words are as follows: 
<note>original Hebrew: ובימה של עץ באמצע וחזן הכנסת עומד עליה עמד אחד מהן לקרוא בתורה היה הממונה מניף בסודרין והן עונין אמין על כל ברכה וברכה</note> 
*And there was a wooden platform in the middle, and the MINISTER OF THE SYNAGOGUE stood upon it. One of them stood there to read from the Law. And the APPOINTED ONE (the Prefect or Official) would wave the cloth, and they would answer "Amen" after him at each and every blessing.*

<margin>Annotations on the New Testament, chapter 5. Shekalim chapter 5, section 1. Tamid chapter 7, section 3 and chapter 7, section 1. See also the Interpreters of Virgil.</margin>
In this passage, the *Appointed One* <note>Memune</note> waving the cloth seemed entirely distinct from the *Chazzan*, the Minister of the Synagogue. I was more easily led to believe this by the authority of Angelo Canini <note>A renowned 16th-century Italian linguist</note>, a most learned man, who cites this passage elsewhere, though in a fragmented form. To this was added the fact that I saw the word *Memune* used everywhere in Hebrew literature to designate *Prefects* to whom the care and oversight of some matter is committed; and I noticed that the duty of waving the cloth in the Temple was performed by the *Sagan* <note>The deputy High Priest</note>, and that he, in that same...

### ON THE OFFICES OF DEACONS Book III.

<margin>
Virgil, *Aeneid* book 5, verse 579.
Suetonius, *Life of Nero*, chapter 22; see also Torrentius's notes on that passage.
Book 12.

In this treatise, he is called the *Appointed One* <note>original Hebrew: ממונה (*Memunneh*); a title for an overseer or official</note>. The *Sagan* <note>A deputy to the High Priest</note> was the man of highest authority and dignity in the Temple after the High Priest; he seemed to have the same relationship to the Levites that the *Prefects of the Synagogue* had to its ministers. I should also mention that it was a custom among the Romans that when Magistrates presided over the games, they gave the signal to begin from a high place, specifically by means of a *mappa*—a small white cloth—which the Praetor would raise as a sign to commence the games or release the chariots from their stalls. No one could unreasonably compare such a cloth to the *Sudarium* <note>A linen wrap or handkerchief</note>. Suetonius writes: *After a meal was set out in the gardens among the servants for the common people as a trial, he presented himself to the eyes of everyone in the Circus Maximus, while some freedman dropped the* CLOTH <note>original Latin: *mappam*</note> *from the place where the Magistrates usually do.* Martial also writes:

->*When the Praetor wished to drop the chalk-white cloth,*<-
->*Hermogenes snatched the cloth from the Praetor.*<-

<margin>
In the same place, Book 2.
Exercise 5, chapter 2.
Petit, *Miscellaneous Readings*, chapter 24.
</margin>
Although these examples might free my opinion from the charge of absurdity, I have nonetheless gladly returned to my first judgment (which is the same judgment held by learned men such as Elias Levita among the Jews, and Morinus and Petit among the Christians) after I more diligently compared the passage in the Babylonian Talmud with that of the Jerusalem Talmud cited just above. Therefore, let us hereafter hold this view: that in the larger Synagogues, while the *Messenger of the Church* <note>original: *Legato Ecclesiae*; referring to the Shaliach Tzibur or prayer leader</note> recited the prayers in a lowly place before the Ark, many people far removed from him—either in the opposite or furthest part of the Synagogue—could not understand his voice distinctly. Thus, they did not know precisely when to respond with *Amen* or the Antiphon. Consequently, the *Minister of the Synagogue* <note>The Chazzan</note> gave a signal with some *Cloth* from the *Platform* <note>original: *Suggesto*; the raised podium or Bimah</note> that the *Blessing* was finished, from which the Synagogue understood that they must respond: *Amen*. As to what kind of cloth this *Sudarium* was, and in what manner the signal was given from the platform, these things are perhaps sought with more curiosity than they can be stated with certainty or solidity.

<margin>
In the *Aruch* <note>A famous 11th-century dictionary of the Talmud and Midrash</note>.
Questions, book 2, chapter 78.
</margin>
It is well-established that the word *Cloth* <note>original Hebrew: סודר (*Sudara*)</note> is of Latin origin, as Rabbi Nathan rightly observed; in the Latin language, it denotes *a linen cloth destined for wiping away sweat* <note>original Hebrew: מטפחת המיוחדת להעביר הזעה</note>, which is called *kapsidrotion* <note>original Greek: καψιδρώτιον</note> by the Greeks. To be sure, Drusius has questioned this elsewhere due to the difference in meaning of this word in common use among the Syrians and the Latins; he preferred to claim it for the Syrians, but if I am not mistaken, he did so without reason. For that difference is not as great as Drusius supposes. Among the Latins, it signifies *a linen cloth destined for wiping away sweat*; among the Syrians, it is *a linen cloth with which they veil the face.*

But who can doubt that those very linen cloths with which the face is veiled were called *sudaria* <note>original Latin: *sudaria*, plural of *sudarium*, derived from *sudor* (sweat)</note>, because they caught the sweat of the head? Suetonius writes: *As he was barefoot and dressed only in a tunic, he put on a cloak of a faded color, and with a* **CLOTH** *held before his face, he mounted his horse, with only four companions.* From this, who would wonder that <term>sudara</term> <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: סודרא; a wrap or turban</note> among the Chaldeans and <term>sudarian</term> <note>original Greek: σουδάριον; a napkin or handkerchief</note> among the Greek writers of the New Testament is used for a linen cloth, or a band, with which the head is veiled? Thus in the Gospel of John regarding Lazarus: *And his face was bound about with a cloth.* <note>John 11:44; original Greek: Καὶ ἡ ὄψις αὐτ͂ σουδαρίῳ περιεδέδετο</note> And concerning our Lord: *And the cloth that was on his head.* <note>John 20:7; original Greek: Καὶ τὸ σουδάριον, ὃ ἦν ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς αὐτ͂</note> However, the linen cloths that were carried in the hands, or with which the body was girded to receive the discharge of sweat, were called *Semicinctia*, or in Greek <term>semikinthia</term> <note>Acts 19:12; narrow cloths or aprons</note>, which are distinguished from *Sudaria* by Luke.

In this case which we are presently discussing, I believe that by *Sudarium* we should understand a certain band or linen cloth which was held in the hands of the Synagogue Minister in the manner of a <term>degel</term> <note>original Hebrew: דגל; a banner or standard</note>. Indeed, we gather this not only from the testimony of Maimonides <note>A renowned 12th-century Jewish scholar</note>, but also from other places in the Talmud in which mention is made of *waving the Sudaria*. Thus, regarding the Deputy <note>original Hebrew: סגן (*Sagan*)</note> who was about to give the signal to the Levites to begin their song, it is said: *And the Deputy waved the cloths.* <note>original Hebrew: והניף הסגן בסודרין</note> The illustrious Peringerus notes: *The Deputy of the Constant Offering (Tamid) stood near the corner holding a banner in his hand. Properly: The Deputy* **WAVED THE CLOTH.** Similarly, the Talmudic writers report that in the execution of a sentence of stoning carried out outside the city, a Minister would ordinarily stand at the door of the court holding a cloth in his hand, which he was to *wave* whenever anyone offered themselves to testify to the innocence of the accused. The text states: *One stood at the door of the house of judgment with the cloths in his hand.* <note>original Hebrew: אחד עומד על פתח בית דין והסודרין בידו</note> By the same example, when the Goat was led to the desert on the solemn Day of Atonement, Talmudic tradition holds that watchtowers were built along the way, and in them stood men *waving cloths* <note>original Hebrew: מניפין בסודרין</note>, so that the High Priest might understand from there at what time the Goat had reached the desert. These passages and examples lead us to think that by *sudarium* we must entirely understand a *certain linen band*, by the waving of which a signal could conveniently be given.

### ON THE DUTIES OF DEACONS, BOOK III, PART II.

<margin>here in chapter 1.</margin>
Since the <term>Chazzan</term> <note>original: *Chazzan*; a synagogue official whose role evolved from a communal attendant or "deacon" to a cantor</note> was the common servant of the synagogue, it is clear in itself that it was primarily his duty to clean the Holy House, guard the Sacred Instruments, and observe other ministerial duties of this kind which the dignity and order of the sacred rites demanded. This has been proven above from Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the famous 11th-century commentator</note> and Elias <note>Elias Levita, a 16th-century Hebrew grammarian</note>; although it requires no further proof, as it is sufficiently demonstrated by the name *Chazzan* itself. Let us take one more example from the *Orach Chajim* <note>The "Path of Life," a primary section of the Shulchan Aruch, the code of Jewish law</note>:

<margin>chapter 148, section 1.</margin>
*It is not permitted for the Minister of the Synagogue to strip the Ark in the presence of the community as long as they are gathered in the Synagogue.* <note>original Hebrew: *Ein shaliach tzibur rashai le'hafshit ha-teivah...*; original Latin translation: *Non licet Ministro Synagogæ denudare Arcam, quandiu Ecclesia in Synagoga congregata est.*</note>

<margin>See Josephus, *Jewish War*, book 1, chapter 5, page 720. Livy, book 30, chapter 17. *Aeneid*, book 8, verse 270; book 11, verse 835.</margin>
The name *Chazzan* is used here for the Chazzanes. Truly, then, these Chazzanes were <term>neokoroi</term> <note>original Greek: *νεωκόροι*; temple wardens or caretakers</note>, or what Livy would call <term>aeditui</term> <note>original Latin: *aeditui*; keepers of a temple</note>, who served in guarding the Holy Houses, sweeping them, and arranging the sacred rites. This was no less true in the religion of the People of God than among the Pagans, who themselves were called "Guardians" by Virgil:

> And the Pinarian house, the **GUARDIAN** of the Herculean rite, 
> established this altar in the grove. <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 8.270</note>

And again:

> But the **GUARDIAN** of the crossroads, Opis, has long 
> sat on the mountain peaks. <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 11.835</note>

<margin>Notes on Eusebius, book 1, chapter 6.</margin>
However, be careful not to confuse such *aeditui* or *Guardians of the Rites* with <term>hierodouloi</term> <note>original Greek: *ἱεροδούλοις*; temple slaves</note>, or *Slaves of the Rites*, such as the <term>Nethinim</term> <note>original: *Nethinæi*; a class of temple servants mentioned in the Bible, traditionally temple laborers</note> were among the Jews, about whom Valesius learnedly discusses elsewhere. For the ordinary wardens of Synagogues and Temples were free-born and honorable men, and they performed no work concerning the sacred rites that was beneath their social standing.

<margin>See the illustrious Prideaux on the *Marmora Oxoniensia*, 116.</margin>
Certainly, among the Pagans, the title of *neokoroi*, though first given to the lowliest ministers who swept the temple, was later claimed with great pride by the Priests themselves. Indeed, the ministers of the sacred rites among the Pagans were also called "Guardians"—those who led others in the words of the rites and watched to ensure that nothing was said contrary to tradition. This is exactly what the Chazzanites did, both by watching over the Readers and by leading the Priests in the words of the Blessing.

<margin>*Natural History*, book 28, chapter 2.</margin>
Pliny writes: *We have seen the highest magistrates supplicate with certain prayers. And so that no words are omitted or spoken out of order, one person leads from a script, while another* **IS GIVEN AS A GUARDIAN TO ATTEND**, *and yet another is placed in charge to command silence.*

Such were the Chazzanites in the most ancient Synagogue, just as I have now described them. But since in all Synagogues not al...

# CHAPTER 21. SYNAGOGUES AND CHURCHES. 1131

Because there was always a supply of proven and trained men to whom the **Acts of Reading and Interpreting the Law**, as well as **Praying**, could be entrusted, it followed that those offices—which were otherwise matters of *communal exercise*—were also assigned to the Ministers of the Synagogue. From then on, they were not only called **חזנים** (*Chazzanim*), **Æditui** (Temple Wardens), **Custodes** (Guardians), or **Observatores Sacrorum** (Observers of Sacred Rites), but also **שליחי צבור** (*Shlichei Tzibur*), meaning **Legates of the Congregation**. For they now solemnly perform the duties of *Reading* and *Praying*; and in larger Synagogues, they have certain others subject to them called *Hypodiaconos* (they call them **שמשים**, *Shamashim* or "Servants"), who perform those more lowly synagogue ministries. This is assumed in the Ritual Books, in which the names **חזן** (*Chazzan*) and **ש"צ** (*Shaliach Tzibur*) are frequently used interchangeably, as is clear from many testimonies cited above where we described the Sacred Rites of the synagogue. Here, however, is a brilliant testimony from the *Colbo* <note>A 14th-century Hebrew work on Jewish law and ritual</note>, from which both points can be made clear:

<margin>Chapter 20, column 13.</margin>
**In a place where it is customary to appoint two Ministers, one for the Morning Service and one for the Additional Service, the first reads from the Torah, and after the reading of the Law and the Prophets he says "May He Bless" [Mi Sheberach], and "Happy are They" [Ashrei], and "Let them Praise" [Yehallelu], and returns the Book of the Law to its place; after which the second stands and says the Small Kaddish and prays the Additional Prayer.** <note>original Hebrew: *U-makom she-nahagu la-asot sheni chazzanim...*; original Latin translation: *Quo loco duos creare solent Synagogæ Ministros...* Note: The "Morning Service" refers to *Yotzer* and the "Additional Service" to *Musaf*.</note>

Behold! Both the Prayers and the Reading of the Law are performed by the Ministers of the Synagogue! Indeed, even when Israelites from the assembly are called today to read from the Law, they do not perform this duty by themselves, except that they read silently and in a low voice, while the Minister of the Synagogue reads in a high and clear voice. Thus it is stated in the Ritual Books:

<margin>*Orach Chajim* chapter 89, § 1.</margin>
**In a place where the custom prevails that the one who goes up to the Torah reads aloud himself: if he has not first reviewed the portion two or three times by himself, he should not go up to the platform.** <note>original Hebrew: *Bi-makom she-nahagu she-ha-oleh le-atzmo korei be-kol ram...*; original Latin translation: *Ubi consuetudo obtinet, ut is, qui vocatur ad legendum in lege...* The "platform" refers to the *Ambo* or *Bimah*.</note>

<margin>Chapter 141, § 2.</margin>
Again: **Two shall not read aloud together; rather, either the one who is called to read reads and the Minister of the Synagogue remains silent, or the Minister of the Synagogue reads and the one called to read does not read aloud. Nevertheless, he must read along with the Minister so that his blessing is not in vain, but he must read quietly so as not to be heard by his own ears.** <note>original Hebrew: *Lo yikre'u shenayim ela ha-oleh korei...*; original Latin translation: *Non legent duo simul alta voce...*</note>

### CHAPTER XXII.

-> The Deacons of the early Christian Church, in respect to their Ministerial Offices, are briefly compared with the Deacons of the Synagogue. <-

<margin>
Apology 2, p. 97.
Chapter 2, 1.
</margin>
**W**ith those sacred rites, for the performance of which all free and trained Israelites were admitted into the Synagogue, the situation in the Christian Church was such that the office of *Praying* was solemnly entrusted to the **Overseer** <note>original Greek: "to Proestoti"</note>, the **Presiding Officer of the Church**, as we understood above from Justin Martyr. For this reason, he is called the **"Angel of the Church"** <note>original Greek: "Angelos tes ekklesias"</note> in the Apocalypse, or, what is the same thing, the **Messenger of the Congregation** <note>original Hebrew: "Shaliach Tzibur"</note>. Likewise, the duty of **Reading the Scripture** was committed to the Deacons, following the example of the **Chazzanim** <note>The "Ministers" or "Cantors"</note> in the Synagogue. That the Christian Church committed the duty of praying to the *Overseer of the Church* was undoubtedly done to avoid all confusion in sacred rites;

<margin>
1 Corinthians 11:5, 14:15, 16.
</margin>
although we may probably conclude from the Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians that a great liberty was also granted in this regard to the believers, who were moved by the Holy Spirit to pour out *Prayers* or *Thanksgivings* outside the regular order. And there is no doubt that Christians continued to use that liberty of theirs for some time after this Epistle was written in certain Churches. But when those extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit began to fail, and since no common level of training was required to pour out prayers solemnly in the Church without set formulas, for the sake of order the Church committed this Duty of Praying to the **Overseer**, for whom it was most fitting in respect to gravity and dignity. I have said that the duty of **Reading the Scripture** was assigned to the Deacons after the example of the Synagogue. For the **Chazzanim**, already from ancient times, whenever other Readers were lacking, had to make up for this deficiency; this is clear enough from a certain testimony of the

### CHAPTER 22. OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

Speaking of the **Deacons of the Synagogue**, their duty among other things was to guard the Book of the Law and also, if necessary, to read from it. In the Christian Church, this was done by the **Readers** <note>original Greek: "anagnostai"</note>, who were a specialized type of **Deacon** <note>original Greek: "diakonon"</note>. In the early days, when the congregation was small, these same Deacons performed all the tasks that the **Presbyters** <note>the Elders or priests</note> did not have the time to manage. Later, these labors were divided: some became **Deacons** <note>original Greek: "diakonoi"</note>, others **Archdeacons** <note>original Greek: "archidiakonoi"</note>, others **Subdeacons** <note>original Greek: "hypodiakonoi"</note>, others **Doorkeepers**, others **Acolytes** <note>original Greek: "akolouthoi"</note> to the Bishops, others **Readers** <note>original Greek: "anagnostai"</note>, and others **Singers** <note>original Greek: "psalmodoi"</note>. Jerome also states that reading in the Church was a duty of the Deacons. Justin Martyr, however, does not say in explicit words that the Holy Scripture was read in Christian assemblies by a Deacon or by any other specific, established person.

<margin>Apology 2 to Antoninus, page 98.</margin>
"The writings," he says, "of the Prophets are read as long as time permits; then, when the one reading has ceased, etc." <note>original Greek: "Ta syngrammata... ton Propheton anaginosketai mechris enchorei; eita pausamenou tou anaginoskontos"</note>. He does not say "when the **Reader** <note>original Greek: "anagnostou"</note> has ceased," <note>original Latin: "cessante Lectore"</note> as if that office had been assigned to a specific person, but rather "the one reading" <note>original Greek: "tou anaginoskontos"</note>, <note>original Latin: "legente"</note>. It is possible that this duty was exercised indiscriminately not only by the Deacon, but also by the **Juniors** who were aspiring to join the Clergy.

<margin>See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 6, chapter 43. Book 2, Epistle 5.</margin>
At the very least, by the following century, **Readers** <note>original Greek: "anagnostai"</note> were already known in the Church as distinct from Deacons. This rank was the lowest among the sacred orders after that of the **Doorkeepers**. Cyprian writes concerning Aurelius, whom he appointed as a **Reader**: *“Such a man deserved the further ranks and greater advancements of clerical ordination, to be judged not by his years but by his merits; but in the meantime, it has pleased us that he begin with the office of reading.”* Certainly, Isidore of Seville, while describing the duties of Deacons (though there is some obscurity in his words), also assigns the office of **Reading** to the Deacons. *“For, just as it is commanded for the Readers to preach the Old Testament, so it is for the Deacons to preach the New.”*

<margin>In the Epistle to Leudefridus. See Ziegler, *On Deacons*, chapter 8, sections 24, 34. Suicer under the word "diakonos".</margin>
And it cannot be denied, as Grotius suggested above, that **Readers** should properly be categorized under the order of Deacons, since the Christian Church in its beginnings recognized no Sacred orders besides those of the **Presbyters** and **Deacons**. Indeed, it is clear from Sozomen <note>a 5th-century church historian</note>, who, speaking of the Church of Alexandria, says: "Here, only the **Archdeacon** <note>original Greek: "archidiakonos"</note> reads this holy book; but among others, the **Deacons** <note>original Greek: "diakonoi"</note> do so." <note>original Greek: "Tauten de ten hieran biblon anaginoskei enthade monos ho Archidiakonos; para de allois diakonoi"</note>. And while in that place only the Archdeacon read that Sacred Volume, elsewhere the Deacons did. That these same Deacons led the Church in the reading and the singing of Psalms is a point we could easily support with many testimonies, if it were certain that Deacons held this office from the very origins of the Church...

### CHAPTER 22. OF THE SYNAGOGUE AND THE CHURCH.

...they are not ministers of food and drink, but ministers of the Church of God. It was the duty of Deacons in the Church to stir the people to attention. <margin>Chrysostom, Homily 19 on Acts.</margin> **Chrysostom** says: *The common minister* <note>original Greek: Κοινὸς... διάκονος</note> *stands crying out with a loud voice, and saying: Let us attend!* <note>original Greek: Πρόσχωμεν; original Latin: Attendamus</note>

It was also the duty of Deacons to instruct the **Catechumens** <term>Catechumens: individuals receiving basic instruction in the Christian faith before being baptized</term> in the knowledge of the mysteries of the Christian Religion, being similar in this to the *Chazzanim* <note>Synagogue attendants</note>, in whom we observed the same thing above. <margin>Chapter 2, page 899. On Luke chapter 19. In Suicer. Epistle 34. Cyprian, Oxford Edition. Cyprian Dissertation 6. On Canon 22 of the Council of Laodicea.</margin> **Theophylact** writes: *The Deacons purify [the mind] through instruction and teaching.* <note>original Greek: Οἱ διάκονοι καθαίρουσι διὰ κατηχήσεως καὶ διδασκαλίας</note> Indeed, in the *African Church*, from the order of *Deacons or Subdeacons*, as Dodwell maintains, the *Teachers of the Hearers* (or Catechumens) were appointed. Furthermore, it was the duty of the Deacons—following the example of the *Chazzanim* in the Synagogue—to give a signal by means of **Oraria** <term>Orarium: a liturgical cloth or stole, used here as a signaling device</term> (that is, handkerchiefs with which they were equipped) to the other Deacons standing in the **ambo** <term>Ambo: a raised pulpit or reading desk in early churches</term> and to the people, indicating when the singing and similar duties ought to begin. **Balsamon** notes: *To carry the Orarium is for Deacons alone. For these, assisting those who celebrate the Sacred rites, and observing the mysteries of the holy prayers and the pronouncements of the Presbyters,* *give notice by means of the Orarium to the Deacons in the pulpit* <note>original Greek: τοῖς ἐν τῷ ἄμβωνι διακόνοις</note> *concerning the proclamation that ought to be made, namely the time for the extended petitions of the Catechumens and the others.* <note>original Greek: διδόασιν εἴδησιν διὰ τοῦ ὠραρίου... τῆς ὀφειλούσης γίνεσθαι ἐκφωνήσεως ἤγουν τοῦ καιροῦ τῆς ἐκτενῆς τῶν αἰτήσεων τῶν κατηχουμένων καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν</note>

<margin>Casaubon on Vopiscus in Aurelian. Severus on Canon 22 of the Council of Laodicea, and Suicer under the word Ὡράριον (Orarium). See Suicer under the word διάκονος (Deacon).</margin> I would not dare to define, however, whether this rite was accepted in the *Christian Church* from its very birth; and if it was accepted, whether that *Orarium* of the *Deacons* does not rather owe its origin to the *Ministry of the Lord’s Table*; therefore, I shall not discuss it further. For I have nothing to add to the observations of the most learned **Casaubon, Beveridge, and Suicer** regarding this word and rite, nor do I care to transcribe them. Likewise, I am not certain whether the Deacons of the *Apostolic Church* presided over the *shorter prayers and the singing of the Church*, as it is established they did in following times; in which case they could otherwise be excellently compared with certain *Chazzanim*. But we do not wish to pursue these matters too anxiously, lest we confuse certainties with uncertainties.

### CHAPTER XXIII.

-> Certain Attributes of the Deacons of the Synagogue and Church are noted, <-
-> showing again their conformity with one another. <-

Nothing now seems to remain to finally complete this treatise of ours, except to briefly discuss certain <term>ATTRIBUTES</term> <note>original Latin: "ACCIDENTIBUS"; in this context, it refers to the non-essential but defining characteristics or circumstances of an office</note> of the Ministers of the Synagogue and the Church. Three things here especially come into consideration: <term>NUMBER</term>, <term>ORDINATION</term>, and <term>SUSTENANCE</term>.

1. Synagogues everywhere generally had *one* <term>CHAZZAN</term> <note>original Hebrew: חזן; the primary attendant or minister of the synagogue</note>, or <term>MINISTER</term>: as is abundantly clear from those things we have discussed above. However, the larger synagogues were able to have—and indeed did have—*several*, as is clear from the testimony produced above from the *Kol Bo* <note>A significant 13th-century Hebrew collection of ritual laws</note>: <margin>Chapter 20, page 13.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: מקום שנהגו לעשות שני חזנים וכו'</note> *In a place where they are accustomed to appoint <term>TWO</term> Chazzans, etc.* If they could have two, then synagogues were able to have even more deacons, as circumstances required. In the earliest Apostolic Churches, however, no one will easily determine exactly how many deacons were established. It is clear that several churches had more than one from the Epistle of Paul to the Philippians, which carries this <margin>Philippians 1:1.</margin> inscription: *Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, <note>original Greek: σὺν ἐπισκόποις καὶ διακόνοις</note> with the <term>BISHOPS</term> and <term>DEACONS</term>.* Just as there were several Bishops (or Presbyters) in the Philippian church, so there were also several Deacons in number. And it seems the affairs of the early Church required several Deacons, both for the administration of the Sacraments—both Baptism and the Lord's Supper—and for the abundance of the needy and miserable whom the Bishops assisted through the Deacons. For Deacons were employed by the Bishop for all ministerial duties, of whatever kind they were, which had respect to the Sacred rites of Religion. And it seems, therefore, that this number of Deacons varied according to the needs of the Church they served; while more were required in larger churches than in smaller ones. This continued until some churches, persuading themselves that those "Deacons of the Tables for Widows"—whom Luke records as being established in the Jerusalem Church outside the regular order and for a time, as it seems—were the types of the genuine Deacons of the Church. They considered themselves bound to this very *sevenfold* number by Apostolic practice; hence the Canon of the Council of Neocaesarea states: <note>original Greek: Διάκονοι ἑπτὰ ὀφείλεσιν εἶναι κα...</note> *There ought to be seven deacons...*

<summary>This page discusses the organizational attributes of deacons, comparing the number of ministers (Chazzanim) in the synagogue to the number of deacons in the early church, noting that while numbers varied by need, some traditions eventually fixed the number at seven based on the Book of Acts.</summary>

2. Furthermore, how much conformity there is in the Ordination of the Deacons of the Synagogue and the Church is abundantly clear from those things which we have argued at length above concerning the ordination of the Prefects of the Synagogue and the Church. <margin>Book 3, Part 1, chapters 14 and 15.</margin> The Synagogues which were in Exile—subject to no Patriarch or Sanhedrin—chose their own Prefects and Ministers through free <term>suffragia</term> <note>original Latin: "suffragia"; referring here to the votes or consensus of the local community</note>; but those others which were subject to the <term>eparchy</term> <note>original Greek: "επαρχια"; meaning a province or the jurisdictional area of a governor or high official</note> of a Patriarch or some Sanhedrin received their Prefects and Ministers from them. This has been proven by us and established with evident testimonies, which would be pointlessly repeated here. Thus the Synagogues of Canaan, Egypt, and Babylonia once received their Ministers from the Patriarchs and high Sanhedrins of those regions; but the Synagogues of the Western Regions, which are subject to no Sanhedrin or Patriarch—such as those of Spain, France, Poland, and Germany—choose their own Prefects and Ministers for themselves. Those Eastern communities also enjoyed the same benefit of liberty after the Patriarchates of those places were finally abolished. Let us understand this matter from Rabbi Karo: <margin>Notes to Rabbi Joseph ben Alexander, Orach Chaim, chapter 53, at number 10.</margin>

For this reason, Rabbi Simcha ruled that even a single individual can block the appointment of a Cantor and say, "I do not wish for such-and-such a person to be the Cantor," unless he had already agreed to him from the beginning. *The Author of the Book Agur wrote: Whoever consents to be a Minister of the Synagogue without*...

### ON THE ATTRIBUTES OF DEACONS, BOOK III, PART II.

...by the common consent of the entire Synagogue; upon [one appointed without it], the Spirit of the Wise does not rest. Indeed, even a single individual can intercede to prevent someone from being elected as a <term>Chazzan</term> <note>The Chazzan is the leader of communal prayer or cantor in a Jewish synagogue.</note>. However, Rabbi Chasdai, drawing from the book *Or Zarua*, dissents from this view. Thus far his argument. Rabbi Kolon, on the other hand, wrote in *Shoresh* 44 that the Prayers of the Church <note>original: "Preces Ecclesiae"</note> are regarded in the same way as the Daily Sacrifice <note>original: "Sacrificium juge," referring to the Tamid sacrifice in the Temple</note>, which was offered to God in the name of the entire community. It is not fitting, therefore, for anyone to be delegated to offer those sacrifices to God who is displeasing to the community. For this reason, Master N. Simcha <note>Likely referring to Simcha of Speyer, a prominent medieval jurist</note> determined that even one person can block someone from becoming a Chazzan by stating that they do not consent to that person; unless, perhaps, they had already consented by their vote at the beginning.

Above all, they are carefully on guard lest the local Magistrate or Prince should interfere in this business. Karo <note>Joseph Karo, author of the Shulchan Aruch</note> recounts from Rabbi Mordechai that it once happened that a certain Prince, as a mark of honor, placed his own hat upon the head of a newly created Chazzan to confirm him in that dignity. But that good man took it poorly, nor did he hide his indignation in the presence of that very Prefect, but said freely: <note>original Hebrew: אדוני אין דיני לקבל ממך עבודת בוראינו</note> *"My lord, it is not my law to receive from you the service of our Creator."* That is, if I am not mistaken: *the Right and Power of worshipping our Creator.*

In a not dissimilar way, matters were conducted in the Assemblies of the Christians. As long as the Apostles presided over the Church at Jerusalem—the mother of all Churches—they were able, by the authority granted to them by the Lord, to ordain whomsoever they wished as Presbyters and Deacons in the Churches. It is doubtful, however, whether they exercised this supreme authority in the ordinary *elections of Prefects and Deacons*, or whether they did not rather consult the Christian common people. Certainly, after the passing of the Apostles and the abolition of the supreme authority of the Jerusalem See, the Churches elected their own leaders by free vote. And although in following times the Bishops claimed for themselves almost the entire right of electing Presbyters and Deacons, nevertheless, it was a matter of religious duty for the holier Bishops not to depart from the ancient custom of consulting the people. 

<margin>Epistles, book 2, Epistle 5.</margin> 
Regarding the *ordaining of Clerics*, Cyprian <note>St. Cyprian (c. 210–258 AD), Bishop of Carthage and an early Christian writer</note> says concerning the appointment of Aurelius as a Lector, in a letter to the Clergy and People of Carthage: *"Dearly beloved brothers, we are accustomed to consult you beforehand, and to weigh the character and merits of each individual by common counsel."* <note>original Latin: "in ordinandis Clericis... fratres charissimi, solemus vos ante consulere, et mores ac merita singulorum communi consilio ponderare."</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how religious leaders are appointed and supported, moving from the democratic election of Deacons in the early Christian church to the financial maintenance of the Chazzan (cantor) in the Jewish Synagogue.</meta>

### CHAPTER 23. SYNAGOGUE AND CHURCH. 1139

...had spoken regarding the choice of the People, he adds: "We observe that the Apostles followed this practice not only in the ordinations of Bishops, but also in the ordinations of **DEACONS**, about which it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: <margin>Acts 6, 4. See also book 3, Letter 9.</margin> *And they called together, etc.*" Regarding the Rite of their Inauguration into office, we have nothing to remark beyond what has been observed in previous sections.

3. It is very clear from our previous dissertation on the *Honoraria, or stipends of the Leaders of the Synagogue*, that the *Chazzans* <note>The author uses 'Chazzanitas' to refer to the Chazzanim or cantors/ministers of the synagogue.</note> were supported by the public, following the example of the *Leaders of the Synagogue*. This is generally assumed by the Jewish authorities and is evident from experience itself. *Rabbi Karo* <note>Joseph Karo, 1488–1575, the famous codifier of Jewish Law.</note>, assuming this fact, raises a question instead as to from where <margin>Notes on Rabbi Asher, Orach Chayim, chapter 53, folio 46.</margin> this stipend should be paid to the *Minister of the Synagogue*: namely, whether all members of the *Synagogue* ought to bear equal costs in paying this honorarium to the *Minister of the Church* <note>Vitringa often uses 'Ecclesia' (Church) to refer to the Jewish congregation or 'Synagoga' interchangeably when discussing their organizational structure.</note>, or whether they should contribute unequal portions according to their means, honors, and wealth—just as individuals are taxed according to the measure of their ability for *Alms* and other burdens borne by the *Church*. He resolves this question based on a response from *Rabbi Hai* <note>Hai Gaon, 939–1038, a prominent medieval Jewish scholar in Babylonia.</note>, showing that those two differing opinions of the *Doctors* <note>Referring to the scholars of the law.</note> regarding this matter—though one might seem to destroy the other—can actually stand together and be perfectly reconciled. 

The *Minister of the Synagogue* has two roles in relation to the *Church*. One role is that by which the *Minister of the Synagogue* pours out the necessary daily and annual *Prayers* for the entire *Church* to fulfill the common duty of the whole congregation. The other role is that by which the *Minister of the Synagogue* observes *certain duties of honor* in cases not absolutely necessary—things which bring a certain dignity to the *Sacred Rites and the People*, such as occurs in *Betrothals, hymns* chanted in the *Synagogue*, and other such duties. To properly value the wage due to the *Minister of the Synagogue* for the necessary duty of *Prayers*, all—both poor and rich—must contribute equally. This is because those necessary daily *Prayers* were substituted for the sacrifices, the costs of which were sustained by the *half-Shekel* <note>original: 'dimidio Siclo'. Every adult Jewish male paid a half-shekel tax for the upkeep of the Temple and communal sacrifices.</note> paid annually by every *Israelite*, where the amount was equal for both the poor and the rich. But as for those other *duties of decorum and honor* performed by the minister of the *Church*, the wage for that labor, properly valued, must be paid from the unequal taxes of the *Church* imposed on each member of the *Synagogue* according to his means, just as all other <term>communal burdens</term> <note>original: 'עולי הצבור' (olei ha-tsibur), referring to the expenses or "yoke" of the community.</note> are borne. From this discourse, it is sufficiently clear how the *Synagogue supports its Ministers*. However, I confess that *what is said here and elsewhere...*

<meta>catchword: concerning</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the historical precedents for the election and financial support of church and synagogue ministers, specifically comparing the Christian deacon's appointment to the Jewish Chazzan's stipend. It explains a compromise in Jewish law where communal prayer costs are shared equally, while ceremonial duties are funded through wealth-based taxation.</summary>

<keywords>Chazzan, Deacons, communal taxes, Joseph Karo, Hai Gaon, Half-Shekel, liturgy, synagogue finance, ecclesiastical history</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the third book of the treatise, wrapping up the discussion on the financial support and status of religious ministers. It continues from the previous page's examination of how Synagogue ministers (Chazzanim) were paid, drawing parallels between Jewish, Christian, and even Pagan Greek models of endowment and clerical support.</meta>

CONCERNING THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF DEACONS, etc. BOOK III. PART...

...are said concerning the *Ministers* of the Synagogue, it should be understood that they refer to such *Deacons* who are simultaneously *Envoys of the Church* <term>Legati Ecclesiae: formal representatives or delegates of the congregation</term>. But the modern Synagogue almost always tends to confuse those two names. I do not know, moreover, whether at some point certain estates were not bequeathed to the Synagogues by pious Israelites, from the revenues of which their *Presidents* and *Ministers* could be sustained, as was a very familiar and frequent custom among Christians. Certainly, as the learned have already observed, something similar was accepted among the Pagans themselves <margin>See Valesius on Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 7, chapter 32. *Shalshelet Ha-Kabbalah* <note>A 16th-century work of Jewish history and tradition</note>, page 20.</margin> in the Athenian Platonic School, *which possessed no small annual revenues from estates that had been donated and bequeathed to that school by studious men.* I have come across one example in Jewish history: the Synagogue of Ezekiel. Thus we read concerning it in the Hebrew Chronicles: <note>original: ויוכין הדרן לכ . סת יחזקאל הוה נחלות וכרמים שנתן לו , אוילמרורד , להתפרנס מהן</note> *Furthermore, Jehoiachin dedicated to that Synagogue of Ezekiel the inheritances and vineyards which Evil-merodach <note>A King of Babylon mentioned in 2 Kings 25:27</note> had given him for his life's sustenance.* 

As for how it was with the Deacons of the Church, this has likewise been very clearly explained in previous sections. They were sustained, along with the rest of the clergy, from the offerings and gifts of the believers, which were distributed among the clergy and the poor. <margin>Book 4, Letter 5.</margin> Cyprian writes *concerning the ordained Readers Aurelius and Celerinus: "Furthermore, know that we have already designated for them the honor of Presbyters, so that they may be honored with the same allowances <term>sportulis: literally 'baskets,' referring to the daily or monthly distributions of food or money given to officials</term> as the Presbyters, and share the monthly divisions in equal quantities."* Let these things, which have been explained above, suffice.

-> Glory to God through Jesus Christ our Lord. <note>original Greek: Δόξα τῷ Θεῷ διὰ Ἰησȣ Χριστȣ τȣ Κυρίῳ ἡμῶν.</note> <-
